10.1001/jamainternmed.2024.2007.headline_claim: A 15-day course of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was safe and generally tolerated in PASC but did not significantly improve core symptoms compared with placebo-ritonavir.
10.1001/jamainternmed.2024.2007.overall: The null finding on pooled core-symptom severity is plausible and carefully hedged, but its main result is not given numerically in the text, and the trial stopped early with an unvalidated composite endpoint. The text also misstates one secondary result: fatigue weeks with mild or no symptoms favoured placebo at P = .02 but is described as non-significant. The safety wording, 'demonstrated the overall safety', is stronger than a 155-person trial with more adverse events on NMV/r supports.

primary_outcome.name: Pooled severity of 6 core PASC symptoms (Likert 0-3) at week 10, adjusted for baseline

issues.title: Text says no significant weeks-with-mild-or-no-symptoms difference except brain fog, but fatigue is OR 0.55, P = .02
issues.explanation: The Results state that, apart from brain fog, no core symptom differed significantly between groups in the proportion of weeks with mild or no symptoms. Table 2 shows fatigue with OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.92), P = .02. That interval excludes 1 at the stated .05 level and points the same way as brain fog, toward fewer mild-symptom weeks on NMV/r. The text therefore hides a second nominally significant result unfavourable to the drug. The result is post hoc and unadjusted for multiplicity, so the effect is on one secondary result only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the protocol or statistical plan that a stricter alpha applied to this post hoc analysis, or a corrected fatigue estimate in the supplement.

quotes.text: A post hoc analysis found no statistically significant difference between the 2 groups in the proportion of total postrandomization weeks with mild or no symptoms for each core symptom

quotes.location: Table 2, Proportion of weeks 1-15 with mild or no symptoms, Fatigue row

issues.title: 'Demonstrated overall safety' claimed from 102 NMV/r participants, with more adverse events and no formal comparison
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the trial demonstrated overall safety. The trial had 102 participants on NMV/r, no formal safety hypothesis or test, and the Discussion compares with a 5-day course for which the trial reports no data. NMV/r participants had more AEs per person (771 events across 102 participants vs 313 across 53) and a much higher rate of dysgeusia, which may have unmasked treatment. Participants on NMV/r also reported slightly higher odds of a more severe most-bothersome-symptom score at 10 and 15 weeks. 'Generally tolerated' is supported, but 'demonstrated safety' is not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety analysis with confidence intervals, or reported 5-day course data from the trial itself.

quotes.text: This randomized clinical trial demonstrated the overall safety of a 15-day course of NMV/r in patients with PASC
We found that a 15-day course of NMV/r had a safety profile similar to the 5-day acute treatment course and was generally tolerated

issues.title: Primary outcome result is given only as 'not significant', with no estimate, CI or P value
issues.explanation: The Results describe the pooled primary outcome qualitatively. No pooled coefficient, OR, CI or P is printed in the text or in Table 2, which lists secondary outcomes only. Readers cannot judge the size or direction of the pooled effect, or what benefit the CI excludes. This matters most here because the trial stopped early and the conclusion is a null result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pooled estimate with CI and P value printed in a figure or in the main text.

quotes.text: there was no statistically significant difference in the pooled symptom severity between NMV/r and PBO/r groups at 10 weeks, adjusted for baseline severity

issues.title: Primary outcome is an unvalidated pooled six-symptom Likert score; authors acknowledge no validated PASC endpoint
issues.explanation: The primary endpoint pools six self-selected symptoms using inverse-variance weighting of proportional odds coefficients. The authors state that no validated endpoint exists. A null result on a non-validated composite is weaker evidence of no effect than one on an established measure. The paper discloses this and frames the study as exploratory, so the headline conclusion is only mildly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the symptom survey was validated before the trial, or that the pooled score tracks a validated measure such as PROMIS.

quotes.text: Core symptoms were selected based on mechanistic rationale, clinical experience, and reported PASC symptoms prevalence and severity.
To date, there are no validated clinical end points or biomarkers of PASC established for clinical trials, to our knowledge.

issues.title: Enrolment stopped for futility at 155 of 200 planned; power was 77% for OR 1.6, so small benefits cannot be excluded
issues.explanation: The trial was designed with at least 77% power to detect an OR of 1.6 with 200 participants. It stopped at 155 randomized (148 with primary data), so power for that effect is lower, and smaller true effects were never well powered. The Discussion states the study does not rule out NMV/r as a therapy, so the conclusion is appropriately cautious. Some Discussion wording ('did not improve') is firmer than the evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confidence intervals for the pooled primary effect excluding clinically meaningful benefit.

quotes.text: We initially determined that a sample size of 200 would provide power of at least 77%
Enrollment was stopped early in June 2023 when the prespecified threshold for futility had been met (conditional power <10%).

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.36874.headline_claim: Lithium aspartate 10 to 15 mg/d was ineffective for treating PCC fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, and a further RCT is needed to test higher dosages.
10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.36874.overall: The primary result is a non-significant difference in a 50-patient, 21-day trial, so 'no large benefit at 10 to 15 mg/d' is supported, but 'ineffective' goes beyond what the wide CI shows and the cognitive half of the primary outcome uses an unvalidated scale. The dose-finding recommendations rest on 3 open-label patients and should be read as hypothesis-generating. The one clear printing error (the Body Pain CI) does not affect conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: Change in sum of FSS-7 and BFSS scores

issues.title: 'Ineffective' conclusion drawn from a non-significant result; CI allows up to 16.6-point benefit on the sum score
issues.explanation: The sample size assumed a 40% difference taken from 10 anecdotal patients, which is probably too large. The primary CI (−16.6 to 9.5) excludes a 40% effect (about 31 points) but not a 15 to 20% effect, which would matter to patients. The trial lasted 21 days at 10 to 15 mg/d. The Conclusions say 'ineffective' without qualification, whereas the data show only that large effects at this dose and duration were not seen. This understates the possible benefit of treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence or non-inferiority margin of at least 20% showing the CI excludes clinically meaningful benefit.

quotes.text: we estimated a 40% intergroup difference for the primary end point and a 48% SD for the placebo group
In this RCT, therapy with lithium aspartate, 10 to 15 mg/d, was ineffective for treating PCC fatigue and cognitive dysfunction.

second_reader.what_stands: The CI for the sum score (-16.6 to 9.5) is compatible with a lithium benefit of up to about 16.6 points (roughly 21% of baseline), so the non-significant P=.59 does not establish that lithium is 'ineffective'; the unqualified wording goes beyond what the data show. The CI does exclude the large (about 40%, roughly 31-point) effect the trial was powered for, and the authors restrict the claim to 10 to 15 mg/d and call for further trials at higher doses, so a more accurate statement is 'no evidence of the hypothesised large benefit at this dose'.

issues.title: Co-primary brain fog scale (BFSS) was invented for the trial and is unvalidated
issues.explanation: The primary outcome sums the validated FSS-7 and a new, unvalidated BFSS. Its responsiveness and minimal important difference are unknown, so a null result on it says little about cognitive dysfunction. The paper itself offers only 3 open-label patients as 'preliminary evidence of BFSS validity'. The fatigue conclusion rests on a validated scale, so the weakness mainly affects the cognitive part of the claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published psychometric validation of the BFSS or a pre-specified validated cognitive outcome showing the same null result.

quotes.text: Due to the lack of a validated cognitive dysfunction scale, a BFSS was developed for this study
providing preliminary evidence of BFSS validity

issues.title: Target serum lithium range of 0.18 to 0.50 mEq/L inferred from 3 open-label completers
issues.explanation: Only 5 of 43 invited patients enrolled, 1 withdrew, and 1 had no dose-finding data. The remaining 3 were open-label, uncontrolled, selected as non-placebo responders and followed after the trial, with regression to the mean and expectation effects possible. The authors still say the data 'suggest' levels of 0.18 to 0.49 mEq/L 'may offer meaningful improvements' and target 0.18 to 0.50 mEq/L 'based on the totality of the data'. The stated range also varies (0.49 in Table 4 and Results, 0.50 elsewhere), and the 0.10 patient had the same dose of 45 mg/d.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised, controlled comparison of higher doses showing a dose-response relationship at these serum levels.

quotes.text: Among 3 patients who completed the dose-finding study, open-label lithium aspartate, 40 to 45 mg/d, was associated with numerically greater reductions
suggest that serum lithium levels between 0.18 and 0.49 mEq/L may offer meaningful improvements in PCC fatigue and/or cognitive dysfunction

issues.title: Body Pain Bother difference 0.1 has CI −5.3 to 0.7, impossible on a 1-5 scale and inconsistent with P = .77
issues.explanation: The printed lower limit is about 5.4 below the estimate, but the upper limit is only 0.6 above it. With SDs of about 1.2 and roughly 25 per arm the standard error is about 0.34, so a CI near −0.6 to 0.8 is expected. A change of −5.3 is also impossible on a 1-5 scale. This is a single misprinted interval; the null result is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The trial protocol or the original table showing −5.3 is a correctly computed bound, which is not possible on a 1-5 scale.

quotes.location: Table 2, Body Pain Bother Questionnaire row

script.explanation: the estimate 0.1 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-5.3, 0.7] (expected about -2.3000) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.9479 (reachable range [0.9206, 0.9744] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.77 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interv

issues.title: No trial registry identifier appears in the supplied text
issues.explanation: The Methods give IRB approval and a protocol supplement but no registry number. Registration may appear in the omitted abstract, so this cannot be settled from the paper as supplied. If truly unregistered, pre-specification of the primary outcome could not be checked, though the protocol is available.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier in the abstract or protocol with the same primary outcome.

quotes.text: The trial protocol is included in Supplement 1.

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.4386.headline_claim: Nonhospitalized patients with PCC generally tolerated all three exercise types without significant symptom exacerbation, so guidelines cautioning against exercise in similar populations may need revision.
10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.4386.overall: The central finding that fatigue change did not differ significantly between groups after any exercise type is consistent across the text and tables, but absence of a significant difference in a small study is presented as evidence of tolerability, and the Conclusions omit significant pain and concentration findings. The guideline-revision recommendation is stronger than the design supports. Several printed numbers are inconsistent (swapped echo differences, IL-6 estimate and P values, a POTS percentage), but none changes the main results.

primary_outcome.name: Change in fatigue VAS from baseline to 48 hours after exercise, patients with PCC vs controls, per exercise type

primary_outcomes.measure: Post-exertional malaise (PEM) symptoms of post-COVID subjects and age/sex matched controls in response to different exercise trials.
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Three exercises trials & 48 hours follow-ups of each trial

issues.title: Tolerability conclusion omits significant PCC pain and concentration differences; guideline revision overreaches
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state exercise was tolerated without significant symptom exacerbation, yet the Results report significantly greater muscle pain (P = .04) and joint pain (P = .009) after HIIT and worse concentration at 48 hours after MICT (P = .03) in patients with PCC versus controls. These secondary findings are uncorrected for multiplicity and may be chance, but the Conclusions do not mention them. The conclusion also rests on a null fatigue test (not an equivalence test) in a small sample at a single 48-hour time point. Advising that guidelines 'may need to be revised' therefore goes beyond what this design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority margin and analysis showing symptom changes fall within it, or a conclusion that names the pain and concentration findings.

quotes.text: nonhospitalized patients with PCC generally tolerated all exercise types without reporting significant symptom exacerbation, performance reductions, or exacerbated inflammation after 48 hours
given that exercise was generally well tolerated, guidelines cautioning against exercise in similar populations may need to be revised
Patients with PCC reported worse muscle pain (mean [SD] VAS ranks, 33.4 [17.7] vs 25.0 [11.3]

second_reader.what_stands: The paper itself reports significantly worse muscle pain and joint pain after HIIT and worse concentration 48 h after MICT in PCC, so 'without significant symptom exacerbation' omits these findings from the Conclusions. The recommendation to revise guidelines goes beyond a small (n = 30 vs 31), non-equivalence-tested study with a 48 h window, a selected PCC phenotype and no correction for multiple VAS tests, although the authors partly temper it ('may need', 'cautiously', 'not generalized') and the pain and concentration differences are modest, uncorrected secondary results, with the primary f

issues.title: Echo mean differences swapped: SV −2.6 mL and LV diameter −9.7 mm; Table 1 implies −9.7 and −2.6
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives stroke volume 59.5 vs 69.2 mL (difference −9.7 mL, 14%) and LV diameter 47.9 vs 50.5 mm (difference −2.6 mm, 5%). The text attaches −2.6 to stroke volume and −9.7 to LV diameter, so the two mean differences and their CIs are swapped. The percentages and P values are right, so the conclusion is not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values are model-adjusted differences defined differently; the matching percentages argue against this.

quotes.text: 14% smaller stroke volume (mean difference, −2.6 mL; 95% CI, −4.9 to −0.2 mL
5% smaller left ventricular diameter (mean difference, −9.7 mm
Stroke volume, mL 59.5 (14.2) 69.2 (18.1)

issues.title: IL-6 time effect: estimate 3.2 pg/mL outside its CI 0.1-0.5, and P = .005 in text vs .02 in legend
issues.explanation: The IL-6 time effect is reported as a mean difference of 3.2 pg/mL with a 95% CI of 0.1-0.5, so the estimate lies far outside its own interval. The text also gives P = .005 whereas the Figure 3 legend gives P = .02 for the same time effect. One or more of these numbers is wrong. IL-6 is a secondary safety/inflammation outcome, and it shows no group difference, so the effect on the conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplement eTable 10 showing a consistent estimate, CI and P for the IL-6 time effect.

quotes.text: mean difference, 3.2 pg/mL; 95% CI, 0.1-0.5 pg/mL

quotes.text: time, P = .02; group × exercise, P = .04
quotes.location: Figure 3 legend, panels C and D

script.explanation: the estimate 3.2 lies outside its own CI [0.1, 0.5]; the estimate 3.2 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [0.1, 0.5] (expected about 0.3000) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Borderline physiologic findings (P .02-.05) among dozens of uncorrected tests support multi-system claims
issues.explanation: Table 1 contains dozens of between-group tests and Table 2 about 60 more, none corrected across outcomes. Findings for stroke volume (P = .02), LV diameter (P = .03), pulse wave velocity (P = .04), isometric strength (P = .02) and deep-breathing HRV (P = .05, CI reaching −0.1) would not survive a correction, yet they feed the 'multiple organ system' conclusion. The strongest results (aerobic capacity, EMG, activity) are robust, so the damage is limited to the secondary multi-system claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or correction across Table 1 outcomes, or an explicit labelling of these findings as exploratory in the conclusions.

quotes.text: patients with PCC had a 14% smaller stroke volume (mean difference, −2.6 mL; 95% CI, −4.9 to −0.2 mL; P = .02)
Isometric knee extension strength was 19% lower in the patients with PCC (mean difference, −37 Nm; 95% CI, −67 to −7 Nm; P = .02)
Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction were performed when significant main or interaction effects were detected.

issues.title: HIIT fatigue change P: Results text gives .08, Table 2 48 h row gives .88
issues.explanation: The Results text reports P = .08 for the HIIT comparison of fatigue change, but the Table 2 fatigue 48 h row prints .88 in the HIIT column. The MICT (.09) and ST (.49) values agree between the two places, which points to a single-digit slip in one of them. Both values are non-significant, so the null primary result is not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplement tables showing the HIIT 48 h fatigue P value, with the printed one being a non-error.

quotes.text: mean [SD] VAS ranks for HIIT: PCC, 29.3 [19.5]; controls, 28.7 [11.4]

issues.title: Observational PCC-control comparison unadjusted for activity, β-blocker use or infection history
issues.explanation: The group effects come from a non-randomized comparison where the model adjusts only for group, time and exercise. Patients spent 43% less time in moderate-to-vigorous activity, 29% vs 6% used β-blockers, and only 52% of controls had verified prior infection. The paper acknowledges inactivity as a possible explanation, but the mechanistic wording ('primary peripheral tissue damage') cannot be separated from deconditioning or medication in this design. This concerns the secondary physiologic aim rather than the tolerability result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Sensitivity analyses adjusting for activity level, β-blocker use and infection history showing unchanged group differences.

quotes.text: patients with PCC spent 43% less time in moderate to vigorous physical activity
It is plausible that our results represent a phenotype indicative of inactivity coupled with primary peripheral tissue damage and neurophysiologic changes
A mixed linear model (fixed effects: group, time, and exercise; random effects: study identification number, exercise order)

issues.title: PCC n is 31 (Results, Table 1) but 30 in Table 2 and Figures 2-3, with no reason given
issues.explanation: The PCC group is 31 in the demographics and Table 1 but 30 in the Table 2 footnote and in the Figure 2 and 3 legends. The Methods claim an intention-to-treat analysis, but the paper does not say why one patient is absent from the symptom and CPET analyses. This is probably a missing-data issue affecting a single participant, so the impact is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The flowchart or supplement stating that one patient had no symptom or CPET data for a specified reason.

quotes.text: For 30 patients with PCC and 31 controls.
Specifically, the study cohort consisted of 31 patients with PCC
according to the intention-to-treat approach

issues.title: POTS 2 of 31 patients is 6% in the text but 7% in Table 1
issues.explanation: Two of 31 patients is 6.5% (6% after rounding down, as printed in the text), but Table 1 prints 7% for POTS and the same 7% for borderline POTS and syncope. The counts sum to 31, so 29 does not explain the difference. This is a trivial rounding or denominator slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the HUTT denominator for the PCC group was 29.

quotes.text: revealed POTS in 2 patients with PCC (6%)
POTS, No. (%) 2 (7)

script.explanation: 2/31 = 6.45%, but the paper prints 7, outside the rounding interval [6.50, 8.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 28.6 rather than 31.

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.50744.headline_claim: A brief outpatient cognitive-behavioral rehabilitation program based on the cognitive activation theory of stress was effective and safe, with sustained improvement in physical function compared with care as usual in patients with post-COVID-19 condition.
10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.50744.overall: The trial shows a statistically significant improvement in self-reported physical function (9.2 points, CI 4.3 to 14.2), but the open-label design, unmatched usual-care control and self-reported outcomes mean part of the effect may reflect expectation or attention. The 'clinically significant' and 'safe' labels go beyond the data, since the estimate is below the authors' own 10-point threshold and the safety data are unvalidated. Substantial and partly differential missing data add further uncertainty.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 Physical Function Subscale (SF-36-PFS) score at T1

issues.title: Open-label trial with usual-care control and self-reported primary outcome; placebo effect not controlled
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation, the control group received no matched attention or sham, and the primary and nearly all secondary outcomes are self-reported. Expectation and attention effects could therefore account for part or all of the 9.2-point difference. The authors state this limitation, yet the Conclusions say the program was simply effective. The conclusion holds only tentatively.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An objective primary or secondary outcome (for example, steps or work attendance) showing a similar benefit.

quotes.text: participants, therapists, and study assistants were not blinded to randomization outcome
The primary outcome measure was participant-reported physical function at T1.
which implies that the placebo effect cannot be controlled for.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with a usual-care comparator and a self-reported primary outcome (SF-36 physical function), and the authors themselves state that placebo and attention effects are not controlled for. This is disclosed and partly discussed, but the Conclusions still state the program was 'effective' without qualifying that the primary and most secondary outcomes are unblinded self-reports. Analysis-stage blinding does not address this bias.

issues.title: 9.2-point primary difference (CI 4.3-14.2) called clinically significant against a stated 10-point threshold
issues.explanation: The Methods say a 10-point SF-36-PFS difference counts as clinically significant. The primary estimate is 9.2 at T1 and 9.0 at T2, both below 10, and the CI lower bounds (4.3, 4.0) fall well under it. The Discussion nonetheless calls the improvement clinically significant, so statistical significance is presented as clinical importance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified minimal clinically important difference below 9 points for this population, or an analysis showing a clinically relevant proportion of responders.

quotes.text: A score difference of 10 points on the SF-36-PFS was considered clinically significant.
score difference, 9.2; 95% CI, 4.3-14.2
reported sustained and clinically significant better physical function

issues.title: MCAR claimed (P = .40) yet allocation and age predict loss to follow-up; 35% missing vs 20% planned
issues.explanation: The authors say missingness was completely at random, but also report that allocation to care as usual and lower age were associated with loss to follow-up. Primary outcome data exist for only 231 of 314 randomized, and the dropout is far above the 20% assumed. The imputation-based ITT result therefore depends on untestable assumptions, and the authors admit non-random missingness cannot be ruled out.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis under missing-not-at-random assumptions (such as tipping-point analysis) giving a similar primary effect.

quotes.text: Analysis of missing data points revealed a missing completely at random pattern
quotes.location: Results, Participants and Study Validity, para 1

quotes.text: Allocation to CAU and lower age were associated with loss to follow-up
quotes.location: Results, Participants and Study Validity, para 1

issues.title: No trial registration identifier appears in the supplied text
issues.explanation: The supplied text names ethics approval and a protocol supplement but gives no registry or registration number. Without it the prespecification of the primary outcome cannot be checked here. This may be an omission in the extract rather than in the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier (for example, ClinicalTrials.gov) with the primary outcome dated before recruitment started on February 22, 2022.

quotes.text: The trial was approved by the Regional Committee for Ethics in Medical Research
the statistical analysis plan is available in

issues.title: 'Safe' rests on a self-composed unvalidated questionnaire; T2 admissions 7 vs 2 and one SAE possibly related
issues.explanation: The safety conclusion relies on an unvalidated, self-composed, unblinded questionnaire summarized descriptively with no formal comparison. Hospital admissions and novel illness were higher in the intervention group at T2, and one of 4 SAEs might have been due to diagnostic delay. The data are reassuring but support 'no clear signal of harm' more than a flat 'safe' claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A validated safety instrument or a prespecified formal comparison of harms showing no excess in the intervention arm.

quotes.text: All safety variables are based on a separate, self-composed questionnaire
a brief outpatient rehabilitation program with a cognitive and behavioral approach was effective and safe.
A total of 4 SAEs in the intervention group were recorded

issues.title: Text gives significant Cohen d range as 0.26-0.51, but anxiety at T1 (P = .05) has d = 0.20
issues.explanation: The Results say significant effects had d from 0.26 to 0.51. Table 2 lists anxiety T1 at P = .05, which meets the paper's own criterion of P ≤ .05, with d = 0.20. The stated lower bound is therefore wrong or the anxiety T1 result is not being counted. This is a minor reporting slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that anxiety at T1 was treated as non-significant (for example, P rounded from just above .05).

quotes.text: varied from 0.26 to 0.51 among the statistically significant differences

issues.title: 227 of 314 completing follow-up implies 28% incomplete, but the paper states 35% incomplete data
issues.explanation: 227 of 314 gives about 72% complete and 28% incomplete follow-up, whereas the paper reports 35% with incomplete data, and repeats it in the Discussion. The figure may use a different definition, such as any missing item at any time point. The paper does not say, so the extent of missing data is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The Figure 1 flow diagram or a definition of incomplete data that yields 35%.

quotes.text: 227 patients completed the entire follow-up period, resulting in a total of 35% of individuals having incomplete data
quotes.location: Results, Participants and Study Validity, para 1

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.0728.headline_claim: Donepezil's efficacy for post-COVID-19 fatigue and psychological symptoms was not confirmed in this RCT in a general population.
10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.0728.overall: The paper reports a clear null result for donepezil on post-COVID fatigue, and the conclusion is appropriately cautious (efficacy not confirmed, phase 2, underpowered acknowledged). The only candidate raised, absent registration details in the text, is a verifiability point that cannot be settled from the paper and does not change the null conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder Fatigue Scale (CFS) score at 3 weeks

issues.title: No trial registry identifier or registration date stated in the report text
issues.explanation: The report points to a prior protocol paper and a supplement but prints no registry number or registration date, so a reader cannot confirm from this text that the primary outcome was fixed in advance. The registration may well exist in the cited protocol report or journal metadata. Because the primary result is null, the gap affects verifiability rather than the direction of the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (with registration date before first enrollment on December 14, 2022) listing CFS at 3 weeks as primary outcome, cited in the protocol report or journal metadata.

quotes.text: The trial protocol was described in detail in a previous protocol report
The primary end point was a change in CFS score and the absolute CFS value

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.34304.headline_claim: A personalised resistance exercise programme for 3 months improved walking distance, health-related quality of life, anxiety, depression, and grip strength after COVID-19, without increasing adverse events or postexertional malaise, and may be a generalizable therapy.
10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.34304.overall: The paper reports a modest, nominally significant primary effect (36.5 m, 95% CI 6.6 to 66.3, P = .02) from an open-label trial with unblinded assessment of an effort-dependent test, extra contact in the intervention arm, and 17.6% missing primary data. The secondary-outcome claims (quality of life, anxiety, depression), the generalizability claim and the broad safety claim go further than the unadjusted, unpowered and partly subgroup-based evidence supports. The numerical slips (Table 1, Table 3, units) are minor and do not change the primary result, but the Table 3 Group B row is wrong and should be corrected.

primary_outcome.name: Incremental Shuttle Walk Test distance at 3 months

issues.title: About 20 secondary outcomes at unadjusted P<.05; conclusion names three nominal hits (P=.02, .01, .002)
issues.explanation: The primary result is itself modest (P = .02, CI 6.6 to 66.3 m). Table 4 shows about 20 secondary outcomes, and only EQ-5D-5L utility (P = .02), PHQ-4 category (P = .01) and handgrip (P = .002) reached P < .05, with no correction. Under a Bonferroni threshold of about .0025 only grip strength would clearly remain. The conclusion nonetheless lists quality of life, anxiety and depression as improved. The anxiety and depression claim comes from a single 4-item screening category score, not separate outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical or alpha-adjusted testing plan in the protocol or statistical analysis plan that covers these outcomes.

quotes.text: All P values were from 2-sided tests and results were deemed statistically significant at P < .05.
appeared to improve walking distance, health-related quality of life, anxiety, depression, and grip strength.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper tests about 18 secondary outcomes in Table 4 at unadjusted P < .05 with no multiplicity correction. Its conclusion names health-related quality of life (P = .02), anxiety and depression (PHQ-4, P = .01) and grip strength (P = .002) as improved, without noting that these are nominal results among many tests. The 'about 20' figure is slightly high, the wording 'appeared to improve' is hedged, and grip strength (P = .002) would survive a Bonferroni correction for 18 tests, while the other two would not. Also, the PHQ-4 result is a single combined category, so 'anxiety' and 'depression'

issues.title: Open-label usual-care comparator, unblinded ISWT assessors and extra staff contact in the intervention arm
issues.explanation: Control participants received no nonroutine contact, while intervention participants were contacted every 2 weeks (daily in hospital). ISWT and interviews were done by staff who knew allocation, and the psychological and quality-of-life outcomes are self-reported. Expectation and attention effects could therefore account for part of the 36.5 m difference and the questionnaire effects. The study supports a benefit of the whole package versus no contact, not of resistance exercise specifically.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that ISWT assessors were blinded or an attention-matched control arm showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Participants in the intervention group received more contact with site staff compared with participants in the control group.

with no nonroutine contacts from research staff.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with a usual-care comparator, the ISWT and interviews were done by assessors who knew the allocation, and the intervention arm had more staff contact; the authors state all three. The limitations are disclosed, but the paper concludes they 'should not undermine the overall validity' and does not discuss how they could inflate the modest primary effect (36.5 m, 95% CI 6.6-66.3) or the patient-reported results.

issues.title: Primary outcome analysed in 192 of 233 (17.6% missing), while text cites 11.2% withdrawal
issues.explanation: The text describes a low withdrawal rate of 11.2% (26 of 233). The primary analysis includes only 192 participants (98 control, 94 intervention), so 41 of 233 randomized (17.6%) contribute no change score, and the reasons for loss to follow-up are stated as unavailable. The result (P = .02, lower CI bound 6.6 m) is not far from the null, so it may be sensitive to this missing data. The headline attrition figure understates the missing outcome data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The eTable 7 imputed analysis (or other sensitivity analysis) giving essentially the same effect and CI, together with a clear account of the non-completers.

issues.title: Generalizability concluded from non-significant interaction tests the authors say were not powered
issues.explanation: The Limitations state the interaction analysis was not powered. The following sentence nonetheless treats absence of significant interactions as support for generalizability. Subgroup CIs are very wide, for example race/ethnicity subgroup 'Other' 17.3 m (−103.6 to 138.1) with n = 13, and sex estimates differ by more than 45 m. Absence of evidence of heterogeneity here is weak support and does not justify the generalizability claim in the Conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified, powered test of effect modification, or confidence intervals narrow enough to exclude clinically important heterogeneity.

issues.title: 'No adverse events' claim rests on hospitalizations and a 99-person malaise subgroup, not a full AE report
issues.explanation: The Discussion and Conclusions say no adverse events or serious adverse events occurred in relation to the intervention and that adverse events were not increased. The main text reports only hospitalizations and deaths, plus a malaise questionnaire completed by 99 of 233 participants after a protocol amendment, measured only at follow-up. Self-reported adverse effects such as musculoskeletal symptoms are not tabulated for either arm. The safety conclusion is plausible but broader than the evidence shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A complete adverse-event table in the supplement showing no intervention-related events, with ascertainment equivalent in both arms.

10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.20687.headline_claim: Goal-oriented cognitive rehabilitation improved self-reported goal attainment in people with long COVID and cognitive impairment, with benefit sustained at 6 months, and provides the first class II evidence supporting its use in routine care.
10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.20687.overall: The primary finding, higher self-rated goal attainment with CR than usual care at 3 and 6 months, is statistically clear and robust to complete-case analysis. Its interpretation as a specific, clinically meaningful and durable benefit is weakened by the unblinded self-rated outcome, the lack of an attention-matched control and 26% attrition. The numeric slips (screened N, drug-type row, P value, effect-size column) are minor individually but suggest weak table checking.

primary_outcome.name: Goal attainment (BGSI), participant-reported, at 3 and 6 months

issues.title: Self-rated primary outcome, unblinded participants, and no attention-matched control (usual care)
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is the participant's own goal rating. Participants knew their allocation, and the control group got variable usual care with less therapist contact. The paper itself says this may introduce expectancy and nonspecific effects, yet the Discussion calls the benefit 'clinically meaningful and durable'. The trial can show that CR participants rated their goals higher, but it cannot separate the specific effect of CR from contact time and expectancy. This weakens the main result, so it stands only as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control arm, or a blinded or objective measure of goal achievement showing the same effect.

quotes.text: participants could not be blinded to group allocation, which is common in behavioral interventions and may introduce expectancy effects
the absence of an active control condition meant greater therapist contact in the intervention group, which may have introduced nonspecific effects

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome is participant-reported, participants knew their allocation, and the comparator was usual care without attention matching, all as the paper itself states. The authors acknowledge these limitations and argue the large, sustained effect makes them unlikely to explain the results, but the design features are as described.

issues.title: Conclusion endorses routine-care use from one 78-person trial with a self-rated primary outcome
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says the findings 'support its use in routine care' and calls the effects clinically meaningful and sustained. The evidence is one small trial with unblinded participants rating their own goals, a variable usual-care comparator, and secondary cognitive and symptom outcomes showing no benefit. A routine-care recommendation goes beyond this. A statement that CR improved self-rated goal attainment versus usual care at 3 and 6 months is what the data support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Replication in a larger blinded or attention-controlled trial, or independent evidence of benefit on functional outcomes.

quotes.text: provide the first class II evidence for a goal-based cognitive rehabilitation intervention for this population and support its use in routine care

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion endorses routine-care use on the basis of one trial of 78 randomized participants (below the planned 88) with a self-rated primary outcome and no attention-matched control. The wording is not hedged. I checked the conclusion's wording against the design and limitations; I did not assess whether 'class II' is the correct grade under a particular classification scheme.

issues.title: Cohen d values in Table 2 do not track the printed differences (e.g., 1.90 gives d = 0.07)
issues.explanation: The reported effect sizes do not match the mean differences and the SDs in Table 1. A 6-month difference of 1.90 on D-KEFS condition 2, with a baseline SD of about 3.2, would be d of about 0.6, but d = 0.07 is printed. This tiny d is then cited in the Discussion as a 'small improvement'. The 3-month C4 difference (0.87, SD about 3.3) would give about 0.26, not 0.48. The d column cannot be relied on, which affects how the secondary results are described. Direction is mixed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of how d was computed (standardiser) that reproduces the printed values.

quotes.text: adjusted mean difference, 1.90 [95% CI, 0.32-3.49]
processing speed at 6 months (Cohen d = 0.07)

issues.title: 26% loss by 6 months, higher in CR at 3 months; durability relies on MAR imputation
issues.explanation: By 6 months, 20 of 78 participants had no outcome data. Loss at 3 months was uneven between arms (5 CR vs 1 TAU). Missing-at-random is asserted, not tested, and the sensitivity analysis agrees with the primary one, which limits the concern. The 6-month cognitive results rest on complete cases only (n = 40 to 44).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Missingness analyses or a delta-adjusted sensitivity analysis showing conclusions are stable under non-ignorable dropout.

quotes.text: By 6 months, these rates declined to 30 participants (75.0%) in TAU and 28 participants (73.7%) in CR groups.
multiple imputation was not used, and complete case analysis is presented

Table 2 gives P < .001 for the same estimate, and the printed CI (0.75 to 1.11) and SE (0.09) imply P well below .001. The text value looks like it was taken from the goal-satisfaction row. issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text value comes from a different model or analysis set than the Table 2 row.

10.1001/jamaneurol.2025.4415.headline_claim: Three remotely delivered interventions (BrainHQ, PASC-CoRE + BrainHQ, tDCS-active + BrainHQ) showed no differential benefit on the modified ECog2 versus their comparators at end of intervention in long COVID cognitive symptoms, and the authors conclude the trial failed to demonstrate differential benefits.
10.1001/jamaneurol.2025.4415.overall: The null headline conclusion is reasonably supported: effect estimates are tightly centred on zero with narrow CIs, secondary outcomes agree, and the authors word the conclusion cautiously. The only confirmed error is a trivial typo (74 vs 174) in a descriptive secondary result. The unvalidated 7-day recall modification of the primary scale is a modest caveat on interpreting the null, not a threat to it.

issues.title: Primary outcome is a self-report ECog2 with a changed 7-day recall anchor and no validation reported
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is a 41-item self-reported scale whose recall window was changed to the past 7 days, and the paper reports no validation or reliability data for this version. Responsiveness to change is therefore unknown, which weakens how firmly a null can be read from it alone. The concern is partly offset by consistent nulls on independent secondary and performance-based outcomes and by the authors' careful 'failed to demonstrate' wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published or supplementary validation data showing the 7-day modified ECog2 has adequate reliability and responsiveness in long COVID.

10.1001/jamaoto.2025.1304.headline_claim: SGB with mepivacaine is not superior to saline placebo for COVID-19-induced parosmia, and SGB should not be recommended as treatment.
10.1001/jamaoto.2025.1304.overall: The null finding on the responder outcome (43% vs 38% at 3 months) is consistent across the text and tables, but the trial stopped at 48 of 114 planned participants and the CI still includes the 25-point difference defined as clinically meaningful, so the firm 'should not be recommended' conclusion overreaches. Several printing errors (baseline sex percentages, the 3-month CI upper limit in the abstract, Table 2 percentage cells) are reporting slips that do not change the overall null interpretation. Late registration is a transparency weakness the paper does not disclose.

issues.explanation: The trial stopped for futility at 48 randomized participants (target 114) and analysed 46 per protocol. The 3-month CI for the responder difference is wide enough to include the 25-point difference the authors defined as clinically meaningful. The abstract, key points and conclusion nonetheless say SGB provides no benefit beyond placebo and should not be recommended; the data support only that no benefit was demonstrated with limited precision. The paper's Limitations paragraph does not mention the early stop or imprecision.

The Limitations section does not mention early stopping, imprecision or per-protocol analysis, and the upper CI bound is inconsistent between Table 2 (23) and the text (33). 10.1002/alz.091999.headline_claim: No conclusion is stated in the supplied text; the only design information is the title, which describes a six-month follow-up study of the cognitive profile of post-COVID-19 patients after cognitive rehabilitation at a public Brazilian centre.

10.1002/clc.70110.headline_claim: Low-level tragus stimulation is a promising adjunctive therapy for POTS following post-acute COVID-19, reducing upright heart rate response, altering HRV, and decreasing NPY levels.
10.1002/clc.70110.overall: The headline claim that tragus stimulation attenuates POTS rests on small-sample physiological surrogate outcomes, reported only as 'p<0.05' with no effect sizes, no flow diagram, no stated blinding or registration, and internal inconsistencies between text and figure captions. The direction of effect is plausible but the conclusion should be read as exploratory and not as evidence of clinical benefit.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Title and conclusion claim therapy for POTS, but only physiological surrogates were measured
issues.explanation: The title states that tragus stimulation attenuates POTS and the conclusion calls it a promising adjunctive therapy. The limitations admit that broader clinical symptoms were not assessed, so only HR, HRV and NPY were studied. A reduction in heart-rate response does not show symptom improvement, and the outcomes are not reported with effect sizes. The follow-up statement also mentions symptoms but none are reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported symptom scores or functional outcomes showing improvement.

quotes.text: this study primarily focused on the effects of LL -TS on physiological parameters
LL -TS represents a promising adjunctive therapy for individuals with POTS following post -acute COVID -19 infection

second_reader.what_stands: Only physiological measures (HR, Holter HR, HRV, NPY, BP) are reported, with no symptom, quality-of-life or functional outcomes, yet the title and conclusion use therapeutic language ('attenuates POTS', 'promising adjunctive therapy'). This is softened because the authors acknowledge the gap in Limitations, the conclusion itself lists the physiological effects, and upright HR rise is the defining feature of POTS; so the problem is overstated framing rather than a concealed gap. Note also that the Methods say symptoms were reassessed at follow-up but no results are given.

issues.title: Minimum HR: text says significantly decreased, Figure 4 caption says no effect
issues.explanation: Results 2.4 states that minimum and maximum HR were significantly decreased at 1 month and 1 year versus sham, and further reduced versus baseline. The Figure 4 caption says LL-TS had no effect on minimum HR and that only average and maximum HR fell. The text also never mentions average HR, which the caption and discussion do. The reader cannot tell which Holter outcomes actually changed, and the Discussion refers to average and maximum HR only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The figure data showing which of the two statements is correct and a correction of the other.

quotes.text: The minimum and maximum HR were significantly decreased at 1 month and 1 year in the LL -TS group compared with the sham LL -TS group (all p <0.05)
(A) LL -TS had no effects on minimum HR during the 24 h -holter.

issues.title: Allocation concealment and blinding not described; unequal arms (26 vs 31) unexplained
issues.explanation: The paper names a web-based randomization table and a similar-looking sham device, but does not say who was blinded or how allocation was concealed. The arms are unequal (26 vs 31) with no stated block or stratification scheme, and there is no flow diagram. The outcomes are mostly objective measurements, so the effect on interpretation is modest, but the sham-controlled claim cannot be fully assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of double-blind design and central concealment, or the trial protocol.

quotes.text: All patients were randomly assigned to either the LL -TS group or the sham LL -TS group using a web -based randomization table.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation for 57 patients; many outcomes tested without multiplicity control
issues.explanation: No power calculation or primary outcome is declared, and 57 patients are analysed for HR, Holter, HRV, LF/HF and NPY outcomes at three time points, with p<0.05 as the threshold throughout. The limitation section admits the small sample, but the conclusion is still phrased as a promising therapy. Findings should be read as exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome with a power calculation, or a protocol with multiplicity handling.

quotes.text: First, the sample size in our study was relatively small, limiting the generalizability of our findings.
Statistical significance was set at p <0.05.

issues.title: Analysis described only as 'two-way ANOVA'; no statistics, effect sizes or exact p reported
issues.explanation: The methods name a two-way ANOVA for between-group comparisons, with no statement of factors, repeated-measures handling or post hoc tests. The results give only 'p<0.05' and no means, SDs, effect sizes or test statistics in the text. Between-group claims at 1 month and 1 year therefore cannot be checked, and baseline imbalance is not addressed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary tables with means, SDs, ANOVA terms and post hoc procedures.

quotes.text: For continuous data with a normal distribution, a two -way ANOVA test was used for comparisons between groups.

issues.title: No trial registration; enrolment window and consent waiver raise questions about prospective design
issues.explanation: No registry number is given for a study described as randomized. The inclusion window begins in December 2019 and one centre's ethics approval waived consent, which sits oddly with a prospective randomized sham-controlled design. Prespecification of outcomes cannot be checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry entry dated before enrolment.

quotes.text: This study was a multi -center randomized study.
the institutional Ethics Committee of Xiangyang Central Hospital reviewed and approved the study, waiving the requirement for patient consent

issues.title: NPY results paragraph describes HR change; 1-year further decline after 1-month therapy unexplained
issues.explanation: The NPY paragraph in Results 2.2 repeats sentences about 'the increase in HR' within the LL-TS group instead of NPY, so the NPY within-group results are not actually reported. The stimulation lasted 1 month, yet HR, Holter HR and NPY are said to fall further at 1 year than at 1 month; the paper does not explain whether stimulation continued or what drove this. The durability claim is therefore unsupported by described methods.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that stimulation continued to 1 year, with NPY within-group data reported.

quotes.text: The peripheral NPY levels during the postural test were significantly reduced at 1 month and 1 year in the LL -TS group compared with the sham LL -TS group (all p <0.05). In the LL -TS group, the increase in HR at 1 month
continuing for a total duration of 1 month.

issues.title: HF change described as 'increased' in text but 'attenuated' in Figure 5 caption
issues.explanation: Results 2.5 says HF significantly increased from supine to standing in the LL-TS group versus sham. The Figure 5 caption says the change in LF and HF was attenuated, grouping HF with LF, which the text says decreased. The caption may refer to the size of the change rather than its direction, so the wording is inconsistent but not necessarily contradictory. Without the figure, the direction of the HF effect cannot be confirmed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 5 panels showing the sign of the HF change in each group.

quotes.text: the HF component of HRV, associated with parasympathetic activity, significantly increased from supine to standing in the LL -TS group compared with the sham LL -TS group
The change in LF and HF from supine to standing was significantly attenuated in the LL -TS group compared with the sham LL -TS group.

10.1002/ctm2.1436.headline_claim: PTIC modifies the physiological network of post-acute COVID-19 sequelae in a sex-dependent way and reduced hyperinflammation after treatment.
10.1002/ctm2.1436.overall: The headline claims that PTIC reduced hyperinflammation and acts differently by sex are weakly supported: they rest on 37 of 89 randomised completers, many uncorrected comparisons, and a descriptive rho contrast (0.17 vs 0.36) in subgroups of 8 to 12 with no interaction test. The findings are hypothesis-generating at best, and the extended-course recommendation for women is not testable with this design.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated as a single primary outcome; relative change from baseline in inflammatory biomarkers and network correlation metrics

issues.title: Sex-dependent effect in title rests on rho 0.17 vs 0.36 in groups of 8 and 12, with no interaction test
issues.explanation: The title and summary claim PTIC acts depending on sex, and that women may need a longer course. The evidence is a single descriptive comparison of two network correlations from tiny, separately analysed subgroups, with no sex-by-treatment interaction test or uncertainty interval. The study was also not designed or powered for sex subgroups, so the difference could easily be noise.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A formal sex-by-treatment interaction test (or bootstrap CI for the rho difference) showing a clear difference.

quotes.text: Polymerised type I collagen modifies the physiological network of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 depending on sex

Women in the PTIC group exhibited a stronger response, evidenced by a lower correlation of the network between baseline and the first-day post-treatment (rho = 0.17) as compared to the male group (rho = 0.36).

second_reader.what_stands: The sex-dependence claim rests in the main text on a single comparison of rho 0.17 (n=8 women) versus 0.36 (n=12 men) with no interaction test, interval or permutation comparison, so a sex difference is not statistically established there. The point that it relies solely on these values is limited, since the supplement (Figures S4-S5, Table S4) may contain other supporting analyses that were not available to check, and the rho p-value above is illustrative only.

issues.title: Only 37 of 89 randomised patients analysed (58% excluded); completer-only analysis, no ITT
issues.explanation: Of 89 randomised, only 37 who completed all assessments were analysed. Excluding about 58% of randomised patients breaks the protection of randomisation, and the paper gives no reasons per arm, no baseline comparison of completers versus non-completers, and no sensitivity analysis. Efficacy and sex-difference conclusions rest on this selected subset.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 52 excluded patients were missing for reasons unrelated to treatment and that results were robust to including them.

quotes.text: Our analysis focused only on patients who had completed all assessments
or a matching placebo ( n = 44)

script.explanation: The participant flow balances arithmetically but 1 transition(s) drop participants with no stated reason: 52 participant(s) drop between 'randomized' and 'analysed' with no stated exclusions. Not itself an error -- papers legitimately omit attrition reasons -- but the reader cannot audit the loss.

second_reader.what_stands: Only 37 of 89 randomised patients (41.6%) were analysed, 52 (58%) were excluded, and the paper states the analysis was restricted to patients who completed all assessments. No ITT analysis, reasons for non-completion or handling of missing data are given in this letter, although the primary trial report may contain them.

issues.title: Dozens of biomarker-by-timepoint comparisons with uncorrected p<.05 support 'reduced hyperinflammation'
issues.explanation: The claim that PTIC reduced hyperinflammation rests on a handful of nominally significant differences (p<.05 or p<.01) among many cytokines, cell ratios and three timepoints. No multiplicity correction is described, and the significant markers differ from timepoint to timepoint. With so many tests, several p<.05 results are expected by chance, and 37 completers give little power or stability.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified correction (e.g. FDR) in the supplement under which these differences remain significant.

quotes.text: We observed significant differences between groups (Figure S3C) on first-day post-treatment in IP-10, IL-8, CRP
Our findings suggest that PTIC reduced the hyperinflammation associated with COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: The letter reports 12 significant between-group differences over three timepoints with only p<.05 or p<.01 thresholds and no stated multiplicity correction, yet concludes PTIC 'reduced the hyperinflammation'. The word 'dozens' and the 'uncorrected' label cannot be verified from the main text, because the number of variables tested and any correction may be in the supplement. The significant markers also include several cell-ratio variables that are not direct inflammation markers.

issues.title: Conclusions that PTIC reduced hyperinflammation and women need longer courses exceed the 37-completer data
issues.explanation: The summary states PTIC reduced hyperinflammation and implies women may need an extended course, but no course-length comparison was made. The data are scattered uncorrected differences in selected markers from 37 completers (17 placebo, 20 PTIC), with no sample-size calculation and no ITT analysis. The recommendation on extended treatment in women is not testable from this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from arms with different treatment durations, or an ITT analysis with corrected p-values supporting the same conclusions.

quotes.text: Administration of PTIC reduced hyperinflammation, leading to a decrease in the correlation between physiological networks
Immunomodulatory drugs, such as PTIC, may necessitate an extended course in women with a robust physiological network.

second_reader.what_stands: The statement that PTIC 'reduced hyperinflammation' is presented as established from 12 uncorrected comparisons in 37 completers, and the advice that women may need an extended course is not tested by any comparison of treatment durations. The latter is worded with 'may', so it is a speculation more than a claim, but both conclusions go beyond what a completer-only, small-subgroup analysis can support and no limitations are discussed.

issues.title: Network correlation (rho) used as recovery metric is not validated and has no uncertainty
issues.explanation: Conclusions about faster recovery and treatment effect rely on rho between network adjacency matrices at baseline and later days, built from correlations filtered at p<.05 in groups of 7 to 12. No validation as a clinical or recovery marker, and no confidence intervals or tests on the rho values, are given. This weakens the network-based claims but is a methodological choice by the authors.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Validation studies linking this network-correlation metric to clinical recovery and showing stability of rho in groups this small.

quotes.text: Network adjacency was calculated using a Spearman correlation matrix, filtered with p < .05.

issues.title: Text contradicts itself on whether PTIC altered more variables in men or in women
issues.explanation: One passage says only a few variables changed in women compared with placebo while many changed in men. A later passage says that, in contrast to women, PTIC in men only transiently affected a few variables. Both cannot describe the same comparison, so the sex-dependent narrative is unclear. This is a wording inconsistency that does not alter any printed number.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Figures S4/S5 showing the two statements refer to different, non-conflicting comparisons.

quotes.text: However, in the groups of female participants, only a few variables showed modifications compared to placebo
In contrast to women, PTIC administration in men only affected transiently a few variables

10.1002/fsn3.3597.headline_claim: Six months of creatine supplementation improves tissue bioenergetics and attenuates clinical features of post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome, and is safe and effective.
10.1002/fsn3.3597.overall: The primary muscle-creatine increase is plausible, but the trial has only 6 participants per arm, many uncorrected tests and a large baseline imbalance in the primary outcome. The fatigue measures showed no between-group effect, yet the conclusion claims attenuated clinical features and recommends creatine as safe and effective. Several text figures (77.8%, 33%, lung pain) do not match Table 2 or the Results, so the conclusion should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Change in vastus medialis muscle total creatine (MRS) from baseline to 6-month follow-up

issues.title: n = 12 justified by a power calculation for d = 0.5, yet used for confident efficacy claims
issues.explanation: The minimal sample of 12 is said to come from G*Power with a medium effect (0.50), alpha .05 and power .80 for two groups and three measurements. The correlation among repeated measures and other inputs are not given. A two-group comparison at d = 0.5 normally needs over 100 participants. With six per arm, the many outcome tests are very imprecise, and the paper's own limitation text notes the small sample. The conclusion still says creatine improves bioenergetics and attenuates clinical features.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Full G*Power inputs (correlation among repeated measures, nonsphericity correction) showing n = 12 is adequate for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: was calculated prior to the study using power analysis
The relatively small size of our sample also restricts

second_reader.what_stands: The stated calculation does not fit its own label. n = 12 cannot give 80% power for a medium d = 0.5 under conventional two-group assumptions, and the calculation concerned one primary outcome (muscle creatine), not the clinical outcomes. The limitations paragraph mentions small sample size only for gender analyses and does not weigh it against the confident efficacy claims ('outcompetes placebo', 'safe and effective'). I could not verify the exact G*Power inputs, so the claim that the calculation is wrong is limited to the mismatch with d = 0.5.

issues.title: Safe and effective recommendation drawn from 6 creatine-treated patients and one mild adverse event
issues.explanation: Safety was judged from an open-ended questionnaire in six creatine participants over six months, with one mild nausea case. This cannot exclude uncommon harms. Efficacy rests on many uncorrected tests in a tiny sample. The recommendation as safe and effective goes beyond what the design can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Larger sample or systematic safety monitoring (laboratory markers, structured adverse event capture) supporting the safety claim.

quotes.text: Creatine induced no major side effects
transient mild nausea

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion recommends creatine 'as a safe and effective intervention' on the basis of 6 creatine-treated patients with one mild adverse event. Such data cannot exclude even common adverse events (the upper bound is about 50% or more), and the limitations section does not mention that safety cannot be assessed at this sample size. The wording is hedged with 'might', but the recommendation still goes beyond what 6 patients can show.

issues.title: Conclusion claims attenuated clinical features; no MFI-20 or exercise-tolerance interaction (p > .05)
issues.explanation: The Results state that no significant interaction was found across the five MFI-20 fatigue subdomains, and time to exhaustion had p = .75. The Discussion and Conclusion highlight pain, concentration and other symptoms. Fatigue is the defining feature of the syndrome, so claiming to 'attenuate clinical features' without stating the null fatigue result overstates the clinical benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion that explicitly states the fatigue outcomes were null and limits the clinical claim to the symptom VAS scores.

quotes.text: No significant interaction effect was found
attenuate clinical features

second_reader.what_stands: The paper found no treatment-by-time interaction on any of the five MFI-20 fatigue dimensions (all p > .05) or on exercise tolerance (p = .75), so the conclusion that creatine attenuates clinical features of the fatigue syndrome is not supported for fatigue or exertional capacity. Seven VAS symptom interactions are nominally significant (p ≤ .03), so the statement has partial support there. This support is weakened because the placebo group improved too, baselines differed between groups, nothing was adjusted for multiple testing, and the sample is n = 6 per arm.

issues.title: Lung pain called a significant drop in Discussion; not significant within creatine group (Results/Table 2)
issues.explanation: The Results say creatine significantly improved symptoms except anosmia and lung pain, and Table 2 carries no significance mark for creatine lung pain. The Discussion nonetheless says participants reported a significant drop in lung and body pain. Placebo lung pain fell almost as much (2.0 to 0.0 versus 2.3 to 0.0), so the interaction p = .02 does not clearly support a creatine-specific lung pain effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion refers to the between-group interaction, together with a creatine-versus-placebo contrast specific to lung pain.

quotes.text: except for anosmia and lung pain
reporting a significant drop in lung and body pain after the intervention

issues.title: Baseline vastus medialis creatine 28.2 vs 20.6 mM between arms; baseline balance untested for primary outcome
issues.explanation: Baseline primary-outcome values differ by 7.6 mM, more than two SDs, and the creatine arm is also about 8 years older. The paper says baseline characteristics did not differ, but this refers to demographics and not to the primary outcome. A change-score analysis of the primary outcome, with no adjustment for baseline, makes the between-group interaction hard to interpret.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted analysis (ANCOVA on change) of the primary outcome giving the same between-group result.

quotes.location: Table 2, Vastus medialis muscle, Creatine baseline
Table 2, Vastus medialis muscle, Placebo baseline

issues.title: About 26 interaction tests at alpha .05 without correction; brain-region findings p = .01 each
issues.explanation: Interaction p-values were computed for 13 tissue sites, 5 fatigue subdomains, time to exhaustion and 7 symptoms, all at p ≤ .05 with no adjustment. The brain-region claims (left frontal, right parietal white matter, p = .01) would not survive even a modest correction across 13 sites. The primary muscle outcome is more robust, but secondary and symptom claims are weakened.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or correction showing the brain-region results survive adjustment.

quotes.text: The significance level was set at p ≤ .05.
to augment creatine levels at vastus medialis muscle

issues.title: Concentration-difficulty drop stated as 77.8%; Table 2 means give 62.5% (4.0 to 1.5)
issues.explanation: The Discussion reports a 77.8% drop in concentration-difficulty scores at 3 months. Table 2 shows creatine means of 4.0 at baseline and 1.5 at 3 months, a 62.5% drop. The method behind 77.8% is not stated, so the quoted figure overstates the change that the table supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated derivation (for example mean of per-participant percentage changes) that yields 77.8%.

quotes.text: significant drop of 77.8%

issues.title: Brain creatine increase 'up to 33%' vs about 30% from Table 2 right parietal white matter means
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives the maximum increase as 33% in right parietal white matter. Table 2 means of 5.3 and 6.9 give about 30%. The gap is small and could reflect a different averaging method, but the printed values do not reproduce it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level data showing a mean per-participant increase of 33%.

quotes.location: Table 2, Right parietal white matter, Creatine baseline
Table 2, Right parietal white matter, Creatine 3 months

issues.title: Supplier-funded trial; funder's role in design, analysis and reporting not stated
issues.explanation: Alzchem GmbH provided the creatine and is a named funder, and the senior author declares an advisory role with the company. The paper does not state whether the funder had any role in design, analysis or reporting. Conflicts are disclosed, but the missing statement leaves independence unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the funders had no role in design, data analysis, interpretation or reporting.

quotes.text: Creatine monohydrate was provided by Alzchem GmbH
and Alzchem GmbH, Trostberg, Germany.

10.1002/hsr2.71367.headline_claim: An individually tailored respiratory physiotherapy programme was feasible for persons with PASC and persistent dyspnoea, and was associated with significant improvements in health-related quality of life and daily functioning.
10.1002/hsr2.71367.overall: The feasibility conclusion (13 recruited, 100% retention, 99% of sessions completed) is supported. The claims of benefit and safety rest on unblinded, uncontrolled pre-post changes in patient-reported scores across about 19 uncorrected tests, with two non-significant results (p = 0.0544 and 0.06) described as improvements. These claims should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (recruitment, retention, and completion of supervised sessions)

issues.title: Benefit and safety claimed from 13 patients in an open-label single-arm pre-post study with PROM outcomes
issues.explanation: There is no control group, participants were unblinded, and the benefit outcomes are self-reported scores compared before and after, so regression to the mean, natural recovery and expectation effects cannot be separated from a treatment effect. The authors acknowledge that time alone cannot be ruled out, yet state the program 'demonstrates' benefit and is 'safe', and recommend it for practice. Safety rests on a single statement that no adverse events occurred in 13 people. Feasibility conclusions are supported, but the benefit and safety claims go beyond the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control comparison, or conclusion wording limited to feasibility and hypothesis generation.

quotes.text: This intervention was able to be implemented in an outpatient setting with minimal resources and was found to be safe and beneficial for participants.
This study demonstrates that an individualized physiotherapy program for persons with PASC is feasible, beneficial for symptom burden
The impact of time alone cannot be ruled out

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does base 'safe and beneficial' and 'demonstrates ... beneficial for symptom burden, and improves health-related quality of life' on 13 participants in an open-label single-arm pre-post design whose efficacy outcomes are mostly self-reported, with no control group, uncorrected multiple testing, and an average 20-week window in which time alone cannot be excluded. The authors do state these limits in the limitations paragraph and call the study a pilot, so the claim is not made without caveats elsewhere, but the penultimate Discussion paragraph and section 4.1 use causal, unhedged wor

issues.title: EQ-5D anxiety/depression (p=0.0544) and cough VAS (p=0.06) described as improved despite p > 0.05
issues.explanation: The Results list anxiety/depression among the significant improvements in individual EQ-5D domains. Table 3 gives p = 0.0544 for that domain, which is above the stated threshold of 0.05. The text also says cough severity was improved, but its p is 0.06. Two non-significant results are therefore reported as significant improvements, which slightly overstates the quality-of-life and symptom benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alpha above 0.0544, or a corrected Table 3 p-value for anxiety/depression below 0.05.

quotes.text: as well as in individual EQ -5D domains of usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression
Level of functioning (PCFS) and cough severity (VAS) were also improved.
Statistical significance was assumed at p -value < 0.05.

issues.title: About 19 secondary comparisons tested at p<0.05 without multiplicity correction; borderline results called benefits
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports 19 secondary-outcome p-values, all judged against an unadjusted 0.05 threshold. With that many tests, a few nominally significant results are expected by chance. Results that would not survive a Bonferroni correction (such as the pain/discomfort and PCFS findings) are still presented as improvements. The strongest results, such as EQ usual activities and EQ-VAS, would likely survive correction. This weakens secondary findings but not the feasibility conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified statement that the secondary outcomes were purely exploratory and hypothesis-generating, with conclusions worded accordingly.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was assumed at p -value < 0.05.
Participants' self -efficacy for managing symptoms improved across all domains.

issues.title: 'Large effect in all domains' of symptom self-efficacy, but one d = -0.78 is moderate by the paper's own bins
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the symptom self-efficacy domains showed a large effect size in all domains. Four d values appear in Table 3: -0.97, -0.78, -0.81 and -0.88. Under the Methods bins (large = 0.8-1.29), the -0.78 for interfering with friends/family is moderate. Only one domain is affected, and it sits right at the boundary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An unrounded d of at least 0.80 for the interfering-with-friends/family domain.

quotes.text: the latter demonstrating a large effect size in all domains
moderate ( d =0.5 -0.79)

10.1002/jbio.202200391.headline_claim: Photobiomodulation delivered by transcranial helmet or whole-body light bed improves cognitive and EEG measures of COVID-19 brain fog, with the authors concluding both modalities are effective.
10.1002/jbio.202200391.overall: The headline claim that either PBM modality improves COVID brain fog is not supported at the strength stated: the study has two active-only arms of n = 7, no control, no primary outcome, a post-hoc choice of the Day 12 timepoint, and no multiplicity handling. Several results are overstated in the text (tPBM Flanker described as significant at p = 0.1, MoCA called significant at p = 0.052). The results can be read as hypothesis-generating at most.

primary_outcome.name: No single primary outcome named; pre- vs post-treatment (Day 1 vs Day 12) changes in MoCA, DSST, Trails A/B, PRT and qEEG P300/Flanker measures

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from pre-post change in two active-only arms without placebo or sham control
issues.explanation: Both arms received active PBM and results are reported as within-arm pre-to-post changes, with no placebo, sham or untreated comparison and no between-group test. Practice effects from repeated cognitive testing, expectation and regression to the mean cannot be separated from any treatment effect. The authors' acknowledgement of the limitation does not support the unqualified conclusion that PBM was effective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or untreated control group, or a comparison against a published learning-effect benchmark for these tests.

quotes.text: As a proof of principle study, the design used only active treatment.
This study is limited by both the number of subjects and the lack of a placebo arm.

second_reader.what_stands: The effect estimates are within-arm pre-post changes with no sham, placebo or untreated comparator, and the paper still concludes effectiveness. However, the lack of a placebo arm and the pilot status are acknowledged explicitly in the paper, so the problem is that the conclusions are stronger than the design supports, not that the limitation is concealed.

issues.title: Title and summary assert effectiveness from an uncontrolled n = 14 pilot with mixed significance
issues.explanation: The title and summary state that either treatment improves brain fog and was effective, but the study has 7 participants per arm, no control, no sample-size justification, no primary outcome and no between-group analysis. Several outcomes were not significant for one or both arms (PRT, TrA for wbPBM, most tPBM qEEG measures) and MoCA p values were 0.052. A pilot of this design can generate hypotheses but cannot support a claim of effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled design with adequate power and a pre-specified primary outcome showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Use of either transcranial or whole-body photobiomodulation treatments improves COVID-19 brain fog
PBM delivered by either whole body or transcranial treatment was effective in improving parameters of brain performance

second_reader.what_stands: The title and summary state effectiveness without qualification, but the evidence is an uncontrolled two-arm pilot of 14 people where about half of the arm-level outcome tests reached nominal significance, with no multiplicity control. The limitations paragraph acknowledges small size and no placebo, yet the title and summary conclusions go further than that design can support.

issues.title: Discussion says each method significantly decreased Flanker time, but tPBM Flanker T had p = 0.1
issues.explanation: The Results report a non-significant tPBM Flanker time change (p = 0.1) and state it was significant only in the wbPBM group. The Discussion nonetheless says each method significantly decreased Flanker response time and increased P300 voltage.
