quotes.text: In the follow-up period, the exercise group was more active and the MFI-20 improved more than in the control group.
Within the groups, only the MFI-20 of the exercise group improved significantly between the 3- and 6-month follow-up.

issues.title: Discussion claims strength improved vs control; Table 3 group-effect p = 0.953, 0.381, 0.594
issues.explanation: The Discussion states exercise improved strength compared to control. The paper's own between-group tests for strength (leg press, rowing, bench press) are non-significant, and controls also improved significantly on leg press and rowing. Only VO2peak and oxygen pulse showed group effects.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group comparison for any strength measure.

quotes.text: Exercise improved endurance capacity, oxygen pulse, and strength compared to control.
A group effect was found for VO2peak ( p < 0.01) and oxygen pulse ( p < 0.05) between exercise and control, respectively.

issues.title: Unqualified 'exercise is safe' rests on 0 events in ~22 exercisers over 4 weeks in screened population
issues.explanation: Safety criteria were defined and no events were reported, which is reassuring. However, with about 22 exercising patients, zero events is compatible with an event rate up to roughly 14% (95% upper bound), and the cohort was pre-screened to exclude cardiac disease. The unqualified 'safe' conclusion and 'important reassurance' go beyond what this sample can establish.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified safety monitoring protocol with a precision statement acknowledging the upper bound on event rate.

quotes.text: Our study, therefore, provides important reassurance that patients post-COVID without elevation of troponin and signs of cardiac diseases can safely perform physical exercise.
Safety of exercise was defined as no new symptoms or worsening of symptoms, no palpitations, no hospitalizations, and no clinical signs of heart failure.

issues.title: Sample size based on VO2peak, not stated primary fatigue outcome; no calculation details given
issues.explanation: The sample size was said to be calculated for VO2peak, but no assumptions, target number or power are reported, and the stated primary outcome is fatigue. The fatigue comparison with 22 per arm is therefore of unknown power, so the null fatigue result cannot be read as absence of effect. The authors partly acknowledge limited sample size, but the abstract conclusion on fatigue is stated without that caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported power calculation showing adequate power for the MFI-20 primary outcome.

quotes.text: The sample size was calculated to achieve a significant training effect measured as an improvement in VO2peak.

issues.title: Follow-up (3 and 6 month) results given without denominators or multiplicity control
issues.explanation: Follow-up comparisons are reported without stating how many participants contributed at 3 and 6 months. Several secondary comparisons across questionnaires and subdomains are tested at p<0.05 with no correction, and the two nominally significant 6-month results (activity and MQOL psychological) are isolated. These should be viewed as exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 with follow-up denominators and a pre-specified multiplicity strategy.

quotes.text: After 6 months, the total physical activity per week was significantly greater in the exercise group than in the control group (exercise 1280 ± 1192 vs. control 644 ± 554, p < 0.05).

issues.title: Abstract attributes fatigue improvement to willingness to participate; no design supports that causal reading
issues.explanation: Both arms improved on fatigue and quality of life with no between-group difference. The abstract attributes the improvement to willingness to participate in a training study, but with open-label design and no no-participation comparison, natural recovery or regression to the mean explain it equally well. This is an interpretive overreach of modest consequence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison with a non-participating cohort showing smaller improvement.

quotes.text: Fatigue and quality of life improve over time in individuals that are willing to participate in a training study irrespective of their allocation.

10.1007/s00394-024-03546-0.headline_claim: Three months of a synbiotic plus zinc supplement appears to improve tissue metabolism and attenuate post-exercise malaise in post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome, possibly through neuroprotective activity.
10.1007/s00394-024-03546-0.overall: The headline claims about improved tissue metabolism and attenuated post-exercise malaise rest on a few isolated P values of 0.02 to 0.05 among roughly 50 uncorrected tests, in a metabolite subset of 11 people. The primary fatigue outcome was null between groups (P = 0.90), so the 'safe and efficient' recommendation is not supported. Retrospective registration and several minor printing inconsistencies add to the caution.

primary_outcome.name: General fatigue (MFI-20) change from baseline to 3 months

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from baseline fatigue at 3 months

issues.title: Null primary fatigue outcome (P = 0.90) followed by Discussion suggesting the synbiotic tackles fatigue
issues.explanation: The primary outcome, change in general fatigue, did not differ between arms (interaction P = 0.90), and placebo reduced fatigue about as much as the synbiotic (-18.4% vs -17.3%). The Results lead with the within-group synbiotic reduction, and the Discussion says the synbiotic might be listed among interventions that tackle fatigue. The between-group data do not support a fatigue benefit; the paper's own Conclusion focuses on other outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group difference in the primary fatigue outcome.

quotes.text: We found no significant interaction effect (time vs . treatment) between interventions across all five fatigue subdomains during the trial.
Synbiotic intake led to a significant reduction in general fatigue
the synbiotic might be listed among promising interventions that tackle fatigue in post-COVID 19 ME/CFS

second_reader.what_stands: The primary fatigue outcome showed no between-group difference (P = 0.90, identical 3.0-point falls), yet the Discussion says the synbiotic might 'tackle fatigue' and calls it 'efficient'. The wording is tentative and the Conclusion does not claim a fatigue effect, but the Discussion does not connect the suggestion to the null primary result.

issues.title: About 54 uncorrected interaction tests; 4 reach P 0.02-0.05 and carry the tissue-metabolism and malaise claims
issues.explanation: The paper tests five fatigue subdomains, time to exhaustion, eight symptom scores and 39 metabolite-region combinations at P <= 0.05 with no correction. Only four interaction tests are significant, with P between 0.02 and 0.05, roughly the number expected by chance across about 54 tests. The Conclusion that the synbiotic improves tissue metabolism and attenuates post-exercise malaise rests on these.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified correction or hierarchy under which these findings remain significant.

quotes.text: The significance level was set at P
appears to improve tissue metabolism and attenuate post-exercise malaise in patients with post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome

second_reader.what_stands: About 55 interaction tests were run at an uncorrected P ≤ 0.05, and only 4 (P = 0.02 to 0.05) came out below it, which is close to the roughly 3 expected by chance. The malaise and tissue-metabolism claims in the Conclusion rest on those 4 results, and the paper does not discuss multiplicity. The Conclusion is tentative, and the tests are not independent, so the exact count of false positives is uncertain.

issues.title: Tissue-metabolism conclusion rests on 11 participants (5 vs 6) with no power calculation for these outcomes
issues.explanation: Metabolite outcomes come from a subset of five controls and six treated participants, selected for reasons the paper does not give. The power calculation covers only general fatigue. The Discussion and Conclusion nonetheless state that the synbiotic improves tissue metabolism, which this subset cannot reliably support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation for the spectroscopy outcomes and an explanation of how the subset was selected.

quotes.text: In a subset of patients (five from the control group and six from the experimental group), tissue levels of choline, creatine and N -acetyl aspartate were determined
The minimal sample size ( n 12) was determined through power analysis

second_reader.what_stands: The tissue-metabolism findings come from 11 participants (5 vs 6) and the only power calculation was for general fatigue. The Conclusion's wording ('appears to improve tissue metabolism') is cautious, but the paper does not say how the subset was selected.

issues.title: Recommended as 'safe and efficient' from 26 participants, open-ended AE reporting and a null primary outcome
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the synbiotic could be recommended as a safe and efficient intervention. Safety was assessed with an open-ended questionnaire in 12 treated participants, which cannot exclude uncommon harms, and the primary fatigue outcome showed no difference from placebo. The recommendation goes beyond what the data support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety analysis in a larger sample and a positive primary outcome.

quotes.text: could be recommended as a safe and efficient intervention for addressing post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome
a transient mild diarrhea was experienced by two female patients

second_reader.what_stands: 'Safe and efficient' is stated in the Discussion on the strength of 26 participants, open-ended adverse-event reporting and a null primary outcome. The mild adverse events listed are real and the Conclusion is more cautious, but a trial this size cannot establish safety and the efficacy claim rests only on secondary, uncorrected results.

issues.title: Registered 2023-08-25, about 11 months after study start; registry lists 32 enrolled vs 26 randomised in paper
issues.explanation: The trial registry shows first submission in August 2023, after data collection began in September 2022, so the registration was retrospective. The primary outcome in the current record matches the paper, which limits concern about outcome switching, but earlier record versions were not checked. The registry's 32 actual enrolments against 26 randomised in the paper is not explained in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version dated before enrolment, or a flow diagram accounting for the 6 additional enrolments.

quotes.text: The study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06013072).
Data collection occurred at the Applied Bioenergetics Lab at the University of Novi Sad between September 2022 and December 2023.

issues.title: Participant aged 66 reported in a trial with an 18-65 year eligibility range
issues.explanation: The eligibility criteria limit enrolment to ages 18-65, but the side-effects paragraph describes a female participant aged 66 who took the synbiotic. Either the age is a typo or an ineligible participant was enrolled. It does not change the efficacy results, but it is an unexplained factual inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected age within 18-65 or a protocol note permitting an age exception.

quotes.text: individuals aged 18-65 years
change in body odor in one female patient (aged 66)

issues.title: Placebo NAA increase attributed to a 12-month follow-up in a trial with only a 3-month follow-up
issues.explanation: The Methods say all measures were taken at baseline and at 3 months, and the intervention lasted 3 months. The brain NAA paragraph nonetheless reports a placebo-group increase at 12-month follow-up. This is a wrong time point with no corresponding assessment in the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of a 12-month assessment in the protocol or registry.

quotes.text: at the 3-month follow-up (post-administration)
expect for a significant increase at right frontal grey matter at 12-month follow-up

issues.title: Industry funding and employee author declared, but funder's role in design, analysis and reporting not stated
issues.explanation: DSM Nutritional Products AG co-funded the trial and supplied the product, and an author is employed there, all of which are declared. The paper does not state whether the funder had any role in design, analysis, interpretation or the decision to publish. This is a reporting gap that matters given the positive framing of secondary results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the funder had no role in design, analysis, interpretation or publication.

quotes.text: and DSM Nutritional Products AG.
the company that supplied the supplements examined in this study

10.1007/s00405-020-06520-8.headline_claim: Combining oral corticosteroids with olfactory training improved olfactory function in persistent COVID-19 dysosmia, supporting its safety and efficacy and motivating randomized trials.
10.1007/s00405-020-06520-8.overall: The data show a larger TDI gain in nine self-selected steroid-treated patients than in 18 patients on training alone, but the design cannot separate treatment from selection, baseline differences or spontaneous recovery, and the between-group evidence is marginal (p=0.046). The conclusion's claim of supported safety and efficacy overstates a hypothesis-generating pilot; only the call for randomized trials is justified.

primary_outcome.name: Change in TDI olfactory score (ΔTDI) between 5 and 10 weeks

issues.title: Conclusion asserts safety and efficacy from 9 self-selected treated patients, no control for recovery
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that the pilot supports safety and efficacy. The basis is 9 steroid-treated patients in a non-randomized, unblinded, unadjusted comparison with no sample-size calculation, and a marginal p=0.046. Safety rests on 3 of 9 patients reporting minor events, with no systematic assessment and far too few patients to exclude uncommon harms. The authors' own limitations paragraph says the findings are not conclusive, which conflicts with the conclusion's wording. This also covers the causal-sounding wording (c9), the safety claim (c8) and the sample size (c3).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomized or adequately powered controlled study showing the same benefit with systematic safety monitoring.

quotes.text: The findings of this pilot study support the safety and efficacy of combining oral corticosteroids and olfactory training
In turn, it is difficult for our preliminary findings to be conclusive about the potential benefits of OCS and OT, and caution is warranted.
Of the nine participants who received OCS, three reported minimal and transient side effects such as abdominal pain and insomnia.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's wording ('support the safety and efficacy') goes beyond what 9 self-selected treated patients, an unadjusted borderline p=0.046, no untreated control and 3/9 reported side effects can show. The overreach is partly tempered because the Discussion openly states that findings are preliminary and non-conclusive and the Conclusion calls for randomized trials, so the paper does not hide the limitation; the issue is the mismatch between the cautious Discussion and the stronger Conclusion sentence.

issues.title: Self-selected allocation (9 OCS+OT vs 18 OT), unadjusted; baseline TDI-1 19.7 vs 24.9
issues.explanation: Patients chose their own group, largely according to their attitude to steroid safety, so motivation, health beliefs and other unmeasured factors may differ between arms. Baseline TDI-1 was about 5 points lower in the OCS+OT arm (19.7 vs 24.9). That leaves more room to improve and more regression to the mean, and the 'NS' label from tiny groups does not show balance. Only unadjusted comparisons were done, and with no untreated group spontaneous recovery cannot be separated from treatment effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomized allocation, or an adjusted analysis (e.g. ANCOVA on TDI-1) with a matched or untreated control showing the same difference.

quotes.text: Only 9 participants volunteered for the OCS + OT group, whereas 18 opted for performing OT alone.
Ideally, larger cohorts and a control group of dysosmic patients would help separate the effect of treatment from spontaneous recovery.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by patient choice (9 OCS+OT vs 18 OT), and the comparison of delta-TDI is unadjusted for baseline. The OCS+OT group started 5.2 points lower on TDI-1 (19.7 vs 24.9), a gap that 'NS' does not rule out as meaningful at these group sizes, and the implied follow-up means are almost equal (about 27.4 vs 27.0). The paper does disclose the non-randomized design, but it relies on the NS baseline test and does not adjust for or discuss the baseline gap, so regression to the mean or a ceiling/floor effect cannot be excluded.

issues.title: Discussion contrasts within-arm significance (p=0.007 vs 0.126); between-group p=0.046 is marginal
issues.explanation: The Discussion presents a significant change in one arm against an insignificant change in the other as evidence of benefit. The difference between 'significant' and 'not significant' is not itself a test. The valid between-group comparison is a single Mann-Whitney p=0.046, on n=9 vs 18 and without a correction or adjustment, so it is marginal and fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group test with a confidence interval, adjusted for baseline, that is robust to this contrast.

quotes.text: participants in the OCS + OT group showed a significant increase of 7.7 points on average in their TDI score, compared to an insignificant 2.1-increase in the OT group

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective interventional comparison of a drug
issues.explanation: The study allocates patients to a drug and a comparator and tests the outcome prospectively, but no registry identifier is given, only an ethics approval number. Without a registered protocol the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be checked against what was reported. This is a transparency gap rather than a demonstrated error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or published protocol dated before TDI-2 testing that lists ΔTDI as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: This pilot prospective study is the continuation of our study on 72 non-hospitalized patients

10.1007/s00406-023-01747-y.headline_claim: A multidisciplinary bio-psycho-social rehabilitation (MBR) program with physiotherapy emphasis is feasible and tolerable for severely affected PCC patients with fatigue, and the authors call for further research on its effectiveness.
10.1007/s00406-023-01747-y.overall: The paper presents itself as a feasibility pilot and its main conclusion, feasibility with an unproven effect on walking distance, is largely supported. Table 2 and Table 1 contain several transcription slips that do not affect results. The 'tolerability' claim and the word 'confirms' go somewhat beyond an uncontrolled sample of 33 without systematic adverse-event reporting.

primary_outcome.name: Change in 6-minute walk test distance (T1 to T2)

issues.title: Uncontrolled 13 improved vs 6 worsened described as 'confirming' WHO recommendation
issues.explanation: The Discussion says more than twice as many patients improved as deteriorated and that this confirms the WHO recommendation that active therapy is possible. The primary outcome change (500.6 to 512.0 m) was not significant, there is no control group, and 14 patients were unchanged. The data are compatible with feasibility but do not 'confirm' a treatment recommendation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison or a test showing the improved/deteriorated split is beyond what chance variation in repeated 6MWT would give.

quotes.text: This confirms the WHO recommendation that active therapy is possible for the majority of patients with PCC and fatigue

issues.title: 'Tolerability' claimed without systematic adverse-event data; 3 dropouts and 6/33 deteriorated
issues.explanation: The Discussion states the study demonstrated feasibility and tolerability. The paper reports no structured adverse-event collection, only reasons for early termination (including worsening fatigue) and a retrospective review of six patients with worse 6MWT. Two of the non-completions were probably linked to the program. The tolerability claim is thinner than worded, though the feasibility claim and the limited scope of the paper are reasonably consistent with the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified adverse-event monitoring protocol with results showing no program-related events beyond those described.

quotes.text: While our study demonstrated the feasibility and tolerability of a rehabilitation program emphasizing active physiotherapy
Furthermore, it is important that adverse events and reasons for early termination are reported.

issues.title: Table 2 FSS counts 29/5 sum to 34 but n = 33; printed 12.1% matches 4/33
issues.explanation: The two FSS categories are printed as 29 and 5, which add to 34, yet the table and text say 33 patients were analysed. The percentages 87.9/12.1 correspond to 29/33 and 4/33, so the second count is probably a typo for 4. The category labels also overlap at exactly 4. This is a small descriptive slip and does not affect the outcome analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary data listing showing 34 patients in the FSS analysis, or a printed category definition that makes 5 correct.

issues.title: Table 1 psychological lessons: total 4 sessions but weekly counts 1+1+1 = 3
issues.explanation: The psychological lessons row gives a total frequency of 4 sessions, but the weekly frequencies below it are 1, 1 and 1, which sum to 3. Every other row with weekly counts adds to its total. The intervention description is therefore inconsistent for this component, though it does not change any results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A program manual showing a fourth psychological session outside the weekly schedule.

quotes.location: Table 1, Psychological lessons (group) row, total frequency column

issues.title: Table 2 has several percentages that do not match counts (29.4, 38.0/62.0, 33.7/67.3, 15.3, 72.3)
issues.explanation: Several percentages in Table 2 disagree with the printed counts and n = 33. Marital status 20/13 prints 60.6/29.4 (should be 60.6/39.4). Education 11/22 prints 38.0/62.0 (should be 33.3/66.7). PHQ-4 depression and anxiety 11/22 print 33.7/67.3, while the same counts in the pulmonary row print 33.3/66.7. Employed 28/5 prints 15.3 for non-employed (15.2), and 'other conditions' 9/24 prints 72.3 (72.7). These are transcription slips in baseline descriptors only; the text itself repeats 'one-third' for PHQ-4 and the results are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator disclosed for these items (e.g. missing data) that reproduces the printed percentages.

quotes.location: Table 2, Marital Status, Living with partner/alone row

10.1007/s00406-024-01792-1.headline_claim: A two-week comprehensive multimodal integrative inpatient program produces significant improvement in fatigue and in self-reported ability to work in patients with chronic post-COVID syndrome.
10.1007/s00406-024-01792-1.overall: The finding that patients' fatigue scores were lower after the program and at six months is plausible as a descriptive observation, but the paper's conclusion that the program is effective is not supported by a single-arm design with selection on high baseline fatigue and about a third of participants missing from the primary analysis. The claim of clinical relevance also lacks a benchmark. The results should be treated as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: MFI-20 total fatigue score

issues.title: Single-arm uncontrolled design cannot attribute fatigue and work-ability changes to the program
issues.explanation: All efficacy claims rest on pre-post change in one cohort with no comparison group. Natural recovery, regression to the mean after selection on high fatigue, and non-specific inpatient effects (rest, removal from work, attention) cannot be separated from the program effect. The authors acknowledge the missing control but still conclude the program is effective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control group showing the same change, or a stated plan treating the study as purely descriptive with conclusions limited to association.

quotes.text: This study lacked a control group and it could be argued that the reduction in fatigue was simply due to the passage of time
it was demonstrated that such a treatment setting can be a meaningful, longer lasting, and effective treatment option for patients suffering from severe PCS.
quotes.location: Discussion, final paragraph of main discussion

second_reader.what_stands: The design is a single-arm, uncontrolled before-and-after study, so the fatigue and work-ability changes cannot be attributed to the program itself, and the authors acknowledge this in the Limitations. Even so, the Discussion says it 'was demonstrated that such a treatment setting can be a meaningful, longer lasting, and effective treatment option' and the Conclusions say the improvement came 'through' the program. This causal wording goes beyond what the design supports.

issues.title: Primary analysis includes 42 of 64 patients (34% missing); no completer comparison or sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Missing questionnaires were excluded test by test, so the primary repeated-measures result rests on a third fewer patients than were enrolled. The paper does not compare completers with non-completers or use any method for missing data. If those who responded at six months differ in outcome, the reported sustained improvement may be biased.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table showing baseline characteristics and T1 fatigue similar in completers and non-completers, or a sensitivity analysis (mixed model or imputation) with similar results.

quotes.text: For statistical analyses, missing values were excluded test by test, resulting in an overall   N MFI-T1-T3 =  42,
Not all of the remaining 64 participants completed the questionnaires at each time point

second_reader.what_stands: The primary repeated-measures analysis uses 42 of 64 eligible patients (about 34% missing; 39% for work ability) as a complete-case analysis, and the text reports no completer comparison or sensitivity analysis. The only partial reassurance is that baseline fatigue means for N=64 and N=42 are close, and Fig. 2 was not visible to me.

issues.title: 'Clinically relevant' and 'effective' conclusions asserted without MCID, control, or objective work data
issues.explanation: The conclusions describe the program as effective and the fatigue change as clinically relevant, yet the paper states no validated cut-off exists for the MFI-20 and offers no minimal important difference. Work ability is a single self-rated item with no objective sick-leave data, but is presented as a positive sign for insurers. Statistical significance of a within-group change is treated as proof of clinical benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A cited MCID for the MFI-20 total score that the observed 9-10 point change exceeds, together with conclusions explicitly limited to uncontrolled association.

quotes.text: There is currently no validated cut-off value for the MFI-20 [1].
Although we can only present data on self-reported ability to work, this is a positive indication for health insurance companies
patients can achieve a significant and clinically relevant improvement in their leading symptom fatigue.

second_reader.what_stands: The claims of a 'clinically relevant' fatigue improvement and an 'effective' treatment rest on a statistically significant before-and-after change, comparison with general-population norms and no MCID or control group. The authors even say no validated MFI-20 cut-off exists, and mean fatigue stays above the 75th percentile of the reference group. The work-ability claim is fairly hedged by the authors as self-reported only, so the missing-objective-data criticism applies mainly to the 'effective' and health-insurance framing, not to an overclaim of objective work outcomes.

10.1007/s00406-024-01904-x.headline_claim: Cognitive training combined with weekly group psychotherapy improves cognitive performance in post-COVID-19 patients, and many cognitive symptoms improve over time.
10.1007/s00406-024-01904-x.overall: The study is openly exploratory and non-randomized, and its own main finding is that cognitive scores improved over time in both groups; only 3 of 19 interactions were nominally significant. The cognitive effects of the intervention cannot be separated from natural recovery, and the recommendation for depression rests on an uncontrolled, completers-only measure. Printed errors (df 109, 0,7%) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Pre-post change in 19 cognitive test variables (Hypothesis 1), with between-group interaction analysis (Hypothesis 2)

issues.title: Non-randomized, unmatched control with higher baseline performance limits group-vs-time inference
issues.explanation: Allocation was by clinical decision and patient preference, the control group was not matched for age or gender and scored higher at baseline on every variable. The three significant interactions (SM, SR, FC) are crossover patterns from lower baselines, which is also what regression to the mean or differential practice effects would produce. The authors caveat causality, but the group-participation inference and conclusion remain weakly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline-adjusted analysis or matched/randomized comparison reproducing the interaction effects.

quotes.text: The allocation to the intervention group and the control group was based on clinical decisions and the patient's preferences.
For all variables examined here, performance of the control group at the baseline measurement was higher than performance of the intervention group.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper really is non-randomized (allocation by clinical decision and patient preference), the groups were unmatched for age and gender, and the authors state the control group's baseline was higher than the intervention group's, with no baseline adjustment in the mixed ANOVAs. This limits group-versus-time inference, though the authors acknowledge it and disclaim causality; the 'all variables' baseline claim cannot be verified because no baseline-by-group table is given.

issues.title: 38 uncorrected tests (19 pre-post, 19 interactions); several key results at p .03-.05
issues.explanation: The authors disclose in Methods that they ran 19 Wilcoxon tests and 19 mixed ANOVAs without correction because the study was exploratory. The disclosure is genuine, but the Results and Discussion still describe significant improvement across domains and interpret three interactions, two of which have p of .046 and .030, as possibly group-related. With 19 tests, about one false positive per family is expected, so the interaction findings are fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pre-specified primary outcome or multiplicity-adjusted results showing the same findings.

quotes.text: Due to the exploratory nature of the study, we decided not to correct for multiple testing.
Only three of 19 variables showed a significant interaction effect of time of testing and group membership.

issues.title: Registration (22 Dec 2022) post-dates start of the July-Dec 2022 intervention; no primary outcome fixed
issues.explanation: The trial was registered after the interventions had started and essentially when they ended. The disclosure is honest, but pre-specification of 19 outcomes and the hypotheses cannot be verified. This weakens confidence in the nominally significant findings, but the paper does not claim confirmatory results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing outcomes and analysis plan were entered before data collection.

quotes.text: DRKS00030974, 22 Dec 2022, retrospectively registered.
All the group interventions took place from July 2022 until December 2022.

issues.title: Recommendation for depression/cognitive impairment rests on uncontrolled BDI-II and mostly time effects
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the intervention may be considered for patients with both cognitive impairment and depression. Depression was assessed only in the intervention group, so the BDI-II decrease cannot be separated from natural recovery, and most cognitive gains appeared equally in the control group. Feasibility is supported modestly (15 of 19 completed, 6 of 15 attended all sessions), so the wording is hedged but still goes beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison of BDI-II between groups showing greater decline with intervention.

quotes.text: Group psychotherapy and neurocognitive training is feasible and may be considered particularly for PC patients potentially complaining of both neurocognitive impairment and  mood  disorders  (i.e.  depression).
Due to the exploratory design of this study aiming for feasibility testing, the BDI-II was only assessed in the intervention group.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis (15 of 19 starters); Hypothesis 1 pre-post tests have no control and mislabelled test
issues.explanation: Only the 15 completers were analysed, excluding 4 who dropped out for physical deterioration, overlapping rehab or other expectations. That omits non-completers and biases toward benefit. The test is called a 'Mann-Whitney test for paired samples', which is the Wilcoxon signed-rank procedure, so the method is mislabelled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis including the four dropouts.

quotes.text: 19 one-sided Mann-Whitney tests for paired samples (one for each variable) were performed using R Studio version 4.2.1.
Two participants left the intervention group due to overlapping rehabilitation programs, one due to deterioration of his physical condition, and one due to other expectations of the group.

issues.title: BDI-II F test prints numerator df 109, impossible with 15 completers (likely 1.09)
issues.explanation: The BDI-II result is printed as F (109, 10.91) = 12.33, p = .004. A numerator df of 109 cannot arise from 15 participants; the pair looks like a dropped decimal (1.09, 10.91 summing to a GG-corrected df ratio of 10). The reported statistic is therefore mis-printed, though the conclusion probably survives.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version or supplement showing df of 109 arising from a legitimate design.

quotes.text: GreenhouseGeisser F (109, 10.91) = 12.33, p = .004
quotes.location: Results, Depressive symptomatology and group satisfaction

issues.title: Diverse participants printed as 0,7% but 1 of 15 is 6.7%
issues.explanation: The intervention group description gives 10 females (67%), 4 males (27%) and 1 diverse (0,7%). One of 15 is 6.7%, and the three shares only sum to 100% with 6.7 (67+27+6.7). The 0,7 is a printed error, trivial for the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; it is a printed value.

quotes.text: 10 females (67%), 4 males (27%), 1 diverse (0,7%)

script.explanation: 1/15 = 6.67%, but the paper prints 0.7, outside the rounding interval [0.65, 0.80]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 142.9 rather than 15.

10.1007/s00431-025-06705-5.headline_claim: Individualized online exercise therapy is feasible, safe, and associated with clinically relevant improvements in physical function, quality of life, and school attendance in pediatric long-COVID.
10.1007/s00431-025-06705-5.overall: The paper reports before-after improvements in a 14-patient exploratory trial, and the between-group contrast was not significant, so the data cannot show that the therapy itself caused the change. The efficacy and scalability wording in the Discussion outruns the design despite the preliminary caveats. The visit labelling mismatch in Fig. 3, the 85% compliance figure and the imputation of follow-up data are secondary reporting problems.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test (6MWT), designated as lead of a group of primary outcomes with handgrip strength and sit-to-stand

issues.title: Benefit claimed from within-arm change; 12-week vs 6-week differences not significant, no untreated comparison
issues.explanation: Both arms improved from visit 1 to visit 3, and the between-arm difference was reported as not significant. Both arms received the same therapy, so the only between-group contrast is 12 versus 6 weeks of exercise, and the paper says there was no no-intervention control. Improvement over about 3 months in long-COVID could reflect spontaneous recovery, learning effects on the 6MWT, or regression to the mean, and the paper reports that 9 of 14 patients recovered. The data therefore cannot support the statement that the study 'demonstrates the beneficial effects' of the therapy. The delayed-start arm could have given a visit 2 comparison but is not analysed as such.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis comparing group 1 with group 2 during the exercise-free 6 weeks (visit 1 to 2) showing a clear treatment effect.

quotes.text: Although intergroup differences (12 week vs. 6-week intervention) were not statistically significant
This study demonstrates the beneficial effects of individualized online exercise therapy on physical capacity, quality of life, and school participation in pediatric patients with long-COVID.
The lack of a no-intervention control group restricts causal attribution.

second_reader.what_stands: The benefit statements ('demonstrates the beneficial effects') rest mainly on within-arm pre/post changes and pooled attendance figures, and the 12-week vs 6-week contrast, which is a dose comparison, was not significant. It is not strictly true that there is no untreated comparison, since group 2 had a 6-week exercise-free period and the one reported interaction (QoL at visit 2) is compatible with a delayed-start effect, but the paper does not analyse or present that contrast as the basis for causal benefit. The authors do partly hedge ('exploratory', 'preliminary', 'hypothesis-generating'),

issues.title: Efficacy and scalability asserted from 14 patients with no power calculation and a non-significant arm contrast
issues.explanation: With 7 patients per arm, no sample-size calculation, no untreated control and a non-significant between-arm difference, the paper still states that its results 'support efficacy' and that the therapy is 'effective' and a 'clinically scalable' model. The abstract also says the findings highlight 'accessible and effective treatment approaches'. These statements go beyond what a 14-patient exploratory study can show, even though other sentences correctly call the work preliminary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation and a significant between-group primary result in an adequately powered trial.

quotes.text: Our results support efficacy based on 6MWT and validated questionnaires.
IOET therefore offers a clinically scalable rehabilitation model that can be integrated into pediatric rehabilitation services
The findings highlight the potential of telemedicine-based rehabilitation strategies as accessible and effective treatment approaches

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy and scalability wording in the Discussion and in the abstract's What is New goes beyond what 14 patients, no stated power calculation and a non-significant arm contrast can show, and scalability was not evaluated. The paper does, however, state the exploratory and underpowered nature of the study in several places, including the Conclusion, so the problem is a mismatch between some strong phrases and the authors' own caveats rather than an absence of caution.

issues.title: 6MWT 396.0 m to 616.3 m labelled visit 3 in text but visit 4 in Fig. 3 caption
issues.explanation: The Results attribute the 396.0 m and 616.3 m 6MWT values to baseline and post-intervention (visit 3), and say performance fell at visit 4. The Fig. 3 caption gives the same numbers, and the same pattern for handgrip, sit-to-stand and CK, as visit 1 versus visit 4. Both cannot be right, so the reader cannot tell which timepoint the headline primary-outcome improvement refers to. The visit 3 reading is the more plausible one, so this is a labelling error that leaves the conclusions intact.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary table S1 showing that 616.3 m is the visit 3 mean and that the caption's 'visit 4' is a typographical error.

quotes.text: Improvements were observed across all measures from baseline (visit 1) to post-intervention (visit 3)
At 3-month follow-up (visit 4), physical performance declined compared to visit 3 but remained above baseline levels

issues.title: 9 of 14 recovered and opted out of follow-up, yet analyses use n = 14 with data 'missing completely at random'
issues.explanation: Nine of 14 participants (64%) are reported to have opted out of further follow-up because they had recovered. Departure because of recovery is related to the outcome, which is hard to square with the statement that missing data were missing completely at random. Missing values were filled by LASSO imputation, and the amount imputed is not reported, so the visit 4 results and the conclusion about 'sustained benefit at 3 months' may largely reflect imputed values. The direction of any bias cannot be determined from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A report showing that all 14 participants completed visit 4 assessments and that few values were imputed.

quotes.text: 9 out of 14 participants (64%) reported full recovery from long-COVID and opted out of further follow-up
Little's MCAR test indicated that the data were missing completely at random.

issues.title: Overall compliance of 85% does not match the group figures (91.7% of 72, 76.4% of 144, about 81.5%)
issues.explanation: Taking n as the number of scheduled sessions, the group percentages are attainable. Pooling them gives (66+110)/(72+144) = 81.5%, not the 85% printed as overall compliance. The denominators (72 and 144) are also not multiples of the 7 patients per arm, and the paper does not say how they were derived. This is a minor reporting inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplement table S1 showing session counts that pool to 85%, for example different denominators from those implied by n = 72 and n = 144.

quotes.text: Group 2 completed 91.7% of sessions ( n = 72)
Overall compliance with the intervention was high

issues.title: Symptom duration of 21 months called 'mean' in Results but 'median' in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Results report a mean pre-inclusion symptom duration of 21 months, and the Discussion calls the same figure a median. Table 2 reports group means of 24 and 19 months, which fit the 'mean' label. No conclusion depends on the difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable beyond confirming the statistic from the raw data.

quotes.text: The mean duration of symptoms prior to inclusion was 21 months.
where the median symptom duration was 21 months before inclusion

10.1007/s00431-026-06840-7.headline_claim: A co-designed online psychology/physiotherapy intervention is acceptable and feasible for young people with post-COVID syndrome in an NHS clinic setting, and no specific benefit was demonstrated on the primary or secondary outcomes.
10.1007/s00431-026-06840-7.overall: The feasibility and acceptability findings are the paper's supportable contribution, with small numbers and an unregistered pilot design. The null efficacy result is weak evidence because usual care was intensive and undefined, breathing retraining reached both arms, and the trial had no power calculation. The claim that BrPD is a predominant cause of breathlessness goes beyond a descriptive baseline assessment.

primary_outcome.name: SDQ Impact Score

issues.title: Undefined, intensive usual care incl. breathing retraining in both arms makes null comparison uninformative
issues.explanation: Both arms received extensive and variable MDT input, and all young people diagnosed with breathing difficulties were referred for physiotherapy (24/32 received breathing retraining). This dilutes any contrast between arms. With n=32 and no power calculation, the absence of a difference cannot be read as absence of benefit; the authors say as much but still write 'no specific benefit was demonstrated'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A defined, comparable usual-care protocol and evidence that controls did not receive breathing retraining.

quotes.text: The results show that there was no standard treatment offered to both control and intervention groups.
The complexity and intensity of the input being received by the controls made it very unlikely that an impact from the intervention would be detected.
All CYP diagnosed with breathing difficulties were referred for physiotherapy.

issues.title: 'Predominant cause of breathlessness' claimed from a descriptive baseline prevalence of BrPD (84-91%)
issues.explanation: The key-points summary says breathing pattern disorders are a predominant cause of breathlessness, but the study only counted how many participants met BrPD criteria. No analysis relates BrPD to breathlessness, and all participants had normal spirometry and gas transfer. The data support 'common', not 'predominant cause'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis linking BrPD status to breathlessness severity, or wording limited to prevalence.

quotes.text: We identified that breathing pattern disorders are common and a predominant cause of breathlessness in teenagers with PCS.
quotes.location: What is known - What is new

quotes.text: Breathlessness, chest pain, and fatigue are highly prevalent in this population with a high incidence rate of BrPD.

issues.title: Table 3: wellness Den df repeats F values and VT2 VO2/kg outcome appears twice with different results
issues.explanation: In the Wellness row of Table 3 the denominator df entries (0.472, 25.381, 1813) are copies of the F statistics (0.472, 25.381, 1.813), not plausible df of about 30. Separately, the VT2 VO2/kg outcome appears as two rows with different F and p values (treatment p=0.56 vs 0.089; time p=0.473 vs 0.018), whereas Table 2 lists only one anaerobic threshold outcome. Readers cannot tell which result is correct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original Table 3 showing sensible df and a single anaerobic threshold row (an extraction artefact).

quotes.text: VT2 VO 2 /kg threshold
Anaerobic threshold VT2 VO 2 /kg
Wellness Score percentage (0-100%)

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported for a randomised pilot; SDQ primary outcome prespecification unverifiable
issues.explanation: The paper reports only an ethics approval number and no trial registration. The SDQ Impact Score is called the primary outcome, but its prespecification cannot be verified externally. Because the authors claim no efficacy and the SDQ result is null, the effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (with date) listing the SDQ Impact Score as primary outcome.

quotes.text: This is a randomised pilot trial assessing acceptability and feasibility of a co-designed intervention.
The primary outcome measure (SDQ impact score) was chosen before the intervention had been co-designed.

issues.title: Unblinded participants and lead researcher (also the intervention physiotherapist) with self-reported primary outcome
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the lead researcher also delivered the intervention, while the primary and most secondary outcomes are self- or parent-reported. This could bias those outcomes toward the intervention. The authors disclose it and make no efficacy claim, so the effect on conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the SDQ was completed independently of the unblinded team and parents, or an effect that survives a blinded outcome.

quotes.text: Participants were allocated after the initial assessment at which point participants (and the lead researcher, CW) were no longer blinded.
There was suspected reporter bias in some of the baseline assessment questionnaires with uninvited parental influence.

issues.title: Chance sex imbalance (2/15 vs 9/17 male) not adjusted for; allocation concealment not described
issues.explanation: Males were 13.3% of controls and 52.9% of the intervention group (p=0.025), but the models contain only time, treatment and their interaction. Allocation concealment is not described, though the method of sequence generation is. In a pilot with no efficacy claim the impact is minor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis adjusting for sex that gives the same results, and a description of concealed allocation.

quotes.text: There were more males in the treatment group.
CYP were assigned into 2 treatment groups using computergenerated block randomisation with variable block sizes

issues.title: Pooled Nijmegen improvement over time (p<0.001) placed alongside breathing retraining in 24 participants
issues.explanation: The improvement in Nijmegen score is a time effect in both arms, and the interaction with treatment was not significant (p=0.265). It is not an analysis of the 24 participants who received retraining and has no untreated comparison. The sentence suggests a link to retraining that the data cannot show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A subgroup analysis with a comparison group showing retraining-specific change, or wording that explicitly attributes the change to natural course.

quotes.text: 24 (75%) participants received physiotherapy clinic sessions for breathing retraining and symptoms within the Nijmegen scores significantly improved over time (P < 0.001).
However, none of the interactions were statistically significant, indicating that there were no variables where the change in baseline to post-treatment differed depending on treatment group.

issues.title: Number of study sites given as two clinics in Introduction but three centres in Limitations
issues.explanation: The Introduction says standard treatment was described in two tertiary PCS clinics, whereas the Limitations say the 66 eligible people were identified across three specialist centres. The setting of the trial is therefore unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement explaining that two clinics ran the service while three centres identified participants.

quotes.text: The study documented symptoms in this population and described standard treatment in two tertiary PCS clinics.
Although 66 young people were identified as potentially suitable for the intervention across three specialist centres

issues.title: Discussion says five onward referral pathways but lists six
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that five onward referral pathways were identified, but the bracketed list names six. One of the two is wrong. Nothing in the results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two of the listed items were counted as one pathway, or a corrected count in the paper.

quotes.text: Five different onward referral pathways to local services were identified
consultant only, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS)/psychology, psychiatrist, and social workers

10.1007/s00508-025-02501-1.headline_claim: Transcutaneous auricular VNS (10Hz, 25Hz, and a 2Hz comparator) is acceptable and feasible in female long COVID patients and is associated with symptom improvement, particularly fatigue and dyspnea, with preliminary evidence of benefit and safety.
10.1007/s00508-025-02501-1.overall: The paper is an exploratory pilot whose own limitations section is candid, but its Summary draws safety and therapeutic-benefit conclusions from within-arm change in about 12 participants per arm, with no inferential tests and an acknowledged non-inert comparator. Feasibility and acceptability findings are the part that can be relied on, subject to unexplained usage counts (up to 249 applications over 12 weeks) and retrospective registration with a primary outcome (HRV) that differs from the paper's stated focus.

primary_outcome.name: Acceptability, feasibility and adherence (paper's stated focus); registry lists heart rate variability as the sole primary

issues.title: Symptom benefit inferred from within-arm pre/post change; no between-group test, 2Hz comparator not inert
issues.explanation: No inferential test of any kind is reported, and no between-arm contrast is shown even though the Methods say intergroup comparisons were made. The authors concede the sample could not detect differences between groups and that the 2Hz arm was not a real control. They also concede that long COVID symptoms may improve with time alone. Improvement in all arms, including 2Hz, therefore says little about an effect of VNS itself. The 10Hz-versus-2Hz differences are also uninterpretable because baselines differ (e.g. MCS 45 vs 42; ISI 10.3 vs 14.2).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-arm contrasts with confidence intervals (adjusted for baseline) showing differences between the active arms and 2Hz.

quotes.text: The sample size was too small to detect differences between individual groups, but the overall population demonstrated improvement with VNS.
the 2Hz group was not a real control group but more a subtherapeutic intervention
the time factor alone could lead to symptom improvement

second_reader.what_stands: The symptom benefit claims (Abstract: 'all VNS treatment groups experienced reduction in symptoms'; Discussion: 'overall population demonstrated improvement with VNS') rest on within-arm baseline-to-12-week changes. No between-group test result is reported, and the 2Hz arm improved on most scales, by more than the active arms on ISI, which the authors themselves call subtherapeutic rather than inert. The authors do disclose the time-effect and comparator limitations and label the work exploratory, and the conclusion is framed around feasibility and acceptability, so the point is true of the sy

issues.title: Up to 249 applications and 6764 min reported against a one-session-per-evening, 12-week protocol
issues.explanation: The protocol is one 30-minute session each evening for 12 weeks, about 84 sessions and 2520 min. Table 2 reports a maximum of 249 applications and 6764 min in the 10 Hz arm. That implies multiple sessions per day, a protocol deviation or a different counting unit, none of which is explained. At the other extreme the 25 Hz arm has a minimum of 3 applications and 21 min, which sits poorly with the 'high adherence' conclusion. Dose is therefore poorly characterised.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 'application' as a device activation (not a session), or confirmation that some participants were allowed multiple daily sessions.

quotes.text: Stimulation was applied to the left ear for 30min each evening, using biphasic waveforms.

issues.title: Summary states VNS 'safe' and likely beneficial from 35 analysed participants and no inferential tests
issues.explanation: The Summary says the treatment 'was found to be safe, with no significant side effects reported' and that VNS 'may offer therapeutic benefits... particularly in reducing fatigue and dyspnea'. With 3-5 participants per arm reporting adverse events and only 35 participants analysed, a safety conclusion is not supported. The benefit claim rests on within-arm change without a control contrast. The paper's closing paragraph is more cautious than its Summary, but the Summary is what most readers will take away.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Summary restricted to feasibility, with adverse events described as mild and common and no efficacy or safety claim.

quotes.text: The treatment was found to be safe, with no significant side effects reported
Vagus nerve stimulation may offer therapeutic benefits for women with long COVID

issues.title: Registered primary outcome (HRV) differs from the paper's stated focus (feasibility) and its symptom headline
issues.explanation: The registry lists heart rate variability as the sole primary outcome. The paper frames feasibility and acceptability as its focus and puts symptom improvements in the Summary, while HRV is reported as unchanged. The paper does not identify a primary outcome or explain the change. Because only the current registry version was seen, whether this was a post-hoc switch cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing feasibility outcomes were registered as primary before recruitment, or a paper statement identifying its primary outcome.

quotes.text: The present pilot study focused on the acceptability, feasibility and adherence to VNS treatment.
Heart rate variability remained stable throughout the trial

issues.title: BFI baseline SD of 4.5 in the 10Hz arm is far out of line with all other BFI SDs (1.4-2.6)
issues.explanation: On the 0-10 Brief Fatigue Inventory, a mean of 5.4 with SD 4.5 would require nearly all participants at the scale extremes. The same arm's follow-up SDs are 2.1 and 2.6, and the other arms are 1.4-1.9 at baseline. This is probably a typographical error, but it affects the apparent size of the 10Hz fatigue reduction, the paper's key symptom claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level BFI data showing a bimodal distribution, or a corrected table.

issues.title: Device manufacturer funded the study; funder's role unstated; authors declare no competing interests
issues.explanation: The company that makes the TENS device funded the study. The paper does not say whether it had any role in design, analysis or reporting. The authors declare no competing interests. The funding is visible, so this is a transparency gap rather than concealment. It matters mainly because the Summary's favourable wording about safety and benefit is not supported by inferential results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the funder had no role in design, data analysis, interpretation or the decision to publish.

quotes.text: The study was supported by Schwa-medico Handelsgesellschaft m.b.H.
declare that they have no competing interests

issues.title: Trial registered 2023-06-20, about 3 months after recruitment began on 3 March 2023
issues.explanation: The paper says it was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov and that recruitment began on 3 March 2023, but it gives no registration date. According to the registry the first submission was on 2023-06-20, after enrolment had started. Retrospective registration weakens the safeguard against changing outcomes, which matters here given the HRV-versus-symptoms mismatch. The paper discloses neither the timing nor its implications.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an earlier registration of the same trial (e.g. another registry) before 3 March 2023.

quotes.text: Recruitment began on 3 March 2023
quotes.location: Material and methods, Trial design and overview

quotes.text: the trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov

issues.title: 12-week median cortisol is 0.29 µg/dl in the text but 0.284 in Table 3
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the 12-week median morning cortisol as 0.29 µg/dl. Table 3 prints 0.284 for the Total column at +12 weeks, which would round to 0.28. The gap is small and both values are within the reference range, so no conclusion depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text value comes from a different calculation (e.g. a mean or a different analysis set) rather than the Table 3 median.

quotes.text: a median of 0.247µg/dl at baseline and 0.29µg/dl after 12 weeks

quotes.location: Table 3, Cortisol row, +12 weeks, Total column

10.1007/s00508-025-02522-w.headline_claim: PEMF is feasible, well accepted and safe, and it produced improvements in fatigue, physical and mental health and work ability in a 20-person pilot, indicating it is an effective approach for post-COVID-19 fatigue.
10.1007/s00508-025-02522-w.overall: The paper supports at most feasibility and acceptability of PEMF in a small pilot; the efficacy and safety statements go beyond descriptive data from 20 patients with no testing or primary outcome. The key 6-minute walk control value at T1 is inconsistent across text, table and Discussion, and several other percentages in the text do not match Table 2, mostly in the intervention's favour. Treat all between-arm differences as exploratory.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue (BFI, MFI); the paper does not designate a primary outcome

issues.title: Efficacy, 'significant' benefit and safety asserted from 20 patients with no inferential testing or sample-size basis
issues.explanation: The authors chose to report no inferential statistics and state that the study has limited power. They nevertheless say effectiveness 'was demonstrated', that 6MWT results were 'significant', and that PEMF 'has been shown to be safe' because no further adverse events were reported. Ten participants per arm, one control group imputed after dropouts, and unstated variability in differences cannot show efficacy or safety. At most the data are hypothesis-generating and support feasibility.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; a pre-specified analysis plan with adequate power would be needed to support these statements.

quotes.text: In summary, PEMF seems to be an effective approach
while the 6 MWT results demonstrated significant improvements favoring the intervention group
The PEMF has been shown to be safe, as no other adverse events were reported.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper asserts efficacy ('effective approach', 'significant improvements', effectiveness 'demonstrated') and safety ('has been shown to be safe') from 20 randomized patients (7 control completers) with no inferential tests, no confidence intervals and no reported sample-size basis, which contradicts its own stated reason for avoiding inference and its limitations statement. The authors do disclose the descriptive design and limited power and frame the conclusion around feasibility and the need for larger trials, so the overreach is concentrated in the Discussion and Results wording rather t

issues.title: Control 6MWT at T1: Results say +11%, Table 2 gives 448.8 to 199.1 m (-56%), Discussion says -246 m
issues.explanation: The Results give the control group's 6-minute walk change at T1 as +11%. Table 2 shows the control mean falling from 448.8 m to 199.1 m, and the Discussion says the placebo group worsened by 246 m. The Discussion figure also differs slightly from the table (about 250 m), so the control T1 value is unreliable whichever source is right. The T1 control-versus-intervention contrast for the key objective outcome therefore cannot be trusted. If the table is right, the intervention advantage at T1 is large; if the text is right, it is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 or participant-level data showing the control T1 mean and the +11% change are consistent with each other and with the 246 m statement.

quotes.text: follow-up assessment at T1: +10% vs. 11%
The placebo group worsened at T1 by 246m

second_reader.what_stands: The paper gives three incompatible descriptions of the control-group 6MWT change at T1: +11% in the Results, a fall from 448.8 to 199.1 m (-56%) in Table 2, and -246 m in the Discussion (which is close to but not exactly the table's -249.7 m). The T2 control value and the other 6MWT figures reconcile with the table, so the 199.1 m entry may be a typographical or extraction error, but the paper does not say so and the contradiction is real as printed.

issues.title: About 30 outcomes, no primary outcome; conclusion highlights improvements and omits null results
issues.explanation: The study assesses around 30 outcomes at two timepoints with no primary outcome and no multiplicity handling. The Conclusion states improvements in physical and mental health, while 30 s sit-to-stand, grip strength, HADS anxiety and current pain did not favour the intervention and two SF-36 subscales were worse at T1. A favourable subset of outcomes receives the emphasis. With no testing and no designated primary outcome, the likelihood of favourable differences by chance is unquantified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a stated analysis plan showing the favourable outcomes were the planned ones.

quotes.text: this study population showed improvements in physical and mental health in the intervention group
There was no difference between the groups in the 30 s STS and hand grip strength

issues.title: Treating staff unblinded; blinding of the physical-performance outcome assessors not stated
issues.explanation: The paper says the staff were aware of allocation. The objective measures (6MWT, sit-to-stand, grip strength) are staff-administered and effort-dependent, and the paper does not say who assessed them or whether they were masked. Knowledge of allocation could influence encouragement and scoring. The 6MWT is the main basis for the 'clinical benefit' statement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 6MWT, 30 s STS and grip strength were measured by assessors masked to allocation.

quotes.text: The treating staff were not blinded to the allocation because we used different spool applicators

issues.title: Several Results percentages differ from Table 2: GH control T2 -8% vs -18%, RE -77% vs -67%, PD-Q T2 +13% vs +33%
issues.explanation: Most percentage changes in the text can be reproduced from Table 2, but a few cannot. Control SF-36 general health at T2 is given as -8% where the table gives about -18%. Control role emotional is given as -77% where the table gives about -67%. Intervention PD-Q at T2 is given as +13% where the table gives about +33%, a worsening of pain that the text understates. These are isolated reporting errors, but they show the text and table were not reconciled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated method for the percentages, such as mean of individual percent changes, with participant-level data reproducing the text values.

issues.title: HADS total, intervention: text -34% and -53% vs Table 2 means implying -24% and -41%
issues.explanation: The Results report larger HADS total improvements for the intervention group than the Table 2 means support. The table means imply about -24% at T1 and -41% at T2. The control percentages are approximately reproducible. Unless the percentages were computed differently, which the paper does not say, the text overstates the intervention advantage on this outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated calculation method and participant-level data reproducing -34% and -53%.

issues.title: 3/10 control dropouts (all worsened, none in intervention); imputation by group, no details
issues.explanation: Three control participants worsened and dropped out with no follow-up visit, while no intervention participant did. T2 control values rest on 7 observed participants plus unreported imputation done within group. Missingness linked to worsening violates the usual missing-at-random assumption. The number of imputations, the imputation model and any sensitivity analysis are not given, so how the T2 between-arm contrasts were affected is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported imputation model and sensitivity analysis (for example worst-case imputation for the dropouts) showing the T2 contrasts are unchanged.

quotes.text: There was no follow-up or end of the study visit in the three drop-outs of the control group, because all three patients worsened remarkably.
data were imputed by group using multiple imputation

issues.title: No trial registry identifier in the supplied text; no primary outcome designated
issues.explanation: The text gives an ethics number and recruitment dates but no registry identifier. Fatigue is called 'obviously the most important parameter', but no outcome is designated primary, so the prespecification of the analysed outcomes cannot be checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier with a prespecified outcome set dated before recruitment.

quotes.text: Recruitment started on 5 July 2023 and ended on 8 July 2024.
was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical University of Vienna (EK-Nr: 1764/2021)

10.1007/s10072-023-07268-9.headline_claim: A dual-task augmented reality rehabilitation protocol improves cognitive function (executive functions) in people with long COVID brain fog, with fatigue and TMS outcomes largely unchanged.
10.1007/s10072-023-07268-9.overall: The cognitive benefit comes from a small, non-randomized, unblinded comparison with preference-based allocation, and rests on two of about nine unadjusted outcomes. The reported analysed numbers are also unclear, since df imply 18 and 12 analysed rather than 20. The paper's own hedging as a pilot means its claim should be treated as tentative at best, and the safety claim is unsupported by reported data.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated as primary; executive function measures TMT-B and FAB showed time x group interaction

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from a non-randomized, preference-allocated comparison of 10 vs 10 participants
issues.explanation: Participants chose the intervention, while controls were those unable to attend. Motivation, mobility, age and sex differences could explain the larger TMT-B and FAB improvement. The control group had no attention-matched activity and assessments were unblinded. The design cannot support attribution of the cognitive gain to the dual-task protocol, and the authors admit this possibility themselves.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomized allocation, or analysis adjusted for baseline differences and motivation.

quotes.text: the groups were not randomized and participation to the dual-task protocol was based on participants' preference
Efficacy of dual-task augmented reality rehabilitation in non-hospitalized adults

second_reader.what_stands: The study is non-randomized, allocation was by preference/logistics, and groups were 10 vs 10, yet the title and aim use 'efficacy'; this is a real mismatch with the design. It is softened because the authors label the work pilot/observational, state the selection-bias limitation openly, and call the evidence preliminary in the conclusion.

issues.title: Two of ~9 outcomes (TMT-B P=0.026, FAB P=0.017) reach significance, no multiplicity correction or primary outcome
issues.explanation: The cognitive finding rests on two interaction tests from a family of at least nine outcomes plus TMS tests. No primary outcome was prespecified, and the Bonferroni correction applies only to post hoc comparisons within an outcome. With a correction across outcomes, neither would be significant. The cognitive benefit should be viewed as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified, registered primary outcome, or significance holding after correction across outcomes.

quotes.text: Bonferroni's correction was applied for the post hoc analyses

second_reader.what_stands: Only two of roughly 11 time x group interaction tests reached P < 0.05 (0.026 and 0.017), no primary outcome was named, and the stated Bonferroni correction covers only post hoc comparisons, not the multiple outcomes. Neither interaction P would survive a correction across outcomes (and the 0.026 would not survive even across the three cognitive tests), so the cognitive finding is exploratory. The count is closer to 11 than ~9.

issues.title: Error df of 11 (HGE) and 16 (cognition, fatigue) vs 18 (TMS) in a 10+10 design with no exclusions described
issues.explanation: With 10 participants per group, a 2x2 mixed ANOVA has error df of 18, as in the TMS results. The cognitive and fatigue interaction tests use F(1,16) and the HGE group effect uses F(1,11), implying about 18 and 12 analysed participants. The paper reports no dropouts, missing data or exclusions, so the analysed sample for the main cognitive findings is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of which participants had missing data for each outcome, or a corrected df.

issues.title: Ten per group with no sample-size calculation in a study titled 'Efficacy'
issues.explanation: There is no power calculation and only 10 per group, so effect estimates are imprecise and prone to chance findings. The authors describe the study as a pilot with preliminary evidence, which limits the harm. The problem is mostly the use of 'efficacy' in the title.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation supporting 10 per group for the reported effect.

quotes.text: the sample size was moderate
this study provides preliminary evidence of the efficacy of a dual-task physiotherapy protocol

issues.title: 'Safe and well-accepted' stated without any reported adverse-event or adherence data
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the protocol was safe, well accepted and could promote adherence. The Results contain no adverse event data, session attendance or adherence figures. With 10 treated participants, safety could not be established statistically in any case.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported adverse events, attendance and adherence data in the paper or supplement.

quotes.text: The proposed protocol was safe and well-accepted

issues.title: MEP increase of 70% has 95% CI 3-150 excluding zero, but P = 0.058
issues.explanation: A 95% CI that excludes zero implies p below .05, but the same estimate is reported as non-significant (p=0.058). The CI is asymmetric around 70, so it may come from a different method than the ANOVA test, though the paper does not say. This is a small inconsistency in a secondary, group-independent TMS result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors stating the CI was computed on a log or ratio scale or by a different method that explains the apparent mismatch.

quotes.text: MEP increased by 70% (95% CI 3-150, P =  0.058)

issues.title: TMT-B change printed as -15.9 s but CI printed as 7.6-24.1 without minus signs
issues.explanation: The TMT-B change is printed as negative, while its 95% CI has positive bounds. The CI is centred on the magnitude of the change, so this is a sign-format inconsistency rather than a calculation error. It affects no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original PDF printing the CI as -24.1 to -7.6.

10.1007/s10103-023-03917-9.headline_claim: Photobiomodulation, transmucosal laser irradiation of blood, and B complex use seem to improve taste and smell perception in patients with COVID-19 related long-term taste impairment, without full recovery after the treatment periods.
10.1007/s10103-023-03917-9.overall: The trial reports no significant between-group differences for taste, taste distortion or smell, with only 3 sham participants analysed and 22% attrition, so the positive conclusion rests on within-group change and descriptive tendencies. The headline claim is not supported by the controlled comparisons; the printed numerical errors are minor by comparison.

primary_outcome.name: Taste overall perception (sum of 0-10 scores for salt, sweet, acid, bitter; 0-40 scale), quantitative hyperconcentrated solutions

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from within-group change and 'tendencies' when all between-group tests, including vs sham (n=3), were null
issues.explanation: All between-group tests for taste, taste distortion and smell were non-significant, and the sham arm had only 3 analysed participants. Improvement is argued from within-group changes and descriptive tendencies versus placebo, which cannot separate treatment effect from natural recovery or chance. The conclusion that the treatments improve taste and smell is therefore not supported by the controlled comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group contrast against sham showing an effect, or a confidence interval for the difference excluding the null.

quotes.text: No statistical differences were found in the final intergroup analysis, for Taste, Taste Distortion, and Smell, despite the tendencies observed through the median and mean results.
it was possible to verify improvement in all groups in comparison to the placebo group, despite the lack of statistical relevance

second_reader.what_stands: Every between-group test printed, including all comparisons against sham (n=3), is null (final sweet p = 0.050 is not below the stated alpha of 0.05 and no pairwise test is significant), yet the Discussion and Conclusions infer improvement 'in all groups in comparison to the placebo group' and that treatments 'seem to improve' taste and smell, based on medians, within-group change and untested frequency tables. The authors do acknowledge the lack of statistical significance and the small sample, which softens but does not remove the mismatch between the null tests and the efficacy wording.

issues.title: 11 of 50 randomised participants (22%) excluded from analyses; completers only, no missing-data handling
issues.explanation: The tables use the 39 completers and the paper describes no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis. The attrition is disclosed, and its effect on the null between-group results cannot be assessed because arm-wise dropouts are not given in the text. It adds to uncertainty but does not by itself alter the interpretation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram showing balanced, reasoned losses and an ITT or sensitivity analysis giving the same results.

quotes.text: was responsible for a 22% dropout rate (50 participants included, 39 finished experimental protocols)

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; six arms of 3 to 8 analysed participants, yet efficacy conclusion drawn
issues.explanation: Alpha, beta and power are stated, but no effect size or required sample size is given. After attrition, arms had 7, 7, 8, 7, 7 and 3 participants, so the study could not detect moderate differences, which the authors acknowledge. This undermines any efficacy claim, and non-significance cannot be read as evidence of benefit either.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-registered sample-size calculation giving the target of about 50 for a stated effect size.

quotes.text: Sample size played another major limitation.
Considered Alpha error was 0.05 (CI 95%), Beta error 0.20, and Power of 0.80.

issues.title: Tukey post hoc p for G4-TLIB smell change printed as 0.001 in Results and 0.01 in Table 5 caption
issues.explanation: The Results text reports the only significant post hoc smell difference (G4-TLIB, initial vs final) as p = 0.001, while the Table 5 caption gives p = 0.01 for the same comparison. Both values are below 0.05, so the significance call is unchanged, but the two printings cannot both be right. It is a minor reporting inconsistency on a secondary, within-group result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two values come from different tests or comparisons, or the original output showing which value is correct.

quotes.text: the statistical difference was only visible in G4-TLIB ( p =  0.001)
was in the G4-TLIB between the initial and final ( p =  0.01)

issues.title: Taste distortion reduction printed as 35% for n = 15 of 39, but 15/39 = 38.5%
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that taste distortion reduction was seen in 35% (15 of 39) of participants, but 15 divided by 39 is 38.5%. The paper attaches no explanation, so the percentage and the count disagree. The result is described as non-significant and does not drive the conclusions.
