issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of the 35% figure on a different base, or source data showing 14 of 39 participants.

quotes.text: The taste distortion reduction tendency without statistical relevance was observed in all groups 35% ( n =  15 of 39)

script.explanation: 15/39 = 38.46%, but the paper prints 35.0, outside the rounding interval [34.50, 36.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 42.9 rather than 39.

issues.title: Registration numbers given but no registration date or registered primary outcome stated
issues.explanation: The paper cites ReBEC and UTN identifiers but does not say when the trial was registered or what the registered primary outcome was. The reader therefore cannot check for outcome switching. This is a reporting gap, not a demonstrated inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry entry showing registration before enrolment with the same primary outcome.

quotes.text: registered in the Brazilian Randomized Clinical Trials Platform (ReBEC) under the number (RBR-3tpvp8t)

10.1007/s10571-026-01736-4.headline_claim: C1-INH treatment was associated with coordinated, phase-specific proteomic modulation across complement, bradykinin, immune, and ECM-related pathways in neurological PASC.
10.1007/s10571-026-01736-4.overall: The paper is an explicitly exploratory, hypothesis-generating proteomic subanalysis of 10 participants, and its hedged wording is largely appropriate. However, the named protein signals rest on within-arm, nominal-p, uncorrected selection from about 7,600 analytes, so they should be read as candidates only, not as demonstrated C1-INH effects. A few internal contradictions (IGFBP1 direction, ITLN1 correlation sign) further reduce confidence in the text's accuracy.

primary_outcome.name: Within-arm plasma protein change (SomaScan) during the C1-INH treatment window

issues.title: Treatment-phase effects rest on within-arm change from baseline, with no placebo-controlled contrast
issues.explanation: Arm 1 (TP1-TP9) and Arm 2 (TP9-TP17) were each compared to their own baseline, and the placebo period was kept only as a contextual reference and not used in the analysis. Without a between-arm or on-drug versus placebo contrast, changes cannot be separated from time, period or sequence effects, in 4 and 6 people. The conclusion's 'associated with' wording is hedged, but 'phase-specific modulation' by C1-INH is still not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis contrasting on-C1-INH with placebo periods (e.g., period-adjusted mixed model) showing the same proteins.

quotes.text: For treatment-phase effects, Arm 1 (TP1-TP9) and Arm 2 (TP9-TP17) were compared against their respective baselines using within-subject paired tests.
placebo results were not used
C1-INH treatment was associated with coordinated, phasespecific proteomic modulation

second_reader.what_stands: Treatment-phase effects rest on paired within-arm change from each arm's own baseline, and the placebo period was explicitly not used as a subtraction or filter. No placebo-controlled contrast is reported, so the changes could partly reflect time, period or sequence effects. The authors label the work exploratory and use 'associated with', and they add a descriptive placebo check, so the gap is acknowledged. The conclusion's 'C1-INH treatment was associated with... phase-specific modulation' still rests on uncontrolled within-arm change.

issues.title: Named protein findings selected on nominal p<0.05 or fold-change among 7,596 analytes without correction
issues.explanation: Proteins were prioritised by nominal p<0.05 or |log2FC|≥0.75 across 7,596 analytes in 4-6 participants per arm, and only enrichment and pooled correlations were FDR-adjusted. At p<0.05 about 380 analytes would pass per comparison by chance alone, and only 11 proteins passed in the treatment phase. The Conclusions nonetheless name NRP2, CD83, CXCL13, C9, KLKB1 and SERPINE1 as signatures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: FDR-adjusted protein-level results showing the named proteins remain significant.

quotes.text: proteins with p-values < 0.05 were  classified  as  nominally significant
consistent modulation of neuroimmune and adaptive markers (NRP2, CD83, CXCL13)

second_reader.what_stands: The named proteins (NRP2, CD83, CXCL13) were selected on nominal p<0.05 or a fold-change cutoff among 7,596 analytes with no protein-level multiplicity correction, and the paper says so. The number of same-direction nominal hits (11) is about what chance would give across two arms, and CXCL13 clears the fold-change cutoff by only 0.01 log2 units. FDR was applied only to pathway enrichment and to the pooled correlations, and the authors repeatedly label the findings exploratory, but the Conclusions still call these markers 'consistent modulation'.

issues.title: IGFBP1 direction in treatment phase inconsistent: downregulated in Results, upregulated in Discussion
issues.explanation: The treatment-phase Results place IGFBP1 among downregulated targets, whereas the Discussion lists it among proteins upregulated during the treatment phase and the full-arc Results call it consistently upregulated. The Results sentence is visibly scrambled in the text, so part of this may be an extraction or typesetting problem. A reader cannot tell which direction the authors found, though it concerns one protein among many exploratory findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Excel 2 showing IGFBP1 direction by arm and window, with the Results list being a typesetting error.

quotes.text: downregulated targets included COL6A3 (collagen type VI alpha 3 chain), defensin 112), IGFBP1 (insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 1)
quotes.location: Results, Directionality of protein expression during treatment

quotes.text: including CD83, CD28, FCMR,  FDCSP,  ATG7,  LSAMP,  and  IGFBP1

issues.title: Reproducibility and placebo check cited as support, though nothing was replicated and placebo data are n=6
issues.explanation: The Limitations say reproducibility of the trends supports their interpretability, but no replication or independent dataset is reported. The Discussion also uses a placebo-window check (Arm 2 only, n=6, not used in analysis) to argue treatment signals are not nonspecific temporal variation, which that check cannot establish. The wording is hedged, so this is a modest overstatement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An independent cohort or within-study replication reproducing the named proteins, plus a formal placebo-versus-active contrast.

quotes.text: the reproducibility and biological plausibility of observed trends support their biological interpretability
consistent with the primary treatment-phase signals not being explained solely by nonspecific temporal variation

issues.title: ITLN1-pain correlation called inverse but printed as positive rho 0.913
issues.explanation: The sentence says pain change correlated inversely with ITLN1 but prints rho as +0.913, while the three other pain associations in the same sentence carry minus signs. By the paper's own convention a positive rho means worsening, so the sign or the word is wrong. It affects one of eight FDR-significant associations in an exploratory analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Excel 6B showing the ITLN1 rho sign matches the text.

quotes.text: Present pain intensity change correlated inversely with ITLN1 (rho 0.913, FDR 0.0112)
positive rho reflects association with increases in symptom scores (worsening)

issues.title: Proteomics in 10 of 36 randomized participants selected by plasma availability, arms of 4 and 6
issues.explanation: Only 10 of 36 randomized participants (28%) were profiled, chosen by availability of plasma at all timepoints, with no comparison to the 26 not analysed. The 4 versus 6 split is attributed to feasibility, not chance, so the arms are not a randomized comparison. This is disclosed as a pilot subset, so it limits generalisation rather than invalidating the exploratory findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline and clinical comparison of the 10 profiled versus 26 unprofiled participants showing no systematic difference.

quotes.text: Proteomic profiling was performed in 10 of 36 randomized participants with plasma available at all predefined collection timepoints.
Randomization  yielded  an  imbalanced  allocation  (Arm  1  n=4;  Arm  2 n=6)

issues.title: Pooled n=10 Spearman correlations across different crossover periods drive 'FDR-significant' associations
issues.explanation: The pooled analysis combines Arm 1 TP1-TP9 and Arm 2 TP9-TP17, which are equal-length on-drug windows but occur in different periods, and the authors acknowledge power and stability differ by arm. With 10 observations, rho around 0.75-0.91 is highly unstable and the eight FDR-significant results are best treated as hypotheses. The authors label them exploratory, so the issue weakens a secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Arm-specific and permutation-based analyses showing the same associations, or replication in an independent sample.

quotes.text: performed a treatment-aligned pooled analysis combining Arm 1 TP1-TP9 with Arm 2
power and correlation stability differ by arm
eight protein-outcome associations remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (FDR < 0.05)

issues.title: Follow-up: 3 significant proteins, then 'confirmed' 23 significant and 18 high-effect proteins
issues.explanation: Three proteins met p<0.05 and 14 met the effect threshold, yet the next sentence says cross-validation 'confirmed' 23 and 18. The larger numbers probably reflect different tests or less strict filtering, but the paper does not say so, and 'confirmed' implies a superset relationship that the counts do not show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Excel 2 showing the 23/18 sets are defined by a different filter and include the primary sets.

quotes.text: we identified three proteins with statistically significant changes (p<0.05) and 14 with strong effect sizes
confirmed 23 significant and 18 high-effect-size proteins with consistent directionality

10.1007/s11055-022-01307-2.headline_claim: Cortexin at 10 and 20 mg i.m. is effective for correcting cognitive and asthenic manifestations of post-COVID syndrome, with anxiolytic and antidepressant effects, and its absence of side effects supports its use for PCS.
10.1007/s11055-022-01307-2.overall: The headline claims that Cortexin is effective, dose-dependent and free of adverse events are not supported by an uncontrolled, open-label, single-cohort before-after design with patient-rated outcomes and no between-dose test. Several descriptive numbers are also internally inconsistent (age SD, CT categories, complaint denominators). Only the observation that post-COVID symptoms were common and that scores improved over 30 days can be taken at face value.

primary_outcome.name: unclear (no prespecified primary outcome named; MFI-20 asthenia score, MMSE and Schulte test reported)

issues.title: Efficacy 'demonstrated' from single-cohort open-label before-after data with no comparator
issues.explanation: All 979 patients received Cortexin and were compared only with their own baseline. There is no untreated or placebo group and no blinding. Post-COVID symptoms often resolve spontaneously, and entry required abnormal scores, so improvement is expected without any drug effect. Outcomes are mostly patient-rated or repeated cognitive tests, and all patients rated efficacy as high. The data cannot support a causal efficacy claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or placebo arm, or blinded outcome assessment, showing the improvement exceeds the natural course.

quotes.text: The efficacy of Cortexin was demonstrated in correcting asthenic and cognitive symptoms in patients with PCS.
All  patients  evaluated  treatment  effi  cacy  as  high  in terms  of  measures  of  subjective  treatment  quality  assessment scales.

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy is stated as 'demonstrated' and 'confirmed' from a single-arm, open-label before-after design with no placebo or untreated comparator, so change over time cannot be attributed to Cortexin. The claim that all patients rated efficacy as high also rests on unblinded, subjective patient scales, with no figures reported.

issues.title: Dose-dependent effect claimed with only within-group p-values and no 10 mg vs 20 mg test
issues.explanation: The reported p-values test change from baseline within each dose group. The claim that 20 mg works better rests on comparing fold-changes (3 vs 3.6 for fatigue, 4.6 vs 5.1 for weakness) and on figure impressions. No between-dose test is shown. The groups are also not shown to be comparable at baseline, and dose allocation is only said to be random. The dose-dependence conclusion is therefore not demonstrated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A printed between-dose test (for example Mann-Whitney on change scores) with baseline-adjusted differences.

quotes.text: In patients receiving Cortexin 10 mg, fatigue decreased almost three-fold ( p < 0.001) and general weakness by a factor of 4.6 ( p = 0.004).
Patients receiving Cortexin 20 mg showed more marked changes: fatigue decreased by a factor of 3.6

second_reader.what_stands: The text and conclusion assert a dose-dependent effect, but the only p-values given are within-group before-after tests, and no direct 10 mg vs 20 mg test is reported in the text or tables. The numeric differences between doses are small and without uncertainty estimates, so a dose-response claim is not supported by what is printed.

issues.title: Anxiolytic/antidepressant effects and zero adverse events claimed without supporting measures or data
issues.explanation: The Conclusions claim anti-anxiety, antidepressant and dose-dependent anxious-depressive effects. No validated anxiety or depression instrument or result is reported. The assessments listed cover asthenia, cognition, attention and subjective treatment quality. The claim of no adverse events rests on a single phone call and one visit, with no event table. Both claims go beyond what is shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Anxiety/depression scale scores by visit and dose, plus a structured adverse event log.

quotes.text: Cortexin was found to have anti-anxiety, antidepressant, and anxiolytic effects, which were more marked at the 20-mg dose.
During the observation period, none of the patients showed any AE or  unfavorable  therapeutic  interactions  with  other  drugs.

second_reader.what_stands: The anxiolytic, antidepressant and 'more marked at 20 mg' claims are not supported by any validated anxiety or depression measure or any printed data in the text or tables, and 'anti-anxiety' and 'anxiolytic' are listed as separate effects. The zero-AE statement is at least stated as a monitored outcome (telephone and visit 3 recording), but it is reported without a denominator, dropout data or detail on how events were elicited, so it cannot be verified from the paper.

issues.title: Complaint frequencies all fit a denominator of 79, not the 979 patients analysed
issues.explanation: The complaint percentages (97.5, 93.7, 92.4, 89.9, 70.9, 69.6, 44.3, 38.0) are all multiples of 1/79 to one decimal. A base of 979 would give steps of about 0.1%. The paper presents them as frequencies in the 979-patient cohort and gives no subsample size. The base of these prevalence figures is therefore unclear, which weakens the prevalence claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that frequencies come from a defined subsample, or patient-level counts out of 979 that reproduce these percentages.

quotes.text: increased fatigue (97.5%), general weakness (93.7%), forgetfulness (92.4%), anxiety (89.9%)

issues.title: Results say 20 mg gave greater asthenia and cognitive effects; Conclusions say no dose effect on cognition
issues.explanation: The Results state that improvements in asthenia and cognitive status were greater with 20 mg. The Conclusions state the dose-dependent effect holds for asthenic and anxious-depressive disorders but not for cognitive impairment. No numbers or between-dose tests are given to settle which is right. The dose-response statements are therefore internally inconsistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 3 data or a between-dose test showing the 20 mg advantage is confined to asthenia.

quotes.text: Marked improvements in terms of asthenia and cognitive status were seen in all patients, with greater effects in patients receiving 20 mg Cortexin
Cortexin had a dose-dependent effect in relation to asthenic and anxious-depressive disorders but not cognitive impairments.

issues.title: Dose assignment called random with no method, concealment or baseline comparison (584 vs 395)
issues.explanation: The paper asserts random dose assignment but gives no sequence generation, concealment or baseline balance by dose. The arms are unequal (584 vs 395), and no baseline data by dose are shown. Any dose comparison therefore rests on an unverified allocation process.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol describing a concealed randomisation scheme and a baseline table by dose arm.

quotes.text: 584  patients  (59.6%)  received  10  mg i.m. and 395 (40.4%) received 20 mg i.m.; doses were assigned randomly.

issues.title: Age SD printed as 4.5 years in abstract but 14.5 years in Methods for the same mean of 54.6
issues.explanation: The abstract gives age as 54.6 ± 4.5 years, while the study-population paragraph gives 54.6 ± 14.5 years with a range of 18-80. An SD of 4.5 is incompatible with that range in a cohort of 979, so the abstract value is probably wrong. It is a descriptive slip that does not affect the efficacy conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or the original-language abstract showing the age SD is 4.5 and the 18-80 range is a different quantity.

quotes.text: mean agonist was 54.6 ± 14.5 years (range 18-80 years)

issues.title: CT lung-involvement categories sum to 903 but only 879 patients had chest CT (979 minus 100)
issues.explanation: The four lung-involvement categories total 903 patients. Only 879 patients had chest CT, since 100 had none. Adding the 100 without CT gives 1003, which is more than the 979 enrolled. Some counts are therefore wrong or the categories overlap. This is a descriptive error with no effect on the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the no-involvement group includes the 100 patients without CT and that one of the other counts is a typo, which would still leave the totals unreconciled.

quotes.text: in 519 (53.1%) there was  no  lung  involvement
chest CT was not  performed  in  100  patients

issues.title: No registration or protocol reference for a program that assigns doses and tests treatment efficacy
issues.explanation: No registry entry or protocol reference is given, so the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be checked against what is reported. Many outcomes are reported without a designated primary one. The observational label may explain the absence, but the dose assignment and efficacy aim make the study interventional in practice.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier or ethics-approved protocol that predates enrolment and lists the outcomes.

quotes.text: The aim of the CORTEX multicenter clinical-epidemiological observational program is to study the prevalence and clinical manifestations of PCS in patients at out-patient neurological clinics

10.1007/s11356-022-22949-2.headline_claim: Mountain spa rehabilitation at high altitude improved health of patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome and can be recommended for their recovery.
10.1007/s11356-022-22949-2.overall: The paper shows before-after changes in 14 patients (10 for lung function and symptoms), but without a concurrent control, blinding or multiplicity control it cannot support the causal claim that rehabilitation improved health, nor the socioeconomic claim. The objective findings (6MWT, some blood indices) are suggestive only, and the recommendation outruns a pilot of this size and design.

primary_outcome.name: Pre-post change in lung function (6MWT, Borg scale), clinical symptoms and platelet mitochondrial bioenergetics; the paper names no primary outcome, and the registry lists five

issues.title: Uncontrolled before-after design in 14 patients cannot attribute changes to rehabilitation; 'randomized' label unsupported
issues.explanation: All treatment inferences compare the same patients at admission and after 16-18 days. The healthy control group received no intervention and was not matched (mean age 51.3 vs 58.7, BMI 25.2 vs 29.9). Spontaneous recovery, other care, regression to the mean and expectation effects cannot be separated from the programme effect, yet the title and conclusions attribute improvement to rehabilitation. The paper also cites a 'randomized controlled' registration without describing any randomisation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or usual-care comparison arm with randomised allocation reported in the paper.

quotes.text: These tests were performed before (MR1) and after mountain spa rehabilitation (MR2).
quotes.location: Materials and methods, Functional capacity of the lungs

quotes.text: The randomized controlled clinical trials registration number is NCT05178225.
Mountain spa rehabilitation can be recommended for the acceleration of recovery of patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: The patient data are a single-group before-after comparison with no concurrent control receiving no rehabilitation, so changes cannot be attributed to the rehabilitation (time since illness, natural recovery, regression to the mean, and unblinded measures are all unaddressed). The paper's only mention of randomization is the registration sentence; the paper describes no randomization, and the registry (allocation randomized, 51 enrolled, masking none, retrospective registration) does not match the 14 patients analysed. I could not check what the other registered participants or arms were.

issues.title: Conclusion claims reduced socioeconomic problems and recommends use; no such outcome measured, no control
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state that spa rehabilitation 'contributes to ... the reduction of socioeconomic problems' and recommend it clinically. No cost, work-return, health-care use or other socioeconomic data were collected, and the design is uncontrolled with n = 14. The listed limitations (short duration, sample size) omit the lack of control and the 29% missing data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported socioeconomic outcome data or a conclusion limited to the measured physiological outcomes.

quotes.text: Spa rehabilitation in high-altitude environment contributes to the acceleration of patients' health and to the reduction of socioeconomic problems.
Limitations of these pilot results include relatively short time of mountain spa rehabilitation (16-18 days) paid by the insurance company and number of patients with postCOVID-19 syndrome ( n = 14).

second_reader.what_stands: No socioeconomic outcome was measured in the paper or in the registered outcomes, and with no control group for the patients, the statements that rehabilitation 'contributes to' acceleration of health and reduction of socioeconomic problems, and the recommendation, go beyond the data. The authors do acknowledge small size and short duration and call the work a pilot, so the limitation is partly weighed, but the missing control group and the absence of any economic measurement are not.

issues.title: HgB (p = 0.056) listed among significant blood-count improvements; glucose p = 0.069 also called improved
issues.explanation: The Results state that MR 'significantly improved blood count' and include HgB with p = 0.056, above the stated alpha of 0.05. The same section says glucose 'improved' at p = 0.069. These are non-significant changes presented as improvements. The effect is limited to wording of one secondary result; the other listed parameters (RBC, HCT, MCV) do meet p<0.05, though no multiplicity correction was applied.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified, different alpha or a statement that HgB was only described as a trend.

quotes.text: MR significantly improved blood count, as the count of RBC ( p = 0.008), HCT ( p = 0.003), MCV ( p = 0.009), and HgB ( p = 0.056) were higher in MR2
quotes.location: Results, Effect of MR on blood count and metabolites

quotes.text: Slightly higher blood glucose level of the patients improved after MR ( p = 0.069, Table 3).
quotes.location: Results, Effect of MR on blood count and metabolites

issues.title: Functional and symptom outcomes available for only 10 of 14 patients (29%) with no explanation
issues.explanation: The 6MWT, Borg score and symptom questionnaire cover 10 of 14 patients and the paper does not say why four are missing or whether they differ from completers. If the missing patients were less likely to improve, effects are overstated. This is a reporting gap in the main clinical outcomes rather than proven bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Explanation that the four were missing for reasons unrelated to outcome (e.g. not scheduled for the test) with baseline comparison.

quotes.text: The functional capacity of the lungs was evaluated in ten of the fourteen patients
quotes.location: Materials and methods, Functional capacity of the lungs

quotes.text: From fourteen patients, ten patients filled out the questionnaire for evaluation of clinical symptoms before and after MR.
quotes.location: Results, Effect of MR on clinical symptoms

issues.title: Unblinded self-reported Borg dyspnoea and symptom counts support the 'improved health' claim
issues.explanation: The Borg dyspnoea score and the 21-item symptom questionnaire are self-reported by patients who knew they were receiving rehabilitation, and the registry lists masking as none. Table 2 gives only raw counts with no test, yet the text says many symptoms improved. Expectation effects may inflate these improvements, so they carry less weight than objective measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded assessment or a sham/control comparison for patient-reported outcomes.

quotes.text: Patients completed a questionnaire (21 questions) before and after MR.
Many clinical symptoms have improved after MR, as breathing difficulty, shortness of breath, chills, heart palpitations, overall fatigue
quotes.location: Results, Effect of MR on clinical symptoms

issues.title: Retrospective registration; registry enrolment 51 vs 14 patients reported; five 'primary' outcomes, no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: The trial was registered about 8 months after the start, so the plan could not be checked in advance. The registered outcomes are broad (five primary outcomes) and match what the paper reports, so selective reporting is not evident, but with many outcomes and no multiplicity adjustment the p values should be read as exploratory. The registry lists 51 participants against 14 patients and 15 controls analysed; the paper does not explain the difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prospective registration records or an explanation that the registry covers a larger multi-arm study.

quotes.text: The randomized controlled clinical trials registration number is NCT05178225.

10.1007/s11357-024-01179-z.headline_claim: A 2-week supervised, low-intensity cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program for long COVID patients produces lasting benefit, with the authors stating it significantly boosts general health and resumption of normal life.
10.1007/s11357-024-01179-z.overall: The headline claim that a 2-week program permanently improves health is not supported: there is no concurrent control for follow-up, no baseline CPET, 62% loss at 3 months, and only 2 of 9 CPET variables differ between months 2 and 3. The study can at most be read as a descriptive, hypothesis-generating series; the intervention description is also internally contradictory.

primary_outcome.name: Respiratory functional parameters, 6MWT and quality of life (Random Forest main outcome); between-group comparison of pulmonary and EQ-5D measures at enrolment

issues.title: Long-term efficacy inferred without concurrent control or baseline CPET; only 2- vs 3-month PR group data
issues.explanation: The control group received a single check-up and no follow-up CPET is reported for it. The only longitudinal outcome analysed (CPET) compares the rehabilitation group at 2 vs 3 months, with no pre-rehabilitation CPET (the Limitations admit this). Such a comparison cannot show that the 2-week program caused any change, as it could reflect natural recovery, home exercise, or selective return of fitter patients. Claims of program efficacy and permanence are therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: CPET data for a concurrent control group, or baseline CPET in the rehabilitation group, showing a change attributable to the program.

quotes.text: the  original study design did not include arrival CPET at the beginning of the rehabilitation program
The data that support the findings

second_reader.what_stands: The CPET data cover only the 2-month vs 3-month visits of the rehabilitation group; there is no baseline CPET and no concurrent control with follow-up, so a long-term benefit of the 2-week programme cannot be inferred from them. The missing baseline CPET is acknowledged in Limitations, but the Abstract and Discussion still speak of lasting or permanent effects. The data-availability sentence (data on request) is not itself a flaw in the point.

issues.title: 'Proved' permanent improvement and 'significantly boosts general health' not supported by the data shown
issues.explanation: The Results say the study 'proved' permanent improvement, and the Conclusion says the program 'significantly boosts general health'. The data are a non-randomized comparison, a 2- vs 3-month CPET comparison with 62% attrition and no baseline CPET, and nothing in the paper tests general health after the program. A change between months 2 and 3 cannot show a permanent effect of a 2-week program.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data with baseline and 3-month outcomes, handling missing data, showing a sustained effect.

quotes.text: Our study  proved  that  2-week  cardiopulmonary rehabilitation permanently improves the participants' performance.
significantly boosts general health

second_reader.what_stands: The wording that the programme 'proved' to 'permanently' improve performance and 'significantly boosts general health' goes beyond the data presented: follow-up was at most 3 months with 38 of 100 participants, there was no baseline CPET or control, only 2 of 9 CPET variables differed (uncorrected), and no general-health outcome change is shown in this paper. The claim about general health may draw on the authors' earlier publication, which was not examined here.

issues.title: Only 38 of 100 attended 3-month CPET; no missing-data analysis, unclear if comparison is paired
issues.explanation: 73 of 100 attended at 2 months and 38 at 3 months, so 62% were lost. Table 3 does not state the n for each column or whether the test was paired, so the 2- vs 3-month difference may compare 73 people with 38 different people. Those who returned may differ systematically (for example, those who felt well or poorly). The significant VO2 changes (p = 0.033 and 0.021) are then not a reliable basis for a 'permanent' benefit claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A paired analysis restricted to the 38 completers, with a comparison of completers and dropouts showing no systematic difference.

quotes.text: only 38 patients participated in the 3-month followup
indicating  a  dropout  rate  of  27%  at  2  months  and  62% at  3  months  in  the  follow-up  phase

second_reader.what_stands: Only 38 of 100 had 3-month assessment, and the paper reports no analysis of missing data (no comparison of completers with non-completers, no sensitivity analysis) and does not say whether the Table 3 comparison is paired or what n each column has. The dropout figures themselves are correctly calculated and openly reported, with attrition explained as non-compliance.

issues.title: Intervention described as low-intensity only, yet HIIT used for severe cases
issues.explanation: The Study design section says only low-intensity exercise was used for patient safety, citing evidence that interval training can be harmful in long COVID. The Interventions section says high-intensity interval training was used in severe cases, with a detailed protocol (60-s maximal bouts, 4-6 cycles). The Discussion repeats the low-intensity claim. Readers cannot tell what exercise the patients received, or whether the safety rationale applied, which limits reproducibility and interpretation of the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that HIIT was only a described alternative and was not delivered to any participant.

quotes.text: In our study, only low-intensity  exercise  training  was  involved,  considering  our patients' safety.
In severe cases, we implemented high-intensity  interval  training.

issues.title: Random Forest 'generalization' claimed without held-out validation, on same 200-person data
issues.explanation: The model was 'trained on the 200 individuals' dataset', repeated ten times, and feature importances are said to 'affirm the reliability and generalization capability' of the model. No external or held-out validation, accuracy values or confidence intervals are given in the text. The outcome is the clinicians' own allocation to rehabilitation, so the model recovers a rule already applied, and says nothing about rehabilitation benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described cross-validation or held-out test with reported accuracy.

quotes.text: Random Forest  was  trained  on  the  200  individuals'  dataset, to predict the outcome.
The selected parameters and their importance collectively affirm the reliability and generalization capability of the developed classification model

issues.title: No trial registry entry reported; only ethics approval number 160/2021
issues.explanation: The paper cites only an ethics approval number and no registry identifier, so prespecification of outcomes cannot be checked. Given that it is labelled an observational quasi-experimental study, registration may not have been required. With many outcomes tested and no multiplicity handling, the risk of selective reporting cannot be excluded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record predating enrollment that lists the same outcomes.

quotes.text: approved by the Ethical Committee of Semmelweis University with the registration number 160/2021

10.1007/s11357-024-01324-8.headline_claim: Post-COVID syndrome shifts resting-state EEG dynamics toward local processing in older adults, and adaptive task-switching training modulates these changes specifically in post-COVID females but not males.
10.1007/s11357-024-01324-8.overall: The headline claims that training modulates post-COVID neural dynamics, particularly in females, are only tentative: the healthy comparison group is non-concurrent and differs in IQ and recruitment, there is no untrained post-COVID arm, and the sex difference rests on significant-versus-non-significant results in small groups. The exploratory pre-training group differences are reasonable as hypotheses, but the efficacy language in the Discussion goes beyond the design.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated as a single primary outcome; the analyses centre on resting-state MSE and SPD changes from PLS analyses

checklist.control: none for post-covid; non-concurrent healthy training group

issues.title: Healthy controls recruited pre-pandemic from a different source and with different IQ than post-COVID group
issues.explanation: The healthy females were recruited before COVID-19 from a lab database, while post-COVID participants were recruited in 2021-2022 through news portals and Facebook. The groups also differ significantly in IQ (131.3 vs 117.9, p = 0.035), and IQ is discussed as a reserve factor. Differences attributed to post-COVID syndrome are therefore confounded with period, recruitment channel and cognitive reserve, and the sample is small (20 vs 16).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrently recruited, IQ-matched healthy comparison group, or analyses adjusting for IQ and recruitment channel.

quotes.text: The healthy old-training group (20 participants, all females) was recruited before the COVID19 pandemic; thus, they did not encounter the virus.
We recruited our participants for the healthy oldtraining group through our database and for the postCOVID old-training group through online news portals  and  Facebook.
the CF  group had significantly higher IQ than the HF  group ( t (34) =   -  2.200, p =  0.035

second_reader.what_stands: The healthy comparison group was recruited earlier (pre-pandemic) from a lab database, whereas the post-COVID group was recruited through news portals and Facebook, and the post-COVID females had about 13 points higher IQ (p = 0.035, d about 0.73). The group comparison is therefore confounded by recruitment source, period and IQ, and IQ was not adjusted for; the paper does mention the high IQ as a limitation but does not treat it as a confound of the group contrast.

issues.title: No untrained post-COVID arm; training effect inferred from pre-post change with time effects dismissed by assertion
issues.explanation: All participants received training, so changes from pre to post in post-COVID groups cannot be attributed to training rather than time, repeated EEG, or practice. The Discussion states time effects cannot be fully ruled out but calls them very unlikely without supporting data. Symptoms did not improve, which cuts both ways.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from an untrained post-COVID group measured at the same interval showing no change.

quotes.text: Even though we cannot rule out time effects entirely,  the possibility  that  the  post-COVID-syndrome-related  neural  changes  resolved  themselves as  time  went  on  is  very  low.

second_reader.what_stands: There is no untrained post-COVID arm, so training effects cannot be separated from time, repeat-testing or spontaneous change. The Discussion dismisses time effects as 'very low' in probability with only an indirect argument (no change in subjective symptoms), while partly acknowledging the limitation with 'cannot rule out time effects entirely'.

issues.title: 'Females but not males' rests on p=0.008/0.006 vs p=0.124/0.068; the joint analysis shows similar pattern
issues.explanation: The claim that training worked only in females compares a significant female PLS result with non-significant male results (n=14), which is not a test of a sex difference. The authors' own combined analysis found one significant latent variable showing a similar pattern in both sexes, with only somewhat larger female design scores. Small n and the lack of a formal interaction test mean the male result is inconclusive rather than null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A formal sex-by-training interaction test showing a significant difference, with adequate power.

quotes.text: for females, LV1 singular  value  =  0.74, p =  0.008;  for  males,  LV1  singular value = 0.56, p =  0.124
quotes.location: Results, Sex differences in the effect of post-COVID syndrome and cognitive training

quotes.text: similar  pattern  of  pre-  to  post-training  changes  in  females  and  males  with  post-COVID  syndrome
our adaptive task-switching training paradigm modified local neural dynamics for females but not for males.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that training modified neural dynamics 'for females but not for males' rests on one subgroup being significant and the other not (p=0.008/0.006 vs 0.124/0.068), with no formal sex x training test; the joint analysis itself shows a similar pattern in both sexes, with only a modest difference in design scores. The claim is stronger than the evidence, particularly for SPD where the male result is p=0.068.

issues.title: Discussion claims training 'improves' neural and cognitive function though design cannot show it
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that the study supports training efficiency in improving neural and cognitive functioning in post-COVID patients. Yet there is no untrained comparison, symptoms did not improve, post-COVID females remained slower than healthy females after training, and 'disappearance' of a group difference is inferred from a non-significant post-training result in small samples. The study could at most suggest a hypothesis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised controlled comparison with an untrained post-COVID arm showing differential neural and cognitive change.

quotes.text: our study supports the efficiency of cognitive training in improving neural and cognitive  functioning  in  post-COVID  patients
Our  post-COVID  participants reported no significant improvement in their subjective symptoms during the adaptive cognitive training procedure.

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion states that the study supports training 'improving neural and cognitive functioning' in post-COVID patients, but with no untrained control, practice effects seen equally in healthy controls, no improvement in symptoms, and a neural 'effect' defined by a non-significant post-training group difference, the design supports at most an association with change over the training period. The authors do hedge elsewhere (exploratory, time effects not entirely ruled out), but the conclusion is worded more strongly than the data allow.

issues.title: MSE/SPD not validated as markers of post-COVID or training benefit; aging and compensation readings are speculative
issues.explanation: The neural measures are not linked here to symptoms or behaviour, and symptoms did not improve. Interpretations as accelerated aging or compensation are offered as hypotheses and the authors say as much. This is a modest weakness of interpretation rather than a clear error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence tying these EEG measures to post-COVID symptoms or outcomes.

quotes.text: In this exploratory study, we investigated how brain dynamics are affected by post-COVID syndrome in older adults.
potentially contributing to accelerated neural aging in this condition

10.1007/s11553-025-01244-1.headline_claim: A telephone-based Post-COVID pacing coaching programme (Covidcare) is practicable and shows a significant reduction in fatigue on the FAS, with the greatest benefit for patients with extreme fatigue.
10.1007/s11553-025-01244-1.overall: The practicability claim is reasonable for a descriptive service evaluation, and the authors state that efficacy cannot be judged without a control group. The statement that those with extreme fatigue benefited most is weakly supported because of baseline selection, no comparator, and a 36% completer sample. The reported statistics (d, p) are internally consistent with the printed means and SDs.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) score from T1 to T2

issues.title: Benefit language drawn from uncontrolled pre-post change (-3.13 FAS points overall) with no comparator
issues.explanation: All results are within-person T1 to T2 changes in a single uncontrolled cohort. The abstract states a significant reduction was 'demonstrated' and that those with extreme fatigue 'benefited', although the Limitations say efficacy statements are possible only with great caution. Without a control, programme effect cannot be separated from natural course, parallel therapies or regression to the mean. Only the practicability claim is reasonably supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control group, or a baseline-to-baseline run-in period, showing no comparable fatigue change without the programme.

quotes.text: Die größte Limitation ist wohl in der fehlenden Kontrollgruppe zu sehen
Weitere Untersuchungen unter kontrollierten Bedingungen sind anzuempfehlen.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no comparator, and the pre-post change of -3.13 FAS points is the only evidence of effect. However, the authors state this limitation clearly and hedge in the Diskussion and Limitationen. The residual problem is that the abstract's 'profitierten' and the Fazit's 'positive Hinweise' read as benefit claims without matching caveats. The overall change also falls just below the paper's own MCID.

issues.title: Only 85 of 239 enrolled (35.6%) have paired FAS data; no description of the 154 excluded
issues.explanation: The effect estimates come from a complete-case subset of about one third of the participants. No baseline characteristics or T1 FAS scores of the 154 without T2 data are given, so selection of who returned the questionnaire cannot be assessed. The limitation is disclosed, but the headline 'benefit' conclusion does not carry it. The direction of the bias is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison of baseline FAS and demographics between responders and non-responders, or a sensitivity analysis imputing T2 for the 154.

quotes.text: meldeten sich insgesamt 239 Versicherte
Eine ist die vergleichsweise niedrige Responderquote von 36%.

second_reader.what_stands: The counts are correct and openly disclosed, but the 154 without paired data are not described beyond a hypothesised reason. Their baseline characteristics are not compared with the 85 analysed, and no sensitivity or missing-data analysis is given. With 64% lacking T2, the analysed subset may not represent all participants. The authors acknowledge the low rate but not this specific risk of bias.

issues.title: 'Extreme fatigue benefited most' rests on baseline-selected subgroups (5.43 vs 2.20) with no between-group test
issues.explanation: The abstract says those with extreme fatigue mainly benefited, based on a larger mean fall in the group chosen for the highest T1 scores. Selection on a high baseline value produces larger apparent falls through regression to the mean even without an effect. No test compares the two subgroups, and the T2 mean of the extreme group (34.30) has a much larger SD than at T1 (8.44 versus 3.26). The comparison of subgroup significance (p = 0.002 versus 0.014) is also not a test of difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison or a test of subgroup by time interaction adjusted for baseline score (for example ANCOVA), showing the extreme group improves more than expected from regression alone.

quotes.text: 30 Teilnehmende (35%) erreichten mit initial mindestens

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's 'Es profitierten v.a. Betroffene extremer Fatigue' rests on baseline-selected subgroups (5.43 versus 2.20 points) with no between-group test. A rough test from the printed values gives p of about 0.07, and regression to the mean is a plausible contributor to the difference. The paper's wording in the Diskussion is more cautious ('mögliche positive Wirkung'), but the abstract states the claim without that qualification.

10.1007/s11845-025-03899-3.headline_claim: Supervised telerehabilitation-based exercise produced greater improvements than an unsupervised home exercise program in dyspnea, pain, functional capacity, and some sleep and anxiety measures in post-COVID-19 syndrome, and is a safe, accessible and effective alternative.
10.1007/s11845-025-03899-3.overall: The direction of the headline finding (supervised telerehabilitation outperforming a brochure for dyspnea, pain and sit-to-stand time) is plausible and the main between-group p-values are internally consistent with Table 2. However, the text contains several mismatches with the tables (effect sizes, MCID statement, depression interaction), the self-reported outcomes were not blinded for participants, and the comparator confounds delivery mode with supervision. The Conclusion's wording on safety and routine-practice adoption goes beyond a small trial in mild-to-moderate patients.

primary_outcome.name: mMRC dyspnea score (no primary outcome designated in the text)

issues.title: Participants unblinded to supervised vs brochure arm; dyspnea, pain, sleep and mood outcomes are self-reported
issues.explanation: The trial is described as single-blind (assessors), and the authors admit participant blinding cannot be guaranteed. Dyspnea (mMRC), pain (NPRS), sleep (PSQI) and anxiety/depression (HADS) depend on patient report. Participants who received attention from a therapist may report better improvement regardless of physiological effect. Only the 5-TST is a performance measure, and even it depends on motivation. The between-group differences are therefore likely inflated to some degree.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants were truly unaware of allocation, or an objective primary outcome showing the same effect.

quotes.text: every effort has been made to blind assessors and participants to group allocation, but this cannot be guaranteed
This single-blind, randomized-controlled, prospective trial was conducted

second_reader.what_stands: Participants cannot plausibly have been blinded to supervised versus brochure allocation, and the paper itself says blinding cannot be guaranteed and labels the trial only single-blind (assessor). The dyspnea (mMRC), pain (NPRS), sleep (PSQI) and mood (HADS) outcomes are patient-reported, so they are exposed to performance and reporting bias, and the paper does not claim participant blinding or test its success. The paper does acknowledge this limitation, and the 5-times sit-to-stand outcome is performance-based and assessed by a blinded evaluator, so it is not affected in the same way.

issues.title: All 4 dropouts (4/32, 12.5%) were in the control arm; completers-only analysis, reasons not reported
issues.explanation: Of 64 randomized, 60 were analysed. The four missing were all controls, with no reasons or intention-to-treat analysis reported. The imbalance in dropout could bias the between-group estimate in either direction. The loss is small, so this weakens rather than invalidates the main results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis with imputed data for the four dropouts showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Four patients in the control group (CG) discontinued treatment, leaving 60 patients to complete the study (TG = 32; CG = 28).
The remaining 64 patients were randomly allocated into two groups.

issues.title: Conclusion calls TR 'safe' and supports routine practice from 32 mild-to-moderate TG patients
issues.explanation: The study enrolled only mild-to-moderate PCS patients and excluded severe cases. It reports 3 minor adverse events in 32 TG patients. The Conclusion nonetheless states TR is 'safe' and supports 'integration into routine clinical practice', without repeating the limitation. The data support feasibility and short-term benefit in this population, not a general safety or effectiveness claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion explicitly restricted to mild-to-moderate PCS, or safety data in a larger or more severe sample.

quotes.text: TR offers a safe, accessible, and effective alternative.
this exclusion may limit the generalizability of the results to more severe cases.

issues.title: Text says 5-TST change exceeded the 1.7 s MCID in both groups; the CG change is 1.5 s
issues.explanation: The Results say the 5-TST change in both groups was greater than the 1.7 s MCID. Table 2 and the same paragraph give the control-group change as 1.5 s (95% CI 0.3 to 2.6), which is below the MCID. The claim of clinically important improvement in the control arm is therefore not supported. This makes the control arm look better than the data show, which slightly understates the between-group contrast.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different MCID for the control analysis, or a CG mean change of at least 1.7 s.

quotes.text: In 5-TST, the change in both groups was greater than the MCID score (1.7 s)

issues.title: 5-TST effect sizes in text (TG 0.88, CG 0.34) disagree with Table 2 (0.591, 0.268)

issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 0.66 is the endpoint difference, or an analysis in which 0.66 is the adjusted change difference.

10.1007/s12325-024-02826-9.headline_claim: Vortioxetine significantly improved self-reported depressive symptoms in post-COVID-19 condition versus placebo, with a larger antidepressant effect in individuals with higher inflammation, metabolic disruption and BMI.
10.1007/s12325-024-02826-9.overall: The finding that depressive symptoms fell more with vortioxetine than placebo comes from a randomized, blinded, ITT trial but is a post hoc, non-primary outcome, and the paper itself calls it preliminary. The biomarker-moderation claim in the Abstract and Key Points is not supported by the single omnibus interaction test presented. Only a minor direction error in the nicotine covariate text was otherwise confirmed.

primary_outcome.name: QIDS-SR-16 total score at 8-week endpoint (the paper's depressive-symptom outcome; the paper does not explicitly label a primary outcome)

issues.title: Biomarker-moderation claim rests on one post hoc omnibus 5-way interaction with no subgroup estimates
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Key Points state that vortioxetine had a greater effect with higher inflammation, metabolic disruption and BMI. The only support is a significant omnibus five-way interaction term from a post hoc model, and the paper reports no effect estimates at different marker levels and no direction or size of moderation. A significant high-order interaction does not show where or in which direction the effect differs. Without multiplicity control or lower-order terms, the moderation conclusion is at best a hypothesis, as the Conclusions section itself says. The baseline p = 0.029 finding does not involve treatment, so it cannot support it either.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported treatment effects stratified by marker level, or a pre-specified analysis plan with multiplicity control showing a consistent direction of moderation.

quotes.text: Notably, individuals with baseline markers of increased inflammation, metabolic disruption, and elevated BMI exhibited a more pronounced antidepressant effect at endpoint.
was not pre-specified in the study protocol as a primary outcome measure or key secondary measure
Greater antidepressant effect with higher inflammation, metabolic disruption, and BMI.

second_reader.what_stands: The moderation claim rests on a single omnibus treatment x time x CRP x TG-HDL x BMI interaction test (chi2 = 21.376 unadjusted, 26.092 adjusted), with no estimates at different biomarker levels, no separate moderator tests, and no direction or size of the interaction in the paper; the 'more pronounced effect with higher inflammation, metabolic disruption and BMI' wording therefore goes beyond what was shown. The paper does acknowledge that the analysis was post hoc and not pre-specified (Methods, Discussion limitations) and frames the finding as a hypothesis in the Conclusions; however, the A

issues.title: Nicotine frequency called associated with lower symptoms, but B = +0.181 on QIDS-SR-16 means higher symptoms
issues.explanation: The Results say frequency of nicotine consumption was associated with lower depressive symptoms. The reported coefficient is positive (B = 0.181, CI 0.066 to 0.297, p = 0.002) for an outcome where higher scores mean worse depression. The data therefore indicate more frequent nicotine use goes with higher symptoms, the opposite of what the text says. This is a covariate in a baseline model and does not affect the treatment comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the outcome was coded so that higher values mean fewer symptoms, or a corrected Table 2 with a negative coefficient.

10.1007/s40120-026-00928-w.headline_claim: taVNS is safe and well accepted, and fatigue and quality of life improved in all groups, but taVNS did not reduce fatigue more than sham, suggesting a possible placebo effect.
10.1007/s40120-026-00928-w.overall: The finding that taVNS did not beat sham on fatigue is reported consistently, but the trial is a pilot-sized study with unclear primary-endpoint definition and inconsistent significance labelling. The 'not superior' conclusion is better read as inconclusive than as evidence of no effect. The NCT number the registry record matched belongs to a different, cited US trial, so no registration comparison for this study is possible.

issues.title: Primary endpoint is MFI-20 in Methods and power calculation, but usage-time incidence (MFI-20 secondary) in Data Analysis
issues.explanation: The Methods and sample-size section treat the MFI-20 fatigue score as the primary endpoint and power the trial on it. The Data Analysis section defines the primary outcome as the proportion of patients exceeding a usage-time threshold and lists the MFI-20 as secondary. The paper's central efficacy claim (taVNS not superior to sham) rests on the MFI-20, so the hierarchy that governs its testing, power and alpha is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registration showing a prespecified co-primary structure (MFI-20 efficacy plus acceptance) with the Data Analysis wording being a drafting slip.

quotes.text: estimated to provide 80% power for the primary endpoint, the MFI-20 questionnaire

second_reader.what_stands: The paper labels MFI-20 as primary in the power calculation and Endpoints list but as secondary in Data Analysis, where the primary outcome is the usage-time incidence; the Endpoints section's two co-primary endpoints partly reconcile this. The inconsistency that remains is that Data Analysis lists MFI-20 as secondary, and the 36-participant power calculation covers only the MFI-20 endpoint, not the usage-time endpoint that the analysis plan treats as primary.

issues.title: Null between-group result in ~12 per arm, acknowledged as pilot-level power, stated as 'not superior to placebo'
issues.explanation: The trial was powered for a 5 to 10 MFI-unit difference with 12 per arm, and the authors say power remains pilot-level. Absence of a significant difference from such a sample does not show taVNS is no better than sham, yet the Key Points and Discussion state this and add that taVNS had no effect beyond placebo. No between-group estimates with intervals appear in the main text to show how large a benefit is excluded. The finding should be read as inconclusive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group MFI-20 differences with confidence intervals excluding the clinically relevant 5-10 unit benefit.

quotes.text: the sample size remains insufficient to allow for more than pilot-level statistical power
In this patient population, taVNS was not superior to placebo.
quotes.location: Key Summary Points, What was learned

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does acknowledge pilot-level power in Limitations, but the Key Summary Points and Secondary Endpoints text state 'not superior to placebo' and 'did not show effects beyond placebo' as if the null were conclusive, with about 13 to 14 participants per arm and no confidence intervals shown in the main text. The limitation is disclosed rather than hidden; the issue is that the headline wording is firmer than a non-significant result at pilot power supports.

issues.title: Significance labelling inconsistent: 'no significant changes' vs p = 0.009-0.043 called significant against a 0.017 threshold
issues.explanation: The Data Analysis states p < 0.017 is the significance threshold, and the Results summary says no within-questionnaire changes were significant. The detailed Results then label many within-group changes significant at nominal levels (e.g. p = 0.043, 0.037, 0.026, 0.024, 0.019, 0.018), which fail the stated threshold. The reader cannot tell which standard was used; the between-group null is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated rule that nominal 0.05 applies to exploratory within-group tests and 0.017 only to the primary pairwise comparisons.

p values below this  threshold  were  considered  statistically significant
'Bodily pain' in Verum2 between visits 0 and 1 with p =  0.043

issues.title: Acceptance endpoint declared met though 10 of ~41 patients had no or incomplete usage logs; self-report only
issues.explanation: The paper says the usage endpoint was achieved, with 36 participants reaching at least 192 min/day, and that no patient-reported duration fell below this. But 8 patients kept no log and 2 had incomplete logs, so objective durations are missing for roughly a quarter of those remaining, and the figure of 236 min/day comes from the remainder. The authors call this a 'minor uncertainty', yet adherence for the unlogged group rests on unverified confirmation and acceptance is judged on completers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Retrieved device log-files for the 10 patients confirming usage of at least 192 min/day.

A minor uncertainty remains due to the above mentioned lack of logfiles

issues.title: Text percentages use n=45 but Tables 3-4 use an unstated denominator of 39 (13.3% vs 15.4%; 7% vs 7.7%)
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives Hashimoto's as 13.3% (n = 6), implying 45 patients, while Table 3 prints 15.4% for the same count, implying 39. Table 4's 7.7% for 3 skin irritations follows the same 39 base, while the text gives 7%. The denominator behind the tables is never defined and matches neither the 45 randomized nor the 41 or 37 later quoted. A minor reporting inconsistency; no conclusion depends on it. The claim that Hashimoto's was the 'only shared characteristic' is also odd with 6 of 45.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that Tables 3-4 are based on 39 patients with available data.

issues.title: Only patients blinded; self-reported fatigue outcome and one participant unblinded himself to sham
issues.explanation: The paper states only the patients were blinded, and the fatigue outcome is self-reported. One participant identified his sham allocation by manipulating the device. Because the result is null, any bias from unblinded staff or broken patient blinding would, if anything, have favoured the active arms, so the main conclusion is not overturned.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that outcome questionnaires were collected and entered without investigator involvement and that investigators had no allocation knowledge.

10.1007/s40121-025-01287-z.headline_claim: A self-help version of an osteopathic-derived routine reduced long COVID fatigue more than wait-list control in this feasibility RCT, and the self-help intervention alone could help support a reduction of fatigue in some people.
10.1007/s40121-025-01287-z.overall: The feasibility findings (recruitment met, 79% retention at 3 months, no serious adverse events) are credible apart from small denominator and prose slips. The efficacy signal is weak: it rests on completers only, on differential dropout, on no between-arm test, and on an open-label wait-list comparison. Using all randomized participants' means, the intervention arm shows no larger reduction. The hedged conclusions should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ-11) from baseline to 3 months

issues.title: Completer-only change (-4.6 vs -2.9) vs all-randomized means (-3.0 vs -3.3); ITT claimed, dropout 30.6% vs 11.8%
issues.explanation: The authors say they adopted an ITT approach but report change only among participants with both 0- and 3-month data. Using Table 3's full-arm baselines, the intervention mean moves from 25.5 to 22.5 (-3.0) while the wait-list moves from 26.3 to 23.0 (-3.3), which is no advantage. The completer advantage comes from a subset with a higher baseline (27.1) and unequal dropout. The benefit signal is therefore sensitive to who remained in the study, and these crude comparisons mix different samples.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A mixed-model or imputation analysis on all 100 randomized participants showing a similar between-arm difference.

quotes.text: rates being 30.6% in the intervention group and 11.8% in the wait-list control group
We adopted an intention-to-treat (ITT) approach, assuming participants utilized the treatment for the group they were allocated to.
a greater reduction in fatiguerelated symptoms was observed when analysis was limited to those participants providing both

second_reader.what_stands: The paper calls its analysis intention-to-treat, but the printed change values (-4.6 vs -2.9) come only from participants with both 0- and 3-month data. Dropout was unequal (30.6% vs 11.8%), and the reported intervention advantage shrinks to about nothing (-3.0 vs -3.3) if all-randomized baselines are used, so the 'larger reductions' claim in the Key Points and Discussion rests on a complete-case analysis with differential attrition. The -3.0/-3.3 figures are my own crude mixed-denominator calculation, not an analysis in the paper, and the authors do disclose that the greater reduction applies

issues.title: Arm difference in CFQ-11 change (-4.6 vs -2.9) has no between-group test or CI; a paired t test is described
issues.explanation: The Methods describe a paired t test for 'intervention vs. wait-list control', but a paired test is a within-person comparison and cannot compare arms. No between-arm estimate with uncertainty is reported. The 1.7-point gap in mean change is small against the SDs of about 6 to 7 at 3 months, so the Key Summary statement of larger reductions is not backed by any inference. The authors' feasibility framing limits the damage.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-arm estimate with CI (or an unpaired or ANCOVA test) showing a clear difference.

issues.title: Unblinded wait-list comparison on self-reported fatigue; benefit signal remains in conclusions despite disclosed bias
issues.explanation: Participants knew their arm because the intervention group received a physical pack, and the outcome is self-reported fatigue. The authors acknowledge possible exaggerated effects, yet the conclusions still cite 'indications of benefit'. The language is hedged, but the design cannot separate the intervention from expectation or waiting effects.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence from an objective outcome or an active or sham control showing the same effect.

issues.title: Stage 1 column: N = 139 in age row, but gender and ethnicity counts both sum to 140
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives 139 stage 1 responses, but female plus male is 140 and White plus other ethnic group is also 140. The percentages are calculated on 140. The recruitment-route row sums to 115, so the stage 1 denominators are inconsistent throughout. This is a small reporting error that does not affect efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote or CONSORT figure showing 140 stage 1 records, with one lacking an age.

issues.title: Text implies 27 wait-list participants at 6 months (45 - 18); Table 3, 59/100 and 56.9% imply 29
issues.explanation: The Results say 18 of the 45 wait-list participants at 3 months dropped out by 6 months, leaving 27. Table 3 gives N = 29, and the 6-month total of 59 and the 56.9% rate both fit 29. The prose error affects retention reporting only, which is a feasibility aim.

issues.explanation: The 38.0% response rate is not 139/391 (35.5%), and the 67.0% recruitment rate is not 100/139 (71.9%). Both could rest on denominators the text does not state. These are feasibility process metrics and do not bear on the efficacy results.

10.1016/j.actpsy.2026.108116.headline_claim: Personalized telerehabilitation showed high recorded adherence and favorable usability, providing preliminary support for feasibility; domain-specific cognitive effects were not established after FDR correction, and exploratory PCA findings require confirmation in larger trials.
10.1016/j.actpsy.2026.108116.overall: The paper's headline claim is mostly feasibility (adherence, usability) plus an explicit statement that domain-level between-group benefit was not established; that claim is largely supported and carefully hedged. The main weaknesses are the non-standard sequential allocation without concealment or registration, and the uncorrected exploratory PC1 result featured in the Conclusion. The apparent direction problems in Table 2 are extraction artefacts from dropped minus signs.

primary_outcome.name: Time x Group interaction on neuropsychological domain scores (pilot feasibility/preliminary effects)

issues.title: Allocation was sequential (intervention filled first, controls drawn after), without concealment or registration
issues.explanation: Participants were not allocated by a concurrent random sequence: the 52 intervention places were filled first and the 36 controls selected afterwards. This can confound group with enrolment time, selection and availability, and the paper describes no allocation concealment and no trial registration. The disease-duration difference (46.5 vs 51 months, p = 0.147) is small, so the main concern is the allocation process rather than a demonstrated imbalance. Between-group comparisons are therefore weaker than in a standard RCT.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a prespecified concurrent random sequence with concealed allocation, or evidence that all candidates were randomized in a single draw.

quotes.text: First, eligible candidates were randomly selected for the intervention group until all available telerehabilitation places were filled
The study was not registered in a public clinical trial registry.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does state that allocation was sequential (intervention places filled first, controls drawn afterwards) and that the study was not registered in a public registry. However, it says each group was 'randomly selected' and does not describe any allocation concealment either way, so 'without concealment' is not stated and cannot be confirmed from the paper; it is an absence of reporting rather than a stated fact. The sequential, place-filling scheme and lack of any described randomization procedure or concealment mean the randomized label is weakly supported.

issues.title: Conclusion cites nominal PC1 difference (p = 0.043) and adherence association despite null FDR-corrected domain tests
issues.explanation: After the domain-level Time x Group tests were non-significant after FDR correction, an unplanned PCA yielded a group difference at p = 0.043 (beta 0.715, SE 0.346), uncorrected for multiplicity. The Conclusion presents this as a finding alongside the adherence association (p = 0.005), without noting that it is nominal, even though the abstract and discussion say so. Disclosure is adequate in the body, but the Conclusion gives the result more weight than a single p just under .05 supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan naming PC1 as a primary outcome, or a multiplicity-adjusted p below .05.

quotes.text: these p -values were not corrected for multiple comparisons
including higher adjusted scores on a global cognitive change component in the intervention group and an association between this component and motor adherence

issues.title: Table 1 alcohol-use chi-square (1.65) does not match counts 4/33 vs 3/46 (about 0.75)

Differences in self-reported symptoms or the PC1 score could therefore reflect contact, expectation or retest effects. The authors acknowledge this and make no efficacy claim, so the effect on the conclusions is small.

issues.title: Complete-case analysis excludes 9 of 88 randomized (10.2%); no ITT or sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: The primary analyses use only participants with both assessments, and no intention-to-treat or imputation analysis is given. Three intervention participants never started and three discontinued for physical reasons, which could be informative dropout. The loss is modest, disclosed, and affects results already described as non-significant.
