issues.title: Reliable-worsening share of 6.7% in intervention group is not attainable with n = 46 (3/46 = 6.5%)
issues.explanation: The text reports 6.7% of intervention participants with reliable worsening in processing speed, yet the analysed intervention group has 46 participants. No whole-number count out of 46 gives 6.7%; 3/46 gives 6.5%. This is probably a typographical slip and affects only a descriptive secondary figure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 5 or the supplement showing a denominator other than 46 for processing speed (for example 45 or 15).

quotes.text: verbal memory and processing speed in 8.7% and 6.7% of intervention participants
Baseline and follow-up outcome data were available for 46 intervention participants

10.1016/j.acvdsp.2021.10.007.headline_claim: Sulodexide in patients with long COVID-19 may be a good intervention to ameliorate chest pain, palpitations, fatigue and neuro-cognitive difficulties associated to endothelial dysfunction.
10.1016/j.acvdsp.2021.10.007.overall: The sulodexide conclusion is not reliable. It rests on a non-randomised comparison with an untreated group that had a different baseline profile, and the symptom benefit is not backed by any reported data. Only the delta EQI difference is quantified, and it is confounded by selection and baseline EQI. The Libreville abstract's 'young people' conclusion also conflicts with its own mean age of 59.1 years.

primary_outcome.name: Endothelial function amelioration (delta EQI) and long COVID-19 symptom evolution

issues.title: Non-randomised sulodexide vs untreated comparison with worse baseline EQI and more comorbidity; causal wording unsupported
issues.explanation: Sulodexide was given to a selected subgroup of patients with endothelial dysfunction and compared with an untreated group that differed at baseline. The treated group had lower EQI and more diabetes, hypertension, coronary disease and long-term medication. The difference in delta EQI (1.26 vs 0.22) could reflect baseline differences, regression to the mean or the 21-day natural course. The conclusion that sulodexide may be a good intervention to ameliorate symptoms uses causal language the design cannot support. No adjustment or limitation is reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised allocation, or an analysis adjusted for baseline EQI and comorbidity (or matched groups) showing the same between-group difference.

quotes.text: A group of patients with endothelial dysfunction (EQI < 2.0) received sulodexide.
Patients in sulodexide group had lower EQI than the non-medical intervention group
Sulodexide in patients with long COVID-19 may be a good intervention to ameliorate chest pain, palpitations, fatigue and neuro-cognitive difficulties

second_reader.what_stands: The paper describes a non-randomised comparison in which the treated group had clearly worse baseline EQI (0.94 vs 1.52) and more cardiovascular comorbidity and medication use, with no stated adjustment. The conclusion uses interventional wording ('may be a good intervention to ameliorate') that goes beyond what this design supports. Only the abstract was available, so the full paper might contain adjustment or limitations that are not visible here.

issues.title: Symptom benefit (primary outcome) asserted with no data, test or named symptom instrument
issues.explanation: Long COVID symptom evolution is a stated primary outcome, and the conclusion rests on it. The abstract reports no symptom scores or proportions, no between-group test, and no instrument or definition of how symptoms were measured. Only the endothelial outcome has numbers. The symptom conclusion is therefore unsupported as presented, and the association with endothelial change is asserted without any correlation shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Full text reporting symptom scores or proportions by arm with a between-group test, using a defined symptom instrument.

quotes.text: patients in sulodexide group presented lower long COVID symptoms especially chest pain, palpitations, fatigue and neuro-cognitive difficulties
Primary outcomes were defined as endothelial function amelioration (delta EQI) and long COVID-19 symptoms evolution during the follow-up.

second_reader.what_stands: Within the abstract, symptom improvement is stated as a primary outcome result without any numbers, test or named symptom measure, so it cannot be checked. This is a limitation of what is reported here; the full paper or poster may contain the data, which was not available to check.

issues.title: Libreville abstract concludes cardiovascular involvement 'affects young people' but mean age is 59.1 years
issues.explanation: The Libreville abstract's conclusion says cardiovascular manifestations in COVID-19 affect young people. Its own results give a mean age of 59.1 ± 13.3 years, with no age-stratified data. The conclusion is therefore not supported by the reported data, although the descriptive counts are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An age-stratified table showing that a large share of patients were young, or a comparison with an older reference population.

quotes.text: Cardiovascular manifestations are frequent in Libreville for COVID-19 and affect young people.
The mean age was 59.1 ± 13.3 years with a predominance of men (sex ratio 1.4).

10.1016/j.admp.2022.101701.headline_claim: An exercise rehabilitation programme improved physical fitness (6-minute walk distance and maximal power) in hospital staff with long COVID, was perceived positively, and is likely to improve work capacity and encourage job retention.
10.1016/j.admp.2022.101701.overall: The finding that walk distance and maximal power rose after the programme in 17 completers is reported with small p-values, but it comes from an uncontrolled retrospective comparison that excludes 12 of 29 participants. The abstract's claim about work capacity and job retention is not supported by any measured work outcome. Treat the results as preliminary, hypothesis-generating pilot data.

primary_outcome.name: Six-minute walk distance (TM6), pre vs post programme

issues.title: Causal benefit claimed from an uncontrolled retrospective pre-post comparison of 17 participants
issues.explanation: All participants received the programme and were compared only with their own earlier values. Improvement in walk distance and power could reflect natural recovery, test familiarity or motivation, not the programme. The paper nonetheless states that the programme 'a permis' the improvement. The conclusion holds only as a tentative association.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group of untreated long-COVID staff showing no similar improvement over the same interval.

quotes.text: Il s'agit d'une étude observationnelle rétrospective, monocentrique.
La participation à un programme de réadaptation à l'effort a permis une amélioration de la fonction musculaire et de la tolérance à l'effort.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper bases its statement that the programme 'a permis une amélioration' on an uncontrolled, retrospective before-after comparison of 17 people, so the causal wording is not supported by the design. The authors do partly soften it by calling the work a pilot study and asking for larger studies to confirm the benefits 'suggérés'.

issues.title: Pre-post efficacy analysed in 17 of 29 (41% not re-tested); 12 non-completers not described
issues.explanation: Only 17 of 29 participants completed the programme and were re-tested, and missing observations were excluded. Those who dropped out may have benefited less, so the conclusion describes the best-case subset. The completers' baseline values differ from the full cohort's, for example maximal power 131.7 W versus 120.2 W, which suggests selective completion. The abstract does not mention the dropout.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline and reason-for-dropout data for the 12 non-completers showing they resembled completers, or a sensitivity analysis including them.

quotes.text: Sur ces 29 patients seulement 17 ont complété le programme de réadaptation à l'effort
Les observations manquantes ont été exclues de l'analyse statistique.

second_reader.what_stands: The pre-post efficacy results come from 17 of 29 people (41% lost to re-testing), and the paper gives no reasons for the dropout and no comparison of the 12 non-completers with the 17 completers. The authors state the rule that missing observations were excluded, so the exclusion is disclosed, but the possible bias from a completers-only analysis is not discussed.

issues.title: Abstract concludes improved work capacity and job retention; no work outcome was measured
issues.explanation: The abstract concludes that the treatment is likely to improve work capacity and job retention. The objective data are only walk-test and exercise-test measures. The work information comes from a self-report questionnaire with 16 of 29 responses, not linked to individuals and with no comparison. Participants' job situations after the programme cannot be attributed to the programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A measured work outcome (sick-leave days, return-to-work or retention) compared before and after the programme or against controls.

quotes.text: This treatment is likely to improve work capacity and encourage job retention.
Il serait intéressant d'évaluer l'effet d'un tel parcours de soins sur la durée des arrêts de travail.

second_reader.what_stands: No objective work outcome (sick leave after the programme, return to work, job retention) was measured or compared, and the authors acknowledge in Perspectives that the effect on sick-leave duration remains to be assessed. A descriptive, self-reported questionnaire from 16 of 29 people did record work status, and the abstract's claim is worded as 'likely', but the claim of improved work capacity and job retention goes beyond the data presented.

issues.title: Responder threshold for maximal power: 50 W in Methods, 20 W in Results (46% responders)
issues.explanation: The Methods define a significant exercise-test improvement as a 50 W gain in maximal aerobic power. The Results report that 46% improved using a 20 W threshold, without saying the definition changed. The 46% therefore does not match the stated definition, and the proportion of responders at 50 W is not reported. The main pre-post power comparison does not depend on this threshold.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that 20 W was a pre-specified or secondary threshold, or that the Methods '50 W' is a typographical error.

quotes.text: si on observait une amélioration de la puissance maximale aérobie de 50 W en post-réhabilitation
En considérant comme significative une amélioration de 20 W de la PMA

10.1016/j.ahjo.2022.100105.headline_claim: EECP significantly improved validated fatigue and cardiovascular-related markers in patients with Long COVID.
10.1016/j.ahjo.2022.100105.overall: The data show that patient-reported scores were higher after EECP in a small, uncontrolled, completers-only retrospective cohort, but they cannot show that EECP caused the change. The abstract's efficacy conclusion goes beyond the design, which the authors acknowledge only in the final Discussion paragraph. A few table-to-summary mismatches and the broad 'all patients benefited' statement add further minor uncertainty.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS Fatigue (change from baseline)

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from 16 patients, no control group, pre-post Wilcoxon tests only
issues.explanation: All evidence is within-patient change from baseline in a single uncontrolled, retrospective cohort of 16 patients treated by one provider. Long COVID symptoms often improve spontaneously, and the patient-reported outcomes (fatigue, SAQ, DASI) are open to expectation effects. The Wilcoxon p-values show that scores changed, not that EECP caused the change. The causal conclusion is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of a concurrent untreated or sham comparison group, or of a stable pre-treatment baseline period showing no spontaneous improvement.

quotes.text: Design: Retrospective analysis of a contemporary, consecutive patient cohort.
A Wilcoxon Signed Rank test was performed to compare the change from baseline

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does infer efficacy from 16 patients with no control group, and the main inferential results are pre-post comparisons. It is not Wilcoxon only, though: the paper also reports a Mann-Whitney U test, a Fisher's exact test and a correlation analysis, and none of these provides a control comparison for treatment effect. Analysis is of completers only (4 excluded).

issues.title: Abstract conclusion states EECP 'significantly improved' markers with no caveat on the uncontrolled 16-patient design
issues.explanation: The abstract's conclusion is phrased as established efficacy in Long COVID, based on 16 patients with no comparator. The limitation and the hypothesis-generating status appear only in the final Discussion paragraph. The Discussion also claims that the study 'supports the use of EECP' for Long COVID.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract that states the uncontrolled design and the hypothesis-generating status alongside the conclusion.

quotes.text: EECP significantly improved validated fatigue and cardiovascular-related markers in patients with Long COVID.
These promising findings are hypothesis generating and should be further explored in a broader clinical investigation.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's concluding sentence says 'significantly improved' without any caveat about the 16-patient uncontrolled design, and the abstract does not give the sample size. The caveat does exist in the paper (the abstract labels the design retrospective, and the Discussion calls the findings observational and hypothesis generating), so the limitation is stated in the body, just not in the abstract conclusion.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis: 4 of 20 treated patients (20%) excluded for non-completion or missing data
issues.explanation: Only patients who completed the prescribed sessions were analysed, and four were dropped without any description of why. If they stopped because of lack of benefit or side effects, the reported improvements overstate what an intended-to-treat group would see. The paper reports no adverse events and no analysis of the excluded patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data showing the excluded patients dropped out for unrelated reasons and had similar outcomes.

quotes.text: Four patients were excluded for not completing EECP therapy and having incomplete data.
All patients completing the prescribed 15 -35 sessions of EECP were included for analysis.

issues.title: Table 1 summary means do not match the listed patient rows (PROMIS-F 5.00 vs 4.63; 6MWT 192.9 vs 200.00)
issues.explanation: Summing the per-patient values printed in Table 1 gives means different from the printed summary row for several outcomes, while the Age mean matches exactly. The summary figures are the headline numbers in the abstract. The differences are small for SAQ and DASI but larger for PROMIS-F and 6MWT, so the reported effects cannot be fully reproduced from the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source table or supplement showing different per-patient values consistent with the printed means, or confirmation that the rows in this text were shifted during extraction.

quotes.text: the PROMIS Fatigue, SAQ, DASI, and 6MWT improved by 4.63 ± 3.42 (p < 0.001)
Six-minute walk (6MWT) distance (n = 13) improved significantly by 200.00 ± 180.14 (p = 0.002)

issues.title: 'All patients benefited' overstated: Table 1 shows zero change in some patients; RDS unchanged in 7 (44%)
issues.explanation: The Results say all patients benefited regardless of baseline severity. Table 1 lists patients with no change on a measured outcome (for example 6MWT change of 0 for patient 12 and DASI change of 0 for patient 16), and 3 patients had no 6MWT data. The paper also reports the RDS unchanged in 7 of 16 patients. The claim is therefore broader than the data, though the RDS is a separate outcome from the one the sentence refers to.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Showing that the sentence is restricted to patients with a measurable improvement, or that the zero entries in Table 1 are extraction artefacts.

quotes.text: All patients benefited independent of severity of baseline symptom
The RDS improved for 7 patients (44%) and remained the same in 7 patients (44%).

10.1016/j.amjmed.2024.04.030.headline_claim: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir may be a potential treatment for long COVID, with the PAX LC trial presented as a methods description of a phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design.
10.1016/j.amjmed.2024.04.030.overall: This is a design-only paper with no efficacy results, so there is no headline treatment conclusion to over- or understate. The only defensible issue is a small inconsistency in the stated CYP3A4 inducer window (28 vs 30 days), which affects no result. The primary outcome, blinding approach and analysis plan are consistent with the registry record.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score change from baseline to Day 28

primary_outcomes.measure: National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS)-29 version 2.1 Physical Health Summary Score

issues.title: CYP3A4 inducer lead-in window printed as 28 days (Table 2) and 30 days (Safety section)
issues.explanation: The exclusion criteria prohibit strong CYP3A4 inducers within 28 days before the first dose, while the Safety section advises avoiding them 30 days before and during the trial. The paper does not say whether one is an eligibility rule and the other is counselling, so the protocol's stated washout is ambiguous. No results depend on it, but a reader implementing the protocol would not know which window applies.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol statement that the 28-day window is the eligibility cut-off and the 30-day statement is separate non-binding guidance, or a corrected single window.

quotes.text: Concomitant use of any medications or substances that are strong inducers of CYP3A4 are prohibited within 28 days prior to first dose of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir
Participants are advised against using strong CYP3A4 inducers 30 days before and during the trial.

10.1016/j.amjms.2025.12.780.headline_claim: Program participation was associated with small improvements in patient-reported health status and modest cost patterns, with an ICER of $31,140 per QALY approaching the Canadian threshold, though the authors call these findings preliminary and associative.
10.1016/j.amjms.2025.12.780.overall: The paper's own abstract and conclusions are appropriately hedged: an uncontrolled pre-post evaluation with small effects, described as preliminary and associative. The reliable core is the descriptive utilization data and the small within-patient changes. The Table 4 improvement percentages use an unstated denominator, the ICER rests on a VAS-based QALY in a small subset, and some Discussion language overreaches. The economic conclusion is the weakest part.

primary_outcome.name: Not specified; PROMs analysed were PCFS, PHQ-9, GAD-7 and EQ-5D VAS

issues.title: QALY gain of 0.046 equals VAS change 4.6/100 although the Canadian EQ-5D-5L value set is stated for economic analyses
issues.explanation: The methods say economic analyses used the Canadian EQ-5D-5L value set, but QALYs were estimated from changes in VAS scores. A VAS rating is not a preference-based utility, and a one-year gain assumes the whole short-term change persists for 12 months and would not have occurred anyway. The ICER of $31,140 per QALY, which straddles the $30,000 threshold, therefore rests on a fragile basis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that the QALY gain was calculated from value-set utilities of the five-domain responses, or a rationale for using VAS.

quotes.text: Changes in EQ-5D-5 L VAS scores among patients with assessments before and after program entry were used to estimate QALY gains over a one-year horizon.
quotes.location: Methods, Healthcare System Utilization and Costs Analysis

quotes.text: valuation for economic analyses used the Canadian EQ-5D-5 L value set
estimated annual gain of 0.046 QALYs per patient

second_reader.what_stands: The reported 0.046 QALY gain equals the VAS change of 4.6/100 exactly, and the Methods say QALYs were estimated from VAS changes, so the QALY estimate appears to rest on the VAS rather than on utilities from the stated Canadian value set. The paper does not report an index-based utility change, so the statement that the value set was used for economic analyses is not reflected in the QALY calculation shown. The calculation also treats the gain as lasting a full year from a single post-visit VAS comparison, which the authors partly flag as a limitation.

issues.title: Symptom and complication tables use N = 3,596, above the 2,287 accepted patients and 1,914 initial visits
issues.explanation: Tables 2 and 3 give prevalence among 'patients' at the initial visit with N = 3,596. The paper reports only 2,287 accepted referrals and 1,914 patients with an initial visit, so 3,596 cannot be a count of unique patients. The paper does not say what the base is. The prevalence figures cannot be interpreted as stated, though they are descriptive and do not carry the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that N counts symptom/complication records or visit-level assessments rather than unique patients.

quotes.text: 1,914 patients had their initial visit to the program
Prevalence of Persistent Symptoms at Initial Visit ( N = 3,596)

issues.title: Abstract reports cost reductions and ICER without noting the non-significant post-visit effect
issues.explanation: The abstract says reductions in inpatient, ambulatory and physician costs were observed. The Results say the before/after-visit variable was not statistically significant, and the Discussion says the declines were not directly linked to program participation. The ICER of $31,140 uses operating cost only and assumes no change in other costs. A reader of the abstract would take the cost reductions as program-related, which the paper's own analysis does not support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract statement that the cost declines were secular trends not attributable to enrolment.

quotes.text: Modest reductions in inpatient, ambulatory, and physician service costs were observed.
was not statistically significant (Table 5)
these reductions were not directly linked to program participation

issues.title: Discussion calls changes 'clinically meaningful' and 'likely attributable' despite sub-MCID change and no control
issues.explanation: The Results state the PHQ-9 reduction of 0.9 did not reach the MCID of 3.7, and that changes cannot be attributed to the program. The Discussion nevertheless describes 'clinically meaningful improvements' and attributes the VAS rise to early intervention. These statements go beyond what the uncontrolled pre-post data support and contradict the paper's own limitations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled comparison data, or Discussion wording confined to the associative language used in the abstract.

quotes.text: did not meet the established minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for the PHQ-9
quotes.location: Results, Functional status, mental health, and quality of life

quotes.text: likely attributable to early intervention

issues.title: Table 4 'Improved n (%)' for PHQ-9, GAD-7 and EQ-VAS uses n = 828, not each row's n (355, 578, 578)
issues.explanation: Table 4 prints 66 (8%), 25 (3%) and 74 (9%) beside rows with n = 355, 578 and 578. Over each row's own n these are 18.6%, 4.3% and 12.8%. They only match if all are divided by the PCFS n of 828. The text then reports 'Only 8%' showing meaningful depression improvement, and the Discussion repeats 8-9%. The denominator is unstated, and the proportions improved among measured patients are understated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote stating that percentages are expressed over all 828 patients with PROMs.

script.explanation: 66/355 = 18.59%, but the paper prints 8, outside the rounding interval [7.50, 9.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 825.0 rather than 355.

issues.title: ICER derived from 264 of 2,287 patients (11.5%) with paired VAS, no sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: The 0.046 QALY gain comes from patients with paired VAS data, which is a small and possibly unrepresentative subset. Paired PROM outcomes cover 355-828 patients. The authors acknowledge selection bias, but no analysis tests how it affects the ICER. The abstract presents the ICER without this qualifier.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison of baseline characteristics of patients with and without paired VAS data, or a weighted/sensitivity ICER.

quotes.text: Follow-up data were only available for a subset of patients, introducing potential selection bias.
among patients with at least one EQ-5D VAS score prior to and following the initial clinic visit

issues.title: Multiple PROMs, EQ-5D domains and subgroups tested at p < 0.05 without correction (one subgroup p = 0.04)
issues.explanation: Many outcomes, domains and PCFS subgroups were tested at an uncorrected 0.05 level. Most headline results have much smaller p-values, but the high-PCFS PHQ-9 result (p = 0.04) and the EQ-5D domain results would be vulnerable. The practical effect is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or multiplicity adjustment plan.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
p = 0.003 for the low PCFS group; p = 0.04 for the high PCFS group
quotes.location: Results, Functional status, mental health, and quality of life

issues.title: Table 5 caption gives N = 264 for utilization/cost rows; text says 1,477 patients had utilization data
issues.explanation: Table 5 is captioned N = 264, yet the text says administrative utilization data covered 1,477 patients. The cost-trend rows presumably use the larger sample, and the 264 belongs only to the EQ-5D VAS and QALY rows. The caption is misleading and the 1,477 is not reconciled with the 1,914 patients seen. This is a labelling problem rather than a changed result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated N for each Table 5 row showing 1,477 for the cost rows.

quotes.text: Healthcare Utilization and Costs Among Participants ( N = 264)
the analysis was limited to patients whose initial clinic visit occurred on or before May 1, 2023

issues.title: Study window ends September 2023 but initial visits are counted to 31 October 2023
issues.explanation: The abstract and Methods give data collection to September 2023, but the cost section counts initial visits to October 31, 2023. The windows could differ by data source, but the paper does not say so. The effect on the conclusions is negligible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the September 2023 window refers only to referrals/PROM collection and not to administrative data.

quotes.text: Between April 1, 2022 and October 31, 2023, 1,914 patients had their initial visit to the program

10.1016/j.apmr.2022.12.184.headline_claim: Virtual and augmented reality training on a Digital Mirror (D-Wall) improved 6-minute walk distance in people with Long COVID, and the authors conclude the medium-performance group approaches normative values.
10.1016/j.apmr.2022.12.184.overall: The poster reports significant within-group gains in 6-minute walk distance after a 10-session programme, but without a concurrent control the gains cannot be attributed to the programme. The claim that the medium group reaches normal levels is not backed by any printed absolute or normative values. The authors' own call for a randomized trial fits treating the conclusions as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: Change in 6-minute walk distance (metres), pre vs post, per subgroup

issues.title: Uncontrolled before-after design used to claim improvement and approach to normative 6MWT levels
issues.explanation: The study has a single cohort measured before and after a 10-session programme, with only external published normative data as a comparator. Without a concurrent control group, the gain in walk distance cannot be attributed to the intervention rather than to spontaneous post-COVID recovery or test familiarity. The comparison with normative data from a different study and population is informal; no between-group statistic or numbers for the normative values are given. The paper itself recommends a randomized trial, which supports reading the efficacy conclusion as tentative at most.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist group with comparable Long COVID patients showing no comparable change, or a quantified comparison with matched normative data.

quotes.text: The study is a before-after trial comparing the affected sample with baseline normotype data.
After the treatment, results are close to normative data of Perera et al, 2006, Geriatrics.
A future randomized control trial aimed at testing whether improvement of this method over a traditional one is suggested.

second_reader.what_stands: The design is uncontrolled and single-arm, and the poster says so ('before-after trial'). It recommends an RCT only to test superiority over a traditional method. The claim that results are 'close to normative data' is stated without any post-treatment or normative numbers in the text. The uncontrolled design as such is disclosed. Improvement is supported only as a within-group Wilcoxon change (p < 0.005), and the approach to normative levels cannot be verified from this abstract.

issues.title: Claim that the medium group reaches normative level has no reported normative or post-treatment values
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the medium-functional group achieves a level similar to normotype subjects, but the poster prints only mean gains (56 ± 65 m and 99 ± 74 m), not absolute pre or post distances or the normative values. A significant pre-post Wilcoxon test shows change, not equivalence to a reference population. The statement that the improvement is 'statistically significantly difference' does not support closeness to normal. Also, the low-performance group had the larger mean gain, so the emphasis on the medium group rests on unreported absolute levels.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Printed pre/post 6MWT distances for each group alongside the Perera et al normative means with a formal comparison or equivalence test showing the medium group within a stated margin of normal.

quotes.text: data support that especially the medium-functional group achieves the similar level of normotype subjects.
MPP increases 56+- 65 meters, LPP increases 99+-74 meters

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract gives no post-treatment 6MWT values, baseline values or normative reference values for either group. The conclusion that the medium group 'achieves the similar level of normotype subjects' therefore cannot be checked against any printed number. It also goes beyond the Results sentence, which says only that both groups are 'close to' the norms. The full poster might contain the supporting data, but this text does not.

issues.title: Author affiliated with Digital Mirror maker TecnoBody while declaring no conflicts; no funder stated
issues.explanation: One author is listed with TecnoBody S.r.l., and the intervention is delivered on the Digital Mirror D-Wall. The disclosure says there are no potential conflicts of interest, and no funding source or company role is stated. An employee or affiliate of the manufacturer evaluating the product is commonly treated as a relevant interest, so readers cannot judge the company's involvement. Whether this is a real omission depends on the author's relationship to the product, which the paper does not give.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that TecnoBody S.r.l. is an unrelated entity from the device's manufacturer, or that the author has no financial or employment tie to the product and the company had no role in the study.

quotes.text: Marco Gidoni (TecnoBody S.r.l.)
The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research authorship and/or publication of this poster.

10.1016/j.apmr.2024.04.014.headline_claim: Asynchronous telerehabilitation was more effective than a booklet-based rehabilitation program in post-COVID-19 patients, improving physical capacity and QoL, and was similar in reducing fatigue.
10.1016/j.apmr.2024.04.014.overall: The between-group evidence is weaker than the Discussion implies: the primary fatigue outcome was null in a small pilot (35 of 50 planned), and the 'more effective' claims rest on a handful of uncorrected secondary tests; the 6MWT difference (79.35 m, p=.008) is the strongest result. Numerous table inconsistencies (ATG post-fatigue data, CI/p mismatches, swapped or miscomputed cells) are mostly small reporting errors but reduce confidence in the tables as a whole. The conclusions are best read as hypothesis-generating for a larger trial.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Pre-intervention (day 1); after intervention (day 84); follow up 1 (3 months after intervention); follow up 2 (6 months after intervention).

issues.title: Pilot with null primary outcome (p=.104, n=35 of 50) claims telerehabilitation 'more effective' and a 'real effect'
issues.explanation: The primary fatigue outcome showed no between-group difference, and recruitment reached 35 of the 50 planned participants, with about nine between-group secondary tests and no multiplicity correction for between-group tests. The Discussion nevertheless presents telerehabilitation as more effective on function and QoL and says the results suggest a real effect, and it cites large within-group fatigue changes in both arms. The data support a hypothesis for a larger trial, not an efficacy conclusion; the Conclusions' wording about 'potential' is more cautious than the Discussion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction showing the 6MWT and 30s sit-to-stand differences survive multiplicity, and conclusions limited to hypothesis generation.

quotes.text: this is the first study to show that asynchronous telerehabilitation could be a more effective option than a home rehabilitation booklet
but the consistency in the results suggest a real effect
without significant differences between groups
quotes.location: Results, Comparison between groups after intervention

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome (fatigue) did not differ significantly between groups (p=.104, CI −0.22 to 2.32, n=35 analysed of 50 enrolled), and the phrase 'suggest a real effect' in a pilot with that result is stronger than the data support. However, the Discussion's 'more effective' claim is hedged ('could be') and tied to named secondary outcomes (6MWT, 30"STST) that were significant, the limitations paragraph openly notes the nonsignificant fatigue result, and the Conclusion describes fatigue as 'similar' between arms; the secondary findings were not corrected for multiplicity, and the Discussion's

issues.title: ATG post-intervention fatigue data differ between Tables 3 and 5 (14 vs 16 low-fatigue; SD 1.29 vs 1.21)
issues.explanation: The same ATG post-intervention data are printed twice with different values. Table 3 gives 14 of 17 ATG participants in the nonfatigue/low category and Table 5 gives 16 of 17. The post-intervention FSS SD is also 1.29 in Table 3 and 1.21 in Table 5, with the same mean of 2.89. The primary outcome therefore has two incompatible versions for the intervention arm, and the between-group fatigue-level test (p=.084) may rest on the wrong one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two tables use different analysis sets or fatigue cut-offs at the post-intervention time point, or a corrigendum with the correct counts and SD.

quotes.location: Table 3, Fatigue level, Nonfatigue/low row, ATG column
Table 5, Fatigue level, Nonfatigue/low row, After Intervention column

issues.title: Discussion lists MCSS as a benefit of telerehabilitation; post-intervention MCSS difference is 0.54, p=.884
issues.explanation: The first Discussion paragraph names the SF-12v2 mental component (MCSS) as an outcome on which telerehabilitation was more effective. Table 3 shows no between-group difference at the end of the intervention, and the Discussion itself later says there is no significant effect on the mental component. The only support is a p=.007 at 3 months quoted in the Results text, with no table or estimate behind it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A tabulated between-group 3-month MCSS comparison with a significant difference, with the Discussion restricting its MCSS claim to follow-up.

quotes.text: could be a more effective option than a home rehabilitation booklet in patients with postacute COVID-19 on several functional status (6MWT, 30”STST) and QoL (SF-12v2 MCSS) outcomes
However, it seems that a multimodal program has no significant effect on the mental component of SF-12v2.

issues.title: Discussion calls 133.05 m the ATG-favouring difference; between-group 6MWT difference is 79.35 m
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the difference was 133.05 m in favour of ATG, which is more than double the 65.45 m from Li et al. 133.05 m is the ATG's own before-after change in Table 5. The between-group difference printed in Table 3 and in the Results is 79.35 m. The comparison with the literature is therefore overstated or not like-for-like.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Li et al. 65.45 m is also a within-group change, in which case the like-for-like comparison would be 133.05 vs 65.45 and only the 'in favor of ATG' wording would be wrong.

quotes.text: whereas in our study the difference was of 133.05 m in favor of ATG

issues.title: Within-group CIs exclude zero but p is non-significant: ATG MCSS (0.31-7.43, p=.069), BRG PCSS (p=.188)
issues.explanation: In Table 5 the ATG MCSS change has a 95% CI of 0.31 to 7.43 yet a paired t-test p of .069; the text then says MCSS 'did not' improve. Table 6 shows the same kind of mismatch for the BRG PCSS: 4.56 (0.46 to 8.67) with p=.188. The CIs and p-values cannot both come from the same test. The error would understate within-group improvement, and the conclusions about which within-group changes are significant are unreliable for these rows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that the p-values come from a different test than the CI (for example a Wilcoxon test), stated in the table.

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0506 (reachable range [0.0500, 0.0513] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.069 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the CI excludes the null (0.0), but the reported p = 0.069 says the result is not significant

issues.title: 30s arm curl between-group difference printed as 2.00 but group means 21.00 and 18.00 differ by 3
issues.explanation: Table 3 lists the 30s arm curl means as 21.00 (ATG) and 18.00 (BRG) but prints the mean difference as 2.00 with CI 1.00 to 6.00, whose midpoint is 3.5. The p-value of .054 is consistent with a difference of 3, so the 2.00 cell appears wrong. This secondary result is not significant either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the difference is adjusted for baseline.

The functionality claim is weakly supported, and the baseline table contains a swapped or mislabelled Sex row and an inconsistent drug count that do not change the efficacy results.

issues.title: Only completers analysed (27 vs 30), no ITT analysis; effects likely overstated; losses not described
issues.explanation: Only participants who completed the treatment plan were analysed, and no intention-to-treat analysis is given. The intervention arm has 27 analysed against 30 in the control arm, and the dropouts are not described in the text. The authors concede this may overestimate effects, yet the conclusion states the program was effective without that qualification. With effect sizes of 1.1 to 1.6 on self-reported outcomes, the missing ITT analysis matters.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis including all randomized participants, with Figure 1 showing the dropouts were few and balanced.

quotes.text: A per-protocol analysis was performed including participants who completed the treatment plan.
we acknowledge that it may overestimate treatment effects compared to an intention-to-treat analysis.

second_reader.what_stands: Only completers (27 vs 30) were analysed and no ITT analysis was done, and the authors themselves state this may overestimate effects; so that part is true but is disclosed, not hidden. The claim that losses are not described cannot be confirmed because the CONSORT figure content is not available in the text, and the loss is small (3 of 60, all in the intervention arm), so the size of any overstatement is not established.

issues.title: Unblinded participants, self-reported outcomes and a booklet-only comparator; effects not separable from expectation
issues.explanation: All outcomes are patient-reported, and participants knew they were receiving an intensive program (about 4 sessions a week, including therapist contact) versus a booklet. Differences such as 2.84 points on pain intensity and 8.07 on the Tampa scale may reflect expectation and attention as well as specific components. Blinded assessors do not help for questionnaires. The paper nonetheless concludes the program itself is effective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control arm or objective outcome measures showing similar effects.

quotes.text: Because of the nature of the intervention, it was not feasible to blind participants.

The control group, in addition to standard medical care, received an educational booklet with information on the main symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition, without follow-up or monitoring by a therapist.

second_reader.what_stands: Participants were unblinded, the outcomes were self-reported, and the comparator was a minimal booklet without therapist contact, so the effects cannot be separated from expectation, attention and other non-specific effects. The authors acknowledge the lack of participant blinding as a limitation but do not discuss the self-report or the unmatched attention control, and do not temper their conclusion accordingly.

issues.title: Conclusion claims improved functionality and system-level value; only WHODAS total differs (P=.039), 7 subscales n.s.
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the program improved functionality, but between groups only the WHODAS total reached significance (P=.039, CI 2.28-30.03), while all subscales showed non-significant differences. The conclusion also recommends integrating PIM into health systems on the basis of a 57-person single-centre per-protocol trial with an 8-week outcome. Neither the per-protocol analysis nor the non-blinding is carried into the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified ITT analysis showing robust functional benefit across WHODAS domains, or a conclusion restricted to short-term pain outcomes.

quotes.text: In conclusion, the PIM program was an effective intervention for the reduction of new-onset persistent pain and improvement of functionality in patients with post-COVID-19 condition.
The integration of interventions such as PIM into health care systems may offer an effective strategy

second_reader.what_stands: Functionality evidence is limited to a single borderline-significant WHODAS total (adjusted P=.039) with all 7 subscale comparisons non-significant, in an unblinded, per-protocol, self-report trial, so the unqualified conclusion of improved functionality is stronger than the data support. The health-system statement is hedged ('may offer') and rests on an 8-week trial with no cost or implementation data, so it is speculation beyond the results rather than a demonstrated finding; also, the printed total mean difference (16.16) does not equal the difference of the printed group changes (about 12

issues.title: Intervention drug percentages (e.g. 22.7%) imply 22 users, but 66.7% of n=27 implies 18
issues.explanation: The intervention drug rows are all multiples of 1/22 (13.6%=3/22, 18.2%=4/22, 22.7%=5/22), which implies 22 users. The stated share on pharmacologic treatment, 66.7% of 27, is 18 users. The control arm is internally consistent (24 users). The discrepancy affects a baseline description only and does not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the drug percentages use a different base (for example users with documented drug type), or a corrected Table 1.

The intervention value of 70% is likewise not attainable at n=27 but equals 21/30. The Sex row therefore appears to have its columns transposed. 10.1016/j.arrct.2025.100516.headline_claim: Outpatient rehabilitation was associated with improved physical function in post-COVID patients, while their quality-of-life deficits persist relative to other rehabilitation groups.
10.1016/j.arrct.2025.100516.overall: The descriptive finding that post-COVID patients improve their 6MWT while keeping lower EQ-5D scores is plausible, but the headline rankings rest on a baseline-coupled score (T2D = 2×discharge − admission), unadjusted age differences of up to 16 years, and a 55.6% complete-case sample. The abstract and Discussion also overstate the significance of improvements and of the QOL gap, and several numbers in the abstract and prose disagree with the tables, though these are minor. Treat the conclusions as tentative and descriptive, not as evidence of rehabilitation efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test distance (6MWT) and EQ-5D-5L index/EQ-VAS; no single primary outcome is designated

issues.title: Between-group conclusions rest on T2D (=2×discharge − admission), claimed free of coupling and regression effects
issues.explanation: The headline comparisons ('highest physical function', 'lowest QOL') use T2D, which the authors define as discharge plus change. This equals twice the discharge value minus the admission value, so it is not baseline-independent and does not remove regression to the mean as the Methods claim. The paper offers no head-to-head comparison with ANCOVA or other baseline adjustment, and the Limitations concede the score needs further testing. The rankings of groups on T2D should be treated as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses showing group rankings are unchanged under ANCOVA or mixed-model baseline adjustment.

quotes.text: using the formula T2D=t2 + D (with D = changes from t1 to t2)
without mathematical coupling or regression effects
further testing in diverse populations is needed to con fi rm its broader applicability

second_reader.what_stands: Between-group conclusions do rest on T2D, which equals 2*discharge - admission. By construction T2D contains the baseline value and the change score, which the paper itself shows are negatively correlated. The claim of freedom from mathematical coupling and regression effects is therefore not supported, and the limitations section does not weigh this. The only caveat offered is that the formula needs further testing in other populations.

issues.title: Age differs by up to 16 years across groups and was not adjusted; abstract's 6MWT/QOL rankings ignore this
issues.explanation: The post-COVID group has a mean age of 44.7 years versus 49.4 to 61.1 in the other groups. The final models adjust only for sex, and the authors say age was left out because it is collinear with diagnosis. The abstract nonetheless states that post-COVID patients showed the highest physical function, outperforming all groups. Part of that ranking may reflect age, and the headline conclusion is tentative until this is addressed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis stratified by age band or with age as a covariate showing the same group ordering.

quotes.text: Wedid not adjust for age or BMI because of strong collinearity between age and diagnostic group
patients with PC were substantially younger than those with orthopedic or COPD diagnoses
outperforming all other outpatient rehabilitation groups

second_reader.what_stands: Age differs by up to about 16 years across groups and was not adjusted, and the abstract's 6MWT and QOL rankings carry no age caveat, although the limitations section does disclose the issue. It is not true that the paper ignores it. The abstract's 'outperforming all other groups' also goes beyond the reported tests, which compare PC with COPD and orthopedic groups only, and it relies on a sex-adjusted PC value set against an unadjusted overall mean.

issues.title: Improvement attributed to rehabilitation from uncontrolled pre-post change; stated aim is 'efficacy'
issues.explanation: All groups were treated and only admission and discharge values were compared, so no effect of rehabilitation can be isolated from spontaneous recovery, regression to the mean or practice effects on the 6MWT. The authors note a strong negative correlation between baseline and change, which is the pattern regression to the mean produces. The introduction frames the work as an assessment of rehabilitation efficacy, which a pre-post cohort cannot supply. The between-group contrasts are the more defensible part of the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A waitlist or usual-care comparison group, or authors restricting all claims to descriptive change.

quotes.text: Monocentric comparative cohort pre-post study.
data-driven assessment of rehabilitation ef fi cacy

issues.title: 749 of 1346 patients (55.6%) excluded, differentially by group, yet sample described as 'consecutive'
issues.explanation: Over half of the patients treated in 2023 are not in the analysis, mostly for missing data. Orthopedic patients were disproportionately excluded for missing 6MWT data, and post-COVID patients are over-represented. Between-group comparisons therefore apply to a selected subset, and the abstract's 'consecutive sample of 597' does not convey this. The no-difference comparison offsets this only partly because it cannot capture missing-not-at-random mechanisms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A breakdown of exclusions by reason and group showing the analysed sample is representative of all 1346.

issues.explanation: The abstract presents the post-COVID 6MWT gain with a within-group P < .001 as the highest of any group. The test of whether gains differ between groups (time x group) was non-significant at P = .094. The pairwise follow-ups used Fisher LSD with no multiplicity correction across 6 groups and 3 outcomes. Gains in cardiovascular, metabolic and orthopedic groups (46.6-47.4 m) are close to each other and the evidence of superiority is mainly over the two smallest groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Multiplicity-adjusted pairwise tests (for example Holm) that still show post-COVID gains exceeding the cardiovascular, metabolic and orthopedic groups.

10.1016/j.arrct.2025.100526.headline_claim: Participants who completed an 8-week symptom-titrated virtual rehabilitation program valued it and reported positive effects, while also reporting challenges sustaining exercise after the program.
10.1016/j.arrct.2025.100526.overall: This is a small qualitative descriptive study, and its themes about participant experience are reasonably supported. The conclusions about 'positive effects' and an 'effective' approach go beyond what perceptions from 13 intervention completers can show, and they depend on the separate parent RCT. The session-length discrepancy is a trivial inconsistency.

issues.title: Perceptions of 13 intervention completers described as 'positive effects' and an 'effective' approach
issues.explanation: All interviewees were intervention-arm completers, selected from consenting participants. They were all happy to have been assigned to the intervention, and no control participants were interviewed. Such data show how participants experienced the program, not that it produced effects. Wording such as 'positive effects' and 'effective rehabilitation approach' attributes causal benefit to the program, with effectiveness resting on the separate parent RCT. The limitation is stated in the paper but not carried into the abstract conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording in the abstract and Discussion that clearly frames the findings as participants' perceived benefits only, with efficacy deferred to the RCT.

10.1016/j.bbi.2026.106892.headline_claim: Temelimab did not show improvement in fatigue compared with placebo in adults with persistent symptoms due to post-COVID condition.
10.1016/j.bbi.2026.106892.overall: The negative primary result (RR 0.9, 0.6-1.2; 49% vs 54% responders) is internally consistent and can be relied on, with the caveat that 13 randomised participants are missing from the primary analysis despite the stated ITT and no-missing-data claims. Several tables and text passages contain transposed or mismatched values, and the secondary-outcome narrative omits the nominally unfavourable PHQ-9 result while overstating a Tower of London benefit, so secondary findings should be read cautiously.

issues.title: Primary responder analysis uses 96 and 94 participants, not 102 and 101, despite 'no missing data' and ITT
issues.explanation: Table 1 lists 102 Temelimab and 101 placebo participants, and the Methods state primary data were not missing and analysis was by intention-to-treat. The primary responder proportions are nonetheless given over 96 and 94 participants, so 13 randomised participants are absent from the primary analysis with no explanation in the main text. The null primary result is unlikely to flip, but the stated analysis population does not match the numbers used.

issues.title: PHQ-9 RR 0.4 (0.2-0.8) favours placebo, yet Abstract and Discussion say no secondary differences
issues.explanation: The Results report that Temelimab patients were less likely than placebo patients to improve on the PHQ-9, with an interval excluding 1. The Abstract and Discussion nonetheless state that secondary outcomes showed no differences, and the paper does not mention this nominal finding as a possible signal of worse depression outcomes or as a likely chance result under multiple testing. The primary conclusion is unaffected, but the secondary-outcome summary is inaccurate and glosses over a result that points against the drug.

Composite BAC and HERV-W ENV baselines are likewise transposed between Tables 1 and 2. Baseline balance as described differs depending on which table is correct, though the discrepancies are small.

issues.explanation: The race and ethnicity counts add up to 101 in the Temelimab column and 102 in the placebo column, the reverse of the stated arm sizes, while age and sex counts match the headers. The percentages also fit those reversed denominators. This is a minor table error with no bearing on efficacy, though it fits the pattern of arm mislabelling in c4.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote explaining non-exclusive race categories or a participant with missing race data in each arm.

quotes.text: Race or ethnic group - N(%)

issues.title: Primary effect reported as RR from logistic models rather than the prespecified OR (RR 0.9, 0.6-1.2)
issues.explanation: The protocol prespecified odds ratios, but the paper reports relative risks 'calculated using logistic regression models' without saying how an RR was obtained. The switch is disclosed with a reason, and the RR agrees with the raw responder proportions, so the null primary result is not in doubt. Only the unspecified derivation method remains a minor reporting gap.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the procedure used (marginal standardisation or log-binomial) and the prespecified OR result showing the same conclusion.

quotes.text: Relative risk estimates were used although the protocol had prespecified odds ratios as the primary analysis.
Relative risk was calculated using logistic regression models in the overall sample

10.1016/j.bbih.2022.100485.headline_claim: LDN is safe in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome and may improve well-being and reduce symptomatology in this cohort.
10.1016/j.bbih.2022.100485.overall: The paper is a small uncontrolled pilot, and its efficacy conclusion is appropriately hedged only in part: the abstract states that LDN is safe, and presents unblinded self-reported pre-post changes in unvalidated single-item scales as a signal of benefit. Several reporting inconsistencies (recruitment dates versus the 333-day median, employment denominator, Table 3 percentages, unexplained lost patients) do not change the picture, but they reduce confidence in the data handling. At most the paper supports a hypothesis-generating signal and tolerability in about 38 starters.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly stated as primary; paper reports 7 Likert questionnaire components and symptom incidence at 2 months. Registry primary outcome is fatigue reduction at 12 weeks.

primary_outcomes.measure: Reduction of fatigue in post-COVID-19 syndrome by treatment with LDN and NAD+

issues.title: Efficacy and safety conclusions drawn from an uncontrolled, unblinded pre-post study of 36 completers
issues.explanation: All the reported improvements are paired within-patient changes in unblinded self-report, with no control group. Natural recovery over about 2 months, placebo response and regression to the mean could explain them, as the authors concede in the limitations. The abstract still concludes that LDN is safe and may improve well-being, with the safety statement based on 2 discontinuations among 38 starters and no comparator. The data support only a hypothesis-generating signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or an external comparator showing that the observed changes exceed those expected without treatment.

quotes.text: No control arm was used in the study, only pre and post analysis was done and the witnessed improvements in symptoms and wellbeing may be due in part of fully to placebo or natural improvement in symptoms.
LDN is safe in patients with PCS and may improve well-being and reduce symptomatology in this cohort.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is an uncontrolled, unblinded single-arm pre-post design of 36 completers with self-reported outcomes, and the paper says so and hedges its efficacy wording ('may improve', 'not possible to solely attribute this to LDN'). What still stands is that the title says 'efficacy' and the Abstract states 'LDN is safe' without qualification. That safety claim rests on 36 completers from 52 enrolled, with adverse events recorded only at clinic reviews and a loss-to-follow-up count that does not reconcile (38 - 2 = 36 versus three further lost).

issues.title: Completers-only analysis; patient accounting unclear (38 started, 2 stopped, 36 completed, 3 'additional' lost)
issues.explanation: The abstract presents 36 of 52 (69.2%) as completing, but 14 never started treatment, so true attrition among starters is small. However, the analysis uses completers only, and the Results arithmetic (38 - 2 = 36) leaves no room for the three extra patients the Discussion says were lost. It is also unclear whether the two patients who stopped for adverse events contributed follow-up data. Efficacy estimates may therefore exclude those who did worst, and the safety denominator is not clearly defined.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The Fig. 1 flow diagram showing every patient accounted for, with the 'three additional' patients located among the non-starters, and a note on whether the 2 discontinuers completed follow-up.

quotes.text: In total 36(69.2%) participants completed the questionnaire at the end of the two-month period.
Albeit three additional patients were lost to follow and it is unknown if they took LDN.

issues.title: Outcomes are seven single-item Likert ratings with varying ranges (1-3 to 1-6) and no validation reported
issues.explanation: Outcomes are single ordinal items with different range lengths, and the anchors are not printed, which makes the direction and size of change hard to interpret. No validation, reliability or minimal important difference is given, and no fatigue measure, the registered primary outcome of the related trial, is reported. Statistically significant median shifts therefore cannot be translated into clinically meaningful improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of these items, or anchors and a minimal important difference showing the changes are clinically meaningful.

quotes.text: The questionnaire explored 7 different components of clinical status using Likert scaling, a symmetrically balanced ordinal scale assessment of each component

issues.title: 22 symptom comparisons at uncorrected p<0.05; chest tightness (.047), cough (.016) emphasised as improvements
issues.explanation: The Methods use p < 0.05 for each test with no multiplicity adjustment. With 22 symptom tests and 7 Likert tests, about one or two nominally significant results would be expected by chance alone. The Results and Discussion nonetheless name the nominally significant symptoms as improvements. The primary Likert findings are less affected, but the symptom-level claims are weak.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or a multiplicity correction showing these symptom results remain significant.

quotes.text: a significant reduction (p < 0.05) seen in low mood, personality change, joint pain, chest tightness and cough
A p value of < 0.05 was deemed significant for individual statistical tests.

issues.title: Recruitment 'June-November 2020' is incompatible with a median 333 days from diagnosis to enrolment
issues.explanation: Patients were said to be recruited between June and November 2020, yet the median time from COVID-19 diagnosis to enrolment was 333 days. Even a diagnosis at the very start of the Irish epidemic could not give that median for enrolment by November 2020. The registry record also gives a study start of January 2021, so the recruitment dates are probably wrong. This leaves the study's timing and the 'at least six months' eligibility unverifiable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected recruitment period (for example 2021) consistent with the 333-day median and the registry start date.

quotes.text: between June and November 2020
The median time from diagnosis of COVID-19 until enrolment was 333 days

issues.title: Table 3 cough baseline 19(37.3) and headache follow-up 24(63.9) do not match n=36
issues.explanation: The Table 3 total is 36, but 19 of 36 is 52.8%, not 37.3%, and 24 of 36 is 66.7%, not 63.9%. The cough count of 19 is the same as the whole-cohort count in the Results (19 of 52, 36.5%), suggesting the wrong group's count was entered. If the true baseline cough count among the 36 completers was lower, the reported cough reduction (p = .016) is overstated. The headache cell is a smaller slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 19 of the 36 completers had cough at baseline (which would make the percentage 52.8%), or a corrected table.

script.explanation: 19/36 = 52.78%, but the paper prints 37.3, outside the rounding interval [37.25, 37.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 50.9 rather than 36.

issues.title: Healthcare worker share is 34.8% in abstract/text (apparent n=46) but 30.8% (16/52) in Table 1
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results give 34.8% for 16 healthcare workers, while Table 1 gives 30.8% out of 52. The text figure only works if the denominator is 46 (those with a documented occupation), which is not stated. A reader would take the two as contradictory, though nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the occupational percentages use only the 46 participants with a documented occupation.

quotes.text: Healthcare workers represented the largest occupational cohort n = 16(34.8%)

issues.title: Employment figures: 'of 50' stated, but 31 (64.6%) and 34 (70.8%) both imply a denominator of 48
issues.explanation: The Results say 50 patients were in employment, but 31 and 34 are reported as 64.6% and 70.8%. Those percentages equal 31/48 and 34/48, and 31/50 would be 62.0% and 34/50 would be 68.0%. Either the denominator or both percentages are wrong. This is a secondary descriptive result and does not affect the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that 48 patients had usable employment data, with the text's 50 being a typographical error.

quotes.text: Of 50 patients in employment, 31 (64.6%, CI 51 -78%)

script.explanation: 31/50 = 62.00%, but the paper prints 64.6, outside the rounding interval [64.55, 64.70]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 48.0 rather than 50.

issues.title: Symptom-duration criterion given as 3 months (Introduction), 12 weeks (abstract) and 6 months (Methods)
issues.explanation: The paper describes the eligible population with three different symptom-duration thresholds. The Methods eligibility criterion (six months) is the one that governs enrolment and is consistent with the reported median time since diagnosis. The mismatch is a descriptive inconsistency, not evidence of a different population.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that the Introduction and abstract refer to the general NICE definition and not the study's entry criterion.

quotes.text: who had symptoms for at least three months
to have any symptoms for at least six months after initial diagnosis

issues.title: LDN regimen described as 2 months (to 2 mg) in abstract but up to 3 mg over 3 months of supply in Methods
issues.explanation: The abstract describes a two-month course ending at 2 mg, whereas the Methods say the dose rose monthly to a maximum of 3 mg and three months were prescribed. The Methods give a reason (clinic delays), but the abstract does not mention that some patients took 3 mg. The actual dose exposure is therefore not clearly reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual dosing records showing the dose actually taken at follow-up.

quotes.text: were prescribed 2 months (1 mg month one, 2 mg month two)
three months of medication was prescribed

10.1016/j.bbih.2024.100733.headline_claim: Treatment with LDN and NAD+ may be beneficial in those with long-term fatigue symptoms resulting from COVID-19.
10.1016/j.bbih.2024.100733.overall: The pre-post improvements are plausibly real as descriptive changes, but without a control, blinding, or objective outcomes, and with 36% missing at week 12, they cannot show that LDN and NAD+ caused benefit. The abstract's responder (52%) and skin irritation (25%) figures do not match the results (47.8%; 30.6%), and the safety and subgroup claims go beyond a 36-person uncontrolled pilot.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 total score (headline outcome; the paper does not name a primary outcome)

primary_outcomes.measure: Reduction of fatigue in post-COVID-19 syndrome by treatment with LDN and NAD+

issues.title: 36% lack week-12 data; responder rate and week-12 means reflect 23 completers of 36 enrolled
issues.explanation: Only 23 of 36 enrolled participants (63.9%) have week 12 data. The abstract's responder figure does not state that it covers completers only; across all enrolled participants 11 responders would be 30.6%. Dropout was highest early, and completer-based estimates may overstate benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (e.g. multiple imputation, worst-case) showing similar responder proportion and effects with all enrolled patients.

quotes.text: Week 12 (N = 23)
Five participants withdrew from the study within the first two weeks of treatment, of whom two were lost to follow-up.
out of the participants who received LDN and NAD + and completed their 12-week assessments, approximately half could be described as responders

second_reader.what_stands: About 36% (13 of 36) of enrolled participants have no week-12 data, and the week-12 means and responder classification are based only on the 23 with data, with no imputation or sensitivity analysis shown; only 5 of the 13 missing are explained as withdrawals. The Discussion does say 'completed their 12-week assessments', but the abstract's '52% responders' is not labelled as completers, does not match 11/23 (47.8%), and is far higher than the 11/36 (31%) responding in the enrolled cohort.

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from uncontrolled open-label pre-post change in self-reported scores
issues.explanation: There is no control group, no blinding, and the outcomes are patient-reported fatigue and quality of life. Pre-post p-values cannot distinguish treatment effect from natural recovery, placebo and selection effects, which the authors acknowledge. The hedged conclusion 'may be beneficial' is tentative at best, and the responder claim suggests a treatment-responsive subgroup that the design cannot identify.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control showing a smaller change.

quotes.text: We conducted an observational open-label pilot study to address the chronic phase of COVID-19 (NCT04604704)
could be attributed partially to the placebo-effect or natural improvements in disease state over time
In conclusion, our study showed that treatment with LDN and NAD + may be beneficial in those with long-term fatigue symptoms resulting from COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy signal rests entirely on uncontrolled, open-label pre-post change in self-reported scores, so the p-values cannot separate treatment effect from placebo, expectation or natural recovery. However, the authors state this limitation clearly and hedge their conclusion ('may be beneficial', RCTs needed), so the paper does not claim proven efficacy; the residual problem is that 'our study showed' and the p<0.0001 framing still lean toward a treatment effect.

issues.title: Abstract responder rate 52% does not match 11 of 23 (47.8%); 12/23 would give 52.2%
issues.explanation: The abstract says 52% of patients were responders at week 12. The Results define 11 responders and 12 non-responders among 23 participants, which is 47.8%. The abstract figure matches the non-responder count instead, so the headline subset proportion is misreported by about four percentage points.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A responder definition or denominator under which 52% of the analysed participants were responders (e.g. 12 of 23 meeting criteria).

quotes.text: We found a subset of 52 % of patients to be responders after 12 weeks of treatment.
Fig. 2A shows a boxplot depicting the mean total SF-36 scores at baseline and week 12 for those who were considered clinically responsive (N = 11) and non-responsive (N = 12).

script.explanation: 11/23 = 47.83%, but the paper prints 52, outside the rounding interval [51.50, 53.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 21.2 rather than 23.

issues.title: Abstract states treatment 'is safe' from 36 uncontrolled participants with 3-4 AE withdrawals
issues.explanation: The sample is too small and uncontrolled to exclude uncommon harms. Self-reported events and withdrawals due to adverse events are reported, but the abstract's safety statement is stronger than the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger controlled safety dataset showing comparable event rates to placebo.

quotes.text: Our data suggest treatment with LDN and NAD + is safe
four patients withdrew due to expected adverse events from LDN

issues.title: Responders defined by SF-36 improvement, then shown to have 'significant' SF-36 improvement (P < 0.0001)
issues.explanation: Responders were selected post hoc as those with more than 20% SF-36 improvement and a week-12 score of at least 55. Testing whether this group improved on SF-36, and contrasting it with non-responders, is circular and says nothing about who benefits from treatment. The responder subgroup is also a post hoc outcome-dependent classification, with no baseline predictors identified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified responder definition in the protocol or registry and an independent outcome used to validate the responder group.

quotes.text: Clinically responsive participants reported a significant increase in SF-36 scores (P < 0.0001)

issues.title: Skin irritation: 25% (abstract) and nine (Discussion) vs 11 of 36 = 30.6% (Results, Table 2)
issues.explanation: The abstract reports skin irritation in 25% of patients and the Discussion says nine participants. The Results and Table 2 list 11 of 36 (30.6%). The summary statements understate the most common adverse event relative to the primary table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explanation that two of the 11 events were not counted as skin irritation attributable to the patch.

quotes.text: The iontophoresis patches were associated with mild, short-lived skin irritation in 25 % of patients.
The most commonly reported adverse event was skin irritation in the location of the NAD + patch (n = 11).
nine  participants  experienced  skin  irritation

script.explanation: 11/36 = 30.56%, but the paper prints 25, outside the rounding interval [24.50, 26.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 44.0 rather than 36.

issues.title: Table 3 baseline N = 36 vs Efficacy N = 31 in text; week 2 N = 30 conflicts with efficacy definition
issues.explanation: The text attributes the Table 3 means to the 31-person Efficacy dataset, but the table header gives baseline N = 36. The Efficacy dataset requires baseline and week 2 data, yet week 2 has only 30 participants. The analysis denominators are therefore unclear, though the means themselves appear to come from the 31.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 3 header and a statement of exactly which participants contributed at each time point.

quotes.text: In the Efficacy dataset group (N = 31), the mean total SF-36 score improved from 36.5 (SD 15.6) at baseline
Week 2 (N = 30)
completed at least baseline and week 2 survey assessments

issues.title: Reported age range 28-69 years exceeds the stated eligibility ceiling of 65 years
issues.explanation: Methods limit eligibility to ages 18-65, but both Table 1 and the Results give a maximum age of 69. Either the eligibility criteria were not applied as described or they were stated incorrectly. This does not change the efficacy results but it is an unexplained protocol deviation or reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the age criterion was amended or that age is computed at a later date than enrolment.

quotes.text: Patients aged between 18 and 65 years were eligible
Ages ranged from 28 to 69 years

issues.title: Female baseline Chalder total: text says 26.6, Table 4 says 26.1
issues.explanation: The sex-specific text gives 26.6 for the female baseline Chalder total, while Table 4 gives 26.1 (SD 4.2). The table value reproduces the overall baseline of 25.9, so the text figure appears to be wrong. This overstates the female baseline-to-week-12 drop slightly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table correction showing 26.6 as the female baseline.

quotes.text: The sum of the Chalder scale decreased from 26.6 at baseline to 15.9 at week 12

quotes.location: Table 4, female, Total Sum of Chalder Fatigue Scale, baseline

issues.title: Adverse-event withdrawals: three in Results vs four in Discussion, with only five withdrawals in total
issues.explanation: The Results say five withdrew, two lost to follow-up and three for medical issues or adverse events. The Discussion says four withdrew for expected LDN adverse events. A fourth such withdrawal cannot be reconciled with five total withdrawals of whom two were lost to follow-up.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow diagram showing four withdrawals for adverse events and six withdrawals in total.

quotes.text: Three participants withdrew due to pre-existing medical issues and/or adverse events that are known to be caused by LDN
four patients withdrew due to expected adverse events from LDN

10.1016/j.bbih.2024.100736.headline_claim: iTBS was well tolerated among 4 individuals with PCC, and active stimulation was associated with positive trends in some symptom clusters compared with sham.
10.1016/j.bbih.2024.100736.overall: This is a four-participant feasibility case series, and its tolerability findings are reasonable as a pilot signal. The efficacy language ('improved', 'compared with sham', 'treatment') goes beyond what descriptive within-person changes in 3 of 4 cases, with two sessions per condition and no inferential testing, can support. The headline conclusion should be treated as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; feasibility and tolerability (primary aim), with secondary trends in Flanker interference, quality of life, and GAD-7

issues.title: Abstract claims active-vs-sham trends but results only show change from baseline in 3 of 4 cases
issues.explanation: The abstract says active stimulation was associated with positive trends compared with sham. The Results report only improvement relative to baseline in 3 of 4 participants for single conditions, with two sessions per condition and no between-condition comparison. With four participants, a fixed condition order confounded with time, and no inferential statistics, the sham contrast is not demonstrated. The claim is hedged as trends, which limits the severity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-participant sham versus active data in Fig. 1 showing consistent differences from sham.

quotes.text: active stimulation was associated with positive trends in some primary symptom clusters as compared with sham stimulation
given that this is a case series and each participant is considered separately, no inferential statistics are possible to compute

second_reader.what_stands: The text-reported results are all change from baseline in 3 of 4 cases, and no sham-vs-active comparison is reported or quantified in the text, so the abstract's 'as compared with sham' is not supported by any stated result. The 'in 3 of 4 cases' wording is accurate for the three reported outcomes, and the paper does not claim inferential tests (it states none are possible), but I could not check whether Fig. 1 visually shows sham against active, so I cannot say the comparison is absent from the figure.

issues.title: Conclusion calls iTBS a 'feasible and well-tolerated treatment' and cites improvements from 4 participants
issues.explanation: The conclusion describes iTBS as a feasible and well-tolerated treatment and reports evidence of improved interference, quality of life and anxiety. Only tolerability data (3 of 4 responding) and descriptive within-person changes exist, with two sessions per condition. The tolerability reading is reasonable for a pilot; the 'improved' and 'treatment' wording is stronger than the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable beyond rewording; the data themselves would need a controlled comparison.

quotes.text: Some evidence of  improved  cognitive  interference,  quality  of  life  and  anxiety  were observed.
The current findings provide further evidence that iTBS could be a feasible and well-tolerated treatment for patients experiencing PCC.

issues.title: Blinding of participants and assessors not described for self-reported outcomes
