issues.explanation: Anxiety, quality of life and function were self-reported, and the paper does not say whether participants or outcome assessors were blinded to sham versus active conditions. The authors concede placebo may account for some patterns, but the abstract and conclusion do not carry that caveat. Whether blinding was adequate cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that participants and outcome assessors were blinded to condition and that blinding was assessed.

quotes.text: self-reported symptoms of anxiety, quality of life, functional abilities were completed online by each participant
even in this case it must be noted that placebo may still account for some of the patterns observed

issues.title: GAD-7 response codes printed as 0, 1, 3, 4 (value 2 missing) for a '4-point scale'
issues.explanation: The Methods describe the GAD-7 as a 4-point scale but list codes 0, 1, 3 and 4, with no code 2. The standard instrument uses 0-3, so this is most likely a typographical slip in the description. It does not by itself show the scoring was wrong, but the anxiety scoring cannot be confirmed from the text. Anxiety is one of the three outcomes highlighted in the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary materials or the administered questionnaire showing the standard 0-3 coding was used.

quotes.text: Responses are given on a 4-point scale
1 = ' two days or less days ' , 3 = ' three or more days ' , and 4 = ' nearly everyday '

issues.title: Mean age 34 years vs ranges; and tolerability counts: 'no adverse events' yet 2 of 3 report scalp tingling
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results say no adverse events occurred, while two of three respondents reported scalp tingling and Table 2 shows one respondent as neutral on discomfort or side effects after sessions. Tingling is a common expected sensation and is reported openly, so the inconsistency is one of labelling. Tolerability also rests on only 3 of 4 participants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocol-defined adverse event definitions that exclude transient scalp sensations.

quotes.text: No adverse events occurred in active or sham stimulation; 2 participants reported  tingling  sensation  on  the  scalp
One of the three participants did not complete the tolerability/side  effect  survey,  and  so  responses  were  based  on  the remaining three.

10.1016/j.bbih.2025.100963.headline_claim: A virtual six-week mindfulness program may improve sleep quality in women with Long COVID dysautonomia, with a favorable effect on inflammatory biology (CTRA decrease).
10.1016/j.bbih.2025.100963.overall: This is an uncontrolled pilot in which every pre-specified primary outcome was null. The insomnia and CTRA findings are secondary, are subject to the limits of a single-arm, completer-only analysis, and the insomnia gain reverted at follow-up. The conclusions can be relied on only as hypothesis-generating, and the 'effective' wording is stronger than the evidence supports. The numeric inconsistencies (N of 16 vs 17, 53 vs 48 transcripts) are modest but should be clarified.

primary_outcome.name: Pre-specified primary outcomes: hemodynamic parameters on orthostatic testing, 6-minute walk distance, and health-related quality of life (SF-20); CTRA gene expression is the reported inflammatory analysis

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline in the composite autonomic symptom score COMPASS-31 for autonomic symptoms
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline / Pre Intervention(1-2 weeks prior to intervention), Post Intervention ( 1-2 weeks post intervention completion)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline in Active Stand Test of hemodynamic symptom parameters, exercise tolerance.
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline / Pre Intervention(1-2 weeks prior to intervention), Post Intervention ( 1-2 weeks post intervention completion)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline of Six Minute Walk in hemodynamic parameters, exercise tolerance
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline / Pre Intervention(1-2 weeks prior to intervention), Post Intervention ( 1-2 weeks post intervention completion)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline in mean score in Health-Related Quality of Life (QOL) SF-20
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline / Pre Intervention(1-2 weeks prior to intervention), Post Intervention (1-2 weeks post intervention completion); 4 weeks post intervention

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute sleep or CTRA changes to mindfulness, yet 'effective' is claimed
issues.explanation: With no control group, changes in insomnia scores and gene expression could reflect regression to the mean, expectancy, group support or time. The authors admit they cannot determine the effect of time on CTRA, but still call the program 'effective' and attribute a 'favorable effect' on inflammatory biology to it. The ISI gain also reverted at 4 weeks. The causal wording outruns the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or wait-list arm showing the same change.

quotes.text: this pilot study was non-randomized and importantly lacked a control group necessary to optimize causal inference
practical, effective, complementary approach that is feasible and acceptable

second_reader.what_stands: The design cannot attribute the sleep or CTRA changes to mindfulness, and the Conclusion's description of the MBI as 'effective' goes beyond what a single-arm study with no significant change in the pre-specified primary outcomes can support. The point is weaker than stated because the authors clearly acknowledge the missing control group in the Limitations and the CTRA discussion, hedge their sleep and biological claims ('may improve', 'may be a favorable effect'), and call for controlled trials; the overreach is confined to the single word 'effective' in the final conclusion sentence.

issues.title: Analysed N is 17 in Table 2 and the survey percentages but 16 completers in the text
issues.explanation: The Results say 16 of 20 completed post-intervention assessments, and the active stand analysis uses N = 16. Table 2 gives N = 17 for both pre- and post-intervention, and the follow-up survey percentages imply 17 respondents. The paper never explains who the 17th person is or why the pre-intervention column drops from 20 to 17. The analysed sample for the headline ISI result is therefore ambiguous.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or note showing 17 participants supplied questionnaire data at post-intervention, with the baseline column also restricted to those 17.

quotes.text: Sixteen participants (80%) completed the post-intervention and 4-week follow-up assessments.
Post-Intervention = 17) Mean
the majority agreed that the experience was helpful (88.24%)

issues.title: Registered primary COMPASS-31 is not named as a primary outcome in the paper
issues.explanation: The registry (NCT05566379) lists COMPASS-31 as a primary outcome alongside the active stand test, 6MWT and SF-20. The paper's list of pre-specified primaries omits COMPASS-31 and presents it among the questionnaire results. Its result was null, so the discrepancy does not inflate the findings. It is still an undisclosed mismatch between registered and reported primary outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing COMPASS-31 was added as a primary after the paper's outcome set was fixed.

quotes.text: Pre-specified primary outcomes were changes in hemodynamic parameters on orthostatic testing, exercise tolerance as assessed by 6-min walk distance, and health-related quality of life.

issues.title: 4 of 20 participants (20%) missing post-intervention; completer-only analysis with no sensitivity check
issues.explanation: Four of 20 enrolled participants did not attend the post-intervention visit, and all post-intervention results use completers. If the dropouts differ systematically (for example, sicker participants), the pre-post changes could be biased. The bias direction is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity or mixed-model analysis including all 20 participants, giving similar results.

quotes.text: Sixteen participants (80%) completed the post-intervention and 4-week follow-up assessments.
In participants who presented for post-intervention testing (N = 16)

issues.title: Pilot of 20 (16-17 analysed) with no power calculation and no multiplicity adjustment
issues.explanation: The sample size of 20-30 was estimated without a stated basis, and 11 questionnaire domains plus multiple gene analyses were tested without correction. ISI p = 0.001 would survive a Bonferroni correction over 11 domains (threshold about 0.0045). The wording is mostly hedged, so this weakens secondary findings only modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis plan designating ISI and CTRA as the sole key outcomes.

quotes.text: a sample size of 20 -30 participants was estimated

issues.title: Conclusion emphasises secondary sleep and CTRA results despite null primaries and ISI rebound
issues.explanation: None of the pre-specified primary outcomes (active stand, 6MWT, quality of life) changed. The conclusion nonetheless highlights improved sleep, a secondary outcome whose gain reverted by 4 weeks, and a CTRA change from an uncontrolled comparison. The caveats are present, but the framing is more favourable than the primary results support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pre-specification of ISI or CTRA as the key outcome of the trial.

quotes.text: No significant changes were observed for the active stand test or 6MWT.
scores reverted toward baseline levels at 4week follow-up

issues.title: CTRA gene set described as 19 + 34 = 53 transcripts in Methods but 48 in Results
issues.explanation: Methods describe a contrast of 19 pro-inflammatory and 34 interferon transcripts, which is 53. The Fig. 2 legend states the CTRA average covers 48 transcripts. The paper does not explain the five-transcript difference, so the exact gene set behind the p = 0.004 result is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 48 of the 53 transcripts passed detection or quality filters.

quotes.text: 19  pro-inflammatory  gene  transcripts  with  34  Type  I interferon
Average expression of 48 pre-specified gene transcripts measuring the Conserved Transcriptional Response to Adversity

issues.title: Post-intervention '30% with COMPASS-31 ≥ 50' is not attainable at N = 16 (or 17)
issues.explanation: The Discussion reports 30% post-intervention against 40% at baseline. Of 16 completers, 4 gives 25% and 5 gives 31.25%. Of 17, 5 gives 29.4%. The percentage therefore implies an undisclosed denominator, and it is another sign of the unclear analysed N.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement of the denominator (for example 20 with imputation) for the 30% figure.

quotes.text: (30% vs 40% with COMPASS-31 ≥ 50)
In participants who presented for post-intervention testing (N = 16)

issues.title: Race/ethnicity rows in Table 1 total 19 of 20 (95%) with no missing category
issues.explanation: The four race/ethnicity categories sum to 19 participants and 95%, against a stated N of 20. Missing data is the likeliest explanation, but the table does not show a missing row. The consequence is trivial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote reporting one missing race/ethnicity value.

quotes.text: Total ( N = 20)
Race/Ethnicity, N (%)

10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101379.headline_claim: Low-dose aripiprazole was associated with improved functional status (FSS) in long COVID, warranting a randomized controlled trial.
10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101379.overall: The paper's actual claim is modest: LDA was associated with improved self-reported FSS in an uncontrolled retrospective series, with randomized testing needed, and that is mostly consistent with its own caveats. The result rests on a completer subset of 50 of 76 patients, concomitant LDN in about 87%, and a locally modified, unvalidated functional scale that the Discussion wrongly calls validated. Several small numeric inconsistencies (denominator of 52, 86.6% vs 86.0%, composite labelled an average, two mean durations) suggest sloppy reporting but do not change the main finding.

primary_outcome.name: Functional Status Scale (FSS)

issues.title: Only significant outcome (FSS) uses a locally modified, unvalidated PCFS; Discussion calls it validated
issues.explanation: The FSS was modified from the published PCFS, and the Methods state the modified version has not been independently validated. The Discussion nonetheless describes it as a validated instrument. The headline result (p = 0.001) depends on this unvalidated, self-reported measure. This weakens confidence in the result and the Discussion wording is inconsistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of the modified scale used in this clinic.

quotes.text: The modified version has not been independently validate
The FSS is a validated 5-point ordinal instrument

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's Methods state that the FSS is a modified version of the PCFS and has not been independently validated. The Discussion then describes 'The FSS' as 'a validated 5-point ordinal instrument' without qualification, which is inconsistent with the Methods. FSS is the only significant outcome in the main 50-patient analysis (p = 0.001). The point overstates in two ways: the modification is disclosed in the Methods, and symptom count was also significant (p = 0.011) in the 33-patient longitudinal subgroup. The Discussion wording applies to the original Klok PCFS, not to the modified scale a

issues.title: Before-after FSS change (3.78 to 3.28) from an uncontrolled retrospective series
issues.explanation: The only comparison is each patient before versus after LDA, with no control group. The FSS change cannot be separated from natural recovery, regression to the mean, concomitant LDN use, or reporting effects. The authors acknowledge this and word their conclusion cautiously, so the design limits the evidence but does not misstate it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not refutable from the paper; a concurrent control group would be needed to settle it.

quotes.text: given the retrospective observational design and the lack of a control group, these findings should be interpreted cautiously
The FSS improved significantly from 3.78 to 3.28 (p = 0.001).

issues.title: Outcome analysis limited to 50 of 76 LDA patients (34% excluded), with a further 33-patient subset
issues.explanation: Patients were included in the outcome analysis only if follow-up surveys were completed, so about a third of exposed patients are missing. The comparison of excluded and included patients on baseline traits cannot show that the excluded patients would have had similar outcomes. Residual selection bias is acknowledged but the FSS result still rests on a completer set.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Outcome or follow-up data for the 26 excluded patients showing similar FSS changes.

quotes.text: lacked completed baseline or follow-up symptom surveys required for outcome assessment
residual selection bias cannot be excluded

issues.title: Weight-change counts total 45 of 50 and percentages (and 53.8% LDN overlap) imply a denominator of 52
issues.explanation: The weight-change counts (25, 18, 2) add to 45, not 50. The printed percentages match a denominator of 52, a number that does not appear anywhere else in the 50-patient cohort. The same denominator seems to have been used for the 53.8% concomitant LDA and LDN figure (28/52). This points to a different dataset or a transcription error. It affects only a side-effect description, not the FSS result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that weight was available for 52 patients, or a corrected table of weight changes with a 50-patient denominator.

quotes.text: 48.1% (n = 25) gained weight (1 -42 pounds), 34.6% (n = 18) lost weight (1 -71 pounds), and 3.8% (n = 2) experienced no change
concomitant use of LDA and LDN documented in 53.8% (n = 28)

script.explanation: 25/50 = 50.00%, but the paper prints 48.1, outside the rounding interval [48.05, 48.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 52.0 rather than 50.

issues.title: No multiplicity correction across 7 symptoms, count, composite, FSS and subgroup tests
issues.explanation: No alpha control is applied across many outcomes and subgroup analyses. The main FSS p = 0.001 would probably survive a correction, but the subgroup findings (p = 0.011 and 0.013) would not. The effect on the headline is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a judgement about secondary analyses.

quotes.text: multiple exploratory comparisons
statistically significant changes were observed in the total number of symptoms (p = 0.011) and FSS (p = 0.013)

issues.title: Composite score printed as 20.36 / 18.62 although defined as an average of seven 0-5 ratings
issues.explanation: The Methods define the composite as an average of seven symptom scores, which cannot exceed 5. Table 1 reports medians of 20.0 and 18.0 and means of 20.36 and 18.62. These equal the sum of the seven individual symptom means, so the composite is actually a sum (maximum 35). The label and description are wrong. The test result (p = 0.121) is probably unaffected because dividing by 7 does not change a rank test, but readers are misled about the scale.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The supplementary data showing the composite was computed as a mean and Table 1 reports a rescaled quantity.

quotes.text: as the average severity across the seven symptoms by summing their individual scores and dividing by the number of symptoms

issues.title: Mean days on LDA printed as 315 (max 1165) and as 204.4 (max 1025) in the same paragraph
issues.explanation: Two different means and two different maximum durations are given for LDA exposure, with no explanation of the populations. Exposure duration matters for judging whether follow-up was long enough, and readers cannot tell which figure applies to the analysed 50 patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the two figures refer to different populations (76 exposed vs 50 analysed, or time on drug vs time to last follow-up).

quotes.text: The mean duration on LDA was 204.4 days (range, 31 -1025 days)

issues.title: 'Only FSS' significant statement omits a significant symptom-count change (p = 0.011) in the 33-patient subgroup
issues.explanation: The Discussion says only FSS improved significantly, but the Results report a significant reduction in symptom count (p = 0.011) in the 33-patient subgroup. The Abstract's null statement on symptom count also covers only the 50-patient analysis. The omission is narrow and slightly understates the findings, and the subgroup result is itself exploratory and uncorrected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The Discussion explicitly limiting the statement to the 50-patient analysis.

quotes.text: Of the outcomes assessed, only FSS showed a statistically significant improvement following LDA treatment
statistically significant changes were observed in the total number of symptoms (p = 0.011)

issues.title: Concomitant LDN use printed as 43/50 = 86.6%, but 43/50 = 86.0%
issues.explanation: The percentage does not match its own count and denominator. The same 86.6% appears again in the Discussion. Either the count or the percentage is wrong, a minor error that affects the description of co-treatment but not the FSS comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected count (for example 43.3 is not possible; a count of 43 gives 86.0%) or a note that LDN status was known for a different denominator.

quotes.text: Most patients also received low-dose Naltrexone (LDN) (43/50, 86.6%)
which was used in 86.6% of patients

script.explanation: 43/50 = 86.00%, but the paper prints 86.6, outside the rounding interval [86.55, 86.70]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 49.7 rather than 50.

issues.title: 'Majority' used for 18 of 50 patients (36%) in the normal BMI range
issues.explanation: The text calls 18 of 50 patients a majority, but 36% is at most a plurality. The same paragraph says 'most patients (n = 18)' are aged 30-40. This is a wording slip that does not change any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A BMI table showing more than 25 patients in the normal range.

quotes.text: the majority (n = 18) had a BMI in the normal range (18.5 -24.9)

issues.title: LDA period ends 10/2023 in the Abstract but 17 September 2023 in the Methods
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Methods give different end dates for the review window. It is a small inconsistency that affects no result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Abstract date reflects follow-up or data extraction.

quotes.text: who received LDA between 5/2021 and 10/2023
between May 18, 2021, and September 17, 2023

10.1016/j.biopha.2023.115723.headline_claim: CCSA shows superior efficacy over placebo in post-COVID asthenic syndrome, based on MFI-20 and MoCA changes and supporting fMRI findings.
10.1016/j.biopha.2023.115723.overall: The claim of superior efficacy is not supported at the strength stated: it rests on two borderline, uncorrected scale results (MFI-20 p = 0.043, MoCA p = 0.023) in 15 per arm, a null FAS-10, and within-group imaging contrasts without a between-group test. Retrospective registration and a headline that departs from the registered imaging primary add further doubt. At most the data suggest a preliminary signal, which matches the Abstract's 'potential effectiveness' rather than the Conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: MFI-20 total score (headline outcome; the paper does not label a primary outcome)

primary_outcomes.measure: Changing patterns of brain activation using task fMRI with a cognitive paradigm

issues.title: Conclusion states 'superior efficacy' from a self-described single-centre pilot of 15 per arm
issues.explanation: The Limitations call the study a small single-centre pilot needing larger studies, and note that MoCA gains may reflect learning over a short follow-up. The Conclusion nevertheless says the study allows the authors to state superior efficacy, including on neuroimaging. With 15 patients per arm, borderline p-values and a null FAS-10 result, the data support only a preliminary signal. The Abstract's 'potential effectiveness' is more consistent with the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A powered, pre-registered primary analysis showing the between-group effect, or a Conclusion limited to preliminary signals.

quotes.text: This is a single centre study, which lets us consider it a pilot, requiring future research including larger amounts of patients.
Thus, the conducted study allows us to state the superior efficacy of CCSA over placebo.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion states 'superior efficacy' of CCSA over placebo from a 30-patient single-centre study (15 per arm) that the authors themselves call a pilot. The limitations section acknowledges the pilot status, but the unqualified conclusion wording is stronger than the evidence supports, and the abstract uses the softer 'potential effectiveness'.

issues.title: Superiority rests on MFI-20 (p = 0.043) and MoCA (p = 0.023) among many uncorrected tests; FAS-10 null
issues.explanation: The paper tests three clinical scales plus task and resting-state fMRI contrasts, and states that the imaging tests are uncorrected. The two scale results used for the superiority claim are borderline (p = 0.043 and 0.023) and were not corrected for the three scales. FAS-10, a third fatigue scale, showed no between-group difference (p = 0.4406). The headline therefore leans on selected nominally significant outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single primary outcome with a hierarchical testing plan, or adjusted p-values remaining below 0.05.

quotes.text: threshold of statistical significance p < 0 ⋅ 001 without correction for multiple comparisons
Differences between groups were not statistically significant (p = 0 ⋅ 4406).

second_reader.what_stands: The paper bases its superiority claim on MFI-20 (p = 0.0434) and MoCA (p = 0.02344) between-group differences, and neither would survive even a simple correction across the three scales. FAS-10 is null (p = 0.4406). The text does not say the scale tests were uncorrected; the 'without correction' statement concerns the fMRI analyses. 'Many' tests is accurate only if the fMRI comparisons are counted. The registry's primary outcome is fMRI, not these scales.

issues.title: Neuroimaging 'superiority' inferred from drug arm having more significant clusters than placebo arm
issues.explanation: Tables 6 and 7 report separate within-group before > after maps at uncorrected thresholds. The CCSA arm shows six clusters and the placebo arm one. The authors contrast these and the Conclusion says superiority is seen with neuroimaging, but no group-by-time interaction test is reported. A difference between 'significant' and 'not significant' is not itself a significant difference, and the decrease in activation is not shown to be a benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group (group x time) fMRI analysis showing a significant difference.

quotes.text: It is shown that activation differences in the group that received the drug include multiple cognitive areas versus only the visual cortex in the group that received placebo
Moreover, the superiority of efficiency is observed not only according to the corresponding scales and questionnaires,  but  also  with  the  use  of  high-tech  neuroimaging techniques.

second_reader.what_stands: The neuroimaging 'superiority' rests on the drug arm showing more uncorrected clusters (6) than the placebo arm (1) in separate within-group analyses, with no direct between-group test of change. A difference in significance is not evidence of a difference between arms, and the activation change is a decrease with an uncertain functional meaning. The within-group fMRI analyses were not corrected for multiple comparisons.

issues.title: Registered 2023-07-10, about 14 months after the study start (2022-05-18) and ethics approval
issues.explanation: The paper cites NCT05939622 without stating when registration occurred. The registry shows first submission on 2023-07-10 and study start on 2022-05-18, and the paper reports ethics approval on 18.05.2022. Registration therefore followed enrolment, so the primary outcome could not have been fixed in advance in a verifiable way. Combined with the shift in emphasis to the scales, this weakens trust in the headline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing an earlier registration before enrolment began.

quotes.text: The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05939622).
the approval of the local ethics committee was obtained (No. 29/3 dated 18.05.2022)

issues.title: Registered primary is task fMRI, but headline superiority is drawn from MFI-20 and MoCA scales
issues.explanation: The paper's stated aim and the registry's primary outcome (change in task fMRI activation, baseline to day 10) are imaging measures, and the paper designates no primary outcome. The Abstract and Conclusion headline instead the MFI-20 and MoCA differences, which were registered as secondary (the registry lists 3 secondary outcomes). Imaging change in the drug arm is reported as a decrease in activation without a between-group test, so the declared primary does not demonstrate superiority.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis plan naming MFI-20 as primary, or earlier registry versions listing it as primary.

quotes.text: To assess executive network using resting-state fMRI and patterns of brain activation using task fMRI
demonstrated clinical superiority in the reduction of asthenic symptoms for the group of patients treated with CCSA

issues.title: Two peaks in Tables 2 and 5 print FWE p of 0.087 and 0.434, above the stated p ≤ 0.05 threshold
issues.explanation: The Methods set an FWE threshold of p ≤ 0.05, and Results 3.2 calls activation in the same areas significant. Table 2 prints the supplementary motor peak as 'P FWEcorr < 0.087' and Table 5 prints the right prefrontal peak as 0.434. Both exceed the stated threshold, so either the cells are mislabelled (the FDR value may be the one used) or these peaks are not significant as defined. These are descriptive within-group activation tables, so the effect on the efficacy conclusion is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the FDR value was the criterion for these two peaks, or a corrected table showing FWE p ≤ 0.05 for them.

issues.title: 'Matched by sex and age' in abstract, but randomized arms differ by 14 years in median age (42.0 vs 28.0)
issues.explanation: The abstract says the 30 patients were matched by sex and age. The study randomized patients, and Results 3.1 reports median ages of 42.0 years for CCSA and 28.0 years for placebo. The difference is not statistically significant, but with 15 per arm that is weak reassurance. The wording of the abstract overstates the balance, and age may matter for the MoCA practice effect the authors mention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of an age-matched allocation procedure, or mean ages that are similar.

quotes.text: The study included 30 patients matched by sex and age with postCOVID asthenic syndrome.
The median age for the CCSA and placebo groups was 42 ⋅ 0 [26 ⋅ 5; 46 ⋅ 5] years and 28 ⋅ 0 [26 ⋅ 0; 43 ⋅ 5] years

issues.title: Table 1 lists two 'Inferior parietal lobule (left)' seeds, the second with positive x = 52
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives two seeds with the same left-hemisphere label. One has x = -46 and the other x = 52, which is a right-hemisphere coordinate. Either the label should read 'right' or the minus sign is missing. The seed list defines regions of interest only, so no efficacy result rests on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original table showing a distinct label (for example right) or x = -52 for the second row.

quotes.location: Table 1, first Inferior parietal lobule (left) row
Table 1, second Inferior parietal lobule (left) row

10.1016/j.bjid.2026.105892.headline_claim: Systemic corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone did not provide significant benefit in patients with persistent post-COVID interstitial lung disease, though the authors note a 6MWT improvement only in the prednisolone arm.
10.1016/j.bjid.2026.105892.overall: The paper's main finding, no clear benefit of prednisolone on lung function over placebo, is reported, but it is weakly supported: small groups, no power calculation, no between-group estimates or CIs, retrospective registration with a different registered primary outcome, and inconsistencies in the dose and several table entries. The within-arm 6MWT finding should not be read as a treatment effect. The 'no benefit' statement is better read as 'no difference detected in an underpowered trial'.

primary_outcome.name: Forced vital capacity (FVC, litres)

primary_outcomes.measure: The rate of radiological, functional and quality of life improvement in prednisolone treatment for persistent interstitial lung disease following SARS-CoV-2.

issues.title: Null result stated as 'no additional benefit' with no between-group estimates or CIs and no power calculation
issues.explanation: The Methods say interpretation rests on effect estimates and 95% CIs, yet the tables give only within-group means, SDs and within-group significance flags for the continuous outcomes. With about 31 to 35 per arm and no sample size calculation, a failure to find significant differences cannot show equivalence. The Abstract's wording could be read as showing that prednisolone does not work, which the data cannot establish. If anything this understates a possible treatment effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group differences with 95% CIs excluding a clinically important FVC benefit.

quotes.text: Interpretation of the findings was based primarily on effect estimates and their corresponding 95% Confidence Intervals
systemic corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone did not provide additional benefits in patients with post-COVID interstitial lung disease.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no between-group effect estimates or 95% CIs for any outcome, despite stating that interpretation relies on them, and it did no power calculation (which it discloses). The conclusion is hedged (small sample, larger trials needed), so the abstract's 'did not provide additional benefits' is a stronger wording than the body supports, but the absence of a power calculation is acknowledged rather than concealed.

issues.title: Prednisolone dose given as 1 mg/kg/day in the Abstract but 0.5 mg/kg/day in Methods
issues.explanation: The Abstract says prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for one month. The Methods say 0.5 mg/kg/day for 30 days, then tapering. The dose is the core of the intervention, and a null result for corticosteroids is interpreted against it. Readers cannot tell what dose was tested, and the Discussion's regimen limitation depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or erratum showing the dose actually delivered, and which statement is a typo.

quotes.text: prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for 1month followed by gradual dose reduction)
Patients in the treatment group received prednisolone at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg/day for 30 days

issues.title: Trial registered 2024-12-04, over three years after the 2021-08-10 start; paper does not disclose this
issues.explanation: The registry shows the study started in August 2021 and was first submitted in December 2024, after enrolment. The paper only states that the study was registered and does not say it was retrospective. A late registration means the prespecified primary outcome and analysis cannot be verified against a contemporaneous record, which matters given the registry and paper outcomes differ.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated protocol or ethics-approved outcome specification predating enrolment, or an earlier registry version.

quotes.text: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov under registration number NCT07380152.

issues.title: Registered primary: composite radiological/functional/QoL at 10 months; paper's primary: FVC (L) at 6 months
issues.explanation: The registry lists a composite improvement rate over 10 months as the primary outcome. The paper names FVC in litres as primary with follow-up to 6 months and reports no analysis of a composite rate. Because registration was retrospective, the paper's choice cannot be checked against an earlier record. All domains were null here, so the practical effect on the conclusion is limited, but the primary outcome in the paper is not the registered one and no explanation is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or protocol listing FVC at 6 months as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: The primary outcome was FVC, expressed in Liters (L).

issues.title: 15% loss (78 randomised, 66 analysed) analysed as modified ITT; Table 2 uses only 29 + 28 = 57
issues.explanation: The authors describe their analysis as approximating modified intention-to-treat and give the reasons for exclusion. This is a defensible choice at this attrition level, but it is not a full ITT analysis, with no imputation or sensitivity analysis. The pulmonary function tables use fewer participants (57) than the 66 stated, which the text does not explain. This weakens confidence in the null findings modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 or supplementary data showing participants lost by arm and reasons, and a sensitivity analysis with all randomised.

quotes.text: Accordingly, the analytical strategy approximated a modified intention-to-treat approach, considering all participants with at least one post-baseline assessment available.
Placebo Group (n ¼ 29)

issues.title: Within-arm 6MWT gain (prednisolone only) highlighted as potential benefit despite no between-group difference
issues.explanation: The Abstract reports that walking distance increased significantly only in the prednisolone group. The Results say no significant between-group differences were detected. A significant change in one arm and not the other is not evidence of a treatment effect, and the unadjusted 6MWT result is one of many outcomes tested. The Discussion nonetheless proposes a beneficial effect on muscular dysfunction. The prednisolone group also started lower with a much larger SD.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant group-by-time interaction for 6MWT with a prespecified hypothesis.

quotes.text: Walking distance increased significantly only in the prednisolone group.
Conversely, the significant improvement in 6MWT distance observed only in the prednisolone group suggests a potential beneficial effect on post-COVID muscular dysfunction.

issues.title: Abstract swaps group sizes: placebo n=31 and prednisolone n=35 versus 35 and 31 in Results and Table 1
issues.explanation: The Abstract gives the placebo group as 31 and the prednisolone group as 35. Results and Table 1 give 35 placebo and 31 prednisolone. The Abstract's own sex percentages fit the Table 1 assignment (placebo 14/35 female = 40%, so 60% male), so the Abstract labels are the ones that are wrong. The slip is cosmetic for the conclusions but misleads anyone reading only the Abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 showing 31 placebo and 35 prednisolone analysed participants, with Table 1 headers being the ones mislabelled.

quotes.text: The placebo group (n = 31) comprised 60% male participants with a median age of 51years
Consequently, the final analysis included 31 patients in the prednisolone group and 35 patients in the placebo group.

issues.title: Table 1 prednisolone ethnicity counts 16 + 24 = 40 in a group of 31; 24 (77.5%) is also not 24/31
issues.explanation: The two ethnicity rows are the only categories shown, yet the prednisolone column counts sum to 40 against n = 31. The Black percentage 77.5% also does not equal 24/31 (77.4%). The placebo percentages likewise carry small rounding slips (71.5% and 28.5% for 25/35 and 10/35). This is a table error affecting a baseline comparability claim. The reported p = 0.78 for ethnicity cannot be reproduced from the printed counts.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 24 Black participants and the White/Asian row being a subset, or a third category dropped from the table.

quotes.location: Table 1, White or Asian row, prednisolone column

issues.title: 'All' parameters improved in both groups, but prednisolone TLC fell from 91.6% to 86.6% (and 5.18 to 4.78 L)
issues.explanation: Results state all spirometric parameters improved from baseline in both groups. In Table 2 the prednisolone group's TLC (% and litres) is lower at V2 than at baseline. The prednisolone baseline TLC (91.6 ± 36.4%) is also far from the placebo baseline (73.9 ± 13.2%) with a very large SD, which sits uneasily with the statement that TLC baselines were comparable. The overall null conclusion is not changed, but the sentence overstates uniform improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors defining 'spirometric' as FEV1 and FVC only and noting TLC separately, with comparable TLC baselines shown.

quotes.text: All spirometric parameters demonstrated improvement from baseline to follow-up visits in both groups

issues.title: CRP 'within normal range (<1.0 mg/dL)' but prednisolone baseline mean 1.06; Discussion says 'mildly elevated'
issues.explanation: Results say CRP stayed within the normal range (<1.0 mg/dL) throughout, yet the prednisolone baseline mean is 1.06 mg/dL, above that limit. The Discussion says CRP remained mildly elevated, so the paper describes the same variable in two opposite ways. The difference is small and does not bear on the between-group conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the normal-range claim refers to medians or to most participants, with data showing that.

quotes.text: C-Reactive Protein (CRP) concentrations remained within the normal reference range
C-reactive protein and D-dimer levels remained mildly elevated throughout the study

10.1016/j.bjpt.2025.101247.headline_claim: In men with chronic post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis, aerobic and combined aerobic/resistance exercise improved ventilatory function, fibrosis grade, dyspnea and QoL, with aerobic exercise improving exercise capacity most.
10.1016/j.bjpt.2025.101247.overall: The benefit of aerobic and combined exercise over resistance exercise and DBE alone on FVC and DLCO is plausible, but the pairwise statistics are internally inconsistent in several places, with p-values smaller than the printed CIs allow. Secondary claims about dyspnea, QoL, exercise capacity and fibrosis rest on unblinded assessments, a formula-estimated VO2max, or a single-reader ordinal CT score, and are stated more firmly than that supports.

primary_outcome.name: Ventilatory function: FVC and DLCO (% predicted)

issues.title: Dyspnea, QoL and exercise capacity assessed by unblinded assessors yet stated as firm benefits in conclusion
issues.explanation: Assessors of exercise capacity, dyspnea and QoL were unblinded, and participants could not be blinded, so these interview-based and effort-dependent outcomes are open to bias. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless present the superiority of aerobic and combined training on these outcomes without qualification. The limitation is acknowledged only in the final paragraph, so the secondary-outcome claims are weaker than presented. The blinded primary outcomes are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that these outcomes were collected by assessors masked to group allocation, or a sensitivity analysis showing results are unchanged.

quotes.text: In contrast, assessors of exercise capacity, dyspnea, and QoL were unblinded due to practical considerations.
Unblinded assessors for exercise capacity, dyspnea, and QoL may have affected results.
could similarly improve ventilatory function, lung fibrosis, dyspnea, and QoL

issues.title: Fibrosis-grade 'improvement' rests on one reader's ordinal 0-4 CT score analysed with parametric ANOVA
issues.explanation: Fibrosis grade is a five-level ordinal score read by a single radiologist. No reader reliability is reported, and a mean difference of 0.6-0.8 grades is analysed with a mixed ANOVA that assumes interval data. The conclusion states that exercise improves lung fibrosis, but the limitations section does not mention this measurement issue or the short 12-week window. A claim of structural improvement is therefore stronger than this evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported inter- or intra-reader agreement for the CT grade and a non-parametric or ordinal analysis giving the same result.

quotes.text: Fibrosis grading was conducted by an experienced radiologist
A mixed 4 × 2 factorial ANOVA assessed
could similarly improve ventilatory function, lung fibrosis, dyspnea, and QoL

issues.title: Pairwise p = 0.001 printed beside 95% CIs whose lower bounds are 0.2-0.4 (DLCO, FVC) and are asymmetric
issues.explanation: Several pairwise comparisons print p = 0.001 although the CI lower limit lies just above zero, which implies a p near 0.04-0.05 on a normal approximation. Several CIs are also not centred on their own mean difference. The CIs and p-values cannot both be correct, which reduces confidence in the pairwise results for the primary outcomes. The comparisons would probably remain nominally significant, but the strength of evidence is overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that CIs are Bonferroni-adjusted while p-values are from a different model, together with the unadjusted CIs; or corrected values in Table 3.

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0525 (reachable range [0.0476, 0.0578] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.001 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Trial dated March-June 2024 (12-week programme) but manuscript received 14 June 2024
issues.explanation: The Methods place the trial between March and June 2024 with a 12-week intervention, and the article was received on 14 June 2024. That leaves very little time for final post-testing, analysis and writing, particularly if enrolment was staggered. It may simply reflect loose date reporting, so it cannot be resolved without exact enrolment and follow-up dates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Exact first-enrolment and last-follow-up dates showing the last 12-week assessment occurred in late May or early June 2024.

quotes.text: This trial, conducted from March to June 2024
quotes.location: Methods, Study settings and ethical considerations

quotes.text: Received 14 June 2024

issues.title: Exercise capacity is formula-estimated VO2max from treadmill time, not measured
issues.explanation: VO2max was derived from time to exhaustion with a fixed linear formula, so every 1 minute of treadmill time maps to 2.94 ml/kg/min regardless of participant. Group differences therefore reflect treadmill time, and comparison to an MCID for measured VO2max is less meaningful. Since the aerobic group trained on a treadmill, practice effects on the test modality may favour that group. The authors acknowledge the limitation and label the outcome 'estimated'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Directly measured VO2max or treadmill time in a non-trained modality showing the same group ordering.

quotes.text: estimated VO2max = 2.94 × (time to exertion in minutes) + 7.65
Limitations include the inability to directly measure VO2max

10.1016/j.brat.2025.104917.headline_claim: CBM-I training for fatigue is acceptable and feasible for people with long-term conditions, shows promise in reducing fatigue and associated symptoms, and a full-scale trial is justified.
10.1016/j.brat.2025.104917.overall: The feasibility conclusions (adequate recruitment, retention above 50%, adherence about 77%, no device-related adverse events) are supported, apart from a few small count slips in the acceptability and adherence percentages. Statements that the intervention shows promise in reducing fatigue are weakly supported: the study was not powered for efficacy and made no inferential tests, the fatigue intervals include zero, and missing-data handling is not described. The large interpretation-bias effect rests on an adapted, unvalidated task and should be read as exploratory.

primary_outcome.name: Interpretation bias index (ambiguous scenarios task) at T1, between-group, adjusted for baseline

issues.title: Conclusion says 'promising effects' on fatigue though fatigue intervals include zero; no inferential testing
issues.explanation: The Methods say effect sizes are descriptive only and the study was not powered for efficacy. Yet the abstract and conclusions say CBM-I 'shows promise in reducing fatigue', and the Discussion says people given CBM-I 'appeared to show lower levels of fatigue'. The CFQ effects are small (g 0.09-0.32), and from the printed SEs the mean-difference intervals include zero at every time point. Depression (PHQ-9) is somewhat better supported, but it is one of about 20 uncorrected descriptive outcomes. This supports a conclusion that a full trial is warranted, not one about fatigue reduction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Table 4 intervals for CFQ that exclude zero in the source PDF, or an explicit statement that the fatigue effects are within chance and only hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: As this was a feasibility study no significance tests were performed, and effect sizes are provided for descriptive reasons only
CBM-I training is an easy to administer, relatively brief digital intervention which shows promise in reducing fatigue and associated symptoms in those with long term health conditions.
Table 4 shows small effect sizes were found for CFQ and PHQ-9 at all follow-up points

issues.title: Large interpretation-bias effect (g = 0.834) rests on a task adapted for new populations without reported validation
issues.explanation: The bias outcome comes from a CFS-specific task re-worded for MS and cancer after consultation with patients. No reliability or validity data for this adapted version are given. The paper also does not say whether training and test scenarios differ in content. The large effect on this task is therefore best read as an exploratory signal, not a confirmed change in the proposed mechanism.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reliability or validity data for the adapted task in the MS and cancer samples, or evidence that test items differ from training items.

quotes.text: The materials were further adapted to tap into fatigue across LTCs by consulting with people with MS or cancer who experience fatigue.

issues.title: Missing-data handling not described despite 'ITT'; T1 retention 68% (FLEX) vs 83% (control)
issues.explanation: By T3 about 30% of participants had no assessment, and at T1 the experimental arm retained fewer participants than control (45/66 against 54/65). The paper says analyses were intention-to-treat but does not say how missing outcomes were handled or whether missingness differed by arm or illness group. Because the efficacy signals rest on available-case mixed models, they are conditional on missing-at-random assumptions the paper does not examine. This does not affect the feasibility finding, which met its criterion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of missing-data handling (for example mixed model under MAR with sensitivity analyses) and a comparison of baseline characteristics of completers and non-completers by arm.

quotes.text: 75.57% (experimental = 45, control = 54) were retained at post-intervention (T1)
All analyses were intention-to-treat.

issues.title: Control interpretation-bias SD printed as 0.11 vs 1.03 in FLEX; raw difference 0.98 vs g = 0.834
issues.explanation: The text reports control M = 0.62 (SD 0.11) and CBM-I M = 1.60 (SD 1.03) for the headline outcome. A ten-fold SD difference on the same scale is implausible and would imply a far larger standardised effect than g = 0.834. The control SD is probably 1.1 with a dropped digit, but the paper cannot confirm that. The printed beta of 0.664 is also given next to the interval of g.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source article or dataset showing the control SD as 1.11.

issues.title: T1 acceptability respondents: arms 47 + 54 = 101 but total printed as 97 (74.05%)
issues.explanation: The text gives 97 respondents (74.05% of 131) but splits them into 47 experimental and 54 control, which sums to 101. The experimental figure of 47 also exceeds the 45 experimental participants reported as retained at T1. One of these counts is misprinted, which leaves the denominators behind the T1 acceptability means in Table 3 uncertain, though the acceptability conclusion is not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT figure or Table 3 footnote giving T1 acceptability n by arm that sums to the printed total.

quotes.text: At T1, 74.05% ( n = 97) participants (experimental = 47, control = 54) provided acceptability ratings.
75.57% (experimental = 45, control = 54) were retained at post-intervention (T1)

issues.title: FLEX non-adherent percentage printed as 16.42% but 11/66 = 16.67%
issues.explanation: The results give 11 of 66 experimental participants as non-adherent and print 16.42%. The count over the arm size gives 16.67%, and the three adherence categories only sum to 100% with 16.67. This is a small reporting slip that does not change any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for the FLEX arm (for example a count of 10.84 of 66, which is not possible) or an erratum stating a different count.

quotes.text: 16.42% ( n = 11) were non-adherent

script.explanation: 11/66 = 16.67%, but the paper prints 16.42, outside the rounding interval [16.42, 16.43]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 67.0 rather than 66.

10.1016/j.brs.2021.10.368.headline_claim: The title states that at-home taVNS given twice daily for 4 weeks reduces Long COVID anxiety and fatigue, and the conclusions say it may reduce anxiety and improve stress and fatigue (first study in the fenced text, P3.112).
10.1016/j.brs.2021.10.368.overall: The headline claim that taVNS reduces anxiety and fatigue is not supported by the data in this abstract, which are pooled before-after changes in 13 people with the randomized comparison withheld. At most, the data are hypothesis-generating and consistent with the hedged 'may reduce' wording. The baseline anxiety figure also lacks a stated denominator.

primary_outcome.name: not stated; GAD-7 anxiety score is the main reported measure

issues.title: Title asserts taVNS reduces anxiety/fatigue from pooled pre-post scores in 13 people, blinded comparison withheld
issues.explanation: The only reported evidence is a fall in GAD-7 from 13.7 to 8.6 to 3.4 across all participants, and the arm comparison is withheld. The 4-week value comes after an open-label phase in which everyone knew they were on active treatment, and the improvement is on a self-rated scale. With 13 participants and no sample-size justification, a causal title ('REDUCES') is not supported. The 'may reduce' conclusion is closer to what the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unblinded randomized results showing a clear active-versus-sham difference in GAD-7 and fatigue at 2 weeks.

quotes.text: AT-HOME TELEMEDICINE CONTROLLED TAVNS TWICE DAILY FOR 4 WEEKS REDUCES LONG COVID SYMPTOMS OF ANXIETY AND FATIGUE
Randomized data remains blinded at abstract deadline.
At home taVNS may reduce anxiety and improve stress and fatigue.

second_reader.what_stands: The title states causally that taVNS reduces anxiety and fatigue, but the only evidence reported is pooled pre-post scores from 13 participants (some on sham for the first 2 weeks, with an open-label second half), while the randomized blinded comparison is explicitly not reported. The abstract's conclusion is more cautious ('may reduce') and calls for further studies, and fatigue has no numbers given at all, so the title overstates what the abstract supports; the claim of intent is not being made, only that the evidence shown cannot separate treatment effect from placebo, natural recovery or r

issues.title: 72.7% anxiety prevalence is not a share of the 13 enrolled (fits 8/11); denominator unreported
issues.explanation: The abstract says 13 subjects were enrolled, but 72.7% cannot be produced by any whole count out of 13. It matches 8 of 11, which suggests two participants are missing from the baseline figure. The abstract does not say who they are, and the 25% at 4 weeks has no stated denominator, so the baseline-to-4-week comparison cannot be checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow or note stating that 11 participants had baseline symptom data (e.g. 2 enrolled but not assessed), with 8 of them reporting anxiety.

quotes.text: we enrolled 13 subjects who were previously COVID positive
Overall, 72.7% of participants reported anxiety as a symptom at the initial visit.

10.1016/j.brs.2023.01.1672.headline_claim: M1-targeted HD-tDCS paired with a rehabilitation program was effective in reducing PASC-related fatigue (and anxiety, with improved quality of life), with 10 sessions over five weeks.
10.1016/j.brs.2023.01.1672.overall: The fatigue improvement favouring active stimulation is probably real in direction, but the headline between-group difference (14.03) disagrees with the paper's own arm means (11.77), and the responder P value (reported < .001, recomputed about .007) and regression reporting are inconsistent. Registration came after the study start, the registered 10-week follow-up is unreported, and the conclusions about recovery and low cost go beyond a single 5-week trial.

primary_outcome.name: Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS) total score at end of treatment (week 5)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: From date of randomization (1 week before intervention beginning) up to 5 weeks (T1) and up to 10 weeks (T2; follow-up)

issues.title: Primary MFIS difference 14.03 does not match the arm reductions 22.11 vs 10.34 (difference 11.77)
issues.explanation: The abstract gives mean MFIS reductions of 22.11 (active) and 10.34 (sham), which differ by 11.77. The Results report a between-group difference of 14.03 (CI 7.78-20.28). Table 2 baseline and week-5 means reproduce the 22.11 and 10.34 exactly, so the 14.03 is not explained by the paper's own data. The primary effect is overstated by about 2.3 points, though it stays significant on either figure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 14.03 is a covariate-adjusted model estimate, with the model output showing it, or corrected raw data in which the arm reductions differ by 14.03.

quotes.text: (mean group MFIS reduction of 22.11 points vs 10.34 points)
mean group difference 14.03 points; effect size 1.2; 95% CI 7.78 e 20.28; P < .001

second_reader.what_stands: The printed arm reductions (22.11 vs 10.34) give a difference of 11.77, which does not equal the reported 14.03 (CI 7.78 to 20.28, centred on 14.03), and the paper does not say how 14.03 was derived. A covariate-adjusted model estimate would be a reasonable explanation, but the paper does not state this, and the adjusted Group coefficient it does print (14.22) is not 14.03 either. The mismatch is therefore real and unexplained in the text, but it is not necessarily an error.

issues.title: Recovery, durability and low-cost claims exceed a single 5-week trial with no follow-up or cost data
issues.explanation: The Discussion says HD-tDCS plus rehabilitation 'improves the chances of recovery' and may reduce public health costs. It also refers to a 'sustained response'. The Conclusion cites 'low cost' as support for clinical application. The trial measured only a change in fatigue score at week 5 and reports no recovery, durability or cost outcomes. Both arms also received rehabilitation and improved, so the incremental benefit of stimulation over rehabilitation alone is the only supported finding. The conclusions go beyond the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported follow-up data showing sustained improvement, or cost data supporting the low-cost claim.

quotes.text: Taken together, HD-tDCS and rehabilitation improves the chances of recovery, offer incentives to treatment compliance and may have an impact on public health costs.
These fi ndings along with the low cost of the therapy and its tolerability suggests its potential application in the clinical practice for the treatment of PASC.

issues.title: Responder OR 0.24 (CI 0.08-0.70) appears inverted and P < .001 does not fit; chi-square gives P about .007
issues.explanation: With 77.14% vs 45.71% responders, the active-vs-sham odds ratio is about 4.0. The printed 0.24 is its reciprocal, with the reference group unstated. The printed P < .001 also fits neither the CI nor the chi-square test the Methods describe. The CI upper bound of 0.70 implies P of about .01, and the 27/35 vs 16/35 table gives chi-square of about 7.3, P of about .007. The responder result is real but weaker than printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated reference category (sham as reference) together with an exact test result that actually gives P < .001 for this 2x2 table.

issues.title: Regression F(7,54) does not match Table 3's five predictors or n = 70; anxiety P = .3 in text vs 0.04 in Table 3
issues.explanation: Table 3 lists five predictors (group, age, sleep difficulty, depression, anxiety), but the text reports an F-test with 7 numerator df and 54 denominator df. That implies 62 analysed participants, not the 70 used elsewhere, and the missing data are not explained. The text says baseline anxiety was associated with response at P = .3, but Table 3 marks anxiety as significant at P = 0.04. The Methods call the model 'mixed linear', while Table 3 is labelled multiple linear regression. The exploratory analysis cannot be reconstructed from what is reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A model specification with seven terms and 62 complete cases, plus a corrected anxiety P value.

quotes.text: A signi fi cant regression equation was found ( F (7,54) ¼ 17.40, P < .001)
Anxiety severity at baseline was associated with lower response (P ¼ .3)

issues.title: Trial registered 2022-03-16, about six months after the 2021-09-14 start, yet described as prospective
issues.explanation: The registry record shows registration after enrolment began. The paper describes the trial as prospective and cites the registry number as if it were a prospective registration. Retrospective registration means the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be verified as fixed in advance. This weakens confidence in the fatigue result but does not by itself invalidate it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version dated before 2021-09-14 or a protocol with a timestamp before enrolment, showing the primary outcome was fixed in advance.

quotes.text: This was a prospective, double-blind, randomized, shamcontrolled clinical trial (NCT05289115)

issues.title: Registry primary time frame includes a 10-week follow-up (T2) not mentioned in the paper
issues.explanation: The registry lists the primary outcome over 5 weeks (T1) and 10 weeks (T2, follow-up). The paper measures outcomes only at baseline and the end of treatment and does not mention T2. The registered follow-up component of the primary outcome is therefore unreported, which limits what can be said about durability. Whether this is a change of plan or an artefact of a later registry edit cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing the T2 follow-up was added only after the trial completed, or a statement in the protocol that follow-up was not undertaken.

quotes.text: The primary and secondary outcomes were measured at the baseline (T0) and at the endpoint (T1).

issues.title: Abstract conclusion gives secondary anxiety and quality-of-life results equal weight with the primary fatigue result
issues.explanation: The abstract conclusion states that the intervention was effective for fatigue and anxiety and improved quality of life. Anxiety and quality of life were secondary outcomes, and the paper does not report the number of comparisons in its Bonferroni correction. Those outcomes' significance depends on which test is used. Whether this is selective emphasis is a matter of judgement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical or Bonferroni-adjusted analysis showing the secondary outcomes remain significant at the corrected threshold.

quotes.text: An intervention with M1 targeted HD-tDCS paired with a rehabilitation program was effective in reducing fatigue and anxiety, while improving quality of life in people with PASC.

issues.title: Table 1 acute-phase categories sum to 37 (active) and 38 (sham) against n = 35 per arm
issues.explanation: The five acute-phase severity categories are presented as a single classification. Their counts add to 37 in the active arm and 38 in the sham arm, and the percentages add to more than 100%. Either some participants are counted twice or some counts are wrong. This is a baseline-description error with little bearing on the efficacy findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote saying the categories overlap (for example cumulative hospital support), or a corrected table summing to 35 per arm.

quotes.text: Active (n ¼ 35)

10.1016/j.brs.2023.01.232.headline_claim: The title states that tDCS combined with cognitive training is efficacious for the neurocognitive symptoms of long COVID-19, while the abstract reports only pilot findings and describes the sham-controlled comparison as still planned.
10.1016/j.brs.2023.01.232.overall: The abstract contains no quantitative results and no controlled comparison, so it cannot support a conclusion that tDCS plus cognitive training is efficacious for long-COVID neurocognitive symptoms. The body is appropriately hedged as preliminary, but the title's 'Efficacy' overstates it. At most it supports a rationale for the planned sham-controlled trial.

primary_outcome.name: A-PASC cognitive and emotional complaints (pilot)

issues.title: Reported cognitive/emotional improvement comes from an uncontrolled pilot with no data; sham trial only planned
issues.explanation: The abstract reports decreased complaints and better recall in a pilot with no comparison group, no sample size and no statistics. Such changes could reflect practice effects, natural recovery or expectation. The paper itself calls them preliminary and says the active-versus-sham comparison is still to come, so the weakness is disclosed; the issue is limited to how far the improvement statements can be read as benefit of tDCS.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Showing the pilot had a concurrent control or that the abstract makes no benefit claim beyond describing within-group change.

quotes.text: Preliminary results from a pilot study a decrease of cognitive and emotional complaints evaluated by A-PASC inventory.
We will compare the ef fi cacy of active vs. sham tDCS, combined with cognitive training, to improve these neurocognitive symptoms.

issues.title: Title claims 'Efficacy' of tDCS plus training; abstract reports only uncontrolled trends and a planned comparison
issues.explanation: The title states efficacy, yet the abstract gives only unquantified pilot observations, describes cognitive changes as 'trends', and says efficacy will be compared against sham in a future trial. Efficacy cannot be established without the controlled comparison, so the title goes beyond what is reported. This is a wording problem; the body is cautious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the title is a programme-assigned label and the authors present the work explicitly as hypothesis-generating only; the abstract body does largely do that.

quotes.text: EFFICACY OF TRANSCRANIAL DIRECT CURRENT STIMULATION AND COGNITIVE TRAINING FOR THE NEUROCOGNITIVE SYMPTOMS OF LONG COVID-19
They showed an improving trend in lexicon assess, and in phonemic verbal fl uency.

10.1016/j.brs.2024.12.534.headline_claim: fNIRS effectively assesses pain-related cortical activation, and tDCS may enhance pain-related brain function and improve chronic pain perception in ADRD.
10.1016/j.brs.2024.12.534.overall: The conclusion about tDCS improving chronic pain perception is only weakly supported by the visible results, which are channel-wise fNIRS statistics and correlations with pain scores. The hedged pilot framing limits the damage, but the causal and practice-changing language overreaches. Because the excerpt is truncated, the design cannot be fully assessed.

issues.title: Pilot abstract infers tDCS improves chronic pain perception from channel t-tests and fNIRS-NRS correlations
issues.explanation: The visible results are channel-level t-statistics (e.g. HbO t = -2.25, p = .03) and correlations between fNIRS channels and NRS pain scores (r = .69, .50). These do not show that tDCS changed pain ratings, yet the conclusion says tDCS leads to improvements in chronic pain perception and signals a potential shift in pain management. The wording is hedged ('may', 'pilot', 'further investigation is warranted'), and the excerpt is truncated, so the full design cannot be judged; the claim is overreaching rather than clearly unsupported. The p-values are uncorrected across many channels.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The full abstract showing a controlled or pre/post comparison in which NRS pain ratings improved significantly after tDCS, with multiplicity addressed.

quotes.text: tDCS may enhance pain-related brain function and modulate pain pathways, leading to improvements in chronic pain perception.
signaling a potential shift in pain management strategies for brain disorders

10.1016/j.brs.2025.04.023.headline_claim: Combining anodal tDCS over the left prefrontal cortex with olfactory training restores smell in persistent COVID-19 anosmia, with a durable effect compared with sham stimulation plus training.
10.1016/j.brs.2025.04.023.overall: The between-group mixed-model results for VAS and SST show a large difference favouring active stimulation, so the efficacy signal is probably real for these subjective and identification-based outcomes. The conclusions on safety, wide applicability, durability and mechanism go beyond a 52-patient single-centre trial with no reported registration, and the placebo-arm statements rest on weak within-arm tests. The analysed-versus-randomized mislabelling in the Abstract is minor and explained by one withdrawal.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline to end of stimulation (t1) in VAS-smell and Sniffin' Sticks identification score

issues.title: No trial registry entry reported; two co-primary outcomes with no multiplicity handling
issues.explanation: The paper describes a randomized trial with an ethics approval number but gives no registry identifier, so prespecification of the primary outcome, analysis and sample size cannot be checked. The primary outcome is defined as the t0-to-t1 change in both VAS-smell and SST, with no adjustment for two co-primary endpoints. Both results are very strong (p < 0.001), so the practical effect on the conclusion is limited, but selective reporting cannot be excluded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prospective registry record matching the reported primary outcomes and analysis.

quotes.text: The study protocol was approved by the Territorial Ethic Committee (244/2023 - DB id 13157).
The detailed sample size calculation can be found in the Supplementary File.

issues.title: Conclusion calls treatment 'safe' and suitable for 'millions' from 35 treated patients with one line on adverse events
issues.explanation: The abstract concludes the treatment is safe and a suitable widespread option for millions, based on 35 treated patients at a single centre recruited from treatment requests across Italy. Safety is supported only by a single sentence saying no adverse events were reported, with no description of how they were monitored. The trial also cannot say whether tDCS or its combination with olfactory training is responsible, as the Discussion itself admits. The generalisation and safety claims are not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety monitoring protocol and a large enough sample to bound the rate of adverse events.

quotes.text: This safe and inexpensive treatment can therefore represent a suitable and widespread option for millions of individuals.
The procedure was well tolerated by all participants and no adverse events were reported.

issues.title: Placebo 'no amelioration' and 77% responder figures rest on within-arm tests; no between-group responder test
issues.explanation: The abstract states that no olfactory amelioration occurred in the placebo group, and the Discussion that OT with sham 'did not achieve any beneficial effects'. These rest on a non-significant Stuart-Maxwell test within 17 patients, which does not show absence of effect, and 1 of 17 placebo patients did move from anosmia to hyposmia. The 77% responder figure is a within-arm result with no formal comparison with the placebo rate. The primary between-group interaction analysis is sound, so this weakens only the secondary categorical claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group test of responder proportions showing a clear difference, or confidence intervals showing the placebo arm cannot be consistent with a modest improvement.

quotes.text: In the experimental group, 27 out of 35 patients (77 %) showed a significant improvement (Stuart-Maxwell test: p < 0.001).
as no patients in the placebo group regained a significant olfactory function

issues.title: Claims of clinical evidence for olfactory-circuit involvement not testable with this design
issues.explanation: The paper concludes that its findings support the involvement of brain olfactory circuits in COVID-19 anosmia. The trial applied tDCS over the prefrontal cortex with simultaneous olfactory training and measured only smell scores, with no imaging or physiological data to show which network was affected. The authors themselves state they cannot separate the contribution of tDCS from olfactory training or of the PFC from the OFC. The mechanistic claim is therefore speculation, not a result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Imaging or neurophysiological data from the trial showing changed olfactory network activity linked to the outcome.

quotes.text: our findings provide important clinical evidence supporting the existing neuroimaging data regarding the involvement of brain olfactory circuits

issues.title: Abstract gives 35 as experimental-arm randomized n; Methods say 36 (35 analysed after one withdrawal)
issues.explanation: The Abstract says 52 patients were randomly assigned with 35 in the experimental arm, but the Methods say 53 were randomized, 36 to the experimental arm. The Results explain that one experimental patient withdrew consent, which accounts for 35 analysed. The Abstract therefore mislabels the analysed numbers as randomized, and the paper does not make clear in text that the analysis excluded a randomized patient. No result depends on this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The abstract being explicitly labelled as reporting analysed participants.

quotes.text: Of the 80 participants screened, 53 were deemed eligible and included in the study.
Except for one patient in the experimental group (withdrawn consent), 52 participants completed the entire trial course.

10.1016/j.brs.2025.08.018.headline_claim: Combined prefrontal tDCS plus cognitive training may improve attention, processing speed and inhibitory control in PASC patients with cognitive complaints, compared with sham tDCS plus cognitive training, though the authors call the findings preliminary.
10.1016/j.brs.2025.08.018.overall: The trial is small and openly described as exploratory. Its positive findings are three nominally significant, uncorrected interaction tests of about 16, driven largely by lower baseline scores in the active arm, since raw endpoint means are nearly the same. The abstract's hedged conclusion is closer to what the data support than some Discussion statements, and the numeric slips (Table 1, Table 3) are minor but indicate limited checking.

primary_outcome.name: Six standardized neuropsychological tests (verbal memory, working memory, executive functioning, attention, language); the paper's headline significant results are FDT inhibitory control, FDT processing speed and TEADI divided attention

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in neuropsychological assessment between experimental groups

issues.title: Headline interactions arise from baseline gaps; raw endpoint means are near-identical (TEADI 123.3 vs 124.3)
issues.explanation: In Table 2 the active arm starts worse on all three headline measures, and by endpoint the arms are essentially equal. The 'greater improvement' in the active arm is therefore consistent with regression to the mean or with a baseline difference, not necessarily with a treatment effect. The limitation section mentions this, but the conclusion still reads the interactions as treatment benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis adjusting for baseline score (ANCOVA) or a randomization-based check showing the interaction persists, with endpoint differences favouring the active arm.

quotes.text: started at numerically lower baseline performance levels

quotes.location: Table 2, TEADI Total score row, baseline tDCS
Table 2, TEADI Total score row, endpoint tDCS

second_reader.what_stands: The raw endpoint means are near-identical for TEADI (123.31 vs 124.31). The tDCS group also started numerically lower on TEADI and on the two significant FDT sub-scores, and the authors acknowledge this as a possible explanation. The paper cannot show that the interactions arise from the baseline gaps: the baseline differences were reported as non-significant, the models are fitted to longitudinal data with covariates, and the adjusted changes in Table 3 differ from the raw ones. So a baseline or room-to-improve explanation is plausible and disclosed, but not established.

issues.title: About 16 primary-outcome tests, no correction; the three positive findings have p = 0.034-0.046
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports about 16 group-by-time tests across six cognitive domains with no multiplicity control and no single prespecified primary endpoint. The conclusions on attention, processing speed and inhibitory control rest on three p-values of 0.034-0.046 with effect-size CIs touching 0. Roughly 0.8 false positives would be expected by chance, and none of the three survives even a modest correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy naming these three subscores as the primary endpoints, or confirmation in an independent sample.

quotes.text: We did not apply correction for multiple comparisons given the exploratory nature of this pilot study.
inhibitory control (effect size [ES] = 0.07, 95 % CI 0 to 0.23, p = 0.046), processing speed (ES = 0.08, 95 % CI 0 to 0.25, p = 0.034)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports about 16 primary sub-score tests without multiplicity correction, and the three positive findings have p = 0.034 to 0.046, none of which would survive a Bonferroni-type adjustment. The authors state this plainly (Section 4, Section 6.3) and label the results preliminary, so the omission is disclosed rather than hidden. The abstract conclusion that tDCS + CT 'might be effective' still rests on these uncorrected p-values.

issues.title: Text says all cognitive tests improved in both groups; TENON delayed hits fell and two RAVLT scores did not improve
issues.explanation: The Results say every cognitive assessment improved significantly (ps < 0.009) in both groups except working memory and FDT reading. Tables 2 and 3 show TENON delayed hits worsened significantly in both arms on a higher-is-better scale, and RAVLT learning over trials fell with a CI spanning zero. RAVLT recognition in the active arm also has a CI that includes zero. The general-improvement narrative, attributed to training, is therefore overstated for these measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source output showing delayed-hits changes are positive on the reported scale, or that the TENON delayed-hits score is error-count based (lower is better), contradicting the Table 2 footnote.

quotes.text: All cognitive assessments presented a significant improvement from baseline to endpoint in both groups

quotes.location: Table 3, Language (TENON) Delayed Hits row, active tDCS + CT
Table 3, RAVLT Learning over trials row, active tDCS + CT

issues.title: Discussion says tDCS 'can enhance' executive function and credits CT for both-group gains; design cannot show either
issues.explanation: Headline wording is cautious, but the Discussion and Future Directions state the effect as established ('can enhance executive functioning') and claim anatomical specificity without any active-site control. The Conclusion also attributes both groups' improvement to cognitive training, which cannot be separated from practice effects and natural recovery, as the authors themselves note. These statements go beyond three uncorrected, borderline results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable beyond the wording itself; a training-only or active-site control arm would be needed to support these statements.

quotes.text: Our findings offer preliminary evidence that combining tDCS with CT can enhance executive functioning in patients with PASC
which might be attributed to the CT delivered
