issues.explanation: With 40 participants, percentages move in steps of 2.5%, so 67.6% cannot occur. The four categories (67.6, 2.5, 7.5, 22.5) sum to 100.1%, consistent with a typo for 67.5%. This is a trivial slip in baseline description.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A denominator other than 40 for this item.

quotes.text: Most participants (67.6%) lost both their sense of taste and smell during their illness.

10.1016/j.ctim.2024.103107.headline_claim: A combined plant extract (CPE) supplement reduced moderate-to-severe long COVID symptoms, particularly fatigue and post-exertional malaise, with an acceptable safety profile, though larger trials are needed.
10.1016/j.ctim.2024.103107.overall: The headline claim is hedged in the abstract, but the evidence is thin: two borderline-significant symptom results (p about 0.02-0.03) from an unvalidated self-report instrument, with no multiplicity control, and a null primary CRP outcome. The placebo reformulation that unblinded 10 participants adds a plausible bias toward overstating benefit, so the results are best read as hypothesis-generating. The numeric slips found (24.4% vs 24.2%, 400 vs 500 mg, CRP wording) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Change in CRP and change in total symptom score (co-primary)

issues.title: No multiplicity control: 2 primary outcomes, 19 symptoms compared, fatigue and PEM highlighted at p about 0.02-0.03
issues.explanation: The trial had two primary outcomes (CRP and total symptom score) and compared 19 individual symptoms, then headlined fatigue and PEM. All tests used an unadjusted 0.05 threshold. With a total symptom score p of 0.029 and fatigue/PEM p-values of 0.020 to 0.027, a modest correction would remove significance, so these should be treated as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or adjusted p-values that keep these results significant.

quotes.text: significantly differences between the treatment groups were observed for fatigue and PEM (pvalue of 0.027 and 0.020, respectively)
two-tailed tests and a significant level set at p-value < 0.05

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states a single unadjusted alpha of 0.05 with no multiplicity correction across 2 primary outcomes and 19 symptom comparisons, and the highlighted fatigue and PEM results (p = 0.027 and 0.020) would not survive a Bonferroni correction for 19 comparisons (0.0026). The total symptom score p = 0.029 would also not meet a 0.025 split across the two primary outcomes. The authors label the trial exploratory and call for confirmation, but their abstract and conclusion still emphasise fatigue and PEM without noting the multiplicity.

issues.title: 10 of 33 placebo participants stopped early after a placebo reformulation that unblinded them; analysis not adjusted
issues.explanation: Ten placebo participants discontinued because the placebo formulation was altered (colorants removed), and the authors acknowledge this led to unblinding and could overstate CPE efficacy. Outcomes are self-reported symptom scores, which are vulnerable to unblinding, and the missing post-discontinuation data were handled by LOCF. No sensitivity analysis excluding these participants or accounting for the change is presented, and the abstract conclusions do not reflect this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis excluding or separately analysing the 10 affected participants that gives the same effect estimates.

quotes.text: In the placebo group, ten participants discontinued the study treatment early due to a modification in the placebo formulation
Another limitation was the early discontinuation of 10 participants in the placebo group, which led to unblinding.

second_reader.what_stands: 10 of 33 placebo participants (30%) stopped early after a placebo formulation change, and the authors state this led to unblinding; this is disclosed, and they argue it may have overestimated the CPE effect. The paper does not say how participants were unblinded or whether the unblinded group knew its allocation, and describes no analysis adjusting for or testing the impact of the discontinuations beyond ITT with LOCF, so 'stopped early and unblinded' is supported but 'unblinded by the reformulation' mechanism is only asserted by the authors.

issues.title: Discussion wording on efficacy and safety is stronger than an exploratory 66-person, 7-day trial supports
issues.explanation: The Discussion states the RCT 'has shown' a significant reduction and gives 'initial evidence on the efficacy and safety', while one of two primary outcomes (CRP) was null and the symptom outcome used an unvalidated, self-reported instrument. The safety claim comes from a 7-day exposure in a small sample. The abstract itself is hedged, so the overstatement is moderate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; rests on interpretation of wording.

quotes.text: This RCT has shown that participants receiving CPE supplementation experienced a statistically significant reduction in the total symptom score
this study provides initial evidence on the efficacy and safety of CPE

issues.title: No power calculation; n=33 per arm with fatigue and PEM findings emphasised
issues.explanation: The sample size was set from pilot-trial guidance rather than a power calculation, and the authors acknowledge this. The trial is labelled exploratory and conclusions are hedged, so the weakness is disclosed. It still limits how much weight the fatigue and PEM effects, which come from 3 vs 12 and 6 vs 17 events, can carry.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a stated design choice.

quotes.text: a sample size of 30 participants per treatment group was determined
the lack of sample size calculation, no assessment of blinding success, a small sample size

issues.title: Primary total symptom score uses a new questionnaire with only expert content validation
issues.explanation: The total symptom score, one of two primary outcomes, comes from a questionnaire developed for this study with only a three-expert IOC check. Reliability and responsiveness were not assessed, a gap the authors acknowledge. Because the symptom benefit rests entirely on this instrument, it supports only tentative conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reliability and responsiveness data for the questionnaire, or replication with a validated instrument such as the FSS.

quotes.text: A self-report questionnaire, specifically developed for this study, was used to assess 19 commonly reported long COVID symptoms
Additionally, the reliability of the long COVID symptom questionnaire was not assessed.

issues.title: Text says CRP fell in both groups, but placebo median rose from 1.93 to 2.10 mg/L
issues.explanation: The Results state CRP decreased in both groups after treatment, but the placebo median went from 1.93 at baseline to 2.10 after treatment. Only the CPE median fell (2.46 to 1.65). The statement is inaccurate as written but does not change the null CRP between-group result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level data showing the placebo group's mean or paired change decreased despite the median rise.

quotes.text: After treatment, CRP levels decreased in both groups, with medians (IQR) of 1.65 (0.87, 5.32) and 2.10 (0.69, 4.66) mg/L, respectively.

issues.title: Listed ingredients sum to 400 mg of a 500 mg capsule; remaining 100 mg unexplained
issues.explanation: The five ingredient masses add to 400 mg, but the capsule is described as 500 mg. The paper does not say what makes up the other 100 mg (excipient or other content), so the true herbal dose is unclear and the 4500 mg/day figure cannot be assumed all active. This is a reporting gap with limited effect on the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper or product specification that the capsule contains 100 mg of excipient or standardized extract not listed.

quotes.text: Each 500 mg capsule of CPE contained dried powders of Citrus aurantifolia (Christm.) Swingle (180 mg), Tiliacora triandra (Colebr.) Diels (110 mg), Cannabis sativa L. (50 mg)

issues.title: Table 1 concomitant medication in CPE arm: 8 (24.4%) but 8/33 = 24.2%
issues.explanation: Table 1 prints 24.4% for 8 of 33 CPE participants, but 8/33 is 24.2%. No integer count out of 33 gives 24.4%. This is a small baseline-table slip and does not bear on any efficacy result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the denominator for this row was not 33 (for example, missing data for one participant).

quotes.location: Table 1, Concomitant medications row, CPE column

quotes.text: CPE (N = 33)

script.explanation: 8/33 = 24.24%, but the paper prints 24.4, outside the rounding interval [24.35, 24.50]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 32.8 rather than 33.

10.1016/j.ctim.2026.103367.headline_claim: A yoga program developed for adults with post COVID-19 condition was feasible, with preliminary effects suggesting benefit on mental but not physical HR-QoL, and adequately powered trials are needed.
10.1016/j.ctim.2026.103367.overall: The feasibility conclusion is reasonably supported, and the abstract and conclusion rightly call the SF-36 analyses underpowered and non-significant. Weaknesses are a few mismatched abstract adherence figures, an uncorrected baseline imbalance, and a Discussion sentence that reads a non-significant MCS difference as suggestive of benefit.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility of the yoga program (recruitment, reach, adherence, acceptability, retention, adverse events)

issues.title: Abstract adherence 95% (≥1/wk) and 65% (≥2/wk) don't fit 13 yoga participants (12/13=92.3%, 9/13=69.2%)
issues.explanation: The abstract reports 65% of yoga participants attending ≥2 sessions/week and 95% attending ≥1/week. With 13 participants, 95% cannot occur, because the nearest values are 92.3% and 100%. The Results counts (3 at ≥3/wk, 6 at 2-3/wk, 3 at 1-2/wk, 1 at ≤1/wk) give 9/13 = 69.2% at ≥2/wk, which matches the Results' 69.3% but not the abstract's 65%. The text also prints 7.6% for 1/13, which is 7.7%. The feasibility conclusion still stands, but the headline adherence figures do not match the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative definition or denominator for the abstract percentages (for example, a per-session or per-week attendance analysis) that yields 65% and 95%.

quotes.text: ≥ 1 session/week = 95%
Adherence  was  slightly  higher  in  the  yoga  group  (69.3%)
(7.6%) attended ≤ 1  sessions/ week

issues.title: Discussion says yoga 'may have beneficial effects' on mental HR-QoL despite MCS p=.054, CI -0.06 to 7.04
issues.explanation: The MCS between-group effect (B = 3.49, 95% CI -0.06 to 7.04, p = .054) was not significant. The data come from 29 participants in an open-label trial with self-reported SF-36, and the groups differed in age and sick leave at baseline. The Discussion nonetheless contrasts a 'beneficial' mental effect with a null physical effect. The physical effect also has a CI spanning zero (-3.60 to 1.00, g = -0.41), so the data do not support treating the two scales differently. The abstract and conclusion are appropriately cautious; the problem is confined to this Discussion sentence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording in the Discussion that frames the MCS result as hypothesis-generating only, with no directional benefit claim.

quotes.text: findings suggested that a 12-week yoga intervention may have beneficial effects on mental, but not physical HR-QoL
There was no statistically significant difference in (between-group) effects on MCS
Preliminary (underpowered) analyses showed no pre-to-post intervention group differences

issues.title: Baseline imbalance in age (56.5 vs 47.1) and sick leave (84.6% vs 37.5%); sick leave not adjusted
issues.explanation: The yoga group was older and far more often on sick leave, and reported lower work capacity at baseline. The mixed models adjust for baseline score, age and sex, but not for sick leave, which may relate to the mental-health outcome. The authors acknowledge that such imbalances 'may either exaggerate or mask' effects. This weakens the between-group MCS and PCS comparisons, which are already framed as preliminary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis that also adjusts for sick leave and work capacity and gives the same MCS estimate.

quotes.text: Participants randomized  to  yoga  were  significantly  older ( p = .004) and more likely to be on sick leave ( p = .010).
adjusted for baseline score, age, and sex

10.1016/j.cyto.2024.156688.headline_claim: Circulating calprotectin is higher in persistent post-COVID hyposmia than in controls and falls after three months of olfactory training, so it holds potential as a biomarker for monitoring treatment response.
10.1016/j.cyto.2024.156688.overall: The finding that calprotectin is higher in hyposmic patients than in controls is plausible but rests on small groups. The claims that it tracks treatment response and that local inflammation is a main driver of persistent olfactory loss are not supported by a single-arm before-after design with no untreated hyposmic comparator. The dispersion data in Table 3 are internally inconsistent with the printed ranges, so the paper's conclusions should be read as tentative and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Serum and nasal supernatant calprotectin concentration, HT0 vs HT1

issues.title: Calprotectin fall after training inferred from a single-arm before-after design with no untreated hyposmic group
issues.explanation: The 36 hyposmic patients were measured once before and once after 12 weeks of training. Both control groups are healthy normosmic people, not untreated hyposmic patients followed over the same period. Post-COVID olfactory loss often improves on its own over months, so the fall in calprotectin and the TDI gain may reflect time rather than training. This weakens the claim that calprotectin tracks treatment response.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from a concurrent untreated hyposmic group showing no comparable calprotectin or TDI change over 12 weeks.

quotes.text: The decrease in calprotectin levels post-olfactory training implies a role in monitoring and evaluating treatment responses.
This group was tested again after 3 months of an olfactory training protocol (HT1).

second_reader.what_stands: The calprotectin fall is inferred from a single-arm before-after comparison of the same 36 patients. There is no untreated hyposmic group, so natural recovery over 3 months, regression to the mean or assay and sampling drift cannot be separated from any effect of training. The authors' Discussion attributes the decrease partly to the training protocol and does not list the missing untreated arm as a limitation, although the abstract's 'implies a role in monitoring' is more cautious.

issues.title: Table 3 SDs exceed the maximum allowed by printed ranges (e.g. CG2 nasal SD 2.00 vs range 2.94-4.82)
issues.explanation: Several SDs in Table 3 are larger than any set of values lying inside the printed range could produce. The clearest case is CG2 nasal supernatant, with SD ± 2.00 against a range of 2.94-4.82. The same problem appears in the CG2 serum, CG1 serum and HT1 serum cells, and for the HT1 nasal SD of 4.64 if the shifted layout is read that way. Either the SDs or the ranges are misreported, so the dispersion data in Table 3 cannot be relied on. The medians, which carry the main comparison, are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the bracketed values are not ranges (for example interquartile ranges or a different dispersion measure), or the raw data showing SDs within the printed ranges.

quotes.location: Table 3, CG2 median (range), nasal supernatant column
Table 3, CG1 SD / CG2 median rows
Table 3, HT1 row, blood samples column

issues.title: 36 patients, no sample-size justification, and biomarker/monitoring claims without accuracy or correlation analysis
issues.explanation: No sample-size calculation is given, and the authors acknowledge the small number of participants. The conclusions use cautious wording, but the abstract and Discussion still describe a monitoring role. No ROC analysis, cutoff performance or calprotectin-TDI correlation is provided to back a biomarker claim. This weakens the biomarker conclusion to a tentative, hypothesis-generating one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported power or precision justification, or ROC/correlation analyses supporting the biomarker and monitoring claims.

quotes.text: The main limitation of our study is the small number of participants.
Circulating calprotectin holds potential as a biomarker in persistent olfactory dysfunctions after COVID-19.

issues.title: Persistent nasal inflammation presented as a main factor in establishing enduring olfactory loss
issues.explanation: The study compares biomarker levels across groups and before and after training. It cannot establish that inflammation is a main factor in the establishment of chronic olfactory disease. The causal wording goes beyond a correlational finding. The Discussion also credits training with modulating pro-inflammatory responses, with no mechanistic evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longitudinal data showing calprotectin elevation preceding and predicting persistence of olfactory loss, or hedged wording presenting this only as a hypothesis.

quotes.text: it allows to indicate the persistence of a local post-acute inflammatory status as a main factor in the establishment of an enduring olfaction disease.

issues.title: Paired HT0 vs HT1 data apparently analysed with Mann-Whitney; no multiplicity handling across several comparisons
issues.explanation: The only test named is Mann-Whitney, which is for independent groups, yet HT0 and HT1 are repeated measures on the same patients. If it was used for that comparison, the pairing was ignored. That would normally understate the significance of the within-patient change. The paper also runs many pairwise comparisons across four groups and two sample types without stating any correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that a paired test (Wilcoxon signed-rank) was used for HT0 vs HT1, with the multiple comparisons declared as exploratory or corrected.

issues.title: Olfactory training called safe without any adverse-event reporting in this study
issues.explanation: The Discussion calls olfactory training an easy and safe therapy without significant side effects. The study reports no adverse events or tolerability data for its 36 patients. The sentence is background and is not part of the headline biomarker conclusion. It is still an unsupported safety statement within the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A citation to safety evidence for the training protocol, or reported adverse-event data from these patients.

quotes.text: Olfactory training is an extremely easy and safe therapy without significant side effects

issues.title: Mean age and NCS values differ between text and Table 2 (52 vs 53 years; NCS 0.6 vs 0.5 in HT1)
issues.explanation: The Methods give a mean age of 52 years for HT0 and HT1, but Table 2 gives 53. The Results say mean NCS is 0.6 in both HT0 and HT1, but Table 2 gives 0.5 for HT1. These are small reporting slips that do not change any comparison. They show that the descriptive reporting was not carefully cross-checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the two values refer to different quantities (for example median versus mean) or a corrected table.

mean value 0.6 in HT0 and HT1 patients

10.1016/j.eclinm.2023.101946.headline_claim: AXA1125 significantly reduced patient-reported fatigue (CFQ-11) versus placebo in fatigue-predominant Long COVID, despite no significant difference in the primary τPCr endpoint, and the authors call for larger multicentre trials.
10.1016/j.eclinm.2023.101946.overall: The primary mitochondrial endpoint was null, and the favourable CFQ-11 fatigue difference (LSMD -4.30, P = 0.0039) comes from a secondary, patient-reported outcome in a 41-patient single-centre pilot. It is a reasonable signal for a larger trial but not demonstration of efficacy or of a metabolic mechanism. Several table and date errors (a placebo change of -2.25 vs -1.60, impossible SDs) lower confidence in the reporting but do not overturn the fatigue result.

issues.title: Pilot with null primary endpoint described as showing 'marked symptomatic improvement' and 'no safety concerns'
issues.explanation: The primary mitochondrial endpoint was not met, with the numerical change in tau PCr going the wrong way. The paper nonetheless frames the secondary patient-reported fatigue result as demonstrating marked improvement. The 41-patient single-centre sample is small and the patient-reported measure is open to placebo and expectation effects. Safety is called a non-issue although treatment-emergent events were more frequent on AXA1125 (52.4% vs 20.0%) in a very small sample. The fatigue signal is hypothesis-generating at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy making CFQ-11 co-primary, or a larger trial confirming the effect.

quotes.text: making this one of the fi rst randomised, double blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials in this disease to demonstrate marked symptomatic improvement.
Treatment with AXA1125 was well tolerated and raised no safety concerns

second_reader.what_stands: The null primary endpoint is clearly disclosed throughout, so it is not hidden. However, 'marked symptomatic improvement' rests on an unadjusted-for-multiplicity, patient-reported secondary endpoint in a 41-person pilot, and the primary estimate pointed the unfavourable way. The Discussion's 'marked' and 'first ... to demonstrate' therefore overstate what a pilot can show, and 'raised no safety concerns' is stronger than the data allow: TEAEs were 52.4% vs 20.0% (my unadjusted P ≈ 0.03), there was one grade 3 event, and 21 patients over 4 weeks cannot rule out safety signals. issues.title: No multiplicity control across secondary and post-hoc outcomes; fatigue result survives only a simple Bonferroni
issues.explanation: The Methods state that no multiplicity allowance was made for the secondary outcomes. The CFQ-11 total result would survive a simple correction across the four stated secondaries, but the subscale and post-hoc findings are more fragile. This weakens secondary claims rather than the main CFQ-11 result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified testing hierarchy for the secondary endpoints.

quotes.text: As this was a phase 2a study, there was no allowance for multiplicity for the secondary outcomes.

issues.title: Post hoc responder analyses used to claim a metabolic mechanism although tau PCr did not improve
issues.explanation: Responders are defined by the fatigue outcome, so differences in other measures between responders and non-responders are exploratory and prone to selection effects. The Discussion nonetheless claims that a 'positive trend' in tau PCr suggests the treatment works through metabolism and oxidative stress. The randomised comparison shows no benefit on tau PCr (longer recovery on AXA1125, P = 0.24). The mechanistic claim is not supported by the trial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified mediation analysis showing tau PCr change mediates the fatigue effect.

issues.explanation: In Table 2 the placebo total Likert score goes from 28.05 to 26.45, a change of -1.60, but the printed mean change is -2.25. The placebo subscale changes (-1.30 and -0.30) also sum to -1.60. With complete data the printed value cannot be right. 10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103358.headline_claim: Rovunaptabin (BC007) improved fatigue and quality of life versus placebo in post-COVID syndrome patients with GPCR functional autoantibodies, with a good safety profile, supporting further larger trials.
10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103358.overall: The safety finding (no significant TEAE difference, expected transient INR/aPTT rise) is reasonably reported, but the efficacy claims rest on a 30-patient exploratory trial with uncorrected secondary endpoints, some barely under 0.05, and the Abstract mislabels t-values as effect sizes. The headline suggestion of a curative, causal therapy is not supported; the results are hypothesis-generating only. The other numeric slips (d48 vs d42, 30 vs 29 at V7, vitality t-value) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Number of participants with treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) to day 28 (co-primary: TEAEs to day 70)

primary_outcomes.measure: Mean change from baseline in score on FACIT-FS scale at Day 30.

issues.title: Dozens of fatigue/QoL endpoints tested uncorrected; several 'significant' p-values are 0.036-0.040
issues.explanation: Each fatigue and SF-36 score was tested separately without correction, across many scales and visits, and only the significant ones are tabulated. Several headline results sit just under 0.05 (FACIT 0.0378, social functioning 0.0396, MCS 0.0357), and even a Bonferroni split over the three fatigue scores (0.0167) would remove FACIT. Yet the Added value and Discussion state a significant improvement in fatigue and quality of life versus placebo without caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or adjusted p-values showing the key fatigue results survive correction.

quotes.text: Thus, each fatigue score was tested separately without correction for multiple testing, as we did not know which of the endpoint would show a potential effect after treatment.
Rovunaptabin showed a significant improvement of self-reported fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that scores were tested without multiplicity correction, and about 20 RCT endpoints (about 40 tests including cross-over) were analysed. Three RCT p-values (0.0378, 0.0396, 0.0357) lie in the 0.036-0.040 range, and only Bell and SF-36 vitality would survive a Bonferroni correction. 'Dozens' is an overstatement for the RCT part alone, and the uncorrected testing is disclosed and the study labelled exploratory.

issues.title: 30-patient exploratory trial concludes possible 'curative and causal therapy' and efficacy vs placebo
issues.explanation: The trial (14 vs 16 participants) had no efficacy power calculation, a primary safety endpoint that was non-significant, and uncorrected self-reported secondary outcomes. The conclusions nevertheless describe a significant improvement in fatigue and quality of life compared to placebo and a potentially curative, causal therapy. The causal link between GPCR-fAAb neutralisation and symptoms is also not shown, as some patients lost the autoantibodies without improvement in a placebo-first subgroup.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation in an adequately powered trial with a pre-specified primary efficacy endpoint.

quotes.text: The data of the present clinical trial suggest that rovunaptabin might offer a novel approach for a curative and causal therapy for an autoimmune subgroup of patients with PCS.
For this initial exploratory pilot study, a sample size of n = 30 was considered sufficient, to obtain data for a subsequent study with an effect size of 0 ⋅ 35.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does hedge and calls for larger trials, but a 30-patient exploratory trial with a safety primary endpoint, uncorrected secondary endpoints, a baseline imbalance and at most 91 days of follow-up cannot support 'curative' therapy. It also cannot support unqualified statements of significant improvement 'compared to placebo'. The paper additionally says it hypothesises a B-cell/plasma-cell immunomodulating mechanism without testing it.

issues.title: Abstract calls t-values 'effect size' (Bell 3.64, FACIT 2.10, FSS -2.66); Table 3 effects are 7.54, 2.91, -0.43
issues.explanation: The Abstract reports the Table 3 t-statistics as 'effect size'. The actual treatment differences are 2.91 (FACIT), 7.54 (Bell) and -0.43 (FSS) points. The label makes the effects look like standardised effects of a size they are not; the 'SD' column in Table 3 is also evidently a standard error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'effect size' is meant as the t-statistic.

quotes.text: Bell score (effect size = 3 ⋅ 64, p = 0 ⋅ 0004)

issues.title: SF36 vitality RCT t-value printed 2.97; estimate/SE gives 4.03
issues.explanation: Table 3 prints t = 2.97 for vitality, but 6.65 divided by the adjacent 1.65 is 4.03. The CI and p = 0.0001 support 4.03, and 2.97 duplicates the cross-over FACIT row. The estimate and p stand; only the t cell appears wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors stating the t-value derives from a different model quantity than estimate/SE.

script.explanation: ratio: 6.65 / 1.65 gives 4.0303, not the printed 2.97. For the printed value to hold the denominator would have to be 2.23906, not 1.65.

issues.title: Summary gives cross-over start as d48; Methods and tables give d42 (V8)
issues.explanation: The Summary says the second treatment was given at d48, but the Procedures section says the switch began on d42 (V8). Table 2 lists cross-over adverse events on day 42, and a 28-day follow-up from d42 ends at d70, matching the co-primary endpoint. The Summary figure appears to be a slip; it does not change any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol amendment showing the second infusion was actually given at d48.

quotes.text: at day 0 (d0) and d48 with a follow-up of 28 days, respectively

issues.title: Text says 30 completed V7; Figure 2 caption gives 13 + 16 = 29
issues.explanation: The Results say 30 participants completed V7 with full primary data, yet the Figure 2 caption counts 13 in sequence A and 16 in sequence B at V7. The Fig. 1 legend also records a missing RCT visit in the rovunaptabin group. The denominator for the V7 efficacy comparisons is therefore unclear, though the discrepancy is only one patient.

10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103633.headline_claim: NR increased NAD+ within 5 weeks but did not significantly improve cognition, fatigue, sleep, or mood versus placebo; exploratory within-group analyses suggested benefits after 10 weeks of NR, warranting larger trials.
10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103633.overall: The finding that NR raises blood NAD+ is well supported despite minor numeric inconsistencies in the fold-change text and Table 1 sample sizes. The trial shows no significant benefit on any cognitive or symptom outcome versus placebo, and the within-group post-hoc benefits lack a controlled comparison. Conclusions about safety and about absence of cognitive effect go somewhat beyond what a small trial with heavy, uneven dropout can show.

issues.title: NR-NR NAD+ fold change at 5 weeks: 2.6 (Abstract, Discussion) vs 3.1 (Results)
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Discussion give a 2.6-fold rise at 5 weeks and 3.1-fold at 10 weeks in the NR-NR group. The Results state an average 3.1-fold rise at both 5 and 10 weeks. The 2.6 figure also appears in the Results as the 15-week value and as the PBO-NR 5-week value, so the true 5-week value is unclear. This does not change the qualitative NAD+ finding, but one reported result is inconsistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 3 or a supplementary table showing a 5-week NR-NR fold change of 2.6 and a 10-week value of 3.1, with the Results sentence being a typographical slip.

issues.title: 'Safe' and 'no significant differences in AEs' stated without a test; NR-NR discontinuation 21.6% vs 9.5%
issues.explanation: The conclusion calls NR 'safe' and the Discussion says there were no significant AE differences, but no AE comparison is reported. Table 2 shows AE-related discontinuation of 8/37 in NR-NR versus 2/21 in PBO-NR, including two definitely related, and treatment-related AEs such as rash and nausea. The small trial and high dropout cannot establish safety. The wording should be 'generally tolerated in this small sample'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified or reported statistical comparison of AE rates between phases or arms showing no meaningful difference with adequate precision.

issues.title: 'Does not meaningfully improve cognition' drawn from an underpowered null with wide CIs and 51% NR-NR dropout
issues.explanation: The paper reports no sample size calculation, ends with 36 completers, and has 51.4% dropout in NR-NR versus 14.3% in PBO-NR. The CIs are wide, for example RBANS total beta 6.08 (95% CI -10.86 to 23.01), so clinically meaningful effects in either direction are not excluded. Missing-at-random is assumed, although AEs and reinfection drove withdrawals. The statement that NR 'does not meaningfully improve cognitive functioning' is stronger than a null result from this design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation or equivalence margin showing the study could exclude a clinically important effect, plus sensitivity analyses for non-random dropout.

issues.title: NAD+ 2.6/2.1-fold and CIs 1.9-3.3/1.6-2.7 printed for both NR-NR (15/20 wk) and PBO-NR (5/10 wk)
issues.explanation: The Results give exactly the same fold changes and CIs for the NR-NR group at 15 and 20 weeks and for the PBO-NR group at 5 and 10 weeks of NR. issues.title: Table 1 NR-NR n = 29 vs 37 assigned to NR-NR in Results and Table 2; 8 participants unaccounted for

issues.title: Post-hoc pre-post NR changes (FSS -3.77, PSQI -0.74, BDI -1.67) read as benefit without a controlled comparison
issues.explanation: The reported improvements in fatigue, sleep and depression come from uncontrolled before-after changes in all participants after 10 weeks of NR, with no multiplicity correction. issues.title: Primary outcomes defined inconsistently: cognition only (Summary) vs cognition plus NAD+ (Methods)
issues.explanation: The Summary and Cognitive assessments sections name cognition (ECog, RBANS, TMT-B) as primary. The Primary analysis section says the primary outcomes also include blood NAD+. 10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103730.headline_claim: Home-based intranasal and transcranial photobiomodulation is safe and feasible and shows potential cognitive benefits for post-COVID-19 brain fog, particularly in adults under 45.
10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103730.overall: The primary composite comparison was not significant (p = 0.088, CI crossing zero), so the trial does not demonstrate efficacy; the positive framing rests on an unadjusted exploratory subgroup (<45, p = 0.028) and one task at selected timepoints. The pilot is honest in places, labelling the work hypothesis-generating, but the 'primary endpoint was met' and 'first controlled evidence of efficacy' statements overstate it. Safety and feasibility conclusions are reasonably supported.

primary_outcome.name: Mean change in Creyos cognitive composite score from baseline to Day 56

issues.title: Null primary composite (p = 0.088) described as 'met' and as first evidence of efficacy
issues.explanation: The prespecified primary endpoint, the Day 56 composite, did not reach significance (difference 0.043, 95% CI -0.007 to 0.092, p = 0.088). Yet the Discussion states the primary endpoint 'was met', the Results say the study 'successfully met its main objective', and the 'Added value' box claims 'first controlled evidence of itPBM's efficacy'. The abstract also says attention tasks 'improved consistently' although the single attention task was non-significant overall at Day 56. These statements are stronger than a null primary result with an exploratory subgroup supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary endpoint definition of 'met' as completion of measurement, with efficacy claims removed from the abstract and boxes.

quotes.text: While the primary endpoint was met as specified, the pattern of results underscores the need for larger, fully powered trials
This indicates that the study successfully met its main objective of evaluating itPBM's potential to alleviate brain fog in PCC.
provides the first controlled evidence of itPBM's efficacy for PCC cognitive impairment

second_reader.what_stands: The pre-specified primary composite did not reach significance (difference 0.043, 95% CI -0.007 to 0.092, p = 0.088), yet the Discussion says the primary endpoint 'was met as specified', the Results say the study 'successfully met its main objective', and the Research in context calls it 'the first controlled evidence of itPBM's efficacy'. The 'met' wording could be read as a feasibility or evaluation objective, and the paper elsewhere calls the result not significant and hypothesis-generating. But the efficacy and 'met' wording is not supported by the primary result.

issues.title: Efficacy claim for under-45s rests on an unadjusted subgroup p = 0.028 with no interaction test
issues.explanation: The conclusion that benefit is concentrated in younger adults rests on one subgroup p-value (0.028) in a trial where the overall effect was not significant. No test of treatment-by-age interaction is reported, many outcomes and timepoints were tested without adjustment, and the subgroup was about 31 people (17 active, 14 sham). The authors admit the analysis is exploratory, but the Interpretation and Research in context still present the age effect as a finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant, prespecified treatment-by-age interaction test, or a multiplicity-adjusted subgroup result.

quotes.text: with significant gains in participants <45 years (prespecified but exploratory, p = 0.028)
showing significant improvements in attention and composite cognitive scores in younger adults (<45 years).
quotes.location: Research in context, Added value of this study

second_reader.what_stands: The under-45 claim rests on a single nominal subgroup p = 0.028 (n = 17 vs 14) with no reported treatment-by-age interaction test and no multiplicity adjustment, while the overall primary was null. The paper does label the analysis as prespecified and exploratory and cautions against subgroup conclusions, but the Summary and Research in context still present 'significant improvements' in younger adults, and the estimates come from the model that adjusts for age stratum, so 'unadjusted' is not quite accurate.

issues.title: Table 3 footnote b labels Feature Match Day 56 (p = 0.133) as significant; same row says not significant
issues.explanation: Footnote b states a statistically significant overall difference at Day 28, Day 56 and Day 84, yet lists p = 0.133 for Day 56. The table row and the Results text say Day 56 was not significant overall. The slip is cosmetic, and the main text clarifies it, but the table's p-value column also prints only '<0.05' for the row.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing Day 56 omitted from the significance statement.

quotes.text: Statistically significant difference favoring Active itPBM in the overall group for the Feature Match task at Day 28 (p = 0.019), Day 56 (p = 0.133)

issues.title: Table 4 MSBQ row says no significant differences but cites an item-level p = 0.011 within the same cell
issues.explanation: The MSBQ specific-symptoms cell states there were no significant differences and gives >0.05 as the p value, but also cites 'Memory' favouring sham at p = 0.011 in older adults. The item-level, subgroup finding is unadjusted and not in the Results text. It is a minor internal inconsistency in how the row is summarised.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the 0.011 is an unadjusted post hoc item test excluded from the summary.
