issues.title: Z-score composite difference 0.043 restated as '4.3%' in Discussion; units mislabelled
issues.explanation: The primary result is a mean z-score difference of 0.043 (95% CI -0.007 to 0.092). The Discussion calls this a 4.3% difference (CI -0.7% to 9.2%). A z-score difference is in standard-deviation units, not percent, so the percentage label is wrong and could mislead readers about effect size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the composite is expressed on a percentage scale.

quotes.text: a 4.3% difference (95% CI -0.7% to 9.2%) on Day 56
a global composite score was calculated by averaging Zscores across all Creyos tasks at each time point

10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103737.headline_claim: REGENECYTE was safe and well tolerated and produced a meaningful and durable reduction in fatigue in post-COVID syndrome.
10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103737.overall: The finding that fatigue scores fell more with REGENECYTE than placebo is plausible and the CFQ-11 p-values are small, but it comes from 20 vs 10 patients, single-blind masking and patient-reported outcomes only. The paper has several internal inconsistencies between text and Table 3 (frailty, mental fatigue, EQ-5D, and individual p-values), plus uncorrected multiplicity. The headline 'meaningful and durable' benefit is best read as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), CTCAE v5.0

issues.title: No sample-size calculation (20 vs 10); abstract states a 'meaningful and durable' fatigue effect without hedging
issues.explanation: The sample size was chosen without formal calculation, and only 10 patients received placebo. The efficacy outcomes are all self-reported questionnaires in a single-blind design. The abstract and interpretation state a durable benefit as established, which is stronger than this design supports. The Discussion's hedging ('preliminary', larger trials needed) does not carry over to the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract that labels efficacy findings as exploratory and preliminary, or confidence intervals showing the effect estimate is precise.

quotes.text: selected without formal calculations
It produced a meaningful and durable reduction in fatigue symptoms
the sample size was relatively small (n = 30)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does state that no formal sample-size calculation was made (20 vs 10, safety-driven, exploratory) and acknowledges the small n as a limitation, so that part is disclosed rather than hidden. However, the Summary's Interpretation says 'meaningful and durable' without hedging, and the Findings say 'significantly and sustainably improved', even though fatigue was a secondary endpoint in a single-site, single-blind, unpowered trial with no confidence intervals or stated multiplicity control. The body text does hedge ('preliminary', 'larger confirmatory trials are needed'), so the point ho

issues.title: Frailty: 'no significant changes' in abstract vs significant between-group FRAIL differences in Results/Table 3
issues.explanation: The abstract and the Research in context box say frailty did not differ between groups. The Results say the REGENECYTE group had a significant, sustained FRAIL reduction compared with placebo, and Table 3 prints between-group p-values of <0.001 (W12) and 0.009 (W26). The paper never reconciles the two statements, so a reader cannot tell whether frailty improved. This is a reporting inconsistency on an exploratory outcome and leaves the main fatigue claim intact.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Table 3 FRAIL p-values come from a different analysis (for example, raw scores rather than level change) with the level-change test shown to be the one the abstract reports.

quotes.text: The REGENECYTE group demonstrated a statistically significant and sustained reduction in total FRAIL scale scores from week 6 to week 26, compared to the placebo group.
While no statistically significant between-group differences of level change were observed at any visit
There were no significant changes in frailty or cognitive scores.

issues.title: Text and Table 3 p-values differ: CFQ-11 Bimodal W26 0.004 vs <0.001; PGI-S W26 0.007 vs 0.003
issues.explanation: The Results text and Table 3 give different between-group p-values for the same week-26 comparisons. For CFQ-11 Bimodal the text says p = 0.004 and the table says <0.001. For PGI-S fatigue the text says 0.007 and the table says 0.003. The paper does not say which test produced which value. Every version is still below 0.05, so the conclusion is unchanged, but the reported results are unreliable at the level of individual p-values.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values come from a different test (for example, change-from-baseline Wilcoxon) than Table 3, with both labelled.

issues.title: Text says mental fatigue and EQ-5D-5L W26 differences were non-significant; Table 3 p-values are 0.002-0.035
issues.explanation: The Limitations say mental fatigue showed no significant improvement. Table 3 prints between-group p-values of 0.002 (W12) and 0.035 (W26) for it. Similarly, the Results say W26 EQ-5D-5L differences versus placebo were not significant, while Table 3 gives p-values of 0.005, 0.009 and 0.022 for three of the dimensions. The paper's wording and its table point in opposite directions, so the reader cannot tell which outcomes differed from placebo.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that Table 3 p-values test raw scores while the text refers to a stricter level-change analysis, with the latter reported.

quotes.text: Second, mental fatigue did not show significant improvement
However, the level changes observed at week 26 across the dimensions of EQ-5D-5L in the treatment group were not statistically significant compared to placebo.

issues.title: Dozens of fatigue, frailty, QoL and cognition comparisons at p<0.05 with no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: Many outcomes (CFQ-11 Bimodal, Likert and two subscales, PGI-S, FRAIL, five EQ-5D domains, EQ-VAS, index, MoCA) were each tested at two or more timepoints against an uncorrected alpha of 0.05, with no hierarchy. The strongest fatigue results are probably robust. Secondary claims about quality of life, mental fatigue and frailty are not protected against false positives.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or adjustment procedure, or an explicit statement that all non-CFQ-11 outcomes are descriptive.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.

issues.title: Discussion extends a 30-patient post-COVID trial to ME/CFS, anti-ageing uses and a 'strong safety profile'
issues.explanation: The Discussion speculates about use in ME/CFS and in broader regenerative and anti-ageing applications, none of which were studied. It also calls the safety profile 'strong' on the basis of 20 treated patients over 26 weeks. The language is hedged, but it goes well beyond the population and data in the trial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Removal or clear labelling of these statements as speculation outside the trial's evidence, with safety described as preliminary.

quotes.text: this therapy may also hold potential for addressing other fatigue-related conditions.
this treatment protocol could potentially be extended to ME/CFS

Our findings support the hypothesis that hUCB-based therapies such as REGENECYTE may warrant further exploration not only for post-COVID recovery, but also for broader regenerative and antiaging applications.

10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.104264.headline_claim: Low-dose prednisolone produces a statistically significant but modest short-term reduction in post-COVID symptom severity (PROMIS), driven mainly by fatigue, though below the prespecified clinical-relevance threshold; B vitamins showed no efficacy.
10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.104264.overall: The central finding, a small statistically significant benefit of prednisolone on the PROMIS composite that is below the prespecified 3-point threshold, is honestly stated and the arithmetic reconciles across tables. Reliance should be limited by the unvalidated composite, the uncorrected secondary and post hoc analyses, and a fatigue headline (-6.4) that cannot be matched to the reported tables. The flagged sample-size and outcome-switching concerns are not real problems.

primary_outcome.name: Change in PROMIS total T-score from day 0 to day 28 (composite of fatigue, dyspnoea, cognitive impairment, anxiety, depression)

primary_outcomes.measure: Pilot phase: Proportion of participants retained after 28 days
Confirmatory phase: Mean difference in PROMIS Total Score from day 0 to day 28

issues.title: Primary outcome is a study-specific PROMIS composite with no psychometric evaluation of the composite itself
issues.explanation: The primary endpoint is a custom composite of five PROMIS domains. The authors rely on validation of the individual domains and did not evaluate the composite. The 3-point clinically meaningful threshold is applied to it without composite-specific anchoring. This weakens how the clinical relevance of the -1.4 result can be interpreted, but it does not change the finding that the effect fell below 3 points.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published validation or MCID anchor study of this exact five-domain composite.

quotes.text: no additional psychometric reevaluation of the composite
assessed using a study-specific composite score derived from the PatientReported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) item banks

issues.title: Fatigue is presented as the driver of the effect via a post hoc, unreconciled -6.4 figure that cannot be matched to Table 2
issues.explanation: The abstract attributes the result mainly to fatigue with -6.4 points and p<0.001, a figure not traceable to Table 2, where the adjusted fatigue effect is -2.0 and the prednisolone-arm within-group change is -4.8. The metric (within-group change versus adjusted difference) is not stated. The paper calls the fatigue analysis both prespecified secondary and post hoc. The recommendation to move to a fatigue-only endpoint and a concluding sentence about fatigue rest on this exploratory result while the primary was only modestly and sub-threshold significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: eFigure S1 showing a PROMIS fatigue-domain between-group difference of -6.4 points with a stated metric, and a protocol listing the fatigue-driver analysis as pre-specified.

quotes.text: future trials may consider a more targeted primary endpoint focused on fatigue alone
quotes.location: Research in context, Implications of all the available evidence
Table 2, Fatigue, Change row, effect of prednisolone

issues.title: No multiplicity control described for secondary outcomes and post hoc timepoints, yet 'all' reported significant
issues.explanation: The Statistical analysis section describes three F-tests with no alpha adjustment and no hierarchy for the secondaries. The Results describe all secondary outcomes as significantly improved in the prednisolone group, and six follow-up timepoints and many within-group paired tests are analysed post hoc. The secondary p-values (0.001 to 0.02) are mostly small, so the pattern is probably robust. Still, the secondary findings should be read as supportive and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statistical analysis plan specifying a hierarchical or alpha-adjusted testing procedure covering the primary and secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: improved in the prednisolone group, including patient-reported symptoms as measured by MYMOP
Three null hypotheses were tested with corresponding F-tests within the models

10.1016/j.eng.2024.03.013.headline_claim: Lianhua Qingke tablets significantly improved the clinical symptoms of patients with long COVID cough and were associated with good safety and tolerance.
10.1016/j.eng.2024.03.013.overall: The main finding, that the trial arm had a shorter time to cough disappearance and better symptom scores, is large and consistent across outcomes. It rests on a self-reported diary endpoint with a placebo comparator, and its strength depends on how well blinding held. The reporting has several internal inconsistencies, notably in the follow-up counts and the PPS exclusions, but none of them undermines the headline result.

primary_outcome.name: Time to disappearance of cough within 14 days (FAS)

issues.title: Follow-up counts (184 control, 221 trial) exceed participants not recovered by day 14 (163, 108)
issues.explanation: Only participants whose cough had not disappeared were to be followed up after the trial. The day-14 rates leave 163 control and 108 trial participants in that group, yet Tables 2 and 3 list 184 and 221. The trial-arm count is about twice the eligible group, so the follow-up population and the 54.81% day-14 rate cannot both be as described. Which participants are in the follow-up tables is unclear, and this weakens interpretation of the follow-up results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Tables 2 and 3 include all participants with a recorded disappearance time, or a corrected flow showing how 221 trial participants qualified for follow-up.

quotes.text: 54.81% (131 of 239 participants) in the trial group
Participants whose cough did not disappear during the trial received an additional follow-up at (30 ± 2) days after the conclusion of the trial.
Cough disappearance at follow-up

issues.title: Primary endpoint is a diary-card cough score of 0 for 24 h, with no validated or objective measure
issues.explanation: The primary endpoint, time to cough disappearance, rests on a self-reported diary score, and the authors concede there are no objective or quantitative criteria. Blinding with a placebo limits bias, but the effect depends on whether participants stayed blinded, and a herbal product with taste or side effects can compromise that. The endpoint is defensible, but the efficacy claim is only as reliable as the self-report and the blinding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the diary score was validated against objective cough monitoring, or that blinding was tested and held.

quotes.text: Cough disappearance was defined as a daytime and nighttime cough score of 0 for the previous 24 h reported on the participant's diary card.
First, there are no objective or quantitative evaluation criteria for the safety and efficacy of Lianhua Qingke tablets.

issues.title: Closing sentence says 4 PPS exclusions; the flow gives 12 (10 beyond the FAS)
issues.explanation: The Results give 12 PPS exclusions, and 482 minus 12 equals the printed PPS of 470. The last sentence of section 3.1 then says 4 participants were excluded from the PPS, which fits neither 12 nor the 10-person FAS-to-PPS gap. It probably refers to non-completers, but this is not stated, and the completer count of 471 plus 11 non-completers (482) also does not match the 480-person FAS.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The flow diagram (Fig. 1) or supplement showing that the 4 refers to a separate step, such as non-completers excluded from the analysis, that sits outside the 12.

quotes.text: 12 were excluded: 2 did not take the trial medication; 4 withdrew consent
2 participants were excluded from the FAS and SS, and 4 were excluded from the PPS.

issues.title: Enrolment start given as March 2023 (Methods) and January 2023 (Results)
issues.explanation: The Methods say enrolment began in March 2023, while the Results say participants were recruited from January 2023. Both end in July 2023. This is a factual inconsistency about the study period. It also matters for judging when the trial was registered relative to enrolment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that January-February 2023 was a screening or site-preparation period before enrolment began.

quotes.text: Participants were enrolled from March 2023 to July 2023.
between January 2023 to July 2023

issues.title: Secondary outcomes and subgroups tested at P < 0.05 without a stated correction (all reported P < 0.001)
issues.explanation: The Methods use an unadjusted two-sided P < 0.05 for all non-primary indicators, and several subgroup tables are also unadjusted. All reported P values are below 0.001, so the omission is unlikely to change any significance decision. The lack of a stated hierarchy is a reporting weakness only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable. A stated hierarchical testing plan would remove the reporting gap.

quotes.text: Other indicators were tested, and a two-sided P < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

issues.title: Text says all baseline P > 0.05, but Table 1 shows hemoglobin P = 0.031
issues.explanation: Section 3.2 states that no baseline characteristic differed significantly (P > 0.05). Table 1 gives a hemoglobin difference of P = 0.031, and the trial arm is higher. This is a small factual error and, for one of about 25 baseline variables, an unremarkable chance imbalance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 showing a different hemoglobin P value.

quotes.text: there was no statistically significant difference in baseline participant characteristics

10.1016/j.ensci.2024.100537.headline_claim: Oral minocycline was effective at ameliorating symptoms in patients with ME including long COVID and post-coronavirus vaccination sequelae, and represents an effective first-line therapeutic option, especially at the initial stage of disease (<6 months).
10.1016/j.ensci.2024.100537.overall: The paper reports a single-arm, unblinded, uncontrolled pilot with subjective outcomes. It cannot show that minocycline is effective, let alone first-line, and the author's own limitations paragraph concedes this. There are also unexplained denominator inconsistencies (47 vs 51, 15 vs 18), a non-significant neuropathic pain result called significant, and a paired design analysed with an independent-groups test. At best the data suggest tolerability and a hypothesis worth testing in a controlled trial.

primary_outcome.name: Performance status (PS) score change, with a decrease of at least 2 points

issues.title: Efficacy and first-line status claimed from an uncontrolled, unblinded 55-patient before-after series
issues.explanation: All patients received minocycline, with no comparison group, no randomisation and no blinding. Improvements on subjective, patient-reported ratings over 6 weeks cannot be separated from placebo response, regression to the mean or the natural course. The author acknowledges this, and also says a large trial is needed to justify first-line use. Yet the abstract and conclusions state flatly that minocycline 'was effective' and 'is an effective first-line therapeutic option'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control analysis showing the observed change exceeds the expected natural course and placebo response.

quotes.text: It represents an effective first-line therapeutic option for these patients in the initial stage.
possible placebo effects could not be excluded
Oral minocycline was administered on a 6-week schedule

second_reader.what_stands: The study is an uncontrolled, unblinded, single-clinician before-after series of 55 patients (51 analysed), with subjective, patient-reported primary outcomes, and no comparator. It cannot support the unqualified statements that minocycline 'was effective' or is 'an effective first-line therapeutic option', which appear in the title, abstract and conclusions. The Limitations section does acknowledge placebo, natural-course and design issues and says a large trial is needed to justify first-line use, so the caveat is stated by the authors, but it is not carried into the title, abstract or concl

issues.title: Before/after comparison: 51 completers in Results text, 47 patients in Table 3 caption and percentages
issues.explanation: The Results say Table 3 compares the 51 patients who completed treatment, but the Table 3 caption says 47. The Table 3 percentages match a denominator of 47. Four completers are therefore unaccounted for in the main symptom comparison. The text counts for neuropathic pain (13) and disequilibrium (21) scale to the same proportions as the Table 3 counts (12 and 19), so they appear to use the 51 base.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 4 completers lacked complete before/after symptom data (or that '47' in the caption is a typo), with the printed counts then reconciling to one denominator.

quotes.text: between the study 47 patients with ME before and after the treatment with minocycline
study 51 ME patients who completed treatment

script.explanation: 46/51 = 90.20%, but the paper prints 98, outside the rounding interval [97.50, 99.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 46.9 rather than 51.

issues.title: 'Initial stage' recommendation rests on an unplanned subgroup split (27/30 vs 14/21) analysed with a Cox model
issues.explanation: The favourable-effect rate was 27/30 (90%) in patients with disease under 6 months, versus 14/21 (67%) in the rest. The conclusion turns this into a recommendation to use minocycline early. The split was not described as pre-specified, and the response is binary (no time-to-event), so a hazard ratio of 3.6 (CI 1.2–10.6) is hard to interpret. Without a control group, shorter-duration patients may simply improve more through natural recovery, which the author concedes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified protocol for the duration analysis and a logistic or time-to-event model that supports the association, with natural-course data from controls.

quotes.text: especially at the initial stage of disease
the disease duration within 6 months was significantly associated with the favorable therapeutic effects

issues.title: Paired before/after symptom proportions described as analysed with Fisher's exact test
issues.explanation: Each patient was assessed before and after treatment, so the symptom proportions are paired. The Methods state that Fisher's exact test (with Yates' correction) was used, which treats the two timepoints as independent groups. The reported p-values therefore do not use the pairing and are imprecise in either direction. Typically this makes the tests conservative, so some p-values (e.g. neuropathic pain 0.052) might change under a paired test.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or output showing that McNemar's (paired) tests were used and that the printed p-values are from them.

quotes.text: Proportional data were analyzed using the Fisher
Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare both median PS scores

issues.title: Neuropathic pain improvement called significant in text and abstract but Table 3 gives p = 0.052
issues.explanation: The Methods set significance at p < 0.05. Table 3 gives p = 0.052 for neuropathic pain in the whole cohort. The Results and the abstract nevertheless list neuropathic pain among the significantly improved symptoms. By the paper's own threshold, that claim is not supported for the whole cohort. Only the long-COVID subgroup (p = 0.045, n=18) crosses the threshold.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified one-sided test or a different stated alpha for this comparison, or a corrected p below 0.05.

quotes.text: Neuropathic pain 12 (25 %) 4 (9 %) 0.052
Significant amelioration of subjective symptoms of fatigue
Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

issues.title: Table 4 long-COVID post-treatment counts/percentages fit n=15 and differ from Table 2 (n=18)
issues.explanation: Table 4 is described as covering 18 long-COVID patients, but its after-treatment percentages (20%, 7%, 13%) only fit a denominator of 15. Several after-treatment counts also differ from the patient-level Table 2: fatigue, post-exertional malaise and unrefreshing sleep show 4 in Table 2 but 3 in Table 4, and brain fog shows 3 versus 2. The before-treatment brain fog percentage (8, 41%) does not fit 8/18 either. The long-COVID subgroup results (89% favourable, symptom p-values) rest on tables that do not reconcile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that 3 long-COVID patients lacked post-treatment data in Table 4, and corrected counts agreeing with the patient-level Table 2.

quotes.text: Orthostatic intolerance 3 (17 %) 1 (7 %) 0.35

script.explanation: 3/18 = 16.67%, but the paper prints 20, outside the rounding interval [19.50, 21.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 15.0 rather than 18.

issues.title: Primary PS outcome is a self-cited 10-point scale based on subjective report, with no validation shown
issues.explanation: The headline 80% responder rate relies on a PS score derived from patient-reported symptom severity, using a scale cited to the author's earlier papers. No validation data or defined meaningful change threshold are given, and the 2-point cut-off is not justified. This limits interpretation of the 80% figure, though the scale is at least described in Table 1.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation (reliability, responsiveness) of this PS scale and justification of a 2-point change as clinically meaningful.

quotes.text: PS was graded on a 10-point scale as below [11]
Based on subjective symptom severity reported by the patients as described previously

issues.title: Symptom positivity judged by a single unblinded clinician-author; PS from patient report
issues.explanation: Symptoms were rated on a Likert scale and dichotomised at 'moderate or worse' after verification by the one author-physician, who also delivered the treatment. There is no blinded rater. This adds ascertainment bias to the already uncontrolled design, but it is largely covered by the no-control issue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that outcome assessment was done by a blinded or independent rater.

quotes.text: After verification by the only doctor (author), the symptom was counted as positive

issues.title: About nine symptom tests at uncorrected p<0.05; orthostatic intolerance (p=0.03) claimed significant
issues.explanation: The paper tests PS plus nine symptoms in the whole cohort and again in the long-COVID subgroup, all at an uncorrected 0.05. The abstract lists orthostatic intolerance as significantly improved at p = 0.03, and this and the neuropathic pain subgroup result (p = 0.045) would not survive any usual multiplicity correction. The strongest results (p < 0.01) are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or adjusted p values that still fall below the threshold for the borderline symptoms.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
Orthostatic intolerance

10.1016/j.explore.2024.04.004.headline_claim: Biosound Therapy showed promising improvement in long COVID symptoms without reported side effects, and a full-scale RCT is feasible if recruitment is moved to a setting with more long COVID patients.
10.1016/j.explore.2024.04.004.overall: The feasibility conclusions are modest and fairly supported, but the efficacy claims rest on unadjusted within-group changes in 9 open-label participants with self-reported outcomes and uncorrected multiple tests. Participant flow, effect sizes and the labelling of the Wilcoxon statistics contain several inconsistencies that make the reported results hard to verify. The efficacy findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Not specified as primary in the paper; GAD-7, PHQ-9, CBS tasks and COVID-19 Persistent Symptom Questionnaire were all assessed at baseline and 4 weeks, with significant intervention-group changes reported for several.

issues.title: Efficacy claims rest on within-group pre-post change in 9 patients; control arm not used for inference
issues.explanation: Only paired baseline-to-4-week changes are tested, and the control group (n = 4) is not compared with the intervention group. The Abstract, Discussion and Conclusion nonetheless state that the intervention group improved and that the clinical data warrant a full trial. With no valid comparator, improvement cannot be attributed to Biosound Therapy. The feasibility conclusions stand more firmly than the efficacy ones.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A valid between-group or interaction analysis showing the improvement exceeds that in controls.

quotes.text: Statistics were not used to confirm differences between groups, but rather to measure differences between pre and post observations.
The intervention group showed promising improvement without reported side effects.

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy claims ('significant improvement', 'promising improvement') rest on within-group pre-post Wilcoxon tests in the 9 intervention patients. The control arm (n=4) is only given its own within-group tests and is never compared with the intervention arm, and this was a stated choice. The paper therefore cannot separate treatment effect from regression to the mean, natural recovery, expectancy or the lack of masking. The caveat that this is a small pilot and that a full RCT is needed is stated, but the improvement wording still reads as efficacy. Also, the arm counts in the text (11 allocate

issues.title: Participant flow: 11 allocated, 1 withdrawal, but 9 analysed; 15 enrolled in Results vs 14 in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Results state 11 were allocated to the intervention and 1 withdrew, which leaves 10, yet 9 intervention participants are analysed. Fifteen enrolled and 13 were analysed, so two people are missing but only one withdrawal is described. The Discussion computes retention as 13 of 14, a third denominator. The flow cannot be reconciled from the text, so the retention figure and the analysed sample are uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 or the supplement showing a second intervention-arm loss, or 10 intervention participants analysed.

quotes.text: Eleven were allocated to the intervention; four to the control.
One participant withdrew from the intervention group due to not having enough time to complete the study.
13 out of 14 participants who enrolled in the study finished it

script.explanation: The participant flow balances arithmetically but 1 transition(s) drop participants with no stated reason: 2 participant(s) drop between 'randomized' and 'analysed' with no stated exclusions. Not itself an error -- papers legitimately omit attrition reasons -- but the reader cannot audit the loss.

issues.title: Open-label design with self-reported primary outcomes (PHQ-9, GAD-7, symptom questionnaire)
issues.explanation: Participants knew their group, and the main benefits are on self-reported scales, including an investigator-developed, unvalidated symptom questionnaire. Expectancy and social desirability could inflate the improvements. The authors list this in the limitations, but the Abstract and Conclusion do not qualify the improvement claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded or objective outcome assessment showing similar improvement.

quotes.text: participant bias may have been in effect because participants were aware if they were in the intervention or control group

issues.title: Six outcome tests at p<0.05 uncorrected; 4 of 6 'significant' results have p 0.02-0.04
issues.explanation: The Abstract lists significant improvements in six outcomes with an uncorrected 0.05 threshold. Four of the six have p between 0.02 and 0.04. Only the PHQ-9 and Double Trouble results would remain significant after a conservative correction. The significant findings are presented as the main results although multiple outcomes and subscales were tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis plan treating these as exploratory or correcting for multiplicity.

quotes.text: A p value less than 0.05 was set as significant.

issues.title: Control-group results for GAD-7, PHQ-9 and CBS tasks not reported though described as insignificant
issues.explanation: The text says all score changes in the control group were insignificant, but Table 2 gives no control means, SDs, z or p for GAD-7, PHQ-9 or the CBS tasks. Only Fatigue and Remembering have control data. Readers cannot check the claim or see how much the controls changed, which is the only available benchmark for the intervention-arm change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Full control-arm statistics for every outcome in the paper or supplement.

quotes.text: All score changes for the control group were insignificant.

issues.title: Effect sizes in text disagree with Table 2 (PHQ-9 0.84 vs 0.89; Remembering 0.74 vs 0.85; GAD-7 0.71 vs 40.5)
issues.explanation: The effect sizes quoted in the Results differ from those in Table 2 for three outcomes. The GAD-7 effect size cell holds 40.5, which is the z value, and the control column holds 45, which looks like a value from another row. The 0.74 given for Remembering also repeats the Fatigue value. Readers cannot tell which effect sizes are correct, and how effect size was computed is not stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The published table layout showing correct values in each cell, with text values being typographical.

quotes.text: PHQ-9 ( z = 45, p = 0.01; large effect size of 0.84)
Remembering ( z = 28, p = 0.02; large effect size of 0.74)
GAD-7 ( z = 40.5, p = 0.04; large effect size of 0.71)

issues.title: Wilcoxon statistics labelled 'z' (40.5, 45, 33.5, 28) are rank-sum V values, not z-scores
issues.explanation: The Results and Table 2 label the Wilcoxon statistics as z, but values like 45 and 40.5 cannot be z-scores for 9 pairs with p = 0.01 to 0.04. They match the V statistic from R. The mislabelling makes the results hard to interpret and means the effect-size calculation is unexplained. The Odd task p-value (V = 3, p = 0.04) also seems high for that V.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Output stating the statistic is V and p computed with tie handling matching the printed values.

quotes.text: PHQ-9 ( z = 45, p = 0.01; large effect size of 0.84)
Double Tasks ( z = 1, p = 0.01; large effect size of 0.85)

issues.title: Trial registered in May 2023, about two years after the April 2021 start
issues.explanation: The registry record was first submitted on 2023-05-05, after the April 2021 start and the December 2021 end of recruitment. The authors disclose this. Retrospective registration means the registry cannot show that outcomes and analysis were fixed in advance, which matters given the number of outcomes tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Dated protocol or earlier registry version showing pre-specified outcomes.

quotes.text: This trial was registered retrospectively due to  discrepancy  related  to  the  device  classification  of  the  Biosound Therapy System.

issues.title: Female share given as 67% in text but 77% in Table 1 (10 of 13)
issues.explanation: The text says 67% (n = 10) of participants were female, but 10 of 13 is 76.9%, which matches Table 1. The text figure is a typographical error. Nothing else depends on it, though the text's 67% and 23% would not sum to 100.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for the text percentage.

quotes.text: 67 % ( n = 10) of participants were female

script.explanation: 10/13 = 76.92%, but the paper prints 67, outside the rounding interval [66.50, 68.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 14.9 rather than 13.

issues.title: Allocation 11:4 under simple randomisation; authors call the process inappropriate
issues.explanation: The authors say the imbalance shows the randomisation process was not appropriate. In fact, such an imbalance can arise by chance with simple randomisation of 15 people. Allocation concealment is not described, and the investigators delivering the intervention enrolled and randomised participants. Because the arms are not compared, the main effect is on feasibility rather than on the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: N/A; judgement on how the imbalance should be interpreted.

quotes.text: The unbalanced allocation ratio demonstrated that the randomization process was not appropriate.

10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2023.01.010.headline_claim: Telepsychotherapy delivered after post-acute COVID-19 illness can reduce anxiety and depression among COVID-19 survivors.
10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2023.01.010.overall: The conclusion that telepsychotherapy 'can reduce' anxiety and depression rests on an uncontrolled, unblinded pre-post change in clinician diagnoses among 14 completers out of 26 eligible patients. It is best read as a descriptive, hypothesis-generating report of feasibility. Table 1 also has several overall-column errors (gender, medical conditions, ventilation duration) that do not affect the main result but reduce confidence in data handling.

primary_outcome.name: Clinician consensus psychiatric diagnosis of depression and anxiety at treatment end, pre/post McNemar test

issues.title: 'Can reduce anxiety and depression' concluded from uncontrolled pre-post change in 14 completers
issues.explanation: The only efficacy evidence is the change in clinician diagnosis from treatment entry to end in 14 completers, with no control group. Spontaneous recovery after COVID, concurrent medical care and regression to the mean cannot be separated from treatment effect. The conclusion that telepsychotherapy 'can reduce' symptoms is stronger than this design supports; the sample is also very small and no sample size justification is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent comparison group, or a conclusion worded as descriptive association only.

quotes.text: Comparison of pre- and post- treatment psychiatric diagnoses indicated a significant resolution of both clinical depression
can reduce anxiety and depression
the naturalistic nature of our study

second_reader.what_stands: The causal-sounding conclusion that telepsychotherapy 'can reduce anxiety and depression' rests on an uncontrolled before-after change in 14 completers out of 26 referred, assessed by clinician diagnosis, with no comparison group and no outcome data for the 12 non-completers. The paper does call the data preliminary and names the naturalistic design and a missing standardized outcome as limitations, but it does not acknowledge the absence of a control group, the completer-only analysis, or the possibility of spontaneous recovery, so the conclusion is stronger than the design supports.

issues.title: Ventilation duration overall mean 64.5 d exceeds both subgroup means (22.7, 59.5); implied pooled ~38.8 d
issues.explanation: The overall mean ventilation duration (64.5 days) is higher than both the completers' (22.7) and the non-completers' (59.5) means, which is arithmetically impossible for a pooled mean. With 9 and 7 ventilated patients the pooled mean should be about 38.8 days. The text repeats 64.5 and uses ventilation duration to describe non-completers as sicker.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the overall figure covers a different set of patients, for example including patients outside the 16 listed.

quotes.location: Table 1, mechanical ventilation duration row, overall

issues.title: Pre-post efficacy reported for 14 of 26 eligible patients (completers only); 12 excluded from outcome analysis
issues.explanation: Diagnostic change is reported only for the 14 completers. The 8 who declined and the 4 who dropped out contribute no outcome data. Completion includes patients who remitted before seven sessions, and non-completers tended to be sicker. The reported resolution therefore overstates what would be expected among all referred patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including all 18 who began (or all 26 referred) with end-of-treatment diagnoses imputed or observed.

quotes.text: Among the 18 who enrolled, 14 patients completed treatment
all patients (100%) met criteria for anxiety at treatment entry

issues.title: Outcome is unblinded clinician consensus diagnosis; PHQ-9/GAD-7 baseline only (n=10, n=9), no end-point scores
issues.explanation: The efficacy result is a yes/no clinician consensus diagnosis, not a validated symptom score, and no blinding of assessors is described. Symptom scales were collected only at baseline in about half the sample, so change in severity cannot be shown. The authors acknowledge the lack of a standardized primary outcome, but the conclusion still speaks of symptom reduction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Post-treatment validated scale scores or blinded assessment of diagnoses.

quotes.text: Baseline PHQ-9 ( n = 10) and GAD-7 ( n = 9) scores were collected for approximately half of the sample
clinical consensus diagnoses of anxiety and depression by clinicians

issues.title: Table 1 'Overall' column inconsistent with subgroups: medical conditions 14/12 vs 10/16; gender 16/10 vs 10/16
issues.explanation: For pre-existing medical conditions the overall column gives 14 (None or one) and 12 (Two or more), but the completed and partial columns add to 10 and 16. For gender the overall column gives 16 male and 10 female, but the subgroups add to 10 male and 16 female, so these look transposed. The medical-conditions row matters because the text says non-completers had more comorbidities and 'Two or more' is the larger group overall.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table correction showing the overall counts were derived from different data than the subgroup columns.

quotes.location: Table 1, pre-existing medical conditions, overall column
Table 1, 'Two or more' row, overall column

issues.title: Table 1 caption says 26 'enrolled in treatment' while text says 18 began therapy and 8 declined
issues.explanation: The caption calls all 26 patients 'enrolled in treatment', but the text says only 18 began therapy and 8 declined. The table itself covers all 26 who met criteria, split into completers and partial/decliners. This is a wording slip in the caption with no effect on any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A caption defining 'enrolled' as 'referred and eligible'.

quotes.text: Demographic and clinical characteristics of 26 patients enrolled in treatment
Among the 18 who enrolled, 14 patients completed treatment

issues.title: Complication rates 'among hospitalized' (n=24) fit a denominator of 26 (34.6% = 9/26, 15.4% = 4/26)
issues.explanation: The paper says complications are reported among hospitalized patients (24), but the neurological and renal percentages can only come from 26. The wording or the denominator is therefore wrong, but the effect is a few percentage points on descriptive complication rates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that complication percentages use all 26 patients as denominator.

quotes.text: with lower rates of neurological (34.6%) and renal (15.4%) complications

10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e29261.headline_claim: Airflow limitation, detected by methacholine challenge or excessive diurnal FEV1 variability, may be present in many long covid patients, and asthma treatment normalised variability and reduced fatigue and dyspnoea.
10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e29261.overall: The detection finding that most of these 30 long covid patients exceeded the 12% variability threshold is reported plainly but cannot be interpreted without a reference group. The treatment-response conclusions come from an uncontrolled before-and-after design in selected high-variability patients, so they are only suggestive, and the authors themselves call for interventional studies.

primary_outcome.name: Detection of airflow limitation (positive methacholine BPT or diurnal FEV1 variability >=12%) in long covid patients

issues.title: No control group: 18.0% to 7.3% variability fall and symptom gains attributed to treatment
issues.explanation: All 29 treated patients were selected because their FEV1 variability was high (or BPT positive) and were compared only with their own earlier values. A fall in variability after selection on high values, plus the natural course of a postviral condition and expectation effects on symptoms, could produce the same pattern without any treatment effect. The Discussion says the treatment 'resulted in normalisation' and cites the objective measure as strengthening the results, which does not address regression to the mean or natural resolution. The detection aim is less affected than the treatment-response aim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo control group showing no comparable fall in variability or symptoms.

quotes.text: The study does not include a control group, but the results are strengthened by the objective normalisation in lung function variability
three weeks ' treatment resulted in normalisation of diurnal lung function variability, absence of dyspnoea and significant reduction of fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: The study is single-arm and open-label, and the paper attributes the fall in FEV1 variability (18.0% to 7.3%) and the symptom improvements to asthma treatment using causal wording, even though it admits there is no control group. The authors' statement that the objective spirometry normalisation 'strengthens' the results does not address natural resolution, regression to the mean, or expectation effects on the self-reported symptom scores.

issues.title: 95% (21/22) 'airflow limitation' rests on a ≥12% variability cut-off with no control group
issues.explanation: The main detection claim depends on a variability threshold applied to home measurements taken morning, evening and around exercise, in 30 consecutive long covid patients with no healthy or non-covid comparison. Without a reference rate, 21/22 positives cannot be read as specific to airflow limitation or to long covid. The maximum-minimum variability measure rises with the number of readings taken. The conclusion that airflow limitation is detectable in 'many' patients is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data showing that variability ≥12% under the same protocol is uncommon in comparable people without airflow limitation.

quotes.text: Excessive lung function variability was defined as ≥ 12% diurnal variability in FEV1.
The current study faces potential limitations of a small and selected cohort and the use of unsupervised app-based lung function tests.

second_reader.what_stands: The 95% (21/22) is arithmetically correct and the ≥12% cut-off is defined in advance and attributed to GINA, but the study has no control or reference group, so the specificity of this threshold for airflow limitation (versus measurement variability from frequent unsupervised app spirometry in a selected LC cohort) cannot be assessed from the paper. The authors acknowledge the small selected cohort and unsupervised tests, yet still describe the 21/22 as documented airflow limitation.

issues.title: Unpaired Mann-Whitney named as the only test for paired pre/post data; p-values unverifiable
issues.explanation: The Methods name only the unpaired Mann-Whitney test, but the headline comparisons are within-patient before/after measures. Either the wrong test was used or the description is imprecise. The direction of the error is likely to understate rather than overstate significance, so the impact is limited. The paper does not report test statistics, so it cannot be checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank (the paired form of the test) was used, or the analysis code.

quotes.text: Statistical analyses were performed with Ledidi Core (Ledidi, Oslo, Norway), using non-parametric Mann -Whitney test.

issues.title: Authors tied to the AsthmaTuner company; conclusions recommend app-based spirometry
issues.explanation: One author is a part-time consultant at MediTuner and another co-founded the company that owns AsthmaTuner, the device used for all variability measurements. These interests are declared, and funding is stated as none. The conclusions recommend daily app-based monitoring, so readers should weigh the findings with this in mind.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: n/a; this is a disclosed interest rather than a refutable error.

quotes.text: Bj ¨ orn Nordlund was part of founding MediTuner AB, the company owning the medical device AsthmaTuner.
An app-based spirometer may potentially be used for illness surveillance and to assess response to treatment.

10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e37920.headline_claim: Herbal medicines (BIT, KOG, CBD) showed feasibility for a clinical trial in long COVID, and the authors state that BIT or KOG show potential efficacy for fatigue while requiring definitive controlled evidence.
10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e37920.overall: The paper's core conclusion, that the design is feasible with good adherence and no drug-related adverse events, is reasonably supported. Efficacy statements for BIT/KOG in fatigue and CBD in cognition cannot be drawn from an uncontrolled, unadjusted analysis with 31% dropout and LOCF. A few text-table inconsistencies (cognitive VAS significance, KOG CFQ, an EQ-5D CI) are small but should be corrected.

primary_outcome.name: Treatment success rate (VAS change >15 points) for fatigue or cognitive dysfunction at 12 weeks

issues.title: Cognitive VAS between-group p = 0.0472 at 13 weeks flagged significant, text says no group difference
issues.explanation: Table 7 flags the between-group p-values for VAS for cognitive dysfunction at 5, 9 and 13 weeks (0.0477, 0.0358, 0.0472) as p < 0.05. The Results text states there was no significant difference between groups at 13, 25 or 37 weeks. The table and the text disagree on one reported result, and the nominally significant differences are not discussed anywhere.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or supplement showing the 13-week p-value was above 0.05, or a stated text-wide convention under which p = 0.0472 was not treated as a group difference.

quotes.text: 25 weeks, or 37 weeks, with no significant difference between groups

quotes.location: Table 7, VAS for cognitive dysfunction, 13 weeks row

issues.title: Many unadjusted between-group and within-group tests across 45 patients, with LOCF at 31% dropout
issues.explanation: Tables 6 to 8 report roughly 90 between-group p-values and many within-group CIs, with no correction for multiplicity. Groups were allocated by syndrome and symptom type, so group comparisons mix indication with treatment effect. LOCF imputation under 14 of 45 dropouts (31%) can bias change scores. The authors state the analysis was exploratory in a pilot, so this weakens secondary significance claims rather than the feasibility conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified statement that all efficacy tests are exploratory with no inferential claims, or a sensitivity analysis on completers or with multiple imputation that agrees with the LOCF results.

quotes.text: the last observation carried forward analysis was employed to handle missing data while evaluating effectiveness
An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was used to compare the different herbal medication groups ( p < 0.05).
Data are presented as mean difference from baseline (95 % confidence intervals).

issues.title: Discussion/Conclusions suggest BIT/KOG efficacy for fatigue and CBD effect on cognition from an uncontrolled pilot
issues.explanation: With no control arm, improvement in fatigue over 6 to 9 months cannot be attributed to the herbal medicines. The Discussion nevertheless says BIT or KOG 'may be considered' with persistent effects, and the Conclusions describe 'potential efficacy'. The CBD cognitive suggestion rests on one secondary CFQ result at 37 weeks that improved in every group (between-group p = 0.9368), while K-MoCA, digit span, BNT and cognitive VAS showed no improvement. The authors partly concede natural course and the lack of controls, but the headline recommendations are not tempered accordingly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or historical natural-history comparison showing the improvements exceed spontaneous recovery, or wording that frames the within-group changes as hypothesis-generating only.

quotes.text: a 12-week administration of BIT or KOG may be considered, with effects persisting not only during the intervention period but also up to six months post-intervention
Significant decrease in CFQ score of the CBD group suggests that CBD might have potential effect for the recovery of cognitive dysfunction
Fatigue symptoms improved significantly in all groups, regardless of the type of prescription administered.

issues.title: Text calls KOG CFQ improvement at 37 weeks significant, but its CI (-11.57 to 3.70) includes zero
issues.explanation: The Results say CFQ improved significantly in the BIT, KOG and CBD groups at 37 weeks. The KOG interval in the same sentence and in Table 7 runs from -11.57 to 3.70, which includes zero, so it is not significant by the authors' own CI. This overstates the cognitive findings. The CBD claim in the Discussion depends on this CFQ result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the KOG interval excludes zero, for example both bounds negative with a different estimate.

quotes.text: the Cognitive Failure Questionnaire score showed significant improvement in the BIT, KOG, and CBD groups at 37 weeks
3.93, 95 % CI: 11.57 to 3.70 in the KOG group

issues.title: EQ-5D-5L CBD 13-week CI upper bound printed as 0.88 in text but 0.08 in Table 8
issues.explanation: The text gives the CBD 13-week EQ-5D-5L 95% CI as 0.11 to 0.88. Table 8 prints the same cell as (0.11, 0.08). An upper bound of 0.88 would be implausibly wide around an estimate of 0.01, so the text is probably the slip. It is a small transcription error that changes no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the true upper bound is 0.88 and the table is wrong, which would still leave a text-table mismatch.

quotes.text: and 0.01, 95 % CI: 0.11 to 0.88 in the CBD group

10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e40453.headline_claim: A 3-month home telerehabilitation programme is safe and effective, improving exercise capacity, leg muscle strength and endurance in post-COVID-19 patients with mild to moderate symptoms.
10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e40453.overall: The paper shows both arms improved in walk distance and sit-to-stand over 3 months, but the between-group tests are null, allocation was by order of entry, and 37% were lost with completers only analysed. The claim that the programme is 'safe and effective' is not supported beyond tentative within-group improvement. Minor numeric slips (BMI row duplicated, effect-size labels, abstract wording) do not change this.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) and pulmonary function (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC, FEF25-75, PEFR)

issues.title: 'Safe and effective' conclusion rests on within-group change; group-by-time interactions are null
issues.explanation: Both arms improved in 6MWD and 1MSTS, and the between-group interactions were not significant (p=0.918 for 6MWD, p=0.342 for 1MSTS). The intervention therefore cannot be shown to cause the improvement beyond natural recovery or the control arm's activity. The Conclusion nonetheless states the programme was shown to be effective and safe. At most the data show improvement over time in both groups, with no demonstrated advantage of the programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant interaction or between-group difference favouring the intervention on a prespecified primary outcome.

quotes.text: Home-based telerehabilitation programs have been shown to be safe and effective, improving exercise capacity, leg muscle strength, and endurance
no significant group-by-time interactions were observed for exercise capacity ( p > 0.05)
Thus, this explains the improvement of the 1MSTS in both groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion says the program is 'safe and effective' for exercise capacity, strength and endurance, but all group-by-time interactions are null (6MWD p = 0.918; 1MSTS p = 0.342), and the control group improved by about as much in 6MWD (56 vs 54 m). The effectiveness claim therefore rests on within-group pre-post change, which the authors themselves attribute partly to the app-based support given to both groups; the safety statement rests on a small sample of 32 completers.

issues.title: Allocation by order of entry labelled 'random'; no concurrent true control; comorbidity imbalance (p=0.019)
issues.explanation: Participants were allocated by order of entry and the authors say true randomisation was difficult because participants entered at different periods. Allocation was therefore predictable and open to selection and time effects. The control arm was a stretching programme with other exercise allowed, and baseline comorbidities differed (no comorbidity 6% vs 43%, p=0.019). Any between-group comparison is confounded, and the Methods wording 'randomly assigned' misdescribes the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation of a concealed random sequence generated before enrolment.

quotes.text: All eligible participants were randomly assigned to either the control or intervention group according to their order of entry into the study, as managed by the assistant researcher.
participants did not enter the study during the same period, making true randomization difficult to implement.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation by order of entry is described as 'randomly assigned' in Methods, while the Limitations section says true randomization was difficult because participants entered at different periods. The paper calls the design quasi-experimental, acknowledges no true control group, and reports a comorbidity imbalance (p = 0.019) among completers. The 'no concurrent control' claim is partly overstated, since both groups were enrolled in the same Dec 2021–Mar 2022 window and the control group was a comparison arm rather than an absent one, but the authors do say participants did not enter at the sam

issues.title: 37% lost to follow-up (differential, 31% vs 44%); only completers analysed; 32 analysed vs 52 planned
issues.explanation: Of 51 enrolled, 19 were lost by 3 months, 18 and 14 remained. The Discussion states 35%, but 19/51 is 37%. Loss was higher in the intervention arm (44% vs 31%). All tables are completer-only, the claimed ITT analysis is not shown, and the analysed sample is far below the 52 targeted, so the null interaction tests are underpowered and results may be biased by who dropped out.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Presented ITT results with imputation showing the same conclusions.

quotes.text: Nineteen participants dropped out by the 3-month follow-up for various reasons (see Supplementary Table S3), leaving 18 in the control group and 14 in the intervention group.
the dropout rate in our study (35 %) remained lower than that reported recently (50 %) [13]
resulting in a total of 52 participants.

second_reader.what_stands: About 37% of participants (19/51) were lost, with a higher loss in the intervention arm (44% vs 31%), and Tables 1–3 and the stated analyses use only the 32 completers. Fewer than planned (32 vs 52) were analysed, and the Discussion's 35% does not match the 37.3% from the printed counts. The authors state that an ITT analysis was also run with similar results but do not show it in the paper, so the claim of completers-only analysis holds for what is reported.

issues.title: Table 2 3-month BMI and %body fat values are identical in both groups and BMI is inconsistent with weight
issues.explanation: The 3-month means and SDs (30.29 ± 10.51 control, 32.58 ± 9.10 intervention) are printed in both the BMI and %body fat rows, although the baselines differ. The BMI values cannot be right given the almost unchanged body weights, since a ~1 kg gain changes BMI by about 0.4, not 2.4 to 5.8. The reported 'significant BMI increase' (effect size 0.76) and the Discussion's use of it to explain poor lung function rest on this row.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the 3-month BMI and %BF values really are identical in both arms.

quotes.location: Table 2, Body mass index row, Post 3-mo F/U

quotes.text: participants in the intervention group showed an increase in BMI (effect size = 0.76)

issues.title: Effect sizes 0.53 and 0.34 called 'large' despite the paper's own thresholds (0.5 medium, 0.8 large)
issues.explanation: The Methods define d = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 as small, medium and large. The Discussion calls d = 0.53 for 6MWD and d = 0.34 for 1MSTS 'large'. By the stated criteria these are medium and small, so the magnitude of improvement is overstated. The 0.53 also does not match the Results (1.06 control, 0.55 intervention).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different threshold scheme stated for these effect sizes.

quotes.text: Effect sizes of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 were classified as small, medium, and large, respectively.
the effect size for improvements in 6 MWD was 0.53, indicating a large effect
with an effect size of 0.34, indicating a large effect

issues.title: Abstract says no between-group differences (p>0.05); Table 2 group main effects for FEV and PEFR are p=0.032, 0.031
issues.explanation: The abstract says no statistically significant between-group differences were found for any outcome. Table 2 flags the group main effects for FEV (p=0.032) and PEFR (p=0.031) as significant. These main effects reflect baseline imbalance rather than treatment effect, and the interaction tests are all non-significant. The wording is imprecise rather than the conclusion being wrong, and it hides a baseline imbalance in lung function.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the abstract that the p>0.05 refers only to group-by-time interactions.

quotes.text: No statistically significant differences were found between the two groups for all outcome measurements ( p > 0.05).

quotes.location: Table 2, Lung function FEV row, Gr F column

issues.title: Dyspnea on exertion p=0.04 in text vs p=0.03 in the Figure 3 caption
issues.explanation: The Results give p=0.04 for dyspnea on exertion, while the Figure 3 caption gives a single p=0.03 for the starred between-group difference. If these are the same comparison the values disagree, but both are below 0.05 and the caption may refer to another symptom. This is a minor reporting inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 3 showing the asterisk on a different symptom than dyspnea on exertion.

quotes.text: Dyspnea on exertion showed a significant difference between the two groups at this time point ( p = 0.04).
Significant differences between the groups using Chi-Square test, p = 0.03

10.1016/j.ijosm.2026.100830.headline_claim: Osteopathic care added to physical therapy improved fatigue and functional status over PT alone at 2 months in long COVID, though the authors describe the trial as exploratory and underpowered.
10.1016/j.ijosm.2026.100830.overall: The paper is candid that it is an underpowered exploratory trial and hedges its conclusion, so the headline claim of potential benefit is not overstated in wording. Support for it is weak, because the outcomes are self-reported in an unblinded trial with extra contact in the intervention arm, and the 2-month time point differs from the registered 90-day one. Several reporting inconsistencies (T3 numbers, adjusted CI versus SMD, descriptive errors) mean the estimates should be treated as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) and Post-COVID Functional State (PCFS) at 2 months

issues.title: FSS 2-month MD CI (-14.47 to -6.35, z about 5) is inconsistent with its SMD 0.45 (CI -0.36 to 1.26)
issues.explanation: The adjusted 2-month FSS difference has a very narrow CI for 12 participants per arm, whereas the standardized effect size for the same contrast has a CI that includes zero. The raw arm SDs of about 14 imply much more uncertainty than the MD CI shows. The 2-month fatigue result may be more precise than the data support, or one of the two sets of figures is misreported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The model output showing the covariate-adjusted SE is about 2 with a SMD that matches, or a corrected Table 3.

quotes.text: mean difference = GLYPH<0> 10.41; 95% CI: GLYPH<0> 14.47 to GLYPH<0> 6.35

quotes.location: Table 3, FSS row, SMD at 2 months

quotes.text: Standardized mean difference calculated from marginal estimates

second_reader.what_stands: The printed FSS MD CI (z about 5.0) and the SMD CI (z about 1.1, spanning zero) imply very different precision, and the SMD 0.45 does not equal MD/SD (about 0.73). The SMD CI matches a plain two-group calculation with n = 12 per arm, while the MD CI is much narrower than raw SDs would give. This is not necessarily an error, since the footnote indicates different bases (marginal versus adjusted), but the paper does not explain the discrepancy, and the two estimates would lead a reader to different conclusions about whether the 2-month FSS difference is distinguishable from zero.

issues.title: Self-reported fatigue and function outcomes, unblinded participants, extra contact in OC + PT arm; no sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Participants and clinicians knew allocation, and both primary outcomes (FSS, PCFS) are patient-reported. The OC + PT arm received additional treatment sessions with no attention-matched control. Expectation and attention effects could therefore account for a large part of the 10-point FSS difference, and the authors state they did not assess this. The benefit conclusion is tentative at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham or attention-matched control, or analyses showing the effect is robust to plausible expectation bias.

quotes.text: It was not possible to blind the clinicians regarding the groups and the participants regarding their treatment.
the absence of measures to assess the influence of expectation effects

second_reader.what_stands: Both primary outcomes are self-reported by participants who knew their allocation. The OC + PT arm had an additional, longer, personal contact with a second practitioner type, and no analysis was done to probe expectation or attention effects; the authors acknowledge this as a limitation. What I could not verify is how much extra contact there was, because the number of sessions attended per arm is not given in the text I had.

issues.title: Text says 2 missed the 3-month assessment, but Table 3 shows 23 of 28 (5 missing), unevenly split by arm
issues.explanation: The Results say only 2 participants did not complete the T3 assessment, which would leave 26. Table 3 gives 13 PT and 10 OC + PT at T3, a total of 23. That means 5 are missing: 1 of 14 in PT and 4 of 14 in OC + PT. The 3-month secondary results therefore rest on more loss than stated, and the loss is concentrated in the intervention arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or text showing that 26 participants had T3 data and that Table 3's T3 n values refer to something else.

quotes.text: only 4 (14%) and 2 (8%) patients did not complete the assessments at T2
OC + PT (n = 10)

issues.title: Registry lists primary outcomes at 90 days; paper's primary time point is 2 months, with 3-month results secondary
issues.explanation: The ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT05012826 lists fatigue and functional status at 90 days as primary outcomes. The paper makes 2 months primary and 3 months secondary, while saying nothing changed. This matters because the PCFS difference is present at 2 months but not at 3 months (-0.26, CI -0.69 to 0.16), so the choice of time point favours the intervention. Earlier record versions were not checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing the primary time frame was 2 months when registered, or 90 days being defined as the 2-month post-intervention assessment.

quotes.text: The primary outcomes were fatigue and functional status, measured 2 months post-randomization.
No changes to trial outcomes occurred after the trial commenced.

issues.title: T3 timing: median 91 days (IQR 91-91) in text versus arm means of 124.0 and 105.4 days in Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results say T3 occurred at 91 days with an IQR of 91-91, meaning at least half the visits were exactly at 91 days. Table 2 gives mean times of 124.0 (SD 23.2) for PT and 105.4 (SD 16.7) for OC + PT. Those means imply many visits well past 91 days, and PT's 124 is about 4 months, so the two statements cannot both describe the same quantity. The paper does not explain the difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition showing the Table 2 row measures a different interval, or a corrected value.

quotes.text: Time to endpoint T3; mean days (SD)

issues.title: Only 28 randomized; sample-size basis inconsistent (90/104/76) and assumes FSS SD 2.0 versus observed ~14-15
issues.explanation: The trial reached 28 participants of a stated 104, and 24 are analysed at 2 months. The sample-size rationale is muddled across several figures and uses an SD of 2.0 on a 9-63 scale where the trial's own SDs are 14-15. Effects estimated from 12 per arm are prone to exaggeration, yet the headline 2-month difference is presented as a benefit signal. The hedging limits the damage, so the conclusion stands only as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A coherent, documented sample-size calculation using a realistic SD showing the 28 achieved could detect the observed effect.

quotes.text: MID) of 1.2 points (SD 2.0) on the FSS
A total of 90 participants (45 per group) would be required to detect this difference with 80% power

issues.explanation: The abstract and Table 2 give 14 randomized to OC + PT, but Table 3 shows 13 at baseline. The Methods say all enrolled participants were analysed by ITT with multiple imputation, yet one baseline value appears absent and is not explained. This is a small reporting gap rather than a randomization discrepancy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one participant lacked baseline FSS/PCFS data and was imputed in the model.

quotes.text: OC + PT (n = 13)
All enrolled participants were  followed  through  the  study  and  included  in  the  analysis

The vaccine-dose rows for PT total 14 with no missing value, so the 'Missing' entry conflicts with the rest of the table. This is a minor descriptive error that does not touch the outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing PT Missing = 0.

issues.title: Discussion gives 57% combined overweight/obesity; Results and Table 2 give 61% (17/28)
issues.explanation: The Discussion states a combined prevalence of 57% for the sample, but Table 2 gives 6 overweight plus 11 with obesity, which is 17 of 28 (61%), the figure used in the Results. The 57% is not reproducible from the table. It is a small error in the comparison with an external cohort.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 57% that matches Table 2 counts.

issues.title: Intubation reported as 1 participant (4.5%); no stated denominator gives 4.5% (1/28 = 3.6%)
issues.explanation: The Results report 1 intubated participant as 4.5%. Against the sample of 28 this is 3.6%, against the 10 hospitalised it is 10%, and Table 2 gives 7.1% of the 14 PT participants. 4.5% corresponds to a denominator of 22 that the paper never defines. It is a small descriptive error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator of 22 for this percentage.

quotes.text: only 1 participant (4.5%) received intubation for mechanical ventilation

10.1016/j.imr.2024.101084.headline_claim: QARP had long-term sustained efficacy for dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough in patients with COVID-19, especially in young and middle-aged patients.
10.1016/j.imr.2024.101084.overall: The 14-month mMRC and MBS improvements are statistically strong but rest on unblinded self-rated scales without multiplicity control. The claim of efficacy sustained to 28 months holds only for MBS, since the 28-month mMRC difference is not significant and the MBS difference is below the paper's own MCID. The claim that the effect is larger in younger patients lacks an interaction test, and several reporting slips (CI sign, 'increased' wording, 'all primary outcomes') need correcting.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline to 28-month discharge visit in mMRC and MBS (ADL also listed in Methods)

issues.title: 'Sustained to 28 months' claimed for mMRC although 28-month mMRC difference is -0.1 (P = 0.220)
issues.explanation: The Methods say the principal outcomes are changes to the 28-month visit. The mMRC difference at 28 months is not significant, and the 28-month MBS difference (-0.4) is below the paper's own MCID of -0.5. Even so, the Conclusions say QARP improved mMRC and MBS at 14 months 'and the efficacy was sustained up to the 28th month'. The Discussion also calls the 28-month mMRC and MBS changes statistically different from control, though it later concedes mMRC was less significant. Only MBS supports the sustained claim, and then modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan making 14 months primary, or a significant 28-month mMRC difference.

quotes.text: QARP rapidly and significantly improved mMRC scores, MBS scores, chest tightness, and cough in COVID-19 patients at 14 months, and the efficacy was sustained up to the 28th month.

quotes.location: Table 2, mMRC T3 row, difference column (P = 0.220)

quotes.text: between the baseline and 28-month discharge visit.

second_reader.what_stands: The mMRC between-group difference at 28 months is small and not statistically significant (-0.1, 95% CI -0.3 to 0.1, P = 0.220), so the Conclusions statement that efficacy for mMRC was sustained to the 28th month is not supported by the table. Only the MBS result (P = 0.024) is significant at 28 months, and the Discussion does concede that mMRC results were weaker; the problem is the overstated wording in the Conclusions, not a hidden result.

issues.title: Unblinded participants rating their own dyspnoea (MBS, mMRC); effects of 0.4-0.6 points are small
issues.explanation: Patients knew their allocation and rated their own breathlessness. Expectancy and attention effects could produce small differences of this size. The control group was not given a comparable attention or sham programme. The paper does not discuss this risk in its limitations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Objective outcome measures pointing the same way, or evidence that participants could not tell the groups apart.

quotes.text: The specific intervention did not allow blinding of patients or the therapist administering the intervention.
However, outcome assessors and data statisticians were not informed of the grouping information to reduce bias.

second_reader.what_stands: Patients could not be blinded and rated their own dyspnoea, and the paper does not address this as a limitation despite relying on patient-reported scales; blinded assessors and statisticians do not remove this risk. The significant between-group effects are 0.4 to 0.6 points, which are at or below the cited MCIDs (-1 and -0.5), so they are small relative to the size of plausible expectation or reporting bias.

issues.title: 'More effective in young and middle-aged patients' concluded without a treatment-by-age interaction test
issues.explanation: The conclusion rests on significant differences in younger participants and none in older ones. No test of whether the effect differs by age is reported, and no subgroup analysis was described in the Methods. A non-significant result in a small subgroup is not evidence of no effect. The age-effect statement is not supported by the analysis presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported treatment × age interaction test that is significant.

quotes.text: QARP was also more effective in young and middle-aged patients than in older patients.
no significant differences were found between the two groups for any outcome at any point during the follow-up period for the older participants

issues.title: 'Significantly superior for all primary outcomes' contradicted by ADL (14-month difference 0.0, P = 0.985)
issues.explanation: ADL is defined as one of the three principal outcomes. Table 2 shows no between-group difference in it at any follow-up (P = 0.853, 0.985, 0.110). The statement that QARP was significantly superior on all primary outcomes is therefore wrong as written. The abstract does acknowledge that ADL showed no difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that ADL was not a primary outcome.

quotes.text: The QARP group showed significantly superior efficacy for all primary outcomes compared with the standard therapies group
The principal result was changes in the scores on the modified Borg dyspnea scale (MBS),the activity of daily living (ADL)

quotes.location: Table 2, ADL T2 row, difference column

issues.title: Three principal outcomes, several timepoints and symptoms tested at 0.05 with no correction
issues.explanation: No multiplicity adjustment is described. The weakest significant findings (28-month MBS, P = 0.024, and the symptom-positivity comparisons) could be chance results. The strongest 14-month results are unlikely to be affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical testing plan, or a stated alpha adjustment.

quotes.text: Here, a 2-tailed P < 0.05 threshold was used to indicate statistical significance.

issues.title: Sample-size inputs (mMRC 0.52 vs 0.95, SDs 0.11 vs 0.92) do not match the trial's scale or direction
issues.explanation: The assumed treatment-group mean (0.95) is worse than the control mean (0.52) on a scale where higher means more severe dyspnoea. The SDs differ by a factor of about 8, and neither fits the trial's baseline mMRC of 2.7-2.9. The calculation therefore cannot be reproduced or relied on to show the sample was adequate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registered protocol showing different inputs, or a clear explanation of the reference study's scale.

quotes.text: the mMRC Scale score in the control group is 0.52 with a standard deviation of 0.11, and the average mMRC Scale score in the treatment group is 0.95 with a standard deviation of 0.92.

issues.title: Abstract says QARP 'significantly increased' MBS scores at 28 months though difference is -0.4 (an improvement)
issues.explanation: On the Borg scale higher numbers mean more breathlessness, so a -0.4 difference is a reduction and a benefit. The abstract calls it an 'increase', which reads as the opposite. This is a wording error with no effect on the analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; it is a wording slip.

quotes.text: significantly increased their MBS scores ( -0.4, 95 % CI ( -0.7, -0.1), P = 0.024)

issues.title: Global COVID-19 totals differ between Introduction (756 M cases, 6.84 M deaths) and Discussion (770 M, 6.97 M)
issues.explanation: The same WHO source is cited for two different sets of global totals. This is background information only and does not touch the trial results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the Discussion figures were taken from a later WHO update.

quotes.text: > 756 million cases of SARSCoV-2 infections globally, including 6844,267 deaths
Over 770 million people have been infected with SARS-CoV-2, with 6.97 million fatalities

10.1016/j.intimp.2024.112673.headline_claim: Combining major ozone autohemotherapy (O3-MAH) with conventional treatment more effectively improves symptoms, lung function and 6MWD in PASC patients than conventional treatment alone, without adverse events.
10.1016/j.intimp.2024.112673.overall: The headline claim that O3-MAH beats conventional treatment for PASC rests on an open-label, single-centre trial with borderline between-group P-values (0.0478, 0.0374), uncorrected multiplicity and baseline imbalance, and the lung-function superiority claim is not borne out by the between-group tests. The safety claim is also stated more strongly than the limited monitoring allows. The printed-number errors found are minor, so the conclusions should be treated as tentative and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Changes in symptom score, 6MWD, and lung function parameters between groups before and after intervention
