issues.title: Conclusion that O3-MAH improves lung function and 6MWD more than control not supported by between-group tests
issues.explanation: Both arms improved on FVC, FEV1 and 6MWD, but after-treatment between-group tests are null for FVC (0.74), FEV1 (0.90), FEV1/FVC (0.61) and absolute 6MWD (0.2633). Only tidal volume (0.0374) and 6MWD %pred (0.0032) differ, the latter despite a null absolute distance. The conclusion nonetheless states superiority on lung function and 6MWD.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, adjusted analysis showing a significant between-group difference in lung function and absolute 6MWD.

quotes.text: more effectively improves symptoms, lung function, and 6MWD in patients with PASC than conventional treatment alone

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of superior lung function is supported by only one of seven between-group comparisons (VT, P=0.0374, not significant after any multiplicity correction), and the others are far from significant (P=0.56 to 0.90). The 6MWD claim is supported by 6MWD%pred (P=0.0032) but not by absolute distance (P=0.2633), so the conclusion overstates the evidence for lung function and is only partly supported for 6MWD.

issues.title: ~10 primary variables and ~45 lab markers tested at P<0.05 uncorrected; key between-group P=0.0478, 0.0374
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is a family of symptom, 6MWD and lung-function variables with no single pre-specified primary endpoint or correction. About 10 post-treatment between-group primary comparisons were run; only three reached P<0.05, two of them barely. The laboratory section adds many more tests, and the post-hoc subgroup analyses (CRP, treatment duration, symptom duration) are additional. The main finding therefore carries a high chance of false positives.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single primary endpoint or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis in which the results survive.

quotes.text: A P-value of ＜0.05 was considered significant.
than the conventional group (P = 0.0478)

second_reader.what_stands: About 10 primary variables and 44 laboratory markers were tested at an uncorrected 0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment or single prespecified primary. Two key between-group results (symptom score P=0.0478, VT P=0.0374) would not survive even a Bonferroni correction across the 10 primary variables, though 6MWD%pred (P=0.0032) would fall just under 0.005.

issues.title: Open-label trial without sham; subjective symptom score is a primary outcome with borderline P=0.0478
issues.explanation: Patients knew they were receiving a 7-day blood-ozone infusion, versus conventional care only. The symptom score is a patient-rated 0-3 scale summed over 13 symptoms, and 6MWD depends on effort. Placebo, attention or expectation effects can therefore explain part or all of the modest between-group difference. The authors acknowledge this, but the conclusion states efficacy without qualification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment of the symptom score, or a sham-controlled arm.

quotes.text: we could not blind the treatments, introducing potential bias and placebo effects.
Symptom severity was categorized into none, mild, moderate, and severe, with corresponding scores of 0, 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with no sham, the authors concede this, and the symptom score is a subjective primary outcome whose between-group P is 0.0478, only marginally below 0.05. Blinded outcome assessment is not described, so the symptom result is vulnerable to bias and placebo effects.

issues.title: Marked baseline imbalance (symptom score, ~15 markers) with unadjusted post-treatment comparisons
issues.explanation: The authors themselves conclude the O3-MAH group had slightly more severe disease at baseline. That many baseline differences is more than chance would suggest under simple randomization with 73 patients. The main between-group comparisons use post-treatment values without adjustment for baseline. The direction of bias is unclear, because greater severity can raise regression to the mean but also lowers the starting point.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or change-score analysis showing the same between-group differences after baseline adjustment.

quotes.text: had a higher symptom score than the conventional group (P = 0.0493)
had slightly more severe disease.

second_reader.what_stands: There is substantial baseline imbalance, including the symptom score (P1=0.0493, medians 10 vs 7) and more than 15 laboratory markers (23 by count of bold baseline P-values in Table 3), and post-treatment between-group comparisons are unadjusted. The imbalance is disclosed by the authors but not handled analytically, and the baseline gap in symptom score is about as large as the post-treatment gap.

issues.title: Safety claim ('without any adverse events') rests on infusion-session monitoring in 35 patients over ~1 week
issues.explanation: The conclusion declares the treatment free of adverse events and a new treatment option for PASC. Adverse-event monitoring is described only for the infusion session through one hour after, and was not systematically compared with the control arm. With 35 treated patients and a 7-day course, the data cannot exclude moderate rates of adverse events, and longer-term effects are unknown. The conclusion is stated more strongly than this single-centre, open-label study supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified systematic adverse-event record covering both arms through follow-up.

quotes.text: without any adverse events, thereby providing new treatment options for PASC.
No participant indicated treatment-related symptoms nor adverse events.
from the initiation of treatment through to one hour post-transfusion
quotes.location: Methods 2.5, Evaluation of symptoms and adverse events

issues.title: Complete-case analysis of 73/80; arm split of exclusions not reported; 15 of 35 O3-MAH patients got ~4 days
issues.explanation: Seven patients were excluded, including some missing only one test, and no intention-to-treat analysis or per-arm accounting is provided. Attrition is small, so the effect on results is probably limited. The shortened courses in 15 of 35 O3-MAH patients, who were still analysed, would if anything understate the effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram showing the per-arm exclusions and a sensitivity analysis including all randomized patients.

quotes.text: Therefore, 73 patients completed the entire study.
Our protocol prescribed a seven-day course of O

issues.title: Text says no significant immune change in conventional arm; lymphocytes rose 1.46 to 1.54, P=0.0229
issues.explanation: The text says no immune or cytokine parameter changed significantly in the conventional group. Table 3 prints a bold, below-0.05 within-group P of 0.0229 for conventional-group lymphocytes, which the text itself treats as a cellular immune indicator. The statement is therefore not accurate. The effect is small and does not change the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that lymphocyte counts are excluded from 'immune parameters', or a corrected P-value in Table 3.

quotes.text: There were no significant differences in immune and cytokine parameters in the conventional treatment group before and after treatment.

issues.title: Myoglobin after O3-MAH: median 28.31 printed below its own Q1 of 38.86
issues.explanation: The post-treatment myoglobin cell reads 28.31 (38.86, 52.91). A median must lie within its interquartile range, so at least one of the three numbers is wrong. The text reports a significant myoglobin decrease in the O3-MAH group (P=0.0010), so the table cell cannot be taken at face value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source data showing a different Q1 (for example 18.86), which would make the cell a simple typo.

issues.title: Post-hoc subgroup with >20 weeks symptoms: median 25 weeks reported with IQR (23, 24)
issues.explanation: The post-hoc subgroup with symptoms over 20 weeks is described as 25 (23, 24) weeks. A median above the upper quartile is impossible. It affects only a descriptive post-hoc subgroup.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The supplementary table showing correct quartiles for this subgroup.

issues.title: Table 1 O3-MAH percentages inconsistent with n=35: 17 (51%) should be 48.6%, 23 (68%) should be 65.7%
issues.explanation: Two O3-MAH-column percentages in Table 1 do not match their counts over the stated n of 35. Shortness of breath is 17 (51%) but 17/35 is 48.6%, and corticosteroids is 23 (68%) but 23/35 is 65.7%. Every other row matches its count. These are baseline descriptives, and the reported P-values are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing different counts, for example 18/35 for shortness of breath, with the percentage then correct.

quotes.location: Table 1, Shortness of breath row, O3-MAH

script.explanation: 17/35 = 48.57%, but the paper prints 51, outside the rounding interval [50.50, 52.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 33.3 rather than 35.

issues.title: Text calls CD16+56 'counts' higher in O3-MAH at baseline; the n/uL row is lower (178 vs 186)
issues.explanation: The text lists CD16+56 counts among the baseline values that were higher in the O3-MAH group. Only the percentage row supports that (22.3 vs 14.91, P=0.0311). The absolute count row shows 178 vs 186 /uL (P=0.2874), which is lower and not significant. This is a small wording slip and does not alter any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sentence refers to percentages, or a corrected table showing a higher count in the O3-MAH group.

quotes.text: cluster of differentiation (CD)16 + 56 counts

quotes.location: Table 3, CD16 + 56, n/uL row, O3-MAH before
Table 3, CD16 + 56, n/uL row, conventional before

10.1016/j.isci.2025.114574.headline_claim: An interpretable logistic regression model with a nomogram (fatigue, SF-36, FEV1/FVC, PSQI, IL-6, CRP, NEUTP) can predict which long COVID patients will respond to low-dose methylprednisolone, providing a decision-support tool for individualized treatment.
10.1016/j.isci.2025.114574.overall: The paper shows moderate discrimination for 'improvement' (AUC about 0.84-0.87 in external cohorts), but only in treated patients with no comparator, and with a change-score outcome that is partly coupled to a predictor. The claims of strong performance, individualized treatment guidance and a drug-mechanism interpretation are not supported. Test-set results are imprecise and non-independent, with specificity of 0.29-0.51 throughout and accuracy no better than assuming everyone responds.

primary_outcome.name: Treatment success defined as an SF-36 total score increase of more than 10 points (MCID)

issues.title: Single-arm data cannot show who benefits from methylprednisolone; 'response' is SF-36 gain >10 points in treated patients
issues.explanation: All 330 patients received the same 8 mg/day for 14 days and no untreated or alternative-treatment group exists. The outcome is any SF-36 rise above 10 points, which would also occur in many patients through spontaneous recovery or regression to the mean. The model therefore predicts who improves, not who benefits from the drug, so the claim that it identifies patients 'who may benefit from treatment' and supports 'individualized treatment' is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the data include a concurrent control arm analysed for treatment-by-predictor interaction.

quotes.text: all patients received methylprednisolone tablets (brand name: Medrol, manufactured by Pfizer, specification: 4mg/tablet) orally at a dose of 8 mg (2 tablets) daily for 2 consecutive weeks
helps identify patients who may benefit from treatment, facilitating more precise treatment decisions

second_reader.what_stands: All patients were treated, and 'response' is defined as an SF-36 gain >10 points. The model therefore predicts who improves on this score after treatment, and it cannot show who benefits from methylprednisolone as opposed to who would improve anyway. The claims that the model 'helps identify patients who may benefit from treatment' and aids treatment decisions go beyond what a single-arm design supports.

issues.title: Discussion asserts methylprednisolone improves outcomes by suppressing inflammation, inferred from single-arm predictors
issues.explanation: The Discussion reads CRP, IL-6 and NEUTP as showing that low-dose methylprednisolone 'can alleviate symptoms and improve clinical outcomes' by suppressing inflammation. A model's feature importances in treated-only data cannot show a drug effect or mechanism. The statements about fatigue, lung function and sleep have the same problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled analysis showing a predictor-by-treatment interaction on the outcome.

quotes.text: suggest that low-dose methylprednisolone can alleviate symptoms and improve clinical outcomes in long COVID by suppressing inflammation and modulating immune function

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion asserts that methylprednisolone improves symptoms and outcomes by suppressing inflammation, based only on baseline predictors in a single-arm cohort. The authors' note that the mechanisms need further verification softens the mechanistic claim, but the causal efficacy statement is still not supported by the design.

issues.title: 'Strong' performance and 'valuable' treatment-decision tool overstated: specificity 0.29-0.51, test accuracy below prevalence
issues.explanation: The model labels most patients as responders: in the test set it correctly flags only 2 of 7 non-responders, and in each external cohort only half. Test accuracy (0.7576) is below the proportion of responders (26/33 = 78.8%), so it does no better than assuming everyone responds. A single baseline variable (CRP, SF-36) reaches an AUC of about 0.72, the same as the 7-variable model on the test set. With no control group the model cannot guide who should get the drug.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Calibration and decision-curve analysis showing net benefit over treating everyone, plus a comparator arm.

quotes.text: The LR model and nomogram demonstrated strong predictive performance and clinical interpretability

second_reader.what_stands: At the reported thresholds the LR model labels about half or more of non-responders as responders (specificity 0.29-0.51), and in the test cohort its accuracy (0.758) is below the 0.788 achieved by predicting everyone responds. Calling performance 'strong' and the tool 'valuable' for treatment decisions is therefore overstated, especially given the very small non-responder groups (7-10 patients) and the wide confidence intervals. Discrimination by AUC is moderate to good in three of four cohorts.

issues.title: Outcome is SF-36 gain >10 points while baseline SF-36 is a top predictor: lower baseline favours 'response'
issues.explanation: Treatment success is defined as an SF-36 increase above 10 points and baseline SF-36 is one of the seven predictors, ranking second in SHAP importance. Patients with low baseline scores have more room to rise and are subject to regression to the mean. Lower SF-36 therefore predicts 'response' partly by construction, and the Discussion reads this as 'more severely impaired patients might benefit more' from the drug.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis of the outcome adjusted for baseline score in a controlled comparison, or a non-change-based outcome.

quotes.text: we predefined an increase of >10 points in the SF-36 total score as the threshold for achieving the MCID and used this criterion to define treatment success
We observed that lower SF-36 scores were associated with higher probabilities of response to methylprednisolone treatment

second_reader.what_stands: Because the outcome is a gain in SF-36 and baseline SF-36 is a leading predictor, the finding that lower baseline scores predict 'response' is partly built into the outcome definition. The authors interpret it as sicker patients 'benefitting more' from the drug, with no control arm and no adjustment for ceiling effects or regression to the mean.

issues.title: Test (n=33, 7 non-responders) and external (n=53, 42) validation give wide intervals, yet performance is called stable
issues.explanation: No sample-size justification is given. With 7 non-responders in the test set, the LR test AUC of 0.72 has a 95% CI of about 0.50 to 0.94 and specificity of 0.29 (CI 0.05-0.70). The external cohorts have only 10 and 8 non-responders. The data cannot distinguish performance in the 0.7-0.9 range from chance-level discrimination in the test set, so 'stable performance' is not established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger validation set, or intervals showing the AUC clearly above 0.7 in all cohorts.

quotes.text: the two external validation cohorts were modest in size

issues.title: 407 patients extracted but 330 analysed; 77 (19%) exclusions not itemised and may inflate response rate
issues.explanation: The Methods say 407 patients were extracted, while the Results analyse 330. Exclusion criteria are listed but the number removed under each is not given, and the excluded group is not described. Because exclusion depends partly on completing treatment and having follow-up, the analysed set is enriched for completers and probably for responders.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram with exclusion counts showing similar baseline characteristics and outcomes in excluded patients.

quotes.text: A total of 407 Long COVID patients who received low-dose methylprednisolone treatment were extracted from the database.
quotes.location: Methods, Experimental model and study participant details

quotes.text: This study ultimately included 330 cases, of which 266 were classified as treatment-effective and 64 as treatment-ineffective.
quotes.location: Results, Patient characteristics and dataset allocation

issues.title: XGBoost accuracy in text (95.54% train, 69.70% test) differs from Tables 2-3 (0.9257, 0.6667)
issues.explanation: The text gives XGBoost accuracy of 95.54% (training) and 69.70% (test), while Tables 2 and 3 print 0.9257 and 0.6667 for the same model name. The text refers to a hyperparameter-tuned model whose results are in no table, so the two sets of numbers may describe different fits, or the text may have mislabelled the F1 score as accuracy. This does not affect the choice of logistic regression, but the reader cannot tell which model each figure belongs to.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or supplement showing the tuned XGBoost model with 95.54% training and 69.70% test accuracy.

quotes.text: Although it achieved a relatively high accuracy rate (95.54%) on the training set

issues.title: LR chosen after comparing six models on the test set, so the test AUC of 0.72 is not independent
issues.explanation: XGBoost was re-tuned after the test result and LR was then selected using performance in the training and test sets. The test results therefore informed model choice and are optimistic as an independent estimate. The external cohorts are a cleaner check, but they are small and show LR specificity of only 0.50.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified selection rule using only cross-validation on the training data.

quotes.text: Therefore, the LR model was selected for downstream analysis.

10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.103328.headline_claim: Tailored exercise did not outperform standard care for HRQoL or upright time in COVID-19-induced POTS, and was associated with reduced upright time, while several secondary outcomes improved in both groups.
10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.103328.overall: The null primary HRQoL result and the reduction in upright time are reported straightforwardly and can be relied on, subject to the open-label design. The Conclusions and Perspectives go beyond the data in endorsing exercise for 'selected individuals', since responder rates were equal across arms. Numeric errors are minor typographical slips.

primary_outcome.name: Change in HRQoL (EQ-5D-5L) and upright time (accelerometer)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in time in upright position and steps per day
primary_outcomes.time_frame: through study completion, an average of 1 year

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: through study completion, an average of 1 year

issues.title: Conclusion endorses exercise despite equal 36% responder rates in both arms and reduced upright time
issues.explanation: The trial found no HRQoL benefit and lower upright time and steps with exercise. About 36% of each arm improved EQ-VAS by 10 points or more, so the 'clinically meaningful improvements in some individuals' cannot be attributed to exercise. The Conclusions and Perspectives nonetheless say exercise may be a reasonable option for selected individuals and support its use. The abstract also highlights a 'trend' in PEM whose credible interval spans 0.13 to 2.75.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that responders were more frequent or larger in the exercise arm, or an adverse-event report showing the intervention is safe and tolerable.

quotes.text: may still represent a reasonable therapeutic option for selected individuals with COVID-19–induced POTS
was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in some individuals, supporting its use as an individualized treatment option.
The exploratory responder analysis of EQ-VAS showed that 36% of participants in each group improved \$10 points.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does report equal 36% responder rates in both arms and a significant 31 min/day greater reduction in upright time with exercise, and the Perspectives sentence says exercise 'was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in some individuals, supporting its use'. Because the control arm improved equally often, that responder rate gives no support for an exercise-specific benefit; the statement in the Perspectives box that 'supporting' use rests on it, which is not justified. However, the paper is not an unqualified endorsement: it states exercise did not outperform standard ca

issues.title: Unblinded participants self-report the HRQoL primary outcome and all questionnaire secondaries
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and completed the EQ-5D-5L and the symptom questionnaires themselves. Only the follow-up test leader was blinded. Expectation effects could therefore have inflated the self-reported outcomes in the exercise arm. The primary HRQoL comparison was null, so the bias risk affects the secondary and responder claims more than the main result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable. The point is a design limitation. It matters less because the primary result is null and the objective outcome is accelerometer-based.

quotes.text: participants and physiotherapists were not blinded due to the nature of the intervention.
This was an open-label, randomized controlled parallel-group trial

issues.title: EQ-VAS time effect 7.155 lies outside its printed CI of 0.5-3.8
issues.explanation: Table 3 gives an EQ-VAS time effect of 7.155 with a 95% CI of 0.5-3.8, which does not contain the point estimate. With P = 0.035 the interval should be roughly 0.5 to 13.8. The error affects only a within-group time effect, not the between-group result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing a consistent interval; this would confirm the slip rather than refute it.

script.explanation: the estimate 7.155 lies outside its own CI [0.5, 3.8]; the estimate 7.155 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [0.5, 3.8] (expected about 2.1500) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0000 (reachable range [0.0000, 0.0000] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.035 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used

issues.title: Steps/day registered as a primary outcome but analysed as a secondary outcome
issues.explanation: The registry lists the primary outcome as time upright and steps per day, plus HRQoL. The paper treats only HRQoL and upright time as primary and labels steps a secondary exploratory outcome. The steps result is unfavourable to exercise (interaction P = 0.004), so the change makes the intervention look better rather than worse.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or the statistical analysis plan showing steps was designated secondary before data collection.

quotes.text: Secondary outcomes were assessed for exploratory reasons and included daily steps, sedentary time, physical and autonomic function, mental health, and symptom burden.

10.1016/j.jbmt.2024.11.037.headline_claim: Eight weeks of supervised Pilates Method (PM) is effective for rehabilitation of individuals with post-COVID-19 syndrome, improving 6MWT performance, post-exercise fatigue and sleep quality.
10.1016/j.jbmt.2024.11.037.overall: The headline claim that eight weeks of Pilates is effective is only weakly supported. The primary 6MWT contrast against the control group is null, and the PG vs SPEG difference is confounded by a significant baseline imbalance with no adjustment. The sleep and fatigue conclusions rest largely on within-group change, uncorrected multiple tests and unblinded self-report in an underpowered sample, and the Table 3 BORG-M contrasts do not match Table 2.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test distance (physical fitness)

issues.title: Effectiveness claimed from within-group change; PG vs CG 6MWT p=0.56 and PSQI between-group p=0.36
issues.explanation: The PG improved from baseline, but the PG did not differ from the control group on the primary 6MWT outcome. The between-group tests for PSQI total and for most sleep components were non-significant. The paper nonetheless concludes PM is effective for walking, fatigue and sleep, and that it shows superiority to supervised exercise. Statistical significance in one arm but not another is not evidence of a difference between arms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group analysis of change, adjusted for baseline, showing PG better than CG on 6MWT and PSQI.

quotes.text: Our findings indicates that eight weeks of PM is effective in improving 6MWT performance, post-exercise fatigue and sleep quality in individuals with PCS-19.
it demonstrates the superiority of PM in individuals with PCS-19
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph on SPE and sleep quality

quotes.text: Although the intervention groups showed a reduction in these values, only the PG showed this statistically significant reduction.

second_reader.what_stands: For 6MWT and sleep quality, the effectiveness claims rest on within-group change (PG significant, others not) rather than on between-group evidence: PG vs CG on 6MWT is p = 0.56 and PSQI total between-group is p = 0.36. The 'superiority of PM' statement for sleep is not backed by any significant between-group test, and the 6MWT contrast with SPEG is confounded by baseline imbalance. The fatigue (BORG-M) claim is partly supported by a significant PG vs CG contrast (p<0.030), so the point is weaker for that outcome.

issues.title: Baseline 6MWT differs across arms (418 vs 509 m, p=0.004) yet between-group tests ignore baseline
issues.explanation: The groups differed at baseline on the primary outcome, and on psychosomatic illness and chronic pain. The between-group analysis is a one-way ANOVA on post-intervention values with no ANCOVA or change-score analysis. Much of the PG-SPEG gap at follow-up was already present at baseline, so the significant PG vs SPEG 6MWT result cannot be read as a treatment effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted analysis (ANCOVA or change scores) showing the same PG advantage.

quotes.text: The groups were homogeneous regards sociodemographic and clinical variables, except for the prevalence of psychosomatic diseases and persistent symptoms after contamination by the disease

second_reader.what_stands: Baseline 6MWT differs materially between arms (418.1 vs 509.0 m, p=0.004 in the text, <0.005 in Table 1), and the between-group comparisons (one-way ANOVA F(2,56)=5.422 and Tukey) use T16 values only, with no baseline adjustment or change-score analysis. This can distort the between-group contrasts in either direction (the PG vs SPEG gap of 103 m versus about 41 m on change scores). The Results sentence calling the groups 'homogeneous' omits the 6MWT, though the imbalance is reported in the next sentence.

issues.title: Randomised 59 vs 84-102 planned; confident efficacy conclusion despite acknowledged shortfall
issues.explanation: The sample-size calculation required 28 per group, or 34 allowing for loss. The trial randomised 59 (20, 20, 19). The limitations paragraph concedes this, yet the paper ends with an unqualified statement that the programme is effective. The primary between-group contrast (PG vs CG) was not significant, which is what an underpowered design would produce.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A revised power calculation showing 59 participants suffice for the primary contrast.

quotes.text: a sample of 28 individuals would be needed for each group
the sample size achieved was below the initially projected sample calculation needed to ensure the desired reliability power of the results

second_reader.what_stands: The study randomised 59 participants against a planned minimum of 84 (28 per group), or 102 with allowance for losses. The limitation is acknowledged, but the abstract-level conclusion and the first Discussion sentence state effectiveness without qualification. The limitations paragraph says only that the shortfall 'does not preclude valuable data', so the conclusion is not tempered by it.

issues.title: Table 3 BORG-M Tukey differences do not match Table 2 post-intervention means (PG-SPEG -0.95 vs -1.3)
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives post-intervention BORG-M means of 0.9 (PG), 2.2 (SPEG) and 2.1 (CG). These imply PG-SPEG of about -1.3 and SPEG-CG of about +0.1. Table 3 prints -0.95 and -0.30, which has the opposite sign for SPEG-CG. The PG-SPEG contrast is reported as non-significant (p=0.09), and one of the two tables is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Tukey comparisons used adjusted or change-score means, or a corrected Table 2 whose means reproduce the Table 3 differences.

issues.title: Seven PSQI components plus total and ~24 within-group tests at alpha 0.05, uncorrected
issues.explanation: The paper adopts 5% significance with no correction beyond Tukey for pairwise ANOVA contrasts. Sleep-quality claims for the PG cite individual components (quality, latency, duration, disorders) that reached only p<0.02 to p<0.03 in paired tests. With 8 PSQI measures, a Bonferroni threshold would be about 0.006, and only the total score would pass.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction, or evidence that PSQI total was the only designated sleep outcome.

quotes.text: It was adopted the value of 5% as the level of statistical significance.
PG individuals showed improvement in other PSQI subscales, such as subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration and sleep disorders

issues.title: Self-reported fatigue (BORG-M) and sleep (PSQI) outcomes in unblinded participants
issues.explanation: Only the assessing investigator was blinded; participants knew their arm. The control group received only a home-exercise guidebook, so expectancy and attention effects could influence reported fatigue and sleep. The paper does not discuss this limitation, though it draws fatigue and sleep conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an attention-matched control or participant blinding.

quotes.text: The investigator who performed the initial and final data collection regarding the assessment/evaluation of the participants was blinded
The individuals were asked about their perception of effort 5 min after performing the 6MWT.

10.1016/j.jesf.2024.04.003.headline_claim: A 4-week moderate-intensity treadmill program with or without non-immersive VR may improve fatigue, cognitive function and sleep quality to the same extent in post-COVID-19 subjects, and participant satisfaction may be greater with VR-assisted treadmill training.
10.1016/j.jesf.2024.04.003.overall: This is a very small (16 completers), retrospectively registered, open-label two-arm exercise study with no non-exercising control. The claims that both programmes improve outcomes, and to the same extent, are not supported by the design, because improvements are within-group and equivalence is inferred from non-significant tests. The satisfaction difference is real arithmetically but rests on unblinded, subjective ratings, and the authors' hedging ('may', 'definitive conclusion cannot be reached') is appropriate but is not carried into the abstract's wording.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale), cognitive function (MoCA), sleep quality (PSQI) are co-equal outcomes, with participant satisfaction labelled secondary

issues.title: 'Same extent' claimed from non-significant between-group tests with 8 per arm and no power calculation
issues.explanation: With 8 per arm and no sample-size calculation, a non-significant between-group result cannot show the two programmes are equivalent. No equivalence margin or confidence interval for the difference is given. The fatigue difference is 2.6 points on a 33-point scale (p = 0.063), which is not trivially small. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless say the two programmes improve outcomes 'to the same extent'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence margin and a confidence interval for the between-group difference lying inside it.

quotes.text: may improve fatigue, cognitive function, and sleep quality to the same extent in COVID-19 survivors
Nonetheless, a definitive conclusion cannot be reached due to the limited sample size

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does infer 'the same extent' / 'similarly' from non-significant between-group tests with 8 per arm, no stated power calculation and no equivalence margin, and the confidence intervals recomputed from the printed data are wide enough to leave clinically relevant differences open, especially for Chalder and MoCA. It is not unqualified, though: the Conclusion uses 'may' and says a definitive conclusion cannot be reached because of the limited sample size, but the abstract and Discussion state sameness more firmly.

issues.title: Benefit claimed from within-group pre-post changes with no non-exercising control, in a recovering population
issues.explanation: The main efficacy message is that both groups improved from baseline, shown by paired t-tests. Without a control group, a baseline-to-follow-up change cannot be credited to the exercise. Participants were recruited 3-4 months after infection and selected for low MoCA scores, so spontaneous recovery and regression to the mean are likely. The Discussion nonetheless explains the improvements through exercise mechanisms. The study can support a hypothesis, not a demonstration of benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent non-exercising or usual-care arm showing smaller change than the exercise arms.

quotes.text: Both groups showed significant improvements in the Chalder Fatigue Scale, the MoCA questionnaire, and the PSQI scores after training compared to baseline (p < 0.05)
Other limitations include the lack of a non-exercising control group

second_reader.what_stands: The reported benefit rests only on within-group pre-post changes, and with no non-exercising control group, in a recently infected and selected-for-low-score population, exercise effects cannot be separated from spontaneous recovery, regression to the mean or expectation. The authors do acknowledge the missing control group in the final Discussion paragraph, but the causal wording ('induced', 'lead to') and the Conclusion's caveat limited to sample size do not carry that limitation through.

issues.title: Table 2 baseline header n=10 per arm, but VR age mean 49.38 only fits n=8; Table 3 and abstract use n=8
issues.explanation: Table 2 labels both arms n = 10, while the abstract and Table 3 analyse 8 per arm. The header is plausibly the randomized population, but the VR age mean of 49.38 cannot come from 10 whole-year ages (it equals 395/8). The gender counts, in contrast, sum to 10. Table 2 therefore mixes two populations, and the baseline comparison cannot be tied to the analysed sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or supplement showing Table 2 covers all 20 randomized participants, with age values that give a mean of 49.38 at n = 10.

quotes.text: Non-VR group (n1 = 10)
Sixteen of twenty post-COVID-19 subjects completed this study (n1 = 8, n2 = 8).

issues.title: Unblinded interviewer and participants; the only significant between-group result is self-rated satisfaction
issues.explanation: All outcomes are questionnaires, and the interviewer, the physiotherapist and the participants knew the allocation. The sole significant between-group finding is satisfaction on a 5-point scale, which is highly open to expectancy and interviewer effects. Participants in the VR arm may simply have rated the novel game format higher. The headline claim that VR 'could' give greater satisfaction should be read in that light.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Assessor-blinded or objectively measured outcomes agreeing with the satisfaction difference.

quotes.text: neither the physiotherapist nor the participants were blind to the exercise programs. Likewise, the interviewer who administered the questionnaires was not blind to patient allocation

issues.title: 20 % loss (4 of 20) with completers-only analysis; arm, reasons and handling of dropouts not given in text
issues.explanation: The analysis covers 16 of 20 randomized participants. The text does not say which arm lost the four people, why they left, or whether baseline values differ for them. The Methods describe no intention-to-treat or missing-data approach. With 8 per arm, one or two dropouts could change the between-group and satisfaction results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 showing balanced dropouts with reasons unrelated to the intervention, plus an analysis including all 20 randomized participants.

quotes.text: Sixteen of twenty post-COVID-19 subjects, recruited by referral from a pulmonologist, completed this study.

issues.title: Post-intervention fatigue p = 0.063 not reproduced from printed means/SDs (non-VR SD 0.66 looks anomalous)
issues.explanation: Table 3 gives post fatigue 10.50 ± 0.66 vs 13.12 ± 3.87 with 8 per arm. An unpaired t-test on these gives t ≈ 1.89 and p of roughly 0.08 (pooled) to 0.10 (Welch), not 0.063. The SD of 0.66 is about one sixth of the baseline SD of 4.39 and of the other arm. Either the SD or the p is mis-printed, or a different test was used. Any plausible correction leaves the result non-significant, so the effect is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data or a corrected SD for the non-VR post fatigue score that reproduces p = 0.063.

quotes.text: Chalder fatigue score (p = 0.063)

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

10.1016/j.jocn.2023.09.005.headline_claim: Donepezil 5 mg/day did not produce statistically significant memory improvement over 12 weeks versus control, though significant within-group gains were seen in two WMS-R subtests in the donepezil arm.
10.1016/j.jocn.2023.09.005.overall: The primary between-group finding is null and the authors say so, but the sample is very small and underpowered, and attrition is not accounted for in the text. The 'noteworthy efficacy' in specific subtests rests on uncorrected within-arm tests that the between-group analysis does not support, so it should be treated as hypothesis-generating at most.

primary_outcome.name: WMS-R subtests and indices (no single primary outcome named)

issues.title: Subtest 'efficacy' claimed from within-arm Friedman tests while between-group GEE was null
issues.explanation: The favourable subtest findings come from testing change over time within the donepezil arm only, while the between-group GEE comparison found nothing significant. A within-arm change cannot be attributed to the drug, because the control arm also improved on most subtests (practice effects, natural recovery). Control arm means rose on Visual Reproduction I and Verbal Paired Associates II too, so the claimed benefit is not shown relative to control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant group-by-time interaction for these subtests, or a pre-specified between-group contrast showing donepezil superior to control.

quotes.text: significant increases in Visual Reproduction I and Verbal Paired Associates II scores were evidenced within the drug-administered group
our results support the notion that donepezil enhances visual reproduction scores I

second_reader.what_stands: The paper bases its claims of subtest-level efficacy (Discussion: 'our results support the notion that donepezil enhances visual reproduction scores I'; Conclusion: 'noteworthy efficacy was observed in specific memory subtests') on within-arm Friedman tests (P = 0.032 and 0.034), while the between-group GEE found no difference for any subtest or index. No between-group test supports these subtest claims, there is no multiplicity adjustment across many subtests, and the control group also improved numerically. The authors do report the null primary result and list small sample size and single-b

issues.title: Only 10 vs 15 analysed with no sample-size calculation; null result is uninformative
issues.explanation: With 25 analysed participants and no reported power calculation, the trial cannot rule out a clinically meaningful effect, nor reliably detect one. The authors acknowledge this limitation and call for larger studies, which tempers the issue. The null between-group result should be read as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation showing adequate power for the planned effect.

quotes.text: The study encompassed 25 participants, comprising 10 individuals in the drug-administered cohort and 15 individuals in the control cohort
Nevertheless, the study has some limitations, including a small sample size

issues.title: Completers-only analysis; numbers randomised and lost not given in text
issues.explanation: The analysis includes only participants who completed 12 weeks, and the text does not say how many were randomised or withdrew per arm. The 10 vs 15 split under simple random allocation suggests possible unequal attrition. Without an intention-to-treat analysis, the between-group comparison could be biased in either direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing few or balanced dropouts, or an ITT analysis giving the same result.

quotes.text: who qualified for and concluded the entire 12-week investigation

10.1016/j.jpsychires.2026.11.021.headline_claim: Adding left-prefrontal tDCS to cognitive training reduced anxiety and daytime sleepiness and improved cognition and psychomotor speed in women with post-COVID cognitive complaints, relative to sham tDCS plus training and training alone.
10.1016/j.jpsychires.2026.11.021.overall: The behavioural results are statistically consistent with the printed F values and eta-squared figures, but they come from 30 participants (10 per arm, about half the calculated need) and show extreme effect sizes. The paper's causal and corroboration language is stronger than this design supports, because of the unverified blinding, the consumer-grade EEG indices and the claim that all gains were confirmed by corrected non-parametric tests (fluency was not). The headline direction is plausible but should be read as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: Baseline-adjusted ANCOVA group effect on post-intervention scores across outcomes (anxiety, sleepiness, cognition, reaction time, EEG markers)

issues.title: 10 per arm versus 19 calculated, with extreme effects and confident causal wording
issues.explanation: The trial enrolled 10 per group against the 19 per group its own calculation required, and that calculation assumed an implausibly large effect (ω² = .82, power .99). Observed effects are very large (BAI mean 44.7 to 5.6, SD falling from 8.8 to 2.2; reaction times about 100 ms faster), which is what small, unblinded-operator samples tend to produce. The Discussion nevertheless says the results are hard to attribute to chance and strengthen causal interpretation. The limitations section and 'confirmation needed' statement temper this, but the headline verbs ('reduced', 'improved') remain unqualified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A replication or a fully powered sample reproducing effects of similar size, or authors framing the findings strictly as hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: the present 10 per group constitute an initial
is difficult to attribute to chance or expectancy

second_reader.what_stands: The paper really has 10 per group against 19 calculated. It reports very large effects (anxiety partial eta-squared .88 and dz 4.36; reaction-time partial eta-squared .71-.74), and it uses causal verbs in the abstract and conclusion ('reduced', 'improved') and says the pattern 'is difficult to attribute to chance or expectancy' and that selectivity 'strengthens the causal interpretation'. The shortfall is not concealed: it is stated in Methods and Limitations, the magnitudes are called 'provisional' or 'preliminary', and the abstract asks for confirmation in larger samples. The remaining probl

issues.title: Fluency gain called confirmed by corrected non-parametric tests, but its Kruskal-Wallis p_FDR is .067
issues.explanation: The Conclusion and Results say the gains were confirmed by non-parametric tests after multiple-comparison correction, and that the K-W tests corroborated the parametric results for all FDR-surviving outcomes. In Table 2 the fluency K-W test gives p = .056 and p_FDR = .067, so it is not significant at the paper's own .05 threshold. Fluency is still listed as an improved domain in the Conclusion. The ANCOVA result for fluency (p_FDR = .002) stands, but the claim of non-parametric confirmation does not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table in which the fluency Kruskal-Wallis p_FDR is below .05, or text restricting the non-parametric confirmation claim to outcomes where it holds.

quotes.text: were confirmed by non-parametric tests after correction for multiple comparisons
Non-parametric Kruskal -Wallis tests corroborated the parametric results for all of these outcomes.

issues.title: EEG arousal and valence indices from a consumer headset are used as objective corroboration
issues.explanation: Cortical arousal (beta/alpha) and frontal valence were derived from an EMOTIV EPOC+ with a limited montage and interpreted relative to each person's baseline, with no reference range. The paper still presents their movement as objective, concordant evidence that reduces the likelihood of expectancy or reporting bias. Because these indices are simplified and not validated against clinical state, they cannot carry that weight. The effect is to make the clinical conclusion look better corroborated than it is.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that these specific indices on this headset track anxiety and arousal in an independent validation sample, or a more cautious reading of them as exploratory.

quotes.text: EEG was recorded with a consumer-grade headset and a limited montage
and no a priori optimal range was assumed

issues.title: 'Double-blind' label with unblinded operator and unverified blinding; self-reported anxiety and sleepiness
issues.explanation: The title and abstract call the trial double-blind, but the stimulator operator knew the allocation and blinding was never checked with an allocation-guess question. Anxiety (BAI) and sleepiness (ESS) are self-reported and show the largest effects. The equal outcomes in sham and CT-only arms partly reassure, but one three-arm trial with 10 per group cannot exclude expectancy as a contributor. The label overstates the level of masking.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A post-study allocation-guess questionnaire showing participants could not distinguish active from sham, plus a record of who ran assessments and delivered training.

quotes.text: Blinding integrity was not formally verified
quotes.location: Section 2.3, Randomization, allocation concealment, and masking

quotes.text: the operator was  not  blinded

issues.title: Discussion says valence shifted from negative, but CT+tDCS baseline in Table 1 is +0.02 (SD 1.03)
issues.explanation: The Discussion describes frontal valence in the CT+tDCS group as moving from negative (right-dominant) to strongly positive. Table 1 gives the baseline mean as +0.02 with SD 1.03, which is neither negative nor distinguishable from zero. The post-intervention value (1.61) is still clearly higher, so the shift itself holds. Only the description of the starting point is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level or median baseline valence data showing a negative group baseline.

quotes.text: to strongly positive (left-dominant)

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2023.111389.headline_claim: Famotidine improves cognitive impairment, depression and anxiety symptoms after COVID-19 and its safety is supported in this 12-week trial.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2023.111389.overall: The cognitive findings (MMSE and MoCA) are consistent across timepoints and tests, although the trial is small, uses a modified ITT with LOCF and has a registration that does not designate a primary outcome. The claims of efficacy in depression and anxiety and of safety are not supported at the strength stated in the abstract and conclusion, because the results rely on uncorrected secondary tests, small effects the authors call clinically minor, and a sample too small for safety conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: MMSE score (change from baseline and score at weeks 6 and 12)

issues.title: Depression and anxiety efficacy claimed despite non-significant HAM-D treatment effect and 'minor' changes
issues.explanation: The abstract conclusion states efficacy in treating depression and anxiety. The paper's own results show that between-group HAM-D scores were not different at weeks 6 and 12 (p = 0.387 at week 12), and that the repeated-measures treatment effect was not significant (p = 0.927). The HAM-D and HAM-A changes are described as minor and possibly not clinically significant, and the HAM-A differences are about 0.3 to 0.6 points. The depression and anxiety claim is therefore not supported at the strength stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified clinically meaningful threshold for HAM-D and HAM-A that the observed differences exceed.

quotes.text: However, this minor reduction might not be considered clinically significant.
Our study supports safety and efficacy of famotidine in treating cognitive impairment, depression and anxiety symptoms induced by COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: The authors themselves call the HAM-D reduction minor and the HAM-A decrease slight and possibly not clinically significant, and the HAM-D treatment main effect (p = 0.927) and endpoint scores did not differ. Yet the Abstract conclusion and Section 5 state efficacy and improvement in depression and anxiety without qualification. The 'non-significant' part applies to the main effect and endpoint comparisons, not the change-score tests, which were nominally significant (p = 0.009-0.042) but partly reflect baseline imbalance and were uncorrected for multiplicity.

issues.title: Eight scale-by-timepoint tests, no multiplicity control; HAM-D and HAM-A p-values 0.009 to 0.042 are fragile
issues.explanation: MMSE, MoCA, HAM-D and HAM-A were each tested at two timepoints at an unadjusted 0.05. The depression and anxiety results (HAM-D p = 0.009 and 0.02; HAM-A p = 0.04 and 0.02 in the abstract) are secondary and would not survive even a simple correction across the eight comparisons. The primary cognitive result is largely unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or adjusted p-values showing the secondary results remain significant.

quotes.text: A p -value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
the famotidine group experienced a larger reduction ( p = 0.009, p = 0.02, respectively)

issues.title: Safety claimed from 25 vs 25 patients with no safety power, though the Discussion denies a definitive conclusion
issues.explanation: The abstract conclusion says the study supports safety. The trial was powered on MMSE, not on adverse events, and 25 patients per arm cannot exclude even moderately higher rates of uncommon events. The Discussion says the sample size prevented a definitive conclusion on risks and benefits, which contradicts the abstract wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A safety analysis with confidence intervals excluding a clinically important excess of adverse events, or a safety-based sample size calculation.

quotes.text: The two groups did not differ in the frequency of adverse effects.
but the small sample size prevented us from making a definitive conclusion about the balance of risks and benefits
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph on famotidine safety and delirium

issues.title: Modified ITT: 10 of 60 randomised patients (16.7%) excluded; 5 later dropouts handled by LOCF only
issues.explanation: The 'ITT' population is actually a modified ITT, since it excludes 10 randomised patients without a post-baseline assessment. LOCF was used for the remaining 5 patients who dropped out between weeks 6 and 12, with no sensitivity analysis. Balanced dropout with a non-clinical reason lowers the risk of bias, but the 50-patient analysis cannot be considered a full ITT estimate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (e.g. mixed model without LOCF) that includes all 60 randomised patients and gives the same result.

quotes.text: Before the first clinical assessment visit, ten patients (five patients from each arm) dropped out due to consent withdrawal due to problems with commuting.
by using the last observation carried forward technique

issues.title: Registration did not distinguish primary from secondary outcomes, so MMSE as primary cannot be verified
issues.explanation: The registry entry listed all outcomes without designating a primary. The paper's choice of MMSE as primary, and the sample size based on it, cannot be checked against the registration. All four scales were significant on at least some comparisons, so the choice has little practical effect on the direction of results, but it weakens the confirmatory status of the cognitive finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry record or protocol showing MMSE designated as primary before enrolment.

quotes.text: the distinction between primary and secondary outcomes was not explicitly delineated

issues.title: Table 1 categories sum to 24, not N = 25: education in both arms, diagnostic method in placebo
issues.explanation: Several mutually exclusive Table 1 variables add to 24 participants in an arm that has 25. This affects education in both arms and diagnostic method in the placebo arm. A missing value per variable would explain it, but no missing data are declared and the percentages use 25 as the base. This is a small reporting inconsistency that does not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one participant per arm had missing education data, and one placebo participant had missing diagnostic-method data.

quotes.location: Table 1, Education, Higher row, famotidine column
Table 1, Education, Higher row, placebo column

issues.title: Placebo sex percentages in Table 1 (46.0%, 54.0%) do not match counts 12 and 13 of 25 (48.0%, 52.0%)
issues.explanation: In the placebo arm 12 females and 13 males make 25 participants, which gives 48.0% and 52.0%. The table prints 46.0% and 54.0%. The percentages sum to 100 but do not match the counts, so either the percentages or the counts are wrong. This is a baseline descriptive slip with no effect on the outcome analyses.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum showing the placebo arm had a different sex split or denominator, so that 46.0% and 54.0% are correct.

quotes.location: Table 1, Sex, Females row, placebo column
Table 1, Sex, Males row, placebo column

script.explanation: 12/25 = 48.00%, but the paper prints 46.0, outside the rounding interval [45.95, 46.10]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 26.1 rather than 25.

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2023.111471.headline_claim: Celecoxib monotherapy significantly improved depressive symptoms (HDRS) compared with placebo in patients with moderate depressive symptoms following COVID-19, with higher response and remission rates at week 6.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2023.111471.overall: The central finding, a larger HDRS decline and higher response and remission rates with celecoxib at 6 weeks, is not undermined by the errors found. These are the stated per-arm N of 28 in the text and Table 1 percentages computed on a denominator of 28; they are reporting slips. The 'safe and well-tolerated' statement goes beyond a 6-week, checklist-only safety assessment in 62 patients, and the study is small and single-centre, as the authors acknowledge.

primary_outcome.name: Average change in HDRS score from baseline to week 6 (study endpoint)

issues.title: 'Safe and well-tolerated' stated from 62 patients, 6 weeks, checklist only, no laboratory monitoring
issues.explanation: The Discussion says celecoxib was safe and well-tolerated. Yet adverse events came only from a 25-item checklist, no laboratory tests were done, and follow-up was 6 weeks in 31 patients per arm. A non-significant difference in adverse events at this sample size does not establish safety, and abdominal pain, constipation and diarrhoea were numerically more frequent on celecoxib. The Abstract and Conclusion are cautious, so this weakens a secondary claim only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limiting the safety statement to short-term, checklist-detected events in the Discussion where it is made.

quotes.text: celecoxib therapy was safe and well-tolerated, and no serious side effect was observed
In this study, we did not conduct laboratory measurements.

issues.title: Text gives 28 + 28 randomized but states 62; all tables use 31 per arm
issues.explanation: The Results say 62 patients were equally randomized to celecoxib (n = 28) or placebo (n = 28), which sums to 56. Every table, the sample-size section and the ITT statement use 31 per arm (62 in total). The withdrawal numbers are not themselves the problem, because LOCF carries those patients forward. The printed 28 is a reporting error that leaves the true randomized arm sizes unclear in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 showing 31 randomized per arm, which would confirm the text 'n = 28' as a typo only.

quotes.text: 62 patients were equally randomized to receive either celecoxib ( n = 28) or placebo (n = 28)
a total of 62  patients  (31  in  each  group)  were  included  in  the  final  analysis

issues.title: Table 1 percentages in several rows use a denominator of 28, not 31 (e.g. sex sums to 103%)
issues.explanation: In the celecoxib column, male 61% and female 42% add to 103%, and the counts 19 + 12 = 31 give 61% and 39%. Marital status (39% / 71%), placebo single (60%) and time since infection (39%, 25%) are also too high for n = 31 and fit n = 28. These are baseline-table reporting errors only. The counts and the analysis N of 31 are unaffected, so the efficacy results are not touched.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that those rows were defined on a 28-person subset, which the table headers and text contradict.

script.explanation: 12/31 = 38.71%, but the paper prints 42, outside the rounding interval [41.50, 43.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 28.6 rather than 31.

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2024.111625.headline_claim: A six-session HRV and temperature biofeedback intervention improved self-reported somatic, anxiety, depressive symptoms, sleep and some quality-of-life domains in long COVID, and may be a promising treatment option.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2024.111625.overall: This is an uncontrolled, self-reported pilot of 20 people (14 at follow-up) with no multiplicity correction, so the improvements cannot be attributed to biofeedback and some are marginal. The authors disclose most limitations and hedge the main claim as 'may be promising', which reduces the harm. The mechanistic, scalability and long-term-relief statements go beyond the data and should be disregarded.

primary_outcome.name: Multiple self-reported primary outcomes: somatic symptoms (PHQ-15), depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), sleep (PSQI), self-efficacy, and health anxiety (HAI-18)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post pilot of 20 cannot attribute improvements to biofeedback; conclusion still favours the treatment
issues.explanation: All participants received the intervention and were compared only with their own baseline on self-reported measures. Placebo effects, provider support, co-enrolled psychotherapy or acupuncture, regression to the mean and natural recovery cannot be separated from any biofeedback effect. The authors acknowledge this but still conclude that biofeedback is promising and could give long-term relief. Their argument that symptoms persist untreated relies on mean time since infection, which does not show that recovery rates are low. The small sample (20, 14 at follow-up) adds imprecision but is secondary to the missing control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist arm showing the same changes only in the biofeedback group, or documented stable symptoms across a pre-treatment baseline period in these participants.

quotes.text: a within-subject design that did not include a comparison or control group
mean enrollment date of our participants was 16.8 months after initial infection, corroborating existing literature, which suggests that most symptoms persist without treatment
the results of this study suggest that biofeedback may be a promising treatment for patients with long COVID

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does have a single-arm pre-post design with n = 20 (16 completers, 14 at follow-up) and cannot attribute improvement to biofeedback, and it says so explicitly. The conclusion is still favourable ('may be a promising treatment ... who have not responded well to standard biomedical approaches', 'could provide long-term relief'), and the argument that a mean of 16.8 months since infection rules out natural remission is weak because it describes only a mean, uses external literature, and the paper also reports no data on prior non-response to standard care. The paper does not overstate c

issues.title: Roughly 17 outcomes at two timepoints tested at alpha .05 with no correction; some headline results are marginal
issues.explanation: The paper tests six primary and many secondary and exploratory outcomes at two time contrasts, all at p ≤ .05 without correction. The authors say so openly, which limits the harm. The Results and Discussion nevertheless state improvements in somatic, depressive and sleep outcomes as findings, although those p-values (.01 to .02 in the omnibus tests) would not pass a conventional adjustment. The strongest results, such as anxiety, are less affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified correction or a hierarchy of primary outcomes under which the somatic, depression and sleep results remain significant.

quotes.text: without accounting for multiple comparisons, thus increasing the possibility of a Type 1 error
Participants reported significant improvements in self-reported somatic, anxiety, and depressive symptoms, and global sleep quality immediately after the six sessions

issues.title: 30% of participants lost by 3 months (14 of 20); missing-data assumptions and dropout comparison not stated
issues.explanation: Six of the 20 enrolled had no three-month data and four of them did not complete the six sessions. Mixed-effects models can handle this under a missing-at-random assumption, but the paper does not state the assumption or compare dropouts with completers. Those who stayed may have been the ones who improved, which would flatter the sustained-effect results. The effect on the conclusion is moderate and cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement and sensitivity analysis showing that dropouts did not differ at baseline and that results hold under plausible missing-not-at-random scenarios.

quotes.text: Of the 20, 16 completed all six sessions of biofeedback, and 14 of the 16 completed the assessments at the three-month post-treatment time point
analyzed using a mixed effects general linear model, as implemented in SAS PROC MIXED, with time as the within-subject factor

issues.title: Mechanism, long-term relief, scalability and low cost asserted without HRV data or follow-up beyond 3 months
issues.explanation: The Discussion says HRV biofeedback may correct the underlying pathophysiology, but neither HRV nor temperature was measured and the study relied only on self-report. The closing paragraph describes the treatment as low cost, scalable and capable of long-term relief, although no costs or implementation outcomes were assessed and follow-up was three months in 14 people. These statements go beyond what a single-arm self-report pilot supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pre/post HRV data showing the change, cost data, and a longer controlled follow-up.

quotes.text: HRV biofeedback may reduce peripheral signals of fight or flight and correct the underlying pathophysiology that sustains long COVID
Biofeedback is a non-invasive, relatively low cost, and scalable treatment option that could provide long-term relief and rehabilitation to patients.

issues.title: Discussion summary omits null self-efficacy and health anxiety, two of the six stated primary outcomes
issues.explanation: Self-efficacy and health anxiety were hypothesised and listed as primary outcomes, and neither improved significantly. The first Discussion paragraph lists only the significant outcomes. The null results are reported in the Results, so readers can find them, but the summary conveys a more uniformly positive picture than the primary-outcome set supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Discussion summary that states the null primary outcomes alongside the significant ones.

quotes.text: we found that patients with various long COVID complaints had significant improvements in somatic symptoms, anxiety, and depressive symptoms, as well as several domains of health-related quality of life, and global sleep quality
Changes to self-efficacy, health anxiety, pain, work absenteeism, and self-reported use of OTC drugs were not significant.

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2024.112021.headline_claim: A short multimodal psychosomatic day-clinic program for post-COVID patients was followed by a significant reduction in symptoms between admission and discharge.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2024.112021.overall: The finding that post-COVID patients have high symptom burden and improve between admission and discharge is descriptive and reasonably supported for completers, but because the study is uncontrolled it cannot show the program caused the improvement. The Abstract also misattributes NIPA statistics to the standard-setting comparison, overstating the depression contrast. The paper hedges causation in places, so the main concern is overreach in the Conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: PHQ-15 somatic symptom burden, admission vs discharge (within-group paired t-test)

issues.title: Single-arm admission-to-discharge change cannot attribute symptom reduction to the program
issues.explanation: All patients were measured only before and after treatment, with no control group. Improvement over 3-4 weeks could reflect time, regression to the mean, co-interventions or activities outside therapy, as the authors concede. The paper hedges on causation, but its headline still presents the reduction as a result of the program, so the evidence supports only an uncontrolled before-after change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist comparison group showing a difference in change.

quotes.text: it was not possible to simultaneously survey a control group
Despite the short duration of treatment, the patients showed a significant reduction in symptoms between admission and discharge.

second_reader.what_stands: True as a matter of design: a single-arm admission-to-discharge comparison cannot separate the program's effect from time, regression to the mean, natural recovery or outside activities, and the authors say so (Sections 4.4 and 4.5, and the abstract). What does not stand is the idea that the paper ignores this; it states the limitation explicitly, and its headline wording reports a change between time points, though phrases such as 'using a multimodal therapy approach' and 'Due to the diversity of symptoms, a multimodal therapy approach is recommended' read somewhat more favourably than the de

issues.title: Abstract gives NIPA statistics (PHQ-9 p=.009, PHQ-15 d=0.79) as the standard-setting comparison
issues.explanation: The Abstract says that compared with standard clinical settings, post-COVID patients had higher burden (PHQ-15 d=0.79; PHQ-9 p=.009, d=0.39). Results 3.1 shows those figures belong to the NIPA comparison. Against standard settings, PHQ-15 is d=0.67 and PHQ-9 is p=.659, d=0.10, i.e. no difference. The Abstract therefore overstates the contrast with standard settings on depression.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Abstract figures pool or refer to the NIPA group, or corrected Results showing p=.009 for the standard setting.

issues.title: Pre-post change reported for 55 completers only; 10 dropouts (15%) had higher baseline distress
issues.explanation: Discharge outcomes exist only for the 55 patients who completed treatment, while the 10 dropouts were more distressed at admission on several scales (anxiety p=.045, compulsion p=.021, PHQ-Stress p=.021). Improvement among completers may therefore overstate the effect in all admitted patients. The effect is modest given only 10 dropouts, but it is a one-directional bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including dropouts (e.g. last observation carried forward) with similar change.

quotes.text: The DG showed higher mental distress based on mean scores in the ISR and PHQ.
At discharge, the TG of the post-COVID sample showed a significant improvement

issues.title: Conclusion recommends the approach and invokes chronification, which the pilot did not measure
issues.explanation: The study had no control, no follow-up and no chronification outcome, yet the Conclusion recommends the multimodal approach and links it to preventing chronification. The recommendation rests on guidelines and uncontrolled within-group change. The wording is mostly framed as guideline intent, so the overreach is moderate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Long-term follow-up data against a control group showing lower chronification.

quotes.text: Due to the diversity of symptoms, a multimodal therapy approach is recommended.
A multimodal therapy approach recommended in the guidelines is intended to counteract a possible chronification

issues.title: No multiplicity correction across about 11 pre-post tests; fatigue result (p=.009) would not survive Bonferroni
issues.explanation: Significance was set at p<.05 for every test with no adjustment. Most reported improvements are small enough to withstand a Bonferroni correction over 11 outcomes, but the fatigue result highlighted in the Abstract (p=.009) would not. Fatigue is a central outcome for this population, so that claim is weaker than presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or a stated correction showing FS remains significant.

quotes.text: Significance was stated at p < .05.

issues.title: 'Prospective' label with registry ID and IRB number dated 2024 for 2022-2023 enrolment; timing unreported
issues.explanation: Patients were treated January 2022 to March 2023, but the ethics reference (IRB-2024-03) and the registry ID (DRKS00033514) suggest approval and registration after the data were collected. The paper does not give the dates, so it is unclear whether 'prospective' describes a pre-planned analysis or routine data analysed afterwards. This affects how much weight the pre-specified framing deserves, not the numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry and ethics records showing approval and registration before January 2022 enrolment.

quotes.text: The study has  been  registered  in  the  German  Registry  for  Clinical  Studies  (ID: DRKS00033514).

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2024.112023.headline_claim: The micro-choice-based intervention for long COVID was safe, highly satisfactory and significantly enhanced health activation and illness perception, with sustained 12-month gains in function, fatigue, sick leave and exercise capacity.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2024.112023.overall: This is an uncontrolled single-arm cohort, so the reported improvements in activation, fatigue, function and sick leave cannot be attributed to the intervention, and the unhedged Conclusion about economic benefit has no supporting data. Several small numeric inconsistencies (63% vs 65%, 75.9 vs 75.4, CSQ-8/9, age range) do not alter the main results. The findings are best treated as descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Completion rates; patient satisfaction (CSQ-8); illness perception (B-IPQ); patient activation (PAM-13)

primary_outcomes.measure: Changes to cognitive and emotional perception of illness
Changes in level of patient activation

issues.title: Uncontrolled, unblinded single-arm study with self-reported outcomes supports sustained-benefit conclusions
issues.explanation: All change is measured before and after in one cohort, so effects of the intervention cannot be separated from natural recovery, regression to the mean or expectation, which is likely for self-reported outcomes such as illness perception and activation. The authors state they cannot attribute the improvements to the intervention, yet the Conclusion lists 'rapid and long-term improvements' and policy implications without that caveat. Results are best read as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control group showing less change over the same 12 months.

quotes.text: The patients served as their own controls, and we cannot claim that the improvements were due to the intervention itself.
alongside rapid and long-term improvements in sick leave, fatigue, functional level, and exercise capacity during follow-up period

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, unblinded, non-randomized design (the registry confirms masking NONE and non-randomized allocation), and the paper does acknowledge this in the Discussion but the Conclusion and Abstract conclusion use causal and 'sustained' wording ('significantly enhanced', 'rapid and long-term improvements', 'We have shown') without repeating the caveat, so the uncontrolled design cannot support attributing sustained benefit to the intervention; what the data support is that outcomes were better at 12 months than at baseline in those who stayed in the study. The 'self-reported out

issues.title: Title and conclusion foreground exploratory sick leave and fatigue results over the primary outcomes
issues.explanation: The paper's title and conclusion highlight sick leave, fatigue and function, which are exploratory or secondary outcomes, while primary outcomes receive less weight. No multiplicity control is applied across many outcomes. The primary outcomes are also reported, so this is an emphasis issue that weakens secondary results only modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol that designates sick leave and fatigue as primary outcomes.

quotes.text: together with significant reduction in sick leave
2.4.3. Exploratory outcomes

issues.title: Cost-saving and welfare implications stated in the Conclusion with no economic analysis
issues.explanation: The paper admits no formal socio-economic analysis was done, yet the Conclusion says the findings have significant implications for reducing costs to employers and welfare systems. No costs, benefits or comparator were measured, and the sick-leave change is uncontrolled. The cost claim is unsupported by the data presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A costing or health-economic analysis of the programme versus usual care.

quotes.text: Although formal socio-economic analyses were not a part of this project, we find it likely that the short and concentrated format of the intervention was highly cost-effective
the findings hold significant implications for alleviating costs and reducing the burden on employers and welfare systems

issues.title: Baseline sick leave is 63% in the abstract but 65% (40/62) in Results and Tables 1 and 3
issues.explanation: The abstract gives baseline sick leave as 63%, while Table 1, Table 3 and the Results give 65% (40/62). The abstract figure is not derivable from the printed counts. This slightly understates the baseline-to-12-month fall in sick leave (65% to 23%), and the headline conclusion still holds.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract uses a different denominator (for example 40/63) or a different population.

quotes.text: Sick leave decreased significantly from 63 % at baseline to 43 % and 23 % at 3 and 12-month, respectively
At baseline 65 % of the employed participants were on sick leave

issues.title: Paper says registration followed first inclusions (approval date 10 Feb 2022); registry record shows 26 May 2021
issues.explanation: The paper itself says the study was posted to ClinicalTrials.gov after the first patients were included and gives a February 2022 approval date, while the registry shows first submission on the study's start date. The timing is internally unclear. Because registered primaries match the paper's, the impact is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing first posting before the first patient was enrolled.

quotes.text: was published at ClinicalTrials.gov after the first patients were included
with an approval date of 10 February 2022

issues.title: 12-month VAS functional level: 75.9 in text vs 75.4 (17.2) in Table 3
issues.explanation: The Results give the 12-month VAS mean as 75.9, while the Table 3 sequence under functional level gives 75.4 (17.2). The screen placed 75.4 in the WSAS row, which is wrong, but the VAS discrepancy of 0.5 points remains. It is small and does not alter any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explicit statement that the text reports model-estimated rather than observed means.

quotes.text: increased from a mean of 52.9 at baseline to 68.7 and 75.9 at the 3 and 12-month follow-up

issues.title: '>90% acceptance' is cited to another study; this cohort's own 78 of about 101 eligible is about 77%
issues.explanation: The Discussion says over 90% of eligible patients accepted participation and cites a different paper.
