This cohort's own flow does not obviously support that figure: after the two stated exclusions about 101 remain and 78 accepted. Because Fig. 2 is not readable here and other exclusions may exist, this cannot be settled from the text. It matters only to the external-validity claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 2 showing that about 85 or fewer patients were eligible and willing, or that the 90% refers to a pooled cohort.

quotes.text: In total, 78 patients met the inclusion criteria and accepted participation in the program
> 90 % of patients who fulfilled inclusion/exclusion criteria accepting participation

issues.title: Satisfaction instrument called CSQ-8 in Methods and Table 2 but CSQ-9 in Statistics and Results
issues.explanation: The Methods describe an eight-item CSQ-8, and the Table 2 note reports the CSQ-8 score, but the Statistics and Results sections call the same score CSQ-9. This looks like a naming slip. It is cosmetic, but it concerns a stated primary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the paper's own Table 2 note settles it as CSQ-8.

quotes.text: Clinical Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8) was used to measure patient satisfaction with health services
The mean CSQ-9 score was 28.7 ± 3.3.

issues.title: Age range upper limit is 67 years in the abstract but 66 years in the Results
issues.explanation: The abstract gives participants' ages as 19-67 years, while the Results give a range of 19-66 years for the same 78 patients. The 67 may be the eligibility ceiling rather than the observed maximum. It is a minor factual slip with no bearing on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract range reflects the eligibility limit rather than the observed range.

quotes.text: included 78 patients with long COVID aged 19 -67 years
Mean age was 40 years (range 19 -66 years)

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2026.112605.headline_claim: A five-week multimodal inpatient psychosomatic programme improves depressive symptoms, mental health-related quality of life, social functioning and coping competence compared with treatment as usual in post-COVID patients with mental health comorbidity.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2026.112605.overall: The study is a non-randomised, preference-allocated interim analysis of completers, so the claim that the programme 'leads to' improvement is only tentatively supported. Of nine uncorrected outcome tests, only coping competence and social functioning survive a multiplicity correction, and the sample-size outcome (PCS) was null. Reporting inconsistencies (83 vs 81 baseline patients, duplicated Table 4 rows) add unreliability but do not change the direction of the conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: Post-COVID symptom severity (PCS score)

issues.title: Self-selected, non-equivalent control group; causal 'leads to' wording; only interval adjusted
issues.explanation: Patients chose their arm, and controls differ in employment, in how they were selected (PHQ-9 >= 10 required only for controls), in assessment timing (31 vs 46 days) and in receiving outpatient psychotherapy (about 37%). Preference-based allocation is confounded with motivation and severity. Only the T0-T1 interval is adjusted for, yet the Discussion states that the programme 'leads to' improvement. The data show associations in a self-selected comparison, not a demonstrated treatment effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis adjusting for baseline outcome, employment and selection criteria that leaves the interactions unchanged, plus softened causal wording.

quotes.text: Group allocation was based on patient preference
with a higher proportion of retired or pensioned participants in the control group (40.8%)
more than one-third of the control group reported outpatient psychotherapy between T0 and T1

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by self-selection, the groups differ significantly on employment status (and the control group was recruited in a different period), and the only covariate adjusted for was the T0-T1 interval, yet the Discussion uses causal wording ('leads to', 'produces'). The authors do disclose selection bias and the contaminated control condition in the limitations, and baseline outcome scores did not differ, so the problem is the mismatch between the stated limitation and the causal wording, not an undisclosed design feature.

issues.title: Nine outcomes tested at p < .05 with no correction; headline depression result is p = .042
issues.explanation: Nine outcome interactions are tested at a nominal two-sided .05 with no adjustment, and the conclusions treat the significant ones as established. Under Bonferroni or Holm correction only social functioning (p = .005) and coping competence (p = .004) remain significant, while the depression interaction (p = .042) is borderline. The conclusion on depression and mental quality of life is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A declared hierarchy of outcomes or correction in the protocol, or a corrected analysis preserving the results.

quotes.text: with a significance level of p < .05 (two-tailed)
Compared with controls, the intervention group showed significantly larger improvements in depressive symptoms

second_reader.what_stands: Nine outcomes were each tested at an uncorrected alpha of .05, and the depression interaction (p = .042, partial eta squared 0.035) is presented as the lead finding in the abstract. Under Bonferroni or Holm correction over nine tests, depression, mental HRQoL (.014) and overall competence (.018) would not remain significant, whereas social functioning (.005) and coping competence (.004) would. The pre-specified primary outcome (PCS) showed no effect, and the paper does not discuss multiplicity.

issues.title: Table 4: identical Group and Covariate statistics printed for SF-36 mental and social functioning rows
issues.explanation: The between-subject Group row (F(1,92) = 0.110, p = .740, partial eta-squared 0.001) and the Covariate row (F = 0.622, p = .432, partial eta-squared 0.007) are identical for the SF-36 mental domain and social functioning outcomes. These are different scales with different distributions, so identical values are very unlikely. At least one set is probably a transcription error. The headline Time x group interactions differ between rows and are not obviously affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Output showing the two models genuinely give identical between-subject statistics, or a corrected Table 4.

quotes.location: Table 4, SF-36 mental domain and social functioning rows, Between-subject Group

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: discontinuers removed and 124 T1 completers cut to 120 analysed
issues.explanation: Intervention patients who discontinued treatment are removed before the baseline count, and the number is not given. Among T1 completers, 73 became 71 and 51 became 49 after protocol-deviation exclusions. Excluding non-completers from a non-randomised comparison favours the programme, because those who tolerate and finish it may do better. No intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Sensitivity or ITT analysis including discontinuers, or a count showing very few discontinued.

quotes.text: After the exclusion of patients without written informed consent or discontinued treatment, 83 patients remained in the intervention group
71 patients from the intervention group and 49 from the control group were included after excluding those with protocol

issues.title: Conclusions foreground secondary outcomes; power-calculation outcome (PCS) showed no group difference
issues.explanation: The sample size was based on a between-group PCS difference, and PCS showed no interaction (p = .874). The abstract and Discussion nonetheless emphasise improvements in psychological outcomes and coping and recommend clinical implementation. The null primary result is reported but not framed as the primary hypothesis being unsupported at T1. Because the study is an interim analysis, this weakens rather than invalidates the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry stating that coping competence or depression was the primary outcome for the T1 analysis.

quotes.text: based on the primary hypothesis of a between-group difference in mean PCS score across follow-up assessments
No group-by-time interaction effects were found for post-COVID symptom severity, fatigue, anxiety, or physical health-related quality of life.

issues.title: Intervention n at T0 given as 83 (Results), 81 (Table 1) and 71 analysed, with no reconciliation
issues.explanation: The Results say 83 intervention patients remained at baseline, while Table 1 and section 3.2 use n = 81. The analysed sample is 71, and Table 2 n values (77-80) differ again. The unexplained 2-patient gap, and the unclear link between the baseline sets, make the analysis populations hard to trace. The headline interaction tests are not directly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or text stating that 2 of the 83 baseline patients were removed (for example for T0-T1 interval) before Table 1.

quotes.text: After the exclusion of patients without written informed consent or discontinued treatment, 83 patients remained in the intervention group
Table 1 Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of the intervention (n = 81) and control group (n = 49) at T0.

issues.title: Registered 15.02.2024, after intervention treatment began in July 2023
issues.explanation: Registration followed the start of intervention treatment by about seven months. A published protocol partly mitigates this, but the paper does not state that the outcomes reported match it. The main weakness is that the pre-specified primary outcome (PCS) shows no effect while secondary outcomes are headlined.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry entry or protocol listing the same outcomes and hypotheses with a date before enrolment.

quotes.text: received inpatient psychosomatic treatment between July 2023 and July 2025
DRKS-ID: DRKS00033562

issues.title: Fatigue benefit suggested from within-arm change (p = .029) despite null interaction (p = .120)
issues.explanation: The Discussion suggests the programme may have reduced fatigue based on a significant pre-post change in the intervention group, even though the controlled comparison was not significant. Pre-post change can reflect regression to the mean or time and does not isolate treatment. The wording is hedged, so the overstatement is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison showing a fatigue interaction effect.

quotes.text: These within-group findings suggest that the inpatient psychosomatic program may have contributed to reductions in fatigue that were not detectable in the between-group comparison.

issues.title: Planned sample: '58 per group' gives 116, not the stated total of 118
issues.explanation: The Methods say the planned total was 118 participants (58 per group), but 2 x 58 = 116. Inflating 98 by 20% gives about 117.6, i.e. roughly 59 per group. This is a small internal inconsistency with no bearing on the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the arms were deliberately unequal.

quotes.text: assuming 20% dropout, the planned total sample was 118 participants (58 per group)

10.1016/j.jpsychores.2026.112920.headline_claim: CBT for post-COVID-19 condition reduces fatigue immediately after treatment, supporting its feasibility and preliminary efficacy in PCC; larger RCTs with active controls are needed to confirm.
10.1016/j.jpsychores.2026.112920.overall: The headline claim that CBT improves fatigue rests on a single borderline ANCOVA result (p=.045) among five uncorrected primary outcomes, in an open-label wait-list pilot where the MMRM between-group difference and the 3-month follow-up were null. The authors disclose most limitations and use hedged wording in the abstract, but the Conclusion's wording ('can lead to improvements', 'high clinical relevance') is stronger than the evidence supports. The result is best treated as a feasibility finding with hypothesis-generating efficacy signals.

primary_outcome.name: Multiple primary outcomes: FSS, PHQ-15, SBQ-LC Breathing and Circulation, DSQ-2 PEM, SSD-12

issues.title: Five uncorrected primary outcomes; fatigue effect p=.045 (BCa p=.049) carries the efficacy conclusion
issues.explanation: Five primary outcomes were analysed at alpha 0.05 with no correction, and only two ANCOVA results reached significance, both just under .05 (FSS p=.045, Breathing p=.044). The authors admit the type I error risk but still conclude that CBT can improve fatigue and call this of high clinical relevance. The sensitivity MMRM did not confirm the between-group fatigue difference at post-assessment (p=.444), so the conclusion rests on one borderline ANCOVA result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or a registered single primary outcome (fatigue), or a correction showing the result survives.

quotes.text: no single primary outcome but a set of primary outcomes were defined a priori
While this approach reflects the multifaceted symptom profile of PCC, it also increases the risk of type I error inflation.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary-outcome set (five in Table 2, six counting PEM) was tested at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05, and the fatigue between-group result (p=.045, BCa p=.049) would not survive any standard correction. That result underpins the efficacy statement in the abstract and conclusion. The authors do disclose the type I error risk in 4.1, and the MMRM interaction (p=.014) points the same way, so the problem is real but openly acknowledged rather than hidden.

issues.title: Conclusion asserts fatigue benefit of 'high clinical relevance' from an unblinded wait-list pilot with null MMRM and follow-up
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says CBT can improve fatigue and that this is highly clinically relevant. The evidence is one borderline ANCOVA (d=-0.58, p=.045) in an open-label, wait-list-controlled pilot; the MMRM between-group fatigue difference at post was not significant (p=.444), no primary outcome was significant at 3-month follow-up, and the authors themselves call the overall interpretation 'inconclusive' because of concurrent treatments. Self-reported fatigue with no blinding and a wait-list comparator is also vulnerable to expectancy effects. The claim should be framed as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded or active-control comparison, or consistent significant fatigue effects across ANCOVA, MMRM and follow-up.

quotes.text: In summary, this pilot RCT indicates that CBT can lead to improvements in fatigue in individuals with PCC
this finding is of high clinical relevance
the overall interpretation remains inconclusive

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion and Discussion call the fatigue finding 'of high clinical relevance' and say CBT 'can lead to improvements in fatigue', based on a wait-list pilot with self-report outcomes, a borderline ANCOVA result, a null MMRM between-group contrast at post (p=.444) and no significant follow-up effects. No clinical-significance threshold is applied. The description 'null MMRM' is overstated, because the MMRM interaction (p=.014) and the within-CBT change (p=.019) were significant. The paper also hedges with 'pilot', 'preliminary' and the call for confirmatory trials, and the 'inconclusive' r

issues.title: Dichotomised, unvalidated PEM outcome (94% positive at baseline) cannot support 'no harm in PEM' reading
issues.explanation: With 94% of participants PEM-positive at baseline, a dichotomised outcome has almost no room to show change, so the null PEM result is uninformative. The Discussion nonetheless uses the high PEM prevalence to say CBT improvements are possible in people with PEM, which the PEM measure cannot confirm either way. The effect on the main conclusion is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the dichotomised PEM score is validated and sensitive to change in a sample with a high baseline prevalence.

quotes.text: the dichotomization of the originally ordinal items might have limited the sensitivity to change, which has not been validated yet

10.1016/j.lanepe.2022.100539.headline_claim: CoQ10 does not significantly reduce the number or severity of PCC-related symptoms compared with placebo, and the authors state that CoQ10 should not be recommended as treatment for PCC.
10.1016/j.lanepe.2022.100539.overall: The central finding, no significant difference between CoQ10 and placebo on EQ-5D or symptom score, is internally consistent and supported by the reported estimates. Reporting slips (a p-value mismatch, a wrong Table 1 percentage, a baseline mean discrepancy) do not change this. The main limits are the unvalidated symptom questionnaire and a 'should not be recommended' conclusion that goes beyond the single dose, duration and timing tested.

primary_outcome.name: Change in PCC-related symptom score and EQ-5D health index at 6 weeks, CoQ10 vs placebo

primary_outcomes.measure: Effect of Coenzyme Q10 treatment in Long Term COVID-19 on number of self-reported symptoms of LTC measured by EQ-5D-5L questionnaire.
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Changes from baseline questionnaire response to questionnaire response after 6 weeks of treatment

primary_outcomes.measure: Effect of Coenzyme Q10 treatment in Long Term COVID-19 on number of self-reported symptoms of LTC measured by Long Term COVID-specific questionnaire.
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Changes from baseline questionnaire response to questionnaire response after 6 weeks of treatment

primary_outcomes.measure: Effect of Coenzyme Q10 treatment in Long Term COVID-19 on severity (symptoms score) of self-reported symptoms of LTC measured by Long Term COVID-specific questionnaire.
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Changes from baseline questionnaire response to questionnaire response after 6 weeks of treatment

primary_outcomes.measure: Effect of Coenzyme Q10 treatment in Long Term COVID-19 on severity (symptoms score) of self-reported symptoms of LTC measured by EQ-5D-5L questionnaire.
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Changes from baseline questionnaire response to questionnaire response after 6 weeks of treatment

issues.title: Symptom-score primary outcome uses a 32-item questionnaire developed for the study without validation
issues.explanation: The PCC symptom score comes from a questionnaire built by the authors from literature and a Danish cohort, with no reported validation or responsiveness data. An insensitive instrument could mask a real effect, so the null symptom-score result is weaker evidence than a validated scale would give. The validated EQ-5D, also null, limits how far this undermines the overall conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation or responsiveness data for the PCC-specific questionnaire.

quotes.text: we developed a scoring system using two questionnaires
The PCC-speci fi c questionnaire consists of 32 questions based on the available literature and prevalent symptoms reported in a Danish cohort of patients with PCC.

issues.title: 'Should not be recommended' is stronger than a null result at one dose, timing and duration supports
issues.explanation: The 'Research in context' implication states categorically that CoQ10 should not be recommended. The data show no significant effect over 6 weeks at 500 mg in patients about 9 months after onset, using an unvalidated symptom scale, and the Discussion says benefit with earlier or longer treatment cannot be excluded. The CI does rule out the 10-point target effect, so the recommendation is defensible for this regimen but is worded more broadly than the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limiting the recommendation to this dose, duration and patient timing, or an equivalence analysis.

quotes.text: Our fi ndings suggest that Coenzyme Q10 should not be recommended as treatment PCC.
quotes.location: Research in context, Implications of all the available evidence

quotes.text: Thus, it cannot be excluded that CoQ10 would signi fi cantly bene fi t patients if administered at an earlier point of time in the course of PCC or even during acute COVID-19.

issues.title: EQ-5D difference 0.01 (-0.02; 0.04) has p = 0.45 in Summary but p = 0.40 in Results
issues.explanation: The Summary and the Results give the same adjusted EQ-5D difference and CI, but print two different p-values. Both are non-significant, so the conclusion is unchanged, but one of the two figures is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two p-values come from different models or analysis sets.

quotes.text: change in EQ-5D health index (with a mean difference of 0.01; 95% CI: -0.02; 0.04; p = 0.45)
the estimated difference was 0.01 (95% CI: -0.02; 0.04), which was not statistically signi fi cant ( p = 0.40)

issues.title: Table 1 BMI 25-30: arm B 17 of 60 printed as 45.0% (should be 28.3%); total 37 as 18.6%
issues.explanation: In the BMI 25-30 row, 17 of 60 in arm B is printed as 45.0%, and the total column prints 37 of 119 as 18.6%. Both percentages do not match their counts; the correct values are 28.3% and 31.1%. This is a typographical error in a baseline table that affects no outcome analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing 17 (28.3) and 37 (31.1), which would confirm the printed values were typos.

script.explanation: 17/60 = 28.33%, but the paper prints 45.0, outside the rounding interval [44.95, 45.10]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 37.8 rather than 60.

issues.title: Baseline PCC symptom score 43.06 (Results, Table 1) vs 42.63 (Discussion) for the whole cohort
issues.explanation: The baseline mean for all 119 participants is 43.06 in Table 1 and Results, but the Discussion describes the entire cohort's improvement as starting from 42.63. A different analysis set could explain it but none is stated. The difference is small and does not affect the treatment comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion figure is based on participants with complete week-20 data.

quotes.text: the mean symptom score at baseline was 43.06 (95% CI: 40.18; 45.94)
had a signi fi cant overall improvement in PCC-related symptom scores (from 42.63 to 35.80)

issues.title: Trial registered 17 days after randomisation began (25 May vs 11 June 2021); outcomes match
issues.explanation: Randomisation began on 25 May 2021 and the registry record was first submitted on 11 June 2021, so registration came slightly after the start. The registered primary outcomes match those reported, and the delay is short, so the risk of outcome switching looks low. Earlier record versions were not checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing the record was public before the first participant was randomised.

quotes.text: From May 25th, 2021, to September 22nd, 2021, 121 participants underwent randomization
The trial is registered with EudraCT, 2020005961-16 and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04960215, and is complete.

issues.title: Pharma Nord named as funder and capsule supplier while the authors declare no competing interests
issues.explanation: The Acknowledgments say Pharma Nord funded the study and the capsules came from the company, yet the declaration states no competing interests. The paper also states the funder had no role in design, analysis or writing, which mitigates the concern. The company's interest would favour a positive result, and the trial was null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that Pharma Nord provided only product with no financial ties to authors or institution.

quotes.text: Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF21OC0066984) and PharmaNord funded this study.
We declare no competing interests.

10.1016/j.lanepe.2026.101744.headline_claim: Immunoadsorption with tryptophan adsorbers was not effective in reducing symptom burden in post-COVID syndrome compared with sham treatment.
10.1016/j.lanepe.2026.101744.overall: The finding of no significant difference between immunoadsorption and sham is consistent across outcomes, and the MoCA result is reasonably tight. The wording 'not effective' is firmer than the wide intervals for PCFS and fatigue outcomes, the per-protocol population is unclear with unequal, outcome-related dropout, and Table 1 and the dropout counts contain small inconsistencies. These are mostly minor reporting errors, so the headline holds only as 'no benefit shown'.

primary_outcome.name: Symptom severity: PCFS, CFS, Bell score, MFI-20, MoCA and handgrip change (six measures, treatment vs sham)

primary_outcomes.measure: Improvement of Post-COVID symptoms as measured by PCFS score
primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 weeks after completion of immunoadsorption and sham-apheresis

primary_outcomes.measure: Change of physical and/or mental fatigue as measured by Chalder-Fatigue-scale
primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 weeks after completion of immunoadsorption and sham-apheresis

primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 weeks after completion of immunoadsorption and sham-apheresis

primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 weeks after completion of immunoadsorption and sham-apheresis

primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 weeks after completion of immunoadsorption and sham-apheresis

primary_outcomes.measure: Change of cognitive impairment as measured by Montreal cognitive assesment (MoCA)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 weeks after completion of immunoadsorption and sham-apheresis

issues.title: Unqualified 'not effective' conclusion rests on wide CIs (PCFS OR 0.41-3.36) in a trial sized only for MoCA
issues.explanation: The sample size was set for a 2-point MoCA difference, not for the other five registered primary outcomes. For PCFS and the fatigue scales the confidence intervals include both meaningful benefit and harm. Absence of a significant difference is stated in the Interpretation as the treatment being ineffective. A conclusion that a clinically relevant benefit was not shown, rather than excluded, is better supported, especially for 21-month-old PCS.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified minimal important difference for PCFS and fatigue scales that all CIs exclude.

quotes.text: We determined that the enrolment of 38 patients would provide the trial with 90% power
Immunoadsorption was not effective in reducing symptom burden in post-Covid syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: The sample size was set only for MoCA, and the PCFS interval (OR 0.41-3.36) is too wide to exclude either a sizeable benefit or harm, so the Summary's unqualified 'not effective' goes beyond what that outcome shows. The main text is more cautious (it states benefit cannot be ruled out in early PCS and that no tangible benefit was found), and the MoCA CI does exclude a 2-point gain. I did not compare the intervals with a clinically important difference for each scale, because the paper gives none.

issues.title: Analysis labelled per protocol; 6 to 7 of 40 left before cycle 2, unequally and for outcome-related reasons
issues.explanation: The authors state the analysis was per protocol and that no intention-to-treat analysis was possible. More patients left after IA (5) than after sham (1 to 2), and both sham leavers reported improvement and feared they would not receive real IA. The Table 2 denominators (37 IA, 34 sham for PCFS) do not match a clean set of 34 completers, so the actual analysis population is unclear. The null conclusion therefore has some uncertainty from informative dropout, and the direction of any bias is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all randomised patients' available periods giving the same estimates, or a flow diagram showing exactly which data entered each model.

quotes.text: The analysis was done 'per protocol'.
precluding any intention-to-treat analysis

issues.title: Dropouts in Discussion (5 after IA + 2 after sham = 7) imply 33 completers, but Results report 34
issues.explanation: The Results give 16 of 21 IA-first and 18 of 19 sham-first patients completing the second cycle, which implies 5 and 1 dropouts (6 in total, 34 completers). The Discussion says 5 left after IA and 2 after sham, which would leave 33. One count is wrong by one patient. This is a small reporting slip, but it concerns the very participants excluded from the per-protocol analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram (Fig. 1 text) showing 2 sham-first dropouts and 19 sham-first participants with one counted as completing for another reason, or a correction of the Discussion count to 1.

quotes.text: 34 patients underwent the second
5 subjects dropped out after an initial round of immunoadsorption

issues.title: Table 1 lists one sham-first patient at baseline PCFS category 1 despite eligibility of PCFS 2 or higher
issues.explanation: The Summary and Methods say all patients had a PCFS of at least 2, yet Table 1 shows 1 patient (5.3%) in category 1, and 1 (2.5%) overall. Either the eligibility rule was not applied, the baseline score differed from the screening score, or the table has an error. It has little effect on the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that eligibility was judged at screening and baseline scores could differ, or a corrected Table 1.

quotes.text: at least 2 on the Post-Covid-19 Functional Scale

issues.title: Table 1 pooled totals impossible: C3c mean 1.07 outside group means 1.11/1.14; C1q total SD 0.25 vs group SDs 0.03/0.04
issues.explanation: A pooled mean must lie between the two group means, but the C3c total is 1.07 while the groups are 1.11 and 1.14. The C1q total SD is 0.25 although both groups have mean about 0.2 and SDs of only 0.03 and 0.04, which would give a pooled SD near 0.035. The total column of the complement rows therefore contains printing errors. These are baseline descriptors and do not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing C3c total 1.12 and C1q SD 0.025 (or a different subset used for the Total column, which the footnote does not mention).

quotes.location: Table 1, C3c row, Sequence IA-Sham column

issues.title: DIAMED (adsorber maker) listed as funder and supplier, yet 'no potential conflicting interests' declared
issues.explanation: The Summary lists DIAMED Medical Technology among funders, and the Methods and Role sections say it provided materials and made the adsorber. The Role of funding source lists only the university and ministry as funders, and the Declaration of interests says there are none. The relationship is not described consistently, which is a transparency gap rather than a threat to the null result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that DIAMED provided only in-kind adsorbers with no financial payment and no author relationships with the company.

quotes.text: DIAMED Medical Technology.
Materials were provided by DIAMED Medical Technology, Cologne, Germany.
The authors declare no potential conflicting interests.

issues.title: Table 2 CFS arm means differ by 3.4 points, yet the reported treatment difference is 0.09
issues.explanation: For the other outcomes the model difference matches the difference of arm means (MFI-20 2.5 vs 2.4, Bell -2.6 vs -2.6). For CFS the post-treatment means are 17.2 (IA) and 13.8 (sham), a raw gap of 3.4 in the direction of more fatigue after IA, but the model estimate is 0.09. The paper does not explain what adjustment produces this, so the CFS result cannot be verified from the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline CFS values or model output showing the period or carry-over adjustment accounts for the 3.3-point gap.

10.1016/j.mayocpiqo.2023.05.002.headline_claim: PSRT reduced somatic and other symptoms within 4 weeks in patients with PASC without identified organ injury, and the benefit persisted to 13 weeks.
10.1016/j.mayocpiqo.2023.05.002.overall: The finding that symptoms fell from baseline in this small single-arm cohort is plausibly real, but the paper's causal efficacy conclusion is not supported by an uncontrolled, unblinded design with self-reported outcomes in a self-selected sample. The remaining problems are scale-description and p-value slips that do not change the main results.

primary_outcome.name: Change in SSS-8 somatic symptom score from baseline to 13 weeks

issues.title: Causal efficacy claim from an uncontrolled, unblinded, self-selected single-arm cohort of 23 with self-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: All 23 participants received PSRT and no comparison group exists. The primary outcome is a self-reported symptom score, and the registry lists no masking. Participants were also screened for being open to a mind-body approach. Despite this, the Discussion speaks of 'efficacy' and the Conclusion says PSRT 'reduced symptomatology' with the benefit persisting. The before-after changes cannot separate treatment effect from expectation, natural course or regression to the mean, so the causal conclusion is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control with comparable outcome data, or a conclusion worded as a descriptive pre-post change only.

quotes.text: In our study, each participant served as their own control; thus, there was no direct comparison group.
Participants were screened for their willingness to consider a mind-body approach for treating long COVID
Other limitations include the subjective reporting of symptoms

second_reader.what_stands: The design facts are as described: a single-arm, unblinded, self-selected cohort of 23 with only self-reported outcomes, and the paper discloses these limitations, including the absent comparator and selection bias. What stands is that the Discussion and Conclusion use causal efficacy wording ('PSRT reduced', 'efficacy of PSRT seen in this study') that the design cannot support, and the argument that prior chronicity makes spontaneous improvement unlikely only partly offsets expectancy, regression to the mean and natural recovery; the paper does not misreport its design.

issues.title: FSS-9 item at 8 weeks: CI (-3,-1) excludes zero but P = .085; Discussion says significant at all time points
issues.explanation: The Results give a median change of -2 with 95% CI -3 to -1 at 8 weeks and say the reduction was significant only at weeks 4 and 13, with P = .085 at week 8. The same CI at weeks 4 and 13 goes with P < .001 and P = .01, and a CI of -3 to -1 implies a p well below .05. The Discussion then says the reduction was significant at every time point, which contradicts the Results. One of the printed values is wrong, but only a secondary item is affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 8-week CI or p was computed by a different method, or a corrected 8-week p or CI.

quotes.text: this reduction was statistically signi fi cant at weeks 4 and 13
this signi fi cant reduction was seen at 13 weeks as well as at every other time point

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the STATED 95% CI is 0.0001 (reachable range [0.0000, 0.0500]), but p = 0.085 is reported; the two reconcile only if the interval is a 80% CI, which is not what the paper says. Either the level, the interval or the p is misreported

issues.title: FSS-9 range printed as 0-63, but 8 summed items scored 1-7 give 8-56
issues.explanation: The paper says the FSS-9 score sums all statements except the first, each rated 1 to 7, so 8 items. That gives a possible range of 8 to 56, not 0 to 63. The reported scores (baseline median 52) are compatible with 8-56, so this is a description error and does not change any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary scoring instructions showing that items are scored 0-7 and nine items are summed.

quotes.text: Scoring ranges from 0 to 63.
on a scale of 1 (Strong Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree)

issues.title: PROMIS-29 physical: four items anchored 1-5 would give 4-20, but range is printed as 0-16
issues.explanation: Four items anchored from 1 to 5 would sum to 4-20, yet the range is given as 0-16 and the scale is called '4-point'. Either the anchors or the range are misreported. The Table 2 footnote that an increase means better health also sits oddly with falling PROMIS scores that the text calls improved. This is a reporting inconsistency and no result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The instrument's actual item coding showing a 0-4 scoring per item.

quotes.text: These scores were summed to represent an overall score, ranging from 0 to 16.
a four-item questionnaire in which participants are asked about their physical functionality

issues.title: MDP described as '4-item' scale, yet scores up to 110 and medians of 54 are reported
issues.explanation: The paper calls the MDP a 4-item scale with items scored 0-10, which would cap the score at 40. It then states a range of 0-110 and reports medians of 54 and IQRs up to 60.5, which are impossible on a 0-40 scale. The item count is therefore the likely error, not the range. Only the description is wrong; the reported results are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the description mismatch stands as printed.

quotes.text: The overall score was summed and ranges from 0 to 110.

issues.title: Power calculation assumed baseline SSS-8 of 5.8, but observed baseline median was 20
issues.explanation: The sample-size justification assumes a baseline SSS-8 of 5.8 falling to 3.2 (a 45% reduction). The enrolled cohort had a baseline median of 20 on the same scale. The calculation therefore does not describe the study population, although the larger observed change means the study was not underpowered for the primary test.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the power calculation used a different baseline or that the enrolled baseline was close to 5.8.

quotes.text: Assuming a baseline SSS-8 of 5.8

10.1016/j.medcle.2022.12.019.headline_claim: Pirfenidone and nintedanib were equally effective in improving PFT parameters, while nintedanib appeared more effective for 6MWT distance and oxygen saturation in post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis.
10.1016/j.medcle.2022.12.019.overall: The headline claims that both drugs improved lung function and were equally effective, and that nintedanib is better for exercise capacity, are weakly supported. The design has no untreated comparator, uses uncorrected multiple tests, and infers equivalence from non-significance in 15 patients per arm. Several table values are also inconsistent, though these affect secondary outcomes.

primary_outcome.name: Not designated; PFT parameters (FVC, FEV1, DLCO), 6MWT, and SO2 at week 12

issues.title: Efficacy of each drug inferred from within-arm change with no untreated comparator
issues.explanation: Benefit is inferred from week 0 to week 12 changes within each arm. There is no placebo or untreated arm, steroids were being tapered over the same period, and post-COVID lung function tends to recover spontaneously. The stated limitations (no early follow-up, small numbers) do not mention this, so the improvements cannot be attributed to the drugs.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated control group showing smaller improvement.

quotes.text: there were significant increases in all PFT parameters, 6MWT, and oxygen saturation compared to week 0
The results of our study showed that both treatment arms provided improvement in PFT results, 6MWT distance, and oxygen saturation levels.

second_reader.what_stands: Both drugs are judged effective from pre/post change within each arm, with no untreated or placebo comparator, so improvement cannot be separated from natural recovery, steroid taper, regression to the mean or ongoing oxygen therapy. The Results sentence is descriptive, but the Discussion and Conclusion language ('provided improvement', treatments 'resolved prefibrotic areas') reads the changes as drug effects. (Table 1 also lacks multiplicity adjustment across many outcomes, which I did not examine further.)

issues.title: 'Equally effective' conclusion drawn from non-significant differences in 15 patients per arm
issues.explanation: The authors conclude both drugs were equally effective, based on non-significant between-group PFT comparisons (for example ΔFVC p=0.17, ΔDLCO% p=0.26) in 15 patients per arm with no sample size calculation or equivalence margin. Absence of significance in such a small trial is not evidence of equivalence; the point differences (e.g. ΔFVC 0.2 vs 0.4 L, ΔDLCO% 9.1 vs 14.6) favour nintedanib numerically.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence margin with a confidence interval inside it.

quotes.text: both agents were equally effective in improving PFT parameters
This prospective study included 30 patients

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion that the agents were 'equally effective' on PFT parameters rests on non-significant between-arm tests in 15 patients per arm, which cannot show equivalence; the CIs recomputed from printed data (e.g. ΔDLCO% about -4.5 to +15.5) are compatible with a substantial difference. The small sample is acknowledged as a limitation, but the conclusion is not tempered accordingly.

issues.title: 'More effective early' claim drawn from baseline-score regression without a comparator
issues.explanation: The claim that therapy works better early comes from a regression with baseline radiological score in treated patients only. Without untreated patients, milder baseline disease predicting larger change could reflect natural recovery or regression to the mean rather than a drug effect. The conclusion that early treatment yields better results is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled analysis with a treatment-by-baseline-score interaction.

quotes.text: These findings suggest that antifibrotic therapy is more effective early in the development of fibrosis.
Early detection and treatment of pulmonary fibrosis may yield more effective results from treatment.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that antifibrotic therapy is 'more effective early' is drawn from a within-sample association of baseline radiological score with change, with no untreated comparator and no test of treatment-by-baseline interaction, so it cannot show differential drug efficacy. In addition, Table 3 as printed has radiological score as the dependent variable and Δ outcomes as predictors, with mixed coefficient signs (ΔDLCO% negative, ΔDLCO/VA% positive) and standardized betas beyond 1, so the table does not cleanly support the stated direction.

issues.title: Pirfenidone heart rate: Table 1 means imply -2.0 bpm change, Table 2 reports -12.9
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives pirfenidone heart rate 100.4 at week 0 and 98.4 at week 12, a 2.0 bpm fall. Table 2 reports a mean change of -12.9 for the same group with the same n of 15. A paired mean change must equal the difference of means, so one table is wrong. Heart rate is a secondary outcome, so main claims are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction showing the Table 1 or Table 2 value was a typographical error, or different analysed sets.

quotes.location: Table 1, Heart rate row, pirfenidone week 0
Table 1, Heart rate row, pirfenidone week 12

issues.title: Table 3 DLCO% and DLCO/VA% coefficients have opposite signs; text describes one direction
issues.explanation: Table 3 states radiological score is the dependent variable, with the change variables as predictors. ΔDLCO% has B = -0.291 and ΔDLCO/VA% B = 0.192, opposite signs, yet the text says lower baseline score goes with greater change in both. The text's direction therefore does not follow from the table for DLCO/VA%, and the model's set-up is hard to interpret.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors clarifying the model specification and that the DLCO/VA% sign is reversed in the table.

quotes.text: lower radiological score at week 0 was associated with significantly greater changes in DLCO%, DLCO/VA% and oxygen saturation values

issues.title: 6MWT superiority (p=0.02) among nine uncorrected between-group comparisons
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives nine between-group tests at alpha 0.05 without correction. The SpO2 result (p=0.005) is borderline against a Bonferroni threshold of about 0.0056, while the 6MWT result (p=0.02) would not survive. The conclusion's wording is hedged, but the 6MWT claim rests on an uncorrected test in a small trial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or a correction retaining significance.

quotes.text: the change in 6MWT distance and oxygen saturation levels were significantly greater in the nintedanib group than in the pirfenidone group
p values <0.05 were considered statistically significant.

issues.title: Radiological score: pirfenidone and nintedanib Table 1 differences (6.0, 5.1) differ from Table 2 changes (5.5, 5.6)
issues.explanation: Pirfenidone means fall by 6.0 in Table 1 but the Table 2 change is 5.5; nintedanib means fall by 5.1 but Table 2 gives 5.6. Rounding cannot explain 0.5 gaps in both arms, so the tables are not mutually consistent. The effect remains large and in the same direction, so the conclusion is little affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of different analysed samples or an unrounded calculation explaining the 0.5 gaps.

quotes.location: Table 1, Radiological score row, pirfenidone week 0
Table 1, Radiological score row, pirfenidone week 12

issues.title: Randomized comparison reports ethics approval but no trial registration
issues.explanation: The paper describes a randomized comparison but gives no registry identifier, so the prespecified outcomes cannot be checked. This matters since many outcomes were tested with no primary outcome declared. Impact on conclusions is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry with a primary outcome predating enrolment.

quotes.text: In the second stage of our study, we aimed to compare the efficacy of antifibrotic treatments in a randomized trial.

10.1016/j.mhp.2024.200359.headline_claim: Audio-guided, mindfulness-based forest bathing may offer a feasible and cost-effective complementary treatment for moderately affected Long/Post-COVID patients.
10.1016/j.mhp.2024.200359.overall: The feasibility finding (about 22% dropout) and the within-group direction of self-reported change can be taken at face value, apart from a minor 46 versus 48 recruitment inconsistency. The paper does not support treatment or cost-effectiveness claims: there is no control group, no blinding, completers only, and no cost data. The Conclusion should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Long/Post-COVID symptom severity (C19-YRS) and fatigue, pre-post change; feasibility (dropout) is the stated study aim

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post study of self-reports 2 weeks apart; treatment-style conclusion not supported
issues.explanation: All outcomes except pulse rate are self-reported before and after the programme, with no control group and no blinding. The reported improvements cannot be attributed to forest bathing, since expectancy, regression to the mean and spontaneous change would produce similar patterns. The authors acknowledge this, but the Conclusion still frames the programme as a treatment option. The results support only feasibility and hypothesis generation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control showing the same change, or a Conclusion limited to feasibility and signal for further testing.

quotes.text: Our study employed a pre-post design without a control group.
may offer a feasible, flexible and cost-effective method for the adjunctive treatment and rehabilitation of moderately affected Long/Post-COVID patients

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, no-control pre-post study of self-reported outcomes about two weeks apart, analysed on completers only, and the authors say it does not permit causal statements. The abstract's conclusion is appropriately modest (further research warranted), but the final Conclusion's 'adjunctive treatment and rehabilitation' and 'cost-effective' wording goes beyond the data: cost was not measured, there was no comparator, and feasibility rested on a 22% dropout rate, so the hedge 'may offer' only partly offsets the treatment-style framing.

issues.title: Conclusion calls the programme cost-effective though no costs or comparator were measured
issues.explanation: Cost-effectiveness needs cost data and a comparison with an alternative, and the study has neither. The 'may offer' wording softens but does not remove the claim, which appears in both the abstract and the final Conclusion. The claim goes beyond what an uncontrolled feasibility study can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Cost data and an economic comparison in the study, or removal of the cost-effectiveness wording.

quotes.text: this approach may offer a feasible and cost-effective method for the complementary treatment of moderate Long/Post-COVID
may offer a feasible, flexible and cost-effective method for the adjunctive treatment and rehabilitation of moderately affected Long/Post-COVID patients

issues.title: Only 36 completers analysed; 5 of 10 withdrawals due to illness or severe symptoms, no ITT analysis
issues.explanation: Completion of all sessions and all questionnaires was a prerequisite for inclusion, so the outcomes describe those who finished. Half of the 10 withdrawals were for acute illness or severe symptoms during the programme, which are plausibly related to the condition being treated. Improvements among completers probably overstate what a full enrolled group would show. No baseline comparison of completers and dropouts is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline data for the 10 dropouts showing they resembled completers, or an analysis including all enrolled participants.

quotes.text: The prerequisite for fulfilled participation in the study was the completion of all forest bathing sessions and all questionnaires
Participants reported acute illness ( N = 2), severe Long/Post-COVID symptoms during the intervention period ( N = 3)

issues.title: Symptom and fatigue outcomes use shortened/altered instruments (8 of 19 items; 2-week FAQ recall)
issues.explanation: The symptom scale was cut to eight items and the fatigue questionnaire's recall period was doubled, with no validation of the adapted versions. Within-person change is still informative, but the severity labels and comparisons with earlier work rest on scoring that was not validated for the modified forms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Validation data for the adapted versions or sensitivity analyses on the original item sets.

quotes.text: containing eight (from originally 19) prominent Long/Post-COVID symptoms was employed
unlike the original, participants were asked about symptoms that had occurred within a period covering the last two weeks (originally: last week).

issues.title: Results state 48 recruited; abstract and Methods state 46 (48 - 10 = 38, not the 36 analysed)
issues.explanation: The Results say 48 participants were recruited and 10 were excluded, which leaves 38, yet 36 are analysed. The abstract and Methods say 46 were recruited, and 46 - 10 = 36 with a 22% dropout. The 48 looks like a typographical slip. It leaves the recruited denominator ambiguous, but the analysed N and the dropout rate are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two people were recruited but never started (screened but not enrolled), explaining 48 versus 46.

quotes.text: In total, N = 48 participants suffering from Long/Post-COVID have been recruited for this study.
A total of N = 46 moderately affected Long/Post-COVID patients
N = 46, N = 36 included; recruited through media

script.explanation: The Results 3.1 cascade: 48 recruited, 10 excluded, 36 analysed does not reconcile: 'recruited' (n=48) minus its 1 stated exclusion(s) (10) leaves 38, but 'analysed' reports 36 -- 2 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

issues.title: About six primary-type ANOVAs, no overall correction; weakest subscale results are p < .05 only
issues.explanation: No family-wise correction is applied across the outcome families. The headline results mostly pass a conservative threshold anyway. Subscale findings at p < .05, such as affective symptoms and mental well-being, would not, but they are secondary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a judgement about whether correction was required in a pilot.

quotes.text: We observed decreased overall Long/Post-COVID symptoms ( p < .001) and fatigue ( p < .001), increased well-being ( p < .001) and a more adaptive use of stress-coping strategies ( p < .01) over time.

10.1016/j.neurom.2026.09.025.headline_claim: Non-invasive autonomic-focused interventions (SAT, tcVNS, or combined) were associated with within-group improvements in multidomain Long COVID symptom burden, with the combined arm showing the broadest descriptive pattern, though active arms did not differ significantly from each other.
10.1016/j.neurom.2026.09.025.overall: The paper is candid that this is an open-label, hypothesis-generating trial, and its claims are mostly hedged to match. Even so, the evidence for any benefit over no treatment rests on self-reported outcomes in unblinded participants, a primary analysis of about half of those randomised with a non-prespecified adherence filter, and within-group change without reported pairwise contrasts against control. The results are best read as exploratory signals, not evidence of efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: SBQ-LC multidomain symptom burden (domain scores)

primary_outcomes.measure: PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 Short Form (Abbreviated PCL-5)

issues.title: Open-label, no-sham monitoring control with only self-reported outcomes cannot separate treatment from expectancy
issues.explanation: Participants knew their assignment, the control arm received no active intervention or sham, and every efficacy outcome is self-reported. Any improvement in the active arms relative to control may therefore reflect expectancy, engagement or placebo response. The authors acknowledge this, but the efficacy signal they report cannot be attributed to the interventions themselves.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham-controlled or expectancy-adjusted analysis, or objective physiological outcomes, showing the same benefit.

quotes.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention, and expectations regarding treatment benefit were not formally assessed at baseline.
Consequently, it did not control for expectancy effects, treatment engagement, placebo responses, or other nonspecific effects associated with receiving an active intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: The design is open-label with a no-sham monitoring control and self-reported outcomes only, so the paper cannot separate intervention-specific effects from expectancy or other nonspecific effects. The authors state this themselves in the Methods, Discussion and Conclusion and frame the findings as hypothesis-generating, so the problem is real but disclosed, not hidden.

issues.title: Primary analysis on 250/501 completers with a non-prespecified ≥50% adherence filter applied to active arms only
issues.explanation: The headline results come from participants with complete data and, for active arms, at least 50% adherence. The threshold was not numerically prespecified and the paper describes its selection inconsistently. Control participants faced no adherence filter, so retained participants may differ systematically by arm. The mixed-model sensitivity analyses are only omnibus and are not labelled as a full ITT analysis of change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or SAP version dated before data collection that fixes the 50% threshold, plus a full ITT analysis of change giving the same effect sizes and active-versus-control contrasts.

quotes.text: Because the specific 50% threshold was selected pragmatically after examination of intervention-engagement patterns rather than prespecified numerically in the original protocol
The threshold was selected without reference to clinical outcomes in the present study
quotes.location: Methods, Intervention adherence and analytic threshold

quotes.text: The final analytic sample therefore consisted of 250 participants

second_reader.what_stands: The primary analysis does use 250 of 501 participants (about 50%), and the authors say the 50% threshold was chosen after looking at engagement patterns, not prespecified numerically, and was applied to active arms only. The filter's direct effect is small (3 participants), and most of the loss comes from missing outcome data; the ITT mixed-model sensitivity analysis is broadly consistent with the primary analysis but not uniformly so, and the paper acknowledges the selection concern.

issues.title: Registry lists PHQ-8, GAD-7, PCL-5, BPQ as primary; paper reports them as secondary, with 4-week not 8-week follow-up
issues.explanation: The current registry entry names eight primary outcomes including the four psychological and autonomic scales that the paper calls secondary. Time frames (weeks 0, 4, 8) also differ from the 4-week study reported. The paper attributes the shortening to a protocol modification but does not describe the change in outcome hierarchy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated registry history or protocol amendment, made before outcome data were available, designating SBQ-LC as the sole primary outcome and a 4-week endpoint.

quotes.text: Secondary outcomes included anxiety symptoms measured by the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) [25]
Following a protocol modification, 541 participants were re-consented and enrolled

issues.title: Benefit framed as within-group change; no active-versus-control contrasts reported, only omnibus 4-group interactions
issues.explanation: The abstract and discussion emphasise within-group improvements in active arms against a control described as showing minimal change. Omnibus Group×Time tests include the control, but pairwise active-versus-control change is not reported, and several domains (movement, muscle/joint) lack a significant interaction. The reader cannot tell the size of any between-arm effect over control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported pairwise Group×Time contrasts (each active arm versus control) with effect sizes and CIs supporting the claimed benefit.

quotes.text: Active intervention conditions demonstrated within-group improvements across multiple SBQ-LC symptom-burden domains
whereas the monitoring-only control condition demonstrated minimal change

issues.title: Nine co-primary SBQ-LC domains plus secondaries tested at α=.05 without correction
issues.explanation: The study defines the primary endpoint as multiple domain scores and applies no multiplicity control, so some significant results are expected by chance. The authors justify this by Type II error concerns and call all findings hypothesis-generating. The impact is limited by that framing, but borderline domain-level results should not be read as confirmed effects.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary endpoint or hierarchical testing plan under which the key results remain significant.

quotes.text: formal correction for multiple comparisons was not applied because such adjustment could increase Type II error

issues.title: Conclusion cites 'clinical relevance' and scalability despite open-label self-report data and a post hoc filter
issues.explanation: The final paragraph says the results highlight potential scalability and clinical relevance for a large population. The trial reports no minimal clinically important differences, cost data, or uptake outcomes, and only about half of participants were analysed. The preceding paragraph and the abstract limit the overreach.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis showing changes exceed established minimal clinically important differences, and feasibility/uptake data from the decentralised delivery.

quotes.text: highlights their potential scalability and clinical relevance for the large population of individuals experiencing persistent multisystem symptoms

10.1016/j.nicl.2022.103218.headline_claim: HBOT improves disruptions in white matter tracts and alters functional connectivity organization of neural pathways attributed to cognitive and emotional recovery in post-COVID-19 patients.
10.1016/j.nicl.2022.103218.overall: The randomized, sham-controlled design is sound, but the imaging conclusions rest on 56 of 79 randomized patients with no ITT analysis. The structural headline comes from one of many uncorrected DTI metrics, and the brain-behaviour links are pooled across arms and partly mismatch the tables. The claims of white-matter improvement and recovery-related connectivity change are tentative, not established..

primary_outcome.name: NeuroTrax cognitive assessment (global cognitive score)

issues.title: Imaging analysed in 56 of 79 randomized (29% lost); no ITT; below the 74 calculated
issues.explanation: Of 79 randomized, 6 dropped out and 17 more were excluded for head motion. All imaging conclusions rest on 28 per arm, with no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis. The achieved sample is well under the 74 participants the paper's own calculation required. Balanced exclusions reduce but do not remove the risk of bias, and the authors themselves note a possible underpowered estimate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis showing the same imaging effects with all randomized participants.

quotes.text: nine patients from the HBOT group and eight patients from the control group were excluded from further analysis due to excessive motion or head motion artifacts
the final analysis included 28 patients from each group

second_reader.what_stands: Imaging was analysed in 56 of 79 randomized patients (about 29% not analysed). It is a completer-plus-motion-screened analysis, not intention-to-treat, and 56 is below the 74 calculated. The 74 was for the primary cognitive outcome rather than for imaging, and the authors flag the dropout and underpowering as a limitation.

issues.title: Structural FA finding (p = 0.007) chosen from many uncorrected DTI metrics and seeds
issues.explanation: Structural connectivity was analysed over many diffusion metrics and several bilateral seed regions with no stated multiplicity correction. The abstract highlights the left-amygdala FA result (F = 7.81, p = 0.007) and concludes that HBOT 'improves disruptions in white matter tracts'. A p of 0.007 among roughly ten metrics times several seeds is only weak evidence. The paper also shows no baseline white-matter disruption in these patients to be 'improved'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single structural outcome, or multiplicity-adjusted p-values below 0.05 for the FA result.

quotes.text: fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusion (MD), radial diffusion (RD), axial diffusivity (AD), linear anisotropy (Cl), planar anisotropy (Cp)
There was a significant group-by-time interaction in the FA of left amygdala tracts postHBOT

second_reader.what_stands: The FA result (p = 0.007) comes from a family of at least about 54 structural metric-by-seed tests with no multiplicity correction stated, and it would not survive a Bonferroni correction even over the nine metrics alone. The seeds were a priori, and the paper does not show that the amygdala FA result was selected after viewing the data. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless present it without caveat.

issues.title: Brain-behaviour correlations pooled over both arms (n = 56); no within-group analysis, causal wording
issues.explanation: Changes in connectivity were correlated with changes in cognitive or BSI-18 scores across all 56 patients combined. Because treatment moves both variables, such correlations can arise from the group effect alone and do not show that connectivity changes drive recovery. The Discussion and abstract nonetheless say the changes are 'attributed to cognitive and emotional recovery'. The correlations are also uncorrected, with p values up to 0.05 in Table 3.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Correlations within each arm or a model adjusting for group showing the same association.

quotes.text: analyzed in the entire cohort (r = -0.350, p = 0.005)
These changes have been correlated with improved psychiatric scores.

second_reader.what_stands: The brain-behaviour correlations (Fig. 2, Fig. 4, Table 4, and r = -0.350 for FA vs BSI-18) are pooled over both arms with n = 56, and no within-group correlations are reported in the main text. The quoted sentence itself is correlational, but the Discussion goes on to say the changes were 'induced by HBOT' and 'may explain the clinical improvement', which is causal language that the pooled correlations cannot support.

issues.title: Abstract says 73 randomized (37/36); Results say 79 randomized, with 73 completing
issues.explanation: The abstract describes 73 patients as randomized to HBOT (37) or sham (36). The Results say 79 were randomized and 37 + 36 = 73 completed the protocol. The abstract therefore drops the six post-randomization losses and understates attrition at the headline level.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing that 73 was the randomized number and the 79 in the text is an error.

quotes.text: 73 patients were randomized to receive 40 daily sessions of HBOT (n = 37) or sham treatment (n = 36)
the remaining seventy-nine were randomized to one of the two arms

issues.title: Conclusion proposes connectivity as eligibility/monitoring tool; study tested neither
issues.explanation: The closing conclusions describe connectivity analysis as a promising treatment eligibility and response monitoring tool. The study reports group-level differences and pooled correlations, with no test of individual-level prediction or monitoring performance. The authors state that follow-up ended 1-3 weeks after treatment. The wording is hedged, so this is a mild overreach.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A predictive or diagnostic-accuracy analysis supporting monitoring or eligibility use.

quotes.text: promising treatment response monitoring tool
promising treatment eligibility and response monitoring tool

issues.title: Results 3.2 correlations and effect sizes do not match Tables 2 and 3 (r 0.361 vs 0.306; ES -0.365 vs 0.329)
issues.explanation: The text reports an executive-function correlation of r = 0.361 (p = 0.007) for SN-FPN, but no such row exists in Table 3; the insula-FPN row reads r = 0.306, p = 0.022. The attention correlation of -0.453 is attributed to DMN-FPN in the text, whereas Table 3 puts 0.453 on a different pair and 0.304 on DMN-FPN. The text also gives ES -0.365 for the insula-PPC connection against 0.329 in Table 2. The key brain-behaviour findings cannot be traced reliably to the tables, and the signs are inconsistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or supplementary table showing the text values belong to rows omitted from Table 3.

quotes.text: SN.AInsula (L) FPN.LPFC (R) EF 0.306 0.0220
DMN.LP (R) FPN.LPFC (L) Attention 0.304 0.0227

issues.title: No trial registry identifier given; protocol cited only by reference
issues.explanation: The paper describes a prospective randomized trial but states no registry number. It defers methodology and clinical outcomes to a protocol and an earlier paper. The primary outcome (cognition) is named but the imaging analyses are not shown to be pre-specified. Without an identifier, a reader cannot check the imaging analyses against a prior plan.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier (given in the companion paper) listing the imaging connectivity analyses as pre-specified outcomes.

quotes.text: Detailed overview of the methodology and results of the clinical outcomes are provided in the study protocol

issues.title: WMH percentages use unexplained denominators: 12 (54%) fits neither 28 nor 37; 17 (47%) fits 36
issues.explanation: The HBOT mild-WMH figure of 12 (54%) implies a denominator near 22, while the control figure of 17 (47%) implies 36. Neither matches the stated 28-per-arm analysed cohort. The reader cannot tell who was rated. This is a minor reporting error with no effect on the main claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator (e.g., 22 rated HBOT patients) in Supplementary Table S2.

quotes.text: 12  (54  %)  patients  had  mild
the final analysis included 28 patients from each group

script.explanation: 12/28 = 42.86%, but the paper prints 54, outside the rounding interval [53.50, 55.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 22.2 rather than 28.

10.1016/j.nrl.2022.06.008.headline_claim: Neuropsychological rehabilitation is an effective tool for treating cognitive-emotional alterations of post-COVID-19 syndrome, although not all patients recover pre-COVID functional level six months after treatment.
10.1016/j.nrl.2022.06.008.overall: The paper is a single-centre, non-randomised clinical-programme report whose conclusion that rehabilitation is 'effective' goes beyond its design. The control group had normal baseline cognition, also improved, and did not differ from the treated group after treatment. Printed numeric slips (p-values and one percentage) are minor, but regression to the mean and practice effects cannot be separated from any treatment effect..

primary_outcome.name: not stated as a single primary outcome; pre-post and between-group changes on neuropsychological tests and HADS

checklist.control: non-randomised concurrent untreated control (patients with normal testing)

issues.title: Non-randomised, untreated control chosen for normal cognition; baseline imbalance; efficacy conclusion drawn
issues.explanation: Patients with impaired testing received cognitive treatment, and those with normal testing formed the control group. The two groups therefore differed at baseline on RAVLT and fluency, with the experimental group worse. Gains in a lower-scoring group are expected from regression to the mean and practice even without treatment, and controls also improved. The design cannot support the unqualified statement that rehabilitation is effective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison with an untreated group with equal baseline deficits, or randomisation of patients with impairment.

quotes.text: pacientes con un rendimiento normal en la exploración neuropsicológica y que, por lo tanto, no realizaron tratamiento cognitivo
En tales variables el grupo control obtuvo mejores puntuaciones que el grupo experimental.
En conclusión, la rehabilitación neuropsicológica es una herramienta eficaz para tratar las alteraciones cognitivoemocionales derivadas del síndrome post-COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was non-randomised and determined by normal baseline cognition, so the untreated comparison group differs from the treated group by construction, and four RAVLT/fluency measures show baseline imbalance favouring controls. Despite this, and with practice effects acknowledged only for controls, the Conclusion states without qualification that the rehabilitation is 'eficaz'; the design supports at most a suggestion of benefit. The authors do report the baseline imbalance and the practice-effect caveat, so the problem is the strength of the conclusion, not concealment.

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from within-group pre-post change; no between-group test of change; post-treatment groups equal
issues.explanation: The paper reports significant pre-post improvements in the treated group but also in controls on several measures. Between-group comparisons after treatment and at follow-up are non-significant. Comparing effect sizes between groups is descriptive and not a test. The efficacy conclusion is therefore not supported by an inferential comparison of change, and the authors' own results show similar post-treatment performance. The unqualified Abstract and Discussion conclusion (also candidate c10) goes beyond this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A group-by-time interaction or between-group test of change scores favouring the treated group.

quotes.text: No se observaron diferencias intergrupales en la valoración postratamiento ni en la valoración de seguimiento (tabla 3).
En el grupo control también se hallaron diferencias estadísticamente significativas entre las puntuaciones de las valoraciones pre y postratamiento.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's efficacy inference rests on within-group pre-post tests and a descriptive comparison of effect sizes, with no formal between-group test of change (no interaction or change-score comparison), and groups do not differ post-treatment. The larger GE changes are numerically visible in the printed means, but without a test, and with baseline imbalance, they cannot show a treatment effect beyond practice or regression toward the mean.

issues.title: Open-label therapy with self-reported HADS outcomes and no stated assessor blinding
issues.explanation: Treatment was delivered at home and nobody was blinded. The anxiety and depression gains rest on the self-reported HADS, which can be influenced by expectation. The paper does not say whether testers knew group membership. This weakens the emotional-symptom result more than the performance-based cognitive results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that assessors were blinded to group allocation.

quotes.text: Los pacientes realizaban el tratamiento cognitivo desde su domicilio a través de la plataforma de telerrehabilitación Guttmann

issues.title: About 11 measures at 3 timepoints and two groups tested at p<0,05 with no correction
issues.explanation: The paper tests around eleven outcomes in several comparison sets using an unadjusted 0,05 threshold. The strongest treated-group results would survive correction. The control-group changes (p of 0,017 to 0,040) and the baseline differences (p of 0,033 to 0,047) would not, and the claim that controls changed 'less' relies on that pattern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or a correction for multiple testing.

quotes.text: se consideraron estadísticamente significativos los valores de p < 0,05

issues.title: Follow-up p-values 0,10 (z=-2,570) and 0,16 (z=-2,418) do not match their z; text calls both significant
issues.explanation: Two pre-to-follow-up results are printed with p-values (0,10 and 0,16) that sit above the paper's 0,05 threshold while the text calls them significant. The accompanying z statistics correspond to p of about 0,010 and 0,016, so the p-values appear to have lost a zero. The significance claims probably stand, but the printed values are wrong. The effect size r = 0,01 printed beside z = -2,570 for fluency is also implausible, since z of this size in a sample of 91 implies r of about 0,27.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or supplementary output showing the exact p-values are 0,10 and 0,16 with a different test or threshold.

quotes.text: fluencia verbal (z = -2,570; p = 0,10; r = 0,01)
quotes.location: Resultados, follow-up pre vs seguimiento paragraph

quotes.text: RAVLT aprendizaje (z = -2,418; p = 0,16; r = 0,36)
quotes.location: Resultados, follow-up pre vs seguimiento paragraph

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.1, but recomputed from the printed z = 2.57 p is at most 0.01018, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: 77,3% (n=17) of returned workers implies 22 workers, but 23 are reported; 17/23 = 73,9%
issues.explanation: The paper says 23 participants had returned to work, and the subgroup counts agree (19 + 4 = 23, 33,3% of 69). It then says 17 of these reported difficulties and gives 77,3%, which fits a denominator of 22. 17 of 23 is 73,9%. The Discussion repeats 77,3%. A similar slip appears for external aids, where 73,9% (n=51) matches 51/69, not 51/56 as the phrase 'of whom' implies. These are descriptive follow-up figures and do not affect the efficacy claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explanation that one returned worker lacked difficulty data (denominator 22).

quotes.text: el 33,3% (n = 23) de los participantes se había reincorporado a su puesto de trabajo
El 77,3% (n = 17) de los pacientes que habían vuelto a trabajar describieron dificultades

script.explanation: 17/23 = 73.91%, but the paper prints 77.3, outside the rounding interval [77.25, 77.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 22.0 rather than 23.

10.1016/j.nrleng.2022.06.007.headline_claim: Neuropsychological rehabilitation is an effective tool to treat cognitive-emotional deficits in post-COVID-19 syndrome, though not all patients recover their pre-COVID functional level months after treatment.
10.1016/j.nrleng.2022.06.007.overall: The headline claim that neuropsychological rehabilitation is an effective treatment rests on a non-randomised comparison with healthy controls and on within-group changes, and so is not supported as stated. Practice effects, regression to the mean and open-label assessment can each explain much of the improvement. The numeric slips found (misprinted P values, 77.3% versus 73.9%) are minor, but follow-up denominators are not reported.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; cognitive and emotional test scores (digit span, RAVLT, verbal fluency, HADS) analysed as multiple outcomes

issues.title: Non-randomised 'control' of patients with normal testing; effectiveness claim rests on pre-post change
issues.explanation: Patients were split by whether they had cognitive deficits, so the treated group started lower on the RAVLT measures and verbal fluency and the controls were untreated because they were healthy on testing. Gains in the treated group can therefore reflect regression to the mean, practice, or spontaneous recovery as well as treatment. The control group also improved on several measures, which shows these non-treatment influences are present. The authors still conclude in the abstract and conclusion that rehabilitation 'is an effective tool', which this design cannot show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised or matched comparison of patients with equal baseline deficits, or an analysis adjusting for baseline score showing a treatment-specific gain.

quotes.text: The remaining 26% (n = 32) presented normal results in the neuropsychological examination and therefore did not receive treatment for cognitive symptoms; these were treated as the control group
The control group obtained better scores on these variables than the study group.
In the control group, we cannot rule out a practice effect that may explain the variations observed between the different evaluations.

second_reader.what_stands: The comparison group was formed by non-random allocation on baseline cognitive test results (normal vs impaired), so it is not a like-for-like control, and the 'effective' conclusion rests on pre-post change within groups. Selection on low scores (regression to the mean), differing room for improvement, and practice effects are all uncontrolled; the authors acknowledge practice effects only for controls and rely on an unshown prior correction for the study group.

issues.title: Benefit inferred from within-group significance and unadjusted r comparisons; no test of differential change
issues.explanation: Intergroup tests found no difference at post-treatment or follow-up. The case for benefit instead rests on the treated group reaching significance on more tests and having larger r values. Comparing significance across groups of 91 and 32 and comparing r values without intervals does not show that the groups changed differently.
