No analysis of group-by-time change or baseline-adjusted change is provided.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A group-by-time test (or baseline-adjusted comparison) showing a significantly larger gain in the treated group.

quotes.text: The study group presented larger effect sizes than the control group for the backward digit span (0.30 vs 0.07)
We did not observe intergroup differences in the post-treatment or follow-up evaluations (Table 3).

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of greater benefit in the study group rests on within-group Wilcoxon significance and side-by-side comparison of r values; no test of differential change (interaction or change-score comparison) and no confidence intervals are provided. The intergroup tests that were run are at single time points only, and the study group started from lower scores.

issues.title: Follow-up covers about 69 of 123 patients; the number followed up and reasons for loss are not stated
issues.explanation: Follow-up percentages in the text imply a base of 69 (for example 18/0.261 and 56/0.812), versus 123 patients in the analysed sample. The paper does not say how many were followed up or how those lost differ. The abstract states the 44.9% unable to do their previous work as a percentage of patients in general, though it refers to about 69. Results about persistence of difficulties may not generalise to the full programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow chart or text giving the number completing follow-up and the reasons for non-completion.

quotes.text: Of the participants surveyed, 26.1% (n = 18) were studying some course before completing treatment.
In the follow-up evaluation, 33.3% (n = 23) of participants had returned to work

issues.title: Open-label design with self-reported HADS and remote telephone testing; emotional treatment given to both groups
issues.explanation: There was no blinding, and assessments were done remotely by telephone before and at follow-up. HADS is self-reported and could reflect expectation. Because both groups received emotional intervention when HADS was 8 or more, mood change is not specific to the cognitive programme. This weakens the secondary mood claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded assessors for follow-up, or statements that the mood outcome is explicitly exploratory.

quotes.text: All participants presenting symptoms of anxiety and depression underwent emotional intervention, regardless of the group in which they were included.

issues.title: 77.3% (n = 17) of 23 workers does not match 17/23 = 73.9%; 77.3% implies 22
issues.explanation: The paper says 23 people had returned to work, then says 77.3% (n = 17) of them reported difficulties. 17 of 23 is 73.9%; 77.3% corresponds to 17 of 22. The same 77.3% is repeated in the Discussion. This is a small slip in a descriptive secondary result and does not touch the main efficacy claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 3 or the raw data showing 22 workers answered the difficulties question, with the paper saying so.

quotes.text: Of the patients who returned to work, 77.3% (n = 17) reported difficulties performing their professional tasks
In the follow-up evaluation, 33.3% (n = 23) of participants had returned to work

script.explanation: 17/23 = 73.91%, but the paper prints 77.3, outside the rounding interval [77.25, 77.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 22.0 rather than 23.

issues.title: About ten outcomes at three timepoints tested at P < .05 with no correction or primary outcome
issues.explanation: No primary outcome or adjustment for multiple comparisons is given. Borderline results (P of .025 to .04) are described as significant. The strong treated-group results would remain significant, so the effect on the conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or adjusted P values showing the main results unchanged.

quotes.text: Values of P < .05 were considered statistically significant in both cases.

issues.title: Follow-up paragraph misprints: P = .10 and P = .16 beside z of 2.57 and 2.42; r = 0.01; 'RAVLT-learning 0 vs 0.30'
issues.explanation: Two comparisons are called statistically significant but are printed with P = .10 and P = .16, which are above .05. The printed z values (2.570 and 2.418) correspond to P of about .010 and .016, so a zero seems to have been dropped. The verbal fluency effect size of 0.01 also does not fit z = 2.57. A later sentence gives a RAVLT-learning effect size of '0 vs 0.30' for the control group versus the study group, which contradicts the earlier 0.39 vs 0.36 and probably refers to another variable. These are transcription errors in a secondary follow-up analysis. The headline conclusion is not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table of the pre-to-follow-up comparisons showing the P values as .010 and .016 and the effect sizes as intended.

quotes.text: and verbal fluency (z = -2.570; P = .10; r = 0.01)
RAVLT-learning (z = -2.418; P = .16; r = 0.36)
The effect sizes were larger in the control group than in the study group for the RAVLT-learning (0 vs 0.30)

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.1, but recomputed from the printed z = -2.57 p is at most 0.01018, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

10.1016/j.pec.2024.108180.headline_claim: The authors conclude that lifestyle self-adjustment strategies are effective for improving quality of life and symptom severity in long COVID-19.
10.1016/j.pec.2024.108180.overall: The headline claim that the programme improves quality of life and symptom severity is only weakly supported: symptom severity is never reported at follow-up, no primary outcome is named and the registered primary (fear-avoidance) is absent, and only three of about 20 uncorrected between-group tests are nominally significant, with null totals. Open self-reported outcomes against a leaflet control add further bias risk, so the result is best read as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Not identified in the paper (registry lists fear-avoidance belief changes as primary)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: At 6 weeks at the end of the intervention

issues.title: Title and conclusion claim improved symptom severity; no end-of-study symptom data are reported
issues.explanation: The title, abstract and conclusion state that symptom severity improved. The only symptom-severity data (C19-YRS) appear in Table 1 at baseline, and Table 3 reports only EQ-5D, WHODAS and WSAS at 6 weeks. The claim about symptom severity therefore has no supporting outcome data in the paper, and the claim of reduced disability is also undercut by the null total WHODAS between-group result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: End-of-study C19-YRS symptom severity results showing a between-group benefit.

quotes.text: Strategies based on lifestyle adjustments are adequate for the improvement of quality of life and symptom severity in the long COVID-19 population.
Outcome measures of the participants included in the study at the end of the study.

second_reader.what_stands: The title, abstract conclusion and discussion claim improvement in symptom severity, yet no end-of-study C19-YRS symptom severity data are reported, so the claim has no direct supporting result in the paper. Only quality of life, disability and functional impairment outcomes are presented post-intervention, with symptom items such as pain/discomfort showing no between-group difference (p=0.660).

issues.title: Registered primary outcome (fear-avoidance beliefs) is absent; paper names no primary outcome
issues.explanation: The prospectively registered record (NCT05477199) lists fear-avoidance belief change as the only primary outcome, at baseline and 6 weeks. The paper never mentions fear-avoidance and designates no primary outcome, instead claiming benefit on quality of life, disability and symptom severity. The reported outcomes appear to be a different set from the registered primary, with no stated reason, so the efficacy claim rests on outcomes not pre-specified as primary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the primary outcome was changed before data collection, or the paper reporting fear-avoidance.

quotes.text: The study was a randomized, single-blind clinical trial registered in Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT05477199.
Strategies based on adjustment to chronic illnesses are effective

second_reader.what_stands: True that the paper names no primary outcome and reports no fear-avoidance measure; the sample-size calculation points to WHODAS only implicitly. Whether fear-avoidance beliefs was the registered primary outcome cannot be verified from the paper alone, since the registry entry is not shown.

issues.title: About 20 between-group tests with no correction; 3 nominal hits (p = 0.004, 0.009, 0.014) back the claim
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports roughly 20 between-group comparisons, each at p <= 0.05 with no adjustment and no designated primary outcome. Only three reach nominal significance (self-care 0.004, anxiety/depression 0.009, WHODAS self-care 0.014); about one false positive is expected by chance from 20 tests. Against a Bonferroni threshold of 0.0025 for 20 tests none survives, so the efficacy conclusion rests on results that do not withstand correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a hierarchical testing plan, or a multiplicity adjustment.

quotes.text: P-value was considered significant when p ≤ 0.05.

second_reader.what_stands: There are about 20 between-group comparisons at alpha 0.05 with no stated correction, and the three nominal hits (0.004, 0.009, 0.014) do not survive Bonferroni or Holm adjustment for 20 tests. The three results are the basis for the abstract's between-group claims.

issues.title: Efficacy conclusion leans on within-group change; most between-group tests (incl. totals) are null
issues.explanation: The abstract cites significant change from baseline in the intervention group as a finding. Within-group change cannot separate treatment from time, regression to the mean, or expectation, and the control group also improved significantly on several subscales. The between-group tests the authors performed show differences only in three subscales and none in total WHODAS (0.492) or WSAS (0.197), so the broad conclusion is only partly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group analysis (e.g. ANCOVA on change) showing a consistent benefit across the main outcomes.

quotes.text: The intervention group showed significant differences from baseline on some subscales of the quality of life, disability, and functional impairment variables.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract and conclusion lean heavily on within-group changes in the intervention arm, while the between-group comparisons are mostly null, including every total score. The three between-group differences are real nominal findings but are limited to the self-care and anxiety/depression items of EQ-5D and WHODAS self-care, and broader claims such as reduced disability and improved functioning are not supported by between-group tests.

issues.title: All outcomes are self-reported and participants were unblinded; assessor blinding adds little
issues.explanation: EQ-5D, WHODAS and WSAS are all self-completed, and participants could not be unaware of receiving 12 sessions versus a leaflet. Blinding the research assistant therefore offers little protection against expectation or response bias, and the limitations section does not mention it. The registry's triple-masking entry differs from the paper's single-blind description.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence participants were masked, or objective outcomes showing the same effect.

quotes.text: The research assistant collecting the data was blinded to the hypothesis of the study and to the patient
It consists of a self-reported measure that

second_reader.what_stands: All reported outcomes come from questionnaires, and participants in the active arm necessarily know they are receiving the programme, so assessor blinding offers limited protection against reporting bias. The paper does not state that participants were unblinded and does not say how the questionnaires were administered, so the extent to which the assessor could influence responses cannot be judged.

issues.title: Text gives p = 0.630 for within-group WHODAS mobility; Table 3 within-group p is 0.018
issues.explanation: The Results sentence lists WHODAS mobility among subscales with significant intervention-group change, but quotes p = 0.630. In Table 3, 0.630 is the between-group p; the intervention within-group p is 0.018. The other p values in the sentence come from the within-group column, so this one was taken from the wrong column. The table's conclusion (significant within-group change) is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 0.630 is a within-group p for mobility, or a corrected Table 3.

quotes.text: mobility (p = 0.630)

issues.title: Only immediate post-programme outcomes at 6 weeks; no follow-up, yet conclusions are unqualified
issues.explanation: Outcomes were measured only at the end of the 6-week programme, and the authors say persistence of effects is unknown. The conclusion nevertheless calls the strategies effective with no qualification on durability. This limits the strength of the claim but does not invalidate the short-term result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A follow-up assessment showing sustained effects.

quotes.text: A second limitation is the absence of a follow-up period

issues.title: Control EQ-5D mobility worsened (2.43 to 2.71) but change printed as +0.28 under an improvement convention
issues.explanation: In every other row the Δ equals baseline minus end-of-study (improvement positive). For control mobility the score rose, so baseline minus end is -0.28, yet 0.28 is printed with no sign. This is probably a lost minus sign. It makes the control arm look as if it improved slightly when it worsened, narrowing the apparent between-arm contrast marginally.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Δ columns are absolute magnitudes, or the raw data.

quotes.location: Table 2, Quality of Life Mobility row, Control Group
Table 3, Quality of Life Mobility row, Δ Control Group

10.1016/j.phrs.2022.106360.headline_claim: Supplementation with L-Arginine plus vitamin C has beneficial effects in Long-COVID, attenuating typical symptoms and improving effort perception compared with a multivitamin combination.
10.1016/j.phrs.2022.106360.overall: The headline claim of a beneficial effect of L-Arginine + Vitamin C rests on a non-randomised, unblinded survey with only post-treatment outcomes, and the unmeasured baseline difference makes causal attribution unreliable. The printed mean symptom score (8.15) is also impossible on the stated 9-27 scale. The direction of the Table 2 differences is striking, but the size of the effect cannot be trusted.

primary_outcome.name: Long-COVID symptom score (physician-rated, 9 symptoms) at 30 days

issues.title: Non-randomised, post-treatment-only survey with no baseline symptoms or adjustment, yet causal benefit claimed
issues.explanation: Treatment was chosen by family physicians, and symptoms were recorded only after 30 days of treatment, with no baseline measure. No adjustment for confounders is reported, and the only balance evidence is age, sex and hospitalisation. Differences as large as 94.4% versus 1.1% severe asthenia could easily reflect who was given which product or who was surveyed. The conclusion of a beneficial effect is therefore not supported by this design. The survey was also administered after treatment had finished, so the study is retrospective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline symptom scores for both groups showing similarity, or an adjusted or randomised comparison giving the same effect.

quotes.text: we did not administer the survey at baseline but only after 30 days.
Our survey indicates that the supplementation with L-Arginine + Vitamin C has beneficial effects in Long-COVID
The survey was distributed to patients who had already received the treatments.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a non-randomised, post-treatment-only survey with no baseline symptom or effort data and only unadjusted comparisons, yet the abstract concludes that the supplementation 'has beneficial effects' and the discussion says it is 'the first to show' benefit. The authors do acknowledge the missing baseline and call for interventional studies, but the causal wording of the conclusion is stronger than the design supports.

issues.title: Unblinded physicians rated symptoms and patients self-rated effort; no control for assessment bias
issues.explanation: The physicians who administered the survey and scored the symptoms knew each patient's treatment, and patients knew what they took. Symptom severity and Borg effort are subjective, so expectation effects could produce large apparent differences. The abstract and conclusions draw no attention to this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded or objective outcome assessment, or evidence that raters did not know the allocation.

quotes.text: Physicians were asked to maintain a ~2:1 ratio (L-Arginine + Vitamin C vs alternative treatment) in administering the survey; therefore, they were not blinded

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that physicians were not blinded and that they scored symptoms, with no measure to control assessment bias, and the limitations section does not discuss this. That the effort scores were patient self-ratings is not stated in the paper, so that part of the point is an assumption.

issues.title: Mean symptom score 8.15 in the L-Arginine group is below the minimum possible total of 9
issues.explanation: Nine symptoms were each rated 1 (absent) to 3 (severe), so a total score cannot be lower than 9. The text reports a mean of 8.15 ± 1.3 for the L-Arginine + Vitamin C group, which is impossible on the stated scale. The total is therefore mis-scored or mis-described, and the headline score comparison cannot be reproduced from the paper. The direction of the effect in Table 2 is still apparent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors specifying a scoring scheme (e.g. items scored 0-2) under which 8.15 is attainable.

quotes.text: 8.15 ± 1.3 vs Alternative
on a scale from 1 to 3 (where 1 is absence of the symptom

second_reader.what_stands: Under the scoring described in the Methods (nine items scored 1-3, summed), a mean of 8.15 is below the minimum possible 9, so the reported figure is inconsistent with the stated scale. The paper never defines the total score, so a different construction (such as 0-2 scoring) or a reporting error cannot be ruled out from the text.

issues.title: Symptom score is an ad hoc 1-3 physician rating of nine symptoms, with no validation or defined summation
issues.explanation: The survey was designed by the authors, and the nine-item score is not shown to be validated or reliable. The summing method is not stated, and the printed totals are not consistent with the scale (see the separate issue on the score range). This weakens the main symptom result, though the outcome is plausible as a rough severity measure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Citation of validation of this instrument, or a defined scoring method with reliability data.

quotes.text: on a scale from 1 to 3 (where 1 is absence of the symptom

10.1016/j.rehab.2022.101709.headline_claim: An 8-week supervised home-based inspiratory/expiratory muscle training (RMT) programme improved quality of life, but not exercise tolerance, in people with long-term post-COVID-19 symptoms.
10.1016/j.rehab.2022.101709.overall: The finding that real inspiratory-based training improves inspiratory muscle strength and lower limb function, and that RMT improves expiratory function, is well supported. The headline claim that only RMT improves quality of life rests on a single borderline contrast against a sham arm that barely changed, with no significant difference from IMT or IMTsham, so it should be treated as tentative. Several summary statements (lung function, grip strength, HRQoL recommendation) are looser than the reported data.

primary_outcome.name: HRQoL (EQ-5D-5L index and VAS) and exercise tolerance (Ruffier test)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from Baseline Health-related quality of life at 8 weeks
Change from Baseline Exercise tolerance at 8 weeks

issues.title: 'Only RMT effective' for quality of life rests on one borderline contrast against a non-improving sham arm
issues.explanation: All groups except RMTsham improved significantly on quality of life from baseline, including IMTsham, and RMT did not differ significantly from IMTsham or IMT. The sole significant between-group result is RMT vs RMTsham on the EQ-5D index (adjusted difference 0.151, 95% CI 0.029 to 0.273); the VAS differences were not significant. The RMTsham arm is the odd one out (little change, 0.628 to 0.684), so the contrast may reflect that arm's weak response rather than a specific RMT benefit. 'Only RMT was effective' is therefore stronger than the data support, as the authors partly concede in the Discussion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified test showing RMT superior to both sham arms and to IMT on the primary HRQoL outcome.

quotes.text: Only an 8-week supervised home-based RMT programme was effective in improving quality of life
except for the RMTsham group
quotes.location: Results, Health-related quality of life and exercise tolerance

quotes.text: the RMT group did not show statistically signi fi cant differences in quality of life compared to the IMTsham
quotes.location: Discussion, Health-related quality of life and exercise tolerance

second_reader.what_stands: The 'only RMT effective' claim does rest on a single between-group contrast, RMT vs RMTsham, because RMT was not significantly better than IMTsham and RMTsham was the only arm that did not improve from baseline, while the near-identical zero-resistance IMTsham arm improved significantly (p=0.003). The contrast is not merely borderline: it is significant on both EQ-5D index and VAS, with an adjusted p of roughly 0.01 or below, although the EQ index CI lower bound is close to zero. The Discussion hedges this (RMT vs IMTsham non-significant, 'interpret with caution'), but the Abstract and Conclus

issues.title: Headline HRQoL contrast is borderline (CI 0.029 to 0.273) with no correction across 2 primary and 7 secondary outcomes
issues.explanation: Pairwise comparisons were Bonferroni-adjusted per the Methods, but no adjustment across outcomes is stated and it is unclear whether the printed CIs are the adjusted ones. The headline contrast is flagged ** (p<0.01) although its CI (0.029 to 0.273) implies an unadjusted p of about 0.016. This is a weak spot rather than a demonstrated error, and it makes the 'only RMT' result fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that the CIs and ** flags are Bonferroni-adjusted and that p<0.01 holds after adjustment, plus a stated plan for the two primary outcomes.

quotes.text: Multiple comparisons with Bonferroni adjustment were performed in the case of signi fi cant ANOVA fi ndings.

quotes.location: Table 2, EQ-5D-5L index, Respiratory vs Respiratory sham, post-intervention

issues.title: Combined training recommended for HRQoL although RMT vs IMT HRQoL difference was -0.060 (CI -0.182 to 0.063)
issues.explanation: The Clinical implications advise combined training over isolated training to maximise HRQoL. The direct RMT vs IMT comparison on HRQoL was not significant and the Discussion says there were no differences other than RMT vs RMTsham. The recommendation is supported for expiratory function but not for HRQoL.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant RMT vs IMT difference in HRQoL in the paper's results.

quotes.text: To obtain the greatest improvements in HRQoL and expiratory muscle function, the use of combined training (inspiratory/expiratory muscles) is recommended over their application in isolation.
with no differences in the other between-group comparisons
quotes.location: Discussion, Health-related quality of life and exercise tolerance

issues.title: Grip strength: Results report significant within-group rises in all 4 groups; Discussion says it 'did not increase'
issues.explanation: The Results say handgrip rose significantly from baseline in all four groups (p = 0.002 to 0.023) but did not differ between groups. The Discussion states flatly that grip strength did not increase and then offers a physiological explanation for the absence of any upper-limb gain. The data support only a lack of between-group difference, probably a general time or sham-attention effect, so the Discussion wording is inaccurate but does not affect a main claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the Discussion sentence refers only to between-group differences.

quotes.text: upper limb muscle strength increased signi fi cantly in all groups
However, upper limb grip strength did not increase.

issues.title: Conclusion says no impact on lung function, yet PEF rose significantly in RMT (d up to 1.2, p<0.001 vs baseline)
issues.explanation: PEF is reported under lung function, with a significant group x time interaction (p = 0.003) and a large RMT advantage over the other three groups. The abstract conclusion and final Conclusions section nonetheless say the programmes had no impact on lung function. The statement is accurate only for FVC, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC, so it understates the PEF finding; it is an inconsistency in how the result is summarised.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explicit definition in the paper placing PEF outside 'lung function'.

quotes.text: Expiratory muscle strength and peak expiratory fl ow showed a statistically signi fi cant and large ( d ≥ 0.87) increase in the RMT group compared with the other 3 groups.
but had no impact on lung function and psychological status.

10.1016/j.rehab.2023.101765.headline_claim: A 90-day exercise training rehabilitation (ETR) course reduced dyspnoea more than standard physiotherapy (SP) in people with persistent breathlessness after COVID-19 ARDS, with an increased physical SF-12 component.
10.1016/j.rehab.2023.101765.overall: The direction of the primary result is plausible, since the effect is large with a CI well away from zero. However, it comes from an open-label trial with self-reported outcomes, a non-matched comparator and a retrospective registration. The estimate is probably inflated. Secondary SF-12 claims are the weakest, with a p-value mismatch, baseline imbalance not adjusted despite the stated ANCOVA, and generalisation beyond ICU survivors.

primary_outcome.name: MDP total score (dyspnoea) at day 90

primary_outcomes.measure: Evaluate the effect of exercise rehabilitation on post-ICU dyspnea

issues.title: Reported differences equal raw day-90 mean gaps, not the ANCOVA baseline-adjusted estimates the Methods describe
issues.explanation: The Methods say between-group differences were tested with an ANCOVA adjusted for baseline. In Table 2 every reported difference equals the simple gap between day-90 means, to within rounding. Because the groups differed at baseline, notably on the SF-12 where ETR began higher, adjusted differences would not match. The SF-12 physical gap of 6.96 includes a 3.65-point head start for ETR, so the reported SF-12 effect is probably overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reporting of model-adjusted means or coefficients showing that the ANCOVA estimates coincide with the raw differences.

quotes.text: were tested using an ANCOVA model adjusted for baseline values
The mean MDP after ETR was 42% lower than after SP at 26.15 vs. 44.76

quotes.location: Table 2, SF-12 Physical component row, baseline ETR

second_reader.what_stands: The Table 2 and Results differences are numerically the raw day-90 mean gaps, and the MDP total CI matches an unadjusted t interval, not the baseline-adjusted ANCOVA estimates the Methods describe. This was checked from printed values only; the paper does not show the ANCOVA output, so I cannot say what the model itself returned.

issues.title: Open-label trial with self-reported primary outcome (MDP); assessor blinding cannot address participant bias
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the primary and secondary outcomes are all patient-reported. The assessor blinding the authors cite as a strength does not protect against expectation effects or differential reporting. The control arm also had a known promise of later ETR. The large treatment effect on dyspnoea may therefore be partly inflated by this bias, and the conclusion should be tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an objective or sham-controlled corroborating outcome showing a comparable effect, or an MDP administered in a way that participants could not influence.

quotes.text: open-label, assessor-blinded trial
The primary outcome was the measurement of dyspnoea in its 3 dimensions, as assessed by the difference in the MDP score

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome (MDP) and both secondary outcomes (mMRC, SF-12) are self-reported in an open-label trial, so the unblinded participants could influence them; assessor blinding does not address this. The paper frames assessor blinding as bias minimisation and does not list unblinded patient-reported outcomes as a limitation.

issues.title: Conclusion generalises to all people with post-COVID dyspnoea; sample was ventilated ICU survivors near Paris
issues.explanation: Participants all had ventilated COVID ARDS, were at least 3 months post-ICU, and lived within 5 km of a participating practice. The final conclusion recommends high-intensity training for 'people presenting with dyspnoea after COVID-19' generally. Most long COVID patients were never ventilated, so the claim goes beyond the population studied.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from non-ICU long COVID patients showing a similar benefit.

quotes.text: received mechanical ventilation for ≥ 48 h following a documented SARS-Cov-2 infection
may therefore be the most appropriate rehabilitation treatment for people presenting with dyspnoea after COVID-19.

issues.title: Conclusion highlights SF-12 physical component after null SF-12 total and mental scores
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says an increased physical HRQOL component was found in the ETR group. The total SF-12 score was not significantly different and the mental component showed nothing. The physical component is a subscale comparison without correction for multiple tests, and it started with a baseline advantage for ETR. This is a modest positive spin on a secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan naming the SF-12 physical component as a key secondary outcome, with a baseline-adjusted estimate showing the same effect.

quotes.text: An increased physical component of HRQOL was also found in the ETR group.
Separate analysis of the SF-12 physical component results, however, revealed a 21% increase of the score

issues.title: SF-12 total: 95% CI 0.22 to 16.25 excludes 0 but p printed as 0.14 (CI implies about 0.04)
issues.explanation: The SF-12 total score difference of 8.24 has a 95% CI that excludes zero, which implies p of about 0.04. The table prints p = 0.14, and the text then calls the groups 'similar'. The physical and mental SF-12 rows show smaller but similar p-value/CI mismatches. This probably understates a secondary result, and it leaves the SF-12 results unreliable as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction or supplement showing the SF-12 total was analysed with a method (e.g. a different CI construction) that gives p = 0.14 with this interval.

quotes.text: Mean SF-12 total scores after the rehabilitation intervention were similar for ETR and SP groups.

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0439 (reachable range [0.0436, 0.0442] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.14 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the CI excludes the null (0.0), but the reported p = 0.14 says the result is not significant

issues.title: Emotional response called 'least decreased' although breathing discomfort fell least (34% vs 36%)
issues.explanation: The Results give reductions of 34%, 48% and 36% for breathing discomfort, sensory and emotional dimensions. The Discussion says the emotional response was the least decreased. By the paper's own percentages breathing discomfort fell least, and by change from baseline the emotional dimension actually fell most. The Discussion then uses this to argue ETR works through physical rather than emotional mechanisms, so that interpretation is not supported by the numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated metric (e.g. absolute points on a common scale) under which the emotional response is demonstrably the smallest reduction.

quotes.text: were 34%, 48% and 36% lower, respectively
it should be noted that the emotional response was the least decreased

issues.title: ETR vs usual care differs in session length (60 vs 30 min), therapist type and standardisation; intensity not isolated
issues.explanation: ETR sessions were twice as long and delivered by specialised pulmonary rehabilitation physiotherapists. SP sessions were shorter, unstandardised and delivered by general physiotherapists. The comparison therefore shows that the ETR package beat usual care, but not that intensity is the active component. The Conclusion nonetheless says high-intensity training may be the most appropriate treatment. Seven participants also received the other treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison arm matched on session duration and therapist expertise, or an analysis showing the effect tracks achieved intensity rather than programme and provider.

quotes.text: Participants in the SP group had the same number of sessions, but they were delivered by general physiotherapist practitioners.
for a shorter duration (30-minute sessions) and without standardisation than those in the ETR group
High-intensity exercise training (ie, longer sessions with a higher target exercise intensity) may therefore be the most appropriate rehabilitation treatment

issues.title: Trial stopped at 60 of 200 planned participants; effect sizes likely imprecise, secondary outcomes underpowered
issues.explanation: The target of 100 per group was not reached, with 27 and 33 randomised, because of recruitment difficulty. The primary result is large and highly significant, so it is likely real in direction, but the magnitude is imprecise. The SF-12 findings are the main casualty, with the authors themselves invoking a lack of power.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A replication or larger trial giving a similar effect size.

quotes.text: the impossibility of recruiting 200 participants as planned forced us to prematurely stop the study.
Using our results to retrospectively calculate the required sample size gave us a participant cohort size of only 40.

issues.title: Registered after enrolment began (paper: 29 Sep 2020; registry first submission 10 Sep 2020; start 7 Aug 2020)
issues.explanation: The trial was registered about 3 to 7 weeks after the first participants were enrolled. Registration after the start means the primary outcome and analysis cannot be confirmed as fixed beforehand. The registry's primary outcome is generic dyspnoea at month 3, which does not pin down the MDP total score. The registration date also differs between the paper and the registry.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or the approved protocol showing MDP total score at day 90 as the prespecified primary outcome before enrolment.

quotes.text: was registered on Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT04569266) on September 29, 2020.
Between August 7, 2020, and January 26, 2022, 487 participants with CARDS were screened for inclusion

issues.title: Recruitment start date is August 7, 2020 in Abstract but July 22, 2020 in Results
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Results give different start dates for the same 487-person screening period ending January 26, 2022. The two dates are about 16 days apart. Nothing in the conclusions depends on this, but it matters for judging how the start date relates to registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that July 22 is the first screening date and August 7 the first randomisation, applied consistently to both passages.

quotes.text: Between August 7, 2020, and January 26, 2022, 487 participants with CARDS were screened for inclusion
Between July 22, 2020 and January 26, 2022, 487 people were potentially eligible

issues.title: Printed percentages do not match counts: 32/60 printed 55% (53.3%); Table 1 SP men 21/33 printed 67% (63.6%)
issues.explanation: The recruitment share is printed as 55% (32/60), but 32/60 is 53.3%. Table 1 has further percentages that do not match their counts, such as the SP men row. These are small reporting slips, with no bearing on the efficacy findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source count showing 33/60 recruited at the lead site and corrected Table 1 percentages.

quotes.text: 55% (32/60) of whomwere recruited from the Groupe Hospitalier Paris Saint-Joseph

script.explanation: 32/60 = 53.33%, but the paper prints 55, outside the rounding interval [54.50, 56.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 58.2 rather than 60.

10.1016/j.rehab.2023.101815.headline_claim: A home-based exercise program with teleconsultation significantly improves effort tolerance, but only for people who had severe effort intolerance at baseline.
10.1016/j.rehab.2023.101815.overall: The whole-population primary result is null, and the authors say so in the Discussion, but the abstract conclusion and Practical implications present the program as effective on the strength of a single, small, post hoc-style subgroup (18 vs 13, p = 0.035) with no interaction test or multiplicity control. The numeric slips (22 vs 23, 74 vs 79 denominators, 62% vs 65%, 80 vs 63 days) are minor but show inconsistent denominators. Treat the subgroup benefit as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Change in effort tolerance measured by the 6-minute walking test (6MWT) at 4 weeks (T1)

issues.title: Null primary result (p = 0.109); efficacy conclusion rests on an untested subgroup (n = 18 vs 13, p = 0.035)
issues.explanation: The primary between-group comparison of 6MWT change was not significant (77.6 vs 49.5 m, p = 0.109). The conclusion that the program 'significantly improves effort tolerance' for severely intolerant people rests on a baseline-defined subgroup of 31 people. No subgroup-by-treatment interaction test is reported and the analysis was not powered for it. Alongside other uncorrected analyses (secondary outcomes, MCID responders, improver odds ratios), this makes the subgroup benefit hypothesis-generating at best. The change-from-baseline design and the small subgroup also leave room for chance and regression to the mean.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction test, or evidence that the subgroup was pre-registered as the primary analysis with multiplicity control.

quotes.text: a homebased exercise program with teleconsultation signi fi cantly improves effort tolerance but only for people who had severe effort intolerance at baseline.
We have shown that the intervention did not produce a higher improvement in effort tolerance compared with Controls in the total study population.
This home-based exercise program was effective in improving their condition after 4 weeks.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary comparison was null (77.6 vs 49.5 m, p = 0.109), and the claim of efficacy in severe-intolerance patients rests on a post hoc-style subgroup of 18 vs 13 (p = 0.035) with no interaction test, no stated multiplicity control and no stated prespecification, so the Abstract Conclusions and the 'was effective' sentence overstate what the data can support. The Discussion and final Conclusion are more hedged, and the paper does report the null overall result openly, so the problem is the strength of the Abstract and Practical-implications wording, not concealment of the primary result. My

issues.title: MCID responder rates use inconsistent denominators: 24/37 = 65%, not 62%
issues.explanation: The Intervention rate of 84% matches 31/37. The Control rate of 62% does not match 24/37, which is 64.9%. It would match a denominator of 39. If the denominators differ, the between-group p = 0.036 may rest on an unequal basis. With 37 in each arm, a simple chi-squared on 31/37 vs 24/37 gives about p = 0.06 (hand calculation).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Control denominator was 39 (or that the test used a different method), with a reproduction of p = 0.036.

quotes.text: 84 % ( n = 31) in the Intervention group and 62 % ( n = 24) in the Control group
A total of 74 individuals completed the study: 37 in the Intervention and 37 in the Control group

script.explanation: 24/37 = 64.86%, but the paper prints 62, outside the rounding interval [61.50, 63.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 38.7 rather than 37.

issues.title: 2-month follow-up available for 55 of 79 randomised (about 30% missing); 'spontaneous recovery' rests on it
issues.explanation: Only 55 of 79 randomised participants (28 and 27) had the T2 6MWT. About 30% were not measured, and the ANOVA used completers only. The Discussion uses the similar T2 distances to suggest a marginal role for the program and spontaneous recovery. Those completers are a self-selected, closer-to-centre subset. This weakens a secondary, exploratory interpretation, not the primary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison showing T2 completers and non-completers are similar at baseline and T1, or a sensitivity analysis imputing the missing T2 values.

quotes.text: Two months after the end of the program the 6MWT was repeated by 55 participants: 28 in the Intervention and 27 in the Control groups (Fig. 1, T2).
In addition, we had a high number of participants lost at the 2-month follow-up (T2).

issues.title: Hypoxia at rest: text gives n = 22 (30%), Table 1 gives 23 (29%)
issues.explanation: The Results text says 22 participants (30%) had hypoxia at rest. Table 1 gives 23 (29%), and its arm counts (13 + 10) add to 23. The two sources disagree on a baseline count. The discrepancy is small and no outcome depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text count excludes one participant lacking an assessment, or a corrected table or text.

quotes.text: 30% ( n = 22) suffered from hypoxia at rest
Hypoxia at rest, n (%) 23 (29)

issues.title: Baseline text divides Table 1 counts by 74 although Table 1 is based on N = 79
issues.explanation: Table 1 reports baseline data for all 79 randomised participants. The baseline text applies the same counts (31 with significant effort intolerance, 59 with desaturation) to a denominator of 74. This yields about 40% and about 80% against 39% and 75% in the table. It is a reporting inconsistency in baseline description, not an error in the outcome analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 31 and 59 counts in the text are for the 74 completers only and differ from Table 1.

quotes.text: about 40% of the 74 ( n = 31) showed signi fi cant effort intolerance at 6MWT

issues.title: Text says in-hospital stay averaged ~80 days; Table 1 acute + rehabilitation stays sum to 63.1
issues.explanation: The text describes an average in-hospital stay of about 80 days. Table 1 lists mean acute care (26.7) and rehabilitation (36.4) days, which total 63.1. No other hospital component is listed. This is a descriptive inconsistency that does not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 'in-hospital stay' that includes additional stays summing to about 80 days.

quotes.text: their in-hospital stay averaged about 80 days
Days in rehabilitation hospital, days 36.4 (15.2)

issues.title: 'Safe' claim rests on 4 weeks of adverse-event counts in 40 participants with one unattributed hospitalisation
issues.explanation: Safety was assessed only in the Intervention group over 4 weeks, with no comparison event rate. The paper reports no adverse events yet also an exercise-period hospitalisation for cardiovascular events judged 'not directly related'. With n = 40, zero events cannot exclude a moderate risk. The claim 'safe' is stronger than this design supports; 'no events observed' would be accurate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Safety data collected in both arms with comparable event rates, or a definition of adverse events under which the hospitalisation is clearly unrelated.

quotes.text: We also found the Intervention program to be safe and feasible, with high participant adherence and satisfaction.
One hospitalization during the study period occurred due to cardiovascular events not directly related to the exercise program .

issues.title: Primary and secondary analyses use 74 completers, not the 79 randomised; no intention-to-treat analysis
issues.explanation: Randomisation was 40 vs 39, but the primary 6MWT comparison and Table 2 use 37 per arm after 5 people left. No ITT or sensitivity analysis is reported. With a small, balanced loss the impact is probably minor, but the stated efficacy analysis is per completer.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported ITT or imputed analysis giving the same primary result.

quotes.text: A total of 74 individuals completed the study: 37 in the Intervention and 37 in the Control group
At T1, 5 participants left the study: attrition rates were 8 % ( n = 3/40) and 5 % ( n = 2/ 39)

10.1016/j.rehab.2024.101853.headline_claim: Telerehabilitation training improved physical activity amounts, exercise self-efficacy and sleep quality in people with long COVID, but did not improve cardiorespiratory fitness or HRQOL.
10.1016/j.rehab.2024.101853.overall: The trial's primary outcome (CRF) showed no benefit, and the positive claims rest on uncorrected secondary self-reported outcomes whose significance depends on the GEE difference-in-differences. The control group fell from a high baseline, and baseline-adjusted ANCOVA comparisons are non-significant. Abstract effect sizes are misprinted as CI bounds, registration was retrospective, and a third of participants were lost with baseline-carried-forward imputation, so the headline conclusion should be treated as tentative at best.

primary_outcome.name: Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), including VO2peak, workload, AT, O2 pulse, FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, HR recovery, VE/VCO2 slope

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Exercise Capacity: Peak Oxygen Uptake (VO2peak) From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Exercise Capacity: Workload (Watt) From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Exercise Capacity: Anaerobic Threshold (AT) From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Lung Function: Forced Expiratory Volume 1 (FEV1) From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Lung Function: Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Lung Function: FEV1/FVC % From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Ventilation/ Perfusion Abnormalities (VE/VCO2) From Baseline to 12 Weeks
Change in Left Ventricular Function: O2 Pulse From Baseline to 12 Weeks

issues.title: PA and self-efficacy 'effects' come from CG decline off a high baseline; baseline-adjusted ANCOVA is non-significant
issues.explanation: Simple randomization left the groups unbalanced at baseline on the outcomes of interest. The CG started at much higher PA (walking 3086 vs 1655) and then fell, while EG within-group changes were not significant (walking p = 0.249, total PA p = 0.168). The ANCOVA between-group comparisons that control for baseline are all non-significant (walking p = 0.439, total PA p = 0.214, self-efficacy p = 0.055). The GEE difference-in-differences is therefore heavily dependent on this analytic choice. The conclusion that telerehabilitation increased PA and self-efficacy is not robust.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A GEE or ANCOVA adjusted for baseline PA and self-efficacy that still shows significant between-group differences.

quotes.text: Interestingly, the CG had initially higher walking behavior and total PA than the EG.
Consequently, we were able to overcome the baseline differences between the groups.
Fifth, as we used simple randomization for group assignment, certain baseline characteristics between the 2 groups became incomparable, increasing the risk of selection bias.

second_reader.what_stands: For walking and total PA, the EG did not change significantly, the CG fell from a significantly higher baseline, and the ANCOVA that adjusts for baseline is non-significant (p=0.439 and 0.214). So the GEE 'effect' is mainly a CG decline plus regression away from a high baseline. For self-efficacy the EG did rise significantly (+1.2, p=0.007) alongside a CG fall, so the claim is only partly true there, although the baseline-adjusted ANCOVA is still non-significant (p=0.055). The Discussion's statement that the CG self-efficacy decline was not significant conflicts with Table 2.

issues.title: Conclusion asserts increased exercise frequency/intensity and better overall health, which were not shown
issues.explanation: The conclusion says telerehabilitation 'can effectively increase exercise frequency and intensity' and improves 'overall health outcomes'. Frequency and intensity were not reported outcomes, and CRF and HRQOL showed no group difference. The evidence is limited to self-reported PA, self-efficacy and sleep over 12 weeks, with the weaknesses described in c9 and c10. The conclusion overstates what the trial supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported frequency/intensity data showing differences between groups.

quotes.text: The personalized and convenient nature of telerehabilitation training can effectively increase exercise frequency and intensity, enhance self-ef fi cacy, and improve sleep quality.
First, there was a lack of longterm follow-up to assess the sustained effect of the telerehabilitation.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion says telerehabilitation 'can effectively increase exercise frequency and intensity', but the paper reports no frequency or intensity outcome and the moderate and vigorous PA results were null. 'Improving overall health outcomes' is also unsupported, because CRF and all four HRQOL domains showed no difference and only a self-reported sleep score improved. The Conclusion omits the paper's own caveats about adherence, dropout and absent long-term follow-up.

issues.title: Positive claims rest on secondary outcomes among ~20 uncorrected tests after a null CRF primary
issues.explanation: The primary outcome (CRF, with many parameters) was null. The conclusion is built on secondary outcomes (PA, self-efficacy, sleep). About 20 outcomes were tested at an uncorrected two-tailed p < 0.05. The registry lists eight primary measures and four secondary outcomes. With even a Bonferroni threshold near 0.0025, the total PA (p = 0.003) and sleep (p = 0.012) findings would not survive. The secondary findings are therefore exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical testing plan or multiplicity adjustment for the secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: The primary outcome was cardiorespiratory fi tness (CRF), and secondary outcomes were physical activity (PA) amounts
All analyses were two-tailed, with p < 0.05 indicating statistical signi fi cance.

second_reader.what_stands: Every positive finding in the abstract and conclusion comes from a secondary outcome, after null results on all CRF parameters. Roughly 22 interaction tests were run at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05. The sleep result (p = 0.012) and the total-PA result (p = 0.003) would not survive a correction across all tests, while the walking and self-efficacy results would. The paper does disclose the null primary result, and 'about 20 tests' fits the Table 3 count of 22.

issues.title: 33% attrition (EG 38% vs CG 27%) handled by baseline-carried-forward imputation
issues.explanation: The post-test was missing for 60 of 182 randomized participants, more often in the EG. LOCF imputed no change for all of them. That biases between-group change estimates in an unpredictable direction, and it treats the dropouts as having exactly zero change. The reasons for dropout (feeling better, reluctance) suggest the data are not missing at random. The trial's PA, self-efficacy and sleep effects, and its null CRF result, are all affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (multiple imputation or mixed model on observed data) giving the same effect estimates.

quotes.text: In the EG, 56 (62 %) participants completed the 12-week homebased telerehabilitation training program with a dropout rate of 38 %.
Missing data were handled using the last-observation-carried-forward method for intent-to-treat analysis.

second_reader.what_stands: About one third of participants (33%) were lost, with higher loss in the EG (38%) than the CG (27%). Their 12-week values were filled by LOCF, which with two time points equals baseline-carried-forward, i.e. an assumption of zero change. The paper reports no sensitivity analysis, such as complete-case analysis, multiple imputation or a mixed model, and it does not test the difference in dropout between arms.

issues.title: Abstract/Results give CI bounds as the group×time estimates for walking, total PA and self-efficacy
issues.explanation: The abstract reports b = -763.3 (walking), -711 (total PA) and -1.19 (self-efficacy). Table 3 gives the interaction estimates as -1684, -2147 and -2.35. The abstract values are the upper CI limits (-736.3 for walking, with digits transposed; -711.0; -1.19). The Results text also drops the minus signs. The significance claims survive, but the effect sizes are understated by roughly a half to a third.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A model in the paper or supplement in which the abstract values are the actual interaction estimates.

quotes.text: The EG had greater walking behavior ( b = -763.3, p < 0.001), total amount of PA ( b = -711, p = 0.003), exercise self-ef fi cacy ( b = -1.19, p < 0.001)

issues.title: Open-label trial with attention imbalance; headline outcomes are self-reported questionnaires
issues.explanation: Participants could not be blinded, and the EG received weekly reminders and monitoring while the CG received none. The positive outcomes (IPAQ, self-efficacy, PSQI) are all self-reported. The assessor-blinded objective outcome (CPET) is the one that showed no effect. This weakens the interpretation of the secondary results as a specific effect of the exercise programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Objective activity monitoring (e.g. accelerometry) confirming the self-reported PA differences.

quotes.text: The CG maintained their usual lifestyles for 12 weeks without exercise reminders
Third, biases were identi fi ed using self-reported questionnaires.

issues.title: Trial called 'prospectively registered' but registered Jan 2022, after recruitment began Oct 2021
issues.explanation: The Methods describe prospective registration. The abstract gives the registration date as 25 January 2022, and recruitment began in October 2021. The registry record shows first submission on 2022-01-24 and study start on 2021-10-12, so registration came roughly three months after start. The outcomes and analyses could therefore have been shaped after participants were already enrolled, and the 'prospective' label is inaccurate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that registration occurred before the first participant was enrolled.

quotes.text: prospectively registered on the ClinicalTrials.gov website (NCT05205460)
Between October 2021 and January 2023
The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05205460) on January 25, 2022.

issues.title: CG self-efficacy fall (12.1 to 10.9) called non-significant, but Table 2 gives paired p = 0.011
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the control group's exercise self-efficacy decreased without statistical significance. Table 2 gives a within-CG paired p of 0.011 for the same change. The text therefore contradicts the table. The significant CG decline also matters for how the EG-versus-CG interaction should be read.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated stricter alpha or correction under which p = 0.011 is non-significant.

quotes.text: scores decreased after 12 weeks, although this decrease was not statistically signi fi cant

issues.title: Abnormal HRR total of 92 exceeds the 1-min (29) and 2-min (43) components, whose union is 52
issues.explanation: The Discussion says 92 of 182 participants had abnormal heart rate recovery. The components given are 29 (1-min), 43 (2-min) and 20 (both), so the union is 52. The 92 is not reachable from its own components. This is a secondary descriptive statement and does not affect the trial results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of abnormal HRR that includes additional criteria and is stated in the paper.

quotes.text: 92 participants had abnormal HRR out of the total 182 participants in both groups (1-min HRR: 29, 2-min HRR: 43, both: 20)

issues.title: Adherence of 26.05 of 36 sessions printed as 74%; arithmetic gives 72.4%
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives average adherence as 26.05 sessions, or 74%, of the 36 prescribed. 26.05 / 36 is 72.4%. The discrepancy is small and does not change the conclusion of limited adherence, but the figures are inconsistent as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative denominator or per-participant averaging that yields 74%.

quotes.text: no participants completed the full 36 sessions, with an average of 26.05 (74 %)

10.1016/j.rehab.2024.101920.headline_claim: Adding respiratory muscle training (inspiratory and expiratory, sham-controlled) to aerobic exercise produced additional improvements in respiratory muscle strength, inspiratory muscle endurance and peak expiratory flow, but no between-group differences in HRQoL, exercise tolerance, psychological distress or DLCO.
10.1016/j.rehab.2024.101920.overall: The primary-outcome result is reported as null, and the headline is mostly supported for respiratory muscle strength and endurance. The remaining problems are modest: the Discussion misstates which HRQoL measures improved within groups, an effect size is mislabelled as large, and the PEF finding is stated more firmly than a borderline, unadjusted secondary result allows.

primary_outcome.name: EQ-5D-5L index (HRQoL) and peak VO2 (exercise tolerance)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline and 1-week post-intervention (9 weeks from baseline)
Baseline and 1-week post-intervention (9 weeks from baseline)

issues.title: Discussion says HRQoL intragroup gains were only in AE+RMT, but EQ-5D-5L index also rose in sham (P < 0.001)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says significant intragroup improvements in HRQoL occurred only in the AE+RMT group. The Results and Table 2 show the EQ-5D-5L index improved significantly in both groups (sham D = 0.108, P < 0.001); only the VAS (and DLCO) was significant in the AE+RMT group alone. The Conclusion's statement that only AE+RMT showed a clinically relevant HRQoL increase over baseline leans on the VAS and is not matched by the index. This makes the within-group HRQoL benefit look more specific to RMT than the paper's own data show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion sentence refers only to the VAS and DLCO, or a Table 2 showing the sham-group index change was not significant.

quotes.text: there were statistically signi fi cant intragroup improvements for these outcome measures only in the AE+RMT group

quotes.location: Results, Health-related quality of life and exercise tolerance

issues.title: PEF benefit (P = 0.044, CI 0.02 to 1.3) stated as a finding despite null interaction and many lung outcomes
issues.explanation: PEF was the only one of several lung function variables with a significant between-group ANCOVA difference, while the group x time interaction for lung function was reported as non-significant. The p-value is just under 0.05 and the CI lower bound is 0.02, with no multiplicity correction across the many secondary outcomes. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless list PEF as an improvement from RMT.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy that made PEF a confirmatory outcome, or a multiplicity-adjusted P below 0.05.

quotes.text: There was no statistically signi fi cant group £ time interaction for lung function outcomes ( P > 0.05)
resulted in improvements in respiratory muscle strength, inspiratory muscle endurance and peak expiratory fl ow

issues.title: IME effect d = 0.7 described as large, though Methods class 0.5-0.7 as moderate
issues.explanation: The Methods define moderate as 0.5-0.7 and large as 0.8 or more. Inspiratory muscle endurance has d = 0.7, yet the Results and abstract describe it as a 'large' improvement and the Discussion attributes the clinically relevant changes in strength and endurance to d >= 0.8. The mislabel is small and the MIP and MEP effects are still large.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that d = 0.7 was rounded from a value of at least 0.75 and classed large on that basis.

quotes.text: moderate (0.5 -0.7) or large ( ≥ 0.8) [28]
due to large effect sizes ( d ≥ 0.8)

quotes.location: Results, Physical function and psychological status

10.1016/j.rehab.2025.102073.headline_claim: SBRT was feasible and well tolerated with high adherence, questionnaires may suit a future primary outcome, and targeting a reduced respiratory rate showed no additional effect over regular SBRT.
10.1016/j.rehab.2025.102073.overall: The feasibility conclusion (high compliance, about 15% dropout) is supported by the data. The efficacy-leaning statements are not: pooled uncontrolled pre-post effects are described as improvements, the Discussion calls a CI-spanning-zero result significant, and the null finding on rate reduction rests on a small, unpowered, exploratory comparison. Several smaller printing inconsistencies (45 vs 47, the 500-minute claim, 0.9 vs 0.98) should be corrected.

primary_outcome.name: Compliance and adherence (session attendance and home exercise diary)

issues.title: 'No additional effect' of rate reduction drawn from 25 vs 22 participants with wide CIs
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion state that rate-reducing SBRT has no positive effect compared with regular SBRT. The between-group comparison was exploratory, unpowered, and uses wide intervals, and respiratory rate itself was available for only 14 outpatients. Absence of a statistically clear difference here is not evidence of absence, as the authors concede in their Limitations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified equivalence margin with CIs lying inside it, or a power calculation for this comparison.

quotes.text: The data suggest that SBRT aimed at reducing the respiratory rate does not have a positive effect compared to regular SBRT.
A controlled and intentional reduction in breathing frequency did not show an additional effect.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion that rate reduction 'does not have a positive effect' / 'did not show an additional effect' rests on 25 vs 22 participants (and 14 for respiratory-rate outcomes) with CIs of roughly +/-0.6 SD or wider that include medium-sized differences in both directions, so the data cannot support absence of an effect; absence of evidence is stated as if it were evidence of absence in the Abstract and Conclusion. The paper does partly acknowledge this in the Results and Limitations ('the effect, if present, is most likely too small to achieve statistical significance'), so the problem is the

issues.title: Discussion says all practised at home >=500 min; Table 2 minimum is 239 min
issues.explanation: The Discussion explains the lack of correlation between home practice and outcome by saying all participants practised at least 500 minutes. Table 2 shows a minimum of 239 minutes (an inpatient in I_IND), so the premise is false for at least some participants. The 'ceiling/threshold' interpretation and the advice about practising every second day lean on this claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Diary data showing the 239-min participant's total was a data entry error or that 500 min refers to a different quantity.

quotes.text: all participants practiced at home for at least 500 min

issues.title: Pooled pre-post changes in both arms presented as improvements; no untreated comparator
issues.explanation: The headline effect sizes (VR-12 physical, GAD-7, PHQ-9) are changes from baseline pooled across both singing arms, with no control receiving standard care. Natural recovery, concurrent rehabilitation and the Hawthorne effect are acknowledged only in the Limitations. The abstract's wording does not carry that caveat, so the quality-of-life and mental-health signals are weaker than presented, although the paper's own conclusion is limited to feasibility and outcome selection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract that states these are uncontrolled pre-post changes in a design with no standard-care arm.

quotes.text: The overall comparison between baseline and follow-up assessments yielded improvements corresponding to medium effects
The study does not directly compare SBRT to the standard of care.

issues.title: Discussion claims 'objective' lung-function gain and 'significant' VR-12 mental gain; CIs include zero
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the study objectively demonstrated improved lung function (resting respiratory rate and FVC) and a significant improvement in the VR-12 mental score. In Table 3 the CIs for FVC (-0.21 to 0.71), respiratory rate at rest (-0.25 to 1.26) and mental score (-0.05 to 0.88) all include zero, the data are uncontrolled pre-post, and the authors elsewhere call lung function change 'relatively small'. These sentences overstate secondary exploratory findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecified analysis with p<0.05 for these changes, or the text clearly using 'significant' in a non-statistical sense.

quotes.text: we were able to achieve a significant improvement in the VR-12 MHC score
Furthermore, we objectively demonstrated an improvement in lung function by reducing the resting respiratory rate and lung function parameters (FVC).

quotes.location: Table 3, VR-12 Mental component score, change from baseline

issues.title: Abstract says 45 participants; Table 1, flow text and Methods give 47
issues.explanation: The abstract's Results describe 45 study participants, but Table 1, Table 3 and the Results text all use 47 completers (55 randomized minus 8 dropouts). The abstract's 81% female and mean age 51.5 match the 47-person table, so the 45 is a misprint. It is a minor reporting error; the findings do not depend on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two participants were excluded from the abstract's descriptive statistics only.

quotes.text: The 45 study participants were predominantly female
Baseline demographics ( n =47)

issues.title: Abstract devotes more space to exploratory within-group effect sizes than to the primary compliance outcome
issues.explanation: The primary outcome (compliance) gets one sentence in the abstract's Results, while three uncontrolled questionnaire effect sizes with CIs get most of the remaining space. The paper itself labels these analyses exploratory. Readers may take away an efficacy signal from a feasibility study, though the conclusion section remains modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract that states effect sizes are exploratory and uncontrolled and gives primary outcome detail beyond a single percentage.

quotes.text: There was a high level of compliance with SBRT, with 96 % of participants completing all training sessions led by vocal coaches.
The study was analyzed in an explorative and hypothesis-generating manner.

issues.title: GAD-7 CI upper limit printed 0.9 in abstract vs 0.98 in Table 3 (truncation, not rounding)
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the upper limit as 0.9 while Table 3 prints 0.98. The difference is 0.08 and looks like truncation rather than rounding. Nothing about the interpretation changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the two printed values are different.

10.1016/j.resp.2024.104360.headline_claim: The authors conclude that 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training improved symptoms in PASC and ME/CFS, which could have been driven by improved parasympathetic activity.
10.1016/j.resp.2024.104360.overall: The headline that IMT improves autonomic function and symptoms in PASC and ME/CFS is only weakly supported: it comes from a small, open-label, uncontrolled pre-post study with about 30 uncorrected tests and completers-only analysis. The clearest signals (MIP, and HRV gains driven largely by healthy controls) do not show an HRV improvement in ME/CFS, and the Discussion overstates some results. The authors' pilot framing and caution partly temper this, but the title and conclusions are more causal than the design allows.

primary_outcome.name: Autonomic function (HRV and COMPASS 31; named as primary in the Introduction; registered as Clinical autonomic function)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute symptom or autonomic change to IMT
issues.explanation: All participants received IMT with no untreated or sham comparator, and questionnaires and 6MWD are open-label and subject to expectation and learning effects. The title and conclusions say IMT improves autonomic function and symptoms, a causal claim this design cannot support. Healthy controls also served as the comparison for the patient groups but were trained too.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised or time-controlled comparison showing the same changes.

quotes.text: a pilot interventional open label single group assignment study
We found that IMT improved symptoms in PASC and ME/CFS

second_reader.what_stands: The single-arm, open-label pre-post design cannot by itself attribute symptom or autonomic change to IMT, and the Conclusion's 'IMT improved symptoms' and the title's 'improves' are stronger than that design allows. The authors do disclose the absence of a time control in the Limitations, so the weakness is acknowledged, but the causal conclusion wording is not fully aligned with it.

issues.title: HRV 'improved in all participants' though ME/CFS RMSSD fell (33.7 to 30.8) and pRR50 was flat (11.4 to 11.7)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says HRV improved in all participants, but the ME/CFS group's RMSSD decreased and pRR50 barely moved. The significance applies to a pooled main effect driven largely by controls (RMSSD 54.2 to 75.7), not to ME/CFS specifically. Parasympathetic improvement in the patient groups is therefore overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Group-by-time post hoc results showing a significant ME/CFS-specific RMSSD increase.

quotes.text: improved HRV (LF, HF, RMSSD, pRR50), resting heart rate, maximal inspiratory pressure and 6MWD in all participants

second_reader.what_stands: The ME/CFS group's RMSSD fell (33.7 to 30.8) and pRR50 was flat (11.4 to 11.7), so 'improved in all participants' is not supported at the group level for those two measures; the improvement is a pooled main effect driven mainly by controls and PASC. It is not true that the paper claims a significant ME/CFS-specific RMSSD or pRR50 gain, and the LF and HF values did move in the stated direction in ME/CFS (LF 59.4 to 55.4, HF 40.1 to 43.7), though by small amounts relative to the SDs.

issues.title: About 30 outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 with no across-outcome correction; many reported p values 0.02-0.04
issues.explanation: Seven DSQ domains, seven COMPASS scores, seven HRV indices, 6MWD, MIP, weight, BP and HR were each tested at 0.05. Holm-Sidak applies only within each ANOVA's post hoc comparisons. Several highlighted findings (resting HR p = 0.037, secretomotor p = 0.023, LF p = 0.035, HF p = 0.034, RMSSD p = 0.034) would not survive correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary endpoint or a family-wise correction retaining these effects.

quotes.text: Significance was accepted at p < 0.05 and all pvalues and statistical markers presented are from significant post hoc testing.
increased  HF  power  (p = 0.034),  increased  RMSSD  (p = 0.034)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper tests roughly 30 or more outcomes at p < 0.05 with no stated correction across outcomes (Holm-Sidak applies only to pairwise post hoc comparisons within each ANOVA), and several headline IMT findings, including all four HRV effects (p = 0.034-0.035) and resting HR (p = 0.037), sit in the 0.02-0.04 range where multiplicity matters. The registry lists chemoreflex, clinical autonomic, vascular and cognitive function as primary outcomes, and the paper does not label any outcome as primary in its analysis, so the status of these findings as confirmatory is unclear; this was not checked be

issues.title: Analysed n inconsistent across tables: control 9 vs 8, PASC 9 enrolled vs 7 analysed, ME/CFS 9 vs 7
issues.explanation: Completers should be 9 controls, 7 PASC and 9 ME/CFS. Tables 1 and 4 use these, but Tables 2 and 3 give 8 controls, and Table 3 gives 7 ME/CFS, with no stated missing data. Group sizes of the analysed sets therefore differ between outcomes without explanation, so the COMPASS 31 ME/CFS findings rest on 7 people, not 9.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 1 control and 2 ME/CFS participants did not complete the questionnaires.

quotes.text: Control (n = 8)
ME/CFS (n = 7)
Control (n = 9)

issues.title: 8 of 33 (24%) dropped out; completers-only analysis, including 2 ME/CFS exits plausibly linked to IMT
issues.explanation: Analysis includes only participants with both visits and no sensitivity analysis. Two ME/CFS dropouts (post-exertional malaise, jaw pain during IMT) may relate to the intervention, so excluding them could favour apparent benefit and understate harm. The paper does mention PEM caution but does not count these as adverse events.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis showing the same results.

quotes.text: Only data with both baseline and follow-up visits completed were included in the analysis.
a temporal mandibular joint disorder with pain during IMT, and post-exertional malaise

issues.title: Discussion claims ME/CFS > PASC for pain and immune symptoms, but Results found no DSQ difference (p >= 0.12)
issues.explanation: The Results report no DSQ differences between PASC and ME/CFS (all p >= 0.12). The Discussion nevertheless lists pain and immune function as greater in ME/CFS than PASC. Only vasomotor function showed a significant difference, so the Discussion statement is stronger than the tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported significant PASC vs ME/CFS differences for pain and immune scores.

quotes.text: There were no differences in the symptom scores between PASC and ME/CFS (all p ≥ 0.12; Table 2)
certain symptoms that were greater in ME/CFS versus PASC implying greater impairment of the autonomic nervous system including pain

issues.title: Pilot with 7-9 analysed per group; title asserts improvement; registry lists 40 enrolled vs 33 in paper
issues.explanation: Group sizes of 7 to 9 give very little power and imprecise estimates, and many significant effects are borderline (p about 0.03). The authors do call it a pilot and urge caution, which tempers this. The registry's enrolment of 40 is not reconciled with 33 in the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry enrolment explained as including screen failures.

quotes.text: As this was a pilot study, the sample size was determined by feasibility and funding.
we caution against  extrapolating  this  data  to  larger  populations  given  the  small sample  size

issues.title: Registry lists chemoreflex and cognitive primaries not reported in the paper
issues.explanation: The registry record has four primary outcomes, but the paper reports only autonomic measures as primary and neither chemoreflex nor cognitive results. Whether this is outcome omission or later record edits cannot be settled from the current registry version alone. The abstract mentions vascular function (p = 0.001) with no methods describing it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the primaries were revised before the data were collected, or a companion paper reporting them.

quotes.text: The two purposes of this study are first to investigate the autonomic function (primary) and symptomatology (secondary)
This project was registered as a clinical trial (NCT05196529)

10.1016/j.rmed.2021.106470.headline_claim: Multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation is useful in post-COVID-19 patients regardless of preexisting cardiorespiratory comorbidity.
10.1016/j.rmed.2021.106470.overall: Both groups clearly improved during rehabilitation, but with no control group and no formal comparison of change between groups, the paper cannot show that rehabilitation caused the improvement or that response is equal regardless of comorbidity. The abstract also misstates which between-group differences were significant, and one P value (DLCO, 9.7%) is inconsistent with its CI. The headline is tenable only as a tentative description of improvement over time.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly named; within-arm pre/post changes in FEV1, FVC, DLCO %-predicted, 6MWD and blood gases were the main reported outcomes

issues.title: Single-arm pre/post design with no control used to conclude rehabilitation is 'extremely useful' for all
issues.explanation: All 95 patients entered a 30-day rehabilitation programme after recovering from COVID-19 pneumonia, with no comparison group. Improvements in spirometry, DLCO, blood gases and 6-minute walk distance over about five weeks cannot be separated from natural post-COVID recovery, learning effects on the 6MWT, or regression to the mean. Many patients also could not do baseline tests, so the paired analyses cover only subsets. The strong wording ('extremely useful', 'must always be prescribed') goes beyond what this design shows; it supports only that patients improved during rehabilitation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from a concurrent or well-matched non-rehabilitated comparison group showing smaller improvement over the same interval.

quotes.text: Immediately  afterwards,  all  patients  began  a  30-day  respiratory rehabilitation program, in addition to the appropriate pharmacological treatment.
Our study shows that a multidisciplinary rehabilitation program is extremely useful in post-COVID-19 patients, regardless of the presence of an underlying cardiorespiratory comorbidity.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is single-arm and uncontrolled, and the paired pre/post improvements cannot separate the effect of rehabilitation from spontaneous post-COVID recovery, regression to the mean, or concurrent pharmacological treatment. The Discussion nonetheless says the study 'shows' the program is 'extremely useful' and that all hospitalised COVID-19 patients should undergo it, which is stronger than the design supports; the abstract's 'may be useful' is better calibrated, and the authors do openly acknowledge the lack of a control group.
