issues.title: 'No difference in response' and 'greater improvement' rest on level comparisons, not change, with wide CIs
issues.explanation: Both groups improved significantly from baseline, but the paper never compares the change scores between groups. Table 2 (titled 'Differences in changes') actually gives between-group differences in pre-rehabilitation and post-rehabilitation levels, which are confounded by baseline differences and unadjusted. The abstract's 'significant greater improvement' for DLco and the Discussion's 'no substantial differences in the response' are therefore both untested. The non-significant results come from small, partly missing samples with wide CIs, so they do not show equal response.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A direct between-group test of the change scores (or a baseline-adjusted model) with CIs excluding clinically meaningful differences.

quotes.text: This leads  us  to  believe  that  there  are  no  substantial  differences  in  the response to physical effort between those with preexisting cardiorespiratory comorbidities and those initially healthy
Table 2 Differences in changes of examined parameters between patients with no un-
Comparison between subjects with no previous pathology and those with preexisting cardiopulmonary comorbidity was made  with  unpaired t -test  and  Welch ' s  correction.

second_reader.what_stands: The between-group comparisons printed are of levels before and after rehabilitation, not tests of the difference in change, even though the Table 2 caption says 'differences in changes'; the 'significantly greater improvement' in DLCO (and FEV1) is therefore inferred from a widening level gap with no test or CI for the change difference. The 'no substantial differences in response' conclusion rests on non-significant results with wide CIs (e.g. 6MWD level gaps with CIs spanning about -2 to 86 m), which cannot establish equivalence.

issues.title: Abstract: DLco the only significant between-group difference; Results/Discussion also report FEV1 (P=0.032)
issues.explanation: The abstract says DLco %-predicted was the only parameter with a significantly greater improvement in the group without comorbidity. Results, Table 2 and the Discussion report a significant FEV1 difference as well (420.9 mL, 95% CI 36.7 to 805.2, P = 0.032). The abstract therefore understates the between-group differences the paper itself reports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract refers to a different analysis (e.g. change scores) in which FEV1 was not significant.

quotes.text: DLco %-predicted  was  the  only  parameter  that  showed  a  significant  greater  improvement
the mean difference in FEV1 between the two groups became 420.9 mL (95% CI: 36.7 -805.2; P = 0.032)
a statistically significant difference between the two groups was observed only in the FEV1 and DLCO%-predicted changes

issues.title: DLCO improvement 9.7% (CI 6.0-13.5) reported as P = 0.016; CI implies P < 0.0001
issues.explanation: For patients without comorbidity, DLCO%-predicted rose by 9.7% with a 95% CI of 6.0 to 13.5, reported with P = 0.016. That CI excludes zero by a wide margin (z about 5), so the P value should be well below 0.001. The same P = 0.016 is printed for the comorbidity group's 3.3% change, where it does fit, so the first value looks like a duplicated entry. The direction of the finding is unaffected, but the stated significance for this result is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors' output showing P = 0.016 for this change, with the printed CI being the erroneous value.

quotes.text: DLCO%-predicted improved by 9.7% (95% CI: 6.0 -13.5%; P = 0.016)

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0000 (reachable range [0.0000, 0.0000] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.016 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

10.1016/j.rmed.2021.106648.headline_claim: Patients referred to ambulatory respiratory rehabilitation after SARS-CoV-2 infection showed improvement in exertional dyspnoea, functional capacity, hyperventilation prevalence and quality of life over follow-up, which the authors take to support screening for hyperventilation syndrome and early rehabilitation referral.
10.1016/j.rmed.2021.106648.overall: The descriptive findings (frequent hyperventilation, persistent dyspnoea in outpatients referred for rehabilitation) are plausible, but the claim that these improve with rehabilitation rests on an uncontrolled cohort in which 25 of 39 patients were analysed and natural recovery cannot be separated out. The abstract and discussion contain a few small numerical inconsistencies (age 50 vs 60, delay 73 vs 84 days, and a hyperventilation p-value that does not match Fisher's test), none of which alone changes the conclusions. The main concern is that the rehabilitation conclusions are stated more strongly than the design allows.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated; within-group change in exertional dyspnoea (mMRC) reported

issues.title: Uncontrolled before-after cohort (n=25) but Abstract and Conclusion say symptoms improve with rehabilitation
issues.explanation: Improvements in dyspnoea, 6-min walk, sit-to-stand, hyperventilation and quality of life are within-patient changes over about 61 days with no comparison group. The Discussion concedes that the design cannot show whether rehabilitation or natural recovery caused them. The Abstract and Conclusion nonetheless say these components improve with rehabilitation and early referral, and the Discussion says 'our data confirm' guidance. The improvements are real as observed changes, but their attribution to rehabilitation is unsupported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical comparison group of similar post-Covid patients not receiving rehabilitation, showing less improvement over the same interval.

quotes.text: We cannot conclude from the design of this study [40] whether these improvements were promoted by rehabilitation program itself or by the natural evolution of the disease.
This component as well as the associated functional disorders can improve with early rehabilitation referral.
This longitudinal observational study was conducted in two ambulatory physiotherapy structures

second_reader.what_stands: The study is an uncontrolled observational before-after cohort, and the paper's own Discussion states that the design cannot separate rehabilitation effect from natural recovery. The Abstract and Conclusion say the outcomes 'may' or 'can' improve with rehabilitation, which is hedged and does not claim proof, but it is not accompanied by the caveat there and the Discussion's statement that rehabilitation 'probably played a role' rests on the delay since onset, not on a comparison. Also, the paired analysis is based on 25 of 39 patients (complete cases only), so 'n = 25' is accurate for the impr

issues.title: Change analysis limited to 25 of 39 patients (64%); 7 lost to follow-up, complete-case only
issues.explanation: Only 25 patients had two assessments. The other 14 comprised 5 who had only recently started, 2 who recovered early and 7 who were lost to follow-up. No sensitivity analysis is given. The loss is partly administrative and partly informative: the early recoverers and the long-duration selection (97 vs 66 days) mean the analysed group is not the whole cohort. The direction of any bias is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including the 14 non-analysed patients, or baseline data showing the 7 lost to follow-up resembled the analysed patients.

quotes.text: Reasons for absence of second assessment were: recent start of rehabilitation ( < 2 months; n = 5), early recovery irrelevant for a second evaluation (n = 2) and loss of follow-up (n = 7)
in the evolution over the course of rehabilitation analysis was performed on complete-cases.

issues.title: Abstract calls non-significant 12 vs 0 hyperventilation difference 'greater'; headline link to dyspnoea untested
issues.explanation: The Abstract describes a 'greater prevalence' of hyperventilation in the PFS group, with a p-value of 0.255 printed in the same sentence. The Conclusion states hyperventilation 'may explain' persistent dyspnoea and altered quality of life, yet no analysis relates hyperventilation status to dyspnoea or quality of life. The screen was added after enrolment began, so only 35 of 39 patients were assessed. The hedging ('may') limits the overstatement, but the headline is stronger than the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis within the cohort showing hyperventilation status is associated with dyspnoea or VQ-11 scores.

quotes.text: greater prevalence of hyperventilation syndrome (n = 12(41%) vs . 0(0%); p = 0.255)
included later a systematic screening for hyperventilation syndrome
Hyperventilation is frequent in long Covid and may explain persistent dyspnoea as well as altered quality of life.

issues.title: Single-centre-pair cohort of 39 (6-10 in comparison group) with no sample-size rationale
issues.explanation: The study enrols 39 consecutive patients with no sample-size calculation. Between-group comparisons involve only 10 patients, or 6 for hyperventilation and lung function. Prevalence estimates such as 34% (12/35) therefore carry wide uncertainty, and the null between-group findings cannot be read as absence of difference. The conclusions are phrased tentatively, so the weakness is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified descriptive aim with confidence intervals showing the prevalence estimates are adequately precise.

quotes.text: 39 consecutive patients were included from April 1st , 2020 to April 1st , 2021.

issues.title: ~20 uncorrected paired tests in Table 2; hyperventilation (p=0.023) and VQ-11 (p=0.041) would not survive correction
issues.explanation: Table 2 reports about 20 within-patient comparisons at an unadjusted 0.05 threshold, with no primary outcome designated. The strongest findings (dyspnoea, 6-MWT, sit-to-stand) are far below any plausible corrected threshold. The hyperventilation composite (p = 0.023) and total quality-of-life score (p = 0.041) are borderline and would not remain significant under a simple Bonferroni correction. Both are featured in the Abstract and Discussion as significant improvements.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or multiplicity plan, or adjusted p-values still below 0.05 for hyperventilation and VQ-11.

quotes.text: reduced from 10(50%) to 3(15%) (p = 0.023)
exertional dyspnoea as well as hyperventilation prevalence significantly decreased and 6-MWT, 3-STS and quality of life significantly improved.

issues.title: p = 0.255 for hyperventilation 12/29 vs 0/6 does not match Fisher's exact test (about 0.07)
issues.explanation: The paper says categorical variables were compared with Fisher's exact test. For 12/29 vs 0/6, the two-sided Fisher p is about 0.07, not 0.255. The result stays non-significant, but the printed p overstates how far the data are from significance, and the Abstract's 'greater prevalence' is closer to the data than the printed p suggests. The finding would be a trend rather than a clearly null result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Different underlying denominators or a stated test that yields p = 0.255 from the data.

quotes.text: all patients presenting with hyperventilation syndrome were in this subgroup (12(41%) vs. 0(0%); p = 0.255)

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.255, but recomputed from every convention tried on this table (Pearson, Yates, Fisher, McNemar, likelihood ratio, Fisher-Freeman-Halton where they apply) p is at most 0.1412, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show. This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Abstract gives non-PFS age as 50 ± 10 yr; Table 1 and Results give 60 ± 10 yr
issues.explanation: The abstract reports the comparison group's age as 50 ± 10 years. Table 1 and Results section 3.2 both give 60 ± 10 years for the same comparison with the same p = 0.002. The overall mean of 48 only reconciles with 60, so the abstract is the wrong figure. It is a reporting slip that does not change the finding that the PFS group was younger.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published erratum or the source data showing the non-PFS mean age was 50.

quotes.text: They were younger (43 ± 14 vs. 60 ± 10yr, p = 0.002)

issues.title: Median delay to referral is 73 days in Abstract/Table 1/Results but 84 days in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Abstract, Table 1 and Results report a median time from onset to rehabilitation of 73 days. The Discussion says patients were referred with a median delay of 84 days, with no explanation. The Discussion then uses this figure to argue that rehabilitation probably contributed to the improvement. The discrepancy is small and the argument holds either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 84 days is a different statistic, such as the median in the 25 patients with two assessments.

quotes.text: Rehabilitation referral was considered with a median delay of 73[34 -178] days after disease onset.
However, patients were referred with a median delay of 84 days after disease onset

10.1016/j.rmed.2023.107362.headline_claim: Three months of prolonged-release pirfenidone was safe and showed therapeutic efficacy in patients with PASC-pulmonary fibrosis, though whether fibrosis stabilises, progresses or improves remains unresolved.
10.1016/j.rmed.2023.107362.overall: The safety description is reasonable for a small open-label pilot, but the abstract's claim of therapeutic efficacy is not supported by an uncontrolled before-after design, as the authors partly concede in the body of the paper. There are also reporting inconsistencies (the mMRC significance claim, the FVC eligibility ceiling, and Table 4 subgroup values). The efficacy results should be treated as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Safety and tolerability (AEs), with pulmonary function, 6MWT, dyspnoea and symptoms reported as efficacy outcomes

primary_outcomes.measure: To investigate the effect of pirfenidone on fibrotic signs induced by COVID19 infection

issues.title: Abstract concludes 'therapeutic efficacy' from an uncontrolled, open-label single-arm 65-patient before-after study
issues.explanation: All efficacy results are baseline versus 3-month changes in one open-label arm, with patient-reported outcomes unblinded and no concurrent control. Patients enrolled within about two months of infection, a period when spontaneous recovery is expected. The authors themselves state they cannot exclude that functional normalisation occurred independently of the drug. The abstract conclusion of therapeutic efficacy therefore goes beyond what the design can show, and contradicts the more cautious final Conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control showing greater improvement than natural recovery.

quotes.text: three months ' treatment with PR-PFD was safe and showed therapeutic efficacy.
we cannot exclude that the functional normalization may have occurred independently of taking PR-PFD
open-label, uncontrolled,  proof  of  concept  study.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's 'showed therapeutic efficacy' is drawn from an open-label, uncontrolled, single-arm before-after analysis of 65 completers, which cannot separate drug effect from spontaneous post-COVID recovery, regression to the mean or co-interventions, and the abstract does not carry the caveat. However, the paper does not hide this: the Discussion, Limitations and final Conclusion explicitly say improvement may have occurred without the drug and that efficacy is not established, so the overclaim is confined to the abstract wording and partly offset by the body text.

issues.title: Table 4 FVC ≥70 group: FEV1 baseline 95 vs 86 in Table 1, and fall to 78 labelled as improvement
issues.explanation: For the FVC ≥70 group, Table 1 reports baseline FEV1 of 86 ± 11 %p. Table 4 reports a baseline of 95 and a 3-month value of 78, with p < 0.001, in a table titled 'improvements'. A fall of 17 points would be a deterioration, and the baseline disagrees with Table 1. Other cells in the same column, such as FVC 76 (91-74), also show reversed interquartile bounds and differ from the Table 1 mean of 81. The subgroup results in Table 4 for this group therefore cannot be relied on as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source table showing different values for these cells.

quotes.location: Table 4, FEV1 row, FVC ≥ 70 %p after 3 months

issues.title: mMRC dyspnea called 'considerably reduced' though overall Table 3 p = 0.134; only Borg dyspnea is significant
issues.explanation: The abstract lists dyspnea among variables that significantly improved, and Results describe a considerable reduction in mMRC. The overall mMRC test in Table 3 is p = 0.134. Exercise dyspnea (Borg, p = 0.010) and the mMRC subgroup comparisons in Table 4 are significant, so some dyspnea measures did improve. The claim is overstated for the mMRC scale as a whole.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A specified analysis showing a significant overall mMRC change, or an abstract that names only Borg dyspnea.

quotes.text: there was a considerable reduction in mMRC and CAT scores after three months

issues.title: FVC ≥70 %p group mean 81 conflicts with eligibility of percent predicted FVC <80
issues.explanation: The Methods require percent predicted FVC below 80 for enrolment. Table 1 gives a baseline mean of 81 ± 10 for the FVC ≥70 group, which cannot happen if every patient met the criterion. Table 4 also describes this same group with a median of 76 (IQR 74-91), which is a different summary of the same baseline. Either the eligibility criterion was not applied as written or the table is wrong. This does not change the safety or efficacy conclusions directly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that FVC ≥70 patients were enrolled on another criterion (e.g. TLC or DLCO) or a corrected Table 1 value below 80.

quotes.text: percent predicted FVC < 80

issues.title: Introduction: IR Cmax called 59.8% higher than PR, but 19.81 vs 7.96 is 149% higher (PR is 59.8% lower)
issues.explanation: The Introduction states that the immediate-release Cmax of 19.81 is 59.8% higher than the prolonged-release Cmax of 7.96. The numbers actually give a PR Cmax that is 59.8% lower than IR, equivalent to IR being about 149% higher. This is a wording error in background text that nothing in the study depends on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the arithmetic is fixed by the printed values.

quotes.text: Cmax,  19.81 μ g/mL, that  was  59.8%  higher than PR-PFD

10.1016/j.rmed.2024.107763.headline_claim: Intermittent hypoxia exposure (IHE) combined with routine treatment improved physical endurance, spirometry, dyspnea and fatigue more than normoxia exposure (NE) in patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC).
10.1016/j.rmed.2024.107763.overall: The direction of the main findings is plausible, with large and consistent between-group differences on several measures. The paper's strength of wording ('markedly improved') outpaces a small trial of acute (1-hour post-exposure) effects with untested blinding on largely subjective or effort-dependent outcomes and no multiplicity control. The numeric slips (alcohol count, COPD percentage, an ambiguous sentence) are minor and do not change the results.

primary_outcome.name: Differences in 6MWD, spirometry, Borg, mMRC, FAS, and CFQ-11 scores between groups before and after interventions

issues.title: Patient-reported and effort-dependent outcomes rest on untested participant blinding to a hypoxia sham
issues.explanation: Borg, mMRC, FAS, CFQ-11, a self-made improvement scale and the 6MWD all depend on participant effort or report. Blinding relied on the claim that participants 'could not sense the difference', with no blinding-success check. The paper does not say whether the investigator who collected outcome data knew allocation. Expectation effects could therefore inflate the between-group differences, especially the modest Borg and mMRC changes and the subjective improvement rates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinding-success assessment showing participants guessed allocation no better than chance, plus a statement that outcome assessors were blind.

quotes.text: Each participant was informed about the two different possible exposures prior to participating in the study, but they could not sense the difference when exposed to NE or IHE.
Subjective feelings of symptom improvements (dyspnea and fatigue) were recorded using a simple, self-made scale

issues.title: About 11 co-primary outcomes at alpha 0.05 with no correction; several 'significant' results are marginal
issues.explanation: The primary outcomes are 6MWD, six spirometry measures and four symptom scales, all tested at 0.05 with no multiplicity control or prespecified hierarchy. The strongest results (p ≈ 0.001) would probably survive correction. The conclusion still claims benefit across spirometry and dyspnea, and several of those p-values (0.013 to 0.042) would not survive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registered, prespecified single primary outcome (e.g. 6MWD change) with the others designated secondary or exploratory.

quotes.text: The primary outcomes were differences in 6MWD, spirometry, and Borg, mMRC, FAS, or CFQ-11 scores between the two groups before and after the interventions.
A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

issues.title: 'Markedly improved' claim rests on assessments 1 hour after the last exposure; modest between-group margins
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that IHE markedly improved endurance, spirometry, dyspnea and fatigue. All post-intervention measurements were taken 1 hour after the final session, so only immediate effects are shown. Between-group differences in some measures are small (median 6MWD change 47.0 vs 23.5 m; Borg change 1.0 vs 0.0 point). The qualifier about future work does not fix the strength of the headline wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Follow-up data showing sustained benefit weeks after exposure, with between-group differences exceeding established minimum clinically important differences.

quotes.text: IHE markedly improved the physical endurance and spirometry of PASC patients and relieved symptoms of dyspnea and fatigue.
the participants were required to undergo the 6MWD and spirometry tests twice (before the intervention and 1 h after the last intervention)

issues.title: Dose-duration claim (≥10 vs <10 days IHE, 35 vs 12 patients) is a non-randomized comparison
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that longer IHE 'resulted in' greater improvements than shorter IHE. The 12 patients with <10 days and the 35 with ≥10 days were not randomly assigned to duration. Reasons for stopping early (or continuing longer) could relate to outcome. Only an association can be claimed, and the subgroup is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that duration was assigned at random or by a prespecified rule independent of patient response.

quotes.text: A longer duration (≥10 days) of IHE resulted in greater improvements in 6MWD, spirometry, and fatigue than shorter duration treatment (<10 days).
Of the 47 subjects in the IHE group, 12 received IHE for <10 days and 35 received IHE for ≥10 days

issues.title: Alcohol history: text says 22 participants, Table 1 arm counts 11 + 10 = 21
issues.explanation: Section 3.1 reports 22 participants with a history of alcohol consumption. The Table 1 alcohol row gives 11 in the IHE arm and 10 in the NE arm, which total 21. One count is wrong. Nothing in the efficacy results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that one participant's alcohol status was counted in the text but not assigned to an arm, or a corrected Table 1 count.

quotes.text: 22 a history of alcohol consumption

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 3 of 98 randomized excluded after allocation, arms of exclusions not reported
issues.explanation: Ninety-eight patients were randomized and 95 analysed, after exclusion of three who received under 7 days of exposure. No intention-to-treat analysis is given and the arm of each excluded patient is not stated. With such a small loss the effect is probably limited, but exclusions after randomization based on exposure received can bias the comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis including the three excluded patients, or a statement that they were evenly or randomly distributed and had outcome data.

quotes.text: Ninety-eight patients were randomly assigned to the two interventions, and three were excluded for receiving IHE or NE for less than 7 days.
Finally, 47 patients in IHE group and 48 patients in NE group completed all the procedures.

issues.title: Sentence says dyspnea/fatigue 'not significantly different' between groups; post-intervention p = 0.006–0.016
issues.explanation: Section 3.2.2 opens by saying dyspnea and fatigue scores did not differ between groups, without naming a timepoint. Table 2 shows post-intervention between-group p-values of 0.013 (Borg), 0.016 (mMRC), 0.001 (FAS) and 0.006 (CFQ-11). The sentence probably means baseline, so this is an ambiguous or misplaced statement rather than a result error. A reader could take it as a null finding at follow-up.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation from the authors that the first sentence refers to baseline values only.

quotes.text: Dyspnea (Borg, mMRC) and fatigue (FAS, CFQ-11) were not significantly different between the two groups.
with better improvements than in the NE group (p = 0.031 for Borg; p = 0.001 for mMRC; p = 0.001 for FAS; p = 0.001 for CFQ-11)

issues.title: COPD in IHE arm: 3 of 47 printed as 6.8%, but 3/47 = 6.4%
issues.explanation: Table 1 lists 3 IHE participants with COPD as 6.8% of the arm. With 47 participants this is 6.4%. The error is small and the associated p-value (0.317) is unaffected in practice. It is a single printing slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the IHE arm denominator for this row was 44 rather than 47.

quotes.location: Table 1, Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease row, IHE column

script.explanation: 3/47 = 6.38%, but the paper prints 6.8, outside the rounding interval [6.75, 6.90]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 44.1 rather than 47.

10.1016/j.rmed.2025.108503.headline_claim: Thoracic spinal manipulation (HVLA) added to pulmonary rehabilitation improved pulmonary function and thoracic mobility more than pulmonary rehabilitation alone in patients with Long COVID.
10.1016/j.rmed.2025.108503.overall: The within-group gains and the larger FVC, FEV1 and rotation differences appear in the tables, but the trial has weak safeguards: allocation concealment is undescribed, there is no sham, and blinding is overstated. Nine outcomes were tested with no correction, and the Conclusion and Discussion go beyond what a 2-week, single-centre, 42-patient trial with no obstructive/restrictive classification can show. The direction of the effect is plausible, but its size and the generalisability claims should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: FVC and FEV1 (pulmonary function); primary outcome not explicitly designated

issues.title: 'Double-blinded' label with no sham; patient awareness likely and assessor blinding not stated
issues.explanation: The paper calls the study double-blinded, but the therapist cannot be blinded. The control arm received no sham manipulation, and the thrust and cavitation 'pop' make it likely that patients knew which arm they were in. The outcomes include effort-dependent spirometry (FVC, FEV1) and tape-measure readings. The paper never says the outcome assessor was unaware of allocation. Because the experimental arm also received extra hands-on contact, the between-group differences cannot be attributed to the manipulation alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that a sham manipulation was used, that patient blinding was tested, and that the assessor was masked to allocation.

quotes.text: It was a double-blinded study, where patients were blinded to the treatment group, and another therapist with training and expertise in physical therapy recorded the pre- and post-outcomes.
Group B (Control) received only pulmonary rehabilitation.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does call the study 'double-blinded' while the control arm had no sham or placebo manipulation, and it gives no method by which patients could be kept unaware of receiving a thrust technique, so patient blinding is unsupported and doubtful; the Limitations section does not discuss this. However, the claim that assessor blinding is 'not stated' is only partly right: a separate assessor is described, but the paper does not say that this person was unaware of allocation, so assessor blinding is implied by the 'double-blinded' label rather than explicitly reported.

issues.title: Chit-method allocation by the recruiting investigator, concealment not described; FEV1 bands 10 vs 6 of 21
issues.explanation: The principal investigator both recruited participants and assigned them by chit draw, and the paper does not say how the allocation was hidden until assignment. Without concealment, selection into arms cannot be ruled out. The FEV1 band imbalance (47.6% vs 28.6% in the 61-70% band) is weaker evidence, because mean baseline FEV1 is nearly the same in both arms. The main concern is therefore the unverified concealment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or registry entry showing allocation was concealed (opaque sealed chits drawn by someone independent of recruitment).

quotes.text: Forty-two subjects were randomly assigned to Group A (experimental) and Group B (control) using the chit method by the principal investigator.
were recruited for the RCT by the principal investigator

issues.title: Nine between-group tests, no primary outcome or correction; p = 0.028 and 0.009 mobility results fragile
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports nine between-group comparisons with no designated primary outcome and no multiplicity adjustment. The stated alpha is an unadjusted 0.05. FVC, FEV1 and rotation (p ≤ 0.0008) would survive a Bonferroni threshold of about 0.0056. Flexion (p = 0.028) and lateral flexion (p = 0.009) would not. The claim of improved 'thoracic mobility' therefore rests partly on results that are not robust to testing nine outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and a stated correction, or a registry entry designating FVC as the sole primary outcome.

quotes.text: The level of significance was determined by p < 0.05 at a 95 % confidence interval.

issues.title: Conclusion of greater 'thoracic mobility' gain omits non-significant extension and all three chest-expansion tests
issues.explanation: The Results say Table 2 shows 'greater improvement' in Group A, but Table 2 only tests change within each arm, so it cannot show a difference between arms. The Conclusion says manipulation gave more improvement in thoracic mobility without noting that extension and all three chest-expansion levels showed no between-group difference (p = 0.302, 0.071, 0.541, 0.061). The Conclusion does not mention chest expansion, a prespecified outcome. The summary is therefore more favourable than the between-group table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion explicitly limited to FVC, FEV1, flexion, lateral flexion and rotation, with chest expansion and extension reported as no different between arms.

quotes.text: The results were statistically significant for all parameters (p < 0.05) in either group with greater improvement in experimental group (Group A).
In the present study, though within-group chest compliance increased, the between-group result was not seen.

issues.title: Claim of generalisability to obstructive and restrictive patterns from 42 young single-centre patients; durability implied
issues.explanation: The paper says the results generalise to patients with obstructive and restrictive respiratory patterns. Yet the sample is 42 young adults (mean age about 24) from one outpatient department with FEV1 of 61-80%. The authors also admit the FEV1/FVC ratio was not recorded, so patterns were never classified. The paper also claims the effects can 'prevent the condition from becoming chronic', although follow-up ended after 10 sessions over 2 weeks. Neither claim is supported by these data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Spirometric classification of participants into obstructive and restrictive patterns, subgroup results, and follow-up data beyond the 2-week treatment period.

quotes.text: The study's strength lies in the fact that with a representative sample size, its results can be generalised to patients with obstructive and restrictive respiratory patterns.
the immediate effects reported can help achieve improvements in pulmonary function in related cases and prevent the condition from becoming chronic.
Recording more parameters, such as FEV1/FVC ratio, can help better understand abnormal respiratory patterns in Long COVID cases.

10.1016/j.visres.2025.108550.headline_claim: Coloured overlays improve reading speed and reading experience in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.1016/j.visres.2025.108550.overall: The finding of a small average reading-speed gain (about 8 wpm) with the overlay in an open, single-session ABBA comparison is plausible. It cannot be separated from expectation effects, and the experience outcome has no comparison condition. The subgroup 'benefit most for those who struggle' and the cortical-hyperexcitability interpretation are not supported by the design. There are also minor numeric inconsistencies (30 vs 29 patients, 83.3% vs 86.2%).

primary_outcome.name: Reading speed (words per minute, Wilkins Rate of Reading test) with versus without overlay

issues.title: No sham or blinded comparison: 8 wpm gain and comfort reports may reflect expectation, not the overlay
issues.explanation: Reading speed with and without the overlay was compared in the same people in one open session, with a fixed ABBA order that handles drift but not expectation or motivation. The comfort outcome is subjective, comes only from patients who knew they were using their chosen overlay, and has no comparison condition. The title's causal wording ('improve reading speed and reading experience') is stronger than this design supports. The conclusion that overlays 'showed promise' stands only as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded sham-tint or randomised-order comparison showing the same gain.

quotes.text: The first and last passage was read with the preferred overlay while the second and third passage was read without an overlay.
There was no significant difference between reading speeds in trial 1 vs 4 (with overlay) or trial 2 vs 3 (without overlay)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no sham or masked comparison: participants knowingly read with their self-selected overlay, so the roughly 8 wpm gain and the comfort comments could partly reflect expectation or motivation. The ABBA order and the trial 1 vs 4 and trial 2 vs 3 checks handle order effects only, and the Limitations section does not mention the lack of blinding or a placebo condition.

issues.title: Abstract reports 83.3% positive effects; Results report 86.2% (25/29); Table 2 lists 30 patients
issues.explanation: The abstract's headline experience figure (83.3%) differs from the Results figure (25 of 29 = 86.2%). The abstract value matches 25 of 30, and Table 2 lists 30 patients even though only 29 were included. The sample used for the experience outcome is therefore unclear. The difference is small and the qualitative message is unchanged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract percentage uses a different, stated denominator or outcome definition.

quotes.text: Most of the patients (83.3 %) experienced positive visuo-perceptual effects when using the overlay.
Twenty-five patients (86.2 %) reported positive effects from reading

script.explanation: 25/29 = 86.21%, but the paper prints 83.3, outside the rounding interval [83.25, 83.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 30.0 rather than 29.

issues.title: Subgroups defined by their own outcome gain used to claim that those who struggle benefit more
issues.explanation: Patients were grouped by how much they improved (5% or 15% or more) and then compared on baseline speed (p = 0.08, and p < 0.001 for the 6 patients). This selection on the outcome produces a lower baseline in the 'responders' by regression to the mean and by percentage-scale arithmetic. The longer time since illness result (p = 0.05) is borderline and unadjusted. The Discussion nonetheless draws a benefit-for-the-struggling conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis of the baseline-by-effect interaction (for example regression of absolute change on baseline in a controlled design).

quotes.text: Six patients read faster by 15 % or more, median 26.3 % (16.0 -70.8 %).
From this it appears that those who struggle more may benefit more from the use of overlays.

issues.title: Abstract links reading gain to cortical hyperexcitability with no neurophysiological data (r = 0.48, n about 21)
issues.explanation: The abstract's closing sentence ties a small, uncontrolled reading-speed gain and a modest correlation with discomfort to cortical hyperexcitability after COVID-19. The study measured no cortical or neural quantity. The hedge softens this, but the mechanistic interpretation still goes beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Neurophysiological or other direct evidence of hyperexcitability in these patients that relates to the overlay response.

quotes.text: seem consistent with the attribution of reading difficulty and perceptual distortion to cortical hyperexcitability

issues.title: Visual acuity categories (28 + 1 + 1 = 30) exceed the 29 included patients
issues.explanation: The Results split distance visual acuity into 28, 1 and 1 patients, which adds up to 30. The paper includes only 29 patients. One count is wrong, or the 30th recruited (excluded) patient was mixed in. The error is descriptive and does not affect the reading-speed result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected count (for example 27 with acuity of 1.0 or better) or a statement that the 30th, excluded patient is included in this tally.

quotes.text: Twenty-eight patients had a visual acuity of decimal 1.0 or better,
one had 0.9 and one had 0.8

issues.title: Error reduction given as 39.7%, but 73 vs 102 errors is a 28.4% reduction from the no-overlay count
issues.explanation: Total errors were 73 with overlay and 102 without, a difference of 29. Expressed as a share of the no-overlay errors this is 28.4%, not 39.7%. The figure 39.7% arises only if the difference is divided by the overlay count. The difference was not significant and is a secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the percentage is deliberately calculated relative to the overlay condition.

quotes.text: The group level difference in number of errors corresponded to 39.7 %, however the difference was not statistically significant.
a total of 73 errors (median 3, min 0 max 8) were made when reading with an overlay and a total of 102 (median 3.5, min 0 max 18) when reading without

script.explanation: Error difference as percent of no-overlay errors (printed 39.7%): 29 / 102 gives 0.284314, not the printed 39.7. For the printed value to hold the denominator would have to be 0.730479, not 102.

10.1016/j.ymthe.2025.01.007.headline_claim: IA therapy in post-COVID ME/CFS patients with elevated ANSR autoantibodies leads to significant reduction in autoantibodies, soluble spike protein and inflammatory cytokines, with moderate improvements in neuropsychological parameters, though it does not influence subjective symptom perception.
10.1016/j.ymthe.2025.01.007.overall: The immunological findings (transient autoantibody, spike and cytokine reduction) are descriptive and reasonably supported, but the claimed neuropsychological and grip-strength benefit rests on an open-label, uncontrolled 12-patient before-after comparison with acknowledged practice effects and no multiplicity control. The authors are candid about limitations and report null patient-reported outcomes, so the conclusion should be read as tentative and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; the paper reports multiple outcomes (ANSR autoantibodies, spike protein, cytokines, CERAD-Plus, hand grip strength, SF-36, self-reported symptoms)

issues.title: Neuropsychological and grip improvement inferred from open-label within-group change in 12 patients, no concurrent control
issues.explanation: Efficacy is inferred from before/after changes in 12 unblinded, uncontrolled patients. The untreated control group shown in the supplement partly addresses practice effects but is not compared directly, and word-learning clearly showed a learning effect. Hand grip and CERAD depend on patient effort, and the self-reported outcomes did not improve, so the 'objective improvement' is open to bias and the conclusion is tentative at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A direct between-group comparison of change scores versus an adequately matched untreated control group.

quotes.text: since post-COVID control patients who did not undergo therapy likewise demonstrated signi fi cant improvement
quotes.location: Results, IA therapy leads to strong decrease section

quotes.text: This study shows that TheraSorb IA therapy has the potential to improve the neuropsychological state of ME/CFS
This is an observational study, and a randomized controlled trial including a placebo group is needed

second_reader.what_stands: The grip and CERAD improvements rest on open-label, uncontrolled pre-post change in 12 patients (no randomisation, blinding or placebo), which the authors acknowledge in the limitations and by calling for an RCT; the claim of 'potential to improve' is hedged accordingly. It is not true that there is no concurrent control at all: untreated post-COVID retest controls were used to screen for practice effects on CERAD sub-tests, and the word-learning result was dropped for that reason. That control does not address placebo, regression to the mean or expectation effects, and no practice-effect cont

issues.title: Methods say all tests are paired, but Fisher, Mann-Whitney and unpaired tests are named elsewhere
issues.explanation: The statistics section says all tests are paired, yet Figure 1 uses an unpaired test against controls and Table 2 names Mann-Whitney U and Fisher's exact test for before/after data. Paired before/after data analysed with unpaired tests would be less powerful (understating changes) and wrong. The paper does not allow the reader to tell which test produced each p value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used for all before/after comparisons.

quotes.text: All applied statistical tests are paired and two-sided.
Unpaired Man-Whitney U Test was performed between control patients and post-COVID patients.
a Fisher ' s Exact Test. b Mann-Whitney U test.

issues.title: 'Notable'/'objectively improved' wording exceeds what an uncontrolled n=12 open-label study supports
issues.explanation: The abstract and Discussion describe 'notable improvement' and 'objectively improved' health status although the design cannot separate treatment from practice and expectation, patient-reported outcomes did not change, and effects are transient. The wording is softened elsewhere ('potential', 'moderate') and an RCT is called for, so the overstatement is moderate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data showing the improvement exceeds untreated controls.

quotes.text: Thirty days post-immunoadsorption therapy, patients exhibited notable improvement in neuropsychological function
The present study shows that the health status of post-COVID patients with ME/CFS symptoms and high ANSR autoantibody levels objectively improved after IA therapy.

issues.title: Dozens of uncorrected tests in 12 patients with no sample-size justification
issues.explanation: The paper tests many autoantibodies, cytokines, T-cell subsets, questionnaires and cognitive measures without correction, in 12 patients and with no power calculation. The authors label the study exploratory, but sporadic significant findings such as the modest hand-grip gain or single T-cell subsets are fragile and should be read as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pre-specified primary outcome with adjusted analysis showing the same results.

quotes.text: p values were not corrected for multiple testing, as this study was of exploratory nature
the small sample size of 12 patients reduces the statistical power, potentially masking signi fi cant changes

issues.title: Table 2 symptom/criteria denominators are 11 versus 12 patients elsewhere, with no stated missing patient
issues.explanation: The abstract and Table 1 describe 12 patients, but every categorical row in Table 2 uses 11 as the denominator. The paper never says one patient lacked symptom data. This is likely missing data, but it is undisclosed. Continuous rows (SF-36 etc.) do not state n.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one patient did not complete the symptom questionnaires or was missing at follow-up.

quotes.text: This observational study includes 12 post-COVID patients

quotes.location: Table 2, Canadian criteria for ME/CFS, Before IA column

10.1016/s1473-3099(23)00685-0.headline_claim: The authors conclude that the synbiotic preparation SIM01 alleviated multiple symptoms of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome at 6 months in adults after acute COVID-19 infection.
10.1016/s1473-3099(23)00685-0.overall: The randomised, placebo-controlled design is sound and the symptom benefits for several domains are plausible, but the primary outcome is a self-reported, investigator-developed instrument with only face and content validation, which limits how firmly 'effective' can be stated. The numerical discrepancies between text and Table 2 are most likely adjusted-versus-unadjusted differences, and the microbiome mechanism claim and the 'safe' claim are stated more strongly than the evidence shown.

primary_outcome.name: Alleviation of PACS symptoms by 6 months, assessed with the PACSQ-14 questionnaire

issues.title: Primary outcome measured with a study-specific questionnaire validated only for face and content
issues.explanation: The primary outcome, symptom alleviation, comes from the PACSQ-14, developed by the investigators and checked only by an expert panel for face and content validity. The authors acknowledge that validated tools were not available, yet the conclusion states SIM01 'was effective'. Without reliability, responsiveness or minimal-important-difference data, the size and meaning of the reported ORs are uncertain, and the Discussion's 'locally validated' wording overstates the validation described in Methods.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published reliability and responsiveness validation of the PACSQ-14 in a comparable population.

quotes.text: validated by an independent expert panel for face and content validity
robust and validated assessment tools for individual symptoms were not available
the use of a locally validated questionnaire to assess PACS symptoms

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome was measured with PACSQ-14, a questionnaire developed for this study, and the main text describes its validation only as face and content validity by an expert panel. The authors acknowledge the lack of globally validated tools and that limits how far the primary outcome can be relied on, but this is a disclosed limitation. The appendix, which I did not see, may contain further validation detail.

issues.title: 'Safe' conclusion rests on any-AE counts (22 vs 25) with no serious adverse event data reported
issues.explanation: The paper concludes SIM01 is safe, based on any-adverse-event counts of 22/232 and 25/231 and a list of mild gastrointestinal events. No serious adverse event count, discontinuations due to adverse events, or severity grading overall is reported, although a DSMC and adjudication committee existed. The data show no signal, but a trial of 232 participants per arm cannot establish safety broadly, and the wording is stronger than the reported evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported serious adverse event count by arm, showing no excess.

quotes.text: SIM01 is a safe and promising treatment for PACS
22 (10%) of 232 individuals in the SIM01 group and 25 (11%) of 231 individuals in the placebo group had adverse events

issues.title: Diversity and richness gains inferred from within-arm tests (p=0·0019 vs 0·61); richness p=0·051 called an increase
issues.explanation: The microbiome claim relies on significant change from baseline in the SIM01 arm and not in the placebo arm, which is not a test of difference between arms. Richness at p=0·051 is described as increased, though it is above 0·05. Between-arm comparisons at 6 months are reported for composition and resistome, so the mechanistic story is partly supported, but the diversity and richness statement is weaker than presented. This affects the mechanism claim rather than the clinical result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-arm test of change in diversity and richness showing a significant difference.

quotes.text: increased bacteria diversity (p=0·0019) and bacteria richness (observed number of species; p=0·051) in the SIM01 group but no difference in diversity (p=0·61)
in the SIM01 group but not placebo group after 6 months of treatment

issues.title: Insomnia listed as non-significant after Bonferroni, yet Table 2 gives SIM01 p=0·0024 (<0·0036)
issues.explanation: The Results list insomnia among symptoms not significant after Bonferroni correction (p>0·0036), but Table 2 reports an insomnia SIM01 p of 0·0024, below that threshold. Table 2 is a multivariable stepwise model, so the p-values may legitimately differ from the unadjusted per-symptom tests in Figure 2. The paper does not say this, so insomnia's status is unclear, and by the Table 2 model it would count as significant, which would understate the benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 2 showing an unadjusted insomnia p above 0·0036, with Table 2 explicitly described as a different adjusted model.

quotes.text: although these results were not significant after Bonferroni correction (ie, p>0·0036)

quotes.location: Table 2, Insomnia, Treatment group SIM01 row

issues.title: Primary outcome uses LOCF/no-change imputation with 12-14% missing at 6 months
issues.explanation: Missing 6-month data (28 of 232 and 32 of 231) were filled by carrying forward the 3-month value or assuming no change. This can bias treatment effect estimates in an unpredictable direction. A multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis is reported as consistent, but only in the appendix.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Appendix multiple-imputation results reproducing the per-symptom ORs and Bonferroni significance.

quotes.text: The last observation carried forward method was used to impute missing data of the primary outcome.
Because the last observation carried forward method expected the data to be missing completely at random

10.1016/s1473-3099(25)00073-8.headline_claim: A 15-day course of nirmatrelvir–ritonavir did not significantly improve PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score at day 28 compared with placebo–ritonavir in people with long COVID, and the fully decentralised design was feasible.
10.1016/s1473-3099(25)00073-8.overall: The central finding, no significant or clinically meaningful PHSS improvement with a 15-day course, is supported by the reported CI. The main caveats are partial unmasking on a patient-reported outcome and a conclusion about 'long COVID' that goes somewhat beyond what a single generic outcome can show. No numerical errors affecting results were found.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS-29 v2.1 Physical Health Summary Score, change from baseline to day 28

primary_outcomes.measure: Number of Participants With No, Mild, Moderate, or Severe Symptoms at Week 10 According to the Core Symptoms Severity Scale Score

issues.title: Masking partly compromised: 67% of placebo arm guessed correctly, dysgeusia 48% vs 6%, on a patient-reported outcome
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is patient-reported, so it is sensitive to participants' beliefs about their allocation. Dysgeusia was much more frequent on active drug, and two-thirds of the placebo group correctly identified placebo. The authors acknowledge masking may not have been fully effective. However, the active arm guessed worse than chance, so the bias direction is uncertain and a large hidden benefit is not implied. This weakens confidence in the null result only modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sensitivity analysis showing no treatment difference among participants who guessed incorrectly or who did not experience dysgeusia.

quotes.text: In the nirmatrelvir–ritonavir group, 19 (41%) of 46 participants correctly guessed their treatment
Conversely, 33 (67%) of 49 participants in the placebo–ritonavir group correctly identified their treatment
this approach might not have been entirely effective in masking participants to their treatment allocation

issues.title: 'Insufficient to treat long COVID' is broader than a null on a generic PHSS in a mixed population
issues.explanation: The data support that this regimen did not improve the PHSS by a clinically meaningful amount at day 28. The authors state the broader inference as insufficiency for long COVID, citing consistency with STOP-PASC. They also say the trial was not powered for individual symptoms and that dose or duration may have been inadequate. The wording is somewhat stronger than the evidence, but the paper's own qualifications largely offset it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to 'this 15-day regimen did not improve general physical health at 28 days'.

quotes.text: The consistency of results across both studies suggests that 15-day treatment with this antiviral is insufficient to treat long COVID.
which was not powered to assess individual symptoms

issues.title: Registry-search status counts sum to 86, not the 92 pharmacological trials, in the background panel
issues.explanation: The Research in context panel says 92 pharmacological trials were found, and gives six recruitment statuses for 'these trials' that add up to 86. The missing six may be statuses such as unknown or withdrawn that were not listed. Either way this is a background literature-search detail and does not affect the trial results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the six remaining trials had unlisted statuses (unknown, withdrawn or suspended), or that the statuses refer to a different subset.

quotes.text: with only 92 trials testing pharmacological interventions
quotes.location: Introduction, Research in context, Evidence before this study

quotes.text: The recruitment statuses of these trials were: 12 not yet recruiting, eight terminated, 35 actively recruiting, one enrolling by invitation, 11 active but not recruiting, and 19 completed.
quotes.location: Introduction, Research in context, Evidence before this study

10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00242-2.headline_claim: Colchicine and famotidine-loratadine gave small, marginal additional 12-week fatigue (FAS) reductions compared with no drug, these effects were not sustained at 24 weeks, and long-term symptom benefit is unlikely with these drugs alone.
10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00242-2.overall: The main conclusion, that the drugs give at most small, transient fatigue benefit and do not support widespread use, is reasonably cautious and mostly survives. The reported drug effects are fragile (borderline p near 0.04, uncorrected, lost in sensitivity analyses) and come from an open-label trial with a self-reported outcome. The remaining issues are small printing inconsistencies and an overreaching claim about specialist care.

primary_outcome.name: 12-week Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) score, adjusted for baseline

issues.title: Within-arm FAS falls (about 3-5 points) attributed to specialist care without a no-care comparison
issues.explanation: All groups received usual specialist care, so a fall in every arm cannot show that the care caused it. Regression to the mean, spontaneous recovery, trial participation and expectation are equally compatible. The paper also states it cannot identify which care elements mattered. The Discussion statement that the fall 'shows the importance' of specialist care goes beyond the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison arm without specialist care showing smaller improvement.

quotes.text: The consistent decrease in FAS scores beyond the MCID across all groups shows the importance of access to and evaluation of specialist care

issues.title: Open-label trial with self-reported fatigue outcome: small 12-week drug effects (about 1.5 points) vulnerable to expectation
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the primary outcome is self-reported fatigue, with no placebo for the no-drug arm. The 1.5-point differences are well below the 3-point MCID the authors cite, so they could readily arise from expectation effects. The authors acknowledge this, and the paper's conclusion is already cautious, so the main message survives. The abstract's reporting of the additional reductions leaves this bias unstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded or objective outcome showing the same differences.

quotes.text: Participants were unblinded to allocation throughout the trial, as were investigators after data lock.
which substantially limits interpretation of results

issues.title: Two borderline 12-week effects (p=0.041, 0.038) uncorrected and lost significance in both sensitivity analyses
issues.explanation: The colchicine and famotidine-loratadine effects are significant only at about p 0.04 with no multiplicity adjustment across three drug comparisons and several outcomes. In the multiple-imputation and 84-day completer analyses the effects were no longer significant. The abstract reports them as statistically significant without these caveats, so the finding is fragile, though the authors' overall interpretation is cautious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary comparison, or significance holding under imputation and completer analyses.

quotes.text: Adjusted analyses showed small, statistically significant FAS reductions in the colchicine
no longer significant at the 5%

issues.title: Rivaroxaban 24-week FAS SD: text gives 8.92 (the famotidine-loratadine value), Table 2 gives 8.73
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the rivaroxaban 24-week score as 33.4 (SD 8.92). Table 2 gives 33.4 (SD 8.73) for rivaroxaban, and 8.92 belongs to the famotidine-loratadine column. One of the two printed values is wrong, most likely the text. No reported test depends on this SD.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the rivaroxaban 24-week SD is 8.92 and the Table 2 value is the slip.

quotes.location: Table 2, Week 24 FAS score row, rivaroxaban column

issues.title: 668 stated as 86% of 750 baseline completers, but 668/750 = 89.1%
issues.explanation: The Results say 668 (86%) of those participants, referring to the 750 with baseline FAS, had a 12-week score. The percentage is 89.1% on that base and 85.9% on the 778 randomised. The primary analysis population is therefore described with an inconsistent denominator. The effect on conclusions is nil.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Text defining the 86% as proportion of all randomised participants.

quotes.text: 668 (86%) of those participants

issues.title: Table 1 age row gives n=197 for no-drug group randomised at n=196
issues.explanation: The no-drug group is stated as 196 randomised participants. The Table 1 age row for that group reports n=197, which is larger than the group. The age n cannot exceed the number randomised, so one printed figure is wrong. The effect on results is probably nil.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected randomisation count of 197 for the no-drug group, which would also change the 778 total.

quotes.location: Table 1, Age, years row, no drug column

quotes.text: or no drug (usual care only; n=196)

issues.title: Discussion says drug differences 'no longer significant by 24 months'; trial follow-up was 24 weeks
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the differences between drug groups and usual care are no longer significant by 24 months. The trial ended at 24 weeks, as the previous paragraph states. This is a wrong unit in one sentence and does not affect the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of a 24-month assessment in the trial protocol.

quotes.text: no longer significant by 24 months

issues.title: Figure 1 legend 24-week percentages for rivaroxaban (82%) and no drug (79%) do not match printed denominators
issues.explanation: Figure 1's legend gives 152 (82%) of 188 and 147 (79%) of 189. The printed counts give 80.9% and 77.8%. The printed percentages fit a denominator of about 186 instead. The legend percentages and denominators disagree, though only a descriptive completeness figure is affected. The no-drug row repeats the same inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that the percentages use a different denominator than the printed one.

quotes.text: 152 (82%) of 188 in the rivaroxaban group
147 (79%) of 189 in the no drug (usual care only) group

issues.title: Table 3 female sex CI 0.521 to 1.579 excludes zero but p=0.32; consistent with a missing minus sign
issues.explanation: As printed, the CI excludes zero while the p value is 0.32, and the estimate 0.529 is not the CI midpoint. With a minus sign on the lower bound, the midpoint is exactly 0.529 and the CI spans zero, matching p=0.32. This is probably a typographical or extraction artefact in a covariate row, not in a drug effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original PDF showing -0.521 with the minus sign present.

quotes.location: Table 3, Female sex at birth row

issues.title: Table 1 poor sleep colchicine: 158/187 printed as 86%, but 158/187 = 84.5%
issues.explanation: The percentage does not match the printed count and denominator. It does match a denominator of 184, so the denominator is probably mistyped. Only a baseline characteristic in one cell is affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source listing showing 187 respondents and 161 cases.

quotes.location: Table 1, Poor sleep row, colchicine column

script.explanation: 158/187 = 84.49%, but the paper prints 86, outside the rounding interval [85.50, 87.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 183.7 rather than 187.

10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00406-8.headline_claim: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for up to 25 days did not improve cognitive, autonomic, or exercise long COVID symptoms, and the authors conclude it provides no measurable clinical benefit.
10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00406-8.overall: The headline conclusion of no benefit on the primary endpoints is well supported: all primary comparisons have wide CIs spanning zero and no estimate favours active treatment. The flagged problems are minor reporting slips (a dropped sign in the text CI and in one subgroup row) and a Summary statement of 'no differences in secondary endpoints' that overlooks a nominally significant exercise secondary result favouring placebo. None of these changes the overall null interpretation.

primary_outcome.name: Proportion achieving clinically meaningful improvement in phenotype-specific PROM at day 90 (cognitive PROMIS 8a, autonomic OHQ item 1, exercise DSQ-PEM)

primary_outcomes.measure: Total Number of Participants Enrolled in Each Appendix

issues.title: Summary says no secondary differences, but exercise secondary 25-day vs placebo is -13·8% (CI -24·9 to -2·8), p=0·01
issues.explanation: The Summary states there were no differences in secondary endpoints. Table 2 shows the exercise secondary endpoint (Endurance Shuttle Walk improvement) was lower with 25-day nirmatrelvir-ritonavir than placebo (16% vs 33%), with a CI excluding zero and p=0·01. The result is nominally significant, in the direction of worse outcome with active drug, and the Results text then says it 'did not indicate a treatment effect'. The result may be a chance finding given unadjusted multiplicity, but it should be reported as such rather than as no difference. The overall null conclusion on benefit is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'no differences' meant none surviving multiplicity adjustment, with the exercise secondary result flagged as nominally significant and favouring placebo.

quotes.text: There were no differences in secondary endpoints, and no safety signals were observed

issues.title: Results text gives exercise 25-day CI as -24·9 to 2·8 (spanning zero) but p=0·014; Table 2 gives -2·8
issues.explanation: The Results paragraph prints the upper CI bound as 2·8 (positive), which would include zero, yet reports p=0·014. Table 2 prints -2·8 for the same comparison, which fits p of about 0·01. The sign slip in the text makes the result look non-significant, which supports the text's wording that there was no treatment effect. The error is minor but it hides a nominally significant secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source documents showing the CI upper bound really is +2.8 with a correspondingly larger p-value.

quotes.text: adjusted difference -13·8% [95% CI -24·9 to 2·8], p=0·014

issues.title: Figure 2C >38 months estimate 0·12 lies outside its printed CI (0·74 to 0·98); lower bound likely -0·74
issues.explanation: The point estimate 0·12 cannot lie outside its own 95% CI of 0·74 to 0·98. The interval would be centred on the estimate if the lower bound were -0·74, so a sign was probably lost in the figure or in text extraction. This is a cosmetic slip in an exploratory subgroup panel and does not affect any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original figure showing the printed lower bound as -0·74.

quotes.text: >38 months

script.explanation: the estimate 0.12 lies outside its own CI [0.74, 0.98]; the estimate 0.12 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [0.74, 0.98] (expected about 0.8600) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

10.1016/s2213-2600(22)00125-4.headline_claim: An online breathing and wellbeing programme (ENO Breathe) can improve the mental component of health-related quality of life and elements of breathlessness in people with persisting symptoms after COVID-19.
10.1016/s2213-2600(22)00125-4.overall: The main claim of effectiveness rests on a borderline MHC result (p=0.047, CI lower bound 0.03) from an unblinded, usual-care-controlled trial with differential withdrawal, and the result is no longer significant under the authors' own BOCF sensitivity analysis. The VAS running result survives Bonferroni correction but is also a self-reported outcome in an open-label design. The conclusions should be read as tentative signals rather than confirmed effectiveness.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline to 6 weeks in RAND SF-36 mental health composite (MHC) and physical health composite (PHC); MHC p shown

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline in RAND-36 (RAND SF-36)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: At baseline, then repeated after 6 weeks.

issues.title: Two co-primary composites (MHC, PHC) tested at 0.05 each; MHC p=0.047 would not survive a 0.025 split
issues.explanation: The sample size was powered for a 5-point difference in MHC or PHC, and both were tested at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05. Only MHC was significant, at p=0.047 with a CI whose lower bound is 0.03. Splitting alpha across the two co-primaries (0.025) would make this non-significant. The secondary VAS running result is narrower than the candidate suggests: p=0.0026 just clears 0.05/18, though it is one of 18 secondary tests and was not designated as a key outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or a single designated primary outcome (for example MHC alone) in the protocol or registry, which would make 0.05 appropriate for MHC.

quotes.text: An α of 0·05 was taken to indicate statistical significance.
regression coefficient 2·42 [95% CI 0·03 to 4·80]; p=0·047

second_reader.what_stands: Two composites were named as the primary outcome and each was tested at 0·05 with no stated multiplicity adjustment. The MHC p=0·047 is above 0·025 and would not be significant under a simple two-way split. The paper does not say whether a hypothesis is deemed met if either composite is significant, so whether a correction was strictly required rests on how the primary hypothesis is read.

issues.title: Unmasked participants self-report primary outcome against a no-attention usual-care control
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and completed the SF-36 and breathlessness VAS themselves. The intervention added six group sessions, a one-to-one session, at least three emails per week, a phone contact and a welcome pack. Usual care was unstandardised and received nothing comparable. The 2.4-point MHC difference and the VAS result cannot be separated from expectation, social contact and attention effects. The authors nonetheless state a causal conclusion of effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched or sham comparator, or evidence from an objective outcome showing the same direction of effect.

quotes.text: outcome measures were collected using a self-completion online form
given the nature of the intervention, double blinding was not possible

second_reader.what_stands: Participants knew their allocation and self-reported the primary outcome against a no-attention, delayed-treatment control, so expectation and response bias could inflate the differences. The paper acknowledges that participants could not be masked, but it phrases this as 'double blinding' and does not weigh the effect on self-reported outcomes in its conclusion.

issues.title: Complete-case analysis (129/150) labelled ITT; withdrawal 22% vs 7%; MHC p goes 0.047 to 0.095
issues.explanation: Table 3 is titled intention-to-treat but analyses 58 of 74 and 71 of 76 participants. Withdrawal was three times higher in the intervention arm, and reasons such as excessive fatigue are plausibly related to outcome. Under baseline-observation-carried-forward imputation the primary MHC result is no longer significant. The sole significant primary finding therefore depends on the missing-data handling.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified multiple-imputation or mixed-model analysis including all 150 participants that reproduced a significant MHC effect.

quotes.text: 16 (22%) participants in the ENO Breathe group withdrew
with the p value for the SF-36 MHC score going from 0·047 in the main analysis to 0·095 in the post-hoc analysis

second_reader.what_stands: The analysis labelled intention-to-treat is in fact a complete-case analysis of 129 of 150 randomised participants, with withdrawal of 22% versus 7%. The main MHC result (p=0·047) loses nominal significance (p=0·095) when missing data are imputed by BOCF. The authors report this openly, but the ITT label is inaccurate and the primary result is sensitive to the missing data.

issues.title: 'Effective' claimed on MHC 2.42 (CI 0.03-4.80), below the 5-point design effect; PHC null; BOCF p=0.095
issues.explanation: The intervention is described as effective on the strength of a borderline primary result: the CI lower bound is 0.03, the point estimate is below the 5-point difference used for the power calculation, and PHC (the other co-primary) shows no effect. The authors' own sensitivity analysis loses significance. The Discussion then says differential withdrawal is unlikely to explain the results. The evidence supports a tentative signal on one co-primary, not a confident claim of effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified MCID for long COVID below 2.4 points together with a robust all-participant analysis giving a clearly significant MHC effect.

quotes.text: The intervention appears safe and was effective at improving the mental component of HRQoL
Overall, the differential withdrawal rate is unlikely to explain the results when considered as a whole

second_reader.what_stands: The word 'effective' is applied to an MHC difference of 2·42 (CI 0·03 to 4·80) whose entire interval lies below the 5-point difference the trial was designed to detect. The point estimate is also below the 3 to 5 point MCID range, the other primary composite (PHC) was null, and the result is no longer significant under BOCF (p=0·095). The authors do discuss the MCID uncertainty and the withdrawal imbalance, but their conclusion still states effectiveness more firmly than these results support.

issues.title: Post-hoc completers-only comparison (40 vs 42) used to claim greater benefit in those who participate most
issues.explanation: The modified per-protocol set keeps participants who attended all sessions in the intervention arm and, in the control arm, those who later completed the programme. Both selections happen after randomisation, so the groups are no longer randomised comparisons. The intervention arm's baseline MHC (30.88) differs from the control (36.23), and included participants had better baseline health than those excluded. The 3.50 versus 2.42 coefficients have overlapping CIs, with no test of difference. The statement of 'substantially greater' effect and benefit 'particularly in patients who participate most' goes beyond this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised or instrumental-variable (CACE) analysis showing a dose-response effect, or a formal test showing the per-protocol effect is greater than the ITT effect.

quotes.text: the modified per-protocol analysis suggests that in people who fully participate in ENO Breathe, the effect of the intervention was substantially greater than usual care
particularly in patients who participate most in the intervention.

10.1017/s0033291723002921.headline_claim: CBT-PCC is feasible, well accepted, and potentially effective as part of inpatient neurological rehabilitation for post-COVID-19 condition, with improvements in subjective fatigue and illness cognitions.
10.1017/s0033291723002921.overall: The feasibility and acceptability findings are reasonably supported for a small uncontrolled study, and the authors acknowledge the lack of a control group. The efficacy signals (fatigue, illness cognitions) are within-group changes with LOCF dilution, no multiplicity control and a retrospective registration, so they are hypothesis-generating only. The safety statement is the most overstated element, given the 85% adverse-event rate and the unclear denominator.

primary_outcome.name: not designated in the paper; pre-post changes across PHQ-15, SSD-12, FSS, PHQ-9, GAD-7, ICQ and HEALTH-49

issues.title: Within-group pre-post changes in 63 uncontrolled inpatients read as support for 'potentially effective'
issues.explanation: With no control group, and the programme added to routine inpatient rehabilitation, improvements in fatigue and illness cognitions over about four weeks cannot be separated from rehabilitation, natural recovery, regression to the mean or expectancy. The authors admit this in the limitations, but the Discussion still says the results support potential effectiveness. The problem is narrower than the screen says: the wording is hedged and the Conclusion does not claim efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control group, or a Discussion that treats the pre-post changes strictly as hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: This study was conducted as a single-group, uncontrolled clinical trial.
our results support that CBT-PCC is feasible, well accepted, and potentially effective as part of inpatient neurological rehabilitation

issues.title: Drop-outs (22/63 without post data) had higher baseline symptoms than the 32 per-protocol completers
issues.explanation: About a third of participants lacked post-intervention data and only 32 met the per-protocol definition. Completers had significantly lower baseline somatic, depressive and anxiety symptoms and less helplessness, so the per-protocol effects (dav up to 0.75) come from a less burdened subgroup. The paper discloses this and reports the ITT sample as the main analysis, so it limits generalisability rather than invalidating a result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Sensitivity analyses showing that results do not depend on completers, such as multiple imputation or a mixed model using all available data.

quotes.text: participants who adhered to the study protocol ( n = 32 [50.0%]
because discontinuation of the study was associated with baseline clinical characteristics

issues.title: LOCF fills 22 of 63 missing post-scores with baseline values, diluting the ITT pre-post effects
issues.explanation: For the 22 participants without post assessment (13 attended no session), the last observation is the baseline value, so their change is set to zero. This assumes no change in a third of the sample, attenuates the ITT effect sizes and distorts the variance. It likely explains why the ITT dav values (0.33 for FSS) are smaller than the per-protocol ones (0.48). The paired t-tests also treat these imputed values as real data, so the ITT p-values are not trustworthy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with multiple imputation or a mixed model giving the same effect sizes.

quotes.text: Missing data at post-intervention assessment were handled using the last observation carried forward (LOCF) method.

issues.title: 'Can be regarded as safe' stated despite 85.4% reporting an adverse event and no comparator or baseline
issues.explanation: Adverse events were measured once, after the intervention, with no control group or baseline, so events caused by the programme cannot be separated from those caused by the rehabilitation stay or by the condition. 85.4% reported at least one event and 29.3% reported severe or extremely distressing ones. The percentages imply about 41 respondents rather than 63, so people who dropped out and may have had worse experiences are probably missing. A flat statement of safety goes beyond what a small, uncontrolled sample of this kind can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated UE-G denominator including all treated participants, and a comparison with adverse-event rates in a control or usual-care group.

quotes.text: At least one adverse event was reported by 85.4% of the participants
Thus, the presented treatment protocol can be regarded as safe.

issues.title: Retrospective registration (DRKS00031219) with no designated primary outcome and recruitment in Feb-Jul 2022
issues.explanation: The trial was registered after the study started, so the registry cannot confirm which outcomes and analyses were planned in advance. Nine outcome tests were run without a stated primary outcome or multiplicity correction, and the reported significant results were selected from them.
