This is disclosed and the study is exploratory, so it weakens only the secondary efficacy signals.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record showing the outcomes and analyses with a date before the first participant was enrolled.

quotes.text: The trial was retrospectively registered at the German Clinical Trials Register (www.drks.de, DRKS00031219).

10.1017/s1355617723007592.headline_claim: Cognitive training, including Speed of Processing Training, has long-term positive benefits for everyday abilities, quality of life and continued independence in older adults, based on the ACTIVE trial.
10.1017/s1355617723007592.overall: This is a conference abstract with no numerical results, so the headline claim of long-term benefit cannot be checked from the text. The main concern is that findings specific to speed of processing training are phrased as benefits of cognitive training generally. Other concerns, such as registration and multiplicity, cannot be assessed from an abstract of this kind.

primary_outcome.name: Not designated; abstract emphasises driving competence and crash involvement over ten years

issues.title: Conclusion generalises to 'cognitive training' while results single out speed training; no effect sizes given
issues.explanation: The Results say only speed of processing training sustained driving and reduced crash risk, yet the Conclusion credits 'cognitive training' in general with long-term benefit on everyday abilities, quality of life and independence. No effect sizes, intervals or p-values are given for any outcome, including quality of life and depression. The wording is broader than the results shown, though this is a conference abstract and the data are promised for the talk.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The full presentation or publication reporting effect sizes and CIs for each training arm on quality of life and independence, showing benefit for all cognitive training types.

quotes.text: Speed of Processing Training was found to sustain driving competence with respect to continued driving relative to other types of training
cognitive training can have long-term positive benefit on the everyday abilities, quality of life, and continued independence of older adults
Positive benefits were also observed for Health Related Quality of Life (HRQoL), and depression.

issues.title: Many outcomes listed with no multiplicity handling stated in the abstract
issues.explanation: The abstract lists cognitive, IADL, mobility, quality-of-life, mortality and health outcomes across three training arms and a control. No correction or primary outcome hierarchy is stated. Whether this matters cannot be judged from an abstract with no p-values.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and analysis plan, or corrected p-values, for the reported driving, crash, HRQoL and depression findings.

quotes.text: Outcomes included measures of cognitive function, measures of IADL (including crash involvement and driving cessation)

10.1017/s1355617723007634.headline_claim: CICT, combining speed-of-processing training with the Transfer Package, shows high promise as an efficacious therapy for brain fog due to PASC, pending confirmation in a large RCT.
10.1017/s1355617723007634.overall: The PASC findings are a nine-person (5 vs 4) pilot with large but very imprecise effects on self-rated outcomes against an untreated waitlist, so they support at most a hypothesis worth testing; 'efficacious' is stronger than the evidence allows, although the authors do call for a large RCT. The only clear printed error is the mean age outside the stated range in the separate stroke case series, which does not affect the PASC conclusions. Missing registration and ethics statements are expected omissions in a conference abstract and cannot be assessed from this text.

primary_outcome.name: Not designated; Mental Clutter Scale and COPM Performance scale both reported

issues.title: 'Efficacious therapy' wording drawn from a 9-person unblinded pilot (5 vs 4) with d = 1.7 and p < .05
issues.explanation: The PASC abstract concludes that CICT 'shows high promise as an efficacious therapy' on the basis of five immediate-CICT and four waitlist participants. With groups this small, effect sizes (d = 1.7) and p < .05 are very imprecise, no sample-size calculation is described, and outcomes are self-rated against an untreated waitlist. The authors' call for a large RCT tempers the conclusion, but the word 'efficacious' and the statement that 'all five' improved meaningfully still lean further than a pilot of this size supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full report with a prespecified sample-size rationale, confidence intervals around the effects, and blinded outcome assessment supporting the efficacy claim.

quotes.text: To date, CICT shows high promise as an efficacious therapy for brain fog due to PASC.
To date, five were enrolled in the immediate-CICT group; four were enrolled in the wait-list group.
These preliminary findings warrant confirmation by a large-scale randomized controlled trial.

issues.title: Self-rated COPM and Mental Clutter Scale outcomes against an untreated waitlist, blinding not described
issues.explanation: The two reported between-group outcomes (COPM Performance and the Mental Clutter Scale) are self-rated, and the comparison group is an untreated waitlist. Participants know their allocation and no blinding or attention control is described, so expectation effects could contribute to the very large d = 1.7. The abstract does not state this as a limitation of the efficacy claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods section describing masked assessors, or objective or performance-based outcomes showing similar between-group differences.

quotes.text: on parallel occasions in the delayed-CICT group (aka waitlist controls)
as measured by the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) Performance scale

issues.title: Stroke case series: mean age 59.7 years lies outside the stated age range 47-55
issues.explanation: The stroke case series abstract gives a mean age of 59.7 years but a range of 47-55. A mean cannot exceed the maximum of its own range, so one of the figures is misprinted (probably the upper bound). This is a factual slip in a different abstract from the PASC trial, and nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full-paper or corrected abstract showing the true range (e.g. 47-75) or a mean consistent with 47-55.

quotes.text: mean age = 59.7 years, (range, 47-55)
quotes.location: Participants and Methods, chronic stroke case series

issues.title: No trial registration statement in the abstract of a randomized PASC pilot
issues.explanation: The abstract describes randomization to immediate or delayed CICT but gives no registry identifier. Within a short conference abstract this is common and does not show that the trial was unregistered. Whether outcomes were prespecified cannot be verified from the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier and registration date preceding enrolment, with matching primary outcomes.

quotes.text: Participants were randomized to CICT immediately or after a 3month delay.

10.1037/rep0000626.headline_claim: CICT is a feasible cognitive rehabilitation method for Long COVID brain fog, with preliminary efficacy on everyday performance, return-to-work, brain fog, fatigue and processing speed, warranting confirmation in a large RCT.
10.1037/rep0000626.overall: The feasibility conclusions (adherence, acceptability, no adverse events) are reasonably supported for a small pilot. The efficacy signal rests on an open-label comparison with usual care, self-reported primary outcome, completers-only analysis of about 13-14 people and uncorrected tests, so it is only a tentative signal. The authors hedge, but the 0.2% argument, the 'hard endpoint' framing and some text-versus-table inconsistencies make the efficacy case look stronger than it is.

primary_outcome.name: COPM Performance scale (change from pre- to post-treatment)

issues.title: Open-label trial vs unmonitored usual care; self-rated primary outcome (COPM) with d=2.6 and no placebo control
issues.explanation: Participants knew they were receiving a 36-hour therapy or no treatment, and the primary outcome (COPM performance) and most secondary outcomes are self-reported. A very large effect (MD 3.7, d=2.6) could therefore partly reflect expectancy or demand effects, which the authors admit cannot be excluded as there was no placebo or active comparison. The employment outcome, offered as a rebuttal, is also self-reported and tiny. The efficacy conclusion is tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment or an attention-matched control showing a similar effect on the primary outcome.

quotes.text: unblinded, open-label, parallel arm, partial-crossover design
Skeptics might argue the substantial advantage in favor of CICT on the primary outcome was due to the operation of demand characteristics
Other important limitations were the absence of long-term follow-up, blinding, and control for placebo effects.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper really is an open-label trial with a self-rated primary outcome (COPM, d=2.6) and no placebo or attention-control arm, and the authors say so themselves in the Methods, Discussion and limitations; this means the effect cannot be separated from expectancy or demand effects. The point is overstated in calling the comparator 'unmonitored', since TAU participants were tested on the same battery at several time points, and the authors partly mitigate the concern with an objective test (SDMT, p=0.042) and the return-to-work finding (p=0.048), though both come from very small samples (about

issues.title: 'All nine outcomes favoured one group (0.2% by chance)' rests on a null MoCA (MD 0.3) and treats correlated outcomes as independent
issues.explanation: The Methods use a sign-test style figure (0.2%) to offset the lack of multiplicity correction. The MoCA is described in the Results as showing no advantage (MD 0.3, 95% CI -3.1 to 3.7, p=0.84, d=0.1), and the GAD-7 was also non-significant, so the 'all nine' count is only a direction count. The nine outcomes are also correlated measures from the same 13-14 people, so the chance calculation assumes independence that is not present. The figure gives little protection against false positives.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated rule that any positive point estimate counts as an advantage, plus an analysis accounting for the correlation between outcomes.

quotes.text: all nine outcomes showed an advantage for the same group; the probability of that occurring by chance was only 0.2%
No advantage for Immediate-CICT over TAU was seen for general cognitive ability: MoCA MD=0.3 points
quotes.location: Results, In-lab Tests of Cognitive Ability

issues.title: Efficacy framing (return-to-work, objective SDMT gain, d up to 3.1) rests on 5 participants, p=0.048/0.042, no correction
issues.explanation: Return-to-work is presented as a 'hard' endpoint that rebuts demand effects. It is self-reported, covers five CICT participants (a Fisher test at p=0.048), and none of the p-values are corrected for multiplicity. The SDMT p of 0.042 comes from a rank-based model, and the authors say the raw-score model gave dissimilar results (relegated to the supplement). Very large effect sizes from about 13 people are likely inflated. The authors' caveats soften this, but the Impact section still states benefits on daily performance and return-to-work.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A multiplicity-adjusted or pre-specified hierarchical analysis in which return-to-work and SDMT remain significant.

quotes.text: with promise of (a) improving performance of cognition-based tasks in daily life and (b) promoting return-to-work
A distinct advantage in favor of Immediate-CICT over TAU was observed in return-to-work, p=0.048
We highlight that the findings about efficacy summarized in this paragraph are preliminary.

issues.title: COPM Satisfaction main effect and group-by-baseline interaction both reported as F(1,9)=22.8, p<0.001
issues.explanation: Two different terms of the same model are given identical test statistics. One of them is probably a transcription slip, and the main-effect CI does not match F = 22.8 under a simple model. Which value is right cannot be determined from the paper. The effect is on a secondary outcome and the direction of benefit is not in doubt.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Output from the analysis showing both terms really have F = 22.8, or a corrected value for one of them.

quotes.location: Results, Performance of Everyday Activities (Satisfaction main effect)

quotes.text: than for those with high baseline scores, F(1,9) = 22.8, p < 0.001

issues.title: Completers-only analysis called 'conservative' despite 2 of 9 TAU participants lost before Baseline 2 and none from CICT
issues.explanation: All analyses exclude two randomised TAU participants who withdrew before Baseline 2, and one more participant was excluded from the COPM, MCS and SDMT analyses. No one was lost from Immediate-CICT, so the loss is one-sided, and the claim that completers analysis is conservative is not shown. The authors themselves say the withdrawals 'may have inflated' the CICT advantage. The effect is probably modest, but it is not an intention-to-treat estimate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis (e.g. multiple imputation) of the primary outcome that reproduces the effect.

quotes.text: All data are reported only on a completers basis because the completers analyses were conservative
Two-of-nine TAU participants withdrew before Baseline 2 testing, which may have inflated the advantage observed for CICT.

issues.title: Discussion says TAU was slower at baseline on SDMT; Table 1 means (42.7 vs 39.1) show the reverse, medians agree with text
issues.explanation: The Discussion uses Table 1 to argue the groups were balanced and says the TAU group processed information more slowly. In Table 1 the TAU mean SDMT is higher (faster) than the Immediate-CICT mean, while the medians in the Results (43 vs 47) support the text. The baseline SDMT is therefore skewed and mean and median disagree on direction, which weakens the balance argument for the SDMT result. The error is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement in the paper that the sentence refers to medians rather than the Table 1 means.

quotes.text: The TAU group processed information more slowly than the CICT group.

issues.title: Immediate-CICT CTAL range reaches 3.9, above the stated inclusion cutoff of 3.5
issues.explanation: Inclusion required a CTAL score of 3.5 or lower, but the beginning-of-treatment range in the Immediate-CICT group extends to 3.9. This may reflect a different measurement occasion or scoring (screening vs treatment start). The paper does not clarify it. It has no bearing on the efficacy conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the inclusion CTAL was scored at screening, separately from the start-of-treatment CTAL.

quotes.text: Inclusion criteria included some impairment in IADL per a Cognitive Task Activity Log score ≤3.5
At the beginning of treatment, the mean Total in the Immediate-CICT group was 3.2 (SD = 0.5, range = 2.4-3.9)
quotes.location: Results, Adherence to and Engagement in CICT

10.1038/s41380-023-02084-1.headline_claim: Clinical improvement in Long-COVID is associated with reduction in autoantibodies, lipids and inflammation following therapeutic apheresis, and the approach may form the basis for objective monitoring and a clinical score.
10.1038/s41380-023-02084-1.overall: The biomarker reductions after apheresis are probably real as before-after changes, but the paper's central framing, that they are associated with clinical improvement, is not supported: no symptom data, control group or non-improver comparison is shown. The conclusions are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: not_specified

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design with improvers only: no control for time, heparin, co-treatments or non-responders
issues.explanation: All 27 patients received apheresis and were measured before and after, with no control group and no non-improving patients. The authors list the missing sham arm as a limitation, and also say that co-treatments (antioxidants, anti-inflammatory drugs, possibly glucocorticoids) may affect outcomes. The title and abstract nevertheless link clinical improvement to the biomarker reductions, though no comparison shows the biomarkers differ between improvers and non-improvers. The title's association with clinical improvement therefore cannot be supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or untreated control group, or data from non-improving patients showing smaller biomarker changes than improvers.

quotes.text: it was not conducted as a randomized controlled trial that included sham experiments of the invasive procedure without therapeutic filters
These components all may have an impact on treatment success
in 27 patients who showed clinical improvement after extracorporeal therapeutic apheresis

second_reader.what_stands: The biomarker analysis is a single-group before-after comparison of 27 patients described as clinically improved, with no control for time, heparin, co-treatments, or non-improvers. The authors acknowledge the lack of a sham arm, heparin, and co-treatments as limitations, and call for future cohorts including non-improvers, so the problem is real but disclosed rather than hidden.

issues.title: Title claims improvement is 'associated' with biomarker reduction, but no symptom data or correlation are reported
issues.explanation: The title and abstract say clinical improvement is associated with reductions in autoantibodies, lipids and inflammation, and propose a clinical score. The paper presents no symptom scores for the 27 patients, no comparison with non-improvers, and no biomarker-symptom correlation; the Discussion admits a clear correlation with symptoms is missing. The safety claim ('extremely safe') likewise has no adverse-event data in this cohort.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported symptom scores and a biomarker-change versus symptom-change analysis in the 27 patients, plus adverse-event data.

quotes.text: This, however, describes only an association and not causality and a clear correlation with symptoms and improvement of patients.
is an extremely safe method
It may therefore form the basis for a more objective monitoring and a clinical score

second_reader.what_stands: No symptom data for the 27 patients and no biomarker-symptom correlation are reported, so the title's 'associated with' and the abstract's 'pattern of biomarkers with clinical symptoms' are not supported by shown analysis. The authors do state in the final paragraph that the data show only an association and not a clear correlation with symptoms, so this limit is disclosed, and 'extremely safe' is asserted without safety data from this study.

issues.title: 'Clearly shows' apheresis is 'powerful' for reducing biomarkers despite no control and an acknowledged association
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the study 'clearly shows' apheresis is a powerful technology to reduce biomarkers, then immediately says it describes only an association. Lipid and fibrinogen reductions are mechanically expected, but the authors' wording is stronger than an uncontrolled pre-post series supports for inflammatory and autoantibody markers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison showing the same reductions relative to sham.

quotes.text: this study clearly shows that extracorporeal apheresis is a powerful technology to reduce biomarkers that have been implicated in the pathogenesis of post-infectious syndromes
This, however, describes only an association and not causality

10.1038/s41386-024-01995-z.headline_claim: A digital therapeutic (AKL-T01) improves select post-COVID-19 cognitive deficits, with associated improvements in quality of life and fatigue, but not sustained attention.
10.1038/s41386-024-01995-z.overall: The primary outcome was clearly null, and the positive conclusions rest on uncorrected secondary and exploratory results, many near p = 0.05, from self-reported measures against an open waitlist with unblinded staff contact. The paper discloses most of these limitations, but the Conclusions and Discussion still read the secondary results as evidence of benefit. They support only hypothesis-generating findings that need an active-controlled replication.

primary_outcome.name: Change in sustained attention (TMB Digital Symbol Matching Task, number correct), group x timepoint interaction

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Cognitive Function, as Measured by Number Correct on the Digit Symbol Matching Task

issues.title: Waitlist control cannot separate specific effect from expectancy on self-reported secondary/exploratory outcomes
issues.explanation: Controls received no game or equivalent contact, while the claimed benefits are mostly self-reported. Participants knew their arm, so expectancy, attention and practice could produce these differences. The authors say an active control is needed to 'confirm conclusions regarding specificity', yet the Discussion states that findings 'support the efficacy' of AKL-T01 for mood.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An active or sham-controlled comparison showing the same self-reported gains.

quotes.text: We did not include an active expectancy-matched control group
suggests potential downstream impact on clinically relevant outcomes

second_reader.what_stands: True: with a waitlist control and no blinding of participants, the design cannot separate a specific intervention effect from expectancy or attention on the self-reported secondary and exploratory outcomes (WHODAS, NeuroQOL, MFIS, GAD-7), and the authors concede this in Limitations. Not fully true that it is unacknowledged: the limitation is stated, though the Discussion still uses causal and 'support the efficacy' wording for these self-reports. Performance-based tasks are less exposed to expectancy, though not immune to it, since the control group received no comparable engagement.

issues.title: Uncorrected testing of many outcomes; claimed benefits rest on p = 0.04 to 0.05 (and one at 0.008)
issues.explanation: Primary, six or more secondary cognitive, two functional, several fatigue subscales, anxiety, depression and memory outcomes were tested without adjustment. The reported benefits have p of 0.05 (disability), 0.05 (quality of life), 0.04 (task switching), 0.04 (fatigue) and 0.008 (anxiety). Only a small number of tests are positive out of many run, so chance findings are plausible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy of outcomes, or adjusted p-values showing the secondary results survive correction.

quotes.text: results were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
Participants in the intervention group also reported reductions in disability and fatigue, as well as improved quality of life, compared to waitlist controls.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper tested many outcomes with no multiplicity adjustment, and several of the benefits it highlights (disability, quality of life, switching, total fatigue) rest on nominal p of 0.04 to 0.05; only simple RT (0.004) and the cognitive fatigue and anxiety results (0.009, 0.008) are lower, and none of these would clearly survive a conventional correction. The lack of correction is disclosed and framed as proof-of-concept, but the Discussion still states these benefits and 'efficacy' without hedging for multiplicity.

issues.title: Null primary outcome (p = 0.95) followed by conclusions foregrounding uncorrected secondary benefits
issues.explanation: The primary outcome showed no effect, yet the Conclusions say some deficits 'may be ameliorated' with improved disability, quality of life and fatigue. The Discussion says the findings 'support the efficacy' of AKL-T01 for mood from an exploratory anxiety result. These claims rest on unadjusted, near-threshold, self-reported outcomes against an open waitlist.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion that explicitly frames secondary and exploratory results as hypothesis-generating only.

quotes.text: Despite the lack of improvement in sustained attention
The digital and scalable nature of this intervention may help address the substantial need for accessible treatments in individuals with long COVID.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome was null (p = 0.95) and the abstract and Conclusions lead with secondary and exploratory improvements that were not corrected for multiplicity, with the 'if replicated' hedge dropped from the Conclusions. The paper does state the null primary result clearly, uses 'may' wording, and notes proof-of-concept status and the lack of an active control, so the null result is not hidden, but the framing is more favourable than the primary result and the uncorrected secondary evidence support.

issues.title: Allocation concealment unreported; unblinded trial managers administered questionnaire outcomes
issues.explanation: The paper does not say how allocation was concealed. The trial managers who ran weekly visits and administered the scales and questionnaires knew each participant's group. The functional and mood outcomes could therefore be influenced by staff contact. The registry lists masking as double, which does not match the unblinded managers described here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of concealed allocation, or evidence that questionnaires were self-completed without manager involvement.

quotes.text: Trial managers administering assessments were not blinded to group assignment
Scales and questionnaires were administered by trial managers.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation reported for 49 vs 49 analysed proof-of-concept trial
issues.explanation: No power calculation is given, and 12 of 110 randomized participants contributed no data. The study is described as preliminary, so the lack of calculation is acceptable, but near-threshold secondary findings from such a sample are fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation for the primary outcome in the protocol.

quotes.text: This report describes the randomized assignments and initial 6-week enrollment period

issues.title: Funder-employed authors with equity analysed the data of a trial of the funder's product
issues.explanation: Akili funded the trial and supplied devices. Four authors were employees with stock or equity, and an employee analysed the data. All of this is disclosed, so it is not hidden, but it increases the importance of independent verification of the positive secondary results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Independent reanalysis of the deidentified data by an unaffiliated statistician reproducing the results.

quotes.text: CM, CAS, DNF, and SHK were employees of Akili Interactive and have owned stock or equity in the company.
CM analyzed the data.

issues.title: WHODAS interaction F printed as 4.02 in Abstract but 4.01 in Results
issues.explanation: The same test (F[1,82]) is reported with different statistics in two places. The p-value is the same either way, so the effect is cosmetic.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version giving one value.

10.1038/s41467-025-57198-7.headline_claim: Therapeutic plasma exchange is safe but did not improve post-COVID-19 condition symptoms, function, fatigue, quality of life or cognition compared with sham.
10.1038/s41467-025-57198-7.overall: The safety finding is reasonably supported, with one minor text-table slip on the most common adverse event category. The efficacy conclusion that TPE is not effective rests on descriptive data from 25 per arm with no effect estimates or intervals, so it should be read as tentative. The paper also treats safety as the sole primary even though the registry lists two functional outcomes as co-primary.

primary_outcome.name: Safety and tolerability of PE vs sham (AEs within 90 days); efficacy measures (PCFS, FSS) listed as secondary in paper

primary_outcomes.measure: Evaluate the safety and tolerability of PE in patients with Post-Acute Covid-19 Syndrome (PCC) comparing to sham plasma exchange (placebo)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Within 90 days from the treatment start

primary_outcomes.measure: Proportion of subjects with Grade 0, 1 o 2 functional disability assessed by the functional status scale (PCFS)
Proportion of subjects with Grade 0, 1 o 2 functional disability assessed by the fatigue severity scale (FSS)

issues.title: Firm 'not effective' conclusion from 25 per arm with no efficacy tests or confidence intervals
issues.explanation: The paper states that no statistical tests were run apart from the primary outcome, and no effect sizes or intervals are reported for any efficacy outcome. It nonetheless says its findings 'demonstrate' TPE is not effective and that any effect is likely small. With 25 per arm and no estimates, absence of an observed difference is not evidence of absence. The safety finding is better supported than the efficacy conclusion, which should be read as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported between-group estimates with confidence intervals that exclude a clinically meaningful benefit.

quotes.text: Due to the exploratory aim of the study no statistical test were conducted with exception of the principal study outcome.
In conclusion, therapeutic plasma exchange is safe, but unlikely to improve the PCC.
Of note, at day 90, 10 (40%) participants in the placebo arm but only 6 (24%) in the TPE arm had improved to a PCFS score 1-2

second_reader.what_stands: With 25 per arm, the paper reports no p-values or confidence intervals for any efficacy outcome in the main text (the Methods state only one chi-square test, on PCFS at days 45 and 90). The Discussion and Results nonetheless use firm wording ('demonstrate... not effective', 'absolute lack of benefit'), and the nominal 24% vs 40% day-90 difference is described only as 'of note'. This is tempered by the explicit small-sample limitation, the exploratory framing, and the hedged final conclusion ('unlikely to improve'), and I could not check the figures or supplement for test results.

issues.title: Registered co-primaries (PCFS, FSS) described as secondary, though PCFS drove sample size and the only test
issues.explanation: The registry lists safety, PCFS-based and FSS-based functional proportions as primary outcomes. The paper declares safety the sole primary and treats functional status and fatigue as secondary. Yet the Methods say the sample size was set for the PCFS proportion and the only formal test was a chi-square on PCFS. The mismatch is undisclosed. Because the efficacy results are null, it does not make the treatment look better, but it blurs which outcome was the confirmatory one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registry versions showing only safety as primary at enrolment, or a protocol stating the PCFS/FSS outcomes were secondary from the start.

quotes.text: The primary endpoint of this trial was safety.
A sample size of 25 subjects per group was stabilished as the minimum necessary to analyse the difference in the proportion of subjects with functional disability 3 or 4 by the end of the study.

issues.title: Text calls administration-site AEs most common in TPE arm (41) but Table 2 lists nervous system disorders at 45
issues.explanation: The Safety text says local administration-site symptoms were the most common adverse events, with 41 (17.4%) in the TPE arm. Table 2 shows nervous system disorders at 45 (19.1%) in that same arm, which is higher. The statement holds only for the placebo arm. This is a small reporting error that does not change the safety conclusion, although it hides a slightly higher neurological AE count with TPE (45 vs 31).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 showing nervous system disorders below 41 in the TPE arm, or text restricting the statement to the placebo arm.

quotes.text: The most common AE reported were local symptoms at the administration site, accounting for 41 (17.4%) in the TPE arm

quotes.location: Table 2, Nervous system disorders row, TPE column

10.1038/s41467-025-59909-6.headline_claim: Remotely delivered Counterweight-Plus weight management is likely cost-effective for long COVID symptoms from an NHS/PSS perspective (ICER ~£14,754/QALY) and potentially cost-saving from a societal perspective.
10.1038/s41467-025-59909-6.overall: The NHS/PSS ICER arithmetic is internally consistent (740.11/0.0501644 = £14,754), and the cost-effectiveness finding is plausible for a 6-month within-trial analysis. It rests on an unblinded wait-list design with self-reported utilities and some unexplained inconsistency between Table 3 and Table 4 adjusted costs. The claims of societal cost-saving, dominance and readiness for implementation at scale are stronger than the data support, since the societal cost CI spans zero.

primary_outcome.name: Trial primary outcome: continuous symptom score for the participant-selected most important LC symptom (within-trial QALY/utility analysis reported here)

issues.title: Open-label wait-list trial: QALY gain of 0.050 rests on unblinded self-reported EQ-5D, with usual-care control
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation, and the control group received no programme and no attention-matched contact for 6 months. The QALY gain comes entirely from self-reported EQ-5D utilities, which are open to expectation and attention effects. The gain also narrowed between 3 and 6 months, as the paper's own description of Fig. 1a shows. The limitations section does not address this, yet the cost-effectiveness conclusion depends on this QALY difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis showing the cost-effectiveness result is robust to a substantially smaller QALY gain, or a discussion of expectation effects.

quotes.text: ReDIRECT was a wait-list RCT, with participants allocated in a 1:1 ratio at baseline to one of two groups: intervention or control
quotes.location: Methods, The main randomised controlled trial (ReDIRECT)

quotes.text: Participants allocated to the control arm received usual care and were given access to the weight management programme 6 months after baseline assessment.
quotes.location: Methods, The main randomised controlled trial (ReDIRECT)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper confirms a wait-list design with usual-care control and a QALY gain of about 0.050 based on participant-completed EQ-5D-5L, with no stated blinding and no discussion of bias from unblinded self-report. The word 'open-label' and the absence of blinding are inferred from the design, not stated by the authors.

issues.title: 'Cost-saving' and 'meets criteria for implementation' claimed despite societal cost CI -£2,282 to +£1,145
issues.explanation: The societal cost difference (-£568.50) has a 95% CI that includes zero, so cost saving is not demonstrated. Societal ICER's upper limit is £40,752/QALY, above the £30,000 threshold. The NHS/PSS ICER's upper limit is £59,951/QALY. Evidence covers only 6 months, relies on an unblinded self-reported QALY gain, and productivity losses are self-reported. Stating that the programme 'dominates' usual care and 'meets the health economic criteria for implementation at scale' is stronger than this evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longer-horizon modelled results, or a societal cost CI excluding zero.

quotes.text: In terms of decision-making, this weight management programme meets the health economic criteria for implementation at scale for people living with LC.
the intervention is predicted to become cost-saving, dominating usual care

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion and Conclusion state definitively that the intervention 'becomes cost-saving' and 'dominat[es] usual care' and 'meets the health economic criteria for implementation at scale', although the societal cost difference CI (-£2,282 to +£1,145) spans zero. The societal ICER's upper limit (£40,752/QALY) exceeds £30,000, and the INMB CIs span zero from both perspectives. The Results and abstract use more cautious wording ('may be', 'potentially', 74% probability), so the overstatement lies in the Discussion and Conclusion rather than the whole paper.

issues.title: Adjusted cost difference in Table 3 (-£502; total +£498) differs from text (-£264.35) and Table 4 (+£740)
issues.explanation: Table 3's adjusted healthcare resource use means (2744 control, 2242 intervention) imply a difference of -£502, while the Discussion gives -£264.35 and the Results give -£47.03 at 6 months. Table 3's adjusted NHS/PSS totals (2744 vs 3242) imply +£498, whereas Table 4 gives +£740.11. The -£264.35 is consistent with Table 4 (740.11 - 1000 = -259.89), so Table 3 appears to come from a different, unexplained adjustment. The headline ICER rests on Table 4, so this is a reporting inconsistency rather than an error in the ICER.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 3 adjusted values are complete-case or single-model estimates, with a reconciliation to the pooled SUR estimates.

quotes.text: an adjusted difference of the intervention group relative to control group of -£264.35
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph on healthcare resource use

issues.title: Missingness 1/354 control vs 36/348 intervention; MAR assumed without sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Almost all missing observations are in the intervention arm (about 10% of its observations against 0.3% in control). The imputation assumes data are missing at random and is not tested against missing-not-at-random scenarios. The overall missingness is small, so the effect is probably modest. Still, the differential pattern could bias the QALY and cost differences in either direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported MNAR or complete-case sensitivity analysis giving similar QALY and cost differences.

quotes.text: Data were assessed to be missing at random (MAR)

10.1038/s41467-025-64831-y.headline_claim: A just-in-time energy management app with activity tracking did not reduce post-exertional malaise versus control; the authors state the intervention was safe and feasible, and suggest the framework should be refined and tested in conditions without high recovery rates.
10.1038/s41467-025-64831-y.overall: The primary null result (no DSQ-PEM interaction, p = 0.614 per-protocol, 0.621 ITT) is reasonably consistent across analyses, but rests on completers below the target sample size and an ITT set smaller than stated. The 'equivalence', 'safe' and 'feasible' claims go beyond a superiority trial, and some secondary results in Table 2 appear duplicated. Treat the main finding as 'no difference detected' rather than demonstrated equivalence.

primary_outcome.name: DSQ-PEM sum score (questions 1-5, 100-point scale)

issues.title: ITT sensitivity analysis described as all 250 randomised but figures show N = 231, unexplained
issues.explanation: The Methods say the intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis covers all randomised participants, and 250 were randomised. Both ITT figure captions give N = 231, so 19 people are missing with no reason or flow count. The analysis is therefore a modified ITT, and the paper does not say how those 19 were handled. Because it is only a sensitivity check and agrees with the main result, the effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or CONSORT box showing that 231 is the number with at least one outcome record in the mixed model, with the 19 excluded accounted for.

quotes.text: In total, 250 participants were randomised (125 per group)
we conducted sensitivity analysis in the form of intention to treat analysis for all participants who were randomised

issues.title: Primary analysis is completers only (161/250, ~36% lost), below the 170 needed for the power calculation
issues.explanation: The primary analysis includes only participants who finished follow-up, and the paper's own ITT is labelled sensitivity. Attrition is about 36%, and 161 analysed is below the 170 required for 90% power. The ITT result agrees, which limits the concern, but the ITT used 231 rather than all 250, and the null conclusion still rests on a reduced and possibly selected sample. Null findings are best read as 'no difference detected' rather than evidence of no effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-registered statement that the per-protocol analysis was primary, together with a full-sample ITT analysis with the same estimate.

10.1038/s41467-026-75991-w.overall: The prespecified primary test was null (p=0.10), and the positive LVEF claim rests on a supportive ANCOVA with a 12% complete-case loss, so the conclusion should be read as tentative at best. Mechanistic and strategy statements go beyond what a neutral confirmatory result and uncorrected exploratory outcomes support.

issues.title: Conclusion reports an LVEF difference though prespecified primary t-test was null (diff 0.74, p=0.10)
issues.explanation: The prespecified confirmatory t-test did not reach significance (0.74 points, CI -0.14 to 1.62, p=0.10). The final conclusion nonetheless states a treatment-associated LVEF difference, relying on the supportive ANCOVA (0.99, p=0.021), and does not mention the null primary result there. Disclosure in the Discussion opening does not correct the conclusion's framing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statistical analysis plan naming ANCOVA as the confirmatory primary analysis.

second_reader.what_stands: The concluding sentence reports a 'modest treatment-associated difference in LVEF' and does not mention that the prespecified confirmatory t-test was non-significant (0.74 points, 95% CI -0.14 to 1.62, p = 0.10); the difference it describes comes from the supportive ANCOVA (0.99 points, p = 0.021). The paper does state the neutral primary result and the exploratory status of the interpretation clearly in the Results, Discussion and Limitations, and the wording is hedged, so the problem is the omission in the final sentence rather than a hidden or misreported result.

issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary sensitivity analyses (multiple imputation) giving the same primary estimate.

issues.title: Discussion says findings support a cardioprotective immunomodulatory strategy despite neutral primary test
issues.explanation: The Discussion first states mechanistic interpretation is exploratory, then says the functional and tissue changes support a targeted cardioprotective immunomodulatory strategy. This rests on the supportive ANCOVA, uncorrected secondary outcomes and subgroups, and many between-group secondary differences are not distinguishable from zero (e.g. T1, T2, perimyocardial enhancement). Support for mechanism or strategy is therefore not established by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy making the tissue-marker and ANCOVA results confirmatory.

quotes.text: supporting a targeted cardioprotective immunomodulatory strategy

issues.title: Volumes called 'increased' in Results but 'stable' in Discussion; between-group EDVI CIs include zero
issues.explanation: The Results state that end-diastolic volumes increased with intervention (LV-EDVI +2.13 ml/m2 within arm), whereas the Discussion says volumes stayed descriptively stable and uses this to argue preload does not explain the LVEF signal. The between-group differences (1.45 and 1.46 ml/m2) are about the same size as, and point the same way as, the LVEF effect, with CIs crossing zero, so a preload contribution is not excluded. The inconsistent wording weakens the argument that loading conditions do not explain the LVEF change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'stable' refers only to between-group differences, with a preload-adjusted analysis showing the LVEF effect persists.

10.1038/s41467-026-77925-y.headline_claim: AER002 was safe and well tolerated but did not produce a group-level benefit over placebo for Long COVID; exploratory analyses suggest greater drug exposure may be associated with response among participants with lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels.
10.1038/s41467-026-77925-y.overall: The central conclusion, that AER002 gave no detectable group-level benefit in this small exploratory trial, is reasonably supported but cannot be read as proof of no efficacy, given the low power and the baseline antibody imbalance that was not adjusted for. The responder, exposure-by-antibody and mechanistic (PET and proteomic) claims are post hoc or uncorrected and should be treated as hypothesis-generating only. Several count inconsistencies (placebo responders 9 vs 6, ENDOPAIN denominators, biopsy counts) need correction but do not change the main findings.

issues.title: Discussion infers biological effect on immune pathways from uncorrected PET (6 vs 4) and unadjusted proteomic signals
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the data suggest AER002 had a biological effect on inflammatory and immune-activation pathways. The PET comparisons (n=6 vs 4) used no multiplicity correction, with no within-arm longitudinal differences, and the Figure 7 legend calls them 'adjusted' while the Methods say they were not. The conclusion goes beyond the evidence and overstates a possible drug effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Multiplicity-corrected PET and proteomic results, or enrichment showing significant immune pathway changes.

issues.title: 'Not efficacious' stated in abstract from an n=36 trial with no sample-size calculation
issues.explanation: No sample-size justification is reported, and the authors concede power only for a large PHSS difference. The abstract nonetheless concludes the drug 'was not efficacious', while the day-90 PHSS difference of -4.1 (95% CI -8.6 to 0.47) is compatible with both no effect and a clinically relevant difference in either direction. The null result supports 'no large effect detected' rather than evidence of no efficacy. This reading understates any possible benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified power calculation or an interval excluding clinically meaningful benefit.

issues.title: Baseline anti-S/S1 antibody imbalance (placebo higher) not adjusted for, though called a strong predictor of improvement
issues.explanation: Placebo participants had higher baseline anti-S (median 124 vs 62.3, p=0.026) and anti-S1 antibodies. The authors then report these as strong predictors of improvement and suggest the imbalance may have masked a drug effect. The primary and secondary mixed models are not shown to adjust for it, so the between-arm comparison may be biased against AER002, and the null conclusion is less secure than it reads. issues.explanation: The abstract highlights that lower baseline antibody and higher drug exposure predicted perceived benefit, a result from unadjusted, post hoc dichotomised models in 36 people. PGIC is subjective and the placebo arm's response rate was higher (about 75%). Exposure in the placebo arm is essentially zero, so exposure effects are tangled with arm assignment. The Results describe the responder analyses as 'pre-specified' while the Methods call the exposure-by-antibody regression 'post-hoc'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registered or SAP-dated specification of the antibody-by-AUC interaction analysis with a multiplicity plan.

10.1038/s41591-024-03384-x.headline_claim: A remotely delivered structured weight management programme (850 kcal/day total diet replacement, then food reintroduction and maintenance) effectively reduces the long COVID symptoms that matter most to participants, and is safe and effective in people with long COVID and overweight.
10.1038/s41591-024-03384-x.overall: The trial reports a modest, nominally significant 6-month benefit on a self-reported, standardised composite symptom outcome, with a large and unambiguous weight-loss effect. Because the design is open-label, attrition was strongly differential and the primary estimate is borderline and below the powered target, the 'robust' and 'safe' conclusion is stronger than the evidence supports. The printing errors (swapped arm sizes in the abstract, a Table 2 SAE miscount) do not change the findings.

primary_outcome.name: Participant-nominated dominant long COVID symptom score (standardised change from baseline)

issues.title: Open-label wait-list trial with self-reported primary outcome; effect of -0.34 SD may reflect expectation
issues.explanation: Participants knew they were receiving an intensive programme and rated their own symptoms, while controls were waiting for the same programme. Such designs are prone to expectation and attention effects, and the primary difference is small and borderline. The weight-loss mediation analysis found no interaction, which does not help separate a specific from a non-specific effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of benefit on objective or blinded-assessed outcomes, or an attention-matched control showing similar effects.

quotes.text: Due to the nature of the diet intervention, participants, researchers and the dietitians who delivered the intervention were aware of group allocations.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with a wait-list control and a self-reported, patient-selected primary outcome, and the effect is -0.34 s.d. with a CI reaching -0.01, so non-specific effects such as expectation could contribute. The paper acknowledges unblinding and extra contact as a limitation but does not name expectation or reporting bias explicitly; the claim that the effect 'may reflect expectation' is plausible but cannot be shown from the paper, and the open-label design is an unavoidable feature of a diet trial rather than an undisclosed flaw.

issues.title: Conclusion claims 'robust' evidence and 'safe' on 16 SAEs and a borderline, unblinded primary result
issues.explanation: The study was powered for the primary outcome, not for safety; 16 serious events in total cannot establish the absence of excess harm, and two were judged related to the intervention. Calling the evidence 'robust' is hard to square with an open-label design, a primary CI reaching -0.01 and a complete-case analysis with imbalanced losses. No multiplicity adjustment was made for the secondary outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety analysis with confidence intervals excluding clinically important excess harm, and robust results to unblinded bias.

quotes.text: these results represent robust randomized trial evidence that remotely delivered dietary weight management
The intervention was safe, with no difference in reported SAEs.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does describe the evidence as 'robust' and the intervention as 'safe' on the basis of a primary result with P = 0.0466 and an upper CI bound of -0.01 in an unblinded trial with self-reported outcomes, differential attrition (19 vs 1 missing at 6 months), and sensitivity analyses in which two of three estimates have CIs including zero; the 16 SAEs (6 vs 10) show no excess but are too few to establish safety, and two gallstone events were attributed to the intervention. The wording is stronger than the data warrant, although the authors do discuss unblinding, extra contact and attritio

issues.title: Borderline primary effect (-0.34 SD, P = 0.0466) below the 0.5 SD target is framed as striking benefit
issues.explanation: The primary result is nominally significant, with the lower CI bound at -0.01 and an estimate smaller than the effect the trial was powered to detect. The attenuation from -0.90 at 3 months to -0.34 at 6 months and the loss of significance in positive-test-only analyses are disclosed but not reflected in the confident framing. Emphasis falls on secondary outcomes such as fatigue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified, defended minimal important difference at or below 0.34 SD and 12-month data confirming persistence.

quotes.text: The symptoms that matter most to individuals improved significantly, with striking improvements in physical and mental fatigue

issues.title: Primary outcome is a standardised, participant-nominated composite with no known clinically important difference
issues.explanation: Each participant's primary outcome is a different symptom scale, standardised to its own subgroup's baseline spread, and 17% used an unvalidated 10-point VAS. The authors acknowledge the measures have not been validated in long COVID and that clinical significance is hard to judge. This makes the size of the primary effect (-0.34 SD units) hard to interpret, though the approach was prespecified and is a reasonable innovation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation or an anchor-based minimal important difference for the standardised composite in long COVID.

issues.title: Complete-case primary analysis labelled ITT; 19/116 vs 1/118 lost by 6 months

Imputation and weighting reportedly give similar results, which mitigates but does not remove concern given the primary P of 0.0466.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Table 4 showing the imputed and weighted primary estimates with CIs excluding zero and a worst-case/tipping-point analysis.

10.1038/s41598-022-15565-0.headline_claim: HBOT improves neurocognitive functions and symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition, with brain perfusion and microstructural changes offered as the likely mechanism.
10.1038/s41598-022-15565-0.overall: The primary cognitive result (global score, p = 0.038) is modest and comes from a completers-only analysis of a small exploratory trial; several reporting inconsistencies exist (abstract N, swapped domain labels, one effect size). issues.explanation: The conclusion states that the benefit can be attributed to increased brain perfusion and neuroplasticity. The evidence is group-level imaging differences with partly uncorrected thresholds and a handful of correlations, without a mediation analysis or proof that the imaging changes preceded or explained the clinical change. issues.title: Attention/executive d and p swapped between text and Table 2; attention p=0.052 called significant
issues.explanation: The text gives attention d = 0.477, p = 0.04 and executive function d = 0.463, p = 0.05. Table 2 gives executive function 0.477 (p = 0.045) and attention 0.463 (p = 0.052). The labels are swapped, and as a result the attention interaction, which is not below the stated alpha of 0.05, is reported as significant. The claim of improved attention (and the abstract's list of significant domains) is therefore not supported at the declared threshold, and p = 0.045 for executive function is also borderline.

issues.explanation: The sample size was calculated from a healthy-adult study assuming a 4.4-point difference with SD 6.7, giving 74 completers, or 85 after allowing for dropout. The trial analysed 73 patients and the observed difference was smaller than assumed. The primary p = 0.038 is therefore a modest, near-threshold result in a small exploratory trial, yet the title and conclusion state that HBOT improves function without qualification.

issues.title: Only completers analysed (73 of 79 randomized); no ITT analysis despite efficacy conclusions
issues.explanation: All reported efficacy results are from the 73 patients who completed the protocol. issues.explanation: The Methods describe a Hochberg correction for the imaging, but the figure caption gives the voxelwise thresholds as uncorrected. The abstract nonetheless presents brain perfusion and microstructure changes as findings. For the clinical outcomes, a Bonferroni correction is declared yet many secondary results are described as significant at p = 0.04-0.05 (e.g. depression p = 0.04, sleep p = 0.042) with no adjusted threshold given. 10.1038/s41598-023-35058-y.headline_claim: The ReCOVery telerehabilitation app is reported as not significantly more effective than treatment as usual on quality of life, while regression models link app use time and self-efficacy/health literacy to improvements in several secondary outcomes.
10.1038/s41598-023-35058-y.overall: The randomised comparison shows no significant benefit of the app, and that null result is reliable apart from a few reporting slips. The abstract's conclusion that app use can contribute to recovery rests on exploratory, uncorrected regression models and is not supported by the trial design. issues.title: Abstract concludes the app 'can contribute to recovery' despite null primary result and exploratory regressions
issues.explanation: The randomised comparison found no benefit on quality of life or on any other outcome (and a nominally worse SF-36 physical result than control). The abstract's final conclusion nonetheless says significant use of the app can contribute to recovery, and its regression results are headlined ahead of the null result. The regressions cannot show that use produced benefit, so the conclusion goes beyond the evidence. The same emphasis on the secondary regression findings appears in the abstract's selection of results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion restricted to 'no benefit shown; exploratory associations in app users warrant testing'.

quotes.text: In conclusion, the significant use of ReCOVery APP can contribute to the recovery of Long COVID patients.
