The abstract is not silent on the null result, which it reports in an earlier sentence, and the wording is conditional on 'significant use'.

issues.title: Exploratory, uncorrected regressions on app minutes (intervention arm) used to claim app benefit
issues.explanation: Models of 3-month change on minutes of app use, self-efficacy, health literacy and other covariates cannot show that app use caused improvement, because use is self-selected and measured only in the intervention arm. Four to ten outcomes were modelled with several predictors each, at p < 0.05, with no correction. The significant paths (e.g. p = 0.036 and 0.021 in the PCSQ model) are of the kind that arise by chance, and the reported R² values are modest. The between-group randomised comparison showed no benefit. The regression results are hypothesis-generating only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Allocation-adjusted or pre-specified models with multiplicity control showing the associations survive.

quotes.text: The independent variables of age, gender, minutes of APP use, increase in self-efficacy, health literacy, and patient activation were introduced into the model.
However, linear regressions model identified significant models of improvement predicted by time of ReCOVery APP use

second_reader.what_stands: The app-use regressions are exploratory and have no stated multiplicity control. They come from a non-randomised dose-response comparison in a small subgroup, and the authors use them to support the view that the app could produce benefit and inform guidelines. The paper does label them as the secondary objective and states the null primary comparison. After a Bonferroni correction across about 9 outcomes, only the Sit-to-Stand association clearly survives.

issues.title: Text reports a 'significant decrease' in symptoms but the only p printed with it is 0.09
issues.explanation: The Results state that a significant decrease in persistent symptoms was found. The p-value quoted in the same sentence is 0.09, and it comes from the between-group comparison at 3 months. No within-group test supports the word 'significant'. The wording is therefore unsupported, although it concerns a secondary outcome only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A printed paired within-group test with p < 0.05 for the symptom count.

quotes.text: a significant decrease was found in the number of persistent symptoms
p -value: 0.09

issues.title: 17 of 52 intervention participants is 32.7%, but text, abstract and Discussion state 25%
issues.explanation: The paper says 17 participants in the intervention group (n = 52) used the app significantly and gives this as 25%. 17/52 is 32.7%. The count or the percentage is wrong, and the 25% is repeated as the adherence figure used to explain the null result. The adherence story is poor either way, so the impact is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of a different denominator (68 participants) or a corrected count of 13.

quotes.text: Only 17 participants (25%) from the intervention group engaged in significant use of the APP

script.explanation: 17/52 = 32.69%, but the paper prints 25, outside the rounding interval [24.50, 26.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 68.0 rather than 52.

issues.title: SF-36 physical at 3 months: p = 0.021 but CI (-16.30; 1.40) spans zero; text says no group differences
issues.explanation: Table 3 prints p = 0.021 for the 3-month SF-36 physical comparison, favouring the control group, yet the CI crosses zero. A difference of -8.5 with these SDs and the group sizes (45 and 42) gives a CI of about -15.7 to -1.3, so the printed interval is inconsistent with the p-value. The Results say there were no differences for the other variables and never mention this one, and the abstract reports only 'no significant differences in favour' of the intervention. A nominally significant primary-outcome difference favouring control is left out.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 3 and a statement that the 3-month physical difference was evaluated and handled in the text.

quotes.text: There were no differences between groups for the other variables.

quotes.location: Table 3, SF-36 Physical Health, 3 months row

script.explanation: the estimate -8.5 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-16.3, 1.4] (expected about -7.4500) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0598 (reachable range [0.0595, 0.0601] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.021 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller int

issues.title: Only per-protocol analysis of 87 of 100 randomised; no intention-to-treat analysis
issues.explanation: Thirteen randomised participants (7 intervention, 6 control) were dropped from all 3-month analyses. The authors describe the study as an effectiveness trial but report only a per-protocol analysis with no ITT or sensitivity analysis. The comparison is no longer fully randomised. The loss is small and balanced, so the effect on the null primary result is probably limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis giving the same conclusions.

quotes.text: To analyze the APP's effectiveness, a per-protocol analysis was performed
The 3-month evaluation was completed by 87 participants, 45 of which belonged to the intervention group and 42 to the control group.

issues.title: Table 2 control-arm gender counts (12 men + 33 women = 45) do not match N = 48 or the women total of 80
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives 80 women overall, but the arm counts 44 and 33 sum to 77. The control arm's 12 men and 33 women sum to 45, not 48. A control count of 36 women would reconcile everything, so one cell appears to be wrong. The error does not affect the main findings. The educational-level row also has an inconsistent percentage (47 of 52 is 90.4%, printed 94.4%).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 showing 36 control women, or a note that three control participants had missing gender.

quotes.text: of the 100 participants, 80 were female and 20 were male

issues.title: Registered 10/02/2022, after recruitment began in January 2022; timing vs randomisation not stated
issues.explanation: The ISRCTN registration date is given as 10/02/2022 while recruitment ran from January to March 2022. Whatever the date format, registration came after recruitment started, and possibly after the study ended. Whether this preceded randomisation and outcome assessment is not stated. The paper cites a published protocol, which partly mitigates the concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record showing registration before the first participant was randomised or a clarified date format and enrolment timeline.

quotes.text: This RCT was registered in the ISRCTN Registry platform (Registry No.: ISRCTN91104012) on 10/02/2022.
The recruitment time was 3 months, from January to March 2022

issues.title: Health literacy scale direction (higher = poorer) is not reconciled with 'increase in health literacy' predictor
issues.explanation: The Methods say higher HLS-EUQ16 scores mean poorer literacy, yet the Discussion and Table 4 speak of an 'increase in health literacy' lowering symptoms. If the raw score change was entered, the interpretation could be reversed. The paper does not say whether the score was reversed or how change was coded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that scores were reverse-coded or that the predictor is the change in the raw score with the stated sign convention.

quotes.text: Higher scores indicate poorer health literacy.
An increase in health literacy predicts a decrease in the number of persistent symptoms.

10.1038/s41598-023-35991-y.headline_claim: A 3-day micro-choice based group rehabilitation for long COVID is safe, highly acceptable, and produces rapid, sustained improvements in fatigue, function, sick leave and exercise capacity.
10.1038/s41598-023-35991-y.overall: The data show large within-person improvements after the programme, but with no control group and unblinded self-report outcomes the paper cannot show that the programme caused them, and 'effective' in the title goes further than the design allows. The numerical slips (mMRC p value, VO2peak % predicted label, abstract p < 0.001) are small and do not change the main results. Safety and durability claims are limited by sample size and a 3-month follow-up, and acceptability is not backed by a reported measure.

primary_outcome.name: CFQ-11 fatigue score at 3 months (paper does not label a primary outcome)

primary_outcomes.measure: Changes to cognitive and emotional perception of illness
Changes in level of patient activation

issues.title: Efficacy and causal attribution claimed from a single-arm, unblinded study with no control group
issues.explanation: All results are within-person changes from baseline, with no comparison arm and no blinding. The authors admit non-specific and attention effects cannot be excluded, yet the title calls the programme 'effective' and the Discussion attributes the improvement to the intervention. Excluding patients who improved while waiting, and the long symptom duration, address spontaneous recovery only partly and do not address expectancy or regression to the mean. The data show improvement after the programme, not that the programme caused it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waiting-list control group showing no comparable change, or the title and conclusions being worded as descriptive only.

quotes.text: Due to the lack of a control group, it is not possible to rule out that the treatment effect can be non-specific and due to attention.
the long duration of symptoms before the intervention makes it less likely that the rapid improvement was due to natural recovery and rather a result of the intervention.
A safe and effective micro-choice based rehabilitation for patients with long COVID

second_reader.what_stands: The study is single-arm and unblinded, and the title ('A safe and effective ... rehabilitation'), the Discussion ('rather a result of the intervention', 'evidence-based reason for hope') and the Conclusion ('yielded strong results') attribute efficacy and causation to the intervention. The paper does acknowledge in the abstract and in the Strengths and limitations section that it is quasi-experimental and that non-specific attention effects cannot be ruled out, and it excludes patients who improved while waiting, so the claim is not made without any caveat. However, the argument against natura

issues.title: Abstract gives p < 0.001 for sick leave and dyspnea; Results give p = 0.02 (sick leave) and 0.03/0.003 (mMRC)
issues.explanation: The abstract attaches p < 0.001 to the reduction in sick leave and dyspnea. In the Results the sick-leave reduction has p = 0.02, and the mMRC dyspnea change has p = 0.03 (text) or 0.003 (Table 3). Only Dyspnea-12 reaches p < 0.001. The abstract overstates the strength of evidence for the sick-leave result, though it remains significant at 0.05.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different, unstated analysis giving p < 0.001 for sick leave (e.g. in the fatigue subgroups) that the abstract is summarising.

quotes.text: Sick leave rates and dyspnea were reduced

quotes.location: Results, Changes in sick leave and functional level

issues.title: 'Safe' and 'sustaining over time' rest on 78 uncontrolled patients followed for only 3 months
issues.explanation: The conclusion says no safety issues were detected and the abstract says improvements were sustained over time. The paper does not describe how adverse events were collected, and 3 patients reported reduced function at some point. With 78 patients, rare harms cannot be excluded, and durability is shown only to 3 months. The wording is stronger than the data, though not unreasonable for a pilot-sized study.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified adverse-event monitoring procedure and longer follow-up data.

quotes.text: Micro-choice based concentrated rehabilitation for patients with long COVID was safe, highly acceptable and showed rapid improvements in fatigue and functional levels, sustaining over time.
No safety issues were detected.

issues.title: Registered primary outcomes (satisfaction, illness perception, activation) not reported; 'highly acceptable' unsupported
issues.explanation: The registry lists completion, satisfaction, illness perception and activation as primary outcomes. The paper centres on fatigue, sick leave, function, dyspnea and exercise capacity, and reports no satisfaction, illness-perception or activation data. The abstract nevertheless calls the programme 'highly acceptable' without a reported measure. Because the paper names no primary outcome, whether this is outcome switching or a separate publication from a broader project cannot be settled here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry version showing fatigue, sick leave and function as pre-specified outcomes for this long COVID cohort, or a separate report of satisfaction data.

quotes.text: The aims of the study were to assess safety, acceptability, potential changes in fatigue, sick leave, functional level, dyspnea, and exercise capacity
safe, highly acceptable and showed rapid improvements in fatigue and functional levels

issues.title: mMRC ≥1 change: Results text gives p = 0.03, Table 3 gives p = 0.003
issues.explanation: The Results give p = 0.03 for the fall in the proportion with mMRC ≥ 1 (69.7% to 57.7%). Table 3 prints 0.003 for the same Wilcoxon test. One of the two is wrong by a factor of ten. Both are below 0.05, so the significance conclusion for this outcome does not change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text p comes from a different analysis (e.g. a different test or population) than Table 3.

quotes.text: while at 3-month follow-up this was reduced to 57.7% (p = 0.03)
quotes.location: Results, Changes in dyspnea, lung function and exercise capacity

issues.title: About 15 outcomes tested at α = 0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment; a few results are marginal
issues.explanation: Many outcomes are tested at two time points without correction. Most are highly significant and would survive adjustment. A handful of secondary results (exercise time p = 0.032, leg discomfort p = 0.043) would not, and the paper does not mark them as exploratory. This weakens secondary claims only slightly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome and hierarchy, or labelling of the remaining outcomes as exploratory.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05.
the results were highly significant and consistent across a number of subjective assessments of symptoms and function and objective tests examining exercise capacity.

issues.title: Text gives baseline VO2peak per kg as 92 (17)% predicted; Table 3 gives 84 (15)%
issues.explanation: The Results attribute 92 (17)% of predicted to VO2peak per kg. In Table 3 that value belongs to absolute VO2peak (mL/min, % predicted), and the per-kg row reads 84 (15). The text therefore overstates baseline per-kg capacity and supports the claim that baseline values were within the normal range. The error is small and affects no test result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 92 (17) figure was intended for the mL/min measure, with the text label a simple slip, would reduce this to a labelling error with no further effect.

quotes.text: a mean ˙ V O2peak kg -1 of 92 (17) % of predicted value
quotes.location: Results, Changes in dyspnea, lung function and exercise capacity

10.1038/s41598-023-36570-x.headline_claim: HBOT promotes cardiac systolic function recovery in patients with post-COVID-19 condition.
10.1038/s41598-023-36570-x.overall: The headline claim that HBOT promotes cardiac systolic recovery is not supported by the prespecified whole-sample comparison (interaction p=0.237) and rests on a post hoc subgroup of 29 patients with one nominal p=0.041 and no multiplicity control. GLS is also labelled primary here although the trial's registered and stated primary outcome is cognitive function. The finding is best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Global longitudinal strain (GLS)

issues.title: Abstract and conclusion rest on a post hoc subgroup (n=16 vs 13, p=0.041); whole-sample p=0.237 omitted
issues.explanation: The abstract reports the post hoc subgroup with reduced baseline GLS (16 HBOT, 13 sham) and its interaction p=0.041, and leaves out the whole-sample interaction (p=0.237). The conclusion that HBOT promotes systolic recovery relies on this one nominal subgroup result, with no multiplicity correction across GLS, GWI, GCW, GWW and GWE or across the two analysis sets. Two of the other Table 4 tests are unreliable (see new issue). The subgroup claim is hypothesis-generating at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified subgroup analysis plan with multiplicity control, or a significant interaction in the full sample.

quotes.text: Compared to the sham group, GLS significantly increased following HBOT
defined as lower than - 20% (Table 4).
HBOT promotes cardiac systolic function recovery in patients suffering from the post-COVID-19 condition.

second_reader.what_stands: The headline claim in the abstract and the unqualified conclusion rest on a post-hoc subgroup (n=16 vs 13, interaction p=0.041), while the whole-sample interaction (p=0.237) is not reported in the abstract. The conclusion that HBOT promotes cardiac systolic function recovery is therefore stronger than the prespecified whole-sample comparison supports; the subgroup result is exploratory and subject to regression to the mean and multiplicity, and the abstract does disclose the reduced-GLS subgroup size but not the null whole-sample interaction.

issues.title: Whole-sample GLS benefit vs sham claimed from within-arm change (p=0.01 vs 0.27); interaction p=0.237
issues.explanation: In the full sample, GLS changed from -19.1 to -20.4 with HBOT (p=0.01) and from -19.5 to -20.0 with sham (p=0.27). The direct between-group test (group-by-time interaction) is not significant, p=0.237. The Discussion nonetheless says GLS was significantly improved by HBOT and exceeded the natural recovery in sham. A significant change in one arm and a non-significant change in the other is not evidence of a difference between arms. The sham arm also moved in the same direction by 0.5 points.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant prespecified between-group test of GLS change in the full sample.

quotes.text: The net effect size was 0.268, and the mixed model analysis was not significant ( p =  0.237) (Table 3).
In the current study, GLS significantly improved following HBOT, compared to the sham protocol.
This recovery in GLS by HBOT exceeded the natural recovery rate observed in the sham group.

second_reader.what_stands: The Results report a non-significant group-by-time interaction for GLS in the whole sample (p=0.237), yet the Discussion states GLS 'significantly improved following HBOT, compared to the sham protocol' and that recovery 'exceeded the natural recovery rate observed in the sham group'. These claims rest on the within-arm contrast (p=0.01 vs p=0.27), which does not test a between-arm difference, so the whole-sample comparative claim is not supported by the paper's own interaction test.

issues.title: Abstract says 60 randomized; Results show 79 randomized and 60 analysed (19 lost)
issues.explanation: The abstract says sixty patients were randomized. The Results say 79 were randomized and only 60 echocardiograms entered the final analysis. The cascade adds up, so the abstract gives the analysed number as the randomized number and hides the 19 post-randomization losses (about 24%).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; the abstract's 'randomized' count conflicts with the Results unless the abstract states it refers to analysed patients.

quotes.text: Sixty patients were randomized to receive
Thus, 79 patients were randomized to either HBOT or sham arms.

issues.title: No GLS power calculation; analysed n=30 per arm and 16 vs 13 in the subgroup, with a confident conclusion
issues.explanation: The sample size is said to be defined in an earlier publication, so adequacy for GLS cannot be checked here. The authors acknowledge the small sample, but the conclusion that HBOT promotes recovery is not tempered accordingly. This compounds the weakness in c8 and c9 rather than standing alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The earlier publication's power calculation showing adequate power for GLS.

quotes.text: A sample size for this study was defined   previously 20.
The main limitation lies in the relatively small sample size.

issues.title: 19 of 79 randomized (24%) not analysed; completers only, handling of missing data not described
issues.explanation: Of 79 randomized patients, 60 had analysable echocardiograms. Reasons include withdrawals, missed assessments, files not transferred and one poor-quality exam per group. Losses are similar across arms, so the bias is probably small, but no sensitivity analysis or missing-data method is described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the mixed model used all available data or an ITT sensitivity analysis giving the same result.

quotes.text: Figure 1 shows the echocardiography examinations of the 30 patients from HBOT and the 30 patients from the sham group that were included in the final analysis.

issues.title: Table 4: identical F=4.585 with p=0.530 and p=0.053; HBOT GWI change 43.8 vs 173.8 from means
issues.explanation: In Table 4, GCW and GWW both print F=4.585, but p=0.530 for one and p=0.053 for the other. The same F with the same degrees of freedom (about 1 and 27) must give the same p, and F=4.585 corresponds to roughly p=0.04. Also, the HBOT GWI change is printed as 43.8, but 2022.6 - 1848.8 = 173.8. These slips do not touch the GLS result, but they show the subgroup table cannot be taken at face value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or supplement showing the intended values.

issues.title: GLS labelled 'primary' here, but the registered and stated trial primary is cognitive function
issues.explanation: The Methods say the trial's primary endpoint was cognitive function, reported in a first publication. The same Methods then list GLS as the primary outcome. The registry lists only NeuroTrax cognitive health as primary. GLS therefore appears to be a secondary or exploratory outcome for the trial, and the 'primary outcome' label overstates its prespecified status. The registry record is the current version only, so earlier changes cannot be checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version showing GLS prespecified as a primary or key outcome with an analysis plan.

quotes.text: The primary end point of this clinical trial was cognitive function which was reported in the first publication
Primary  outcomes-Global  Longitudinal  Strain.

10.1038/s41598-023-45072-9.headline_claim: SSRIs contribute significantly to reduction of post-Covid symptoms in PCS patients, with brainfog and sensory overload improving most, though the authors state this is an exploratory uncontrolled study and a placebo effect cannot be ruled out.
10.1038/s41598-023-45072-9.overall: The study shows that self-reported scores improved in patients who chose to take SSRIs, but the uncontrolled, open-label, self-reported design cannot support the causal and mechanistic conclusions drawn. Numeric slips (93 vs 95 denominators, ratio 1:5.8) are minor; the abstract's 10% is an extraction artefact and matches 9.5%. The headline should be read as a hypothesis-generating signal only.

primary_outcome.name: Not pre-specified; three outcome measures (open question outcomes, Score List, Bell score) reported with no designated primary

issues.title: Causal efficacy claimed from an uncontrolled, open-label before-after cohort of self-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: All benefit estimates are within-patient changes (before vs after, with huge Bayes factors such as 9.6 × 10^17), with no control arm, no blinding and self-reported outcomes. These tests show that scores changed, not that the SSRI caused the change; placebo, expectancy, regression to the mean and natural recovery are not separated. The Bell baseline was completed retrospectively, and baselines for 61 patients were reconstructed after they had already started treatment. The Discussion says the study 'shows' the SSRI contributes significantly to symptom reduction, which this design cannot establish.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo comparison group, or conclusions limited to describing within-patient change without causal wording.

quotes.text: We had no control group. Therefore, a placebo effect cannot be ruled out.
quotes.location: Discussion, Strength and weakness of the study

quotes.text: show that an SSRI contributes significantly to the reduction of PCS symptoms
Working with self-reporting is always vulnerable to biases.
quotes.location: Discussion, Strength and weakness of the study

second_reader.what_stands: The design is an uncontrolled, open-label, self-reported before-after cohort (with baseline reconstructed retrospectively for about two-thirds of patients), yet the Discussion states that an SSRI 'contributes significantly' to symptom reduction, which is a causal efficacy claim. The authors do acknowledge the lack of a control group, placebo, natural recovery and self-report bias, so the limitation is disclosed; the problem is the mismatch between that disclosure and the unhedged causal wording.

issues.title: Conclusion claims clinical evidence for five neurobiological mechanisms from a questionnaire without biomarkers
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says clinical evidence for five of seven mechanisms (HPA axis, brain stem, ANS, CNS, circulation) was found in this study. The data are self-reported symptom scores and anecdotes, with no cortisol, coagulation, kynurenine or cytokine measures. Symptom improvement cannot show which biological pathway is responsible. This goes beyond even the already uncontrolled efficacy evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Biomarker or physiological measurements in this cohort linking SSRI response to the proposed mechanisms.

quotes.text: Clinical evidence for five of the seven possible explanatory mechanisms of an SSRI in PCS were found in this study.
this treatment can contribute to considerable reduction of symptoms, especially brainfog and sensory overload.

second_reader.what_stands: The study measured only self-reported symptoms and functioning, with no biomarkers, so it cannot provide clinical evidence for specific neurobiological mechanisms; the Conclusion's claim that evidence for five of seven mechanisms was 'found' overstates what a symptom questionnaire can show. The Discussion's mechanism sections are mostly hedged as hypotheses, and the authors recognise the need for biomarkers, so the overstatement is mainly in the Conclusion wording.

issues.title: Outcomes are an ad hoc open-question rating, an unvalidated Bell score and a custom 8-item list
issues.explanation: The 63.4% response figure rests on a rating guideline developed for this study, and the Bell score is acknowledged as not validated. The authors argue their strong mutual correlation supports reliability, but correlated self-reports share the same expectancy and recall biases. The Bell score baseline was asked retrospectively. Missing score list (18) and Bell (15) data further restrict those analyses to completers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Validation evidence for the rating guideline and Bell score in PCS, or blinded objective outcome data.

quotes.text: We developed a guideline for rating the answers to this Open question outcomes.
The Bell score is a widely used instrument in research on (chronic) fatigue, although not validated.
quotes.location: Discussion, Strength and weakness of the study

issues.title: 63.4% response is attached to n = 93 in Results but n = 95 in Discussion; 59/95 would be 62.1%
issues.explanation: The Results and Table 2 base the 63.4% response on the 93 patients who answered the open question (25+27+7 = 59 responders in categories 2-4). The Discussion attaches the same 63.4% to all 95 patients, which is not the denominator that produces it. This is a labelling slip that slightly changes how the headline figure reads. The two missing responders are not counted as non-responders anywhere.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two additional patients also responded, giving 60/95 = 63.2%, or a corrected Discussion denominator.

quotes.text: 63.4% of patients (n = 93) reported decrease in symptoms after treatment with an SSRI
63.4% (n = 95) of patients reported a reasonably good to strong decrease in symptoms

issues.title: Comorbidity '80%, n = 93' fits 76/95, not 76/93 (81.7%)
issues.explanation: The text says 76 patients (80%, n = 93) had comorbidity. 76/93 is 81.7%, but 76/95 is exactly 80.0%, so the denominator label looks wrong. This is the same kind of 93 vs 95 labelling inconsistency seen for the response rate. It is a minor descriptive slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that comorbidity data were missing for 2 patients with a different count.

quotes.text: 76 patients (80%, n = 93) had comorbidity

script.explanation: 76/93 = 81.72%, but the paper prints 80, outside the rounding interval [79.50, 81.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 95.0 rather than 93.

issues.title: Male-female ratio 1:5.8 in text vs 80 women/15 men (1:5.3) in Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results give a male-female ratio of 1:5.8, but the Table 2 gender row gives 80 women and 15 men. That is 1:5.3. A ratio of 1:5.8 matches no subset of counts printed in the paper. It affects only a descriptive statistic.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated different denominator or sample for which the ratio is 1:5.8.

quotes.text: male-female ratio 1:5.8
Gender (f/m)80/15

10.1038/s41598-024-51904-z.headline_claim: Amantadine reduces post-COVID-19 fatigue and is safe and tolerable over two weeks of treatment.
10.1038/s41598-024-51904-z.overall: The direction of the result (lower self-reported fatigue scores in the amantadine arm) is plausible but cannot be attributed to the drug with confidence, because the trial was open-label with no-treatment controls and fully subjective outcomes. There are also internal numerical inconsistencies (the mislabelled SDs in Table 1, the unreproducible baseline VAFS p-value, and the 'less than half' claim for FSS) that weaken confidence in the reporting. The safety claim is stronger than a 30-patient, two-week study can support.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) and Visual Analog Fatigue Scale (VAFS) change over two weeks

issues.title: Open-label, no-treatment control with only self-reported fatigue scales; drug effect confounded with expectation
issues.explanation: Both primary outcomes are self-rated, participants and examiners knew the allocation, and the controls got neither placebo nor any substitute. Part or all of the large between-group difference (VAFS drop 4.53 vs 1.37) could reflect expectation or reporting bias. The authors acknowledge this in the limitations but still conclude a substantial, favourable effect, so the effect is best read as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An objective outcome or a blinded, placebo-controlled replication showing the same effect size.

quotes.text: The study was designed open-labeled; Therefore, all the participants and examiners knew the treatment allocation.
the control group received no treatment
This study was not doubleblinded, and we did not use a placebo for the control group.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with a no-treatment (not placebo) control, and both primary outcomes are patient-reported fatigue scales, so the drug effect cannot be separated from expectation or placebo response. The authors acknowledge this in the limitations and recommend a double-blind trial, but the Abstract and Conclusion still state a causal, 'substantial' drug benefit without that caveat.

issues.title: Safety/tolerability claimed from 30 treated patients over 2 weeks, with a severe-AE dropout excluded from analysis
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the results reveal the safety and tolerability of the treatment. Yet one of 33 randomized amantadine patients withdrew for severe nausea and abdominal pain and was excluded from the analysis, and no adverse-event data were collected in controls. The study also had no follow-up past two weeks. A cautious statement of short-term tolerability would fit; a general safety claim does not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified safety analysis including all randomized patients and a comparison with the control arm.

quotes.text: Our results reveal the safety and tolerability of two-weeks treatment with Amantadine in post-COVID-19 patients.
All reported side effects were transient and tolerable for patients, except for one who stopped taking the drug due to severe nausea and abdominal pain

issues.title: Table 1 age/BMI group 'SDs' (1.52, 1.68; 0.75, 0.82) are incompatible with totals 8.98 and 4.43; p<0.0001 doubtful
issues.explanation: The total age SD (8.98) and BMI SD (4.43) are 4 to 6 times the group SDs, which is arithmetically impossible for a pooled sample whose group means differ by only about 2 years or 1.5 kg/m2. The group values behave like standard errors. Treating them as SDs gives the printed p < 0.0001 for age and BMI, but treating them as SEs gives p about 0.3 and 0.17. The reported baseline age and BMI imbalance, and the authors' limitation built on it, are therefore probably an artefact of the mislabelling.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw age/BMI data showing group SDs of about 1.5 (which would contradict the total SD of 8.98) or a correction to Table 1.

issues.title: Baseline VAFS p = 0.087 does not match means/SDs 7.90 ± 0.60 vs 7.34 ± 0.58 (t about 3.7, p < 0.001)
issues.explanation: On the printed summary values the baseline VAFS groups differ markedly, with the amantadine group starting higher. That is incompatible with the claim of no significant baseline difference. The same SDs reproduce the FSS baseline p, so the discrepancy is specific to VAFS. If the printed SDs are right, the arms were imbalanced at baseline and the VAFS change comparison is unadjusted for it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw VAFS data or a stated non-parametric test that yields p = 0.087 for these groups.

quotes.location: Table 2, VAFS, Amantadine group, Before treatment
Table 2, VAFS, Control group, Before treatment

quotes.text: were not different from each other significantly ( P -value = 0.087, and P -value = 0.053, respectively)

issues.title: Discussion says both scales fell below half of baseline, but FSS fell only to 53.5% (53.10 to 28.40)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the FSS and VAFS averages both reached less than half their initial value. This holds for VAFS but not for FSS, where the amantadine group fell by 46.4%. The error is a modest overstatement of the size of the effect and does not change the direction of the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'average of both' refers to a pooled or relative measure that actually falls below 50% for FSS, which the printed means do not support.

quotes.text: since the average of both reached less than half of the initial value after two weeks of treatment with Amantadine.

quotes.location: Table 2, FSS, Amantadine group, After treatment

issues.title: Peripheral edema printed as 0.03% (1) in a group of 30; one patient is 3.33%
issues.explanation: Table 3 gives 0.03% for one patient with peripheral edema, but one of 30 patients is 3.33%. The other rows use the correct n = 30 denominator, so this is a transcription error in one cell. It changes no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for edema (about 3,333 patients), which is impossible here.

script.explanation: 1/30 = 3.33%, but the paper prints 0.03, outside the rounding interval [0.02, 0.04]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 3333.3 rather than 30.

issues.title: Allocation concealment not described; 'simple randomization' only, and reported imbalance rests on suspect Table 1
issues.explanation: The paper gives no sequence-generation or concealment procedure, so allocation integrity cannot be checked in an open-label trial. The authors attribute age and BMI imbalance to simple randomization, but that imbalance depends on group dispersion values that look mislabelled (c3). The concern is therefore mainly about under-reporting of the randomization procedure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry describing a concealed allocation sequence.

quotes.text: using simple randomization with a 1:1 ratio
due to the simple randomization method that we used for allocating patients some features including age and BMI were not statistically similar in both groups.

10.1038/s41598-024-52763-4.headline_claim: Active prefrontal (DLPFC) tDCS was not superior to sham tDCS for fatigue, neuropsychiatric symptoms, anxiety, depression, quality of life or cognition in long COVID.
10.1038/s41598-024-52763-4.overall: The paper reports a small, unpowered trial with no detectable difference between active and sham tDCS, and the numeric errors found are minor typos that change no result. The 'true negative' framing in the Discussion goes beyond what a 33-patient trial with a very wide CI and a baseline imbalance favouring sham can support. The null finding is better read as inconclusive.

primary_outcome.name: Change in FIS total score from baseline to end of treatment (week 4)

issues.title: Unpowered n=33 trial concludes results are 'true negatives'; primary CI -11.1 to 34.5 is wide
issues.explanation: No sample size calculation was done, and 33 patients were analysed. The Discussion nonetheless says the data 'reflect true negative results rather than false negatives', leaning on a Bayes factor of 0.163 whose prior is not given. The primary between-group CI is very wide and includes differences in favour of active tDCS. The data show no detectable effect, not evidence that tDCS does not work.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified equivalence margin or Bayes factor prior, with a CI excluding clinically meaningful benefit.

quotes.text: Therefore, we believe our data reflect true negative results rather than false negatives.
At the time of study design, we could not rely on any RCT with this clinical population to estimate the sample size needed for the expected outcome
The Bayesian factor (BF10 = 0.163) for the primary outcome (FIS total score) suggests that the observed data are about 6.12 times more likely under the null hypothesis

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is small (n=33, no sample size calculation reported) and the primary CI (-11.1 to 34.5, width about 45.7 points) is wide and compatible with both a meaningful benefit and no effect, so the claim that the data 'reflect true negative results rather than false negatives' is stronger than the data and the paper's own limitations support. The paper does, however, acknowledge the small sample in its abstract and conclusion and the BF arithmetic is internally consistent (1/0.163 ≈ 6.1), so the problem is the overstated Discussion sentence and the unreported Bayes factor prior, not a hidden

issues.title: Baseline FIS total 101.6 (sham) vs 77.2 (active), p=0.01; covariate-adjusted but still favours sham
issues.explanation: The sham arm began with much more fatigue than the active arm in the primary outcome. The authors acknowledge this and adjusted for baseline score in the model, so it is not undisclosed or unaddressed. Greater regression to the mean in the higher-baseline group may still have favoured sham. This weakens the 'true negative' reading of the primary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis showing the treatment estimate is unchanged when restricted to participants with overlapping baseline FIS ranges.

quotes.text: The main limitation of our study was the differences in baseline FIS scores between the active and sham groups.
baseline score, age, BMI, PASC duration, depression (PHQ-9), and anxiety (GAD 7) as covariates

issues.title: Sham A-PASC change CI lower bound: text -26.7 vs Table 2 -28.65 (text interval not centred on -16.6)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the sham-arm A-PASC change as -16.6 with a 95% CI of -26.7 to -4.6. Table 2 gives the same estimate with a CI of -28.65 to -4.55. Only the table interval is symmetric around the estimate, so the text lower bound is most likely a typing error. No conclusion depends on it, since the interval excludes zero either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or the raw output showing the sham interval really is -26.7 to -4.6 with an estimate other than -16.6.

quotes.location: Table 2, A-PASC Total row, sham V0-V2 column

issues.title: Table 1 lists 5 mild COVID-19 cases per arm (10 of 33) despite 'moderate or severe' eligibility
issues.explanation: The Methods say participants needed a history of moderate or severe COVID-19. Table 1 shows 5 mild cases in each arm, 10 of 33 in total. This is either a protocol deviation or an inconsistent definition of severity. The table's '2002' entries are garbled and should read 3 severe cases per arm. The trial's null result does not hinge on this, but the sample did not match the stated eligibility.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that severity was classified differently from the eligibility wording (for example by acute-phase care versus a later rating), or that the Table 1 'mild' column is mislabelled.

quotes.text: with a history of moderate or severe COVID-19 infection
The severity of COVID-19: mild/moderate/severe 5/8/2002 5/9/2002 0.99

issues.title: Table 2 physical FIS active change at FU-4W printed -4.58 but its CI implies -4.50
issues.explanation: The printed active and sham changes (-4.58 and -4.93) differ by 0.35, not the printed 0.43. The active interval -9.38 to 0.38 is centred on -4.50, which reproduces 0.43. So one cell, the active estimate, appears to be mistyped. The error is small, and the between-group difference stays nonsignificant either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw model output showing an active LS mean of -4.58 with an asymmetric CI and a 0.35 difference.

quotes.location: Table 2, FIS physical row, active V0-V3
Table 2, FIS physical row, active vs sham V0-V3

issues.title: Screening reported to May 2023 but recruitment stated to end March 2023
issues.explanation: The Results say 71 patients were screened from April 2022 to May 2023. The Methods say recruitment ran from March 2022 to March 2023. Screening runs two months past the stated recruitment end. It is unclear whether this is a loose use of the word recruitment or a date slip. It has no bearing on the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that screening of non-eligible patients continued after enrolment closed, or that the May 2023 date is a typo.

quotes.text: Seventy-one patients were screened for eligibility between April 2022 and May 2023
Recruitment for the study ran from March 2022 to March 2023.

10.1038/s41598-024-53091-3.headline_claim: HBOT improves quality of life, sleep quality, psychiatric and pain symptoms in long COVID patients, and these improvements persist about one year after the last HBOT session.
10.1038/s41598-024-53091-3.overall: The short-term improvements come from the earlier sham-controlled RCT, but this follow-up has no comparator and relies on self-reported questionnaires in an unblinded cohort, so the 'lasting effect' conclusion is only tentatively supported. Persistence is argued from non-significant tests in 31 patients, and permanence and mechanism are overstated. The text also contains several printing errors against Table 2: effect sizes, PSQI p-values and one percentage.

primary_outcome.name: No primary outcome named in the paper; SF-36, PSQI, BSI-18 and BPI are all reported

issues.title: Lasting-effect claim rests on an HBOT-only, unblinded, self-reported follow-up with no control group
issues.explanation: Only the 31 HBOT completers were followed, and the sham group was largely crossed over to HBOT (27/39), so there is no comparator at 1 year. All outcomes are self-completed questionnaires from participants who know they were treated. Persistence is shown only as no significant change between the short-term and long-term scores of the same people. Natural recovery of long COVID, expectancy and response bias cannot be separated from a lasting treatment effect. The 'RCT' label in the title overstates what this analysis can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent, blinded control group followed to 1 year, or objective outcome data showing the benefit beyond what natural recovery would produce.

quotes.text: they could not serve as a proper control group for the current study.
The current long term evaluation confirms that the new protocols of HBOT has an effective lasting effect on long covid patients more than 1 year after their treatment.

second_reader.what_stands: The lasting-effect claim rests on 31 HBOT-treated patients with no control group at long term and only self-reported questionnaires with no described blinding. The authors acknowledge the missing sham comparison in the limitations. The discussion and conclusion nonetheless say the follow-up 'confirms' an 'effective lasting effect' and 'permanent' changes. What the data support is narrower: scores after HBOT did not significantly change between 1-3 weeks and about 16 months, with no comparator to separate treatment effect from natural recovery, expectation or regression to the mean. The paper d

issues.title: Discussion calls the changes 'permanent' and 'brain injury recovery' with no imaging at follow-up
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the findings reinforce that these are permanent changes driven by constant microstructural changes, i.e. brain injury recovery. This follow-up has only questionnaires at about 16 months (486 ± 73 days), with no imaging or objective measures. Permanence and a structural mechanism cannot be inferred. The wording presents speculation as if it were established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longitudinal imaging or objective measures at follow-up that track with the symptom changes.

quotes.text: these are permanent changes driven by constant microstructural changes

issues.title: Results text effect sizes for physical functioning, limitations and pain disagree with Table 2 (e.g. 10.73)
issues.explanation: The SF-36 paragraph gives ES1/ES2 as 0.59/0.16 (physical functioning), 1.08/10.73 (physical limitations) and 0.86/0.62 (pain). Table 2 gives short-term/long-term values of 0.16/0.59, 0.73/1.08 and 0.62/0.86. Two pairs are swapped and the physical limitations pair is garbled, with a value of 10.73 that appears nowhere in the table. The table's ES long-term column also looks like long term versus baseline (e.g. pain 4.59/22.57 = 0.20 does not give 0.86), although the caption defines ES2 as long term versus short term. The text, table and caption therefore use ES labels inconsistently. The error is confined to this passage and does not change the table's own conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or supplementary table showing the text values are correct and Table 2 columns are mislabelled, with 10.73 explained.

quotes.text: ES1 = 0.86 vs ES2 = 0.62, respectively, Table 2

issues.title: Text gives p1 < 0.001 for five PSQI items; Table 2 shows 0.013, 0.002 and 0.007 for three of them
issues.explanation: The Results say short-term improvement in global score, sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbances and daytime dysfunction all had p1 < 0.001. In Table 2, sleep quality has p1 = 0.013 (corrected 0.052), sleep disturbances 0.002 and daytime dysfunction 0.007. Sleep quality is not significant after the Bonferroni correction the authors declare. The abstract's claim of improvement 'across five sleep domains' is therefore stronger than the table supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source output showing p1 < 0.001 for these domains and the table values being a different contrast.

quotes.text: including the global score, sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbances, and daytime dysfunction (p1 < 0.001)

issues.title: Persistence inferred from non-significant paired tests (n = 31); text says p2 > 0.5 but Table 2 has 0.14
issues.explanation: Persistence is concluded because short-to-long-term changes were not statistically significant, with no confidence intervals or equivalence test. With 31 patients, a non-significant test is weak evidence of no change. Some uncorrected p2 values are small: physical functioning 0.014 and physical limitations 0.044. The BSI-18 text says p2 > 0.5, but Table 2 gives 0.32, 0.37 and 0.14. The near-zero mean changes make approximate maintenance plausible, but 'no difference' is stated more firmly than the analysis allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pre-specified equivalence margins with confidence intervals for long-minus-short change lying inside them.

quotes.text: long term scores were not statistically different from the beneficial effects evaluated 1-3 weeks after HBOT

issues.title: Completer-only follow-up: 6/37 (16%) declined; 31/40 (77.5%) of allocated HBOT patients analysed
issues.explanation: Only patients with both short-term and long-term data were analysed. The authors compared baseline characteristics but not short-term outcomes of completers versus decliners. If decliners responded less well, persistence could be overstated. The loss is moderate and the baseline comparison is reassuring, so the effect on conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Short-term outcomes of the six decliners being similar to those of the 31 analysed.

quotes.text: Of those, six declined their participation in long term evaluation.

issues.title: Table 1 long-term column prints 1 (2.7%) for chronic neurological disease; 1/31 = 3.2%
issues.explanation: In the long-term cohort (n = 31) one patient with chronic neurological disease should be 3.2%. The printed 2.7% equals the 37-patient column's figure. The diabetes row, with the same count, prints 3.2. Nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the denominator for this cell was 37.

quotes.text: Chronic neurological impairment\disease

script.explanation: 1/31 = 3.23%, but the paper prints 2.7, outside the rounding interval [2.65, 2.80]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 37.0 rather than 31.

10.1038/s41598-024-61827-4.headline_claim: A decentralised clinical trial platform can technically conduct most study procedures needed to evaluate non-pharmacological interventions for Long COVID, but recruitment, imposter participants and attrition threaten a fully powered trial.
10.1038/s41598-024-61827-4.overall: The feasibility conclusion is cautious and mostly supported by the descriptive data: limited recruitment, imposter participants and high attrition are reported openly. The issues found are small (a one-participant difference in week 12 counts, a 'reasonable use' claim resting on 28 responders, and an over-worded recruitment statement). None changes the main conclusion that a fully powered decentralised trial should not proceed without mitigation.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility outcomes (ability to achieve the recruitment target, retention and attrition, data completeness); no between-group efficacy outcome reported

issues.title: 'Reasonable levels of use' rests on 28 of 85 randomised (33%) who answered the feasibility questionnaire
issues.explanation: Intervention use was measured only in the 28 participants who completed the Week 12 questionnaire, a group likely to be more engaged than the roughly two-thirds who did not respond. The Discussion nonetheless says the interventions were delivered with reasonable use. Use was lowest in the app arm, and interviewees said they used the interventions mainly in the first 2 to 3 weeks. The claim therefore overstates what the data show about engagement in the whole randomised sample, though the headline feasibility conclusion does not depend on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Usage data (for example platform logs or delivery records) covering all randomised participants and showing similar levels of use.

quotes.text: Furthermore, the study interventions were delivered successfully to study participants with reasonable levels of use following treatment allocation.

The feasibility questionnaire was completed by 28 participants at Week 12 and showed that most of participants who had completed the questionnaire (n = 24, 85.7%) had used the interventions at least once.

issues.title: Week 12 PROM completers: 38 in text vs 39 in four Table 2 columns (SBQ-LC and other columns 38)
issues.explanation: The Results text says 38 participants completed the PROMs at week 12. Table 2 shows 38 for the SBQ-LC but 39 for FACIT-F, GAD-2, COVID-19 recovery and MRC dyspnoea. The text and table do not agree, and the paper does not explain why completion would differ by one across PROMs. The gap is one participant and does not affect the feasibility conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text figure refers only to the SBQ-LC, or that one participant completed all other PROMs but not the SBQ-LC at week 12.

quotes.text: just under half completed the PROMs at week 12 (n = 38)

issues.title: 'We have shown' recruitment rose after each social media post, from uncontrolled weekly counts
issues.explanation: The limitations section says recruitment 'increased after each' social media post, although a before-after weekly count with no comparison cannot show that the posts caused the rise. The same section concedes it could not say which recruitment methods worked best. The week 3 spike of 111 sign-ups was attributed to imposters and not to a post. The statement is an overreach in wording, with little effect on the paper's conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Recruitment data timed against each post that show a clear, attributable rise (for example sign-up source tracking) and exclude the imposter surge.

quotes.text: However, we have shown that recruitment increased after each time we posted the study advert on social media.
In addition, we posted the recruitment advert on social media at weeks 2 and 4, explaining the slight surge in recruitment after weeks 2 and 4 (Fig. 1).

10.1038/s41598-024-68100-8.headline_claim: Daily self-administered gastrocnemius electrical stimulation for 4 weeks increased ankle dorsiflexion strength in individuals with persistent musculoskeletal PASC.
10.1038/s41598-024-68100-8.overall: The finding that active stimulation raised dorsiflexion strength relative to sham is statistically strong for such a small trial (n = 18, interaction p < 0.001), but it comes from a retrospectively registered secondary analysis and rests on very few participants. The claim that the gain is linked to improved gastrocnemius activation is not supported, since GVA did not differ between groups. The IADL effect size in the Discussion (d = 1.2) contradicts Table 2 and should be disregarded.

primary_outcome.name: Ankle dorsiflexion strength (dynamometry during MVC) and gastrocnemius voluntary activation (GVA) via sEMG

primary_outcomes.measure: Gastrocnemius Muscle Endurance (Muscle Sustained Contraction) in Response to Electrical Stimulation

issues.title: Conclusion links strength gain to improved gastrocnemius activation although GVA had no group effect (p = 0.894)
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says the strength findings 'were associated with improvement of gastrocnemius muscle activation'. The between-group interaction for GVA was null (p = 0.894; percentage GVA p = 0.896), and the paper's first hypothesis, that GVA would improve, was not supported. The only supporting evidence is a correlation of change scores in the 10 IG participants (rho = 0.782), which does not establish a mechanism. The Abstract also does not state the null result for a stated primary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group GVA analysis showing greater activation gains in the IG, or a mediation analysis linking GVA change to the strength effect.

quotes.text: These findings were associated with improvement of gastrocnemius muscle activation.
There were no significant differences for GVA ( p =  0.894, d  =  0.032, Fig. 3c)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no group difference in GVA (p = 0.894; % improvement p = 0.896), so the Conclusion's statement that the strength gain was associated with 'improvement of gastrocnemius muscle activation' is not supported as a treatment effect on activation; the evidence is only a within-IG correlation of changes (rho = 0.782, p = 0.008, n = 10), which does not show that E-Stim improved activation or mediated the strength gain. The Conclusion does use 'associated', and the Discussion frames the finding as a correlation, but the Conclusion omits that the activation outcome itself showed no betw

issues.title: Discussion cites IADL effect size d = 1.2 ('very large'); Table 2 IADL effect sizes are 0.101 to 0.655
issues.explanation: The Discussion uses a 'very large' IADL effect size of 1.2 to argue for longer follow-up. Every IADL effect size in Table 2 is 0.655 or smaller, and the within-group IG change (p = 0.058) has d = 0.366, which the paper's own scale calls small. The text value is not supported by the table, and it makes a non-significant secondary outcome look more promising.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of which contrast or computation yields d = 1.2 for IADL (for example an unreported subgroup or per-protocol analysis).

quotes.text: Noteworthy, the very large effect size (d = 1.2) of this outcome shows potential for longer explorations.

quotes.location: Table 2, Lawton-Brody IADL row, IG BL vs 4W

issues.title: Allocation concealment not described; 18-participant completer analysis with imperfect sham blinding
issues.explanation: Randomisation was by a computer-generated list with 'sequential allocation', and concealment is not described. One control participant was excluded, and the analysis covers 18 completers (10 IG, 8 CG). The Limitations also say 3 control participants recognised the sham. With 8 controls, these points make the large percentage-improvement gap fragile, although a 5% dropout alone is not a serious threat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation (e.g. in the parent trial) of concealed allocation and an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis giving the same strength result.

quotes.text: one participant in CG withdrew from the study due to non-compliance. In total, 18 participants successfully completed all assessments and interventions over a 4-week period.
three patients in the CG recognized they had a sham device during the study, however they were not unblinded

issues.title: GVA is called a primary outcome but is not among the registered primary outcomes (endurance, ankle strength)
issues.explanation: The registry lists muscle endurance and ankle strength as primary outcomes. The paper designates dorsiflexion strength and GVA as primary and does not say that GVA was added post hoc for this secondary analysis. The strength outcome plausibly matches the registration. The unregistered GVA outcome was null and underlies the activation claims in the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing GVA and dorsiflexion strength as primary outcomes, or a statement in the paper that these outcomes were prespecified.

quotes.text: This is a secondary analysis of a double-blinded randomized controlled trial

issues.title: Registered 01/20/2022, about two months after recruitment began in November 2021
issues.explanation: The paper reports a registration date of 01/20/2022, while recruitment ran from November 2021 to May 2022. Participants were therefore enrolled before registration. The registry also gives a study start of 2021-08-18 and a first submission of 2022-01-18. Combined with the outcome mismatch, the prespecification of the primary outcomes cannot be verified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the first participant was enrolled after 01/20/2022 or that the protocol with its outcomes was lodged before enrolment.

quotes.text: The protocol was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05198466, 01/20/2022).
through the ClinicalTrials.gov website information from November 2021 to May 2022

issues.title: 3 s active + 6 s rest phases imply about 20 s/40 s per minute, not the stated 24 s/36 s
issues.explanation: A 3 s active and 6 s rest cycle lasts 9 s. Repeated across a minute it gives about 20 s of contraction and 40 s of relaxation (one third duty cycle), not the 24 s and 36 s stated. The hourly totals (24 min and 36 min) repeat the same figures. This is a description of the dose, not an outcome analysis, so it affects interpretation of the intervention only slightly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A device specification showing the active phase is 3 s per burst with multiple bursts per cycle, giving 24 s of activity per minute.

quotes.text: referred to as the active phase, lasting 3 s
resulting in 24 s of muscle contraction × 36 s of muscle relaxation

issues.title: Stimulation frequency given as 21-129 Hz in Methods and 20-121 Hz in Discussion
issues.explanation: The paper gives two different ranges for the same device output. The difference may reflect rounding or a different unit, but the paper does not say. It does not affect any reported result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion range refers to a different quantity (for example a pulse rather than a packet rate) or the manufacturer's specification.

quotes.text: These packets were delivered at a frequency of 21 to 129 Hertz (packets per second).
elicits electrical pulses at low and high frequencies (20-121 Hz)

10.1038/s41598-024-71055-5.headline_claim: Individually tailored endurance and strength exercise is safe and feasible for patients with PCC-POTS, and shows tentative improvements in symptoms, function and HRQoL, supporting an RCT.
10.1038/s41598-024-71055-5.overall: The feasibility conclusions (safe, deliverable, measurable, completion about 96-100%) are reasonably supported by the single-arm data. The efficacy wording is not: the design has no control group, about 25 uncorrected tests were run, the ActivPAL outcomes did not change, and the Conclusion still says effectiveness was shown. There are also a handful of small printing inconsistencies (the 6MWT HR row, WAI completeness, adherence percentage) and one misclassified result (resting HR rise listed as an improvement).

primary_outcome.name: Process feasibility (recruitment, adherence, safety, acceptability of intervention and measures); the paper also lists ActivPAL physical activity/posture and EQ-VAS as primary outcomes in Table 1

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Measured before and after the intervention period of 12-16 weeks to detect a change

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in time in upright position and steps per day
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Measured before and after the intervention period of 12-16 weeks to detect a change

issues.title: Conclusion claims effectiveness on primary outcomes from an uncontrolled study where posture outcomes did not change
issues.explanation: This is a single-arm, non-randomised pilot with no control group, so pre-post changes cannot be attributed to the exercise programme. Yet the Conclusion says the results show effectiveness on primary and secondary outcomes. The ActivPAL posture outcomes, listed as primary, showed no significant change. The strong wording is not supported, although the other conclusions on feasibility are reasonable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusion reworded to limit claims to feasibility and uncontrolled, hypothesis-generating changes.

quotes.text: The tentative results of this study show the effectiveness of the intervention on primary and secondary outcomes
The data illustrates the changes in time in various postures, which did not change significantly.
since the study did not include a control group

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion says the results 'show the effectiveness of the intervention on primary and secondary outcomes', yet the design is uncontrolled and one of the two primary outcome domains (posture/time upright, with steps showing only a small untested change of about 350 steps/day) showed no significant change, so that wording overreaches. It is softened by 'tentative', the Discussion's explicit no-control-group caveat, and the call for an RCT, and the EQ-VAS primary outcome did improve (MD 11.0, p < 0.001), so the overstatement is one of wording rather than an unacknowledged limitation.

issues.title: About 25 outcomes tested at uncorrected p < 0.05, then described as significant improvements
issues.explanation: Table 6 reports roughly 25 paired tests with a single uncorrected threshold of 0.05, with no primary outcome and no adjustment. Several 'significant' results are marginal. With this many tests and no control group, some nominally significant changes would be expected by chance, so the favourable outcome summary is weaker than stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary outcome or a stated multiplicity correction.

quotes.text: An effect or difference was considered significant if its p-value < 0.05.

issues.title: Resting HR rose 71.5 to 75.1 bpm (p = 0.043) but is listed among 'improvements'
issues.explanation: The Discussion names HR at rest among outcomes that showed improvement. Table 6 shows resting heart rate going up by 3.56 bpm, a statistically significant change in the unfavourable direction for a tachycardia condition. This is a misdescription of one result and contributes to an overly favourable summary of the physical-function findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors' justification that a higher resting HR is a desirable change in this population.

quotes.text: improvements were demonstrated in physical functions, capacity, and health-related quality of life (HR at rest, 6MWT, Frändin/Grimby and EQ-VAS)

issues.title: Table 6, 6MWT HR at 6 min: MD 11.71 and CI 22.79 to -2.33 do not match means (diff 4.7) or each other

It also does not match the printed pre and post means, which differ by 4.7. The row's values appear to have been shifted or mis-printed, but the outcome is non-significant (p = 0.181) and secondary, so the effect on conclusions is small.

Table 6 analyses 21 participants for WAI, a third figure. None of the three can be reconciled from the paper. This is a small reporting inconsistency in a feasibility metric.

quotes.text: except for the WAI questionnaire where only 68% of the participants had complete data

issues.explanation: Table 4 uses N = 25 at all three time points, but 26 were included and all completed the intervention. Only one participant is described as missing the post measurement. The missing-data percentages therefore rest on a denominator the paper does not explain. This slightly affects the feasibility figures only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one participant had no questionnaire data and was excluded from Table 4.

The mismatch concerns a feasibility figure and, if anything, understates adherence relative to the printed sessions.

10.1038/s41598-024-78651-5.headline_claim: High-dose wearable TENS produced a greater reduction in pain-related functional interference (BPI-I) than low-dose TENS at 4 weeks in long-COVID patients with fibromyalgia-like symptoms, and was feasible and acceptable.
10.1038/s41598-024-78651-5.overall: The headline claim of greater pain-interference reduction with high-dose TENS rests on a between-group difference that mostly reflects baseline imbalance, since the change from baseline differs by only about 0.26 points. The fatigue and gait benefits come from within-arm changes, while all between-group tests are null. This pilot supports feasibility, but not efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: Functional interference from pain (BPI-I), between-group at 4 weeks

primary_outcomes.measure: Mean Change in Functional Interference From Pain From Baseline to 4 Weeks (Blinded Phase)

issues.title: Primary BPI-I difference of 2.61 mirrors baseline imbalance (5.54 vs 3.17); change difference is ~0.26
issues.explanation: Baseline BPI-I was much higher in the placebo group (5.54 vs 3.17, p = 0.021), and no covariate adjustment was made. The 4-week 'mean difference' of 2.6 matches the difference in end-of-study scores, which is mostly the baseline gap of 2.37. The arms' actual changes from baseline are small and similar (0.198 vs 0.454) and the paper itself says within-group improvement was not significant. The headline claim of a 'greater decrease' in BPI-I is therefore not supported by the reported changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A covariate-adjusted or change-score analysis showing a significant group-by-time effect on BPI-I of similar magnitude.

quotes.text: Baseline BPI-I was significantly higher in the PG than the IG (Table 2).
No covariates adjustments were made due to low sample size.
However, within-group comparison did not show significant improvement (Table 3).

second_reader.what_stands: The 2.61 is a 4-week between-group difference in level, and about 2.37 of it was already present at baseline (5.54 vs 3.17). The difference in change from baseline is only about 0.26, and neither within-group change is significant. The abstract and Results call 2.61 a 'greater decrease' in the IG and attribute it to TENS. No covariate adjustment was made, so the baseline imbalance is not accounted for.

issues.title: Fatigue and gait benefits claimed from within-arm changes; all between-group fatigue and gait tests were null
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion say TENS reduced interference from fatigue and gait alterations. The supporting numbers are changes from baseline in the high-dose arm only (GFI +6.08 in 5 patients; stride time, cadence, double-support). Between-group comparisons at 4 weeks are not significant for GFI (0.867 all, 0.161 FM subgroup) and for every gait parameter in Table 4 (0.24 to 0.90). The Discussion's 'demonstrates the benefit' goes beyond a 25-patient pilot whose main comparison is also compromised (see c8).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant between-group (group-by-time) tests for GFI and gait in the main paper, with the multiplicity of secondary outcomes accounted for.

quotes.text: Daily TENS therapy showed potential in reducing functional interference from pain, fatigue, and gait alterations in long-COVID individuals.
Baseline BPI-S and GFI did not significantly differ between groups (Table 2), nor did they show significant differences at 4 weeks (Table 3).
Our study demonstrates the benefit of highdose TENS

second_reader.what_stands: The fatigue claim rests only on a within-arm change in a 5-person subgroup, and the between-group GFI tests are null, both overall (p = 0.867) and in the subgroup (p = 0.161). The gait claims are framed as changes from baseline, and every 4-week between-group gait comparison in Table 4 is null. However, the paper reports a significant time x group effect for cadence and stride time in a supplementary table I could not see, so 'all between-group gait tests were null' is not fully supported. The Discussion statement that the study 'demonstrates the benefit' concerns pain interference, where the

issues.title: Table 3 FM subgroup: text SE 10.61 conflicts with table SE 2.188; table BPI-I p = 0.08 conflicts with text p = 0.125
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the SE of the IG-FM GFI change as 10.61, but Table 3 prints 2.188. Only 2.188 reproduces p = 0.005. For the FM BPI-I between-group comparison, the text says p = 0.125 while Table 3 says 0.08. The table's CI (-3.183 to 0.39) implies p of about 0.125, and 0.08 is the within-group IG-FM p-value copied into the between-group row. Both FM-subgroup errors favour the text-level story only slightly, and the conclusions drawn from them are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction notice or supplementary table showing SE 10.61 and p = 0.08 are the intended values for these analyses.

quotes.location: Table 3, FM sub-group GFI, IG row

quotes.text: mean difference = 1.39, p = 0.125

issues.title: Table 1 and text disagree: swapped cancer/osteoarthritis p, PT split 4/1 vs 2/3, memory 10/13 printed as 80%
issues.explanation: The text gives p = 0.03 for cancer and 0.01 for osteoarthritis, but Table 1 gives the reverse. The Limitations say 4 PG and 1 IG patients had concurrent physical therapy, while Table 1 shows 2 PG and 3 IG. Table 1 also prints 10 (80) for memory difficulty in a 13-patient group, when 10/13 is 76.9%. These are small errors that do not change the findings, but they show the baseline reporting was not carefully checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the printed values are correct, for example a different PG denominator for memory difficulty.

script.explanation: 10/13 = 76.92%, but the paper prints 80, outside the rounding interval [79.50, 81.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 12.5 rather than 13.

issues.title: Primary BPI-I CI (-4.543, 0.689) includes 0 but p = 0.008; likely a lost minus sign on the upper limit
issues.explanation: As printed, the CI includes zero and is not centred on -2.616, which conflicts with p = 0.008. With a minus sign on 0.689 the interval is exactly centred on the estimate and matches the p. The more serious problem with this primary result is in c8, not in this sign.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original PDF showing -0.689 as the upper CI limit.

script.explanation: the estimate -2.616 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-4.543, 0.689] (expected about -1.9270) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Acceptability 'above 70% in all categories' contradicted by PG perceived usefulness of 61.4%
issues.explanation: Both the Results and the Discussion say acceptability exceeded 70% in all categories or both groups. The paper's own PU figure for the placebo group is 61.4%, below 70%. A secondary feasibility statement is therefore overstated, and the placebo group's lower usefulness rating is glossed over.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A threshold defined differently, such as a composite score across items above 70% in each group.

quotes.text: reported device acceptability above 70% during the blinded study phase

issues.title: Device manufacturer's in-kind support disclosed, but its role is not stated and not in competing interests
issues.explanation: The device maker, NeuroMetrix, provided in-kind support and the trial tests its device against a low-dose version of the same product. The paper does not say whether the company had any role in design, analysis or writing. The competing-interests section mentions only a consultancy with a different company.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the manufacturer had no role in design, data analysis or manuscript content.

quotes.text: in-kind support provided by Neurometrix Inc., based in Massachusetts, USA, which is the manufacturer of the Quell
No additional potential conflicts of interest were reported.

10.1038/s41598-024-82412-9.headline_claim: Vascular photobiomodulation significantly reduces pain and interference with daily activities (walking, work, sleep, enjoyment of life) in post-COVID-19 tension-type headache and orofacial pain compared with simulated treatment.
10.1038/s41598-024-82412-9.overall: The claim that VPBM outperforms sham rests on a per-protocol subset (12 v 16) while the intention-to-treat VAS comparison is null (p = 0.189), and the abstract presents within-group p-values as between-group differences. The trial is small, has a vague registered outcome and no sample-size calculation, and the BPI findings are uncorrected multiple comparisons. The supportable conclusion is that pain fell in both arms, with a possible per-protocol-only difference that needs confirmation in a larger trial.

primary_outcome.name: VAS pain intensity (per-protocol before/after comparison between groups); registry lists headache and orofacial pain at four weeks

issues.title: Superiority over sham claimed from per-protocol VAS (p = 0.001, 12 v 16); ITT difference null (p = 0.189)
issues.explanation: The conclusion and abstract state significant pain reduction compared with sham. That rests on the per-protocol analysis of 28 completers, while the ITT between-group VAS comparison (the primary outcome) was not significant. The conclusion and abstract do not say this. Per-protocol completers after non-random dropout can overstate a treatment effect against sham. The supported reading is that VPBM and sham both reduced pain, with a between-group difference only in completers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified per-protocol primary analysis, or a conclusion that explicitly limits the superiority claim to completers and reports the null ITT result.

quotes.text: no statistically significant difference was found between the groups (p = 0.189)
The comparison of pain improvement between the two groups showed a significant difference (p = 0.001)
VPBM demonstrated significant pain reduction in individuals experiencing orofacial pain (OFP)

second_reader.what_stands: The superiority-over-sham claim in the Conclusion rests on the per-protocol VAS comparison (p = 0.001, n = 12 v 16), while the ITT comparison on the same outcome was null (p = 0.189) and the conclusion does not mention this. The PP population is a post-randomization subset (28 of 34 analysed, 40 randomized), so the stronger result may be subject to attrition-related bias, and the paper's own Discussion acknowledges that the pooled analysis found no significant difference. The PP-based claim is not wrong as a PP result, but it is stated more strongly than the ITT result supports.

issues.title: Abstract cites within-VPBM p-values as between-group differences; 11 uncorrected BPI items, sleep between-group p = 0.082
issues.explanation: The abstract says differences were seen between the two groups and then quotes p = 0.010, 0.011, 0.009, 0.012 and 0.016, which are the VPBM within-group p-values in Table 7. The between-group p-values for those items are 0.041, 0.011, 0.021, 0.082 and 0.043, and sleep is not significant. Around 11 BPI items were tested at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05, so the few nominal hits (p of 0.011 to 0.043) are weak evidence for the conclusion that VPBM reduces interference with walking, work, sleep and enjoyment of life.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or correction for the BPI items, or an abstract that reports the between-group p-values.

quotes.text: These differences were evident in the average pain experienced in the previous week (p = 0.010)
Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05.
