second_reader.what_stands: The abstract quotes within-VPBM-group p-values (0.010, 0.011, 0.009, 0.012, 0.016) as evidence of differences that it also describes as between-group, and for sleep the between-group p is 0.082 (not significant) while the abstract lists sleep alongside the others. Between-group p-values for the other cited items (0.041, 0.011, 0.021, 0.043) are nominally below 0.05 but come from about 11-12 BPI items with no correction across items, so none would survive a Bonferroni threshold of roughly 0.004-0.005; the exact item count (11 versus the 12 rows I count) I could not settle.

issues.title: Registered primary outcome is vague; paper has no single prespecified primary and headlines BPI items
issues.explanation: The registry primary outcome is 'headache and orofacial pain' at four weeks, with no named instrument. The paper measures VAS, BPI and HIT-6, and the abstract headlines BPI items rather than VAS. Whether the primary outcome changed cannot be determined from the current record alone, but the lack of one clearly specified primary outcome allows selective emphasis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original registered protocol or earlier record versions naming VAS as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: The following assessments were conducted to measure the primary outcome:
The primary outcome analyzed in the PPA

issues.title: Modified ITT: 6 of 40 randomized excluded, 12 of 40 (30%) non-completers, LOCF imputation
issues.explanation: Only 34 of 40 randomized participants entered the 'ITT' analysis, and 28 completed the protocol. Excluding randomized participants and using last observation carried forward means even the ITT result is not a full randomized comparison. The loss is substantial for a trial this small. This makes both analyses tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flowchart showing balanced, trial-unrelated losses and a sensitivity analysis including all 40 randomized participants.

quotes.text: A total of 40 patients participated in the study and were randomized into two study groups
The data analysis and follow-up were conducted for 34 participants who underwent at least two interventions.

issues.title: Table 1 total energy 1440 J is double the 720 J implied by 180 J x 4 sessions
issues.explanation: Table 1 lists 180 J per session and 4 sessions, which gives 720 J in total, but the table prints 1440 J. The Methods also state four weekly sessions. The dosimetry total is therefore wrong or the schedule is misreported, which matters for reproducing the protocol, though it does not alter the clinical results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol stating eight sessions or two applications per session, which would reconcile 1440 J.

quotes.text: Total irradiated energy (J)
totaling four sessions

issues.title: Registry start date (2022-05-10) precedes registration; paper reports data collection from Oct 2022
issues.explanation: The registry labels the record as retrospective because the recorded start predates submission. The paper reports data collection beginning on 30 October 2022, after registration, which supports its claim of prospective registration. The registry enrolment of 59 versus 40 randomized in the paper also differs. Neither point is resolved by the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the start date was an anticipated date and that enrolment began after registration.

quotes.text: prospectively registered at the Clinical Trial Registry (ClinicalTrials.gov) under No. NCT05430776 (24/06/2022)

issues.title: Table 2 headed n = 14/20 but HIT-6 percentages and VAS means match the n = 12/16 per-protocol set
issues.explanation: The Table 2 column headers give 14 and 20 participants, yet the HIT-6 percentages are only possible with denominators of 12 and 16, and match Table 6. The baseline VAS means equal those in Table 3 for the 12/16 set. Table 2 therefore mixes analysis sets, so the baseline comparability it shows cannot be tied to a single population. The effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 2 rows were computed on different subsets, or the unrounded counts for the 14/20 set.

quotes.text: VPBMgroup (n = 14)

10.1038/s41598-024-82584-4.headline_claim: An individualized, symptom-titrated exercise program is effective in reducing fatigue and improving HRQoL and physical performance in post-COVID condition, and is safe and feasible in commercial fitness facilities.
10.1038/s41598-024-82584-4.overall: The large FSS reduction in the intervention arm probably reflects a real short-term difference, but it comes from an open-label, wait-list comparison with a self-reported primary outcome. Only completers (118 of 174) were analysed despite the 'intention-to-treat' label. The 'proof', 'effective' and 'safe' language and the 'confirms the benefit' reading of a non-significant PEM result go beyond the evidence, and the flow text is internally inconsistent though it can be reconciled.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) from PRE to POST

issues.title: 'Intention-to-treat' analysis excludes 56 of 174 randomized (32.2%); only completers with PRE and POST data analysed
issues.explanation: The analysis set requires data at both PRE and POST, so the 56 randomized participants who dropped out or never started (more in INT than CON) are not in the model. Calling this 'intention-to-treat' and invoking mixed-model MAR handling overstates what was done. Dropouts in an open-label trial often had low expectancy or poor early experience, so results among completers may favour the intervention. The authors list attrition as a major limitation, but the abstract and conclusion still state effectiveness without qualification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all 174 randomized participants (for example multiple imputation or worst-case) giving the same FSS result.

quotes.text: All individuals with at least one data point at both PRE and POST were included in the intention-to-treat analysis, regardless of the number of actual training sessions.
One major limitation of this study is the relatively high attrition rate.

second_reader.what_stands: The analysis is not intention-to-treat as the term is normally used. It is a completers or available-case analysis of the 118 who had POST data, with 56 of 174 (32.2%) excluded, and more if the 50 non-starters count as randomized. The authors do call attrition a major limitation, but they still describe the analysis as ITT, and their 174 denominator does not make clear that the 50 non-starters sit outside it.

issues.title: Open-label wait-list design with self-reported fatigue (FSS) as primary outcome; bias not discussed
issues.explanation: Participants learned their allocation after baseline testing and the primary outcome is a questionnaire. The FSS change of -1.14 in INT versus -0.23 in CON could be partly expectancy or reporting effects, especially against a wait-list with no attention control. The objective measures (grip strength, step test) are effort-dependent and tested by facility staff who knew the allocation, so they are not clearly protected either. The limitations section does not mention this, yet the conclusion states efficacy without qualification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that outcome assessors or participants were blinded, or an attention-control comparison showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Participants received information about their allocated group after the PRE diagnostics.
The severity of perceived fatigability was assessed using the fatigue severity scale (FSS) 48-50 .

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with a wait-list comparator and a self-reported primary outcome, and the paper never discusses the resulting risk of performance or expectation bias in the FSS result. Blinding itself was not feasible, and the objective strength and endurance outcomes partly support the finding. The omission lies in the limitations section and the strength of the conclusions.

issues.title: 'Proof' of effectiveness and unqualified 'safe' claim from an exploratory, open-label, unpowered 10-week trial
issues.explanation: The authors say the trial was exploratory with no power calculation, yet write that their results 'proof' the program is effective for HRQoL and 'the overall burden of disease' (not measured), and the conclusion calls it effective and safe. Safety rests on 'no adverse events were recorded' with no stated systematic collection, only 10 weeks of follow-up, and a 32% dropout. The HRQoL and strength results (p = 0.018 to 0.031) were not corrected for the many outcomes tested. The primary FSS effect looks robust in size, but the language goes well beyond what the evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified adverse-event monitoring protocol with reported events per arm, and a multiplicity-adjusted analysis keeping the secondary results significant.

quotes.text: Our results proof that an individualized and symptom-titrated exercise program is effective in improving HRQoL and the overall burden of disease.
Other than that, no adverse events were recorded.
we did not perform an a priori sample size calculation or power analysis.

second_reader.what_stands: 'Proof' of effectiveness and unqualified claims of safety are stronger than an exploratory, open-label, unpowered 10-week trial with 32% attrition and no stated multiplicity control can support. The authors do mention the missing power calculation, and the FSS and PEM data do not show a mean worsening in the intervention group. The 'no adverse events' statement is weakly supported because the methods describe no systematic adverse-event recording and report nothing for CON.

issues.title: Results text says 50 non-starters 'additionally' to 56 dropouts, but 174 - 56 = 118 already
issues.explanation: The Results say 50 randomized people never commenced and 'additionally' 56 ceased between PRE and POST. Subtracting both from 174 would leave 68, not the 118 analysed. The percentages elsewhere (32.2% overall, 29.4% CON, 34.8% INT) and the arm sizes in Table 2 (60 and 58) only work if the 56 is the total loss from randomization, including the 50 non-starters. The flow description is therefore misworded or internally inconsistent. The numbers can be reconciled, so this is a reporting error rather than a threat to the result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 3 showing 50 non-starters and 56 PRE-to-POST dropouts as separate groups, with a different analysed total.

quotes.text: A total of 174 people were randomized of which 118 were included in the final analysis.
Additionally, 56 participants (CON: 25; INT: 31) ceased participation between PRE and POST.
Between PRE and POST 32.2% of all participants (CON: 29.4%; INT: 34.8%) ceased the intervention.

issues.title: Non-significant PEM change (p = 0.065) described as 'confirming the benefit' of the program
issues.explanation: The time-by-group effect on PEM was not significant (p = 0.065), and the Discussion elsewhere concedes there were no effects on PEM. Yet the same section says the reduction 'confirms the benefit' for moderate PEM. A null secondary result should not be described as confirmation, and the PEM result cannot be used to argue the program does not worsen PEM beyond showing no clear difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified PEM analysis with a significant interaction, or wording that treats PEM only as a safety signal with no benefit claim.

quotes.text: Regarding the descriptive values (no statistical significance), a reduction in PEM was observed in the intervention group, which confirms the benefit of symptom-titrated exercise for moderate PEM in PCC patients.

10.1038/s41598-025-07461-0.headline_claim: A 16:8 time-restricted eating plus weekly 1-2 day fast with a no-sugar diet reduces Long COVID symptoms more than a mild 14:10 TRE plus no-sugar diet, and both interventions reduce symptoms.
10.1038/s41598-025-07461-0.overall: The finding that LC symptom scores fell more during fasting than during mild TRE is plausible, but it comes from an open-label, self-reported, completer-only analysis with predictable ID-parity allocation. The 10-week overall reduction has no control group. The registration statement conflicts with the registry record, and there are minor numeric slips (BMI 25.9 vs 25.5, 58% vs 55.2%) that do not change the main results.

primary_outcome.name: Change in LC-Score and change in numLCsym during 4 weeks of Fasting vs 4 weeks of TRE

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Before and after 4 weeks of Fasting treatment or TRE treatment

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Number of Long COVID Symptoms, Per Treatment
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Before and after 4 weeks of Fasting treatment or TRE treatment

issues.title: Crossover sequence assigned by even/odd REDCap ID by the enrolling investigator, yet called randomized
issues.explanation: Participants were assigned to sequence AB or BA by whether their ID number was even or odd, and the investigator who enrolled them made the assignment. This is a predictable alternation rule, not a concealed random sequence, and the paper still describes the trial as randomized throughout. A crossover design limits the consequences, but assignment knowledge could influence who was enrolled and when, and the open-label self-reported outcome makes this more consequential. The label 'randomized' and the claim of being a randomized trial are stronger than the method supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol showing IDs were issued from a concealed computer-generated random sequence, independent of the enroller.

quotes.text: Dr. Bunker enrolled all participants and randomly assigned them to crossover trial treatment arms based on whether their REDCap identifier was even or odd.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does state that the enrolling investigator assigned sequence by even/odd REDCap ID, which is a deterministic, non-concealed, alternation-type rule rather than a true random sequence, yet the study is labelled 'randomized' throughout. The paper does not say the investigator could choose the ID or knew the next one in advance, so selection bias is possible but not demonstrated. The crossover design and the non-significant sequence and carryover tests (p = 0.268 and p = 0.303) limit how much sequence imbalance would matter.

issues.title: Open-label trial with self-reported primary outcomes; superiority of fasting stated without caveat
issues.explanation: Both primary outcomes are self-reported symptom counts and severities, and participants knew which regimen they were on. The Limitations mention the reliance on patient-reported symptoms but not the lack of blinding, and the Abstract and Conclusions state that fasting was significantly superior. The between-treatment difference (-10.2 vs -2.8 LC-Score points) could partly reflect expectation or effort. The finding of a difference is plausible, but its size and attribution to fasting itself are uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Objective outcome measures concordant with the self-reports, or a blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: Due to the nature of the interventions, the trial was not blinded.
This trial relied on patient-reported symptoms and severity assessment since there are no available biomarkers  for  Long  COVID.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with participant-reported primary outcomes, and the Abstract and Conclusions state that fasting was superior without mentioning that unblinded self-report can inflate a difference between a more burdensome and a milder arm. The authors do disclose non-blinding in Methods and the reliance on self-report, and the general bias caveat, in Limitations, so the problem is the lack of caveat in the headline claims rather than a hidden design feature. The registry's 'SINGLE' masking also does not match the paper's 'not blinded'.

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 58 of 77 who began (24.7% lost) analysed, with no sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: All efficacy results come from the 58 participants who completed all 10 weeks. The 19 who began but did not complete are not analysed, and the reasons are not reported in the text. Dropout from a demanding fasting regimen is likely related to the outcome, so completer-only estimates probably look better than an analysis of everyone who began. The size of the bias cannot be assessed from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or imputed analysis of all 77 giving similar treatment differences.

quotes.text: 58 participants (75%) successfully completed the 10-week study as designed and, thus, comprised the analytic sample.
The 'attempted treatment' sample consisted of 77 participants

second_reader.what_stands: The paper analyses only the 58 completers out of 77 who began (24.7% not analysed), calls this the analytic sample, and reports no intention-to-treat, imputation or sensitivity analysis. The reasons for non-completion cannot be read from the text, so the size of any bias is unknown, but completer-only analysis of an unblinded, self-reported crossover trial with this level of attrition leaves the results open to attrition bias.

issues.title: Paper says registered before enrolment; registry shows first submission 2023-01-03, after 2022-11-04 start
issues.explanation: The Methods say the trial was registered before screening and enrolment began. The paper also says prescreening began in November 2022, and the registry record gives a study start of 2022-11-04 and a first submission of 2023-01-03. The ethics approval date printed as 19/01/2024 falls after enrolment began and is not explained. The registration statement is therefore inconsistent with the registry. Registration after enrolment began allows outcome definitions to drift, though the registered primary outcomes do match the paper's.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry record version dated before 2022-11-04, or documentation that the first enrolment came after 2023-01-03 and that the original IRB approval was earlier than the printed date.

quotes.text: was registered at clinicaltrials.gov prior to initiation of screening and enrollment
Between November 2022 and April 2024, a total of 424 individuals were prescreened via pragmatic electronic means.
This randomized crossover clinical trial (NCT06214455) (19/01/2024) was approved by the Pacific Northwestern University of Health Sciences Institutional Review Board

issues.title: 10-week LC-Score fall of 51.8% presented as treatment effect, without a control and despite a run-in fall of 6.7
issues.explanation: The Abstract credits the 'no-sugar diet, TRE and Fasting' regimen with a 51.8% fall in LC-Score and a 40.6% fall in numLCsym over 10 weeks. There is no untreated or no-diet comparison, and the 2-week run-in on the TRE regimen alone already lowered LC-Score by 6.7 points. Regression to the mean, natural recovery and expectation in an open-label, self-reported trial could contribute to the change. The Discussion's argument for a chronic, stable illness rests partly on a figure for one subgroup.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group showing no comparable change over 10 weeks.

quotes.text: Altogether, the 10-week regimen of a nosugar diet, TRE and Fasting decreased the mean LC-Score by 51.8% (p  < 0.0001) from 37.8 to 18.2.

issues.title: Sample-size target not reported; enrolment stopped early for logistical reasons
issues.explanation: The paper says sample size was estimated but gives no target or assumptions, and says enrolment was stopped early because of slower recruitment and volunteer-team limits. Early stopping not based on outcomes is a limited concern, but the intended sample size is unknown, and the registry lists 77 as actual enrolment. The result is based on 58 completers, so effect sizes may be imprecise. This weakens the confidence of the stated conclusions rather than refuting them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The protocol sample-size calculation with a target at or below the analysed n.

quotes.text: enrollment was stopped early due to challenges involving the conduct of a trial by an all-volunteer team and slower than anticipated subject enrollment

issues.title: Initial mean BMI is 25.9 in the text but 25.5 for all 58 subjects in Table 1
issues.explanation: The weight-loss paragraph gives 25.9 kg/m2 as the initial mean BMI of the analytic sample. Table 1 gives 25.5 for all subjects and 25.9 only for males. The 4.6% figure follows from 25.9, whereas 25.5 would give 4.7%. This is a small reporting slip that does not touch the main efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 25.9 refers to a different population, such as the 77 who started the study.

quotes.text: from the initial mean of 25.9
quotes.location: Results, Adverse events and weight loss

quotes.text: BMI, mean (SD)</th><td>25.5 (4.2)
quotes.location: Table 1(a), BMI row, All subjects column

issues.title: Fasting-related flare-ups: 32 of 58 printed as 58%, but equals 55.2%; Conclusions say 55%
issues.explanation: The Figure 7 caption gives 32 of 58 participants as 58%, but 32/58 is 55.2%. The Conclusions print 55% for the same group. The figure caption therefore disagrees with its own count and with the Conclusions. The value 58% appears to be carried over from the separate 'share of flare-ups during Fasting' statement. It is a minor reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 58% uses a different denominator for the same statement.

quotes.text: 32 of 58 participants (58%) reported one or more fasting related flare-up.
While 55% of participants reported one or more transient treatment-related flare-up

script.explanation: 32/58 = 55.17%, but the paper prints 58.0, outside the rounding interval [57.50, 59.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 55.2 rather than 58.

10.1038/s41598-025-09772-8.headline_claim: Combining tDCS with cognitive training is a feasible, safe and effective approach for reducing fatigue and enhancing cognition in post-COVID patients, with the M1 target slightly more effective than DLPFC.
10.1038/s41598-025-09772-8.overall: The feasibility and safety findings are plausible, but the stated conclusions that the treatment is 'effective' and that M1 is more effective for fatigue are not supported: there is no control arm, and the primary FSS group-by-time interaction was non-significant. There are also several reporting inconsistencies (swapped group sizes, overall percentages that do not reconcile with group percentages, an impossible total SD, malformed regression df). Of these, only the misleading comparative claims bear on the conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) physical fatigue

issues.title: 'Effective' conclusion drawn from uncontrolled pre-post change in two active arms, with null primary between-group result
issues.explanation: Both arms received active tDCS plus cognitive training, with no sham or single-treatment arm. The reported improvements are time effects (pre-post), which cannot be separated from placebo, practice effects, regression to the mean or natural fluctuation, as the Discussion itself concedes. The Abstract nevertheless concludes the combination is an effective approach. Only the feasibility and safety conclusions fit this design, and even the safety summary has inconsistent numbers (see c9).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison against a sham or no-stimulation arm, or an Abstract and Conclusion confined to feasibility and within-group change.

quotes.text: These findings indicate that tDCS combined with cognitive training is a feasible, safe, and effective approach for reducing fatigue and enhancing cognition in post-COVID patients.
the current design does not allow us to disentangle the individual effects of each intervention

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that tDCS plus CT is 'effective' rests on pre-post change in two active arms with no sham or CT-alone comparator, and the only between-arm primary test (FSS interaction p = 0.172) was null, so the causal 'effective' wording in the Abstract and Conclusion goes beyond the design. The paper does state this limitation openly and asks for confirmatory randomized trials, so the problem is the strength of the headline wording rather than an undisclosed weakness.

issues.title: M1 superiority for fatigue claimed in Abstract and Conclusion despite non-significant FSS and MFIS interactions
issues.explanation: The primary FSS time-by-group interaction was non-significant (p = 0.172), as were all MFIS interactions. Yet the Abstract and Conclusion say M1 + CT was slightly more effective in reducing fatigue, and the Discussion says M1 + CT showed 'greater effects' on the primary objective. The only supports are a sleep interaction (p = 0.047, a secondary outcome) and ecological assessments, which are not the registered primary measure. The comparison between targets was the primary objective, and it did not show a difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant pre-specified between-group FSS effect, or a statement that the claim is exploratory and based on secondary measures only.

quotes.text: The M1 + CT group showed a slightly higher efficacy in reducing fatigue and improving sleep quality than the DLPFC + CT group.

quotes.location: Table 2, FSS row, Time x Group interaction

quotes.text: While both stimulation targets were beneficial, the primary motor cortex target appeared slightly more effective in reducing fatigue and improving sleep quality.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's own primary (FSS) and MFIS between-group interactions are all non-significant (FSS p = 0.172), yet the Abstract and Conclusion state that M1+CT was more effective for fatigue, and the Discussion says M1+CT showed 'greater effects' on the FSS. Only the PSQI interaction (p = 0.047, unadjusted across many outcomes) and a borderline EMA physical fatigue interaction (p = 0.050) point in that direction, and the word 'slightly' softens the claim but does not remove the mismatch.

issues.title: Abstract says both groups improved sleep quality; Results report no significant change in DLPFC+CT
issues.explanation: The Abstract says both groups showed significant improvement in cognition, anxiety, depression, pain and sleep quality. The sleep result is a significant time-by-group interaction (p = 0.047, not the p bonf column) driven by M1 + CT, with no significant changes in DLPFC + CT. The Abstract therefore overstates the sleep result for one arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A within-group test showing a significant sleep improvement in DLPFC + CT.

quotes.text: Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in cognition, anxiety, depression, pain, and sleep quality.
with no significant changes in the DLPFC + CT group
quotes.location: Results, Secondary clinical outcomes, sleep paragraph

issues.title: Discussion says M1 beat DLPFC on both physical and cognitive ecological fatigue; cognitive effect non-significant, physical p=0.050
issues.explanation: The Discussion says M1 + CT showed significant improvement in both physical and cognitive ecological fatigue compared with DLPFC + CT. For cognitive fatigue the Results say no significant time-per-group effect was found. For physical fatigue, the interaction is reported as significant at a corrected p of exactly 0.050, which is not below 0.05. The claim is unsupported for cognitive fatigue and only borderline for physical.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported significant time-by-group interaction for cognitive fatigue, or an unrounded p for physical fatigue below 0.05.

quotes.text: Worth to highlight, M1 + CT group revealed a significant improvement in ecological fatigue assessment (both physical and cognitive) compared to DLPFC + CT group.
but no significant time-per-group effect was found
quotes.location: Results, Ecological momentary assessment, cognitive fatigue sentence

issues.title: Depression text claims DLPFC improved 'compared to' M1 from separate within-group tests; interaction p=0.820
issues.explanation: The Results say DLPFC + CT showed a significant improvement compared with M1 + CT, but the numbers are separate within-group paired tests (p < 0.001 vs p = 0.052). The only between-group tests are non-significant: the shift rates (19.4% vs 6.5%, p = 0.051), which in fact numerically favour M1, and the BDI-II interaction (p = 0.820). The wording is a difference-in-significance inference, not evidence of a between-group difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A group-by-time test on BDI-II showing a significant DLPFC advantage.

quotes.text: paired-t-test showed that DLPFC + CT group showed a significant improvement (p < 0.001) compared to the M1 + CT group
quotes.location: Results, Secondary clinical outcomes, depression paragraph

quotes.text: 19.4% for the M1 + CT, and 6.5% for the DLPFC + CT
quotes.location: Results, Secondary clinical outcomes, depression paragraph

issues.title: Overall percentages (25%, 14.7%, 14.28%) do not reconcile with group percentages and group sizes
issues.explanation: The overall percentage shifting out of fatigue diagnosis is printed as 25%, but group rates of 29.03% (of 31) and 25% (of 32) give 26.98% overall. At follow-up 14.7% is printed against group rates giving 15.87%. Separately, 14.28% reported side effects overall, yet the group rates are given as 6% and 7%, both lower than the overall figure. The group-level tables are the more interpretable; the overall figures are used in the Discussion as evidence of efficacy and safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-group counts that reproduce the overall figures, e.g. a different denominator stated for the 6% and 7% side-effect figures.

quotes.text: 29.03% for the M1 + CT, and 25% for the DLPFC + CT
quotes.location: Results, Primary outcome: fatigue, MFIS paragraph

quotes.text: At follow-up, 14.7% of patients remained with no fatigue diagnosis
quotes.location: Results, Primary outcome: fatigue, MFIS paragraph

quotes.text: 14.28% of the patients reported adverse effects

issues.title: Abstract gives M1+CT n=32 and DLPFC+CT n=31; Table 1 gives 31 and 32
issues.explanation: The Abstract assigns 32 completers to M1 + CT and 31 to DLPFC + CT. Table 1's headers say the opposite, and its percentages (26/31, 25/32, 2/31) only work with the Table 1 assignment. The totals (63) agree, so only the group labels are wrong. Nothing depends on it, but a reader of the Abstract gets the group sizes the wrong way round.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT figure showing 32 patients analysed in the M1 + CT arm, together with a corrected Table 1.

quotes.text: n = 32 in the M1 + CT group and n = 31 in the DLPFC + CT group

issues.title: Evolution (months): Total SD 7.91 is below both what group SDs allow (~15) and the DLPFC SD (19.83); Total mean also off
issues.explanation: The total-sample SD cannot be smaller than the pooled within-group SD, which here is about 15.3. The total mean 32.02 also does not equal the size-weighted group means (about 32.8). The group-level t test is consistent with the group SDs, so the Total column is the unreliable one. This is a baseline descriptive and affects no efficacy result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 total SD of about 15, or a footnote that the Total column uses a different metric.

quotes.location: Table 1, Evolution (months) row, DLPFC + CT column

issues.title: Completers-only analysis of 63 of 67 randomised; dropout allocation not stated and Methods say all completed 15 sessions
issues.explanation: Efficacy outcomes are analysed only in the 63 completers; no intention-to-treat analysis is given. With 6% loss this likely changes little, but the arm of each dropout is not reported in the text, and the statement that all participants completed all sessions conflicts with four withdrawals. This matters little to the headline conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis including the four dropouts with per-arm allocation, showing the same results.

quotes.text: Among the patients who started the treatment, 94% completed the trial.
All participants completed the 15 sessions.

issues.title: Regression F statistics print malformed degrees of freedom (e.g. F(- 2.13), F(- 3.74), F(2.91))
issues.explanation: The two cognition models give negative degrees of freedom and the two fatigue models give decimal values like 2.91 and 3.66. F degrees of freedom must be positive whole numbers, so none of the four is a usable value. The regression results (depression and pain-functionality as predictors) cannot be checked from the text. These are secondary exploratory analyses.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original article typography showing standard df such as F(1,61), with R2 consistent with those df.

quotes.location: Results, Predictors of fatigue and cognition improvements
Results, Predictors of fatigue and cognition improvements
Results, Predictors of fatigue and cognition improvements

10.1038/s41598-025-13905-4.headline_claim: The pilot shows limited feasibility of a 12-week unsupervised aerobic exercise program, with statements about efficacy restricted, though weak indications of reduced symptom severity and improved wellbeing were seen.
10.1038/s41598-025-13905-4.overall: The main conclusion, that adherence to an unsupervised programme was limited and feasibility was modest, is supported and carefully hedged. The efficacy language ('weak indication') relies on an exploratory tally of positive-direction DID whose chance interpretation is not justified, and every DID interval spans zero. The numeric problems found are minor typographical slips (an impossible CI upper limit, a copied CI, a loose comorbidity statement).

primary_outcome.name: Adherence to the intervention procedure (feasibility)

issues.title: VO2peak gain of 1.8 ml/kg/min (AT, within-group) called comparable to a trial effect; ITT DID is -0.25
issues.explanation: The discussion compares the as-treated intervention group's pre-post change in VO2peak with that of a supervised RCT, as if it supported efficacy. That figure is a within-group change in a post-randomisation subset. In the ITT analysis the intervention gain (0.79) was smaller than the control gain (1.04), and the AT DID is 1.42 with CI -5.64 to 8.48. The comparison flatters the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group, ITT-based comparison showing a VO2peak difference comparable to the cited trial.

quotes.text: The mean difference in relative VO2peak (1,8 ml/kg/min) from baseline to follow-up in the present AT population is comparable

issues.title: 'Not expected by chance' inference from 25/33 positive-direction DID; all DID CIs include zero, no group tests
issues.explanation: The authors state that no group differences were tested. They then use the 25/33 positive-direction proportion (CI 0.58-0.89) to suggest the pattern is not due to chance, and the abstract reports a weak indication of efficacy. The parameters are not independent, the direction rule is partly arbitrary, and no DID interval excludes zero, so the chance statement is not supported by the design. The feasibility conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis plan treating the sign tally as a valid exploratory test, with a correlation-aware calculation showing the pattern is unlikely under the null.

quotes.text: This indicated that the proportion of positive DID may not have been expected by chance.
no hypotheses were stated, no group differences were tested, no outcome efficacy cut-offs were provided
However, there was some weak indication for efficacy of the intervention to reduce self-rated severity of symptoms and to improve overall wellbeing.

issues.title: Per-protocol proportion CI printed as 0.67 [0.48, 9.82]; an upper limit above 1 is impossible
issues.explanation: The per-protocol proportion of positive-direction DID is given with an upper confidence limit of 9.82, but a proportion cannot exceed 1. It is almost certainly a typo for about 0.82. Nothing else in the paper depends on it, so the effect is limited to one reported interval.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published correction or supplementary table showing the PP interval as 0.48 to 0.82 would show this is only a typo; it would still be a printing error.

script.explanation: 9.82 lies outside [0.0, 1.0], which a proportion cannot do. The extraction was verified against the paper's own text, so this is not a misreading on our side: the value as printed cannot be what the label says it is. The likeliest innocent explanations are a typesetting error or a mislabelled row -- both worth asking the authors about, and neither something this review can settle.

issues.title: Table 3 quality-of-life standardised DID 0.03 [-1.18, 0.47] repeats the CI of the row above
issues.explanation: The standardised CI for quality of life does not centre on its point estimate and matches the health-status row exactly. Dividing the raw CI by the baseline SD gives roughly -0.71 to 0.78. One interval in the ITT table is therefore wrong, though no conclusion changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or source output showing -1.18 to 0.47 is the true standardised interval for quality of life.

quotes.location: Table 3, Quality of life (1-4) row, standardized DID

issues.title: Headache baseline 4.67±3.06 (intervention) and 4.11±2.67 (control) identical in PP (n=14/23) and AT (n=17/26)
issues.explanation: The PP and AT analyses contain different participants, yet headache baseline mean and SD are identical to two decimals in both groups of both tables. This could be innocent if the reclassified participants lacked headache data, but the paper does not say so. It may be a carried-over cell.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Stating the number of participants with non-missing headache data in each analysis set, and showing the extra AT participants contributed no headache baseline values.

issues.title: 'Orthopaedic diseases most reported' does not hold in controls or overall (asthma/allergy 28/54 vs 27/54)
issues.explanation: The text says orthopaedic diseases were the most reported comorbidity, quoting 54% and 46%. Table 1 shows asthma and/or allergy at 60.7% in the control group, and overall it is marginally more common than orthopaedic disease. The statement holds only for the intervention group. This is a minor descriptive slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The text restricted to the intervention group, or a definition of comorbidity that excludes asthma/allergy.

quotes.text: Orthopaedic diseases were the most reported comorbidities (previous or current) at T0 with 54% in the intervention and 46% in the control group
quotes.location: Results, Description of study population, para 3
Table 1, Asthma and/or allergy row, control group

10.1038/s41598-025-23760-y.headline_claim: Exercise training modulated the serum extracellular vesicle RNA profile in response to acute exercise, mainly by downregulating immune, inflammatory and mitochondrial genes, so EV RNAs may serve as biomarkers of long COVID recovery and as mediators of systemic adaptation.
10.1038/s41598-025-23760-y.overall: The null findings, no viral RNA and no resting or direct pre/post training DEGs, are reasonably reported. The headline claim that training modulated the EV RNA profile and that EV RNAs act as functional mediators rests on a single-arm pilot of 14 completers and on a significant-versus-non-significant comparison, so it is only tentative. Several small numeric inconsistencies (work rate %, duplicated lab row, pathway counts, 46% vs 42.9%) add to the need for caution but do not change the overall picture.

primary_outcome.name: Serum EV RNA differentially expressed genes (q < 0.05), peak exercise vs rest after training (headline analysis; registry primary is peak VO2 at 10 weeks)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in aerobic capacity (Peak Oxygen Uptake) at 10 weeks after rehabilitation comprehensive (normal intensity) pulmonary rehabilitation program.

issues.title: Both direct pre- vs post-training EV RNA contrasts are null; conclusion credits training with modulation
issues.explanation: Neither direct comparison of pre- and post-training EV RNA found any DEG, at rest or at peak exercise. The positive finding, 53 DEGs at peak vs rest only after training, is a difference between a significant and a non-significant within-time comparison. With n=14, that pattern can arise from noise and threshold effects. The conclusion that training modulated the EV RNA response goes further than the direct tests support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A formal training-by-exercise interaction test showing a significant difference between the pre- and post-training exercise responses.

quotes.text: no DEGs were found at peak exercise between pre- and post-training time points
exercise training modulated the EV RNA profile in response to acute exercise

second_reader.what_stands: Both direct pre- vs post-training contrasts (at rest and at peak exercise) gave no DEGs at q < 0.05, and no formal training-by-exercise interaction test is reported. The conclusion that training 'modulated the EV RNA profile in response to acute exercise' therefore rests on 53 DEGs versus 0 DEGs in two separate within-visit contrasts, which is a difference in significance rather than a tested difference.

issues.title: Conclusion calls EV RNAs functional mediators and links them to symptom improvement; no outcome link or functional test
issues.explanation: The Discussion says EV RNA signatures were not correlated with clinical outcomes, and the pathway analysis is described as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. The Abstract and Conclusion nonetheless speak of molecular mechanisms underlying symptom improvement and of EV RNAs acting as functional mediators of adaptation. An association of 53 genes at the FDR threshold in 14 people with no control group cannot show mediation. The wording outruns the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses linking EV RNA changes to individual symptom or fitness change, or functional experiments showing EV RNAs mediate the adaptation.

quotes.text: may not only serve as potential biomarkers of long COVID recovery but also act as functional mediators of systemic adaptation
highlights potential molecular mechanisms underlying symptom improvement

second_reader.what_stands: No analysis links EV RNA changes to symptom or fitness outcomes, and no functional experiment was done, yet the conclusion describes EV RNAs as possible 'functional mediators of systemic adaptation' and the abstract points to mechanisms underlying symptom improvement. The authors do state in the Discussion that no correlation with outcomes was done and that the pathway findings are exploratory, and the conclusion is hedged with 'may', so the overreach is one of framing rather than an undisclosed gap.

issues.title: Single-arm design: training effect on EV RNA cannot be separated from time, recovery or repeat testing
issues.explanation: All 14 participants had the same sequence, with sampling before and after 10 weeks of training. There is no comparison group, so changes cannot be attributed to training rather than spontaneous recovery, repeat CPET exposure or batch and time effects. The authors say this in the Discussion and limitations, but the abstract and conclusion still state that training modulated EV gene expression.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent non-training control group analysed alongside the participants.

quotes.text: we cannot distinguish the effects of exercise training from spontaneous recovery
quotes.location: Discussion, EVs as mediators of exercise adaptation

quotes.text: our study lacked a control group
Acute exercise and exercise training modulated EV-associated gene expression in long COVID

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is a single-arm pre/post study with no control group, so any training effect on EV RNA cannot be separated from time, spontaneous recovery or repeat testing; the authors say so in the Discussion and Limitations. The problem is acknowledged but not resolved: the abstract ('Acute exercise and exercise training modulated EV-associated gene expression') and conclusion use causal training language without that caveat.

issues.title: Peak work rate gain printed as 16% in Results but 10.3% in Discussion; Table 1 means give 11.5%
issues.explanation: The same cohort and measure is given two different percentage gains, 16% in the Results and 10.3% in the Discussion. Neither matches the Table 1 means (139 to 155 W). The reader cannot tell which figure is right. This is a reporting inconsistency in a secondary fitness result and does not touch the EV RNA findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 16% is the mean of individual changes and 10.3% is a different quantity, or a corrected figure that reconciles them.

quotes.text: Peak work rate increased by 16% (Table 1).
increases in peak work rate (10.3%)
quotes.location: Discussion, EVs as mediators of exercise adaptation

issues.title: 7 of 21 enrolled (33%) not analysed; no account of dropouts or comparison with completers
issues.explanation: The paper says 21 participants were enrolled and 14 completed all exercise trials. It gives no reasons for the other 7, no flow diagram and no comparison of completers and non-completers. The sequencing analysis uses only completers, so results may not represent those enrolled. Because the claims are exploratory and not about efficacy, this weakens interpretation rather than invalidating it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow account showing the 7 non-completers left for reasons unrelated to training or response and resembled completers at baseline.

quotes.text: Fourteen out of 21 subjects completed all exercise trials and the study.
14 subjects completed exercise training, and their demographics are presented in Table 1.

issues.title: Post-training absolute VO2 SD printed as 0.07 versus 0.69 pre; flagged significant
issues.explanation: The post-training SD of 0.07 L/min is about one tenth of the pre-training SD of 0.69, which is implausible for the same participants after training. It is probably a mistyped 0.7, but as printed it affects the stated significance of the paired test. The 7.4% gain also does not equal the change in the printed means.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing post-training SD of 0.07.

issues.title: Troponin and Pro-BNP both reported as 6.8±2.2 in Table 1
issues.explanation: Two different screening analytes with different units of scale and normal ranges have an identical mean and SD in Table 1. This most likely reflects a duplicated or mis-pasted row. The text uses these values only to say they were 'within normal ranges', so nothing else depends on them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source laboratory data showing both analytes truly have mean 6.8 and SD 2.2.

quotes.text: High Sensitivity Troponin (normal<15 ng/L)
Pro-BNP (normal<253 ng/L)

issues.title: Discussion cites 21 of 44 inactivated pathways for the resting comparison, which has 68 inactivated
issues.explanation: In the Results, V24T0 vs V2T0 has 68 inactivated pathways, and 44 inactivated belongs to V24T1 vs V24T0. The Discussion paragraph on the resting comparison uses 44 and links it to 'acute exercise after training'. The two comparisons are mixed up, so the claim that 21 of the inactivated pathways were inflammation-linked is not tied to a clear pathway set.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pathway lists showing 44 inactivated pathways in the V24T0 vs V2T0 comparison.

quotes.text: including 32 activated and 68 inactivated pathways
21 (e.g., STAT3, SAPK/JNK, PDGF, and C-type lectin receptor pathways) of the 44 inactivated pathways
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph on resting pathway changes

issues.title: Exercise intolerance 6/46% in Table 1 and text; 6 of 14 is 43%
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives 6 participants with exercise intolerance as 46%, and the text repeats 46%. Six of the 14 completers is 42.9%. The other symptom rows are consistent with a denominator of 14. The slip is small and affects only a descriptive figure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the denominator for this symptom was not 14 (for example 13 participants).

quotes.text: Exercise Intolerance (6/46%)

script.explanation: 6/14 = 42.86%, but the paper prints 46, outside the rounding interval [45.50, 47.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 13.0 rather than 14.

issues.title: EV RNA analysis is not the registered primary outcome (peak VO2 at 10 weeks); only the current record was seen
issues.explanation: The registry lists change in peak oxygen uptake at 10 weeks as the only primary outcome. This paper's central results are EV RNA differential expression, which the record does not list as primary. It is presented as a pilot, exploratory analysis and the VO2 result is also reported. Whether this is a real switch cannot be settled from the paper and the current record alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing EV RNA as a registered secondary or exploratory outcome from the start.

quotes.text: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified (q < 0.05)
Peak oxygen uptake increased after training by 7.4%

issues.title: Registered 2022-05-10 after the February 2022 start; registration not prospective
issues.explanation: The paper states the study began in February 2022, and the registry record was first submitted on 10 May 2022. Registration therefore followed enrolment, so it cannot show that outcomes were fixed before data were seen. This matters little for a descriptive pilot but weakens any claim that the analysis plan was pre-specified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing an earlier first submission, before enrolment started.

quotes.text: single-center pilot clinical trial was conducted from February 2022 to December 2023
Clinical trial registration number : NCT05398692.

10.1038/s41598-025-27036-3.headline_claim: HT-PS23 may be a feasible and well-tolerated intervention for relieving cognitive or physical symptoms associated with long COVID, with improvements in cortisol, CTT2 errors, breathing difficulty and appetite loss versus placebo.
10.1038/s41598-025-27036-3.overall: The paper's own conclusions are hedged as preliminary, but the benefit claims rest on four nominally significant secondary results among roughly 70 uncorrected tests, in a completer-only analysis with unbalanced dropout. The registered primary outcome (CGI-S) was null, and registration was retrospective. The feasibility and safety conclusions are better supported than the efficacy claims.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated as a single primary outcome; the paper reports multiple outcomes (cortisol, CTT2 color errors, breathing difficulty, appetite loss)

primary_outcomes.measure: Clinical Global Impression scales of Severity rated by clinician（CGI）

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 31 of 39 randomised (20.5% lost), losses 6/20 HT-PS23 vs 2/19 placebo
issues.explanation: All baseline and outcome tables cover only participants who completed the trial. Dropouts and exclusions were 6 of 20 in the HT-PS23 arm and 2 of 19 in placebo, so the analysed groups are no longer the randomised groups. Some exclusions (re-infection, antibiotics, <80% compliance) are post-randomisation and could be related to treatment or outcome. This weakens the between-group comparisons that the headline findings rest on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis including all 39 randomised participants showing the same results.

quotes.text: Table 1 .  Comparisons of baseline characteristics between the two groups in those completed the 6-week trial.
One participant in the placebo group and three in the HT-PS23 group dropped out after being infected with COVID again during the intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: Only 31 of the 39 randomised participants (20.5% lost) are analysed, and losses are unbalanced: about 6/20 (30%) in the HT-PS23 arm versus 2/19 (10.5%) in placebo. No ITT or imputed analysis is reported. The per-arm randomised counts are derived by arithmetic from the dropout text, and they reconcile exactly with the printed total.

issues.title: Four p<0.05 results among roughly 70 uncorrected tests (Tables 2-3) are headlined as improvements
issues.explanation: Tables 2 and 3 report Mann-Whitney tests for well over 60 outcomes, each at p<0.05 with no correction. At that rate about three or four nominally significant results are expected by chance alone, which is what was found (cortisol 0.006, CTT2 colour errors 0.018, breathing 0.016, appetite 0.030). None would survive even a modest correction. The headline benefit claims therefore rest on selected nominal results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or limited set of primary tests, or adjusted p-values that remain significant.

quotes.text: HT-PS23 group showed notable improvements in cortisol level
The HT-PS23 group exhibited significant improvements in cortisol levels during the 6-week intervention period (U = 51, p =  0.006).

second_reader.what_stands: Four favourable p<0.05 results come from about 68 uncorrected tests, a count close to what chance alone would give at alpha 0.05 (about 3.4). They are headlined as improvements in the abstract and conclusions, and none survives a Bonferroni or Holm correction. The paper's pilot framing and request for caution soften this, but it never mentions multiplicity.

issues.title: Registered primary CGI-S was null; abstract and conclusions headline cortisol, CTT2, breathing, appetite
issues.explanation: ClinicalTrials.gov lists clinician-rated CGI-S as the only primary outcome. The paper reports no significant CGI-S difference (p = 0.696) but never labels it primary, and the abstract and conclusions feature the four nominally significant secondary results instead. Selecting favourable secondary outcomes for the headline overstates benefit. This also covers the screen's spin flag (c7).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the primary outcome was CGI-S only as a placeholder, or a protocol designating cortisol or CTT2 as primary before data collection.

quotes.text: did not show significant changes between the HT-PS23 and placebo groups
provides preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and safety of using the psychobiotic

second_reader.what_stands: The registered primary outcome, CGI-S, shows no between-group difference (p=0.696). The paper never identifies it as primary, and the abstract and conclusions foreground the four nominally significant secondary results instead. The registration was retrospective. I cannot verify from the current record whether the registered outcomes were changed after registration. The 'feasibility and safety' framing and the explicit caution do temper the conclusion, but the abstract and conclusions still do not report the null primary result.

issues.title: Registered 2023-04-11, about 3 months after study start 2023-01-16; paper lists 16/01/2023
issues.explanation: The paper presents 16/01/2023 beside the registration number as if it were the registration date. The registry's first submission is 2023-04-11, after the start date, so registration was retrospective. Retrospective registration weakens confidence that outcomes were fixed before data were seen, which compounds the primary-outcome concern. This also covers c9.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing a record created before 2023-01-16.

quotes.text: The clinical trial registration number for this study is NCT05813899 (16/01/2023).
quotes.location: Declarations, Ethics approval and consent to participate

issues.title: Text says both groups increased HEPA activity; HT-PS23 HEPA-active fell 10 to 8, placebo flat at 16
issues.explanation: The Results state that both groups increased engagement in health-enhancing physical activity. Table 1 and Table 2 show HEPA-active falling from 10 (71%) to 8 (57%) in the HT-PS23 group and staying at 16 (94%) in placebo. The Discussion correctly says the HT-PS23 group had a lower proportion, so the Results sentence contradicts both the table and the paper's own later text. This is a secondary outcome and does not touch the headline claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 or per-participant data showing HEPA-active counts rising in both arms.

quotes.text: both groups showed increased engagement in health-enhancing physical activity (HEPA) over the course of the trial
quotes.location: Results, Changes over time between the two groups, para 2

quotes.text: The IPAQ results showed a lower proportion of participants in the HT-PS23 group engaging in health-enhancing physical activity post-intervention

issues.title: Sample size of 24 stated without outcome or effect size; 31 analysed across many outcomes
issues.explanation: The power statement gives only alpha and power, with no target outcome, effect size or variance, so it cannot be checked. A pilot of 14 versus 17 has little power for individual symptom or biomarker contrasts. The authors acknowledge this, which limits the problem to the abstract's wording of 'notable improvements'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A documented power calculation for a named primary outcome, with effect size, that the analysed sample satisfies.

quotes.text: At an a priori determined α level of 0.05 and a power of 0.80, a total sample size of 24 is required
the small sample size was a major limitation, and a larger sample size is required to confirm the efficacy of probiotics

10.1038/s41598-025-96555-w.headline_claim: A brief awe intervention improves psychological health in people with long COVID, reducing stress and depressive symptoms and increasing well-being.
10.1038/s41598-025-96555-w.overall: The direction of the findings (lower stress and depression, higher well-being than waitlist) is plausible, but the evidence is weak. It comes from 68 completers, an unblinded waitlist control, self-report outcomes and no intention-to-treat analysis, so the claims of 'efficacy' and 'robustness' go beyond what the design supports. The text and table discrepancies are small and do not change the results.

primary_outcome.name: Well-being (MHC-SF); the registry's sole primary outcome

issues.title: Unblinded waitlist control with self-reported outcomes cannot separate awe effects from expectancy
issues.explanation: The control group received nothing during the comparison period, and every outcome is a self-report questionnaire. Participants in the intervention group knew they were receiving an awe programme, so expectancy, attention and demand effects are confounded with any true effect. The authors concede this only in the final limitations paragraph. The Discussion still says the findings 'demonstrate the efficacy' of the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An active or attention-matched control arm, or evidence of an objective or blinded-assessor outcome showing the same effects.

quotes.text: The study design was a single-blind, waitlist-control, RCT.
as opposed to a wait-list control as we did here, which would help reduce demand characteristics and possibilities of placebo effects.
quotes.location: Limitations and Implications for Future Work

second_reader.what_stands: With a waitlist control, participants aware of their allocation, and only self-reported outcomes, the design cannot separate an awe-specific effect from expectancy, demand or placebo-type effects. The authors name this limitation themselves, but the Discussion still states that the findings 'demonstrate the efficacy' of the intervention.

issues.title: 'Robust' efficacy claimed from large effects in 30 vs 38 completers with a waitlist control
issues.explanation: The abstract and Discussion say the medium-to-large effects (d = 0.78-0.96) 'demonstrate the robustness' of the findings and 'the efficacy' of the intervention. Large standardised effects from a very small, completer-only, unblinded sample are likely to be imprecise and inflated, so they are not evidence of robustness. The paper also extends the result to chronic clinical conditions in general. The supported conclusion is preliminary, hypothesis-generating evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confidence intervals for d that exclude small effects, or an independent replication in a larger, adequately controlled sample.

quotes.text: Effect sizes ranged from medium to large ( d =  0.78-0.96), demonstrating the robustness of these findings.
These findings demonstrate the efficacy of our novel intervention in promoting reductions in depression symptoms and improvements in well-being
positions awe as a promising avenue to improve psychological health in chronic clinical conditions like long COVID.
quotes.location: Limitations and Implications for Future Work

second_reader.what_stands: The large d values are arithmetically correct, but they come from a small completers-only comparison (30 vs 38) against an unblinded waitlist control. The confidence intervals are wide (roughly 0.3 to 1.3 for d around 0.8), and effect sizes from small completer samples tend to be overestimated. Calling the findings 'robust' and saying they 'demonstrate efficacy' is therefore stronger than the design supports, even though the authors list small size and the need for replication as limitations.

issues.title: Efficacy estimated only in completers (30 vs 38); no ITT analysis despite 'substantial attrition'
issues.explanation: The authors state that intention-to-treat analysis was not done because it required complete T2 data. They also say attrition was substantial. The between-group tests therefore cover only those who finished, and the number randomized and lost per arm is not given in the text. Dropout could relate to outcomes or to the arm (the arms differ in size, 30 vs 38), and the claim of no differences is a weak safeguard at this sample size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis giving similar effects, or a CONSORT diagram showing negligible and balanced attrition.

quotes.text: Also, an intention-to-treat analysis was not conducted due to the requirement for complete T2 data from all randomized participants.
Although there was substantial attrition, there were no significant differences between those that dropped out and those that completed the intervention.
quotes.location: Limitations and Implications for Future Work

second_reader.what_stands: All efficacy estimates come from participants with complete T2 data only, with no ITT or sensitivity analysis, even though the authors describe attrition as substantial. The 'no significant differences' check between completers and dropouts cannot rule out bias from differential or outcome-related dropout. I could not check the actual attrition size or its split by arm, because those figures sit in Fig. 1 and the supplement.

issues.title: Awe-group change scores in text (depression -2.31, anxiety -0.33) differ from Table 2 mean differences (-2.25, -0.30)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the awe group's depression change as -2.31, but the Table 2 means (12.87 to 10.62) differ by -2.25. Anxiety shows the same pattern (text -0.33, table 2.95 to 2.65 = -0.30). The control group and the stress and well-being rows agree with the table to rounding. The gaps are small and probably reflect different numbers of respondents at T1 and T2. They do not change the significance of any result, but the paper does not say which numbers are right.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that change scores are computed only among participants with both T1 and T2 values, while Table 2 means use all available data at each time point (with the respective ns).

issues.title: Registry lists well-being as sole primary outcome; paper treats four outcomes as co-primary and headlines depression
issues.explanation: The registry record names well-being at one month as the only primary outcome, while the paper frames four outcomes as primary hypotheses without a correction for multiple outcomes. Depression is highlighted in the abstract and Discussion as a novel finding. All outcomes are reported and the key p-values are small (0.001-0.002), so the practical effect on the conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The pre-specified analytic plan or an earlier registry version listing depression as a primary or key secondary outcome.

quotes.text: This work is the first to document that awe can have salutary effects on psychological health, such as reducing symptoms of depression.
This study is the first RCT to show the effects of awe on depression symptoms.

issues.title: Intervention developers deliver and evaluate their own programme; funder role and any interests not described
issues.explanation: Two authors delivered the intervention, one of them affiliated with a company (Live Conscious), and the funding came via a donation awarded to two of the authors. The paper states no competing interests and says nothing about the funder's role in design, analysis or reporting. Whether any real interest exists cannot be determined from the text, but the developers-as-evaluators arrangement is worth disclosure in an unblinded trial with subjective outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that no author or affiliated organisation has any financial or commercial interest in the intervention, and that the funder had no role in the study.

quotes.text: Live Conscious, Hawi, HI, USA.
The authors declare no competing interests.
This research was supported in part by an anonymous philanthropic donation to the UC Davis School of Medicine awarded to Javier E. López, and Michael Amster.

10.1038/s41598-026-41182-2.headline_claim: A single bout of the six-minute step test acutely improves brachial artery endothelial function (FMD%) in individuals with long COVID.
10.1038/s41598-026-41182-2.overall: The main claim that a single 6MST acutely improved FMD in long COVID rests on an uncontrolled pre-post comparison. The unchanged control group helps but is not a rest-only comparator, and the control group is non-equivalent. The paper also contains several small reporting errors (percentages, the FEV1/FVC row, a text-table mismatch, Baecke sums) and overstated secondary wording. The FMD change is a plausible descriptive finding, but the causal and clinical wording is not supported.'

primary_outcome.name: Brachial artery FMD response (pre- to post-6MST)

issues.title: Pre-post FMD rise (4.53% to 6.83%) is claimed as an exercise effect with no rest-only comparator
issues.explanation: The study is a single-session, cross-sectional, pre-post comparison with no non-exercise session and no randomisation. The title says the test 'acutely promotes' endothelial function and the conclusion says it 'elicited' an improvement, yet the Methods state the design cannot infer causation. The unchanged control group gives some reassurance. But the long COVID group started well below controls, so regression to the mean and session effects are not excluded. The causal wording also covers the interpretation as a clinical effect, so the headline is only tentatively supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A rest-only session in the same participants showing no FMD change, or a reported significant group×time interaction with a non-exercise comparison.

quotes.text: A single bout of submaximal aerobic functional capacity test acutely promotes endothelial function in long COVID patients
The 6MST elicited an acute improvement in brachial artery endothelial function in individuals with persistent symptoms following COVID-19.
this study is not able to infer causal relationships between the variables analyzed

second_reader.what_stands: The 4.53% to 6.83% FMD rise is a single-arm pre-post change with no rest-only or sham comparator (the control group also exercised), so it cannot be attributed to the 6MST as an exercise effect. The authors do state the design cannot infer causality, but the title, abstract, discussion and conclusion still describe the rise as an exercise-elicited improvement, which the design does not support.

issues.title: Controls were chosen to be risk-factor-free, so group FMD differences and unadjusted change comparisons are confounded
issues.explanation: Controls had no hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia or regular medication, while the long COVID group had 19-31% of each. The between-group claim of attenuated FMD in long COVID therefore cannot separate long COVID from these comorbidities. The statement that this 'does not compromise the internal validity' is not supported by this design. The within-group acute change is less affected, but the acute-change comparison between groups is also unadjusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison matched or adjusted for comorbidity and medication that gives the same attenuated FMD.

quotes.text: it does not compromise the internal validity of comparisons between Long COVID participants and healthy controls
the lack of control for potential confounding variables such as inflammatory biomarkers, age, physical activity level, and body composition

issues.title: Rehabilitation recommendation calls exercise 'safe, feasible, and effective' from one uncontrolled FMD measure
issues.explanation: The Clinical implications section recommends structured low-intensity exercise bouts as a safe, feasible and effective approach for rehabilitation. The study measured only a transient vascular marker once, had no safety monitoring beyond termination criteria, and no clinical or sustained outcome. Seven participants stopped the test early. The recommendation goes beyond what a single-session, non-randomised design can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocolised safety data and a sustained clinical or functional outcome from an interventional study.

quotes.text: the incorporation of structured low-intensity exercise bouts into rehabilitation programs may represent a safe, feasible, and effective approach

issues.title: Abstract and conclusion cite a 'greater diastolic BP response', but peak-minus-rest change was similar (p = 0.297)
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion say the long COVID group had a greater diastolic blood pressure response. Table 2 shows the groups differed in DBP level from rest onward, with similar changes from rest to peak and from peak to recovery. A higher resting level is not a larger exercise response. The wording therefore overstates a secondary finding, and the Discussion repeats it as 'greater cardiovascular responses'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A defined 'response' measure, such as DBP area under the curve, showing a significant group difference.

quotes.text: greater diastolic blood pressure response
although delta changes from peak to recovery were similar between groups

issues.title: FEV1/FVC printed as 1.01 and 1.03 in Table 1, inconsistent with FEV1 2.98 L and FVC 3.68 L
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives a mean FEV1/FVC of 1.01 (COVID) and 1.03 (control). A true FEV1/FVC cannot exceed 1, and the printed mean FEV1 and FVC imply about 0.81. The row is mislabelled or mis-computed. It affects only the finding that lung function was similar between groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the row is a different quantity (for example a ratio of percent-predicted values) with values that reproduce 1.01 and 1.03.

issues.title: Roughly 40 Table 2 comparisons tested at p < 0.05 uncorrected; borderline HR findings interpreted
issues.explanation: Table 2 tests dozens of haemodynamic outcomes with no correction across outcomes, and a few reach only p = 0.038 to 0.049. The authors warn about multiple comparisons in one paragraph but still interpret the heart-rate result. This affects the secondary cardiovascular findings, not the FMD claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome with the cardiovascular measures labelled exploratory.

quotes.text: Although some variables showed statistically significant differences ( p <  0.05), these results may be influenced by multiple comparisons and should be interpreted with caution.

issues.title: Text gives mMRC score 2 as 65%, but the table gives 9 of 26 (35%)
issues.explanation: The Results text says most patients scored 1 (27%) and 2 (65%) on the mMRC. Table 2 lists 7 (27%) for score 1 and 9 (35%) for score 2. The 65% figure belongs to PCFS score 2, so the text overstates dyspnoea severity in the long COVID group. It is a descriptive error that does not touch the FMD result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected data table showing 17 of 26 patients with mMRC 2.

quotes.text: scores of 1 (27%) and 2 (65%)

issues.title: Controls described as free of preexisting risk factors, yet Table 1 lists stress (6) and former smoking (3) in controls
issues.explanation: The Limitations section calls the control group free of preexisting risk factors. Table 1 shows 6 controls with stress and 3 former smokers. The cardiometabolic risk factors are indeed absent in controls, so the inconsistency is narrow. It still matters because the same sentence is used to defend the group comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 'risk factors' that explicitly excludes stress and smoking history.

quotes.text: healthy young adults without preexisting risk factors or regular medication use

issues.title: Control Baecke domain means sum to 7.37 but the final score is printed as 7.02
issues.explanation: The COVID column's domains add up to the printed final score, but the control column's do not. The control gap of 0.35 exceeds any rounding effect. One of the control domain scores or the final score is mistyped, or the control column rests on different data. It concerns a baseline activity comparison only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement that the final score is computed differently, or that control domain means use different participants.

quotes.location: Table 1, Occupational domain row, control column
Table 1, Sports domain row, control column
Table 1, Leisure domain row, control column

10.1038/s41598-026-44806-9.headline_claim: A remotely delivered, one-to-one physical activity coaching programme is feasible, safe, and may improve PA, sedentary behaviour, functional capacity, symptoms and HRQoL in people with Long COVID, with a fully powered trial warranted.
10.1038/s41598-026-44806-9.overall: The feasibility conclusion (recruitment 89%, retention 92%, adherence 83%) is reasonably supported for a pilot. The efficacy claims are exploratory: they come from an unblinded pilot of 50 with imbalanced baselines, unadjusted primary models and a changed outcome hierarchy relative to the registry. The abstract and Conclusions are mostly hedged ('may improve'), so the problems are modest and chiefly reporting inconsistencies (sex split, baseline text, risk differences) and some Discussion over-wording.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (recruitment, retention, adherence)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Physical activity (PA) patterns (steps/day) from baseline (pre-intervention), at 12 weeks (post-intervention), 6 months and 12 months
Change in Physical activity (PA) patterns (time spent in light PA per day) from baseline (pre-intervention), at 12 weeks (post-intervention), 6 months and 12 months
Change in Physical activity (PA) patterns (time spent in moderate-to-vigorous PA per day) from baseline (pre-intervention), at 12 weeks (post-intervention), 6 months and 12 months
Change in Physical activity (PA) patterns (time in sedentary behaviour -lying or sitting- per day) from baseline (pre-intervention), at 12 weeks (post-intervention), 6 months and 12 months
Change in functional capacity (six-minute walking test) from baseline (pre-intervention) at 12 weeks (post-intervention), 6 months and 12 months
Change in functional capacity (one-minute sit-to-stand test) from baseline (pre-intervention) at 12 weeks (post-intervention), 6 months and 12 months

issues.title: Baseline imbalance (time since COVID 31 vs 46 months, lung function, dyspnoea, higher EG steps); adjusted results not shown
issues.explanation: The coaching arm had better lung function, lower dyspnoea and higher baseline steps, which could favour the EG. The primary models are unadjusted, and the sensitivity models, which the paper says give slightly smaller effects, are not shown in the main text. With n=50 the effect size is uncertain. This is acknowledged, and the direction of effect appears robust.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted estimates in Additional file 4 showing negligible change in effect sizes.

quotes.text: Baseline between-group differences were observed in time since acute infection, lung function and dyspnoea.
yielded results which were consistent in direction, although of slightly lower magnitude but still clinically relevant

issues.title: Printed risk differences exceed differences of the printed proportions in many rows (e.g. 36 vs 44, 32 vs 40, 46 vs 51)
issues.explanation: The footnote defines risk difference as the absolute difference in proportions. Several rows give larger values than the printed percentages imply. Examples are ITT <5000 steps at 6 months (52% vs 16% = 36 points, printed 44), ITT 3 months in the second proportion block (52% vs 20% = 32, printed 40) and per-protocol 3 months (57% vs 11% = 46, printed 51). This pattern runs through the proportion rows, for example the ITT mMRC>=2 row (60% vs 4% = 56, printed 66). The RDs look model-derived but are labelled as raw differences, so the effect sizes are overstated relative to the counts shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods or supplement stating that RDs are model-estimated marginal differences, with the estimated proportions shown.

quotes.text: Risk difference represents the absolute difference in proportions between groups.
from baseline to six-month followup: 36% to 16% vs. 52% to 52%
quotes.location: Results, Physical activity and sedentary behaviour

issues.title: Paper's primary outcome (feasibility) differs from registry primary outcomes (PA, 6MWD, 1minSTS); change not disclosed
issues.explanation: The registry lists steps, light PA, MVPA, sedentary time, 6MWD and 1minSTS as primary outcomes, with follow-up to 12 months. The paper names feasibility as primary and presents the registered outcomes as secondary or exploratory, without saying the hierarchy changed. All registered outcomes are reported, so this is a transparency problem rather than selective omission. The paper does hedge efficacy as preliminary, which limits the damage.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version already listing feasibility as primary, or a paper statement explaining the change.

quotes.text: Primary outcome: feasibility
Preliminary efficacy and effectiveness

issues.title: Discussion says the intervention 'effectively increased' PA, and 'safe' is stated for 25 coached participants
issues.explanation: The study was explicitly not powered for hypothesis testing, was unblinded for participants, and lost 20% of participants by six months. Unqualified causal wording in the Discussion ('effectively increased') and the unqualified 'safe' go beyond what a pilot of 25 per arm supports. The abstract and Conclusions are more cautious, so the headline effect is only partly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: N/A; the issue is wording relative to the design.

quotes.text: This intervention effectively increased PA and reduced sedentary behaviour
this was not intended for hypothesis testing but rather to ensure adequate precision in estimating variability

issues.title: Unblinded participants and coaches; fatigue, dyspnoea and HRQoL (patient-reported) gains stated in abstract
