issues.explanation: Only assessors were blinded. FACIT-FS, mMRC and EQ-5D-5L are self-reported and could be influenced by knowing the allocation and by the coaching contact. The authors acknowledge this in the limitations, but the abstract reports these gains without the caveat. The between-group differences for these outcomes are therefore of uncertain size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; blinding status is stated.

quotes.text: Outcome assessors were blinded to group allocation, although participants and intervention providers were not, due to the nature of the intervention.
quotes.location: Methods, Randomisation, allocation concealment and blinding

quotes.text: This may have influenced interaction dynamics and, potentially, patient-reported outcomes.

issues.title: Abstract sex split (EG 80% F, CG 76% F) conflicts with Table 1 (PA coaching 72% F, usual care 80% F)
issues.explanation: The abstract gives 80% female for the coaching arm and 76% for usual care. Table 1 gives 18/25 = 72% female for coaching and 20/25 = 80% for usual care. The abstract's 76% matches the pooled sample, not the control arm, and the 80% appears to be attached to the wrong arm. This is a reporting slip with no effect on results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published correction or protocol showing the abstract used different group definitions.

quotes.location: Table 1, Female/male row, PA coaching column

issues.title: Roughly 25 outcomes at two timepoints; Bonferroni applied over only three comparisons per analysis
issues.explanation: The correction covers three comparisons within each analysis, not the full set of outcomes, so the family-wise error rate across all outcomes is not controlled. Borderline results, such as MVPA +7[1;14] and sedentary time -71[-141;-2] at 3 months, are the most fragile. The strongest results are unlikely to be affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or key-outcome set, or a family-wise adjustment across outcomes.

quotes.text: Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds were applied separately for between-group (p<0.017; three comparisons)

issues.title: Results say 'no other' baseline differences, but Table 1 stars FEV1pp (94 vs 104) and FVCpp (90 vs 100)
issues.explanation: The Results name only dyspnoea as differing at baseline and then say no other significant differences were seen. Table 1 stars FEV1pp and FVCpp as significant between-group baseline differences, and the Discussion concedes lung-function and time-since-infection imbalances. The Results sentence is therefore inaccurate, and it understates baseline imbalance where the main findings are reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Text clarifying that 'other' refers only to non-lung-function variables.

quotes.text: No other significant differences were observed.

issues.title: Usual-care arm received the tracker and weekly reporting; no attention-matched control
issues.explanation: Controls were not a no-intervention group, since self-monitoring is itself a behaviour-change technique. This probably understates the PA effect, but the lack of attention-matching could inflate patient-reported outcome differences. The paper discloses both issues.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable.

quotes.text: participants received the same activity tracker and submitted weekly PA reports
the use of usual care rather than an attention-matched control intervention may have introduced attention or expectation bias

10.1038/s41598-026-51787-2.headline_claim: A six-week multi-component rehabilitation programme gives substantial, immediate and sustained (six-month) benefits in long COVID, validating its clinical efficacy.
10.1038/s41598-026-51787-2.overall: The data suggest that pooled patients improved on respiratory muscle strength, walking distance and several symptoms from baseline to six months. The design does not support attributing this to the programme or calling it durable. The six-month analysis merges arms and compares only with baseline, uses a per-protocol set of 75 of 109 randomised, and the abstract wording overstates retention. A secondary symptom figure (muscle and joint pain) is also internally inconsistent.

primary_outcome.name: 6MWD, PImax and PEmax (respiratory muscle strength)

primary_outcomes.measure: Physical endurance improvement assessment of 6 MWT distance and outcome of treadmill stress test.

issues.title: Six-month benefit and 'behaviour change' claims rest on a merged cohort with no concurrent comparator
issues.explanation: For the follow-up, the intervention and sham-IMT groups were merged and changes were tested only against the cohort's own baseline. This design cannot attribute improvement at six months to the programme, because spontaneous recovery from COVID is expected over this period. The Conclusions nonetheless call the programme effective, say it facilitates long-term behavioural change, and say it beats the natural course, using literature cohorts as the comparison. No physical-activity data were collected to support the behaviour-change mechanism. This undermines the causal framing of the main sustained-benefit conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A 6-month between-arm comparison, or a concurrent usual-care cohort, showing a persistent difference favouring the programme.

quotes.text: the intervention and control groups were merged
Direct comparison between baseline and 6-month follow-up outcomes confirmed a statistically significant and clinically meaningful impact of the rehabilitation programme.
offers a more favourable recovery trajectory than the natural course of the disease

second_reader.what_stands: The six-month benefit and 'more favourable trajectory than the natural course' claims rest on a pooled single cohort with before/after comparisons only, with no concurrent untreated comparator, and the natural-course comparison is to differing published cohorts. The 'behavioural change' statement is a speculation not supported by any measured activity or behaviour outcome, though the Discussion does partly hedge it as plausible; the Conclusions state it more firmly.

issues.title: Efficacy shown only in per-protocol set: 75 of 109 randomised analysed (about 31% excluded), no ITT
issues.explanation: Only participants attending at least 12 of 18 sessions and completing follow-up were analysed, which is 75 of 109 randomised. The Discussion says this confirms effectiveness under optimal compliance, but the conclusions are stated for the programme generally. Excluding about 31% of randomised participants can inflate benefit if non-completers did worse. No ITT sensitivity analysis is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat analysis of all 109 randomised participants with similar results.

quotes.text: Of the 123 individuals, 109 were randomised to either the intervention or control group.
Eligibility for final analysis required attendance at ≥ 12 of 18 training sessions, resulting in a study population with a mean adherence of 0.89.
confirming intervention effectiveness under optimal compliance

second_reader.what_stands: The reported results cover 75 of 109 randomised participants (about 31% not analysed) using a per-protocol set defined by at least 12 of 18 sessions plus complete data, and no ITT analysis is presented. The per-protocol design is disclosed and the Discussion frames it as 'under optimal compliance', but the Abstract and Conclusions still speak of validated clinical efficacy without that qualification; the reason for each of the 34 exclusions cannot be determined from the extracted text.

issues.title: 6-month muscle/joint pain: overall 77% (58/75) exceeds both sex-specific rates in text (56% women, 24% men)
issues.explanation: Table 3 gives 58 of 75 (77%) with muscular or articular pain at 6 months. The Results text says 56% of women and 24% of men reported it. An overall rate cannot exceed both subgroup rates. One of the two reports is wrong, or the text refers to something else without saying so. This affects a secondary symptom result, not the primary outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text percentages refer to a different quantity (for example pain change or a different time point) that reconciles with the Table 3 count.

quotes.text: Muscle and joint pain was reported by 56% of women vs 24% of men (p = 0.003)

issues.title: Abstract claims 'statistically significant retention' vs post-rehab values; Time 2→3 tests are mostly non-significant
issues.explanation: The abstract describes statistically significant retention of improvements compared with post-rehabilitation values. The Time 2→3 comparisons mostly show no significant change, which is an absence of evidence of decline, not a significant finding of retention. Where changes are significant (6MWD p=0.02 and chest expansion p=0.001), they are further increases. The real result is only 'no clear decline', and the wording overstates it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence or non-inferiority analysis of Time 2 vs Time 3 showing retention within a stated margin.

quotes.text: The six-month follow-up analysis demonstrated statistically significant retention of improvements in functional and qualitative parameters compared with post-rehabilitation values

issues.title: Registered primary outcomes (quality of life, treadmill test) are not reported; paper names 6MWD and PImax/PEmax
issues.explanation: The registry lists quality of life and a treadmill stress test among primary outcomes, and neither appears in the results. The paper's own primary outcomes are 6MWD and PImax/PEmax. Because only the current registry version was seen and the paper says the protocol was unchanged, selective reporting cannot be confirmed. It remains an unexplained omission.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing quality of life and treadmill outcomes were added after the data were collected, or a companion paper reporting them.

quotes.text: The primary outcomes of this study were functional exercise capacity, measured by the six-minute walk distance (6MWD)
The study protocol remained unchanged after participant enrollment commenced.

issues.title: Exploratory baseline-capacity subgroup (p=0.026, uncorrected) presented as an abstract conclusion
issues.explanation: The abstract conclusion says the greatest gains are in patients with lower baseline capacity, and the Discussion calls the intervention a high-priority therapy for them. This rests on a single uncorrected subgroup comparison (p=0.026, r=0.257) within a merged uncontrolled cohort. Regression to the mean could produce the same pattern. It should be framed as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified subgroup analysis with an interaction test, and a control arm showing the baseline-by-treatment interaction.

quotes.text: with the greatest functional gains in patients with lower baseline capacity
Those with lower baseline capacity (<75%) achieved substantially greater improvements

issues.title: 'Durable' and 'long-term' benefit claimed from a single six-month follow-up
issues.explanation: The only follow-up is at six months, yet the Discussion states the programme shows durable efficacy and confirms the longevity of effects. The data support, at best, persistence of group-level improvement to six months without a control comparison. The wording overreaches the design, though the authors elsewhere say longer follow-up is warranted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Follow-up data beyond six months, or rewording claims to 'at least six months'.

quotes.text: The six-week rehabilitation programme demonstrated durable efficacy in improving pulmonary function
reinforcing the long-term effectiveness of the implemented rehabilitation programme

issues.title: Registry start date (1 June 2022) precedes registration (7 July 2022); paper dates start to July 2022
issues.explanation: The registry shows a study start of 1 June 2022 and first submission on 7 July 2022, which is retrospective by about five weeks. The paper says the project began on 8 July 2022 and data collection on August 2022. If the paper's dates are right, registration was prospective. The discrepancy is small and cannot be resolved from the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Enrolment records showing the first participant was enrolled after 7 July 2022.

10.1038/s41598-026-52301-4.headline_claim: Speleotherapy improves respiratory muscle strength, quality of life and lung function in adult asthma and dysfunctional breathing across asthma, COPD and Long COVID, with a favourable safety profile, while the pre-specified asthma primary endpoint (FeNO) did not change.
10.1038/s41598-026-52301-4.overall: The null primary endpoint (FeNO) is the only pre-specified asthma result, and the favourable conclusions rest on open-label patient-reported outcomes, a post-randomisation-excluded analysis set, and retrospective registration. The headline benefit claims should be treated as exploratory; sample size figures are also internally inconsistent between sections.

primary_outcome.name: FeNO (asthma); lung function and MIP/MEP (COPD, Long COVID)

issues.title: Secondary and exploratory results framed as demonstrated benefit despite null primary endpoint
issues.explanation: The pre-specified asthma primary endpoint was null, yet the Discussion states the study demonstrates improvement and a favourable benefit-risk profile. Many secondary outcomes were tested across three diseases with a post hoc subgroup, and harms were collected non-systematically, so 'no relevant harms' cannot support a benefit-risk conclusion. The Conclusion itself calls these results exploratory, which conflicts with the Discussion wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Systematic harms collection and a pre-specified hierarchy of testing in which the secondary outcomes were confirmatory.

quotes.text: No relevant harms were observed, supporting a favourable benefit-risk profile of speleotherapy as an adjunctive, non-pharmacological intervention.
Adverse events were assessed non-systematically by patient self-report
secondary outcome results should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in future studies.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper discloses that the primary endpoint was null and labels the secondary results exploratory in its Conclusion. However, the Abstract, results headings and Discussion present the secondary and patient-reported results as benefit, and the benefit-risk statement rests on unsystematic harm monitoring. The framing is therefore more favourable than a null primary endpoint supports, but it is not an undisclosed or unhedged claim throughout.

issues.title: Open-label, no-treatment control; headline gains rest on patient-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: Participants and assessors were unblinded, and the control group received nothing, so expectation and attention effects cannot be separated from a true effect. The clinically relevant gains highlighted in the Abstract are all self-reported, while the objective primary endpoint was null. The Discussion treats response bias as unlikely, which the design cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham or attention-matched control, or blinded objective outcomes showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Due to the nature of the intervention, participants and care providers were not blinded to group allocation. Outcome assessors and data analysts were not blinded.
this appears unlikely to have substantially influenced the results,

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with a no-treatment control and no blinded assessment, and the headline benefits are predominantly self-reported. The authors acknowledge possible placebo response, but their reason for dismissing it is weak. Some objective, effort-dependent measures (lung function, MIP/MEP) also moved, so 'rest on PROs' is true of the main claims but not of every reported gain.

issues.title: 25 of 233 randomised excluded after randomisation (7 for <12 sessions), contradicting 'analysed as randomised'
issues.explanation: Of 233 enrolled, 25 (10.7%) were removed, including 7 for attending fewer than 12 sessions and 5 for illness during therapy. These exclusions are post-baseline and likely fall mostly in the intervention arm, so the analysis is closer to per-protocol than intention-to-treat. The Methods nonetheless state participants were analysed as randomised, and exclusions by arm are not given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram by arm showing exclusions occurred before randomisation or were balanced, and a sensitivity analysis including all randomised participants.

quotes.text: Participants were analysed in the groups to which they  were  originally  randomised.
fewer than 12 therapy sessions completed (n = 7)

second_reader.what_stands: About 11% of those enrolled (25 of 233) were left out of the analysis, including 12 for events after therapy had begun (illness during therapy, fewer than 12 sessions). This is not an intention-to-treat analysis and conflicts with the statement 'analysed as randomised'. The paper says 'enrolled', not 'randomised', and gives no arm breakdown of exclusions, so the exact number randomised and the direction of any bias cannot be determined.

issues.title: Limitations give group sizes 115/64/47 (total 226); Results and Abstract give 107/59/42 (total 208)
issues.explanation: The Limitations section reports larger sample sizes for every diagnostic group than the Results and Abstract. The Limitations figures sum to 226, which matches neither the 233 enrolled nor the 208 analysed. The power statements in that section are tied to these unexplained numbers, so the reader cannot tell what sample the power claims refer to.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Limitations numbers are pre-exclusion or per-protocol counts, with a flow diagram reconciling 226 to 233 and 208.

quotes.text: For the asthma group ( n =  115), the planned sample size of 80 was reached
In the COPD group ( n =  64), the power was 0.8; in the Long COVID group ( n =  47), it was 0.7.
In  the  total  cohort  of  patients  with  bronchial  asthma  (n = 107;  intervention:  54;  control:  53)

issues.title: Trial registered July 2025, after recruitment ended (Sept 2024) and follow-up finished (Jan 2025)
issues.explanation: Registration followed completion of all follow-up by about six months, so the primary endpoints and analysis plan cannot be checked against a contemporaneous record. The paper asserts no changes after commencement, but that claim cannot be verified. Multiple primary endpoints per group and a post hoc under-70 subgroup add to the risk of flexible reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated protocol or ethics submission pre-specifying the endpoints and analysis.

quotes.text: Trial registration: DRKS00033365 (retrospectively registered).
follow-up for all outcomes was completed on 10 January 2025

issues.title: Later-phase 'all eligible included' and sex imbalance undermine randomisation; no adjustment for sex or centre
issues.explanation: The Methods say that in later phases all eligible patients were included, which implies allocation may not have followed the random sequence for some participants. The Limitations admit unequal sex distribution between groups. Analyses are unadjusted Mann-Whitney tests, so imbalance in sex or diagnosis is not accounted for. The arm size differences alone are not a defect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Allocation records showing all participants followed the random sequence, and sex-adjusted analyses giving the same results.

quotes.text: In  later  phases,  all  eligible  patients  were  included  to  meet  the  target  sample  size,  which  may  have  led  to  imbalances in sex and diagnosis distributions.
Despite  randomization,  an  unequal  gender  distribution  occurred  between  groups,  which  may  limit  the interpretability of results.

issues.title: Study organised by speleotherapy association that paid the lead author and statistician; funder role not stated
issues.explanation: The German Speleotherapy Association, which the lead author leads, paid both the lead author (€10,000) and the analysing statistician (€7,735). The conflicts are disclosed, but the paper does not say what role the association had in design, analysis or reporting. Analysts were unblinded and the sponsor has an interest in a positive result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A funder-role statement confirming independence in design, analysis and reporting.

quotes.text: Martin Mogk, from the company moreData, was commissioned by the German Speleotherapy Association to conduct the statistical analysis of the study and received an honorarium of €7,735.
he received an honorarium of €10,000 from the German Speleotherapy Association for organizing and supervising the present study.

issues.title: Blood CO2 measure labelled SpCO2 in Abstract but pCO2 in Results for p = 0.026; comparison also differs
issues.explanation: The Abstract reports an SpCO2 increase at T2 in CO2-rich centres with p=0.026. The Results attribute p=0.026 to pCO2 and describe it as a difference between high- and low-CO2 caves, not an increase within CO2-rich centres. The measure and the comparison are therefore described inconsistently. This affects only the secondary CO2 subproject.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Additional file 8 showing SpCO2 and pCO2 are the same variable and the within-centre T2 increase has p=0.026.

quotes.text: In CO₂-rich speleotherapy centers, both SpCO₂ (p = 0.026)
PetCO 2 and pCO 2 were significantly higher at T2 in Bindweide/Ennepetal ( p <  0.001 and p =  0.026, respectively)
quotes.location: Results, high vs low CO2 caves

10.1038/s43856-025-00829-3.headline_claim: Vaccination in unvaccinated individuals with Long COVID was associated with improved overall health for most participants, with some worsening; immune signatures (IFN-β, CNTF, sIL-6R) may predict non-improvement or improvement.
10.1038/s43856-025-00829-3.overall: The descriptive finding that about two-thirds of 16 participants reported feeling better at 12 weeks is reliable only as a description of this small open-label cohort; with no control group and a single self-rated outcome it cannot show that vaccination caused improvement. The immune-predictor findings rest on tiny subgroups, many analytes and an inconsistently specified PLS model, and should be treated as hypothesis-generating only. Internal reporting inconsistencies (PLS components, excluded surveys, subgroup counts) are minor individually but reduce confidence in the details.

primary_outcome.name: Overall health condition (better, same, or worse) after first COVID-19 vaccine dose

primary_outcomes.time_frame: The measure will be reported both longitudinally, over the 3 months following the participant post-vaccination (reporting the result at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks post-vaccination), and as a cross-sectional result at the end of the study (week 12).

The measure will be reported both longitudinally, over the 3 months following the participant post-vaccination (reporting the result at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks post-vaccination), and as a cross-sectional result at the end of the study (week 12).

issues.title: Symptom improvement after vaccination claimed as 'evidence' from a 16-person uncontrolled, unblinded pre-post study
issues.explanation: With no control group, self-reported 'better' at 12 weeks (10/16) cannot be attributed to vaccination; the authors themselves note Long COVID symptoms fluctuate and that the design cannot estimate benefit or harm. Yet the Discussion states the study provides evidence for symptom alleviation. The conclusion is only tentative at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent unvaccinated comparison group showing a lower improvement rate than the vaccinated participants.

quotes.text: this study provides evidence for alleviating symptoms among Long COVID participants upon vaccination
Symptom and immune changes may be a result of the natural course of disease not due to the vaccine.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a 16-person, uncontrolled, unblinded pre-post design with self-reported outcomes and no tests of the symptom changes, so the sentence 'provides evidence for alleviating symptoms ... upon vaccination' is stronger than the design supports. The point is only partly right because the authors state these limitations repeatedly, including that changes may be the natural course of disease, and the conclusion itself is cautious ('most people improved or stayed the same'). The inconsistency is in that single sentence's wording, not in an undisclosed limitation.

issues.title: Predictor claims for IFN-β, CNTF and sIL-6R rest on groups of 3, 2 and 7 participants and 162 analytes
issues.explanation: The PLS and mixed-model results compare outcome groups of 3, 2 and 7 participants across 162 analytes, with no sample-size calculation (target 50–100, 16 enrolled). A model with 162 features and about 12 people can fit almost anything, and a cumulative pseudo-R-squared of 0.98–0.99 suggests overfitting. The conclusion calls these 'top predictors' even though the Discussion calls the possibilities speculative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: External validation of the signature in an independent cohort, or a stable result under leave-one-out testing.

quotes.text: We prospectively sought to enroll 50–100 participants
The top predictors of participant non-improvement upon vaccination were stable elevated levels of IFN-β and CNTF.

second_reader.what_stands: The IFN-β, CNTF and sIL-6R claims rest on comparing groups of 3 (Same/Worse), 2 (Transient) and 7 (Better) participants against 162 analytes, with multiplicity adjustment only within analyte across groups and not across analytes, and a PLS model with 8 components (4 in the Methods) and pseudo-R2 of 0.99 fitted to about 12 people. The authors flag this as preliminary elsewhere, but the Conclusion's wording of 'top predictors' is stronger than that base supports, and the group totals (12) do not match the 11 immunophenotyped participants stated in Results.

issues.title: PLS model reported with 4 components in Methods but 8 in Results and Figure 4; R-squared 0.98 vs 0.99
issues.explanation: The Methods describe a final PLS model reduced to 4 components with cumulative pseudo-R-squared 0.98, whereas the Results and Figure 4 legend describe 8 components with 0.99. It is unclear which model produced the VIP-ranked predictors (IFN-β, CNTF, sIL-6R) that appear in the conclusion. The predictor claims cannot be traced to a single specified model.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 4-component model was a cross-validation step and the 8-component model was the final one, with both fits reported.

quotes.text: Final analysis involved reduction to 4 principal components
Final analysis involved reduction to 8 components
determined by Partial Least Squares (PLS) optimized at eight components

issues.title: 35 of 162 analytes called significant using Tukey adjustment within each analyte only, not across analytes
issues.explanation: The mixed models were adjusted for multiple group comparisons within each parameter, but no correction across the 162 analytes is described. With groups of 2 and 3, a number of the 35 'significant' factors would be expected by chance, yet the interferon and sIL-6R findings headline the conclusions. The paper handles multiplicity properly elsewhere (Bonferroni for correlations), so this part is the weak link.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported FDR- or Bonferroni-adjusted p-values across all 162 analytes showing IFN-β, CNTF and sIL-6R remain significant.

quotes.text: adjusted for multiple comparisons within each parameter using the Tukey method
Thirty-five factors were found to be significant amongst these subgroups

issues.title: Primary outcome is one unvalidated self-rated change item in an unblinded study
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is a single self-reported question comparing current health with health before the vaccine, with a 'not sure' response and no validated instrument. In an unblinded cohort that expected a benefit, this item is open to expectation and recall effects. This weakens the 10/16 improvement figure, but the measure is a reasonable patient-centred choice for a pilot.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Validation data for this item or concordant change on a validated instrument (e.g. a PROMIS or SF-36 measure) collected in the same participants.

quotes.text: Overall health change was measured with the question, “Would you say that your overall health, as compared to your health before the vaccine, is worse, better, or the same?”

issues.title: Exclusion of surveys: Results exclude 4 early surveys, Discussion says 3 participants (incl. 12-week) excluded
issues.explanation: Results say two 2-week and two 6-week surveys were excluded and all 16 12-week surveys kept. The Discussion says surveys from three participants were excluded and describes their 12-week responses (1 better, 2 same). These accounts cannot both be right, and the 12-week 10/16 'better' headline depends on which is correct. The Results also repeat the survey counts in a second, redundant sentence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion refers only to the excluded 2- and 6-week surveys of those participants, and a reconciliation of 3 participants with 4 surveys.

quotes.text: we included 14 2-week surveys, 14 6-week surveys, and 16 12-week surveys
Surveys from three participants were excluded from the analysis because their submissions were out of order or on the same day
Among these participants at 12 weeks, one reported overall better health and two reported the same health

issues.title: Immune assays are secondary in the paper but registered as a primary outcome (NCT04895189)
issues.explanation: The registry lists two primary outcomes, surveys after vaccination and immune assay findings. The paper treats immune response only as a secondary outcome. Since the immune findings feature in the conclusions, the gap in outcome status is worth noting, but the registry history is not available to show whether it was in place at the start.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing immune assays were added as a primary outcome only after the paper's analysis plan was fixed, or were always labelled secondary.

quotes.text: The primary outcome was whether individuals’ overall health condition improved, stayed the same, or worsened after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine.
Secondary outcomes included changes in symptom prevalence and severity and associated changes in immune response to the COVID-19 vaccine.

issues.title: Outcome groups for plasma models total 12 (3+2+7) but immunophenotyping was done on 11 participants
issues.explanation: The linear mixed models on plasma analytes use three outcome groups of 3, 2 and 7 participants (12 in all). The Results say immunophenotyping assays were completed in 11 of 16. The number of participants contributing plasma data is therefore unclear, and 7 'Better' participants differ from the 10 who were better at 12 weeks without explanation of the classification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow for plasma analytes showing which 12 (or 11) participants contributed samples at each timepoint.

quotes.text: Immunophenotyping assays were completed on a subset of 11 out of 16 participants
those who did not improve or felt worse at weeks 6 and 12 post-vaccination (

issues.title: Minor descriptive inconsistencies: age minimum 21 vs 22, baseline Q1 13.8 vs 14.5, 15 vs 14 symptoms listed
issues.explanation: Several descriptive values disagree within the paper: the youngest age (21 in text, 22 in Table 1), the first quartile of the baseline symptom count (13.8 vs 14.5 for the same median of 23), and the number of most frequent symptoms (fifteen announced, fourteen listed). The text also says all participants tested positive and then that two did not report positive tests. These are cosmetic and do not change the findings, but they indicate limited proofreading.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrigendum or source data showing a single consistent value for each quantity.

quotes.text: The median age of the 16 included participants was 54 years (range 21–69)
The median number of symptoms per participant before vaccination was 23 (Q1–Q3 14.5–27, min-max 3–43

10.1038/s43856-026-01486-w.headline_claim: Personalised multimodal therapy (nutritional counselling plus pacing-based physiotherapy) is feasible and safe, and exploratory physical performance outcomes show potential improvement that grows over longer follow-up.
10.1038/s43856-026-01486-w.overall: The feasibility findings (recruitment, adherence, study burden) are reasonably reported, but the clinical message of growing PMT benefit rests on non-significant between-group intervals, within-arm change and a secondary-outcome highlight, in a pilot with differential follow-up and a confounded control. Safety is claimed on non-systematic adverse event capture. Numeric slips are minor and do not change conclusions..

primary_outcome.name: 1-min sit-to-stand (1-MSTS) change from baseline at 12 weeks

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from Baseline Repetitions Sit-To-Stand's in one minute at 12 weeks

issues.title: Growing PMT benefit inferred from within-arm change and unadjusted trends; all between-group CIs include 0
issues.explanation: The primary 12-week 1-MSTS difference is 0.97 [-1.75, 3.70], and the 18-week difference of 2.14 [-1.26, 5.54] and the 6-MWT differences also span zero. Yet the paper explains the widening gap as 'mainly due to' change in the PMT group, and the abstract, plain-language summary and conclusion highlight growing differences at T3 (a non-primary timepoint). The control arm also improved (3.18 [0.62, 5.74] at T3), and nothing tests whether the gap actually grows. The data support only a small, imprecise, uncertain between-group difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A formal test of group-by-time interaction (e.g. mixed model) showing a growing between-group difference with an interval excluding zero.

quotes.text: This is mainly due to an observed increasing effect in the PMT group
quotes.location: Results, Physical performance and sample size calculation

quotes.text: showed potential improvement in both groups
The estimated effect between the groups increased over the trial duration
quotes.location: Results, Physical performance and sample size calculation

second_reader.what_stands: For both physical-performance outcomes (1-MSTS, 6-MWT) every between-group CI at every time point includes 0, and the 'increasing effect' rests on point estimates and on within-arm changes (with a control arm that also improved and with attrition-affected subsets), not on a tested between-group trend. This is tempered by the authors' labelling of the study as exploratory with no hypothesis testing and their hedged wording, but the Conclusions' 'appear to become more pronounced' and the plain-language summary's 'might offer extra benefits' still lean further than the data support.

issues.title: Future-RCT size of 41 powered on within-group T0-T3 increase; attrition inflation 32 to 41 should give about 44
issues.explanation: The sample size is framed as establishing an increase in 1-MSTS from T0 to T3, which is not the between-group question a definitive RCT would address. Inflating 32 for 27.7% attrition by multiplication gives 41, while allowing for 27.7% loss properly (dividing by 0.723) gives about 44. The abstract's 'would require 41 participants' is thus likely an underestimate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors' G*Power output showing 32 is already per-arm or that the 41 includes a different attrition adjustment.

quotes.text: the required sample size to establish an increase in 1-MSTS repetitions from T0 to T3
quotes.location: Results, Physical performance and sample size calculation

quotes.text: Taking into account the attrition rate of 27.7% at T3, a total sample size of 41 participants should be recruited for the future RCT.
quotes.location: Results, Physical performance and sample size calculation

issues.title: Differential follow-up (22/33 control vs 27/32 PMT at 12 weeks) analysed as available cases only
issues.explanation: At T2, 22 of 33 control participants (33% lost) and 27 of 32 PMT participants (16% lost) contributed 1-MSTS data. Only available data were analysed with no imputation or sensitivity analysis, and the discussion does not address possible bias from differential loss. This weakens the interpretation of the between-group estimates, but the study is a pilot with no inferential claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (multiple imputation or worst-case) giving similar between-group estimates.

quotes.text: No imputation was performed for missing data.
Analyses used all available data, with varying sample sizes.

issues.title: Safety 'demonstrated' from non-systematic self-reported adverse events in a 65-person pilot
issues.explanation: Adverse events were collected only if participants chose to report them, with no systematic ascertainment and no per-arm event counts. The abstract nevertheless says the study 'demonstrated overall safety', and the plain-language summary says it 'was safe'. A small pilot with unstructured AE capture can at most show no major safety signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified systematic AE collection protocol with per-arm event tables showing comparable rates.

quotes.text: The study demonstrated overall safety and feasibility despite a high study burden.
adverse events (AE) were collected non-systematically through participant self-report

issues.title: PMT vs non-protocolised physiotherapy by different therapists cannot isolate nutrition or 'synergy'
issues.explanation: The control received unprotocolised physiotherapy chosen by each participant, while PMT therapists received structured training in a pacing approach. Nutritional counselling, physiotherapy content and therapist differences are therefore all confounded. A synergy of nutrition with physiotherapy cannot be inferred even if the between-group gap were real, and fidelity in the control arm was not assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A factorial or nutrition-only comparison design, or documented equivalent physiotherapy content across arms.

quotes.text: determined at the discretion of each physiotherapist and therefore not protocolized
the potential synergistic effect of the nutritional optimisation and the supervised pacing-based physiotherapy

issues.title: Physical fatigue subscale (T3 CI excludes 0) singled out among 5 MFI subscales x 3 timepoints
issues.explanation: The paper describes the physical fatigue subscale as showing growing between-group differences, alongside 1-MSTS and 6-MWT, while stating the other subscales showed no notable patterns. With many outcomes and timepoints and no adjustment, one interval excluding zero is within what chance would produce. It is a secondary outcome and cannot support the growing-effect narrative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy naming physical fatigue as a key secondary outcome, or an adjusted analysis retaining the finding.

quotes.text: The preliminary between-group differences of the 1-MSTS, the 6-MWT and the physical fatigue subscale
The other subscales showed no notable patterns.

issues.title: 6-MWT T1 between-group lower CI bound is -18.7 in Results text but -18.07 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results text prints the lower bound of the 6-MWT between-group difference at T1 as -18.7, while Table 2 prints -18.07 for the same cell. The interval is centred on the estimate only with -18.07, so the text value is the slip. No conclusion changes, since the interval spans zero either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The underlying dataset showing -18.7 as the actual bound (which would break the CI symmetry).

quotes.location: Results, Physical performance and sample size calculation, para 2
Table 2, 6-MWT, Change between T1 and T0

issues.title: Total-sample protein intake printed as 734 g/day while group means are 75 and 72
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives the total-sample protein intake as 734 ± 21, but the PMT and control means are 75 and 72, so the total must lie between them (about 73.4). This is almost certainly a dropped decimal point, whether in the paper or in extraction. Nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The published PDF showing 73.4 in this cell.

quotes.location: Table 1, Protein intake g per day, Total sample

issues.title: T1 attrition 18.5% (53/65 retained) vs 52 participants with 1-MSTS data at T1
issues.explanation: The reported T1 attrition implies 53 retained participants, whereas the 1-MSTS data at T1 come from 52 (27 + 25). The number of participants contributing data differs by outcome (MFI-20 has 54), so this is probably a difference between attrition and missing outcome data. The one-participant gap does not affect conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The CONSORT diagram (Fig. 1) showing 12 withdrawals at T1 and one retained participant missing the 1-MSTS.
