PMTT1 n = 27, controlT1 n = 25

10.1051/bioconf/20236505039.headline_claim: Complex rehabilitation combining drug therapy with head micropolarization and translingual neurostimulation is an effective rehabilitation approach for neurological manifestations of post-COVID syndrome / chronic fatigue syndrome.
10.1051/bioconf/20236505039.overall: The headline claim that adding micropolarization and translingual neurostimulation is effective is not supported by this design: allocation is non-randomised and undescribed, no between-group test is reported, and the conclusion is stated more strongly than the evidence allows. The numbers in Table 1 are directionally favourable to the main group, so a benefit is possible but unproven.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; Table 1 reports asthenia, MMSE, autonomic, Epworth, anxiety and depression questionnaires

issues.title: Non-randomised 69 vs 51 allocation with no stated method; add-on effect cannot be attributed to the devices
issues.explanation: Patients were 'divided' into a main group (69) and a control group (51) with no stated method, concealment, blinding or sham. The groups differ by the devices, but also possibly by who chose them, when they were treated and how much attention they received. Similar baseline means are reassuring but cannot show comparability on unmeasured factors. Any between-group difference therefore cannot be causally attributed to micropolarization/TLNS.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of random or concealed allocation, or a pre-specified allocation rule with baseline comparability tests and blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: The  patients  were  divided  into  2  groups:  the  main  group  (MG)  -  69  patients  and  the control group (CG) - 51 patients.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper gives no allocation method (it says only 'divided into 2 groups'), so it is not described as randomised, and the unequal 69 vs 51 split with no blinding or sham means the add-on effect of the devices cannot be isolated. What I cannot say from the text is that the allocation was in fact non-randomised, because the paper does not state it either way; baseline values are closely matched.

issues.title: 'Significantly better' MG vs CG claim has no between-group test; asterisks only on MG and undefined
issues.explanation: The paper states that the MG had significantly better indicators on every scale, but reports no statistical test, p-value or confidence interval. The only marker is an undefined asterisk on MG after-treatment values. The control group also improved substantially, so the within-group significance of one arm says nothing about the difference between arms. Multiplicity across six scales is not addressed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group analysis of change (or ANCOVA on follow-up adjusted for baseline) with p-values showing the differences on all scales.

quotes.text: there  are  significantly  better indicators for all indicators of the questionnaires and scales.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that the MG had 'significantly better indicators for all indicators', but reports no between-group test, p-value or alpha, and the asterisks in Table 1 appear only on the MG after-treatment column without a footnote defining them. Under one assumption (± as SEM) the MMSE difference of 0.8 would not be significant, so the claim of significance for all indicators is not supported by anything printed.

issues.title: Conclusion says the therapy 'proven' effective despite non-randomised design, no tests and no safety data
issues.explanation: The conclusion presents the complex rehabilitation as proven effective and the discussion says the results 'confirm' that neuronal connections are repaired. The design (unblinded, non-randomised, no between-group test, single post-treatment timepoint, no adverse-event reporting) supports at most a tentative signal. The mechanistic claim is not tested by any outcome measured.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomised, blinded evidence with a formal between-group test and safety reporting.

quotes.text: have proven to be a complex effective rehabilitation of this category of patients.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion says the therapy has 'proven' effective, yet the paper reports no stated allocation method, no statistical tests, no blinding or sham, no follow-up and no adverse-event or tolerability data. That wording is stronger than the evidence presented supports.

issues.title: Outcome instruments cited only to a handbook; no primary outcome designated
issues.explanation: MMSE and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale are established, but the asthenia, autonomic and anxiety/depression questionnaires are cited only to a clinical guide, with no validation or reliability data. No primary outcome is named, and the raters are not described. This weakens, but does not by itself invalidate, the secondary readings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of the named questionnaires in this population and a pre-specified primary outcome.

quotes.text: the higher the score, the higher the asthenia

issues.title: Treatment duration, timing of 'after treatment' assessment and any follow-up are not stated
issues.explanation: The paper reports one after-treatment timepoint without stating the length of treatment, the timing of reassessment or any follow-up. Post-COVID fatigue is described in the introduction as undulating, so a single early assessment cannot show lasting benefit. No attrition is reported, with all 120 apparently analysed, which is unusual and unexplained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods stating treatment length, assessment timing and follow-up, with attrition accounting.

quotes.text: The results of treatment confirmed the effectiveness  of  the  proposed  conservative  therapy.

10.1055/a-2134-2142.headline_claim: Post-COVID pulmonary rehabilitation produced sustained improvement in patient-reported outcomes (dyspnoea, depression, anxiety, fatigue, pain, QoL) over 6 months in patients with acute/persistent symptomatic COVID-19 (AFS) and post-COVID syndrome (PCS).
10.1055/a-2134-2142.overall: This supplement describes the time course of patient-reported outcomes after rehabilitation in a single uncontrolled cohort, so the improvements are descriptive and cannot be attributed to rehabilitation itself. Several tables contain printing errors (many wrong CIs in Table S10, sign slips in S6, a p-value and df typo in S5 and S8) that appear to be typographical and do not change the overall pattern of results, but individual cells cannot be relied on without correction.

primary_outcome.name: Belastungsdyspnoe (exertional dyspnoea, 11-point NRS)

issues.title: Table S10: at least eight 95% CIs do not match their change estimates (sRtot, BNP, CRP, Pimax, TLCO, TLC)
issues.explanation: Several change estimates in Table S10 lie outside, or far from the centre of, their printed 95% CIs. The BNP subgroup CIs are centred on the same size of change with the opposite sign (+35.35, +44.41). Other rows carry a single wrong bound (sRtot PCS, Pimax PCS, TLCO PCS, TLC AFS) or a wrong estimate (CRP AFS and PCS). The CIs are therefore unreliable, and some significance conclusions drawn from them (for example TLCO PCS marked * though its CI spans 0) cannot be trusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected or original table showing the CIs and estimates are consistent, for example CIs reported for T1-T2 rather than T2-T1.

script.explanation: the estimate -4.74 lies outside its own CI [-3.63, 2.48]

issues.title: Single-arm cohort with open-label self-reported outcomes: pre-post change cannot be attributed to rehabilitation
issues.explanation: All patients received the same programme and change is estimated against their own baseline, with no comparison group and no blinding of subjective outcomes (dyspnoea NRS, PHQ-9, BFI). Improvement from T1 to T2 may partly reflect natural recovery post-COVID, regression to the mean or expectation. The paper's model labelled 'Nur Reha-Effekt' and its pre-post effect sizes should be read as descriptive trajectories, not effects of rehabilitation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The main text framing results purely as descriptive course with no rehabilitation-effect claims, or a comparison with an untreated cohort.

quotes.text: Das dreiwöchige PR-Programm mit individueller Verlängerungsoption
Zur Abschätzung standardisierter Prä-Post-Effektstärken (ES)

issues.title: Age-GAD-7 correlation at T1 has p = 0.710 in Table S8 but p = 0.071 in Table S7 (r = -0.139 vs -0.140)
issues.explanation: The same correlation at baseline is given two p values differing by a factor of ten. A p of 0.710 is implausible for r near -0.14 with N about 221, since other rows with similar r have p near 0.04 to 0.10. Probably a typographical slip with no effect on the main conclusions, but one of the two tables is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the two tables use different models or samples such that a different p is expected.

quotes.location: Table S8, Alter row, GAD-7 column

issues.title: Table S6 BFI: women's T2-T3 CI [0.08; -0.11] is inverted; T1-T4 CIs also have wrong-sign bounds
issues.explanation: The women's BFI T2-T3 CI has its upper bound below its lower bound, so it cannot contain the estimate 0.44. The T1-T4 intervals for women (-1.11 [-1.56; 0.66]) and men (-0.45 [-0.79; 0.11]) are also off-centre in a way that suggests dropped or wrong minus signs. If read literally, the T1-T4 CIs would change the significance reading for both groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original typeset table showing correctly signed bounds.

issues.title: Table S5 pain column: df printed as 1 for chi-square 6.973 and 1.094, but p values correspond to df 3
issues.explanation: Two pain-column cells report (1) degrees of freedom, whereas every other cell uses 3 and the printed p values only fit df = 3. The error appears to be in the df label and not the p, so no conclusion changes. It does mean the table cannot be read at face value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A model specification where the pain-by-sex test genuinely has 1 df and p = 0.073 is a typo.

quotes.location: Table S5, Geschlecht row, Schmerzen column
Table S5, Geschlecht row, Schmerzen column

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.073, but recomputed from the printed chi2 = 6.973 p is at most 0.008277, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Table S11 GROC T4, AFS: CI [-2.27; 0.71] not centred on mean -1.49 (likely missing minus on upper bound)
issues.explanation: The printed interval around -1.49 has midpoint -0.78. Changing the upper bound to -0.71 gives a midpoint of exactly -1.49. Whether this is a typesetting or extraction effect or an original error cannot be settled here. The effect is limited to one cell of a secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The typeset original showing -0.71.

quotes.location: Table S11, T4, AFS, 95% KI (comparison with pre-COVID)

10.1080/09602011.2024.2338613.headline_claim: Cardiopulmonary rehabilitation was efficient in reducing perceived stress and symptoms of depression in long COVID, with no between-group difference in cognitive performance.
10.1080/09602011.2024.2338613.overall: The null cognitive finding is reasonably reported, but the positive mood claims come from a small complete-case sub-study with unblinded self-report, no correction for about 20 outcomes, and no power basis. The Conclusion's 'efficient' is stronger than this supports, and the within-arm depression claim is not backed by its own CIs. The baseline table also shows internal inconsistencies, with MoCA values that appear to be completer data.

primary_outcome.name: Cognitive performance (composite z-scores; the paper names no single primary outcome)

issues.title: Stress and depression findings rest on self-report with unblinded participants and a no-intervention control
issues.explanation: The only positive results are on self-completed questionnaires (PSS, GDS). Participants knew their allocation, and controls were told to maintain usual habits with no attention control. Expectation and demand effects could therefore produce part or all of the differences. The Conclusion states efficacy without noting this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an attention or sham control, or objective corroboration of the mood effects.

quotes.text: single-blinded (assessors blinded to intervention group)
Questionnaires measuring psychological health and sleep quality were explained to participants, who then completed them online.
quotes.location: Methods, Psychological health and sleep quality

second_reader.what_stands: The stress and depression results (PSS, GDS) come from self-reported questionnaires completed by participants who could not be blinded, compared against a no-intervention control with no attention or sham condition. The paper blinds only assessors, does not discuss this bias in its Limitations, and still concludes the programme was 'efficient' at reducing stress and depression.

issues.title: About 20 outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 with no correction; GDS p = 0.015 would not survive
issues.explanation: The paper reports many cognitive, composite and questionnaire tests, with no multiplicity control or declared primary outcome for this sub-study. The depression result (p = 0.015) does not meet even a 5-outcome Bonferroni threshold, and the stress result (p = 0.002) is only marginal under stricter corrections. The Conclusion nevertheless states efficacy as established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction applied to these outcomes.

quotes.text: A signi fi cant group di ff erence was observed for the GDS ( p = 0.015) and PSS scores ( p = 0.002).
Missing values were not imputed and a complete-case analysis where a twotailed signi fi cance level of 0.05 was pertained for the statistical tests.

second_reader.what_stands: About 20 group-comparison tests were run at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05, and the paper states no correction, so the claim is accurate. Under Bonferroni, the GDS result (p = 0.015) would not survive whether 20 or only 5 tests are counted, whereas PSS (p = 0.002) would survive the 5-test threshold and just meet the 20-test threshold of 0.0025.

issues.title: No power basis for psychological outcomes; complete-case n = 32 of 40 supports only a tentative efficacy claim
issues.explanation: The sample size was set for VO2peak, not for cognition or mood, and only 32 of 40 randomized participants (17 control, 15 rehab) were analysed, with no imputation or ITT analysis. Baseline imbalances exist, for example GDS 11.38 vs 15.14. Despite the disclosed limitation, the Conclusion states efficacy without qualification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power or precision calculation for GDS and PSS, or an ITT analysis giving the same effects.

quotes.text: First, the small sample size constrains the statistical power of the results and their generalizability.
The present study is a sub-study from the COVID-Rehab study and therefore there is no subject calculation speci fi c to the variables presented.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper confirms there is no power calculation for the psychological outcomes, and the analysis is a complete-case n = 32 of 40 randomized (20% excluded, reasons only in the supplement). The authors do acknowledge low power in Limitations, so the problem is not undisclosed; what remains is that their conclusion calls the programme 'efficient' for stress and depression, which is stronger than the evidence supports.

issues.title: Table 1 baseline MoCA (24.71 ± 3.92; 27.27 ± 1.94) equals the analysed-sample values and is not attainable at n = 19
issues.explanation: Table 1 is supposed to describe all 38 baseline participants (19 per arm), while Table 3 describes the 32 completers. Yet the control and rehab MoCA means and SDs are identical to two decimals in both tables. These means are attainable only with n = 17 and n = 15, so the Table 1 row appears to carry completer data. That undermines the baseline comparison (p = 0.055) that the paper uses to describe baseline imbalance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw MoCA data for the 38 baseline participants reproducing the Table 1 means and SDs.

issues.title: Within-arm depression 'improvement' stated though both arm CIs include zero (rehab -2.39, -5.25 to +0.46)
issues.explanation: The text says depression worsened for controls and improved for the rehabilitation group. Neither within-arm adjusted change excludes zero. Only the between-group difference is supported, and it is not accompanied by its own effect size and CI.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group difference with a CI excluding zero, and within-arm tests showing change.

quotes.text: This result means that depression scores worsened for the control group and improved for the rehabilitation group.

issues.title: 40 randomized vs 38 in Table 1 ('all participants'), with no reason given in the text
issues.explanation: The Results say 40 people were randomized and that Table 1 covers all who initially took part, yet Table 1 is headed n = 38 and the percentages imply 19 per arm. The two-person gap is not explained in the main text, and the flow chart is only in the supplement. This is a reporting gap that does not change any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow chart showing 2 randomized participants excluded or lacking baseline data before Table 1.

quotes.text: Table 1 presents the characteristics of all the participants who initially took part in the experiment.
From these, forty met the inclusion criteria and engaged in the study.

issues.title: Long COVID duration: text 424 days vs Table 1 total 417.25 days (group means imply about 425.6)
issues.explanation: The text gives 424 days, while Table 1 gives 417.25 for the total. With 19 per arm, the group means of 473.80 and 377.40 imply about 425.6, which is neither figure. The difference is probably due to different denominators or missing values, but it is not explained. It has little bearing on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-group n for this variable showing missing values that reconcile 417.25 and 424.

quotes.text: The mean span of long COVID symptoms was 424 days (min -max: 113 -863)

10.1080/09638288.2022.2032408.headline_claim: An intensive, interdisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation programme produces significant improvement in neuromuscular, respiratory, and functional outcomes in post-ICU COVID-19 survivors.
10.1080/09638288.2022.2032408.overall: The paper shows that patients improved on most measures between admission and discharge, but a single-arm design with no control group cannot separate programme effect from natural recovery and test learning, and the causal wording in the title and Implications goes beyond it. There are several small numeric inconsistencies (6MWT gain 61.13 vs 161.13, FIM gain 25.40 vs 21.63, MIP percentages). The FIM one touches the minimal-important-difference comparison.

primary_outcome.name: No single primary outcome is named; the paper reports pre-post (T0 vs T1) changes in MRC score, MIP/MEP, PCF, Brief-BESTest, TUG, 1-min STST, 6MWT, FAS, and FIM

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute gains to rehabilitation; Implications and title wording go beyond it
issues.explanation: All findings are within-patient changes from admission to discharge with no control group. Spontaneous recovery after critical illness, test learning and selection could each produce the gains. The authors concede causality cannot be reported, yet the title says rehabilitation 'can improve' outcomes and the Implications say it 'results in significant improvement'. The Conclusion hedges with 'seems to be beneficial'. The size of any programme effect is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control group showing smaller gains over a comparable period.

quotes.text: we have no group control and it is not possible to report on the causality of the observed findings
An  intensive  and  interdisciplinary  inpatient  rehabilitation  results  in  significant  improvement
seems to be beneficial for these patients to regain their functional independence

second_reader.what_stands: A single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute the gains to rehabilitation, and the authors say so in their limitations (no control group, causality not assessable, learning effect, natural evolution). The Implications bullet nonetheless uses causal wording ('results in significant improvement') without a hedge; the title ('can improve') and Conclusion ('seems to be beneficial') are softer and partly qualified, so the overreach is mainly in the Implications bullet.

issues.title: Total FIM change 25.40 exceeds the difference of printed means (118.63 - 97.00 = 21.63)
issues.explanation: Total FIM means are 97.00 at T0 and 118.63 at T1, each with 2 missing, which implies a gain of about 21.6 points. The paper prints and repeats a gain of 25.40. The authors compare their gain to a 22-point minimal important difference, and 25.40 clears it while 21.63 does not, so the discrepancy bears on how the result is read.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level data showing the paired subset had different T0 and T1 means from the printed column means.

quotes.location: Table 4, FIM Total row, T0 column
Table 4, FIM Total row, T1 column

quotes.text: mean  improvement  of  25.40 ± 11.33  points  was  seen  in  the total  FIM  score

issues.title: Seven discharge measures only for stays >21 days; 6MWT based on a subset (about 29 of 42)
issues.explanation: Patients with shorter stays have no discharge value for the Brief-BESTest, respiratory strength, PCF, 1-STST, TUG, 6MWT and FAS, and are treated as missing. For most measures about 5-6 of 42 patients are missing, but for the 6MWT 12-13 are missing and 19 have no MID result. Gains therefore describe a length-of-stay-selected subset, and statements like 'all patients improved' apply only to those assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis or baseline comparison showing patients with short stays did not differ from those assessed twice.

quotes.text: Only patients hospitalized in our rehabilitation centre longer than 21 days completed the second evaluation
Otherwise,  these  were  considered missing values.

issues.title: 6MWT gain printed as 61.13 m in Table 4 but 161.13 m in Discussion; means imply about 162 m
issues.explanation: Table 4 gives the 6MWT change as D = 61.13 ±88.49, while the Discussion gives 161.13 ± 88.49 m. The T0 and T1 means (345.00 and 507.00 m) differ by about 162 m, so 161.13 is the consistent value and the table entry looks wrong. The table figure understates the gain by 100 m, but the result stays strongly significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original published table showing 161.13 and the 61.13 arising only from text extraction.

quotes.text: We  found  a  walking  distance  improvement  of  161.13 ± 88.49 m

issues.title: Results claim significant improvement in all assessments, but Borg dyspnea (p=1.000), Borg exertion and gait are not significant
issues.explanation: The Results state a statistically significant improvement in every assessment between T0 and T1. Table 4 shows no change in final Borg dyspnea (p = 1.000), final Borg exertion (p = 0.310) and gait (p = 0.569). The statement is too broad, though these are secondary measures and the main outcomes are still significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors defining 'assessments' to exclude perceived-exertion and gait descriptors.

quotes.text: A  statistically  significant  improvement  was  verified  in  all  the assessments performed between T0 and T1

issues.title: Table 4 MIP at T1: 4 (11.90) and 32 (88.90) sum to 100.80%; 4/36 is 11.1%
issues.explanation: The two mutually exclusive categories below and above the lower limit of normal at T1 add to 100.8%. The count of 4 out of the 36 patients with data gives 11.1%, not 11.90%. This is a small slip that does not affect the main findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the percentage was computed on an unrounded or different denominator that gives 11.90 for 4 patients.

quotes.location: Table 4, MIP < LLN row, T1 column
Table 4, MIP > LLN row, T1 column

script.explanation: 4/36 = 11.11%, but the paper prints 11.9, outside the rounding interval [11.89, 11.91]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 33.6 rather than 36.

10.1080/09638288.2022.2111467.headline_claim: Physical exercise (resistance and aerobic training) positively affects functional status and work ability in health care workers with post-COVID syndrome, with more severely affected participants benefiting more.
10.1080/09638288.2022.2111467.overall: The headline claim that exercise 'safely' improves post-COVID functional status and work ability cannot be relied on as stated, because the study is single-arm with no control and the authors themselves assume causation. The work-ability and mental-health claims rest on cross-sectional correlations, and the 'more severe benefit more' claim rests on a significant-versus-non-significant comparison. The numeric slips (height row, sex ratio, unexplained 32 versus 28) are minor by comparison.

primary_outcome.name: VO2peak (relative VO2peak during cardiopulmonary exercise testing)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change of maximum oxygen uptake (VO2max) over time-points (baseline - 4 weeks - 8 weeks) assessed during cardio-pulmonary exercise testing (CPET)

issues.title: No control group yet improvements are declared 'safe to assume' to result directly from exercise
issues.explanation: All 28 participants received the same exercise programme, with no inactive comparator. Improvements over 8 weeks may reflect natural recovery from post-COVID symptoms (mean time since diagnosis about 6 months), practice effects on the tests, regression to the mean and non-blinded assessment. The authors acknowledge the lack of a control group but then say it is 'safe to assume' the improvements result from exercise, and conclude they 'can safely conclude' a positive effect. The main conclusion is therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist arm showing no comparable change.

quotes.text: A  study  limitation  is  the  lack  of  an  inactive  control  group.
it  is  safe  to  assume  that  the  measured improvements directly result from the exercise intervention.
we  can  safely  conclude  that  physical  exercise  with  its  effects  on both  endurance  and  strength  positively  affects  post-COVID  functional status

second_reader.what_stands: The paper acknowledges having no control group but then states it is 'safe to assume' the improvements 'directly result' from exercise and 'safely conclude' a positive effect, which a single-arm pre-post design cannot support. Natural recovery, practice effects and regression to the mean are not addressed.

issues.title: 'More severe cases benefit more' based on significant-vs-non-significant within-group changes and CI overlap
issues.explanation: The claim rests on VO2peak improving significantly in the SSG (+2.4, p < 0.001) but not in the MSG (+1.27, p = 0.096), and on a graphical look at confidence intervals. A difference in significance is not a test of a difference in effect, and no interaction test is reported for VO2peak or the 6MWT. The only formally significant group effect (30 s STS) went the other way, and the SSG started at a lower fitness level, so regression to the mean cannot be excluded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant group-by-time interaction for VO2peak and 6MWT favouring the SSG.

quotes.text: More  severe  cases  of  post-COVID  fatigue  seem  to  benefit  more compared  to  those  with  mild  symptoms.
the SSG improved more than the MSG;  findings  were  vice  versa  for  the  30 s  STS.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that more severe cases benefit more rests on a significant-versus-non-significant contrast within groups for VO2peak and on visual inspection of CI overlap, with no reported significant group-by-time difference for VO2peak or 6MWT. The one formally significant between-group difference (30 s STS) favours the mild group, and the paper's hedge 'seem' does not offset this.

issues.title: Work-ability and mental-health benefit claims rest on cross-sectional correlations, not change from exercise
issues.explanation: The Implications say that increases in performance are 'directly related' to improvements in work ability and that exercise positively affects mental dimensions. The supporting analyses are correlations and ordinal models of WAI and psychological scores on performance measures at each time point (Tables 2 to 4), not a demonstrated change in WAI caused by exercise. WAI change is not reported in this text. With n = 28 and many correlations the results are imprecise (e.g. WAI vs 30 s STS r = 0.5, CI 0.16 to 0.74).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported pre-post change in WAI and psychological scores with a control or an interaction analysis.

quotes.text: In  health  care  workers  suffering  from  post-COVID  syndrome,  increases  in  physical  performance  are directly related to improvements in work ability.

second_reader.what_stands: The work-ability and mental-health links are supported by correlations between performance and outcomes at each time point and a repeated-measures ordinal model, not by an analysis relating change in performance to change in WAI or psychological scores, so 'directly related' is stronger than the evidence. It is not strictly cross-sectional, since the model uses repeated measures, and the pre-post improvements in psychological scores are reported separately.

issues.title: Planned N=32 versus 28 analysed, with no participant flow; registry lists 46 enrolled
issues.explanation: The Methods say 32 participants 'were included', while Table 1 and all analyses use 28. The paper gives no flow diagram or account of what happened to the other 4, and the registry record shows 46 enrolled. Without this the analysed set cannot be judged for selective loss, although the primary analysis uses mixed models that tolerate some missing data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow account showing 32 (or more) recruited, with reasons for the exclusion of those not analysed.

quotes.text: a total of N ¼ 32 participants were included in the study
Total, N ¼ 28

issues.title: Table 1 height row repeats 170.0 (10.0) in all three columns; CI -0.1 to 0.04 and p 0.693 do not fit
issues.explanation: Total, MSG and SSG columns all show 170.0 (10.0) for height. Identical means and SDs for groups of 10 and 18 would give a difference of exactly 0, yet a p of 0.693 and a CI of -0.1 to 0.04 are printed. The row appears to have been filled in or transcribed incorrectly. It affects only a baseline descriptive, not any efficacy result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw height data showing the identical summaries and a correct CI.

quotes.text: Height (cm)

quotes.location: Table 1, Height row, MSG and SSG columns

issues.title: Discussion gives SSG female:male ratio 9:1 and MSG 1:1.5; Table 1 gives 16:2 (8:1) and 6:4 (1.5:1)
issues.explanation: The Discussion states a 9:1 ratio in the SSG, but Table 1 shows 16 females and 2 males, which is 8:1. The MSG ratio is written as 1:1.5, whereas Table 1 shows 6 females to 4 males, i.e. 1.5:1 in the other direction. The error is minor and the sex-difference argument is only speculative commentary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sex breakdown with 18 SSG participants in a 9:1 split (impossible with n = 18, which would give 16.2:1.8).

quotes.text: this ratio increased  to  9:1  in  the  SSG  while  decreasing  to  1:1.5  in  the  MSG

quotes.location: Table 1, Sex, Female row, SSG column

10.1080/09638288.2023.2242783.headline_claim: EME is a feasible self-management education intervention for post-COVID-19 fatigue, with promising effect sizes that warrant a future trial.
10.1080/09638288.2023.2242783.overall: The feasibility findings (recruitment around 57%, follow-up 76% and 70%) are reasonably supported, apart from a small inconsistency in the recruitment rate. The efficacy-type statements are weak: the design is single-arm and uncontrolled, the sample is very small, some pairwise changes described as significant have CIs that include zero, and the MFIS dispersion values look like standard errors. The conclusions about 'significant effect sizes' and small-sample trial needs should be read as exploratory only.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (recruitment, procedures, follow-up rates); secondary exploratory outcomes SEPECSA, MFIS, OSA, SF-36 PCS/MCS

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design with within-subject ANOVA only; changes cannot be attributed to EME
issues.explanation: All 17 participants received EME in the context of a broader multidisciplinary rehabilitation programme, and no comparator was used. The only analysis is a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA over time. Improvement may therefore reflect natural recovery from long COVID, regression to the mean, co-interventions or expectation. The authors acknowledge that the reported changes may be a cumulative effect of the whole programme. The study can show feasibility, but it cannot show an EME effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical comparison group, or explicit framing of the outcome data as purely descriptive with no effect language.

quotes.text: The results lack a control group
the reported changes, particularly  in  fatigue,  may  be  a  cumulative  effect  of  the  entire program

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design analysed only with within-subject repeated-measures ANOVA, so observed changes cannot be attributed to EME specifically; concurrent rehabilitation components, natural course and regression to the mean are not separable. The authors acknowledge this in the Limitations and Discussion, so it is a design limitation they disclose, not a hidden flaw, though some summary wording is stronger than the design allows.

issues.title: Feasibility study (n=17, 13 at T2, no control) states 'significant effect sizes' and small-sample RCT needs
issues.explanation: The Conclusion and Implications report 'significant' or 'large' effect sizes from partial eta-squared of a within-group ANOVA in 13 to 17 people. The Discussion then infers that only a relatively small sample would be needed for a 90% powered RCT. Pilot-derived within-group effect sizes are imprecise, likely inflated, and cannot support power calculations or efficacy statements. The MFIS change did not reach the minimal clinically important difference (13.8) and the pairwise BL-T2 CIs include zero, so the 'significant' wording is overreaching.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording that treats effect sizes as exploratory only, with confidence intervals around them and no sample-size inference.

quotes.text: As a result, a relatively small sample size would be needed for a 90% powered RCT.
The data revealed significant effect sizes in fatigue impact,  self-efficacy  in  performing  energy  management  strategies, and competency in daily activities.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does describe 'significant effect sizes' (a term that conflates statistical significance with magnitude) and infers a small RCT sample from a 17-person, 13-at-T2, uncontrolled pilot, with wide confidence intervals and no printed sample-size result. It is a feasibility study that explicitly calls the results 'promising' and says they warrant further investigation, and the sample size for the pilot was intentionally small, so the weakness is in wording and the strength of the RCT-planning inference, not in a concealed claim of efficacy.

issues.title: T2 data from 13 of 17 (23.5% missing) with unstated handling in the repeated-measures analysis
issues.explanation: Four of 17 participants did not return the T2 questionnaire, and the paper does not say whether the repeated-measures ANOVA used only the 13 completers or imputed values. Table 3 shows BL and T1 for all 17, so the omnibus p values and effect sizes may rest on a different, smaller sample than the table suggests. Whether the non-responders differ in fatigue is unknown, so the T2 results may be biased in either direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the ANOVA was run on complete cases or with a stated imputation, together with a comparison of completers and non-completers at baseline.

quotes.text: 13/17 returned filled (76.5%)

issues.title: MFIS 'SD' values (4.22, 4.07, 5.40) match standard errors implied by the CIs, not SDs
issues.explanation: For MFIS at baseline the CI of 51.11 to 69.51 with n=17 implies SE of about 4.3 and SD of about 18. The printed 4.22 matches the SE. The same holds at T1 (CI 44.28 to 62.03, SD 4.07) and T2 (CI 37.86 to 61.37, n=13, SD 5.40). The MFIS row therefore appears to report SE under an 'SD' label. This understates the true variability and does not match the other rows. It does not change the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw MFIS data or a table note showing that the parenthesised values are SDs and the CIs were computed differently.

issues.title: Text calls OSA and MFIS BL-to-T2 changes significant, but both printed CIs include zero and lack the 'a' marker
issues.explanation: The Results say OSA increased significantly and the MFIS difference was significant between BL and T2. The Table 3 pairwise CIs are [-0.29, 10.90] for OSA and [-23.66, 2.27] for MFIS. Both include zero, and neither cell carries the 'significant at .05' marker. Only the omnibus repeated-measures test is significant. The claimed pairwise significance, which feeds the conclusion on fatigue impact and competency, is not supported by the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted pairwise p values below .05 for these two contrasts, with the CIs reported on a different (unadjusted or differently computed) basis and labelled as such.

quotes.location: Table 3, OSA, Within-group Δ from bl, T2 column
Table 3, MFIS, Within-group Δ from bl, T2 column

quotes.text: increased  statistically  significantly  between  BL  and  T2
quotes.location: Results, Outcomes and treatment effect size

issues.title: Recruitment rate printed as 56.6% in Results but 53% in Discussion for 17 of 30 eligible
issues.explanation: The Results give 17 of 30 eligible participants as 56.6%, and the Discussion calls the recruitment rate 53%. Both cannot describe the same 17/30. The Results figure is also slightly truncated, since 17/30 is 56.7%. This is a small reporting slip, but recruitment rate is a core feasibility outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated different denominator for the 53% (for example a different eligibility count) in the paper or the flowchart.

quotes.text: recruitment rate:  56.6%
sufficiently  high  recruitment  rate  (53%)

10.1080/13548506.2024.2439180.headline_claim: The authors conclude that a multimodal asynchronous telerehabilitation programme with therapeutic education may be more effective than a booklet-based rehabilitation programme for depression, stress and social support after COVID-19 discharge.
10.1080/13548506.2024.2439180.overall: The headline claim that telerehabilitation provides substantial benefits over booklet rehabilitation is only weakly supported: all post-intervention DASS-21 totals are null, and the supportive results come from level-category tests near p=0.05 without multiplicity control, in a small unblinded self-report pilot. The paper's primary outcome also differs from the registered Fatigue Severity Level outcome. Several abstract and Discussion statements about social support and 3-month stress do not match the tables, so the findings are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: DASS-21 total score (depression, anxiety, stress)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Pre-intervention (day 1); after intervention (day 84); follow up 1 (3 months after intervention); follow up 2 (6 months after intervention).

issues.title: Null DASS-21 totals (p=0.729) but conclusion of 'substantial benefits' and 'better results' than booklet
issues.explanation: After the intervention the groups did not differ on any DASS-21 total score (total p=0.729, depression p=0.458, stress p=0.967). The abstract and conclusion rest on level-category tests (p=0.048 and p=0.033) and later subscores, while the binary depression and stress splits are not significant (p=0.121, p=0.105). With 35 participants and these mixed results, 'substantial benefits' and 'first study to show ... better results' go well beyond the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary analysis on the level categories with a multiplicity-adjusted significant result, or a conclusion limited to hypothesis generation.

quotes.text: the ATG did not differ from the BRG in the total score of each questionnaire after intervention
This pilot study suggests that a multimodal rehabilitation program using asynchronous telerehabilitation provides substantial benefits
This is the first study to show that asynchronous telerehabilitation achieves better results than a home booklet-based rehabilitation

second_reader.what_stands: The DASS-21 total at post-intervention is null (p=0.729) and the abstract's 'substantial benefits' and the Discussion's 'first study to show... better results' are stronger than the totals support, given non-significant totals for DASS-21, anxiety and stress at all points and large BRG within-group improvement. The claim is not baseless, since depression totals and level distributions and 6-month MSPSS favour the ATG, and the paper does elsewhere call the findings preliminary and in need of confirmation.

issues.title: Paper's primary outcome (DASS-21) differs from the registered primary (Fatigue Severity Level), which is not reported
issues.explanation: The paper names depression, anxiety and stress as the primary outcome. The registry record lists only Fatigue Severity Level as primary, with DASS-21 not among them, and the paper reports no fatigue results after baseline. The outcome that the headline conclusion rests on is therefore not the registered one, and the registered one goes unreported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or the published protocol listing DASS-21 as primary, or a report of the fatigue outcome elsewhere.

quotes.text: Primary outcome: depression, anxiety, and stress
The aim was to analyze the preliminary changes in depression, anxiety, stress, and social support comparing both groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper designates DASS-21 as its primary outcome while the current registry record lists Fatigue Severity Level as the only primary, and post-baseline fatigue results are not reported in the manuscript. Whether the registered primary was changed over time cannot be determined because earlier registry versions were not retrieved, and the paper may report fatigue in a separate publication.

issues.title: Dozens of unadjusted between-group tests at 4 timepoints; headline p-values 0.048, 0.033, 0.036
issues.explanation: The only multiplicity correction described is for the Wilcoxon tests; all between-group comparisons use alpha 0.05. Across DASS-21 and MSPSS totals, subscales and level categories at post, 3 and 6 months, a handful of nominally significant results is expected by chance. The headline claims (depression p=0.048, stress p=0.033, 6-month depression p=0.036) sit close to the threshold and would not survive any plausible correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary comparison, or adjusted p-values that remain significant.

quotes.text: In the Wilcoxon test, type I error will be divided by the number of tests done.
The significance level was 0.05 for all statistical analyses.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states a multiplicity correction only for the within-group Wilcoxon tests; roughly 40 between-group tests across four timepoints were run at an unadjusted 0.05, and the headline p-values (0.048, 0.033, 0.036) would not survive any conventional adjustment. The tests are partly correlated and the study is labelled a pilot, so the p-values are best read as exploratory, but the paper does not describe them that way.

issues.title: Social-support claims in abstract and Discussion contradict Tables 2 and 5 (3-month total p=0.213; post p=0.880)
issues.explanation: The abstract reports 'notably higher social support' at 3 months (p=0.038), but that p belongs to the 'other/general' subdomain; the total MSPSS at 3 months is p=0.213. The Discussion also says the ATG was significantly better on global MSPSS at the end of rehabilitation, yet Table 2 gives p=0.880 for that comparison. Only the 6-month total (p=0.028) is supported, so the social-support benefit is overstated in the places readers look first.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis showing a significant total-MSPSS difference at 3 months or at end of intervention, or a table correction showing the printed p-values belong to the total score.

quotes.text: notably higher social support at 3- and 6-month follow-ups (p=0.038, p=0.028 respectively)
at the end of rehabilitation and at the 6-month follow-up, the ATG was significantly better on the global MSPSS

issues.title: Self-reported DASS-21/MSPSS outcomes in participants who knew their allocation; assessor-only blinding
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they had the app or the booklet, and all primary and secondary outcomes are self-report questionnaires. Blinding the assessor does not remove expectancy effects on self-reported mood. Differences of the modest size seen here could partly reflect this, and the conclusion does not account for it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An objective or observer-rated primary outcome, or an attention-matched sham comparator for expectancy.

quotes.text: which is a set of 3 self-reported questionnaires designed to measure the negative emotional states
The use of a double-blind design would further minimize these biases

issues.title: Discussion claims significant 3-month stress-level advantage for ATG; Table 4 gives p=0.512
issues.explanation: The Discussion says a level-by-level analysis at 3 months showed significant ATG advantages for both depression and stress. Table 4 supports this only for depression (p=0.010); the stress-level comparison at 3 months is p=0.512. One of the two claimed 3-month benefits is therefore not present in the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 4 showing a significant 3-month stress-level p-value.

quotes.text: a level-by-level analysis of the subscales also showed statistically significant differences in favor of the ATG in reducing depression and stress levels
Stress Level Peer 0.512 FFH

issues.title: Table 7 footnote says Mann-Whitney for within-group changes, contradicting Methods (Friedman/Wilcoxon)
issues.explanation: The footnotes of the within-group tables state that Mann-Whitney U tests were used, which would ignore pairing, while the Methods say Friedman and Wilcoxon tests were used. The layout of the tables suggests the paired tests were run and the footnote is wrong, but the paper does not say so. Any mistake would affect only the within-group results, not the between-group comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that Friedman/Wilcoxon were run and the footnote is a copy error.

quotes.text: U Mann-Whitney test was used in all the analyses
Friedman and Willcoxon test were performed to compare the intervention effects

issues.title: Recruitment from February 2021 precedes the April 4, 2021 protocol version and the registry start date
issues.explanation: The paper states recruitment began in February 2021, but cites ethics approval for a protocol dated April 04, 2021. The registry record lists a study start of April 2021 and first submission in March 2021. This may reflect an earlier approved version or screening before enrolment, but it is not explained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Ethics approval documents for an earlier protocol version dated before February 2021, or a statement that February 2021 refers to screening only.

quotes.text: between February 2021 and March 2022
current protocol version dated April 04, 2021

issues.title: Table 1 percentages mix bases: BRG 8 (58.80) should be 44.4% of 18; 'Some limitation' pair sums to 95.2%
issues.explanation: In Table 1 some BRG percentages do not follow the same denominator as the ATG cells in the same row. Hospital rehabilitation BRG 8 (58.80) is not 8 of any denominator in the table, and in 'Some limitation' the BRG 7 (38.90) is a column share while ATG 9 (56.30) is a row share. These are baseline descriptive errors; they do not affect the outcome analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote defining a different base for these rows, or counts that give the printed percentages.

quotes.text: Hospital rehabilitation (yes) n (%) 18 (51.40) 10 (55.60) 8 (58.80)

script.explanation: 8/18 = 44.44%, but the paper prints 58.8, outside the rounding interval [58.79, 58.81]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 13.6 rather than 18.

issues.title: Text gives p=0.30 for 6-month family support; Table 5 gives p=0.030 (same d=0.45)
issues.explanation: The Results text prints p=0.30 for family support at 6 months while calling it a significant improvement. Table 5 shows p=0.030 with the same effect size, so the text value is almost certainly a typographical slip. Nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the Table 5 value is p=0.030.

quotes.text: significant improvements in family and other support compared to BRG (p=0.30, d=.45; p=0.015, d=.56)

issues.title: Text gives within-ATG anxiety effect size d=.94; Table 6 gives 0.96
issues.explanation: The Results text and Table 6 give different effect sizes for the same ATG pre-post anxiety change. The difference is small and does not change the description of a large effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated different effect-size formula for the text value.

quotes.text: notably the improvement in anxiety (d=.94)

10.1080/17476348.2026.2684077.headline_claim: Bovhyaluronidase azoximer improved exercise tolerance (exertional desaturation and dyspnea) in long COVID pulmonary sequelae and raised FVC recovery in patients with cardiovascular comorbidity, despite the primary FVC endpoint being negative.
10.1080/17476348.2026.2684077.overall: The primary endpoint was clearly null, and the paper says so. The positive messages (improved exercise tolerance, subgroups who 'benefit most') rest on secondary and post-hoc results. Two of the three headline secondary findings have q = 0.056, above the stated 5% level. The subgroup claims were not supported by interaction tests, and the trial was registered about two years after enrolment began. Treat these as hypothesis-generating at best, with a small unexplained discrepancy in the FAS exclusion counts.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline in percent predicted FVC (ppFVC) by Day 71

issues.title: Two exercise-tolerance findings with BH q = 0.056 are called 'robust' and 'survived' adjustment at a 5% level
issues.explanation: The Methods set significance at 5%. The Discussion says exertional desaturation (Day 71) and exertional dyspnea (Day 180) are 'robust' to BH adjustment with q = 0.056, and the limitations paragraph says these findings 'survived multiplicity adjustment'. A q of 0.056 is above 0.05, so by the paper's own rule only the cardiovascular subgroup finding (q = 0.016) survived. The central 'increased exercise tolerance' claim therefore rests on findings that miss the stated threshold after adjustment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified FDR threshold of 10% or more for the secondary endpoints, stated in the protocol or SAP.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was determined at the 5% level using twosided hypothesis tests.
both robust to Benjamini–Hochberg multiplicity adjustment (q = 0.056)
Three findings survived multiplicity adjustment and remained significant after additional adjustment for baseline imbalances

second_reader.what_stands: Two exercise-tolerance findings have a printed BH q of 0.056, which is above the paper's stated 5% significance level, yet the Discussion calls them 'robust' to BH adjustment and the limitations paragraph says they 'survived' adjustment. Only the cardiovascular-subgroup finding (q = 0.016) meets 0.05 as stated; the paper does not state a looser FDR threshold in the main text, though the supplementary tables could not be checked.

issues.title: Discussion and plain-language summary name subgroups that 'benefit most' despite failed interaction tests and adjustment
issues.explanation: The Discussion and plain-language summary say that females, people over 60 and those infected earlier would benefit most, and that BA 'significantly increased' FVC recovery in the early-infection subgroup. But the sex and age effects were not supported by interaction testing, and the infection-date result (p = 0.022) did not survive multiplicity adjustment. The authors state there were over 20 comparisons and that findings are hypothesis-generating, yet the summary written for patients states them as findings of benefit. This overstates evidence from a trial with a null primary endpoint.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant interaction tests that survive multiplicity adjustment for sex, age and infection date.

quotes.text: were not supported by interaction testing
Bovhyaluronidase azoximer significantly increased FVC recovery rate by Day 180 in patients who were infected with SARS-CoV2 before the median date of 14 February 2022
Our data suggests that patients who would benefit most from BA treatment are females, over 60 years old, and who were infected with earlier variants of SARS-Cov-2.

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion and plain-language summary name females, those over 60 and those infected before 14 February 2022 as the patients who 'would benefit most' and who showed 'meaningful improvements', although the Results report failed interaction tests (p = 0.108, 0.133) and a result that did not survive multiplicity adjustment for the infection-date subgroup. The paper's later hypothesis-generating caveat and the Conclusion's focus on the cardiovascular subgroup soften this, but the stronger wording remains in the Discussion and the plain-language summary.

issues.title: FAS exclusion reasons sum to 39 (16+14+9) but 392 randomized minus 376 in FAS is only 16
issues.explanation: The Results say 392 were randomized and 376 entered the FAS, which means 16 were excluded. The three stated reasons for FAS exclusion (16, 14 and 9) add up to 39. The text does not say how these reconcile, so the analysis population is not clearly documented. The null primary result is probably unaffected, but the FAS definition cannot be verified from the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The CONSORT figure showing that the 14 and 9 patients were excluded before randomization, or that the reasons overlap within the 16 excluded patients.

quotes.text: The Full Analysis Set (FAS) included 376 patients (186 in the BA group and 190 in the Placebo group).
16 patients did not meet the inclusion criterion of lung abnormalities affecting more than 10% of lung tissue
9 patients did not meet other inclusion criteria or met exclusion criteria

script.explanation: The participant flow does not reconcile: 'randomized' (n=392) minus its 3 stated exclusion(s) (39) leaves 353, but 'FAS' reports 376 -- 23 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

issues.title: Day 180 dyspnea 'decreased by 47%' is the odds reduction (OR 0.53); the proportions imply about 34%
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the proportion of patients with exertional dyspnea fell by 47% at Day 180. The Results print about 25% (BA) vs 38% (Placebo), a relative reduction of about 34%. The 47% equals 1 minus the odds ratio (0.53), so it describes odds, not the proportion of patients. This makes the benefit look larger than the printed proportions support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Model-based proportions at Day 180 that differ markedly from the printed approximate 25% and 38%, giving a 47% relative reduction.

quotes.text: approximately 25% of patients in the BA group versus 38% of patients in the Placebo group exhibited increased dyspnea after the 6-MWT
the proportion of patients exhibiting exertional desaturation and dyspnea after exercise decreased by 61% and 47%, at Day 71 and Day 180

issues.title: Abstract concludes 'increased exercise tolerance' after a null primary, resting on two q = 0.056 secondary endpoints
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion state the null primary result but then present increased exercise tolerance as the take-away. That claim is based on exertional desaturation and dyspnea, neither of which meets the adjusted 5% level, while walking distance and the ≥50 m walk endpoint showed no significant difference. The abstract describes the null primary as 'clinically insignificant' rather than a failure to show an effect. The wording is hedged, but the conclusion is stronger than the secondary evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy making desaturation and dyspnea key secondary endpoints with an adjusted threshold above 0.056.

quotes.text: While the primary objective yielded clinically insignificant results, patients treated with BA showed increased exercise tolerance although further investigations are required to confirm findings.
the proportion of patients achieving ≥50 m increase in 6-MWT distance, cough severity, or quality of life assessment

issues.title: Trial registered 2024-04-24, after enrolment (April 2022) and completion (Sept 2023), not stated in the paper
issues.explanation: The ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT06383819 was first submitted in April 2024, about two years after the first patient was randomized and after the last patient completed. The paper states the registration number without noting that it was retrospective. Because the registered primary outcome matches the paper, the main risk is that secondary outcomes and subgroups cannot be checked against a prospective plan, which matters for the secondary and subgroup findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prospective registration record (for example a version dated before April 2022) or a statement of registration timing in the paper.

quotes.text: First patient randomization occurred on 28 April 2022 and the last patient completed the study on 4 September 2023.
The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06383819).

issues.title: Baseline imbalance favouring BA in lung damage, 6-MWT distance and exertional dyspnea (adjusted for)
issues.explanation: At baseline the BA arm had less lung damage, longer walks and less post-walk dyspnea, the same domains where benefit is claimed. The analyses adjust for baseline outcome values and sensitivity analyses reportedly agree, which reduces the concern. The imbalance is still a limitation for secondary exercise-tolerance findings, which already sit near the significance boundary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary adjusted and IPTW results showing unchanged effect sizes and confidence intervals for the exercise endpoints.

quotes.text: Patients in the BA group had notably a lower percentage of lung damage, less exertional dyspnea, and greater distances in the 6-MWT.
Although exercise-related baseline characteristics favored the BA arm, additional statistical adjustment for these imbalances did not change the three findings

issues.title: Abstract omits significant excess of adverse events (37.2% vs 25.0%, p = 0.012) while reporting benefit
issues.explanation: Any adverse event occurred in 73/196 (37.2%) BA patients and 49/196 (25.0%) placebo patients, a statistically significant difference. The abstract's results and conclusion do not mention this, and the plain-language summary says BA 'may offer small benefits'. The conclusion section does mention it, so it is disclosed, but the abstract's benefit-only framing makes the net picture look more favourable than the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract or summary that reports the adverse event imbalance alongside the efficacy results.

quotes.text: Seventy-three (37.2%) patients in the BA group and 49 (25.0%) patients in the Placebo group experienced AEs a statistically significant difference
patients treated with BA showed increased exercise tolerance although further investigations are required to confirm findings

issues.title: FAS removed 16 post-randomization (10 BA vs 6 placebo) for ineligibility; complete-case, no imputation
issues.explanation: Attrition is low (4.1%), but the analysis set excludes randomized patients who turned out to be ineligible and uses complete cases only. Exclusion after randomization is acceptable if it was blinded and based on baseline data, but the paper does not say who made the decisions or when. The imbalance (10 vs 6) is small. This is a minor limitation to the secondary findings rather than a threat to the null primary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that FAS exclusions were adjudicated blind to arm before unblinding, or an ITT sensitivity analysis giving the same results.

quotes.text: Analysis was conducted under a completecase framework with no attempt to impute missing values.
The Full Analysis Set (FAS) included 376 patients (186 in the BA group and 190 in the Placebo group).

10.1080/21679169.2025.2479676.headline_claim: A 4-week pulmonary telerehabilitation programme did not improve functional capacity, symptoms, cognition, anxiety, depression, HRQoL or fatigue compared with usual medical care in people with persistent respiratory post-COVID sequelae.
10.1080/21679169.2025.2479676.overall: The finding of no statistically significant difference in 1-minute STS is probably reliable as a statement about the data, but the stronger conclusion that telerehabilitation 'did not improve' outcomes is not well supported, because only 14 of 24 intervention participants were analysed and the CI includes the MCID. There are also several reporting errors in Tables 1-3 (sign flips, a misprinted CI, rows that do not match other tables), none of which alone changes the null result but which reduce confidence in Table 3, the PtR-X comparison.

primary_outcome.name: 1-minute sit-to-stand test (repetitions)

issues.title: Primary analysis uses 14 of 24 PtR and 25 of 26 controls; 'did not improve' is drawn from an underpowered completer set
issues.explanation: The analysed PtR group is 14 against 24 randomised, with 10 of 11 dropouts in that arm. The sample size required 42 and 39 were analysed, and no ITT or sensitivity analysis is given. The primary between-group CI (-3.0 to 4.6) includes both no effect and the 3.5-repetition MCID used for the sample size. The conclusion that PtR 'did not improve' outcomes therefore goes beyond what a non-significant result in a completer analysis can show. The limitation is disclosed but the conclusion does not reflect it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis of all 50 randomised participants (or multiple imputation / sensitivity analyses) giving the same null result with a CI excluding the MCID.

quotes.text: with  10  of  these  being  from  the  PtR  group
did not improve functional capacity, symptoms, cognition, anxiety, depression, hRQol, or fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: The numbers hold: Table 2 reports 14 of 24 PtR and 25 of 26 control participants, 39 against the 42 required, with 10 of the 11 dropouts from the PtR arm. The conclusion that PtR 'did not improve' outcomes rests on non-significant results from this reduced and unbalanced set. The primary CI (-3.0 to 4.6) cannot exclude the 3.5-repetition MCID, and power at the observed SD was well below 80%. The authors do acknowledge that the dropout may have reduced power, but they still state no improvement rather than no detectable effect. Whether the mixed model excluded dropouts entirely is not fully cer

issues.title: Table 3 has several rows incompatible with Tables 1-2 (energy/fatigue 45.0 vs 23.1; functional disability 4.8)
issues.explanation: In Table 3 the control energy/fatigue baseline is 45.0 ± 7.6 and its within-group change is -1.1. Table 2 gives 23.1 ± 20.7 with a change of +7.9, and Table 1 gives 24.0 ± 20.4. The PtR-X functional disability baseline (4.8 ± 2.6) and global perceived health (2.3 ± 2.3) are also far from Table 1 and 2 values (about 14-16 and about 5). The SF-36 role-physical baseline is identical across groups (22.8 ± 35.3). Control reassessment SDs also differ between tables (MoCA 2.4 vs 2.6). Some Table 3 rows look misplaced or duplicated, so the PtR-X comparison cannot be fully trusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 3 or an explanation of a different scoring or scale for these rows.

issues.title: PtR-X denominator is 25 in the MCID sentence but n = 27 in Table 3
issues.explanation: The Results report 12 of 25 PtR-X participants (48%) reaching the MCID, while Table 3 labels the PtR-X group n = 27. The paper never explains the two missing participants. The percentage is internally correct for 25 but the denominator is not reconciled with the analysed group. This is a secondary, post-hoc responder figure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 2 PtR-X participants lacked a reassessment 1-minute STS, so the responder analysis used 25.

10.1089/can.2022.0135.headline_claim: Formula C, a CBD-rich hemp whole-flower product, appears to be safe and efficacious in people with post-acute COVID-19 syndrome.
10.1089/can.2022.0135.overall: The headline claim that Formula C is safe and efficacious is not supported: the placebo contained therapeutic terpenes, both groups improved similarly, and no between-group significance was shown. Safety statements are also overstated given a withdrawal for an adverse event. The study is a small, underpowered exploratory pilot whose results are at most hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS and PGIC change scores (comparative change from baseline to end of each treatment period)

issues.title: Placebo contained therapeutic terpenes, so Period 1 comparison lacks a true inert control
issues.explanation: After Group 2 improved in Period 1, the placebo was retested and found to contain therapeutic terpene levels, and the study continued 'despite no longer having a true placebo'. Both groups improved similarly on PGIC, so a between-group difference cannot be attributed to Formula C. The Methods also call the trial both 'open-label' and blinded, and allocation concealment is not described. This weakens the only controlled comparison and the efficacy conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the placebo terpene levels are below any active threshold and that the blind and allocation concealment were intact.

quotes.text: After observing improvements in Group 2 during the Period 1, a decision was made to submit the placebo for additional laboratory testing and it was determined that therapeutic levels of terpenes were present in the hempseed oil.
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, Hemp product description

quotes.text: Decision was made to continue the study despite no longer having a true placebo.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that the placebo hempseed oil contained terpenes, which the authors call therapeutic levels. It also reports that Group 2 improved during Period 1 and that the study continued 'despite no longer having a true placebo'. The Period 1 comparison therefore lacks an inert control, and the authors acknowledge this as a limitation. What is not shown is that the placebo terpene amounts caused the improvement, because natural recovery, expectancy and regression to the mean are equally possible.

issues.title: Conclusion says 'efficacious' although no between-group difference was shown and placebo improved similarly
issues.explanation: The authors concede they 'did not achieve complete statistical significance as outlined in the protocol', and that PGIC improved similarly across both groups. Group 2 improved as much as or more than Group 1 over day 0-28, so the data do not isolate an effect of Formula C. The Conclusion nonetheless says the product appears efficacious, which the design and results do not support; the within-group significance in Group 1 (anxiety p = 0.006, dyspnea 0.013, sleep 0.041, one-tailed, uncorrected across 10 tests) is a weak basis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group test showing significantly greater improvement with Formula C than placebo.

quotes.text: Although we did not achieve complete statistical significance as outlined in the protocol, clinical benefits were observed.
appears to be safe and efficacious in

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's word 'efficacious' is not supported by the reported data. The only evidence of benefit is within-group, one-sided, uncorrected change, and the placebo group improved by similar or larger amounts on most measures. The Discussion itself concedes that significance was not achieved as planned, and the Conclusion hedges ('appears to be') and lists limitations. Even so, 'efficacious' goes beyond a result that does not distinguish active product from placebo.

issues.title: Discussion says placebo reached significance; Group 2 results report no significant symptom change
issues.explanation: The Results say that for Group 2 (placebo then open-label) improvements in anxiety, dyspnea, depression, fatigue, sleep and pain 'none reached statistical significance', with only marginal p < 0.1 for two symptoms. The Discussion then says placebo use achieved relief 'also reaching statistical significance'. No reported placebo-period test supports this, so the text is internally inconsistent. The error makes the placebo look more active than the data show, which mainly muddies interpretation of the control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported test showing significant within-group placebo-period change (e.g., PGIC Wilcoxon in Group 2) that the Discussion refers to.

quotes.text: However, the use of the placebo also achieved relief for some symptoms, also reaching statistical significance.
but none reached statistical significance

issues.title: Conclusion says no adverse events; one participant withdrew for an adverse event
issues.explanation: The Conclusion states there were no adverse events, yet the withdrawals paragraph reports one participant leaving because of lightheadedness and euphoria. The investigator judged it unrelated, so the claim might be read as 'no related adverse events', but that is not what is written. The safety statement is overstated, though the event was non-serious and the paper elsewhere reports no serious events.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that the conclusion refers only to product-related events and that the event occurred on placebo only.

quotes.text: There were no adverse events or safety concerns with utilizing Formula C in this patient population.
withdrew due to an adverse event of lightheaded sensation and euphoria

issues.title: 31 randomized vs target 60, no power calculation, yet 'efficacious' concluded
issues.explanation: The study enrolled 31 of a planned 60 with no sample-size calculation, and analyses use 10-12 per group. For an exploratory pilot this is acceptable, but the Conclusion states the product 'appears to be safe and efficacious'. The paper's own data do not support that wording, which is the main concern and is covered under the spin issue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified pilot framing with conclusions limited to feasibility.

quotes.text: Target number for enrollment was 60
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, Design and objectives

issues.title: Analyses on completers only; 8/31 withdrawals and 2 randomized non-dosed excluded
issues.explanation: Eight of 31 (25.8%) withdrew, including two randomized participants never dosed, and tables use available-case data (N = 10-12). No intention-to-treat analysis is described. Withdrawals were similar across arms in proportion (3/15 vs 5/16), so bias direction is unclear, and it is secondary to the other design problems.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or mixed-model analysis including all randomized participants showing the same results.

quotes.text: There were eight withdrawals, (3/15) from Group 1 and (5/16) from Group 2.
two participants were randomized but not dosed

It is a minor unexplained inconsistency in one cell.

These are disclosed, but the funder's role in design, analysis and writing is not stated. This is context for the favourable conclusion rather than a separate defect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the funder had no role in analysis and interpretation, with independent statistical analysis.

10.1093/ajrccm/aamag162.1100.headline_claim: Implementing a diet high in fermented foods in patients with Long COVID appears to have some signal for improvement in neuropsychiatric symptoms, with a larger trial needed to clarify statistical significance.
10.1093/ajrccm/aamag162.1100.overall: The conclusion is worded cautiously for a pilot, but the 'signal' of benefit rests on separate within-arm paired tests, with no between-arm comparison, and only completers are described. The results are hypothesis-generating at best, and the abstract does not show that the diet outperforms usual diet.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Treatment 'signal' rests on separate within-arm paired t-tests; no between-arm comparison of change reported
issues.explanation: Changes from baseline were tested separately in each arm with paired t-tests, and the abstract contrasts which arm reached significance. A significant result in one arm and not the other does not show the arms differ. The control arm also improved on quality of life, so some improvement is not specific to the diet. The concluded 'signal' for treatment benefit is therefore not supported by a randomized comparison, though the wording is tentative and a larger trial is called for.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group comparison (e.g. ANCOVA or a difference in change scores with CI) in Table 1 or the full poster showing the treatment arm improved more than control.

quotes.text: Questionnaire scores were evaluated for changes using a paired t-test, with statistical significance defined as a p-value <0.05.
Those in the control arm only had improvements in reported overall quality of life. Intra-group changes can be seen in Table 1.
Implementing a diet high in fermented foods in patients with LC appears to have some signal for improvement in neuropsychiatric symptoms.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's methods describe only within-arm paired t-tests (plus a Spearman correlation), and the results are framed as 'intra-group changes' (treatment improved on anxiety, PTSD and quality of life; control improved on overall quality of life only), with no between-arm comparison of change reported in the text. The 'signal' conclusion therefore rests on a contrast of significant vs non-significant within-arm results, which does not by itself show a treatment effect. However, the content of Table 1 is not visible here, so the point that no between-arm comparison appears anywhere in the ful

With about 12% loss in a small trial, a completer analysis can favour the treatment if dropout differed by arm. The effect on the conclusion is limited because attrition is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow showing balanced dropout with reasons and a sensitivity or ITT analysis giving the same results.

10.1093/brain/awad377.headline_claim: Vortioxetine improved depressive symptoms and health-related quality of life in post-COVID-19 condition, and showed a pro-cognitive effect after adjustment for baseline CRP, while the unadjusted primary cognitive outcome was not significant.
10.1093/brain/awad377.overall: The unadjusted primary cognitive analysis was null, and the paper's positive cognitive conclusion rests on adjusted, CRP-moderated and subgroup analyses that are exploratory, uncorrected for multiplicity and from an underpowered sample. The depressive-symptom and HRQoL gains are more convincing, though still uncorrected secondaries from a modest, industry-supplied trial with some reporting slips (AE denominators, caption P values).

issues.title: Null primary DSST result reframed as pro-cognitive effect via adjusted/CRP-moderated models
issues.explanation: The registered primary outcome (combined DSST change) was not significant between groups (P=0.361; interaction P=0.720). The abstract conclusion nevertheless states that adjusting for CRP showed a significant pro-cognitive effect, resting on covariate-adjusted and moderator analyses not shown to be prespecified, and on a CRP-subgroup (P=0.045). These should be labelled hypothesis-generating; the discussion's later hedge does not correct the abstract's claim.

10.1093/braincomms/fcad117.headline_claim: Anodal tDCS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex may improve physical fatigue in post-COVID syndrome, and the study confirms tDCS safety in this condition.
10.1093/braincomms/fcad117.overall: The headline claim that tDCS may improve physical fatigue rests on one subscale interaction (P = 0.034) that is uncorrected across outcomes, while the registered primary measure, MFIS-total, was null. The authors do call the study a preliminary pilot, but the abstract and the 'confirms safety' wording go beyond what 47 patients support. The remaining defect is a minor participant-flow inconsistency in the screening counts, with no bearing on the results.

primary_outcome.name: MFIS-total (change in fatigue)

issues.title: Primary MFIS-total interaction null (P=0.184); abstract headlines uncorrected MFIS-physical subscale (P=0.034)
issues.explanation: The primary outcome, MFIS-total, showed no significant time-by-group effect. The abstract nonetheless leads with an improvement in physical fatigue, a subscale that was not the registered primary measure. That result comes from many tests across outcomes, with multiplicity correction applied only to post hoc comparisons within an outcome. The physical-fatigue finding is therefore hypothesis-generating at best, and the Discussion's claim of a 'positive effect' goes beyond the primary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified protocol or registry entry naming MFIS-physical as the primary endpoint, or a cross-outcome multiplicity adjustment under which the physical-subscale interaction remains significant.

issues.title: 'Confirms the safety' of tDCS claimed from 47 patients, 8 sessions and 1-month follow-up
issues.explanation: The safety data are nine mild adverse events (headache, dizziness) across 47 patients, balanced between arms. That supports good short-term tolerability in this sample. It cannot rule out rarer or longer-term harms, so 'confirms the safety' overstates the evidence even though the pilot caveat follows in the next sentence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to 'was well tolerated in this small sample', or a larger safety dataset.

The discrepancy is in the screening and enrolment count only. The 47 analysed participants and the group sizes are consistent with each other and with the registry, so it affects reporting accuracy, not the results.
