issues.title: Retrospectively selected external control, imbalanced at baseline, with unadjusted comparisons
issues.explanation: The control group was retrospectively picked from hospital records, not randomised, and differed at baseline in time from symptom onset (43 vs 34 days, P<0.001), IL-6, SARS-CoV-2 positivity and antibiotic use. The efficacy comparisons are unadjusted Wilcoxon tests, and baseline pulmonary function was never measured. Differences in lung and lung-function outcomes cannot be attributed to MSCs with confidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted analyses (e.g. propensity weighting or covariate adjustment) showing the same effect.

quotes.text: These controls were retrospectively selected from the same hospitals' information systems by study physicians.
The median time from symptom onset to hospitalization was 43 (IQR: 38-53) days in the MSC group and 34 (IQR: 23-46) days in the control group
Moreover, the control group was external and short of randomization.

second_reader.what_stands: The control group was retrospectively selected from hospital information systems, was external and non-randomized, and differed at baseline in time from symptom onset to hospitalization (43 vs 34 days), antibiotic use, IL-6, viral positivity, and some blood counts. All efficacy comparisons are unadjusted. The Results text says baseline was 'generally balanced' and the authors acknowledge the onset delay and the lack of randomization in the limitations. The Methods list matching variables, and the Discussion says matching included 'comorbidities, clinical onset', but Methods do not list those a

issues.title: ~30 pulmonary-function tests plus imaging and symptoms, uncorrected; only 9 nominal P<0.05 highlighted
issues.explanation: Table 3 alone has 4 outcomes x 5 timepoints x 2 severity strata = 40 tests. Nominal significance was claimed for isolated results (VCmax/FEV1 in moderate patients, one DLCO timepoint in severe patients), plus imaging and pain results, with no correction or primary outcome. Several are borderline (P=0.036 to 0.045). Some positive findings would be expected by chance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary endpoint or multiplicity-adjusted results.

quotes.text: A value of P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
significantly improved VCmax

second_reader.what_stands: The paper tested dozens of outcome, time point and subgroup comparisons (30 pulmonary function tests, 40 with 6-MWD, plus imaging and symptoms) at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05, and the nominal significant results are highlighted without multiplicity adjustment. My count of highlighted nominal P<0.05 results is 10 (7 PFT, 1 imaging, 2 pain), not 9, and the conclusion is worded as a trend and preliminary, which limits but does not remove the issue.

issues.title: Day-28 follow-up 47/52 (90%) MSC vs 35/58 (60%) control; complete-case analysis, no imputation
issues.explanation: Analysis was limited to patients with follow-up data and missing values were not imputed. Control follow-up at day 28 was only 60% versus 90% for MSC, and baseline lung-function was never measured. The reasons for missingness are not given, so selective retention could bias the between-group differences. The authors only note loss to follow-up as an inevitable challenge.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis or comparison of baseline characteristics of completers vs non-completers in each arm.

quotes.text: Ultimately, 47/52 patients in the MSC group and 35/58 patients in the control group at day 28
Missing values were not imputed.

second_reader.what_stands: Day-28 follow-up was 47/52 (90%) in the MSC group vs 35/58 (60%) in the control group, and the analysis used available data only with no imputation, so differential attrition could bias the comparisons. The authors acknowledge loss to follow-up as a limitation, but they do not assess its effect with any sensitivity analysis.

issues.title: 'Confirmed' safety and benefit in both moderate and severe patients from a small non-randomised study
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the study 'confirmed' safety and underscores benefit for both moderate and severe patients, yet there was no imaging benefit in moderate patients and lung-function gains were scattered and uncorrected. The final conclusion is hedged ('trend', 'preliminary'), which softens the problem. Safety (similar AE rates, one grade 3 event) is reasonably supported, though 52 patients cannot exclude rare events.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; wording is a judgement.

quotes.text: This study confirmed MSCs' safety and observed significant improvements in pulmonary function and ground-glass lesion volumes in severe patients.
These findings underscore MSC therapy's potential benefits for both moderate and severe COVID-19 patients

issues.title: Table 2 any-AE grade 1-2 cell: 18 (36.54%) but 18/52 = 34.62%; 36.54% is the 19-patient total
issues.explanation: The text reports 19 MSC patients (36.54%) with any AE. Table 2 prints 18 (36.54) in the grade 1 or 2 column, and 18/52 is 34.62%. The 18 plus 1 grade 3-4 patients reconciles to 19, so only the percentage in that cell is mislabelled. Nothing depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the grade 1-2 cell intentionally shows the overall percentage.

quotes.text: 19 patients (36.54%) in the MSC group

quotes.location: Table 2, any adverse event row, MSC grade 1 or 2

script.explanation: 18/52 = 34.62%, but the paper prints 36.54, outside the rounding interval [36.53, 36.55]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 49.3 rather than 52.

10.1097/md.0000000000041583.headline_claim: Adding an evidence-based eHealth education tool to pulmonary rehabilitation reduces kinesiophobia in post-COVID-19 patients with musculoskeletal symptoms, and may improve long-term outcomes, though it did not add benefit to physical outcomes.
10.1097/md.0000000000041583.overall: The headline claim that the eHealth education tool significantly reduces kinesiophobia and may improve long-term outcomes rests on one borderline p = .048 among about 25 outcomes in 12 unblinded patients. The outcome is not a registered primary, there is no multiplicity control, and the effect size and adverse-event figures are internally inconsistent. At best the paper supports a hypothesis for a larger trial, not a conclusion about efficacy or safety.

primary_outcome.name: Not clearly identified in the paper; registry lists manual grip strength, SF-36 quality of life, exercise capacity (6MWT) and CAT as primary outcomes; the paper's only significant result is Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia-11 at posttreatment

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from base line and at the end of each of the six weeks

primary_outcomes.measure: Quality of life according to Short- Form 36 Questionnaire (SF - 36)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from base line and at the end of each of the six weeks
Change from base line and at the end of each of the six weeks
Change from base line and at the end of each of the six weeks

issues.title: One p = .048 among ~25 outcomes in 12 patients, with no multiplicity control, drives a confident efficacy claim
issues.explanation: The only significant result is the post-treatment kinesiophobia comparison (p = .048) from 6 vs 6 patients. About 25 outcomes were tested across several time points with no correction. Under these conditions one borderline p-value is weak evidence. The Discussion nevertheless says the intervention was 'particularly effective' and the Conclusions say it 'significantly' reduced kinesiophobia. The limitations section mentions small size but does not temper these statements.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary outcome of kinesiophobia, or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis keeping p below the adjusted threshold.

quotes.text: resampling tests based on permutations were used
indicating that the telemedicine intervention was particularly effective in reducing the fear of movement
Twelve patients referred from the ICU

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports one nominal p = .048 among roughly 22 or more tested outcomes in 12 patients, with no stated multiplicity adjustment. It nonetheless calls this the main finding and says the intervention was 'particularly effective' (the Discussion does add that physical outcomes were null). The p value would not survive any standard correction, and the effect size and its CI also look inconsistent with Z and n.

issues.title: Conclusions assert long-term benefit and safety/effectiveness not shown by 12 patients and null 7/9-month results
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the tool significantly reduces kinesiophobia and may improve long-term outcomes. The Discussion calls the programme 'safe and effective in addressing long-term disease consequences'. The paper shows no significant long-term difference and no significant benefit on pain, mobility or function. Safety evidence comes from adverse-event percentages that disagree between Results and Discussion. The stated hypothesis of sustained improvement at 7 and 9 months is not supported by the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant long-term between-group differences in a prespecified outcome, with consistent adverse-event counts.

quotes.text: significantly reducing kinesiophobia
is safe and effective in addressing long-term disease consequences.

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion's statement that rehabilitation 'is safe and effective in addressing long-term disease consequences' is not supported. The study has 12 patients, a null between-group result on every visible 7- and 9-month comparison, and adverse-event percentages that differ between Results and Discussion. The Conclusion's wording ('significantly reducing kinesiophobia', 'potentially improving long-term outcomes') is hedged and acknowledges limited physical impact, but it still leans on a single P = .048 result, and no long-term benefit is shown.

issues.title: Patient-reported kinesiophobia is the only positive result; participants knew allocation and got extra contact
issues.explanation: Telehealth patients received six additional one-hour education sessions that controls did not. The paper has no attention-matched control. The one significant outcome is a self-completed questionnaire, so expectation and extra attention could produce the difference. The statement about 'proper blinding' covers staff and statistician only, and the registry lists masking as none.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants did not know their allocation, or an attention-matched control arm with the same contact time.

quotes.text: All the patients were instructed not to discuss their treatment with other patients or evaluators.

second_reader.what_stands: Kinesiophobia (Tampa, P = .048) is the only outcome with P < .05 at posttreatment. It is a self-reported measure in a trial where participants were necessarily aware of an arm that had 6 extra hours of therapist contact, and the registry records no masking. The paper does not state that participants knew their allocation, and its blinding language overstates what could be masked.

issues.title: Registered primaries (grip, SF-36, 6MWT, CAT) not reported as such; headline is kinesiophobia, and SF-36/CAT are absent
issues.explanation: The paper lists 'various outcome measures' with no stated primary. The registry's four primary outcomes were grip strength, SF-36, exercise capacity and CAT, with no TSK among them. The paper uses EuroQoL-5D instead of SF-36, has no CAT results, and builds its conclusion on the TSK result. A registered-primary versus reported mismatch like this could let an unplanned outcome become the headline. The extent cannot be settled without the registry history.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing TSK as a prespecified primary or the registered outcomes having been changed before data collection, or a protocol designating TSK-11 as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: The effectiveness of the interventions was assessed using various outcome measures.
There were no significant differences between the outcome variables

second_reader.what_stands: The paper designates no primary outcome and does not mention the four registered primaries as such. SF-36 and CAT are absent (EuroQoL-5D appears instead, unexplained), and the headline result is Tampa kinesiophobia, which is not among the registered primaries. Grip strength and 6-minute walk are reported but null. This is based on the current registry record only.

issues.title: Effect size r = 0.812 does not match Z = 1.936 with N = 12 (r ≈ 0.56)
issues.explanation: The paper defines r as a nonparametric effect size, normally Z divided by the square root of N. For the reported Z = 1.936 and 12 participants this gives about 0.56, a moderate effect on the paper's own thresholds, not a 'large' one. The narrow confidence interval is also hard to reconcile with a borderline p of .048. The description of a 'large and significant' effect is therefore not supported by the printed statistics.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative effect-size formula under which r = 0.812 follows from the data.

quotes.text: R = 0.812, 95% confidence interval [0.715-0.893]

issues.title: Adverse-event percentages differ between Results and Discussion (25/33/34% vs 22/11/5%) and are unattainable with n=12
issues.explanation: The Results report 25% respiratory events, 33% respiratory plus musculoskeletal, and 34% respiratory plus neurological. The Discussion, describing the same follow-up, gives 22%, 11% and about 5%. In a 12-patient trial the 34%, 22%, 11% and 5% values cannot be a count out of 12. The 34% for respiratory plus neurological events also exceeds the roughly 5% given for neurological events overall. The lower Discussion figures then support the conclusion that the programme is safe.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion figures refer to a different denominator or time window, with adverse-event counts per arm that reconcile with both sets of percentages.

quotes.text: Respiratory adverse events were observed in 25%
22% of the patients reported respiratory adverse events
occurring in approximately 5% of the cases

issues.title: Methods describe a 17-item Tampa scale but Results report the 11-item version (mean 16.00)
issues.explanation: Methods describe a 17-item scale scored 1 to 4, with a minimum total of 17. The Results and table use the 11-item version, where 16.00 is attainable. The reader cannot tell which instrument was administered for the only significant outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors confirming the TSK-11 was used and the 17-item description was an error.

quotes.text: Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia, consisting of 17 items scored from 1 to 4
with a lower score in telehealth (16.00 ± 2.71 vs 23.17 ± 5.49 points)

issues.title: Chance baseline imbalance in medication, exercise and bereavement with 6 patients per arm
issues.explanation: Analgesic use (0 vs 3), no exercise (1 vs 4) and loss of family members (1 vs 3) differ between arms. No adjustment is possible or reported at this size. The claim of 'no baseline differences' rests on non-significant tests with 6 per arm, which carry little weight.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is expected under randomization at this sample size.

quotes.text: Loss of family members, n (%)

10.1097/phm.0000000000002089.headline_claim: A rehabilitation program for post-COVID-19 ongoing symptoms is feasible and may improve symptoms and health-related quality of life, with the authors noting causality cannot be demonstrated.
10.1097/phm.0000000000002089.overall: The central finding, that symptoms and EQ-5D improved after rehabilitation, is reported consistently in Table 1 but is a pre-post change in one uncontrolled group, so it cannot be attributed to the programme. The abstract also has two misprints (breathlessness r and the pain P sign), the strongest-correlation claim is wrong, and the safety claim rests on one sentence. The paper is hedged ('may improve'), so the conclusion is usable only as preliminary, hypothesis-generating evidence..

primary_outcome.name: Changes in NRS symptom intensity (breathlessness, fatigue, pain) and EQ-5D index/VAS from before to after rehabilitation

issues.title: Benefit inferred from paired pre-post change in one uncontrolled cohort (also covers c5)
issues.explanation: All results are before-after differences in a single group, tested with paired t tests. No comparison group exists, so the P values show change over time and not an effect of rehabilitation. Natural recovery, regression to the mean (enrolment required NRS of 5 or more) and expectation effects are not separated from the programme. The authors acknowledge this and use cautious wording in the abstract, so the claim is weaker than a causal one, but the Conclusions still present the improvements as the programme's outcome and recommend access to rehabilitation resources.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical comparison group, or evidence on the expected natural course of NRS and EQ-5D over a similar period.

quotes.text: A paired t test was used to compare changes before and after the rehabilitation program
the lack of a control group
These observational findings support the importance of access to rehabilitation resources for post -COVID-19 patients

second_reader.what_stands: The inference rests on paired pre-post change in one uncontrolled cohort of completers, selected on high baseline symptoms, so the changes cannot be attributed to rehabilitation (natural recovery, regression to the mean, and expectation effects are not excluded). The authors do acknowledge this in the limitations and abstract hedging, so the paper is not wholly unaware of it; but the Conclusions ('provides evidence for... safety', 'significant reduction... has been noted', 'support the importance of access to rehabilitation') and the Discussion's support for implementing rehabilitation provisi

issues.title: Abstract gives breathlessness-EQ-5D r = -0.533 (called low); Results give -0.378 and -0.368
issues.explanation: The abstract reports the breathlessness correlation with EQ-5D as -0.533 and calls it low. The Results give -0.378 (index) and -0.368 (VAS), which are low on the paper's scale. On the paper's own scale (0.51-0.70 = moderate), -0.533 would be moderate, so the abstract contradicts both the Results and its own label. The abstract's contrast between pain/fatigue and breathlessness is therefore not supported by the figures it prints.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary correlation table (Table S1) showing breathlessness r = -0.533 and the Results text as the error.

quotes.text: and low for breathlessness ( -0.533, P < 0.001)
showing low negative correlation with EQ-5D index (Pearson r = -0.378, P < 0.016)

issues.title: Completers-only analysis; analysed n (about 44) not stated and does not match 50 minus 7 dropouts
issues.explanation: The Methods exclude patients with any missing data, and the Results mention seven dropouts. The paper never states how many patients were analysed. The Table 1 means (e.g. 5.614, 2.705, 4.568) are whole-number multiples of 1/44, which implies about 44 analysed. That matches neither 50 nor 43 (50 minus 7). Patients who stopped attending are absent from the outcomes, which would flatter the results if dropouts did worse; with 12-14% missing, the effect is probably small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the analysed n (44) and a participant flow showing how 50 and seven dropouts reconcile.

quotes.text: All analyses were performed excluding patients if missing data were observed.
There were seven dropouts because of work circumstances.

issues.title: Conclusion asserts 'safety' on the strength of one sentence saying the programme was well tolerated
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the study provides evidence for the feasibility and safety of the programme. The only safety information is that the programme was well tolerated by all subjects. The Methods describe no adverse event definition or systematic recording, and the 7 dropouts are attributed to work circumstances without any check for adverse effects. Feasibility is reasonably supported, but the safety claim is stronger than the data in a small series with no stated adverse event monitoring.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A documented systematic adverse-event record for all participants showing no events.

quotes.text: This study provides evidence for the feasibility and safety of a rehabilitation program
The physiotherapy program was well tolerated by all the subjects

issues.title: Fatigue called strongest correlation (r = -0.531) though pain is stronger (r = -0.609)
issues.explanation: The Results state that fatigue has the strongest correlation with quality of life, at r = -0.531 with the EQ-5D index. The next sentence reports pain with the same index at r = -0.609, which is stronger. The Results also give an identical r = -0.449 (P < 0.004) for fatigue-VAS and pain-VAS, which may be a copying slip. The ranking of symptoms by correlation strength, which the Discussion builds on, is not reliable as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Table S1 showing the intended ranking, or a definition of 'strongest' that excludes pain.

quotes.text: The strongest correlation emerges between the reduction of fatigue and the improvement in quality of life being Pearson r coefficient = -0.531
The reduction of pain shows moderate correlation with EQ 5D index (Pearson r = -0.609, P < 0.001)

issues.title: Abstract prints pain NRS change as P > 0.001; Results and Table 1 give P < 0.001
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the P value for the pain change as P > 0.001. The Results and Table 1 give P < 0.001. The sign is reversed in the abstract, so as printed the abstract does not report a significant pain change. Nothing else depends on it, because the full text is consistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; the full text confirms the abstract is the typo.

10.1097/phm.0000000000002350.headline_claim: An 8-week face-to-face rehabilitation program reduces dyspnea, fatigue and anxiety, increases exercise capacity, and improves memory and attention in patients with persistent COVID-19 symptoms.
10.1097/phm.0000000000002350.overall: The paper shows that both groups improved over 8 weeks, but it cannot show that the supervised program caused more improvement than remote monitoring. Allocation was by participant preference, about half the allocated participants were not analysed, and the direct between-group comparisons for fatigue, dyspnea and exercise capacity were all non-significant. The Conclusion and the safety claim go beyond the evidence; the only numeric error found (Table 4 REC n labels) is minor.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue, dyspnea (PFSDQ-M), and exercise capacity (ISWT)

issues.title: Benefit claimed from within-arm change; primary between-group deltas non-significant (p=0.292, 0.608, 0.186)
issues.explanation: Dyspnea fell significantly in the rehabilitation arm (p=0.001) but not the remote arm, and this is read as proof that rehabilitation works for dyspnea. The direct between-group comparisons of change were not significant for fatigue (p=0.292), dyspnea (p=0.608) or exercise capacity (p=0.186). A significant change in one arm and not the other is not evidence that the arms differ. Both arms improved, so the data are equally compatible with time or the remote-monitoring contact.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group interaction (for example ANCOVA on follow-up adjusted for baseline) favouring rehabilitation for the primary outcomes.

quotes.text: There was no difference between the baseline dyspnea score ( _p_ =0.901) and in the deltas between groups ( _p_ =0.608; d=0.08).
quotes.location: Results, Fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise capacity

quotes.text: Of the main sequelae, fatigue improves naturally, whereas dyspnea requires rehabilitation.
An 8-week face-to-face rehabilitation program can reduce symptoms of dyspnea, fatigue, and anxiety, increase exercise capacity

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcomes (fatigue, dyspnea, ISWT) showed no significant between-group difference in deltas (p=0.292, 0.608, 0.186), yet the Abstract and Conclusion say face-to-face rehabilitation reduces dyspnea, fatigue and increases exercise capacity, resting on within-arm change; the Abstract's 'dyspnea requires rehabilitation' rests on a significant-vs-nonsignificant contrast that the direct comparison does not support. Mitigating: the ISWT comparison was underpowered (27%) and the paper does report that both groups improved on fatigue and exercise capacity.

issues.title: Self-selected allocation to rehabilitation vs a booklet-and-calls arm cannot isolate a program effect
issues.explanation: Participants picked their arm by availability and preference. Baseline differences (for example education, smoking, sex) were not adjusted for, and the groups received different contact and attention. The authors admit the allocation 'interferes with the validity of our results', yet the Conclusion states causal benefit ('can reduce symptoms'). The design supports a tentative, hypothesis-generating reading at most.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomised allocation, or an analysis adjusting for baseline covariates showing the same between-group differences.

quotes.text: Volunteers chose to participate in the face-to-face rehabilitation or remote monitoring based on their availability and preference.
We understand that this form of allocation interferes with the validity of our results.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by participant choice and availability, so program effect is confounded with unmeasured factors (motivation, work schedule, transport, education), and the authors concede this threatens validity. The comparator was an active minimal-support arm, and the paper's own between-group tests were non-significant, so the design cannot isolate a program effect; the authors acknowledge the allocation limitation but their Conclusion still attributes benefits to the program.

issues.title: About 52% of 77 allocated were not analysed (40/77); completers-only analysis, loss similar in both arms
issues.explanation: Of 77 allocated, only 37 were analysed. Reasons for withdrawal included clinical improvement and scheduling or transport problems, so completers may differ from dropouts. No intention-to-treat or missing-data analysis is reported. The screen's claim of differential loss is not borne out: loss was about 50% in the rehabilitation arm and about 55% in the remote arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis including all 77 allocated participants with consistent results.

quotes.text: 35 withdrew from participating, and five were considered losses
Others reported clinical improvement and expressed interest in not continuing the research.

second_reader.what_stands: About 52% of the 77 allocated participants (40/77) were not analysed, the analysis included completers only, and attrition was similar across arms (50% vs 55%). Attrition reasons included clinical improvement, which may be outcome-related, so completers-only results may be biased; the authors do list dropout among limitations but do not analyse its effect.

issues.title: Protocol 'shown to be safe, feasible' with no adverse-event reporting and 52% non-completion
issues.explanation: The clinical implications state the protocol 'has been shown to be safe, feasible, and accessible'. The Results contain no adverse-event data and no safety outcome. Feasibility is doubtful when about half of allocated participants withdrew or were lost, many citing schedule or transport barriers. These statements go beyond what this small non-randomised study measured.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported adverse-event log showing no serious events during supervised sessions, or a revised claim limited to what was measured.

quotes.text: In addition, the protocol has been shown to be safe, feasible, and accessible to scientific and clinical communities.
Many dropouts occurred because the participant's work schedule was incompatible with the rehabilitation schedule

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no adverse-event data, so 'safe' is asserted without supporting evidence, and with about half of the rehabilitation arm not completing, largely for schedule and transport reasons the authors themselves cite, 'feasible' is only supported for the subset who stayed. The statement in the Clinical implications is stronger than the reported data allow.

issues.title: Analysed 37 vs 82 planned (41 per group); between-group exercise delta had 27% power
issues.explanation: The sample-size calculation required 41 per group, and the study analysed 22 and 15. The between-group exercise comparison reached only 27% power, so non-significant differences cannot be read as equivalence, and nominally significant secondary findings are fragile. The calculation used a different outcome (6MWT) from the ISWT primary outcome. This weakens the between-group conclusions but is mostly the same issue as c5.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified justification that the study was a feasibility pilot with no efficacy conclusions intended.

quotes.text: the estimate was 41 participants per group.
between deltas (p=0.186; d=0.47; power 27%)
quotes.location: Results, Fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise capacity

issues.title: Table 4 REC row labelled n=21 and n=14, but counts and percentages fit n=22 and n=15
issues.explanation: The REC row of Table 4 is labelled n=21 (face-to-face) and n=14 (remote). The percentages beside the counts only work with 22 and 15, which are the group sizes everywhere else in the paper. Either the n labels are wrong, or the percentages were computed on a different base than the one stated. This is a labelling inconsistency affecting a secondary outcome only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one participant per arm had missing REC data and that percentages were calculated on the full group, or a corrected table.

quotes.location: Table 4, REC row, remote monitoring group

script.explanation: 13/21 = 61.90%, but the paper prints 59.1, outside the rounding interval [59.05, 59.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 22.0 rather than 21.

10.1097/phm.0000000000002559.headline_claim: An individualized, supervised cardiopulmonary rehabilitation program was effective in improving cardiorespiratory fitness, ventilatory efficiency, and symptom burden in individuals with long COVID.
10.1097/phm.0000000000002559.overall: The main finding, a larger VO2peak gain with rehabilitation than with no intervention (ANCOVA P = 0.003, +2.7 vs +0.3 mL/kg/min), is reasonably supported, although it comes from a small trial analysed on completers only and labelled ITT. Claims on ventilatory efficiency, symptom burden and lung function rest on uncorrected marginal P values, unblinded self-report, or results the paper itself shows did not change. The paper also leaves unclear which arm had 17 and which 18 participants.

primary_outcome.name: Change in VO2peak (mL/kg/min) at 8 weeks

issues.title: ~50 secondary tests at P<0.05 uncorrected; ventilatory-efficiency and symptom claims rest on P 0.016-0.045
issues.explanation: The methods apply a two-tailed 0.05 level to all tests, with secondary outcomes analysed like the primary. The conclusions claim improved ventilatory efficiency and symptom burden, resting on marginal uncorrected P values (VE/VCO2 0.032, VT1 0.045, impact scales 0.016 to 0.026). With this many outcomes, several nominally significant results are expected by chance, so these claims are tentative. The primary VO2peak result is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or multiplicity adjustment under which these secondary results remain significant.

quotes.text: A two-tailed significance level of 0.05 was used for all statistical tests.
Secondary and tertiary outcomes were analyzed in the same way as primary outcomes.

second_reader.what_stands: No multiplicity adjustment or exploratory label is stated. About 44 between-group tests appear in the main tables (more than that including within-group and supplementary tests), all judged at P<0.05. The abstract and conclusion state ventilatory-efficiency and symptom-burden benefits that rest on unadjusted P values of 0.016 to 0.045 (VE/VCO2 P=0.032, VO2 at VT1 P=0.045, three impact scales 0.016 to 0.026). The primary outcome (VO2peak, P=0.003) is unaffected, and the strongest impact-scale results (P=0.002 and <0.001) are less exposed than the P 0.016 to 0.045 results.

issues.title: Unblinded no-treatment control for self-reported symptom and QoL outcomes claimed as benefits
issues.explanation: Control participants kept their daily habits, with no attention or sham component, and knew they were waiting for rehabilitation. The symptom impact scales and SF-36 are subjective, so expectation, attention and waitlist effects cannot be separated from the programme's effect. The conclusion that the programme reduced symptom burden is therefore weaker than stated. The objective fitness results are less exposed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of participant-blind outcome collection or an attention-matched control arm yielding similar symptom results.

quotes.text: control group: individuals maintained their daily habits during an 8-wk period
all symptom impact scales improved significantly in the rehabilitation group compared to the control group

issues.title: Discussion claims improved lung function though spirometry was unchanged; 'clinically significant' untested
issues.explanation: The Discussion says rehabilitation could improve lung function, but the Results state spirometry did not change in either group. The opening paragraph also says the findings demonstrate clinically significant improvements without comparing any change to a clinical threshold. These statements go beyond what was measured. The VO2peak and exercise findings themselves are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Spirometry gains in the rehab group relative to control, or a cited MCID that the observed changes exceed.

quotes.text: These original findings suggest that rehabilitation interventions could play an essential supporting role in improving lung function and general fitness in people with long COVID.
quotes.location: Discussion, VE/VCO2 Slope and Respiratory Efficiency

quotes.text: Spirometry parameters did not change in either group
The findings of this study demonstrate clinically significant improvements in enhancing cardiorespiratory fitness

issues.title: Analysis labelled intention-to-treat is a complete-case analysis of 35 of 40 randomized, no imputation
issues.explanation: The Methods claim an intention-to-treat analysis but say missing values were not imputed, and the Results state that 35 of the 40 randomized patients completed testing at both visits. The ANCOVA (F(1,32)) therefore covers completers only. The paper does not report which arms the 5 missing participants came from or why they were lost, so potential bias from dropout is unquantified. The effect on the main VO2peak result is probably small given the modest attrition.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all 40 randomized participants (e.g., multiple imputation) that gives the same VO2peak result.

quotes.text: Missing values were not imputed, and analysis was conducted on an intention-to-treat basis.
A total of 35 patients completed the CPET at both baseline and end of study

issues.title: Arm sizes inconsistent: Table 3, Table 1 sex row and Results text imply control 18/rehab 17, headers say 17/18
issues.explanation: Table headers give control n = 17 and rehab n = 18. The mutually exclusive PCFS and MRC categories in Table 3 sum to 18 for control and 17 for rehab, and the Results text says 17 rehab participants completed. Table 1's sex percentages also fit control 18 / rehab 17, while other Table 1 rows fit the printed headers. The total of 35 completers is unaffected, but the paper does not make clear how many analysed participants were in each arm, so per-arm statistics and adherence figures cannot be fully trusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flowchart showing the per-arm completer counts, with the table column labels confirmed to be correct and the Table 3 counts shown to include a participant outside the arm.

quotes.text: Of the 17 people randomized in the rehabilitation group and completed the study

issues.title: Respiratory reserve called a significant group difference (all P < 0.05) but ANCOVA P = 0.054
issues.explanation: The Results list respiratory reserve among variables with a significant group difference, all P < 0.05. Table 2 gives its intergroup ANCOVA P as 0.054, which is not significant at the paper's own 0.05 level. The Discussion repeats that respiratory reserve improved significantly versus control. This is one secondary result misreported, and the main claims do not depend on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 showing an ANCOVA P below 0.05 for respiratory reserve.

quotes.text: maximal ventilation, VE/VCO2 slope, respiratory reserve, peak power output, t ½VO2 (an index of the efficiency of the recovery) and heart rate at peak exercise (all P < 0.05)

issues.title: Recruitment from August 2021 may predate registry submission (2021-09-02) despite 'prospectively registered'
issues.explanation: The paper says recruitment began in August 2021 and that the trial was prospectively registered. The registry record gives first submission on 2021-09-02 and study start on 2021-09-15. If any participant was enrolled in August, registration was not strictly prospective. The paper does not date the first enrolment, and the primary outcome matches the registry.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A first-randomisation date after 2021-09-02, or confirmation that August 2021 refers only to screening and referral contacts.

quotes.text: Individuals with long COVID were recruited between August 2021 and February 2023
The study was prospectively registered in Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05035628)

issues.title: Control mood impact score described as 'decreased' though the impact score rose 4.88 to 5.94
issues.explanation: Results say the moral/mood scale scores decreased significantly in control. Table 4 shows the impact score rising, and higher means more impact, so mood worsened. The word 'decreased' is ambiguous or wrong for this scale, though the Discussion describes the finding correctly as a decline in mood. It is a wording slip with no bearing on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors stating they meant mood itself decreased, which the Discussion wording already suggests.

quotes.text: only the moral/ mood scale scores decreased significantly in the control group ( P = 0.021)
quotes.location: Results, Quality of Life and Impact Scales

quotes.text: Impact on morale, mood4.88 ± 3.405.94 ± 2.95

10.1101/2022.08.29.22279327.headline_claim: A three-month endurance training rehabilitation (ETR) course decreased dyspnoea in long-COVID patients after CARDS compared with standard physiotherapy (SP).
10.1101/2022.08.29.22279327.overall: The primary result (MDP difference of -18.61, CI -27.78 to -9.44) is statistically strong, but it is a self-reported outcome from an early-stopped, open-label trial registered after enrolment began, so the size of the benefit is uncertain. The secondary quality-of-life results are unreliable as printed, because the SF-12 CIs and p-values do not agree and the physical-dimension claim has no multiplicity control. Several smaller reporting errors (intervention duration, sample-size arithmetic, percentages) lower confidence in the manuscript's care without changing the main direction of the finding.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile (MDP) total score, baseline to day 90

primary_outcomes.measure: Evaluate the effect of exercise rehabilitation on post-ICU dyspnea

issues.title: Open-label trial with patient-reported primary outcome; assessor blinding cannot protect it
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they were receiving the structured programme or usual physiotherapy, and the primary outcome (MDP) is a self-rated symptom score. Part of the 18.6-point difference could reflect expectation or attention effects. The conclusion that ETR 'decreased dyspnoea' is stated without that caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supporting objective outcomes (e.g. exercise capacity) pointing the same way, or evidence that patients were unaware of the hypothesis.

quotes.text: open-label, assessor-blinded trial
in order to minimise the biases due to the open nature of this type of trial

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label and its primary outcome (MDP) is a self-reported dyspnoea score, so participant knowledge of allocation can still influence it, and assessor blinding cannot remove that. The Discussion presents the blinded assessor as minimising bias from the open design, without acknowledging that this protection is limited for patient-reported outcomes. The limitations section does not discuss this. Assessor blinding is not worthless, since it may limit administration bias, but it does not protect against participant-level bias.

issues.title: SF-12 D-90 CIs (unadjusted-looking) disagree with p-values: total CI 0.22-16.25 excludes 0 but p=0.14
issues.explanation: The SF-12 total difference of 8.24 has a 95% CI of 0.22 to 16.25, which implies p of about 0.04. The paper prints p=0.14 and calls the groups 'comparable'. The same mismatch appears for the physical dimension (CI implies p of about 0.002, printed 0.016) and the mental dimension (CI implies about 0.48, printed 0.72). The Methods say all secondary outcomes use baseline-adjusted ANCOVA, but the CIs seem to be raw differences, so estimates, CIs and p-values do not come from one analysis. Readers cannot tell which SF-12 results hold.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that CIs are unadjusted while p-values are from the ANCOVA, or the adjusted estimates and CIs that match the printed p-values.

quotes.text: mean difference 8.24 [95% CI 0.22 to 16.25]; p=0.14

quotes.location: Table 2, SF-12 Total score row, D-90 difference column

quotes.text: between-groups differences were tested using an ANCOVA model adjusted for baseline values

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0439 (reachable range [0.0436, 0.0442] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.14 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the CI excludes the null (0.0), but the reported p = 0.14 says the result is not significant

issues.title: Quality-of-life claim rests on one uncorrected secondary result (SF-12 physical, p=0.016); no safety data
issues.explanation: About eight secondary and sub-dimension tests were run at alpha 0.05 without adjustment. The final conclusion that ETR improved the physical dimension of quality of life rests on p=0.016, which would not survive a simple correction across them. The primary dyspnoea claim is unaffected. No adverse events are reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity plan naming the physical dimension as a key secondary outcome.

quotes.text: Secondary outcomes were analysed in the same way.
A six-week ETR program did improve dyspnoea and the physical dimension of quality of life

issues.title: Intervention length given as three months, 10 weeks and six weeks
issues.explanation: Randomisation says both arms lasted three months with two sessions a week. Procedures say 10 weeks, and the Discussion's final conclusion refers to a 'six-week' ETR programme. The actual dose (about 12, 20 or 26 sessions) is therefore unclear, and the conclusion describes a different programme from the one tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or appendix stating that the programme lasted a single, consistent duration.

quotes.text: both for a duration of three months (two sessions per week)
at the rate of two one-hour sessions per week for 10 weeks
A six-week ETR program did improve dyspnoea

issues.title: Registered about 7 weeks after screening began (22 Jul 2020), after the registry start date of 7 Aug 2020
issues.explanation: The trial was registered after recruitment started, so the primary outcome and analysis plan were not publicly fixed beforehand. The registered primary outcome is broad dyspnoea at month 3, which is consistent with the MDP outcome, so the practical risk is modest. The registration date in the paper (29 September 2020) also differs from the registry's first-submission date (10 September 2020).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A time-stamped protocol or earlier registry version showing the MDP primary outcome fixed before the first patient was randomised.

quotes.text: was registered on Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT04569266) on September 29, 2020.
Between July 22, 2020 and January 26, 2022, 871 patients were assessed for eligibility

issues.title: Stopped at 60 of 200 planned patients; effect size likely imprecise and optimistic
issues.explanation: Only 30% of the planned sample was randomised, and the authors justify the shortfall by saying the observed effect was larger than assumed. A large observed effect in a small, early-ended open trial tends to overstate the true effect. The primary result is still statistically clear, so the finding is best read as tentative in magnitude, not refuted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable as a refutation; a larger confirmatory trial would settle the magnitude.

quotes.text: to prematurely interrupt the study
we estimated that 100 persons would need to be enrolled in each group.

issues.title: Sample size of 100 per group does not match stated 90% power (MCID 12, SD 30, alpha 0.05 gives about 131)
issues.explanation: With a difference of 12, SD of 30, two-sided alpha 0.05 and 90% power, a t-test needs about 131 per group. 100 per group corresponds to roughly 80% power. The planned total of 200 was therefore under-sized for the stated power, though this has little bearing on the observed result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different stated SD, MCID or power that yields 100 per group.

quotes.text: Using these values, a Student t-test, a two-sided alpha of 0.05, and 90% power, we estimated that 100 persons would need to be enrolled in each group.

issues.title: Discussion claims a 'more than 50%' MDP decrease; ETR arm fell 45.0% (47.56 to 26.15)
issues.explanation: The Discussion cites a more than 50% decrease in the MDP score after ETR. Table 2 shows the ETR mean going from 47.56 to 26.15, a 45% fall. The SP arm also fell (48.64 to 44.76), so the between-group difference is about 41.6% of the SP follow-up mean. The statement overstates the effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported analysis showing a greater than 50% relative reduction in MDP total.

quotes.text: the more than 50% decrease of MDP score after a three-month ETR course we have identified

quotes.location: Table 2, MDP Total score row, D-90 ETR

issues.title: Paris Saint-Joseph share printed as 55.17% but 32/60 = 53.33%
issues.explanation: The paper says 60 patients were randomised and 32 were recruited at Paris Saint-Joseph, which is 53.3%. The printed 55.17% corresponds to a base of 58. This is a minor arithmetic or denominator slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the percentage was calculated on 58 patients and why.

quotes.text: Most patients were recruited in the Groupe Hospitalier Paris Saint-Joseph (n=32, 55.17%)
of whom 60 underwent randomisation

script.explanation: 32/60 = 53.33%, but the paper prints 55.17, outside the rounding interval [55.16, 55.18]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 58.0 rather than 60.

issues.title: Allocation concealment not described; 7 of 60 patients received the other arm's programme
issues.explanation: The paper does not say how the sequence was hidden from those enrolling patients. Seven patients received the other arm's programme, but analysis was by ITT, so this would if anything bias towards no difference. It is an unexplained gap rather than a demonstrated flaw.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol statement describing central or opaque allocation concealment.

quotes.text: Patients in the control group received a prescription for SP
Four patients assigned to the ETR group received the SP program, while three patients assigned to the SP program received the ETR program.

issues.title: Table 1 SP smoking/ethylism percentages use denominator 32 (5/32=15.62%) under n=33 header
issues.explanation: The SP column header says n=33, but 5 smokers, 7 former smokers and 4 with ethylism are printed as 15.62%, 21.88% and 12.50%. These are 5/32, 7/32 and 4/32, whereas 5/33 would be 15.15%. One missing value is the likeliest explanation, but it is undisclosed. Nothing in the efficacy results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote stating that one SP patient had missing smoking and alcohol data.

script.explanation: 5/33 = 15.15%, but the paper prints 15.62, outside the rounding interval [15.61, 15.63]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 32.0 rather than 33.

10.1101/2022.09.28.22280467.headline_claim: A home-based personalized computerized cognitive training program improves cognitive dysfunction in people with Long COVID, as shown by a before-and-after feasibility study.
10.1101/2022.09.28.22280467.overall: The paper shows that scores on an unsupervised online battery rose after 8 weeks of home training in 73 self-selected people, but with no comparator it cannot show the training caused the rise, and the efficacy framing is only partly offset by the authors' own caveats. Numeric reporting is mostly sound apart from one mis-rounded percentage (memory 82% vs 86.3%), and the secondary analysis uses an unpaired test on paired data.

primary_outcome.name: Change in CAB z-scores across five cognitive domains (pre- vs post-test, 8 weeks)

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from a single-arm pre/post design with no control and a 73-person self-selected sample
issues.explanation: Every participant received the training and was compared only with their own baseline on a repeated online cognitive battery. Practice effects, regression to the mean and natural recovery over 8 weeks could produce the whole improvement. The stated conclusion that the program could ameliorate cognitive dysfunction is therefore not supported beyond hypothesis-generating level, although the authors do hedge and ask for controlled trials.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical untrained comparison group, or test-retest data on the CAB in untrained Long COVID participants, showing much smaller change.

quotes.text: This was a single-center before-and-after study.
without a control group
This before-and-after study constitutes the first piece of evidence suggesting that a home-based digital therapeutic program could ameliorate cognitive dysfunction in PASC.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy-type inference rests on a single-arm pre/post design with no control and a self-selected sample of 73, and the paper's wording ('evidence suggesting', 'demonstrating that individuals obtained better cognitive scores after the CCT') goes beyond what that design can show, since practice effects and regression to the mean are not addressed. However, the authors label it a feasibility study, openly state the lack of a control group and unknown denominator, and call for controlled trials, so the paper does not claim definitive efficacy.

issues.title: Primary outcome is a vendor CAB z-score composite; reliability for repeat testing in Long COVID not shown
issues.explanation: Cognitive change is measured with a commercial self-administered battery whose domain scores average several sub-tests. The paper cites prior adaptation studies but gives no repeat-testing reliability, practice-effect data or minimal important difference for Long COVID. Changes in z-scores cannot be read as validated clinical improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published test-retest and practice-effect data for the CAB at 8-week intervals, with a reference value for meaningful change.

quotes.text: The z-score in each of the cognitive domains was obtained for each participant and used as the main outcome measure.
The calculation of the cognitive score in each of the five domains is done by averaging the scores of the individual cognitive skills that constitute them

issues.title: Kruskal-Wallis (independent-groups) test used as non-parametric check on paired pre/post data
issues.explanation: The sensitivity analysis treats pre-test and post-test scores as if they came from different people. This ignores the pairing, so the reported chi2 and effect sizes do not correspond to the paired design and cannot truly validate the parametric result. It probably understates significance, so the direction of the findings is unlikely to change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the analysis was run as a paired (Friedman/Wilcoxon) test and only mislabelled.

quotes.text: a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA was run to validate the results

issues.title: Memory: 63 of 73 improved is printed as 82%, but 63/73 = 86.3%
issues.explanation: The Results text gives 63 (82%) of participants improving in memory. Dividing 63 by 73 gives 86.3%, and the other four domains in the same sentence are rounded correctly. The error understates the memory improvement rate slightly and does not change any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different memory denominator or count stated by the authors (e.g. 60/73) showing 82% is correct and 63 is the typo.

quotes.text: 63 (82%) in memory
quotes.location: Results, paragraph on post-test score improvements

script.explanation: 63/73 = 86.30%, but the paper prints 82.0, outside the rounding interval [81.50, 83.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 76.8 rather than 73.

issues.title: Vendor supplied platform and norms free of charge, yet no interests declared; funder role not stated
issues.explanation: The Acknowledgements say the vendor provided the platform, CAB and normative dataset free of charge, and the study evaluates that vendor's training and test. The competing-interests statement says there is no interest in the materials discussed and does not describe any funder role. This does not show bias but the declaration is not reconciled with the in-kind support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the vendor had no role in design, analysis or reporting, and a conflicts statement that discloses the in-kind support.

quotes.text: This research was partially funded by the BBVA Foundation (JAD) and by the Comunidad de Madrid (JAD), and by resources available to the authors.
Cognifit Inc. for providing access to the platform, the CAB and its normative dataset free of charge.

10.1101/2022.10.04.22280680.headline_claim: Immunodaat (elderberry extract, 250 mg twice daily for 30 days) added to standard care was reported to reduce post-COVID physical and mental symptoms, improve quality of life, energy and stamina, and to be safe and effective compared with standard care alone.
10.1101/2022.10.04.22280680.overall: The reported improvements in symptoms and quality of life come from an open-label comparison against standard care with no placebo, using mostly subjective outcomes and many uncorrected comparisons, so the efficacy claim is weak. Table 4's sample sizes, the contradictory safety statements and the inconsistent p-value labels in Table 2 further reduce confidence. The 'safe and effective' and 'normalise' conclusions are not supported by 74 participants over 30 days.

primary_outcome.name: Post-clinical recovery from COVID-19 (signs, symptoms and lab parameters) over 30 days

issues.title: Open-label, standard-care-only comparison with subjective symptom and QoL outcomes drives the efficacy claim
issues.explanation: Participants knew they were taking the extract, the control arm got no placebo, and the main effects are VAS, symptom grades by an unblinded investigator, PSS, ISI and WHO-QOL scores. Expectation and reporting bias, and the extra attention in the treated arm, could produce much of the reported difference. The objective lab outcomes show no difference. The efficacy conclusion is therefore not supported by this design. This covers c4 as well.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment or a placebo-controlled replication showing the same effects.

quotes.text: An open labeled, comparative, randomized, multi-centric, prospective clinical study
while subjects in control group were given only the standard care for Post Covid
These signs and symptoms were graded as mild, moderate or severe by the investigator

second_reader.what_stands: Participants and assessors knew the allocation, and the comparator was standard care with no placebo. The efficacy claim rests on symptom counts, investigator severity grading and self-reported VAS/QoL scales, all of which are open to expectation and assessor bias. The paper never names open-label bias as a limitation. The objective laboratory outcomes show no between-group difference.

issues.title: 'Safe and effective', 'normalise' and 'confirmed safety' drawn from 74 open-label participants over 30 days
issues.explanation: The trial has 74 participants, no sample-size calculation, open-label allocation and 30 days of follow-up. Even so, the abstract calls the product 'safe and effective' and the discussion says the results 'confirmed the safety'. 'Normalise' also overreaches: fatigue persisted in 4 of 37 (10.8%) treated subjects, and many other symptoms persisted. A trial this small and short cannot confirm safety, and the authors themselves ask for larger studies. This covers c5 as well.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger, blinded, adequately powered trial with pre-specified safety monitoring.

quotes.text: Immunodaat™ can be considered as a safe and effective natural ingredient in the management of Post COVID-19 or long COVID condition.
These findings confirmed the safety of use of Immunodaat® capsules in Post COVID-19 recovery or long COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: 'Safe and effective', 'normalize' and 'confirmed the safety' are stronger than 74 open-label participants followed for 30 days can support. The sample is too small to rule out uncommon adverse events, the follow-up is short, and the outcomes are unblinded. Residual symptoms remain at day 30, so 'normalize' overstates the results. The Abstract's 'no adverse effect' also conflicts with the reported minor adverse events. The Conclusion's call for larger studies partly offsets this, but only in that section.

issues.title: Table 2 labels 2/37 vs 5/37 significant for joint pain but not for headache; other small differences also 'significant'
issues.explanation: Joint pain and headache show identical 30-day counts (2/37 vs 5/37), yet one is marked p<0.05 and the other p>0.05. A count comparison of 2/37 vs 5/37 is not significant by a standard chi-squared or Fisher test. Several other symptoms labelled significant (dizziness 1 vs 5, altered mood 3 vs 8, insomnia 3 vs 8, anxiety 2 vs 8) also have small counts that do not obviously reach p<0.05. The text then reports these as treatment benefits, so the number of symptoms with a real difference is overstated. Anxiety is also printed as 2 (2.70%), but 2/37 is 5.40%.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A named test with a reproducible analysis showing p<0.05 for joint pain, and a corrected Table 2.

quotes.text: A significantly lower number of subjects in Immunodaat® group showed symptoms likefatigue, myalgia, weakness, joint pain, mental confusion, dizziness, alteration of mood, insomnia and anxiety at the end of the study.
quotes.location: Assessment of change in the Symptoms of Post COVID-19, Table 2 text

quotes.text: Cough, Headache, GI disturbance, Palpitation, and Shortness of Breathwere observed in a few subjects at the end of the study in both the groups and the difference was found to be non-significant.
quotes.location: Assessment of change in the Symptoms of Post COVID-19, Table 2 text

second_reader.what_stands: Joint pain (2/37 vs 5/37) is labelled significant while headache with identical counts is not, and the joint-pain difference gives roughly p about 0.4 on the printed counts. Confusion, dizziness, altered mood and insomnia are also labelled significant on differences that do not reach p<0.05 under standard unadjusted tests. Only fatigue, myalgia and weakness are clearly supported, with anxiety borderline. The test used is not stated, and no correction was applied for 14 comparisons.

issues.title: Table 4 analyses 31 vs 30 participants; text says all 74 (37 per arm) completed, no dropouts
issues.explanation: The Sample Size section says all 74 subjects completed with no dropouts, and Tables 1-3 and 5-9 use 37 per arm. Table 4 (stress, anxiety, concentration) uses 31 and 30, so 13 participants are missing from this analysis with no explanation. Either the text or the table is wrong, and if the table is right the missing-data handling is undisclosed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow or note showing that 13 participants lacked VAS data, or a corrected Table 4 with n=37 per arm.

quotes.text: All 74 subjects completed the study and there were no drop outs.
Immunodaat® Group (n=31)
Control Group (n=30)

issues.title: No funding or competing-interest statement although the product developer is named
issues.explanation: The product is described as developed by Lodaat Pharma. No funding source, sponsor role or competing-interest declaration appears in the paper. For a trial of a proprietary product with a favourable efficacy conclusion, readers cannot assess the sponsor's influence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published funding and conflict statement showing the sponsor's role.

quotes.text: developed  by  Lodaat  Pharma and composed of Elderberry extract

issues.title: Safety text says no adverse events/effects, then lists abdominal discomfort and distension
issues.explanation: The Results state the capsules did not produce any adverse events, and the Abstract says subjects had no adverse effect. The same paragraph, and the Discussion, then report minor adverse events of abdominal discomfort and distension. No counts, arm allocation or causality assessment are given. The abstract's 'no adverse effect' statement therefore contradicts the paper's own results, and the safety claim is stated more strongly than the data allow. This covers c11 as well.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the minor events occurred in the control arm or were judged unrelated, with counts per arm.

quotes.text: did not have any adverse effect with the use of
as they did not produce any adverse events
Minor adverse events were temporary andincluded abdominal discomfort and distension of abdomen

issues.title: Dozens of uncorrected symptom, scale and lab comparisons with no stated statistical methods
issues.explanation: The paper compares 14 symptoms, 8 severity items, 3 VAS items, ISI, PSS, 5 WHO-QOL items, energy and stamina, and about 20 lab values. It names no tests and gives only p-value thresholds, with no multiplicity control. The significant subset is emphasised in the abstract and conclusion. Some effects are large, so the impact on the conclusions is uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction, or adjusted p-values that remain significant.

quotes.text: Overall quality of life, energy levels and stamina levels improved with the use of Immunodaat™.

issues.title: Primary outcome is a loosely defined bundle of graded symptoms and labs with no single endpoint
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is 'signs/symptoms/lab parameters' compared over 30 days, with symptoms graded by the investigator. The paper defines no composite score, no direction of benefit, and no responder criterion. Which result counts as the primary result is therefore left open, which makes selective emphasis easier.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The CTRI registration showing one pre-specified primary endpoint with a defined analysis.

quotes.text: The primary study outcome was to evaluate comparative changes in post-clinical recovery from COVID19

issues.title: Abstract omits that the blood-parameter component of the primary outcome showed no between-group difference
issues.explanation: The primary outcome includes blood parameters (hematology, ESR, CRP), and Table 9 shows 'p >0.05 for all values'. CRP is not reported anywhere. The abstract features only the symptom and QoL gains. Readers get a one-sided picture of the primary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract or results text that states the null laboratory findings and reports CRP.

quotes.text: blood related parameters, including hematology, ESR and CRP from baseline to 30 days was performed between the groups

10.1101/2022.10.07.22280732.headline_claim: PSRT, a psychophysiologic mind-body programme, reduces somatic symptom burden in PASC patients without identified organ injury, with benefit persisting over 13 weeks.
10.1101/2022.10.07.22280732.overall: The large within-person improvements in SSS-8 are reported consistently across Tables 2 and 3, and the arithmetic checks. However, with no control group, open-label delivery and self-reported outcomes, the study supports only a signal of improvement. It does not support the stated conclusion that PSRT reduced symptoms. The numeric slips found are minor and do not change any main result.

primary_outcome.name: Change in somatic symptom severity (SSS-8)

issues.title: Causal efficacy claimed from an uncontrolled, open-label single-arm cohort of 23 with self-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: All 23 participants received PSRT and were compared only with their own baseline. The primary outcome (SSS-8) is self-reported and unblinded, so expectancy, regression to the mean, natural recovery and the group-class experience cannot be separated from a treatment effect. The Conclusions nonetheless say PSRT 'reduced' symptoms and that the benefit 'persisted'. The large before-after changes show improvement over time, not efficacy. Many secondary outcomes were also tested within-group without multiplicity adjustment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group showing no comparable change, or conclusions reworded as an uncontrolled pilot signal rather than efficacy.

quotes.text: All participants received PSRT and served as their own control.
In our study, each participant served as their own control; thus, there was no direct comparison group.
PSRT reduced symptomatology across multiple domains within four weeks; this benefit persisted over the 3 month study period.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, open-label, uncontrolled cohort of 23 with self-reported outcomes, and the Conclusions use causal language ('PSRT reduced symptomatology') without a comparator, even though the Limitations section acknowledges the lack of a comparator group and subjective reporting. The authors' argument that symptoms were long-standing and refractory is an inference, not a control, and the Limitations section's own note that this mitigates the concern 'somewhat' is not carried into the Conclusions.

issues.title: FSS-9 exercise item: CIs and p-values conflict at 4 weeks (CI -3,1; p<0.001) and 8 weeks (CI -3,-1; p=0.085)
issues.explanation: For the single FSS-9 exercise item, the 4-week CI includes 0 but p<0.001 is printed. The 8-week CI excludes 0 but p=0.085 is printed, and it is identical to the 13-week CI, which has p=0.010. At least one CI or p-value for this item is misprinted. The item is a secondary belief measure, so the main results are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source document or data showing the 4-week CI is (-3, -1) and explaining how the 8-week p and CI were derived (different CI method from the Wilcoxon p).

quotes.text: median difference from baseline at 4 weeks: -2 (95% CI: CI: -3, 1), p<0.001

issues.title: Results text prints SSS-8 4-week CI as (11.4, -5.7); Table 2 gives (-11.4, -5.7)
issues.explanation: The running text gives an impossible interval whose lower bound is positive and above its upper bound. Table 2 gives the same cell as (-11.4, -5.7), which is centred on the -8.5 estimate. The text GI estimate at 8 weeks also lacks its minus sign. This is a typographical slip with no effect on any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that the source document prints a minus sign before 11.4 and that the loss occurred only in text extraction.

10.1101/2022.10.10.22280907.headline_claim: An 8-week face-to-face rehabilitation program reduces dyspnea, fatigue and anxiety, increases exercise capacity, and improves memory and attention in patients with persistent COVID-19 symptoms.
10.1101/2022.10.10.22280907.overall: The paper reports that both groups improved, but the between-group comparisons on the primary outcomes are non-significant and underpowered, and allocation was self-selected with 52% attrition and completers-only analysis. The conclusion that the face-to-face program reduces symptoms and improves cognition is therefore not supported as a causal claim; the data fit a tentative, hypothesis-generating reading. Minor denominator inconsistencies in Tables 1 and 4 do not change this.'

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue and dyspnea (PFSDQ-M) and exercise capacity (ISWT), three co-primary outcomes

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from within-group changes; between-group deltas non-significant (p=0.292, 0.608, 0.186)
issues.explanation: The primary outcomes (fatigue, dyspnea, exercise capacity) improved in both groups and did not differ between groups in change. Dyspnea 'only' improved in the rehabilitation group is a contrast of significant versus non-significant within-group tests, not a group difference. The exercise-capacity comparison had 27% power, so the null result is uninformative, and the same limited power applies to the cognitive comparisons. Improvement could reflect time, regression to the mean or the booklet and monitoring, yet the conclusion and the discussion ('exercise improves the cognitive function') state a program effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis showing a significant between-group difference in change (for example ANCOVA on baseline) for the primary outcomes.

quotes.text: There was no significant difference between groups for distance covered at baseline ( p =0.479) or between deltas (p=0.186; d=0.47; power 27%).
quotes.location: Results, Fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise capacity

quotes.text: Dyspnea in ADLs was significantly reduced only in the face-to-face rehabilitation group ( p =0.001; d=0.54).
quotes.location: Results, Fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise capacity

quotes.text: An 8-week face-to-face rehabilitation program can reduce symptoms of dyspnea, fatigue, and anxiety, increase exercise capacity

second_reader.what_stands: None of the primary or anxiety between-group delta comparisons reached significance (p=0.292, 0.608, 0.186; anxiety 0.077). The conclusion that the face-to-face programme reduces dyspnea, fatigue and anxiety and increases exercise capacity rests on within-group changes. For fatigue and exercise capacity the control arm improved significantly too, and the dyspnea claim rests on a significant-versus-non-significant contrast. The authors do add that some improvement occurs over time and that the sample was small, but the headline conclusion is not tempered accordingly.

issues.title: Arm chosen by participant preference with no adjustment; conclusion worded causally
issues.explanation: Allocation depended on availability and preference, so arm membership is tied to work schedule, transport, motivation and other factors that can affect outcomes. Differences in schooling and smoking are visible in Table 1, and no covariate-adjusted analysis is given. The authors acknowledge the limitation in the discussion, but the conclusion still attributes improvements to the program.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Covariate-adjusted or propensity-based between-group analyses giving the same conclusions.

quotes.text: Volunteers  chose  to  participate  in  the  face-to-face  rehabilitation  or  remote monitoring based on their availability and preference.
We understand that this form of allocation interferes with the  validity  of  our  results.

second_reader.what_stands: Arms were self-selected and the analysis has no adjustment for confounders. Yet the Conclusion uses causal wording ('can reduce', 'increase', 'improve') without carrying forward the allocation caveat. The Limitations section does acknowledge the validity problem, so it is disclosed, but it is not reflected in the strength of the conclusion.

issues.title: 40 of 77 included participants (52%) lost; completers-only analysis with no arm-wise attrition shown
issues.explanation: Only 37 of 77 included participants were analysed. Dropout reasons include 'clinical improvement', which, if more frequent in one arm, could bias the results in either direction. The text does not report dropout by arm or compare dropouts with completers. Results describe adherent completers, not the effect of offering the program.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Arm-wise dropout counts and an ITT or sensitivity analysis showing the same conclusions.

quotes.text: 35 withdrew from participating
and 37 participants were included (Figure 1)

second_reader.what_stands: The arithmetic is right: 40 of 77 (52%) did not contribute data, and all analyses are completers-only on 37 participants, with no intention-to-treat or missing-data handling. The loss is partly acknowledged (small sample, reasons given). Arm-wise attrition is not given in the text, and whether Figure 1 shows it cannot be determined from the supplied material.

issues.title: Protocol 'shown to be safe' with no adverse-event data reported
issues.explanation: The clinical implications state that the protocol has been shown to be safe and feasible. No adverse events, safety monitoring or event counts are reported in the Results. With 22 participants and heavy dropout, safety could not be established in any case. Feasibility is also doubtful given that 35 of 77 withdrew.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported adverse-event table or a statement of systematic safety monitoring with zero or few events.

quotes.text: In addition, the protocol has been shown to be safe, feasible, and accessible to scientific and clinical communities.

issues.title: Cognitive and anxiety claims rest on a few nominal p values (0.031, 0.039, 0.003) among dozens of tests
issues.explanation: Many secondary outcomes and time points were tested at an unadjusted 5% level. The memory and attention claims in the conclusion come from p values of 0.039 and 0.031 in within-group tests. These are fragile if multiplicity is considered. The anxiety result (p=0.003) is stronger but is also within-group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or correction showing the cognitive findings remain significant.

quotes.text: A significance level of 5% was considered statistically significant.
improve memory and attention in patients with persistent symptoms of COVID-19

issues.title: Table 1 remote-group skin colour: White 12 + Brown 2 = 14, but n=15; 20% implies 3
issues.explanation: The two mutually exclusive skin-colour categories for the remote group add to 14, not the stated 15 participants. The printed 20% for Brown corresponds to 3 of 15, not 2. One participant is unaccounted for or one count is wrong. The group comparison p value (0.481) may be affected slightly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one remote participant had missing skin-colour data, with percentages computed over 10 or a different base.

quotes.location: Table 1, White row, remote monitoring column

script.explanation: 2/15 = 13.33%, but the paper prints 20, outside the rounding interval [19.50, 21.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 10.0 rather than 15.

issues.title: Table 4 REC rows: percentages use n=22 and n=15 although the rows are labelled n=21 and n=14
issues.explanation: In the RAVLT recognition (REC) rows the printed percentages match the full group sizes (22 and 15), not the stated REC denominators (21 and 14). Either one participant per group lacked REC data and the percentages are wrong, or the n labels are wrong. The REC results are secondary, but the McNemar and between-group p values depend on which denominator is right.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that REC percentages are computed over all allocated participants, or a corrected table with consistent denominators.

quotes.text: REC (n=14)
quotes.location: Table 4, remote group REC row label

script.explanation: 13/21 = 61.90%, but the paper prints 59.1, outside the rounding interval [59.05, 59.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 22.0 rather than 21.

10.1101/2022.12.02.22282982.headline_claim: TMS was followed by significant improvement in QIDS, PHQ9, GAD7 and PS in Long-COVID and Post-Vaccine patients, and higher initial fatigue (PS) was associated with poorer depression improvement.
10.1101/2022.12.02.22282982.overall: The finding that scores fell after 10 TMS sessions is descriptive only: it comes from completers with no control group, and the authors' attribution to TMS goes beyond what they concede the design can show. The fatigue-moderation claim rests on a single borderline p=0.04 coefficient from a ratio outcome with a non-dedicated fatigue measure, and should be read as exploratory. Reporting inconsistencies (exclusion counts and the Discussion's no-difference statement) are minor by comparison.

primary_outcome.name: Partial regression coefficient of PS (%) at first visit in MANCOVA, with improvement in QIDS (%) as the dependent variable

issues.title: Fatigue finding rests on a borderline p=0.04 (CI 0.01-0.98) in an unregistered retrospective analysis, uncorrected
issues.explanation: The fatigue conclusion is based on one coefficient at p=0.04, repeated across three overlapping models that share the same data. No multiplicity control is applied across predictors, models, scales and the Table 2 pairwise tests. The primary outcome is stated in the Methods, but the retrospective design with no registration means it cannot be shown to be pre-specified. The fatigue claim is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that the PS-delta QIDS hypothesis and analysis were pre-specified, or replication.

quotes.text: considered p <0.05 (two-tailed) statistically significant.
No significant correlations were obtained except for this combination, by the way.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does rest the fatigue finding on a borderline result (p=0.04, CI 0.01 to 0.98, repeated at p=0.04 in Model 3) from a retrospective analysis with no multiplicity correction, and the stated alpha is the unadjusted 0.05. The authors did designate the PS coefficient as the primary outcome and acknowledge unmeasured confounding in the limitations, though they do not discuss the fragility of p=0.04 or the absence of registration, and the number of secondary tests and models examined is not corrected for.
