issues.title: Improvement attributed to TMS, and TMS 'validity' claimed, from an uncontrolled before-after study of completers
issues.explanation: All patients received TMS and were compared with their own baseline, with no control group. The authors acknowledge that this cannot show TMS works, yet they attribute QIDS, PHQ9 and GAD7 gains to TMS and describe the study as elucidating TMS validity. Spontaneous recovery, regression to the mean and placebo response cannot be separated, so the efficacy claim is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or untreated control showing the same improvement difference.

quotes.text: We thus attributed the improvement in QIDS, PHQ9, and GAD7 to TMS.
It is impossible to conclude from this before-and-after study alone that TMS ameliorates psychiatric/physical symptoms.
The present study is the first report to elucidate the validity of TMS and the factors underlying it for psychiatric symptoms after COVID-19 and its vaccination.

second_reader.what_stands: The improvement is attributed to TMS on the basis of external literature from an uncontrolled before-after analysis of 60 completers (those who finished 10 sessions), and the Discussion opens with a claim to have elucidated TMS 'validity', which the data cannot support (no control, regression to the mean, spontaneous recovery, and completer selection are not excluded). However, the authors state the design limitation several times, decline to attribute the PS improvement to TMS, and call the QIDS/PHQ9/GAD7 attribution an inference from prior trials, so the criticism applies to the wording of t

issues.title: Only completers analysed: 60 of 113 eligible patients; 26 discontinuers and 27 one-session patients excluded
issues.explanation: Patients who stopped between sessions 2 and 10 (26) and those who had a single session (27) were left out, so the analysis covers only those who finished 10 treatments. Patients who dropped out may have responded poorly or experienced side effects, so improvement among completers likely overstates what would be seen in all treated patients. No comparison of excluded and included patients is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat style analysis, or data showing that excluded patients resembled completers.

quotes.text: We excluded patients who discontinued treatment before the end of 10 TMS sessions

issues.title: Discussion says no group difference in improvement rates, but Table 4 shows p<0.05 for delta QIDS (50 vs 83.77)
issues.explanation: The Discussion twice says improvement rates did not differ between Long-Covid and Post-Vaccine patients. Table 4 gives a significant unadjusted difference for delta QIDS, and the Results say Long-Covid patients seem to improve better. The adjusted MANCOVA no longer shows a difference, but the Discussion does not say so. This is a reporting inconsistency affecting the claim that the groups follow the same course.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Text explicitly limiting the Discussion statement to the covariate-adjusted analysis.

quotes.text: There were no significant differences between both groups in the rate of improvement of QIDS, PHQ9, GAD7, and PS with TMS.
The recovery rate of each symptom also did not differ between the two groups (Table 4).

quotes.location: Table 4, delta QIDS(%) row, Post-Vaccine column

issues.title: Ratio outcome (post/pre) with low baseline scores underpins the PS-QIDS association; coupling with baseline not addressed
issues.explanation: Improvement is defined as post-score divided by baseline score, so the outcome depends on the baseline QIDS in its denominator. Baseline QIDS medians are low (6 and 7), so small score changes give large percentages and values pile up at 100. The PS coefficient (0.50, CI 0.01-0.98) is borderline, and the paper does not test it against an absolute change or a post-score model adjusted for baseline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis using absolute change or post-score adjusted for baseline that gives the same PS association.

quotes.text: To calculate the improvement rate, we divided the score after 10 TMS procedures by the score at the first visit
PS_Initial visit(%)

issues.title: Fatigue is inferred from Performance Status (range 0-9), a functional scale rather than a fatigue questionnaire
issues.explanation: The central predictor is PS, which the authors describe as one reference indicator in ME/CFS criteria. It reflects functional impairment, which can be affected by depression, so overlap with the QIDS outcome is possible. The authors use cautious wording in places, but the title and conclusions refer to fatigue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Validation data showing that PS tracks fatigue scales independently of depression in this population.

quotes.text: We used PS as an indicator of fatigue symptoms.
Although it is impossible to conclude that a person has ME/CFS solely because of a high PS

issues.title: Long-Covid exclusions (11, 11, 21) leave 57, not 46; first-time-only count of 11 conflicts with its total of 27
issues.explanation: For Long-Covid, 100 cases minus the three printed exclusion groups gives 57, but 46 were analysed. The first-time-only line prints 11 and 5 yet a total of 27. The totals (27 and the final 60) fit a Long-Covid first-time-only count of 22, so the printed 11 is probably a typo. The analysed sample is probably right, but the flow as printed does not add up.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 (an image not available in the text) showing the Long-Covid first-time-only exclusion as 22 and a consistent cascade.

quotes.text: Long-covid group: 100 cases, Post-Vaccine group: 29 cases, 129 cases in total
Long-covid group: 11 patients, Post-Vaccine group: 5 patients, 27 patients in total
Long-covid group: 21 patients, PostVaccine group: 5 patients, 26 patients in total

script.explanation: The Long-Covid cascade from Methods section 6 does not reconcile: 'Long-covid cases selected' (n=100) minus its 3 stated exclusion(s) (43) leaves 57, but 'analysed' reports 46 -- 11 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

10.1101/2023.05.31.23290798.headline_claim: EchA Marine, a sea urchin egg supplement containing Echinochrome A, is an effective and natural treatment that improves quality of life in Long COVID patients, particularly pain/discomfort and mobility.
10.1101/2023.05.31.23290798.overall: The headline claim of an effective and safe treatment is not supported: the trial is small (46 analysed), has no power calculation or safety data, tests seven outcomes without correction (only pain and TTO survive Holm), and was registered after enrolment began with different primary outcomes. Tables 1 and 2 and the figure legends contain printed F-value errors, though the p-values and sums of squares are internally consistent, so the final-condition differences are real as reported but should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: EQ-5D-3L five dimensions (quality of life), final values compared between groups

primary_outcomes.measure: Change of symptoms over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) during rutine medical checkup.
Change of lung capacity over four times (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) assessed during spirometry.
Change of walking distance during a six minutes walk test (6MWT) over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks)
Change of depression measured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via the Beck Health Questionnaire.
Change in the quality of life meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via visual analog scale of EuroQol (EQ-VAS).
Presence or absence of Myocarditis meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via electrocardiogram.
Change in the cognitive function meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via Trial Making test (TMT).
Change in the cognitive function meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via Phonological verbal fluency test.

issues.title: Claims of effective, safe treatment improving 'all dimensions' rest on 46 patients, 2 of 5 dimensions, no safety data
issues.explanation: The paper states the supplement is an effective and safe treatment improving all dimensions, but only 2 of 5 dimensions reached p < 0.05 (and only pain survives correction, see c7). No adverse-event data or sample-size calculation are reported. The authors argue that statistical significance despite a small sample shows robustness, which is the opposite of how small samples behave (significant results from small samples are more likely to overestimate effects). Improvement in non-significant dimensions is inferred from the absence of level-3 scores in the treatment group, which is an unsupported descriptive comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported adverse-event data, a prespecified power calculation, and significant effects in all claimed dimensions after correction.

quotes.text: EchA Marine® is an effective and natural treatment option for improving the quality of life of Long COVID patients.
These findings are especially encouraging given the safety and natural origin of the supplement.
despite the small sample size, the results were statistically significant

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion's claims that EchA Marine is an effective and safe treatment improving all dimensions rest on 46 patients, significant between-group differences in only 2 of 5 dimensions (mobility, pain) at final assessment, and no reported safety data. The statement that the small sample still gave 'robust' results is not supported, and the 'all dimensions' inference comes from the absence of level-3 responses plus TTO and VAS, not from significant tests in the other three dimensions.

issues.title: Paper names EQ-5D dimensions as primary; registry primaries include only EQ-VAS of these, and 7 are unreported
issues.explanation: The registry lists eight primary outcomes, including EQ-VAS, but not the five EQ-5D dimensions or TTO that carry the paper's headline. Seven registered primaries (symptoms, spirometry, 6MWT, Beck depression, myocarditis, TMT, verbal fluency) are not reported. The paper presents no explanation, and only the current record was available, so earlier versions were not checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing the EQ-5D dimensions as primary, or a companion paper reporting the other registered primaries.

quotes.text: quality of life, analyzed on the basis of its 5 dimensions and 3 levels
All detailed information regarding this medical trial can be found on ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05531019.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does name the 5 EQ-5D dimensions as the primary outcome, and it reports no safety results even though safety was to be evaluated. Whether the registered primaries include only EQ-VAS, and whether 7 are unreported, cannot be checked from this paper alone.

issues.title: Table 1 basal F values copy Table 2 final F values; legend F for pain (3.415) is a sum of squares
issues.explanation: All seven basal F values in Table 1 are identical to the final F values in Table 2 and contradict the basal sums of squares and p-values beside them (for example F = 6.738 with p = .256 for mobility). The Figure 2 legend gives F = 3.415 for pain, which is the sum of squares; Table 2 gives F = 8.863. The Figure 3 legend also says the groups differed significantly at baseline on VAS and TTO, although the F and p values it cites are the final ones and Table 1 shows p = .734 and .358. The baseline-balance claim appears to hold in the p-values, but the printed statistics are unreliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source SPSS output showing the basal F values as printed, with matching p-values.

quotes.text: Mobility Basal Between groups .333 1 .333 6.738 .256
Treatments presented significant differences both in Basal and Final conditions

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.256, but recomputed from the printed f = 6.738 p is at most 0.01278, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Registered 2022-08-19, about 11 months after enrolment began in September 2021
issues.explanation: The paper reports recruitment from September 2021 to October 2022, and the registry gives a study start of 2021-09-22 with first submission on 2022-08-19. The outcomes could therefore have been specified after data collection began. The paper's description of prospective selection does not mention this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an earlier registration or a protocol dated before September 2021.

quotes.text: between September 2021 and October 2022

issues.title: Seven outcomes tested at alpha 0.05; only 2 of 4 significant results survive Holm correction
issues.explanation: Five dimensions, VAS and TTO were each tested at 0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment. Mobility (p = .013) and VAS (p = .022) do not survive a Holm or Bonferroni correction for seven tests. Pain (p = .005) and TTO (p = .003) do. TTO and VAS are linked to the dimensions, so these seven tests are not independent, which makes the correction conservative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated hierarchy or prespecified primary endpoint among the seven outcomes.

quotes.text: A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

issues.title: 47 patients 'selected' in Methods versus 46 randomised/analysed; registry lists 54 enrolled
issues.explanation: The Methods say 47 patients were selected, while the Results and every ANOVA (df 1,44) use 46 (22 placebo, 24 treatment). The registry record lists 54 actual enrolments. The paper has no participant flow, so the missing patient(s) and any post-randomisation losses cannot be traced.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT-style flow showing one pre-randomisation exclusion and explaining the registry figure of 54.

quotes.text: We  carefully  and  prospectively  selected  47  patients  of  both  sexes
A  total  of  46Long  COVID  patients  were  recruited  to  participate  in  this  multicenter

10.1101/2023.06.28.23291986.headline_claim: VSL#3 probiotic supplementation reduced Chalder Fatigue Scale scores versus placebo over 4 weeks, with the reduction persisting 4 weeks after treatment, and generally improved gastrointestinal symptoms in Long COVID.
10.1101/2023.06.28.23291986.overall: The primary finding (lower Chalder Fatigue score with VSL#3, p=0.0079) comes from a small pilot of 38 with no sample-size calculation and a percentage-change analysis, so it is suggestive but not firm. The secondary GI and SF-36 claims are uncorrected and some Table 1/Table 2 entries are internally inconsistent, though these errors do not touch the primary result. The supplied registry record (NCT04809974) is for a different trial than the paper's NCT05874089, so registration timing and outcome matching could not be verified.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder Fatigue Scale (Likert) percent change from baseline to week 4 (t4)

primary_outcomes.measure: Effect of Niagen on NAD+ and Cognitive Functioning

issues.title: Pilot of 38 with no sample-size calculation, analysed on % change without baseline adjustment, yet efficacy stated as met
issues.explanation: With 19 per arm, no power calculation and an analysis of percentage change by Mann-Whitney test (no baseline adjustment), the primary result is imprecise. The paper nonetheless says the trial 'successfully met its primary endpoint' and that the benefit persisted at t8. The Discussion's 'preliminary' and 'pilot' caveats do not change that confident wording in the Results and Highlights. The conclusion is better read as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size justification and a baseline-adjusted analysis giving the same effect, with t8 numbers reported.

quotes.text: These results indicate that the trial successfully met its primary endpoint and treatment beneficial effects persisted at least 4 weeks following treatment discontinuation.
quotes.location: Results, VSL#3 Treatment significantly reduced Fatigue

quotes.text: 19 were administered the probiotic VSL#3®, while the other 19 were given a placebo
quotes.location: Results, Demographic characteristics of the population

second_reader.what_stands: True: the study is a 38-participant pilot (the paper itself says so), no sample-size calculation is reported, the primary comparison is a Mann-Whitney test on unadjusted percentage change with no baseline adjustment, and the Results sentence states the primary endpoint was met without qualification. Not fully true: the Discussion hedges ('preliminary', 'pilot', 'further work is needed'), baseline CFS was similar between arms, and I could not check registration or a pre-specified sample size because the supplied registry record belongs to a different trial.

issues.title: Acid regurgitation called non-different in text, but Table 2/Fig 4 give p=0.0159 (VSL#3 median +33.33%)
issues.explanation: The Results say acid regurgitation did not vary between arms, but Table 2 and the Figure 4 caption report p=0.0159 for this comparison. The table row is also internally odd: a VSL#3 median of +33.33% sits outside its printed interquartile range (-60.0;0.0). The nominally significant difference may be in the unfavourable direction for VSL#3, and the text hides it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing a p-value above 0.05 for acid regurgitation, or an explicit statement that the difference is significant and unfavourable.

quotes.text: did not vary between treated and placebo arms
Acid Regurgitation variation % 0 (0.0;0.0) 33.33 (-60.0;0.0) 0.0159

issues.title: Screening to 9 May 2023 leaves no room for t8 follow-up by the 28 June 2023 posting if late patients were included
issues.explanation: A patient screened on 9 May would complete a 2-week run-in, 4 weeks of treatment and 4 weeks of follow-up around mid-July, after the preprint date. The paper does not give the date of the last randomisation or last t8 visit. If only early enrollees reached t8, the t8 claims rest on fewer than 38 patients, which the paper does not state.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Stated dates of last randomisation and last t8 visit before 28 June 2023, or a flow chart showing t8 completion for all participants.

quotes.text: through  May  9,  2023
persisted 4 weeks post treatment, at the end of the study (timepoint t8

issues.title: General Health and Pain rows share placebo 0 (-21.7;19.2) and p=0.2258; VSL#3 General Health IQR excludes its median
issues.explanation: The two SF-36 rows are identical for placebo and for p, and the VSL#3 intervals differ only by a sign. The General Health VSL#3 cell shows a median of 0 below its lower quartile of 3.6, which is impossible as printed. This may be a copy or transcription slip. It affects secondary SF-36 domains that were reported as non-significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the two domains genuinely have identical distributions, or a corrected Table 2.

quotes.text: General Health variation % 0 (-21.7;19.2) 0 (3.6;55.6) 0.2258

issues.title: Secondary claims (GI p=0.0429, fatigue/physical domains p=0.0279/0.0193) rest on about 20 uncorrected tests
issues.explanation: Roughly 20 secondary comparisons were tested at p<0.05 with no correction. The statements that VSL#3 'generally ameliorates gastrointestinal symptoms' and improves physical functioning rest on p-values of 0.0429, 0.0279 and 0.0193. With this many tests, a few nominally significant results are expected by chance. These should be treated as exploratory, not confirmatory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy of secondary endpoints or a multiplicity correction under which these results stay significant.

quotes.text: These data indicate that VSL#3® generally ameliorates gastrointestinal symptoms in Long-COVID patients.
quotes.location: Results, VSL#3 Treatment ameliorates gastrointestinal symptoms

issues.title: 'No conflicts of interest' declared although VSL#3 maker funded the trial and supplied the product
issues.explanation: The authors declare no potential conflicts of interest, but the Funding section states the manufacturer of VSL#3 gave a grant and supplied the probiotic. The sponsor's role in design, analysis and reporting is not described. For a positive efficacy claim about that company's product, the conflicts declaration should reflect the relationship.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sponsor had no role in design, analysis or reporting and that the authors have no financial ties to it.

quotes.text: Conflicts of Interest: the authors declare no potential conflicts of interest
This study received a financial non-conditioning grant by Actial Farmaceutica s.r.l. which also provided the probiotic product.

issues.title: Interstitial pneumonia arm percentages (31.6%, 28.9%) use n=38 instead of n=19 (should be 63.2%, 57.9%)
issues.explanation: In Table 1 the arm counts 12 and 11 are shown with percentages calculated over all 38 participants rather than over the 19 in each arm. The correct arm shares are 63.2% and 57.9%. The p-value of 0.75 is consistent with the counts, so only the percentages are wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote stating that percentages in this row are of the total sample.

quotes.text: Interstitial pneumonia, n (%) 23 (60.5) 12 (31.6) 11 (28.9)

script.explanation: 12/19 = 63.16%, but the paper prints 31.6, outside the rounding interval [31.55, 31.70]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 38.0 rather than 19.

issues.title: Total hospital stay mean 13.1 d (SD 16.8) is outside arm means 16.55/20 d and SDs 29.4/38.4
issues.explanation: The overall mean must lie between the two arm means when the same hospitalised patients are pooled, but 13.1 is below both 16.55 and 20. The total SD of 16.8 is also far below both arm SDs, which is not possible for a pooled set. The row is inconsistent, though it is a baseline characteristic and does not affect the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the total and arm figures were computed over different patient sets, or corrected values.

quotes.text: Hospitalization, days (± SD) 13.1 (±16.8)

quotes.location: Table 1, Hospitalization days row, placebo column
Table 1, Hospitalization days row, VSL#3 column

issues.title: Text gives 20 males as 47.4%, but 20/38 = 52.6%; 47.4% is the female share
issues.explanation: The Results state 20 males (47.4%), yet 20 of 38 is 52.6%. The Table 1 percentage of 47.4 matches 18/38, the female count. This is a minor labelling error with no bearing on the efficacy findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 47.4% is the male proportion (i.e. 18 males).

quotes.text: the sample consisted of 20 males (47.4%)
Male/Female, n (%) 20/18 (47.4)

script.explanation: 20/38 = 52.63%, but the paper prints 47.4, outside the rounding interval [47.35, 47.50]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 42.2 rather than 38.

10.1101/2023.09.09.23295208.headline_claim: HRV biofeedback breathing is feasible for people with Long Covid and seems to be potentially improving symptoms of Long Covid and dysautonomia.
10.1101/2023.09.09.23295208.overall: The feasibility finding (home use, high completion) is reasonably supported, although the adherence rate is inconsistently reported. The claim that HRV-B 'seems to improve' long covid symptoms rests on 13 participants in an uncontrolled, open-label design with self-reported outcomes and uncorrected multiple tests. Table 4 has internal inconsistencies, including the effect sizes and the change column. Efficacy statements should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: C19YRS-m (Modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale) symptom severity

issues.title: Improvement attributed to HRV-B from a 13-person uncontrolled open-label pre-post study with self-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: All outcomes are before-after changes in one group, tested with within-participant Wilcoxon tests. The primary outcome (C19YRS-m) is self-reported and unblinded. There is no comparator to separate treatment from time, expectation or regression to the mean. The statements that the intervention 'seems to have a potential effect on improving LC symptoms' and that there was 'statistically significant improvement' therefore go beyond what the design can show. The authors also say effect size was not an aim and no sample size calculation was done.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or sham comparison showing the same change.

quotes.text: This was a phase 2 uncontrolled open-label feasibility study of a home technology-based HRV-B in 15 individuals with LC.
There was a statistically significant improvement in LC symptoms, functional ability, quality of life and dysautonomia scores.
the intervention seems to have a potential effect on improving LC symptoms, particularly those related to dysautonomia

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does base its improvement claims on a single-arm, open-label pre-post design (13 analysed of 15 enrolled) with mostly self-reported outcomes, and the 'Strengths' bullet and Results text state significant improvement without noting that the design cannot attribute change to HRV-B. However, the abstract, discussion and limitations repeatedly label the study as a feasibility study, use hedged wording ('seems', 'potential effect') and call for a controlled trial, so the causal attribution is tempered rather than asserted outright. The strongest wording problem is the 'Strengths' bullet a

issues.title: Adherence of 92% does not match 720 sessions (13 x 56 = 728 gives 98.9%; 15 x 56 = 840 gives 85.7%)
issues.explanation: The paper reports 720 completed sessions as a 92% compliance rate. Twice-daily practice for 4 weeks is 56 sessions per person. For the 13 analysed participants 720 sessions is about 99%, and for 15 enrolled it is about 86%. Adherence is a core feasibility outcome, and the printed rate fits neither denominator.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator (for example a different session schedule) that gives 92% from 720 sessions.

quotes.text: There was a 92% compliance rate with the breathing intervention as a total of 720 sessions were completed over the 4-week period.

issues.title: Table 4 Cohen's d values (0.047, 0.007, 2.03) are incompatible with the printed means and SDs
issues.explanation: The effect sizes for COMPASS-31 and EQ5D-5L are close to zero although the mean changes are about a third to half of an SD. The WHODAS d of 2.03 is implausibly large for a change of about 7 points against SDs near 19. The text calls the C19-YRSm effect size 'large'. The d column cannot be used to judge effect sizes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative definition of d that reproduces these values from the data.

quotes.text: The effect size for C19-YRSm was large.

issues.title: About 15 outcomes tested at p<0.05 without correction; RMSSD p=0.047 and WHODAS p=0.02 would not survive
issues.explanation: Seven questionnaire outcomes and eight Fitbit outcomes were tested with no multiplicity adjustment. The Abstract lists RMSSD (p=0.047) and WHODAS (p=0.02) as significant. Under a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/15 ≈ 0.0033, only the C19YRS-m severity and functional ability scores pass. The physiological finding (RMSSD) is the borderline one, and the paper states that it supports the mechanism.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan limiting confirmatory testing to the primary outcome.

quotes.text: There was a statistically significant improvement in C19YRS-m (p=0.001), EQ5D Global Health Score (p=0.009), COMPASS-31 (p=0.007), RMSSD (p=0.047) and EHODAS (p=0.02).

issues.title: Breathing intervention described as 6 weeks in one sentence but 4 weeks everywhere else
issues.explanation: The Methods, aims and Table 1 describe a 4-week breathing phase inside a 6-week study. One sentence in the Equipment section says the breathing intervention lasted 6 weeks. The dose is therefore stated inconsistently, although the 4-week reading is clearly the intended one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or statement that breathing practice actually continued through all 6 weeks.

quotes.text: The breathing intervention lasted for 10 minutes twice daily for a total of 6 weeks.
for 10 minutes twice daily for a total of 4 weeks (Figure 1)

issues.title: Participant 11 age band 10-20 straddles the stated minimum age of 18
issues.explanation: Inclusion required age 18 or over, yet participant 11 is listed as 10-20. The band is compatible with an 18-19-year-old, but an age band reaching 10 is odd for an adult-only study. It is likely a banding or typing slip, with little effect on the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The participant's actual age being 18 or over.

quotes.text: age ≥ 18 years

issues.title: Table 4 'Change' does not equal post minus baseline means (COMPASS-31 -7.6 vs -6.06; C19YRS severity -5 vs -6.08)
issues.explanation: For COMPASS-31 the printed means give a change of -6.06, but -7.6 is printed. For C19YRS-m symptom severity the means give -6.08 and -5 is printed. The column is undefined, probably medians and rounded, so it cannot be reconciled with the printed means.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Change column reports median paired differences.

issues.title: Post-hoc exclusion of participant 12 with no sensitivity analysis; completers-only analysis (13/15)
issues.explanation: One of the two exclusions (participant 12) was decided after outcome assessment, for illness at the final visit. The listed exclusion criteria are baseline ones, so the claim that it was 'encompassed by our exclusion criteria' is not clearly supported. Only completers were analysed and no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified rule excluding participants ill at final assessment, or results showing the same findings with participant 12 included.

quotes.text: Participant 12 was unwell during the final assessment with an acute respiratory infection.
2 participants were excluded from analysis, therefore a total of 13 individual datasets were analysed.

10.1101/2024.07.04.24309908.headline_claim: CICT is a feasible cognitive rehabilitation method for Long COVID brain fog, with promise for improving everyday cognitive task performance and promoting return-to-work; larger trials are warranted.
10.1101/2024.07.04.24309908.overall: The feasibility conclusion is reasonably supported for a pilot, but the efficacy claims rest on 14 completers in an open-label trial with self-rated outcomes, a usual-care control, one-sided post-randomisation attrition and no multiplicity correction. The very large effects and the return-to-work claim should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) Performance scale, pre- to post-treatment change

issues.title: Open-label, usual-care-controlled trial with self-rated primary outcome (COPM d=2.6) and no blinded assessment
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the primary outcome and most secondary outcomes are self-reported, with a control that received no therapy for cognition. A very large effect on COPM Performance (MD 3.7, d=2.6) can therefore reflect expectation, attention and demand effects. The authors' rebuttal relies on self-reported employment in five people, which is not independent evidence. The conclusion is tentative at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded assessor rating the primary outcome, or an attention-matched control arm.

quotes.text: Participants in this pilot RCT with an unblinded, open-label, parallel arm, partialcrossover design
Skeptics might argue the substantial advantage in favor of CICT on the primary outcome was due to the operation of demand characteristics
Other important limitations were the absence of long-term follow-up, blinding, and control for placebo effects.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper itself describes an open-label trial against a no-treatment (TAU) control, with a self-rated primary outcome (COPM Performance, d=2.6) and no blinded assessment. The authors state this as a limitation, address demand characteristics in the Discussion, and call the findings preliminary. The registry's 'SINGLE' masking entry is not reflected in the paper's description, and the open-label design is acknowledged rather than concealed.

issues.title: 'All nine outcomes' favoured CICT (p=0.2%) conflicts with the null MoCA result (p=0.73, d=0.2)
issues.explanation: The Methods justify skipping multiplicity correction by saying all nine outcomes favoured the same group, with a 0.2% chance probability. The Results state that no advantage was seen on the MoCA (p=0.73), and the GAD-7 was also non-significant (p=0.09). The sign-based argument ignores that outcomes are correlated and mostly non-significant, so it does not substitute for multiplicity control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'advantage' meant only the sign of the point estimate and that the 0.2% figure was not used to claim significance.

quotes.text: all nine outcomes showed an advantage for the same group; the probability of that occurring by chance was only 0.2%
No advantage for Immediate-CICT over TAU was seen for general cognitive ability

issues.title: No power calculation; 14 completers (7 per arm) support only tentative effect-size claims
issues.explanation: With seven per arm, effect sizes (d=2.6, -3.1, -1.8) are imprecise and prone to overestimation, and the many secondary tests were not corrected. The authors do frame the study as a pilot and call for a large RCT, which limits the harm. The remaining issue is that the efficacy language in the Results and Discussion is stronger than n=14 allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a limitation of the design rather than an error.

quotes.text: Power calculations were not performed to determine a sample size sufficient to reliably detect statistically significant changes for this pilot.
The small ( n =14) and ethnically homogenous (93% European American) sample raises questions about the generality of the findings.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis (2 of 9 TAU participants excluded after randomisation); ITT results not shown
issues.explanation: Randomised participants who withdrew before Baseline 2 (2 of 9 TAU) were excluded from all analyses, and the ITT analyses said to be less favourable are not presented. All withdrawals were in the control arm, so the retained comparison may favour CICT. The authors acknowledge this possibility, but the headline results do not reflect it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reporting the ITT analyses with the same direction and similar magnitude of effect.

quotes.text: All data are reported on a completers basis because the completers analyses were more conservative than the intention-to-treat analyses; all the drop-out occurred in the TAU group
Two-of-nine TAU participants withdrew before Baseline 2 testing, which may have inflated the advantage observed for CICT.

issues.title: 'Promoting return-to-work' claimed from a 5-vs-5 self-reported comparison with p=0.048
issues.explanation: Four of five Immediate-CICT participants were employed after treatment versus none of five TAU participants, with p=0.048 and no correction. The outcome is self-reported and only borderline significant, and the groups differed in time since onset. Presenting this as evidence that CICT promotes return-to-work, and as a rebuttal to demand effects, goes beyond what this comparison can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Independent verification of employment status and a prespecified return-to-work outcome showing a similar effect in a larger sample.

quotes.text: CICT has promise for reducing brain fog, improving performance of everyday tasks, and promoting return-to-work
return-to-work might be considered a 'hard' endpoint because of its binary nature
A distinct advantage in favor of Immediate-CICT over TAU was also observed in returnto-work, p =0.048
quotes.location: Results, Efficacy: Everyday Activities and Employment

issues.title: FAS ANCOVA reported with df (1,10) although the stated exclusion does not cover FAS
issues.explanation: Only COPM, MCS, SDMT and MoCA are said to lack data for one excluded participant, yet FAS is reported with error df 10 whereas PHQ-9 and GAD-7 have df 11. Either FAS also lacks a participant (undisclosed) or the df is mis-stated. The effect on conclusions is minimal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplement data showing a missing FAS value for a participant.

quotes.text: he was excluded from the efficacy analyses of these measures

10.1101/2024.12.13.24318856.headline_claim: BC007 (Rovunaptabin) showed a significant improvement in fatigue, severity of fatigue and quality of life in an autoimmune subgroup of post-COVID syndrome patients, and is well tolerated, suggesting it might offer a novel curative and causal therapy.
10.1101/2024.12.13.24318856.overall: The paper's efficacy and 'curative' conclusions rest on a small, exploratory trial with many uncorrected secondary tests and a crossover analysis that assumes no carry-over. The safety statement is also stronger than a non-significant, underpowered comparison permits. The numerical slips found (a Vitality t-value, a Figure 3 legend count) are minor, and the registry flags concern a different trial.

primary_outcome.name: Occurrence of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) from V2 to V7 (day 28), comparing sequence A vs sequence B; co-primary TEAEs to V13 (day 70)

primary_outcomes.measure: Part A: Number of Participants With Abnormal Laboratory Values and/or Adverse Events That Are Related to Treatment
Part B: Conversion rate from positive GPCR AAB to negative immune status
Part C: Conversion rate from positive GPCR AAB to negative immune status

issues.title: Conclusion claims 'curative and causal therapy' from an exploratory 30-patient, 91-day pilot with no power calculation
issues.explanation: The authors say the trial was not designed to investigate effectiveness, that n=30 was 'considered sufficient' for a pilot, and that follow-up was at most 91 days. Yet the Conclusion states significant improvement and suggests BC007 might be a curative and causal therapy. Secondary endpoints with no multiplicity control, a crossover with untested carry-over, and a short follow-up cannot establish this. The data support hypothesis generation, not a claim of cure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of durable benefit beyond 91 days in a confirmatory trial with pre-specified efficacy endpoints and multiplicity control.

quotes.text: The clinical trial was not designed to investigate effectiveness of BC007
suggest that BC007 might offer a novel curative and causal therapy

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's wording 'might offer a novel curative and causal therapy' goes beyond what an exploratory 30-patient, 91-day pilot with a safety primary endpoint and unadjusted multiple secondary outcomes can support, and the Conclusion does not repeat the Discussion's caveats. It is not accurate to say the paper has no basis for its sample size or presents the trial as confirmatory, since n=30 is justified as a pilot size, the Discussion explicitly says the trial was not designed to investigate effectiveness, and the Conclusion is phrased with 'suggest' and 'might'.

issues.title: Dozens of secondary scales tested at alpha 0.05 with no correction; only significant results tabulated
issues.explanation: The paper uses a 5% significance level with no adjustment across many questionnaires and two analysis sets. Table 2 lists only the scores that reached significance, and several of those have p-values just under 0.05. With this many tests, a few nominally significant results are expected by chance. The conclusion that fatigue, severity and quality of life improved is therefore much weaker than its wording suggests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity adjustment, or a designation of one fatigue endpoint as the main secondary endpoint.

quotes.text: Only scores showing a significant treatment of BC007 are shown.
No treatment effects of BC007 were observed on DSQ-PEM, walking distance (6MWT)

second_reader.what_stands: The Statistical Analysis section states a 5% level and no multiplicity correction or hierarchy for the many secondary scales, and the Table 2 footnote confirms that only significant scores are tabulated there, so several results sit near p=0.04-0.05. This is mitigated because the full set of scores is given in supplementary tables 9-27 and the Results text reports the null findings for DSQ-PEM, 6MWT and the Borg scales, so the selective tabulation is not hidden; I did not check the supplementary tables.

issues.title: Crossover estimates assume no carry-over or period effect despite a 14-day gap and claimed prolonged benefit
issues.explanation: The crossover contrast is estimated 'assuming no carry over or period effects', and no washout was used beyond a 14-day break. The Discussion says one infusion produced a prolonged improvement and that fAAb changes persisted, which makes carry-over plausible. The carry-over assumption is not tested, so the crossover results (FACIT, Bell, CCC, Vitality, General health) are less secure. The pre-crossover between-group results are not affected by this point.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified test of sequence-by-treatment interaction showing no carry-over, or sensitivity analyses restricted to first-period data that give the same crossover conclusions.

quotes.text: A linear model similar to the one above was applied to estimate the cross-over difference (assuming no carry over or period effects)
no specific washout phase was necessary prior to randomisation
Although patients received only a single infusion of BC007, the patients experienced a prolonged improvement of their symptoms.

issues.title: 'No higher AE rate' claimed although first-period TEAEs were 42.9% on BC007 vs 18.8% on placebo (ratio 2.29)
issues.explanation: The paper treats the non-significant Poisson test (p=0.1299) as evidence that BC007 caused no higher rate of adverse events. The first-period point estimate is more than double on BC007, and the interval (0.71 to 8.52) is compatible with a large excess. The overall conclusion of good tolerability may well be right, but this trial cannot show it. The Discussion statement 'no higher rate of AEs' goes beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority margin for safety, or an analysis showing the first-period excess was explained by events unrelated to treatment.

quotes.text: six of 14 in sequence A (42·86%) and three of 16 in sequence B (18·75%)
no statistical difference was observed (p=0·1299, Poisson -test)
no higher rate of AEs was observed compared to placebo

issues.title: Figure 3 legend gives 14 sequence A participants at V14 although one was withdrawn after day 28
issues.explanation: One sequence A participant was withdrawn after day 28 and 29 participants completed the trial. The legends for Figures 3 and 4 nevertheless give n=14 for sequence A at V14, which cannot be reached after a withdrawal. The legend is wrong, or the withdrawal and completion counts are. This changes no reported estimate, but it leaves the denominators at the late visits unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the withdrawn participant's V14 data were collected, or a corrected legend.

quotes.text: One participant, assigned to sequence A, was withdrawn due to acute COVID-19

issues.title: Table 2 SF-36 Vitality (until day 28): printed t = 2.97 but 6.65/1.65 = 4.03
issues.explanation: In every other row of Table 2 the t-value equals the treatment effect divided by the SD column. For Vitality until day 28 that ratio is 4.03, but the paper prints 2.97. The printed p of 0.0001 and the confidence interval agree with 4.03, so the t-value cell is the one that is wrong. It is probably a copy of the crossover FACIT value, and it changes no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing a different effect or SD that gives t = 2.97 and is consistent with p = 0.0001 and the CI.

script.explanation: Vitality until day 28: effect / SD vs printed t: 6.65 / 1.65 gives 4.0303, not the printed 2.97. For the printed value to hold the denominator would have to be 2.23906, not 1.65.

10.1101/2025.06.12.25329489.headline_claim: Pycnogenol 200 mg daily did not improve health status (EQ-VAS) compared with placebo over 12 weeks in post-COVID-19 condition; both groups improved clinically relevantly, suggesting non-therapeutic effects.
10.1101/2025.06.12.25329489.overall: The primary conclusion, that Pycnogenol did not improve EQ-VAS over 12 weeks (β=0.54, 95% CI -3.45 to 4.54, p=0.79), is well supported by a registered, randomized, blinded design with 152 of 153 analysed. The issues are minor: an abstract that omits three nominal secondary differences, an unreconciled discontinuation count, unadjusted multiplicity, and speculative attribution of the placebo improvement.

primary_outcome.name: Health status (EQ-VAS), change from baseline to 12 weeks

issues.title: Abstract says no secondary-endpoint differences, but Results report 3 nominal differences (p=0.014, 0.036, 0.048)
issues.explanation: The abstract states that no between-group differences were observed in secondary endpoints. The Results report lower sedentary time (p=0.014) and dyspnea (p=0.036) in the Pycnogenol group and higher TAC at 15 min (p=0.048). The abstract omits these nominal findings, although they are small, unadjusted and discussed as hard to attribute to the product's mechanism. This is an inconsistency in the abstract, not an error in the primary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract statement qualified as 'no consistent' or 'no differences after multiplicity adjustment'.

quotes.text: No between group differences
Sedentary time, min.day -1-22.47-40.27 to -4.670.014
Linear regression analysis showed a statistically significant difference in TAC at the measurement timepoint 15min

issues.title: Discussion lists nominal secondary differences as findings, while later doubting them
issues.explanation: The opening of the Discussion says the Pycnogenol group 'reported improvements in dyspnea severity, appeared to engage in less sedentary behavior' and had higher TAC. These are unadjusted nominal p-values among many tests, and the primary was null. The authors later caveat the differences, and the main conclusion is correctly null, so the effect is limited to the framing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Discussion that framed these explicitly as exploratory and unadjusted in the Principal Findings.

quotes.text: the Pycnogenol ® group reported improvements in dyspnea severity, appeared to engage in less sedentary behavior, and had a marginally higher total anti-oxidative capacity.
difficult to attribute to the expected mechanisms of action of the study product

issues.title: Roughly 40 secondary/biomarker tests with no multiplicity adjustment; 3 nominal hits at p 0.014-0.048
issues.explanation: Table 2 and Table 3 report about 40 secondary models without any stated correction or exploratory label for the set. With that many tests, about two nominal p<0.05 results are expected by chance; three were found, and one (TAC 15 min) has a CI bound of 0.00. The nominal findings should be read as hypothesis-generating. The primary conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified multiplicity strategy or an explicit exploratory label for all secondary outcomes.

issues.title: Improvement in both arms attributed to non-specific effects without an untreated comparison
issues.explanation: Both arms improved on EQ-VAS (5.4 and 7.9 units), and the abstract and conclusion attribute this to non-therapeutic or non-specific effects such as care attention. With no no-treatment arm and no measures of those factors, regression to the mean, measurement effects and natural recovery cannot be excluded. The wording is hedged but still goes beyond the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from an untreated or waiting-list control arm showing smaller improvement.

quotes.text: highlighting the potential of non-specific therapeutic effects, including care attention, emotional support, and symptom monitoring

issues.title: Pycnogenol discontinuations for side effects: stated 5, itemised reasons total 4
issues.explanation: The text says five Pycnogenol participants stopped product because of side effects but lists only four reasons (2 GI, 1 dermatological, 1 other). The placebo group reconciles (1 GI + 1 dermatological = 2). One Pycnogenol discontinuation is unaccounted for in the text; the supplement may resolve it. No conclusion depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Table 8 listing a fifth reason category for the Pycnogenol group.

quotes.text: Five participants from the Pycnogenol ® group and two from the placebo group discontinued
one from each group due to dermatological complaints

10.1101/2025.07.24.25331961.headline_claim: Home-based intranasal and transcranial photobiomodulation (Vielight Neuro RX Gamma) is safe and feasible and shows encouraging evidence of cognitive benefit in post-COVID-19 cognitive impairment, particularly in adults under 45.
10.1101/2025.07.24.25331961.overall: The primary composite did not differ significantly between groups (difference 0.043, 95% CI -0.007 to 0.092, p=0.088), so the paper's 'first controlled evidence of efficacy' and age-specific benefit claims rest on uncorrected subgroup and single-task results from a small pilot analysed per protocol. There are also internal inconsistencies in secondary reporting (Feature Match Day 56, mobility direction). The safety and feasibility findings are more reliable than the efficacy claims.

primary_outcome.name: Change in composite cognitive score (mean of seven Creyos tasks) from baseline to Day 56

primary_outcomes.measure: The change in the combined results of 7 Creyos items: Spatial Planning, Monkey Ladder, Rotations, Feature Match, Paired Associates, Token Search, Polygons.

issues.title: Primary composite p=0.088 (CI -0.007 to 0.092) presented as active PBM improving cognition and 'first controlled evidence of efficacy'
issues.explanation: The primary endpoint difference of 0.043 had a 95% CI of -0.007 to 0.092 and p=0.088, so no benefit over sham was shown. Yet the Summary says active PBM 'showed greater improvement', the Discussion cites 'encouraging evidence', and the Added value section claims 'first controlled evidence of PBM's efficacy'. The conclusion that efficacy was shown, relying on the under-45 subgroup (p=0.028) and Feature Match, is not supported by the pre-specified primary analysis, which was null and run in a per-protocol set of 41.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary analysis showing a significant between-group difference, or wording limiting claims to hypothesis-generating signal.

quotes.text: Active PBM showed greater improvement in composite cognitive scores (p=0.088), with significant gains in participants under 45 years (p=0.028).
provides the first controlled evidence of PBM's efficacy for PCC cognitive impairment
quotes.location: Research in Context, Added value of this study

second_reader.what_stands: The primary composite difference was not statistically significant (p=0.088, CI -0.007 to 0.092 spanning zero), and the paper says so in Results and Table 3, but the Summary, Discussion and Research in Context word it as active PBM improving composite scores more and describe the study as providing 'the first controlled evidence of PBM's efficacy' for PCC cognitive impairment. That efficacy wording is stronger than a pilot whose primary endpoint was not met and whose positive results come from an unadjusted age subgroup and a single component task can support, although the paper elsewhere call

issues.title: Under-45 composite (p=0.028) and Feature Match headlined from many uncorrected, nominal tests
issues.explanation: After a non-significant overall primary (p=0.088), the under-45 subgroup (p=0.028) and individual component tasks (7 tasks, several timepoints, 2 age strata, plus many secondary items) were tested with no multiplicity correction and no reported group-by-age interaction test. The significant results are single nominal p-values just below 0.05, and the Summary and Added value sections still headline them as significant improvements. The conclusion that PBM works 'particularly in younger patients' is therefore hypothesis-generating only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, alpha-controlled hierarchy or a significant treatment-by-age interaction test supporting the age effect.

quotes.text: No adjustments for multiple comparisons were made for secondary outcomes and timepoints due to the exploratory nature.
A pvalue < 0.05 is interpreted as statistically significant for hypothesis generation.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does state that no multiplicity adjustment was made and that p<0.05 is for hypothesis generation, and the under-45 composite (p=0.028) and Feature Match findings come from among many unadjusted nominal tests across age strata, tasks and timepoints. However, the methods text refers to secondary outcomes and timepoints, whereas the under-45 composite is a subgroup of the primary endpoint; the age subgroup is called pre-specified in Results but the registry record lists no age-stratified analysis (registry lists only the overall primary outcome, and earlier record versions were not retr

issues.title: Table 3 footnote calls Feature Match Day 56 significant (p=0.133); Results list only Day 28 and Day 84
issues.explanation: The Table 3 footnote says the overall-group Feature Match difference was statistically significant at Day 56 while printing p=0.133, which is not below the stated 0.05 threshold. The Results text names only Day 28 and Day 84 as significant. The table row also says active was better 'by Day 28 onward', overstating consistency of the Feature Match effect, which the Discussion calls 'significant improvements across groups'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the Day 56 p-value was mistyped and is actually below 0.05, or that the footnote was meant only to list the timepoints tested.

quotes.text: Statistically significant difference favoring Active PBM in the overall group for the Feature Match task at Day 28 (p=0.019), Day 56 (p=0.133), Day 84 (p=0.017)
significant improvements in Feature Match accuracy for the active group compared to sham were observed at Day 28 (p = 0.019) and Day 84 (p = 0.017)

issues.title: EQ-5D mobility p=0.007: text and Discussion favour sham, Table 4 favours active PBM
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion state the <45 sham group had significantly greater mobility improvement (p=0.007). Table 4 reports the same p-value but says active PBM improved more. Both cannot be right. If sham was better, the table misstates a significant result against the active arm, which understates harm or a negative secondary finding for PBM; Table 4 as printed makes the treatment look better.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary tables showing the direction of the mobility difference and which statement is correct (this would resolve which is wrong, not the inconsistency).

quotes.text: The <45 sham PBM group showed significantly greater improvement in the mobility domain at Day 56 (p = 0.007)
Active PBM improved more (greater reduction in mobility limitations)

issues.title: Primary MMRM run only in per-protocol set (41 of 43); two active-arm exclusions, no ITT primary shown
issues.explanation: The primary efficacy analysis is stated to be in the per-protocol population, which dropped two active-arm participants after randomization (one for non-compliance). No ITT or sensitivity result for the primary composite is given in the paper. With a null primary the impact is limited, but the analysed set departs from randomized groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT MMRM of the primary composite giving essentially the same estimate and p-value.

quotes.text: Two active group participants were excluded from the PP analysis (one for incomplete Day 56 assessments, one for non-compliance), resulting in 41 PP participants (21 active, 20 sham).
fixed effects for group, visit, group-by-visit interaction, age stratum, and baseline score covariate in the PP population.

issues.title: Registered 2023-05-10, about 5 weeks after the 2023-04-01 start; registered primary matches paper
issues.explanation: The registry record NCT05857124 was first submitted after the recorded study start, so registration was retrospective, though the paper does not say so. The registered primary outcome (composite of seven Creyos tasks to Day 56) matches the paper's, so the main risk of outcome switching is not evident. The registry lists 36 as actual enrollment while the paper randomized 43, and earlier record versions were not checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing an earlier first submission before 2023-04-01.

quotes.text: was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05857124)
Enrollment occurred from April 2023 to September 2024.

issues.title: Table 4 MSBQ row says no significant differences yet cites sham-favouring Memory item p=0.011
issues.explanation: The MSBQ specific-symptoms row says 'No significant differences' with p > 0.05 (NS) but also reports a nominally significant sham advantage on 'Memory' at p=0.011 in older adults. This is most likely an item-level result placed in a summary cell, so the row is internally unclear rather than clearly wrong. The effect is limited to one secondary row.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote or supplement stating the p > 0.05 applies only to the overall symptom comparison and the Memory item is a separate item-level test.

quotes.text: No significant differences (trend toward sham reporting less fatigue,
'Memory' in Sham was superior at Day 56

10.1109/jiot.2022.3188914.headline_claim: Weekly telerehabilitation with telecoaching after early education improves physical activity, exercise tolerance and inspiratory muscle strength in post-acute COVID-19 patients, according to this pilot study.
10.1109/jiot.2022.3188914.overall: The paper is mainly a technical description with a small 14-patient pilot, and the authors call the results preliminary. Its efficacy language in the abstract and conclusion is stronger than the data support: the key result compares responder shares (6/7 vs 3/7) without a reported between-group test, and one headline figure (41.9%) is arithmetically impossible with seven patients. The technical feasibility conclusions are more reliable than the clinical ones.

primary_outcome.name: Daily number of steps per day at post-treatment (five weeks)

issues.title: Headline 85.7% vs ~42.9% responders has no reported between-group test; 6/7 vs 3/7 is not significant
issues.explanation: The abstract's evidence of benefit is the share of patients with any increase in steps in each arm, with no between-group effect size, test statistic or p-value in the text. Any increase counts as a responder, regardless of magnitude. With 6/7 versus 3/7 responders the difference is well within chance for this sample size (Fisher exact p about 0.27), so the claimed potential to improve activity is not demonstrated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A printed between-group test on change in steps per day showing significance in Table I.

quotes.text: 85.7% of patients in telerehabilitation versus 41.9% educational group
in the educational group, there was an increase in physical activity in 41.9% of patients

second_reader.what_stands: The 85.7% vs ~42.9% responder comparison is reported without any visible between-group test in the text, and my recomputation (6/7 vs 3/7, Fisher exact p about 0.27) shows it would not be significant; the 41.9% figure is also an impossible proportion for n=7 and is presumably 42.9%. However, I could not see Table I or Fig. 4, which might contain a test on step counts, and the authors present the figure descriptively and call the study preliminary rather than claiming a significant difference for it.

issues.title: Conclusion attributes improved physical condition to telerehabilitation from a 14-patient pilot
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the pilot shows early education then telerehabilitation can improve physical activity, exercise tolerance and inspiratory muscle strength. Inspiratory strength rose significantly in both arms, so it cannot be credited to telecoaching, and the activity and exercise-tolerance differences between arms are not tested or are small (6/7 vs 3/7; 5/7 vs 3/7). Whether the effect comes from the intervention versus supervision, time or chance is not established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests with adequate precision showing superiority on these outcomes.

quotes.text: early disease-specific education on post-COVID conditions followed by telerehabilitation with telecoaching can improve patients' physical condition
A significant increase in inspiratory muscle strength was observed in both groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion states that telerehabilitation with telecoaching can improve physical condition on three outcomes without caveat, drawing on 14 patients, non-significant (by recomputation) between-group differences for activity and exercise capacity, and an inspiratory strength gain seen in both arms. The paper's Discussion does label the work preliminary and calls for a larger study, which softens but does not remove the overreach in the Conclusion sentence.

issues.title: 41.9% of 7 educational-group patients is impossible; nearest value is 42.9% (3/7)
issues.explanation: The paper states seven patients per group, so possible percentages are multiples of 14.3% (3/7 = 42.9%, 2/7 = 28.6%). The printed 41.9% in the abstract and results matches no whole number of patients. The headline primary-outcome comparison therefore contains a wrong figure, though the likely intended value (42.9%) is close and the comparison barely changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that group sizes or denominators differed (e.g., a count other than 7 underlying 41.9%).

quotes.text: 85.7% of patients in telerehabilitation versus 41.9% educational group
seven patients in each group

issues.title: Control received no weekly contact, so supervision and attention effects are confounded with telecoaching
issues.explanation: The control arm did unsupervised home exercise while the experimental arm had weekly supervised video lessons with feedback on step counts. Any difference could reflect contact and supervision rather than the sensor-based telecoaching, and neither patients nor assessors were blinded, with a step-count outcome that coaching directly targets. This is a defensible pragmatic comparison for a pilot but limits interpretation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control or a claim limited to the supervised package.

quotes.text: The educational group continued unsupervised home exercise training only.
had a telerehabilitation lesson with telecoaching with a physiotherapist once per week

10.1111/bcp.15988.headline_claim: The CBD-dominant cannabis-based medicinal product was safe and well tolerated, and demonstrated feasibility in long COVID, with efficacy requiring future placebo-controlled trials.
10.1111/bcp.15988.overall: The paper is an honest feasibility report: recruitment shortfall, open-label design and lack of efficacy inference are all disclosed, and the primary outcomes match the registry. The only point that needs trimming is the unqualified 'safe' claim for long COVID from 12 uncontrolled participants, plus the mild efficacy-trend wording; otherwise the conclusions stand as feasibility findings.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility measures: recruitment rate, tolerability (retention), and number of side effects

primary_outcomes.measure: Tolerability for the treatment of long COVID

issues.title: 'Safe' stated for long COVID from 12 uncontrolled participants; no serious AEs but 145 side effects reported
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Discussion call the drug 'safe' for people with long COVID based on 12 participants without a control group. Twelve people can rule out only very common serious harms. Side effects were universal (145 across 12 people) and 4 of 22 adverse events were moderate, so 'well-tolerated' is supportable as a description of this sample, but 'safe' in the wider population is not established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to 'well tolerated in this small sample' with a stated confidence bound on serious AE rates.

quotes.text: The study drug was safe and well-tolerated, demonstrating feasibility of CBD-dominant cannabis-based medicinal products in individuals diagnosed with long COVID.
Given our findings that the drug is welltolerated and safe for people with long COVID

issues.title: Single-arm design cannot attribute apparent PROM improvements to drug; paper discloses this but hints at benefit
issues.explanation: The trial had no control arm, so any change in anxiety, depression, sleep or quality of life cannot be attributed to the drug. The authors state this repeatedly and frame the primary aims as feasibility. A residual hint of benefit ('trend that the study drug may improve some health measures') remains in the Discussion, but it is hedged and does not drive the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; a feasibility design with explicit caveats is acceptable, and the hedged trend wording is the only residual concern.

quotes.text: In the absence of a control group, it is not possible to determine the sources of this apparent improvement in health.
quotes.location: 3.2.1 PROMs and Fitbit data, point iv

quotes.text: our data suggess a trend that the study drug may improve

issues.title: 5 of 12 had shortened drug exposure (supply issues) yet 100% retention is cited as tolerability evidence
issues.explanation: Tolerability was defined by withdrawals due to side effects, and none occurred, so 100% retention is arithmetically correct. But 5 of 12 (42%) received a shorter course than planned, so the 'high retention' claim reflects less than full planned exposure for those participants. The paper discloses this, and the effect is small on the feasibility conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that tolerability was assessed only up to the earliest taper point for all, or that early-taper participants had equivalent exposure at the key dose.

quotes.text: Due to supply issues with the study drug, 3 participants tapered off the drug at month 4 (final visit at month 5) and 2 participants tapered off the drug at month 3
we attained 100% retention, consistent with the low rate of reported adverse events and side effects

10.1111/cts.13826.headline_claim: Growth hormone treatment improved self-reported fatigue, depression, mood and quality of life in symptomatic PASC patients with low glucagon-stimulated GH, but symptoms returned after treatment ended.
10.1111/cts.13826.overall: The paper is an uncontrolled, open-label pilot of 13 analysed patients with self-reported primary outcomes, so the reported symptom improvements cannot be attributed to GH, and the 'first study to show' claim is not supported. There are also minor reporting inconsistencies (sleep in the Highlights, BMI p-value, physical performance wording) and an unexplained difference between registered and reported primary outcomes. The results are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Subject-reported symptom severity (fatigue, depression, mood, quality of life, sleep)

primary_outcomes.measure: Lean Body Mass as Measured by Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) at Baseline
Lean Body Mass as Measured by Dual Energy X-Ra Absorptiometry (DEXA) at 6 Months
Fat Mass as Measured by Dual Energy X-Ra Absorptiometry (DEXA) at Baseline
Fat Mass as Measured by Dual Energy X-Ra Absorptiometry (DEXA) at 6 Months

issues.title: Causal efficacy conclusions drawn from a single-arm, open-label before-after design with no comparator
issues.explanation: All participants received GH with no control group, so improvements in self-reported symptoms cannot be separated from placebo or expectancy effects, natural recovery or regression to the mean. The paper concedes the lack of placebo but still describes a 'convincing treatment response' and states that GH improved symptoms. The washout rebound is compatible with both a drug effect and fading expectancy. Participants and assessors were unblinded and the main outcomes were all self-reported, which compounds the problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or placebo-controlled comparison showing the same effect.

quotes.text: The small sample size and lack of a placebo group for comparison are both limitations of this study.
demonstrated a convincing treatment response for subject-  reported outcomes despite the small sample size

second_reader.what_stands: The design is single-arm and open-label, and the paper states causal efficacy ('GH treatment improved...', 'convincing treatment response') on the strength of unblinded self-reported outcomes. It never weighs placebo or expectancy effects as an alternative explanation, and the withdrawal rebound is treated as supportive without a control. It is not accurate to say the limitation is hidden: the lack of a placebo group and the small sample are acknowledged, and the Conclusions call for larger studies and describe the effect as non-curative.

issues.title: Pilot of 13 analysed, uncontrolled participants concludes it is first to show GH reduces PASC symptoms
issues.explanation: The Conclusions assert GH treatment 'reduces' neurologic PASC symptoms and the Highlights suggest physicians should consider GH testing. A small open-label single-arm pilot can only be hypothesis-generating. The language implies demonstrated efficacy that the design does not support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to a preliminary, hypothesis-generating signal.

quotes.text: the first  study  to  show  that  GH  treatment  reduces  neurologic  PASC  symptoms
we present a pilot study to determine if individuals with neurologic PASC symptoms experience symptom relief with GH treatment.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions state this is 'the first study to show that GH treatment reduces neurologic PASC symptoms', based on 13 analysed participants with no comparator and subjective outcomes, in a study the authors call a pilot. That wording is stronger than the design supports, because a pilot can suggest but not show an effect. The paper's own request for larger studies and its description of the effect as non-curative partly soften this, and the priority claim itself cannot be verified from the paper.

issues.title: Highlights claim significant sleep improvement; Results give p = 0.081 (non-significant)
issues.explanation: The Study Highlights list sleep among symptoms with significant improvement. The Results and Discussion state that sleep quality did not change significantly (p = 0.081) and PSQI stayed in the poor range. The summary overstates one secondary result relative to the paper's own data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported significant PSQI result (e.g. a significant post-hoc contrast) in Table S2 that the main text omitted.

quotes.text: had significant improvement in fatigue, sleep, depression, mood, and quality of life
quotes.location: Study Highlights, What does this study add

quotes.text: Average sleep quality did not change significantly with GH treatment ( p = 0.081)

issues.title: Paper's primary outcomes (symptom scores) differ from registered primaries (DEXA lean and fat mass)
issues.explanation: The current registry record lists DEXA lean and fat mass as primary outcomes, while the paper declares subject-reported symptom severity primary and reports DEXA as exploratory. The paper does not explain the change, and the registered primary results were null while the declared primary ones were positive. Only the current registry version was seen, so earlier registrations may have differed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing symptom outcomes were registered as primary before enrolment.

quotes.text: Subject-  reported  outcomes  of  symptom  severity  were the primary outcomes of this study.
Body composition was assessed using dual-  energy X-  ray absorptiometry (DEXA) (GE Lunar iDXA; GE Healthcare; Chicago, IL) to determine lean and fat mass.

issues.title: Per-protocol style analysis: 13 of 17 baseline subjects analysed, one excluded post hoc for weight loss
issues.explanation: Of 17 baseline participants, 4 are not in the analysis: three dropped out or were terminated and one was excluded for weight loss over 45 kg. No intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is given, and the exclusion is partly outcome-related. The flow is fully accounted for, and the direction of bias is uncertain, though completers analyses tend to favour the treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis giving the same results.

quotes.text: One subject was excluded from the final analysis due to profound weight loss during the study ( > 45 kg).
Two  subjects  withdrew  and  one  was  terminated due  to  COVID  reinfection  after  1 month.

issues.title: BMI p-value is 0.948 in the text but 0.197 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The same paired BMI comparison is given two different p-values. Table 2 (0.197) fits the body mass result (p = 0.168) far better than the text value. Both are non-significant, so the conclusion about body composition is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors explaining that the two p-values come from different tests or sets.

quotes.text: Body mass index (BMI)30.30 ± 6.630.80 ± 6.80.197

issues.title: Conclusions say no physical performance change, yet submaximal walk and torque gains are reported (p = 0.003-0.043)
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state treatment came without changes to physical performance, but Table 2 reports significant uncorrected increases in 25% effort walk (p = 0.003), 50% effort walk (0.030), total distance (0.007) and submaximal torque. The authors do distinguish maximal from self-metered measures in the Discussion, so the contradiction is partly one of summary wording. The statement is internally inconsistent and these results are uncorrected exploratory findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusions qualified to maximal-effort performance only.

quotes.text: without changes  to  body  composition,  physical  performance, metabolism
The distance walked at subject-  perceived 25% effort  and  50%  effort  both  significantly  increased  with treatment.

10.1111/hex.70079.headline_claim: The personalised health behaviour support programme was safe, feasible and acceptable, and compared with usual care it improved physical activity and respiratory symptoms, supporting a definitive larger trial.
10.1111/hex.70079.overall: The feasibility findings (recruitment, retention, acceptability) are reasonably supported by the data. The efficacy and safety claims in the conclusion go beyond what an unblinded, unpowered pilot with completer-only, unadjusted analyses and no control-arm symptom data can show. The registration was retrospective despite being described as prospective, and a few printed numbers (CAT sign, CIs for handgrip and MVPA, session count) are internally inconsistent.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility of recruiting and randomising adults with post-COVID syndrome (recruitment, randomisation, completion, acceptability)

issues.title: Pilot conclusion states efficacy vs usual care; diary symptom reductions had no control comparison
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that, compared with usual care, the programme improved physical activity and respiratory symptoms, and that this was supported by reductions in self-reported symptoms. The trial was not powered for efficacy, had about 12-15 analysed per arm, and made no multiplicity adjustment across roughly 15 outcomes. The diary-based symptom reductions exist only for the intervention arm. Safety rests on zero adverse events in 17 participants. The data support feasibility and a hypothesis-generating signal, not demonstrated efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified efficacy hypothesis with multiplicity control, or usual-care diary data supporting the symptom comparison.

quotes.text: when compared to usual care, the personalised health support programme improved PA and respiratory symptoms
Although not powered to detect change
self -reported diaries were not provided to the usual care group

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion says that, compared with usual care, the programme 'improved PA and respiratory symptoms' in a pilot the authors say was not powered to detect change, with unadjusted, uncorrected tests; steps, movement intensity and CAT do have between-group CIs excluding zero, but the other PA outcomes (sedentary time, MVPA, ISWT) do not. The diary-based reductions in fatigue, breathlessness, sleep and migraine come from the intervention arm only (the usual care group had no diaries, as the limitations section states), so they cannot support a comparison with usual care and are not a controlle

issues.title: Between-group CIs inconsistent with printed SDs: handgrip 1.2 (0.5-3.2) too narrow, MVPA 9 (-29 to 47) too wide
issues.explanation: The handgrip difference of 1.2 kg has a CI of 0.5 to 3.2, whose midpoint is 1.85 rather than 1.2. With SDs of 3.0 and 3.4 and about 15 and 12 completers, the interval should be about -1.4 to 3.8 and include 0. So the interval would make a non-significant difference look significant. The MVPA CI (-29 to 47) is about 5 times wider than SDs of 11 and 7 imply (about 2 to 16). One of these figures is wrong, so the reported handgrip result cannot be relied on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or a statistical appendix showing unequal analysed numbers or different SDs that reproduce these intervals.

quotes.text: with a between -group difference (+1.2 (95% CI 0.5 -3.2) kg; Table 3)

script.explanation: the estimate 1.2 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [0.5, 3.2] (expected about 1.8500) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Unadjusted change-score tests on completers only, with baseline imbalances and within-group contrasts
issues.explanation: Between-group comparisons use change scores without adjustment for baseline, in about 15 vs 12 completers. Arms differ at baseline in symptom duration and some outcomes. The text contrasts within-group changes (improved vs 'not improved'), which is not itself a comparison between groups. This weakens secondary results and makes the efficacy statements tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA) analysis or ITT analysis giving similar estimates.

quotes.text: Differences between groups were assessed by independent samples t -tests or Mann -Whitney U test of within -person change scores for each group.
but not the usual care group (+5 (72) VMU; Table 3)
