issues.title: Signposting-only control and unblinded assessment confound programme effect with attention
issues.explanation: The intervention arm received an interview, seven one-to-one sessions and daily diaries. The control arm was given only website signposting, and the research team knew allocation. Differences in subjective outcomes (CAT, symptoms) and unblinded functional tests may partly reflect contact and expectation. This is a recognised pilot limitation, but it is not carried into the efficacy wording of the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment or an attention-matched control arm showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Participants allocated to usual care were signposted with information about the digital self -help available in their local area
a lack of ability to blind the research team to the study allocation

issues.title: Described as prospectively registered, but registry first submitted 2023-02-28, after recruitment began
issues.explanation: The paper states that the trial was prospectively registered. Its own dates (August 2022 to March 2023) put the start before the registry's first submission on 28 February 2023. The registry itself lists start 1 November 2022 and labels the registration retrospective. The 'prospective' statement is therefore not accurate, and the registry cannot be used to show the outcomes were fixed in advance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or a registration date before the first participant was enrolled.

quotes.text: was prospectively registered on the clinicaltrials.gov website (NCT05752331)
was conducted between August 2022 and March 2023

issues.title: CAT between-group difference printed as +4 in text but -4 in Table 4 (CI -6 to -1)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the CAT between-group difference as +4 points with a 95% CI of -6 to -1. An estimate of +4 cannot lie inside that interval. Table 4 and the within-group changes (-4 vs 0) support -4, so the text has a sign error; the reported direction of benefit is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected or errata version showing the text intentionally reports the sign of a different scale direction.

quotes.text: with a between -group difference (+4 points (95% CI: -6 to -1) points; Table 4)

issues.title: Seven support sessions stated, yet results describe sessions six to eight and an IQR of 7-8
issues.explanation: Methods and the start of the adherence paragraph describe seven support sessions. The same paragraph reports attendance at 'sessions six to eight' and an IQR reaching 8. The number of sessions offered is therefore unclear, which affects how adherence should be read.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the interview counts as a session, or that an eighth session was offered, in a protocol or supplement.

quotes.text: Engagement with the seven virtual self -management support sessions
15 (88%) completing sessions six to eight

10.1111/hex.70299.headline_claim: A digital personalised combined lifestyle intervention (physical activity and diet counselling with a nutritional supplement) is feasible and well received by patients with post-Covid-19 condition, and may improve physical activity and dietary quality and be integrated into routine care.
10.1111/hex.70299.overall: The finding that the digital intervention was acceptable and well attended is supported by the descriptive data. The Conclusion's recommendation of routine integration to enhance recovery, and the lung-function and well-being benefits implied in the Discussion, are not supported. They rest on an uncontrolled, self-selected comparison, within-arm significance testing and post-hoc adherence groups. The only numeric inconsistency found is a minor one in the supplement compliance count.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (compliance, experiences and perceived effectiveness)

issues.title: Feasibility study concludes routine-care integration 'to enhance recovery' and improved psychological well-being
issues.explanation: The design is non-randomised, with a self-selected control, no pre-specified efficacy outcome and no between-arm testing. Even so, the Conclusion says the findings suggest routine integration 'to enhance patient recovery', and the Discussion cites improved physical and psychological well-being. Table 3 shows no change in EQ-5D or HADS, and the evidence for improved lifestyle is self-reported and based on respondents only. The closing caveat about future randomised studies only partly offsets the earlier recommendation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled, adequately powered comparison showing improved clinical outcomes, or a conclusion limited to feasibility and acceptability.

quotes.text: These findings suggest the integration of digital personalised CLIs into routine post‐Covid‐19 care to enhance patient recovery.
thereby suggesting the potential of implementing CLIs in the management of PCC by improving physical and psychological well‐being
EQ‐5D scores did not change over time in both groups

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's 'integration into routine care to enhance patient recovery' and the Discussion's 'improving ... psychological well-being' go beyond a non-randomised feasibility study with only within-group paired tests: EQ-5D did not change in either group, HADS counts were 1-3 patients with no test, and improvements such as FFMI and fatigue also occurred in controls or cannot be separated from natural recovery. The claim is partly softened because the authors' final sentence calls for larger randomised studies for objective outcomes, and the psychological claim rests on qualitative reports,

issues.title: Health benefits inferred from significant vs non-significant within-arm change; self-selected control, no between-arm test
issues.explanation: The Results say lung function rose in the intervention arm but not in the control arm, which implies a difference between arms without testing one. The two groups were formed by voluntary participation with a cap of 50, so they are not comparable. Natural post-Covid recovery is also visible, since FFMI rose in both arms, and no between-arm or adjusted comparison, baseline adjustment or multiplicity control is reported. Pulmonary data exist for only 25 intervention and 13 control patients, and baseline DLCO differs (75.2 vs 65.8). The apparent benefit on pulmonary function and fatigue therefore cannot be attributed to the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-arm (group by time) test, adjusted for baseline, showing a difference in change in pulmonary function.

quotes.text: while no changes were observed in the control group
Specific interaction effects could, however, not be established due to the small sample size and associated power constraints
Measured in 25/13 patients of the intervention/control group.

issues.title: NS subgroup analysed by post-hoc adherence (22 stoppers and 7 biomarker decliners moved to 'no NS')
issues.explanation: The 'with NS' group contains only patients who kept taking the supplement and whose plasma n-3 levels rose, while 29 others were reassigned to 'without NS' after the fact. Adherers typically differ from non-adherers, and the classification used a post-treatment biomarker. The finding that pulmonary function rose only 'with NS' is therefore confounded by adherence and by the way the groups were built. The paper does not claim the NS works, so this weakens a secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis by original NS allocation (offered vs not offered), or a prespecified adherence definition independent of the outcome biomarker.

quotes.text: Twenty‐two patients prematurely stopped using the NS during the intervention and were allocated to the intervention group without NS for the analysis.
these were therefore considered non‐compliant and analysed in the intervention group without NS

issues.title: Supplement compliance of 16/46 does not reconcile with 24 users minus 7 decliners minus 2 excluded (15)
issues.explanation: Of 24 patients taking the supplement, 7 were reclassified as non-compliant and 2 were excluded for missing bloods, which leaves 15 (17 if the exclusions are ignored). The Discussion reports 16 of 46 as 'good compliance', and the 46 is not explained, since the intervention group is 47 and 41 completed. The Discussion also calls the same compliance 'low' in the next sentence. This is a small reporting inconsistency in a secondary component and does not affect the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram (Figure 2) showing that one of the 2 excluded patients was among the 7 decliners and that 46 is a defined denominator would reconcile the counts.

quotes.text: of whom 24 patients had NS based on their self‐reported compliance
Furthermore, two patients were excluded from the analysis because of missing blood sampling data at study visit 2.
demonstrating good compliance in 16 of the 46 patients (35%)

issues.title: No registration of the nested intervention study is reported
issues.explanation: The paper gives an ethics number but no trial registry identifier for the intervention. Without registration, the health outcomes cannot be checked against a prespecified plan. Because the aims are feasibility and description, the effect on the conclusions is minor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier for the cohort or intervention with prespecified feasibility outcomes.

quotes.text: This proof‐of‐concept study was a nested intervention within a multicentre prospective observational cohort study in the Netherlands.

10.1111/hex.70357.headline_claim: The LISTEN personalised self-management intervention was not cost-effective from an NHS/PSS perspective over 3 months but was cost-saving and dominant from a societal perspective, and the authors describe it as highly cost-effective from a societal perspective.
10.1111/hex.70357.overall: The NHS/PSS finding (higher cost, tiny QALY gain, not cost-effective) is reasonably reported. The societal 'highly cost-effective' conclusion is stronger than the evidence allows: all societal intervals include zero, about 37.5% of data were imputed under an untested MAR assumption, and the societal NMB does not reconcile with its own cost and QALY differences. The remaining slips (Table 7 hours, small scenario-table differences) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Ox-PAQ routine activities domain score (primary clinical effectiveness outcome in the CEA)

issues.title: Societal 'highly cost-effective' claim although cost, QALY and NMB CIs all include zero; 3-month horizon
issues.explanation: The summary calls the intervention highly cost-effective from a societal perspective. Yet the societal cost difference (-£607, CI -£1690 to £477), the QALY difference (0.005, CI -0.004 to 0.014) and the NMB at £20,000 (CI -£175 to £2292) all include zero. The NHS/PSS analysis, the primary perspective, found the intervention not cost-effective, and the authors' own text says the clinical analysis could not show firm meaningful benefit. The 3-month horizon (which the authors say is likely insufficient) adds further uncertainty. 'Highly' is not supported; 'probably cost-saving, with substantial uncertainty' would be.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Societal CIs excluding zero, or a headline conclusion worded as uncertain/probable rather than 'highly cost-effective'.

quotes.text: from a societal perspective, the LISTEN intervention was highly cost -effective
interpreted with caution based on the short follow -up horizon

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does call the societal result 'highly cost-effective' (4.3, also 'may be highly cost-effective' in 4.2) although the cost, QALY and NMB 95% CIs all include zero and the horizon is 3 months; the claim rests on the 95.4% CEAC probability. It is not unqualified: the same paragraph says to interpret with caution because of the short follow-up, small differences in costs and effects, and the lack of NHS/PSS evidence, and Section 4.1/4.2 acknowledge the horizon and that differences were not statistically significant, so the problem is the strength of the wording relative to the uncertainty

issues.title: About 37.5% incomplete EQ-5D/CSRI data handled by MAR imputation with no sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Only 62.5% of participants returned complete questionnaires, and the cost and QALY results, including the societal dominance result, rest on imputation assuming data are missing at random. No analysis tests departures from that assumption. Lost-work costs, the main driver of the societal result, have only 159 to 172 respondents per arm at 3 months out of 270 and 274 randomised. The text also says 67 imputed datasets were 'equivalent to' the percentage with complete data, which does not match the stated 62.5%.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified MNAR or complete-case sensitivity analysis giving similar societal results, or a correction explaining the 67 vs 62.5% figures.

quotes.text: The proportion of participants returning complete EQ -5D and CSRI questionnaires was 62.5%.
Assuming data were missing at random, multiple imputation by chained equations using predictive mean matching
Rubin's rules [31] were used to combine the 67 imputed datasets equivalent to the percentage of participants with complete data

issues.title: Societal NMB £1058 at £20,000 is about £340 above what cost saving £607 and 0.005 QALYs imply
issues.explanation: With a QALY gain of 0.005 and a cost saving of £607, the NMB at £20,000 should be roughly £707 (at most about £717 allowing for rounding). The paper reports £1058, and £1114 at £30,000. The difference between the two thresholds implies a QALY gain of about 0.0055, so the gap of about £340 sits in the cost term, not the QALY term. This makes the societal result look stronger than the printed cost and QALY differences support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement explaining that societal NMBs were estimated differently from the mean cost and QALY differences, or a corrected NMB near £700.

quotes.text: demonstrating a cost reduction of £607 (95% CI, -£1690 to £477)
with an adjusted mean difference of 0.005 QALYs (95% CI, -0.004 to 0.014)

issues.title: Table 7 shows 628.00 h for 15-min prep/notes; 1256 sessions x 15 min = 314 h (costs fit 15 min)
issues.explanation: Section 3.4 and the Table 7 labels say preparation and note-writing were cut to 15 minutes per session, but both rows print 628.00 h, which is the 30-minute figure. The £17,221.45 cost on each row matches half of the 30-minute cost implied by Section 3.1, so the costs appear to be right and only the hours column is wrong. No headline result depends on the hours cell.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 628 h is the unreduced 30-min figure, or a costing workbook showing 628 h used in the £17,221.45 calculation.

quotes.text: reduced from 30 min each to 15 min each
Session preparation (15 min assumed)

issues.title: Usual-care adjusted NHS/PSS cost £1378.58 (Table 3) vs £1399.74 (Table 6) though only intervention arm changed
issues.explanation: The scenario changes only the intervention cost, yet the usual-care adjusted mean cost differs by about £21 between Tables 3 and 6. The societal usual-care mean also appears to move, from 7054.38 to 7032.38. The cost reduction implied for the intervention arm also differs between perspectives. Re-estimation could explain this, but the paper does not say so and the effect is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the scenario models were re-run with new imputations/adjustment, or a clean Table 6 showing usual care at 1378.58.

10.1111/hex.70399.headline_claim: The LC-OHP is feasible and acceptable for people with long COVID, and trends in the data show promise for improvements across outcomes, supporting a fully powered RCT.
10.1111/hex.70399.overall: The feasibility and acceptability conclusions are reasonably supported by recruitment (60 of target 60), completion (50/60, 83%) and adherence data. The statements of potential benefit across all outcomes and an early advantage over control rest only on within-arm trends with an improving control group, and should be read as hypothesis-generating at most.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (recruitment, retention, adherence) and acceptability

issues.title: Feasibility trial claims improvement across all outcomes and a 3-month advantage over control without between-arm analysis
issues.explanation: The Results report only within-group direction of change, with the control group also improving on most measures and a caution that comparisons need to reflect baseline scores. The Summary nevertheless says the programme has potential to improve all outcomes and that the intervention group seems better than control at 3 months. Within-arm change and an unadjusted direction cannot show a between-arm difference, so these statements go beyond the evidence, though the main feasibility conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supporting File S1 showing between-arm differences in change with baseline adjustment and intervals that support the 3-month advantage claim.

quotes.text: These initial data suggest the LC -OHP has the potential to lead improvements across all outcomes at 3 and 6 months.
Additionally, those in the intervention group seem to have more favourable outcomes in the short -term (3 months) compared to the control group.
Outcomes scores in the control group also demonstrated some improvements apart from self -efficacy (GSE) at 6 months.

10.1111/hex.70517.headline_claim: PCE-CfD (person-centred experiential counselling for depression) was effective for depression, anxiety and functioning in people with Long Covid treated in an NHS Talking Therapies service, with outcomes exceeding NHS targets and supporting its continued use.
10.1111/hex.70517.overall: The pre-post improvements are internally consistent: the Cohen's d values match t/sqrt(31). They come from a single uncontrolled cohort of completers only, with 18.4% of treated patients excluded. The claim of high efficacy and benchmark-beating recovery is therefore not supported as stated, and the data support at most an encouraging, descriptive finding..

primary_outcome.name: PHQ-9 pre-post change (paired t-test)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post data (n=31) used to claim PCE-CfD is 'highly efficacious' for Long Covid depression
issues.explanation: All evidence is within-group change in one uncontrolled cohort, plus comparison of recovery percentages with national service targets. Neither can separate treatment effect from natural recovery, regression to the mean or concurrent care in the Post-Covid service. The authors say this themselves in section 5.4 but still describe the therapy as highly efficacious and effective, so the stated conclusion goes beyond the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or matched comparison group, or wording limited to describing observed change without efficacy claims.

quotes.text: the study used an uncontrolled before‐and‐after design
PCE‐CfD was deemed to be highly efficacious with people with Long Covid in this evaluation.
The significant improvements observed in patient‐reported outcomes provide valuable evidence supporting the continuation of PCE‐CfD being offered within NHS TTAD services

second_reader.what_stands: The data are indeed a single-arm, uncontrolled pre-post series of 31 completers, and the Discussion's phrase 'highly efficacious' is a causal-sounding label that this design cannot support; the paper's own Limitations section says as much. However, the paper does not rest on that claim unqualified: the abstract-level and concluding language is cautious ('encouraging', 'not generalisable', 'further research is recommended'), so the overstatement is confined to specific wording rather than the paper's overall conclusion.

issues.title: Outcomes analysed in 31 completers only; 7 of 38 treated patients (18.4%) excluded
issues.explanation: Seven patients who began treatment were left out of all outcome analyses, so recovery and improvement rates describe only people who finished. Completion was judged by the therapist at discharge, and dropout is often linked to poor response. The 90.32% and 77.42% figures are therefore likely higher than an intention-to-treat figure, yet they are compared directly with national targets and called highly efficacious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat analysis including the 7 non-completers that gives similar recovery and improvement rates.

quotes.text: These patients were excluded from all outcome analyses, but a comparison analysis was performed
we excluded clients who did not complete the treatment, as indicated by the therapist at discharge

second_reader.what_stands: Outcomes were analysed in 31 completers only, with 7 of 38 (18.4%) excluded, which is a per-protocol-type analysis that can inflate apparent effectiveness and recovery rates. The paper discloses this, notes the non-comparability with national figures, and recommends intention-to-treat in future, so the issue is a real analytic limitation that is acknowledged, not concealed.

issues.title: Table 1 maximum of 24 sessions exceeds the stated 20-session limit for PCE-CfD
issues.explanation: The therapy is described as time-limited to up to 20 sessions, yet Table 1 gives a maximum of 24 for the 31 completers. The paper does not say whether the protocol was exceeded or sessions were counted differently. This weakens how well the treatment dose is described, but it does not change the outcome results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 20-session cap is a guideline, or that extensions beyond 20 sessions were permitted.

quotes.text: time‐limited in nature (up to 20 sessions)
PCE‐CfD count

issues.title: All outcomes are unblinded patient self-report questionnaires
issues.explanation: Every outcome is self-reported by patients who knew they were being treated, so expectancy and social-desirability effects could add to the measured improvement. The bias is shared by all routine service data, and the paper discusses it only in general terms. It adds to, but does not independently change, the uncontrolled-design problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Independent clinician-rated or blinded outcome assessment agreeing with the self-reports.

quotes.text: Data collected consisted of patient self‐reported questionnaires that were completed before and after treatment.

issues.title: Therapist ethnicity percentages (87.5%/12.5%) imply 8 therapists, not the 9 stated
issues.explanation: The table note says 9 therapists delivered treatment, but the ethnicity split of 87.5% and 12.5% can only come from 8 (7/8 and 1/8). One therapist's ethnicity is probably missing and not mentioned. This is a trivial reporting gap that does not touch any outcome result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that ethnicity was missing for one therapist.

quotes.text: The therapist ethnicity breakdown is 87.5% White British, Irish or European and 12.5% Asian or Asian British.
For the 9 PCE‐CfD therapists, the gender breakdown included 7 Females, 1 Male and 1 Non‐binary.

10.1111/jebm.12465.headline_claim: QJYQ is a safe Chinese herbal medicine that can bring benefits to patients with post-COVID-19 condition, based on improved mMRC and Borg scores at 14 days added to standard rehabilitation.
10.1111/jebm.12465.overall: The headline of benefit on breathlessness and exertion rests on a small, open-label, 14-day comparison using patient-reported scales, with an unexplained GEE effect size and no multiplicity control. The safety claim goes further than 14 days of data allow. The direction of benefit is plausible, but the magnitude and certainty are weakly supported.

primary_outcome.name: mMRC scale (breathlessness) and Borg scale (perceived exertion and fatigue), both at 14 days

issues.title: Open-label, no placebo; both primary outcomes (mMRC, Borg) are patient-reported, differences small
issues.explanation: Participants knew they were receiving an herbal granule on top of standard rehabilitation, and the outcomes are subjective symptom ratings. Expectation and detection bias could produce differences of the size seen (about 0.14 mMRC points and 0.5 Borg points at day 14). The conclusion nonetheless states that benefit was demonstrated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that outcome assessors were blinded, or objective corroborating outcomes (e.g. 6MWD) that also favoured QJYQ.

quotes.text: This study was a randomized, open-label clinical trial to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of QJYQ for patients with PCC.
First, it was an openlabel study without placebo control, rather than the double- blind trial, which might cause selection bias and detection bias.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with no placebo (acknowledged by the authors) and both primary outcomes, mMRC and Borg, are self-reported, so unblinded participants could influence them. The observed between-group differences at 14 days (-0.14 on mMRC, -0.48 on Borg) are small relative to the scales; the paper does not state a minimal important difference, so clinical relevance is not assessed, and the conclusion does not weigh the blinding limitation against the 'benefit' claim.

issues.title: mMRC GEE β = -0.626 (CI width 0.95) does not match observed group differences of -0.02 to -0.15
issues.explanation: The observed mean mMRC differences are tiny (baseline +0.02, day 7 -0.15, day 14 -0.14) with SEMs of 0.03-0.05. The headline GEE estimate is about four times larger and its interval far wider than these data suggest. The model specification is not given, so readers cannot tell what the β represents, and the 6MWD β of 0.006 is on a scale that cannot be matched to the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated GEE specification (link, covariates, time coding) under which β = -0.626 is the expected effect.

quotes.text: The GEE estimated difference of the mMRC scale was [ β (95%CI) =-0.626 ( -1.101, -0.151); p = 0.010].
After 14 days of treatment, the score was 0.20 ± 0.03 in the QJYQ group and 0.34 ± 0.04 in the control group.

second_reader.what_stands: The reported mMRC beta (-0.626) is much larger than any observed between-group difference printed in Table 3 (+0.02, -0.15, -0.14), and the paper does not define the GEE model (covariates, time parametrisation, correlation structure) that would explain this; the CI and p-value are internally consistent with the beta. The mismatch is not necessarily an error, since model-based estimates can differ from raw means, so it is an unexplained inconsistency rather than a demonstrated miscalculation; the Borg beta (-0.395) is within the observed range and is not subject to this concern.

issues.title: Two primary outcomes at α = 0.05 each with no correction; Borg p = 0.026 exceeds Bonferroni 0.025
issues.explanation: No multiplicity strategy is stated for two primary outcomes, yet the conclusion treats both as confirmed. The Borg result (p = 0.026) is above the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.025. The subgroup findings are also uncorrected, though the authors label them exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified rule that either primary suffices, or a protocol that names one primary.

quotes.text: The GEE estimated difference of the Borg score was [ β (95%CI) =-0.395 ( -0.744, -0.046); p = 0.026].
Statistical tests were two-sided, and the significance level was set at α = 0.05.

issues.title: 'Safe' concluded from 14-day, open-label data; relatedness judged by unblinded investigators
issues.explanation: Liver-enzyme shifts were no more frequent with QJYQ (ALT 9 vs 10, AST 4 vs 8), which is reassuring. But a short course in an open-label trial, with attribution left to investigators who knew the allocation and no full adverse-event table, supports 'no safety signal observed' rather than a flat claim of safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full adverse-event table by arm with blinded causality assessment.

quotes.text: Theresults of this study provided evidence that QJYQ is a safe Chinese herbal medicine which can bring benefits to patients with PCC.
Noneoftheabnormalities in ALT and AST was considered to be related to QJYQ and SRTs by the assessment of clinical investigators.

issues.title: Males mMRC subgroup CI (-1.988, 0.053) spans zero but p = 0.039; fits an upper bound of -0.053
issues.explanation: The printed interval includes zero, which is incompatible with p = 0.039 and with the text calling QJYQ better in males. The estimate (-1.021) sits at the midpoint of (-1.988, -0.053), and that interval gives p of about 0.039, so the upper bound is probably a sign error. The correct bound would confirm the finding, so this is a reporting slip in an exploratory subgroup.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 4 showing the males interval as (-1.988, -0.053) in the original publication.

quotes.location: Results 3.2, subgroup analysis of mMRC, males

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0499 (reachable range [0.0497, 0.0501] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.039 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the CI includes the null (0.0), but the reported p = 0.039 says the result is significant

issues.title: Mean imputation for 4 dropouts (1.03%) in ITT analysis
issues.explanation: Mean imputation understates variance and is not a recommended approach. With about 1% missing data the impact on the primary results is very small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with complete cases or model-based imputation giving the same estimates.

quotes.text: following the intention to treat (ITT) principle with the mean imputation applied for missing data.

10.1111/pcn.13716.headline_claim: High-dose vitamin D supplementation may benefit patients with post-COVID syndrome by reducing fatigue, alleviating anxiety, and improving cognitive symptoms, with minimal side effects.
10.1111/pcn.13716.overall: The trial is a small, placebo-controlled, 8-week study with complete follow-up, and its hedged abstract conclusion ('may benefit') is broadly consistent with its nominal results. However, three positive findings at P 0.011-0.024 among about nine uncorrected outcomes, weak allocation concealment and an unsupported 'cost-effective' recommendation mean the benefit claims are tentative at best. One table cell (DASS-depression change) is misprinted but does not affect any conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: CFQ-11 fatigue and DASS-21 depression/anxiety subscales (primary outcomes as stated in Methods; Results also highlight CFQ, DASS-anxiety, ACE)

issues.title: About nine outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 uncorrected; three benefit claims rest on P = 0.011-0.024
issues.explanation: The trial tested CFQ, PSQI, two DASS subscales, ACE, two TMT measures, IL-6 and CRP, each in adjusted GEE models, with no multiplicity control. The three claimed benefits have P = 0.024, 0.011 and 0.012, and none would survive even a simple Bonferroni threshold across nine outcomes (about 0.0056). The authors acknowledge the type I error risk in the limitations, but the Conclusion presents fatigue, anxiety and cognition benefits as findings. Of the stated primary outcomes, only one of two (DASS-anxiety) was significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single primary outcome or hierarchical testing plan in the registry/protocol, or adjusted P values that remain below the corrected threshold.

quotes.text: increasing the risk of type I errors due to multiple comparisons
The results indicated statistically significant reductions in fatigue symptoms (CFQ, coefficient -3.5, P 0.024)
quotes.location: Results, Effectiveness of vitamin D supplementation

second_reader.what_stands: About nine outcomes were tested at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05 with no single primary outcome. The three claimed benefits (P = 0.011, 0.012, 0.024) would not survive Bonferroni or Holm correction for nine tests. The authors do acknowledge multiple comparisons in the limitations, but the conclusions are not tempered to match.

issues.title: Conclusion calls vitamin D 'cost-effective' and recommends it for deficient patients; no cost or subgroup data
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says incorporating vitamin D into PCS treatment appears to be a cost-effective and safe approach. The study collected no cost data, did not analyse by deficiency status, and had null results for depression, sleep, TMT, IL-6 and CRP, with the positive results uncorrected for multiplicity. The recommendation therefore goes beyond what an 80-patient, 8-week trial can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An economic analysis or a pre-specified deficiency-subgroup analysis supporting the statement.

quotes.text: appears to be a cost-effective and safe approach
While further evidence is necessary regarding the effects of vitamin D in PCS

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion calls supplementation 'cost-effective' and recommends it especially for deficient patients, but the paper reports no cost or cost-effectiveness data and no analysis by baseline deficiency. The recommendation therefore goes beyond what the trial measured, even though the sentence is hedged with 'appears to be' and an acknowledgement that more evidence is needed.

issues.title: 13 covariates in a GEE on 80 participants; adjusted coefficients nonetheless match raw change differences
issues.explanation: The primary models adjust for 13 covariates with only 80 participants, and the authors say this may have inflated effect estimates. Comparing the Table 2 raw change scores with the adjusted coefficients shows close agreement for CFQ and DASS-anxiety, so overfitting does not visibly drive those results. The covariate burden still adds model uncertainty and lacks a stated rationale, since randomization should make most adjustment unnecessary. It weakens confidence modestly rather than undermining any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified unadjusted or minimally adjusted analysis giving the same estimates and P values.

quotes.text: The inclusion of many covariates in our GEE analysis may have led to overfitting and inflated treatment effect estimates.

issues.title: Same researcher generated the allocation list, enrolled and assigned participants; no concealment described
issues.explanation: The paper says the main researcher generated the randomization, enrolled participants and assigned them. The list was kept inaccessible only to assessors, so nothing shows the enroller was blind to upcoming allocations, and blocks of four are guessable. Selection bias at enrolment therefore cannot be excluded. Balanced baseline data (Table 1) are reassuring, and the main effect is on self-reported outcomes assessed by blinded assistants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocol or registry text showing centralized or sealed opaque allocation concealed from the enrolling researcher.

quotes.text: The main researcher generated randomization, enrolled participants, and assigned them to groups.
it remained inaccessible to assessors until the completion of the last patient's follow-up

issues.title: Primary outcome defined inconsistently: DASS subscales named, sample size based on fatigue, CFQ/ACE headlined
issues.explanation: The Methods name DASS-depression and DASS-anxiety as the primary outcomes, yet the sample-size calculation uses fatigue scores, and the Results and Conclusion lead with CFQ fatigue and ACE cognition. DASS-depression, a named primary, was null. Without the registry entry it cannot be shown that primary outcomes changed, but the paper's own account of which outcome is primary is internally inconsistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registered primary outcome (TCTR20221013001) listing fatigue, anxiety and cognition as co-primary outcomes in advance.

quotes.text: In this study, we employed the subscale scores of DASS -depression and DASS -anxiety as our primary outcomes.
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, Outcomes and measurements

quotes.text: assessing vitamin D efficacy in post-COVID fatigue using visual analog scale fatigue scores

issues.title: DASS-depression vitamin D change printed -1.7 but 8th-week 3.6 minus baseline 5.6 gives -2.0
issues.explanation: In Table 2 the vitamin D group's DASS-depression means are 5.6 at baseline and 3.6 at week 8, so the change should be -2.0, but the table prints -1.7. The placebo row (5.0 to 4.7, -0.3) and the other rows reconcile, so this cell looks wrong. The corrected unadjusted difference would favour vitamin D slightly more. The adjusted result is non-significant (P = 0.085) and is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level data (Mendeley dataset) showing a mean individual change of -1.7 for the vitamin D group, e.g. from different denominators or timing.

quotes.location: Table 2, DASS - depression, Vitamin D row, mean difference column

10.1111/sms.14240.headline_claim: An 8-week supervised, tailored multicomponent exercise program improved quality of life, fatigue, depression, cardiovascular fitness and muscular strength in people with post-COVID-19 condition more than WHO self-management recommendations did.
10.1111/sms.14240.overall: The finding that supervised exercise improved fitness and strength more than a leaflet is plausible, but it comes from a small, unblinded trial with no named primary outcome and about 30 uncorrected comparisons, so the quality-of-life, fatigue and mood claims are tentative. The wording 'highly effective' and 'safe' goes beyond the data. Several text-table mismatches (final HR, Likert CFQ-11, brain fog, Table 1 denominators) are reporting slips that do not alone overturn the main results.

primary_outcome.name: not named in paper (registry lists 'Changes in subject clinical status')

issues.title: 'Highly effective' (NNT 1.82 on estimated VO2max) and 'safe' claims from 39 participants, unblinded
issues.explanation: The Discussion calls exercise highly effective based on an NNT of 1.82 for an estimated VO2max gain of at least 1 ml/kg/min. This outcome is a submaximal estimate in a small, unblinded trial. 'Safe' rests on the absence of reported adverse events in 19 exercised patients, with no stated surveillance method. The wording is stronger than the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified adverse event surveillance protocol and a larger or confirmatory trial supporting the effect.

quotes.text: meaning that physical exercise is highly effective in these patients
may be an effective, safe, and well-  tolerated intervention in post-  COVID-  19 conditions

second_reader.what_stands: 'Highly effective' rests on an NNT of 1.82 that cannot be reproduced from the printed means and SDs (these give roughly 4 to 9). It concerns a submaximal-test estimate of VO2max in 39 participants, unblinded, with a threshold borrowed from cardiopulmonary disease populations. 'Safe' rests on zero reported adverse events in 19 participants, which cannot rule out an event rate of about 16%. The paper also does not describe how adverse events were collected, and it withdrew participants with attendance below 85%.

issues.title: About 30 outcomes tested at p<0.05 with no primary outcome; many headline p-values are 0.02-0.045
issues.explanation: Table 2 compares about 30 variables by ANCOVA at an unadjusted 0.05 level. Bonferroni is stated only for the fitness ANOVA. Many of the claimed benefits (SF-12 PA 0.024, FSS 0.024, PHQ-9 0.021, VO2max 0.035, HR 0.045, PCSF 0.033) have p-values that would not survive any reasonable correction. The main finding is therefore best read as hypothesis-generating for those outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a hierarchical testing plan or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis showing the main results hold.

quotes.text: The significance level was set at p < 0.05.
with Bonferroni adjustment was used to analyze the differences between groups for physical fitness markers

second_reader.what_stands: Table 2 tests about 30 outcomes at an unadjusted p<0.05, and the paper names no primary outcome. Many of the significant results lie between 0.018 and 0.045, and none would survive a Bonferroni correction across 30 tests. The correction was applied only to the Figure 1 fitness ANOVA, and the sample size calculation hints at VO2max as the intended primary outcome without stating it.

issues.title: Unblinded supervised exercise vs leaflet; headline gains in self-reported fatigue, QoL and mood
issues.explanation: The exercise arm had supervised sessions three times a week and the control arm had a self-management leaflet. The paper does not describe any blinding of assessors or outcome handling. The fatigue, quality-of-life and depression results are self-reported and may reflect expectation or attention effects. This weakens those results as evidence of a specific exercise effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of blinded outcome assessment and of how self-report questionnaires were collected without knowledge of allocation.

quotes.text: Participants from the experimental group completed 8 weeks of a tailored and supervised
to follow the WHO guidelines: Support for Rehabilitation

second_reader.what_stands: The comparison is supervised exercise against an unsupervised leaflet, with no attention-matched control. Participants cannot have been blind to allocation, and the paper reports no blinding procedure. The headline fatigue, quality-of-life and mood gains are self-reported and so open to expectation and attention effects. The registry's single masking does not remove this for patient-reported outcomes.

issues.title: Final HR change in Results (-50.0% vs -13.3%, p = 0.01) contradicts Table 2 (about -1.2% vs -6.8%, p = 0.045)
issues.explanation: The Results give the final heart rate change as -50.0% vs -13.3% with p = 0.01. These are the same figures as the Likert CFQ-11 change. Table 2 shows only small HR changes and a group-effect p of 0.045. The HR sentence is therefore misreported, and the cardiovascular claim rests on a weaker p-value than the text states.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text HR percentages and p come from a different analysis (for example a mean of individual percent changes) with matching data.

quotes.location: Table 2, Final HR row, exercise post

issues.title: No named primary outcome; sample size based on aerobic capacity; registered primary is a broad 'clinical status'
issues.explanation: The paper never names a primary outcome. The power calculation uses aerobic capacity, while the Discussion emphasises quality of life and fatigue. The registered primary outcome is too general to match to any one measure. It cannot be determined from the paper whether the headline outcomes were those prespecified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history or protocol that defines the primary outcome as VO2max or a specific scale and the statistical analysis plan.

quotes.text: We hypothesized that the intervention would
significantly improve health markers for the quality of life and fatigue

issues.title: Table 1 exercise-group percentages use denominator 18 in some rows and 19 in others
issues.explanation: Most exercise-group percentages in Table 1 correspond to 19 participants (for example 8/19 = 42.1%). Other rows give percentages that only fit 18 (for example 12 (66.7), 11 (61.1), 7 (38.9), 2 (11.1), 6 (33.3)). The analysed n at baseline is therefore inconsistent, and the paper does not say whether a participant was dropped or missing data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table note explaining missing data for those rows.

quotes.location: Table 1, Brain fog row, exercise column

issues.title: Likert CFQ-11: -50.0%/-13.3%, p=0.008 in Results vs -48.2%/-11.7%, p=0.02 in Discussion; Table 2 p=0.018
issues.explanation: The same fatigue comparison is given with two sets of percentage changes and three different p-values across Results, Discussion and Table 2. The Results percentages match the table means, but the Discussion values do not and the calculation basis is not stated. The effect is still significant in every version, so the conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion uses mean individual changes and that p = 0.008 comes from a distinct test.

quotes.text: Likert CFQ-  11: -50.0% versus -13.3, p = 0.008
Likert CFQ-  11 score (-48.2% vs. -11.7%, p = 0.02)

issues.title: Planned n = 38 (19 per group) vs 39 randomised (20/19); no CONSORT flow or analysed n per outcome
issues.explanation: The target was 38, but 39 were randomised with 20 in control. This difference is trivial by itself. More relevant, the paper says it followed CONSORT yet gives no flow diagram. It reports one dropout, but not how many were analysed for each outcome. The registry lists 83 enrolled participants, which is not explained in the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow diagram showing 39 randomised and the analysed n per outcome, with the 83 registry count explained.

quotes.text: we recruited 19 participants per group ( n = 38)
randomly assigned into control ( n = 20) and exercise ( n = 19) groups

issues.title: Discussion gives brain fog 55.5% but Table 1 counts (10+11 of 39) give 53.8%, same as memory problems
issues.explanation: Brain fog and memory problems have identical counts in Table 1, yet the Discussion gives them different percentages. The counts support 53.8% for both. This is a minor reporting slip in a descriptive sentence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different symptom count for brain fog in the full dataset.

quotes.text: brain fog [55.5%], memory problems [53.8%]

issues.title: Adherence rule: 85% stated but 20 of 24 sessions is 83.3%
issues.explanation: The Methods define the attendance threshold as 85% and equate it with 20 of 24 sessions. 20/24 is 83.3%. A cosmetic inconsistency in a protocol description.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the arithmetic is simple.

quotes.text: Attendance ≥ 85% (at least 20 of the 24 scheduled sessions)

script.explanation: 20/24 = 83.33%, but the paper prints 85.0, outside the rounding interval [84.95, 85.10]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 23.5 rather than 24.

10.1113/ep092099.headline_claim: A 12-week supervised HIIT scheme preserved left ventricular mass at 12-month follow-up in people previously hospitalised for COVID-19, whereas LVM decreased in the standard care group, with no between-group effect on pulmonary diffusing capacity, symptoms or functional capacity.
10.1113/ep092099.overall: The central finding (a 9.7 g between-group LVM difference from a prespecified randomised comparison) is reported with generally sound methods. It comes from a trial that recruited about 58% of its planned sample, and the effect disappears when LVM is indexed to body surface area. The headline should be read as tentative, and several small numeric slips (participant counts, a Table 4 percentage, a sign on the LVSV difference) need correcting but do not change the main result.

primary_outcome.name: Change in left ventricular mass (LVM, grams) by cardiac MRI from baseline to 12 months

issues.title: Preserved-LVM claim rests on absolute LVM; BSA-indexed difference null (P = 0.24) and HIIT body weight rose
issues.explanation: The headline says HIIT preserved LVM and 'specifically' targets cardiac effects of COVID-19. The between-group difference is significant for absolute LVM (P = 0.0182) but not once indexed to body surface area (2.51 g/m2, P = 0.24). The HIIT group also gained significant fat-free mass and weight, and the authors note LVM follows these closely. This limitation appears only in the Discussion, not in the highlights or abstract, so the headline is more certain than the data support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A BSA- or lean-mass-adjusted LVM analysis showing a significant between-group difference.

quotes.text: LVM was maintained in the HIIT but not the standard care group
as indicated by the lack of statistically significant differences when using BSA-indexed measures

second_reader.what_stands: It is true that the 'preserved LVM' claim in the Abstract rests on absolute LVM (9.68 g, P = 0.018), that the BSA-indexed difference is not significant (2.51 [-1.71, 6.73], P = 0.24), and that HIIT body weight rose by 3.61 kg more than control; the Discussion itself notes the BSA-indexed null and links LVM to weight/fat-free mass. What does not stand is any suggestion that this is undisclosed: the caveat appears in the Discussion, but not in the Abstract, Highlights or Conclusion, and the indexed CI is wide enough that it neither confirms nor excludes a real effect (roughly half the absolute d

issues.title: Recruited 28 of 48 planned participants (14 per arm); significant LVM result with wide CI, shortfall not discussed
issues.explanation: The sample size calculation required 24 per arm, but only 14 per arm were randomised. The LVM result (9.68 g, 95% CI 1.72 to 17.64, P = 0.0182) is borderline in precision and could be inflated. The limitations section does not mention the shortfall or its effect on power. The hedged wording keeps the conclusion tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A revised power calculation showing adequate power with 14 per arm, or a statement in the limitations addressing the reduced sample.

quotes.text: Inclusion of 24 participants in each group would provide a statistical power ((1 -β ) × 100%) of 86% with a two-sided significance level of 0.05
A total of 28 participants were included in the final ITT analysis at 12months(HIIT: n = 14, control: n = 14).

issues.title: Pre-hospital activity imbalance (control 9/14 vs HIIT 2/14 light) and BMI difference not addressed
issues.explanation: Controls were far more often in the lowest pre-hospital activity category than HIIT participants, and mean BMI differed by 3.6 kg/m2. The analysis adjusts only for sex. Because the authors themselves attribute the control LVM decline partly to inactivity, this baseline difference could contribute to the between-group LVM difference. This is probably chance imbalance but is not examined.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis adjusting for pre-hospital activity and BMI that leaves the LVM difference unchanged.

quotes.text: Physical activity level before hospitalisation ( n )
The cause of this remains speculative, but it may either reflect diseasespecific effects on the heart

issues.title: Analysed numbers disagree: 13 per arm (Fig 2), 14 per arm (Tables 2-3), 22 cMRI completers vs 23 implied
issues.explanation: The Figure 2 legend gives n = 13 per arm for the ITT analysis, while the Table 2 and Table 3 notes give n = 14 per arm for the same analysis. The text says 24 completed follow-up and 22 had cMRI. The Figure 1 caption accounts for only 4 non-attenders and 1 missed MRI, which would give 23. The size of the primary-outcome analysis set cannot be pinned down, though the error is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT figure showing a second MRI exclusion, and a statement that Figure 2 plots 13 per arm for a stated reason (e.g. unanalysable images).

quotes.text: White is the control (standard care) group ( n = 13) and black is the intervention (HIIT) group ( n = 13).
Data are provided for the intention-to-treat analysis (control group [standard care], n = 14; intervention group [HIIT], n = 14).
Thus, a total of 22 participants completed cMRI at 12 months.

issues.title: LVSV between-group difference printed as -3.91 but its CI [-6.50, 14.32] is centred on +3.91
issues.explanation: The LVSV between-group estimate is printed as -3.91 mL, yet the interval -6.50 to 14.32 has its midpoint at +3.91. A symmetric Wald interval cannot be centred 3.91 above its estimate, so the sign is most likely wrong. The direction of the LVSV effect is therefore misreported, although the P value (0.455) is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source output showing a negative estimate with an asymmetric (e.g. bootstrap) interval.

quotes.text: between-group difference -3.91 [ -6.50, 14.32] mL, P = 0.455

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.4616 (reachable range [0.4608, 0.4624] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.455 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Table 1 relative VO2peak: both arms 22.3 ± 7.8 but total 22.8 ± 7.6
issues.explanation: Both groups print identical values (22.3 ± 7.8) with n = 14 each, so the combined mean must be 22.3. The Total column prints 22.8 ± 7.6. One of the three entries is mistyped. This is a baseline descriptive and does not affect the trial's results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the group means really are 22.3 and 22.8 and the printed duplicates are a transcription slip.

quotes.location: Table 1, VO2peak (mL/min/kg), Control and Intervention columns

issues.title: Table 4 HIIT 12-month column: 1 of 13 printed as 7.1% (should be 7.7%)
issues.explanation: In the HIIT 12-month column the 10 is shown as 76.9% (denominator 13), but each of the three 1s is shown as 7.1%, which is 1/14. The counts sum to 13, so the percentages in that column do not share one denominator. The percentages as printed sum to about 98%. This is a minor reporting error in a descriptive table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a 14th HIIT participant was in the 12-month PCFS denominator for those rows only.

quotes.text: intervention group (HIIT, n = 13)

script.explanation: 1/13 = 7.69%, but the paper prints 7.1, outside the rounding interval [7.05, 7.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 14.1 rather than 13.

issues.title: No trial registry identifier given in the paper
issues.explanation: The article does not print a trial registration number. It points to a protocol paper and a pre-analysis SAP on OSF instead. The SAP largely mitigates concern about outcome switching, but a registry ID in the paper itself would allow checking.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record (e.g. ClinicalTrials.gov) with matching primary outcome, registered before enrolment.

quotes.text: the study protocol has been published elsewhere (Rasmussen et al., 2021)
The statistical analysis plan is provided elsewhere and was published online in detailed form before any analyses were conducted

10.1126/scitranslmed.adu4284.headline_claim: Larazotide as adjuvant therapy was associated with faster spike antigen clearance, faster gastrointestinal symptom resolution, and faster return to usual activities than placebo in children with MISC, and may be safe.
10.1126/scitranslmed.adu4284.overall: The headline claims of faster spike clearance, faster GI recovery and faster return to usual activities rest on Fisher P values that cannot be reproduced from the printed counts, and the prespecified day-21 GI endpoint was null. Only the win-ratio analysis and the safety observations remain, and both are tentative in 11 to 12 children. The conclusions should be read as hypothesis-generating at most.

primary_outcome.name: Proportion of children with improvement in GI symptoms with no MISC progression, through day 21

primary_outcomes.measure: Evaluate the efficacy and safety of AT1001 versus placebo on mitigating symptoms of MIS-C
Determine proportion of participants with improvement in MIS-C related GI symptoms and no progression of disease

issues.title: Spike-clearance Fisher P values (0.002, <0.001, <0.0001) impossible for 3 vs 5 children; counts give P≥0.1
issues.explanation: Fig. 3B compares 3 placebo with 5 larazotide children, and the legend gives the clearance counts. The smallest two-sided Fisher P with groups of 3 and 5 is about 0.036, so P = 0.002, P < 0.001 and P < 0.0001 cannot arise. The legend counts (1/3 vs 3/5 by day 7, 1/3 vs 4/5 by day 14, 2/3 vs 5/5 by day 21) give non-significant P values. The headline claim of accelerated spike clearance is therefore not supported by the stated tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that these P values come from a different test or a larger set of samples, or a corrected figure where the counts reproduce them.

quotes.text: P = 0.002, P < 0.001, and P < 0.0001, respectively
quotes.location: Results, Larazotide accelerates clearance of spike protein antigen

quotes.text: n = 8 children: three in the placebo group and five in the larazotide

second_reader.what_stands: With the counts the paper itself gives (3 vs 5 children), the two-sided Fisher P values are about 1.0, 0.46 and 0.38 at days 7, 14 and 21, so the reported 0.002, <0.001 and <0.0001 cannot be reproduced. The text and legend also disagree on the placebo denominator (4 vs 3), but the alternative denominator does not change this conclusion.

issues.title: Day 7 and 14 GI recovery Fisher P<0.001 not reproducible: 1/5 vs 4/6 gives two-sided P≈0.24
issues.explanation: The text reports P < 0.001 for GI recovery at days 7 and 14. The legend counts are 1 of 5 placebo and 4 of 6 larazotide at both days, and the exact test on these counts is nowhere near 0.001. With groups of 5 and 6 no table can reach P < 0.001 under any outcome split of this kind. The claimed significance of the primary-type GI endpoint is not supported by the printed counts.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level data showing different counts, or a stated different test that gives P < 0.001.

quotes.text: P < 0.001) and day 14
and 4, 4, and 4, respectively

second_reader.what_stands: The printed counts give a two-sided Fisher P of about 0.24 at both day 7 and day 14, not P<0.001. The text's own statement that day 21 showed no difference also fits these counts.

issues.title: Return-to-health/activities Fisher P=0.002 inconsistent with 2/5 vs 4/6 (two-sided P≈0.57)
issues.explanation: The text reports P = 0.002 for return to usual health and usual activities at days 14 and 21. The legend gives 2 of 5 placebo and 4 of 6 larazotide children at both days, which is a small, non-significant difference. Neither this nor the identical P for activities can be produced from these counts. The claim of faster return to usual activities is not supported by the printed numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the P value refers to a different comparison, or corrected counts that reproduce 0.002.

quotes.text: Fisher’s exact test, P = 0.002
quotes.location: Results, Larazotide has lasting impact on quality of life and recovery

quotes.text: and two, four, and four, respectively

second_reader.what_stands: The printed counts (2/5 vs 4/6) give a two-sided Fisher P of about 0.57 for both return to usual health and return to usual activities, not 0.002. The 'greater in larazotide' statement is a difference of proportions that is nowhere near significant on these counts.

issues.title: Null day-21 primary GI endpoint presented as faster GI resolution in Abstract and Discussion
issues.explanation: The primary efficacy endpoint is GI improvement through day 21, and the Results admit no significant difference by day 21. The Abstract and Discussion nonetheless state that larazotide produced faster GI resolution, based on day 7 and 14 comparisons that were not shown to be prespecified. The disclosure in Results does not carry into the headline claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registered or protocol-specified analysis of GI recovery at days 7 and 14 as the primary comparison.

quotes.text: Children treated with larazotide displayed faster resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms

second_reader.what_stands: The prespecified primary endpoint (GI improvement through day 21) shows no difference, and the Abstract and Discussion present 'faster resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms' without saying that the primary comparison was null. The Results text does disclose the null day-21 result, and the faster-recovery claim rests on day 7 and 14 comparisons whose reported P values do not match the printed counts.

issues.title: 12 of 20 planned children, no power calculation; efficacy stated more firmly than the data allow
issues.explanation: The trial enrolled 12 children against a planned 20, with no formal sample size justification. The authors accept that group differences may reflect cohort differences rather than drug. Despite that, the Discussion states that the evidence supports use of larazotide and that it serves as a beneficial adjuvant, which a 6 vs 5 or 6 comparison with several irreproducible P values cannot establish.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified exploratory framing of the efficacy outcomes throughout, with no claim of benefit.

quotes.text: A sample size of 20 was planned, balancing feasibility
it is possible that intrinsic differences between the cohorts contributed

second_reader.what_stands: It is true that only 12 of 20 planned children were enrolled and that no power calculation is reported. The shortfall and the possibility of cohort imbalance are acknowledged. However, parts of the text ('we show that larazotide serves as a beneficial adjuvant', 'supports the use', 'should be considered') are stronger than a 12-child study with several irreproducible P values can support, and the stated ITT population (12) differs from the 11 or fewer analysed.

issues.title: Registry primary GI outcome time frame is 24 weeks; paper defines primary window as day 21
issues.explanation: The current registry record gives a 24-week time frame for the GI primary outcome, whereas the paper evaluates it through day 21 (where it is null). The paper also reports the long-term follow-up, so nothing is hidden, but the difference is not explained. Earlier registry versions are unavailable, so it cannot be settled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registered record history showing day 21 was the original timeframe.

quotes.text: no progression of MISC through day 21
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, Primary and secondary end points

issues.title: 'Validated the safety profile' from 12 children and recommendation for other forms of PASC
issues.explanation: Safety is based on 11 treated children with 52 vs 50 mild or moderate events, which cannot exclude uncommon adverse effects. The Discussion says the safety profile was validated, and the Conclusion recommends considering larazotide in other forms of PASC that were not studied. These statements go beyond a small phase 2a trial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to 'no safety signal was observed in this small cohort' and no recommendation beyond MISC.

quotes.text: we validated the safety profile of larazotide
larazotide should be considered as an adjuvant

issues.title: Primary GI endpoint analysed as ad hoc ≥90% PedsQL recovery; clinical-manifestation component not reported
issues.explanation: The Methods define the primary endpoint as improvement in PedsQL GI score and in clinical manifestations. The Results instead analyse a caregiver-reported 90% recovery threshold and show no clinical-exam component. The threshold appears chosen after the fact and the authors note that no validated MISC measure existed, which limits how the GI result can be interpreted. The drug-effect conclusion on GI symptoms is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry predefining the 90% threshold and the composite.

quotes.text: recovery from gastrointestinal symptoms (90% or greater across all gastrointestinal symptom categories)
validated assessments of MISC or other forms of PASC were not yet available

issues.title: 'ITT = all randomized' stated, but most analyses use 11 children (placebo n=5, spike antigen placebo n=3)
issues.explanation: The Methods say the primary analysis was on all randomized participants (12). The primary GI outcome and Fig. 4 analyses have five placebo children, and Table 1 shows four placebo children with spike antigen, against three in the spike analyses. The excluded child (non-completer of dosing, in the placebo group) is dropped without explanation, so the analysis is not the stated ITT set. With such small groups, removing one child can alter the comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the non-completing child had no outcome data for any assessment, with a sensitivity analysis including that child.

quotes.text: Four children in the placebo group (one of whom did not
quotes.location: Results, Larazotide accelerates clearance of spike protein antigen

quotes.text: Three children in the placebo group and five children

issues.title: Dozens of Fisher tests across days and domains with no correction or hierarchy; only correlation matrix adjusted
issues.explanation: Efficacy is tested at days 7, 14, 21 and later, across GI domains, health, activities, irritability and spike clearance. The Methods describe no correction for these binary tests, and the conclusions cite the comparisons that came out significant. This weakens the secondary and exploratory claims, though the win ratio is a single prespecified composite.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified testing hierarchy or adjusted P values for the binary endpoints.

quotes.text: Multiple comparisons were completed with
Additional binary end points were analyzed by Fisher’s

issues.title: Follow-up counts in Fig. 4 do not fit one larazotide patient lost after day 112 (placebo 3 at day 140, 5 at day 168)
issues.explanation: The text says one larazotide patient was lost to follow-up after day 112. Yet the legend still has five larazotide respondents at days 140 and 168 while day 112 is five, and the placebo respondents go 4, 4, 3, then 5. Response numbers can rise if missed visits were later completed, but this is unexplained. The effect is minor, because late follow-up is secondary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that responses at day 112 were missing for a patient who later returned data, or a corrected legend.

quotes.text: one patient assigned to the larazotide group completed dosing
quotes.location: Results, Design of the clinical trial

quotes.text: 9 children (four in the placebo group and five in the larazotide

issues.title: Table 2 placebo musculoskeletal 6 (10%) of 50 events should be 12%; placebo organ counts sum to 51
issues.explanation: The placebo musculoskeletal cell prints 6 events and 10%, but 6 of 50 is 12%. The placebo organ-system counts also add to 51 against a total of 50, and a count of 5 would fix both. It is a transcription slip with no bearing on the safety conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote explaining that percentages use a different base.

quotes.text: Musculoskeletal 2 (4) 6 (10)

script.explanation: 6/50 = 12.00%, but the paper prints 10, outside the rounding interval [9.50, 11.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 60.0 rather than 50.

10.11336/jjcrs.14.10.headline_claim: Rehabilitation in a convalescent ward improved respiratory, physical, and mental/functional conditions in moderate-to-severe COVID-19 patients, showing the ward can provide effective rehabilitation.
10.11336/jjcrs.14.10.overall: The descriptive finding that measures such as walking distance, SPPB, PCFS and FIM improved over the stay in 16 patients is plausible, but the claim that the ward provides effective rehabilitation is not supported by an uncontrolled, unblinded, completer-only series. Statistical handling is thin for small, skewed data, and Table 1 has two wrong percentages that do not affect the findings.

primary_outcome.name: not designated; multiple outcomes compared across admission, 4 weeks, and discharge

issues.title: Uncontrolled, unblinded before-after series used to conclude the ward provides effective rehabilitation
issues.explanation: All 16 patients were measured at admission, 4 weeks and discharge, with no comparison group and no blinding. Patients recovering from acute COVID-19 would be expected to improve spontaneously, so the changes cannot be attributed to the rehabilitation. Several outcomes are self-reported and open to expectation effects. The authors nonetheless state that the ward can provide effective rehabilitation, a causal claim the design cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A contemporaneous control group or historical comparator showing smaller recovery without rehabilitation.

quotes.text: This study was conducted as an observational study with no previous data for comparison
This result indicated that a convalescent rehabilitation ward can provide effective rehabilitation to
HADS  is  a  selfevaluation questionnaire

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is an uncontrolled single-group before-after series with no stated blinding, and it concludes that the convalescent ward 'can provide effective rehabilitation', which a design with no comparator cannot establish, since natural recovery cannot be separated from the effect of the ward. The authors do note small sample and single-site limits and report residual impairment at discharge, but they do not acknowledge the lack of a control group or of blinding as limits on the efficacy conclusion; the absence of blinding is an omission in reporting rather than something the paper states.

issues.title: Parametric repeated-measures ANOVA on skewed or ordinal data at n=16; mMRC p=0.050 starred as significant
issues.explanation: Several outcomes have SDs as large as or larger than their means, and others are ordinal scores. The paper does not report the Shapiro-Wilk results or the ANOVA statistics, so the validity of the post-hoc p-values cannot be judged. The mMRC admission-vs-4-weeks comparison is printed as 0.050 yet marked as p<0.05 and described as significant. Results are also unadjusted across eight outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported Shapiro-Wilk results showing normality, or a non-parametric sensitivity analysis giving the same conclusions.

quotes.text: The Bonferroni test was performed as a post-hoc test.
established a significance level of 5% for each item

issues.title: Analysis restricted to 16 of 17 patients; the patient who relapsed and returned to acute care is omitted
issues.explanation: Seventeen patients were enrolled, but the one who relapsed with worsening pneumonia was removed before analysis. All analysed patients are therefore those who did well enough to be discharged home. This favours the rehabilitation story and inflates apparent improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including the 17th patient's available data, showing the conclusions are unchanged.

quotes.text: returned to the acute care hospital
One patient was transferred to an acute care hospital due to acute aggravation, but all other patients were discharged to their homes.

issues.title: Table 1: hypertension 9 (62.5%) and depression 1 (16.7%) do not match n=16 (should be 56.3% and 6.3%)
issues.explanation: Table 1 is stated to describe 16 patients. Hypertension is printed as 9 (62.5%), the same count as dyslipidemia, which is correctly given as 56.3%. Depression is printed as 1 (16.7%), but one of 16 patients is 6.3%. These are two wrong cells in a baseline table; no efficacy result depends on them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that these percentages use a different denominator, or a corrected table showing 56.3% and 6.3%.

quotes.text: Table 1. Patient characteristics.( n = 16).

script.explanation: 9/16 = 56.25%, but the paper prints 62.5, outside the rounding interval [62.45, 62.60]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 14.4 rather than 16.

issues.title: Discussion's '57 days after onset' is unclear against median 32.0 days to ward and 57.5 hospital days
issues.explanation: The Discussion says improvements were confirmed about 57 days after onset. Table 1 gives a median of 32.0 days from onset to ward admission and a median of 57.5 days in hospital. If the latter is the ward stay, discharge would be nearer day 90 after onset. The hospital-days measure is undefined, so the timing statement is ambiguous rather than demonstrably wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition showing that hospital days run from onset, or the paper stating the ward-only stay.

quotes.text: approximately 57 days after onset

quotes.location: Table 1, convalescent ward admission from onset row

10.1136/annrheumdis-2022-eular.3861.headline_claim: A 2-week complex rehabilitation program including interval hypoxic-hyperoxic training (Reoxy therapy) reduces pain, breathlessness, depression and anxiety and improves functional status and general health in patients with OA and post-COVID syndrome.
10.1136/annrheumdis-2022-eular.3861.overall: The OA/post-COVID abstract is a small three-arm trial (13/9/14) with a 2-week follow-up. Its results are presented mostly as within-arm percentage changes, with no named between-group tests, no comparator data and no multiplicity handling. The confident conclusion of efficacy should be treated as preliminary. The RA abstract has a minor, unexplained drop from 111 to 102 patients.

primary_outcome.name: not specified (pain VAS reported first)

issues.title: Small three-arm trial (13/9/14) with no sample-size basis; efficacy conclusion stated without caveat
issues.explanation: Only 36 patients were randomised, so each arm has 9 to 14 people. No sample-size calculation is reported, and the follow-up is only 2 weeks. The conclusion reads as confirmed efficacy rather than a preliminary signal. Large percentage changes in small arms are unstable, so the confident wording goes beyond what this design can support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation or a full-paper version showing the trial was adequately powered for its primary outcome, or a conclusion worded as preliminary.

quotes.text: 36 patients with OA (78% females, age of 43 to 68 years, generalized OA, OA of the knee or hip joints) where included in the randomized placebo-controlled study.
reduces pain, breathlessness, depression and anxiety, improves functional status and general health in patients with OA and post-COVID syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: The arms are 13/9/14 (sum 36), and the abstract gives no sample-size justification or power calculation. The conclusion states efficacy in definitive terms without any caveat about small size or preliminary nature. The abstract format may explain the missing detail, but it does not remove the lack of caveat in the conclusion.

issues.title: About seven outcomes tested at p<0.05 with no primary outcome or multiplicity handling stated
issues.explanation: Pain, Lequesne, WOMAC, anxiety, depression, general health and breathlessness are each reported as significant, with no primary outcome named and no correction described. With this many tests, a few borderline p<0.05 results could arise by chance. Whether the authors corrected is not stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or a stated multiplicity correction.

quotes.text: anxiety level on Spielberger-Khanin test - by 40,9% (p<0,05)
Joint pain and general health on 100-mm VAS, Lequesne and WOMAC indexes, Spielberger-Khanin anxiety test, Beck depression inventory and breathlessness on Modified Borg scale

issues.title: Headline percentage gains are study-arm-only changes; between-group tests, effects and comparator data are unreported
issues.explanation: The percentages quoted are changes within the Reoxy group from baseline. The comparison with placebo and control is reduced to one sentence saying p<0.05 on every parameter, with no test, estimate, interval or comparator data. Readers cannot judge how much of the improvement beyond placebo or standard care is attributable to the treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table giving baseline and 2-week values for all three arms with the between-group test and effect estimates.

quotes.text: decreased by 49,6% (p<0,05)
In the study group there were statistically significant differences from the placebo group

issues.title: RA abstract: 111 women in Methods, 102 in the step-count subgroup analysis, 9 unexplained
issues.explanation: The RA abstract says 111 women were studied, but the later subgroup analysis uses 102 patients, with no account of the 9 missing. The gap is probably a data-availability issue for the step-count grouping, but it is not stated. The effect is small, and the main fatigue results are not tied to a specific denominator.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 9 patients lacked step-count data (or were otherwise excluded), or that the 111 was the enrolled number and 102 the analysed number.

quotes.text: The study included 111 women with RA
patients (n=102) were retrospectively  divided  into  two  groups

issues.title: Randomised trial abstract gives no registration or protocol reference
issues.explanation: The abstract describes a randomised placebo-controlled study but gives no registry identifier, ethics approval or protocol reference. This prevents checking the outcomes against a prior plan. It is a limitation of the abstract format more than evidence of a problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier or ethics approval statement in the full publication.

quotes.text: included in the randomized placebo-controlled study.

10.1136/bjsports-2022-106681.headline_claim: Home-based exercise training (HBET) improves physical domains of health-related quality of life, increases functional capacity and reduces some persistent symptoms in survivors of severe/critical COVID-19, and is presented as an effective and safe strategy.
10.1136/bjsports-2022-106681.overall: The primary result (higher SF-36 physical component score with exercise) is nominally significant, but it rests on an unblinded, self-reported outcome against a minimal-contact control, and its p-value is smaller than the printed CI implies. The secondary claims about functional capacity and symptoms depend on a few uncorrected borderline p-values among many nulls, and 'safe' rests on an informal staff statement in 50 participants. Registration concerns raised by the screen are not supported by the paper's own recruitment timeline.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 physical component summary (change from baseline to 16 weeks)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline on quality of life assessed by the SF-36 health survey questionnaire at 16 weeks.

issues.title: Self-reported SF-36 primary outcome in unblinded participants versus a minimal-contact control
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the primary outcome (SF-36 physical component summary) is a questionnaire the participants complete themselves. The control group received general advice and a check-in every 2 months, so there was no attention or activity placebo. The authors concede that benefits may be partly placebo effects, but the conclusion still says HBET 'improves' physical HRQoL. The size of the true effect is therefore uncertain, and the objective secondary outcomes were mostly null on intention-to-treat analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of a credible attention-matched or sham control, or concordant improvements in blinded objective measures supporting the SF-36 result.

quotes.text: it was not possible to blind the participants to the intervention; therefore, the benefits may be partially explained by placebo effects
CONTROL patients were contacted by phone or text message every 2 months
