second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome (SF-36 physical component summary) is self-reported, participants were unblinded, and the control arm received only a minimal check-in every 2 months with no attention-matched contact, so expectation and attention effects could inflate the between-group difference. The authors do acknowledge this in the limitations, but the estimate is not discounted for it and the conclusion is stated without that caveat; the assessor-blinded objective outcomes give only limited corroboration (sit-to-stand borderline at p=0.048, other ITT objective outcomes null).

issues.title: Functional and symptom conclusions rest on 3 uncorrected p-values (0.048, 0.020, 0.025) among dozens of tests
issues.explanation: Dozens of secondary outcomes were tested at alpha 0.05 without any correction across outcomes. The claims of increased functional capacity and reduced persistent symptoms rest on the sit-to-stand result (p=0.048, lower CI bound 0.01) and two symptom proportions (p=0.020 and 0.025), while handgrip, timed-up-and-go, PCFS, fatigue, dyspnoea and total symptoms were not significant. With this many comparisons, a few such p-values are expected by chance, so these conclusions are tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or multiplicity-adjusted p-values for these outcomes that remain significant.

quotes.text: Significance level was set at p ≤0.05.
reduces some persistent symptoms in this population

issues.title: 'Effective and safe' conclusion rests on an informal staff judgement of adverse events in 50 participants
issues.explanation: The paper has no prespecified safety outcome or described ascertainment procedure, and says only that no adverse events were reported 'according to our medical staff'. With 25 exercisers, the data cannot rule out uncommon harms such as post-exertional symptom exacerbation. The conclusion states the programme is safe and effective without qualification, while the limitations say results cannot be extrapolated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, systematically collected adverse-event protocol with event counts by arm and attribution rules.

quotes.text: This model of exercise emerges as an effective and safe therapeutic strategy
were reported according to our medical staff
We cannot extrapolate our results to other clinical populations

issues.title: SF-36 p-values smaller than their CIs imply: primary p<0.001 (CI implies ~0.003); vitality p=0.015 (CI implies ~0.05)
issues.explanation: For the primary outcome, EMD 16.8 with 95% CI 5.8 to 27.9 gives SE of about 5.6, z of about 3.0 and p of about 0.003, yet p<0.001 is printed. For vitality, EMD 15.1 with CI 0.2 to 30.1 gives z of about 1.97 and p of about 0.05, yet p=0.015 is printed. The CI and p appear to come from different contrasts or models, and this is not explained. The primary result stays nominally significant, but the reported strength of evidence is overstated and the vitality finding is borderline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that the printed p-values come from a different contrast or test than the printed CIs, or corrected values.

quotes.text: EMD: 16.8 points

script.explanation: the reported 'p < 0.001' is unreachable at the STATED 95% confidence level (recoverable p [0.0027, 0.0031]); it reconciles only if the interval is a 99% CI, which is not what the paper says. Either the level, the interval or the p is misreported

issues.title: Discussion gives fatigue severity ES 0.79; Table 4 FSS row prints ES 0.71
issues.explanation: The Discussion reports effect sizes of 0.90 and 0.79 for total symptoms and fatigue severity. Table 4 prints 0.90 for symptoms per patient but 0.71 for the FSS score. One of the two figures is wrong. The FSS between-group difference is not significant (p=0.173), so the slip affects a descriptive claim only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 0.79 comes from a different, labelled analysis, or an erratum showing Table 4 is the misprinted value.

quotes.text: fatigue severity (ES: 0.90 and 0.79, respectively)

10.1136/bmj.o1212.headline_claim: An online singing-based breathing and wellbeing programme (ENO Breathe) significantly reduces breathlessness and improves quality of life in people with long covid.
10.1136/bmj.o1212.overall: The primary finding, a 10.48 point reduction in breathlessness versus usual care in a single-blind randomised trial, is reported plainly, but this is a short news summary with no confidence intervals or p-values. The unqualified quality-of-life claim and the attender-only subgroup findings should be read cautiously; the effect on quality of life is limited to mental health scores.

primary_outcome.name: Breathlessness while running (0-100 scale)

issues.title: Opening says quality of life improved; only mental health improved slightly, physical health did not
issues.explanation: The opening summary says the programme significantly reduces breathlessness and improves quality of life. The results paragraph says only mental health scores improved slightly and physical health scores did not. The unqualified headline claim therefore overstates the quality-of-life finding, though the primary breathlessness result is reported correctly and the nuance is given a few paragraphs later.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the headline that quality-of-life gains were limited to the mental component, or a primary quality-of-life result showing significant overall improvement.

quotes.text: has been found to significantly reduce breathlessness and improve quality of life for people with long covid.
Mental health scores on a quality of life measure also improved slightly, although physical health scores did not.

issues.title: Lead author attributes gains to breathing techniques and delivery style, which the design cannot separate
issues.explanation: The quoted author attributes improvement to both the breathing techniques and the creative, humane delivery. A comparison with usual care tests the whole package, so it cannot apportion benefit between components. The wording is hedged ('suggests') and the focus-group data may partly inform it, so this is a weak interpretive point.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Qualitative or mediation data in the trial report supporting the separate contribution of each component.

quotes.text: Our study suggests that the improvements in symptoms experienced by participants resulted from both practical breathing techniques learnt, but also the creative, humane, and positive way the programme is delivered.
quotes.location: 'Can we end on a high note?' section

issues.title: Wider benefits reported only for participants attending all sessions, not labelled as non-randomised
issues.explanation: The summary reports improvements in wider respiratory symptoms, anxiety and quality of life only among those who attended all sessions. Restricting to attenders breaks the randomised comparison and favours adherers. The primary result is presented separately first, and no figures are given, so the weight placed on this is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The trial report showing these were pre-specified secondary analyses on the full randomised sample or a per-protocol analysis clearly labelled as such.

quotes.text: Patients who attended all the sessions were also found to have improvements in a wider range of respiratory symptoms, anxiety, and quality of life.

10.1136/bmj.q346.headline_claim: A supervised eight-week online group rehabilitation programme (Regain) can improve health-related quality of life compared with usual care in adults with long covid, with improvements sustained at 12 months and an acceptable safety profile.
10.1136/bmj.q346.overall: The trial shows a small, statistically significant patient-reported improvement versus a minimal-contact usual-care comparator, but it is unmasked and the effect size is only 0.03 with no threshold for importance. The claim of clinical benefit is plausible but is stated more confidently than the design and effect size support.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS preference score (health-related quality of life) at 3 months

issues.title: Unmasked trial with patient-reported primary outcome and a 0.03 PROMIS difference
issues.explanation: Neither participants nor practitioners could be masked, and the primary outcome (PROMIS preference score) is self-reported. With a small effect of 0.03, even modest expectation or reporting bias could account for a meaningful share of the difference. The limitation is acknowledged but the conclusion of clinical benefit is still stated firmly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of objective outcomes agreeing with the self-reported benefit, or sensitivity analyses showing no expectation effect.

quotes.text: the inability of trial participants or Regain practitioners to be masked to treatment allocation
patient reported outcomes measurement information system (PROMIS) preference score 0.03

issues.title: 'Clinical benefit' stated for a 0.03 PROMIS difference with CI lower bound 0.01 and no threshold
issues.explanation: The primary effect is 0.03 with a 95% CI of 0.01 to 0.05, and no minimal important difference is given in the text. Calling this clinical benefit and 'high quality' evidence is stronger than the effect size and the unmasked design support. Also, P=0.02 is printed for a CI of 0.01 to 0.05 which is consistent only roughly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified minimal important difference for the PROMIS preference score that the effect and CI exceed.

quotes.text: provided the first high quality randomised controlled trial evidence of clinical benefit and lack of harm

issues.title: Minimal-contact usual-care comparator (one advice session vs eight weeks of group sessions)
issues.explanation: The control received a single online session while the intervention involved eight weeks of supervised group contact. Attention and social contact differences cannot be separated from the programme's specific components. This is a reasonable pragmatic choice but limits attribution to exercise or psychological content.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The trial aimed at pragmatic effectiveness versus standard care, which would make the comparator appropriate by design.

quotes.text: online session of advice and support with a trained practitioner

10.1136/bmjmed-2024-001068.headline_claim: The personalised Listen self-management intervention produced non-significant short-term improvements in routine activities versus usual care, with improvements in emotional wellbeing, fatigue, quality of life and self-efficacy.
10.1136/bmjmed-2024-001068.overall: The primary result is non-significant (P=0.052), and the authors themselves say firm conclusions are not possible. The headline claim is reasonably hedged, although the Results text and the discussion of secondary outcomes lean favourable, and no multiplicity control was applied. The main printed error is the 554 vs 544 randomised count, which does not change the findings. The registry flag concerns a different trial and does not apply.

primary_outcome.name: Ox-PAQ routine activities domain score at three months

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10)
Change in Perceived Medical Condition Self-Management Scale
Change in the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale
Change in Quality of Life Enjoyment and Satisfaction Questionnaire
Change in Adapted Illness Intrusiveness Rating

issues.title: Randomised total given as 554 (277 per arm) in abstract/text but 544 (274 + 270) in Tables 1, 3 and 4
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results say 554 participants were randomised, 277 per arm. Table 1 and Table 4 list 544 (274 usual care, 270 intervention), and Table 3 uses 270 for the intervention arm. The abstract's own percentage of women (394, 72.4%) fits 544 and not 554. The correct total should be confirmed, and the text figures look wrong. The efficacy results do not depend on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT figure or supplement showing 554 randomised with 10 excluded from Table 1 for a stated reason, and 72.4% computed on a 544 subset.

quotes.text: 554 participants were randomly assigned to the trial intervention
Total sample (N=544), no. (%)

script.explanation: 394/554 = 71.12%, but the paper prints 72.4, outside the rounding interval [72.35, 72.50]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 544.2 rather than 554.

issues.title: Null primary outcome (P=0.052) described as greater capacity; unadjusted, self-reported secondary gains highlighted
issues.explanation: The primary analysis was non-significant, yet the Results text says the intervention group had greater capacity for daily activities, and the covariate-adjusted model B is called significant. The conclusions list improvements in wellbeing, fatigue, quality of life and self-efficacy. These are open-label, self-reported outcomes tested without multiplicity control. The authors do caveat bias, so the overstatement is moderate, but the framing is more favourable than the primary result supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or multiplicity correction showing the secondary results survive adjustment, and wording that kept the primary result as null.

quotes.text: Our primary analysis indicated that people who had received the Listen intervention had greater capacity for daily activities
a statistically significant improvement in the primary outcome

issues.title: Primary analysis had 410 follow-up scores vs 474 needed for 90% power; 15% attrition assumed, ~25% seen
issues.explanation: The sample size calculation needed 474 analysable participants, inflated to 558 for an assumed 15% loss. Only 410 of 544 randomised (about 75%) provided 3-month data, so power fell below the planned 90%. A non-significant primary result (P=0.052) is therefore less informative, and this works against showing an effect. The authors mention the loss to follow-up only briefly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A recalculated power analysis showing 410 analysable participants still gives about 90% power for the primary effect, or multiple-imputation results with the full randomised sample.

quotes.text: Assuming 15% loss to follow-  up, the overall recruitment target was set to 558 participants.
Follow- up (N=410), mean (SD)

10.1136/bmjopen-2023-083224.headline_claim: A 6-week theatre-based wellness programme is perceived as acceptable and has a range of potential positive psychosocial impacts for people with long COVID, supporting a larger clinical trial.
10.1136/bmjopen-2023-083224.overall: The paper's central conclusions are about acceptability and feasibility: uptake of 20 of 21, 19 of 20 completing, 16 of 20 at follow-up. These are reasonably supported, and the efficacy language in the conclusion is appropriately cautious. The Discussion's descriptions of 'significant' improvements and quantitatively identified reductions in loneliness overreach for a single-arm, unpowered study, but this affects only secondary, exploratory material.

primary_outcome.name: not designated; feasibility and acceptability (uptake, retention, attendance) with exploratory change in health and well-being measures

issues.title: Discussion treats uncontrolled, uncorrected paired changes (n≈16) as programme effects, incl. non-significant ones
issues.explanation: The study has one arm and no comparison group, and the quantitative outcome tests are exploratory, unpowered and uncorrected across many measures. Even so, the Discussion calls the fatigue change 'overall significant improvements'. It also says reductions in loneliness and increased social support were 'identified quantitatively' and explained by programme mechanisms, though the paper says only self-rated health and CFS showed evidence of change. Regression to the mean, natural recovery and expectation effects cannot be separated from any programme effect. The hedged conclusion survives, but these Discussion statements overreach.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison, or multiplicity-adjusted evidence that the loneliness, social-support and fatigue changes exceed what is expected without the programme.

quotes.text: outcome assessments showed overall significant improvements in fatigue
Reductions in loneliness and increased perceived social support (identified quantitatively) were supported through mechanisms of increased sense of community
No causal associations can be inferred between the programme and outcomes as there was no comparison group.
quotes.location: Strengths and limitations of this study

10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094386.headline_claim: Ten HBOT sessions did not show more short-term benefit than sham treatment in long covid patients, both groups improved, and HBOT has a favourable harm profile.
10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094386.overall: The null primary result (PF p=0.87, RP p=0.57, FAS, n=79 analysed of 80) is internally consistent and can be relied on, as can the null secondary results. The sex-difference and 'sufficient in selected cases' messages rest on non-significant or exploratory per-protocol analyses and are overstated, and the safety conclusion is stronger than Table 5 supports. Several tables carry denominator and typographic errors, but they do not change the main findings.

primary_outcome.name: RAND-36 PF and RP mean change from baseline at 13 weeks (PF p=0.87; RP p=0.57)

issues.title: Non-significant sex subgroup (all p>0.05, no interaction test) promoted as 'important' in abstract and conclusions
issues.explanation: The primary result is null, yet the abstract and conclusions emphasise a 'notable' or 'important' sex difference, and say 10 sessions 'may already be effective for women'. The subgroup results in the text have p values of 0.648 (PF), 0.067 (RP), 0.051 and 0.053 in the per-protocol sets, none significant, with no interaction test and no multiplicity adjustment. Per-protocol sets are also not randomised comparisons. The finding is hypothesis-generating at most and should not be presented as a discovery.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sex-by-treatment interaction test with p<0.05 and multiplicity control.

quotes.text: Both groups improved, with a notable sex difference.
10 sessions may already be effective for women
Although it did not reach statistically significant evidence.

second_reader.what_stands: All sex-subgroup comparisons have p>0.05, and no interaction test is reported. Despite that, the abstract and conclusions describe a 'notable'/'important' sex difference and say 10 sessions 'may already be effective for women', with no non-significance caveat in those places. The discussion does acknowledge non-significance, and the conclusion's 'may' and call for further study soften the claim somewhat. A rough interaction check (z about 1.5, p about 0.13) does not support a clear sex difference either.

issues.title: Treatment-count breakdown: 'four' with <5 sessions but arm split 3+4=7; placebo categories sum to 44
issues.explanation: The Results say four subjects had fewer than five treatments, but the arm split given is three HBOT and four placebo, which is seven. The placebo categories (32 completed, 4 under five, 8 with five to nine) also add to 44, more than the 40 randomised or 41 in the safety set. The overall total of 80 fits 'four', so the placebo figure of four appears wrong, and it may be one. This is a reporting slip in the dose-exposure description. It does not change the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A per-arm exposure table showing the placebo under-five count is one, or another reading of the sentence that makes the arm counts sum to four.

quotes.text: four subjects had less than five treatments (three in HBOT and four in placebo)
15 subjects had five to nine treatments (seven in HBOT and eight in placebo)

issues.title: 'Favourable harm profile' stated though probably-related AEs were 49% vs 24% and severe AEs 3 vs 0
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusions call the harm profile favourable and say HBOT 'seems safe'. Table 5 shows probably-related AEs in 19 of 39 (49%) on HBOT versus 10 of 41 (24%) on sham, severe AEs 3 versus 0, and discontinuation 15% versus 7%. The Results text says AE frequency was similar and the Discussion offers alternative explanations, but the headline conclusion does not carry these caveats. AEs were collected only to week 13, with only SAEs recorded after week 6. A phase II trial of 80 patients can only tentatively support a safety statement, so 'favourable' overstates it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group safety comparison showing no meaningful difference in related or severe AEs, or an AE rate that excludes the unblinded-chamber effects.

quotes.text: HBOT has a favourable harm profile.
In 19 subjects (49%), AEs were probably related to HBOT

issues.title: '10 sessions could be sufficient' rests on exploratory per-protocol 52-week responder result (p=0.012)
issues.explanation: The null FAS primary result is followed by per-protocol and completers-only analyses at 52 weeks (PPAS p=0.024, PPS10 p=0.012), selected after randomisation and with no multiplicity control. The authors flag them as exploratory and the conclusion is worded as hypothesis-generating. The Discussion sentence on sufficiency still reads more positively than the evidence allows. The FAS PF responder p was 0.033, one of many nominal comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, multiplicity-controlled analysis in the randomised population showing a 52-week benefit.

quotes.text: This suggests that 10 treatments, two to three times a week, could be sufficient in selected cases.
which was liberal and not sufficient to confirm efficacy

issues.title: Responder-table denominators contradict their notes and each other (Tables 3, 4, 6); some percentages fit no n
issues.explanation: Table 3 is labelled PPAS but its note gives the FAS denominators (n=40; 39), while Table 6 (also PPAS) gives n=37; 35 at week 13. Table 6 percentages imply other denominators again: week 13 placebo 19 (50.0%) implies 38, not 35, and the week-26 placebo 19 (57.1%) fits no listed n. The week-52 total 37 (48.0%) should be about 55%. 13/32 is 40.6% in Table 4 but printed 40.1% in Table 6. Table 4 week-13 percentages use 40 and 40 although the note gives 39 for placebo. The week-52 PF comparison (p=0.024 in PPAS) is one of the figures affected, so readers cannot tell which denominators were used. This is a reporting problem and the main findings stay null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The protocol or supplement stating that missing and deceased subjects were counted as non-responders and which denominators applied, together with corrected percentages.

quotes.text: At week 13: n=37; n=35, week 26: n=36; n=35, week 52: n=35; n=32 (HBOT; placebo).

script.explanation: 37/67 = 55.22%, but the paper prints 48.0, outside the rounding interval [47.95, 48.10]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 77.1 rather than 67.

issues.title: Results text gives a five-unit responder threshold for Table 6; table and Methods use 10 units
issues.explanation: The Results describe the PPAS 52-week responder analysis (p=0.024) as a change of at least five units. The Table 6 note defines it as at least 10 units, and Table 4 and the Discussion also use 10. The text is almost certainly wrong, but a reader cannot be sure which threshold the p-value rests on. The error sits in the sentence that reports one of the paper's few significant findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary analysis output showing a five-unit threshold was used for the PPAS table.

quotes.text: change of at least five units in the physical
Proportion of subjects with at least 10 units of improvement from baseline.

issues.title: Table 1 Total column has several cells that do not match the arms (snus 0.5%, 93.0%, mean 25.0, mean 12.0)
issues.explanation: In the Total column, 4 of 80 is printed as 0.5% (should be 5.0%) and 75 of 80 as 93.0% (should be 93.8%). The total general-health mean (25.0) is below the HBOT mean (28.8) and equals the placebo mean, though with equal-sized arms it should lie between them. The chair-stand total of 12.0 is above the mean of the arm means (about 11.6). These are baseline descriptive errors that nothing in the efficacy analysis depends on, but they show the table was not carefully checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing these totals are correct and the arm cells are what is mistyped; the totals would still disagree with the arms.

quotes.location: Table 1, Daily user Swedish snus, Total
Table 1, Full time work/study before COVID-19, Total

script.explanation: 4/80 = 5.00%, but the paper prints 0.5, outside the rounding interval [0.45, 0.60]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 800.0 rather than 80.

10.1136/bmjresp-2022-001237.headline_claim: Early data from the Your COVID Recovery digital programme show symptom and quality-of-life improvements in people with long COVID, supporting further evaluation in an RCT.
10.1136/bmjresp-2022-001237.overall: The paper honestly describes itself as early, observational data, but its Conclusion that the programme 'demonstrates improvements' and can be offered at scale goes beyond a single-arm, completers-only service evaluation. Within-group changes (CAT about 4.2 points, VAS about 11 points) are probably real as descriptions but cannot be attributed to the programme. The numerical slips found are minor.

primary_outcome.name: EQ-5D-5L VAS score (pre vs post programme)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post service evaluation cannot attribute CAT/EQ-5D improvement to the programme
issues.explanation: All results are baseline-to-follow-up changes in one uncontrolled group of completers. Natural recovery, regression to the mean, concurrent clinical care and expectation effects cannot be separated from any programme effect. The paper itself cites the lack of natural recovery in other cohorts but does not test it here. The data support description of change, not effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group showing less change over the same interval.

quotes.text: the data in this study are  uncontrolled  and  a  randomised  controlled  trial  of the Your COVID Recovery ® digital  platform versus best usual care would be important.
The CAT total scores decreased significantly following the Your COVID Recovery ® digital programme (pre=19.8 (7.2); post=15.6 (7.6), p<0.01)

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, uncontrolled pre-post service evaluation, so improvement in CAT and EQ-5D-5L (VAS and some dimensions; the Index Value change was not significant) cannot be attributed to the programme, and regression to the mean, natural recovery, concurrent care and the selection of complete-case completers could all contribute. The authors do state in the Discussion that the data are observational and uncontrolled and that an RCT is needed. However, the wording in the Results and Conclusion ('demonstrates improvements ... following a light touch intervention', 'impact', 'evaluate

issues.title: Only 110 completers with pre and post data analysed; no denominator of starters or dropouts
issues.explanation: Only participants with both pre and post datasets were extracted. The paper does not report how many registered, started or dropped out, so the completion rate and any selection bias cannot be judged. Completers are plausibly those who benefited, so improvement estimates are likely too favourable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A report of all registered users and a sensitivity analysis including non-completers.

quotes.text: Those with complete preintervention and postintervention  datasets  were  extracted  from  the  site  from  the  first patient  completing  the  programme
Table 1 Characteristics of 110 participants who completed the Your COVID Recovery ®  digital programme

issues.title: Conclusion says data 'demonstrate' improvement and support offering at scale; design and data do not
issues.explanation: The Conclusion asserts the data demonstrate symptom improvement after a light-touch intervention that can be offered at scale. The data are uncontrolled, completers-only, and say nothing about delivery at scale or the support actually given. The caveats sit in the Discussion, not in the Conclusion, so the headline wording outruns the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Conclusion that framed the findings as descriptive and hypothesis-generating only.

quotes.text: These early  data  are  encouraging  as  it  demonstrates improvements  in  symptoms  after  a  COVID  infection following a light touch intervention, which can be offered at scale.
We do not have data on the level of support provided to participants.

issues.title: No primary outcome or multiplicity control across ~20 pre-post tests; usual activities p=0.029 fragile
issues.explanation: About 20 separate tests (VAS, index, five EQ-5D dimensions, CAT total and eight items) are run at p<0.05 with no designated primary outcome and no correction. Most results are strongly significant, so the conclusion is little affected, but the usual-activities result (p=0.029) would not remain significant after correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was set at p<0.05.
usual activities (p = 0.029)

issues.title: EQ-5D index mean difference 0.1 sits outside the CI midpoint (-0.04 to 0.11)
issues.explanation: The reported mean difference of 0.1 lies near the upper end of the CI -0.04 to 0.11, whose midpoint is 0.035. A symmetric CI around a mean of at least 0.05 would not run to -0.04. Either the CI or the mean difference is misprinted; it affects one secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded mean difference near 0.035 or a corrected CI.

quotes.text: with  a  mean  difference  of  0.1  (0.3)  (95%  CI -0.04 to 0.11)

script.explanation: the estimate 0.1 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-0.04, 0.11] (expected about 0.0350) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Text says all CAT items p<0.005 but Table 2 sleep item is p=0.006
issues.explanation: The Results text says every CAT symptom item except phlegm improved at p<0.005. Table 2 gives the sleep item p=0.006, which does not meet that threshold. The sleep item is still significant at the pre-specified 0.05 level, so only the wording is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that a different threshold applied to the sleep item, or a corrected p-value in Table 2.

quotes.text: improved significantly preintervention to postintervention (p<0.005), apart from the phlegm item score (p=0.168)

10.1136/bmjresp-2022-001377.headline_claim: Outpatient rehabilitation added to usual care is associated with significantly greater improvements in fatigue, respiratory symptoms, functional capacity, mental health and HRQoL than usual care alone after severe COVID-19 pneumonia, and rehabilitation 'facilitates recovery' that 'otherwise would remain incomplete with usual care'.
10.1136/bmjresp-2022-001377.overall: The finding that Rehab patients had better self-reported symptoms than a self-selected, transport-limited usual-care group is plausible, but the non-randomised allocation, open-label design and subjective primary outcomes mean the causal conclusion is not supported as stated. The objective 6MWT improvement was equal in both arms. The results are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: CAT score and fatigue questionnaires (CFQ-Likert, CFQ-bimodal, FACIT, FSS) at 8 weeks

issues.title: Non-random allocation by transport access confounds Rehab vs usual-care comparison (distance 3.6 vs 6.3 km)
issues.explanation: Patients were in the rehabilitation arm only if they could physically attend; those who could not formed the usual-care arm. The groups differ significantly in distance to the centre, and attendance ability may track unmeasured factors such as income, support or health. Differences at 8 weeks therefore cannot be attributed to rehabilitation with the certainty the conclusion implies; the authors themselves call for randomised trials.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that attendance ability was unrelated to prognosis, e.g. adjusted analyses incl. distance, SES and comorbidity showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Patients who could participate in the supervised rehabilitation programme comprised the intervention group (Rehab, n=25), whereas  patients  who  were  unable  to  participate  (due to  logistical/transport  issues)  comprised the UC group (n=27).
The rehabilitation centre-home distance was significantly greater in the UC group (table 1).

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was non-random and determined by ability to reach the centre, and the groups differed significantly in distance (3.6 vs 6.3 km, p=0.002). The analysis adjusts only for baseline outcome values, so any factor tied to transport access could confound the Rehab vs UC comparison. The authors disclose non-randomisation and the distance gap as a limitation, but the analysis does not address it and the conclusions are not tempered accordingly. Table 1 does not show a measured variable that explains the outcome differences, so the size of the confounding cannot be determined from the paper.

issues.title: Causal conclusion ('facilitates recovery', incl. depression) from a non-randomised 8-week comparison
issues.explanation: The conclusion asserts that rehabilitation facilitates recovery that would otherwise remain incomplete, in a self-selected comparison with no longer follow-up. It also lists depression among the improved domains, although HADS-Depression did not differ between groups (p=0.627); only BDI did. Exercise 'effective' is also not tested against any control in the training data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to association, and a design or adjusted analysis addressing selection.

quotes.text: In  conclusion,  rehabilitation  facilitates  recovery  of respiratory symptoms, fatigue, depression/anxiety, cognitive impairment and HRQoL that otherwise would remain incomplete with usual care.
Randomised controlled trial studies are needed to confirm the benefits of rehabilitation post-  COVID-  19 compared to usual care.
quotes.location: Abstract, How this study might affect research, practice or policy

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion's causal wording ('facilitates recovery', 'otherwise would remain incomplete') goes beyond a non-randomised 8-week comparison with unadjusted confounding by distance and transport access. The inclusion of 'depression' rests on BDI alone, since HADS-Depression showed no between-group difference (p=0.627). It is not true that the paper ignores the issue: the abstract and discussion use 'associated with', the lack of randomisation is stated as a limitation, and an RCT is explicitly called for.

issues.title: Open-label design; all primary outcomes self-reported; objective 6MWT showed no between-group difference
issues.explanation: Every primary outcome (CAT and fatigue scales) is a patient-reported questionnaire, and participants knew their allocation. Expectation and reporting bias could inflate the apparent benefit, and this is not acknowledged as a limitation. The one objective functional measure, 6MWT, improved by about 60 m in both groups with no between-group difference (p=0.501).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded assessment of outcomes or objective corroborating endpoints showing between-group differences.

quotes.text: The CAT is an eightitem questionnaire that was developed to assess COPD symptoms  and  qualify  health  status  impairment.
The FSS is a nine-  item questionnaire that rates the severity of fatigue symptoms.

issues.title: No trial registration reported; prespecification of primary outcomes and analysis unverifiable
issues.explanation: The paper describes a prospective interventional study but gives no registry number. Without a registered protocol, the choice of CAT and four fatigue scales as primary outcomes, and the many secondary tests, cannot be checked against a prior plan. This limits confidence rather than showing a specific error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment listing the same primary outcomes.

quotes.text: This was a prospective, interventional, non-  randomised parallel  assignment  two-  arm  study  that  was  conducted from January until August 2021.

issues.title: Threefold workload increase vs stated 10% weekly increments (about 2.4-fold)
issues.explanation: The prescription states weekly 10% increments of baseline work rate from a 50% start, which would give about 2.4-fold over 8 weeks. The paper reports a threefold increase. The difference could come from how increments were applied or measured, and the figure data are not in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 3 data or supplement showing the actual work-rate progression, or a definition of the increment that yields threefold.

quotes.text: The workload was increased weekly by 10% of the baseline work rate
training intensity increased threefold from the first to the last training session

issues.title: Attrition quoted as 16% but 8/52 = 15.4%; ANCOVA said to include lost patients
issues.explanation: The abstract states 16% attrition, while the counts given in Results (4 + 4 of 52) yield 15.4%. Separately, Methods say baseline values of patients lost to follow-up were included as covariates, which cannot recover their missing 8-week outcomes, so analysis is effectively complete-case with 8 patients missing. Differential reasons for dropout (4 non-completers in Rehab for commitments or embolism) are not analysed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing 8.3 of 52 equivalent differently defined attrition, or sensitivity analyses with multiple imputation.

quotes.text: A 16% attrition rate was
In the UC group, four patients failed to attend the re-  evaluation visit at 8 weeks (figure 1).

script.explanation: 8/52 = 15.38%, but the paper prints 16, outside the rounding interval [15.50, 17.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 50.0 rather than 52.

10.1136/bmjresp-2022-001439.headline_claim: A 12-week home-based inspiratory muscle training programme resulted in a significant improvement in exercise capacity and quality of life in postdischarged patients with long COVID and reduced aerobic capacity, compared with usual care.
10.1136/bmjresp-2022-001439.overall: The primary result (higher peakVO2 with IMT, about +4.5 mL/kg/min) is large and consistently reported, though from a small, unblinded-participant trial against no treatment. The QoL conclusion rests on within-arm comparisons, the secondary and policy claims (cost, equivalence to supervised training, CIx benefit) go beyond the data, and registration was about six weeks after the study start. The headline benefit on exercise capacity is reasonably reliable but should be read as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: Peak oxygen consumption (peakVO2, mL/kg/min) at 12 weeks

issues.title: QoL benefit claimed from within-arm significance only; no between-group QoL comparison reported
issues.explanation: The QoL conclusion rests on usual activities, anxiety/depression and VAS changing significantly within the IMT arm but not within usual care. A difference in significance between arms is not a test of the treatment effect. Baseline imbalances (VAS 70 vs 79; anxiety/depression median 2 vs 1) and unblinded self-reported outcomes with an untreated control add further uncertainty. The abstract-level and Conclusions statement that IMT improved QoL is therefore not directly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group adjusted QoL differences with CIs and p values (in figure 4 or supplement) showing a significant treatment effect.

quotes.text: A  significant  improvement  in  usual  activities
quotes.location: Results, Effect of IMT on health-related QoL

quotes.text: Visual analogue scale

second_reader.what_stands: In the text and Table 1, the QoL benefit rests on within-arm significance (IMT arm significant, UC not), and no between-group QoL estimate, CI or p value is printed; the baseline imbalance in VAS and anxiety/depression makes this more consequential. I could not see Figure 4, so I cannot rule out that it shows between-group contrasts, and the Methods do describe a covariate-adjusted model that may have been used.

issues.title: Claims of low cost and equivalence to supervised exercise training unsupported by a 26-patient trial vs no treatment
issues.explanation: The trial compared IMT with no physical therapy in 26 patients at a single centre. It cannot show that IMT is an effective alternative to supervised exercise programmes, and no costs were measured. Safety is based on 13 treated patients over 12 weeks. The assessor-blinded but participant-unblinded design with an untreated control also means part of the effect may be non-specific.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A head-to-head comparison with supervised training and an economic analysis within the study.

quotes.text: may offer an accessible physical therapy model, requiring minimal infrastructure resources
quotes.location: Key points, How this study might affect research, practice or policy

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's Key points and Clinical implications describe home IMT as an effective alternative to supervised exercise training with low cost and minimal infrastructure, but the only comparator was usual care and no cost or head-to-head data are reported. The IMT arm also had weekly physiotherapist visits, which the 'minimal infrastructure' wording does not acknowledge.

issues.title: Secondary findings (CIx p=0.046, QoL dimensions) claimed as benefits with no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: About ten secondary comparisons (VE/VCO2, CIx, five EQ-5D dimensions, VAS, within- and between-arm) were run with no correction. The CIx effect (p=0.046) and one or two QoL dimensions are nominally significant and are presented in the Discussion as established benefits. The primary peakVO2 result is not affected, but these secondary claims are tentative at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or adjusted p values showing the CIx and QoL effects survive correction.

quotes.text: the mean of CIx significantly increased in those patients allocated to the IMT group
quotes.location: Results, Effect of IMT on HR response to maximal exercise

issues.title: VE/VCO2 slope IMT within-group CI (-2.75 to -0.69) excludes 0 but p=0.214; unit mL/kg/min is wrong
issues.explanation: The IMT-arm within-group change is printed with a 95% CI that lies entirely below zero, yet the p value is 0.214 and the text calls the change non-significant. The estimate -1.03 is also not the midpoint of -2.75 to -0.69 (midpoint -1.72). A sign slip in the upper bound (should be +0.69) would make all three numbers agree. The unit is also given as mL/kg/min for a dimensionless slope. This affects one secondary within-group result only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The trial dataset or supplementary tables showing the CI is actually -2.75 to 0.69 (or another interval consistent with p=0.214).

quotes.location: Results, Secondary endpoints, VE/VCO2 slope, paragraph 2

script.explanation: the estimate -1.03 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-2.75, -0.69] (expected about -1.7200) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0500 (reachable range [0.0478, 0.0523] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.214 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller

issues.title: Registered 2022-03-12, about six weeks after the 2022-01-30 study start (registry record)
issues.explanation: According to the ClinicalTrials.gov record, the trial was first submitted after enrolment had begun. The paper presents registration without this caveat and says all outcomes of the 'registered protocol' are reported. The registered primary outcome (peak oxygen consumption) matches the paper, so the practical risk of outcome switching for the primary is low. The registry lists no secondary outcomes, so the secondary endpoints cannot be checked against registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the record was first posted before 2022-01-30, or the first participant being enrolled after 2022-03-12.

10.1136/bmjresp-2025-003653.headline_claim: The five-phase, one-to-one primary care pulmonary rehabilitation programme is a safe and effective intervention that may improve functional exercise capacity, fatigue and dyspnoea in patients with long COVID.
10.1136/bmjresp-2025-003653.overall: The primary 6MWD benefit at 12 weeks (+39 m, CI 18 to 59, supported by a blinded assessor and an ITT mixed model) is reasonably credible but comes from an underpowered trial. The wider conclusion ('safe and effective', improvements in fatigue and dyspnoea) outruns the evidence: it rests on open-label self-reported outcomes, uncorrected secondary analyses and an unreported control-arm safety comparison. The Discussion also foregrounds a larger 55 m estimate over the primary 39 m.

primary_outcome.name: Change in 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) from baseline to 12 weeks

issues.title: Open-label, no-attention control undermines patient-reported fatigue and dyspnoea claims
issues.explanation: Only the 6MWD assessor was blinded. Patients knew their allocation and the control group had no sessions, attention or placebo. The fatigue (CIS-fatigue, CAT, mMRC) benefits are self-reported and may reflect expectation or contact effects. Yet the conclusion states that fatigue and dyspnoea improve, and the control is described as accounting for spontaneous recovery.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an attention-matched or sham control, or blinded assessment of fatigue and dyspnoea giving similar effects.

quotes.text: The trial was open-  label, but the primary end point measurement (6MWD) was performed by a blinded assessor.
Our trial showed that primary care PR may decrease fatigue,  compared with usual care.

second_reader.what_stands: The fatigue (CIS-fatigue) and dyspnoea (mMRC) outcomes are patient-reported, the trial was open-label, and the control group got no PR and no attention comparator. Blinding was applied only to the 6MWD assessor, and the limitations section does not discuss the risk of bias from unblinded self-report. The paper does hedge the claims ('may decrease', 'potentially observed'), so it is not true that the paper makes unqualified claims. I did not check the online supplement or whether the mMRC mixed model was significant.

issues.title: 'Safe and effective' conclusion after a 76/134 trial called 'not definitive for any outcome'
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the trial is not definitive for any outcome, with 57% of the target sample. Safety is supported only by a list of eight AEs (four PEM) and one SAE in the intervention arm, with no control-arm comparison. The conclusion still calls the programme 'safe and effective' and extends it to fatigue and dyspnoea, which rest on unblinded self-report and uncorrected secondary analyses. The primary 6MWD result is supported more strongly than the wording implies.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified safety analysis with control-arm AE comparison, or a conclusion worded as preliminary.

quotes.text: is therefore not definitive for any outcome
There were eight AEs (four PEM, two musculoskeletal issues, one nausea and one atypical chest pain) and one unrelated SAE
is  a  safe  and  effective  intervention  that  may  improve  functional  exercise  capacity,  fatigue and  dyspnoea  in  patients  with  long  COVID.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper itself says results are 'not definitive for any outcome' yet closes with 'is a safe and effective intervention', so the strongest wording in the conclusion is not matched by the paper's own caveat, although the efficacy part is softened with 'may improve'. The safety claim rests on 8 AEs and 1 unrelated SAE in 39 treated patients, with no control-group AE comparison reported, so 'safe' is an assertion the data cannot firmly support. The primary 6MWD result is statistically clear, so 'effective' for functional exercise capacity is not unsupported.

issues.title: Dyspnoea and CAT claims rest on uncorrected secondary tests across ~15 outcomes
issues.explanation: Secondary and exploratory outcomes were tested by linear regression and chi-squared tests with no correction across outcomes. Holm correction was applied only across time points within mixed models. The dyspnoea benefit named in the conclusion comes from mMRC at p=0.014 in this uncorrected analysis, and the authors admit the regression effects were not seen with the mixed model. Dyspnoea and CAT effects should therefore be treated as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity adjustment across secondary outcomes, or a mixed-model confirmation of mMRC and CAT effects.

quotes.text: a significant intervention effect was found for the CAT
these latter intervention effects should be confirmed in a trial powered for these outcomes

issues.title: Discussion cites a 55 m 'overall' 6MWD effect, not the 39 m primary 12-week estimate
issues.explanation: Results report +39 m (CI 18 to 59) at 12 weeks from the prespecified mixed-model contrast. The Discussion instead reports a 55 m improvement from a supplement analysis and aligns it with a 61 m meta-analytic effect. Readers see a larger effect than the primary estimate, and the difference between the two analyses is not explained in the main text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Main-text explanation that the 55 m overall estimate is the same contrast on a different scale and that the 39 m value is the primary estimate.

quotes.text: The intervention group showed a mean improvement (overall treatment effect) of 55 m
The linear mixed model estimated the treatment effect at week 12 as +39 m

10.1136/bmjresp-2026-004177.headline_claim: A 3-week symptom-based rehabilitation programme improved HRQoL compared with usual care in people with post-COVID condition, with some benefits persisting at 3 months.
10.1136/bmjresp-2026-004177.overall: The primary result (PCS difference 2.9 points, CI 0.2 to 5.7, p=0.038) is statistically significant but small and imprecise. It rests on an open-label comparison with unstructured usual care and a self-reported outcome, and on a complete-case analysis with unequal loss between arms (29% vs 14%). The headline claim of improved HRQoL holds only tentatively, and the control-arm N of 87 in the outcome table is a text-extraction artefact, not a real discrepancy.

primary_outcome.name: Physical HRQoL (SF-12 PCS) change from baseline to 3 weeks

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline Quality of life assessed by Short Form - 12 Questionnaire at week 4 and week 12

issues.title: Open-label trial vs unstructured usual care with self-reported primary outcome (PCS difference 2.9, CI 0.2-5.7)
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and every outcome was a self-reported questionnaire. The comparator was usual care with no attention control, so the 3-week gain may partly reflect expectation, the effect of a 3-week inpatient stay, or reporting effects rather than the programme content. The authors note that assessor bias is minimised, but this does not address participant-level bias, and the conclusion states the benefit without that caveat. The primary estimate is also small and imprecise, and no minimal important difference exists to judge it against.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham or attention-control arm, or objective or blinded-assessor outcomes that show a similar effect.

quotes.text: participants could disclose their group allocation during assessments
administered at the discretion of their outpatient clinicians
favouring the REHAB group (mean difference 2.9 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 5.7, p=0.038)

second_reader.what_stands: The trial was open-label for participants, compared with usual care that was explicitly unstructured and left to outpatient clinicians' discretion (no attention-matched control), and the primary outcome (SF-12 PCS) was self-reported, so the 2.9-point difference (95% CI 0.2 to 5.7, p=0.038) is vulnerable to expectation and reporting bias; the Limitations passage only addresses assessor bias, not participant-level bias. The authors do disclose the lack of blinding and the lack of a known minimal important difference, and the point estimate and CI are arithmetically coherent, so the issue is a di

issues.title: Differential loss (47/66 REHAB vs 57/66 control analysed) and complete-case primary analysis labelled ITT
issues.explanation: Of 132 randomised, 104 entered the primary analysis. About 29% of the REHAB arm and 14% of the control arm were lost. The primary test is a complete-case t-test, although it is called a completer analysis of the ITT population. Unequal loss can bias a self-reported outcome. Sensitivity analyses reportedly agree, which limits but does not remove the concern, since the imputation results are only in the supplement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Full imputed-data primary results showing the same estimate, or a CONSORT diagram showing the losses were unrelated to allocation.

quotes.text: Control group (n=57)
Of these, 104 participants were included in the completer
quotes.location: Results, Trial flow and participant characteristics

issues.title: Primary effect is imprecise (d 0.43, CI 0.02-0.82; analysed 104 vs 110 needed) yet concluded as significant improvement
issues.explanation: The sample was sized for d=0.54, but the observed d was 0.43 with a lower CI bound close to zero. The analysed n was 104, slightly below the 110 required. The primary p value (0.038) is only just under 0.05. The authors' wording of 'significantly improved' is accurate for the test, but the CI shows the data are consistent with a trivial effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A replication or larger trial with a narrower CI, or a prespecified minimal important difference that the lower bound clears.

quotes.text: Accounting for an anticipated dropout rate of 20%, the targeted sample size was 132 participants (66 per group).
with a Cohen's d of 0.43 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.82)

issues.title: Registry lists SF-12 at weeks 4 and 12; paper makes PCS at 3 weeks primary and 3 months secondary
issues.explanation: The registry record names SF-12 quality of life at weeks 4 and 12 as the primary outcome, without naming a component. The paper designates the PCS at 3 weeks as primary and the 3-month result as secondary. The time points are only loosely aligned and the paper does not discuss how the registered outcome maps onto the reported one. This cannot be settled without the registry history.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing PCS at the end of the programme was specified as the primary outcome before data collection.

quotes.text: (end of the REHAB or usual care period)
Trial registration number NCT05172206.

issues.title: Summary box says 'individuals with PCC' while the Discussion limits findings to those with sufficient functional capacity
issues.explanation: The summary and Conclusion state benefits for people with PCC generally. The authors state elsewhere that the findings apply only to people able to walk and exercise. The trial was single-centre and delivered as inpatient care. The qualifier appears in the Discussion but not in the summary statements.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A summary statement that carries the functional-capacity qualifier.

quotes.text: people with PCC who retained sufficient functional capacity
significantly improves physical and mental quality of life, as well as depression and anxiety

10.1136/rmdopen-2023-003061.headline_claim: A self-evidence-based digital care programme is associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in PROMIS-measured health-related quality of life across multiple domains in adults with autoimmune diseases, AID-associated conditions and long COVID.
10.1136/rmdopen-2023-003061.overall: The paper shows that completers of an uncontrolled, unblinded programme reported improved PROMIS scores. The causal wording in the title and the 'wide applicability' claim are not supported by this design, which also leaves out 35% of eligible participants and has a funder-affiliated author team. The numeric slips (subgroup totals, one text percentage swap, two declining subgroup cells) are minor and do not change the overall findings.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS29+MSx domain T-scores, baseline to end of programme (no single primary outcome is named)

issues.title: Causal 'improves HRQoL' claim rests on an uncontrolled, unblinded pre/post design with self-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: All 202 completers were compared only with their own baseline, with no control group, no blinding and patient-reported outcomes, and the end of the programme was set individually. The reported gains cannot be separated from regression to the mean, expectancy or placebo effects, natural change over time or concurrent treatment changes. The title, the 'wide applicability' claim and the call to increase funding go beyond what this design can show; only an association is supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent matched comparison group, or a randomised or waitlist control showing the same change.

quotes.text: participants were not randomised or blinded
as the current study is unblinded

second_reader.what_stands: The design is uncontrolled, unblinded, pre/post with self-reported PROMIS outcomes, and the title ('improves HRQoL') and Discussion opening ('has the potential to meaningfully improve') use causal-leaning language that this design cannot support. However, the authors openly state these limitations, mention placebo effects and exaggeration of effect size, and use 'associated with' in the Key Messages and summary, so the causal claim is overstated in the title rather than asserted without caveat.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis: 110 of 312 (35.3%) eligible participants have no outcome data; 'no attrition bias' inferred
issues.explanation: Only the 202 of 312 eligible participants who completed the programme and had end-of-programme scores were analysed. People who dropped out, perhaps because it did not help, are not in the results, so the gains describe completers only. The statement that there was 'no attrition bias' rests on non-significant baseline comparisons, which cannot rule out bias, and no analysis tests how sensitive the result is to the missing 35%.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis (for example multiple imputation or worst-case imputation) showing similar gains in all 312 starters.

quotes.text: Of the remaining 312 individuals, 202 (64.7%) completed BL and EOP information and were included in the study.
suggesting no attrition bias

second_reader.what_stands: The analysis is completers-only: 110 of 312 eligible participants (35.3%) have no EOP outcome data, and no imputation or sensitivity analysis is reported. The Results inference of 'no attrition bias' from a non-significant comparison of baseline characteristics is not justified, because baseline similarity does not show that post-baseline outcomes among dropouts would have matched completers; the authors partly acknowledge this in the limitations paragraph, though the Results wording stays unqualified.

issues.title: MIC-exceedance rests on a post hoc subset chosen by baseline score; all-comers miss MIC in 3 domains
issues.explanation: The claim that average improvements exceeded MIC in every domain applies only to those who were abnormal at baseline in each domain. Selecting people by a low baseline score tends to produce larger apparent change through regression to the mean. In the full cohort, cognitive function, physical function and depression changes are smaller than the paper's MIC thresholds, and under 60% of the subset individually reached MIC. The text mostly makes these qualifications visible, so this weakens a secondary claim rather than a main one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis of the severity-stratified change against a comparison group or with adjustment for regression to the mean.

quotes.text: The average changes reported by all-  comers in this study generally fall within the above parameters.
Statistically significant improvements,  exceeding  MIC  thresholds,  were  seen in  multiple  PROMIS29+MSx  domains

issues.title: Diagnosis subgroup n values sum to 208, not 202; 'remaining 183' implies 189 non-No-AID
issues.explanation: The ten diagnosis groups in Tables 2 and 4 add up to 208 participants, but the study has 202. Removing the 19 with no autoimmune diagnosis leaves 189 by the table counts, while the text says 183. The paper does not say whether participants were counted under more than one diagnosis, so the subgroup results cannot be reconciled with the total population.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote or appendix stating that some participants carry more than one primary diagnosis, giving 6 double-counted individuals.

quotes.text: the remaining 183 individuals
quotes.location: Results, paragraph on 19 participants without autoimmune diagnosis

quotes.text: Distribution of diagnoses*

issues.title: Text claims improvement in every domain per diagnosis group; IBD cognition (-0.8) and MS physical function (-0.9) fell
issues.explanation: The Results state that trends toward improvement appeared in every domain in every diagnosis group. Table 4 shows a mean change of -0.8 for cognitive function in IBD and -0.9 for physical function in MS, and for these higher-is-better domains that is a decline. The statement is therefore slightly too strong, though both groups have only 12 people and the overall conclusion is not changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that these two cells had a sign error in the table, such as a corrected table with positive values.

quotes.text: Trends  toward  improvement  were  seen  in  every domain in each diagnosis group

quotes.location: Table 4, Cog func row, IBD column
Table 4, Phys func row, MS column

issues.title: Company evaluates its own product; funder's role in design, analysis and reporting not stated
issues.explanation: The study was funded by Mymee, which provides the programme, and several authors are employees, owners or advisors of the company. These conflicts are declared, but the paper does not say what role the funder had in study design, data analysis or the decision to publish. Given an uncontrolled design with favourable framing, an independent statement of funder involvement would help readers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the funder had no role in analysis, interpretation or the decision to publish, or independent statistical analysis.

quotes.text: This study was funded by Mymee.
NB is a paid consultant for Mymee and has ownership in the company.

issues.title: Text swaps Native Hawaiian/PI (1.5%) and Multiracial (1.0%) percentages relative to Table 1 counts (2 and 3)
issues.explanation: The text gives 1.5% for Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander and 1.0% for Multiracial participants. Table 1 lists 2 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (1%) and 3 Multiracial (1%) participants, which correspond to about 1.0% and 1.5% respectively. This is a cosmetic slip in the demographic description that does not affect any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing 3 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander and 2 Multiracial participants and a mislabelled table.

quotes.text: (1.5%),  Multiracial  (1.0%)
Native Hawaiian/ other Pacific Islander

script.explanation: 2/202 = 0.99%, but the paper prints 1.5, outside the rounding interval [1.45, 1.60]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 133.3 rather than 202.

10.1136/spcare-2023-004595.headline_claim: Astragalus root extract reduces the prevalence of post-COVID-19 chronic fatigue syndrome in nurses and can be safely used by people with CFS.
10.1136/spcare-2023-004595.overall: The large 13.8% vs 80% difference in CFS at end of treatment suggests a real signal, but the primary comparison used an inappropriate paired test, and flow and attrition reporting is contradictory (64 vs 59, 'no missing data'). The safety and 'long-term effect' conclusions exceed what a 59-person, 30-day trial with 30 days of follow-up can show. Treat the efficacy finding as tentative and the safety claim as unsupported.

primary_outcome.name: Proportion of nurses meeting DePaul-based CFS criteria at end of intervention (30 days)

issues.title: 64 randomised vs 59 analysed: 5 participants lost, yet 'no missing data' and no per-arm attrition reported
issues.explanation: The Results say 64 nurses were randomised, then say the primary outcome was lost for 5 of '59 randomised' participants. The same paragraph also states there were no missing data. Arm sizes (29 and 30) sum to 59, so the analysis excludes 5 people. Their arm, timing and reason are not given, and the analysis is not described as intention-to-treat. This leaves the attrition and the randomised-by-arm numbers unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram showing 59 were randomised (with 5 excluded before allocation) and 64 as an eligibility count, with no post-randomisation losses.

quotes.text: The remaining 64 participants were then randomly assigned to either the intervention or placebo group.
The primary outcome measure was lost for 5 of the 59 randomised participants at the time of the intervention
There were no missing data in this study

issues.title: Between-group CFS proportions compared with McNemar test, which is for paired data
issues.explanation: Table 2 labels the between-group p-values (both 0.0001) as McNemar tests, and the Results say the same. The arms are independent groups of different people, so McNemar's test does not apply; a chi-square or Fisher exact test is appropriate. The headline effect is probably robust, but the primary-outcome p-values are not reliable as reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the arms were matched or paired in the analysis, or an independent-groups test reproducing the reported p-values.

quotes.text: ‡Mc-Nemar test.
The McNemar test showed there was a statistically significant difference between these two groups

issues.title: 'Can safely use' conclusion rests on non-significant blood-pressure change and no reported adverse events in 59 nurses
issues.explanation: Safety was not a pre-specified outcome and is assessed only through blood pressure differences that were not significant. A 59-person, 30-day trial cannot exclude uncommon or longer-term harms. The unqualified statement that people with CFS can safely use the extract goes beyond what the data show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified safety analysis with adequate sample size and follow-up showing no excess adverse events.

quotes.text: As a result, people with CFS can safely use the root extract of this plant.
oral administration of Astragalus root extract is considered safe

issues.title: 'Long-term' persistence claimed from a time effect seen in both arms and only 30 days post-treatment
issues.explanation: The Discussion cites the decline in CFS over time as proof that the extract's effects persist after treatment stops. The same decline occurred in the placebo arm, and the interaction showing a different time trend between groups is non-significant. Follow-up is only 30 days after the end of treatment. Persistence at one month is plausible, but 'long-term' is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longer post-treatment follow-up with a significant group-by-time interaction or a sustained between-group difference.

quotes.text: a third assessment 60 days after the start of the administration
Group (control)×time
the number of people suffering from CFS decreased statistically significantly over time in the control group

issues.title: Table 1 baseline statistics inconsistent: Children p=0.014 vs text 'no significant differences'; t=10.07
issues.explanation: Table 1 prints a significant baseline difference for number of children (p=0.014), while the text says no baseline characteristic differed (p>0.05). The printed means and SDs do not support that t or p: the difference of 0.14 children is small relative to its standard error. Work experience shows t=10.07 with p=0.286, which is incompatible. These baseline-table errors cast doubt on the data handling but not the primary results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw baseline data showing the printed t and p values were correct, with the means or SDs mistyped.

quotes.text: there were no statistically significant differences between the two groups (p>0.05; table 1)

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

issues.title: Control group at 1-month follow-up labelled n=53 although 21 (70%) implies n=30
issues.explanation: The text gives the control denominator at 1 month as 53, whereas elsewhere the control group is 30 and 21/30 = 70%. No arm could have 53 participants in a 59-person trial. This is a typographical inconsistency that does not change the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; Table 2 and the printed percentage both show n=30.

quotes.text: 21 (70 %) in the control group (n=53)

10.1136/thorax-2022-btsabstracts.361.headline_claim: Routinely used cardiometabolic tests indicate higher future risk in adults after severe COVID-19 than in healthy controls, which the authors say supports interventions such as aerobic exercise training.
10.1136/thorax-2022-btsabstracts.361.overall: The headline claim that survivors of severe COVID-19 have a higher future cardiometabolic risk, and need exercise interventions, rests on a single cross-sectional comparison with non-concurrent controls who were selected to be comorbidity-free and are described inaccurately. The data show only unadjusted differences in markers, with no tests or intervals. The conclusion should be read as tentative at best. The abstract also contains separate overstatements in the P229 conclusions..

primary_outcome.name: No primary outcome named; cardiometabolic measures (BMI, blood pressure, glucose, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, VO2 peak, PWV) compared between groups

issues.title: Non-concurrent historical controls, selected to be comorbidity-free, with no adjustment, limit the comparison
issues.explanation: Controls were recruited to a different study and chosen to have no pre-existing conditions, while 26 of 38 survivors had at least one comorbidity and BMI differed. Differences in BMI, blood pressure, HOMA-IR and PWV may reflect pre-existing disease, selection or study conditions rather than COVID-19. The authors acknowledge this is unclear, but the Results and the first Conclusion still present a higher-risk profile after COVID without that caveat. Only unadjusted summaries with no confidence intervals or p-values are shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses adjusted for comorbidity and BMI, or a concurrent matched comparison group measured with the same protocol.

quotes.text: Historical adult age and sex matched healthy controls with no pre-existing conditions recruited prospectively to a different study were used as a comparator group.
It is unclear whether acute COVID-19 further contributes to pre-existing cardiometabolic risk.

second_reader.what_stands: The comparator is a non-concurrent historical group from a different study, selected to be largely comorbidity-free (88.2% with none vs 31.6%), and the paper reports no adjustment for comorbidity, so group differences cannot be attributed to COVID-19. The authors partly acknowledge this ('unclear whether acute COVID-19 further contributes'), but they do not list the control selection as a limitation, and the control group is smaller than stated for some measures (n=9 to 12).

issues.title: Cross-sectional data presented as showing higher future risk and supporting exercise interventions
issues.explanation: The study measured risk markers once, with no outcome follow-up, so it cannot show 'future risk'. The recommendation of aerobic exercise rests on the authors' own admission that it is unclear whether COVID-19 contributed to the risk profile. The study did not test any intervention. The data support only a descriptive difference in markers between two non-comparable groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longitudinal outcome data or an intervention arm in the same study.

quotes.text: routinely used clinical tests of cardiometabolic risk indicate higher future risk for adults post-COVID compared to healthy controls
our small exploratory study supports the need for interventions such as aerobic exercise training

second_reader.what_stands: The study is cross-sectional and uncontrolled for comorbidity, so it measures current risk markers, not future risk, and the paper tested no intervention; the 'higher future risk' and 'supports the need for interventions' statements go beyond the data. The softening is that the authors call the study small and exploratory and cite external evidence for exercise, so the recommendation is an extrapolation and not a claimed trial result.

issues.title: P229 claims CPET-guided treatment improves outcomes from an uncontrolled series (20 of 32 retested)
issues.explanation: Only 20 of 32 patients had a second CPET, and 14 of those improved symptoms. There was no control group, and the treatment is not described. Regression to the mean, natural recovery and selective retesting could explain the changes. The AT stayed low, and 6 patients had no symptom improvement. The causal statement in Conclusion 2 is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison, or evidence that retesting was unselective and the treatment was standardised.

quotes.text: A targeted treatment programme based on CPET improves symptoms and physiological parameters in long covid patients.
20 patients underwent a second CPET.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that the CPET-guided programme 'improves symptoms and physiological parameters' is drawn from an uncontrolled series in which only 20 of 32 patients (62.5%) were retested, with no comparison group, no statistics, and baseline and follow-up means computed on different subsets. The observed changes are small (+2.8 and +5.2 percentage points), the AT did not improve, and the treatment itself is not described, so causal wording is not supported.

issues.title: Controls described as having no pre-existing conditions, yet Table 1 shows 2 of 17 with comorbidities
issues.explanation: The Methods say the comparator controls had no pre-existing conditions. Table 1 shows only 15 of 17 (88.2%) with zero comorbidities, one with one comorbidity and one with more than two. The description of the control group is therefore not accurate as written. The effect is small, and it slightly narrows rather than widens the survivor-control contrast.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The control study protocol showing that these two controls were counted as having comorbidities only through a different definition (e.g. treated and well controlled conditions), or a corrected Table 1.

quotes.text: Historical adult age and sex matched healthy controls with no pre-existing conditions

quotes.location: Table 1, Comorbidities row 0, healthy controls column
Table 1, Comorbidities rows 1 and More than 2, healthy controls column

issues.title: P229 conclusion lists impaired oxygen pulse, but peak oxygen pulse reported as normal (88.9% predicted)
issues.explanation: The Results report a flattened oxygen pulse curve but a normal peak value (88.9% predicted). Conclusion 1 states long covid is associated with impaired oxygen pulse without that qualification. Readers of the conclusion alone would overestimate the abnormality. The inconsistency is real but narrow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that 'impaired oxygen pulse' refers specifically to the early-flattening curve rather than the peak value.

quotes.text: but peak oxygen pulse was normal (mean 88.9%)
Long covid is associated with impaired peak oxygen uptake, ATand oxygen pulse.

10.1152/japplphysiol.00078.2023.headline_claim: HIIT is an efficacious exercise intervention for increasing left ventricular mass in individuals previously hospitalized for COVID-19.
10.1152/japplphysiol.00078.2023.overall: The primary result (LVM +6.8 g, 95% CI 0.8 to 12.8, p=0.029) is internally consistent, and the study is described as a randomized, investigator-blinded trial. The main weakness is that 'efficacious' is stated without qualification on the basis of 28 participants and a lower CI bound near zero. Only the abstract was available, so registration, power calculation and flow could not be assessed.

primary_outcome.name: Left ventricular mass (LVM) by cardiac MRI

issues.title: 'Efficacious' conclusion rests on 28 participants and a CI of 0.8 to 12.8 g, with a lower bound near zero
issues.explanation: The abstract ends with an unqualified statement that HIIT is efficacious for increasing LVM. The evidence is one small trial (28 participants) with a single significant primary result whose CI is wide (0.8 to 12.8 g). The data support a probable increase of uncertain size, possibly small, which needs replication. Because the abstract also reports that the secondary outcomes (DLCOc, other lung function metrics, KBILD) showed no between-group differences, 'efficacious' is stronger than the evidence warrants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation showing the trial was powered for this LVM difference, together with the full paper hedging the conclusion as preliminary or in need of replication.

quotes.text: HIIT is an efficacious exercise intervention for increasing LVM in individuals previously hospitalized for COVID-19.
LVM increased in the HIIT vs. standard care group with a between-group difference of 6.8 [mean, 95%CI: 0.8; 12.8] g; p=0.029.

10.1152/japplphysiol.00489.2022.headline_claim: An individualized, supervised concurrent training program, with or without inspiratory muscle training, was safe and more effective than WHO self-care recommendations and inspiratory muscle training alone in outpatients with post-COVID-19 conditions.
10.1152/japplphysiol.00489.2022.overall: The paper's strongest result is for lower-body and upper-body strength, where supervised concurrent training outperforms the leaflet and inspiratory-training arms, but the headline claim of superior cardiovascular fitness is not supported by the null VO2max between-group comparison. Participant flow is internally inconsistent (80 versus 83), the control is unsupervised with self-reported outcomes, and no sample-size justification is given, so the symptom conclusions are tentative. The Discussion also overstates RM-alone effects.

primary_outcome.name: Estimated VO2max (mL/kg/min), with maximal and submaximal muscle strength described as primary
