issues.title: Conclusion claims superior cardiovascular fitness although the VO2max between-group comparison was null
issues.explanation: The estimated VO2max, named a primary outcome in the Discussion, showed no significant difference between groups. The Abstract conclusion, New & Noteworthy and Perspective nevertheless say the supervised program is more effective for regaining cardiovascular fitness. The support rests on within-group pre-post changes in CT and CTRM, which do not show superiority over the leaflet group. The Perspective also calls self-care 'highly inefficient', even though the control group improved on several measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group (interaction or ANCOVA) result for VO2max favouring CT/CTRM over CON.

quotes.text: no significant differences between groups were detected in the estimated V̇ o 2max
was safe and more effective than self-care recommendations and inspiratory muscle training alone, to regain cardiovascular and muscular fitness

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no significant between-group difference in estimated VO2max, yet its abstract conclusion, Discussion and Perspective say concurrent training was more effective than self-care and inspiratory training alone for cardiovascular fitness. The supportable claim is limited to within-group VO2max improvements in CT and CTRM, with superiority shown for strength, fatigue and depression but not for estimated VO2max.

issues.title: No sample size calculation; 17-23 per arm; many outcomes; confident superiority conclusions
issues.explanation: The paper reports no sample size calculation, and arms of 17 to 23 participants give little power for between-group comparisons. Many outcomes were analysed with a Bonferroni adjustment declared but no stated family of tests. The Limitations mention sample size only in terms of generalisability, not precision, while the conclusions are stated confidently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified power calculation for VO2max or strength, or a registry record stating the target sample size.

quotes.text: First, the sample size and the characteristics of the participants, it does not allow the results to be generalized
A 2 (group) × 2 (time: pre vs. post) factorial analysis of variance with Bonferroni adjustment was used to analyze the differences between groups.

issues.title: Paper's primary outcomes (VO2max, strength) differ from the single registered 'clinical status' outcome
issues.explanation: The registry lists one generic primary outcome, 'Changes in subject clinical status', while the paper calls estimated VO2max and muscle strength the primary outcomes and symptoms secondary. The paper does not say how its primary outcomes map to the registered one. This cannot be settled without the registry history.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing VO2max and strength were prespecified as the primary outcome measures.

quotes.text: was more effective in improving the primary outcomes (estimated V̇ o 2max and maximal and submaximal muscle strength)
Outcome of exercise test was the estimated V̇ o 2max (mL/kg/min).

issues.title: Randomized N reported as 80 but group sizes sum to 83; the 3 dropouts are only implicit; no flow diagram
issues.explanation: The Abstract says 80 were randomized, and Table 1 and the Abstract give group sizes of 20/17/23/20. The Results say 80 were 'included in the per-protocol analysis' with group sizes 21/25/17/20, which sum to 83. Three dropouts (one CT, two CTRM) reconcile the two sets, so about 83 were probably randomized, but the paper never says so and gives no CONSORT flow. Randomized and analysed numbers are therefore mislabelled and the attrition denominator is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow or statement that 83 were randomized and 80 analysed, with the Results group sizes defined as the randomized allocation.

quotes.text: Eighty patients were included in the per-protocol analysis, per group: CT ( *n* = 21), CTMR ( *n* = 25), RM ( *n* = 17), and CON ( *n* = 20).
Three patients dropped out of the study for reasons unrelated to symptom worsening
concurrent training (CT, number of subjects ( *n* ) = 20;

script.explanation: The Per-protocol group sizes against stated total does not reconcile: the arms of 'per-protocol analysed' sum to 83, but the stage reports n=80 -- 3 participant(s) appear or vanish between the total and its own breakdown.

issues.title: Discussion credits RM group with significant dyspnea and fatigue gains; Results show only SF-12 PA
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the multicomponent groups and the RM group each had significant improvements in quality of life, dyspnea and fatigue over time. The Results and Table 2 show the RM group significant only for SF-12 PA. RM mMRC, FSS and CFS changes carry no significance mark. The Discussion therefore overstates the inspiratory-training-alone effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Within-group test results showing significant RM pre-post changes in mMRC, FSS and CFS.

quotes.text: Changes were also observed in SF-12 PA domain for RM group.

Only in the multicomponent training groups (CT and CTRM) and the RM group, were there significant improvements in health-related quality of life, dyspnea (mMRC), and fatigue (both FSS and CFS-Linkert) over time.

issues.title: Efficacy based on per-protocol completers only; about 3 dropouts, none analysed; no ITT
issues.explanation: Efficacy was determined only in participants who completed the assigned program, and supervised arms required at least 20 of 24 sessions. No intention-to-treat analysis is given. With only 3 dropouts the effect on results is probably small, but the dropouts are all from the exercise arms, which makes completers somewhat favourable to exercise.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis including the 3 dropouts giving the same between-group results.

quotes.text: Determination of efficacy was based on the per-protocol (PP) population, which consisted of all participants who were randomized and completed the assigned programs.
Attendance ≥ 85% (at least 20 of the 24 scheduled sessions) was mandatory to continue in the study.

issues.title: Unsupervised leaflet control bundles supervision and attention with exercise; self-reported outcomes
issues.explanation: The control arm received an emailed leaflet with no monitoring, while the CT arms had coach and medical supervision at three sessions a week. For the self-reported symptom, fatigue and depression outcomes, the between-group differences cannot be separated from contact, attention and expectation. This fits a 'versus usual care' question but not a causal claim about the training itself.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control or blinded outcome assessment showing the same symptom differences.

quotes.text: As in real-life practice, indications were not directly supervised nor adherence monitored
All sessions were directed by certified strength and conditioning coaches and conducted under medical supervision.

issues.title: Abstract says CT improved significantly in dyspnea; the CT mMRC pre-post change is P = 0.063
issues.explanation: The Abstract says both CT and CTRM improved significantly for dyspnea. The Results show that the CT group's mMRC change was not significant (P = 0.063), though dyspnea symptom prevalence did fall in CT in Table 1. The statement holds for CTRM and for symptom prevalence in CT, but not for the mMRC scale in CT.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An Abstract that specified dyspnea as symptom prevalence rather than the mMRC scale.

quotes.text: The CT and CTRM groups improved significantly for dyspnea and fatigue, as did the health status.
and GAD-7 < 10 and mMRC in the CT group (both *P* = 0.063)

issues.title: Attendance rule says >=85% but '20 of 24' sessions is 83.3%
issues.explanation: The methods define the mandatory attendance threshold as 85%, equal to at least 20 of 24 sessions. 20/24 is 83.3%, and meeting 85% would need 21 sessions. The slip is minor and the realized mean attendance (88%) was above either threshold.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol defining 20/24 as the required threshold with the 85% only approximate.

quotes.text: Attendance ≥ 85% (at least 20 of the 24 scheduled sessions) was mandatory to continue in the study.

10.1155/2023/6687803.headline_claim: EECP was associated with reduced symptom burden, improved physical capacity and HRQoL in patients with PASC-associated angina and microvascular dysfunction, suggesting EECP may be beneficial for managing PASC.
10.1155/2023/6687803.overall: The study is a 10-patient, open-label, single-arm pilot, so it can only generate hypotheses. The claims of 'objective benefit' and of demonstrated benefit go beyond the data, since 6MWD change was not significant and was driven by one patient. Treat the findings as exploratory only; a few small table-text errors do not change this.

primary_outcome.name: Symptom burden (patient-reported PASC symptoms, angina and fatigue); 6MWD also reported as physical capacity outcome

issues.title: Single-arm, open-label pre/post design cannot attribute symptom gains to EECP
issues.explanation: All 10 patients received EECP and were compared only with their own baseline, with no control or sham arm and no blinding. The main improvements are patient-reported (angina, fatigue, symptom burden, HRQoL), so expectation, attention from the treatment course and natural recovery cannot be separated from a treatment effect. The conclusion that EECP is associated with benefit is therefore tentative at best.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or usual-care control group showing the same pre/post changes relative to control.

quotes.text: Limitations include the small sample size, the lack of a control group, and randomization.
EECPtreatment was associated with a reduction in symptom burden, improvement of physical capacity, and HRQoL

second_reader.what_stands: A single-arm, uncontrolled pre/post design cannot attribute the symptom changes to EECP, and the paper concedes the lack of a control group and calls for controlled studies. The Conclusions are hedged ('associated with'), but the Abstract and Discussion word the results causally ('demonstrates', 'benefits from EECP'), and the limitations omit placebo, expectation and regression-to-the-mean effects for the self-reported outcomes.

issues.title: 'Objective benefits' claimed though 6MWD change (+29.5 m, SD 54.9) was not significant
issues.explanation: The abstract and Discussion state that patients had subjective and objective benefits, and the conclusion cites improved physical capacity. The only objective measure, 6MWD, rose by a mean of 29.5 m (SD 54.9), which the authors say was not statistically significant. This mean is strongly influenced by one patient (+173.5 m), and the median gain is 21 m. The claim of objective benefit is not supported by the data presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant, controlled improvement in an objective measure such as 6MWD.

quotes.text: Tis pilot study demonstrates that patients with PASCassociated angina and MVD experienced subjective and objective benefts from EECP.
However, the improvement was not statistically signifcant.
Tese fndings suggest that EECP may be benefcial for the management of PASC.

second_reader.what_stands: The 6MWD gain (+29.5 m, SD 54.9) is not statistically significant (t about 1.70, p about 0.12), and one patient's +173.5 m drives much of the mean. The paper nonetheless claims 'objective benefits' in the Abstract and Discussion, 'improvement of physical capacity' in the Conclusions, and says that EECP 'may be beneficial for the management of PASC', without carrying the non-significance into those statements.

issues.title: 10-patient pilot, no sample-size calculation; many unadjusted outcomes with only p<0.05 reported
issues.explanation: With 10 patients and no power calculation, effect estimates are very imprecise. Many outcomes (symptoms, 6MWD, HADS, eight RAND-36 subscales) were assessed with no correction for multiplicity, and only 'p<0.05' is given for the symptom findings. This is acceptable for a pilot but weakens any confident reading of the symptom results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a power calculation, or multiplicity-adjusted results.

quotes.text: An interventional pilot study was performed, including 10 patients

issues.title: Text gives physical function +7.5; Table 3 PF row is 6.3 (7.5 is the role-physical row)
issues.explanation: The Results name physical function as a top-three improvement at +7.5. Table 3 gives 6.3 (12.4) for physical function, and 7.5 (37.4) belongs to role-physical (RP). The ranking sentence is therefore wrong for this subscale, but the effect is small and no conclusion depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 3 showing PF mean change 7.5, or a statement that the text refers to RP.

quotes.text: physical function (+7.5)

10.1155/2023/7068326.headline_claim: AIR significantly reduces fatigue and increases energy in people with Long COVID, and is more effective than an active health-and-wellness control.
10.1155/2023/7068326.overall: The within-group improvement in fatigue under AIR is fairly consistent, but the headline claim of superiority over an active control is not well supported: month 3 was not significant, LOCF and completer analyses were null, 60% of participants were lost with differential retention, and the energy superiority claim rests on within-arm changes alone. The conclusions should be read as preliminary evidence of improvement in both arms, not as demonstrated AIR superiority.

primary_outcome.name: General fatigue (MFI), change over time, AIR vs active control

issues.title: Energy superiority over control claimed from within-arm changes; no between-group difference (all p ≥ 0.274)
issues.explanation: The Conclusion and Abstract say AIR gave more significant energy results than the active control, and cite an energy gain of 18.26 versus 10.40. Those are separate within-group changes. The between-group comparison was not significant at any time point (month 3 p = 0.335), the group-by-time interaction was also not significant (p = 0.084), and AIR started with the lower baseline energy score. The data show both arms improved similarly, and do not show AIR superior on energy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant group-by-time interaction or between-group difference in energy change from baseline.

quotes.text: Moreover, the AIR intervention yielded more signifcant fatigue reduction and energy enhancement results than an active control group.
However, no signifcant diference was found between groups at any time interval, as shown in Table 2.
the absolute increase in mean scores for energy for the AIR group (18.26) was almost twice that of the active control group (10.40)

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion and abstract claim energy results superior to the active control, but the only support is the larger within-arm change (18.26 vs 10.40) and larger within-arm effect size; the interaction (p = 0.084) and every between-group comparison (p >= 0.274) are non-significant. AIR also started 3.3 points lower, so the larger raw change is partly consistent with a lower baseline. The authors do state the null between-group result in the Results, but the conclusion does not carry that qualification.

issues.title: 60% attrition, differential by arm; between-group fatigue benefit appears only under EM imputation
issues.explanation: Only 40 of 100 randomized completed all measures, with 46% retention in AIR versus 34% in control. Between-group fatigue differences were significant at months 1 and 2 only with EM imputation; under LOCF (p = 0.116, 0.167, 0.115) and completer analyses (p = 0.117, 0.132, 0.146) no between-group difference was significant. The claim that the methods returned 'nearly identical results' is not borne out for the between-group comparison, so the superiority claim depends on the imputation model applied to a majority of missing data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (e.g. mixed model under MAR with auxiliary variables or multiple imputation) showing the between-group difference persists.

quotes.text: Notably, the retention rate for the AIR group was higher ( n � 23; 46%) than that for the control group ( n � 17; 34%).
Tere was no signifcant diference between groups at any time interval (baseline: p � 0 . 286, month 1: p � 0 . 116, month 2: p � 0 . 167, and month 3: p � 0 . 115).
Both approaches returned nearly identical results.

second_reader.what_stands: Attrition of 60% (40% completers), with 46% vs 34% retention by arm, is correct and disclosed, and between-group fatigue differences are significant only under EM imputation (M1 p = 0.004, M2 p = 0.048), not under LOCF (p >= 0.115) or completers (p >= 0.117). The claim that the three approaches gave 'nearly identical results' holds for within-arm changes but not for the between-group comparison. The retention difference between arms is small and was not tested, so 'differential' attrition is a descriptive observation rather than an established bias.

issues.title: Fatigue superiority over control stated without qualification; month 3 p = 0.058, month 2 p = 0.048
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Conclusion say AIR yielded more significant fatigue results than the active control. The between-group difference at month 3, the end of the intervention, was not significant (p = 0.058), month 2 was borderline (p = 0.048), and LOCF and completer analyses found no between-group differences. The within-group AIR effect is robust, but the claim of superiority over an active control is only tentative and is stated more strongly than the evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary endpoint at month 1 or 2 with multiplicity control, or a significant between-group result at month 3.

quotes.text: Additionally, the AIR group experienced more signifcant outcomes than the active control group.
approaching a signifcant diference at month 3 with a small efect size

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract and conclusion state superior fatigue reduction versus control without qualification, while month 3 is p = 0.058 and month 2 is a borderline p = 0.048, and the advantage disappears under LOCF and completers analyses. The Results section does describe month 3 as 'approaching' significance, so the qualification is present there, but not in the abstract or conclusion. The interaction under EM (p = 0.001) does support a differential time course under that analysis.

issues.title: No trial registration or prespecified primary outcome reported for the randomized trial
issues.explanation: The paper reports IRB approval but no trial registry identifier or protocol, so the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be checked against a prespecification. This matters because fatigue and energy were both analysed with several imputation methods and multiple between-group comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry made before enrolment listing the same primary outcome and analysis.

quotes.text: approved by the Institutional Review Board (or Ethics Committee) of Luther College (protocol code 30.20 and October 22, 2020)

issues.title: Table 1 baseline fatigue difference printed 0.05; printed means 17.54 and 17.04 give 0.50
issues.explanation: The baseline row of Table 1 prints a between-group difference of 0.05, but the two printed means differ by 0.50. Every other row of the table matches its means. This is a typographical slip in a baseline row and does not affect any between-group result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the baseline means were different from those printed, such that the difference is genuinely 0.05.

10.1155/ijcp/5641307.headline_claim: Both taVNS and sham taVNS reduced fatigue severity in post-COVID syndrome, with sham taVNS reported as superior to taVNS.
10.1155/ijcp/5641307.overall: The paper's fatigue result is internally contradictory: the abstract says taVNS beat sham while the conclusion says sham was superior, and the supporting p-values in Tables 3 and 4 do not follow from the printed statistics. The autonomic claims rest mainly on within-arm changes and the sample is small, so the paper supports only a tentative, hypothesis-generating reading, which the authors partly acknowledge.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue severity (FSS)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: After the evaluation of the patients on the first day of participation in the study, the final evaluation was completed at the end of the 10th session (10 days later).

issues.title: Abstract says taVNS beat sham on FSS (p=0.022) but concludes sham was superior; the data favour taVNS change
issues.explanation: The abstract results say taVNS was more effective than sham in decreasing FSS, yet the abstract conclusion and Results 3.2 say sham was superior. The sham arm's lower post-treatment FSS (4.79 vs 5.05) reflects its lower baseline (5.16 vs 5.57). The change from baseline was larger with taVNS (about -0.52 vs -0.37), as the Discussion itself notes. The 'sham superior' headline therefore contradicts both the abstract results and the paper's own change-score data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the conclusion refers to unadjusted post-treatment scores, together with a baseline-adjusted analysis showing no taVNS advantage.

quotes.text: taVNS was more effective than sham taVNS in decreasing FSS
with sham taVNS being superior to taVNS

second_reader.what_stands: The paper contradicts itself. The abstract Results and Section 3.4 favour taVNS on FSS change, while the abstract Conclusion, Section 3.2 and Section 5 say sham was superior or had the greater decrease. The change data (0.52 vs 0.37) favour taVNS, so the 'sham superior' statement is not supported by the change scores. The 0.15-point difference itself is small and its p-value is questionable (see i15).

issues.title: Autonomic conclusion rests on within-arm changes; between-group RMSSD, SNS, LF/HF showed no difference
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says taVNS may increase parasympathetic dominance and reduce sympathetic activity. This rests on significant change within the taVNS arm but not the sham arm, which is not a valid comparison of the arms. Between-group tests after treatment were null for RMSSD, SNS index and LF/HF, and the Discussion itself says the within-group changes could be nonspecific or placebo-related and that the stimulation does not shift sympathovagal balance. The conclusion goes beyond what the paper's own tests show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant between-group (or interaction) tests for RMSSD, SNS index and LF/HF.

quotes.text: The present study suggests that taVNS may have a potential to impact autonomic regulation by increasing parasympathetic dominance and reducing sympathetic activity in patients with PCS.
suggesting that auricular vagal stimulation does not shift sympathovagal balance towards parasympathetic dominance.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of reduced sympathetic activity rests on a within-arm SNS index change, and the RMSSD and LF/HF improvements are also within-arm only. Between-group comparisons showed no difference for these, and the authors' own Discussion says the RMSSD result argues against a parasympathetic shift. The PNS index and LF power do have between-group support, and the Conclusion is hedged, so the overall statement is weaker than 'no support' but still overreaches for the sympathetic claim.

issues.title: Table 4 p-values do not follow from printed t (FSS t=-1.151 gives p≈0.26, printed 0.022); abstract relies on them
issues.explanation: For the FSS change-score comparison Table 4 prints t = -1.151 yet p = 0.022; with 40 degrees of freedom that t corresponds to p of about 0.26. The HF and LF rows show the same pattern (t = -0.990, p = 0.042; t = 5.126, p = 0.029). Cohen's d (-0.355) matches the t value, so the p-values appear to be the erroneous entries. The abstract claim that taVNS was more effective for FSS and LF/HF power depends on these p-values. Table 3's post-treatment FSS t of -0.571 with p 0.034 similarly does not fit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or a corrected table showing p=0.022 for this comparison, for example from an ANCOVA-based test.

quotes.text: taVNS was more effective than sham taVNS in decreasing FSS

script.explanation: The printed t = -1.151 supports p no smaller than 0.25616, but the paper reports p = 0.022 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

second_reader.what_stands: In Table 4 the printed p-values for FSS (0.022), HF power (0.042) and LF power (0.029) do not follow from the printed t statistics and sample size. The FSS t of -1.151 corresponds to p of about 0.26, so the abstract's claim that taVNS was more effective in decreasing FSS (p = 0.022) is not supported by the paper's own numbers. Only the PNS index p-value is reproducible.

issues.title: Planned d=0.80, alpha 0.05, power 0.80 needs about 26 per arm; 21 per arm enrolled, and no N is stated
issues.explanation: The paper says the sample size was set a priori for d=0.80, power 0.80 and alpha 0.05, but never states the resulting N. A two-sample t test with those inputs needs about 26 per group, not 21. Observed effects (d about 0.2 to 0.45) are far smaller than planned, as the authors admit. The effectiveness statements in the abstract ('both ... were effective') are therefore based on a trial underpowered even for its own assumption.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A printed G*Power output showing 42 total participants suffices under the stated inputs.

quotes.text: based on an assumed large effect size
This implies that a larger-sample size of approximately 32 per group would be needed for adequate power.

issues.title: Registered primary outcome is HRV (10 sessions); paper foregrounds fatigue FSS and 20 sessions
issues.explanation: The registry lists HRV as the only primary outcome with a 10-session endpoint. The paper's title, abstract aim and conclusion centre on fatigue and it reports a 20-day protocol without naming a primary outcome or explaining the change. Because fatigue is neither registered as primary nor declared primary in the paper, its status as the main result cannot be verified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing fatigue was registered as primary or the protocol changed before data collection.

quotes.text: The aim of this study was to investigate and compare the effectiveness of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) and sham taVNS in fatigue in individuals with PCS.
Each participant received the taVNS every day for 20 days

issues.title: Table 2 height 172 vs 164 cm (t=3.025) printed with p=0.738; baseline 'similar' claim unsupported
issues.explanation: The height means and SDs imply a clear baseline difference (about 8 cm, t near 3.2, p near 0.003), yet the table prints p = 0.738 and the text says groups were similar. Other Table 2 rows have the same mismatch (age t=0.222 with p=0.413; BMI t=0.112 with p=0.219). The baseline balance claim is therefore not supported by the table as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Corrected Table 2 with consistent t and p, or raw baseline heights.

quotes.text: The groups were similar in terms of physical characteristics (Table 2).

issues.title: Participant blinding unverified for a self-rated fatigue outcome with a no-current sham
issues.explanation: Fatigue was self-rated on the FSS, and the sham group received no current while the active device was run at perceptible intensities, so participants may have guessed their allocation. No blinding check was reported. The paper discloses this limitation and does not claim taVNS efficacy, so the effect on the stated conclusion is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant allocation-guess questionnaire showing blinding was maintained.

quotes.text: this study has an assessor-blinded design and is not double-blind
In both groups, FSS scores decreased significantly over time, indicating that part of the improvement may be related to natural recovery or nonspecific effects.

issues.title: Registry flags registration as retrospective; paper dates conduct to June-Dec 2023, after registration
issues.explanation: The registry start date precedes first submission, so the record is flagged retrospective. The paper dates enrolment to 1 June to 1 December 2023, after the January 2023 submission, and calls the study prospective. The mismatch is probably a registry date entry issue but cannot be settled from the paper alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the start date was a planned value, or dated recruitment records.

quotes.text: between 1 June and 1 December 2023
approved on 26/10/2022

issues.title: Results text gives taVNS post-treatment FSS SD as 0.10; Table 3 gives 1.10
issues.explanation: The Results text prints 5.05 ± 0.10 for the taVNS group after treatment, while Table 3 prints 5.05 ± 1.10. The Table 3 value is consistent with the reported effect size, so the text appears to be the error. A reader of the text alone would see an implausibly tight spread.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the SD is 0.10.

quotes.text: 5.05 ± 0.10 in the taVNS group

issues.title: Post-treatment FSS cut-point counts: arms sum to 23 and 17, not the stated 24 and 18; arms of 16 and 24, not 21 and 21
issues.explanation: The post-treatment categories (<4 and >=4) are mutually exclusive, but the per-arm counts add to 23 and 17 rather than 24 and 18. The sham arm counts sum to 16 and the taVNS arm to 24, though each arm has 21 participants. The stated totals (24+18=42) fit the whole sample but not the arm counts, so at least two numbers are wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing counts that sum to 21 per arm and to the stated totals.

quotes.text: 54% of the participants ( n � 24) (sham taVNS: 9, taVNS: 14)
46% of the participants ( n � 18) (sham taVNS: 7, taVNS: 10)

issues.title: Results 3.4 'mean differences' of 53 (HF) and 6.85 (LF) are after-treatment values, swapped, not Table 4 deltas
issues.explanation: The text reports mean pre/post differences of 53 for HF power and 6.85 for LF power. In Table 4 the HF delta is 0.30 and the LF delta is -70.4; 6.85 is the HF after-treatment value and 53 is the LF after-treatment value. The text therefore misassigns two table cells to the wrong parameters and the wrong quantity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the text's differences come from a different analysis.

quotes.text: 53 (HF power), and 6.85 (LF power)

issues.title: Table 2: 10 of 21 males printed as 52% (should be 48%); chi-squared 3.422 for identical distributions
issues.explanation: Ten of 21 is 47.6%, and 11 of 21 is 52.4%, so the printed 52% and 48% are swapped. Both arms have the identical sex split (10 male, 11 female), which gives a chi-squared of 0 and p=1, not 3.422 and p=0.116. The table's sex row is thus wrong in two ways, though it has no effect on the main findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator that makes 10 correspond to 52%.

quotes.text: Male 10 (52)
Sham taVNS ( n =21)

script.explanation: 10/21 = 47.62%, but the paper prints 52, outside the rounding interval [51.50, 53.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 19.2 rather than 21.

10.1155/ijcp/7692776.headline_claim: The authors conclude that ReCOVery APP did not significantly improve quality of life in Long COVID patients over 6 months, and that adherence, professional support and longer-term studies need investigation.
10.1155/ijcp/7692776.overall: The null primary result (no significant SF-36 improvement at 6 months) is the paper's main conclusion, and it is reasonably reported, though based only on a completers analysis of 80 of 100 participants. The favourable statements about secondary outcomes and symptom regression go beyond the data, and several Table 3 and Table 4 values do not match the text or each other. These are mostly reporting slips and overstated secondary claims, and they do not reverse the primary finding.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 quality of life (physical and mental health components)

issues.title: Physical-health regression: text b -0.723 and PAM b 0.777, p 0.51 differ from Table 4 (-0.654; 0.765, p 0.061)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives -0.723 for number of symptoms, but Table 4 prints -0.654. For PAM the text gives b 0.777 and p 0.51, but the table gives 0.765 and p 0.061. The text calls this a 'tendency towards significance', which fits p 0.061 rather than 0.51, so the text p looks like a typo for 0.051 or 0.061. The text-versus-table differences affect only exploratory coefficients in a non-significant model, but the authors need to say which numbers are right.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values come from a different (for example bootstrapped) model, with the corresponding output provided.

quotes.text: increases in physical health-related quality of life could be predicted by experiencing a lower number of symptoms
quotes.location: Results, paragraph on first regression model

issues.title: Abstract claims a 'decrease in symptoms' effect, but the model uses T2 symptom level among many T2 covariates
issues.explanation: The abstract and discussion say that a decrease in symptoms is related to better mental quality of life. The model enters the 6-month symptom count, not the change, together with other 6-month variables measured at the same time as the outcome. This is an exploratory association, and it does not show that symptom reduction produced the improvement. The physical-health model was non-significant (p = 0.065), and the health-literacy coefficient is negative while the text calls it a 'better scores' relationship.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A model using change in symptoms (T2-T0), adjusted for baseline symptoms, that gives the same association.

quotes.text: In the second model, improvement in mental health-related quality of life (T2-T0) was included as dependent variable.
Linear regression analyses revealed a signifcant relationship between the decrease in the number of symptoms and the improvement in mental health-related quality.
Number of symptoms (T2)

issues.title: Table 3 T2 means for PAM (31.46) and ISI (12.05) do not reconcile with T0 and the T2-T0 change
issues.explanation: For PAM, T0 is 39.75 and T2 is 31.46, which implies a change of about -8.3. The table prints +0.71, and Table 2 shows PAM at 6 months near 40 in both arms. For ISI, T2 minus T0 is 0.03, but the printed change is 0.47. Table 2 arm means weighted by n give about 12.5, so the printed 12.05 looks like a transposition. These are transcription errors in an all-participants secondary table, and they do not touch the primary comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors' dataset (Zenodo) showing PAM T2 about 40.5 and ISI T2 about 12.5 with the printed changes.

issues.title: Efficacy analysed only in 80 of 100 randomised (completers); no ITT or missing-data analysis
issues.explanation: All between-group comparisons use only participants who completed the 6-month assessment, and 8 reinfected people were excluded. The paper reports no intention-to-treat or imputed analysis, and Table 2 shows 42 of 52 and 38 of 48 remaining. The groups also differed at baseline in SF-36 physical health (29.06 versus 35.58, p = 0.053), and this was not adjusted for. The null primary conclusion is tentative rather than overturned.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis giving the same null result for the SF-36 comparison.

quotes.text: To analyze the efectiveness of ReCOVery APP, a perprotocol analysis was performed.
Intervention group had 52 participants in T0, 47 participants in T1, and 42 participants in T2.

issues.title: Text claims greater intervention improvement in five secondary variables; none is significant (e.g. mental QoL p 0.559)
issues.explanation: The Results state that the intervention group improved more on mental quality of life, cognition, emotional wellbeing, activation and health literacy. Table 2 gives p-values of 0.559, 0.097, 0.878, 0.194 and 0.793 for these changes, so no between-group difference is shown. Health literacy actually fell more in the intervention arm. The Conclusions then cite the cognitive 'positive trend' as a sign of benefit and link it to adherence, but the paper reports no adherence analysis. These statements overstate secondary findings on a trial whose primary result was null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests (adjusted or unadjusted) showing significant advantages for these five outcomes.

quotes.text: the intervention group improved to a greater extent from the beginning of the project (T2-T0) in the following variables: mental health-related quality of life, cognitive status, emotional wellbeing, activation, and health literacy.

quotes.location: Table 2, SF-36 mental health, T2-T0 row

quotes.text: the positive trend observed in cognitive status suggests that aspects of the intervention may be benefcial

10.1159/000528188.headline_claim: Olfactory training improves subjective olfactory function and reduces parosmia in post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction, and should be recommended as a first-intention treatment for post-viral olfactory dysfunction.
10.1159/000528188.overall: The paper's recommendation of OT as first-line treatment for all post-viral OD is not supported: the only objective, prespecified primary outcome was null and the supporting subjective and parosmia findings rest on within-arm tests, a borderline sparse-cell chi-squared and completers only. At most the study suggests hypotheses for a properly powered, blinded trial. Reporting slips such as SE labelled as SD are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Amelioration of objective olfactory function (UPSIT-40 score)

issues.title: Null primary UPSIT-40 result, yet OT recommended as first-line for all post-viral OD
issues.explanation: The prespecified primary outcome (objective olfactory function by UPSIT-40) showed no group, time or interaction effect. The conclusion nevertheless recommends OT as first-intention treatment for all post-viral OD patients. That rests on unblinded-prone subjective ratings, a borderline parosmia comparison and a quality-of-life gain seen equally in placebo. For a self-described pilot, this recommendation is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified adequately powered analysis showing a between-group benefit on UPSIT or other objective measures.

quotes.text: We did not observe any effect of OT on scores in a validated test of olfactory function
it should therefore be recommended as a first-intention treatment option to all patients presenting with post-viral OD.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary objective outcome (UPSIT-40) showed no effect, and the supporting findings are weak: the subjective gain had a non-significant group-by-time interaction (p = 0.091), and the parosmia result is fragile (see i9). Even so, the Conclusion recommends OT as first-line for all post-viral OD. Safety and low cost may justify offering OT, but the data do not show efficacy. The study was also limited to post-COVID OD, so 'all post-viral OD' goes beyond the population studied.

issues.title: Subjective improvement claimed from within-arm tests after non-significant group×time interaction (p = 0.091)
issues.explanation: The interaction of group and time, the test of whether OT differs from placebo, was not significant (p = 0.091). The authors then tested each arm separately and treated 'significant in the intervention arm, not in placebo' as a treatment effect. A difference in significance is not a significant difference, and both arms improved numerically. The conclusion that OT improves subjective function is therefore not shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group difference in change scores for the subjective outcomes.

quotes.text: the interaction of group*time showed a trend (F(1,39) = 2.99; p = 0.091). We therefore decided to carry out post hoc tests by comparing scores for both groups.
the effect is significant in the intervention group but not in the placebo group

second_reader.what_stands: The between-group test of whether the subjective improvement differs by arm was not significant (p = 0.091). The claim of a subjective effect of OT rests on the intervention arm reaching significance within itself while the placebo arm did not. A significant change in one arm and a non-significant change in the other does not establish a difference between arms. The Conclusion's 'OT leads to improved subjective olfactory function' therefore overstates what the data show.

issues.title: Parosmia reduction claimed from a borderline post-only chi-squared (p = 0.049) with a sparse cell
issues.explanation: After training, 14/19 vs 21/22 reported parosmia, tested by a chi-squared with p = 0.049. One cell (placebo without parosmia, n = 1) has expected count well below 5, so an exact test would likely give a larger p. The intervention arm moved only from 80% to 74%, and the difference partly reflects an increase in the placebo arm. The stated N of 42 also differs from the 41 implied by the counts. The conclusion that OT reduces parosmia is fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An exact test or adjusted model on all participants giving p well below 0.05 with a within-person change difference.

quotes.text: 14/19 participants from the trained group indicated parosmia, while this number was 21/22 in the placebo group
The frequency of parosmia was significantly lower after OT.

second_reader.what_stands: The only support for 'significantly lower after OT' is a post-only between-group χ² of p = 0.049, with an expected cell count of about 2.8; an exact test gives about p = 0.08. The intervention arm's parosmia rate barely changed (80% to 74%), and most of the difference at follow-up comes from a rise in the placebo arm (86% to 95%). No test of change over time or of the group-by-time interaction is reported. Denominators also differ between time points (20 vs 19 in the intervention arm), and the printed N of 42 does not match the 41 that reproduces the statistic. The claim that parosmia frequenc

issues.title: Analyses restricted to 41 of 50 randomised (19 vs 22); no ITT analysis or CONSORT flow
issues.explanation: Only participants returning at follow-up were analysed, with different loss per arm (5 vs 3), and no imputation or ITT analysis is shown. Reasons for dropout are not given. This weakens the secondary findings, though it does not create the main problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis giving the same results with all 50 randomised participants.

quotes.text: At follow-up, a total of 41 participants returned, namely 19 from the intervention group and 22 from the placebo group.

issues.title: Subjective and parosmia outcomes prone to expectation; blinding success with odorless placebo not assessed
issues.explanation: The headline benefits are self-reported yes/no or 0-10 ratings, while the placebo vials contained no odor. Participants may have inferred their allocation, and the authors themselves attribute the quality-of-life gain in both arms to placebo-type effects. Blinding was not tested, so the subjective results are open to bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinding-success questionnaire showing participants could not identify their arm.

quotes.text: This may very well be a placebo effect, as patients may have felt empowerment in face of their olfactory deficits
placebo control trials with OT are difficult because we can suppose participants could ask a third party to sniff the vial

issues.title: Pooled self-evaluation dispersions (0.28-0.40) labelled SD but match SEs; subgroup SDs are 1.8-3.0
issues.explanation: The Results label 0.29, 0.36, 0.28 and 0.40 as SD, yet the subgroup SDs for the same 0-10 ratings are 1.8-3.0. Values of this size fit standard errors with n about 41. The mislabelling is a reporting slip that does not change any test result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing a pooled SD of about 0.29 on the 0-10 scale (not possible given the subgroup SDs).

quotes.text: average scores before training: (mean [SD]) 4.3 (0.29) points
before: 3.8 [1.9] points; after: 5.4 [1.8] points

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported for a randomized trial
issues.explanation: The paper gives an ethics approval number but no registry identifier, so prespecification of the primary and secondary outcomes cannot be checked. This is a transparency gap rather than a demonstrated problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prospective registry entry listing UPSIT-40 as primary and the same secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: The protocol, its amendments, and other documents were approved by the Medical Research Ethics Committee of the CIUSSS MCQ (MP-2021-486).

10.1159/pps/aemag017.headline_claim: Immersive VR exercise therapy is feasible, safe, and acceptable for post-COVID fatigue, with a potential clinical signal favouring VR, although the primary between-group difference was not significant.
10.1159/pps/aemag017.overall: The primary comparison was null (3.03 points, p = 0.15), and the authors say so, but the Conclusion still claims a signal favouring VR from non-significant exploratory contrasts and calls VR safe from a small pilot. The paper has real internal inconsistencies about Con-EG attrition (38 vs 47 with primary data) plus a sign error in the primary CI. Only the descriptive conclusion that VR was feasible and that both arms improved is reasonably supported.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) from baseline (T0) to post-intervention (T1)

issues.title: Con-EG: 12 of 50 left before T1 (38 left) but 47/50 reported with primary-endpoint data
issues.explanation: The paper says 12 Con-EG participants discontinued before the post-intervention assessment, and the CONSORT legend says all dropouts occurred before T1 completion. Yet the complete-case set, responder and worsening analyses use 47 Con-EG participants. Other Con-EG denominators also differ (38 implied by 21 = 55.3%; 46 in the global-impression percentages). The statement that missing data were small (<7%) and the responder and worsening comparisons cannot all be right. The missing-data handling and the secondary comparisons would need to be rechecked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Showing that the 12 Con-EG dropouts still contributed T1 FSS data (for example through late assessment), or that 47 is a typographical error for 38 with the downstream percentages recomputed.

quotes.text: with three participants in the VR-EG and 12 participants in the Con-EG discontinuing participation prior to the post-intervention assessment
[47/50 (94.0%)] in the Con-EG had no missing data for the primary endpoint
quotes.location: Results, Participant Population for Sensitivity Analyses

quotes.text: only 21 participants (55.3%) in the Con-EG met this benchmark
quotes.location: Results, Adherence to the Study Protocol

second_reader.what_stands: The paper gives incompatible Con-EG denominators. 12 of 50 left before T1, which leaves 38 and matches the 21/38 = 55.3% adherence figure. Yet 47/50 are reported as having complete primary-endpoint data and 47 are used in the responder and worsening analyses, as against the stated <7% missingness. The paper does not say which counts are correct, so the complete-case, responder and worsening analyses for Con-EG cannot be verified. I only checked internal consistency of the counts, not the underlying data.

issues.title: Null primary (p = 0.15) and non-significant exploratory outcomes presented as a signal favouring VR
issues.explanation: The primary between-group difference is 3.03 points with p = 0.15, below the 6.3-point threshold, and the 3- and 12-month differences are also non-significant. The responder comparison (39.5% vs 34%, p = 0.59) shows no difference, and the worsening comparison (p = 0.073) is not significant, yet the Conclusion cites both as a consistent pattern favouring VR. Pointing out that only the VR group's within-group change exceeded 6.3 points does not show a between-group difference. All of these outcomes were analysed post hoc or without multiplicity adjustment, so a signal is not supported; at most the data are compatible with a benefit or none.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified, adequately powered test showing a between-group benefit on responders or worsening.

quotes.text: suggests a potential clinical signal favoring immersive VR
Only the VR-EG exceeded the predefined clinically relevant reduction of at least 6.3 points.
A clinically relevant improvement of ≤ -6.3 points on the FSS was achieved by 17 of 43 participants (39.5%) in the VR-EG and 16 of 47 participants (34%) in the Con-EG

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion does rest its 'potential clinical signal favoring immersive VR' on a primary outcome with p = 0.15 and on secondary or post hoc outcomes that were non-significant (responders p = 0.59, worsening p = 0.073) or untested (PGIC, exertion). It also omits the null primary result from that sentence. The wording is hedged ('potential', 'exploratory'), the null primary and nonsignificant follow-ups are reported elsewhere, and larger trials are called for, so this is a case of overly favourable framing rather than a claim of efficacy.

issues.title: Per-protocol analysis described as correcting for higher Con-EG dropout; no per-protocol estimate in the text
issues.explanation: The Discussion says all sensitivity analyses, including a per-protocol analysis that corrects for the much higher dropout in the comparison group, supported the results. A per-protocol set removes non-adherent participants; it does not adjust for missing outcomes, and the Results text reports no per-protocol estimate or its size. With 24% vs 6.5% attrition and arm-differential adherence, robustness to missing data and to non-adherence is asserted rather than shown in the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The per-protocol estimate and CI in Table S4, along with a missing-data sensitivity analysis (for example multiple imputation) with similar results.

quotes.text: All sensitivity analyses supported the adequacy of results, including the per-protocol analysis correcting for the much higher dropout rate in the comparison group.
only 21 participants (55.3%) in the Con-EG met this benchmark
quotes.location: Results, Adherence to the Study Protocol

issues.title: Sample size based on 0.9-point item-mean difference (about 8.1 FSS points) versus observed 3.03
issues.explanation: The design assumed a between-group difference of 0.9 on the 1-7 item-mean FSS, equivalent to about 8.1 points on the 9-63 sum scale used in reporting. That exceeds the paper's own 6.3-point MCID and is 2.7 times the observed difference of 3.03. The trial could therefore detect only a very large advantage, and its null result is uninformative for effects of 3 points or so. The authors partly acknowledge underpowering.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A justification that 8.1 sum-scale points is a clinically expected effect from prior data, or a corrected assumed difference.

quotes.text: a mean difference of 0.9 (SD = 1.5) in FSS scores between groups was anticipated
A sample size of 45 participants per group provided 80% power to detect this difference

issues.title: Registration dated 16 June 2023, three months after stated start of recruitment in March 2023
issues.explanation: The trial register entry post-dates the stated start of recruitment. If participants were enrolled before registration, the trial is not strictly prospectively registered and the primary outcome could not be verified as fixed in advance. The paper supplies no first-randomisation date, so this cannot be resolved here. The primary outcome (FSS change) is the same as the protocol described, which limits practical concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A first-randomisation date after 16 June 2023, or a registry history showing an earlier record.

quotes.text: Recruitment took place between March 2023 and April 2024
The trial was preregistered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00032059) on June 16, 2023.

issues.title: 'Safe' stated flatly from 46 VR participants; 'infrequent' AEs described while 61% had an AE and 87% had vertigo
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says VR is safe, feasible and acceptable without qualification, from a 46-participant pilot where the authors admit AE ascertainment differed between arms. The Results call adverse events infrequent while 60.9% of VR participants had at least one and 87% had vertigo (all mild or moderate, transient). Absence of severe events in 46 people cannot exclude a modest rate of harm. The Con-EG dropout (24% vs 6.5%) also complicates the 'acceptable' claim for the comparator rather than for VR.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety endpoint with an adequately powered or confidence-interval-based safety conclusion.

quotes.text: this exploratory randomized controlled trial shows that immersive VR exercise therapy is feasible, safe, and acceptable for patients with post-COVID fatigue
Adverse events were infrequent and generally mild across both study arms.

issues.title: VR participants told their allocation after randomisation; patient-reported outcomes and 'double-blind' wording
issues.explanation: Participants in the VR arm were told that their intervention was VR, and the primary outcome and most secondary favourable outcomes (global impression, perceived worsening, FSS) are self-reported. The differential dropout (12 Con-EG vs 3 VR-EG, 11 of them citing dissatisfaction) suggests the control arm perceived itself as the less attractive arm. This makes expectancy effects a plausible contributor to the self-reported VR advantages that the Conclusion relies on. The 'double-blind' description in the limitations is not accurate for participants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence from a credibility/expectancy measure showing equal expectations across arms at T1.

quotes.text: Following randomization, only participants assigned to the VR-EG were informed about the VR-based nature of their intervention.
although an active comparator and double-blind procedures were used to minimize expectancy effects

issues.title: Primary FSS difference 3.03 printed with CI –1.02 to –7.06; upper bound sign wrong (should be about +7.06)
issues.explanation: The printed interval has reversed bounds and does not contain the estimate. Read with a positive upper bound it is centred on 3.03 and matches p = 0.15 and the two within-group reductions. This is a typographical error in the headline primary result, not a change in the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the printed interval itself is impossible as written. It would be dismissed only if the journal's typeset version shows +7.06.

issues.title: Attendance reported as up to 14 of 12 scheduled sessions
issues.explanation: The Methods schedule 12 sessions, but the Results say completers attended at most 14 of the 12 scheduled sessions. Either the range or the schedule is misreported, or extra sessions were delivered without being described. This does not affect the main findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that make-up sessions beyond 12 were allowed, or a corrected range.

quotes.text: All participants who completed the study attended at least 10 and no more than 14 of the 12 scheduled sessions.
quotes.location: Results, Adherence to the Study Protocol

quotes.text: Participants in both groups completed 12 supervised training sessions over 6 weeks

10.11604/pamj.2023.46.65.36615.headline_claim: Six weeks of respiratory muscle training improved persistent symptoms, lung function and exercise tolerance in COVID-19 survivors, and the authors describe it as a safe and effective option.
10.11604/pamj.2023.46.65.36615.overall: The headline claim that respiratory muscle training/pulmonary rehabilitation is safe and effective rests on within-group pre-post changes in a small non-randomised study; every between-group test in Table 3 is non-significant and the control arm also changed on several measures. The paper's text also misdescribes the control-arm results and uses undisclosed, shifting denominators. Benefit is plausible but not demonstrated.

primary_outcome.name: Persistent symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, cough, chest pain) at 6 weeks

issues.title: Benefit claimed from within-arm change; all between-group (factorial ANOVA) tests non-significant
issues.explanation: The conclusion of benefit rests on pre-post Wilcoxon tests within the training arm. The between-arm factorial ANOVA in Table 3 is non-significant for every outcome (e.g. FEV1 L p=0.806, 6-MWD p=0.477), and the control arm also improved in several measures. The data therefore do not show that training did better than no training, and the paper never discusses this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group comparison of change scores or an interaction test showing a significant group-by-time effect.

quotes.text: Comparison of means between T0 and T6 was performed using Wilcoxon test.
A significant improvement in dyspnea, cough, fatigue, and chest pain was noted in G1 after 6 weeks (Table 2).

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusions of benefit (Results, Discussion, Conclusion) rest on within-G1 pre/post Wilcoxon tests, while all 13 between-group factorial ANOVA p-values in Table 3 are non-significant (0.093 to 0.97); the paper does not discuss this. For the Table 2 symptom outcomes no between-group test is reported at all, so the claim there is based solely on within-arm change versus a non-significant change in a 12-patient comparison arm.

issues.title: Non-randomised 12-patient control, allocation undescribed, matched on age, sex, BMI only
issues.explanation: Patients were not randomised and the paper does not say how they came to be in G1 or G2. Matching on three variables leaves baseline lung function and exercise capacity unbalanced (FEV1 93.7% vs 81.4%, DLCO 66% vs 76%). Group differences other than training could account for the comparisons, so the control only weakly supports a causal reading.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of allocation showing it was independent of patient characteristics and baseline balance on outcome variables.

quotes.text: The groups were matched based on age, sex and BMI.

second_reader.what_stands: The control group is a non-randomised 12-patient group, the allocation procedure is not described, and matching is stated only on age, sex and BMI (not on baseline severity or outcome values), with visible baseline differences in several functional measures. The paper does not claim randomisation, and the small sample size and need for further studies are acknowledged only in general terms.

issues.title: 'Pulmonary rehabilitation safe and effective' stated, though only respiratory muscle training was tested
issues.explanation: The key-points box says the study demonstrated that pulmonary rehabilitation was a safe and effective option. The Discussion concedes that the intervention was respiratory muscle training only and is not complete pulmonary rehabilitation. With no significant between-group effect and a small non-randomised design, 'demonstrated' effectiveness is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the wording and limitation are both printed.

quotes.text: The present study demonstrated that pulmonary  rehabilitation  was  a  safe  and effective  therapeutic  option  in  prolonged COVID-19;
Secondly, it involved only respiratory muscle training which  is not considered as  complete pulmonary rehabilitation

second_reader.what_stands: The key-message bullet states that pulmonary rehabilitation was safe and effective, although the intervention tested was a chest-physiotherapy/respiratory muscle training program that the authors themselves say is not complete pulmonary rehabilitation. The limitation is disclosed in the Discussion but not carried into the summary bullet, and the safety statement rests on a single sentence ('no severe adverse events') in a 30-patient group.

issues.title: Table 2 percentages use denominators 29 (G1) and 9 (G2), not headers n=30 and n=12; missing data unexplained
issues.explanation: Table 2 headers give G1 n=30 and G2 n=12, but the percentages only fit denominators of 29 (22/29=75.9%) and 9 (7/9=77.8%). The paper does not say that 1 G1 and 3 G2 patients lack symptom data, nor why. The analysed set for the symptom outcomes is therefore undisclosed, especially in the small control arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or text stating that 29 G1 and 9 G2 patients had symptom data at both time points.

script.explanation: 7/12 = 58.33%, but the paper prints 77.8, outside the rounding interval [77.75, 77.90]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 9.0 rather than 12.

issues.title: Unblinded training with self-reported symptom outcomes (dyspnea, fatigue, cough, chest pain)
issues.explanation: Patients knew whether they were in the training group, and the symptom outcomes were from a questionnaire. The paper calls for double-blind studies in future, implying this one was not blinded. This adds a bias risk for the symptom results beyond the lack of a between-group test.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors or patients were blinded.

quotes.text: multicenter  double-blind studies with complete rehabilitation programs are required.
Persistent symptoms were obtained using a standardized questionnaire.

issues.title: Text says only FEV1 (%) improved in controls, but Table 3 has p<0.05 for G2 FEV1 (L), TLC (L) and 6-MWD
issues.explanation: The Results claim only FEV1 (%) increased significantly in G2, but Table 3 reports p=0.042 (FEV1 L), p=0.043 (TLC L) and p=0.018 (6-MWD, which fell). Controls therefore also changed significantly in several measures the paper credits to training. The text understates the control-arm changes, which makes the training effect look more specific than the table supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Table 3 G2 p-values for FEV1 (L) and TLC (L) are misprinted.

quotes.text: However, only FEV1 (%) increased significantly  in the control group.

issues.title: Table 1 G2 comorbidity percentages use denominator 11 (18.2, 63.6, 9.1), not 12; obesity row duplicates hypertension
issues.explanation: Several G2 comorbidity percentages in Table 1 only fit a denominator of 11, while the header and text give 12; the hypertension row (7, 58.3%) uses 12. The obesity row also repeats the hypertension counts (20, 13, 7) with a different G2 percentage, so it looks like a copy error. These are baseline-table slips that change no main result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one G2 patient lacked comorbidity data.

script.explanation: 2/12 = 16.67%, but the paper prints 18.2, outside the rounding interval [18.15, 18.30]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 11.0 rather than 12.

issues.title: Respiratory rate p-values in text (G1 0.02, G2 0.01) are swapped versus Table 3 (G1 0.013, G2 0.018)
issues.explanation: The text and Table 3 attach the respiratory rate p-values to opposite groups. The values 0.013 and 0.018 round to 0.01 and 0.02, matching the text's numbers in swapped order. Both remain below 0.05, so no conclusion changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; it is a printed inconsistency of trivial size.

quotes.text: FR (cycles/min)

10.11606/issn.2317-0190.v30i4a214740.headline_claim: A physiotherapy rehabilitation program improved SF-36 physical functioning, physical aspects and pain domains and handgrip strength in people with post-COVID-19 syndrome, without changing six-minute walk distance, pain or perceived exertion.
10.11606/issn.2317-0190.v30i4a214740.overall: The study is a small, non-randomised waitlist comparison with substantial baseline imbalance, and its conclusion of programme-induced improvement rests mainly on within-group changes; the group-by-time interaction is significant only for SF-36 physical function (p = 0.033) and not for role-physical, pain or handgrip. The Borg results are described inconsistently across the paper. The conclusions should be treated as exploratory and not as evidence of efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: not designated; SF-36 domains, six-minute walk test, handgrip strength, Borg scale and VAS all reported with equal weight

issues.title: Conclusion credits programme with gains where group-by-time interaction is non-significant (p=0.736, 0.367, 0.3)
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion state that the programme improved role-physical, pain and handgrip, based on significant time effects within the intervention group. The two-way ANOVA interaction, which is the test of a differential effect versus the waitlist, is not significant for these outcomes. Waitlist controls also rose on several of them (handgrip 23.70 to 26.40; pain 51.1 to 66.7). The causal conclusion therefore exceeds what the controlled comparison shows, and only physical function has a significant interaction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant group-by-time interaction tests, or a pre-specified within-group primary analysis for these outcomes.

quotes.text: Observou-se no GI aumento significativo (p<0,05) da qualidade de vida nos domínios de capacidade funcional, aspectos físicos e redução da dor e aumento da força de preensão palmar.

quotes.location: Table 2, Preensão palmar row, GI column

second_reader.what_stands: For physical aspects, pain and grip strength, the group-by-time interaction is non-significant (0.736, 0.367, 0.3), and the GC changed as much as or more than the GI (pain +15.6 vs +6.1; grip +2.7 vs +1.0 kgf). The conclusion that the programme improved these outcomes therefore rests only on within-group tests, with no demonstrated difference from the GC. It does not hold for functional capacity, where the interaction is significant (p=0.033) and the GI rose while the GC fell. The meaning of the letters A and B in Table 2 is not stated, so it cannot be confirmed from the paper.

issues.title: Non-randomised convenience allocation; GI sicker and less active than waitlist GC (n=23 vs 10)
issues.explanation: Participants were allocated by convenience to treatment (23) or waitlist (10), and the groups differ strongly at baseline in hospitalisation, ventilatory support, age and physical activity. The intervention group started lower on most outcomes, so it had more room to improve and may regress toward the mean. No adjustment is made, and the conclusion nevertheless states the programme improved outcomes. The authors do note the heterogeneity as a limitation, but the headline claim ignores it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Covariate-adjusted analyses, or baseline-matched groups, showing the same interaction effects.

quotes.text: alocados por conveniência em dois grupos
O GC era mais jovem e com mais indivíduos praticantes de atividade física.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by convenience and not randomised, with 23 patients receiving treatment and 10 waiting. The GI was older, had more hospitalisation and ventilatory support, did less exercise, and had worse baseline SF-36 and walk-test values than the GC. The authors disclose most of this in the Results, Discussion and limitations, but the baseline imbalance remains and the groups are not comparable.

issues.title: Borg effort reported as increased, improved, significant and unaltered; table shows GI 2.50 to 1.86, interaction p=0.258
issues.explanation: The Results say perceived effort increased significantly in the intervention group, but Table 2 shows Borg falling from 2.50 to 1.86. The abstract and discussion call the Borg result a significant between-group finding and an improvement. The conclusion says effort was not altered. The only significant Borg term is the group main effect (p = 0.016), which reflects a baseline difference (GC 0.80 vs GI 2.50), not an intervention effect; the interaction is p = 0.258. The paper therefore gives four mutually inconsistent statements about one outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explicit statement that the significant Borg effect is a group main effect only, with consistent wording in Results, abstract, discussion and conclusion.

quotes.text: No GI houve aumento significativo da percepção de esforço nos momentos antes e depois da intervenção quando comparado ao GC.
sem alterar os níveis de capacidade funcional no TC6', de percepção de dor e esforço

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 10 waitlist controls vs 23 treated, yet definite efficacy conclusion
issues.explanation: With 33 participants and only 10 controls, the interaction tests have little power and the estimates are imprecise. The authors acknowledge the low number, but the conclusion uses the language of established benefit. The study is better read as exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-study sample-size justification, or hedged exploratory wording in the conclusion.

quotes.text: o baixo número amostral se deve à dificuldade de encaminhamento dos profissionais
O programa de intervenção fisioterapêutica, personalizado, foi capaz de melhorar os domínios de capacidade funcional

issues.title: 11 outcomes x 3 effects tested at 5% with no primary outcome; correction only for post hoc contrasts
issues.explanation: Eleven outcomes were each tested with three ANOVA terms at an uncorrected 5% level, and no primary outcome was named. Bonferroni correction applied only to post hoc pairwise contrasts. A few nominally significant results (e.g. interaction p = 0.033) are then emphasised, so some could arise by chance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A declared primary outcome or a pre-specified multiplicity strategy across outcomes.

quotes.text: O teste post hoc de Bonferroni foi utilizado para comparar análise inter e intragrupos.
Um nível de significância de 5% foi definido para todas as variáveis.

issues.title: EVA pain after-intervention mean for GC printed as 40,20, while the baseline mean is 0,20 (same SD 0,63)
issues.explanation: Table 2 prints the GC post-intervention VAS mean as 40,20, which is impossible on a 0 to 10 pain scale and inconsistent with the baseline value. It is most likely a typographical error for 0,20. It does not change any conclusion, but the table is wrong as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original data showing a GC mean of 40.2 on the scale used.

10.11606/issn.2317-0190.v31i3a225573.headline_claim: Photobiomodulation therapy showed no effect compared with placebo on functional capacity and muscle performance in people after SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) infection.
10.11606/issn.2317-0190.v31i3a225573.overall: The paper's conclusion that TFBM has no effect is not well supported: 15 participants, no sample-size calculation and wide confidence intervals allow only an inconclusive reading. The analysis model is not clearly specified, and the abstract misreports several Table 2 values, though none of these changes the non-significant results. Registration and allocation concealment are not reported.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: No-effect conclusion drawn from 7 vs 8 participants with no sample-size calculation and wide CIs
issues.explanation: With 7 and 8 analysed participants and no power calculation, a non-significant result cannot show the absence of an effect. The reported 95% intervals (for example -16,59 to 12,73 kgf for peak force) are wide relative to plausible effects. The conclusion that TFBM had no effect is stronger than the data support; 'inconclusive' is the supportable reading. A single session of therapy given without exercise also limits what any negative finding can say.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified power calculation or an equivalence margin showing that the sample could rule out a clinically important difference.

quotes.text: A TFBM não apresentou efeito quando comparada ao placebo na melhora capacidade funcional e desempenho muscular em indivíduos pós SARS da amostra estudada.
Dentre as limitações apresentadas estão o baixo número amostral

second_reader.what_stands: With 7 vs 8 participants, no stated sample-size calculation, and CIs spanning roughly ±14 kgf and ±2.5–3 s, the data cannot exclude clinically meaningful effects, so 'não apresentou efeito' overstates what a non-significant result shows. This is softened because the conclusion says 'da amostra estudada', the low sample is listed as a limitation, and larger studies are requested. The abstract's conclusion does not carry the 'da amostra estudada' qualifier.

issues.title: Analysis model unspecified: ANOVA with Tukey named, but between-group contrast and p = 0.974/0.151 not defined
issues.explanation: The Methods name ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for the pre/post comparison, while the Results give single p values (0,974 and 0,151) and per-arm confidence intervals with no description of which contrast they test. It is unclear whether the between-group effect of interest (change in the active group vs change in placebo) was actually tested. No baseline adjustment is described. The null finding therefore rests on an analysis that cannot be reproduced from the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the ANOVA design showing that p = 0,974 and 0,151 are the group x time interaction tests.

quotes.text: Para comparar as variáveis pré e pós intervenção foi utilizado o teste estatístico ANOVA com pós-hoc de Tukey.
com (p= 0,974) para o pico isométrico

issues.title: Abstract post-TFBM values differ from Table 2: peak force 34.31 vs 31.34; TSLC5 SDs 1.75/2.09 vs 2.09/1.50
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the active group's post-intervention peak force as 34,31 ± 13,50, but Table 2 gives 31,34 ± 13,50. The abstract's TSLC5 SDs (active 1,75; placebo 2,09) also do not match Table 2's post values (active 2,09; placebo 1,50). The abstract version makes the active arm look about 3 kgf higher than placebo, whereas Table 2 gives roughly 0.2 kgf. Neither version is significant, so the conclusion does not change, but the abstract misreports the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published erratum or raw data showing that 34,31 and the abstract SDs are the correct values and Table 2 is the one in error.

quotes.text: obteve média (34,31 ± 13,50)

quotes.location: Tabela 2, Pico de Força Isométrico, Pós-TFBM, TFBM ativa

issues.title: Allocation concealment not described; the person delivering the intervention generated the Excel randomisation
issues.explanation: The therapist who applied TFBM or placebo also generated the allocation with Excel's random function, and no concealment mechanism is described. This leaves open the possibility of selection or allocation bias. Blinded assessors and participants, and the single-session design, reduce its practical impact.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of concealed allocation (for example opaque envelopes prepared by someone else) or enrolment completed before the sequence was generated.

quotes.text: O fisioterapeuta responsável pela intervenção foi responsável também pela randomização feita utilizando a função = ALEATÓRIO( ) da ferramenta Excel

issues.title: 3 of 18 randomised participants excluded without stated reasons or arms; analysis on 15 completers
issues.explanation: The Results state that 18 were randomised and 3 excluded, but give no reasons or allocation arms in the text. Analysis covers only the 15 who remained, not all randomised participants. The effect on the comparison cannot be judged from the text, and the CONSORT figure may supply the detail.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing the 3 exclusions occurred before randomisation or allocation, or were balanced across arms for stated reasons.

quotes.text: Os 18 participantes foram selecionados e randomizados para participar da pesquisa, sendo 3 excluídos.

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported; primary outcome not designated
issues.explanation: The paper gives an ethics approval number but no trial registration. It also does not name a primary outcome among fatigue, peak force and the sit-to-stand test. Selective reporting of outcomes therefore cannot be ruled out, although the results reported look complete.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: sob o parecer de nº 5.479.217

issues.title: Heights in Results text given as '165 cm (± 0,10 cm)' and '1,70cm' — mixed units; Table 1 uses metres
issues.explanation: The Results text writes mean height in cm but the SD (0,10) and the placebo mean (1,70) in metres. As printed, 165 cm with SD 0.10 cm is impossible for a 152–182 cm range. Table 1 gives the correct metre values, so this is a cosmetic slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; Table 1 already shows the intended unit is metres.

10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a2426.headline_claim: Symptom-based REHAB was superior to usual care for quality of life over the long term in post-COVID patients with predominantly fatigue symptoms (PCC-f), but not in the cognition (PCC-c) or soma (PCC-s) clusters.
10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a2426.overall: The finding of a QoL benefit in the fatigue cluster is plausible, and the reported CIs and p-values are internally consistent. The cluster contrast (benefit in PCC-f only) is not supported, because it rests on significance differences in small completer-only subgroups with no interaction test or multiplicity control. The arm and cluster counts do not reconcile, and 'long-term' and 'natural recovery' overstate a single 3-month follow-up against usual care.

The conclusion states that REHAB is superior in PCC-f but not in PCC-c or PCC-s, based on p<0.05 in one cluster and not in the others. The non-significant clusters have wide CIs that include effects similar to the PCC-f estimate, and no test of difference between clusters is given. The data support a PCC-f QoL signal, not evidence that the other clusters do not benefit.

The fatigue result (p=0.005) is the stated primary aim and is more robust. The grip strength result (p=0.037) and the eosinophil result (p=0.022) are isolated hits that would not survive correction, yet the conclusion states strength improvement as a finding.
