10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a2913.headline_claim: Nintedanib did not improve FVC at 180 days compared with placebo in patients with ILD findings following COVID-19-related lung injury, and serious adverse event incidence was similar between groups.
10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a2913.overall: The abstract's headline null result on FVC is internally consistent: the mean difference, CI and P=0.74 agree. The conclusion is worded cautiously as 'did not improve'. The CI is wide, from roughly -139 to +98 mL, so it supports 'no demonstrated benefit' and not 'no effect', and the abstract does not state a sample-size rationale.

primary_outcome.name: Change in baseline forced vital capacity (FVC, mL) at 180 days

issues.title: Null FVC result (-20.17 mL, 95% CI -138.54 to 98.20) is imprecise; no target sample or power stated
issues.explanation: The abstract does not state a target sample size or the difference the trial was powered to detect. The 95% CI for the FVC difference runs from about -139 mL to +98 mL, so it cannot rule out a modest benefit or a modest harm from nintedanib. 'Did not improve' is a fair description of a non-significant result, but it should not be read as showing no effect. Whether this matters depends on the full paper's sample-size justification, which an abstract cannot be expected to give.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full report or protocol showing a pre-specified sample-size calculation, with a clinically relevant FVC difference that the 103 participants gave adequate power to detect. Alternatively, a stated minimal important difference lying outside the 95% CI.

10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a3028.overall: The abstract reports plausible, internally consistent effects on exertional desaturation and dyspnea, but gives no primary outcome, sample sizes per arm or multiplicity control, and is industry-funded. The headline 'sustained benefit in high-risk groups' rests on unlabelled subgroup analyses of FVC and should be treated as exploratory.

issues.title: Day 180 FVC subgroup results (age, sex, CVD) presented as sustained benefit without overall FVC result
issues.explanation: The abstract gives p-values only for the FVC responder proportion in three subgroups (older, female, CVD) and no overall FVC result or interaction tests. It is not stated whether these subgroups were prespecified or exploratory. The conclusion nonetheless states evidence of sustained benefit in 'high-risk groups', which suggests that the overall FVC result was likely not significant and the subgroup findings are being highlighted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified subgroup plan with significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction tests, and a reported overall FVC result consistent with the claim.

The overall FVC result may exist in the full study but is not in this abstract. The sustained-benefit wording therefore rests on unadjusted subgroup p-values alone, and the full-text analysis plan could not be checked here.

10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a3183.headline_claim: Symptom-based REHAB improves quality of life and mental health in fatigue and somatic symptom clusters of post-COVID condition compared with usual care, but not in the cognition cluster, where only anxiety improved.
10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a3183.overall: The abstract openly presents itself as a subgroup analysis, so the registered primary outcome is not misreported, but its cluster-specific conclusions are exploratory. They rest on very small arms, about nine uncorrected comparisons and no interaction tests. The conclusion also credits the somatic cluster with a QoL benefit that the Results do not show. The findings are best taken as hypothesis-generating.

issues.title: Cluster-level 'benefit' claims rest on uncorrected subgroup tests in arms of 7 to 29, without interaction tests

Differences between 'significant' and 'non-significant' clusters are also not tested against each other, so the contrast between clusters, and the conclusion drawn from it, is tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified cluster-by-treatment interaction analysis with multiplicity control showing the same pattern, or a statistical analysis plan naming these subgroup tests as confirmatory.

issues.explanation: Only 104 of 132 randomized participants are analysed, and the abstract does not give the randomized numbers per arm, the reasons for loss or whether missing data were imputed. Completer-only analysis can bias between-group differences if dropout differs by arm. The full paper may resolve this, but the abstract cannot.

10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a3185.headline_claim: The authors conclude that the Fatigue Severity Score is effective for assessing Long COVID fatigue outcomes, that tailored interventions improve fatigue severity, and that multimorbid patients have poorer outcomes.
10.1164/ajrccm.2025.211.abstracts.a3185.overall: The headline claim that tailored interventions are effective and that FSS is a suitable outcome rests on an uncontrolled cohort in which only 102 of 297 patients are analysed, with no psychometric support for FSS. The multimorbidity finding is conditioned on improvement and is exploratory at best. The data support a descriptive statement that many engaged patients reported lower FSS at follow-up, not effectiveness.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Fatigue Severity Score (FSS) after tailored interventions

issues.title: Effectiveness of tailored interventions inferred from an uncontrolled single-group pre-post change in FSS
issues.explanation: The study reports FSS change in patients who received tailored interventions, with no comparison group. Improvement in fatigue over time can reflect natural recovery from Long COVID, regression to the mean, or patients being seen when symptoms were at their worst. The conclusion about effectiveness of the interventions therefore cannot be supported by this design, though the hedged wording softens it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of a concurrent or historical untreated comparison group, or a statement that the claim is purely descriptive.

quotes.text: Nonetheless, the study provides insights into the effectiveness of tailored interventions in improving

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract infers that tailored interventions are effective from a pre-post change in FSS in a single group with no control, and it names no limitation about natural recovery or regression to the mean. The wording is hedged ('insights', 'certain groups'), but the causal framing is still not supported by the design described.

issues.title: Multimorbidity conclusion drawn from a comparison restricted to the 91 improvers, with small unreported subgroups
issues.explanation: The abstract compares FSS change by comorbidity only among patients already classed as improved, then concludes multimorbid patients have poorer outcomes. Selecting on improvement removes the patients with no change or worsening, so the comparison cannot show who does worse overall. Only the size of the no-comorbidity group (32 of 91) is given, the other group's size is missing, and no sample-size justification is reported; the authors do concede a small sample. The finding is at most an exploratory signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis of all 102 engaged patients (for example, change in FSS or proportion improved by comorbidity status) showing the same difference.

quotes.text: Of the improved group, 32 had no co-morbidities, showing significantly more change in FSS score than
Despite a small sample size, results suggest poorer outcomes for multimorbid individuals.

second_reader.what_stands: The comparison is indeed restricted to the 91 improvers, and the subgroup means, spreads, exact p value, and the multimorbid group size (59 only by subtraction) are not reported, so 'poorer outcomes for multimorbid individuals' goes beyond a within-improvers difference in change size. The authors do flag the small sample size, and the 32 versus 59 split is not itself tiny, so the subgroups are not 'small' in the sense of a handful of patients.

issues.title: Outcomes reported for 102 of 297 patients (34%); 195 (66%) unaccounted for, so improvement rate may be inflated
issues.explanation: The Methods describe 297 patients, but the Results cover only the 102 who 'engaged'. The abstract does not explain what happened to the other 195 or whether they differed. If non-engagers had no follow-up FSS because of poor response or worsening, the 91/102 improvement figure is biased upward, and it is not an intention-to-treat estimate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow description showing the 195 were not eligible for or not yet due for follow-up, or that they did not differ at baseline from the 102.

quotes.text: A study on 297 Long COVID patients at

second_reader.what_stands: Outcomes are reported for only 102 of 297 patients (34%), with no account of the other 195, so the 89% improvement figure applies only to engaged patients and could overstate improvement in the whole clinic cohort. Whether it is actually inflated cannot be said, because 'engaged' is undefined and the reason for missing follow-up is not given; the abstract does word its result as 'out of 102 engaged patients' rather than claiming it for all 297.

issues.title: Conclusion that FSS is effective for Long COVID fatigue assessment rests on no psychometric data
issues.explanation: The Background says FSS as an outcome in Long COVID is unexplored, yet the Conclusion says it is effective for assessing fatigue outcomes. The abstract reports no validity, reliability, minimal important difference or responsiveness analysis. A change in score in an uncontrolled cohort does not show that the instrument measures fatigue well in this population.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported validity, reliability or responsiveness analysis of FSS in this cohort.

quotes.text: The study suggests that FSS is effective in assessing Long COVID fatigue outcomes.

10.1164/rccm.202309-1572oc.headline_claim: Six weeks of inspiratory muscle training improved exertional dyspnea and inspiratory muscle endurance in people with long COVID and diaphragm weakness, and the authors conclude it could be a potential therapy.
10.1164/rccm.202309-1572oc.overall: The finding that diaphragm weakness persists is observational, and the trial evidence for IMT is small (9 per arm), open-label, unadjusted for multiplicity, and mostly rests on within-arm changes and borderline between-group P values. The claims about improved inspiratory strength are suggestive at best; the claim that IMT improves dyspnea is not established by the between-group results.

primary_outcome.name: Change in inspiratory muscle fatiguability (time to task failure) from before IMT to after 6 weeks of IMT

issues.title: Dyspnea benefit claimed from within-arm significance; between-group dyspnea differences not significant
issues.explanation: The dyspnea improvement is presented through significant pre-post changes in the IMT arm and 'no changes' in the sham arm. Table 2's between-group P values for the dyspnea scales are non-significant (mMRC 0.18, Borg 0.24) or borderline (CRQ 0.05). Difference in significance is not evidence of a treatment effect, so the claim that IMT improved dyspnea is not established by these comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant pre-specified between-group test (e.g., ANCOVA) for Borg or mMRC dyspnea.

CRQ dyspnea is borderline (P=0.05, CI reaching -0.01), yet the Discussion calls it significant. The Conclusions are hedged ('could be a potential therapy'), which softens but does not remove the issue.

issues.title: Open-label trial: participant-terminated endurance and self-reported dyspnea outcomes exposed to expectation bias
issues.explanation: The trial is labelled open-label; the primary endurance outcome ends when the participant stops, and dyspnea is self-reported. Analysts were blinded, which helps only for data processing, not for effort or reporting. The limitation is acknowledged but the conclusions are not tempered accordingly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants were effectively blinded to allocation and that task-failure was objectively terminated.

quotes.text: prospective, open-label, sham-controlled randomized trial of IMT
Participants were then asked to breathe continuously through the IMT device until task failure
the largely open-label nature of the IMT study means that the possibility of unknown biases cannot be excluded

second_reader.what_stands: The paper calls the trial open-label, and both its endurance endpoint (participant-terminated) and its dyspnea endpoints (self-reported) depend on effort or perception, so expectation effects are possible. The paper does not say whether participants knew their arm, and blinded analysts and a sham device partly mitigate this. The limitation is acknowledged only generically and expectation bias is not named.

issues.title: 9 per arm, powered for within-person change only, yet conclusions compare IMT with sham
issues.explanation: The authors say the study was powered for intraindividual differences, not between-group ones, but the sham-controlled comparison is the basis of the claims. With 9 per arm and many outcomes tested without multiplicity adjustment, the between-group findings (several near P=0.05) are fragile. The conclusions are partly hedged, but the claim that sample size was sufficient for the primary outcome is not well supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample size calculation for the between-group primary endpoint.

quotes.text: our study was powered to detect intraindividual differences in the study parameters and not intergroup differences
IMT was found to improve global inspiratory muscle strength

second_reader.what_stands: With 9 per arm and power stated only for within-person change, the between-group comparisons against sham are underpowered and unadjusted for many outcomes. The paper discloses this itself, and the Conclusions are mostly phrased as within-group effects. The Discussion and the 'At a Glance' box still lean on the sham comparison for the claim that IMT works.

issues.title: P=0.05 results called significant despite stated P<0.05 criterion (within-arm and between-group endurance)
issues.explanation: The Methods define significance as P<0.05, yet the within-arm rise in time to task failure is reported at P=0.05 and described as significant. Rounding to two decimals might hide a value just below 0.05, but the paper does not show this. Since time to task failure is the primary endurance outcome, the borderline P matters for the headline endurance claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Exact P value below 0.05 (e.g., 0.046) from the authors' software output.

issues.title: 4 of 18 declined 6-week physiological measurements; arm split and handling not reported
issues.explanation: Four participants declined measurements at 6 weeks but answered questionnaires, so the 6-week physiological persistence claim rests on 14 people with unreported arm balance and no stated method for missing data. issues.title: Null twPdi result reframed as non-dynamic metric; the Discussion claims significant primary-outcome between-group difference
issues.explanation: The established diaphragm-strength measure (twPdi) did not change with IMT, and the paper explains this away as a static metric. Yet the Discussion asserts the sample 'was sufficient to demonstrate a significant between-groups difference in the primary outcome', although Table 2's between-group P for time to task failure is 0.05 and the text elsewhere says the study was not powered for between-group comparisons. Title and Conclusions refer to diaphragm weakness-related dyspnea 'improved' by IMT, which the null twPdi does not support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group primary-outcome P clearly below 0.05 from the prespecified analysis.

quotes.text: No signi fi cant changes in twPdi were seen in either the treatment or the sham arm

issues.title: Within-group nonnormal data tested with Kruskal-Wallis, a test for independent groups
issues.explanation: The Methods state Kruskal-Wallis was used for within-group comparisons of nonnormal data, which is a test for independent samples. It may be a mislabel for a paired or repeated-measures test (Wilcoxon or Friedman), which the paper does not clarify. If the test was actually applied as written, the within-group P values underpinning the dyspnea and endurance claims are unreliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors confirming a paired nonparametric test was used.

issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published reliability and validity data for this protocol in the online supplement.

quotes.text: The primary outcome for this part of the study was the change in inspiratory muscle fatiguability

Table 2, sham arm, before training, time to task failure

10.11648/j.ajcem.20261404.16.headline_claim: Adding osteopathic correction to breathing exercises and chest massage in a 14-day rehabilitation program is significantly more effective than breathing exercises and massage alone for post-COVID respiratory muscle strength, ventilation, exercise tolerance, dyspnea, anxiety/depression and quality of life.
10.11648/j.ajcem.20261404.16.overall: The direction of the findings (better respiratory pressures, volumes and symptom scores with osteopathy added) is plausible, but the paper is too inconsistent and under-reported to support its confident 'standard of care' conclusion. Abstract effect sizes disagree with the Results and Table 1, the baseline HADS in the text disagrees with the table, and several printed between-group p-values do not follow from the table's means and SDs. There is also no randomization or blinding detail, no sample-size calculation, no registration and no follow-up beyond 14 days.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 87 patients, 2-week outcomes, yet recommended as a standard of care
issues.explanation: The paper reports no sample-size justification, and the Limitations call the sample small. Despite this, the Conclusions recommend osteopathy as a standard component of rehabilitation, and the Discussion says a 'sustained effect' was produced although no follow-up beyond day 14 was measured. The conclusion goes beyond what a single-centre trial with immediate post-course outcomes can support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified power calculation and follow-up data showing durability.

quotes.text: The sample was relatively small, with a predominance of women (71.3%)
These data support the recommendation of a comprehensive approach including osteopathy as a standard component of medical rehabilitation

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no sample-size calculation, assesses outcomes only at the end of a 14-day course in 87 patients, and still recommends osteopathy as a standard component of rehabilitation. The limitations mention small size only in relation to generalising to men and do not mention the short follow-up. They do not temper the standard-of-care recommendation.

issues.title: Between-group p-values in Table 1 do not match the group means/SDs (FVC, MEP, Stange, SpO2)
issues.explanation: Recomputing between-group t-tests from the Table 1 post-treatment means and SDs gives FVC p about 0.14 (printed 0.03), MEP about 0.19 (printed 0.04) and Stange about 0.05 (printed 0.02). SpO2 goes the other way: p about 0.016 (printed 0.09), so the text's 'not significant' SpO2 finding is not supported by the table. MIP gives about 0.04 against 0.02 printed. If the tables are correct, the superiority claim for FVC and MEP is not supported at 0.05.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted or non-parametric analysis described in the paper that reproduces the printed p-values, or corrected SDs in Table 1.

quotes.location: Table 1, FVC row, main group After
Table 1, FVC row, comparison group After
Table 1, SpO2 row, comparison group After

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

second_reader.what_stands: For FVC, MEP, Stange and SpO2, the printed between-group p-values cannot be reproduced from the printed group means and SDs with an independent-samples t-test. FVC, MEP and Stange come out non-significant (about 0.14, 0.19 and 0.05) where the table prints 0.03, 0.04 and 0.02, and SpO2 comes out about 0.016 where the table prints 0.09. The MIP value is a smaller gap (0.036 vs 0.02), and the VC and 6MWT values match. A non-parametric test for some rows cannot be excluded, but the paper does not say which rows used which test.

issues.title: Ten outcomes tested at p<0.05 without correction or a designated primary outcome
issues.explanation: About ten outcomes are tested within and between groups at an uncorrected 0.05 level, and no primary outcome is named. Several of the between-group p-values in Table 1 lie between 0.01 and 0.04, and these would not survive a Bonferroni correction (0.005). The strongest results (6MWT, mMRC, HADS, EQ-5D) would survive. The claim of superiority across all key parameters is therefore weaker for the respiratory-strength and volume outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome, or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis keeping the respiratory results significant.

quotes.text: Differences were considered significant at p < 0.05.
Between-group differences after treatment were statistically significant in favor of the main group for all key parameters (p<0.05), except SpO2 (p=0.09).

issues.title: Baseline HADS 8.5 ± 3.1 in Results vs group baselines 15.6 and 15.3 in Table 1
issues.explanation: The Results give an all-patient baseline HADS of 8.5 ± 3.1, with 51% scoring at least 8. Table 1 gives baseline means of 15.6 and 15.3 in the two groups, so the pooled mean should be about 15.5. A mean of 15.5 with SD about 5 would put almost all patients at 8 or above, not 51%. One of the two baselines is wrong, which affects the reported HADS change and its size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or data statement showing the text figure was a different HADS measure or subset, or that Table 1 baselines are mislabelled.

quotes.text: HADS score – 8.5 ± 3.1 points (51% of patients had ≥8)

quotes.location: Table 1, HADS row, main group Before
Table 1, HADS row, comparison group Before

issues.title: Abstract effect sizes (FVC 10.9%, VC 12.4%, MIP 24.6%, HADS 5.2) disagree with Results/Discussion
issues.explanation: Several headline effect sizes in the abstract do not match the Results, Discussion or Table 1. FVC is 10.9% in the abstract but 9.5% in the Results, and VC is 12.4% against 10.2%. MIP is 24.6% against 32.5% for the same 14.4 cm H2O change, and HADS is 5.2 points against 6.2 (15.6 to 9.4). The abstract mixes absolute and relative changes without saying so, and some of its values fit no base at all. The direction of the effects is unchanged, but a reader cannot tell which figure is the effect size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that abstract percentages are relative changes on a defined base that reproduces all four values.

quotes.text: increase in MIP in the main group by 14.4 cm H2O (32.5%)
Anxiety and depression levels decreased by 5.2 points on HADS (p<0.001)

issues.title: Blinding of patients and outcome assessors not described despite a sham comparator and subjective endpoints
issues.explanation: A sham osteopathic correction was used, but the paper never states who was blinded or whether the sham was credible. The patient-reported outcomes (mMRC, HADS, EQ-5D) and the effort-dependent 6MWT are open to expectation effects if blinding failed. This weakens the secondary conclusions on dyspnea, mood and quality of life more than the objective spirometry results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or methods statement that patients and assessors were blinded and the sham was tested for credibility.

quotes.text: The comparison group (n=43) received breathing exercises and massage on the same schedule but with a sham osteopathic correction.
dyspnea (mMRC) decreased from 1.6 to 0.3 points (p=0.0001)

issues.title: Abstract contrasts within-group significance, and between-group tests use post-values only without baseline adjustment
issues.explanation: The abstract supports efficacy by saying the comparison group's changes were mostly not significant, which is a difference in significance and not a test of difference between arms. Table 1's between-group p is for post-treatment values only, with no change-score or baseline-adjusted analysis, although baselines differ slightly (for example VC 82.4 vs 83.8, SpO2 96.7 vs 96.9). This weakens the secondary results, but the table does supply a direct between-group comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted or change-score between-group analysis showing the same differences.

quotes.text: whereas in the comparison group the dynamics were not significant for most parameters.
Within-group comparisons – paired t-test or Wilcoxon test; between groups – independent samples t-test or Mann–Whitney U test.

issues.title: Randomization and concealment not described; 112 examined to 87 analysed with no flow account
issues.explanation: The study is labelled randomized, but the paper gives no sequence-generation or concealment method. It reports 112 people examined and 87 analysed without a flow diagram or arm-wise numbers for the 25 exclusions. Without these details the reader cannot judge selection or allocation bias, and baseline comparability rests on a single 'p>0.05' sentence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial protocol or CONSORT diagram stating the randomisation procedure, concealment and the timing of the 25 exclusions.

quotes.text: A total of 112 individuals were examined; after applying exclusion criteria, 87 patients were included in the analysis
The groups were comparable in age, sex, severity, and time since illness (p>0.05).

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective randomized study run in 2021-2023
issues.explanation: The paper describes a prospective randomized trial but gives no registry or identifier, so reported outcomes cannot be checked against a prospective plan. This matters because ten outcomes are reported and no primary outcome is designated. Whether it was registered cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry made before enrolment that matches the reported outcomes.

quotes.text: A prospective randomized parallel-group study was conducted at the Primorsky Institute of Vertebroneurology and Manual Medicine (Vladivostok) during 2021–2023.

issues.title: SpO2 rise given as 0.9% in text but Table 1 means differ by 1.1 (96.7 to 97.8)
issues.explanation: The Results say SpO2 rose by 0.9% in the main group, but Table 1 gives 96.7 before and 97.8 after, a difference of 1.1. The baseline in the text (96.8%) also differs slightly from the table. The mismatch is small and SpO2 is not a headline outcome, so it changes one reported number only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text value comes from a different measurement set (for example a per-protocol subset) or unrounded means giving 0.9.

quotes.text: SpO<sup>2</sup> increased by 0.9% on average (p=0.01)

quotes.location: Table 1, SpO2 row, main group Before
Table 1, SpO2 row, main group After

10.1177/03000605221148435.headline_claim: Mechanical ventilation during ICU care, rather than neuropsychological or psychological factors, predicts greater functional gains after multidisciplinary rehabilitation in COVID-19 survivors, and early rehabilitation is supported regardless of initial neuropsychological functioning.
10.1177/03000605221148435.overall: The finding that no admission neuropsychological, psychological or fatigue measure predicts functional gain is a tentative null result from a small retrospective cohort. The efficacy of the programme and the 'crucial' role of ventilation rest on an uncontrolled pre-post comparison and post hoc, minimally adjusted analyses. Several text-level inconsistencies (age predictor wording, percentage, fatigue direction, P/F label) are minor but show sloppy reporting.

primary_outcome.name: FIM motor, cognitive and total scores, T0 vs T1 (rehabilitation effectiveness and predictors of change)

issues.title: Efficacy 'confirmed' from uncontrolled pre-post FIM change with no comparator
issues.explanation: All FIM improvement is measured from admission to discharge in one retrospective cohort with no control group. Natural recovery after acute illness, regression to the mean and the length of stay are all confounded with treatment. The Discussion and Conclusions nonetheless state that efficacy was 'confirmed' and highlighted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical comparison group, or an expected spontaneous-recovery trajectory showing the observed gain exceeds natural recovery.

quotes.text: This real-practice retrospective pre-post intervention cohort study was conducted without a control group
confirmed the efficacy of the proposed multidisciplinary treatment in the context of COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that it has no control group, yet the Discussion says the pre-post FIM improvement 'confirmed the efficacy' of the program and later says the results 'highlight the efficacy'. An uncontrolled pre-post change cannot separate treatment effect from spontaneous recovery, and the lack of a comparator is not listed among the limitations. The ethical justification for having no control group is stated, but it does not make the efficacy claim supportable.

issues.title: Post hoc, unadjusted ventilation finding framed as a 'crucial' causal factor
issues.explanation: The ventilated group was younger, at higher nutritional risk and had lower baseline FIM scores than the non-ventilated group. The REs index is a share of the potential gain, so lower baselines can mechanically produce higher REs. The ventilation result emerged from correlation screening of dozens of variables with no multiplicity control, and the subgroup analysis was added post hoc. The Abstract and Discussion nonetheless call respiratory assistance 'crucial', a causal reading that this uncontrolled exploratory design does not support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A model adjusting for baseline FIM, nutritional status and age that retains the ventilation effect, or a prespecified hypothesis on ventilation.

quotes.text: Because of this clear-cut, but not a-priori expected, result, data were further analyzed focusing on the subgroup of participants
quotes.location: Results, Subgroup analyses of the role of mechanical ventilation

quotes.text: Respiratory assistance may represent a crucial factor for short-term neuropsychological disease after-effects.
patients who had received mechanical ventilation reported significantly lower scores in the motor and total FIM scale

second_reader.what_stands: The ventilation result is post hoc in emphasis (described as unexpected, then followed by a subgroup analysis), is unadjusted for baseline FIM, ICU severity beyond a P/F ratio, and for multiplicity, and the REs ratio mechanically favours the lower-baseline ventilated group; the language 'crucial factor' and 'crucial role' is stronger than a non-randomised association supports. It is not fully post hoc, since ventilation was among the collected variables and was disclosed as unexpected, and the paper does show an association with FIM change. The abstract's link to 'neuropsychological disease af

issues.title: Absence of predictive role asserted for a small sample and a limited, mostly verbal test battery
issues.explanation: The abstract says neuropsychological and psychological functioning does not play a predictive role, based on non-significant coefficients in 66 patients with no power calculation. The Discussion admits the tests were few, mostly verbal and self-reported. A lack of significance in a small sample is not evidence of no effect, so the wording is firmer than the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confidence intervals for the neuropsychological coefficients excluding clinically meaningful effects.

quotes.text: not play a predictive role
The present work adopted a restricted number of neuropsychological tests, mostly focusing on verbal (and not visuospatial) domains.

issues.title: Text says age predicted motor and total REs, but the regressions give age P = 0.74 and P = 1
issues.explanation: The regression paragraph opens by saying age and mechanical ventilation were significant predictors of motor and total REs. The model results that follow say age was not significant (P = 0.74 motor; P = 1 total), and only ventilation was. The Discussion agrees that ventilation was the only significant predictor, so the opening sentence is a misstatement. The conclusions are not changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A model table showing age with P < 0.05 in the motor or total REs regression.

quotes.text: age and the use of mechanical ventilation were found to be significant predictors of the motor and total FIM REs scores.
but not age (B ¼ -0.07; t ¼ -0.32; P ¼ 0.74) was found to significantly predict the motor REs score

issues.title: Five depressed patients given as 13.33% of the 45-patient subgroup; 5/45 = 11.11%
issues.explanation: In the ventilated subgroup the paper reports five patients above the HADS depression cut-off as 13.33%. Five of 45 is 11.11%, while 13.33% corresponds to six patients. The same paragraph prints 11.11% for five patients on Digit Span Forward. It is a small reporting slip that affects no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing six depressed patients, or a different denominator of 37.5 (not a whole number).

quotes.text: scores above the normative cut-off were reported in five patients (13.33% of the subgroup) for the depression scale
quotes.location: Results, Neuropsychological and psychological functioning in mechanical ventilation subgroup

script.explanation: 5/45 = 11.11%, but the paper prints 13.33, outside the rounding interval [13.32, 13.34]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 37.5 rather than 45.

issues.title: Ventilated subgroup sentence says 86.67% scored lower than the Chalder cut-off; full sample says higher
issues.explanation: For the whole sample, 87.88% scored higher than the Chalder cut-off of 4. For the ventilated subgroup the paper says 86.67% scored lower than the same cut-off. The subgroup mean of 6.55 in Table 1 and the Discussion's statement that most participants reported fatigue show 'lower' is wrong. This is a wording error with no effect on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the subgroup's fatigue scores were mostly below 4, which would conflict with the Table 1 mean of 6.55.

quotes.text: The majority ( n ¼ 58 [87.88%]) of the current sample scored higher than the cutoff of 4 for the Chalder Fatigue Scale total score.
39 patients (86.67% of this subgroup) reported a score lower than the normative cut-off for the Chalder Fatigue Scale - total score

issues.title: Mean 'P/F ratio' 12.22 (range 6-22) in days; P/F > 100 mislabelled as severe ARDS
issues.explanation: The text gives the mean P/F ratio as 12.22 with a range of 6-22 'days', which cannot be a P/F ratio and contradicts the statement that all participants had P/F above 100. The same sentence calls P/F > 100 a severe level of ARDS, while the Berlin definition places severe ARDS at 100 or below. The ARDS severity description and the P/F summary are therefore unreliable, but nothing in the main analysis depends on them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary table showing that 12.22 is the mean of a different variable and that the actual P/F values were above 100.

quotes.text: all included participants reported a severe level of ARDS (i.e., P/F > 100 mmHg)
The mean P/F ratio was 12.22

10.1177/09727531241306849.headline_claim: A combined Bhramari and Sheetali Pranayama intervention can significantly improve pulmonary function and heart rate variability in post-COVID patients, a valuable non-pharmacological approach to support recovery.
10.1177/09727531241306849.overall: The directional finding that both pranayama groups improved spirometry and HRV more than an inactive control is plausible, but rests on an unblinded, unregistered, small single-centre trial with no tabulated outcome data and inconsistent p-values. The 'wellbeing' and 'holistic benefit' claims are unsupported by any measured outcome, and the intervention duration is not stated.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; pulmonary function (FVC, FEV1, PEFR) and HRV (SDNN, RMSSD) reported together

issues.title: No blinding or concealment statement; no-intervention control; unmeasured 'subjective wellbeing' claimed
issues.explanation: The control group did no activity, and nothing says outcome assessors or analysts were blinded or that allocation was concealed. Spirometry effort is participant-dependent, so unblinded testing could bias results. The conclusion also cites subjective wellbeing improvements although no wellbeing outcome is reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that assessors were blinded and allocation concealed, and a reported wellbeing measure.

quotes.text: Group A was the control group; they did not do pranayama.
The improvements in both physiological measures and subjective wellbeing indicate a holistic benefit of this intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no blinding or allocation-concealment statement, uses a no-intervention control (so effects cannot be separated from attention or expectation, and the PFT effort-dependent outcomes are open to bias), and the conclusion claims improved 'subjective wellbeing' although no wellbeing outcome was defined, measured, or reported. Participant blinding being infeasible is a fair mitigating point, but it does not cover the absent assessor-blinding or concealment statement or the unsupported wellbeing claim.

issues.title: Conclusion claims 'holistic benefit' and recovery support beyond measured short-term physiological outcomes
issues.explanation: The conclusion asserts improvement in subjective wellbeing and a holistic benefit, but only spirometry and two HRV indices were measured, with no symptom, wellbeing or safety outcomes, and no stated intervention duration. The limitations are acknowledged in the Discussion but do not temper the conclusion. The study also offers no direct comparison of the combined technique versus each, despite 'combined' wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported wellbeing or symptom outcomes and safety data supporting the claim.

quotes.text: The improvements in both physiological measures and subjective wellbeing indicate a holistic benefit of this intervention.
The sample size was relatively small, and the study was conducted at a single centre.

issues.title: FVC and RMSSD p-values (P<.04, P<.02) conflict with later 'all P<.01' for same contrasts
issues.explanation: The Results report FVC differences versus control at P < .04 and Sheetali RMSSD at P < .02, but the Between-Group section says all FVC, FEV1 and RMSSD differences versus control had P < .01. Different tests (Tukey versus earlier) might explain it, but this is not stated and no exact p-values are given. Readers cannot tell which p-values apply.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Exact p-values showing the Tukey-adjusted contrasts are below .01 and that the earlier values were a different analysis.

quotes.text: mean difference 0.5 L, P < .04
mean difference 4.8 ms, P < .02
compared to the control group (all P < .01)

issues.title: Five outcomes tested at alpha .05 with no primary outcome or across-outcome correction
issues.explanation: FVC, FEV1, PEFR, SDNN and RMSSD were each tested at P < .05, and the sample size was powered for HRV only. Tukey handles pairwise comparisons within an outcome but not across outcomes. Some reported p-values (P < .05 for PEFR) are borderline, so the conclusion on those could be fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or a correction showing key results remain significant.

quotes.text: A P value < .05 was considered statistically significant.
both Bhramari and Sheetali groups had significantly greater improvements in FVC, FEV1 and RMSSD compared to the control group (all P < .01)

issues.title: Outcome data not tabulated; analysis on change scores unspecified, no baseline adjustment
issues.explanation: The Methods describe ANOVA and within-group paired tests but do not say the ANOVA used change scores, and no post-intervention means or SDs are tabulated (only figures and mean differences). Baseline PFT differences (FEV1 P = .12) are not adjusted for. This limits verification but does not show the result is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A results table of pre/post means and SDs per group with ANCOVA or change-score analysis.

quotes.text: Paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to compare pre- and post-intervention results within the groups.

issues.title: Table 1 Sheetali sex counts 17/1 sum to 18, not the 30 participants stated
issues.explanation: Table 1 prints Sheetali gender as 17/1, which sums to 18, but the Methods state 30 per group and 30 Sheetali participants were analysed. This is most likely a dropped digit (17/13) and affects only a baseline descriptor. It does not alter the outcome results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 or dataset showing 17/13, or an explanation for the missing 12 participants.

quotes.text: participants were randomly allocated to one of the three groups-30 each.

issues.title: No trial registry identifier for a randomised intervention trial
issues.explanation: The paper calls itself an RCT and gives an ethics reference but no registry number, so the HRV primary outcome and sample size assumptions cannot be checked against a protocol. This weakens confidence in outcome selection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier (for example CTRI) with a prospective registration date.

quotes.text: This is a randomised controlled trial (RCT) study designed to examine  the  combined  effects  of Bhramari and Sheetali Pranayama in post-COVID-19 patients.

issues.title: Table 1 prints Bhramari BMI 248 and RMSSD 273, evidently dropped decimal points
issues.explanation: Table 1 shows Bhramari BMI as 248 ± 2.9 and Bhramari RMSSD as 273 ± 5.2, which are physiologically impossible and clearly meant to be 24.8 and 27.3. These are typographical slips in baseline data; the intended values are consistent with the other groups. The problem is cosmetic but visible in the published table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the values are printed as stated, but the intended values are evident.

10.1177/1357633x231188394.headline_claim: Cardiopulmonary telerehabilitation using functional exercises improved exercise and functional capacity and quality of life in individuals after COVID-19 hospital discharge.
10.1177/1357633x231188394.overall: The positive step-count findings (6MST, 2MSWT) are probably real in direction, but the paper's text overstates between-group evidence for VO2peak and 30CST. Table 2 has several totals that do not add up, the baseline statement contradicts the table, and analysis covers completers only with minimal controls and partly self-reported outcomes. The conclusion that quality of life improved rests on one self-reported physical-function domain and is not well supported.

primary_outcome.name: not specified as primary; 6MST steps used as principal functional outcome

issues.title: Text claims between-group gains in VO2peak (table p=0.600) and 30CST (p=0.050 not <0.05)
issues.explanation: The Results summary says physical tests, estimated VO2peak and SF-36 PF improved 'within and between groups (p<0.05)'. Table 3 gives a between-group p of 0.600 for VO2peak, and the next paragraph and Discussion say VO2peak did not differ between groups. For 30CST the between-group p is 0.050, which does not meet the stated p<0.05 criterion. The summary therefore overstates the between-group evidence for two outcomes, and the within-group changes cannot show a treatment effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Table 3 columns showing the 0.600 and 0.050 values belong to different tests than the between-group comparison.

quotes.text: estimated VO2peak (6MST), and exercise capacity (SF-36 questionnaire PF) within and between groups ( p <0.05)
VO2peak (6MST) in the present study was signi fi cant only within groups

second_reader.what_stands: The Results sentence claiming improvement 'within and between groups (p<0.05)' for all listed outcomes including VO2peak is contradicted by Table 3 (between-group p = 0.600) and by the paper's own following paragraph and Discussion, so it is an overstatement of the summary sentence rather than a claim the paper maintains. For 30CST, the between-group p of 0.050 does not meet the stated p<0.05 threshold, so the between-group claim for that outcome is not supported at the stated alpha, though rounding of the printed value cannot be excluded.

issues.title: Table 2 Total column does not equal TG + CG for men, CVD, diabetes, ICU and pulmonary disease
issues.explanation: For five characteristics the Total count differs from the sum of the two arms, even though the arms are mutually exclusive and sum to 57. The differences are 2 (men), 4 (cardiovascular disease), 1 (ICU), 3 (diabetes) and 1 (pulmonary disease). The Total column, and the text figures taken from it (56% men, 65% cardiovascular disease, 42% diabetes), are therefore unreliable. The per-arm counts also feed the baseline comparison that the authors rely on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 or the raw data showing the Total column counts are right and the arm counts are misprinted.

quotes.location: Table 2, Cardiovascular diseases row, Total column
Table 2, Diabetes mellitus row, Total column

issues.title: Only assessors blinded; self-reported SF-36 PF and self-paced home tests open to expectation bias
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation, and SF-36 PF is self-reported. The control arm was minimal (one session plus a diary), so differences could partly reflect attention or expectation. The paper does not say how assessor blinding was kept during videoconference tests. This weakens the PF finding more than the objective step counts.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of how assessor blinding was maintained, and sensitivity analyses using objective outcomes.

quotes.text: Also, the assessors were blinded in this trial.
Moreover, PF (SF-36 questionnaire) improved for both groups but more in TG.

issues.title: Conclusion claims improved 'quality of life' based only on SF-36 physical functioning
issues.explanation: Methods state that only the SF-36 PF score was analysed. The final conclusion says quality of life improved. The Discussion itself compares with studies using the total SF-36 score, which was not measured here. The claim is also made across six outcomes with no stated primary outcome or correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses of other SF-36 domains or the total score supporting a quality-of-life benefit.

quotes.text: The physical functioning (PF) score was considered for analysis.

Therefore, cardiopulmonary telerehabilitation using functional exercises improved exercise and functional capacity assessed using 6MST, 30CST, and 2MSWT and the quality of life of individuals after COVID-19 hospital discharge.

issues.title: Table 3 dispersion values (e.g. 30CST ±0.5, 6MST ±4.2) look like SEs, not the labelled SDs
issues.explanation: The footnote says values are mean ± SD, but several spreads are very small for walking and chair-stand tests in a heterogeneous post-COVID group. If they are SEs, the stated dispersion understates variability and any p-values derived from them could be inflated. The F and eta-squared columns (e.g. F = 646, eta-squared 0.93 for 30CST) appear inconsistent with the between-group p of 0.050.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or the SPSS output confirming the values are SDs.

issues.title: Baseline 'homogeneous (p<0.05)' contradicts Table 2 showing CVD imbalance (71% vs 45%, p=0.01)
issues.explanation: The Results state that groups were homogeneous with 'p<0.05', which is the threshold for a difference. The Discussion repeats that groups were similar. Table 2 flags cardiovascular disease as different between arms (71% vs 45%). The unadjusted between-group analyses ignore this imbalance, which is probably chance but could bear on functional comparisons. The printed p of 0.01 also does not match the arm counts, which give about 0.04.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum clarifying the intended sign, plus an analysis adjusted for cardiovascular disease giving the same between-group results.

quotes.text: Groups were homogeneous, considering baseline data ( p <0.05).
*groups were different ( p <0.05).

issues.title: 10 of 67 randomized (14.9%) dropped before analysis; completers-only analysis without ITT
issues.explanation: 67 were randomized (33 TG, 34 CG) but Table 2 and Table 3 analyse 28 and 29. Losses were equal in the two arms and attributed only to 'withdrawal', and no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is given. Post-allocation withdrawals could be related to treatment burden, so the completer estimates may be optimistic. The effect on the conclusion is modest given the balanced losses.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis giving the same between-group differences.

quotes.text: Overall, 67 individuals were eligible for telerehabilitation and divided into TG ( n = 33) and CG ( n = 34).
The reasons for exclusion after allocation were withdrawal.

issues.title: Analysed n = 57 versus calculated target 64; unclear whether 64 includes the 10% dropout
issues.explanation: The calculation uses d = 0.7, power 0.8 and a 10% dropout allowance, giving 64. Only 57 were analysed. If 64 already allows for dropout, 57 is about as expected; if it excludes dropout, the completed sample is short. No primary outcome or multiplicity plan is stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The sample-size calculation specifying the outcome and whether 64 is before or after dropout inflation.

quotes.text: reaching the sample size of 64 individuals.
Total ( n = 57)

10.1177/1357633x251333903.headline_claim: Telerehabilitation improved dyspnea, exercise capacity, respiratory muscle strength and fatigue in post-COVID-19 patients, and was not better than home exercise, with the program's dyspnea benefit exceeding no-intervention controls.
10.1177/1357633x251333903.overall: The finding that telerehabilitation and home exercise lower dyspnea and fatigue relative to no exercise is reasonably supported for week 6, but the trial is very small (12 per arm) and the TRG was not better than home exercise. The claims of complete dyspnea resolution, effectiveness for exercise capacity and respiratory muscle strength, and long-term maintenance go beyond the interaction results. Table errors (education p, week-12 SmO2 deltas) and unreported registered primaries are secondary issues.

primary_outcome.name: Dyspnea (mMRC) and exercise capacity (6MWT), described as the primary outcomes

issues.title: Effectiveness for exercise capacity and MIP claimed despite non-significant interactions (p=0.062, 0.086)
issues.explanation: The Conclusion states telerehabilitation was effective for exercise capacity and respiratory muscle strength and that gains are maintained long term. These claims rest on within-group changes, since the interaction tests that the authors call their central hypothesis were not significant for 6MWT distance or MIP, and TRG was not better than home exercise. Only dyspnea and fatigue show a between-group difference against the control group, and only at week 6. 'Long term' here means a 6-week follow-up in 36 participants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group test for 6MWT and MIP, or a pre-specified analysis in which within-group change was the primary comparison.

quotes.text: Telerehabilitation has been found to be effective in improving dyspnea, exercise capacity, respiratory muscle strength, and fatigue parameters.
could be achieved and maintained in the long term
The group × time interaction was considered the central hypothesis of interest.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion and Discussion state that telerehabilitation was effective for exercise capacity (6MWT distance) and respiratory muscle strength (MIP), and that exercise capacity gains were maintained long term. The prespecified central test (group × time interaction) was non-significant for both (p=0.062, 0.086), and the week-12 6MWTD change was not significant within the TRG. The only supporting evidence is within-group change and effect sizes, with no demonstrated advantage over the control or home-exercise groups. A narrower caveat: the percent-of-expected 6MWT distance (6MWTED) did show a

issues.title: Week-12 Δ Reco-Test SmO2 repeats Δ Reco-Rest in all groups (CG 3.31 vs 7.13 implied)
issues.explanation: At week 12 the Δ Reco-Test SmO2 cell is identical to the Δ Reco-Rest cell in each group, including the SD. For CG, recovery minus test SmO2 is 7.13, not 3.31. The same pattern appears for HEG (8.09 printed, 17.42 implied) and TRG (4.93 printed, 8.31 implied). The affected variable is a secondary, non-significant outcome, so the conclusions are barely touched, but the table is unreliable at these cells.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source table showing a different Reco-Test value, or a definition of Reco-Test that matches the printed week-12 numbers.

quotes.location: Table 2, CG Week 12 column, SmO2 rows
Table 2, HEG Week 12 column, Δ SmO2 rows

issues.title: Registered primaries physical activity and ADL unreported; other registered primaries relabelled secondary
issues.explanation: The registry lists eight primary outcomes at 6 weeks, but the paper names only dyspnea and exercise capacity as primary and calls the rest secondary. Physical activity and activities of daily living, both registered primaries, do not appear in the Methods or Results at all. The relabelling is mostly harmless because the main reported outcomes were registered, but the omission and the reclassification mean the pre-specified outcome set was not reported as registered.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the primary list was reduced before data collection, or a supplement reporting physical activity and ADL.

quotes.text: The primary outcomes were dyspnea and exercise capacity, whereas the secondary outcomes included muscle oxygenation, pulmonary functions, and fatigue.

issues.title: Dyspnea 'resolved completely' with telerehabilitation, but TRG mMRC is 0.42-0.50 and CG also improved
issues.explanation: The Discussion says dyspnea was resolved completely with telerehabilitation. The mean mMRC in the TRG was still about 0.4-0.5 at weeks 6 and 12, and the control group also improved without intervention, with the TRG advantage over CG shown only at week 6. The wording overstates what the data show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level data showing mMRC of 0 in all TRG participants.

quotes.text: dyspnea in individuals who have previously had COVID-19 was resolved completely with telerehabilitation

issues.title: Education baseline p printed as 0.06 in Results text but 0.006* in Table 1
issues.explanation: The Results text gives p = 0.06 for the education imbalance, while Table 1 prints 0.006 with a significance asterisk. The text also lists education as an exception to baseline similarity, which only makes sense for a significant p, so the text figure appears to be a typo. This is a small reporting slip, and the Discussion already treats the imbalance as real.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two different tests were used for education in the text and the table, or a corrected version of the text.

quotes.text: education level ( p = 0.027 and 0.06, respectively)

quotes.location: Table 1, Educational Status row, p column

issues.title: Baseline imbalance in BMI (p=0.027) and education (p=0.006); allocation concealment not described
issues.explanation: Education and BMI differ across the arms at baseline, and the primary-education share is 83% in TRG versus 8% in CG. The paper discloses this and states it disadvantages the TRG, but the mixed ANOVA is unadjusted and concealment is not described. This is more likely chance imbalance in a very small trial than a randomization failure, and it cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of central or sealed allocation concealment and covariate-adjusted analyses giving the same results.

quotes.text: with differences observed in BMI and educational level, disadvantaging the TRG

10.1177/14799731241255967.headline_claim: A combined respiratory (Powerbreathe Plus inspiratory training plus aerobic exercise) and olfactory/gustatory rehabilitation plan is a therapeutic option against respiratory and neurological sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
10.1177/14799731241255967.overall: The direction of benefit is plausible and the reported group-by-time p-values are small, but the control arm was untreated with no sham, most clinical scores are self-reported, and Table 2 is internally inconsistent (MIP SD, MMRC range, FVC total, MBS direction). The 31-day, young, non-severe population limits the broad therapeutic-option conclusion, and the registered primary time frames (1 year, 1 week) were not the ones reported.

primary_outcome.name: Forced vital capacity (FVC), named as the primary variable for the sample-size calculation

issues.title: No-treatment control without sham; subjective dyspnoea and smell/taste outcomes are self-reported
issues.explanation: The control group received no therapy and no attention control, and participants knew their allocation. Dyspnoea and smell/taste scores were sent by participants themselves, so expectancy and attention effects cannot be separated from the intervention effect. Effort-dependent spirometry and MIP are also open to motivation effects. The efficacy conclusion is therefore weaker than stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of blinded outcome measurement for self-reported outcomes or an attention-control arm.

quotes.text: control group: did not receive any treatment
both groups sent their dyspnoea-related scores via email to the investigators.

second_reader.what_stands: The control arm received no intervention and no sham or attention control, so participants knew their allocation, and the dyspnoea (Borg, MMRC) and smell/taste (SSTQ) outcomes were self-reported by participants (emailed or recorded telematically), so assessor blinding does not protect them from expectation or response bias. This does not apply to spirometry and PImax, which were measured in the laboratory by researchers stated to be blinded, though those were also not shielded from participant effort effects given the unblinded design.

issues.title: Parametric ANOVA and Eta2 used for ordinal dyspnoea scales summarised as medians in Table 1
issues.explanation: Table 1 treats MBS and MMRC as non-normal ordinal data (median, IQR, Mann-Whitney), yet Table 2 analyses them with repeated-measures ANOVA and Eta2. The effect-size labels are also applied loosely (Eta2 0.439 and 0.57 named differently from the stated bands). This weakens the precision of the dyspnoea effects but not necessarily their direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with ordinal/non-parametric methods giving the same conclusions.

quotes.text: A linear general model of analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed
MBS                          | 6 (2) <sup>b</sup>          | 5 (I) <sup>b</sup>

issues.title: Reported 31-day assessments differ from registered 1-year spirometry and 1-week smell/taste primary outcomes
issues.explanation: The registry lists spirometry at 1 year and smell/taste at 1 week as primary outcomes. The paper assesses everything at day 31, names FVC as the primary variable, and states that no later evaluation was done. The registered time frames were therefore not reported, and the paper does not explain the difference. Earlier registry versions were not seen.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing day-31 assessments, or a stated explanation of the time frame change.

quotes.text: A treatment plan was carried out for 31 days
we did not carry out a third evaluation in both groups at the end of the study to observe whether the results obtained were maintained over time

issues.title: Conclusion generalises to all post-COVID patients from young, non-severe participants followed for 31 days
issues.explanation: The abstract conclusion presents the programme as a therapeutic option for patients with post-COVID sequelae generally. The trial enrolled only 18-45-year-olds (median ages 22-23) without severe symptoms, had no sham control, and measured outcomes only at day 31 with no durability follow-up. The limitations are stated in the Discussion but not in the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion explicitly restricted to young adults with mild persistent symptoms and short-term effects.

quotes.text: is a therapeutic option against respiratory and neurological sequelae in patients who have suffered such sequelae due to the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
The study did not evaluate patients with severe symptoms.

issues.title: Baseline IG MIP SD is 10.25 in Table 1 but 4.601 in Table 2 for the same mean 70.04
issues.explanation: The intervention group's baseline MIP has the same mean (70.04) in both tables but an SD of 10.25 in Table 1 and 4.601 in Table 2. Both cannot be right, and the Table 2 MIP SDs (about 4.3-4.9) are all far smaller than Table 1's. A smaller SD in the repeated-measures analysis would inflate the apparent effect sizes for MIP, so the MIP result would need recomputing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction or supplementary data showing the true baseline SD, with the other table being a typo.

quotes.location: Table 2, MIP cmH2O block, IG group row, Pre column

issues.title: Table 2 MBS values as printed show a larger CG fall (5.87 to 1.38) than IG (6.52 to 5.55)
issues.explanation: As printed, the control group's Borg score drops by 4.5 points while the IG's drops by about 1, which would contradict the claim of IG benefit and the statement that the CG maintained or worsened symptoms. The table is heavily garbled (rows and group labels are displaced), so the printed values may belong to different cells. The paper cannot be used to say which assignment is correct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original (non-extracted) Table 2 showing correct row alignment.

quotes.location: Table 2, Dyspnea MBS row, Post column

quotes.text: the IG group showed a statistically significant improvement (p < .05) among the different measurements

issues.title: Table 2 MMRC block prints means of 6.19 and 3.465 on a 0-4 scale
issues.explanation: The MMRC scale runs from 0 to 4, yet the MMRC block contains a pre mean of 6.19 and a post mean of 3.465 attached to CG. The values look like they belong to another outcome (e.g. Borg) shifted by a row. Either way, the printed Table 2 cannot be read reliably for the MMRC comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original table layout showing 6.19 belongs to the MBS CG row.

quotes.location: Table 2, Dyspnea MMRC row, CG group, Pre column

quotes.text: with grades ranging from 0 to 4
quotes.location: Outcome measures, Modified Medical Research Council (MMRC)

issues.title: Enrolled number is 220 in the abstract but 209 in the Methods; 200 analysed
issues.explanation: The abstract says the study was conducted in 220 patients, 200 of whom completed it, while the Methods say 209 were recruited. Both figures are described as the starting population, and the text does not say how 220 or 209 fell to 200. The flow chart may reconcile this but is not readable here. Only the enrolment description is affected; the analysed n of 200 is consistent throughout.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing 220 assessed/eligible and 209 randomised, with the abstract wording meaning screened patients.

quotes.text: conducted in 220 patients with a medical diagnosis of COVID-19
in the end 209 patients were recruited

issues.title: About 8 outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 with no correction and no primary outcome analysis
issues.explanation: Seven or eight outcomes were each tested at 0.05 without adjustment, and the registry lists spirometry and smell/taste as primary while the paper does not designate a primary outcome in its analysis. Most stated p-values are below .01, so correction would probably change little for those, but borderline items such as the FVC time effect (p < .003) are less secure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary outcome and a hierarchy for the rest.

quotes.text: For all analyses, p - value <0.05 (for a confidence interval of 95%) was considered as statistically significan.
showing statistically significant differences in all variables except FEV1.

issues.title: Desired power stated as 90% in sample-size calculation and 80% in statistical analysis
issues.explanation: The sample-size paragraph uses 90% power (98 per group), while the statistical analysis section says 80% power. Only one can describe the design. The actual enrolment of 100 per group meets either figure, so no result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 80% refers to a different analysis than the a priori calculation.

quotes.text: a desired statistical power of 90%
quotes.location: Materials and methods, Participants (sample size calculation)

quotes.text: with a desired power of 80% (b error of 0.2)

10.1177/14799731261454679.headline_claim: A remote, group-based yogic breathing intervention is feasible for people with dysregulated breathing after COVID-19, and the exploratory outcomes suggest it may improve breathlessness (CRQ-D, NQ).
10.1177/14799731261454679.overall: This is a small, openly labelled feasibility trial, and its feasibility findings (31% of those starting completed more than 75% of sessions) can be relied on as tentative. The efficacy signals are not supported: the intergroup differences are null, the favourable results are within-arm or based on 5 completers, and several Table 2 and text entries are inconsistent (fatigue and 4MGS significance, EQ5D and CRQ-D p-values, a sign slip). Conclusions about clinical benefit in breathlessness should be treated as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (attendance and completion: >75% attendance plus visit 2 assessment)

checklist.n_analysed_primary: 27 (13 intervention + 14 usual care) in itt; 5 intervention completers in per-protocol

issues.title: Benefit claimed from significant within-arm CRQ-D/NQ change while intergroup differences are null
issues.explanation: The paper reports improvements in CRQ-D (p<0.001) and NQ (p=0.04) in the intervention arm but not in usual care. It uses this contrast to describe a clinical improvement, even though the direct between-arm comparison is not significant. A difference between 'significant' and 'not significant' is not itself evidence of a difference, and usual care also moved in the same direction (CRQ-D +0.27, NQ -1.60) without a control for regression or attention effects. With 13 versus 14 analysed and unblinded participants, the data cannot show benefit. The Discussion's 'insightful indicators' wording adds to this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified ANCOVA or between-arm comparison of change scores showing a significant intervention effect on CRQ-D or NQ.

quotes.text: a clinical improvement was found in CRQ-D scores in the intervention group, with a mean difference of 0.77 (95%CI 0.29, 1.25; p=<0.001) but not in usual care 0.27 (95%CI -0.31, 0.85; p=0.33)
The NQ clinically improved with the intervention: -2.69 (95%CI -5.26, -0.12; p=0.04) but not in the usual care -1.60 (95%CI -4.69, 1.49; p=0.29).
The data presented in this feasibility study provides insightful indicators that may well be transferable to other populations

second_reader.what_stands: The Results text presents within-arm significance (CRQ-D 0.77 and NQ -2.69 in the intervention arm, versus non-significant changes in usual care) as improvement 'with the intervention', although the intergroup differences are null and the CIs overlap. The Discussion also calls the findings 'insightful indicators that may well be transferable' to asthma and COPD, which goes beyond a null, underpowered comparison of 13 versus 14 participants, with only 5 of 16 completing. This is softened by the authors' explicit statements that intergroup differences were not significant, that the study was unp

issues.title: Text says no significant fatigue/4MGS change; Table 2 shows fatigue p=0.02 and 4MGS intergroup CI excluding 0
issues.explanation: The Results state that fatigue, 4MGS and other measures showed no significant change within or between groups. Table 2 gives a within-group fatigue change of -4.00 (95% CI -7.37 to -0.63, p=0.02) in the intervention arm. It also gives a 4MGS intergroup difference of 0.86 (0.03 to 1.69), which excludes zero, with a within-group p of 0.05. The blanket 'no significant change' sentence therefore does not match the table. The 4MGS difference is in the direction of slower walking with the intervention, so the sentence also hides a possible adverse signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sentence refers only to between-group tests of mean differences in the original units, or a corrected Table 2 in which the fatigue and 4MGS cells differ.

quotes.text: There was no significant change for dyspnoea (D12), Borg scale, RPE, breath-hold, fatigue, 4MGS, physical activity score or EQ5D for both within or between group analysis.

quotes.location: Table 2, Fatigue row, intervention mean difference

issues.title: Per-protocol 'primary' analysis restricted to 5 completers vs 14 usual-care participants, reported as improvement
issues.explanation: Per-protocol analysis is named as primary, but the intervention set is only the 5 of 16 who attended more than 75% of sessions and had a post visit. Selecting on attendance can favour those who felt better, and the comparator is the full usual-care group, which has no matching selection. The CRQ-D gain in completers (p=0.02) is described as a clinical improvement alongside an NQ change with p=0.11 that is not significant. The intergroup tests in the supplement were null, and the ITT analysis does not show a between-group difference either. This weakens the evidential value of the headline per-protocol results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A per-protocol comparison against matched usual-care completers, or an intergroup test showing a significant effect.

quotes.text: Per protocol analyses was set out as the primary analyses to gain a better understanding of the effect of the intervention on outcomes
clinical improvements in the CRQ-D of 0.71 (95% CI; 0.14, 1.28; p=0.02), and a reduction in the NQ of -2.36 (-5.40, 0.67; p=0.11) were observed in the completers (n=5)

issues.title: Feasibility called the primary objective, but registry primaries are breathlessness and function; Table 2 labels them primary
issues.explanation: The registry record lists breathlessness and function at 7 weeks as the primary outcomes. The paper instead defines feasibility as the primary objective and calls CRQ-D and 5RCTS 'other key outcomes', then labels them 'Primary Outcomes' in Table 2. This leaves it unclear which endpoints were pre-specified as primary and which were demoted or promoted. Because the efficacy results are not significant between groups, the practical effect is small, but readers cannot tell which analysis was confirmatory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registry versions or the protocol showing feasibility as the original primary outcome, with CRQ-D and 5RCTS registered as exploratory.

quotes.text: Primary objective: To evaluate the feasibility (attendance and completion) of a 6-week online, remote breathing intervention
Other key study outcomes to guide future studies were a) change in breathlessness

issues.title: EQ5D intervention p printed as 0.00 although 95% CI (-5.98, 12.29) spans zero (implied p about 0.47)
issues.explanation: A p of 0.00 would mean strong significance, but the printed CI includes zero. A paired t-test with n=13 and this CI gives a p of about 0.47. The Results text calls EQ5D non-significant, so the table cell is the error. This is a single wrong cell with no effect on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the p-value column for EQ5D is a different statistic, or a corrected table with p of about 0.47.

quotes.location: Table 2, EQ5D row, intervention mean difference

script.explanation: the paper reports p < 0.005, but the p recoverable from the printed interval at the stated 95% level is [0.4982, 0.5001], and no common confidence level reaches below the claimed bound; the CI includes the null (0.0), but the reported p < 0.005 says the result is significant

issues.title: Usual-care 5RCTS change printed as +1.69 but CI (-4.52, 1.15) and means imply -1.69 (a sign slip)
issues.explanation: The usual-care 5RCTS mean difference lies outside its own CI, and the week 0 and week 7 means (14.94 to 13.26) show a fall, not a rise. The sign is missing in the table and in the Results. As printed, the usual-care arm looks worse on a timed test, when it actually became about 1.7 s faster. That is about the 1.7 s MCID, while the intervention arm slowed by 2.48 s. The error is limited to one cell, but the corrected sign reverses how the arms compare.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 5RCTS change was calculated as week 0 minus week 7 for usual care only, which is not supported by the intervention-arm sign convention.
