10.1177/17534666231167354.headline_claim: A pulmonary telerehabilitation program for not-vaccinated post-COVID-19 patients with respiratory sequelae has proven its benefits in cardiorespiratory variables, dyspnea and anxiety.
10.1177/17534666231167354.overall: The headline claim of proven benefit is not supported: it rests on an unblinded, non-randomized waitlist comparison analysing only completers (100 of 148), with unadjusted baseline imbalances and self-reported outcomes. Several table entries (control SpO2 median, EG post anxiety medians of 50, Table 1 percentages) are internally impossible, so the individual effect sizes cannot be taken at face value. The direction of improvement in the intervention arm is plausible, but its size and attribution to the programme are uncertain.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; outcomes include respiratory rate, heart rate, SpO2, Mahler's dyspnea index, STAI anxiety, EQ-5D quality of life

primary_outcomes.measure: Euroqol-5d european quality of life-5 dimensions
Euroqol-5d european quality of life-5 dimensions

issues.title: 'Has proven its benefits' conclusion from non-randomized, unblinded, completers-only waitlist comparison
issues.explanation: The conclusion states the programme has proven benefits, but the evidence is an unblinded comparison of self-selected sequential groups, restricted to completers, with several table errors and unadjusted baseline differences. Such a design supports a tentative signal at most. The limitations section omits these threats.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion hedged to the design, or a randomized/adjusted analysis supporting the claim.

quotes.text: has proven its benefits in cardiorespiratory variables and dyspnearelated anxiety.

second_reader.what_stands: The wording 'has proven its benefits' is stronger than a non-randomized, unblinded, completers-only comparison with baseline imbalance and self-reported outcomes can support; the results are better described as an association or as preliminary evidence. The authors do disclose the non-randomized design, but the Limitations section omits the main threats to validity.

issues.title: Unblinded comparison with self-reported or self-measured outcomes
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and nearly all outcomes depend on self-report or self-measurement at home. Waitlist controls have no expectation of benefit, so differences in dyspnoea, anxiety and quality of life may partly reflect expectation. The paper acknowledges self-reporting only as a consequence of confinement, not as a bias risk.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded or objectively measured outcomes assessed by an independent assessor.

quotes.text: Participants were confined in the first wave of the pandemic, with no possibility of geographical mobility, so variables were self-reported.

second_reader.what_stands: Participants and presumably assessors knew group assignment (registry masking NONE, no blinding described), and the outcomes were self-reported questionnaires or self-measured with participants' own oximeters, so they are susceptible to expectation and measurement bias. The paper discloses the self-report but does not list it, or the lack of blinding, among its limitations.

issues.title: Non-randomized waitlist comparison (first 74 vs next 74) with baseline imbalance and no adjustment
issues.explanation: The first 74 sign-ups were assigned to the programme and the next 74 to a waiting list, so groups differ by time of enrolment and possibly by who joined early. Baseline trait anxiety, EQ-5D and cough differed significantly, and the between-group comparisons use unadjusted percentage changes. The effect of the programme cannot be separated from selection and period effects. Note the registry record describes the trial as randomized, which the paper contradicts.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of true random or concealed allocation, or analyses adjusting for baseline and enrolment period with similar results.

quotes.text: in order of arrival, in groups of 20, and the control group (CG) was composed by patients in the waiting list
The first 74 were assigned to the EG and the following 74 were inscribed  in  a  waiting  list

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by order of arrival (first 74 vs next 74 on a waiting list), not randomised, and at least three baseline variables (cough, trait anxiety, EuroQol-5D) differed significantly between completers, with no adjusted analysis. The paper does state it is non-randomized, so the design is disclosed, but the imbalance is not addressed in the analysis or the conclusions.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis: 100 of 148 analysed (32% lost), no ITT or missing-data handling
issues.explanation: Only participants who completed all 10 sessions regularly were analysed, and dropout reasons are not given. Excluding non-adherers biases per-protocol estimates toward patients who tolerate and benefit from the programme. The same loss in each arm does not remove this bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis including dropouts with similar results.

quotes.text: Only data from patients who had completed the protocol regularly and successfully were included.
50 subjects of each group completed the protocol.

second_reader.what_stands: Analysis is restricted to completers (100 of 148, 32% not analysed) with no ITT analysis, imputation or sensitivity analysis, and reasons for loss are not reported by arm. Completion was defined as attending all 10 sessions regularly, so the completer set is selected on adherence, which can bias the estimated benefit; the paper does not list this as a limitation.

issues.title: Between-group percentage-change test labelled paired Wilcoxon; no baseline-adjusted comparison
issues.explanation: Table 5 compares percentage changes between independent groups, but its footnote names the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which is for paired data (the methods say Mann-Whitney for between-group). Percentage change of medians near zero and a baseline-imbalanced waitlist group makes these comparisons fragile. The test actually used is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that Mann-Whitney U was used for Table 5 and a baseline-adjusted analysis of change scores.

quotes.text: Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for the comparisons.
Percentage changes in pre-post intervention were calculated and compared between EG and CG.

issues.title: Registry (randomized, n=40, Borg primary) differs from paper (nonrandomized, n=148, Mahler-based sample size)
issues.explanation: The registered design and outcomes differ from what the paper reports: randomized vs nonrandomized, 40 vs 148 participants, Borg dyspnoea and effort scale vs Mahler's index as the sample-size outcome. Borg results are not reported. Without a stated primary outcome in the paper, the many significant outcomes cannot be judged against a pre-specified one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the changes were made before data collection and the primary outcome was declared.

issues.title: Control-group SpO2 median 92 lies outside its own IQR (95-98) in Tables 2 and 3
issues.explanation: A median cannot be below the 25th percentile. The control SpO2 is printed as 92 (95-98) pre and 92 (95.5-98) post. Either the median or the quartiles are wrong, so the control SpO2 data cannot be interpreted as printed. SpO2 is one of the outcomes behind the oxygenation claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or raw data showing the median is within the stated IQR.

issues.title: Table 4: post-intervention state and trait anxiety medians printed as 50, outside IQRs near 12-25
issues.explanation: The EG post medians for state and trait anxiety are printed as 50, while their IQRs are 15-25.25 and 12.75-23.25. A median cannot sit outside its IQR, and 50 would be higher than the pre values (26.5 and 20), i.e. worse, contradicting the text claiming significant improvement. The medians appear to be erroneous, so the size of the anxiety change cannot be read from the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or corrected table showing post medians inside the printed IQRs.

10.1177/19412711261418482.overall: The headline claim that IMT improved total aerosol deposition and perfusion is only partly supported. Aerosol deposition shows between-group differences, but the perfusion claim rests on within-arm change, since the total-lung between-group test is p = 0.053, with baseline imbalance, uncorrected multiplicity and an outcome set that differs from the registry. issues.title: Conclusion claims cost-effectiveness and rehabilitation benefit; only scintigraphic counts in 19 people measured
issues.explanation: The study measured planar scintigraphy counts, SpO2 and MIP over 8 weeks in 19 participants. It measured no symptoms, function, drug-delivery efficacy or cost. The statements that IMT 'may represent a cost-effective tool' and 'support the use of IMT as a rehabilitation strategy' go beyond the data, and the authors themselves say translation to symptoms is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A cost or clinical-outcome analysis within the study.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no cost or cost-effectiveness data, and the only efficacy outcomes are scintigraphic counts (plus MIP and SpO2) in 19 people, so 'cost-effective' and 'support the use of IMT as a rehabilitation strategy' go beyond the data. issues.title: Regional lung borders drawn from activity patterns with no anatomical reference; reproducibility not assessed
issues.explanation: Right/left lung counts depend on borders set from the radioactivity itself on each visit, with no CT or transmission scan and no reproducibility data. Since borders follow the activity, they may track the very change being measured. The authors acknowledge the limitation, but the region-specific claims (right-lung-only perfusion effect) are the ones most affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported inter- and intra-observer agreement for region delineation.

issues.title: About 18 uncorrected tests across region, modality and group; no single primary endpoint designated
issues.explanation: The paper tests total, right and left lungs for both inhalation and perfusion, within and between groups, plus SpO2 and MIP, all at p < 0.05 with no correction. Several between-group p-values (0.053, 0.079) sit near the threshold, and the abstract highlights those that cross it. The significant subset is more likely to include chance findings than the nominal alpha suggests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or family-wise correction showing the key results survive.

issues.title: Sample size based on MIP effect size (1.4688), not on the scintigraphic primary outcome
issues.explanation: The power calculation used inspiratory pressure differences from a prior IMT trial, not radiopharmaceutical counts. It therefore says nothing about the ability to detect changes in deposition or perfusion. The stated 'final sample size of 18 with 9 per group' also sits oddly with a 15% dropout allowance and with 10 enrolled in the IMT group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power calculation based on scintigraphic count changes.

issues.title: Paper says all outcomes were registered; registry lists only aerosol deposition as primary, no others
issues.explanation: The paper names inhalation and perfusion scintigraphy as primary and SpO2, MIP and adverse events as secondary, and states all were registered before enrolment. The current registry record lists a single primary outcome (radioaerosol deposition at 3 minutes) and no secondary outcomes. The perfusion claim in the conclusion therefore rests on an outcome not in the registered set, unless earlier record versions show otherwise.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry record history showing perfusion and the secondary outcomes were listed before enrolment.

10.1177/19458924221113124.headline_claim: Four-week olfactory training with 8 essences (advanced) was not superior to classical 4-essence training, while olfactory function improved overall after training in post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction.
10.1177/19458924221113124.overall: The trial's null comparison of 4 vs 8 essences is reported consistently, but it rests on small, unequal groups with no sample-size calculation, randomisation description or registration. The claim that training itself improved smell comes from an uncontrolled pre/post change (mean UPSIT +1.5), so it should be treated as descriptive only. issues.explanation: All participants received training, so the pre/post rise (UPSIT 25.2 to 26.7, P = .002; VAS rises) cannot be attributed to training rather than spontaneous recovery or retest effects. The authors cite short recovery periods for COVID-related smell loss and the improvement in UPSIT is below the ≥4-point change they define as clinically relevant. The training-effect claim in the Conclusion is therefore stronger than this design allows. The between-arm comparison, the study's actual aim, is not affected by this.

10.1177/19458924221120116.headline_claim: Intranasal 1% sodium gluconate improves olfactory function (anosmia to hyposmia) and lowers nasal calcium in post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction, and supports sodium gluconate as a useful therapy.
10.1177/19458924221120116.overall: The between-group difference in TDI and calcium is large and internally consistent with the printed t statistics, so some real effect on the surrogate outcomes is plausible. However, the control-arm change scores do not match their own means, there is no registration, the sample-size basis is not a power calculation, and the 'useful therapy' conclusion exceeds a one-month trial whose mean gain falls below the authors' own clinical threshold. The headline should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Change in TDI olfactory score (Snif'n Sticks) at 1 month

issues.title: 'Useful therapy' conclusion exceeds a 1-month, 50-patient trial whose mean gain (5.24) is below the paper's own 6-point threshold
issues.explanation: The paper defines a clinically significant improvement as an increase of more than 6 TDI points. The mean gluconate gain is 5.24, and the final mean TDI of 16.80 sits just above the 16.5 anosmia cut-off. Follow-up is one month, with no registration and no analysis linking calcium change to TDI change, yet the conclusion calls the treatment useful and attributes the benefit to calcium chelation. The statistical difference is clear, but the clinical-usefulness and mechanism claims go beyond what the trial shows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Responder analysis showing most gluconate patients exceeded the 6-point threshold with durable benefit, or longer follow-up data.

quotes.text: An individual increase of more than 6 points was regarded as a clinically signi fi cant progression of olfactory function.
intranasal sodium gluconate can represent a useful therapy for persisted olfactory dysfunction post-COVID-19 infection

second_reader.what_stands: True: the trial is 50 patients with 1 month of treatment, the mean TDI gain (5.24) is below the paper's own >6-point individual threshold, the post-treatment mean (16.80) is barely above the anosmia cutoff, and the paper never reports how many patients met the >6-point criterion, yet the Conclusion calls the spray a 'useful therapy'. Not established: the mean being under 6 does not mean most individuals failed the threshold (an estimated ~37% could exceed it), and the authors do acknowledge small sample, short follow-up and a still-low final TDI in the Discussion, though not in the Conclusion

Statements about improvement after zinc and steroids cannot be attributed to treatment, because there is no control group and about 40-47% of patients were lost before retesting. The one numeric slip (statistics for '17' patients are actually for 18) is minor.

issues.title: Treatment effect inferred from uncontrolled, within-group pre-post change (no control, no between-group test)
issues.explanation: All patients received the same prednisolone and zinc, and improvement is judged only against each patient's own baseline with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The limitation is stated in the Discussion, but the title and conclusion still present improvement 'after treatment with oral zinc and steroids'. No between-group comparison exists.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo comparison group showing a difference in recovery.

The reported ranges (6-31, 14-34) and means (20.06, 25.28) only fit if patient 6 is included. Excluding patient 6, the means would be about 19.41 and 25.18 (pre: 330/17, post: 421/17), with maxima 29 and 33. The p = 0.001 is probably also from the 18-patient set. The effect on the result is small.

10.1177/20552076241234432.headline_claim: A 4-week personalised digital physiotherapy programme produced a statistically significant improvement in quality of life in patients with Long COVID, with high satisfaction and values above the MCID, and the authors describe the intervention as effective and feasible.
10.1177/20552076241234432.overall: The paper shows that scores on SF-12 and EuroQol-5D improved over 4 weeks in 32 completers of a single-arm programme, and that participants reported high satisfaction. The title and Discussion claim effectiveness, which this uncontrolled completers-only design cannot support, and the MCID and safety statements are also weaker than worded. The numeric slips are minor and do not change the findings.

primary_outcome.name: Health-related quality of life (SF-12 PCS-12 and MCS-12; EuroQoL-5D)

issues.title: Title and Discussion call a single-arm pre-post programme 'effective' despite no control group
issues.explanation: All quantitative results come from one uncontrolled group measured before and after 4 weeks, analysed in completers only. The authors acknowledge that the design cannot establish causation, yet the title and Discussion assert effectiveness. The data support only that scores improved over 4 weeks, not that the programme caused it. This combines the no-control design problem and the overstated wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or a design permitting causal attribution of the change.

quotes.text: Digital physiotherapy is a satisfactory and effective method to improve the quality of life in Long COVID patients
Overall, only a 4-week digital physiotherapy program was effective in improving the quality of life of our participants
limiting the study ' s ability to conclude a causal association between an intervention and an outcome
quotes.location: Limitations and strengths of the study

second_reader.what_stands: The title and the Discussion state flatly that the programme is 'effective' for quality of life, although the design has only pre and post measurements in one group with no comparator, so improvement cannot be attributed to the intervention (natural recovery, regression to the mean and expectation effects are not separable). The Limitations section does acknowledge the lack of randomization and the Conclusions call for randomized trials, which partly softens this, but the headline claims remain causal and unqualified.

issues.title: 'Values above MCID' compares a 0.87 sum-score change with a 0.26 MCID defined for the EuroQol-5D index
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state that the changes exceed the MCID. For the EuroQol-5D, the 0.87-point change is on the 5-15 sum score used here, while the cited MCID of 0.26 refers to the EuroQol-5D index. The SF-12 thresholds come from a low back pain population. The claim of clinically meaningful improvement is therefore not well supported by the comparisons made, and the MCID assessment method is not described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 0.26 MCID applies to the 5-15 sum score used in this study.

quotes.text: A previous study found that a change of at least 0.26 for the EuroQol-5D questionnaire index represented MCID in patients with Long COVID syndrome.
In this research, an improvement of 0.87 points was obtained with an effect size (medium) of 0.56.

issues.title: Analysis limited to 32 completers; number enrolled and lost not stated in the text
issues.explanation: The quantitative results include only participants who completed the 4 weeks. No enrolled, screened or withdrawn counts are given in the text, so selective loss of non-responders cannot be excluded. If those who dropped out did worse, the improvement would be overstated. The effect cannot be settled without the Figure 2 contents.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow figure showing all enrolled participants completed and were analysed.

quotes.text: A total of 32 participants completed the 4-week intervention and were included in the analysis.

issues.title: 'Safe' conclusion based on spontaneous patient report of no adverse effects; no AE monitoring described
issues.explanation: The safety statement appears in the limitations section and rests on patients reporting no adverse effects. No structured adverse event monitoring, symptom worsening measure or denominator is described. With 32 completers, absence of reports gives little assurance of safety. The claim is weaker than worded, but it is a secondary claim, not a headline one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of systematic adverse event collection that found none.

quotes.text: with patients reporting no adverse effects during the intervention
quotes.location: Limitations and strengths of the study

quotes.text: we regard our intervention to be feasible, safe and consistent with our objectives
quotes.location: Limitations and strengths of the study

issues.title: EuroQol-5D change called an 'increase of 0.87' though the score fell from 9.18 to 8.31 (lower is better)
issues.explanation: The Results describe the EuroQol-5D change as an increase of 0.87 points. Table 2 shows the score falling, and the Methods say higher scores mean worse quality of life, so the fall is an improvement. A reader relying on the text alone would infer deterioration. The wording is wrong in direction, though the table and Discussion ('improvement of 0.87') make the intent recoverable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the table and Methods settle the direction.

quotes.text: Additionally, the EuroQoL-5D questionnaire showed a medium effect size with an increase of 0.87 points.
In this case, the EuroQol-5D higher scores are indicative of worse quality of life.

issues.title: Text cites item 10 as the 'acceptable way' item (SD 0.75); Table 3 places that wording and SD at item 12
issues.explanation: The Results list the lowest-scoring items as 5, 8 and 10, quoting item 10 as 'I find Telemedicine an acceptable way...'. In Table 3 that statement is item 12 (4.43 ± 0.75), and item 10 is 'I do receive adequate attention' (4.93 ± 0.24), one of the highest-scoring items. The text also omits the mean for that item. This is a labelling error with no effect on the main results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different item numbering in the administered questionnaire that matches the text.

quotes.text: 10.-' I find Telemedicine an acceptable way to receive health care services '
10. I do receive adequate attention

issues.title: No trial registration reported although the study is called a trial and follows CONSORT
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval but no registry identifier. Without a registry entry, the choice of SF-12 and EuroQol-5D as outcomes and the paired t-test analysis cannot be checked as prespecified. This matters more for a study that claims effectiveness. It is a transparency gap rather than evidence of outcome switching.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record dated before enrolment with the same outcomes.

quotes.text: This trial has the approval of the Andalusia Ethics Committee with HIP version 281020.
based on the consolidated standards of reporting trials criteria

issues.title: Baseline EuroQol-5D mean given as 9.1 in text and Discussion but 9.18 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results text (and the Discussion) give the baseline EuroQol-5D mean as 9.1, while Table 2 prints 9.18 with the same SD of 1.53. The table value is the one consistent with the reported change of 0.87. The difference is small and does not alter any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the text value was deliberately truncated, or a different baseline subset.

quotes.text: The average score in the EuroQol- 5D was 9.1 (SD 1.53)

issues.title: TSQ items scored 1 to 5 in Methods but described as a 0 to 5 Likert scale in Results
issues.explanation: The Methods define a 1-5 scale and a total range of 14 to 70. The Results describe item means as lying on a 0-5 scale. The 14 items times 1 to 5 give 14 to 70, so the Methods are the consistent version and the Results text is a slip. No reported value depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a 0-5 version of the TSQ was used.

quotes.text: The questionnaire items were scored on a 5-point Likert scale, from 1, strongly disagree, to 5, strongly agree.
ranged from 3.84 to 4.93 on a Likert Scale (0 -5)

10.1177/20552076261428205.headline_claim: Both digitally delivered multimodal interventions (IVR and online self-guided) were associated with multidomain changes in cognitive and functional outcomes in adults with post-COVID condition, with the IVR format showing improvements in global cognition, immediate recall, recognition memory and response inhibition relative to passive control.
10.1177/20552076261428205.overall: The study is an openly non-randomized, unblinded, completers-only comparison with a control group assessed largely at another site, so its estimates are best treated as exploratory and cannot be read as effects of the interventions. The headline claims of cognitive and functional benefit rest on marginal, uncorrected contrasts, some without a significant omnibus test. The two numeric flags about Table 3 look like omnibus-versus-contrast confusion in the table layout, not errors.

primary_outcomes.measure: Differences between groups in scores of global cognition

issues.title: Self-selected intervention format and hand-picked controls; Discussion still uses causal wording
issues.explanation: The protocol and registry specify randomization, but no randomization was carried out. Participants chose IVR or online according to availability and access, and controls were invited directly. Group differences therefore mix treatment effects with who chose what, and the Discussion states that the IVR intervention 'led to' improvements. The Conclusions' 'associated with' wording is more careful, but the study design cannot support the effectiveness claims as stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that allocation was random or concealed, or an analysis that models selection into format and gives the same results.

quotes.text: Participants eligible for an intervention were allowed to choose between the IVR and the online formats according to their availability for in-person sessions, access to technology, and scheduling constraints.
Compared to the control group, the IVR intervention led to improvements in global cognition, immediate recall and recognition memory, and response inhibition.

second_reader.what_stands: Format was self-selected and controls were directly invited rather than allocated by a random or participant-choice process. The Discussion sentence 'the IVR intervention led to improvements' is causal wording that does not fit this non-randomised design, and the Conclusions and most other passages use associative wording. 'Hand-picked' is a characterisation: the paper says controls were invited directly but does not say what criteria were used.

issues.title: Control group assessed mostly at another hospital; only schooling adjusted, no covariates for behavioural outcomes
issues.explanation: Most controls were assessed at a different hospital, so site, examiner and setting are confounded with group. Baseline groups differed in schooling (p<.001), diabetes (p=.004) and labour change (p=.030), and only schooling was adjusted for, and only in the cognitive models. Behavioural outcomes (EQ-5D, WHODAS, MAAS) had no adjustment, although baseline differences there were large (EQ-5D baseline difference of about 0.7 SD between online and control). The behavioural contrasts remain open to confounding by site and selection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis adjusting for site and the imbalanced covariates, or a site-balanced control sample, giving similar estimates.

quotes.text: For logistical reasons, most control assessments were conducted at a different location, the Hospital Santa Maria (Lleida, Spain)
Schooling (years of education) was included as a covariate in the cognitive outcome models due to baseline group differences, while no covariates were included in the behavioral outcome models.

second_reader.what_stands: Most controls were assessed at a different hospital from both intervention arms, so site is largely inseparable from group. Only schooling was adjusted in cognitive models and nothing in behavioural models, although other baseline imbalances (labour status, diabetes, and baseline behavioural scores) are shown. The authors acknowledge the site issue as a limitation but did not adjust for it.

issues.title: Only completers analysed (129 of 172), with differential dropout and no ITT or imputation
issues.explanation: The analysis set is the 129 participants who completed and met the 80% adherence rule, and the authors state that no ITT analysis was done and no imputation was used. Dropout differed by arm and by labour status, so the completer comparison favours those who persisted. Effect estimates for the interventions are therefore likely to be optimistic, and conclusions about 'real-world' effectiveness are weakened.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis giving the same group differences.

quotes.text: no intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis was performed.
Participants who did not reach ≥ 80% adherence were excluded from the primary (per-protocol) analysis.

second_reader.what_stands: Only 129 of 172 enrolled participants were analysed, with no ITT analysis and no imputation, and attrition differed by arm (about 10% in controls, 27-28% online, 25-33% IVR depending on whether adherence exclusions are counted). The authors report this and flag retention as suboptimal, but the results rest on a completers-only sample and the missing-at-random assumption is untested.

issues.title: Global cognition 'improvement' reported though MoCA interaction p = .055; no correction across ~26 outcomes
issues.explanation: The Conclusions list improvement in global cognition for IVR, but the MoCA group-by-time interaction was non-significant (p = .055), and the supporting contrast (IVR > control, p = .001) was run although the stated rule required a significant omnibus test. Other highlighted effects (recognition p = .047, commission errors p = .046, contrast p = .038) are marginal and uncorrected across outcomes, which the authors themselves call exploratory. The headline cognitive benefits therefore read as firmer than the evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity-adjusted analysis in which these contrasts remain significant.

quotes.text: the time-by-group interaction approached signi fi cance
The IVR format was associated with improvements in global cognition, immediate recall, recognition memory, and response inhibition.

second_reader.what_stands: The omnibus MoCA interaction is p=.055, yet the Discussion and Conclusions state that IVR was associated with improved global cognition, and a post hoc contrast was reported despite the stated rule requiring a significant omnibus test. No correction was applied across outcomes (the authors say so and call the findings exploratory), but there are about 37 outcomes in Tables 2-3, not ~26.

issues.title: Post scores are baseline-residualised, so 'decline in controls' cannot be read as absolute deterioration
issues.explanation: Post-intervention scores were converted to standardized residuals from a regression on baseline, so the pre-post time effect is forced to be about zero and group changes are only relative to each other. The Discussion nonetheless says the interventions prevent 'the functional decline observed in the control group'. The data as analysed cannot show absolute decline, and regression to the mean from unequal baselines (e.g. EQ-5D) cannot be separated from true change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw pre/post scores in the control group showing an actual decline, with an analysis modelling raw scores.

quotes.text: postintervention scores were expressed as standardized residuals from a linear regression predicting postscores from baseline values
also in preventing the functional decline observed in the control group

second_reader.what_stands: Post scores are baseline-adjusted residuals, so a negative control value means worse than predicted from baseline across the pooled sample, not an absolute fall in raw performance. The Discussion's statements about 'functional decline' and 'progressive deterioration' in controls therefore cannot be read as absolute deterioration from the data presented.

issues.title: Unblinded participants and assessors with self-reported secondary outcomes interpreted as true change
issues.explanation: Neither participants nor outcome assessors were blinded, and the registry planned single masking. The secondary findings the authors highlight (MAAS, EQ-5D, WHODAS) are self-reported, so expectation could contribute to the differences against a passive control. The cognitive tests are performance-based and less exposed to this, so the issue is narrower for the primary outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded assessment or an active-attention control showing the same self-report effects.

quotes.text: Outcome assessors were not blinded to group assignment.
Scores on the MAAS scale increased in the online group compared to the control group, suggesting that participants who followed the online intervention experienced an overall increase in mindfulness.

10.1177/21501319251325639.headline_claim: A combination biofeedback approach may be delivered remotely and asynchronously alongside standard long COVID treatment to effectively reduce symptom burden in patients with LC.
10.1177/21501319251325639.overall: The paper supports feasibility and acceptability of the device in a small single-arm sample, with consistent stress, distress, cognition and QoL changes from baseline. Its Discussion conclusion that the device was effective is not supported by an uncontrolled, unblinded design, and several reported details (the sleep direction, anxiety result, follow-up dates, registered primaries) need correction or clarification. Treat the efficacy results as exploratory signals only.

primary_outcome.name: Frequency of S-EEG device usage (paper's primary aim: feasibility); registry primaries are change in stress and anxiety at 3 months

issues.title: Single-arm open-label pre-post design cannot show the device is effective; Discussion says it was
issues.explanation: All 45 patients received the device alongside standard long-COVID care, with no control group and no blinding. Improvements from baseline cannot be separated from natural recovery, concurrent treatment, regression to the mean or expectancy. The Discussion nonetheless concludes the device 'was effective' and 'provides significant benefits', which the design cannot support; it supports feasibility and hypothesis generation only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control arm, or restriction of the conclusions to feasibility and exploratory signal.

quotes.text: This study was designed as an open-label clinical trial with no control group
Combining biofeedback and mindfulness training elements, the S-EEG device intervention provides significant benefits to symptom burden in LC patients across multiple domains.

second_reader.what_stands: The first half holds: a single-arm, open-label pre-post design cannot separate a device effect from placebo, regression to the mean, natural recovery or concurrent standard LC treatment, and the authors concede this in the limitations. The paper does not hide the design, but the Discussion and Conclusion still use causal and efficacy wording ('provides significant benefits', 'was effective'), which exceeds what the design supports and sits uneasily with the paper's own description as a feasibility pilot with exploratory outcomes.

issues.title: Sleep reported as improved although score rose 52.7 to 56.2 on a scale where higher means worse sleep
issues.explanation: Methods say a higher sleep score means more sleep problems. Table 3 shows the score rising from baseline at every follow-up (day 90 +3.0, day 180 +4.1, all significant). Results and Discussion nevertheless list sleep among the significantly improved domains. Either the sleep result is a worsening, or the scale direction is misstated; as written, sleep cannot be counted as an improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the scale used was scored with higher = better sleep (for example a scoring manual or the raw data direction).

quotes.text: with the higher number indicating problems with sleep and lower numbers indicating no problems with sleep

second_reader.what_stands: As printed, the sleep score rises from 52.7 to 56.2 (delta +3.0, P = .003) on a scale the Methods define as higher = more sleep problems, yet the Results and Discussion call this an improvement. The paper gives no scoring note that would reverse the direction, so either the labelling or the interpretation is inconsistent; I could not check which from the paper alone. Additionally the Methods name the instrument both 'PROMIS t-score' and 'ASCQ-Me 5-20 raw score', which makes the scale's actual direction in Table 3 uncertain.

issues.title: Registered primaries (stress, anxiety at 3 months) are reported as secondary; paper's primary is device use
issues.explanation: The registry lists change in stress and in anxiety at 3 months as primary outcomes. The paper names frequency of device use as primary and does not say that the registered primaries were changed. Of the registered outcomes, stress improved, but the dedicated anxiety scale (STAI) did not. Without a statement of the change, readers cannot tell whether the framing was pre-specified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing device use as primary, or a protocol stating the efficacy outcomes as exploratory.

quotes.text: frequency of S-EEG usage
Trial registration: NCT5199233. Registered 18 Jan 2022

issues.title: About 8 outcomes at 4 timepoints plus 3 cognitive tests at P < .05 uncorrected; borderline results counted
issues.explanation: The paper used paired t-tests at P < .05 on roughly 32 outcome-time comparisons plus cognitive tests and mixed models, with no correction. Highly significant results (stress, distress, cognition, QoL) are robust to this. Self-efficacy (P = .040, .028) and the Double Trouble result (P = .030) are not, yet they are included in the headline claim of improvement across domains.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated adjustment, or labelling of all efficacy tests as hypothesis-generating with borderline results not counted.

quotes.text: In all cases, P < .05 was considered statistically significant.

issues.title: Anxiety claimed as significantly reduced although STAI-Y1 was non-significant at all four timepoints
issues.explanation: The Discussion states significant decreases in anxiety. This rests on the adapted Emotional Distress-Anxiety t-score; the standard State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-Y1), also a registered-type anxiety outcome, shows no significant change at days 30, 60, 90 or 180. The mixed results are mentioned in Results but not weighed in the headline claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated rationale that the emotional distress form is the pre-specified anxiety outcome, with STAI treated as supplementary.

quotes.text: statistically significant decreases in symptom burden

issues.title: Last enrolment 28 Jul 2023 and study end 31 Oct 2023 (~95 days) cannot allow 180-day follow-up for all 45
issues.explanation: The paper says every participant was followed for 180 days and Table 3 reports Day 180 outcomes for all 45. A participant enrolled on 28 July 2023 would reach day 180 in late January 2024, after the stated study end. The dates or the day-180 sample therefore need explanation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Corrected dates (for example a 2024 study-end date) or an explanation of how late enrollees contributed day-180 data.

quotes.text: Study participation concluded on October 31, 2023.
They were followed for 180 days

issues.title: Dose-response from self-selected usage within one arm read as support for a device effect
issues.explanation: The association between sessions in the prior week and symptom change comes from unrandomised, self-selected usage. People who feel better may use the device more, so the pattern does not show that more use causes more improvement. The wording is associative, but it is offered as support for effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomised assignment of usage intensity, or sensitivity analyses addressing reverse causation.

quotes.text: was used more frequently

issues.title: Text gives lowest weekly device use as 73% (week 13); Table 2 shows 69% in week 12
issues.explanation: The Results describe weekly use as ranging from 100% to 73%. Table 2 shows 31 of 45 (69%) used the device in week 12, which is lower than any value in the text range. This understates the drop in use slightly and affects only a descriptive adherence figure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the range was meant to describe only the start and end weeks.

quotes.text: ranged from 100% (week 1) to 73% (week 13)

issues.title: Questionnaire item counts and ranges do not agree for CD-RS10, self-efficacy and sleep scales
issues.explanation: The resilience scale is described as 5 items scored 0-4 but with a 0-40 range; the self-efficacy range starts at 5 though 4 items scored from 1 give 4; the sleep range ends at 20 though 5 items scored up to 5 give 25. These are description errors, and the analyses use means and changes rather than totals. They leave it unclear how the scales were actually scored, but the main results do not depend on them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The instrument manuals showing the printed ranges are the ones actually used.

quotes.text: from 0 (Not true at all) to 4 (True nearly all the time)
from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident)

issues.title: Week-1 median 542 min over a median 9 sessions (~60 min each) far exceeds the instructed 10 min per session
issues.explanation: Participants were told to use the device up to 10 minutes per session. Table 2 reports a median of 542 total minutes from 9 sessions in week 1, about 60 minutes per session, with a 75th percentile of 1283 minutes (over 21 hours in a week). The minutes metric may not mean active meditation time, which matters because device use is the primary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition showing that the 'total minutes' field counts something other than active session time.

quotes.location: Table 2, study week 1, Number of sessions

issues.title: Trial registration number printed as NCT5199233 (missing a zero) vs NCT05199233 elsewhere
issues.explanation: The registration section gives NCT5199233, which is not a valid NCT format. The data-availability statement gives NCT05199233, which matches the registry record. It is a typographical slip that makes the registration harder to trace.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the two strings differ.

quotes.text: Trial registration: NCT5199233. Registered 18 Jan 2022
within Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05199233)

10.1177/21501319261473073.headline_claim: Handheld transcutaneous cervical VNS is feasible and safe in Long COVID and is a promising, accessible modality for LC symptom management, though the findings are exploratory.
10.1177/21501319261473073.overall: The null primary and secondary results are reported honestly in the Results and Conclusions, and the paper only supports feasibility and exploratory trends from 18 open-label participants. The main reliability problem is the Discussion's claims of 'significant differences in fatigue' and 'three positive trials', which contradict the paper's own data; the 'safe' and 'promising' wording is stronger than n=8 supports.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Post-COVID Functional Status Grade (PCFS), baseline to week 12

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Post-COVID Functional Status Score

issues.title: Discussion claims significant fatigue differences; Table 2 shows PROMIS-F p=0.292, CI -13.2 to 4.3
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the study 'did find significant differences in fatigue', and later says 'three trials demonstrating benefit' and 'three positive trials'. The Results, Table 2 (PROMIS-F estimate -4.5, 95% CI -13.2 to 4.3, p=0.292) and the Conclusions all say nothing reached significance. The Discussion statements misstate a null secondary result as positive and contradict the rest of the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis in which fatigue reached significance (e.g. a different fatigue measure such as PC-FSS or an unadjusted test), which the paper does not report.

quotes.text: The present study examined this hypothesis further and did find significant differences in fatigue in LC participants
However, from ANCOVA adjusting for baseline values no significant differences were detected for any of the scales.
Given there are now three trials demonstrating benefit either with taVNS or the current study’s tcVNS device

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion sentence that the study 'did find significant differences in fatigue' contradicts the paper's own Table 2 (PROMIS-F ANCOVA estimate -4.5, 95% CI -13.2 to 4.3, p=0.292), its Results, and its Conclusions, which all say no outcome reached statistical significance. The claim of 'three trials demonstrating benefit' is likewise stronger than this trial's own data support, although the paper elsewhere properly labels the fatigue findings exploratory and flags the open-label limitation.

issues.title: 'Safe' and 'promising' conclusions rest on 8 treated patients and null efficacy results
issues.explanation: The Conclusions call tcVNS 'both feasible and safe' and 'promising' after a 12-week trial with 8 treated participants, 2 mild adverse events, and no significant effect on any outcome. The Conclusions do caveat that findings are exploratory and not evidence of benefit, so the efficacy overreach is softened. The word 'safe' and 'promising' still go beyond what 8 participants can establish, and the Discussion's 'positive trials' framing adds to this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Larger safety data or a prior safety record in this population sufficient to support the word 'safe'.

quotes.text: This pilot trial demonstrates that the use of a handheld external transcutaneous cervical vagus nerve stimulation (tcVNS) device is both feasible and safe
tcVNS represents a promising and accessible modality for management of LC symptoms

issues.title: Open-label design with self-reported primary and secondary outcomes (no sham control)
issues.explanation: All clinical outcomes are patient-reported and participants knew their allocation, so expectation effects could drive any apparent trend. The authors acknowledge this in the Discussion and Conclusions, and the results are null, so the bias would favour tcVNS if anything and no significant benefit is claimed. It limits how much the 'favourable trends' can be read, not a hidden flaw.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a stated design feature.

quotes.text: This was an open-label randomized controlled pilot
Additionally, the open-label design of this trial represents a significant limitation.

issues.title: Figure 1 caption says PCFS change baseline to Week 1; Methods and Results say week 12
issues.explanation: The caption of Figure 1 describes the change in PCFS 'from baseline to Week 1', while the Methods define the primary endpoint as baseline to week 12 and the Results cite Figure 1 for week-12 grades. This is most likely a typographical slip in the caption (Week 12), and the p=0.535 is described as the week-12 comparison in the text. It is a small labelling error with no effect on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation from the figure axis/labels that the data shown are week-12 data (the caption is then simply a typo).

quotes.text: Change in Post-COVID Functional Status (PCFS) grade from baseline to Week 1.
The change in PCFS grade from baseline to week 12 did not differ significantly between groups (Wilcoxon rank sum test p=0.535).

issues.title: DHEA analysed in 6 of 8 tcVNS and 9 of 10 control at week 12 without explanation of missing samples
issues.explanation: The Results say all participants completed the study including final assessments, yet Table 3 shows DHEA at week 12 with N=6 (tcVNS) and N=9 (control), and N=5 for the tcVNS delta. Cortisol and IL-6 have full N. The missing DHEA samples are not explained, so the DHEA comparison rests on 15 of 18 participants. This is a minor reporting gap that weakens a secondary lab result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that all week-12 visits occurred but some DHEA assays failed, which would explain the lower N.

quotes.text: all (100%) participants completed the 12-week study including the final assessments

10.1177/26924366251403292.headline_claim: A supervised telerehabilitation inspiratory muscle training program is safe, feasible, low-cost, and improves inspiratory muscle strength, endurance, and dyspnea in patients with long COVID after severe infection.
10.1177/26924366251403292.overall: The finding that supervised IMT improves MIP is plausible and likely survives, but the effect size is stated more strongly in the abstract than the adjusted Table 2. Non-random allocation with substantial baseline imbalance, an open-label subjective dyspnea outcome with extremely wide ORs, uncorrected multiplicity and an unsupported safety claim make the broader conclusions tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; the paper names MIP/inspiratory muscle performance and TDI dyspnea as the focus, with the group x time interaction described as the primary effect of interest for continuous outcomes

issues.title: Open-label design with patient-reported TDI dyspnea outcome and OR 12-56 with very wide CIs
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the dyspnea outcome is subjective, so expectation effects may contribute to the dyspnea benefit. The paper acknowledges the lack of sham only in limitations, while the conclusion states dyspnea improvement flatly. The OR CIs (e.g., 2.92-58.41, 9.36-507.83) show how imprecise the estimates are.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded or objective dyspnea endpoint showing the same effect.

quotes.text: the absence of a sham IMT group limits our ability to distinguish intervention effects from potential placebo responses.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is open-label with no sham, the dyspnea outcome (TDI) is patient-reported and so susceptible to expectancy effects despite blinded assessors, and the ORs of about 12-56 have extremely wide CIs (up to 507.83). The authors flag the missing sham group, but the abstract and conclusion still present the dyspnea benefit as established, and the very large ORs should be read as imprecise and likely inflated by bias and the non-random design.

issues.title: Non-random, convenience/sequential allocation with baseline imbalance (intubation 82% vs 25%) supports causal claims only weakly
issues.explanation: Participants were allocated by convenience-based nonrandomized stratification and the IMT group was sicker at baseline (stay 32.7 vs 19.1 days, intubation, lower FVC). Allocation by availability can relate to adherence and outcome, and baseline-worse groups can show regression toward the mean. The unqualified conclusion that IMT improves strength, endurance and dyspnea is therefore not firmly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Concealed, independent allocation or evidence that allocation was unrelated to prognosis.

quotes.text: Participants were allocated to the IMT or control group using convenience-based, nonrandomized stratification
quotes.location: Methods, Study design and participants' recruitment

quotes.text: Due to sequential assignment, the IMT group ultimately included individuals with more severe baseline impairment

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was non-random, convenience/sequential, and produced large baseline imbalance (intubation 82% vs 25%, hospital stay 32.7 vs 19.1 days, lower FVC in IMT), so causal inference rests on a PS adjustment that cannot rule out residual confounding. The authors acknowledge this as the primary limitation, yet the abstract and conclusion still use causal wording ('improves'), and the Methods' claim of balanced key characteristics is at odds with Table 1.

issues.title: Abstract MIP effect (+31.6 vs +6.7 cmH2O) does not match Table 2/Discussion DD of 20.5 cmH2O
issues.explanation: The abstract presents MIP gains of +31.6 (IMT) versus +6.7 (control) cmH2O, which imply a between-group gap of about 25. Table 2 and the Discussion give an adjusted difference-in-differences of 20.5 (9.9-31.0), and Table 2 changes are 29.6 and 9.3. The abstract thus overstates the headline MIP effect relative to the adjusted analysis the paper describes as primary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract values are unadjusted raw changes from a different analysis, with supporting data.

quotes.text: maximal inspiratory pressure (+31.6

issues.title: No multiplicity control across ~15 LMM outcomes; endurance effect (p = 0.050) is marginal
issues.explanation: Sample size was computed for MIP only and was exceeded, so the MIP finding is not underpowered. However, around fifteen continuous outcomes and three TDI domains were tested at alpha 0.05 without correction, and secondary findings such as endurance time (p = 0.050) and FVC % predicted (p = 0.026) are weakly supported. The Discussion nevertheless reports endurance as significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy of outcomes or multiplicity adjustment.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
The IMT group showed significant increases in the endurance time (difference: 62.4 sec; p < 0.05)

issues.title: Conclusion calls the program 'safe' but no adverse-event data are reported
issues.explanation: The abstract and the Discussion describe the program as safe, yet no adverse events, withdrawals or safety monitoring results are given. The paper only notes none dropped out and adherence was high. The safety claim is therefore unsupported by the data presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported adverse-event record showing none or few events.

quotes.text: A supervised, telerehabilitation IMT program is a safe, feasible, and low-cost intervention
These findings support IMT as a structured, safe, and accessible rehabilitation strategy

issues.title: Abstract endurance effect (p = 0.04, CI excludes 0) vs Table 2 DD 62.4 sec, CI -1.6 to 126, p = 0.050
issues.explanation: The abstract reports a significant endurance-time difference (p = 0.04) with different numbers from Table 2, where the adjusted CI crosses zero and p is 0.050. The Results text also gives p < 0.05 for t48.2 = -1.98, which is borderline at best. The conclusion that endurance improved rests on a result that is marginal in the primary adjusted analysis and presented more strongly in the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Explanation that abstract values come from a different, prespecified analysis.

issues.title: No trial registration is reported for a prospective interventional study
issues.explanation: The paper lists an ethics protocol number but no trial registry identifier, so the primary outcome and analysis cannot be checked against a prespecified plan. The paper does not state a primary outcome other than saying the DD served as the primary effect of interest. Whether registration was required is arguable for a quasi-experimental design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment.

quotes.text: The study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of the hospital (protocol number: 34115720.5.0000.0068)
quotes.location: Methods, Study design and participants' recruitment

issues.title: Abstract says no lung-function difference, but FVC % predicted DD 5.47 (p = 0.026) is reported
issues.explanation: The abstract states no between-group differences in lung function, while Results and Table 2 report a significant FVC % predicted difference (p = 0.026). The authors discuss it later, so the omission is a summary inaccuracy rather than hidden data. It likely reflects a single uncorrected result among many and is unimportant to the headline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Abstract wording restricted to absolute spirometric values.

quotes.text: No between-group differences were observed in lung function or functional capacity.
A significant improvement was also observed in the FVC % of predicted (t47.4 = -2.29, p = 0.026)

issues.title: Text male percentages (65%, 51%) differ from Table 1 counts (62.5%, 55.2%)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives 65% males in controls and 51% in the IMT group, but Table 1 counts give 62.5% and 55.2%. The difference is small and does not affect the analysis, though the text direction (more males in control) is still right.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 with counts matching 65% and 51%.

quotes.text: There were more male participants in the control group (65%) compared with the IMT group (51%).

script.explanation: 15/24 = 62.50%, but the paper prints 65, outside the rounding interval [64.50, 66.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 23.1 rather than 24.

issues.title: MIP correlation r = 0.58 reported with p = 0.03, though r = 0.52 gives p < 0.001
issues.explanation: With about 53 participants an r of 0.58 corresponds to p far below 0.001, as the smaller correlations show. The printed p = 0.03 is therefore inconsistent, probably a typo. The conclusion is unaffected because the association remains significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Correlation computed on a much smaller subset.

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.03, but recomputed from the printed r = 0.58 p is at most 6.693e-06, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show. This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Figure 3 panel descriptions in the text conflict with the caption
issues.explanation: The text assigns Borg dyspnea to Panel A, breaths to B, load to C and duration to D, but the caption gives A load, B duration, C breaths, D Borg. A reader cannot tell which description is right. No result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure itself showing which panel is which and a corrected text.

quotes.text: Panel A illustrates
Inspiratory load progression (% of baseline MIP)

issues.title: Statistical analysis says baseline vs. 4 months; study and Table 2 use 12 weeks
issues.explanation: The analysis section names a 4-month time point while the intervention and tables are at 12 weeks. This is almost certainly a typographical inconsistency but leaves the time of analysis formally ambiguous.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocol showing a 4-month assessment.

quotes.text: baseline vs. 4 months
The intervention lasted 12 weeks
quotes.location: Methods, Study design and participants' recruitment

10.1177/27536130231174236.headline_claim: Pre-post changes in PSS-10, GAD-2, and MYMOP measures suggest these PROMs are feasible outcome measures for IMGV in Long COVID, with the authors stating the design cannot establish efficacy.
10.1177/27536130231174236.overall: The paper's modest claim that the PROMs are feasible to collect is reasonably supported, but any evidence of benefit is weak: it comes from 14 of 27 enrolled participants with no control group and no multiplicity handling. The Conclusion's 'powerful enough' wording is not supported, and the Results contain internal inconsistencies (df of 3 instead of 13, 'not significant' beside p = .007 and p = .004). The CIs that appear to include 0 are text-extraction artefacts of dropped minus signs, not real inconsistencies.

primary_outcome.name: Not prespecified as a single primary outcome; PSS-10 total, GAD-2, SSS items, and MYMOP outcomes were all analysed pre-post

issues.title: Conclusion calls findings 'powerful enough' to support implementation while saying power cannot be assessed
issues.explanation: The Conclusion first says power cannot be commented on given the small sample, then says the findings are 'powerful enough' to support a hybrid study that implements the intervention. An uncontrolled, 14-person, complete-case pilot with 48% loss cannot show benefit, so this wording goes beyond what the data support. The feasibility conclusion about the measures is reasonable; the implementation endorsement is not supported by the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to the feasibility of the measures, with no endorsement of implementation based on outcome changes.

quotes.text: these findings are powerful enough to support a hybrid study design that tests adaptation while simultaneously implementing Integrative Medical Group Visits for Long COVID patients.
Given the small number of participants, it is not possible to comment on the power of these measures to detect changes in Long COVID symptomatology.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion does use 'powerful enough' to justify simultaneous implementation right after saying power cannot be commented on. The wording is loose, because 'powerful' can be read non-statistically, and the paper elsewhere clearly states the study is uncontrolled, not powered for efficacy, and that a larger controlled study is needed. The tension is therefore real in the Conclusion's phrasing and in the strength of the inference drawn from 14 uncontrolled completers (a 48% non-completion rate), but it is not a contradiction in the paper's stated limitations.

issues.title: Results say pre-post changes 'not significant' yet report p = .007 and p = .004 at alpha .05
issues.explanation: The Results state that changes in pre and post means were not significant. The same paragraph reports PSS-10 and primary-symptom changes with p = .007 and p = .004, below the stated alpha of .05. Readers cannot tell which statement the authors intend. The sentence understates the study's own nominally significant findings, though the paper elsewhere cautions against reading them as efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A declared multiplicity-adjusted alpha below .004, or a statement that the sentence refers to clinical significance only.

quotes.text: Changes in pre and post means were not significant in this pilot study.
There was also a difference in the primary complaint score between the pre (M = 4.7, SD = .9) and post (M = 3.5, SD = 1.3); t (3) = -3.5, P = .004 scores.

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post paired tests described as improvement and 'promising' despite no control group
issues.explanation: All inference is from paired pre-post tests in one uncontrolled group, so regression to the mean, natural recovery and non-specific effects cannot be separated from any benefit of the group visits. The authors acknowledge this and call the work a feasibility study. Even so, they describe participants as having 'improved' and the results as 'promising', and use this to support implementation. The problem is narrower than the screen claims, because the primary conclusion is about measure feasibility.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Language confined strictly to feasibility, with no use of 'improved' or 'promising' for outcome changes.

quotes.text: This limits the ability to assert that improvements in measures were due to the intervention.
Despite these limitations, the results of this study are promising and contribute to this important area of research.

issues.title: 13 of 27 enrolled (48.1%) lack post data; complete-case improvements may not represent enrolled sample
issues.explanation: Only 14 of 27 enrolled participants contributed paired data, and the analysis ignores everyone else. The paper reports that completers differed in age and days since diagnosis. Participants who stayed and could be reached may also be those who benefited, so the pre-post gains may be biased upward. The dropout rate is disclosed, but the Discussion still states 'improvement' without qualifying it for this selection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all enrolled participants (for example multiple imputation) giving similar estimates.

quotes.text: There were 13 out of 27, or 48.1%, of study participants who did not complete the study
People who completed the study were on average 5 years older and had a mean 285.4 (SD 116.1) days since their COVID-19 diagnosis

issues.title: Paired t-tests printed as t(3) although 14 completers imply 13 degrees of freedom
issues.explanation: The Methods and Table 3 state a paired analysis of 14 participants, which gives 13 degrees of freedom. The Results print t(3) for both the PSS-10 and the MYMOP primary symptom. With 3 df, t = 3.2 would give p of about .05, not .007, so the df label is wrong and the p-values only fit 13 df. This is a reporting slip; the reported p-values appear to be correct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the tests were run on 4 pairs, or a corrected df of 13 in the source article.

quotes.text: There was a difference in PSS-10 between the pre (M = 21.9, SD = 6.6) and post (M = 18.5, SD = 5.7); t (3) = -3.2, P = .007 scores.
We performed a complete case analysis using the fourteen participants who completed the intervention and both assessments.

script.explanation: The printed t = 3.2 supports p no smaller than 0.0457335, but the paper reports p = 0.007 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

issues.title: GAD-2 score range stated as 0 to 3 for a summed score, but mean pre score is 3.71
issues.explanation: The Methods state that GAD-2 scores range from zero to 3 while also saying the two items are summed. A summed two-item score runs from 0 to 6, and Table 3 reports a pre mean of 3.71, which is above the stated maximum. The range is misprinted, and the cut-off of 3 only makes sense on a 0-6 scale.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that each item is scored 0-3 and the total range is 0-6.

quotes.text: Scores range from zero to 3. The 2 items are summed.

10.1177/27536130251385551.headline_claim: Triphala supplementation at 1000 mg/day for 8 weeks may help reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in individuals with post-COVID-19 condition.
10.1177/27536130251385551.overall: The headline claim that Triphala reduces oxidative stress and inflammation rests mainly on within-arm changes, since all four primary biomarkers lacked significant between-group differences at post-intervention. The paper hedges as preliminary, but its Discussion language on efficacy and safety goes beyond what this small, retrospectively registered trial can show.

primary_outcome.name: Oxidative stress and inflammatory biomarkers (MDA, protein carbonyl, IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha)

issues.title: Biomarker 'reductions' rest on within-arm tests; all four post-intervention between-group tests p>.05
issues.explanation: The Discussion says MDA, protein carbonyl, IFNg and TNFa were significantly reduced, based on before/after tests in the Triphala arm only. The between-group comparisons for all four primary biomarkers were not significant (p=.289, .184, .187, .051). Significance within one arm and not in the other is not evidence of a treatment difference. Only the mean-change comparisons for carbonyl (p=.048) and TNFa (p=.001) favour Triphala, and these are unadjusted for multiplicity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary analysis showing significant treatment-by-time interaction for these biomarkers.

quotes.text: We found that the concentrations of MDA, protein carbonyl, IFNγ , and TNFα were significantly reduced
Between-group comparisons showed no statistically significant differences in post-intervention MDA
quotes.location: Results, Oxidative Stress and Antioxidant Status

second_reader.what_stands: The four 'significantly reduced' statements in the Discussion rest on within-Triphala-arm pre/post tests, and all four post-intervention between-group tests are above .05 (TNFα borderline at .051). However, the paper also reports significantly greater mean change in Triphala than placebo for protein carbonyl (P = .048) and TNFα (P = .001), so it is not true that every between-group comparison was non-significant; the point holds for post-intervention values only.

issues.title: Discussion asserts 'beneficial efficacy' though most primary between-group outcomes were non-significant
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the findings support the beneficial efficacy of Triphala and may offer an alternative approach for managing COVID-19, while the Conclusion admits most primary outcomes did not differ between groups. The Conclusion is hedged ('may help'), but the Discussion's efficacy language and the extension to inflammation-related conditions are not supported by a trial with null between-group primary results. The hedging is partial, so the problem is narrower than a pure null-presented-as-positive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant between-group differences on the pre-specified primary outcomes.

quotes.text: Our findings support the beneficial efficacy of Triphala supplementation in attenuating oxidative stress, inflammation, and clinical symptoms.
as most primary outcomes did not show statistically significant differences between the Triphala and placebo groups

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion sentence asserting 'beneficial efficacy' is stronger than the between-group evidence, since all four post-intervention primary comparisons were non-significant and several improvements also occurred in placebo. The paper does, however, qualify this in the Study Limitations and Conclusion (preliminary, 'may help', 'most primary outcomes' non-significant), and a few between-group differences (TNFα and protein carbonyl change, headache, respiratory symptoms) were significant, so the overstatement is in that one sentence rather than across the whole paper.

issues.title: 12 completers (7 placebo, 5 Triphala) had <80% adherence despite an 80% withdrawal criterion
issues.explanation: The Methods say participants consuming less than 80% of the supplement were to be withdrawn. The Discussion reports only 30/37 (placebo) and 32/37 (Triphala) with high adherence, so 7 and 5 completers were below the cutoff yet analysed. This is an inconsistency between the protocol and what was done, and the analysis is effectively not per-protocol as described. It dilutes exposure in both arms and likely biases toward the null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the withdrawal criterion was applied only to non-consumption at a different level, or that the low-adherence group refers to a different adherence measure.

quotes.text: failure to consume at least 80% of the prescribed supplement
30 (81.08%) in the placebo group and 32 (86.49%) in the Triphala group had high adherence to the intervention protocol

issues.title: Trial registered 21 Dec 2023, after recruitment (May-Aug 2023) and after the last visit (22 Oct 2023)
issues.explanation: The registry record was first submitted two months after the final participant visit, so the registration was retrospective. The four registered primary outcomes match the paper's biomarkers, but without earlier record versions it cannot be shown they were fixed before data collection. The paper does not disclose the retrospective registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version dated before 9 May 2023 with the same primary outcomes.

quotes.text: Participants were recruited between 9 May 2023 and 15 August 2023
registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06208761)

issues.title: Headache (p=.016) and respiratory (p=.025) benefits claimed from uncorrected secondary comparisons
issues.explanation: Bonferroni is stated only for post hoc comparisons within the ANOVA, not across the many biomarker, symptom and body-composition outcomes. Headache p=.016 and respiratory p=.025 would exceed a Bonferroni threshold across even the five symptom scales (0.05/5 = .01). The Conclusion nonetheless lists these as improvements.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or correction across outcomes.

quotes.text: Notably, the Triphala group had significantly greater reductions in headache severity compared to placebo
Improvements were also observed in clinical symptoms, including fatigue, headache, and respiratory complaints.

issues.title: 'Determined as safe' rests on creatinine and ALT in 74 completers over 8 weeks
issues.explanation: The safety claim is based on two laboratory markers, a small sample and a short duration, among completers only. The same paragraph recommends longer-term toxicity evaluation, which softens but does not remove the firm wording. Safety was not a powered outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger or longer trial with systematic adverse event ascertainment in all randomized participants.

quotes.text: the supplementation regimen used in this study was determined as safe
future studies with longterm Triphala protocols should evaluate toxicity further

10.1177/27536351241227261.headline_claim: A home-based diaphragmatic-breathing HRV biofeedback intervention is feasible for people with Long Covid and seems to have a potential effect on improving LC symptoms, particularly dysautonomia-related ones.
10.1177/27536351241227261.overall: The feasibility conclusion (home HRV-B is usable by people with Long Covid) is reasonably supported by 92% compliance and positive participant feedback. The suggestion of symptom benefit rests on an uncontrolled, open-label pre/post comparison of 13 completers with self-reported outcomes and uncorrected tests, so it can only be read as hypothesis-generating. The authors disclose the limitations and call for a controlled trial, which tempers but does not remove the efficacy wording.

primary_outcome.name: C19-YRSm (symptom severity subscale; reported as within-participant pre/post change)

issues.title: Single-arm pre/post design with no control; efficacy wording goes beyond what it can show
issues.explanation: All 13 analysed participants received the intervention and were compared with their own baseline over 6 weeks, so change cannot be separated from natural recovery, regression to the mean, or expectation. The paper states feasibility as its aim and calls for a controlled trial, which is appropriate. However, the closing summary and the Results still describe symptom improvement and a 'large' effect as if attributable to HRV-B, so the efficacy language is stronger than the design allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control comparison, or conclusions limited strictly to feasibility.

quotes.text: This was a phase 2 uncontrolled open-label feasibility study of a home technology-based HRV-B in 15 individuals with LC.
the intervention seems to have a potential effect on
The effect size for C19-YRSm was large.

second_reader.what_stands: The design is single-arm pre/post with no control, which the authors state in the Methods and Limitations, and the conclusion is hedged ('seems to have a potential effect'; the Discussion calls for a controlled trial). However, 'The effect size for C19-YRSm was large' is stated without qualification and is true only of symptom severity (d=1.09); the other C19-YRSm subscales are moderate (d 0.54-0.66). The Results also say 'statistically significant improvements' with no caveat that a pre/post comparison without a control cannot separate the intervention from placebo, regression to the mean or

issues.title: 15 outcomes tested at 0.05 uncorrected; RMSSD p=0.048 is the sole significant Fitbit result of 8
issues.explanation: Seven PROM outcomes and eight Fitbit outcomes were each tested with Wilcoxon tests at 0.05 with no correction or stated primary hypothesis for the HRV measures. The RMSSD result (p = 0.048, d = 0.27) is the only significant one of eight Fitbit measures and would not survive correction. The paper describes the RMSSD improvement as 'significant' and uses it to support a dysautonomia effect, though it does acknowledge the effect is weaker.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy naming RMSSD as the key HRV outcome, or correction-adjusted p-values.

quotes.text: There  was  a  significant  difference  in  RMSSD,  a  HRV measure reflecting parasympathetic activity, 14 between preHRV-B and post HRV-B phases (Table 5).
Fitbit RMSSD summaries

issues.title: Effect sizes described as 'large' from n=13 pre/post with no uncertainty intervals
issues.explanation: The authors justify omitting a sample size calculation because the study is a feasibility study not aimed at estimating effect size. Yet the Results call the C19-YRSm effect 'large' and the Discussion treats the effect sizes as evidence of benefit. With 13 participants, Cohen's d (1.09 for severity) has a very wide uncertainty interval, and no confidence intervals are given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confidence intervals around the effect sizes showing a lower bound that still indicates a clinically important change.

quotes.text: A formal sample size calculation was not required for this feasibility study as it did not mimic a definitive randomised trial
The effect size for C19-YRSm was large.

issues.title: Table 3 BP-change 40% unattainable with n=13 (5/13=38.5%, 6/13=46.2%)
issues.explanation: Table 3 is described as the NASA Lean Test results for the 13 participants, but no whole-number count out of 13 gives 40%. The denominator behind the BP figure is therefore different from 13 or the value is misprinted. This is a secondary baseline descriptor and does not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that BP data were valid for only 10 (or 5, 15) participants, or a corrected percentage.

quotes.text: Table 3 shows the results of the NLT for the 13 participants.
Percentage of participants with significant BP changes

issues.title: 2 of 15 enrolled (13.3%) excluded; completers-only analysis with a post hoc exclusion
issues.explanation: The analysis covers 13 of 15 enrolled participants. Participant 6 did not complete the study and participant 12 was dropped because of an infection at the final assessment, a decision the paper links to the exclusion criteria. The exclusions are disclosed, but no analysis including all 15 is given, so the sensitivity of the results to these two is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis including participants 6 and 12 that gives similar results.

quotes.text: Participant 12 was unwell during the final assessment with an acute respiratory infection.
therefore this participant was removed from data analysis

issues.title: Table 2: 2 of 13 printed as 15.9% for tricyclics and SSRIs; 2/13 = 15.4%
