issues.explanation: Two medication rows list 2 (15.9) in a table of 13 participants. Two of 13 is 15.4%, so 15.9 is a misprint, repeated in both rows. Other percentages in the table are right, and nothing in the results depends on this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the denominator for medication history was not 13.

quotes.text: Tricyclic antidepressants n (%)

script.explanation: 2/13 = 15.38%, but the paper prints 15.9, outside the rounding interval [15.85, 16.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 12.6 rather than 13.

10.1177/27536351241308176.headline_claim: A 12-week asynchronous tele-mindfulness intervention seems feasible and effective in reducing anxiety, depression and PTSD symptoms and increasing resilience and self-efficacy in previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
10.1177/27536351241308176.overall: The finding that TG improved more than n-TG on anxiety, depression and PTSD scores is large in the reported data, but it rests on a self-selected, unadjusted control group that differs at baseline in length of stay and fitness. The paper also contradicts itself on this and uses causal wording in its Clinical Message. The registration was retrospective and does not list the stated primary outcomes, and the multiplicity-adjusted q-values are not valid BH values. Treat the conclusions as preliminary feasibility evidence, not demonstrated effectiveness.

primary_outcome.name: Anxiety (BAI) and depression (PHQ-9), Time x Group effect in linear mixed model

primary_outcomes.time_frame: At the beginning of early rehabilitation
At the beginning of early rehabilitation
At the beginning of early rehabilitation
At the beginning of early rehabilitation

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in 1 minute sit-to-stand test between two time points
Change in Short form health survey between three time points
primary_outcomes.time_frame: At the beginning of early rehabilitation, Month 3, Month 6
At the beginning of early rehabilitation

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in 6-minute walking test between two time points

issues.title: Clinical Message asserts effectiveness from a non-randomised, self-selected comparison
issues.explanation: The design cannot separate the programme's effect from selection into the programme or from extra clinician contact. The authors acknowledge this, yet the Clinical Message states the intervention is effective in reducing anxiety, depression and PTSD symptoms and in increasing resilience and self-efficacy. The wording goes beyond what an unblinded, self-selected, unadjusted comparison with no prespecified analysis plan can support. 'Associated with' or 'preliminary evidence' would match the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised or adequately adjusted comparison with consistent effects.

quotes.text: seems feasible and effective in reducing anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms
The T-MBI applied revealed positive effects in reducing anxiety, depression, PTSD symptoms
the absence of a randomized controlled group, strongly influences the quality of the project and the conclusions achieved

second_reader.what_stands: The Clinical Message does state effectiveness ('seems feasible and effective') on the basis of a non-randomised, self-selected comparison, and the Discussion also says 'positive effects'. This is moderated by hedging ('seems') and by a limitations paragraph that explicitly says the lack of randomisation strongly affects the conclusions and that results require caution; the statistical associations themselves are strong and FDR-adjusted, but the causal wording is stronger than the design supports.

issues.title: Self-selected, unadjusted control group differs at baseline (LOS 50.7 v 28.4 d; 6MWT 266.7 v 342.5 m)
issues.explanation: Allocation depended on patients' acceptance and technology access, not randomisation. The groups differed significantly at baseline in length of stay and 6MWT (both p<.001). The Discussion nonetheless says the groups did not differ on baseline clinical variables, then admits the differences in the same paragraph. The Time x Group effects on anxiety and depression are therefore confounded by selection and unmeasured motivation, and no adjustment was made. The apparent TG benefit is also partly open to regression to the mean, since TG had higher baseline BAI and PHQ-9.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses adjusted for LOS, 6MWT and baseline scores that give the same Time x Group effects, or a propensity-matched analysis.

quotes.text: Patients who refused or did not have the chance to accept the intervention
the patients in the control group did not differ significantly from the experimental group in terms of baseline clinical and demographic variables
Conversely, patients who were more physically impaired and with a history of longer hospital LOS more frequently refused TG

second_reader.what_stands: Controls were self-selected and matched only on age and sex; Table 2 shows the numbers in the question (LOS 50.7 vs 28.4 d; 6MWT 266.7 vs 342.5 m, both P<.001), and the analysis models show no adjustment for them. The limitations sentence saying groups did not differ significantly at baseline is inconsistent with this, although the authors do go on to acknowledge the LOS and impairment differences in the next sentences.

issues.title: Described as 'previously registered' but registered 2020-10-29, after enrolment began (June 2020)
issues.explanation: The paper presents the trial as previously registered. The registry shows first submission on 2020-10-29, with a stated study start of 2020-03-30, and the paper's own enrolment period begins in June 2020. The registration was therefore retrospective and did not constrain outcomes or analyses. The registry also anticipated 200 participants versus 88 analysed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing a registration date before the first enrolment.

quotes.text: previously registered on ClinicalTrials
This quasi-experimental study was conducted at the Ferrara University Hospital between June 2020 and December 2021

issues.title: Table 5 FDR q-values are impossible for Benjamini-Hochberg (e.g. p = .929 gives q = 0.048)
issues.explanation: BH-adjusted q-values are at least as large as the raw p and rise with p. Table 5 prints q = 0.048 for p = .929 and q = 0.041 for p = .496, and q ranges only between about 0.001 and 0.048 across all rows regardless of p. They look like ranks or scaled values, not adjusted p-values. The Time x Group significance is read from raw p, so the multiplicity claim is not demonstrated even though the correction is said to be applied. The raw p-values for the key BAI and PHQ-9 interactions are small enough that they would probably survive a proper correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of how q was computed that reproduces the printed values from the raw p-values.

quotes.location: Table 5, MCS-12 Time x Group row

issues.title: Paper's primary outcomes (BAI, PHQ-9) do not appear among the eight registered primary outcomes
issues.explanation: The paper names anxiety (BAI) and depression (PHQ-9) as primary outcomes. The registry record NCT04615390 lists eight primary outcomes, all physical or functional (Borg, heart rate, oxygen saturation, sit-to-stand, walking tests, SF-12), and no psychological measure. So the stated primary outcomes cannot be checked against a prespecified plan. The record shown is the current version only, so this is a mismatch with the registration and not proof of a change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing BAI and PHQ-9 listed as outcomes before enrolment, or a statement that this paper is a psychological sub-analysis with prespecified outcomes.

quotes.text: We focused on anxiety and depression as primary outcomes

issues.title: Baseline sex t-tests use df 72 and 67 while 88 participants are analysed elsewhere (df 86)
issues.explanation: Table 3 compares 56 men and 32 women, which gives df = 86 for a two-sample t-test. The PCS-12 and MCS-12 rows use df = 72 and IES-total uses df = 67, with no mention of missing data. The likeliest cause is undisclosed missing questionnaire data. The odd part is that IES-total has fewer cases than its subscales.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the number of complete cases per questionnaire, or a flow diagram showing missing baseline SF-12 and IES-total data.

issues.title: Table 2 percentages wrong in three rows: High school 53.2/46.8, Divorced 11.4/9.1, ICU total 46.5
issues.explanation: Several percentages in Table 2 do not match their own counts and column denominators. High school graduates are 22/44 (50.0%) in TG and 25/44 (56.8%) in n-TG, but 53.2% and 46.8% are printed, which are the swapped row shares of 47. Divorced/Widowed are 4/44 (9.1%) and 5/44 (11.4%), but the printed values are swapped. ICU total is 47/88 = 53.4%, printed as 46.5. The counts are correct and no conclusion changes, but the mislabelled percentages could mislead on baseline balance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or source table showing these percentages computed on a different, stated denominator.

quotes.location: Table 2, High school row, TG column
Table 2, ICU row, Total sample column

script.explanation: 22/44 = 50.00%, but the paper prints 53.2, outside the rounding interval [53.15, 53.30]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 41.4 rather than 44.

10.1182/blood-2024-210709.headline_claim: RegeneCyte (cord blood HPC) is safe, well-tolerated, and significantly improves fatigue symptoms in post-COVID syndrome.
10.1182/blood-2024-210709.overall: The abstract reports interim, descriptive data from 15 of 30 planned subjects with no between-group test, yet concludes that the product is safe and significantly improves fatigue. Those claims are not supported by what is shown; at most the data are hypothesis-generating. The sponsor affiliation of most authors alongside a no-conflict statement adds reason for caution.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder Fatigue Scale (CFQ-11) fatigue severity at week 12

issues.title: 'Demonstrate safe and significantly improves' claimed from preliminary data on 15 of 30 subjects, no test shown
issues.explanation: The abstract says the interim data from the first 15 subjects 'demonstrate' that the product is safe, well tolerated and 'significantly' improves fatigue. No p-value, effect size or interval is reported, and safety evidence is limited to a statement of no lab trends; adverse events and tolerability data are not shown. The conclusion ('profound fatigue reduction', 'viable treatment option') goes well beyond a 15-subject interim look in a phase IIa study.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group test with adequate precision plus adverse-event data for the full safety population supporting the safety and tolerability wording.

quotes.text: These findings demonstrate that RegeneCyte® is safe, well-tolerated, and significantly improves fatigue symptoms in post-COVID syndrome patients.
Preliminary data from the first 15 subjects show no trends in the changes of clinical safety laboratory parameters

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract concludes that the treatment is 'safe, well-tolerated, and significantly improves fatigue' from preliminary data on about half of the planned 30 subjects (likely roughly 10 vs 5), with no statistical test, p-value, confidence interval, baseline values or adverse event data reported. The safety claim rests on 'no trends' in lab values only, and the word 'significantly' is unsupported by any shown analysis; the denominators I give for the arms are inferred, not printed.

issues.title: Authors employed by product developer StemCyte, yet 'No relevant conflicts of interest to declare'
issues.explanation: The product is developed by StemCyte Inc., and most authors list StemCyte affiliations. The disclosure statement nevertheless says there are no relevant conflicts, and no funder or sponsor role is described. This does not by itself show bias, but it should be weighed alongside the promotional wording of the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that the authors' actual disclosure forms declare the StemCyte employment and sponsorship, with the abstract text simply truncated.

quotes.text: RegeneCyte® (HPC, cord blood, hUCB), developed by StemCyte Inc.
Disclosures No relevant conflicts of interest to declare.

10.1183/13993003.02152-2024.headline_claim: Both face-to-face and remote exercise-based rehabilitation added to usual care significantly improve exercise capacity compared with usual care alone in people hospitalised with COVID-19 who have post-COVID syndrome.
10.1183/13993003.02152-2024.overall: The face-to-face result (52 m, CI 19-85, p=0.002) is reasonably supported for exercise capacity. The remote result is borderline (34 m, CI 1-66, p=0.047), below both the assumed 50 m and the stated MCID, and the paper overstates it. The immune and secondary-outcome claims are exploratory and stated more strongly than the data allow, and several text and table numbers need correction.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Incremental Shuttle Walking Test distance (metres), pre to post 8-week intervention

issues.title: Exploratory immune substudy (n 8-18 per group, uncorrected) presented as 'beneficial immunomodulatory effects'
issues.explanation: The immune data come from a small subset of face-to-face and usual-care participants, with several subsets tested and no multiplicity adjustment. Only some subsets have significant interactions, one at p=0.04, and the CD4+ total is not significant. The shareable abstract and closing statements nonetheless present beneficial effects on the immune system as a finding. The data support only a hypothesis for further study.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified immune analysis plan with multiplicity control and complete sample, showing the interaction effects persist.

quotes.text: Rehabilitation improved short-term exercise capacity in long COVID replicated by real-world evidence and had beneficial immunomodulatory effects
Improving exercise capacity may have important secondary beneficial effects on the immune system in post-COVID syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: The immune data come from a small exploratory subset (8-18 per group), with no stated multiplicity correction, no clinical or functional immune endpoints, and some effects driven by decline in the control group, so 'beneficial immunomodulatory effects' in the shareable abstract is stronger than the evidence supports. The body of the paper does acknowledge the small substudy size and hedges the Discussion ('may have'), so the overstatement is mainly in the abstract wording and in the Discussion claim that immune changes are linked to exercise capacity, which was not tested.

issues.title: Remote benefit (34 m, CI 1-66, p=0.047) stated as significant under 'fully powered' with no alpha split for two comparisons
issues.explanation: Two active arms are each tested against one usual-care arm at two-sided 0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment stated. The face-to-face result (p=0.002) would survive a split, but the remote result (p=0.047) would not at 0.025. The Discussion presents both modes as significantly improving exercise capacity and the trial as fully powered, and recommends both, which overstates how firmly the remote result is established. The conclusion for remote rehabilitation is better described as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol statement that the two comparisons are separate prespecified hypotheses with no family-wise control, plus conclusions worded as tentative for remote.

quotes.text: In this fully powered RCT, we demonstrated that both face-to-face and remote exercise-based rehabilitation significantly improve exercise capacity compared to usual care alone
of 34 (1 -66) m in favour of the intervention (p=0.047)
The sample size was based on a mean difference between groups of 50 m in the primary outcome (ISWT)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states alpha of 0.05 for each of two comparisons against usual care and describes no multiplicity adjustment; the remote result (p=0.047) would not meet a Bonferroni threshold of 0.025, and the paper does not discuss this. 'Fully powered' is supportable for the 50 m design effect (44 per group; 149 analysed), but not for the smaller observed remote effect of 34 m with a lower CI bound of 1 m, so describing remote benefit as significant and the trial as fully powered is stronger than the borderline evidence warrants. Separate comparisons each at 0.05 is a legitimate design choice, and

issues.title: Remote ISWT difference of 34 m (CI 1-66) described as exceeding the 35 m MCID
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the between-group improvements for both programmes exceed the 35 m MCID. The primary adjusted remote difference is 34 m, below that threshold, and its confidence interval runs from 1 m to 66 m, so the data cannot show the effect exceeds the MCID. Only the face-to-face result (52 m, CI 19-85) is clearly above it, and even there the lower limit is below 35.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the MCID comparison refers only to face-to-face, or a remote adjusted difference of at least 35 m.

quotes.text: with a mean (95% CI) difference of 34 (1 -66) m in favour of the intervention
These between-group improvements exceed the established minimal clinically important difference (MCID) (35 m)

issues.title: Secondary physical outcomes called 'clinical improvements' where 95% CIs include zero; no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: Several secondary comparisons with intervals that include no difference are described as clinical improvements, and the Discussion says the other physical outcomes improved 'above the established MCID'. No correction for the many secondary tests is mentioned. These outcomes are supportive rather than primary, so the effect is on secondary claims only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified statement that secondary outcomes are judged by point estimate versus MCID and are hypothesis-generating only.

quotes.text: There were clinical improvements in the SPPB compared to usual care for both the face-to-face and remote interventions
we found potential improvements in several other physical outcomes above the established MCID when compared to usual care

issues.title: Results text for 4-m gait speed disagrees with Table 2 (remote 1.5 vs 0.04; face-to-face CI -0.01 vs 0.02)
issues.explanation: The Results sentence gives the remote 4MGS difference as 1.5 m/s with CI -0.05 to 0.14, but the estimate lies far outside its own interval and Table 2 prints 0.04. For face-to-face, the text CI of -0.01 to 0.21 crosses zero while Table 2 gives 0.02 to 0.21, which does not. The text also calls both 'clinical improvements', so the printed text misstates one value and the significance of another.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version or supplementary table showing 1.5 m/s and a CI of -0.01 to 0.21 are the true analysis outputs.

quotes.location: Table 2, 4MGS row, Remote versus usual care

issues.title: Allocation ratio depends on access stratum; stratum not in the model and baseline groups differ in age
issues.explanation: Participants who could use both programmes were randomised 1:1:1, while others were randomised 2:1 to the single programme they could use. So each active arm and the usual-care arm contain different mixes of access strata, which relate to age and digital literacy. The model adjusts for several covariates but the paper does not say it adjusts for or stratifies by access stratum. The randomised comparison is therefore less clean than a simple three-arm design, though the authors disclose it and the direction of any bias is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including access stratum as a covariate or stratifying variable giving similar effect estimates.

quotes.text: Those unable to access one of the interventions (either face-to-face or remote) were randomised in a 2:1 ratio in favour of the remaining intervention.
this led to some differences between groups with those unable to attend remote programmes being older

issues.title: 'Not harmful' inferred from within-group symptom improvement; adverse events not reported by arm
issues.explanation: The authors infer safety from improved fatigue and symptoms across all three groups, plus two serious adverse events judged unrelated. Neither arm allocation of those events nor PESE exacerbation rates are shown. The trial is small, so it could not detect rare harms. The wording is cautious, so this weakens a supporting claim only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary table of adverse events and PESE by arm showing no excess in intervention arms.

quotes.text: Measures of fatigue and symptoms improved across all three groups
suggesting that the rehabilitation exercise was not harmful in appropriately selected patients
There were two reported serious adverse events during the study period

issues.title: Table 2 cells with estimates outside their own CIs: remote 4MGS change 0.33 (0.04-0.11); PHQ-9 post 4.50 (4.87-7.13)
issues.explanation: Two Table 2 cells print point estimates that lie outside their own 95% intervals, so at least one number in each cell is wrong. The remote 4MGS change should be near 0.07 and the PHQ-9 post-trial mean near 6. Other cells show similar slips (usual-care 4MGS change printed as 0.01 (0.07 - 0.05)). These are transcription errors in secondary outcomes that do not alter the stated conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing these exact estimate and interval pairs are correct (e.g. asymmetric intervals from a non-Wald method).

issues.title: Per-protocol counts: 60/62 printed as 98% (=96.8%) and arms sum to 138 not 140
issues.explanation: The per-protocol sentence gives 60 of 62 usual-care participants as 98%, but this is 96.8%. The three arm counts (40, 38, 60) add to 138, whereas the same sentence states 140 in the per-protocol analysis. Denominators for the remote and usual-care groups also do not match the baseline table. The per-protocol numbers are supplementary to the primary ITT result, so the effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 or supplementary table S3 giving usual-care per-protocol n of 61 or 62 and a total of 140.

quotes.text: 60 out of 62 (98%) usual-care participants completed 75% of the intervention and the follow-up measures
140 out of 181 participants were included in the per-protocol analysis

script.explanation: 60/62 = 96.77%, but the paper prints 98, outside the rounding interval [97.50, 99.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 61.2 rather than 62.

issues.title: Discussion gives 94 participants unable to take either intervention; Results counts 53 + 42 = 95
issues.explanation: The Results show 86 participants could access both programmes, 53 could not attend face-to-face and 42 could not access remote, which totals 181 and implies 95 with a restriction. The Discussion twice says 94. It is a one-person discrepancy that does not affect any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing one participant counted in both exclusion groups or excluded for another reason.

quotes.text: the number of participants unable to uptake either intervention (94 out of 181, 52%)
53 (29%) were unable to attend a face-to-face programme
42 (23%) were unable to access a remote intervention

10.1183/13993003.02930-2021.headline_claim: High-dose prednisolone was not better than low-dose prednisolone for clinical, radiological, physiological or health-related quality of life outcomes in symptomatic post-COVID-19 diffuse parenchymal lung abnormalities.
10.1183/13993003.02930-2021.overall: The finding of no demonstrable superiority of high-dose over low-dose prednisolone is reasonably reported, with appropriate hedging and a stated lack of placebo. The weaker point is the suggestion that a lower dose may be sufficient, which a small superiority trial without a non-inferiority margin cannot support. The numeric issues found are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Proportion of subjects with a complete radiological response (at least 90% reduction in diffuse lung abnormalities on CT) at 6 weeks

primary_outcomes.measure: Proportion of subjects with a complete radiologic response

issues.title: 'Lower dose may be sufficient' drawn from an underpowered superiority trial with no non-inferiority margin
issues.explanation: The trial was designed as a superiority comparison. No sample-size calculation is reported, and the primary outcome difference has a wide 95% CI (-0.20 to 0.08 for complete radiological response). Failure to show superiority of high dose does not show that low dose is sufficient. There is also no placebo arm, so the claim rests on absence of evidence at about 65 per arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority margin with a sample-size calculation, with the CI excluding that margin.

quotes.text: However, our study does indicate that a lower glucocorticoid dose may be sufficient once a decision is made to treat persistent PC-DPLAS.

issues.title: Within-arm improvements in SpO2 and 6MWD described as 'significant' without a placebo arm
issues.explanation: The Discussion reports significant improvements in oxygen saturation and walk distance in both groups, and similar improvement to prior studies 'even with low-dose prednisolone'. With no untreated control and short follow-up in a recovering post-COVID population, such change cannot be attributed to prednisolone. The authors do state that spontaneous recovery is plausible, which largely mitigates this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the caveat is already stated by the authors.

quotes.text: We also found significant improvements in oxygen saturation and 6-min walk distance in both groups.
It is plausible that our subjects, although significantly symptomatic,

issues.title: Hyperglycaemia 21/65 vs 19/65 printed with p=0.20, inconsistent with the counts
issues.explanation: The counts 21 (32.3%) vs 19 (29.2%) differ by about 3 percentage points in 65 per arm. Standard tests give a p value far larger than 0.20, around 0.7. The printed p appears wrong. It does not change any conclusion, since the comparison is non-significant either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated adjusted or alternative test that yields p=0.20 for this row.

10.1183/13993003.03101-2021.headline_claim: Eight weeks of home-based inspiratory muscle training (IMT) improves breathlessness, respiratory muscle strength and aerobic fitness in people with long COVID, and is an efficacious home-based rehabilitation strategy when used as prescribed, despite no between-group ITT effect on the K-BILD total score.
10.1183/13993003.03101-2021.overall: The randomised primary comparison (K-BILD total, ITT) was null, and the positive efficacy claim rests on a per-protocol comparison whose K-BILD row labels in Table 3 look offset from Table 1. The 'ITT' set contains only completers (148 of 281), the trial was open-label with a waitlist control and self-reported outcomes, and several smaller numerical inconsistencies need correcting. Objective gains in inspiratory muscle strength are the most credible finding; claims of improved quality of life and efficacy are tentative.

primary_outcome.name: K-BILD total score (health-related quality of life)

issues.title: Efficacy claimed in title and abstract despite a null ITT primary outcome; benefit rests on per-protocol analysis
issues.explanation: The primary outcome, K-BILD total, showed no between-group difference in the ITT analysis. The only positive result comes from a per-protocol comparison between adherent IMT participants and all controls, which breaks randomisation and favours participants who did well. Even that result is in doubt because the Table 3 K-BILD labels are offset (see the K-BILD table issue). The title ('enhances recovery'), the shareable abstract ('effective') and the conclusion ('efficacious') go beyond what the randomised comparison supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified per-protocol or CACE primary analysis, or a significant ITT result on the primary outcome including all randomised participants.

quotes.text: There was no between-group difference post-intervention for K-BILD total score in the ITT population
Our findings thus indicate IMT may be an efficacious home-based rehabilitation strategy during recovery from COVID-19.
represents an effective, home-based rehabilitation strategy

second_reader.what_stands: The title ('enhances recovery') and the shareable abstract ('represents an effective... strategy') are stronger than a null ITT primary outcome supports, and the primary-outcome benefit appears only in the post-hoc adherence-defined per-protocol set. However, the paper discloses the null ITT result, cautions about withdrawals and nonadherence, and the conclusion is hedged ('may be'). Some ITT secondary outcomes, notably TDI, were significant.

issues.title: 'ITT' analysis includes only 148 completers of 281 recruited; withdrawers differed; Table 1 is completers only
issues.explanation: Only participants who completed post-intervention testing (148 of 281 recruited, about 53%) were analysed, so the 'ITT' result is a completers analysis. Those who withdrew were younger and had higher MIP, so the dropouts differ from completers and the loss may differ by arm. The Methods attribute the age, sex and time-since-COVID summary of 281 adults to Table 1, but those figures match the 148 completers, so baseline data for everyone randomised are not shown. The authors acknowledge the dropout, but the headline claims do not reflect it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram showing per-arm numbers randomised and lost, and an analysis (e.g. multiple imputation) including everyone randomised.

quotes.text: 148 (IMT: n=111; controls: n=37) participants completed the post-intervention testing and were included in the ITT analysis
Those who withdrew following the pre-intervention testing were significantly younger (42.1±13.0 versus 48.4±11.4 years; p<0.001)
281 adults (age 46.6±12.2 years; 88% female; 9.0±4.2 months post-acute COVID-19) (table 1)

second_reader.what_stands: The analysis labelled ITT is a completer analysis of 148 of 281 recruited. The 'ITT' label therefore does not protect against attrition bias, and the withdrawers differed at baseline: they were younger and had higher MIP. The summary characteristics quoted for the 281 participants are those of the 148 completers. The authors do acknowledge the withdrawals and possible self-selection, so this is a labelling and generalisability problem that is disclosed, not hidden.

issues.title: Open-label waitlist control, no sham, with self-reported primary and breathlessness outcomes
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they were doing IMT and were compared with a waitlist group, with no sham device. The primary outcome (K-BILD) and the key breathlessness outcome (TDI) are self-reported, so expectation and learning effects cannot be separated from a true effect. Objective strength measures (MIP) are less vulnerable but are not the claimed clinical benefit. This makes the quality-of-life and breathlessness conclusions tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham-controlled or assessor-blinded comparison showing similar K-BILD and TDI effects.

quotes.text: a learning effect may have been evident in the IMT group as no sham IMT protocol was utilised
compared 8 weeks of IMT with a ' usual care ' waitlist control

second_reader.what_stands: The trial compares IMT with a waitlist 'usual care' control and no sham, and its primary and breathlessness outcomes are self-reported, so expectation and learning effects could inflate the apparent benefit. The authors acknowledge the lack of a sham but do not report any blinding of participants or assessors. The objective strength outcomes depend on participant effort on the training device.

issues.title: Table 3 K-BILD row labels are offset by one row from Table 1 (e.g. control 'Total' 59.7 vs Table 1 total 56.6)
issues.explanation: Table 3's control pre-intervention K-BILD values match Table 1 only if every row label is moved by one position, so 'Total' holds Table 1's breathlessness values and 'Chest symptoms' holds Table 1's total. If the labels are wrong, the per-protocol result of IMT 67.8 versus control 59.8 for K-BILD total is actually a different domain. The true per-protocol total row would then show no between-group marker. That is the only analysis behind the claimed primary-outcome benefit. The same shift explains why the text and the markers disagree for the psychological and chest domains.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 3, or the authors' data, showing the printed labels are right and the control pre-intervention values simply differ from Table 1.

quotes.location: Table 3, K-BILD Total row, control pre-intervention
Table 1, K-BILD Total row (control); also Table 3 Chest symptoms row

second_reader.what_stands: As printed, the Table 3 K-BILD row labels are cyclically offset by one row from Table 1: the 'Total' row holds the breathlessness-and-activities values, and the 'Chest symptoms' row holds the total values. Which row the post-intervention values and the #/¶ significance marks belong to is therefore uncertain. The text's statements about which domains improved cannot be checked reliably against Table 3 until the labels are corrected. Table 3 also has a header typo, 'IMT (n=37)' post-intervention versus n=87 pre-intervention.

issues.title: Several small Table 2/3 and text inconsistencies: control FIT/SMIP, TDI SDs of 0.2/0.3, IMT n=37, markers
issues.explanation: The same 37 controls give different post-intervention values in Table 2 and Table 3 for FIT (22.3±25.9 vs 22.0±27.6) and SMIP (478.0±225.0 vs 464.2±226.8). The per-protocol TDI SDs (0.2 and 0.3) are an order of magnitude below the ITT SDs (2.0, 1.7) while the p-value is identical, which looks like a typo. Table 3's post-intervention IMT header says n=37 rather than 87. Table 2 marks the IMT intensity-gradient change as significant while the text says this occurred in the per-protocol population only, and Table 3 carries no marker for it. None of these alters the main conclusions, but each result needs correcting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors' explanation that the per-protocol control values were re-estimated from a different model, and corrected SDs and header.

10.1183/13993003.congress-2022.2629.headline_claim: Pulmonary rehabilitation improves quality of life and functional capacity in patients with long COVID-19 syndrome.
10.1183/13993003.congress-2022.2629.overall: The headline claim that pulmonary rehabilitation improves QoL and function in long COVID is not supported by this design: allocation was by patient choice, the comparison group had five patients with very different baselines, and only within-group changes were tested. The PR arm's improvements are suggestive but the data are hypothesis-generating at best.

primary_outcome.name: Not specified; abstract names QoL, emotional status and functional capacity

issues.title: Self-selected usual-care arm (n=5) differs markedly from PR arm at baseline (HADS anxiety 12 vs 4)
issues.explanation: Patients who declined rehabilitation formed the comparison group, so arm membership reflects patient choice. The baseline table shows the UC group was worse on several measures (HADS anxiety 12±6 vs 4±5, FACIT 20 vs 27, steps/day 2264 vs 4463). Any difference in change cannot be attributed to rehabilitation, and regression to the mean and selection effects remain open. The baseline differences run in both directions across measures, but the design cannot support a causal efficacy claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that allocation was random or that baseline-adjusted between-group analyses show the same effect.

quotes.text: Patients in the UC declined PR and instructed to be physically active.
HADS (anxiety)4±53±312±69±6

second_reader.what_stands: The usual-care arm was formed by patients declining PR, not by randomisation, and Table 1 shows it started with much higher HADS anxiety (12±6 vs 4±5, about 1.5 SD apart) and worse values on most other baseline measures. The paper reports no baseline comparison or adjustment. The wording 'markedly' is a fair description, but the baseline differences were not formally tested by the authors, and with n=5 the estimates are imprecise.

issues.title: Benefit inferred from within-arm significance only; no between-group comparison is reported
issues.explanation: Only within-group p values are flagged, and significance appears mostly in the PR arm, while UC is non-significant with n=5. A significant change in one group and a non-significant change in another is not evidence that the groups differ. The conclusion of improvement is therefore not supported by a direct comparison, though the PR arm's own changes are suggestive. This is the analytic side of the same weakness as the non-randomised design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group or baseline-adjusted comparison showing a significant difference in change.

quotes.text: Asterisks denote within group differences at p<0.05
PR improves QoL and functional capacity in patients with long COVID-19 syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: The only tests reported are within-group (before vs after), and the efficacy conclusion rests on asterisks that appear only in the PR arm. No between-group comparison, interaction test or adjusted effect is reported, so 'PR improves' is not supported by the stated analysis. The raw changes in some outcomes (e.g. FACIT, 6MWD) point in favour of PR, but this is not a tested comparison, and for EQ-5D VAS the UC arm improved by almost as much as the PR arm.

issues.title: Unqualified efficacy conclusion from 15 non-randomised patients (10 vs 5), no sample-size justification
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that PR improves QoL and functional capacity as a fact. It rests on 15 patients, a self-selected 5-person comparison group, no between-group test and no sample-size calculation. The results can at most suggest a benefit worth testing in a randomised trial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion worded as preliminary, or a powered between-group analysis supporting the claim.

quotes.text: PR improves QoL and functional capacity in patients with long COVID-19 syndrome.
an interim analysis

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion is stated unqualified despite 15 patients (10 vs 5), non-random self-selected allocation, clear baseline imbalance and no between-group test; the title's 'interim analysis' is the only hint of preliminary status. The claim of 'no sample-size justification' is true of the abstract text but cannot be taken as evidence that none exists in the full study, since conference abstracts are short.

10.1183/23120541.00031-2024.headline_claim: Lactoferrin supplementation showed no efficacy over placebo for long COVID symptoms; the fatigue improvement seen in both arms is attributed to placebo or Hawthorne effects.
10.1183/23120541.00031-2024.overall: The null between-arm result is probably reliable as a finding of no detectable difference, but the stated conclusion of 'no efficacy' goes beyond what a 72-patient trial with an optimistic power calculation and no confidence intervals can show. There are also several internal numeric inconsistencies (responder percentages, Table 1 percentages, Discussion versus Results on CFQ). These are mostly reporting errors that do not reverse the main finding.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) score, T0 to T6

issues.title: Non-significant result in 72-patient trial presented as demonstrating lack of efficacy
issues.explanation: The authors conclude lactoferrin has 'no efficacy' and that they 'demonstrate the lack of efficacy'. The trial was powered only for a 20% difference in MCID responders with assumptions that look optimistic, enrolled 72 patients, and reports no confidence intervals for between-arm differences. A non-significant test cannot exclude a modest benefit. The limitations paragraph concedes that small differences might be significant with a larger sample, but the conclusions are not softened.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported between-arm confidence intervals excluding the clinically relevant difference of 20 percentage points or 4 FAS points.

quotes.text: indicating no efficacy of lactoferrin on long COVID symptoms
we demonstrate the lack of efficacy of lactoferrin supplementation in long COVID
Small variations between the study arms might be significant in a study with a greater sample size.

second_reader.what_stands: A non-significant (Holm-adjusted p=1.0) result in a trial of 72 randomised patients (about 65 analysed), powered only for a 20-percentage-point difference and reporting no confidence intervals, is described as 'demonstrating' and 'indicating' no efficacy; absence of significance does not establish absence of effect. The authors partly mitigate this in the limitations (small variations might be significant with larger samples; dose and duration uncertain) and the Conclusion is more measured, but the Discussion's headline wording is stronger than the data support.

issues.title: Discussion lists CFQ improvement in placebo arm at 6 weeks (Results p=0.19) and says no improvement continued
issues.explanation: The Discussion says cognitive failure improved in the placebo arm during the first 6 weeks. The Results say there was no CFQ improvement in either arm (placebo p=0.19). The Discussion also says improvement did not continue after 6 weeks, yet the Results report a significant placebo CFQ decrease between 6 and 12 weeks (p=0.013). The narrative summary does not match the reported tests, though the null between-arm conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary table S1 showing a significant placebo CFQ improvement at T6 and no later CFQ change.

quotes.text: for depression and cognitive failure in the placebo arm
There was no improvement for the CFQ score in either study arm between baseline and 6 weeks (lactoferrin p=1.0 and placebo p=0.19)
In the placebo arm, the CFQ score decreased between 6 and 12 weeks (p=0.013)

issues.title: MCID responder percentages 19 (54.3%) and 21 (62.8%) match no arm denominator (36 randomised, 32/33 completers)
issues.explanation: The primary-outcome responder percentages cannot be reproduced from the counts and arm sizes. 21 (62.8%) matches no integer denominator, and 19 (54.3%) implies 35 participants in the lactoferrin arm, although 36 were randomised and 4 were lost. The denominator used is not stated. The direction of the null result is unlikely to change, but the primary responder analysis cannot be checked as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated analysis denominator per arm (e.g. from supplementary figure S1) that reproduces both 54.3% and 62.8%.

quotes.text: 19 (54.3%) and 21 (62.8%) from the lactoferrin and placebo arms, respectively
Seven participants were lost to follow-up; four in the lactoferrin arm and three in the placebo arm

script.explanation: 21/33 = 63.64%, but the paper prints 62.8, outside the rounding interval [62.75, 62.90]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 33.4 rather than 33.

issues.title: Placebo/Hawthorne effect inferred from within-arm fatigue change; natural recovery cannot be excluded
issues.explanation: Fatigue fell in both arms (FAS 33.5 to 28.0 placebo, 33.5 to 27.0 lactoferrin), and the Conclusion attributes this to a Hawthorne or placebo effect. A two-arm placebo-controlled design has no untreated group to separate placebo effect from natural history, usual care or regression to the mean. The Discussion itself cites a natural decrease in fatigue in this period. The attribution is stated more firmly than the design supports, though it is hedged with 'could be'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from a no-treatment or waiting-list arm in the same population showing smaller change.

quotes.text: This suggests that the observed improvement could be due to Hawthorne or placebo effect.
A recent longitudinal study showed a natural decrease in fatigue symptoms between 6 weeks and 6 months after acute infection

10.1183/23120541.00838-2024.headline_claim: A supervised, twice-weekly, 8-week water- and land-based exercise programme improved lung function, in terms of some dynamic spirometry parameters, in children with post-COVID-19 condition.
10.1183/23120541.00838-2024.overall: The significant FEV1 and FVC interactions mostly reflect decline in the control group. The abstract and Conclusion go further than the paper's own Discussion, which says no actual lung function change was seen and the study was not powered for it. Several table and text mismatches (duplicated LAND boys cells, an implausible AQUA girls CI, narrative direction claims) and uncorrected multiple outcomes make the sex-specific and FVC claims especially fragile; the FEV1 group difference is the sturdiest result.

primary_outcome.name: Exercise capacity and fatigue (registered and stated as primary; reported elsewhere, ref 21; the lung-function outcome analysed here is stated as secondary)

issues.title: Abstract and Conclusion say lung function 'improved'; Discussion says no actual change observed, study not powered
issues.explanation: The shareable abstract and Conclusion state flatly that the programme improved lung function. The Discussion says no actual changes in lung function could be observed, that it is difficult to say with confidence that the intervention will improve lung function, and that the study was not powered for lung function. The significant interactions come mainly from the control group's decline, within-group tests were not significant, and the outcome was secondary and uncorrected. The headline claim is stronger than the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of significant within-group improvements in exercise arms on a prespecified, adequately powered lung function outcome.

quotes.text: improved lung function, in terms of some dynamic spirometry parameters, in children with post-COVID-19 condition
no actual changes in lung function could be observed in the children who participated in our intervention
our study was not powered for changes in lung function

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion and shareable abstract state that lung function 'improved', while the Discussion says 'no actual changes in lung function could be observed' and the limitations paragraph says the study was not powered for lung function, so the paper's wording is internally inconsistent. The strongest evidence of benefit is a significant interaction for FEV1 and FVC driven partly by a decline in the control group and by girls' within-group gains; boys' within-group changes were not distinguishable from zero, and the % predicted post hoc tests found no within-group differences. The 'not powered'

issues.title: Sex-specific 'increases' and girls-versus-boys explanations rest on descriptive cells, no sex interaction test
issues.explanation: The Discussion says all parameters increased in girls and only some in boys, and offers physiological reasons for the sex difference. The reported model includes only GROUP and REPETITION, and the post hoc tests found no significant within-group differences. The sex comparison is based on pre-post means in groups of 8 to 15 children, with no GROUP x REPETITION x SEX test. These statements are exploratory at best, and the explanatory discussion overreaches.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported three-way interaction with sex, or within-group tests showing significant increases in the exercise arms.

quotes.text: the post hoc test did not detect any significant differences within groups
The main method used was an analysis of variance (ANOVA) for repeated measures used to test the interaction between GROUP (3) (fixed factor) and REPETITION (2)

issues.title: AQUA girls FEV1/FVC %: difference -11.62 (CI -51.64 to 28.39) incompatible with SDs of about 6-7 and n=8
issues.explanation: The reported CI for the AQUA girls' FEV1/FVC difference spans about 80 percentage points, though the pre and post SDs are 7.23 and 5.96 with n=8. The point estimate (-11.62) also differs from post minus pre (-7.08). Other rows with similar SDs and n have CIs about a fifth as wide. The row is internally inconsistent, and the text elsewhere describes an 'upward trend' for FEV1/FVC in AQUA.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired data showing an unusually variable difference in one or two children, with SD of differences about 50.

quotes.location: Table 3, FEV1/FVC % row, AQUA mean difference

issues.title: LAND boys: identical mean difference and CI (0.03, -9.09 to 9.15) for FVC % pred and FEV1/FVC %
issues.explanation: Two different outcomes in LAND boys, with different n, means and SDs, share the same mean difference and CI to the second decimal. For FVC % pred the printed difference of +0.03 also disagrees with the printed pre and post means, which fall by 2.3. At least one of the two rows is mis-transcribed, so the LAND boys results for these outcomes cannot be trusted as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the two rows genuinely yield the same difference and CI, or a corrigendum correcting one row.

quotes.location: Table 2, FVC % pred row, LAND mean difference
Table 2, FVC % pred row, LAND pre
Table 2, FVC % pred row, LAND post

issues.title: Narrative summaries of change contradict Tables 2-3 (AQUA girls FEV1/FVC fell; LAND boys; largest AQUA rise)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says all spirometric parameters increased in girls in both exercise groups, but AQUA girls' FEV1/FVC fell from 85.56 to 78.48. The Results name FVC % pred as the largest AQUA girls' increase, but FEV1 % pred rose more. The text says only FEV1 % pred improved in LAND boys, though FEV1 (L) and FEV1 Z also rose slightly. The authors' narrative summaries of the sex-specific findings do not match their own tables. Errors go in both directions, but the 'all parameters increased' statement flatters the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the statement is explicitly limited to % predicted values and that the FEV1/FVC fall is a table error.

quotes.text: Our study showed increases in all spirometric parameters in girls in the exercising intervention groups, regardless of the type of training (AQUA and LAND group)

issues.title: Allocation list chosen from five random versions by lowest baseline MANOVA F; sequence of steps unclear
issues.explanation: The authors prepared five random allocation versions and used the one with the lowest MANOVA F value for baseline characteristics. This is a covariate-balancing step layered on randomisation. The paper does not say when baseline data were available, whether the choice was prespecified, or whether the restriction was accounted for in the analysis. If the list was chosen after seeing baseline data, concealment and the randomness of allocation are weakened. The effect on the lung function results is probably modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or protocol showing the five lists were compared on a simulated or pre-enrolment covariate set before any participant was allocated, with the rule prespecified.

quotes.text: Assignment to groups was prepared in five random versions.
The allocation providing the lowest F value for MANOVA was used when comparing the basic characteristics of the subjects.

issues.title: Six or more correlated spirometry indices tested at alpha 0.05 with no multiplicity control; FVC findings fragile
issues.explanation: The paper tests several correlated spirometry indices at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05 and gives no hierarchy. The FEV1 interactions (p<0.01) are fairly robust, but the FVC interaction is only p<0.05, and the FVC % pred interaction came with no significant within- or between-group difference at all. The conclusion that lung function 'improved' on both FEV1 and FVC rests partly on these less certain results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary lung function index, or adjusted p-values showing the FVC interactions remain significant.

quotes.text: The level of statistical significance was set at α =0.05.
The interaction was significant for absolute FEV1 values ( F (2,64)=6.80; p<0.01, η 2=0.18)

issues.title: Completer-only, valid-spirometry analysis: 86 randomised, 74 completed, about 67 in the F test (22%)
issues.explanation: The analysis uses only children who completed the programme and produced technically acceptable spirometry, with pairwise deletion of missing data. About a fifth of randomised children are absent from the lung function ANOVA. There is no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis. If dropout or failed spirometry differed by arm or baseline function, the between-group differences could be biased.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 or supplementary data showing balanced, small attrition across arms and a sensitivity analysis including all randomised children.

quotes.text: 74 participants completed the intervention.
Missing data was pairwise removed.

issues.title: Power calculation equates d=0.50 with eta-squared 0.04; paper's own moderate benchmark is 0.06
issues.explanation: The sample size section calls d=0.50 / eta-squared 0.04 a moderate effect, while the analysis section defines moderate as about 0.06. The two quoted effect sizes are not equivalent. The calculation also omits the correlation among repeated measures, so it cannot be reproduced. This does not by itself change any result, and the authors state the study was not powered for lung function.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A G*Power input screenshot showing the stated parameters give n=69 for the stated effect size.

quotes.text: η ² values of approximately 0.01, 0.06 and 0.14 could be considered small, moderate and large, respectively

10.1183/23120541.01142-2024.headline_claim: Deupirfenidone did not improve 6MWT or Dyspnoea-12 over placebo; the authors conclude that most PASC patients improve regardless of intervention and that the drug's safety and tolerability support a Phase IIb IPF trial.
10.1183/23120541.01142-2024.overall: The headline conclusion of no benefit on 6MWT or Dyspnoea-12 rests on the primary analysis, which is internally consistent with p=0.70 and similar improvements in both arms. The only flagged problem is a probable typographical slip in one baseline SD, which does not bear on any efficacy or safety result.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline to day 91 in 6-minute walk test distance

primary_outcomes.measure: Change From Baseline in Distance Walked During the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)

issues.title: Table 1 placebo age SD of 132.5 years is impossible for an 18-80 population (overall SD 12.4)
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives the placebo arm's age as 52.7 (132.5) years. An SD of 132.5 years cannot occur when eligibility was limited to ages 18-80, because the largest possible SD in that range is about 31 years. It also conflicts with the overall SD of 12.4 stated in the text. The value is probably a decimal-point slip for about 13.25, which would fit the overall SD. Nothing in the efficacy or safety conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source table or the trial's statistical report printing a placebo age SD consistent with 18-80 (for example 13.25), which would show the 132.5 in this text is an extraction artefact and not a printed value.

quotes.location: Table 1, Age, years row, placebo column

quotes.text: Overall mean (SD) age was 54.7 (12.4) years
Eligible patients were aged 18 -80 years

10.1183/23120541.01434-2025.headline_claim: An individualized 8-week tele-rehabilitation program improves health status, symptoms and fatigue and is feasible and safe in non-hospitalized long COVID, though the primary mobility outcome did not differ between groups.
10.1183/23120541.01434-2025.overall: The primary result is clearly reported as null, so the paper does not claim a primary-outcome effect. The claimed secondary benefits did not survive the authors' own multiplicity correction and rest on a comparison with no corrected significant findings, and the safety framing is weakened by one-armed adverse-event monitoring and inconsistent AE counts (45 vs 50, 46% vs 52%). Several sign slips in the abstract and per-protocol text are minor reporting errors that do not alter conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: AM-PAC Basic Mobility score

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in the basic mobility domain of the Activity Measure for Post-Acute Care (AM-PAC)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline, Week 8 (up to 1 week), and at 6 months.

issues.title: Secondary 'benefits' concluded though none of 25 outcomes survived FDR correction and the primary was null
issues.explanation: The Methods say none of the 25 Table 2 outcomes remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg control at an FDR of 0.25. Yet the abstract reports greater improvements in pain, health status, fatigue and dyspnea, and the final conclusion says secondary outcomes 'demonstrated benefits'. With a null primary outcome and no corrected secondary signals, these results are at most hypothesis-generating. The control group also improved on several measures, and the per-protocol analyses add further uncorrected comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy, or secondary results surviving correction.

quotes.text: none remained statistically significant after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure using an FDR threshold of 0.25
Secondary outcomes demonstrated benefits of the individualized tele-rehabilitation program

second_reader.what_stands: By the paper's own statement, none of the 25 Table 2 outcomes remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg (even at a lenient FDR of 0.25) and the primary outcome was null. Yet the final Conclusion says secondary outcomes 'demonstrated benefits', and the FDR result is not reconciled with that wording anywhere in the Results, Discussion or Limitations. The authors do acknowledge the null primary and use hedged language elsewhere, and my own BH check on the rounded printed p-values did not reproduce 'none', so the FDR statement itself could not be verified.

issues.title: Related adverse events: text says 45 (13 grade 1) but Table 3 sums to 50 (18 grade 1)
issues.explanation: The Results report 45 related adverse events, 13 of them grade 1 and 32 grade 2. Adding the Table 3 cells gives 50 events, 18 of them grade 1 (14 definite plus 4 possible), with grade 2 still 32. Five grade 1 events are therefore unaccounted for between text and table. The related-event burden is understated in the text, which bears on the safety conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that five grade 1 table events were reclassified or duplicated.

quotes.text: (45 adverse events reported by 30 participants)
Grade 1 (mild symptoms, medication intervention not indicated) (13 adverse events))
Multisystem b (brain fog, headaches, etc.)

issues.title: Discussion and Conclusion give 52% with related adverse events; Results imply 30/65 = 46%
issues.explanation: The Discussion and final conclusion state that 52% of the intervention group reported at least one related mild or moderate adverse event. The Results and ad hoc analysis give 30 participants with such events and 35 without, out of 65. That is 46%, not 52%. The two figures cannot both describe the same quantity, and the source of 52% is not shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of the 52% showing it uses a different participant set or event definition.

quotes.text: While 52% of participants in the intervention group reported at least one mild or moderate adverse event related to the intervention
(45 adverse events reported by 30 participants)

issues.title: 'Safety and clinical relevance' claimed though control adverse events were unmonitored and primary outcome null
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the study offers important insights into safety and clinical relevance. Adverse events were collected only in the intervention arm, so there is no comparison and the excess risk of the programme cannot be estimated. About half of intervention participants had related events, and 28 were PEM-related. The primary mobility outcome showed no benefit. The safety wording is defensible as descriptive, but it is stronger than a 132-person unmonitored-control design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adverse-event data from the control arm, or conclusion wording limited to describing events in the intervention arm.

quotes.text: our study offers important insights into feasibility, safety and clinical relevance
Adverse events were not monitored in the control group

issues.title: Abstract drops minus signs: AM-PAC CI printed 0.91 to 2.13 and fatigue MD 0.90, versus -0.91 and -0.90 in Results
issues.explanation: The Abstract prints the primary-outcome CI as 0.91 to 2.13 around an MD of 0.61, which excludes the estimate. It also prints the fatigue MD as 0.90 beside a CI of -1.78 to -0.02, which also excludes the estimate. Results and Table 2 give -0.91 to 2.13 and -0.90. These look like sign slips in the abstract; they do not change any conclusion, but a reader of the abstract alone would see the primary CI as excluding zero and fatigue as worsening.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The published PDF abstract showing the minus signs, which would make this a text-extraction loss.

quotes.text: difference in change: 0.61; 95% CI -0.91 to 2.13

issues.title: Per-protocol pain estimate printed +0.45 lies outside its CI (-0.84 to -0.06); likely -0.45
issues.explanation: In the per-protocol paragraph the pain/discomfort difference is printed as 0.45 while its CI is entirely negative. The CI midpoint is -0.45, so the sign appears to have been dropped. The text still calls this a benefit in favour of the intervention, which fits -0.45. The comparison to the -0.36 unadjusted value is not an inconsistency, since the populations differ. Impact is limited to one exploratory per-protocol value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: eTable 7 showing the value as -0.45 (an extraction loss in this text).

quotes.text: EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort (difference in change: 0.45; 95% CI -0.84 to -0.06)

script.explanation: the estimate 0.45 lies outside its own CI [-0.84, -0.06]; the estimate 0.45 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-0.84, -0.06] (expected about -0.4500) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Per-protocol comparison of 36 progressors vs all 66 controls is post-randomization and uncorrected
issues.explanation: Progressors were defined after randomization by ability to progress exercise, while all controls were retained. Effects in the subset (e.g., VAS 11.48, SF-12 physical 4.04) are larger than in the ITT analysis and are reported as 'in favor of the intervention'. The authors disclose the bias risk and the comparison is exploratory. It does not drive the abstract's headline, so the effect is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified per-protocol plan with a matched or CACE-style comparison.

quotes.text: Per-protocol analysis comparing the control group (n = 66) to participants who progressed in the intervention group (n = 36)
The per-protocol analysis excludes non-progressors but still compares the remaining participants to all controls, which may introduce bias.

10.1183/23120541.01552-2025.headline_claim: A 3-month prednisone regimen starting at 0.5 mg/kg/day is as effective as the longer standard 6-month regimen for post-COVID organising pneumonia and halves the rate of adverse effects.
10.1183/23120541.01552-2025.overall: The 6-month DLCO noninferiority result (CI −5.06 to 7.38 against a 10-point margin) is supported in the mFAS and per-protocol sets, despite early stopping at 82 of 120. The safety claim of halved adverse effects is overstated because the drug-specific complication outcomes did not differ, and the efficacy conclusion omits the 12-month DLCO CI that exceeds the margin and the significant FEV1 difference. The remaining issues are minor reporting inconsistencies in the p-value, SD and table labelling.

primary_outcome.name: Change in DLCO (% predicted) from baseline to 6 months, baseline-adjusted, mFAS

issues.title: 'Halves adverse effects' rests on any-type nonsevere complications; prednisone-related ones did not differ
issues.explanation: The headline says the shorter regimen halves the rate of adverse effects. This comes from the 56.4% vs 22.5% contrast for nonsevere complications of any type, an open-label secondary outcome with no multiplicity adjustment. The outcomes that actually reflect steroid toxicity (prednisone-related, severe or nonsevere) showed no significant difference, and severe any-type events were not lower. The safety half of the conclusion is therefore overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the extra complications in the control arm were adjudicated as steroid-attributable, or a pre-specified safety endpoint showing a difference.

quotes.text: and halves the rate of adverse effects
Only 23% of patients treated with the experimental regimen experienced any adverse side-effects, compared to 56% of those treated with the conventional regimen.
No differences between the groups were observed in severe complications or in complications of any degree related to prednisone treatment

second_reader.what_stands: The 'halves the rate of adverse effects' statement rests only on nonsevere complications of any type (56.4% vs 22.5%). Prednisone-related complications (severe or nonsevere) and severe complications of any type did not differ significantly. Describing the any-type nonsevere result as 'adverse side-effects' without that qualification overstates the safety advantage. The 56.4% vs 22.5% figures themselves are correctly reported.

issues.title: 'As effective' conclusion omits 12-month DLCO gap (upper CI 14.17 > margin 10) and FEV1 difference favouring control
issues.explanation: At 12 months the control arm improved more (22.26 vs 15.50), and the CI for the difference reaches 14.17, beyond the 10% noninferiority margin, so noninferiority is not supported at that time point. FEV1 also improved significantly more with the standard regimen (p=0.033). The Discussion and concluding statements describe the short regimen as as effective and say other secondary variables did not differ, without mentioning these findings. Efficacy is only supported for the 6-month DLCO primary endpoint.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified statement that only 6-month results define efficacy and a discussion that explicitly reports the 12-month and FEV1 findings as limitations.

quotes.text: The difference between groups at 12 months was 6.75%
reached statistical significance, with a p-value of 0.033
may be as effective as the longer standard regimen

second_reader.what_stands: The primary 6-month noninferiority result holds, but the 12-month DLCO difference (6.75, upper CI 14.17, beyond the margin of 10) does not show noninferiority, and the 6-month FEV1 difference (6.75, p=0.033, 95% CI 0.57 to 12.93) favours control; neither is weighed in the 'may be as effective' conclusion. Because the primary endpoint was defined at 6 months, the margin is not formally breached at the prespecified timepoint, and the conclusion is hedged with 'may', so the omission is a matter of incomplete caveating rather than a contradicted primary result. The FEV1 finding is unadjusted for m

issues.title: 82 randomised (41 per arm) but mFAS is 79 (39/40); reason for 3 exclusions not stated in text
issues.explanation: The trial randomised 82 patients, 41 per group. The mFAS, described as the intention-to-treat-based primary population, contains 79 (39 control, 40 experimental). The main text does not say why three randomised patients were left out, and the 79 is also described as the number who completed the regimen, which blurs the analysis population with completers. Excluding randomised patients post hoc from the primary analysis departs from strict ITT, though the effect on the noninferiority result is probably small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The supplementary flow diagram showing the three patients were excluded for a pre-specified, arm-independent reason (for example never receiving any treatment).

quotes.text: recruitment was halted after randomisation of 82 patients (41 per group)
Among the patients who were randomised and included in the mFAS population, 79 (96.34%)

issues.title: Discussion extends findings to noninfectious organising pneumonia and any post-COVID sequelae
issues.explanation: All participants had post-COVID organising pneumonia from one centre, and the primary outcome was 6-month DLCO. The closing paragraph says the findings may have implications for organising pneumonia from other causes, including noninfectious forms. An earlier sentence refers to patients with any post-COVID respiratory sequelae. These generalisations are beyond what this population supports, although the wording is tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the second sentence summarises a separate cited trial and the authors flag that the present data do not extend beyond post-COVID organising pneumonia.

quotes.text: may also have implications for the management of organising pneumonia from other aetiologies, including noninfectious forms
For the treatment of patients with any post-COVID-19 respiratory sequelae, a low-dose prednisone regimen can be as effective as one with a higher dose

issues.title: WHO Clinical Progression Scale p-value is 0.3755 in the text but 0.646 in Table 3
issues.explanation: The Results text gives p=0.3755 for the between-group comparison on the WHO Clinical Progression Scale. Table 3 prints 0.646 for the same scale. The text also quotes 12-month percentages that Table 3 (6-month data) does not show. Both p-values are non-significant, so the interpretation is unchanged, but one of the two printed values is wrong or the analyses are not described consistently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text p refers to a separate 12-month analysis not shown in Table 3, with the 12-month proportions given.

quotes.text: with no significant differences (p=0.3755
quotes.location: Results, Secondary end-points, clinical progression paragraph

issues.title: Table 3 FEV1/FVC entries (82.24, 81.68) are 6-month levels under a 'change from baseline' header
issues.explanation: Under the header 'Changes from baseline at 6 months', the FEV1/FVC rows show values near the baseline levels (82.48 and 82.96). A true change would be near zero. The values appear to be adjusted 6-month means, and the between-group difference of 0.56 is their difference. The row is mislabelled or mis-entered, and readers could not tell from the table which it is.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocol or supplement text defining this entry as a change from baseline of +82.24 (implausible), or a corrected table.

quotes.text: Changes from baseline at 6 months

quotes.location: Table 3, FEV1/FVC % of theoretical value row, Control change column

issues.title: Table 1 total-column FVC SD printed as 2, while arm SDs are 24.7 and 21.6
issues.explanation: The pooled SD of baseline FVC cannot be smaller than both group SDs by an order of magnitude. The value 77.8±2 is almost certainly a truncated value of about 23. Nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source PDF showing the total SD as a value near 23 and the 2 being only a text-extraction truncation.

quotes.location: Table 1, FVC % of the theoretical value row, Control column

10.1186/s12868-025-00989-x.headline_claim: Four consecutive daily sessions of anodal tDCS over the left dlPFC did not produce consistent improvements in subjective or behavioural state fatigue in long COVID, while an occipital alpha interaction is read as a potential stabilizing effect on cortical excitability.
10.1186/s12868-025-00989-x.overall: The null findings on subjective and behavioural state fatigue are reported plainly, but they come from a small trial powered for a different (trait) outcome, so they are weak evidence of no effect. The only stimulation-related positive finding, the occipital alpha interaction (p = 0.020), was uncorrected across many omnibus tests and is carried into the Conclusions as a 'potential stabilizing effect', so it should be treated as exploratory at best.

primary_outcome.name: Subjective and objective state fatigue during the AX-CPT (secondary outcomes of this report; the trait-fatigue primary outcome is reported elsewhere)

issues.title: Only stimulation-related finding (occipital alpha interaction, p = 0.020) is uncorrected across many omnibus tests
issues.explanation: The authors ran many omnibus F-tests (VAS, accuracy, RT, SD RT, theta, alpha, p50, several Go/No-Go models) and corrected only post hoc comparisons. The single stimulation × assessment interaction that reached significance, p = 0.020, would not remain significant under any reasonable family-wise or FDR correction across these tests. The Conclusions nevertheless build a 'stabilizing effect' statement on it. This also covers the selective-emphasis candidate c3.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single alpha hypothesis or omnibus correction under which p = 0.020 remains significant.

quotes.text: no adjustments were made for omnibus F-tests
electrophysiological findings suggest a potential stabilizing effect on cortical excitability, as reflected in attenuated occipital alpha reactivity

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that no adjustment was made for omnibus F-tests. 10.1186/s12872-024-04196-0.headline_claim: Home-based breathing and chest mobility exercises added to standardized home-based cardiac rehabilitation could potentially improve respiratory muscle strength and cardiorespiratory functional capacity in long COVID patients with cardiovascular comorbidities.
10.1186/s12872-024-04196-0.overall: The headline claim of improved cardiorespiratory functional capacity rests on unadjusted post-intervention comparisons with modest p-values (.016 to .032), no multiplicity control, and a baseline 6-MWT imbalance that accounts for most of the 52 m gap. The stress-test and VO2 outcomes were non-significant, and the conclusion on respiratory muscle strength is not supported by any measurement. The effect is best read as exploratory and tentative, with several small reporting errors (METS Δ, VO2 p in the Discussion, bottom chest p, the power-calculation unit) that do not alter the picture.

issues.title: About a dozen outcomes tested at p<.05 with no correction; the main positive results have p = .016 to .032
issues.explanation: The paper tests at least four primary and many secondary outcomes at an unadjusted 0.05 level. The three significant primary results (PCF .016, PEFR .031, 6-MWT .032) are all above a Bonferroni threshold for four primary outcomes. The stress-test results were non-significant. The claim of improved functional capacity is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing order or correction, or a statement that these results are exploratory.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was set at p < .05

second_reader.what_stands: About 11 outcomes were tested at an unadjusted p<.05, and the three main positive results (PCF, PEFR, 6-MWT) have p = .016 to .032. They would not meet even a Bonferroni threshold for the 4 registered primary outcomes. The one qualification is that the bottom chest result (p = .01) falls just outside the quoted range.

issues.title: Follow-up 6-MWT, PEFR and PCF compared without baseline adjustment; 6-MWT change difference is about 12 m, not 52 m
issues.explanation: Table 3 compares 12-week values only, though the outcomes are defined as changes from baseline. The intervention group started 41 m higher on the 6-MWT, and also higher on PEFR and PCF. Using change scores, the 6-MWT difference shrinks to roughly 12 m, and the significant 52 m difference largely reflects baseline. The functional-capacity claim is weaker than presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA) analysis, or a change-score comparison, still showing significant between-group differences.

quotes.text: Their 6-WMD also significantly increased

second_reader.what_stands: Follow-up 6-MWT, PEFR and PCF were compared as raw endpoints without baseline adjustment. The 6-MWT difference in change is about 12 m, not the 52 m quoted in the Discussion, because about 41 m of the gap was present at baseline. PEFR and PCF differences in change (about 43 and 47 L/min) remain roughly half the headline follow-up gaps, but I cannot say whether any of these would remain significant after adjustment.

issues.title: Conclusion claims improved respiratory muscle strength (not measured) and recommends the intervention
issues.explanation: The paper never measures respiratory muscle strength, such as inspiratory or expiratory pressures. The VO2 and METS outcomes were non-significant and were only estimated rather than measured. The study has 46 patients in a single centre with 12 weeks of follow-up. The conclusion that the intervention 'can be recommended' goes beyond these data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Respiratory muscle strength data in the trial, or conclusions limited to the outcomes actually measured.

quotes.text: improve respiratory muscle strength and cardiorespiratory functional capacity

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion's 'improve respiratory muscle strength' is not backed by any direct strength measurement. Only PEFR and PCF, which are indirect proxies, were measured, and the limitations do not mention this gap. The wording is hedged ('could potentially'), and the paper does ask for larger confirmatory studies. However, 'can be recommended for individuals with persistent fatigue' goes beyond a small trial in which fatigue was not an outcome and the estimated exercise-capacity measures showed no difference.

issues.title: Paper's primary outcomes omit the registered 6-MWT, which drives the sample size and the functional-capacity claim
issues.explanation: The registry lists four primary outcomes including change in 6-minute walk test at 3 months. The paper names only PC, PFR and stress tests as primary. Yet it bases the sample size on the 6-MWT and uses that result to support the functional-capacity conclusion. This is an inconsistency in how primary outcomes are labelled rather than demonstrated switching. It matters because the stress-test primary outcomes were non-significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or earlier registry version listing 6-MWT as secondary, or the paper explicitly labelling it primary.
