10.1186/s12879-023-08002-8.headline_claim: HBO2 appears to have a favorable safety profile for PCC considering the absence of SAE, but an unexpected high frequency of AE was observed.
10.1186/s12879-023-08002-8.overall: The paper is an interim, descriptive safety report on 20 subjects, and its baseline-versus-norm findings are plausible despite some mislabelled reference dispersions. The conclusion of a 'favorable safety profile' is not well supported given a 60% AE rate, 65% of AEs at least possibly drug-related, and no by-arm AE data in the paper itself. It should be read as tentative, and the efficacy question is untouched.

primary_outcome.name: RAND-36 physical functioning (PF) and role physical (RP) at 13 weeks

issues.title: 'Favorable safety profile' concluded from 20 subjects with 60% AE rate and no by-arm AE data in the paper
issues.explanation: The conclusion calls the safety profile favorable because no serious AEs occurred. Yet 31 AEs occurred in 60% of 20 subjects, 20 of which were at least possibly related to the study drug, and the paper does not report AEs by treatment arm. With no between-group figures and only 20 participants, the data cannot distinguish an HBO2 effect from a sham effect, and the absence of SAE in 20 people carries little weight.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: By-arm AE counts in the paper or supplement showing AE rates and relatedness comparable between HBO2 and sham arms, with a confidence interval supporting the safety claim.

quotes.text: HBO2 appears to have a favorable safety profile for PCC considering the absence of SAE but an unexpected high frequency of AE was observed.
Thirty-one AEs were recorded, at least one in 60% of subjects.
The number of patients experiencing an AE compared descriptively between groups.

second_reader.what_stands: True that the conclusion of a 'favorable safety profile' rests on 20 subjects, a pooled 60% AE rate (12 of 20) and zero SAEs (compatible with a true SAE rate up to about 15%), and that the main text gives no AE counts by arm even though it says arms were compared descriptively. Not fully true that no by-arm information exists: the AE listings are in Additional file 1, which I could not see. The authors also hedge ('appears') and openly flag the high AE frequency as unexpected, and 64.5% of AEs (20 of 31) were at least possibly drug-related, which sits uneasily with 'favorable'.

issues.title: Norm-group dispersions implausibly small: VAS SD 1.05 vs 95% CI 81-89; 6MWT SD 18, CST SD 1.23
issues.explanation: The reference VAS is printed as 85.1 with SD 1.05 but a 95% CI of 81-89, whose half-width of about 4 implies a much larger SD unless the sample were tiny. The reference 6MWT (SD 18 against a mean of 662) and chair stand (SD 1.23 against a mean of 25) dispersions look similarly small and may be SEs or other quantities labelled as SDs. The labelling inconsistency does not change the conclusion that baseline values are far below norms, but the norm comparisons cannot be reproduced as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source reference table showing that the reference SD is 1.05 or that the printed value is an SE with a CI computed on a different basis.

issues.title: JK listed both as receiving a consulting fee for this trial and as declaring no financial interests

The fee is disclosed, so nothing is concealed, but the statement is internally contradictory. The effect on the findings is negligible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the consulting fee was not considered a competing interest by the journal's policy.

10.1186/s12879-025-10984-6.headline_claim: MYP plus (Myelophil plus Aquilariae Lignum) may have pharmacological potential for managing fatigue and/or brain fog associated with Long COVID, given the observed improvements in an uncontrolled pilot study.
10.1186/s12879-025-10984-6.overall: The paper's own conclusion is appropriately modest: preliminary evidence of potential benefit from an observational pilot. Still, the large pre-post changes in self-rated outcomes cannot be attributed to MYP plus without a control group or blinding, and the biomarker-based mechanistic language is not supported by non-significant results. The one numerical discrepancy (TGF-β post value) is minor and does not alter any conclusion.

issues.title: Single-arm, open-label study with self-rated outcomes and only within-group paired tests; effect not attributable to MYP plus
issues.explanation: All 50 patients received MYP plus with no control arm and no blinding. The primary outcome (mKCFQ11) and the key secondary outcomes (fatigue and brain fog VAS, MFI-20, SF-12) are self-rated. Efficacy rests on paired before/after t-tests, which cannot separate drug effect from natural recovery (mean time since COVID was about 20 weeks), regression to the mean after enrolment on severe scores, or expectancy. The very large drops (mKCFQ11 75.3 to 40.5) therefore cannot be attributed to MYP plus. The hedged conclusion limits the damage, but the Discussion reads the changes as treatment effects.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo comparison group showing a between-group difference, or blinded or objective outcome assessment.

issues.explanation: The Discussion calls a non-significant IFN-γ change a 'slight upward trend' and says it suggests MYP plus 'may have contributed' to enhanced immune activity and symptom improvement. 10.1186/s12890-024-02965-3.headline_claim: Virtual pulmonary rehabilitation, delivered by video conference or self-directed pre-recorded videos, is feasible and safe for individuals with post COVID syndrome, and video-conference delivery can improve sit-to-stand capacity.
10.1186/s12890-024-02965-3.overall: The feasibility, safety and satisfaction conclusions are reasonably supported by this small pilot, and the registered primary outcomes match the paper. The statement that video-conference PR improves sit-to-stand rests on a single uncorrected p = 0.012 comparing 8 against 6 completers, with unequal dropout and no control arm, so it should be read as hypothesis-generating only. Several text-table slips (technical difficulties, Cohen's r, dropout rate) are minor but indicate loose reporting.

issues.title: Claim that video PR 'can improve' sit-to-stand rests on one unadjusted p = 0.012 in 8 vs 6 people, no control
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state that PR via video conference can improve sit-to-stand capacity, and the Discussion says it 'improved significantly' in PR VC. The data are a between-arm comparison of median changes in 8 versus 6 completers, with no untreated comparator. The within-group change in PR VC has a CI spanning zero, and the p-value is partly driven by a fall in the other arm. The feasibility and safety conclusions are reasonably supported, but the efficacy statement is not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison with an untreated or usual-care arm, or pre-specified within-group tests with a CI excluding zero.

quotes.text: The  results  also  suggested that  PR  via  video  conference  can  improve  sit-to-stand capacity  in  this  group  of  patients.
Despite this, we  demonstrated that  virtual  PR programs can be feasible, safe, and potentially beneficial for individuals  with  PCS.

second_reader.what_stands: The 'can improve' claim rests on one unadjusted, uncorrected Mann-Whitney p = 0.012 (secondary, exploratory outcome among ~27 between-group tests) comparing 8 with 6 participants, between two active arms with no no-treatment control, and no CI is given for the between-arm difference. The paper does hedge in places ('suggested', 'potentially beneficial', small sample size, no control group acknowledged), so the problem is that the Conclusions' and Discussion's wording ('can improve', 'improved significantly, indicating... could help functional recovery') is stronger than this evidence supports,

issues.explanation: Of 19 randomised, 14 were analysed: 8 of 9 in PR VC and 6 of 10 in PR SD. Efficacy comparisons use completers only with no sensitivity analysis. The text quotes a 29% dropout rate, but the counts given (3 dropouts after starting among 17 starters, or 5 of 19 post-randomisation) do not produce 29%. The unequal loss could bias the sit-to-stand contrast.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator giving 29% and a sensitivity analysis showing the sit-to-stand difference is robust to the missing participants.

Five reach nominal significance, including FEV1/FVC (p = 0.030), three DSQ-SF items and sit-to-stand (p = 0.012). With this many tests, a few such results are expected by chance. 10.1186/s12890-024-03047-0.headline_claim: Pulmonary rehabilitation improves physical and mental health indices in patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC).
10.1186/s12890-024-03047-0.overall: The data show that patients' functional and dyspnea scores were better after a rehabilitation program, but the design (55 patients, no control, retrospective) cannot attribute that improvement to rehabilitation, and the authors' language ('robust evidence', 'effective treatment') goes beyond it. The mental-health claim rests on HADS alone, since PHQ-9 did not improve. Table 1, Table 2 and the narrative on predictors contain denominator, sign and layout inconsistencies, so the predictor findings are unreliable, though the main pre/post differences are not much affected.

primary_outcome.name: Pre- to post-rehabilitation changes in 6MWT, TUG, CR reps, gait speed, MMRC, SOBQ, HADS, CAT and PHQ-9

issues.title: Uncontrolled pre-post change in 55 patients is presented as strong evidence PR is effective
issues.explanation: All efficacy results are within-patient changes before and after a 3-month program, with no comparison group. Natural recovery from PASC, regression to the mean and use of self-reported scales cannot be separated from rehabilitation. The paper's own Limitations say it cannot distinguish natural recovery from the intervention, yet the Discussion calls the evidence 'robust' and PR 'an effective treatment'. The data support improvement over time in patients who attended PR, not an effect of PR.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or matched control group showing no comparable improvement over the same period.

quotes.text: As an observational study, it lacks randomization and a control group, which are crucial for reducing biases and bolstering result validity.
The study does not clearly distinguish improvements from natural recovery versus those from PR intervention.
There were significant improvements in mobility, dyspnea scales, functionality, and mental health.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is an uncontrolled pre-post analysis of 55 patients, and the Discussion calls it 'strong' and 'robust' evidence that PR is effective and an 'effective treatment', wording the design cannot support because natural recovery, regression to the mean and lack of blinding are not separable from PR effect. This is tempered because the Limitations section explicitly acknowledges the missing control group and natural recovery, and the Conclusion is milder ('supports PR as an integrated model of care') and calls for RCTs; the mental-health claim is also overstated since PHQ-9 did not improve.

issues.title: Table 1 categorical rows do not reconcile to n=55 (smoking 88, alcohol 58, drug 110; hypertension 55+51)
issues.explanation: Several mutually exclusive categories in Table 1 add to more than the 55-patient cohort, for example smoking 36+51+1 = 88 and alcohol 1+2+53+2 = 58. Hypertension shows 55 (100%) 'No' and 51 (93%) 'Yes', while the text gives 26 (47%) with hypertension. The text figure matches the Asthma 'Yes' row, so the table's cells look shifted or mislabelled. The baseline table cannot be relied on for comorbidity prevalence, and hypertension and CKD are used as predictors in Table 4. The main pre/post results do not depend on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 or the source file showing that the printed cells are a conversion artefact and that category counts sum to 55.

issues.title: Stepwise selection of many predictors in 55 patients; selected effects interpreted mechanistically
issues.explanation: Predictors of change were chosen by stepwise selection from a large candidate set in a cohort of 55, with several rare categories (for example CHF n=2, ILD n=1 per Table 1). Such estimates are unstable and their p-values are optimistic, and some estimates here are very large (for example ICS -58.59 on SOBQ from n=3). The authors nevertheless interpret them as risk factors that limit improvement. The main pre/post results do not depend on this analysis.

issues.title: Text reads negative Table 4 change-score estimates as worse outcomes (TUG, MMRC, SOBQ, HADS, CAT, PHQ-9)
issues.explanation: Table 4 models post minus pre change, so negative estimates mean more improvement than the reference group. The Results and Discussion nevertheless describe DM, ILD, outpatient status and inpatient therapies as increasing TUG time, and also report CKD, ICS, CHF and active alcohol use as linked to higher scores. These all have negative estimates. The authors then draw clinical interpretations from them (for example 'increase in psychological distress'). Either the table signs or the narrative are wrong, so the predictor findings cannot be taken at face value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the models were coded with post-minus-pre reversed for these outcomes, or a corrected table whose signs match the text.

quotes.text: showed an increase in time taken to complete the TUG test
quotes.location: Results, Effect of pulmonary rehabilitation, para 2
Table 4, HADS, Chronic Heart Failure row

issues.title: Mean changes for TUG, SOBQ, CAT and MMRC differ from post minus pre means (e.g. TUG -3.50 vs -3.26)
issues.explanation: For four outcomes the printed mean change differs from the printed post mean minus pre mean by more than rounding. The likeliest reason is that pairs with missing data were handled differently in the means and in the paired test, but the paper never reports how many patients contributed to each outcome. The differences are small relative to the effects and do not change any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-outcome analysed n showing that pre and post means were computed on different subsets than the paired differences.

issues.title: Author affiliated with the evaluated PR provider; 'no competing interests' declared
issues.explanation: The program evaluated was delivered by Lifeline Physical Therapy, with which the study partnered, and one author lists Lifeline as their affiliation. The paper declares no competing interests without addressing this relationship. The affiliation is visible but the statement does not say whether the author has a financial interest in a favourable result of the program.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the affiliated author has no financial or other interest in the provider's results or program.

quotes.text: Lifeline Physical Therapy, Warrendale, PA, USA
Our study partnered with Lifeline Physical Therapy
The authors declare no competing interests.

10.1186/s12890-026-04249-4.headline_claim: Isolated inspiratory muscle strength training improves functional exercise capacity, quadriceps muscle oxygenation, peripheral muscle strength, dyspnea and fatigue in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome and CT-confirmed pulmonary involvement.
10.1186/s12890-026-04249-4.overall: The large 6-MWT and respiratory/peripheral muscle strength gains in the IMST arm are consistent across tables, but they come from an unblinded-in-practice comparison with a less supervised control arm, and the primary outcomes differ from the registered one. The claim of improved muscle oxygenation and oxygen utilization is not supported by the between-group tests, and several smaller reporting inconsistencies (eligibility, p-value asterisks, text-table mismatches) lower confidence in the overall reporting.

primary_outcome.name: 6-MWT distance (paper lists this with quadriceps muscle oxygenation as its primary outcomes)

issues.title: Muscle oxygenation 'improved' by IMST rests on within-arm change; resting SmO2 between-group p = 0.120
issues.explanation: The Discussion says IMST increased resting muscle oxygen saturation. That rests on a within-group pre-post p of 0.031, while the between-group effect in Table 3 is p = 0.120. The only significant between-group oxygenation effects (ΔSmO2, ΔSmO2 average) reflect a decline in controls rather than a rise in the IMST arm. The Conclusions' claim that IMST improved muscle oxygenation, a named primary outcome, is not supported by the between-group tests. Many oxygenation outcomes were tested with no multiplicity control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group analysis of resting SmO2 or the other oxygenation measures showing a significant benefit of IMST over control.

quotes.text: increased significantly within the group

second_reader.what_stands: The claimed improvement in muscle oxygenation is supported at rest and for SmO2min only by within-arm change; the between-group tests are non-significant (resting p=0.120, min p=0.391, max p=0.105). The only significant between-group SmO2 effects (ΔSmO2, ΔSmO2average) reflect a fall in the control arm while the IMST arm stayed unchanged (+0.20), so the 'improved' wording in the Conclusions overstates it.

issues.title: Registered primary outcome (oxygen consumption) is not reported; paper's primaries are SmO2 and 6-MWT
issues.explanation: The registry lists oxygen consumption on day one as the only primary outcome. The paper declares muscle oxygenation and 6-MWT as primary and does not report oxygen consumption or explain the change. The 6-MWT result is large, but readers cannot tell whether the primary set was chosen after seeing the data. The Acknowledgements suggest oxygen consumption was part of the original thesis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing muscle oxygenation and 6-MWT as primary, or a statement explaining that oxygen consumption is reported in a separate paper.

quotes.text: The primary outcomes were peripheral muscle oxygenation and functional
This study was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry (NCT05231395) on February 9th, 2022
Investigation of the effects of inspiratory muscle training on oxygen consumption

second_reader.what_stands: The registered primary outcome (oxygen consumption) is neither measured nor reported in the paper, whose stated primaries (SmO2 and 6-MWT) differ from it, and the paper does not explain or acknowledge the change; the Acknowledgements only hint that VO2 belongs to a wider thesis. Earlier registry versions were not checked, so it is unknown whether the registered outcome was altered before or after enrolment. The paper is also internally inconsistent on primaries, since the Conclusions add peripheral muscle strength.

issues.title: Control arm had phone follow-up only versus weekly supervised IMST sessions, with no sham device
issues.explanation: The IMST group received weekly supervised sessions and the control group only phone follow-up. The authors acknowledge this may have caused non-specific effects such as motivation or attention. The training effect cannot be separated from the supervision effect, especially for patient-reported dyspnea and fatigue and for effort-dependent performance tests. The 'triple blind' label is questionable because participants and trainers could probably tell the interventions apart.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the control arm received equally frequent supervised contact, or a sham-controlled sensitivity analysis showing the same effects.

quotes.text: the IMST group received weekly supervised sessions, whereas the control group was followed up by phone.
This difference in supervision may have introduced non-specific treatment effects

second_reader.what_stands: The control arm received phone follow-up and a home breathing programme with no device or sham load, while the IMST arm had weekly supervised sessions, as the authors acknowledge. The paper discloses this and proposes a sham in future studies, but still lists the triple-blind design as a strength, and non-specific attention effects on the subjective outcomes (dyspnea, fatigue) cannot be excluded.

issues.title: Exclusion criteria list diabetes, heart failure and CVD, yet Table 1 reports them in both arms
issues.explanation: The Methods list diabetes mellitus, heart failure and cardiovascular disease as exclusion criteria. Table 1 shows 4 participants with diabetes and 1 with heart failure in each arm, and 4 and 6 with coronary artery disease. Either the criteria were not applied as written or the Methods are misstated. The study population is therefore not what the eligibility text describes, which affects generalizability and safety interpretation more than the effect estimates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the exclusions applied only to uncontrolled or severe forms of these conditions.

| Diabetes mellitus                         | 4 (20%)
| Heart Failure                             | 1 (5%)

issues.title: Conclusions claim improved oxygen utilization and benefit for long-term hypoxemia that were not shown
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say IMST improves oxygen utilization, may help problems of long-term hypoxemia and promotes comprehensive recovery. The study did not measure oxygen consumption and resting SpO2 was normal in both arms (about 95% vs 94%). The muscle oxygenation evidence is weak (see the within-arm inference issue), and the study ended at 8 weeks. These statements go beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported oxygen consumption or hypoxemia outcomes showing a between-group benefit of IMST.

issues.title: Discussion FSS changes (14.96, 1.15) do not match Table 4 means (15.15, 0.87)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says fatigue fell by 14.96 points in the IMST group and 1.15 in controls. The Table 4 pre- and post-training means give falls of 15.15 and 0.87. The 6-MWT changes in the Results do match Table 2, so this is a localized reporting inconsistency. The direction of the fatigue effect is unchanged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values are adjusted or imputed estimates, or a table with different FSS means.

quotes.text: decreased  by  14.96  points
while the control group's decreased by 1.15 points

issues.title: Table 2 marks treatment-effect p = 0.051 and 0.057 as significant despite a p < 0.05 footnote
issues.explanation: The footnote defines asterisks as p < 0.05, but Δ HR (p = 0.051) and resting DBP (p = 0.057) carry them. Both values exceed the stated threshold. Neither is a primary outcome, so the effect on the conclusions is small, but it makes secondary hemodynamic results look significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote stating that asterisks include values up to p = 0.06.

quotes.text: *Statistically significant p-values ( p < 0.05)

issues.title: Sleep duration SD of 888.35 min/day (mean 394.25) is impossible; neighbours are 83-115
issues.explanation: Table 4 gives pre-training sleep for the IMST group as 394.25±888.35 min/day. Sleep is bounded between 0 and 1440 minutes, so the SD cannot exceed 720, and the post-training SD is 83.01. This is almost certainly a typographical slip. Sleep is a non-significant secondary outcome and nothing depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing a genuine SD above 720, which is arithmetically impossible for this range.

quotes.location: Table 4, Sleep duration row, pre-training IMST

issues.title: LCADL described as 4 subscales of 4 items each but also as 15 items (75 points)
issues.explanation: The Methods say the scale has 15 items in 4 subgroups 'each with 4 items', which would be 16 items. Table 4 subscale ranges imply 4, 6, 2 and 3 items, summing to 15, so only the description is wrong. This is a cosmetic slip that does not affect results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the inconsistency is within the Methods text.

(each with 4 items)

10.1186/s12903-023-02952-w.headline_claim: Low-level diode laser 940 nm therapy is effective in restoring taste sensation in patients with post-COVID-19 dysfunction.
10.1186/s12903-023-02952-w.overall: The direction of the result (earlier and more complete taste recovery with laser than placebo light) is plausible from the reported p-values. However, the paper gives no effect sizes, the trial is small (18 per arm) and has one session with 4-week follow-up, and the registry does not clearly match the reported outcome and sample. Several internal inconsistencies (Group II time since recovery, energy density, smoking p-value) lower confidence in the reporting but do not by themselves overturn the finding.

primary_outcome.name: Recovery of taste sensation (time to taste restoration / restoration status at 1 week, 4 weeks, and 1 month)

issues.title: Group II time since recovery 0.93 ± 0.28 months cannot coexist with a 4-week (≈0.92 month) minimum
issues.explanation: Inclusion required taste loss lasting at least four weeks after recovery, which is about 0.92 months. A group mean of 0.93 months with every one of 18 patients at or above 0.92 leaves almost no room for spread, so the largest possible SD is about 0.04, not 0.28. Either the eligibility criterion was not applied as written, or the variable was measured differently from how the paper describes it. This affects the baseline description more than the efficacy result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the time variable is measured from a different origin (e.g. onset of COVID-19, or a tolerance below 4 weeks), or the individual patient values.

quotes.text: for at  least  four  weeks  after  COVID-19  recovery
0.93 ± 0.28 months in Group II

issues.title: Group I about 6.5 years younger with fewer comorbidities; outcome analysis unadjusted in 18 per arm
issues.explanation: Group I averaged 38.2 years versus 44.8 in Group II, and had fewer comorbidities (33% vs 50%). The authors state that age plays a significant role in chemosensory recovery. With 18 per arm, chance imbalance can be material, and the outcome comparisons are not adjusted. This is a modest weakness rather than evidence of failed randomization.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis adjusted for age and comorbidity giving the same treatment effect.

quotes.text: The mean age of the cases in Group I was (38.22 ± 12.90) years, whereas, in Group II, it was (44.78 ± 16.67) years.

issues.title: Blinding asserted but not operationalised; allocation concealment not described; patient-reported taste responses
issues.explanation: The outcome depends on patients saying whether they perceive each taste. Blinding is stated in one sentence, with no account of how the placebo was made indistinguishable from a 1 W 940 nm treatment, or how allocation was concealed from the person assigning patients. The same operator delivered both treatments. The risk of bias is moderate rather than established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of allocation concealment and of placebo/assessor masking, e.g. blinded assessor logs or a blinding-integrity check.

quotes.text: The  patients  and  assessors  were  blinded throughout the period of the study.
The patient was  indicated  whether  the  perceived  flavor  was  sweet, salty,  bitter,  or  acid.

issues.title: Registered primary outcome at 6 weeks vs paper's 1–4 week assessments; registry enrollment 40 vs 36 analysed
issues.explanation: The registry lists a taste survey at 6 weeks as the primary outcome and 40 participants enrolled. The paper defines the primary outcome as recovery of taste with assessments up to 4 weeks and reports 36 patients, with no mention of the registered time point or the 4 missing participants. The mismatch cannot be resolved from the paper alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry history showing the primary outcome and time frame were unchanged and equivalent, and an explanation of the 4 participants not in the paper.

quotes.text: The primary outcome measure was the recovery of taste sensation.
36 patients (18 in each group)

issues.title: Unqualified 'effective' conclusion from 36 patients, one centre, one session, 4-week follow-up, no effect sizes
issues.explanation: The conclusion says laser therapy is effective in restoring taste in post-COVID patients, without hedging. The data are 18 per arm, a single centre, a single session and follow-up to 4 weeks only. No effect sizes or confidence intervals are given, and the limitations paragraph mentions only age and sample size. The direction of the finding is supported, but the strength and generality of the claim are not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Effect estimates with confidence intervals and a replication or longer follow-up showing sustained benefit.

quotes.text: The findings  of  this  study  indicate  that  low-level  laser therapy is effective in restoring taste sensation in patients with  post-COVID-19  dysfunction.
The present study had several limitations.

issues.title: Smoking history p = 0.153 does not match counts 6/18 vs 5/18 (expected p near 1.0)
issues.explanation: Table 1 reports 6 (33.3%) current smokers in Group I and 5 (27.7%) in Group II with p = 0.153. A difference of one patient in 18 per arm gives a p-value near 1, not 0.153. The error does not change the conclusion that the groups are not significantly different, but it shows the baseline table was not reliably computed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 0.153 refers to a different test, e.g. smoking intensity or pack-years, rather than the current-smoker split.

quotes.text: Current smokers6 (33.3%)5 (27.7%)0.153

issues.title: Stated 4 J/cm² energy density does not follow from 1 W for 6 min on a 15 mm spot; treated area not given
issues.explanation: The delivered energy is 360 J. On a single 15 mm spot that is about 200 J/cm², far above the 4 J/cm² stated. The figure is only reachable if the beam covered roughly 90 cm², which the paper does not state. The dosimetry is therefore not reproducible from the text, though this does not directly change the outcome comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the irradiated area or fluence per pass that yields 4 J/cm².

quotes.text: The total time of the laser was 6 min on tissue
had an energy density of 4 J/cm2

10.1186/s12906-025-04784-3.headline_claim: Balneotherapy with aquatic exercises can alleviate several post-COVID symptoms, particularly musculoskeletal pain and fatigue, though larger RCTs are needed to confirm the results.
10.1186/s12906-025-04784-3.overall: The main finding, that balneotherapy plus aquatic exercise improved pain and fatigue scores relative to usual care, rests on an open-label, retrospectively registered trial with only self-reported outcomes and a complete-case analysis labelled ITT. Direction conventions in the figures and tables are unclear, and several printed numbers are wrong (text CI, Table 5 totals, Table 4 estimates), though none is large enough to overturn the findings. The claims of 'clear effectiveness' and an 'excellent safety profile' are stronger than the evidence supports, and the results are best read as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline in questionnaire scores (PCFS, mMRC, SF-36, PSQI, HADS, MFE-30, VAS), compared between groups

primary_outcomes.measure: Differences in questionnaire scores in follow-up time points compared to baseline between both groups
primary_outcomes.time_frame: 2 months i.e., baseline, post-balneotherapy (or one month post-baseline in the control group), and 1 month post-balneotherapy (or 2 months post-baseline in the control group)

issues.title: Open-label trial vs usual care with only self-reported outcomes supports effectiveness claims weakly
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation, the control group received no comparable attention or placebo, and every outcome is a self-reported questionnaire or VAS. Expectation, attention and contact effects cannot be separated from any true effect of balneotherapy plus exercise. The Discussion names this as a limitation but still states 'clear effectiveness' and the Conclusions say BT can alleviate several symptoms. The conclusion should be tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham or attention-matched control arm or objective endpoints showing the same effects.

quotes.text: This study was designed as a prospective open-labelled randomized controlled trial
to continue with usual pharmacological care and regular daily activities
The  unblinded  design  and  short  follow-up  were  perhaps  the  most  important  limitations

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is an open-label, usual-care-controlled trial with exclusively self-reported outcomes, so its effectiveness claims are only weakly supported because expectation and attention effects cannot be separated from a treatment effect. The authors acknowledge the unblinded design, short follow-up and self-report in their limitations and ask for larger RCTs, but still describe 'clear effectiveness' in the strengths paragraph, which is stronger than this design allows.

issues.title: Fig 2/3 captions state improvement directions contradicting the SF-36 and PSQI scale definitions
issues.explanation: SF-36 is defined as 0 (worst) to 100 (best), yet the Fig 2 caption says a decrease indicates improvement. PSQI is 0 (best) to 21 (worst), yet the Fig 3 caption says an increase indicates improvement. The SF-36 betas are negative and the PSQI, HADS and VAS betas positive, and all are called improvements, which only works if the sign convention is control minus treatment. That convention is never stated, so a reader cannot verify the direction of the effect from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the GLM group coding (control as comparison group) and corrected figure captions, or the supplementary change-score table showing BT improving on each scale.

quotes.text: A decrease in follow-up scores vs. baseline indicates improvement in the scales.
Each subdomain ranges from 0 (worst) to 100 (best)
An increase in the follow-up scores vs. baseline indicates improvement in the scales.

issues.title: 'Intention-to-treat' label but only 90 of 98 randomised were analysed (complete cases)
issues.explanation: The paper describes 98 participants as the intention-to-treat population, but the outcome analyses include 47 of 51 BT and 43 of 47 control participants. Two BT participants withdrew because of adverse effects, who would be expected to have worse outcomes, so analysing completers likely favours the intervention. Attrition is small, so the impact is limited, but the ITT label is not accurate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with imputed data for the 8 missing participants showing unchanged effects.

quotes.text: 98 were finally included in the intention-to-treat study according to eligibility criteria.
Finally, 47 patients from the intervention group and 43 from the control group completed the study (Fig. 1) and were included in the outcome analyses.

issues.title: Described as 'prospective' but registered in March 2023, about a year after the registry's study start
issues.explanation: The paper calls the trial prospective and gives the registration date as 13/03/2023. According to the registry, the study started on 2022-03-29, around 11 months before it was first submitted on 2023-03-09. The 15 outcome scales were all treated as primary, with no single prespecified primary outcome. Retrospective registration limits confidence that outcomes and analyses were specified before data were seen.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history or a protocol showing the outcomes were fixed before the first participant was enrolled, or enrolment starting after March 2023.

quotes.text: This  study  was  designed  as  a  prospective  open-labelled randomized  controlled  trial  (RCT:  NCT05765591;  date 13/03/2023).

issues.title: 'Excellent safety profile' and 'clear effectiveness' stated despite 33% adverse effects and open-label design
issues.explanation: 17 of 51 participants in the BT arm reported adverse effects, two withdrew because of fatigue and dizziness, and events were only recorded during BT in the BT arm. This does not support 'excellent safety'. Several of the improvements listed (sleep, mental health) were lost one month later, and the design is unblinded, so 'clear effectiveness' is stronger than the evidence permits.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adverse-event data collected equally in both arms over the full follow-up showing low event rates.

quotes.text: with acceptable tolerability and an excellent safety profile
showing  clear  effectiveness  in  diminishing some symptoms
the adverse events were monitored during BT.

issues.title: One-month energy/fatigue CI in text [-24.23;-10.66] differs from Table 4 [-24.32;-8.71]
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the one-month energy/fatigue beta of -16.52 with the CI from the post-balneotherapy column. Table 4 prints [-24.32;-8.71] for the one-month column. The text interval is narrower and does not centre on -16.52, so the prose slightly overstates the precision of a headline follow-up result. The conclusion that the effect persisted is unaffected, since the table interval still excludes zero.

issues.title: Table 4 mMRC and PCFS estimates are not centred in their CIs (likely dropped decimal digits)

For PCFS one-month, beta 0.16 with CI [-0.281;0.313] has a midpoint of 0.016, matching a beta of 0.016. issues.title: Table 5 fatigue and weakness rows: 10 + 10 = 20 but total printed as 16/17

10.1186/s12913-024-11679-5.headline_claim: Physical and mental health rehabilitation improves quality of life in patients with long-term post-COVID-19 condition and is likely to be a cost-effective use of NHS resources.
10.1186/s12913-024-11679-5.overall: The cost-effectiveness findings are probabilistic and reported with wide uncertainty. The base-case analysis used imputation, so the complete-case concern does not undermine it. The 'likely cost-effective' conclusion is reasonable, but the statements that the intervention improves quality of life and has demonstrated clinical effectiveness go beyond the paper's non-significant EQ-5D QALY and cost differences in an open-label trial. The Table 3 CI misprint is trivial.

issues.title: Conclusion says QoL improves; own EQ-5D QALY gain 0.026 (CI -0.005 to 0.052) and cost difference span zero
issues.explanation: The base-case incremental QALYs and costs both have intervals including zero, and the authors say the credible region runs from dominated to dominant. 10.1186/s12916-023-03237-3.headline_claim: The micro-choice concentrated group rehabilitation was highly acceptable and produced clinically and statistically significant improvements in functioning, illness perception and self-rated health across chronic low back pain, long COVID and type 2 diabetes at 3-month follow-up.
10.1186/s12916-023-03237-3.overall: This is an open, single-arm pilot, and its main findings of high acceptability and satisfaction are descriptive and can be relied on. The claims of efficacy and of a 'generic', trans-diagnostic effect are weaker than stated, because there is no control, the outcomes are self-reported, the diabetes group did not improve on functioning, and the registered patient-activation outcome is not reported. Table 3 gives an exact McNemar p of .054 for all patients, above the stated alpha of 0.05, and none of the subgroup p values (1, .134, .210) is significant either.
