issues.title: BIPQ2 (8-item sum) pre mean 20.79 is below its 4-item subset BIPQ1 mean 22.30
issues.explanation: The Methods describe BIPQ2 as the complete questionnaire (sum of eight items scored 1-10), and the Table 2 footnote says it also includes the four BIPQ1 items. A sum of eight items scored 1-10 must exceed the 4-item subset by at least 4 points, yet the BIPQ2 mean (20.79) is below the BIPQ1 mean (22.30). BIPQ2 is therefore most likely the four remaining items and is mislabelled, which leaves the BIPQ1 versus BIPQ2 contrast, and the claim that effects were 'not expected' on the rest, hard to interpret as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that BIPQ2 comprises only the four items not in BIPQ1 (with the footnote and Methods wording corrected), or item-level data showing the sums are consistent.

quotes.text: Also includes the BIPQ items

issues.title: Uncontrolled, open pre-post design with self-reported outcomes; Discussion says results 'clear' and spurious change 'low'
issues.explanation: All efficacy findings come from baseline-to-follow-up change in a single, unblinded group. Self-report outcomes such as illness perception, functioning and self-rated health are open to expectancy effects, and patients enrolled at peak severity are prone to regression to the mean. The authors concede they cannot attribute improvement to the intervention, yet go on to call the improvement 'clear' and the spurious explanation unlikely. As a pilot, the design supports only a tentative signal, which fits the word 'promising' but not 'clear'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waiting-list control, or objective outcome data, showing similar improvement.

quotes.text: In this open non-randomized pilot study
Since this was a pre-post design with patients as their own controls
we argue that the likelihood of the results being spurious

issues.title: Registered primary 'patient activation' not reported; headline WSAS not among registered primaries
issues.explanation: The registry record lists four primary outcomes: completion rates, satisfaction, change in illness perception, and change in patient activation. The paper reports the first three but never mentions patient activation, and puts the functional-impairment measure (WSAS), which is not a registered primary, at the centre of its conclusions. Because earlier versions of the record were not retrieved, this is selective reporting rather than a proven switch, and the effect on the conclusion is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The protocol or an earlier registry version showing patient activation was removed or moved, and WSAS pre-specified as the main outcome; or patient activation reported elsewhere.

quotes.text: increase the patients' level of functioning
The study was registered in Clinical
quotes.location: Methods, Ethical considerations and data protection

issues.title: Conclusions state generic functional improvement; type 2 diabetes WSAS (p = .11) and EQ-5D were not significant
issues.explanation: The Conclusions report significant improvement in functioning, illness perception and self-rated health, and describe a 'generic' approach, without saying that the diabetes group (n about 61) did not improve significantly on WSAS or on the EQ-5D index and VAS. The Discussion also says it 'seems clear' the outcomes improved trans-diagnostically. The null result is acknowledged earlier in the paper, so the issue is a headline that is broader than the data for one of the three diagnostic groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Conclusions sentence that explicitly excludes diabetes from the functioning and self-rated health findings.

quotes.text: but not for diabetes patients
as well as the illness perception and self-rated health status were found

issues.title: Ethics approval number printed as 2020/101638 in Methods but 2020-101648 in Declarations
issues.explanation: The same regional ethics approval is cited with two different numbers (101638 and 101648). At least one is a typographical error. This has no bearing on the results but makes the approval harder to verify.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the ethics board issued two reference numbers for this project.

quotes.location: Methods, Ethical considerations and data protection

quotes.text: Regional Etisk Komité Vest 2020-101648
quotes.location: Declarations, Ethics approval and consent to participate

10.1186/s12962-026-00748-7.headline_claim: A brief cognitive-behavioural outpatient rehabilitation programme was cost-effective, dominating care as usual in non-hospitalised post-COVID-19 patients, and should be implemented in clinical care.
10.1186/s12962-026-00748-7.overall: The trial shows a higher EQ-5D-based QALY gain and lower reported costs for the intervention, and the arithmetic of the headline figures is internally consistent. However, both effect and cost inputs are self-reported in an open-label, single-centre study, with coarse cost measurement and heavy imputation. The confident recommendation to implement is stronger than this evidence supports.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 Physical Function Subscale (SF-36-PFS) at T1

issues.title: Open-label trial: self-reported EQ-5D-5L and utilisation drive the QALY gain and the dominance claim
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation while completing the self-reported EQ-5D-5L and the health-care utilisation questionnaire. Both the QALY gain (0.056) and the cost savings come from these outcomes. Expectation or disappointment effects could inflate the intervention-versus-usual-care gap. The limitations section mentions the lack of blinding, but the conclusion is stated without qualification. The registry's SINGLE masking entry conflicts with the paper's statement and does not mitigate the bias for self-reported outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that outcomes were collected or verified by blinded assessors or from registries, or an attention-matched control arm producing similar utility differences.

quotes.text: the lack of blinding to group allocation
The EQ-5D-5L responses were transformed into utilities and valued using the Norwegian tariff
In summary, increased QALYs and reduced costs, the intervention 'dominates' the CAU.

second_reader.what_stands: The QALY gain comes from self-reported EQ-5D-5L collected from participants who knew their allocation. The cost difference rests on self-reported yes/no utilisation, with about 21-28% of it imputed. The paper lists the lack of blinding as a limitation, but its conclusion does not discuss how this bears on the dominance claim. The arithmetic itself is consistent with the printed figures, apart from the small gap between adjusted and unadjusted QALY differences.

issues.title: Costs built from binary self-developed questionnaire, assumed visit counts and one hospital's tariff
issues.explanation: Utilisation was recorded as yes/no on a self-developed questionnaire, with free text coded by one author. Visit numbers were assumed from national averages. One Norwegian hospital trust's valuation of a 24-hour stay was applied to all admissions. Roughly 21-27% of utilisation data were missing and imputed. The authors say precise cost estimation is difficult, yet the dominance conclusion is reported with high certainty. The direction of any bias is unclear, so the cost savings are less secure than the confidence intervals suggest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry-based utilisation data or a validated resource-use instrument showing similar cost differences.

quotes.text: Quantification of visits and valuation of visits was challenging due to only binary data and free text comments
These numbers were used for every hospital stay in the study,

second_reader.what_stands: The costs are built from yes/no questionnaire data, assumed (not observed) visit counts taken from national means, website prices for private rehabilitation, and a single hospital trust's valuation applied to all stays. The authors acknowledge this as a limitation. The supplement was not available, so I could not check how much each assumption moves the cost difference.

issues.title: Implementation recommendation exceeds single-centre, open-label, 12-month cost analysis
issues.explanation: The authors call the programme a cost-effective solution for public health services and say it should be implemented. The evidence is one centre, no blinding, a 12-month horizon, assumed cost inputs, and imputation of 26-28% of EQ-5D data. Limitations are listed but do not temper the conclusion. The complete-case analysis halves the QALY gain, and one extremely expensive CAU patient shifted mean CAU cost by about 12,000 NOK.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Multicentre replication, blinded or registry-based outcomes, or longer follow-up confirming the savings.

quotes.text: and should be implemented in clinical
This study shows that robust public health services with outpatient treatment for PCC is a cost-effective solution.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion ('should be implemented in clinical care') and the Discussion ('This study shows ... is a cost-effective solution') are stronger than a single-centre, unblinded, 12-month analysis with assumed cost inputs can support. The authors do state the limitations in their own section. The recommendation is nonetheless worded without qualification and goes beyond what the evidence shows.

issues.title: Heterogeneous, undefined usual-care comparator including costly inpatient rehabilitation
issues.explanation: CAU is any PCC treatment available outside the centre, and its content is not characterised. Inpatient rehabilitation in CAU was the main cost driver. The authors note that a different comparator could change incremental cost and effect, but the dominance result does not reflect this. The finding is therefore specific to this comparator mix.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with a defined, less costly standard-care comparator showing the same dominance.

quotes.text: Care as usual is a relevant comparator, but standard care varies

10.1186/s12967-022-03488-3.headline_claim: Oral anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate (AEO) at 500-1000 mg BID or 1000 mg TID reduces physical and mental fatigue in ME/CFS and Long COVID, supporting further development with longer randomized placebo-controlled studies.
10.1186/s12967-022-03488-3.overall: The paper is an open-label, uncontrolled proof-of-concept whose 'highly significant' fatigue reductions come from within-group comparisons with baseline on self-reported scales, so they cannot show that oxaloacetate caused the improvement. In addition, several reported figures are inconsistent (text versus table values for Long COVID, the placebo percentage, adverse-event denominators, and the Long COVID responder column), and the historical-placebo comparison is poorly defined. The results are hypothesis-generating only, and the efficacy and safety wording in the Key Points and conclusion goes further than the design allows.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder Fatigue Scale change from baseline (Likert and bimodal scoring), with clinical response defined as bimodal score of 4 or less

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from uncontrolled, unblinded, within-group baseline comparisons of self-reported fatigue
issues.explanation: All arms received active treatment with no concurrent control, no blinding, and no randomization. Significance was tested by comparing each group to its own baseline with Student's t-test, with no correction for the many outcomes and time points. The only comparator is a historical placebo rate from a different trial. The 'highly significant' reductions and 'clinical efficacy' therefore show change after treatment, not an effect of the treatment, and the study cannot support its Key Points and conclusion as written.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control arm, or a between-group analysis against a matched placebo group with blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: Significance was calculated from student's T Test scores in Excel by comparison to baseline.
There was no blinding in this study.
As there was no placebo group (only historical placebo), there was no randomization into a separate group.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy conclusions rest on open-label, uncontrolled, within-group changes from baseline in self-reported fatigue, with no concurrent control. Any placebo response, regression to the mean, or expectation effect would be indistinguishable from a treatment effect. The authors do disclose the lack of blinding and of a concurrent control and recommend randomized trials, but the headline wording ('highly significant', 'clinical efficacy') is stronger than this design supports.

issues.title: '75.0% (57/76)' and '62.8% (27/43)' improvement over placebo use an undefined measure vs a responder-rate placebo
issues.explanation: The paper states that 75.0% of ME/CFS and 62.8% of Long COVID patients 'saw improvement' over what historical placebo would give. The criterion for improvement is not defined, and does not match the clinical-response definition (bimodal 4 or less) used for the placebo benchmark and in Table 2, where only 5+8+8 = 21 of 76 ME/CFS patients (27.6%) qualified. The comparison makes the treatment look much better than the paper's own responder data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated, prespecified definition of improvement applied identically to the treated and historical placebo patients.

quotes.text: 62.8% (27/43) of the Long COVID patients saw improvement over historical placebo.
75.0% of the ME/CFS participants (57/76) saw an improvement in  fatigue  over  what  would  be  expected  by  placebo

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does not define what counts as 'improvement over placebo' for the 75.0% (57/76) and 62.8% (27/43) figures. The 5.9% placebo benchmark is used both as a mean percent change and as a responder rate, with an inconsistent denominator and a citation that does not match the text. These two figures cannot be verified or compared with the placebo figure from the information printed in the paper.

issues.title: Long COVID Likert 6-week reductions in text (22.5%, 27.9%) match ME/CFS cells, not Long COVID table (36%, 25.3%)
issues.explanation: The Results text reports Long COVID 6-week Chalder Likert reductions of 22.5% (500 mg BID) and 27.9% (1000 mg BID). The Long COVID table gives 36% and 25.3% for those rows, while 22.5% and 27.9% are the ME/CFS Overall Likert 6-week values in Table 3. The text appears to quote the wrong population, so the Long COVID Likert effect is misreported in prose (understated for 500 mg, overstated for 1000 mg), and the claimed dose-related improvement in Long COVID cannot be read consistently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Long COVID table columns are not Likert 6-week values, or that the text values come from a different analysis of the Long COVID groups.

quotes.text: highly significantly  reduced  fatigue  levels  by  27.9%  from baseline  at  6-weesks
quotes.location: Results, Long COVID 1000 mg BID paragraph

quotes.text: by  22.5%  in  6  weeks
quotes.location: Results, Long COVID 500 mg BID paragraph

issues.title: 'Safe and tolerable' conclusion rests on small uncontrolled safety data with 9/22 Long COVID dropouts unexplained
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that 1000-3000 mg daily was safe and tolerable. The supporting data are a short paragraph of non-severe events with inconsistent denominators, no reasons for the substantial Long COVID dropout, and no safety-specific design. The data are compatible with good tolerability but are too thin to state it as a conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow diagram with reasons for withdrawal showing no dropout was related to adverse effects, and consistent adverse-event denominators.

quotes.text: 1000-3000 mg anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate daily was both safe and tolerable in this population for the duration of the trial.
The  high  dropout  rate  was  probably due to the recruitment of the COVID portion of the trial from social media

issues.title: 9 of 22 Long COVID 1000 mg BID patients dropped out; last-observation-carried-forward is undeclared in Methods
issues.explanation: Roughly 41% of the Long COVID 1000 mg BID arm dropped out, and their earlier values were carried forward, which is mentioned only in the Discussion. The authors report that completers improved by 47.5% on Likert versus 27.9% (text) or 25.3% (table) in the analysed arm. Which numbers are imputed is not shown in the tables, so the Long COVID dose response and the efficacy estimates for that arm are not interpretable, and the carry-forward tends to understate the effect among those who stayed in.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow diagram and a prespecified missing-data method showing results for completers and imputed data separately.

quotes.text: Improvement  at  the  higher  dosage  of 1000 mg BID in Long-COVID patients was lower due to 9 out of 22 dropping out of the trial, and the continuation of the previous data forward.
drop-out  rates  were  higher in the Long COVID groups than in the ME/CFS groups

issues.title: Funder's officer analysed the data; funder role in design and reporting not stated
issues.explanation: The funding and the author's position at the funding company are declared. However, the company officer analysed and interpreted the data, and nothing says who designed the trial, who had access to the raw data, or whether the funder influenced reporting. Data are available only on request. With an unblinded design and a marketed product, this adds to the risk of favourable interpretation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the sponsor's role, independent statistical analysis, or deposited raw data.

quotes.text: AC analyzed and interpreted the patient data regarding patient survey responses.
Author Alan Cash is an officer in a pharmaceutical company that provided the funding for this clinical trial.

issues.title: Historical placebo response 5.9% equals 2/34, not 2 of the 29 non-dropouts the text describes (6.9%)
issues.explanation: The text says 34 patients were given placebo, 5 dropped out, and only two of those who did not drop out improved (5.9%). With 29 completers, 2/29 is 6.9%, and 5.9% is only reached with a denominator of 34. The Results then describe the same 5.9% as a mean Likert improvement over baseline, so it is unclear what the comparator quantity is. The comparator for the paper's 'compares well with historical placebo' claim is therefore mis-specified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source placebo trial reporting 2 responders among 29 completers with 5.9% computed on another basis, or the authors clarifying that 5.9% is on all 34 randomized.

quotes.text: 34  patients  were  given placebo,  5  dropped  out  of  the  study.
Only  two  patients (5.9%) of the patients that did not drop out saw clinical improvement

script.explanation: 2/29 = 6.90%, but the paper prints 5.9, outside the rounding interval [5.85, 6.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 33.9 rather than 29.

issues.title: Long COVID 'reached 4 or less' figures (46.8%, 20.7%) match the 'Bimodal' column, not '4 or Below' (45.5%, 23.8%)
issues.explanation: Table 2 and the conclusion present 46.8% (500 mg BID) and 20.7% (1000 mg BID) as the percentage of Long COVID patients who got to 4 or less on the bimodal scale. In the Long COVID table those values sit in the 'Bimodal' column, while the '4 or Below' column shows 45.5% and 23.8%. The ME/CFS rows use the responder column, so the two populations are summarised with different measures. The effect on the headline is small for the 500 mg group but changes the ranking of the two Long COVID doses' responder rates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation from the authors that the Long COVID columns are mislabelled and the 'Bimodal' column holds the responder percentage.

quotes.text: (% of Treated Patients that reduced the Chalder Fatigue Bimodal Score to 4 or less)
up to 46.8% of Long  COVID  fatigue  patients achieved  clinical  efficacy

issues.title: ME/CFS adverse-event denominators (26 for 500 mg BID, 24 for 1000 mg BID) differ from group sizes (23, 29)
issues.explanation: The adverse-effects paragraph gives 2/23 and 1/26 for the 500 mg BID group, which has N = 23, and 2/24 for the 1000 mg BID group, which has N = 29. The same group is given two different denominators in one sentence, and the 1000 mg BID denominator matches the TID group. The adverse event rates cannot be computed reliably, which matters because the conclusion calls the doses safe.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow diagram showing that the stated safety denominators are the actual numbers analysed for safety in those arms.

quotes.text: Insomnia (1/26 in the 500 mg BID group)
2/24 in the 1000 mg BID group

issues.title: 'Improving at 6 weeks over 2 weeks' does not hold for several ME/CFS 500 mg BID measures
issues.explanation: The Results state that fatigue reduction improved from 2 to 6 weeks. In Table 3 for ME/CFS 500 mg BID the overall bimodal reduction goes from 25.0% to 23.7%, mental fatigue from 19.4% to 17.5%, and the treated percentage at or below 4 is unchanged at 21.7%. The general statement holds for the higher-dose groups but is not true for the lowest dose.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the statement was explicitly limited to the Likert score or to the higher-dose groups.

quotes.text: The reduction in fatigue was also seen with increased time of dosage, improving at 6 weeks over 2 weeks.

10.1186/s12967-022-03660-9.headline_claim: Treamid, a 4-week oral treatment at 50 mg daily, improved clinically significant FVC and/or DLCO and dyspnea in patients recovering from COVID-19 pneumonia, was well tolerated, and can be safely administered after COVID.
10.1186/s12967-022-03660-9.overall: The primary two-arm result (41% vs 17%, p=0.036) is a modest positive finding from a small exploratory trial whose size was derived from a single-arm design. The Discussion statement that the data 'clearly showed' benefit including improved lung function, the safety claim, and the women-subgroup claim all go beyond the evidence, while secondary lung-function outcomes are null. Text-table slips on AEs and the safety set are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Proportion of patients with clinically significant improvement in FVC and/or DLCO at week 4 vs baseline (mITT)

primary_outcomes.measure: Rate of clinically significant change in FVC and/or DLCO at Week 4 relative to the baseline value

issues.title: 'Clearly showed' benefit and improved lung function rest on p=0.036 and 0.031, with null lung-function secondaries
issues.explanation: The primary comparison is only modestly significant (p=0.036 mITT, 0.031 PPS) in 59 patients, and the sample size was derived from a single-arm design. The DLCO component is not significant (p=0.056). Table 2 shows no between-group difference in FEV1, FVC, TLC, FRC or DLCO, and no multiplicity control was applied across the many secondary outcomes. 'Clearly showed ... improving lung function' therefore overstates what a small phase 2 trial supports, which is at best a signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable as a numeric issue; it would soften if the text called the findings preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: The  here  described  data  clearly  showed  the  beneficial  effects  of  Treamid in the treatment of long-COVID patients
There  was  no  difference  in  clinical  response  regarding pulmonary function (FEV1, FVC, TLC, FRC, and DLCO)

second_reader.what_stands: The claim holds: the statement that the data 'clearly showed' benefit and 'improved lung function' rests on a composite responder endpoint (p=0.036 mITT, p=0.031 PPS, the latter being the same endpoint in a different population), while every continuous lung-function secondary (FEV1, FVC, TLC, FRC, DLCO) showed no between-group difference, and the DLCO responder component was p=0.056. The authors do hedge elsewhere (small, exploratory, larger trials needed), so the problem is the strength of the discussion sentence relative to the evidence, not an absence of caveats; the post hoc women-only TLC

issues.title: Post hoc women-only analysis (19 vs 14) with unadjusted p-values and AIC-selected models reported as 'more effective'
issues.explanation: The women-only analysis was post hoc, had no multiplicity adjustment, and used models chosen from eight candidates by AIC. Many of the 33-patient comparisons are non-significant or differ by test (Borg median regression p=0.208). Reporting that Treamid 'was more effective in women' goes beyond what a subgroup chosen after the fact can support, though the label 'exploratory' is stated beside it. It does not drive the primary conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sex-by-treatment interaction test on the primary endpoint, or replication in the planned larger trial.

quotes.text: The corresponding pairwise comparisons of adjusted changes in  modified Borg dyspnea score, TLC and lung damage for  women  of  Treamid  and  placebo  groups  were  made without p-value adjustment.
An exploratory analysis showed that Treamid was more effective in women

issues.title: 'Safely administered' concluded from 29 Treamid-treated patients, 28 days dosing and 2-week follow-up
issues.explanation: Safety was descriptive only, in 29 treated patients. Grade 2 AEs occurred in 2 Treamid patients and none on placebo, and two treatment-related AEs were seen on Treamid. A study of this size cannot exclude uncommon harms, so the safety claim is stronger than the data allow, although the paper elsewhere asks for larger trials.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger safety database or an explicit statement that safety conclusions are preliminary.

quotes.text: Treamid  was  well  tolerated  and  can  be  safely  administered  to  patients  discharged  after  COVID.

issues.title: Sample size from a single-arm A'Hern design (26 patients, one-sided alpha) but analysed as a two-arm comparison
issues.explanation: The target of 60 patients was set from a single-arm, single-stage design with one-sided alpha 0.05. The primary comparison is a two-sided two-group test with 29 vs 30 patients. The trial is therefore not powered for the comparison it reports, and the modest p-values (0.031 to 0.036) are fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power calculation for the two-arm comparison in the statistical analysis plan.

quotes.text: the population size was determined according to single-arm, single-stage A'Hern design [26]

issues.title: Respiratory tract infection AE assigned to placebo in text but to Treamid (1 case) in Table 5
issues.explanation: The safety text lists respiratory tract infection among the additional mild AEs of the placebo group. Table 5 shows the single case in the Treamid column and none in placebo. The table's grade 2 row (3 Treamid events) only adds up if the infection belongs to Treamid, so the prose misattributes a Treamid AE to placebo. This is a minor reporting error with no effect on the main results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary AE listings showing the respiratory infection occurred in a placebo patient and that the table column is wrong.

quotes.text: respiratory tract infection, myodynia, and mitral valve prolapse in placebo group
Table 5 Summary of the observed adverse events in Treamid and placebo groups of SS population
quotes.location: Table 5 caption (Respiratory tract infection row: Treamid 1, placebo 0)

issues.title: Safety set lists 31 placebo patients although one placebo patient received no drug (mITT 30)
issues.explanation: The safety set is defined as patients who received at least one dose and is stated to include 31 placebo patients. A footnote says one placebo patient did not receive the drug, which is why the mITT has 30. The safety set denominator, and so the placebo AE percentages (for example 9/31 = 29.0%), include a patient who was not exposed. The effect is small, but the definition and the count disagree.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that the patient did receive at least one dose and was excluded from efficacy for another reason.

quotes.text: The safety population (SS) included 60 patients (29 in Treamid and 31 in placebo) who received at least one dose of study drug.
quotes.location: Results, Study enrollment and patient characteristics

quotes.text: One patient in the placebo group did not receive the drug and was therefore not included in the efficacy analysis.

10.1186/s12984-024-01340-x.headline_claim: Home-based pulmonary rehabilitation is effective, safe, and improves exercise capacity, fatigue, dyspnea and quality of life in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome, and can be considered an adjunctive, low-cost therapy.
10.1186/s12984-024-01340-x.overall: The direction of benefit on 6MWT is plausible and the control arm also improved, but the unblinded usual-care design and completer-only analysis make the large effects on subjective outcomes uncertain. The conclusions on safety and economic advantage are not supported by any data in the paper.}

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance

issues.title: Unblinded usual-care comparison with extra contact in rehab arm; subjective outcomes prone to expectation effects
issues.explanation: The control group received no exercise and no equivalent contact, while the rehab group had weekly tele-monitoring and face-to-face visits at 2, 4, 8 and 12 weeks. Blinding of participants and outcome assessors for the follow-up measures is not described, and the fatigue, SF-36 and mMRC outcomes are self-reported. The size of the benefit on these outcomes therefore cannot be separated from attention and expectation effects, which weakens the secondary claims more than the walk-test result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of blinded outcome assessment and an attention-matched control, or analysis showing the effect is robust to these.

quotes.text: Tele-monitoring was conducted and regulated on a weekly basis to follow patient adherence to exercise.
quotes.location: Methods, Therapeutic procedure for rehabilitation group

quotes.text: Our results also showed significant improvement in the control group (received usual medical care) when compared to baseline values at the end of the three months of study

issues.title: Conclusion claims safety and economic advantage; no adverse event or cost data were reported
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says HBPR 'has its own economic advantage and more safety measures', is 'safe' and 'low-cost'. The Results contain no adverse event reporting, no safety outcome and no costs or resource use. With 60 analysed patients, the absence of reported events cannot establish safety either.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported adverse event monitoring and a cost analysis within the trial.

quotes.text: HBPR has its own economic advantage and more safety measures.
is effective, safe, and has a potential direct effect on exercise capacity, fatigue, dyspnea, and quality of life

issues.title: Completer-only analysis of 60 of 68 randomized; no ITT or sensitivity analysis for 11.8% dropout
issues.explanation: Eight randomized patients (four per arm) were lost and the analysis covers only 60. No intention-to-treat or missing-data sensitivity analysis is given. With balanced and modest loss this probably does not reverse the findings, but it leaves the estimates unprotected against attrition bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or worst-case imputation analysis giving similar between-group differences.

quotes.text: Eight patients (four in each group) dropped out for follow-up assessments due to non-specific reasons, so the analysis of the data is applied to 60 patients

10.1186/s12991-024-00494-1.headline_claim: Higher CRP, TG-HDL ratio and BMI are associated with poorer DSST cognition in post-COVID-19 condition, and vortioxetine showed a between-group DSST improvement at 8 weeks (p = 0.047) that the authors hypothesise is concentrated in participants with high baseline markers.
10.1186/s12991-024-00494-1.overall: The baseline association of the CRP x TG-HDL x BMI interaction with DSST is reported with a minor wording error on age, and the Poisson model choice is unclear but not shown to be wrong. The claim that high-marker patients respond to vortioxetine rests on a whole-sample, marginal result (p = 0.047, CI lower bound 0.008) with no subgroup contrast and no multiplicity control, so it is at best exploratory, as the authors partly acknowledge.

primary_outcome.name: Composite DSST score change from baseline to week 8 (adjusted ITT GEE)

primary_outcomes.measure: Least Square Mean Change in Baseline to Week 8 on Z-score in Combined Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST)

issues.title: Benefit attributed to high-marker participants, but only whole-sample difference (0.621, p = 0.047) is reported
issues.explanation: The Discussion says there was a significant between-group difference among vortioxetine participants with high baseline markers. The reported pairwise comparison is in the full ITT sample, with a lower CI bound of 0.008, and no high-marker subgroup contrast or marker-level estimates are shown. The five-way interaction p-value does not identify who benefits. The subgroup claim and the Conclusion's suggested treatment-response profile are not supported by the numbers presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Estimated marginal means at specified high and low marker levels showing a significant treatment difference in the high-marker stratum.

quotes.text: a significant between-group difference, at the endpoint among vortioxetine-treated participants who exhibited high baseline markers of inflammation, metabolic disruption and elevated BMI
difference = 0.621, SEM = 0.313, p = 0.047
quotes.location: Results, Effects of metabolic disruption ... comparing vortioxetine and placebo

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion attributes the between-group difference and improvement to participants with high baseline inflammation, metabolic disruption and BMI, but the only between-group estimate reported (0.621, SEM 0.313, p = 0.047) is a whole-sample ITT contrast with no stated marker levels, no definition of 'high' and no stratified estimate. The significant five-way interaction suggests moderation but does not itself show the benefit lies in high-marker participants, and the claim is partly tempered by the paper's hypothesis-generating caveat and the Conclusion's hedged wording ('may positively resp

issues.title: Poisson GLM for DSST total score: link, overdispersion and coefficient scale not stated
issues.explanation: The baseline association comes from a Poisson GLM on the DSST total score. A raw DSST score is a count-like variable, so Poisson is not clearly wrong, but the paper does not report the link function, overdispersion checks or how coefficients should be read. The screen's claim that the outcome is a z-score is not supported by the Table 2 note, which says total score. The baseline finding is also cross-sectional and described by the authors as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reporting the log link, a dispersion statistic near 1, or a sensitivity analysis with a linear or negative-binomial model giving the same result.

quotes.text: A generalized linear model (GLM) with a poisson probability  distribution  was  conducted
Dependent variable: DSST total score

issues.title: Many unadjusted models and interactions; marginal p = 0.047 and a five-way interaction uncorrected
issues.explanation: Unadjusted and adjusted GEE models, multiple interaction terms and several contrasts were tested at alpha 0.05 with no stated correction. The key between-group result has a CI lower bound of 0.008 and p = 0.047, so it would not survive even modest adjustment. The authors call the work hypothesis-generating, which limits but does not remove the problem, since the Conclusion still hypothesises a response profile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan limiting the confirmatory tests to the one contrast, or adjusted p-values remaining below 0.05.

quotes.text: the treatment x time x CRP x TG-HDL x BMI interaction (χ 2 = 12.979, p = 0.011)
quotes.location: Results, Effects ... comparing vortioxetine and placebo

quotes.text: we would conceptualize our results as hypothesis-generating rather than hypothesis-confirming

issues.title: Age called a significant DSST predictor despite p = 0.081 and a CI spanning zero (-0.033 to 0.002)
issues.explanation: The Results say age and the three-way interaction both had a significant negative association with DSST. Age has p = 0.081 and a 95% CI that includes zero, against a stated two-sided alpha of 0.05. Only the interaction (p = 0.023) meets the threshold. This is a wording error affecting one covariate and not the main interaction claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alpha of 0.10 for covariates, or a corrected p-value for age below 0.05.

quotes.text: age (β = -0.016; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.033-0.002; p = 0.081)
both had a significant negative association with performance on the DSST

issues.title: Lundbeck sponsorship declared but its role in design, analysis and publication not described
issues.explanation: The paper states Lundbeck sponsored the work and discloses an author's Lundbeck fees, but says nothing about the sponsor's role in design, analysis or the decision to publish. The registry names a different lead sponsor, which makes the relationship unclear. Disclosure is present, so this is a missing detail, not a hidden conflict.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sponsor had no role in analysis, interpretation or the decision to publish.

quotes.text: This work was sponsored by H. Lundbeck A/S, Copenhagen, Denmark.
speaker/consultation fees from Lundbeck, Janssen, Alkermes

10.1186/s13020-022-00654-z.headline_claim: Individualized Chinese medicine treatment over 3 to 6 months improved clinical symptoms, body constitution balance and lung function in hospital-discharged COVID-19 patients.
10.1186/s13020-022-00654-z.overall: The study is a single-arm observational series with no control group, so improvements over time cannot be attributed to Chinese medicine, yet the conclusion states it provided evidence of benefit. Several smaller numeric inconsistencies (dry cough count, age coefficient, an age effect from a model without age, subgroup denominators) and omitted quality-of-life declines further weaken confidence. The results are best read as descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Change in CM diagnostic pattern and clinical characteristics (CM syndrome checklist)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in CM Diagnostic Pattern & Clinical Characteristics using CM Syndrome Differentiation Assessment
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from Baseline the CM Diagnostic Pattern & Clinical Characteristics at 9 months

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Body Constitution Scores using Body Constitution Questionnaires Assessment
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from Baseline the Body Constitution at 9 months

issues.title: Single-arm uncontrolled study; improvements over time attributed to Chinese medicine
issues.explanation: All 150 participants received CM, and the mixed models estimate change across visits, which cannot be separated from spontaneous post-COVID recovery. The paper itself cites spontaneous resolution of symptoms and lung function in post-COVID patients. The conclusion that the study 'provided evidence' for CM benefit on symptoms, constitution and lung function is therefore not supported by this design; at most it is hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or usual-care comparison group showing differential improvement.

quotes.text: This  study  provided  evidence  for  individualized  CM  treatment on COVID-19 rehabilitation
It was found that CM treatment had a highly significant effect on the distance achieved by participants in the 6MWT
A cross-sectional study by Mandal et al. showed some spontaneous  resolution  of  symptoms  and  restoration of  lung  functions  in  post-COVID  subjects

second_reader.what_stands: The study is single-arm with no control group, and its improvements over time (6MWT, LFQ, symptoms, body constitution) are attributed to CM in the Conclusion ('provided evidence for...'), with causal wording such as 'CM treatment had a highly significant effect' and 'CM could facilitate the resolution'. The paper cites spontaneous recovery (Mandal et al.) but does not list the lack of a comparator among its limitations or temper the attribution. The authors do call the study observational, so the design itself is not hidden; the problem is the causal attribution it cannot support.

issues.title: Better recovery in 43 'without syndrome' participants asserted without between-group test
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the group without the two CM syndromes showed better response to CM treatment. This is based on percentages in Table 6 with no test of group difference, a small subgroup of 43, and a near-zero starting 'healthy' proportion (2.63%). This group was healthier-defined at baseline, so regression and ceiling effects explain the pattern at least as well as differential response.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A formal interaction test showing a differential effect.

quotes.text: Interestingly, this sub-group of participants showed better recovery compared to those with the two CM Syndromes.

issues.title: Significant QoL declines in 3 of 4 domains omitted from the conclusion
issues.explanation: Quality of life fell significantly in psychological, social and environment domains from V1 to V4, and psychological and social at V7. The conclusion lists only benefits and does not mention these declines. The authors attribute them to unrecorded confounders without evidence, so the negative signal is not weighed against the positive claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion or discussion that weighs the QoL declines against the claimed benefits.

quotes.text: quality of life in the aspects of psychological, social, and environment aspects were decreased upon CM treatment
achieving balance in body constitution, and improvement of lung functions

issues.title: Age effect on 6MWT: text says 1.03 m/year, Table 9 estimate is -0.9610
issues.explanation: The Results state that each additional year of age lowers 6MWT distance by 1.03 m. The fixed-effects table gives an Age estimate of -0.9610 m, which does not round to 1.03. The direction is the same but the size of the reported effect is inconsistent, and the age effect is a secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different model output in which the age coefficient is -1.03, with Table 9 showing the wrong version.

quotes.text: the distance achieve in 6MWT will decrease by 1.03 m

issues.title: LFQ age effect (-0.11/year) reported although Model 2 and Table 11B contain no age term
issues.explanation: The Methods define Model 2 with only time points and CM symptoms, and Table 11B lists no age coefficient. Yet the Results say LFQ falls by 0.11 per year of age. The figure is unsupported by any reported analysis, and the model description or the text is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An unreported model including age that produces -0.11, together with a corrected Methods description.

quotes.text: Model 2 = lmer (LFQ Scores ~ Time Points + CM Symptoms + (1|subjects), data).
the score obtained in LFQ will decrease by 0.11

issues.title: CM syndrome checklist used as primary outcome without reported validation in post-COVID patients
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is a syndrome-scoring checklist drawn from tools developed for other populations, with no validation or reliability reported here. The scoring scale is described ambiguously. The symptom-reduction conclusion depends on an instrument whose responsiveness in this population is unknown. Also, practitioners delivering treatment did the unblinded assessments.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published validation of the checklist in post-COVID patients.

quotes.text: Symptom severity was graded upon a four-point scale (0, 2, 4, 6 and 0,  1,  2,  3)

issues.title: Many outcomes, time points and subgroups tested at p<0.05 without correction
issues.explanation: Dozens of tests are run across symptoms, body constitutions, 6MWT, LFQ, QoL domains and subgroups with a single unadjusted threshold of 0.05. Marginal results such as P=0.017, 0.031 and 0.046 would not survive correction. The headline LFQ and 6MWT mixed-model results with P<0.001 are less affected, so the issue is narrower than claimed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or adjusted p-values showing the same conclusions.

quotes.text: A  P-value  of < 0.05  was  considered  statistically significant.
quotes.location: Methods, Data collection, management, and analysis

issues.title: CM called a 'favorable alternative' to Western care from untested visit counts that rebound at V8
issues.explanation: Non-flu Western consultations fall from 42 visits at V1 to 22 at V7, then rise to 38 at V8 when treatment stops. No test or control exists, and CM was given alongside Western care, not instead of it. The statement that CM is a favourable alternative is not supported by these descriptive counts.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison of consultation rates with a formal test.

quotes.text: This observation suggested CM as a favorable alternative medical care for these patients in Hong Kong.
An observable decrease in participants requiring for non-flu related western medicine consultations was found during the CM treatment period.

issues.title: Table 3A subgroup percentages use denominators 108/42, but group sizes are 107/43
issues.explanation: Table 3A and the text give 107 participants with and 43 without the CM syndromes. The percentages in the same table only reproduce with 108 and 42 (for example 69/108 = 63.89%, 22/42 = 52.38%). One participant is therefore classified differently in the headcounts and the percentages. The effect on the comparisons is negligible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that the percentage denominators exclude one participant for a stated reason.

script.explanation: 69/107 = 64.49%, but the paper prints 63.89, outside the rounding interval [63.88, 63.90]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 108.0 rather than 107.

issues.title: Dry cough: text says 69 of 150, Table 2 says 70; 46.67% matches 70
issues.explanation: The Results text gives 46.67% as 69 of 150, but Table 2 lists 70 participants. 70/150 equals 46.67%, whereas 69/150 equals 46.0%, so the text count is the slip. Nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source dataset showing 69 participants with dry cough.

quotes.text: Dry cough7046.67

script.explanation: 69/150 = 46.00%, but the paper prints 46.67, outside the rounding interval [46.66, 46.68]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 147.8 rather than 150.

10.1186/s13063-024-08473-3.headline_claim: A tailored 4-week supervised aerobic training program alleviated persistent long COVID-19 symptoms and improved exercise tolerance compared with a self-management control group.
10.1186/s13063-024-08473-3.overall: The exercise-capacity result (peak VO2, exercise time, load) is the better-supported finding, though from 24 open-label patients with baseline imbalance. The symptom-relief and mental-health claims are weaker: the total-symptom interaction is non-significant (P = 0.097), the symptom outcome is an unvalidated unblinded self-report against a minimal-contact control, and the mental-health conclusion contradicts the paper's own results. A few printed numbers (AT VO2 P, several percentages) are wrong but do not change the main findings.

primary_outcome.name: Not labelled as primary; sample size was based on peak VO2 (mL/kg/min). Symptom count and CPET variables are also reported as headline outcomes.

issues.title: Symptom and depression benefits asserted from within-group change; total symptom count group*time P = 0.097
issues.explanation: The Discussion says fatigue and muscular pain improved compared with control, yet individual symptoms were never compared between groups; muscular pain went from 1 to 0 in training and stayed at 1 in control. Depression is said to be relieved in training although PHQ-9 group*time was 0.721 and the control group also fell. The total symptom count interaction was 0.097, so only the post hoc responder comparison supports alleviation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests for each named symptom showing significance, and a significant total-symptom interaction.

quotes.text: We did not conduct intergroup comparisons for individual persistent symptoms separately.
the number of physical symptoms such as fatigue and muscular pain symptoms significantly improved
while the depression score significantly decreased in the training group

second_reader.what_stands: The depression benefit is asserted from within-group change alone (PHQ-9 group*time P = 0.721, and control also fell by about 1.1 points), and individual-symptom claims (fatigue, muscular pain, chest discomfort) have no between-group test, as the authors concede; the total symptom count interaction was P = 0.097. The overall symptom claim is not wholly unsupported, because the authors did report a between-group responder comparison (8/12 vs 2/12, P = 0.013), which is a different outcome from the symptom count.

issues.title: Symptom improvement claim rests on unblinded self-report on an unvalidated questionnaire, minimal-contact control
issues.explanation: The trial is open-label and the symptom outcome is patient-reported using a questionnaire the authors designed, with no validation or scoring detail. The control group got self-management advice and two calls versus 12 supervised sessions, so expectancy and attention differences could produce part of the symptom difference. The headline claim that training alleviated symptoms is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Validation data for the questionnaire and a blinded or objective symptom assessment.

quotes.text: This was a single-center, parallel-group, open-label, randomized, controlled trial.
assessed using a designed questionnaire at 4 weeks compared to baseline
Control patients were contacted by telephone or WeChat at 2 and 4 weeks

second_reader.what_stands: The symptom improvement outcome comes from an open-label trial, using a self-described 'designed questionnaire' with no stated validation, and the control group got only two brief contacts versus 12 supervised sessions, so expectation and attention effects are not separated from exercise effects. The limitations section does not mention unblinding or the unvalidated instrument. (The objective CPET outcomes are not affected by this concern, and I did not assess them here.)

issues.title: About 30 outcome comparisons at P ≤ 0.05 with no multiplicity control; secondary P values 0.024 to 0.042
issues.explanation: The paper tests many fitness, lung, mental-health and symptom outcomes with a single unadjusted alpha. Peak VO2 would survive adjustment, but several secondary 'significant' results sit just under 0.05 and would not. This weakens the secondary claims rather than the main exercise-capacity result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary endpoint with hierarchical testing.

quotes.text: The significance level was set at P ≤ 0.05.

issues.title: Conclusion cites mental-health benefit though all group*time P values for mental outcomes are 0.37 to >0.99
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say exercise may play a substantial role in recovery of mental health, but every mental-health and quality-of-life interaction was non-significant, as the Discussion itself concedes. The two sections contradict each other, and the headline statement goes beyond the evidence. The safety wording is less clearly a problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group effect on a prespecified mental-health outcome.

quotes.text: Exercise may play a substantial role in the recovery of cardiopulmonary functions and mental health when suffering long COVID-19.
Exercise-trained patients did not exhibit greater improvement in quality of life and mental health compared to the control group.

issues.title: Baseline imbalance in sex (33% vs 83% women) and peak VO2 (20.49 vs 25.30 mL/kg/min)
issues.explanation: Training started with much lower peak VO2 and far fewer women than control. A lower starting value leaves more room for improvement and regression to the mean, which could inflate the training-versus-control change. Only gender was adjusted for, so the headline peak VO2 interaction may be overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis adjusted for baseline peak VO2 giving a similar interaction.

quotes.location: Table 3, Peak VO2 mL/kg/min row, training baseline

issues.title: AT VO2 (mL/kg/min) group*time P: text 0.041 (significant), Table 3 prints 0.056
issues.explanation: The text reports a significant between-group difference in AT VO2 (mL/kg/min) with P = 0.041, but Table 3 gives 0.056 for the same interaction. At the paper's own alpha of 0.05 the table value is not significant. The text therefore claims one more significant exercise-capacity improvement than the table supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or the underlying output showing the interaction P is 0.041.

issues.title: Median of 12.5 sessions reported against a 12-session, 4-week protocol
issues.explanation: The programme is described as 12 supervised sessions, yet the median attended was 12.5. That is only possible if some patients did extra sessions, which the paper never explains. It does not alter any efficacy result but leaves actual exposure unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that extra or makeup sessions were permitted beyond 12.

quotes.text: consisting of 12 supervised aerobic training sessions on a cycling ergometer
with a median count of 12.5 (interquartile range = 2) sessions

issues.title: O2 pulse % pred called a significant rise; within-group CI (-4.87, 18.70) spans zero
issues.explanation: The text says O2 pulse showed a significant increase in the training group, but the within-group change in % pred has a CI spanning zero and no star. Only the interaction P = 0.042 is significant, even though neither arm's own change is. This is an odd pattern that the text does not describe accurately.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors clarifying that the sentence refers to the interaction test.

quotes.text: also revealed a significant increase in the training group from baseline to 4 weeks

issues.title: Printed percentages inconsistent with counts: 8/12 shown as 67.8% (twice), 7/12 as 56.3%
issues.explanation: The responder rate in the training group is printed as 8 (67.8%), but 8 of 12 is 66.7%. The same 67.8 is printed for 8/12 in Table 1 (CVD, control), and 7/12 is printed as 56.3 rather than 58.3. The counts are consistent with the reported chi-square, so these are reporting slips that change no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; arithmetic is exact for counts out of 12.

quotes.text: There were 8 (67.8%) patients in the training group

script.explanation: 8/12 = 66.67%, but the paper prints 67.8, outside the rounding interval [67.75, 67.90]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 11.8 rather than 12.

issues.title: Control FEV1/FVC change printed -3.12 versus -3.5 from the printed means
issues.explanation: The control group means 88.67 and 85.17 differ by 3.50, but the within-group difference is printed as -3.12. The difference may reflect covariate-adjusted model estimates, but the paper never says the column is model-based. No efficacy claim depends on it, since pulmonary function was non-significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that within-group differences are adjusted model estimates.

10.1186/s13063-026-09769-2.headline_claim: Hospital-based rehabilitation and telerehabilitation improved fatigue, physical functioning and episodic disability compared with a home programme, with no significant difference between the two rehabilitation modes for most outcomes.
10.1186/s13063-026-09769-2.overall: The large advantage of both supervised rehabilitation modes over the home programme appears real, since the t statistics and CIs are strongly significant, although the self-reported primary outcome was unblinded. The between-group p values throughout appear to be Levene-test significances, so the claims of no difference between hospital-based and telerehabilitation (and several significance labels) are unreliable; physical functioning differs by about 37 points. Text-table mismatches and baseline table errors add to the doubt about reporting quality.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder fatigue scale score, post-intervention between-group comparison

issues.title: Between-group p values (e.g. p = 0.246 beside t = -4.97, CI -4.25 to -1.82) do not belong to the t statistics
issues.explanation: In Tables 3-6 the between-group p values contradict the t statistics and CIs beside them. Hospital vs telerehab fatigue has t = -4.97 and a CI excluding 0 but is called non-significant (p = 0.246). Physical functioning has MD 36.90 (t = 20.83) at p = 0.178, and DALYs t = -4.508 at p = 0.793. FRC has t = -0.39 and a CI spanning 0 but p = 0.004. In each row the p matches the printed F, as a Levene test would, so significance labels are unreliable. The authors' conclusion that hospital-based and telerehabilitation are 'comparable' therefore rests on mislabelled p values: hospital-based physical functioning (67.4) far exceeds telerehabilitation (30.5), and fatigue differs by 3 points.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Output showing that the printed p values are the t-test significances (for example a table where p is computed with the t and df shown), or a correction of the tables.

quotes.text: no statistically significant difference between hospital-based rehabilitation and telerehabilitation (mean difference (MD) = − 3.04; 95% CI − 4.25, − 1.82;

quotes.location: Results, Change of physical functioning level

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0000 (reachable range [0.0000, 0.0000] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.246 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding; the CI excludes the null (0.0), but the reported p = 0.246 says the result is not significant

second_reader.what_stands: In these three rows the printed p value belongs to the adjacent F statistic, probably a Levene variance test, and not to the t statistic. The correct t-test p is below 0.001 for fatigue (t = -4.97) and physical functioning (t = 20.83), and about 0.70 for FRC (t = -0.39). The text therefore calls fatigue and physical functioning 'no significant difference' although both CIs exclude zero, and implies a significant FRC difference although its CI includes zero. I checked only these three rows, not every row in the tables.

issues.title: Text says no significant FRC change in home programme (p > 0.05); Table 4 gives p = 0.030
issues.explanation: The Results state that functional residual capacity, SaO2 and total lung capacity showed no significant changes in the home programme group (p > 0.05). Table 4 lists p = 0.030 for the home programme FRC change (2198.91 to 2213.69). This understates the improvement in the comparator arm and makes the contrast with the active arms look cleaner than the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing the HP FRC p value is above 0.05.

quotes.text: with no significant changes in the home programmes group

issues.title: Conclusion says 'home programmes showed comparable efficacy', contradicting results showing HP clearly inferior
issues.explanation: The Conclusion first says rehabilitation was significantly better than home programmes, then says home programmes showed comparable efficacy. The Results and Discussion show HP fatigue 25.35 vs 13.61 and 16.64, and disability worsening in HP. The sentence is probably a misplaced reference to HBR and TR being comparable, but that claim is itself weakened by the mislabelled p values (see c1).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors confirming the sentence refers to HBR vs TR and revising it.

quotes.text: However, home programmes showed comparable efficacy.
While HBR and TR were more effective than HP

issues.title: Self-reported primary outcome with unblinded participants and unmatched contact in the control arm
issues.explanation: Only assessors were blinded, yet the primary outcome (Chalder fatigue) is a self-administered questionnaire completed by participants who know their arm. The home programme arm got far less supervision and attention than the other two arms, with no attention control. The size of the fatigue difference versus HP may therefore be partly an expectation or contact effect. Calling the design 'assessor-blinded' as a strength overstates protection for this outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants were unaware of arm assignment, or objective corroboration (e.g. performance measures) of the fatigue difference.

quotes.text: This scale is a self-administered questionnaire consisting of 11 items on a 4-point Likert scale
The study adhered to blind design, with assessors blinded.

issues.title: Results text swaps the HBR-vs-HP (-11.74) and TR-vs-HP (-8.70) fatigue differences relative to Table 3
issues.explanation: The text attributes MD -8.70 (p = 0.023) to hospital-based vs home programme and -11.74 (p < 0.001) to telerehabilitation vs home programme. Table 3 and the group means show the opposite assignment. A reader of the text would conclude telerehabilitation had the larger fatigue benefit, which the data contradict.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or dataset showing the text labels are correct and the group means in Table 3 are mislabelled.

issues.title: Cardiorespiratory benefit claimed from uncorrected tests across about eight outcomes and three pairwise contrasts
issues.explanation: Eight cardiorespiratory outcomes and three pairwise contrasts each were tested at p < 0.05 without adjustment. The Discussion claims significant cardiorespiratory improvement versus home programmes, citing PR, FRC and SaO2 only, while blood pressure showed no between-group differences. This weakens the secondary cardiorespiratory conclusion, not the fatigue result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or adjusted analysis showing the cardiorespiratory effects remain significant.

quotes.text: Specifically, improvements were observed in PR, FRC, and SaO₂.
The significance level was set at p < 0.05.

issues.title: No ITT analysis: 137 of 145 randomised analysed (5.5% excluded), withdrawals in week 1 dropped
issues.explanation: The analysis excluded dropouts and anyone who withdrew within the first week, and states no ITT analysis was used. With only 8 participants lost (48/48/49 randomised vs 46/45/46 analysed), the bias is probably small, but differential dropout cannot be assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all 145 participants with similar results.

quotes.text: This study did not employ an intention-to-treat analysis.
Participants who withdrew within the first week were also excluded from the analysis.

issues.title: Home programme arm allowed unrecorded pharmacological or alternative treatments
issues.explanation: Participants in the HP arm could receive pharmacological or other treatments of their choice, and these were not recorded, so the comparison is against unstandardised usual care. This limits interpretation of what the contrast isolates but probably does not explain the large differences seen.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Records showing co-intervention use was balanced across arms.

quotes.text: Participants could also receive support with pharmacological interventions or any other alternative treatments of their choice.

issues.title: Telerehabilitation called a scalable alternative despite no cost data and unequal physical functioning outcomes
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the comparable effectiveness of HBR and TR suggests telerehabilitation is feasible and scalable in resource-limited settings. The trial reports no cost or implementation outcomes. The premise of comparable effectiveness also rests on p values that do not match the t statistics (see c1).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Cost, adherence or delivery data supporting scalability and corrected tests showing HBR and TR are equivalent.

quotes.text: telerehabilitation may serve as a feasible and scalable alternative to hospital-based care, particularly in resource-limited settings

issues.title: Telerehabilitation post-intervention physical functioning printed as 30.79 and as 30.49
issues.explanation: The within-group result gives a post-intervention mean of 30.79 (CI 28.76-32.32) while the among-group comparison gives 30.49. The between-group MDs (36.90 and 5.31) are consistent with 30.49 only. One of the two values is a typo and the CI cannot be reconciled with certainty.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the mean is 30.79 and that the MDs were computed from different values.

quotes.text: telerehabilitation: 30.49 ± 5.88

issues.title: Female share printed as 30.5% in Table 1 but 44/145 = 30.3% (text)

script.explanation: 44/145 = 30.34%, but the paper prints 30.5, outside the rounding interval [30.45, 30.60]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 144.3 rather than 145.

10.1186/s13102-024-00817-5.headline_claim: A 3-month individualized app-based physical activity (telerehabilitation) intervention did not significantly improve exercise capacity, fatigue or HRQoL in post-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared with a waiting control group; the authors conclude no effect on exercise performance or mental/physical capability was observed.
10.1186/s13102-024-00817-5.overall: The null finding for VO2peak is reported consistently in Table 2, but the trial is severely underpowered (12%, no sample size calculation) and uses a completer analysis. The authors' conclusion that the intervention was not effective is therefore stronger than the data support; the CI cannot exclude a clinically important benefit. The other problems are reporting slips (6 vs 3 months, mismatched baseline values, an impossible anxiety total, a wrong Table 2 note, two registration numbers) that do not change the main result..

primary_outcome.name: change in peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) from baseline to 3 months, intervention vs control

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 12% power (810 needed), yet low power is read as showing ineffectiveness
issues.explanation: The trial had no a priori sample size and reports 12% post hoc power for the primary outcome, with 810 patients needed for 80% power. The authors nevertheless say the weak power supports the conclusion that the intervention was not effective. A trial this underpowered cannot show absence of effect. The VO2peak between-group CI of -1.8 to 0.8 includes the 1.0 ml/min/kg clinically important difference they cite.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample size calculation or an equivalence/non-inferiority analysis showing the CI excludes the MCID.

quotes.text: was 12%.
We did not perform an a priori sample

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does state that no a priori sample-size calculation was done, that post hoc power was 12%, and that 810 patients would have been needed. It then reads this low power as supporting the conclusion that the intervention was not effective, which does not follow: low power means the trial could not reliably detect an effect, and the wide CI is compatible with both no effect and a clinically relevant one. The Discussion and Conclusions do also say that effects were 'not observed' and attribute this to training intensity and disease severity, which partly tempers the point, but the Limitati

issues.title: Table 1 anxiety: total 7.1 ± 4.8 lies outside both group means (4.9 ± 0.9, 4.7 ± 0.8)
issues.explanation: A pooled mean must lie between the two group means. Here the total of 7.1 is above both group means (4.9 and 4.7). The group SDs of 0.9 and 0.8 are also implausibly small against a total SD of 4.8. The baseline anxiety figures in Table 1 cannot all be correct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 showing different anxiety group values that average to 7.1.

Table 1, anxiety severity row, IG column

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 10 of 72 randomized (13.9%) not analysed, no ITT or missing-data handling
issues.explanation: The paper analyses 62 of 72 randomized patients, restricted to those with complete baseline and follow-up data. The reasons for the 10 missing are not given in the text, and their arm distribution is unclear. Without an intention-to-treat analysis, the between-group result does not estimate the effect of assignment. Because the study reports a null result and concludes the intervention was not effective, that conclusion rests on completers only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Fig. 1 showing arm-wise reasons for loss unrelated to treatment, plus a sensitivity analysis including all randomized participants.

quotes.text: Of the 72 randomized patients, 62 were examined at baseline and after the 3-month study period

issues.title: Null result attributed to patient severity rather than the training method, without a test
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the lack of improvement is likely due to disease severity and not to the training method. The study has no comparison with milder patients and no analysis of severity as an effect modifier. The explanation relies on other studies and is untested here, although it is hedged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified severity-by-treatment interaction analysis supporting the statement.

quotes.text: it is likely that the lack of improvement is due to differences in disease severity

issues.title: Primary outcome timing stated as 6 months in Methods but 3 months elsewhere
issues.explanation: The design paragraph says the primary outcome was assessed at baseline and after 6 months. The primary outcome definition, the aims and all results describe a 3-month intervention with assessment after 3 months. The follow-up time of the primary endpoint is therefore stated inconsistently, though the data appear to be 3-month data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry showing a 6-month assessment actually took place and was not the reported endpoint.

quotes.text: at baseline and after 6 months

issues.title: Baseline values in Results text differ from Table 1 (VO2peak SDs, IG mean; CG depression 7.7 ± 5.0 vs 7.5 ± 4.8)
issues.explanation: Baseline figures in the Results text do not match the same cells in Table 1. IG VO2peak is 21.6 ± 6.3 in text vs 21.5 ± 6.1 in the table, and CG is 23.3 ± 6.7 vs 23.3 ± 6.5. CG baseline depression is 7.7 ± 5.0 in text vs 7.5 ± 4.8 in the table. The differences are small and unexplained, so one of the two sources is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values come from a different analysis set, with the numbers matching it.

issues.title: Table 2 note says no within-group significance, but FAS fell significantly in both groups (p < 0.01)
issues.explanation: The Table 2 note says no significant differences were found within groups. The same table shows FAS drops of -3.3 and -3.0 points, which the Results report as significant (p < 0.01) in both groups. The note is incorrect for FAS. The physical-activity result (p = 0.02) is not in Table 2 and is not part of the contradiction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the note was meant to apply only to between-group tests.

The FAS score decreased in both the IG

issues.title: Two different DRKS trial registration numbers printed (DRKS00026245 vs DRKS0002793)
issues.explanation: The Methods and the Declarations give different registry numbers for the same trial. The second has one digit fewer, so it is probably a typo. Registration status and consistency with the pre-specified primary outcome cannot be checked from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record showing which number is correct; a typo would then be confirmed.
