10.20953/1817-7646-2023-1-28-35.headline_claim: Adding ammonium glycyrrhizinate for 30 days to standard therapy provides rapid regression of respiratory and general post-COVID symptoms and normalises spirometry in children after COVID-19 lung involvement.
10.20953/1817-7646-2023-1-28-35.overall: The paper reports a small, open-label, non-randomised comparison of 40 children with baseline imbalance, and its symptom-score differences cannot be attributed to the drug. The conclusions about quality of life, prognosis and an anti-inflammatory mechanism are unsupported by any measured outcome. At most the data suggest a hypothesis for a randomised trial.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; cough and weakness symptom scores (VAS) and spirometry normalisation are the headline outcomes

issues.title: Non-randomised allocation with unadjusted baseline imbalance in age and CT severity (n=20 vs 20)
issues.explanation: Children were assigned to the drug or no-drug group without any described allocation method. The groups differ at baseline: the study group is younger (35% vs 10% aged 7-11) and more often has CT-3 (55% vs 30%). Baseline severity could drive differences in recovery, and no adjustment is made. A causal drug effect cannot be separated from selection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of concealed random allocation or an analysis adjusted for age and CT severity showing the same effect.

quotes.text: остальные 20 пациентов составили контрольную группу (КГ)

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was non-randomised (no method described), and the groups differ in age and CT severity at baseline (CT-3 55% vs 30%; age 12+ 65% vs 90%), with no adjustment in the analysis. The authors do not discuss this imbalance. The imbalance is not statistically significant by a rough Fisher check, and baseline cough and weakness scores were similar, so the direction of any resulting bias on the main outcomes is unclear.

issues.title: Quality-of-life, prognosis and anti-inflammatory claims not measured in a 30-day, open, non-randomised n=40 study
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the drug significantly improves quality of life and prognosis and demonstrates an anti-inflammatory effect. The study measured only symptom scores and some spirometry over 30 days. Nothing measured quality of life, prognosis or inflammation. With 20 children per group, no sample-size calculation and non-random allocation, these claims go well beyond the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Measured quality-of-life or inflammatory outcomes, or a randomised design with longer follow-up supporting these claims.

quotes.text: улучшить прогноз заболевания
объективно демонстрирует

second_reader.what_stands: The quality-of-life, prognosis and anti-inflammatory conclusions are not supported by anything measured: no quality-of-life tool, no follow-up beyond 30 days and no inflammatory markers were used, and the spirometry data are not quantified. In the conclusion, 'объективно демонстрирует' overstates what an open, non-randomised, n=40 comparison with imbalanced groups can show.

issues.title: Open-label comparison with patient/parent-reported symptom scores as the significant outcomes
issues.explanation: The significant between-group findings (cough and weakness scores, symptom frequency) rest on scores reported by patients or parents who knew whether they received the drug. There is no placebo or blinding. Expectation effects could by themselves produce the 1.85 vs 0.75 cough-score difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that outcome assessors and participants were blinded, or a placebo control.

quotes.text: оценку кашля по шестибальной визуальноаналоговой шкале

second_reader.what_stands: There is no blinding or placebo described and the significant results are symptom scores reported by patients or parents (cough and weakness), which are open to expectation effects. The objective spirometry outcome is reported only qualitatively, without values or a test, so it cannot offset this.

issues.title: Four symptoms, three visits and spirometry tested without correction; headline generalises from two significant symptoms
issues.explanation: Cough, weakness, dyspnoea and sputum were each compared at several visits with p<0.05 and no multiplicity correction. Only cough and weakness differ between groups, while dyspnoea and sputum improved equally in both. The abstract's statement of faster regression of symptoms overgeneralises. The spirometry normalisation claim has no data table or test.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome of cough or weakness, or spirometry data with a between-group test.

quotes.text: статистически значимых различий между группами выявлено не было
В основной группе в сравнении с контролем, отмечен достоверно более быстрый регресс выраженности симптомов.

issues.title: Fisher p-values for cough (0.01) and weakness (0.005) do not reproduce from counts; two-sided about 0.02 and 0.01
issues.explanation: Counts printed in the Results allow the two-sided Fisher tests to be recomputed. For cough (14/20 with cough vs 20/20) the two-sided p is about 0.02, against the printed 0.01, which equals the one-sided value. For weakness (10/20 vs 18/20 still weak) it is about 0.01 against 0.005. The reported values look one-sided or computed another way, contrary to the stated two-sided test. The significance conclusions survive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that one-sided tests were used, or different underlying counts than those printed.

10.20953/1817-7646-2024-2-7-14.headline_claim: Standard sanatorium rehabilitation activities help children recover from post-COVID-19 syndrome, and these activities can be recommended as a mandatory programme.
10.20953/1817-7646-2024-2-7-14.overall: The paper is an uncontrolled descriptive study of 61 children, and its conclusion that the sanatorium programme aids recovery and should be mandatory is not supported by the design. The admission-state descriptions are broadly usable, but there are small numeric inconsistencies (fat-metabolism text vs table, girls 65,3% of 61, 46,8% vs 46%). The probiotic efficacy claim is likewise unsupported by any comparison.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Efficacy of sanatorium programme and 'mandatory' recommendation drawn from an uncontrolled single cohort of 61
issues.explanation: All 61 children received the programme and there is no comparison group, so improvement cannot be attributed to the programme rather than to time, natural recovery or expectation. Outcomes at discharge are clinician-supervised self-reports in an open-label setting, with no sample-size calculation and no statistical test of pre-post change. The conclusion that the programme aids recovery and should be mandatory is therefore not supported; the study mainly describes admission characteristics.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group with a pre-post comparison showing the programme's effect beyond natural recovery.

quotes.text: Общепринятые оздоровительные санаторные мероприятия содействуют реабилитации детей с постковидным состоянием и могут быть рекомендованы как обязательная программа.
Общеоздоровительные мероприятия способствовали клинико-лабораторным восстановительным процессам.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's claim that the standard sanatorium programme promotes rehabilitation and can be recommended as mandatory is drawn from a single uncontrolled cohort of 61 children with a 6-11 day stay. It has no comparison group, no defined outcome measure and no reported test of change, so the efficacy and 'mandatory' wording is not supported by the design. I did not see the figure data, so I could not check whether Figs 2a/2b contain quantitative discharge results.

issues.title: Probiotic efficacy asserted for a non-randomised 33-child subgroup with no comparison or test
issues.explanation: The paper states that repeat bacteriological testing confirmed the effectiveness of the probiotic, and that improvement was faster in children who received it. The 33 children were not randomised or compared with untreated children, and no test is reported for the microbiota change or the time difference. The microbiota improvement also appears in children who were not given the probiotic, so the programme and probiotic effects cannot be separated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison with an untreated group, with a statistical test of the difference in microbiota change and time to recovery.

quotes.text: подтвердило результативность назначения

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that repeat testing 'confirmed the effectiveness' of the probiotic in 33 children, but there is no randomisation, no comparison with the 28 children not treated, and no statistical test. The reported improvement could reflect the sanatorium regimen or natural change, so efficacy of the probiotic is not established. The shorter time to improvement in the probiotic group is given without a test and the comparison figures are not clearly defined.

issues.title: Text says neutral fat and fatty-acid salts found in all children; table gives 90,5% for both
issues.explanation: The Results text says neutral fat, fatty acids and fatty-acid salts were detected in all children. The table gives 100% only for fatty acids and 90,5% for neutral fat and for salts. The table's percentages also appear to rest on about 21 children, not the 61 in the study, and the paper does not say so. This is a reporting error on a secondary descriptive result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the coprology table covers a subset and that 'all' refers to that subset's detected cases.

quotes.text: Нейтральный жир, жирные кислоты и соли жирных кислот обнаружены  у  всех
Обнаружено / Detected

issues.title: Girls reported as 65,3% of 61 children; no whole count gives 65,3%
issues.explanation: With 61 children, 39 girls is 63,9% and 40 is 65,6%, so 65,3% cannot be a share of 61. Either the count, the percentage or the denominator is wrong. The error is small and affects only the demographic description.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that sex data were available for a smaller number of children (e.g. 49) whose girls make up 65,3%.

quotes.text: по гендерному признаку - девочек (65,3%)
In 61 children aged 4 to 17 years

issues.title: Abdominal pain at COVID onset: 46,8% in Methods, 46% in Results; 46,8% does not fit n = 61
issues.explanation: The same finding is given as 46,8% and as 46%. The 46% fits 28 of 61, but 46,8% corresponds to no whole count of 61 children (it would fit 22/47). This is a minor internal inconsistency in a background characteristic.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two passages use different denominators or time windows.

quotes.text: 46,8%  случаев  возникали боли в животе
quotes.location: Patients and methods, acute COVID-19 onset

quotes.text: 46% в начальном дебюте COVID-19 возник болевой абдоминальный синдром

10.20969/vskm.2022.15(1).26-33.headline_claim: Medium-term therapy with the adaptogen Trekrezan in patients with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 and post-COVID syndrome reduces symptom severity, increases exercise tolerance, reduces asthenia on the MFI-20 scale, and shortens the inpatient stay.
10.20969/vskm.2022.15(1).26-33.overall: The claim that Trekrezan helps patients with ongoing symptomatic COVID-19 rests on an open-label study with predictable odd/even allocation and mainly patient-reported outcomes. Several Table 2 p-values cannot be between-group comparisons, the exercise-tolerance claim has no reported data, and the dyspnoea and quality-of-life claims have none either. Only a modest, tentative MFI-20 and bed-day difference can be taken from the paper, with considerable risk of bias.

primary_outcome.name: Asthenia severity on the MFI-20 scale (no primary outcome is labelled in the text)

issues.title: Allocation by odd/even enrolment number, labelled 'simple randomisation', is predictable and not random
issues.explanation: Patients were assigned to Trekrezan or control by odd or even sequence number. This is a predictable alternation rather than randomisation, and no allocation concealment is described. Selection and baseline imbalance can therefore bias every between-group comparison the conclusions rest on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of a concealed computer-generated sequence, or an explanation of why the alternation could not be foreseen by enrolling staff.

quotes.text: нечетные номера (1, 3, 5 и так далее) составили 1-ю группу
четные номера (2, 4, 6 и так далее) вошли во 2-ю группу

second_reader.what_stands: The described odd/even allocation is a predictable, non-random (alternation) scheme, so calling it simple randomisation is inaccurate and allocation concealment is absent. The 53/50 split is not exactly what strict alternation of 103 patients would give, and the paper does not explain the one-patient difference.

issues.title: Open-label design with self-reported MFI-20 and self-rated improvement as key outcomes
issues.explanation: The study is open-label with no placebo. The main efficacy results are patient-rated fatigue (MFI-20) and self-rated improvement, plus length of stay, which depends on unblinded discharge decisions. These outcomes are open to expectation effects, so the reported advantage of Trekrezan cannot be attributed confidently to the drug.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded outcome assessor, a placebo or sham control, or objective outcomes that show the same advantage.

quotes.text: Данное исследование является открытым
оценка выраженности астении по шкале MFI-20

second_reader.what_stands: The study is explicitly open-label with no placebo, and its main efficacy results (MFI-20 and self-rated improvement) are patient-reported and so prone to bias from knowing the treatment. Objective endpoints exist but are not the focus of the asthenia claim, and the paper does not discuss this limitation.

issues.title: Conclusion says Trekrezan increases exercise tolerance; no walk-test result is reported
issues.explanation: The Conclusion states that Trekrezan increases exercise tolerance. The walk test is listed in the Methods (and the abstract says 6-minute, the Methods '3 or 6'), but no walk-test values or comparison appear in Results or Table 2. That conclusion is unsupported by data in the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or paragraph reporting walk-test results for both arms with a between-group comparison.

quotes.text: increases exercise tolerance
тест с 3 или 6 мин ходьбой

second_reader.what_stands: No walk-test, Borg or other exercise-tolerance result is reported anywhere in the paper, although the methods list a walk test and the Conclusion claims increased exercise tolerance. The claim has no supporting data presented, and the reported SpO2 shows no between-group advantage.

issues.title: Table 2 p<0.001 values are undefined and not between-group; dyspnoea and quality-of-life results are not shown
issues.explanation: Significant reductions in dyspnoea and improved quality of life are claimed with no data or test shown. Table 2 gives p < 0.001 for every row without saying whether it is within-group or between-group. For subjective improvement (85% vs 74%), SpO2 (93.1 vs 93.3) and DLCO (68.7 vs 67.9) the printed numbers cannot give a between-group p < 0.001, so the stated significance appears to be within-group change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement that the Table 2 p values are between-group (for example ANCOVA on change), with dyspnoea and quality-of-life scores reported for both arms.

quotes.text: a statistically significant decrease in the degree of shortness of breath
improvement in the patient's quality of life were revealed

second_reader.what_stands: The Table 2 p<0.001 values have no stated comparison or test, and several cannot be between-group results from the printed numbers (SpO2, CRP, DLCO and subjective improvement give no significant between-group difference by simple recalculation; MFI-20 and bed-days give p≈0.003 and ≈0.001 by unadjusted two-sample tests). Dyspnoea and quality-of-life results are asserted in the text and abstract but no values, scale or p-values are shown; only a baseline quality-of-life score of 75/100 is given. The statistic used may have been a within-group or a different test; the paper does not say.

issues.title: Post-treatment CRP given as identical 2.5±3.4 mg/L in both groups; group-specific values missing
issues.explanation: Table 2 prints the same post-treatment CRP mean and SD for both groups, and the text presents it as one average for both. This looks like a pooled value rather than two group results. The CRP outcome therefore cannot be compared between arms, and the SD is larger than the mean.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Group-level post-treatment CRP data showing that the two groups genuinely had identical mean and SD.

quotes.text: снижался в обеих группах и составил в среднем 2,5±3,4 мг/л

issues.title: Manufacturer sponsorship and grant disclosed, but sponsor's role in design, analysis and reporting not stated
issues.explanation: The study was supported by the manufacturer of Trekrezan and the authors received a grant. The paper does not say what part the company had in design, data analysis or the decision to publish. This is a modest transparency gap for an open-label study with favourable subjective outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sponsor had no role in design, data analysis, interpretation or the decision to publish.

quotes.text: Авторы получили грант на проведение
quotes.location: Declaration of financial and other relationships

issues.title: Discussion calls all 69 coughs non-productive, but Results say 8 of the 69 were productive
issues.explanation: Results say 69 patients (67%) had cough and 8 of them had productive cough. The Discussion then says 69 patients (67%) had non-productive cough. Both cannot be true; the non-productive count should be about 61. The general conclusion that cough is mostly non-productive is unaffected, and the issue has no bearing on the treatment comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion figure refers to cough without sputum complaints in a different subset, or a corrected count of 61.

quotes.text: В данном исследовании у 69 пациентов (67%) наблюдался  непродуктивный  кашель

issues.title: No trial registration or protocol reported for a study described as randomised and comparative
issues.explanation: The paper presents a prospective comparative trial but gives no registration number or protocol. The reader therefore cannot compare the Methods' endpoints (symptom resolution and adverse events) against the efficacy claims actually reported, such as MFI-20, DLCO and length of stay. This weakens confidence in the outcome selection rather than showing any specific change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or approved protocol listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: устное согласие на участие в исследовании

10.20969/vskm.2022.15(5).22-26.headline_claim: Hepatoprotectors improve liver function markers during early post-COVID-19 rehabilitation, and ursodeoxycholic acid has the most pronounced effect on normalising ALT and total and direct bilirubin.
10.20969/vskm.2022.15(5).22-26.overall: The finding that all three hepatoprotectors lowered ALT and other markers more than observation alone is plausible, but it rests on a non-randomised, unblinded comparison with unadjusted tests and no correction for multiple comparisons. The claim that ursodeoxycholic acid 'normalises' ALT and bilirubin is contradicted by Table 2, where values remain well above controls. The direct bilirubin claim also conflicts with the paper's own Results text.

primary_outcome.name: Serum liver enzymes and bilirubin (ALT, AST, GGT, LDH, ALP, total and direct bilirubin, albumin); ALT and bilirubin emphasised in conclusions

issues.title: Non-randomised, undescribed allocation to four therapy groups, yet one drug is ranked best
issues.explanation: Patients were divided into four groups 'depending on the therapy', with no randomisation, allocation rule, or adjustment described. Group 0 is an observation group, and the control group is 20 healthy volunteers. Baseline lab values match across groups, but unmeasured differences (timing, severity, co-treatments, adherence) could affect recovery. Ranking ursodeoxycholic acid above the other agents is therefore only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation of randomised or rule-based allocation, or a covariate-adjusted analysis giving the same ranking.

quotes.text: depending on the therapy, the patients were divided into 4 groups
Ursodeoxycholic acid has the most pronounced effect on normalization of alanine aminotransferase, total and direct bilirubin levels.

second_reader.what_stands: Non-randomised, undescribed allocation is true: the paper says only that patients were 'distributed' or 'divided' into four groups by therapy, with no randomisation or allocation rule, and it ranks ursodeoxycholic acid best in the abstract and conclusion on the basis of unadjusted comparisons with some baseline differences (for example lower starting ALT and ALP). The ranking is overstated for direct bilirubin: the Results state direct bilirubin dynamics and final values were comparable across groups, so the claim of the 'most pronounced effect' on direct bilirubin is not supported by the pape

issues.title: Direct bilirubin: Results say groups comparable, Table 2 shows ** vs group 0, conclusion says UDCA best
issues.explanation: The Results state that direct bilirubin dynamics and end-of-month concentrations were comparable in all therapeutic groups. Table 2 marks the ursodeoxycholic acid end value (3.18) as significantly different from group 0 (3.93, **), and the glycyrrhizic acid group (3.78) carries a ^ mark against ursodeoxycholic acid. The abstract and conclusion then credit ursodeoxycholic acid with the most pronounced effect on direct bilirubin. The text, table and conclusion do not agree, so the direct bilirubin part of the headline claim is not clearly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Results text, or a pre-specified between-group test showing a UDCA advantage for direct bilirubin, with Table 2 marks matching the text.

quotes.text: Динамика концентрации прямого билирубина была  сопоставимой  во  всех  терапевтических  группах.

quotes.location: Table 2, direct bilirubin row, UDCA group

quotes.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid has the most pronounced effect on normalization of alanine aminotransferase, total and direct bilirubin levels.

issues.title: Eight markers, four groups, many pairwise tests, no correction; only paired t-test is named
issues.explanation: The paper tests eight markers across four groups, at baseline and end, with many pairwise comparisons at p<0.05 and p<0.01, and describes no correction. The only test named is a paired Student t-test, which does not suit between-group comparisons of relative change, and no test is named for the group comparisons. The strongest ALT results (p<0.001) are probably robust. The weaker marginal differences, including those cited in the bilirubin and ALP rankings, are less reliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated correction (for example Bonferroni or Tukey) or an ANOVA or mixed model for between-group comparison, with the key differences still significant.

quotes.text: Динамическое сравнение проводилось с использованием парного критерия Стьюдента.
в группе урсодезоксихолевая кислота относительная динамика показателя достоверно превышала динамику в остальных группах
quotes.location: Результаты и обсуждение, paragraph on total bilirubin

issues.title: 'Normalisation' claimed, but UDCA-group ALT (58.93) and direct bilirubin (3.18) stay above control
issues.explanation: The conclusion says ursodeoxycholic acid normalises ALT and bilirubin. In Table 2, the end-of-month ALT in this group is 58.93, over twice the healthy mean of 26.00 and still marked ### (different from controls). Direct bilirubin is 3.18 against 1.80 in controls, also marked ###. Only total bilirubin (18.81 vs 16.95) approaches normal, though it is also marked ###. The data show a marked reduction, not normalisation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that end values in the UDCA group are not statistically or clinically different from healthy controls.

quotes.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid has the most pronounced effect on normalization of alanine aminotransferase, total and direct bilirubin levels.

10.20969/vskm.2025.18(6).64-71.headline_claim: Enhanced external counterpulsation improves lung volumes and exercise tolerance in patients with post-COVID ventilatory dysfunction and supports its inclusion in comprehensive rehabilitation.
10.20969/vskm.2025.18(6).64-71.overall: The headline claim that EECP improves respiratory function in post-COVID patients is only tentatively supported: allocation is undescribed, there is no blinding or sham, the sample is 15 per arm, and many outcomes are tested without correction. Some lung-volume gains (TLC, FVC, FRC) do differ between groups at 1 month, but the highlighted FEV1 and VC results and the exercise outcomes rest largely on within-group changes, and DLCO did not change. The abstract also mislabels FVC as vital capacity.

primary_outcome.name: Lung volumes (TLC, VC, FVC, FEV1, FRC), DLCO and 6-minute walk distance; no single primary endpoint is labelled

issues.title: Allocation method to EECP vs control not described; non-blinded, no sham, no adjusted analysis (n=15 vs 15)
issues.explanation: The paper states that patients 'were distributed' into two groups of 15 without saying how, and the control group received no sham procedure. Allocation is not concealed or blinded, and effort-dependent outcomes (spirometry, walk test, Borg dyspnoea) are open to bias. Baseline values are not identical (for example TLC 65 vs 57%, BMI 32.8 vs 29.8, DLCO 50 vs 43), and no adjusted analysis is given. A causal claim that EECP 'improves' function is therefore only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a random or concealed allocation procedure, or an adjusted or change-score between-group analysis showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Пациенты были распределены в основную группу (n=15) и группу сравнения (n=15).
Пациенты из группы сравнения получали только оптимальную медикаментозную терапию сопутству -ющих заболеваний

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does not describe how patients were assigned to EECP or control, does not mention blinding, uses no sham procedure, and performs no adjusted analysis (only unadjusted Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests in 15 vs 15). Baseline comparability is reported in Table 1, but that does not remove the risk of allocation bias or of expectation effects on subjective outcomes such as the Borg dyspnea score and the effort-dependent 6MWT and spirometry.

issues.title: FEV1 and VC claimed as improved from within-group p; between-group p 0.349 and 0.053; no 6MWT between-group test
issues.explanation: FEV1 (65→82%, within p=0.041) is listed as a key improvement, yet at 1 month the groups do not differ significantly (p=0.349); VC is borderline (p=0.053). A significant change in one arm alongside a non-significant change in the other does not show a difference between the arms. For the 6MWT (313→352 m) and dyspnoea, only within-group p values are given for the treated arm. The statement that function 'improves' is thus supported for some volumes (TLC, FVC, FRC) but not clearly for FEV1, VC or exercise capacity, and DLCO was unchanged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests of change from baseline (or adjusted for baseline) that are significant for FEV1, VC, 6MWT and Borg score.

quotes.text: whereas no significant changes were observed in controls.

quotes.location: Table 2, ОФВ1,% row, Через 1 месяц (main group; between-group p 0,349)
Table 2, ЖЕЛ,% row, Через 1 месяц (control; between-group p 0,053)

second_reader.what_stands: For FEV1 and VC the paper's claim of improvement rests on within-group Wilcoxon tests; the between-group p-values at 1 month are 0.349 (FEV1) and 0.053 (VC), so superiority over control is not shown for these two, and for 6MWT no between-group test or control follow-up value is reported. The claim for TLC, FVC and FRC is better supported (between-group p<0.001, 0.004, <0.001), although these are also unadjusted comparisons of follow-up values without a test of change scores.

issues.title: Pilot of 15 vs 15 with no sample-size calculation yields a confident recommendation for rehabilitation use
issues.explanation: The study is described as pilot and the small sample is acknowledged. The abstract nevertheless concludes that EECP improves respiratory function and supports its inclusion in rehabilitation programmes. A 30-patient, single-centre, non-randomised study with a 1-month follow-up supports a hypothesis-generating conclusion at most.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample-size calculation, or conclusions worded explicitly as preliminary.

quotes.text: Основным ограничением данного исследования является небольшая выборка.
Целью данного пилотного исследования явилась оценка эффективности метода УНКП
supporting its inclusion in comprehensive rehabilitation programs

second_reader.what_stands: There is no sample-size calculation, no multiplicity handling, no stated allocation method, and the English abstract's conclusion ('improves... supporting its inclusion in comprehensive rehabilitation programs') is firmer than a non-randomised, unblinded 15 vs 15 pilot with 1-month follow-up supports. This is partly mitigated because the study is labelled a pilot and the main text names the small sample as its main limitation and uses softer wording ('может способствовать'), so the overreach is mainly in the abstract and in the Discussion's blanket statement about prior studies.

issues.title: Abstract 'vital capacity 56.5→73%, p=0.006' is the FVC row; Table 2 VC row is 57→70, p<0.001
issues.explanation: The abstract's 'vital capacity' values (56.5→73%, p=0.006) match the forced vital capacity (ФЖЕЛ) row of Table 2. The vital capacity (ЖЕЛ) row shows 57→70% with a within-group p<0.001. One reported result is therefore attributed to the wrong measure. The VC result is also less clearly separated from control at 1 month (between-group p=0.053) than the abstract suggests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the abstract's 'vital capacity' deliberately denotes FVC.

quotes.text: vital capacity (56.5→73%, p=0.006)

issues.title: About 8 outcomes tested at p<0.05 without correction; FEV1 p=0.041 and FRC p=0.018 would not survive
issues.explanation: Seven lung-function measures and the 6MWT and Borg score were each tested at a nominal 0.05 with no primary outcome and no adjustment. With roughly eight to nine comparisons, a Bonferroni threshold would be about 0.006. The FEV1 (p=0.041), FRC (p=0.018) and 6MWT (p=0.007) within-group results would not pass it. The claimed benefits therefore rest partly on nominal significance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A declared primary outcome and a hierarchical or corrected testing plan.

quotes.text: Различия считались статистически значимыми при p < 0,05.

issues.title: Compression pressure 220-280 mmHg in abstract vs 220-240 mmHg in Methods
issues.explanation: The abstract and the Methods give different upper limits for the compression pressure of the same intervention. Nothing in the text reconciles them, so the dose actually delivered is unclear. This does not change the reported results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that pressure was titrated within 220-280 mmHg and 220-240 mmHg was the typical value used.

quotes.text: compression pressure 220-280 mmHg
давление компрессии 220-240 мм рт.ст.
quotes.location: Материалы и методы, treatment course paragraph

issues.title: No trial registration or prespecified primary outcome reported for a prospective interventional study
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval and consent but gives no registry number or prespecified outcome. Without it, selection of outcomes among the many tested cannot be checked, which compounds the multiplicity concern. Whether the study was registered is not determinable from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry that predates enrolment and lists the same outcomes.

quotes.text: Исследование было одобрено Локальным этическим Комитетом Сеченовского Университета (протокол №19-23 от 26.10.2023).

issues.title: Baseline FVC median in treated arm is 56.00 in Table 1 but 56.50 in Table 2
issues.explanation: Table 1 and Table 2 report the same baseline FVC for the treated group with identical quartiles [54.00; 61.00], but the medians differ (56.00 vs 56.50). The abstract uses 56.5. Small, but it shows the tables were not fully reconciled. Text also reports 'mean' VC values (57.27%, 58.73%) while the tables give medians.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the tables use different rounding conventions or different baseline subsets.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-10999234/v1.headline_claim: A 12-week exercise-based telerehabilitation program was associated with improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and gait speed in individuals with long COVID, and was well tolerated and feasible.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-10999234/v1.overall: The fitness (VO2peak, AT) and gait-speed improvements are plausible and statistically supported after BH correction, but should be treated as tentative. Loss to follow-up was large and unequal (14.0% vs 31.7%), the CPET primaries were imbalanced at baseline, and gait speed and symptoms do not match the registered primary outcomes. Participants were also not blinded, which adds to the uncertainty about the size of the effects.

primary_outcome.name: Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2peak, anaerobic threshold), gait speed, and long COVID symptoms (co-primary outcomes)

primary_outcomes.measure: Systolic blood pressure in mm Hg
Diastolic blood pressure in mm Hg

issues.title: Differential dropout (14.0% TG vs 31.7% ACG; 28/120 lost) with results resting on a missing-at-random assumption
issues.explanation: 28 of 120 participants (23.3%) had no post-test data, and loss was more than twice as high in the control arm. Dropout was attributed partly to work-related time constraints that prevented the post-intervention CPET. The primary CPET-based outcomes are therefore analysed as 'ITT' only under a missing-at-random assumption that cannot be verified. The paper's own sensitivity analyses showed that significance varied for several outcomes. The fitness and gait conclusions are therefore more tentative than the headline wording suggests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary analyses (multiple imputation, tipping-point or baseline-characteristic comparison of dropouts) showing the group effects on VO2peak, AT and gait speed are unchanged in direction, size and significance.

quotes.text: Overall, 49 participants (86.0%) in the TG and 43 (68.3%) in the ACG completed the intervention, yielding dropout rates of 14.0% and 31.7%, respectively.
work-related time constraints caused dropout and prevented some participants from completing the post-intervention CPET assessment

second_reader.what_stands: Dropout was clearly differential (14.0% vs 31.7%, 28/120 lost) and the primary GEE analysis explicitly relies on missing-at-random. It is not true that this goes unexamined: the paper reports multiple-imputation and per-protocol sensitivity analyses and discusses reasons for ACG dropout, though the limitations section does not name attrition bias and the work-time reason (possibly unrelated to outcome) cannot verify MAR.

issues.title: Gait speed and symptoms reported as co-primary but absent from registered primaries; 5 registered primaries unreported
issues.explanation: The registered primary outcomes (NCT05922865) are VO2max, AT, working load, breathing reserve, resting HR, O2 pulse, SBP and DBP. The paper's primary outcomes are CRF, gait speed and symptoms, and gait speed supports one of the two headline conclusions. Working load, breathing reserve, resting HR and blood pressure are not reported in the paper's text. The paper describes symptoms as prespecified co-primary yet says the symptom assessments were incorporated after the trial began. Without the registered protocol history this cannot be settled, but as published the primary-outcome set differs from the registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or the approved protocol listing gait speed and symptoms as primary, or a supplementary table reporting the unreported registered primaries.

quotes.text: Primary outcomes included cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), gait speed, and long COVID symptoms.
Following the commencement of the trial, additional CRF measures (heart rate recovery [HRR]) and long COVID symptom assessments were incorporated
Because cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂peak), gait parameters, and long COVID symptom burden were prespecified as co-primary outcomes

second_reader.what_stands: Against the current registry record, gait speed and long COVID symptoms are described in the paper as prespecified co-primary outcomes but are not registered primaries, and five registered primaries (working load, breathing reserve, resting heart rate, systolic and diastolic BP) are not reported in the main text; the paper discloses only that HRR and symptom assessments were added after the trial began. Earlier registry versions were not seen and the 5 registered secondaries were not examined, so whether gait or symptoms were registered elsewhere, or the registered primaries are in the supplem

issues.title: Baseline imbalance in both CPET primaries (VO2peak p=0.041, AT p=0.013) plus weight, PSQI and QOL under simple randomization
issues.explanation: Groups differed at baseline on the primary fitness outcomes and on several secondary ones, and the authors acknowledge the imbalance. The Results also state that no significant between-group baseline differences were observed, which conflicts with the body weight, PSQI and QOL baseline differences reported later (the claim may refer only to Table 2). A baseline imbalance on the outcome itself can distort the estimated change through regression to the mean. The paper does not show that the GEE model adjusted for baseline values, so the size of the VO2peak and AT effects is less secure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Table 4 or the supplement showing the GEE models adjusted for baseline values, or results unchanged in an ANCOVA on follow-up values adjusted for baseline.

quotes.text: At baseline, groups differed significantly in VO₂peak (t=2.07, _p_ =0.041) and AT (t= 2.51, _p_ =0.013).
Third, simple randomization resulted in baseline group imbalances, which were addressed using GEEs and the BH procedure.
Baseline body weight significantly differed between the groups

issues.title: Fatigue/symptom co-primary is an unvalidated binary self-report checklist in unblinded participants
issues.explanation: The symptom outcome is a presence/absence checklist that was added after the trial started, rather than a validated instrument. Participants knew their allocation, so self-reported symptoms are open to expectation effects. The authors acknowledge the limitation, and the headline conclusion does not rely on symptoms. This weakens only the secondary-type fatigue claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the checklist was prespecified in the protocol and validated against a recognised symptom instrument, or a conclusion that does not rely on the fatigue result.

quotes.text: Long COVID symptoms were assessed using a structured checklist based on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention description of post-COVID conditions
The absence of validated symptom severity scales limited interpretation of the clinical magnitude of improvement.

issues.title: Commercial device (KNEESUP, Conzian) used; supplier of devices and company role not stated
issues.explanation: The intervention depends on a commercial brace, tracker and app, and the paper does not say whether the manufacturer supplied the devices or had any role in design or analysis. A statement of no competing interests is given, and the funders listed are non-commercial. Nothing in the text shows a financial tie, but the absence of a statement about the device supply leaves this unresolved from the paper alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the devices were purchased or loaned at arm's length and that the manufacturer had no role in the study.

quotes.text: The authors declare no competing interests.
Reproduced with permission from Conzian Ltd., Taipei, Taiwan.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-1452186/v1.headline_claim: Supervised group telerehabilitation appears to be feasible and safe for people with Long-COVID, with efficacy to be examined in a future study.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-1452186/v1.overall: The paper is a small randomised pilot that makes a modest feasibility claim and explicitly disclaims efficacy inference, which the data support. The flagged completion figure reconciles: 9/11 = 81.8% matches the abstract's 82%, and the Table 2 follow-up n of 9 is explained by the two early withdrawals.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility outcomes (recruitment rate, adherence, completion rate, adverse events, technological issues)

10.21203/rs.3.rs-2521799/v1.headline_claim: Significant use of the ReCOVery APP can contribute to the recovery of Long COVID patients, although the randomized comparison found no significant between-group differences.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-2521799/v1.overall: The randomised comparison shows no significant benefit on the primary or any secondary outcome, so the abstract conclusion that the APP contributes to recovery is not supported by the trial design. Several tables have transcription errors (Table 2 counts, Table 3 Sit-to-Stand cells, Table 4 CIs, the adherence percentage), which makes the secondary regression findings less reliable. The per-protocol and open-label limitations are real but matter little for a null result.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 quality of life (physical and mental health)

issues.title: Null primary SF-36 result and no between-group effects, yet abstract concludes the APP can contribute to recovery
issues.explanation: The primary outcome (SF-36) and every secondary outcome showed no significant difference between groups, and physical health at 3 months nominally favoured the control group. The abstract's conclusion rests on regression models within a mostly non-adherent intervention arm, which cannot separate the effect of app use from patient motivation or recovery trajectory. The discussion likewise states that the intervention group showed 'more improvement' in several domains, although none reached significance against control. The randomised comparison does not support a benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, significant between-group difference on the SF-36 or a randomised dose-response analysis showing an effect of app use.

quotes.text: In conclusion, the significant use of ReCOVery APP can contribute to the recovery of Long COVID patients.
although without attaining significant improvement as compared to the control group.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary SF-36 outcomes and all other between-group comparisons in Table 3 are non-significant (the authors say so themselves), yet the abstract's last sentence states that significant use of the APP 'can contribute to the recovery' of patients, a conclusion that rests only on non-randomized, exploratory regressions of minutes of use. The authors do report the null result and low adherence elsewhere, so the null is not hidden, but the concluding sentence is stronger than the between-group evidence supports.

issues.title: Sit-to-Stand T1-T0 cells are inconsistent with the means; control cell -0.28 (4.84) duplicates another row
issues.explanation: In Table 3 the control group's Sit-to-Stand change is printed as -0.28 (4.84), identical to the intervention group's affective state change. The control means rise from 10.92 to 11.28, which is a gain of 0.36. The intervention change printed as 0.32 also differs from 10.65 - 9.87 = 0.78. The discussion states that the control group 'worsened', relying on the questionable cell, which exaggerates the apparent contrast with the intervention group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Original data showing a control change of -0.28 (4.84) in completers, with the repeat in the affective row a coincidence.

quotes.text: The intervention group's baseline score on the Sit-to-Stand Test improved, whereas that of the control group worsened.

issues.title: Only per-protocol analysis of 87 of 100 randomised; 13 post-randomisation exclusions, no ITT sensitivity
issues.explanation: Efficacy was analysed only for the 87 completers, with exclusions for reinfection and for missing sessions or the evaluation. Excluding randomised participants for non-attendance breaks the randomised comparison, and the effect of this cannot be assessed from the paper. Because attrition is modest and balanced and the result is null, the impact on the conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis giving the same null between-group results.

quotes.text: a per-protocol analysis was performed, comparing baseline, 3 months, and the 3-month-baseline differences between both groups using Student T.
4 due to reinfection and 9 for their failure to attend a face-to-face session or the evaluation session.

issues.title: About 13 outcomes and several regression models tested without multiplicity adjustment; borderline p = 0.021-0.036
issues.explanation: Thirteen outcomes were compared at two time points plus change scores, and four regression models were fitted with no correction or pre-specified primary model. Several of the reported 'significant' predictors have p = 0.021 and 0.036, which would not survive a modest correction. These models also rely on small samples (about 45 in the intervention group) with several covariates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A declared analysis plan treating these models as hypothesis-generating only, with the conclusions worded accordingly.

quotes.text: However, significant models did show a decrease in the number of persistent symptoms, and an improvement in cognitive functioning (MoCA), physical functioning (Sit-to-Stand Test), and Community social support (PCSQ).

issues.title: Adherence reported as 17 participants (25%) of the intervention group, but 17/45 = 37.8% and 17/52 = 32.7%
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results state that 25% of intervention participants made significant use of the APP, giving 17 participants. Seventeen participants correspond to 32.7% of the 52 randomised or 37.8% of the 45 completers. The paper therefore understates adherence, which is central to its interpretation that the app failed because of poor adherence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A defined denominator of about 68 or a corrected count showing 13 participants.

quotes.text: Only 17 participants (25%) from the intervention group engaged in significant use of the APP

script.explanation: 17/52 = 32.69%, but the paper prints 25, outside the rounding interval [24.50, 26.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 68.0 rather than 52.

issues.title: Table 4 regression estimates lie outside their own CIs and the PCSQ predictors differ between table and text
issues.explanation: In Table 4 the MoCA coefficient is 0.346 but its 95% CI runs from -0.538 to -0.154, which does not contain the estimate. The gender coefficient is -2.454 but its CI is 0.928 to 8.732, again excluding it. The Results text says community social support was predicted by APP minutes and health literacy, whereas Table 4 lists self-efficacy. These models underpin the paper's abstract claims, so their direction and predictors cannot be confirmed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Original regression output showing consistent estimates and CIs and the correct PCSQ predictor.

quotes.text: Finally, improvement in community social support was predicted by the minutes of APP use and an increase in health literacy.

script.explanation: the estimate 0.346 lies outside its own CI [-0.538, -0.154]; the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0004 (reachable range [0.0004, 0.0004] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.001 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Table 2 gender and education cells do not match group sizes (44/52 printed 84.5%; 47/52 printed 94.4%; control 12+33=45)
issues.explanation: The women percentage in the intervention group is printed as 84.5%, but 44/52 is 84.6%. The education row prints 47 (94.4%), but 47/52 is 90.4%, and the same row gives 5 (9.6%), which implies 47. The control group gender counts (12 men + 33 women) add to 45, not 48, and the total of 80 women implies 36 in the control group. These are reporting slips in the baseline table; they do not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 36 control women and 47/52 intervention participants with secondary or university studies, with the printed values being typesetting errors.

script.explanation: 44/52 = 84.62%, but the paper prints 84.5, outside the rounding interval [84.45, 84.60]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 52.1 rather than 52.

issues.title: Open-label trial with self-reported SF-36 primary outcome and no blinded outcome assessment described
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the primary outcome is self-reported. Assessors of outcomes are not described as blinded. This limits any positive claim, though the primary result was null so it mainly affects the weight given to the secondary regression findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors were blind to allocation, or an objective primary outcome.

quotes.text: An open-label randomized clinical trial was conducted using two parallel groups
all participants were informed of the assigned intervention during the RCT.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-3010169/v1.headline_claim: EchA Marine (sea urchin egg extract, Echinochrome A) is an effective and safe treatment option for Long COVID patients, improving quality of life, particularly pain/discomfort and mobility.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-3010169/v1.overall: The claim that the supplement is an effective Long COVID treatment is not well supported: it rests on 46 analysed patients, two of five EQ-5D dimensions (one of which would not survive correction for multiple tests), end-point-only ANOVA on ordinal data, a retrospectively registered trial, and an unexplained switch away from the registered primary outcomes. The reported statistics also contain several transcription errors (the Table 2 F column and the captions). At most, the data are hypothesis-generating for pain and quality-of-life scores.

primary_outcome.name: EQ-5D-3L quality of life dimensions (EuroQol); paper's stated primary outcome is quality of life across the five dimensions

primary_outcomes.measure: Change of symptoms over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) during rutine medical checkup.
Change of lung capacity over four times (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) assessed during spirometry.
Change of walking distance during a six minutes walk test (6MWT) over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks)
Change of depression measured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via the Beck Health Questionnaire.
Change in the quality of life meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via visual analog scale of EuroQol (EQ-VAS).
Presence or absence of Myocarditis meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via electrocardiogram.
Change in the cognitive function meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via Trial Making test (TMT).
Change in the cognitive function meassured over time-points (baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks) via Phonological verbal fluency test.

issues.title: 'Effective treatment' and 'improved all dimensions' claimed from 2 of 5 EQ-5D dimensions in 46 patients
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Discussion say the supplement is effective for Long COVID and improved all dimensions. In fact only pain/discomfort and mobility reached p<0.05, three dimensions showed no difference, and the seven registered primary outcomes beyond EQ-5D are not reported. The inference of improvement across all dimensions rests on the absence of a '3' value in the treated group, which was not tested. A cautious conclusion of a possible benefit in pain and mobility, needing replication, is all the evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant effects on all dimensions or pre-registered confirmatory results for the registered primaries.

quotes.text: The dietary supplement EchA Marine® is an effective treatment option for Long COVID patients.
This indicates that the supplement improved all dimensions studied

second_reader.what_stands: The paper claims an effective treatment and 'improved all dimensions' although only 2 of 5 dimensions differed between groups at the end, and the 3 other dimensions were not significant. The 'all dimensions' inference rests on the absence of level-3 responses in one arm, which is not a test, and there is no baseline-adjusted or change analysis.

issues.title: Analysed 46 of 100 planned; significance in a small trial called 'robust'
issues.explanation: The trial reached under half its planned sample (46 analysed versus 100 planned), and the power calculation was for a success-rate difference that is not what was analysed. The Discussion argues that significance despite the small sample shows the results are robust. That inverts the usual reading: with low power, significant findings tend to be exaggerated and fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified rationale for stopping at 50 and a confidence interval narrow enough to exclude a trivial effect.

quotes.text: Thus, a total of 50 patients per group will be included.
Considering that, despite the small sample size, the results were statistically signicant, and can be seen to be robust

second_reader.what_stands: Only 46 of the 100 planned participants were analysed, so the trial fell far short of its stated sample size, and the authors still describe the significant results as 'robust'. With 46 analysed, 4 dropouts excluded, and 7 tests with no multiplicity adjustment, a significant p-value does not establish robustness.

issues.title: Final scores compared by one-way ANOVA on 3-level ordinal data, with no baseline adjustment or change testing
issues.explanation: Only end-of-study scores were compared between arms, using one-way ANOVA on 3-level ordinal ratings. Baseline scores were not used as a covariate, and no within-arm or change-from-baseline tests were reported. Despite that, the Results state that the placebo 'did not have a significant effect' and that the supplement 'achieved a significant decrease', which are claims about change that were never tested. With 46 patients, small baseline imbalances (for example mobility, where baseline MS is .333) could drive the final difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or ordinal analysis adjusted for baseline, or change-from-baseline tests, giving the same findings.

quotes.text: One-way analysis of variance was used to compare quality of life scores between patients in the treatment group and the placebo group.
The most signicant effect was observed in the reduction of pain and discomfort, where the placebo did not have a signicant effect.

second_reader.what_stands: Final scores were compared with one-way ANOVA on 3-level ordinal data, and no baseline-adjusted or within-group change test was reported, so statements that placebo 'did not have a significant effect' are not backed by any reported test. A final-score comparison is acceptable under randomisation with similar baselines, so that choice alone is not an error. The Table 2 F column repeats Table 3 values and does not match its own sums of squares, and the Figure 1 legend gives a sum of squares (3.415) as F.

issues.title: Paper reports EQ-5D as sole primary outcome; seven of eight registered primary outcomes are not reported
issues.explanation: The registry lists eight primary outcomes, and the paper reports only EQ-5D dimensions plus TTO/VAS, with no mention of the other registered measures. Readers cannot tell whether those were measured, dropped, or reported elsewhere. Selective reporting of the outcomes that came out significant would inflate the apparent effect, and the paper gives no explanation for the change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry history showing EQ-5D as the primary from the outset, or a companion paper reporting the other registered outcomes.

quotes.text: The main outcome measures were the values of the dimensions of health of EuroQol 5-Dimension (EQ-5D) questionnaire.
The safety and ecacy of the product will also be evaluated.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports only EQ-5D based outcomes, and seven of the eight registered primary outcomes (symptoms, spirometry, 6MWT, Beck depression, myocarditis, TMT, phonological fluency) have no results in the paper; safety and efficacy are mentioned but not reported. The claim that EQ-5D is the sole registered primary is not exact: the registered primary is EQ-VAS, which the paper reports as VAS, and the registry record could not show whether outcomes changed over time.

issues.title: Seven EQ-5D outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 without adjustment; mobility (p=0.013) would not survive Bonferroni
issues.explanation: The authors tested seven outcomes with no multiplicity control and highlight two as significant. With 0.05/7 = 0.007, pain/discomfort and TTO stay significant, but mobility (p=0.013) and VAS (p=0.022) do not. The Abstract presents mobility as a key finding without caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or a stated correction showing mobility remains significant.

quotes.text: A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically signicant.
Although values were not signicant in other dimensions

issues.title: Safety asserted in Discussion but no adverse event data reported despite stated safety evaluation
issues.explanation: The Methods say safety would be evaluated, and the Discussion calls the findings encouraging given the 'safety' of the supplement. The Results contain no adverse-event counts, withdrawals due to harm, or reasons for the four dropouts. Safety is therefore asserted rather than shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table of adverse events by arm and reasons for the four non-completers.

quotes.text: These ndings are especially encouraging given the safety and natural origin of the
The safety and ecacy of the product will also be evaluated.

issues.title: Table 2 F column copies Table 3 F values; figure captions misstate baseline significance and one F
issues.explanation: Every F value in the baseline table (Table 2) is identical to the matching final-condition F in Table 3, even though the baseline mean squares give very different ratios. For example, TTO basal is .064/.074 = 0.87, not 9.746. The captions add two further errors. Figure 2 says VAS and TTO differed significantly at baseline, which contradicts Table 2 (p=.734, .358) and the Results text. Figure 1 gives F=3.415 for pain/discomfort, but that is the mean square, and Table 3 gives F=8.863. The p-values and sums of squares are internally consistent, so the main results hold, but the reported statistics cannot be taken at face value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 with F values equal to MS between / MS within, and a Figure 2 caption restricted to final-condition tests.

quotes.text: Treatments presented signicant differences both in Basal and Final conditions (F 1,44 = 5.632 p= 0.022; F 1,44 = 9.746 p= 0.003; α =0.05)

issues.explanation: The Results text says 60% of both arms were male, but Table 1 gives 64% and 62.5%. The text attaches p=0.163 to BMI and p=0.249 to age, while Table 1 attaches them the other way round. The reported sex test (chi-square 2, p=0.153) does not fit the near-identical Table 1 proportions. These are baseline-comparability errors that do not change the efficacy results, but they show weak proofreading of the statistics.

issues.title: Recruitment end stated as December 2022 (Abstract, Results) but October 2022 (Methods)
issues.explanation: The recruitment window differs by two months between sections of the paper. This is a minor inconsistency that does not affect the effect estimates, but it leaves the actual enrolment period unclear.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-3733202/v1.headline_claim: Supervised, tailored mixed exercise for 8 weeks is safe and effective in improving physical capacity and wellbeing in people with post-COVID condition (PCC).
10.21203/rs.3.rs-3733202/v1.overall: The paper is an exploratory, non-randomised pilot with 15 vs 10 participants; the safety observations are plausible but the claim that exercise is 'effective' rests on two nominal interaction p-values (0.043, 0.040) with no multiplicity control, while other physical tests were null. The molecular findings are descriptive and explicitly underpowered. The headline conclusion should be read as tentative feasibility and safety evidence only.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Non-randomised 15 vs 10 study without power calculation concludes exercise is 'effective'
issues.explanation: Participants were assigned sequentially (not randomised) to exercise (n=15) or no-exercise (n=10), with no sample-size calculation, no registration, and open assessment. Two of six physical capacity interactions reached p just under 0.05 with no multiplicity correction, while the others (6MWT 0.524, HGS 0.657, TUG 0.577, sit and reach 0.761) did not. Baseline groups also differed (weight, BMI), and the abstract concludes the program is effective for general physical capacity and wellbeing. The data support at most a tentative signal of feasibility and safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a power calculation, randomised allocation, or multiplicity-adjusted significant results across the physical tests.

quotes.text: Twenty-five women and men with PCC were assigned sequentially to exercise (n = 15) and
Supervised exercise adapted to the level of fatigue and ability is safe and effective in PCC
Two obvious limitations of this study are the small sample size

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is indeed a non-randomised (sequential allocation) 15 vs 10 comparison with no power calculation described, and its abstract conclusion calls exercise 'safe and effective'. The claim is narrower than it looks because the authors call the study proof-of-principle, name small sample size as a limitation, say the study was underpowered for sex effects, and the main Conclusions section only says 'safe' and 'does not result in post-exertion malaise'. The 'effective' wording rests on 2 of 6 physical tests reaching p of about 0.04 without correction, and non-randomisation is not listed as a

issues.title: Results text attaches 'all p<0.001' to the group comparison; interaction p-values are 0.043 and 0.040
issues.explanation: The Results say STS-30 (p=0.043) and bicep curl (p=0.040) improved to a greater extent in the exercise group 'as compared to the control group (all p<0.001)'. Figure 2 shows p<0.001 applies to the main effect of time, while the group-by-time interaction is 0.043 and 0.040. The sentence therefore misattributes p<0.001 to the between-group difference, which could make the between-group effect look stronger than it is. The abstract and figure values are consistent with each other.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the p<0.001 refers only to the time effect, or a separate between-group test with p<0.001.

quotes.text: to a greater extent in the exercise group as compared
quotes.location: Results, Positive impact of tailored exercise regimen
Results, Positive impact of tailored exercise regimen

issues.title: Completers-only analysis (>=20/24 sessions); one exercise dropout excluded, no ITT
issues.explanation: The methods require attendance of at least 20 of 24 sessions to be included in analysis, and results describe only the 25 who completed. One exercise-group dropout is mentioned; the six other exclusions are not clearly assigned to arms, so the allocated denominator per group is unclear. Since adherent completers are analysed, effects may be somewhat optimistic, but with so few losses the effect on the conclusions is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing all allocated participants analysed, or that no one was excluded for low attendance and exclusions occurred before allocation.

quotes.text: One participant dropped out in the exercise group because the research centre was too far.

10.21203/rs.3.rs-3744463/v1.headline_claim: Supervised 8-week tailored mixed exercise is safe and effective in post-COVID-19 condition, improving physical capacity and wellbeing, with systemic molecular markers (oxidative stress, plasma proteomics) that can be monitored.
10.21203/rs.3.rs-3744463/v1.overall: The headline claim that tailored exercise is safe and effective is only weakly supported: allocation was sequential and non-randomised, groups were unbalanced, the sample is 25 completers, and the two between-group results are marginal (p=0.040, 0.043) without multiplicity control. Safety and feasibility are the better-supported conclusions. Several text-versus-table inconsistencies (p<0.001, handgrip, PASE direction, counts) are minor but indicate loose reporting.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; physical capacity tests (Bicep Curl and STS-30) reported as the main improvements

issues.title: N=25, no sample-size calculation, no multiplicity control; 'safe and effective' rests on p=0.040 and p=0.043
issues.explanation: With 15 vs 10 participants, no power calculation, six capacity tests plus PASE, HGS and symptoms tested at alpha 0.05 without correction, the two marginal results would not survive adjustment. The limitations are acknowledged, but the abstract conclusion states efficacy without qualification. Also, safety in 15 exercisers cannot exclude uncommon harms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome and sample-size justification, or multiplicity-adjusted significance.

quotes.text: Supervised exercise adapted to the level of fatigue and ability is safe and effective in PCC patients
Two obvious  limitations  of  this  study  are  the  small  sample  size
quotes.location: Limitations and strengths of the study and future research

second_reader.what_stands: N=25, no stated sample-size calculation and no multiplicity adjustment are all true, and the two headline p-values (0.040, 0.043) would not survive any correction across the six capacity tests. However, the authors explicitly flag the small sample as a limitation, and 'safe' is supported by absence of reported adverse events and stable fatigue rather than by those p-values, so the claim is overstated rather than unacknowledged.

issues.title: Abstract concludes 'effective' for 'physical capacity and wellbeing' despite null symptom/fatigue results
issues.explanation: Symptoms and fatigue did not change, wellbeing was not measured, and only two capacity tests showed marginal between-group differences in a non-randomised sample. The abstract conclusion of effectiveness is stronger than this evidence supports. The main-text conclusion on safety is better supported but rests on 15 participants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A measured wellbeing outcome showing benefit.

quotes.text: is safe and effective in PCC patients in improving their general physical capacity and wellbeing
The exercise regimen had no significant impact on altered taste and smell, anxiety, neurological symptoms, general pain, asthma

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's 'effective ... wellbeing' is broader than the data: no wellbeing or quality-of-life measure was collected, symptoms and fatigue showed no improvement, and only two of six capacity tests were significant at p~0.04. It is not accurate to say the nulls were concealed, because they are reported and the fatigue result is framed as showing no harm, and the PASE interaction (p=0.007) does support a narrower claim about physical activity.

issues.title: Sequential (non-random) allocation of 15 vs 10 participants with baseline imbalances; efficacy claimed
issues.explanation: Participants were allocated sequentially, so group membership could depend on enrolment timing and is predictable. Groups differ at baseline in weight, waist and sex mix. Causal efficacy claims from between-group differences are therefore weakened, and the paper concludes 'effective' without that caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that allocation was concealed and unrelated to participant characteristics.

quotes.text: participants were allocated sequentially to one of the two groups: control (usual care) or exercise (8 weeks of mixed tailored supervised exercise)

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was sequential (non-random) with unequal groups of 15 vs 10, and Table 2 shows baseline differences in weight, waist, sex mix, PCC duration and PASE, with the text's description of which parameters differ not matching the table's p-values. Efficacy is claimed in the abstract conclusion, although the Discussion and Limitations are more tentative and the study is labelled proof-of-principle.

issues.title: Results text gives p=0.043/0.040 then 'all p<0.001' for the same physical capacity comparisons
issues.explanation: The Results quote p=0.043 (STS-30) and p=0.040 (bicep curl) and then attach 'all p<0.001' to the sentence about greater improvement in the exercise group. These cannot all describe the same between-group comparison. Likely p<0.001 is the time effect, but as written the text overstates the strength of the between-group evidence. The between-group results themselves are only marginally significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that p<0.001 refers solely to the main effect of time, with the interaction p values as 0.040 and 0.043.

quotes.text: significantly improved with time but to a greater extent in the exercise group as compared to the control group (all p<0.001)
Bicep Curl (p=0.040) and STS-30 (p=0.043) improved to a greater extent in the exercise group than in the non-exercise group.

issues.title: Open-label design; self-reported PASE (p=0.007) and fatigue outcomes with no blinding or control-group fatigue data
issues.explanation: Participants necessarily knew their allocation, and PASE and symptoms are self-reported. Fatigue, the basis of the 'no post-exertion malaise' claim, was recorded only in the exercise group before sessions, so there is no comparator. The PASE benefit may reflect expectation or reporting effects.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Report of assessor blinding and a control-group fatigue measure.

quotes.text: Participants of the exercise group were questioned on their fatigue level before each training session
General fatigue was measured in the exercise group only as a proxy a potential post-exertion malaise.

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 7 of 32 enrolled (22%) not analysed; adherence of 20/24 sessions required
issues.explanation: Of 32 who agreed, 25 were analysed, and the methods require at least 20 of 24 sessions to be included. This is a per-protocol estimate, and no intention-to-treat analysis is given. Only one exclusion was clearly treatment-related, so the bias is probably modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT analysis giving similar estimates.

quotes.text: Participants had to attend at least 20 of the 24 sessions to be included in final analyses.
One participant dropped out in the exercise group because the research centre was too far.

issues.title: Handgrip strength (p=0.089) described as significantly improved in the Discussion
issues.explanation: Results describe only a tendency (p=0.089), but the Discussion says upper body was significantly improved 'as shown by significant improvements in biceps curl and handgrip strength'. Handgrip does not meet the stated p≤0.05 criterion. This inflates a secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A test of HGS with p≤0.05 reported anywhere.

quotes.text: a tendency for a significantly greater progress for HGS (p= 0.089)
Nevertheless, upper body was also significantly improved by 8 weeks of RT

issues.title: PASE fell in no-exercise group (229.20 to 202.80) but Discussion says it improved
issues.explanation: Results show the control PASE decreasing by 26.4 points, yet the Discussion states it improved less dramatically and draws a conclusion about natural recovery. The printed data contradict the interpretation. The exercise-vs-control PASE difference is, if anything, larger than the Discussion implies, but the interpretive statement is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the Discussion refers to a different measure (e.g. physical capacity tests) rather than PASE.

in the noexercise group, which indicates that physical capacity improves over time in PCC patients

issues.title: Resting heart rate called a significant decrease in both groups; Table 2 time effect is p=0.057
issues.explanation: The text says resting heart rate decreased significantly, while the only reported test for time is p=0.057, above the stated p≤0.05 threshold. The claim is not supported by the printed statistic. It is a secondary measure with no bearing on the headline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A separate within-group test showing p<0.05 for each group.

issues.explanation: The text says 7 of 10 no-exercise paired samples showed no significant change, yet the sex breakdown adds to 6. Either the total or a subgroup count is wrong. It affects a secondary proteomics description only.

issues.explanation: The same characteristic of the same 25 participants is counted as 10 in Table 1 and as 11 when the Table 2 group counts are added. This is a minor reporting inconsistency with no bearing on efficacy.

issues.title: Text names weight and BMI as baseline differences; table shows only waist at p=0.036 (weight 0.060, BMI 0.077)
issues.explanation: The text identifies weight and BMI as the baseline differences, yet the table's only p<0.05 is waist circumference, while weight (0.060) and BMI (0.077, an interaction term) are not significant. Baseline imbalance in body size between non-randomised groups is real, but the text misreports which variable. Minor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Table footnote showing italic p values as tendencies and an explanation that tendencies were counted as differences.
