issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or usual-care control arm showing less change, or external data on spontaneous recovery over 8 months in comparable patients.

quotes.text: Significant improvement was seen in all parameters in long-term results with telerehabilitation programs
This study was proved the positive effects of two different telerehabilitation methods on activity, functionality, resting, and post-exertion hemodynamic parameters at long-term follow up.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of 'proved' positive effects of both programmes rests on pre-post change within each arm; no untreated or usual-care control arm exists, so change from natural recovery over 8 months cannot be separated from programme effect. The paper also says the study 'proved' and 'proven' benefits without acknowledging this limitation, and its listed limitations do not mention the missing control.

issues.title: Baseline saturation lower in VCG-ST (p=0.019, 0.008); promised covariate adjustment not reported
issues.explanation: The arm that is said to improve more in saturation started significantly lower, so larger gains are expected from regression toward the mean and a ceiling in the other arm. The Methods say baseline-imbalanced variables would be used as covariates, but no adjusted result is presented. The saturation superiority claim therefore cannot be separated from the imbalance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported ANCOVA or mixed-model with baseline saturation as covariate retaining the group effect.

quotes.text: The baseline mean oxygen saturation of VCG-ST was less than the MAG-AT group at rest ( p= 0.019)
Any variable with a significant difference in the baselines between the two groups would be used as covariance in the comparison.

second_reader.what_stands: The baseline imbalance in saturation (p=0.019 at rest, p=0.008 after exertion, VCG-ST lower) is stated in the text, and the Methods promise covariate adjustment, yet the Results never say that adjustment was done or give adjusted estimates. Because Tables 2 and 3 are empty in the supplied text, it cannot be excluded that a table footnote reports adjustment, so 'not reported' is established only for the main text.

issues.title: Videoconferencing superiority rests on two saturation p-values (0.031, 0.004) among many uncorrected tests
issues.explanation: About ten outcomes were each tested at alpha 0.05 across time points with no multiplicity control. The post-exertion saturation result (p=0.004) is more robust, but the resting result (p=0.031) would not survive a correction. The superiority is also confined to one outcome type and entangled with the baseline imbalance in that same measure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome (resting saturation) or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis retaining significance.

quotes.text: The significance level was set at p< 0.050.
A significant improvement was seen in oxygen saturation, when analyzing the between-group effect at rest ( p= 0.031) and postexertion ( p= 0.004).

issues.title: Same unblinded physiotherapist delivered and assessed; Borg dyspnoea/fatigue and IPAQ are self-reported
issues.explanation: One physiotherapist trained, supervised and assessed every participant, online, and the assessments of dyspnoea and fatigue are subjective. This can bias the within-group claims of improved symptoms. Blind analysis does not remove assessment bias, though the oximetry-based comparison is less exposed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Assessments by an independent blinded assessor, or demonstration that the subjective outcomes were not driving the conclusions.

quotes.text: The lack of a blinded evaluator was another limitation of this study.
Outcomes were measured at baseline assessment, post-treatment, and followup (8 months after baseline assessment) by the same physiotherapist.

issues.title: Conclusion asserts 'safe' and 'relatively inexpensive' with no cost data and 27 participants
issues.explanation: No costs were collected, and the authors acknowledge this as a limitation, yet the Conclusion states inexpensiveness as a finding. Safety rests on no recorded adverse events in 27 patients, which is too few to rule out a clinically relevant event rate. The limitation is disclosed in the Discussion but not carried into the headline conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A cost analysis of both programmes and a larger safety dataset.

quotes.text: Telerehabilitation programs are safe, useful, and relatively inexpensive ways to improve symptoms
Unfortunately, the lack of cost analysis was a limitation of the study.

issues.title: Target of 32 not reached (27 analysed); post hoc power of 86% used; null between-group results read as similarity
issues.explanation: Fewer participants than planned were analysed, and the one-tailed calculation assumed an effect of d=0.25 that is smaller than a conventional moderate effect. Post hoc power derived from the observed saturation difference is circular. The non-significant between-group results for other outcomes are interpreted as showing both methods work similarly, which this sample cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample size for the primary comparison that was met, or equivalence margins with confidence intervals.

quotes.text: assuming a dropout rate of 10%, 32 participants were needed.
the number of cases that met the inclusion criteria and volunteered within the specified time period was below our expectations

10.2340/jrm-cc.v7.24581.headline_claim: A multidisciplinary team assessment for post-COVID-19 condition is not fully convincing as beneficial, but since participants perceived it as helpful, it seems to be of some value.
10.2340/jrm-cc.v7.24581.overall: The paper's main finding, no significant change in any questionnaire after six months, is reported honestly, but with 13-14 patients per test it cannot show absence of change either. The added conclusion that the assessment 'seems to be of some value' rests on an uncontrolled, unblinded helpfulness rating from 13 of 22 patients, and the supporting sex difference (p = 0.012) comes from a chi-square on cells too small for it (exact p about 0.035). The paper's own wording is hedged, so the headline holds only as tentative.

issues.title: 'Some value' concluded from one self-rated helpfulness item (10/13) in an uncontrolled, unblinded pilot
issues.explanation: All objective-ish and validated measures (HADS, MFS, OGQ, activity, sick leave) showed no change, yet the conclusion says the assessment has value because patients said it was helpful. The rating comes from 13 of 22 enrolled patients, with no comparator, no blinding, no information on the rehabilitation actually received, and likely expectation and courtesy effects. Satisfaction does not show benefit, so only a tentative reading is supported. The lack of a control group also means that natural recovery cannot be separated from any effect, in either direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison or validated measure showing improvement attributable to the assessment.

quotes.text: the team assessment seems to be of some value
There was no control nor follow-up questions regarding compliance.

second_reader.what_stands: The 'some value' conclusion rests on one self-rated item answered by 13 of 22 enrolled patients (10 rated it helpful, mostly 'small-moderate'), in a single-arm, unblinded pilot with no control group, no compliance data and no power calculation, while all validated outcome measures showed no significant improvement. The authors do soften the claim ('not fully convincing', 'seems to be', call for controlled studies), so the overstatement is moderate and is partly offset by their caveats. Nonetheless the item cannot show value of the assessment as distinct from expectation, attention or natural c

issues.title: 7 of 22 (31.8%) lost to follow-up; completer-only analysis and underpowered drop-out comparison
issues.explanation: Seven of 22 patients withdrew and all outcomes, including perceived helpfulness, come from the 15 who remained (13 answered the helpfulness item). The drop-out analysis found no differences, but with 7 dropouts it could not detect meaningful ones. Patients who stayed in are plausibly more likely to rate the assessment helpful, so the 76.9% figure may be too favourable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline characteristics and symptom scores of dropouts shown to be similar with adequate precision, or a sensitivity analysis treating dropouts as unhelpful.

quotes.text: seven had withdrawn from the study

issues.title: Pilot of 15 analysed without power calculation; non-significant changes cannot show lack of effect
issues.explanation: With 13-14 patients per comparison and no sample-size calculation, the non-significant pre-post tests cannot distinguish no change from a real change. The authors state this limitation, and their wording is cautious. The limitation weakens the null findings rather than inflating a claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size rationale or confidence intervals showing clinically important changes can be excluded.

quotes.text: the lack of power calculation, as well as the small size of the population

issues.title: Sex difference in helpfulness (8/8 vs 2/5, p=0.012) matches an uncorrected chi-square on tiny cells; exact p about 0.035
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results report that 100% of women but 40% of men found the assessment helpful (p = 0.012). From a 2x2 table of 8/0 vs 2/3, the printed p reproduces Pearson chi-square, which is inappropriate when expected counts fall below 5. A Fisher exact test gives roughly 0.035, so the difference is much less certain than stated. It is also one of several unplanned subgroup comparisons, and the discussion builds an explanation about gender expectations on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that an exact test was used and gave 0.012 (it cannot with these counts), or different underlying counts.

quotes.text: all the women 100% ( n =  8) perceived it as being helpful, compared with 40% ( n =  2) of the men ( p =  0.012).
Differences between the participants and the non-participants were analyzed using the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test and the Chi-square test.

issues.title: Men's baseline: groceries 80% vs travelling 67%, though text says travelling highest for all groups
issues.explanation: The text says travelling had the highest gap frequency for all groups. For men at baseline, Table III shows shopping for groceries at 4 gaps (80%) and travelling at 4 gaps (67%), so travelling is tied by count and lower by percentage. This is a small overstatement in the description of one subgroup and does not affect any outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the comparison is by count or pooled across groups, or a corrected Table III showing travelling highest in men at baseline.

quotes.text: Travelling was the item with the highest frequency of gaps for all groups.

issues.title: Hospitalisation 33.3% (n=5) is labelled as share of respondents but equals 5/15, not 5/12 (41.7%)
issues.explanation: The Demographics text says that among those who provided hospitalisation information, 33.3% (n = 5) were hospitalised. Table I shows 3 of 15 had missing data, so 12 answered, and 5/12 is 41.7%. The 33.3% is the share of all 15 participants. This is a minor labelling error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 33.3% was intentionally given over all 15 participants and the text wording is just loose (which would make it a wording slip only).

quotes.text: hospitalization  occurred  in  33.3%  ( n =  5)
Missing data 3 20.0
quotes.location: Table I, Hospitalized during infection block

script.explanation: 5/12 = 41.67%, but the paper prints 33.3, outside the rounding interval [33.25, 33.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 15.0 rather than 12.

10.2340/jrm.v54.3972.headline_claim: Adding manual diaphragm release to inspiratory muscle training improves maximal inspiratory pressure, dyspnoea, fatigue, lactate, 6-minute walk distance and blood pressure more than inspiratory muscle training alone in men with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.2340/jrm.v54.3972.overall: The direction of the PImax and blood pressure results is plausible, but the paper has several internal inconsistencies: baseline BP outside its own entry criterion, an ITT claim with a completer analysis (error df 58 vs 52 analysed), a Table I n mismatch, and misattributed percentages in the Discussion. The headline claim of superiority across all outcomes should be treated as tentative until the analysed population and the data tables are reconciled.

primary_outcome.name: PImax (maximum static inspiratory pressure) at 6 weeks

issues.title: Baseline SBP/DBP ranges (max 159/98 mmHg) lie wholly below the stated stage II entry criterion (160-179/100-109)
issues.explanation: Eligibility required stage II hypertension of 160-179/100-109 mmHg, yet Table I shows the highest baseline SBP as 159 and 158 mmHg and the highest DBP as 98 mmHg in both arms. No participant could have met the stated criterion at baseline. Either the criterion or the reported baseline data are wrong, and the conclusion about 'hypertensive patients' rests on that population.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the criterion applied to screening readings and that baseline readings were taken after a run-in or treatment.

quotes.text: hypertension at stage II (160-179/100-109 mmHg)

second_reader.what_stands: The baseline SBP and DBP ranges printed in Table I (max 159/98 study, 158/98 control) lie entirely below the stated stage II entry criterion of 160-179/100-109 mmHg, so either the criterion was not applied as written or it is misreported. The paper does not explain this, though a difference between screening and baseline measurements cannot be excluded.

issues.title: ITT claimed but only 52 of 60 completers analysed; F(1,58) df implies 60 and Table I % use n=30
issues.explanation: The paper says data were analysed by intention-to-treat, yet states that only the 52 completers were included in the analysis and describes no imputation. The ANOVA error df of 58 implies 60 observations, and Table I percentages are calculated on 30 per arm while headers say n = 26. The analysed population is unclear, and the 13% loss after randomisation is handled as a completer analysis, which can inflate between-group differences.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of imputation or a full 60-participant analysis, and the reconciliation of Table I counts with n = 26.

quotes.text: data was analysed using the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle (21)
completed the study and were included in the data analysis

second_reader.what_stands: The paper says it used ITT but analysed only the 52 completers with no imputation described, which is not ITT; the F(1,58) degrees of freedom imply 60 analysed participants rather than 52, and the Table I categorical counts and percentages are based on 30 per group despite the n = 26 column headers. Which sample size the test statistics actually used cannot be determined from the paper.

issues.title: Abstracts say 52 allocated and all completed; Methods says 60 randomised with 8 dropouts
issues.explanation: The abstract states 52 men were randomly allocated and the lay abstract says 52 were enrolled and all completed. Methods says 60 were randomised (30 per arm) and only 52 completed, with 8 dropouts. The headline numbers therefore leave out a 13% loss after randomisation, and the registry lists actual enrollment of 90, which the paper does not reconcile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram showing 52 randomised with no post-randomisation losses, and an explanation of the registry's enrollment of 90.

quotes.text: Fifty-two  men  with  post-COVID-19 syndrome were allocated randomly to the study and control groups.
Sixty patients were randomly assigned to the study ( n = 30) and control groups
A  total of 52 men with post-COVID-19 syndrome were enrolled,  and all completed the study.

issues.title: Discussion gives 0.95% BP reduction for the study group; Table II shows 0.95% is control DBP, study is 16.67%/18.08%
issues.explanation: The Discussion states the study group had a 0.95% reduction in both SBP and DBP relative to control. Table II gives 0.95% as the control group's DBP change, while the study group changed by 16.67% (SBP) and 18.08% (DBP). The text understates the reported effect and conflates the two arms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 0.95% denotes a between-group difference, which would not match any value in Table II.

quotes.text: A significant reduction in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure (by 0.95%, p < 0.001)

quotes.location: Table II, DBP study group, % improvement

issues.title: FSS reductions of 51.57%/17.65% in Discussion copy lactate values; FSS means give 33.9% and 6.4%
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives FSS reductions of 51.57% (study) and 17.65% (control), identical to the lactate percentages in Results. The FSS means printed in Results imply far smaller changes. The fatigue effect in the Discussion is therefore overstated by the repeated figures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different FSS scoring (e.g. percent of score range) that yields 51.57% and 17.65% from the printed means.

quotes.text: a reduction in FSS mean score by 51.57%, p < 0.001 in the study group

issues.title: Control PImax baseline SD is 17.52 in Table I but 7.52 in Table II; control change SD 33.12 also implausible
issues.explanation: The same pre-intervention PImax control SD is printed as 17.52 in Table I and 7.52 in Table II. The control change SD of 33.12 in Table II exceeds both pre and post SDs (7.52 and 5.86), which is hard to reconcile. The PImax control data in Table II are therefore unreliable, though the main PImax contrast still clearly favours the study group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original data table showing which SD is correct and a change SD consistent with it.

issues.title: Conclusion generalises to 'hypertensive patients' from men aged 30-45 with mild-moderate fibrosis
issues.explanation: The Conclusion recommends DR for 'these patients' (hypertensive post-COVID-19 patients) without restating the restriction to men aged 30-45, BMI 25-29.9, low-moderate activity. The trial was single-centre with 52 completers. The wording is somewhat broader than the sample supports, though the title and abstract name men.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion that explicitly restricts the recommendation to men aged 30-45 with the studied profile.

quotes.text: improves long-term symptoms in hypertensive patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome, suggesting that DR should be considered for use with these patients.
men aged 30-45 years
participant selection was limited to men with moderate COVID-19 syndrome only

issues.title: No sham or attention control for hands-on DR; participants unblinded for subjective outcomes
issues.explanation: The control arm received IMT only, with no sham manual contact, so extra therapist time and expectation could contribute to differences in subjective outcomes such as dyspnoea and fatigue. The paper says participants were blinded, which is implausible for a hands-on technique versus none. The add-on design answers a pragmatic question, but the effect cannot be attributed to DR itself.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants received a sham manual procedure indistinguishable from DR.

quotes.text: while the control group received IMT only
while the participants and outcome analyser were blinded to the group assignment

10.2340/jrm.v56.25491.headline_claim: Incentive spirometry or diaphragmatic breathing added to standard care was associated with better clinical improvement than standard care alone in post-COVID-19 condition with diaphragmatic dysfunction.
10.2340/jrm.v56.25491.overall: The direction of benefit for IS and DB over standard care is plausible, with large follow-up differences in several measures. But the trial is small, open-label, unregistered and uses a self-reported primary outcome with no sham control, so the size of the effect and the IS-over-DB claim are unreliable. Table III also appears to present reciprocal ORs, and the 'all parameters' claim overstates the G2 FEV1/FVC result.

primary_outcome.name: mMRC dyspnoea scale (clinical improvement)

issues.title: Open-label trial with self-reported mMRC primary outcome and no sham or attention control
issues.explanation: Patients knew whether they were doing supervised-style twice-daily breathing training or standard care alone. The primary outcome, mMRC, is a self-assessed dyspnoea scale, so expectation and extra-attention effects could account for part of the difference. Blinded assessors help for the ultrasound measures but not for patient-reported outcomes. The size of the effect is therefore likely overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that mMRC was administered by blinded assessors with a sham or attention-matched control arm, or concordant objective outcomes of similar magnitude.

quotes.text: While patients and investigators were not blinded regarding patients' allocation to interventional groups
This is a self-assessment tool that measures the impairment caused by breathlessness during daily activities.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label for patients and investigators, its primary outcome (mMRC) is described as a self-assessment tool, and the control arm is standard care alone with no sham or attention control. The authors disclose the lack of blinding and note that assessments were done by unaware independent staff, but this cannot remove expectation or performance bias from a patient-reported primary outcome, and the paper does not say how mMRC was actually collected.

issues.title: Table III ORs for IS (0.03) and DB (0.14) are the inverse of the improvement odds implied by the counts
issues.explanation: With standard care as reference, the reported improvement counts imply ORs well above 1 for IS and DB. The printed univariate ORs (0.06, 0.14) match the reciprocals of those values, so the outcome or reference coding appears reversed relative to how Table III and the text describe it. The direction of benefit is not in doubt. But the table as labelled says the opposite of the text, and the COVID-severity OR flips from 0.12 (univariate) to 10.79 (multivariate), so the coding is unclear throughout.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the model was fitted with non-improvement as the event, or with standard care coded as the comparator, that is printed in the paper or its supplement.

quotes.text: 11 patients (55.0%) in G2, and 3 patients (15.0%) in G3 showed improvement

issues.title: 'Significant improvement in G2 in all parameters' contradicted by G2 FEV1/FVC p = 0.069
issues.explanation: The Results and Abstract state that G1 and G2 improved significantly in all parameters. Table II gives the G2 within-group change in FEV1/FVC as p = 0.069, which is above the stated alpha of 0.05. The G2 SpO2-6MWT and other rows are significant, so the error is narrow but the summary statement is not accurate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated different alpha or an adjusted analysis showing the G2 FEV1/FVC change as significant.

quotes.text: revealed significant improvement in G1 and G2 in all parameters at the end of follow-up

quotes.location: Table II, FEV1/FVC block, p-value row

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 20 per arm with multivariable model and three-way claims
issues.explanation: No sample-size justification is given, and each arm has 20 patients. The multivariable logistic model uses several predictors on about 29 improvers, which gives very wide CIs (for example 1.83-63.47). The authors acknowledge the small sample, so this weakens the precision of secondary comparisons such as IS versus DB rather than the main direction of effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation showing adequate power for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: The findings of the present study may be limited by the small sample size and the short duration of followup.

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a randomized intervention study
issues.explanation: The Methods mention only ethics committee approval and consent. No registry identifier or prespecified protocol is cited, so the primary outcome and the improvement definition cannot be checked against a prior plan.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier with a registration date before enrolment and a matching primary outcome.

quotes.text: The study protocol was approved by the ethical committee of Al-Azhar Faculty of Medicine and all patients provided informed consent before participation.

issues.title: 'Proved to be superior' and 'useful' wording stronger than an open-label 60-patient trial supports
issues.explanation: The main conclusion is hedged. But the Discussion and Lay Abstract use definitive language ('proved to be superior', 'are useful') although the design is unblinded for the self-reported primary outcome, with no sham control or registration and a small sample. The IS-over-DB claim rests on secondary measures with no multiplicity handling.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmatory results from blinded, registered trials with adequate power.

quotes.text: While both interventions proved to be superior to standard care, IS provided better 6MWT as compared with DB.

issues.title: Binary 'improvement' on mMRC is never defined and its between-group test is not reported
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is described as clinical improvement on mMRC. The responder threshold is not defined, and the 75%/55%/15% proportions have no reported chi-square result. The logistic regression that carries the main inference depends on this unstated definition.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated responder definition (for example a drop of at least 1 mMRC point) and a reported test of the responder proportions.

quotes.text: 11 patients (55.0%) in G2, and 3 patients (15.0%) in G3 showed improvement

issues.title: Benefit narrative leans on within-arm significance versus non-significance in G3
issues.explanation: The Results and Abstract contrast within-arm changes (significant in G1 and G2, not in G3) as if this established a between-arm difference. Between-group follow-up comparisons are tabulated, but no baseline-adjusted or change-score comparison is reported. The follow-up differences in mMRC and 6MWT are large, so this weakens the presentation more than the finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported baseline-adjusted or change-score between-group test for each outcome.

quotes.text: However, no significant improvement was found in G3.

10.2340/jrm.v58.44926.headline_claim: Adding an incentive spirometer to standard rehabilitation improved peak expiratory flow and reduced dyspnoea in adults with post-COVID-19 condition, supporting its use as a low-cost adjunct for respiratory symptom management.
10.2340/jrm.v58.44926.overall: The direction of the PEF and dyspnoea results is plausible, but the headline PEF p (0.007) does not match its own CI (implied about 0.04), the analysis does not follow the stated change-score method, and the sample size and power statements are wrong. Open-label, patient-rated dyspnoea, retrospective registration and a changed primary-outcome set further limit confidence, so the conclusions are tentative rather than firm evidence of benefit.

primary_outcome.name: Peak expiratory flow (L/min), MRC dyspnoea scale, EQ-5D-5L VAS (three primaries as stated in the paper)

issues.title: Patient-rated MRC dyspnoea and effort-dependent PEF in an open-label trial with no sham device
issues.explanation: Participants knew they had received a spirometer, and the MRC grade is a patient-selected rating. PEF is also effort-dependent. The 1-point MRC advantage and the PEF gain may therefore partly reflect expectation or extra attention, and the abstract conclusion does not carry this caveat. The assessor-blinding statement appears only in the Limitations and is not described in the Methods.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham-device control, or a blinded objective dyspnoea measure showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Blinding of participants was not feasible, as those in the intervention group were provided with an incentive spirometer.
quotes.location: Methods, Study design, randomization, and blinding

quotes.text: Dyspnoea severity was evaluated using the original Medical Research Council (MRC) Dyspnoea Scale
quotes.location: Methods, Assessment tools and outcome measures

quotes.text: improved peak expiratory flow and reduced dyspnoea in adults with post-COVID-19 condition

second_reader.what_stands: Both headline outcomes depend on the participant: MRC is self-rated and PEF is effort-dependent. The trial was open-label for participants and therapist, with no sham device in the control arm. Assessor blinding, if it occurred as the Limitations describe, does not remove this expectation or effort bias, and the conclusions state the benefits without this caveat. What does not stand is any suggestion that the trial had no blinding at all: the paper reports a blinded outcome assessor in the Limitations, and the registry lists single masking.

issues.title: Sample size of 23 per group and 'achieved power 92%' do not follow from the stated inputs (about 45 and 77%)
issues.explanation: The paper's own inputs (SD about 84 L/min, difference 50 L/min, two-sided alpha 0.05, 80% power) require about 45 per group, not 23. At 41 per group the power is about 77%, not 92%. The observed PEF SDs (106 and 171 L/min) are larger than the 84 assumed, so power for the primary comparison is lower still. This leaves the trial modestly powered and weakens the reassurance given about its precision.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A documented calculation showing 23 per group suffices with different effect size or SD inputs, or a paired-design rationale.

quotes.text: a minimum of 23 participants per group (46 total) was required to detect this difference
the achieved power was approximately 92% to detect a 50 L/min between-group difference in PEF

issues.title: PEF headline difference 65.85 is the follow-up mean difference, not the stated change-score difference (89.02)
issues.explanation: The Methods say follow-up comparisons used change scores, but the PEF 'between-group difference' of 65.85 L/min is simply experimental minus control follow-up means. The change-score difference implied by the reported means is 89.02 L/min. The reported estimate, CI and p therefore do not correspond to the analysis the Methods describe, and the table footnote contradicts the Methods. The effect of the point estimate is understated, but the reported CI and p cannot be tied to a defined analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that PEF was analysed by follow-up comparison, or an adjusted model whose estimate equals 65.85.

quotes.text: using change scores (post-intervention minus baseline)
a mean PEF increase of 200.73 L/min from baseline to 1 month, compared with 111.71 L/min in the control
Between-group differences at 1 month are presented as raw mean differences

issues.title: Paper's primary outcomes (PEF, MRC, EQ-VAS) differ from registered primaries (Barthel, MRC, PEF)
issues.explanation: The registry record names Barthel Index as a primary outcome, whereas the paper presents Barthel as secondary and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L VAS) as primary. The paper also describes the primaries as 'prespecified'. Because the swapped outcomes were both null and the headline outcomes were registered, the effect on the conclusion is limited, but the primary-outcome set is not the registered one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original registered record or protocol listing EQ-5D-5L as primary and Barthel as secondary.

quotes.text: PEF, MRC, and EQ-5D-5L (VAS) are the primary outcomes.
No statistically significant between-group differences were observed at 1 month for the Barthel Index
with peak expiratory flow, dyspnoea, and quality of life as the prespecified primary outcomes

issues.title: Trial registered 2023-04-12, after the 2022-12-21 study start and 1 January 2023 start of data collection
issues.explanation: According to the registry the protocol was registered about three and a half months after the study began and after data collection had begun. The paper does not mention this and describes its primary outcomes as prespecified. This weakens the ability to confirm that outcomes and analyses were fixed in advance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated protocol or ethics-approved outcome list predating enrolment.

quotes.text: The study protocol was registered in the Clinical Trial database (https://clinicaltrials.gov; No: NCT05813873).
Data collection occurred from 1 January 2023 to 30 September 2023.
quotes.location: Methods, Study design, randomization, and blinding

quotes.text: with peak expiratory flow, dyspnoea, and quality of life as the prespecified primary outcomes

issues.title: Conclusions call rehabilitation 'highly effective' and the spirometer 'safe' without a design that can show either
issues.explanation: The Implications section credits rehabilitation with large improvements in both arms and calls it 'highly effective', but both arms received it and there was no untreated comparison. The 'safe' conclusion rests on an uncontrolled statement that no adverse events were reported over 4 weeks in 82 patients. These claims go beyond what a two-arm add-on trial can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A usual-care-only arm showing smaller gains, and a prespecified safety monitoring plan.

quotes.text: suggesting that structured rehabilitation alone is highly effective
across both the intervention and control groups
is a safe, low-cost, and effective adjunct to standard pulmonary rehabilitation for this patient population

issues.title: Baseline symptom paragraph gives n = 42 per group; trial and Table I use 41 per group
issues.explanation: The baseline symptom paragraph states both groups had n = 42, but 82 participants were randomized, 41 per group. Table I uses 41 as the denominator for the same counts. This is a printed slip with no effect on any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 42 participants per group were actually analysed.

quotes.text: 14 patients experienced fatigue, 31 reported muscle weakness
rehabilitation plus incentive spirometer, n = 41

10.2340/jrm.v58.44931.headline_claim: Adding inspiratory muscle training to physical exercise may improve inspiratory muscle strength and reduce cough frequency in adults with post-COVID-19 condition and inspiratory muscle weakness.
10.2340/jrm.v58.44931.overall: The primary finding of a greater MIP gain with IMT is statistically significant and reported with appropriate caveats about the small sample, though its clinical meaningfulness is interpreted generously. The cough benefit rests on a single uncorrected exploratory secondary test and should not be treated as an established effect. Within-group secondary findings are weak support and are mostly flagged by the authors themselves.

primary_outcome.name: Change in maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP), % predicted

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Measured before and after the intervention period of 8 weeks to detect a change

issues.title: Cough benefit (CI -1.1 to -0.1) is 1 of ~26 uncorrected secondary tests yet appears in the conclusion
issues.explanation: Cough frequency is one of many secondary outcomes tested at p<0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment, and the paper itself calls these analyses exploratory. Its confidence interval almost touches zero. The abstract, lay abstract and final conclusion nonetheless list reduced cough as a benefit alongside the primary result. The CAAT cough item is also a 1-5 ordinal score analysed as continuous. With this many unadjusted tests, one nominally significant result is weak support for a named benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy placing cough as a key secondary outcome, or a multiplicity-adjusted result still significant for cough.

quotes.text: Secondary outcomes were considered exploratory; therefore, no adjustment for multiple testing was applied.
For cough frequency, assessed using the cough item of the CAAT, a statistically significant between-group difference was observed, favouring the intervention group
this study suggests that IMT, when added to physical exercise, may improve inspiratory muscle strength and reduce cough frequency

issues.title: MIP difference of 18 is below the 22.1 MCID, yet CI reaching it is read as potential clinical meaningfulness
issues.explanation: The primary between-group difference (18 points) is below the MCID of 22.1, and the CI of 5 to 30 spans trivial to large effects. The discussion argues that the CI including the MCID suggests clinically meaningful potential, and supports this with a responder OR whose CI is 1.31 to 38.32. The data are equally compatible with a clinically negligible effect, so the statement about clinical meaning is stronger than the estimate supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority-to-MCID analysis or a larger trial showing the difference at or above 22.1.

quotes.text: the 95% confidence interval encompassed it, suggesting the potential for a clinically meaningful effect
quotes.location: Discussion, first paragraph on primary outcome

quotes.text: with a mean between-group difference of 18 percentage points (95% CI: 5 to 30)

issues.title: Discussion contrasts significant within-group changes with none in controls despite null between-group tests
issues.explanation: For 1-min STS, PSFS and EQ VAS the between-group differences were not significant (e.g. STS 10, CI -2 to 22; EQ VAS 7, CI -3 to 16). The discussion nevertheless contrasts the intervention group's significant change with the control group's non-significant change, and discusses the EQ VAS change as exceeding the MCID. A difference in significance between arms is not evidence of a difference between them. The authors partly flag this, so the effect on the conclusion is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable beyond the authors' own caveat; a significant interaction or between-group test for these outcomes would resolve it.

quotes.text: The intervention group demonstrated within-group improvements in functional capacity (1-min STS), activity limitations (PSFS), and selfrated health (EQ VAS), whereas no such changes were observed in the active control group.

10.23736/s1973-9087.22.07702-4.headline_claim: Home-based pulmonary rehabilitation (HPR) is as effective as inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation (IPR) for physical capacity, pulmonary function and quality of life in post-COVID-19 patients, and is a good alternative to IPR.
10.23736/s1973-9087.22.07702-4.overall: The finding that both groups improved in 6MWT, strength and quality of life is plausible, though the HPR 6MWT gain is stated inconsistently (+72 m versus +62 m in the table). The claim that HPR is equivalent to or a good alternative to IPR is not supported: it rests on a non-significant interaction in 17 completers, no test against the 50 m margin, and an SD far larger than the one used in planning. Allocation-related dropout, completer-only analysis and unblinded assessment add to this, so the conclusion is at best tentative.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test distance (6MWT)

primary_outcomes.measure: Distance walked in the 6-min walk test (6 MWT).

issues.title: Equivalence concluded from non-significant interaction (P=0.420) in 17 patients; no non-inferiority test, SD far above planned
issues.explanation: The trial was designed as non-inferiority with a 50 m margin, but no between-group difference with a confidence interval was compared with that margin. The conclusion that HPR is 'as efficient' and a 'good alternative' rests on a non-significant interaction test in 17 people. The design assumed an SD of 40 m while observed 6MWT SDs were about 88-137 m, so the study could not exclude a clinically important difference. The authors call the results preliminary, but the conclusion still says the hypothesis is confirmed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group difference in 6MWT change with a confidence interval lying entirely within the 50 m margin.

quotes.text: we calculated that minimum 8 participants were required for each group.
This confirms that our hypothesis that HPR is a good alternative to IPR for post-acute COVID-19.
Home pulmonary rehabilitation was as efficient as IPR to improve physical capacities

second_reader.what_stands: Equivalence/non-inferiority is concluded ('confirms that our hypothesis that HPR is a good alternative') from a non-significant interaction (P=0.420) in 17 analysed patients, with no non-inferiority test or confidence interval against the 50 m margin. Observed 6MWT SDs (88-137 m) are 2 to 3 times the planned 40 m, so the study is underpowered for that design. The authors do call the results preliminary and ask for more participants, which partly tempers but does not remove the overstatement. The planned n of 8 per group is arithmetically reproducible under a one-sided alpha, and the paper does

issues.title: 5 of 22 randomised (22.7%) withdrew over allocation dissatisfaction; completer-only analysis
issues.explanation: Five randomised patients (3/12 IPR, 2/10 HPR) refused to take part because they disliked their assigned group, and only the 17 completers were analysed. Dropout tied to the allocation itself can make the groups non-comparable, and randomisation is no longer protecting the comparison. For an equivalence claim, completer analysis is not a conservative choice. The limitation is acknowledged but the conclusions do not reflect it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including all randomised participants, or evidence that the dropouts were balanced and unrelated to allocation.

quotes.text: These five patients refused to take part in the study because they were not satisfied with the group they were assigned by randomization.
Statistical analysis was completed only for participants who completed the entire study.

second_reader.what_stands: 5 of 22 randomised participants (22.7%) withdrew, all citing dissatisfaction with their randomised group, and only the 17 completers were analysed, so the results are not intention-to-treat and the exclusion is plausibly linked to allocation. The authors disclose this in the Limitations, and the arm-wise dropout rates are similar (25% vs 20%). The risk of bias remains, especially with so small a sample.

issues.title: HPR 6MWT gain printed as +72 m, but Table III means (542 to 604) give +62 m
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion report a 72 m improvement in the home group on the primary outcome. The Table III pre- and post-HPR means differ by only 62 m. One of the figures is wrong, and the home group's primary-outcome gain is overstated by 10 m if the table is right. The qualitative finding of improvement in both groups is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level data or a corrected table showing the HPR mean change is 72 m (for example a pre-HPR mean of 532).

quotes.text: + 95m in IPR group <italic toggle="yes">vs.</italic> +72m in HPR group, P<0.001

issues.title: Results say no significant lung-function or dyspnea change; Table IV gives p=0.034, 0.011, 0.009
issues.explanation: The Results state that no significant improvement was seen in pulmonary function or dyspnea. Table IV shows significant time effects for dyspnea, FVC and TLC, and the Discussion calls them significant improvements. The text and the Results sentence cannot both be right, so a reader cannot tell what the authors found. The between-group conclusion is not changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Results sentence refers only to FEV1 and FEV1/FVC, or corrected p values.

quotes.text: We did not observe any significant improvement on pulmonary function test or dyspnea score in both groups
In contrast, TLCO, FVC and dyspnea show significant improvements

issues.title: Unblinded assessors and patients; self-reported fatigue, dyspnea and QoL outcomes, including the only group difference
issues.explanation: The staff who delivered the rehabilitation also performed all testing, and nobody was blinded. Fatigue, dyspnea and quality of life are self-reported and susceptible to expectation effects, and the single reported group difference (general fatigue, favouring IPR) is one of them. The limitation is disclosed but not reflected in the conclusions. The primary 6MWT outcome is less exposed, so the effect on the main conclusion is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment, or objective-only primary and key secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: Outcome assessors were not blinded to group allocation.
Only IPR was efficient to reduce general fatigue

issues.title: Text says no baseline difference in any variable, but Table I flags height (169.1 vs 177.3 cm) as significant
issues.explanation: The Results assert that no variable differed at baseline, and say this 'confirms that there was no selection bias'. Table I marks height as significantly different between groups, and the printed means and SDs support that. Other baseline imbalances, such as pre-test 6MWT of 447 vs 542 m and sex split of 5/4 vs 7/1, are untested with n=17. The statement of baseline equivalence is overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the asterisk is an error and that height did not differ between groups.

quotes.text: No significant difference between groups was observed in any of the variables measured during the pre-rehabilitation session.

quotes.location: Table I, Height row, HPR column

quotes.text: *Significative difference with IPR group with P<0.05.

issues.title: MFI general fatigue post-IPR SD printed as 48.8 against a mean of 12.0
issues.explanation: The post-IPR cell for general fatigue gives mean 12.0 with SD 48.8, while neighbouring SDs for this subscale are 3.8-7.8. An SD four times the mean on a bounded 4-20 subscale is implausible and is probably a misprint of 4.8. This same cell carries the asterisk supporting the 'only IPR reduced general fatigue' claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing an SD of 48.8 for that cell.

quotes.location: Table V, MFI general fatigue row, Post-IPR

10.23736/s1973-9087.24.08487-9.headline_claim: A 12-week endurance or concurrent exercise program leads to comparable improvements in VO2peak in non-hospitalized people with PCS, with no definite conclusion on the superiority of either modality.
10.23736/s1973-9087.24.08487-9.overall: The finding that the exercise programmes raise VO2peak is supported tentatively: the interaction is significant (P=0.002 or 0.004, depending on where one reads it) and the control group changed little. However, it comes from a per-protocol analysis of 42 of 66 randomised participants with an open-label design. The secondary claims about fatigue and HRQoL rest on within-group changes despite non-significant interactions, and so are not reliable.

primary_outcome.name: VO2peak (peak oxygen consumption, mL/min/kg)

issues.title: Efficacy analysed in 42 of 66 randomised (36.4% lost), completers only, no ITT analysis
issues.explanation: Only participants who completed the programme and met 80% adherence were analysed, so the randomised comparison is no longer preserved. Dropout was 10/24 (ED), 8/22 (CT) and 6/20 (C), and the 2 worsening-symptom discontinuations were in the training groups. The VO2peak benefit is therefore an estimate for adherent completers and probably overstates the effect in the randomised population. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but the Discussion and Conclusions still state efficacy without qualification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or multiple-imputation analysis of all 66 randomised participants giving similar VO2peak effects.

quotes.text: we did not include an intention-to-treat (ITT) approach in the data analysis
In total, 42 participants were analyzed.
had to exceed 80% for retention of participants

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy outcomes were analysed in 42 of 66 randomised participants (36.4% lost, with somewhat unequal loss across arms), using completers/per-protocol data only. The authors state they did not perform an ITT analysis and note this as a limitation. They also describe the 80% adherence requirement as a condition for retention in the analysis.

issues.title: Fatigue benefit inferred from within-group change despite null interaction (FSS P=0.206)
issues.explanation: The between-group time*group tests for FSS (P=0.206), SF-36 subscales (0.254, 0.313) and total (0.258) were non-significant. The control group also improved on SF-36 and symptom count. The claim of meaningful fatigue reduction from exercise comes from comparing significant within-arm changes with a non-significant control change, which is not a valid between-group inference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group (exercise vs control) contrast for FSS or a pre-specified analysis showing a treatment effect on fatigue.

quotes.text: Despite the absence of significant interaction effects in the secondary outcomes, the greater within-group improvements in leg strength, fatigue and HRQoL point towards the benefits of both exercise interventions.
Both exercise interventions led to meaningful reductions in fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: The fatigue benefit is argued from significant within-group changes in ED and CT, even though the group-by-time interaction for FSS was not significant (P=0.206), so a between-group advantage over control is not demonstrated. The paper partly tempers this by acknowledging the null interactions, limited magnitude and low power, but the Conclusion's wording 'led to meaningful reductions in fatigue' is stronger than the between-group evidence supports.

issues.title: Untested 'almost two-fold' SF-36 total advantage of ED over control highlighted despite null interaction (P=0.258)
issues.explanation: The Discussion highlights an almost two-fold greater SF-36 total improvement in ED than in control and attributes it to better physical function and less fatigue. No between-group test is reported, and the time*group interaction was non-significant. The attribution to physical function and fatigue is also not tested, since the SF-36 subscale interactions were non-significant too.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group test of ED vs C change in SF-36 total showing significance.

quotes.text: However, when comparing the total SF-36 score in ED and C, an almost two-fold increase in favor of endurance exercise was found
This may be attributed to an enhanced physical function and reduced fatigue.

issues.title: 'Effective and feasible' stated despite 36.4% dropout; 92.6% adherence is among completers only
issues.explanation: The Discussion calls exercise feasible, but 24 of 66 randomised participants left the study and two training-group participants stopped for worsening symptoms. The adherence figure of 92.6% describes only those who stayed. The claim is therefore stronger than a trial with this attrition supports, though the authors do report the dropout and the adverse events.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adherence and feasibility measures reported for all randomised participants showing acceptable retention.

quotes.text: Our investigation shows that exercise is effective and feasible at improving
an unexpectedly high overall dropout-rate of 36,4% occurred in this study

issues.title: VO2peak time*group interaction P printed as 0.002 in text but 0.004 in Table II
issues.explanation: The Results give the VO2peak time*group interaction as P=0.002, while Table II prints 0.004 for the same effect. Both values are below 0.05, so the significance conclusion is unchanged. Still, one of the two is wrong, and this is the primary-outcome interaction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text and table P values come from different analyses (for example, different post-hoc or corrected tests), or a corrected table.

quotes.text: a significant time*group interaction (P=0.002

issues.title: Identical HRV values across cells: SDNN post 44.5 (17.0) in ED and CT; RMSSD ED pre = post 37.2 (19.6)
issues.explanation: Table II prints identical mean and SD for SDNN post in ED and CT (44.5 (17.0)), identical SDNN pre SDs in those groups (21.2), and identical RMSSD pre and post cells in ED (37.2 (19.6)). Each coincidence is possible, but together they raise the chance of a transcription slip in the HRV rows. HRV is a secondary outcome and the paper reads it as showing no exercise effect, so the impact is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The underlying HRV data or a corrected table showing distinct values for these cells.

quotes.location: Table II, SDNN (ms) row, ED Post and CT Post columns
Table II, RMSSD (ms) row, ED Pre and Post columns

issues.title: CT pre-intervention mMRC 8 of 14 printed as 56.7%; 8/14 is 57.1%
issues.explanation: Table II gives the CT pre-intervention mMRC count of 8 with a group size of 14 and a percentage of 56.7. The arithmetic gives 57.1%. This is a small printing error that affects no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the CT group contained a different number of participants at this assessment, such that 56.7% corresponds to the printed count.

quotes.location: Table II, mMRC score ≥1 row, CT Pre column

script.explanation: 8/14 = 57.14%, but the paper prints 56.7, outside the rounding interval [56.65, 56.80]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 14.1 rather than 14.

10.23736/s1973-9087.24.08634-9.headline_claim: Pulmonary telerehabilitation (PTRP) is feasible and highly effective for restoring functional capacity and quality of life after COVID-19 pneumonia, regardless of supervision type (remote vs hybrid), with the gain maintained long term.
10.23736/s1973-9087.24.08634-9.overall: The headline claim that the telerehabilitation programme is highly effective regardless of supervision is only weakly supported: efficacy comes from uncontrolled pre/post changes in 30 completers of 49 randomised (with much higher dropout in the remote arm), the G1 vs G2 equivalence rests on an underpowered null, and the comparison with non-rehabilitated patients is non-randomised and unadjusted. Feasibility and large within-patient gains are plausible, but causal efficacy and equivalence are not established. The numeric slips (text/table P values) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk distance (6MWD)

issues.title: Efficacy analysed in 30 of 49 randomised patients; dropout unequal (G1 15/28, G2 4/21), no ITT
issues.explanation: Only completers entered the randomised analyses, and dropout was much higher in the remote arm than in the hybrid arm. Completers are a selected group; the paper itself says many stopped because they felt better. Conclusions about equivalence and high effectiveness therefore rest on a non-randomised subset and could be biased in either direction, most likely favouring the programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or missing-data-adjusted analysis giving the same between-arm and within-arm results.

quotes.text: There was a significant discontinuation rate, with only 13 patients from G1 and 17 from G2 having completed the rehabilitation program.
Secondly, a total of 39% of the participants dropped out of the study, with the main reason (42%) being an improvement in symptoms and functional ability

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy tables and tests use only the 30 completers out of 49 randomised, with markedly unequal dropout (15/28 vs 4/21), and no ITT or missing-data handling is described. The paper does disclose the 39% dropout and gives improvement in symptoms as the main reason (42%), but the reasons are not broken down by arm.

issues.title: Efficacy of PTRP inferred from within-arm pre/post 6MWD gains (164.5 m, 154.2 m) without a randomised control
issues.explanation: The randomised trial compares two forms of the same programme, so it has no no-treatment arm. The 164.5 m and 154.2 m gains are before/after changes that include spontaneous recovery after COVID-19. Calling the programme 'highly effective' from these changes is not supported by the randomised design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised or properly adjusted comparison against a no-rehabilitation control showing the same gain.

quotes.text: The statistical method used was the Wilcoxon paired-samples test.
had a 6MWD increase of 164.5 m and 154.2 m respectively

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy claim for PTRP from the randomised study rests on within-arm pre/post 6MWD changes (about 164.5 m and 154.2 m) with no randomised no-treatment control, so natural recovery, learning effects on repeat 6MWT and regression cannot be separated from the programme effect. The only control comparison is the separate non-randomised cohort.

issues.title: 'Safe' and quality-of-life improvement claims rest on one sentence and uncontrolled, completer-only pre/post data
issues.explanation: Safety is supported only by the statement that no adverse events were reported, with no description of how events were collected in 49 randomised patients, 19 of whom left. Quality-of-life improvement is likewise a before/after change in completers with no control arm, and some within-time P values (e.g. Mental component P=0.050) are borderline. The strong wording is not matched by the evidence. Efficacy overreach is covered in the other issues.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described adverse-event monitoring protocol covering all randomised participants, and a controlled quality-of-life comparison.

quotes.text: No incidents or adverse events were reported as a result of participation in the program.
The PTRP was found to be a feasible and highly effective intervention for restoring functional capacity and improving quality of life, regardless of the type of supervision.

second_reader.what_stands: The safety claim rests on one unsupported sentence (no stated method of recording adverse events; no data on the 19 dropouts), and the quality-of-life improvement claim rests on uncontrolled pre/post SF-36 data from the 30 completers only. The mental component effect is borderline (P=0.050) and several domains did not improve, so 'highly effective ... improving quality of life' is stronger than the data support.

issues.title: IG vs NIG gain (140.5 m vs 16.8 m) is non-randomised, completer-only and unadjusted for baseline imbalance
issues.explanation: The conclusion that the programme improved capacity versus advice alone rests on a comparison of non-randomised groups that differ on illness severity and follow-up timing. The intervention group contains only completers, which favours the programme. The direction of severity imbalance (IG sicker) could also understate benefit, since sicker patients have more room to recover or recover differently. Causal wording is stronger than this design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis adjusted for baseline severity and including all 49 randomised patients, giving similar effect.

quotes.text: The increase in 6MWD for IG was 140.53 m, while for NIG it was 16.8 m (P=0.002) (Mann-Whitney test).
participation in the PTRP improved functional capacity compared with those who were simply advised to resume physical activity during recovery.

second_reader.what_stands: The IG vs NIG comparison is non-randomised, uses only IG completers (30 of 49 started), and the quoted 140.5 vs 16.8 m difference is a Mann-Whitney test of unadjusted change scores, despite baseline imbalances in illness severity and desaturation. The baseline 6MWD of IG was lower (not significantly), which could also favour a larger gain through regression to the mean. A T1-adjusted ANOVA is mentioned only for SpO2; 6MWD adjustment is unclear.

issues.title: G1 vs G2 equivalence concluded from underpowered null (power 0.554, n=13 vs 17; planned 30 per arm)
issues.explanation: The data cannot rule out a meaningful difference between remote and hybrid supervision: power was 0.554 even for a large effect, and the analysed sample is half the target. The authors still conclude the two modalities work equally well and rely on post-hoc power of within-group tests. Absence of a significant difference is not evidence of equivalence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence or non-inferiority analysis with confidence interval inside a stated margin.

quotes.text: We did not reach the calculated sample size, so we might not detect a difference between the test groups.
The resulting power of the test was 0.554.

second_reader.what_stands: The G1 vs G2 'similar results' and 'regardless of the type of supervision' conclusions rest on a non-significant test (P=0.496) with only 0.554 power and 30 of 60 planned patients, and no formal equivalence test between arms is reported. My approximate CI from the printed summary statistics is wide and does not exclude differences beyond the 50 m margin. The authors do acknowledge the shortfall in the Limitations.

issues.title: Pain domain T2 P: 0.820 in text vs 0.193 in Table II (0.820 appears in Table III)
issues.explanation: The text cites P=0.820 for the G1 vs G2 Pain comparison at T2, but Table II prints 0.193. The value 0.820 is the IG vs NIG baseline Pain P in Table III. Either way the comparison is non-significant, but the text appears to quote the wrong table. The text also reads similarity as 'improvement with the intervention', which a between-group P does not show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 0.820 is from a different, ANOVA-based test of the same comparison.

quotes.text: which became similar after the intervention (T2) (P=0.820)

issues.title: 114 eligible minus 49 randomised is 65, but NIG is 37; 28 patients not accounted for in text
issues.explanation: The text says 114 were eligible and 49 began the program, then describes the 'remaining eligible patients' as forming a NIG of 37. The 28-patient gap is not explained in the text. It may be accounted for in Figure 2, which cannot be read here, so this cannot be settled from the paper text alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 2 showing 28 eligible patients excluded or lost before NIG enrolment with reasons.

quotes.text: Among the 114 patients who were eligible for PTRP, only 49 began their participation
The remaining eligible patients who were not included in the PTRP were re-evaluated and comprised a non-intervention group (NIG) of 37 patients.

issues.title: Mental component summary T1 P: 0.327 in text vs 0.154 in Table I
issues.explanation: The Results text gives P=0.327 for the baseline between-group comparison of the Mental component summary, while Table I prints 0.154 for the same row. Both are non-significant, so no conclusion changes, but the two printings disagree and the paper does not say they come from different tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text P comes from an ANOVA group-effect test and the table P from Mann-Whitney.

quotes.text: In the Mental component summary, G1 and G2 were similar at T1 (P=0.327)

10.23937/2469-5718/1510259.headline_claim: Short-term hyperbaric oxygen therapy (10 sessions at 2.0 ATM) improves fatigue (Chalder) and functional status (PCFS) in patients with long COVID, supporting its use as an effective treatment.
10.23937/2469-5718/1510259.overall: The claim that HBOT is 'an effective treatment' cannot be relied on, because the study is a 12-patient open-label, uncontrolled pre-post series with self-rated outcomes and completers-only analysis. The within-patient improvements are plausible as hypothesis-generating pilot signals. The numeric slips are small: the Discussion PCFS endpoint of 1.2 vs 1.5, a Table 3 CI inconsistent with its p, and the mean age.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder fatigue scale score (baseline to 10 treatments)

issues.title: Uncontrolled, open-label, self-reported pre-post study used to conclude HBOT is 'an effective treatment'
issues.explanation: All 12 patients received HBOT and were compared only with their own baseline on self-rated fatigue and function scales, with no control, blinding or sham. Regression to the mean, expectation, natural recovery and the placebo effect of ten hours of treatment cannot be separated from a treatment effect. The authors list this as a limitation yet state that the results reaffirm HBOT as an effective treatment. A hypothesis-generating claim is all this design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or untreated control group showing a between-group difference.

quotes.text: First, there was no control group
The results our pilot study confirms Robbins study in that a short course of hyperbaric oxygen (10 sessions)

second_reader.what_stands: The study is uncontrolled and single-arm, with self-reported scales (Chalder, PCFS) assessed before and after treatment, and the authors state 'there was no control group and the placebo effect... cannot [be] minimized'. Despite that, the Discussion says the results 'confirm' Robbins and 'reaffirm the use of hyperbaric oxygen as an effective treatment', and the closing paragraph calls HBOT 'an effective treatment modality', which goes beyond what an uncontrolled pre-post design can show. Two caveats: the paper does describe itself as a pilot and acknowledges the limitation, and I did not verif

issues.title: Discussion gives PCFS after treatment as 1.2; Results and Tables 4-5 give 1.5
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the PCFS improved from 2.3 to 1.2. The Results and Table 4 give 1.5 after ten treatments, and Table 5 reports an improvement of 0.8, which matches 1.5. The Discussion figure implies an improvement of 1.1 instead of 0.8, so it slightly overstates the functional gain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The underlying data showing a mean PCFS of 1.2 after ten sessions, with Table 4 and the Results being the errors.

quotes.text: improvement from 2.3 to 1.2
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph 'Our results also showed significant improvement'

quotes.text: as well as the PCFS (2.3 to 1.5, p = 0.005)

issues.title: 3 of 15 enrolled (20%) excluded from analysis; completers only, 'all patients' wording refers to 12
issues.explanation: Results describe only the 12 completers, and 'all patients' refers to them. Two dropouts could not complete the schedule, so they may differ from completers and their outcomes are unknown. No analysis includes them, so the improvement applies to those able to finish ten sessions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline and available follow-up data on the three dropouts showing similar outcomes.

quotes.text: Of the 15 enrolled patients, three patients dropped out of the study

issues.title: PCFS, a functional-status scale, is presented as a measure of neurocognitive function
issues.explanation: The Discussion says improvement in 'neurocognitive functions (Post Covid Functional Scale)' was demonstrated. The PCFS is a self-reported scale of functional limitations in daily life, not a cognitive test. No cognitive testing was done, so the neurocognition claim and the neuroplasticity explanation are unsupported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A validated cognitive assessment showing improvement.

quotes.text: neurocognitive functions (Post Covid Functional Scale)

issues.title: Planned six-month follow-up is not reported; only a statement that all 12 felt helped
issues.explanation: The authors planned six-month follow-up, and reinfection in five of 12 made the data problematic. No outcome scores are shown for the seven others, while a favourable subjective statement ('all 12 patients felt the hyperbaric treatment helped') is given. Durability of the effect is therefore unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Six-month Chalder and PCFS data for the seven non-reinfected patients.

quotes.text: five of the 12 were re-infected with Covid-19

issues.title: Table 3 Chalder 5-to-10 row: CI (0.6, 6.3) excludes 0 but p = 0.1; 2.8 is not its midpoint
issues.explanation: A 95% CI that excludes zero would imply p below 0.05, yet the row prints p = 0.1. The estimate 2.8 also sits well below the interval midpoint of 3.45. A dropped minus sign on the lower bound is the likeliest cause. The paper's conclusion about this step (not significant) is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original PDF showing a lower bound of -0.6, i.e. an extraction loss of the minus sign.

script.explanation: the estimate 2.8 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [0.6, 6.3] (expected about 3.4500) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Average age 49 in Methods vs mean 48.1 in Table 1
issues.explanation: The Methods give an average age of 49 for the 12 analysed patients. Table 1 gives a mean of 48.1 for the same group. The difference is small and does not bear on the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors stating that 49 is a median or was computed on a different set.

quotes.text: average age of 49 (range 27-73)

10.24075/brsmu.2024.034.headline_claim: Adding systemic ozone therapy to drug therapy in patients with post-COVID asthenic syndrome allows normalization of TNFα, IL1β and IL6 levels and complete reduction of PCAS clinical manifestations in 94.2% of cases, and is an effective, pathogenetically substantiated strategy for outpatient combination treatment.
10.24075/brsmu.2024.034.overall: The headline claim of effective, safe add-on ozone therapy rests on an open-label, unregistered trial with no sham, no designated primary outcome and scale-based outcomes, so it is better read as a tentative signal than as demonstrated efficacy. Several numeric inconsistencies were found (7 comparison patients missing from the CGI-S table, a wrong ISI percentage, mismatched sex totals), but they are individually small and the direction of the reported differences is not obviously changed by them.

primary_outcome.name: unclear: no single primary outcome is named; the paper reports cytokine levels (TNFα, IL1β, IL6) and mental-status scales (MFI-20, MoCa, ISI, HARS, CGI-S) at day 30

issues.title: 'Highly effective and safe' and '94.2% normalisation' go beyond an open-label 30-day study
issues.explanation: The paper concludes that ozone add-on therapy is 'highly effective and safe' and achieves normalised cytokines plus complete symptom resolution in 94.2% of cases. The 94.2% is a CGI-S rating from an unblinded assessment, not a patient-level count of cytokine normalisation. Safety rests on one sentence reporting no adverse events with no described monitoring. The favourable findings therefore support a tentative signal of benefit rather than the confident conclusion stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety monitoring protocol with patient-level data, and patient-level cytokine values showing normalisation in 94.2% of the index group.

quotes.text: Thus, according to the findings, the use of systemic ozone therapy to complement drug therapy is highly effective and safe in patients with PCAS.
No adverse events were reported for patients of the index group and comparison group during the study.

second_reader.what_stands: 'Highly effective and safe' and 'normalization'/'complete reduction in 94.2%' are stated more firmly than an open-label, 30-day study with unblinded subjective outcomes, unadjusted multiple tests, no sham control and no defined AE surveillance can support. A zero-event safety result in 70 treated patients cannot establish safety, and no limitations are discussed. The conclusion's 'one effective ... strategy' wording is somewhat more cautious than the Discussion's wording.

issues.title: Open-label add-on infusion with no sham; scale-based outcomes (MFI-20, ISI, HARS, CGI-S) not blinded
issues.explanation: The index group received 10 intravenous ozone infusions in addition to the drug, while the comparison group received the drug only, with no sham procedure. Neither participant nor assessor blinding is described. The main efficacy results are symptom scales and a clinician global rating that are sensitive to expectation, which could produce part or all of the between-group differences (for example 94.2% vs 62.9% CGI-S 'no disease'). The efficacy claim on clinical outcomes should therefore be treated as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of blinded outcome assessors (or a sham infusion) and of assessment procedures that were independent of treatment knowledge.

quotes.text: the patients' mental status was assessed using the MFI-20, MoCa, ISI, HARS, and CGI-S scores before and after treatment
sodium chloride solution (daily, course of 10 procedures, the first  three  procedures  involving

second_reader.what_stands: The paper describes an add-on ozone infusion versus drug alone, with no sham or placebo infusion and no stated blinding of patients or raters. The subjective, scale-based outcomes (MFI-20, ISI, HARS, CGI-S, and MoCa to a lesser extent) are therefore exposed to expectation and observer bias. The cytokine ELISA results are objective, but the paper does not say whether laboratory staff were masked, so I checked the scale outcomes only.

issues.subtype: CGI-S sum mismatch in comparison group, after treatment
issues.title: Comparison-group CGI-S after treatment accounts for 63 of 70 patients (44 + 19 + 0 + 0)
issues.explanation: After treatment the comparison group's CGI-S rows are 44 no disease, 19 mild, 0 moderate and 0 severe, which is 63 patients out of 70. The paper also states that all patients completed the trial, and the index group sums correctly to 70. Seven comparison patients (10%) are unaccounted for, so either a category is wrong or the percentages (62.9% + 27.1% = 90.0%) are incomplete. The headline CGI-S contrast (94.2% vs 62.9%) is built on this table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or supplement showing where the other 7 comparison patients fall (for example moderate disorder), or a statement that 7 patients had missing CGI-S data.

quotes.location: Table 3, CGI-S no disease row, comparison group after treatment
Table 3, CGI-S mild disorder row, comparison group after treatment

issues.title: No primary outcome; ~13 between-group tests at uncorrected 0.05, so IL1β, IL6 and MoCa results are fragile
issues.explanation: The Methods set a single threshold of p < 0.05 and do not designate a primary outcome or apply any multiplicity correction. The three cytokines, five scales and CGI categories were all compared. The strongest results (MFI-20, ISI, HARS, CGI-S, TNFα) would survive a strict correction, but the IL1β, IL6 and especially MoCa (p = 0.046) differences are only nominal, and the cognitive benefit is weakly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and hierarchical testing plan, or adjusted p-values showing the secondary results remain significant.

quotes.text: The differences were considered significant at р < 0.05.
MoCa score was higher by 10.9% ( р = 0.046)

issues.title: Only Mann-Whitney and chi-squared tests are named, but paired within-group changes and 'Δ' p-values are reported
issues.explanation: Within-group before/after p-values and the between-group 'difference of changes' p-values are reported, yet the Methods list only an independent-samples test and chi-squared. Applying an unpaired test to repeated measurements, or leaving the test for Δ unspecified, makes several reported p-values hard to reproduce. Several categorical within-group p-values also look implausible (for example 41/70 to 0 reported as p = 0.001). The between-group conclusions are probably robust given the large differences, but the exact p-values cannot be verified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that paired tests (for example Wilcoxon signed-rank) and a named method for the Δ comparison were used.

quotes.text: The Mann-Whitney U test was used for comparative analysis of quantitative parameters

issues.title: Randomization described only as 'based on the treatment method'; sequence generation and concealment not given
issues.explanation: No sequence generation, concealment or allocation procedure is reported, and the phrase 'based on the treatment method' is ambiguous. Equal group sizes and balanced baseline data are reassuring but do not exclude selection effects, particularly since patients paid for their own drug and an infusion course may have influenced who agreed to be in each arm. The causal interpretation of the between-group differences depends on this step.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or methods addendum describing computer-generated sequence and concealed allocation.

quotes.text: Patients  were  randomized  into  two  groups  based  on  the treatment method.

issues.title: No trial registry entry reported for a randomized trial run in 2022–2023
issues.explanation: The article reports ethics approval (October 2021) and a study period of 2022–2023 but gives no registry identifier. Without one, the prespecified outcomes and analysis cannot be checked, which compounds the lack of a designated primary outcome noted under multiplicity. This is a transparency gap rather than a demonstrated error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier and a registration date before enrolment.

quotes.text: the study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the S.I. Georgievsky Medical Academy, V.I. Vernadsky Crimean Federal University (protocol No. 10 dated 16 October 2021)

issues.title: Comparison-group baseline MoCa/MFI-20/HARS medians differ between Table 1 and Table 3
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives the comparison group's baseline MoCa median as 24.1, but Table 3 gives 24.5; MFI-20 is 81.3 vs 81.6 and HARS 20.9 vs 20.7. The index group's baselines are identical across the two tables. The Table 3 percentage change for the comparison MoCa (+4.9%) matches 24.5, so one of the tables is wrong. The differences are small but bear on baseline balance and the computed changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explanation that Table 3 uses a different baseline measurement or subset than Table 1.

quotes.location: Table 1, MoCa AFS row, comparison group
Table 3, MoCa AFS row, comparison group before treatment

issues.title: Methods give 77 females / 63 males in total; group counts of 43+44 and 27+26 give 87 / 53
issues.explanation: The first Methods paragraph says the 140 patients included 77 females and 63 males. The group descriptions in the same section and Table 1 give 43 + 44 = 87 females and 27 + 26 = 53 males. The sex split of the whole sample is therefore stated inconsistently, though nothing in the efficacy analysis depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 77/63 figure refers to a subset (for example completers of a particular assessment) rather than all 140 randomized patients.

quotes.text: 140 patients (77 females and 63 males)

issues.title: Within-group changes misstated: ISI -81.3% (medians imply -72.5%); MoCa +17.1% (medians imply +17.8%)
issues.explanation: Table 3 and the Discussion give the index-group ISI decrease as 81.3%, but the printed medians (18.2 to 5.0) imply 72.5%. The index-group MoCa increase is given as 17.1% where 24.2 to 28.5 implies 17.8%. Other rows in the same table reproduce exactly from their medians, so these two entries are inconsistent with the paper's own method.
