10.32782/2226-2008-2024-3-6.headline_claim: Adding sulodexide to basic antihypertensive and antidiabetic therapy in patients with hypertension and type 2 diabetes after COVID-19 increases the effectiveness of complex treatment, reducing post-COVID symptoms and improving blood pressure, ankle-brachial index and quality of life.
10.32782/2226-2008-2024-3-6.overall: The conclusion that sulodexide increases the effectiveness of treatment is not reliably supported: allocation was by therapy in an open, non-randomised comparison with unblinded patient-reported outcomes. BP and ABI benefits rest on within-group changes with no between-group test. Several numbers are inconsistent (group size 45 versus 43, percentages based on n=60, one miscalculated cell), so the data cannot be taken at face value.

primary_outcome.name: Frequency of post-COVID syndrome symptoms at 3 weeks (no outcome explicitly designated as primary)

issues.title: Open, therapy-based allocation described as randomised; causal efficacy conclusion not supported
issues.explanation: Results call the 87 patients 'randomized', but Methods describe an open comparison in which groups were formed by therapy, with no randomisation or concealment method. Outcomes are largely patient-reported symptoms, assessed unblinded, and the groups differ at baseline in BMI and SBP. Under this design differences between groups cannot be attributed to sulodexide, so the conclusion that it increases treatment effectiveness is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described randomisation and concealment procedure, or blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: 87 patients were randomized to the study after past COVID-19
quotes.location: Results and their discussion, first paragraph

quotes.text: open comparative study with a prospective set of patients under inclusion and exclusion criteria
contributes to increasing the effectiveness of complex treatment

second_reader.what_stands: The paper says 87 patients were 'randomized' but its Methods describe an open study in which patients were 'divided into 2 groups depending on therapy', with no randomisation method, concealment or blinding reported, so allocation appears therapy-based and not random. The conclusion that sulodexide 'contributes to increasing the effectiveness' of treatment is a causal claim that this open, non-randomised design (with some unexplained sulodexide use in the control group and inconsistent group size of 45 vs 43) does not support.

issues.title: BP, ABI and symptom benefit versus control inferred from within-group p-values, no between-group test
issues.explanation: Blood pressure and ABI results are tested only between visits within each group. The paper concludes that the drug gave an additional BP reduction and ABI rise compared with control, but never tests the difference in change between arms. The control group's SBP also fell by 15.2 mmHg against 19.6 mmHg in the main group, a small difference that may well not be significant. The same pattern applies to the symptom rates in Table 2.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or between-group test of change showing a significant treatment difference.

quotes.text: but this decrease was significant only in the main group (Table 3)
quotes.location: Results and their discussion, before Table 3

quotes.text: The reliability of the difference in indicators between the 1st and 2nd visits of each group is indicated by p.

second_reader.what_stands: The BP and ABI claims of benefit over control rest only on within-group visit 1 vs visit 2 p-values (Table 3 note), with no between-group or interaction test reported, and 'significant in one group but not the other' is not evidence of a difference between groups. A rough comparison of visit-2 values using the printed ± (assuming SEM) gives non-significant between-group differences (SBP p about 0.15, DBP about 0.26, ABI about 0.27 and 0.43). Symptom outcomes in Table 2 likewise report only within-group p-values, so the same inferential gap applies; I did not test Table 2 symptom between-group

issues.title: Basic-therapy percentages use a base of 60 per group, not 43/44; 14 control patients said to get sulodexide
issues.explanation: The paragraph on background therapy gives percentages that match groups of 60 (16/60 = 26.7%), not the 43 and 44 analysed. It also states that 14 control patients and 16 main-group patients 'additionally received sulodexide'. If true, this means contamination of the control group, and the numbers cannot be reconciled with the stated group sizes. The comparability of background therapy is therefore not shown for the analysed sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement from the authors that this paragraph describes another subset with n=60 per group, and that no control patients received sulodexide.

quotes.text: 16 (26.7%) of the main group additionally received sulodexide capsules

script.explanation: 16/43 = 37.21%, but the paper prints 26.7, outside the rounding interval [26.65, 26.80]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 59.9 rather than 43.

issues.title: Main-group size is 45 in the abstract but 43 in Methods and all tables (45+44=89, not 87)
issues.explanation: The abstract says the main group had 45 patients, while Methods and Tables 1-3 say 43. Only 43 + 44 matches the stated 87. The same discrepancy appears in Table 1, where 9 (20.0%) hospitalised in the main group fits n=45 (9/45 = 20.0%) but not n=43 (9/43 = 20.9%). It is unclear which group size the percentages were computed on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction from the authors confirming 43 as the group size throughout and showing that 20.0% was a typing slip.

quotes.text: The first, main group, consisted of 45 patients who additionally used sulodexide capsules
Group I (main) (n=43)

issues.title: Control group 1st visit '1 PCS symptom': 37 (79.6%) but 37/44 = 84.1%
issues.explanation: The count of 37 out of 44 control patients is 84.1%, not 79.6%. The printed percentage matches 35/44, so either the count or the percentage is wrong. This affects one table cell, and the visit 1 to visit 2 comparison in the control group uses this value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 35 patients, or a different control denominator at visit 1.

quotes.location: Table 2, Patients having 1 PCS symptom, control 1st visit

script.explanation: 37/44 = 84.09%, but the paper prints 79.6, outside the rounding interval [79.55, 79.70]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 46.5 rather than 44.

issues.title: No trial registration reported; outcomes cannot be checked against a prespecified plan
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval but no registry entry for a prospective comparative study, and designates no primary outcome. This makes selective outcome reporting impossible to rule out among the many symptoms and BP measures reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record dated before enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: Protocol approved by the Commission on Bioethics of ONMedU

10.32782/2522-1795.2023.14.9.headline_claim: Physical therapy tailored to astheno-vegetative syndrome is presented as pathogenetically and practically justified for postpartum women with post-COVID syndrome after caesarean section, to improve vegetative status and reduce fatigue and drowsiness.
10.32782/2522-1795.2023.14.9.overall: The finding that the programme group scored better than the comparison group on the questionnaires is plausible but rests on a small, non-randomized, unblinded comparison with no allocation description, no sample-size justification and no stated limitations. The efficacy and 'pathogenetic' justification conclusions should be read as tentative, and a text-table mismatch on FSS adds minor doubt about reporting.

primary_outcome.name: Astheno-vegetative syndrome indicators (Wayne questionnaire, Epworth sleepiness scale, Fatigue Assessment Scale, Fatigue Severity Scale)

issues.title: Non-randomized main vs comparison groups (14 vs 15) with no allocation method and no adjustment
issues.explanation: The two caesarean/COVID-19 groups were not randomized, and the paper does not say how women came to be in the programme or in the comparison group. Apart from baseline scores on the four scales, no baseline data are given for them (only a pooled mean age). The comparison group also received only general recommendations, with no matched supervised contact. Differences such as motivation, access to the rehabilitation centre or compliance may therefore explain part of the gap, which the authors themselves partly attribute to better 'compliance'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of random or concealed allocation, or a baseline table and adjusted analysis showing the two caesarean groups were comparable and the effect unchanged.

quotes.text: The main group consisted of 14 women after caesarean section, suffered from COVID-19 during pregnancy, and performed a proven physical therapy program for 2 months
The comparison group consisted of 15 women after caesarean section who suffered from COVID-19 during pregnancy, recovered during pregnancy and the postpartum period

second_reader.what_stands: The main and comparison groups (14 and 15 women) were evidently not randomised, since the paper describes no randomisation or other allocation procedure, and the analysis is unadjusted t-tests with only a one-sentence assertion of baseline homogeneity. The paper therefore does not allow confounding by allocation or adherence to be excluded.

issues.title: Conclusion says programme is pathogenetically justified; supported only by small non-randomized comparison
issues.explanation: The conclusions describe the programme as 'pathogenetically and practically justified' for improving vegetative status, fatigue and drowsiness. The evidence is a 14 vs 15 non-randomized comparison with no limitations section, no effect sizes and no follow-up beyond two months. The data show a short-term difference on questionnaires, not a demonstrated mechanism or a proven benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion explicitly limited to a tentative short-term difference, with stated limitations on design and sample size.

quotes.text: in order to improve the vegetative status, reduce the feeling of fatigue and weakness, and reduce pathological drowsiness.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion's 'pathogenetically justified' wording rests on introductory literature, not on any mechanism measured in this study. The empirical support is a small, non-randomised comparison of self-reported scales, and the paper includes no limitations discussion. The favourable between-group differences (about 10 points on FAS and 11 on FSS) are real as reported, and the authors do not claim proof of mechanism, so the point holds only for the strength of the wording.

issues.title: No sample-size justification for 14 vs 15 women; confident programme-efficacy conclusion drawn
issues.explanation: The paper gives no sample-size calculation and no confidence intervals or effect sizes. The reported SDs are very small for questionnaire totals (about 1 to 2 points), which makes the p<0.05 contrasts look decisive but leaves precision and generalisability untested. The small, single-centre sample supports only a tentative conclusion, yet the conclusion is stated firmly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample-size calculation showing adequate power for the primary outcome, or a larger replication.

quotes.text: Methods. 44 women were examined at the beginning of the late postpartum period.

The results of the women of the main group on the investigated indicators of astheno-vegetative syndrome were statistically significantly better (p<0.05) than those of the women of the comparison group.

issues.title: Four scales, several group contrasts at uncorrected p<0.05, no primary outcome named
issues.explanation: The authors test four scales across three groups and two timepoints at alpha 0.05 with no correction and no named primary outcome. Pairwise Student tests across three groups also inflate false positives. Because the printed contrasts are large and consistent across scales, this probably weakens rather than overturns the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement designating one primary outcome, or adjusted p-values that stay below 0.05.

quotes.text: The condition of women was assessed according to the results of the Wayne questionnaire, Epworth sleepiness scale, Fatigue Assessment Scale, Fatigue Severity Scale.

issues.title: No trial registration or ethics approval statement reported for the two-month intervention study
issues.explanation: The paper reports informed consent but no registry entry, protocol or ethics committee approval. Without them the outcomes and analyses cannot be compared with a prespecified plan. This matters little for the conclusion in a small observational-style comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or ethics approval number given in the full publication.

quotes.text: The main group consisted of 14 women after caesarean section, suffered from COVID-19 during pregnancy, and performed a proven physical therapy program for 2 months

issues.title: Text says main-group FSS not different from control (p>0.05) but Table 1 marks it significantly different
issues.explanation: The Results text states the main group's Fatigue Severity Scale values did not reach the control group level (p>0.05). In Table 1 the main group's post-programme FSS (35.16) carries the asterisk meaning a significant difference from the control group (31.15). The text and table cannot both be right, so it is unclear whether the main group matched the control group on this scale.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the asterisk or the text p-value is a typographical error, with the correct test result.

quotes.text: але не досягнули рівня КГ (р>0,05)
quotes.location: Results, paragraph on Fatigue Severity Scale

10.32782/2522-1795.2024.18.13.headline_claim: A developed 3-month physical therapy program for older adults with post-COVID syndrome and sarcopenia produced a statistically significantly greater reduction of sarcopenia signs than the general clinical-protocol rehabilitation group.
10.32782/2522-1795.2024.18.13.overall: The study shows large pre/post improvements with the multimodal programme, but the superiority claim over the standard protocol rests on undescribed randomisation, unadjusted t-tests, and dispersions that appear to be SEs rather than SDs. Internal inconsistencies (p>0.05 vs a significance marker, a knee-endoprosthesis conclusion, an 8.5% vs 9.4% gain) lower confidence in the reporting. The direction of benefit is plausible, but its size and statistical certainty are not well established.

primary_outcome.name: Hand grip strength (kg) and SPPB/Edmonton Frail Scale changes; sarcopenia parameter dynamics (no single primary outcome named)

issues.title: EFS overall improvement given as p>0.05 in text but marked significant in Table 3; 'all parameters' claim not borne out
issues.explanation: The Results text says the overall Edmonton Frail Scale improvement (23% in ОГ1, 46% in ОГ2) was p>0.05, whereas Table 3 flags the ОГ2 post-treatment total (9.02 to 4.88) as significantly changed. The abstract and conclusions say every studied parameter improved significantly, but Table 3 shows no significance marker on medication use at all. It also shows none on the pre/post change in social support for ОГ1, or in continence for ОГ2. The text and table cannot both be right, and the 'all parameters' claim overstates the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or the original data showing the p>0.05 refers to a different comparison and that every subscale did change significantly.

quotes.location: Table 3, Загальний бал row, ОГ2 після ФТ

за всіма досліджуваними параметрами (р<0,05)

issues.title: Conclusion 1 describes patients with a knee endoprosthesis, absent from the study population
issues.explanation: Conclusion 1 says low strength and frailty were found in elderly patients with a knee joint endoprosthesis and sarcopenia. The study population is post-COVID patients with sarcopenia, and no knee replacement is mentioned in the inclusion or exclusion criteria. The first conclusion therefore describes a population the paper did not study, which points to a text error. It does not change the data, but it undermines the reliability of the conclusions section.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants had knee endoprostheses, such as a baseline characteristics table or inclusion criterion.

quotes.text: колінного  суглоба  та  саркопенією

issues.title: Allocation described only as 'blind randomized'; no method or concealment, arms of 34 and 41
issues.explanation: The 75 post-COVID patients were said to be split by a 'blind randomized method', but no sequence generation, concealment, or what was blinded is reported. The arms differ in size (34 vs 41), and no baseline table with sex, age or comorbidity by arm is shown. The non-infected control group was not part of the randomisation. The between-arm superiority claim therefore rests on an allocation that cannot be assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of computer-generated or otherwise concealed allocation, plus a baseline table showing balance between arms.

quotes.text: сліпим  рандомізованим  методом
Основну групу 2 (ОГ2) становили 18 чоловіків, 23 жінки

issues.title: Superiority of ОГ2 rests on unadjusted Student's t-tests; headline stresses within-group change from baseline
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusions emphasise 'statistically significantly better ... compared with baseline', which is a within-group result and does not show superiority over the standard protocol. The ОГ1 vs ОГ2 comparison (● marker) is a bare Student's t-test with no adjustment for baseline values, no between-group difference with CI, and no exact p-values. For a randomised comparison this is only weak support for the claimed advantage of the programme, though the post-treatment gaps in the tables are large.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or change-score comparison between arms with confidence intervals showing the same advantage.

quotes.text: за  критерієм  Стьюдента
р<0,05 - статистично значуща різниця між відповідними параметрами ОГ1 та ОГ2

issues.title: SPPB total 5.50±0.17 (n=34) is impossible as an SD; dispersions look like standard errors
issues.explanation: The paper says dispersion is given as S (standard deviation), but the SPPB total is an integer score. A group of 34 with mean 5.50 must have an SD of at least about 0.5, yet ±0.17 is printed. Grip strength dispersions (±0.35 to 0.74 kg in n=16-23 groups) are also much smaller than expected for older adults. The tables therefore probably show SEs, and if the t-tests treated them as SDs the significance would be overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw SPPB score data for ОГ1 showing an SD of 0.17, which is arithmetically impossible for integer scores with this mean.

quotes.location: Table 2, Загальний бал, ОГ1 До ФТ

issues.title: Dozens of subscale comparisons at α=0.05 with no primary outcome or multiplicity control
issues.explanation: Grip strength, SPPB subscales and total, and nine EFS subscales plus total are each compared across several group pairs at an uncorrected 0.05. No primary outcome is named. Headline totals are well separated and likely survive correction, but isolated significant subscales cannot be interpreted confidently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or a correction showing the main findings unchanged.

quotes.text: Критичний  рівень  значимості у разі перевірки статистичних гіпотез у цьому дослідженні приймали рівним 0,05.

issues.title: Pre-COVID sarcopenia established retrospectively by questionnaire; no registration or protocol reported
issues.explanation: Inclusion requires sarcopenia before infection, established retrospectively with a frailty questionnaire cited from a review. Pre-infection status is therefore based on recall and is not a measured diagnosis. The paper reports no trial registration and no sample size calculation. This weakens confidence in who was enrolled but does not directly affect the pre/post comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registration record or documented pre-COVID sarcopenia assessments.

quotes.text: ретроспективно встановлена за опитувальником «Вік не перешкода» [4]

issues.title: Grip-strength gain for ОГ1 men printed as 8.5% but Table 1 gives 9.4%
issues.explanation: The text reports an 8.5% gain in grip strength for ОГ1 men. Table 1 values (22.54 to 24.66 kg) give 9.4%. The other three percentage gains in the same sentence agree with the table. The error narrows the apparent gap between ОГ1 and ОГ2 slightly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded data showing the ОГ1 men's gain is 8.5%.

quotes.text: 8,5% у  чоловіків  ОГ1

10.32782/2522-1795.2024.18.3.4.headline_claim: A three-month physical therapy program with a geriatric focus (exercise, Otago program, massage, occupational therapy, nutrition, education) produced a statistically significantly better effect on astheno-vegetative syndrome indicators than the standard post-COVID rehabilitation protocol in elderly patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome and sarcopenia.
10.32782/2522-1795.2024.18.3.4.overall: The finding that the new program improved autonomic and fatigue measures more than standard care is directionally plausible but only weakly supported: allocation and blinding are undescribed, outcomes are subjective or lightly reported, tests are unadjusted and effect sizes absent. Two reporting inconsistencies (MG1 fatigue called moderate, and the isometric DBP direction) show the text and tables do not fully agree.

primary_outcome.name: Astheno-vegetative syndrome indicators (Wayne's questionnaire, Kerdo index, isometric load test, HRV spectrogram, Fatigue Assessment Scale, Fatigue Severity Scale); no single primary outcome identified

issues.title: Superiority over standard care claimed on all indicators with only bare p<0.05 and no effect sizes, adjustment or multiplicity control
issues.explanation: The conclusions say the program was significantly better than baseline and than the standard protocol on the studied indicators. Between-group significance is marked only for some Table 3 cells and the Wayne questionnaire text, Table 2 lacks SDs entirely, and Table 1 shows no between-group marker; all tests are unadjusted Student tests across about ten outcomes with no baseline adjustment or correction. The direction of benefit is plausible, but the strength and breadth of 'better on the studied indicators' is not demonstrated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reporting of between-group tests with effect sizes and CIs for each indicator, with baseline adjustment and multiplicity control.

quotes.text: The results of MG2 patients were statistically significantly better than MG1 (p<0.05)
The critical level of significance  when  testing  statistical  hypotheses in this study was taken to be equal to 0.05.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does support the claim that superiority over the standard protocol rests on bare p<0.05 statements. The abstract and Conclusion 2 say MG2 was significantly better 'on the studied indicators', and the Wayne passage gives only 'p<0.05'. There are no exact p-values, between-group effect sizes or CIs, no baseline adjustment, and no multiplicity control across about 9 outcomes. It is overstated to say 'all indicators' or 'no effect sizes': the Results limit the MG2 advantage to 'individual tests', within-group percentage changes are printed, and the missing between-group markers in Tables

issues.title: Text says both groups reached moderate fatigue; MG1 post-program FAS 35.40 is above the 35-point severe cutoff
issues.explanation: The Results state that fatigue in both main groups fell to a moderate level on the Fatigue Assessment Scale. Methods define moderate as 22-34 and severe as more than 35, and MG1's post-program mean is 35.40, which is in the severe range. Only MG2 (27.05) is moderate, so the standard-protocol group's improvement is overstated in text. The cutoffs also leave 34-35 undefined, which makes the boundary slightly ambiguous.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that moderate was defined with a cutoff above 35.4, or that the text refers only to MG2.

quotes.text: there was a decrease in the feeling of fatigue of the main groups to a moderate level
more than 35 points - severe fatigue
quotes.location: Materials and methods, Fatigue Assessment Scale paragraph
Table 3, Fatigue Assessment Scale row, MG1 after program

issues.title: Isometric-test DBP rise lower in patients (9.57, 10.02) than CG (14.30) while text says patients' rise is greater
issues.explanation: The text says the blood pressure rise during the isometric test was pathological and more pronounced in patients than controls. Table 1 shows lower baseline values in both patient groups than in controls, and 'improvement' is described as an increase toward and beyond the CG value (MG2 15.05). Either the table, the text or the interpretation of the direction is wrong, so this test cannot be read as evidence of sympathetic predominance or of improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors clarifying that the table reports a different quantity or that the values are mislabeled.

quotes.text: Test with isometric load, increase in DBP for 3 minutes
with a more  pronounced  negative  trend  in  patients  who  suffered from the coronavirus disease

issues.title: Randomization described only as 'blind randomized method'; no sequence, concealment, blinding, or sample-size rationale
issues.explanation: Allocation of 75 patients to 34 vs 41 is stated as randomized, but there is no method, concealment or description of who was blinded, and no sample-size calculation. The sex imbalance is small and not itself a problem. Subjective outcomes (Wayne, FAS, FSS) are patient-reported, so unblinded participants who know they got the new program could inflate the apparent advantage.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of the sequence generation, concealment and blinding procedures.

quotes.text: The representatives of this group were divided into two subgroups by a blind randomized method.

issues.title: No trial registration identifier reported for an allocated interventional comparison
issues.explanation: No registry or registration date is given, so the pre-specified outcomes cannot be checked. With around ten outcomes and no primary outcome named, selective emphasis cannot be excluded, but the paper reports all listed measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry preceding enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: The research protocol was discussed, approved and  approved  at  the  meeting  of  the  Bioethics Commission  of  Vasyl  Stefanyk  Precarpathian National University.

10.32902/2663-0338-2023-1-20-24.headline_claim: The combination of Xavron, Tivorel and Xylate is pathogenetically justified and safe for Long-COVID patients, reduces asthenic syndrome, and thereby reduces cognitive 'brain fog' manifestations.
10.32902/2663-0338-2023-1-20-24.overall: The association between comorbidity and fatigue is plausible but rests on unadjusted correlations in a small sample whose size is unclear. The efficacy and safety conclusions depend on pre-post changes in 20 untreated-controlled patients, with no usable control data, no randomisation or blinding, and one apparently mis-transcribed MMSE entry. The headline claims of benefit and safety, and especially of a cognitive effect, are not supported as stated..

primary_outcome.name: Not prespecified; MOND (neurological deficit) and FAS (fatigue) reported as pre-post changes

issues.title: Efficacy rests on pre-post change in 20 treated patients; the 30-patient group's data are not shown
issues.explanation: Every efficacy result (MOND, DASS-21, FAS) is a before-after Wilcoxon change in the 20 treated patients. The comparison group of 30 is not described, and Table 2 contains no data for it. A single sentence mentions a between-group MOND difference without numbers or direction. There is no randomisation, blinding or sample-size justification, so the pre-post changes cannot be attributed to the drug combination, yet the conclusions state benefit confidently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table of outcomes for the 30-patient group with a between-group analysis adjusted for baseline, showing a difference favouring treatment.

quotes.text: Отже, 50 хворих були розбиті на дві групи: перша - 20 осіб і друга - 30 осіб.
Зміни виразності неврологічного дефіциту в 30 пацієнтів із Long-COVID (МОНД) другої групи після завершення курсу лікування були достовірно нижчими, ніж у першій дослідній групі (р<0,05).
Особливо помітною була різниця у виразності втоми з 28,8±4,1 до 20±1,2 (p<0,01)

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy figures reported in Table 2 and the abstract are within-group pre/post changes in the 20 treated patients, and there are no data for the 30-patient group, so the one reported between-group comparison (p<0.05) cannot be checked. The wording that efficacy 'rests on' pre-post change alone is slightly too strong, because the paper does assert a between-group comparison, but it is unsupported by any shown data, test or definition of the groups.

issues.title: Conclusion 4 claims reduced 'brain fog' although the authors report no significant MMSE change (p=0.845)
issues.explanation: The authors report no significant cognitive change on MMSE and write that cognitive improvement would need a longer, individualised approach. The conclusions nonetheless say the combination reduces cognitive manifestations of Long-COVID through lower asthenia. Brain fog was not measured directly, and no mediation analysis links fatigue change to cognition. The MMSE p-value is itself questionable (see c2), but even so the stated conclusion is not what was reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A direct cognitive or brain-fog measure showing improvement, with an analysis linking it to the fatigue change.

quotes.text: достовірно значущих змін у когнітивний сфері за шкалою MMSE (p=0,845) не спостерігалося
позитивно впливає на редукцію когнітивних проявів Long-COVID у вигляді «мозкового туману»

second_reader.what_stands: Conclusion 4 claims a positive effect on cognitive manifestations ('brain fog') although the only cognitive measure (MMSE) showed no significant change by the authors' own report (p=0.845), and no brain-fog-specific measure or mediation analysis supports the claim. The claim rests on patient-reported better concentration and the FAS reduction, which is a weaker basis than the conclusion's wording implies. Separately, the MMSE p-value in Table 2 duplicates the Table 1 correlation result (0.047, p=0.845), so the pre-post MMSE test itself is unclear.

issues.title: Table 2 MMSE 'Wilcoxon' entry 0,047 (p=0,845) duplicates the Table 1 correlation; pre-post means imply a real change
issues.explanation: Table 2 is footnoted as Wilcoxon, yet its MMSE entry is the same coefficient and p as the Table 1 Pearson correlation between comorbidity and MMSE. A mean rise of 0.7 points with SDs of 0.7 and 0.5 in 20 patients would normally give p well below 0.01. The 'no cognitive change' result, which the authors then discuss at length, therefore looks like a transcription error and may understate an MMSE change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level MMSE data showing a Wilcoxon p of 0.845 for the pre-post change.

issues.title: 'Safe' claimed from 20 patients over 10 days with 2 hypertensive crises (10%) and no comparator event rate
issues.explanation: The conclusion calls the combination safe. The evidence is 20 treated patients, 10 days of exposure, 2 hypertensive crises and no formal adverse-event monitoring or control-group comparison. The events are disclosed in the results, but the conclusion does not reflect them. The data support only that no serious events were observed in a very small sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled safety analysis with event rates in both groups showing no excess of hypertensive events.

issues.title: Causal wording ('directly depends', 'independent of severity') from unadjusted correlations in ≤50 patients
issues.explanation: The conclusions say asthenia directly depends on chronic disease and that comorbidity is a risk factor for Long-COVID regardless of acute severity. The evidence is unadjusted Pearson correlations in patients who all already had Long-COVID plus cerebral ischaemia. There is no control group without Long-COVID, so comorbidity as a risk factor for Long-COVID cannot be assessed. Acute severity was not analysed. Only an association with fatigue and neurological score among already-affected patients is supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison with patients lacking Long-COVID, adjusted for covariates and stratified by acute severity.

quotes.text: Коморбідність є важливим чинником ризику розвитку Long-COVID незалежно від тяжкості перебігу інфекції SARS-CoV-2 у гострому періоді.

issues.title: MOND outcome scale is the authors' own; only a conference resolution cited, no validation data
issues.explanation: The first reported outcome, MOND, is a scale the authors developed. No reliability, responsiveness or validation data are given. issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published validation of MOND showing reliability and sensitivity to change.

issues.explanation: The text gives p=0.001 for r=0.56 'for the whole sample', but Table 1 prints p=0.01 for the same coefficient. Neither value matches a sample of 50, since r=0.56 at n=50 gives p of about 0.00003. The table value matches n=20, so the sample behind the correlations is unclear. 10.3310/nihropenres.14236.1.headline_claim: Non-invasive taVNS did not significantly improve fatigue at 8 weeks compared with sham or placebo stimulation in post-COVID fatigue.
10.3310/nihropenres.14236.1.overall: The headline conclusion, that taVNS did not improve fatigue at 8 weeks, matches the primary results (all p > 0.4) and is not overstated in the Abstract. The reliability of the null is limited by completers-only analysis with uneven attrition and with both control arms below the target sample size. The exploratory material (per-protocol subgroup, FIS result, neurophysiological associations) is uncorrected for multiplicity and is framed more favourably in the Discussion than the evidence allows.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Fatigue Visual Analogue Scale (F-VAS) from baseline to week 8

issues.title: Discussion cites unshown post hoc per-protocol (n=59) improvements as support for taVNS despite null primary results
issues.explanation: The primary ITT and CACE analyses showed no benefit, and the Abstract concludes taVNS did not improve fatigue. The Discussion then reports that VAS, FIS and peripheral fatigue 'improved significantly in the taVNS group' among 59 adherent participants and says this supports taVNS as a potential therapy. The subset is selected on post-randomisation adherence, the claim rests on within-group change, and no numbers or between-group test are given. The result is exploratory and cannot support an efficacy inference. This also covers the separate per-protocol-selection candidate c4.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified per-protocol analysis with between-group estimates and multiplicity control showing the effect.

quotes.text: In that per-protocol analysis, VAS, FIS scores and peripheral fatigue measured by twitch interpolation improved significantly in the taVNS group.
These results support taVNS as a potential therapy for pCF mechanistically

issues.title: Secondary FIS result (p = 0.03, CI 0.7 to 18) and 12-predictor models reported without multiplicity control
issues.explanation: About nine questionnaire outcomes, each with two comparisons, plus two 12-predictor neurophysiological models at two timepoints, are tested without any stated correction. The one significant questionnaire result (FIS placebo vs taVNS, p = 0.03, lower CI limit 0.7) would not survive even a modest correction. The Discussion cautions about multiple testing, but the Abstract and the 'modest signals of potential benefit' wording still highlight it. The primary null conclusion is unaffected, so only the secondary and exploratory findings are weakened.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or a multiplicity adjustment under which the FIS result remains significant.

quotes.text: should be interpreted with caution in light of multiple testing
Total Fatigue Impact Scale (FIS) scores, as one of the secondary outcomes, revealed modest signals of potential benefit.

issues.title: 'ITT' analyses use completers only: 90 of 114 (21%) analysed, with 13% vs 22% vs 28% loss by arm
issues.explanation: The Methods call the analyses intention-to-treat or modified ITT, but they were performed only 'in the randomised population who completed the study'. Loss was 13% in taVNS and 22% and 28% in the control arms, and no sensitivity analysis for non-completers is shown. Both control arms fell below the 32 per arm the sample-size calculation required. Completers-only analysis with differential dropout can bias the estimated effect in either direction, so the null primary result is less secure than 'ITT' suggests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including all 114 randomised participants (for example multiple imputation) that gives the same null primary result.

quotes.text: The primary analyses were conducted on the 90 participants who completed the trial: 34 in the taVNS group and 28 in each of the sham and placebo groups
Both primary and secondary analyses were performed in the randomised population who completed the study

issues.title: Abstract says no week-8 neurophysiological associations; multivariable model shows one (p = 0.019)
issues.explanation: The Abstract says regression analyses found associations with baseline neurophysiological measures at 16 weeks but not 8 weeks. Results 3.3.1 and Table 4 report a significant week-8 association for STR_StartReact_1DI in the multivariable model. Only the lasso analysis found nothing at week 8. The discrepancy is small and affects an exploratory result, not the primary conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An Abstract that specified the lasso analyses only, or a correction to the Results.

quotes.text: In the taVNS group, regression analyses showed associations between fatigue and baseline neurophysiological measures at 16 weeks, but not 8 weeks.
At week 8, a multivariable linear model identified a significant negative association between STR_StartReact_1DI and F-VAS (p = 0.019)

issues.title: taVNS good + moderate adherence sums to 103.34%, unlike sham and placebo, which sum to 100%
issues.explanation: The sham and placebo adherence percentages sum to 100%, which implies exhaustive, exclusive categories. The taVNS values (26.67% and 76.67%) sum to 103.34%, which would need 31 of 30 participants. One figure is misprinted, probably the moderate value (73.33% would fit). The adherence classification feeds the CACE analyses, but those results are null either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the categories are nested (moderate includes good) and a table of counts per arm.

quotes.text: The proportions classified as moderate adherence rates were 76.67% in the taVNS arm, 86.36% in the sham, and 70.83% in the placebo group.
The proportions of participants classified as good adherence were: 26.67% in the taVNS arm, 13.64% in the sham, and 29.17% in the placebo group.

10.33545/26648504.2024.v6.i1a.24.headline_claim: Pulmonary rehabilitation offered to long COVID patients produced perceptible benefits in MMRC grade, six-minute walk distance, cough score and biomarkers, and should be offered to all such cases unless contraindicated.
10.33545/26648504.2024.v6.i1a.24.overall: The paper is an uncontrolled retrospective before-after series, and its causal and long-term quality-of-life conclusions are not supported. Within-group improvement in the 61 patients classed as cured is largely built into how groups were defined, and the statistics appear to ignore pairing. Several labelling and arithmetic inconsistencies (Ns, Table 5 sums, text-table mismatches) lower confidence in the reporting but do not alter the basic picture.

primary_outcome.name: No single primary outcome named; objectives list MMRC dyspnoea grade, oxygen saturation, cough score and six-minute walk distance

issues.title: Causal benefit of rehabilitation claimed from an uncontrolled retrospective before-after series
issues.explanation: The study is a retrospective chart review of 71 inpatients with no comparison group and no blinded assessment. Improvements in SpO2, dyspnoea and cough over three weeks may reflect natural recovery or the concurrent drug treatments described in the Discussion. The conclusion nonetheless states that rehabilitation has a 'positive impact on outcome'. The design cannot support that causal claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group of comparable long COVID inpatients without rehabilitation showing smaller change.

quotes.text: long COVID cases who was admitted and managed in the post COVID
Sixty-one patients in fully recovered group show remarkable improvement

second_reader.what_stands: The paper draws causal conclusions about rehabilitation (including an 'immune-modulatory role') from an uncontrolled retrospective before-after series in which co-interventions and natural recovery are not separated from the effect of PR. The Discussion lists retrospective design and single-centre as limitations, but the Conclusion does not temper the causal wording.

issues.title: Conclusion claims long-term quality-of-life benefit and universal use from 3-week, 71-patient uncontrolled data
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says rehabilitation resulted in 'long-term quality of life' benefit and should be offered to all such cases. The study measured no quality-of-life outcome and followed patients for only about three weeks. The authors also state small sample, single centre and retrospective data as limitations, and the sample is selected (ward inpatients, exclusion of patients on ventilation or with SpO2 <90%). The universal recommendation and the long-term claim go beyond the evidence. There is also no sample-size justification, and the 10-patient group cannot support any conclusion on non-responders.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported quality-of-life data and follow-up beyond discharge supporting the claim.

quotes.text: hence it should be offered to all such cases unless otherwise contraindicated
resulted in perceptible benefits and long-term quality
Small sample size,

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of long-term quality-of-life benefit is not supported: no QoL measure and no follow-up beyond about 3 weeks are reported. The recommendation for all cases rests on 71 uncontrolled, selected patients (10 of whom showed no meaningful improvement), and the stated limitations are not reflected in the Conclusion.

issues.title: Improvement shown only in the 61 patients classed as cured; groups are defined by the outcome itself
issues.explanation: Patients were split into full and partial recovery according to whether they were discharged cured or on home oxygen. Table 3 then shows large improvement in the 61 cured patients, which is largely built into the grouping. Table 4, for the 10 not cured, shows no change in most measures. No analysis for all 71 patients is given, so the overall benefit of rehabilitation is not estimated, and the 'remarkable improvement' headline reflects selection by outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis of change in all 71 patients regardless of discharge category.

quotes.text: and the part recovery category was discharge with home oxygen support
Before PR (N=61)

second_reader.what_stands: The headline improvements in Table 3 are reported only for the 61 patients classed as cured, a group defined by the outcome itself, and the Observations text calls this 'remarkable improvement'; no analysis of all 71 together is given. It is not true that the 10 others are hidden, since Table 4 reports them, and it shows no significant change in 6MWD, MMRC or cough score (SpO2 did rise 87 to 91, P=0.01).

issues.title: Before-after changes in the same patients appear analysed with an unpaired test
issues.explanation: The Methods describe an unpaired test for comparing two variables, and no paired test (paired t, Wilcoxon, McNemar) is mentioned. Tables 3 and 4 compare before and after values in the same patients. The Table 4 SpO2 p-value matches an unpaired calculation. Chi-square comparisons of before and after categories on the same patients are also not valid. P-values for within-patient change are therefore of uncertain validity, though the large Table 3 effects probably survive a correct paired analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or output showing paired tests were used for the before-after comparisons.

quotes.text: The  unpaired  test  was  used  to  compare  two discrete  variables.
Before PR (N=61)

issues.title: Cough outcome is an ad hoc 0-3 grade the authors 'hypothesized', not a validated scale
issues.explanation: The cough score was defined by the authors and has no stated validation or reliability. It is reported as a mean of grades and used in the conclusion as evidence of benefit. With unblinded retrospective scoring, a change in this measure carries limited weight.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Citation of a validated cough scale or inter-rater reliability data for this grading.

quotes.text: 1 for cough on exertion, 2 for nocturnal cough, 3 for cough at rest

issues.title: Text says partly recovered group had no significant improvement but Table 4 SpO2 rose 87 to 91, p=0.01
issues.explanation: The Observations state that the 10 partly recovered patients showed no significant improvement in mean SpO2, MMRC and cough score. Table 4 reports mean SpO2 rising from 87±4 to 91±2 with p=0.01. The text therefore misdescribes the table for SpO2; MMRC, cough and 6MWD do appear unchanged. The Discussion's 'not much improvement' repeats the same simplification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the p=0.01 was not meant as significant, or a corrected Table 4 SpO2 p-value.

quotes.text: no significant improvement

issues.title: Table 5 obstructive airway column: outcomes 27+4=31 but N=30 (90% + 13.33% = 103%)
issues.explanation: The obstructive airway disease column has N=30, but its two mutually exclusive outcomes add to 31 and the percentages add to 103.3%. The four diagnostic columns' N sum to 30+15+14+11=70, not 71, while their outcome counts sum to 71 (61 cured, 10 on oxygen). So the OAD denominator is probably 31, or one count is misprinted, and the 42.3% share in the text depends on which.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level data showing one OAD patient was counted in two categories, or a corrected N.

quotes.text: Obstruction airway diseases (N=30)

quotes.location: Table 5, Discharged with o2 support, obstruction column

issues.title: Baseline SpO2 (87±4 partly recovered; 90.03±3.89 fully recovered) is hard to reconcile with exclusion at SpO2 <90%
issues.explanation: Exclusion criteria remove patients with oxygen saturation under 90%, yet the partly recovered group's baseline mean is 87±4. The fully recovered group's baseline mean of 90.03 with SD 3.89 also implies many values below 90, since values cannot exceed 100. Either the exclusion refers to a different time point or measurement condition, or the criteria were not applied as written. The paper does not say which.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the exclusion SpO2 was measured on supplemental oxygen or at an earlier time point than the tabulated baseline.

quotes.text: saturation less than 90%

issues.title: Table 4 headers say N=61 for a 10-patient group; Table 3 caption says N=71 for 61 patients
issues.explanation: Table 4 is captioned as the partly recovered group (N=10) but both data columns are headed N=61, which is the fully recovered group size. Table 3 has the reverse slip: its caption says N=71 while its columns say N=61, and the data are the 61 fully recovered patients. The counts inside the tables fit the 10 and 61 patients, so these are labelling errors, but they make it easy to misread which patients each table covers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; the headers and captions are printed as described.

quotes.text: Table 4: Change in variable after pulmonary rehabilitation therapy -part recovered group (N=10)
Before PR (N=61)

issues.title: Dozens of p-values at alpha 0.05, no declared primary outcome or correction
issues.explanation: Tables 1 to 5 report many p-values at an unadjusted 0.05 threshold with no designated primary outcome. The headline Table 3 results are so extreme that correction would not change them. Borderline subgroup findings (e.g. Table 4 SpO2 p=0.01, Table 1 alcohol p=0.01) are the ones affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or adjusted p-values.

quotes.text: P value of less than 0.05 was considered significant.

issues.title: Text gives non-IPF ILD 3 and IPF ILD 2 on home oxygen; Table 5 gives 2 and 3
issues.explanation: The Observations list the oxygen-support patients as OAD 4, non-IPF ILD 3, IPF ILD 2, pneumonia 1. Table 5 shows non-IPF ILD 2 (14.29%) and IPF ILD 3 (27.28%). The two ILD counts are swapped between text and table. The text also cites 'Table 3' for these data, but they are in Table 5.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source record showing the text order is correct and the table columns are mislabelled.

quotes.text: OAD-4,  non  IPF ILD-3,  IPF  ILD-2,  and  pneumonia-1

quotes.location: Table 5, Discharged with o2 support, non-IPF column

issues.title: Table 2 IMV share printed as 2.28% but 2/71 = 2.82%
issues.explanation: Invasive mechanical ventilation in 2 of 71 patients is 2.82%, but the table prints 2.28%, apparently transposed digits. Nothing else depends on the value, though the whole table also contains minor rounding slips (e.g. 3/71 printed 4.22%).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator stated for this row that gives 2.28%.

script.explanation: 2/71 = 2.82%, but the paper prints 2.28, outside the rounding interval [2.27, 2.29]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 87.7 rather than 71.

10.33590/respiramj/93u1v2yd.headline_claim: Adding a 12-week synchronous virtual maintenance program after inpatient rehabilitation did not improve SF-12 physical component score beyond rehabilitation alone, but work ability improved more and adherence and satisfaction were high, which the authors take to support virtual maintenance as a feasible and scalable model.
10.33590/respiramj/93u1v2yd.overall: The primary result is null, and the abstract says so plainly. The positive tone of the conclusion rests on one uncorrected secondary result (WAI, p=0.03), on open-label self-report data, and on adherence and satisfaction figures from one centre over 15 weeks. Feasibility is reasonably supported; benefit and scalability are not. The primary estimate also appears to have a dropped sign.

primary_outcome.name: Change in SF-12 physical component score (PCS) from T1 to T3

issues.title: Null primary outcome; conclusion rests on one uncorrected secondary result (WAI, p=0.03)
issues.explanation: The primary outcome (SF-12 PCS) showed no between-group difference (p=0.84). Of roughly nine secondary effectiveness outcomes (MCS, EQ-5D, WAI, PSQI, GAD-7, PHQ-9, sit-to-stand and others), only WAI differed, with p=0.03 and a lower CI bound of 0.2. No multiplicity adjustment or exploratory label is given, yet the conclusion says the work-ability gain 'indicates' that continued support may enhance participation-related recovery. With about nine secondary tests, one p of 0.03 is weak evidence for that claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or multiplicity plan naming WAI as a key secondary outcome, or a WAI result that survives adjustment for the number of secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: except for WAI score, which improved significantly more in the INT than in the control group
the observed improvement in work ability indicates that continued structured support may enhance participation-related recovery beyond the initial rehabilitation phase.

issues.title: 'Scalable model for long-term care' claimed from single-centre, 15-week data; feasibility itself is supported
issues.explanation: Adherence of 85.5% and high satisfaction in 90 participants at one centre support feasibility. They do not show scalability, because multi-site delivery, staffing, cost and generalisability were not assessed. Follow-up ended at 15 weeks, so 'long-term' is not tested. Two authors are shareholders of the company that helped deliver the intervention, which makes unqualified wording more of a concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Multi-site delivery data, longer follow-up, or a cost or resource analysis showing scalability.

quotes.text: High adherence and patient satisfaction support synchronous virtual maintenance programs as a feasible and scalable model for long-term PCC care.
In this single-center RCT, participants with PCC were randomized (1:1)

issues.title: Open-label design with patient-reported outcomes; blinding not described, relevant to the WAI finding
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they received the virtual program or usual care. All effectiveness outcomes except the sit-to-stand test are self-reported questionnaires. An expectation effect could inflate the WAI difference of 2.4 points, which is the one positive secondary result. The abstract does not say whether outcome assessment or analysis was blinded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full-text statement of blinded outcome assessment, or an attention-matched control.

quotes.text: followed by usual care (control) or by a 12-week virtual, synchronous maintenance program (intervention, INT)

issues.title: Primary outcome Δ=0.4 is not at the midpoint of its CI (-3.8 to 3.1); a sign appears to be missing
issues.explanation: A Wald-type difference should sit at the centre of its 95% CI. The CI of -3.8 to 3.1 is centred at -0.35, which fits Δ=-0.4 but not +0.4. The sign of the primary between-group difference is therefore ambiguous. The null conclusion is unaffected, since the interval spans zero either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The full-text primary analysis table showing Δ=0.4 with a non-Wald interval, or a corrected estimate of -0.4.

10.33667/2078-5631-2022-35-8-14.headline_claim: A Bacillus subtilis metabiotic (Bactimunal) for 28 days, one capsule twice daily, is effective and safe for gastrointestinal symptoms and asthenia in patients with post-COVID syndrome.
10.33667/2078-5631-2022-35-8-14.overall: The headline claim of efficacy and safety rests on a small open-label comparison against no treatment, using self-reported scores, with an undescribed randomisation method. The improvements in group 1 are large, but they cannot be separated from expectation effects, and the microbiota results come from 10 selected, uncontrolled patients. The numeric errors found (Enterococcus text/table, UPM percentage, misprinted count, SD) are small and do not change the conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: GSRS total symptom score (primary outcome not explicitly designated in the paper)

issues.title: Open-label no-treatment control with self-reported GSRS and asthenia outcomes
issues.explanation: Group 2 received no supplement or placebo, and the outcomes are patient-reported symptom scores. Improvement in group 1 (GSRS total 45.2 to 25.5 vs 42.2 to 38.9 in group 2) can reflect expectation, attention or other non-specific effects as well as the product. The Discussion nonetheless states that the study shows therapeutic efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of blinded outcome assessment or a placebo arm.

quotes.text: не получала какихлибо дополнительных лекарственных препаратов или БАД
Наше исследование показывает терапевтическую эффективность метабиотика

second_reader.what_stands: The control group received nothing (no placebo), no blinding is described, and the primary outcomes (GSRS, ШАС) are symptom questionnaires, so the comparison is open-label with subjective outcomes that are open to expectation effects. The Discussion's statement of 'терапевтическая эффективность' and the conclusion that the product is 'эффективным' go beyond what such a design can show, and the paper does not list this as a limitation. The one point I could not confirm from the text is that the questionnaires were strictly patient-completed rather than administered by a clinician, though this i

issues.title: Randomisation method not described; baseline characteristics reported for group 2 only (sex, no table)
issues.explanation: The paper says patients were randomised but gives no method or concealment. Group 1's sex distribution is not given and there is no baseline comparison table. Age differs by 4.5 years between groups, which may be chance. Allocation adequacy cannot be assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a computer-generated sequence with concealed allocation and a baseline table.

quotes.text: Пациенты были рандомизированы в две группы.
из них 16 женщин и 4 мужчины

issues.title: Microbiota findings come from 10 selected, uncontrolled patients in group 1 with unpaired tests
issues.explanation: Stool PCR was done only in 10 patients from the treated arm, chosen for diarrhoea scores of 15 to 18, with no control-arm stool data. Before/after changes (for example Akkermansia 0/10 to 6/10) cannot be attributed to the product. The tests named (Pearson chi-square, Fisher) assume independent groups, whereas these are repeated measures on the same 10 people.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Paired analysis and stool data from an untreated comparison group showing the same changes are specific to treatment.

quotes.text: Дополнительно 10 пациентам группы 1 проводилась оценка состояния толстокишечного микробиоценоза
из группы 1 с выраженностью диареи от 15 до 18 баллов

issues.title: 'Safe' concluded from zero reported adverse events in 20 treated patients, collection method not stated
issues.explanation: The conclusion declares the metabiotic effective and safe. The only safety information is one sentence reporting no adverse events. No adverse event collection method is described, and 20 treated patients over 28 days give little power to detect uncommon events. No sample-size justification is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described systematic adverse event collection procedure and a safety claim limited to short-term tolerability.

quotes.text: Нежелательных явлений при приеме метабиотического препарата зарегистрировано не было.
является эффективным и безопасным.

issues.title: Enterococcus increase: text says 4 (40 %) patients, table shows 2 (20 %) at baseline
issues.explanation: The Results text says 4 (40 %) patients had increased Enterococcus spp. before treatment. The table row for Enterococcus > 10^8 shows 2 (20 %), and its p = 0.470 fits 2/10 vs 0/10. One of the two figures is wrong; the table is the better-supported one. The error does not change the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text counts a different Enterococcus threshold than the table's > 10^8 category.

quotes.text: у 4 (40 %) пациентов выявлялось увеличение представительства Enterococcus spp
Enterococcus spp. < 10 8 Enterococcus spp. > 10 8

issues.title: UPM > 10^4 at baseline: table prints 8 (70 %), but 8 of 10 is 80 % as in the text
issues.explanation: The table gives 8 (70 %) for patients with opportunistic flora above 10^4 before treatment, while the text says 8 (80 %). With n = 10, 8 patients is 80 %. The printed p = 0.023 matches 8/10 vs 2/10, so the percentage is the error. This is a small typographical error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the count was 7 and the text and p are the wrong figures.

quotes.text: у 8 (80 %) пациентов, у 4 (40 %) УПМ определялись в сочетаниях
УПМ > 10 4

script.explanation: 8/10 = 80.00%, but the paper prints 70, outside the rounding interval [69.50, 71.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 11.4 rather than 10.

issues.title: Bacteroides fragilis/F. prausnitzii row prints count 80 against n = 10; percentage implies 8
issues.explanation: The baseline cell reads 80 (80 %) in a column with n = 10, which is impossible as a count. The percentage and p = 0.470 point to a count of 8. It is a trivial misprint, possibly introduced in text extraction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original PDF showing '8 (80 %)'.

quotes.text: Bacteroides fragilis / Faecalibacterium prausnitzii < 100

issues.title: Group 1 baseline asthenia SD printed as 7.9 in abstract and 7.8 in Results
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the baseline asthenia score of group 1 as 51.5 ± 7.9. The Results give 51.5 ± 7.8. The discrepancy is tiny and does not affect any conclusion, but one of the figures is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction notice stating that both values are the same SD at different rounding.

quotes.text: выраженность астении до лечения составила 51,5 ± 7,9 балла
выраженность астении составила 51,5 ± 7,8 балла

10.3389/fcogn.2025.1692578.headline_claim: Four weeks of 40 Hz vibratory and auditory treatment (VAT) improved selective attention and response inhibition in long COVID patients, and the improvement was linked to increased plasma BDNF.
10.3389/fcogn.2025.1692578.overall: The paper is an open-label pilot with 10 participants per arm, no sham, no power calculation, and ANOVA results printed with impossible degrees of freedom and inconsistent effect sizes. The flanker and BDNF findings are at best hypothesis-generating, and the claim that cognitive gains are linked to BDNF rests on one pooled regression with unexplained statistics.

primary_outcome.name: Cognitive test score changes and neurotrophin levels (flanker task group-by-session interaction; BDNF)

issues.title: Open-label, no-device control (no sham, unblinded assessors) confounds VAT with expectancy and attention
issues.explanation: Controls received nothing and the study was open-label, with no assessor blinding. Improved flanker scores, heart-rate readings taken by participants on a phone app, and any other outcome sensitive to motivation could reflect expectation, contact or practice rather than VAT. The authors concede this but still report increased attention as a finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham-controlled or blinded-assessor replication showing the same flanker and BDNF effects.

quotes.text: whereas the control group did not use any device but followed the same data collection procedures
The absence of sham and assessor blinding could introduce expectation bias, and therefore a more rigorous follow-up study is necessary to solidify any findings from this study.

second_reader.what_stands: The design is open-label with no sham and no assessor blinding, so any VAT effect is confounded with expectancy, the Hawthorne effect, and extra contact and attention. The authors state this limitation themselves in the Discussion, but they do not carry it into their abstract or conclusions.

issues.title: ANOVA interactions printed as F(1,1); F, p and partial eta squared cannot all be right
issues.explanation: Every group-by-session ANOVA is reported with error df of 1, which is impossible for 20 participants and, taken literally, gives raw p well above the printed adjusted p. The printed partial eta squared values (0.41, 0.22, 0.365) also do not match the F statistics under any single plausible error df. The flanker and BDNF headline results therefore cannot be verified from the reported statistics.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplemental Table 1 showing the correct df and unadjusted p values that reproduce the printed F, partial eta squared and adjusted p values.

second_reader.what_stands: The printed df of (1,1) cannot be correct for n = 20, and with those df the printed p values are impossible. The flanker triple is internally consistent if df2 is about 17-18. The BDNF pe2 (0.22 vs about 0.35 expected) and the heart-rate pe2 (0.365 vs about 0.72 expected, with an adjusted p that looks too large for F = 46.92) cannot be reconciled with the printed F and the stated sample. The paper does not say what model or df produced them.

issues.title: BDNF-flanker link rests on one pooled change-score regression whose F and R2 imply only ~8 residual df
issues.explanation: The claim that the cognitive improvement is linked to BDNF rests on a single regression of change scores. It is not shown to hold within arm, and it does not control for group. The printed F and adjusted R2 are not consistent with a 20-point regression, and the number of points used is not stated. Per-person counts (6/10 vs 1/10 with BDNF increases) are descriptive and do not establish mediation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A within-arm or group-adjusted regression with stated n, and a corrected R2/F pair.

quotes.text: Linear regression between the change in flanker test and change in plasma BDNF value was found to be statistically significant ( F = 37.79, R 2 adjusted = 0.825, p adjusted = 0.003; Figure 3B)

second_reader.what_stands: The only BDNF-flanker evidence is a single regression of change scores, and its F and adjusted R2 imply about 7 residual df (n of about 9), not 18. That is about 7 rather than 8 df, and the paper does not explain the missing observations. The text does not say whether the regression is pooled across arms, so I could not confirm that point.

issues.title: Mechanism and rehabilitative-tool conclusions exceed a 10-per-arm open-label pilot with no sham
issues.explanation: The summary links cognition gains to BDNF and extends VAT's usefulness to other populations. The evidence is a 20-person unblinded comparison with no power calculation, one pooled correlation, and ANOVA statistics with impossible df. These support at most a hypothesis worth testing in a blinded trial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this concerns the strength of the wording relative to the design.

quotes.text: This improvement was linked to an increase in plasma BDNF, suggesting a possible mechanism for VAT.
We propose that VAT may be a useful rehabilitative tool for LC as well as other targeted populations

second_reader.what_stands: The hedged language and the stated causation caveat soften the claims, but the summary and abstract still present a BDNF mechanism and a 'useful rehabilitative tool' on the basis of a 10-per-arm open-label pilot with no sham. That pilot has inconsistent ANOVA reporting and a correlation that rests on about 9 observations. These claims go beyond what the data can support, though the authors do not assert causation outright.

issues.title: No trial registration reported; primary outcome stated only broadly
issues.explanation: No registry ID is given, so the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be checked against a prospective record. The stated primary outcome covers many cognitive tests and several neurotrophins, so the focus on the flanker task and BDNF cannot be confirmed as pre-specified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment naming the flanker task and BDNF as primary outcomes.

quotes.text: The primary outcome of this study was cognitive test score changes and neurotrophin levels, whereas all others were secondary.

issues.title: Abstract/Discussion say 20 recruited or randomized; Methods say 22 recruited, 20 completed
issues.explanation: The Methods and Table 1 give 22 recruited with 20 completing. The Abstract says twenty patients were randomized and the Discussion says twenty were recruited. The paper never gives a flow of 22 to randomization to analysis, or which arms the two dropouts came from. This is mostly a wording problem, but the randomized N and the per-arm denominators (10 and 10) are not clearly stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow showing 22 enrolled, 20 randomized after 2 early exclusions, and 20 analysed.

quotes.text: Twenty-two participants with self-reported cognitive symptoms post-COVID were recruited into this study, two of which were lost to follow-up.
Twenty patients who self-reported cognitive impairment after infection of COVID-19 were recruited in this study

10.3389/fcvm.2022.866113.headline_claim: Sulodexide significantly improves long-lasting post-COVID-19 endothelial dysfunction and alleviates chest pain and palpitations.
10.3389/fcvm.2022.866113.overall: The directional finding that sulodexide-treated patients improved more than untreated patients may be real, but the paper's wording ('proves', 'significantly improves', 'alleviates') goes beyond a non-randomised, open-label study with an untreated control, undescribed allocation and completer-only analysis. The control chest-pain recovery is misprinted (43.6% vs 51.3%), which modestly inflates the headline contrast, and the palpitations result would not survive multiplicity correction. The conclusions should be read as a preliminary signal requiring placebo-controlled confirmation.

primary_outcome.name: Change in long-COVID symptoms (chest pain, palpitations) from T0 to T1 and delta EQI at 21 days; between-group p < 10^-3 reported for chest pain and delta EQI

issues.title: Open-label, untreated control with no placebo; headline chest-pain and palpitation results are subjective
issues.explanation: Controls received nothing and no blinding of patients or assessors is described. The highlighted chest-pain and palpitation recoveries are symptom reports, which are vulnerable to expectation and placebo effects. Controls also recovered substantially without treatment (43.6% to 70.5% across symptoms), so the size of any true drug effect cannot be separated from expectation and natural recovery. The disclosure in the limitations does not temper the headline claim that sulodexide 'alleviates' these symptoms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of blinded outcome assessment, or sham/placebo control, in the protocol or supplementary material.

quotes.text: The control group adhered to the study protocol without any medical treatment
At 21 days, the sulodexide group presented significantly less chest pain
The need of placebo-randomized study is warranted to confirm such results.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is open-label with an untreated control and no placebo, and the headline chest-pain and palpitation outcomes are symptom reports with no described blinding. The authors state the need for a placebo-randomized study, but the abstract and conclusion do not carry that caution. Separately, the control chest-pain recovery figure (43.6%) does not match its own counts (20/39 = 51.3%), which I noticed in passing; it is outside the point asked.

issues.title: Discussion says the study 'proves' sulodexide is effective for >80% of patients; design cannot support this
issues.explanation: The 80% figure is the within-arm recovery rate, not a treatment effect: untreated controls also recovered in roughly half to two thirds of cases. A non-randomised, unblinded 3-week study cannot prove efficacy, and the authors themselves say a placebo-randomised study is needed. The title and conclusion state improvement as fact rather than as a preliminary signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised, placebo-controlled replication or adjusted analyses that account for spontaneous recovery in controls.

quotes.text: is also the first to prove that targeting these symptoms by sulodexide could be an effective solution for more than 80% of patients within a short-time medication of 3 weeks
Our results support that targeting this cause with sulodexide accelerates patients' recovery

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion's wording that the study 'proves' sulodexide is effective for more than 80% of patients is not supported by a non-randomised, open-label, 3-week study in which untreated controls also improved substantially and most between-group differences were not significant. The paper's Limitations and 'other trials are warranted' soften this, but the sentence itself is overstated, and the 80% figure applies to some symptoms only and to within-group recovery rather than the treatment effect.

issues.title: Allocation method unstated in a non-randomised study; all outcome comparisons unadjusted
issues.explanation: The study is called quasi-experimental and the process by which patients were put in the sulodexide or control group is never described. Baseline tables show broadly similar groups, but only unadjusted bivariate tests are used for outcomes, and no adjustment or matching is described. Selection by clinicians or patients, or differences in care-seeking, cannot be excluded, which weakens the causal reading of the group differences.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated allocation procedure (for example, alternate assignment independent of clinician choice) plus adjusted analyses giving similar effects.

quotes.text: This is a prospective multicenter quasi-experimental casecontrol study.
The study population was assigned to a sulodexide group (144 patients) or a no-medical treatment group (146 patients).

second_reader.what_stands: The excerpts supplied do not state how patients were allocated to sulodexide or no treatment, and all between-group outcome comparisons are unadjusted, even though the Methods mention risk ratios that are not reported. Baseline tables look balanced, which lessens but does not remove the concern. Whether Figure 1 describes allocation cannot be seen from the extracted text.

issues.title: Control chest-pain recovery printed 20/39 (43.6%); 20/39 is 51.3%, and 43.6% is repeated in the abstract
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives 20 of 39 recovered in the no-treatment group but prints 43.6%, which equals 17/39. The T1 count of 19 (39 minus 19 = 20 recovered) supports 20, so the percentage is the wrong figure. The corrected contrast is about 83.7% vs 51.3% (a gap of about 32 points, not 40), and a chi-square on 36/43 vs 20/39 gives p of roughly 0.0016, not the printed p < 10^-3. The headline chest-pain effect is still significant but is overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level data showing 17 of 39 control patients recovered with more than 19 symptomatic at T1, or an erratum correcting the table.

quotes.location: Table 2, Chest pain row, no-medical treatment %Recovery

script.explanation: 20/39 = 51.28%, but the paper prints 43.6, outside the rounding interval [43.55, 43.70]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 45.9 rather than 39.

issues.title: Non-attenders at day 21 excluded from analysis; number excluded and reasons not reported
issues.explanation: The Methods say patients who did not attend the 21-day visit were excluded from analysis, but no counts of enrolled versus analysed patients or reasons for missing the visit are given. No intention-to-treat analysis is presented. The results are completer-only, and the amount of attrition cannot be judged from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing negligible and balanced losses (Figure 1 may contain it), or a sensitivity analysis counting missing patients as non-recovered.

quotes.text: Patients who did not attend the scheduled 21day visit were excluded from the data analysis.

issues.title: Nine symptom tests at alpha 0.05 without correction; the palpitations claim (p = 0.009) would not survive Bonferroni
issues.explanation: Nine symptom comparisons were each tested at p < 0.05 with no correction or hierarchy. The palpitations claim in the title and conclusion rests on p = 0.009, which exceeds a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/9 = 0.0056. Chest pain would likely survive. This weakens one of the two named symptom claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol-specified hierarchical testing order or a stated correction under which palpitations remained significant.

quotes.text: The value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
palpitations (85.2 vs. 52.9%, p = 0.009)

issues.title: Sulodexide headache recovery printed 24/30 (80%) but T0 is 31; 24/31 = 77.4%
issues.explanation: The sulodexide group had 31 patients with headache at T0 and 7 at T1, so 24 recovered out of 31. The table divides by 30 and prints 80%. The error is small and the headache comparison is non-significant either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that one headache patient was excluded from the recovery analysis for a stated reason.

script.explanation: 24/31 = 77.42%, but the paper prints 80, outside the rounding interval [79.50, 81.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 30.0 rather than 31.

issues.title: Table 1 prints 61 (16) for monitor/palpitations total; 61/290 = 21.0%, as the text says
issues.explanation: The Table 1 total column gives 61 (16%) for ambulatory monitoring and for palpitations, but 61 of 290 is 21.0%. The Results text states 21%. This is a cosmetic inconsistency that does not affect any analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: None; the arithmetic is unambiguous.

quotes.text: Only 61 (21%) patients had ambulatory 24-h cardiac monitor.

script.explanation: 61/290 = 21.03%, but the paper prints 16, outside the rounding interval [15.50, 17.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 381.2 rather than 290.

10.3389/fdgth.2025.1504217.headline_claim: Individually tailored ICBT with weekly therapist support is feasible for psychological symptoms related to the COVID-19 pandemic in its final phase, with significant within-group reductions in depression and anxiety, though larger studies are needed to draw further conclusions.
10.3389/fdgth.2025.1504217.overall: The paper is a small single-arm feasibility study, and its limits (no control, 37.5% dropout, completers only) are largely acknowledged. Its feasibility conclusion is reasonable, but statements that ICBT is 'effective' and 'beneficial' are not supported by this design. The numeric problems are minor (a garbled Table 4 cell, and an ISI direction that conflicts with the means), but the secondary effects are uncorrected and fragile.

primary_outcome.name: BDI-II and GAD-7 (pre- vs post-treatment change)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change between baseline, end of treatment after eight weeks and follow-up at 12 months after treatment termination.
Change between baseline, end of treatment after eight weeks and follow-up at 12 months after treatment termination.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis (15/24, 37.5% dropout) is described as ITT-consistent; no missing-data handling
issues.explanation: Nine of 24 enrolled participants (37.5%) have no post-treatment data, and all outcome tests use only the 15 completers. The Methods describe this as in line with intention-to-treat, but analysing only those who completed follow-up is not ITT. Completers were more highly educated than non-completers, and the sample was already small and self-selected. The pre-post improvements may therefore be over-optimistic for everyone who started treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (for example multiple imputation or last observation carried forward) on all 24 participants giving similar changes in BDI-II and GAD-7.

quotes.text: This was in line with an Intention-To-Treat approach.
the study had a drop-out rate of 37.5% (9 participants)
Complete Case Analysis (CCA) was conducted, whereby only participants who completed the post-treatment measurement were included
