second_reader.what_stands: The analysis is a complete-case (completers-only) analysis of 15 of 24 enrolled participants (37.5% missing) with no imputation or other missing-data handling, yet Sec 2.5 describes it as in line with ITT, which is not the usual meaning of ITT. The authors do acknowledge the information loss as a limitation, and they report that completers differed from non-completers in education, but the ITT wording remains inaccurate.

issues.title: Uncontrolled pre-post feasibility data (n=15 completers) described as showing ICBT is effective and beneficial
issues.explanation: There was no control group, no sample-size calculation, and only 15 of 24 participants were analysed. Improvements could reflect regression to the mean, the natural course of symptoms, the end of the pandemic or other life events. The authors acknowledge this, yet the Discussion says ICBT 'remains a relevant and beneficial intervention' and the Conclusions say ICBT is 'feasible and effective'. They also argue that significant decreases show that power is 'sufficient', which does not follow. The claims of effectiveness go beyond what a single-arm feasibility study can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist comparison showing a larger improvement in the treated group, or conclusions limited to feasibility.

quotes.text: our results indicate that ICBT in many ways is feasible and effective for psychological symptoms during the last phase of a pandemic
Overall, the fi ndings indicate that individually tailored ICBT remains a relevant and bene fi cial intervention
Despite a low number of participants, decreases in psychological symptoms were identi fi ed, indicating that there is suf fi cient power at least to some extent.

second_reader.what_stands: Uncontrolled pre-post data from 15 completers (with 37.5% attrition) are used to support the statements that ICBT is 'effective' and 'beneficial', which a design without a control group cannot show. This runs against the paper's own caveats (no control condition, small sample, CCA) and its abstract conclusion, which is limited to feasibility, and the reasoning that significant findings show 'sufficient power' is also not sound.

issues.title: About 11 secondary outcomes tested at uncorrected p<.05; several cited effects have p between .025 and .041
issues.explanation: Eleven symptom measures plus two knowledge scores were tested with the Wilcoxon test at alpha .05 without any multiplicity correction. Several secondary results are marginal (KEDS p = .041, IES-6 p = .025, UCLA-LS-R p = .027, knowledge weighted score p = .028), and KEDS was not significant in the paired t-test (p = .057). The Discussion nevertheless says effects on 'some of the secondary outcome measures were shown'. Some of these results may be chance findings. This weakens only the secondary claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction for the secondary outcomes under which these results remain significant.

quotes.text: Thus, effects on primary and some of the secondary outcome measures were shown.
Signi fi cance testing was two-tailed, and results were interpreted as signi fi cant at p < .05.

issues.title: ISI reported as significantly increased (Mdn 15 to 16) while Table 3 mean falls 15.40 to 12.67
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion say insomnia symptoms significantly increased after treatment. Table 3, however, shows the mean ISI falling by about 2.7 points, and Table 4 shows lower means in both post-COVID subgroups. The 'increase' therefore seems to rest on a one-point difference in medians. A reported rise in insomnia may be a misreading of direction, which would understate the treatment effect. The paper cannot settle this without the signed-rank direction or the raw data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired ISI data showing that most non-zero differences were increases and that the sign-rank statistic corresponds to a post-treatment rise.

quotes.text: were signi fi cantly higher ( Mdn =16.00) than pre-treatment ( Mdn =15.00), T =24.00, p =.039

issues.title: Table 4 raw knowledge SD of 14.80 (n=5, range 0-16) is impossible; adjacent weighted cell also garbled
issues.explanation: The raw knowledge score can only range from 0 to 16, so an SD of 14.80 is impossible for five people, and a mean of 11.80 with that SD is impossible too. The weighted-score cell for the same subgroup reads '2.59 (2.59)', where the mean is implied to be about 14.8 from Table 3. The cells for this subgroup appear shifted or mistyped. This is a secondary descriptive table, so nothing in the main results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table, or the raw data, showing that the SD for this subgroup is within 0-8.

quotes.location: Table 4, Knowledge test, Raw score, Probably not post-COVID pre-treatment
Table 4, Knowledge test, Weighted score, Probably not post-COVID pre-treatment

quotes.text: Thus, the total for the raw score ranged from 0 to 16

10.3389/fdgth.2025.1689846.headline_claim: The study demonstrates the feasibility of combining heart rate variability with activity and sleep features to predict next-day fatigue levels in individuals with post-COVID fatigue.
10.3389/fdgth.2025.1689846.overall: The paper is a small, single-cohort feasibility study; its headline performance (XGBoost R2 0.789, MAE 3.18) is likely optimistic because random 5-fold CV places the same participants in training and test folds. The Discussion repeats several numbers that contradict Table 4, and the claim that combined HRV and activity data beats either alone is untested. These weaken the strength of the conclusions, though the 'feasibility' framing is broadly reasonable.

primary_outcome.name: Next-day VAS fatigue prediction performance (XGBoost R2, MAE, correlation)

issues.title: Random 5-fold CV mixes same-participant days across train and test; reported R2 0.789 may not generalise
issues.explanation: Observations from the same participants appear in both training and test folds, so the models can learn person-specific patterns (age, sex, stable HRV profile) rather than predicting fatigue in new people. The authors admit this may overestimate performance, but the abstract and conclusions describe the results as strong accuracy without that qualifier. Stratified-by-fatigue folds, not grouped by participant, do not remove the problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A grouped (participant-level) CV or a held-out-participant test showing similar performance.

quotes.text: may include data from the same participants in both training and test sets within a fold
it may overestimate model performance compared to true cross

second_reader.what_stands: The paper uses random (not participant-grouped) 5-fold CV, so same-participant days appear in both training and test sets, and the authors themselves say this may overestimate performance relative to cross-participant generalisation. The reported R2 of 0.789 should be read as a within-participant-leaking estimate; the size of the inflation is not quantified in the paper. The paper discloses this properly in Methods and Limitations, but the Abstract and Conclusions still describe the performance as 'strong' without this caveat.

issues.title: Claim that combining HRV and activity data beats either domain alone is untested (no single-domain models)
issues.explanation: The conclusions state that integrating physiological and behavioural data gives superior prediction compared with either domain alone. The only comparison reported is XGBoost versus Random Forest, plus models with and without treatment-condition variables, so no evidence compares the combined feature set with single-domain sets. The sample-size caveat is a lesser issue for a pilot.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported performance of HRV-only and activity/sleep-only models in the paper or its supplement.

quotes.text: provides  superior  prediction compared to either domain alone
could be expanded for more robust validation

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions state that integrating HRV and activity/sleep data 'provides superior prediction compared to either domain alone', but no HRV-only or activity-only model was fitted, so this comparison was not tested. The feature-importance rankings show both domains contribute but do not show that combining them improves prediction over either alone.

issues.title: Analysis dataset size is 383 (Table 1, folds) or 389 (Results, Discussion); days per participant also inconsistent
issues.explanation: Table 1 and the cross-validation fold sizes give 383 observations, while Results and Discussion give 389 for the same dataset. The per-participant data description is also inconsistent: the 3.5-day average does not reproduce either total, and the minimum is 1 day in Results against a 2-day exclusion rule and a 2-11 range elsewhere. The sample description cannot be reconciled, though model results are unlikely to change materially.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 389 includes observations removed before modelling, and that the days-per-participant figures use a different unit than model rows.

quotes.text: included  389  observations
approximately  306 observations
Participants  with  less  than  2  days of complete data were excluded

issues.title: Morning-activity advice drawn from unstable subgroup R2 (0.792 vs afternoon 0.070 ± 0.985)
issues.explanation: Subgroup R2 values with SD near 1 in the afternoon group cannot support a ranking of time-of-day predictability, and predictability of fatigue is not evidence that promoting earlier activity reduces fatigue. The behavioural recommendation goes beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Subgroup sample sizes and an analysis showing activity timing change alters fatigue.

quotes.text: promoting earlier daily  activity  may  represent  a  viable  behavioral  strategy
afternoon (R2 = 0.070 ± 0.985)

issues.title: Discussion misstates MAE (3.04/6.54 vs 3.18/6.14) and claims r >0.88 and R2 >0.8 that Table 4 contradicts
issues.explanation: The Discussion's interpretation of model performance uses numbers that differ from the paper's own Table 4 and Results. Both MAEs differ, and the stated thresholds (correlation above 0.88, R2 above 0.8) fail for Random Forest (0.864, 0.691) and for XGBoost R2 (0.789). Tabulated values still show good performance, but the Discussion slightly inflates it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Discussion values come from a separate analysis that is clearly labelled.

quotes.text: The  achieved  mean  absolute  errors  of  3.04  and  6.54
significant variance explained (R2  score  >0.8)
a mean absolute error of 3.18 ± 0.63

issues.title: Age summary inconsistent: 47.9 ± 12.0 (Table 1) vs 47.3 ± 11.5 (Results), and range starts at 0 despite 18-65 eligibility
issues.explanation: Two age summaries for the same 68 participants disagree, and the range minimum of 0 is impossible given adult eligibility of 18-65. This suggests a coding error in the age variable, which is also a model input. Overall impact on the conclusions is likely small, but age is reported as an important predictor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing ages all >=18 and a stated reason for two different summaries.

quotes.text: mean  age  of  47.3 ± 11.5  years
adults aged 18-65 years

issues.title: 68 of 114 enrolled analysed (40% excluded for incomplete data) with no comparison of excluded participants
issues.explanation: The analysed participants are those with complete HRV, accelerometer and questionnaire data, a selected, more adherent subset. Real-world feasibility of the approach is therefore likely overstated, since 40% of enrolled people could not supply usable data. The paper notes technical reasons but does not frame this as a feasibility finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison showing included and excluded participants were similar, or a reported flow of reasons.

quotes.text: While the trial enrolled 114 participants, not all had complete datasets

issues.title: Treatment suggestions drawn from correlational feature importances, though hedged
issues.explanation: Feature importance in a predictive model does not show that modifying autonomic function would reduce fatigue. The paper hedges this in the same section, so the overreach is limited to suggestive wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: N/A; wording judgement.

quotes.text: these  associations  are  correlational  and  should not be interpreted as causal

issues.title: Discussion swaps Sham (23) and Placebo (21) group sizes relative to Table 1 and Results
issues.explanation: Table 1 and Results give Sham n = 23 and Placebo n = 21. Discussion 4.1.1 gives Placebo n = 23 (33.8%) and Sham n = 21 (30.9%). One of the two sets of labels is wrong; the effect on the conclusions is minor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Allocation records showing which arm has 23 participants.

quotes.text: and placebo ( n = 21 participatns)
Placebo  ( n = 23  participants,  33.8%)

10.3389/fimmu.2025.1698271.headline_claim: Combined IMC-2 plus a 15-day Paxlovid course produced greater patient-reported fatigue improvement than IMC-2 alone in Long COVID, suggesting potential synergy and justifying a larger randomized placebo-controlled trial.
10.3389/fimmu.2025.1698271.overall: The between-arm fatigue difference is a patient-rated, open-label, self-selected comparison in about 24 patients, so it supports only hypothesis generation for a randomized trial, as the authors partly state. Arm sizes (12 vs 15 IP, 24 vs 21 unique) and one table difference are inconsistent, so even the descriptive results are not fully reliable. Claims of efficacy, synergy and durable benefit go beyond what this design shows.

primary_outcome.name: PGIC fatigue rating at day 120

issues.title: Self-selected, open-label comparison with patient-rated outcome cannot attribute the fatigue difference to Paxlovid
issues.explanation: Patients chose IO or IP, were not randomized, were not blinded, and rated their own improvement on the PGIC. Any difference of 2 points (p < 0.0001) could reflect who chose which arm, expectation of a more intensive regimen, or placebo effect, and no adjustment is made. The authors acknowledge this, but the between-arm comparison is still presented as statistically significant evidence of efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomized or blinded allocation, or adjusted analyses showing balance and a persistent effect, which this single-site series does not provide.

quotes.text: Patients who consented to off-label use of IMC-2 to treat Long COVID symptoms could take IMC-2 alone (IO) or combine it with a 15-day Paxlovid course (IP).
It was an open-label case series, in which both selection bias -arising from patients actively seeking care -and the placebo effect may have influenced the observed outcomes.

second_reader.what_stands: The IO vs IP allocation was self-selected, open-label and judged only by patient-rated global change, so the 2-point fatigue PGIC difference cannot be attributed to Paxlovid; allocation, expectation and placebo effects are confounded with treatment. The authors do disclose selection bias and placebo effect and call for a blinded randomized trial, so the limitation is acknowledged, but the abstract's 'statistically significant improvement' framing and the 'potential synergy' wording in the Conclusion still go beyond what this design supports.

issues.title: IP group is 12 patients in abstract/Table 1 but 15 in durability and adverse-event sections; 24 total vs 21 unique
issues.explanation: The abstract, results and Table 1 describe 12 IP patients, while the durability section says all 15 IP participants completed follow-up. The IP adverse-event percentages (26.6%, 13.3%, 40%, 86.7%) are whole-patient fractions of 15, not 12. The 24 total is 12 + 12 although three crossovers appear in both arms, and the Table 1 sex counts imply 21 unique patients. The analysed population for the primary comparison and for durability therefore cannot be pinned down.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram or patient listing showing 15 distinct IP exposures (12 IP-only plus 3 crossovers) and that the day-120 comparison used the stated 12 patients.

quotes.text: Twelve received the IO protocol, and 12 received the continuous IP combination.
All 15 participants in the IP group completed all three follow-up timepoints.
quotes.location: Results, Durability of treatment response in the IP cohort

quotes.text: most commonly increased fatigue (40% of patients) and dysgeusia (86.7% of patients)
quotes.location: Results, Adverse event and side effect reporting

issues.title: 'Efficacy' and 'potential synergy' claimed from a self-selected pilot with no Paxlovid-alone or placebo arm
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the findings provide preliminary evidence of efficacy, and the Conclusion proposes a potential synergy between IMC-2 and Paxlovid. Synergy needs a comparison with each component alone, which was not done. The durability conclusion also treats absence of a significant change across timepoints in a few patients as proof of sustained benefit. The hedging language limits, but does not remove, the overreach.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limited to feasibility and hypothesis generation, or data from a Paxlovid-alone or placebo comparator.

quotes.text: These findings provide promising preliminary evidence of feasibility and ef fi cacy, highlighting the potential utility of combination antiviral therapies
The results of this case series suggest a potential synergy between IMC-2 and Paxlovid

issues.title: Data collection to February 2024 is hard to reconcile with complete 731-day follow-up in all IP patients
issues.explanation: Data are said to be collected until February 2024, and 731 days after a February 2024 start would be February 2026, after the December 2025 acceptance. Complete 731-day follow-up in every IP patient is only possible if all started by about late 2023. The paper does not state whether the period refers to enrolment or to end of follow-up.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-patient protocol start dates showing all IP patients began by late 2023, or a statement that the period refers to enrolment only.

quotes.text: Data presented in this case series were collected from patients with Long COVID attending a single Alabama-based clinic from April 2022 to February 2024.

issues.title: Dysautonomia 10-point PGIC difference printed 2.6; printed means give 2.3
issues.explanation: Table 3 gives IO 1.8 and IP 4.1 but a mean difference of 2.6 points. The difference of the printed means is 2.3, which rounding of one-decimal means cannot account for. One of the three numbers is wrong, and the reported effect for this secondary outcome is overstated if 2.6 is the error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing unrounded means whose difference is 2.6, for example if a different set of patients or a changed IO mean was used.

quotes.text: Dysautonomia (PGIC: 10-point Likert) 1.8 (± 3.2) 4.1 (± 1.5) IP response is 2.6 points greater (1.2)

issues.title: Two non-compliant patients removed from analysis (24 of 26 who opted in); no intention-to-treat analysis
issues.explanation: One patient per arm was removed for non-compliance, and results are for the remaining 24. The impact is likely small, but whether these two patients had worse outcomes is unknown, and the analysis cannot be called intention-to-treat. In an unblinded series this adds a further potential for favourable selection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including the two excluded patients that gives the same fatigue difference.

quotes.text: one patient in each group was noncompliant with the protocol and was subsequently removed from the analysis

10.3389/fmed.2023.1149922.headline_claim: A 12-week blended digital and community-based rehabilitation programme significantly improved breathlessness, functional capacity, wellbeing and HR-QoL, and reduced healthcare utilisation, in people with long COVID, and is scalable and effective.
10.3389/fmed.2023.1149922.overall: The paper shows large pre-post improvements among 601 completers, but with no control group, no reported denominator of those who started, and self-reported and unblinded outcomes, it cannot show that the programme caused them. The conclusions of effectiveness, scalability and remote-delivery effectiveness go beyond what this design supports; the improvements are best read as descriptive and probably optimistic.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Dyspnea-12, DASI, WHO-5 and EQ-5D-5L utility from Week 0 to Week 12 (multiple outcomes; no single primary named)

issues.title: Causal effectiveness claimed from a single-arm pre-post service evaluation with no control group
issues.explanation: All 601 participants received the programme and were compared only with their own baseline. Natural recovery, regression to the mean, attention and social-contact effects cannot be separated from the programme effect. The paper nevertheless titles and concludes that the programme produced improved outcomes and is effective. The rebuttal that benefits 'exceed any improvements reported without intervention in the literature' is not a concurrent comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or matched control group, or an analysis showing the observed change exceeds that of an untreated long-COVID comparison cohort.

quotes.text: First, a control group was not included. Therefore, we cannot directly attribute all of the observed benefits to the LC rehabilitation programme
The present study has demonstrated the clinical effectiveness of a scalable LC rehabilitation model for improving physical, mental, and HR-QoL outcomes.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is a single-arm pre-post service evaluation and still uses causal language ('demonstrated the clinical effectiveness', 'in response to', 'suggest that the underlying pathology is responsive to exercise'). The authors do acknowledge the missing control group, so the limitation is disclosed; what stands is that the acknowledgement is partial ('not all' benefits) and sits beside an unqualified effectiveness claim.

issues.title: Completer-only analysis of 601 with no reported number enrolled, withdrawn or lost before Week 12
issues.explanation: The primary analysis includes only participants who completed the programme and provided Week 0 and 12 outcomes. The number who enrolled, started or dropped out is not given, and there is no flow diagram. People who stopped because they did not benefit or felt worse are missing, so the improvements are likely to be overestimated. The size of the bias cannot be assessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow showing the number enrolled and started, with few non-completers or similar baseline characteristics among those lost.

quotes.text: Complete case analysis was conducted for the 601 participants who completed the Nuffield Health COVID-19 Rehabilitation Programme and provided the relevant outcome measures at Weeks 0 and 12.
The primary analyses were conducted in 601 participants who completed the LC rehabilitation programme and provided outcome measures at Week 0 and 12.

second_reader.what_stands: The analysis is explicitly completer-only (complete case, 'completed the programme'), and the supplied text reports no number enrolled, started, withdrawn or lost before Week 12, so attrition and potential selection of better responders cannot be assessed. I could not check whether a flow diagram exists in figures or supplementary material that were not included as text.

issues.title: Conclusions of effectiveness, scalability and effective remote delivery exceed uncontrolled completer-only data
issues.explanation: The conclusion states the model 'meets the urgent need for an effective intervention' and that the first 6 weeks 'demonstrate the effectiveness of remote programme delivery'. Neither can be shown from uncontrolled pre-post change among completers at 12 weeks. Healthcare-utilisation reductions rest on 3-month self-recall versus the preceding period with no comparator.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled evidence that outcomes exceed untreated or usual-care trajectories, and data on non-completers and delivery costs supporting scalability.

quotes.text: The blended and community design of this rehabilitation model makes it scalable and meets the urgent need for an effective intervention to support patients experiencing LC.
Improvements observed during the first 6 weeks of the programme also demonstrate the effectiveness of remote programme delivery.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusions that the programme is 'effective', that its design 'makes it scalable', and that first-6-week improvements 'demonstrate the effectiveness of remote programme delivery' go beyond uncontrolled, completer-only pre-post data; scalability and remote-delivery effectiveness were not directly measured. The data do show improvements in outcomes among completers and delivery at 51 sites, which supports a narrower claim of feasibility and observed improvement.

issues.title: Eight of eleven authors employed by the programme provider evaluate their own service
issues.explanation: Authors employed by Nuffield Health designed, delivered and evaluated the programme, and the paper favours an effective, scalable conclusion for that organisation's model. Employment is disclosed, but the roles of the provider in data collection (by its own specialists), analysis and interpretation are not described. This raises the risk of favourable interpretation without showing any specific error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that independent analysts handled the data and the provider had no role in interpretation or the decision to publish.

quotes.text: JS, KD, AI, MH, LM, ZL, DD, and BK were employed by Nuffield Health.

10.3389/fmed.2025.1649667.headline_claim: Individualized pulmonary rehabilitation produced durable improvements in clinical and psychological outcomes after severe COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, maintained at 1 year regardless of 12, 24 or 36 sessions, suggesting a shorter program may suffice.
10.3389/fmed.2025.1649667.overall: The paper's central claim, that rehabilitation produced benefits maintained for a year irrespective of number of sessions, is only weakly supported: there is no control group, dose groups were assigned by response, only 45% of eligible patients were analysed, and the study was underpowered (0.67). The tables also contain impossible SD/range values and baseline columns that disagree across tables, and the 36s text reuses 24s p-values, so individual results should be treated with caution. Overall the data support recovery over time in completers, not a demonstrated durable programme effect or dose equivalence.

primary_outcome.name: not stated as a single primary outcome; the authors report repeated-measures changes across spirometry, 6-MWD, HGS, fatigue (FAS), functional status (PCFS), dyspnoea (mMRC) and SF-36 domains

issues.title: No control group: 'PRP produced improvements maintained at 1 year' rests on within-group change only
issues.explanation: All 60 patients received rehabilitation and there is no comparison group, no blinding, and no randomisation. Improvement from baseline at 12-24 months after severe COVID-19 is expected to occur partly without treatment. The conclusion nevertheless says PRPs 'produced' improvements and that the benefits were 'maintained' because of them. The data show recovery over time in treated patients, not an effect of the programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical comparison cohort showing smaller recovery without rehabilitation.

quotes.text: In this experimental repeated measures study, sixty patients were included
Importantly, these benefits were maintained 1 year after the intervention, regardless of the number of sessions (12, 24, or 36).
a limitation of this study is that it is not a randomized clinical trial

second_reader.what_stands: The study has no control group, so improvements 'produced' by the PRP and 'maintained at 1 year' rest on within-group pre/post/1-year change only and cannot be attributed to the program versus natural recovery. The authors acknowledge non-randomisation but not the absence of any comparator, and the Conclusion's wording is causal.

issues.title: Dose-independence conclusion drawn from response-adapted groups, small n and no equivalence test
issues.explanation: Patients were not randomised to 12, 24 or 36 sessions. The number of sessions was determined by treadmill performance, so the groups differ at baseline and 'dose' reflects response. Absence of a significant difference among groups of 17-25 patients, with stated power of 0.67, is not evidence of equivalence. The conclusions that a shorter programme 'may be sufficient' and that a personalised programme 'will sustain' results irrespective of initial severity are not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised comparison of session numbers, or an equivalence analysis with pre-specified margins showing similar 1-year outcomes after adjusting for baseline severity.

quotes.text: Those who did not meet the criterion continued until completing 24 sessions
The statistical power (1β err prob) of the sample analyzed was 0.67.
Therefore, irrespective of the initial severity on admission, conducting a personalized PRP treatment will sustain the achieved results 1 year later.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that results are sustained 'irrespective of the initial severity' and that a shorter program 'may be sufficient' rests on non-randomised, response-adapted groups, n of 17-25 per group, power of 0.67 and tests of difference only, so absence of significance is not evidence of equivalence. Moreover, Table 5 itself shows several significant between-group differences at 1 year (FAS, PCFS, bodily pain), and the 12s group is not comparable to the others at baseline, so the stated dose-independence is not established; the limitation about power is noted by the authors but not weighed in the

issues.title: Only 60 of 133 eligible patients analysed (completers who attended follow-up); no ITT or non-responder comparison
issues.explanation: Inclusion required having completed the programme and attended follow-up, and many eligible patients did not take part (49 of 74 in the 12s group, 17 of 34 in the 24s group, 7 of 25 in the 36s group). Those lost may differ in outcome. The 1-year maintenance claim therefore applies to patients who completed the programme and returned for follow-up. Participation was not compared with non-participation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data showing that participants and non-participants had similar baseline and outcome characteristics, or an analysis imputing missing 1-year outcomes.

quotes.text: Inclusion criteria were (a) having gone through the PRP at Hospital El Carmen (HEC), (b) having completed the PRP, and (c) having attended follow-ups with a bronchopulmonary specialist.
In the 12s group, 25 patients were included, 49 did not participate because

second_reader.what_stands: Only 60 of about 133 eligible patients (45%) are analysed, all of them completers who were reachable at 1 year, with very unequal retention by arm (34% in 12s vs 72% in 36s), and no ITT, sensitivity or non-participant comparison is given; the authors cite losses and power but do not discuss attrition bias. The 133 total is my sum of the printed numbers, since the Results text does not state it directly and Figure 1 was not available to me.

issues.title: 36s Results text reuses 24s p-values; disagrees with Table 4 (HGS 0.048, FAS 0.026/0.002, PF 0.039)
issues.explanation: The 36s paragraph gives p-values that equal the 24s group's, while Table 4 gives different ones. Left HGS is 0.048 in the text and 0.001 in Table 4, and total FAS is 0.002 vs 0.001. The text also says the 36s FAS scores fell significantly from baseline to 1 year, but Table 4 marks only the pre-post comparison. This weakens the durability statement for fatigue in this group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source output showing the 36s group truly has these p-values and Table 4 is the erroneous one.

quotes.text: In the right (p = 0.001) and left (p = 0.048) HGS, there was a significant increase in strength after completing PRP compared to the baseline assessment.
the physical (p = 0.001), mental ( p = 0.026), and total ( p = 0.002) FAS scores decreased significantly between the baseline assessment and the 1-year re-assessment
PF ( p = 0.039; p = 0.004, respectively), VT ( p = 0.005; p = 0.004, respectively)

issues.title: Impossible mean/SD/range combinations in Tables 1 and 4 (e.g. SD 19.17 for range 11-32)
issues.explanation: Several cells report an SD that no data within the printed min-max range could produce, or a mean equal to the maximum with a non-zero SD. The 36s Total FAS post-PRP SD is 19.17 for values between 11 and 32, and the right HGS SD is 48.63 for values between 10 and 40. The 24s BMI mean equals its maximum yet has SD 5.42. These are wrong values in the tables, so the affected means, SDs and ranges (and any tests based on them) cannot be trusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw participant data showing these SDs and ranges are attainable (they are not, given the printed ranges and n).

quotes.location: Table 4, Total FAS row, Post PRP column

issues.title: 'No differences among groups at 1 year' contradicted by Table 5 (physical/total FAS p=0.008, PCFS p=0.037, BP)
issues.explanation: The final paragraph states there were no differences among the three groups at 1 year. Table 5 and the Results report significantly lower fatigue (physical and total FAS) and PCFS in the 12s group versus the other groups, and significant differences in bodily pain and diabetes prevalence. These differences largely mirror baseline differences, which were not adjusted for. The summary statement is inaccurate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Wording limiting the claim to spirometry, exercise capacity and strength outcomes.

quotes.text: There were no differences among the three groups (12s vs. 24s vs. 36s) at the 1-year re-evaluation.
the physical FAS score was significantly lower in the 12s group compared to the 36s group ( p = 0.008)
quotes.location: Results, final results at 1 year per group

issues.title: Baseline values in Table 1 disagree with pre-PRP values in Tables 2-4 (24s HRQoL = post-PRP values)
issues.explanation: The 24s baseline HRQoL entries in Table 1 are identical to the post-PRP entries in Table 3, not the pre-PRP ones (physical functioning 67.35 vs 45.00; mental health 66.18 vs 30.88). Other baseline cells also differ: 36s STST 15.22 (Table 1) vs 25.22 (Table 4), 12s MIP 65.79 ± 23.71 vs 67.60 ± 27.01, and 24s 6-MWD max 582 vs 562. At least one version of each is wrong. The baseline between-group comparisons and the size of some pre-post changes are therefore unreliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or erratum that Table 1 and the pre-PRP columns come from different assessments, or source data showing the printed values are correct.

quotes.location: Table 3, Physical functioning row, Pre PRP column
Table 4, STST row, Pre PRP column

issues.title: p = 0.05 and p = 0.050 described as significant (24s FVC; baseline FEV1)
issues.explanation: Two results are called significant with printed p-values of 0.05 and 0.050, which sit exactly on the stated α of 0.05. Whether they count as significant depends on rounding and on a strict versus inclusive threshold. They are borderline, with no multiplicity adjustment across many outcomes, and should not be presented as clear findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded p-values below 0.05.

quotes.text: there was a significant increase in the absolute value of FVC between baseline and the completion of the PRP ( p = 0.05)
FEV1 was significantly higher in the 12s group compared to the 36s group ( p = 0.050)

issues.title: No trial registration or protocol reported; unclear whether analysis was prospectively planned
issues.explanation: No registry identifier is given and no primary outcome is specified. There are about 25 outcomes with no multiplicity correction, so prespecification cannot be checked. The selection of completers who attended follow-up suggests assembly after the fact.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registration record or protocol dated before enrolment naming the outcomes and analysis.

quotes.text: Assessments were conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and 1 year after the intervention.

10.3389/fmed.2026.1720578.headline_claim: Ten sessions of major blood ozonation (MBO) improved fatigue, anxiety, depression, sleep quality and quality of life in patients with post-COVID syndrome, and the treatment may be preferred in patients with persistent symptoms.
10.3389/fmed.2026.1720578.overall: The reported before-and-after improvements are internally consistent apart from a swapped pair of p-values and a wrong vaccination percentage. They come from a single-arm retrospective series of 40 completers, so they cannot show that MBO caused the improvement. The Conclusion's recommendation goes beyond what this design supports, so the headline should be treated as tentative at best.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; FACIT Fatigue Scale is the first-listed and most prominent outcome

issues.title: Single-arm retrospective pre-post series used to claim MBO efficacy and recommend its use
issues.explanation: All 40 patients had MBO, and each p-value tests change from baseline within the same patients (Wilcoxon signed-rank). Placebo response, natural recovery of post-COVID symptoms over time, regression to the mean and co-interventions are not excluded. The Conclusion nonetheless says improvement 'was detected' and that the treatment 'may be preferred', which a pre-post comparison cannot support as a treatment effect. Limitations are acknowledged only in the Discussion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical comparison group, or evidence that symptoms in untreated post-COVID patients do not change over the same interval.

quotes.text: Lack of prospective studies and lack of a control group are other limitations of the study.
The treatment may be preferred after COVID-19 infection in patients with persistent symptoms.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, retrospective pre-post record review with no control group, yet the Aim and Conclusion present the results as efficacy ('improvement ... was detected') and say MBO 'may be preferred' in post-COVID patients. The authors do list the missing control group and non-prospective design as limitations and call for further studies, but the efficacy language and the recommendation go beyond what an uncontrolled pre-post design can support (it cannot separate treatment effect from natural recovery, regression to the mean or placebo/expectation effects).

issues.title: About 25 uncorrected tests; marginal SF-36 and PSQI subscale findings (p=0.034-0.043) are fragile
issues.explanation: Five questionnaires plus 7 PSQI components and 9 SF-36 subscales were each tested at 0.05 with no correction and no designated primary outcome. The main fatigue, anxiety, depression and pain results are strong enough to survive adjustment. The claims of improved sleep disturbance, daytime dysfunction and energy/fatigue (p = 0.034, 0.039, 0.043) would not survive correction. The Conclusion's broad 'quality of life and sleep' claim rests partly on these.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome with the remaining analyses labelled exploratory, or a stated correction method.

quotes.text: a significant improvement was detected in daytime dysfunction (<italic>p</italic> = 0.039)
fatigue (<italic>p</italic> = 0.043)

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 5 of 45 (11%) excluded for missing data, plus exclusion of irregular attenders
issues.explanation: Five of 45 enrolled patients were dropped for missing data with no description of who they were. The Methods also exclude patients who did not attend sessions regularly. Patients who did poorly or had side effects may have stopped attending, so the 40 analysed patients may be those who benefited. No sensitivity analysis is offered.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline characteristics of the excluded patients showing they resemble the analysed ones, or an analysis counting non-completers.

quotes.text: Due to missing data, five patients were excluded from the study, and a total of 40 patients were evaluated.
patients who declined the treatment or did not attend the MBO sessions regularly were also excluded

issues.title: No adverse-event data reported although the Conclusion recommends an invasive blood-ozone procedure
issues.explanation: The paper reports no adverse events, discontinuations for tolerability, or contraindication screening outcomes for MBO, an intravenous procedure. A recommendation that the treatment 'may be preferred' needs a safety statement. Reasons for the 5 exclusions are also missing, so the paper cannot show that none was treatment-related.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of adverse events (or their absence) among the treated patients.

quotes.text: The treatment may be preferred after COVID-19 infection in patients with persistent symptoms.

issues.title: Text swaps Beck depression (p=0.001) and anxiety (p=0.002) p-values relative to Table 3
issues.explanation: The Results prose gives p = 0.001 for depression and p = 0.002 for anxiety. Table 3 gives 0.002 for depression (Z = -3.066) and 0.001 for anxiety (Z = -3.433). The Z values fit the table, so the prose is wrong. Both results are significant either way, so no conclusion changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Table 3 rows are mislabelled, or Z values that give p = 0.001 for depression.

quotes.text: Notably, there were significant improvements in the Beck Depression Inventory (<italic>p</italic> = 0.001) and Beck Anxiety Inventory scores (<italic>p</italic> = 0.002)

script.explanation: The printed z = -3.066 supports p no smaller than 0.00216219, but the paper reports p = 0.001 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

issues.title: Vaccinated patients printed as 85% (n=24) of 40; 24/40 is 60%
issues.explanation: The Results say 85% (n = 24) of the 40 evaluated patients were vaccinated. A count of 24 out of 40 is 60%, and 85% would be 34 patients. The vaccination figure cannot be trusted, though it is a descriptive item and no outcome depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for vaccination status, such as missing vaccination data, that makes 24 equal 85%.

quotes.text: It was determined that 85% (<italic>n</italic> = 24) of the patients were vaccinated.

script.explanation: 24/40 = 60.00%, but the paper prints 85, outside the rounding interval [84.50, 86.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 28.2 rather than 40.

10.3389/fmed.2026.1809451.headline_claim: Nebulized 3D-cultured MSC-EVs give faster early relief of post-COVID chronic cough (superior at day 6, comparable at day 14) with good tolerability.
10.3389/fmed.2026.1809451.overall: The headline claim that nebulized EVs give faster early cough relief rests on a non-randomized, unblinded comparison with no sham arm and a subjective outcome, with nominally significant day-6 results that are uncorrected for multiplicity. One of those results (total effective rate, P=0.035) recomputes to about 0.07. The data support at most a hypothesis-generating signal and acceptable short-term tolerability, not demonstrated efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: Cough Evaluation Test (CET) improvement at day 6, efficacy categories

primary_outcomes.measure: Adverse reaction (AE) and severe adverse reaction (SAE)

issues.title: Non-randomized, unblinded comparison with no sham nebulization on a patient-reported cough score
issues.explanation: The study is described as non-randomized, and the control arm received no nebulization at all. The primary CET score is subjective, so patients who know they are inhaled something may report faster improvement. The day-6 advantage therefore cannot be attributed to the EVs themselves. The authors concede the bias in the limitations, yet still describe efficacy in the Discussion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of concealed random allocation, blinded outcome assessment, or a sham-controlled arm.

quotes.text: while the control group did not receive any EVs treatment during the same period
the absence of a placebo nebulization for the control group may introduce bias
This was a pilot, non-randomized, controlled clinical study

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a non-randomized comparison in which only the EV group received nebulization, with no sham nebulization and no reported blinding, and the primary outcome is a patient-reported cough score. The authors openly list the missing placebo as a limitation, but the design weakness itself is real.

issues.title: 'Demonstrates' faster relief and 'favorable efficacy' claimed from a non-randomized, open pilot
issues.explanation: The Conclusion states the pilot demonstrates faster early relief, and the Discussion says the findings suggest favorable efficacy. The design (no randomization, no placebo, subjective outcome, no multiplicity control) supports only a hypothesis-generating signal. The authors' own limitation about bias is not carried into the conclusion's wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusion worded as hypothesis-generating only.

quotes.text: this pilot study demonstrates that nebulized 3D-EVs provide faster early relief of post-COVID chronic cough
Our clinical trial findings suggest a favorable therapeutic efficacy and safety profile for MSC-EVs treatment

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's verb 'demonstrates' and the Discussion's 'favorable therapeutic efficacy' are stronger than a non-randomized, open-label pilot with a patient-reported endpoint and an effect confined to day 6 can support. The paper partly offsets this by calling the day-6 result one to interpret with caution, describing the work as initial evidence, and recommending placebo-controlled trials, so the overstatement is one of wording in the Conclusion and the first Discussion paragraph rather than of the paper's overall stance.

issues.title: No primary timepoint or multiplicity control across day-6, day-14, time-to-resolution and immune outcomes
issues.explanation: The paper tests several clinical endpoints and timepoints at nominal P<0.05 with no correction and no named primary timepoint. The day-6 findings (P=0.023 and P=0.035) and the time-to-resolution result (P=0.037) are all close to the threshold. The immune plasma-cell result is one of many subsets tested. These positive findings are therefore weak evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary endpoint and timepoint, or a correction for multiple tests.

quotes.text: P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
significantly higher rate of significant improvement (22.5% vs. 5.0%,

issues.title: Day-6 total effective rate 67.5% vs 47.5% (27/40 vs 19/40) gives p about 0.07, not the printed 0.035
issues.explanation: The printed counts imply a chi-square statistic near 3.3, which gives p near 0.07. The paper prints P=0.035 and calls the difference significant. The day-14 comparison (85% vs 80%) also gives p near 0.56 against the printed 0.452. If the 0.07 value is right, one of the two day-6 'significant' results is not significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a different test or the full 3-category table produced P=0.035.

quotes.text: a significantly higher total effective rate (effective + significant effective) than the control group (67.5% vs. 47.5%,

issues.title: Text gives Dec 2022-Jan 2023 infections; Table 2 ranges start 2022/11/17 and 2022/10/21
issues.explanation: The Results say both groups were infected in the same December 2022 to January 2023 outbreak. Table 2 shows ranges beginning on 2022/11/17 (treatment) and 2022/10/21 (control), so some patients were infected 1 to 2 months earlier. The control arm also reaches back about a month further, so the groups are less comparable than the text implies. This is a small reporting inconsistency and does not affect the main result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 2 ranges include earlier infection dates and that most patients fell in Dec-Jan.

quotes.text: were infected with COVID-19 during the same outbreak period from December 2022 to January 2023

quotes.location: Table 2, COVID-19 infection time row, control column

issues.title: Registered retrospectively (Apr 7, 2023) after first enrolment (Feb 15, 2023)
issues.explanation: The registration came about 7 weeks after the first patient was enrolled, so the registered outcomes cannot be checked against the analysis plan before data were seen. The paper discloses this plainly. The risk is that day-6 and time-to-resolution were chosen after seeing early data, which cannot be ruled out here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the day-6 and time-to-resolution outcomes were listed at registration.

quotes.text: Due to administrative delays, the study was registered retrospectively at
The first patient was enrolled on February 15, 2023.

10.3389/fmolb.2022.1016352.headline_claim: Mountain spa rehabilitation combined with ubiquinol supplementation accelerates recovery of platelet mitochondrial function and improves symptoms in post-COVID-19 patients, and the combined programme can be recommended.
10.3389/fmolb.2022.1016352.overall: The mitochondrial deficit in post-COVID patients and the rise in platelet CoQ10 with supplementation are plausible descriptive findings in a small pilot. The claim that ubiquinol itself accelerates recovery, and the treatment recommendation, are not supported: there is no placebo, no between-arm test of respiratory change, a third time point of 8 patients, and some non-significant results are worded as significant. Registration came after enrolment began.

primary_outcome.name: Platelet mitochondrial CI-linked OXPHOS and ET capacity (MRQ group, change over rehabilitation)

issues.title: Ubiquinol effect inferred from within-arm change and significant-versus-ns, with no MR vs MRQ test of mitochondrial outcomes
issues.explanation: The conclusion that ubiquinol accelerates mitochondrial recovery rests on paired tests within each arm and on one arm reaching p<0.05 while the other did not. The Methods describe no between-arm test of the change in respiration, so the claim that MRQ improved more than MR is not tested directly. With no placebo, small unequal arms (10 and 14 patients in lung tests) and an age gap, the benefit cannot be attributed to ubiquinol.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A group-by-time interaction test or between-arm comparison of respiratory changes showing MRQ > MR.

quotes.text: Paired Student´s t -tests were used for evaluation the difference between the MR1 and the MR2, the MRQ1 and the MRQ2, and between the MRQ1 and the MRQ3 groups.
Dry cough and shortness of breath improved signi fi cantly in the MRQ group, not in the the MR group.
in both cases representing only half of that achieved during the same time in patients simultaneously supplemented with CoQ10.

second_reader.what_stands: The ubiquinol effect on mitochondrial outcomes rests on within-arm paired tests, a significant-vs-nonsignificant contrast, and a descriptive 'half' comparison. No MR vs MRQ test is reported for mitochondrial or symptom outcomes. A between-arm test does exist, but only for blood count deltas (Section 3.3).

issues.title: Pilot data (14 and 22 patients, no sample-size calculation) used for a causal ubiquinol claim and treatment recommendation
issues.explanation: The study is called a pilot, enrolment was set by sanatorium admissions, and no power calculation is given. Yet the Abstract and Summary assert a significant or crucial role of ubiquinol and recommend the combination to patients. The supporting correlations combine repeated measures from the same patients and cannot show cause. The evidence supports a hypothesis, not a treatment recommendation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled, adequately powered trial or between-arm analysis supporting the causal claim.

quotes.text: Mountain spa rehabilitation with supplementary CoQ10 therapy could be recommended to the patients with post C19.
The correlation analysis con fi rmed crucial role of supplemented CoQ10 in the regeneration of CIlinked platelet mitochondrial function.
The total number of patients in the study was limited by the number of patients admitted and treated in the Sanatorium

second_reader.what_stands: Small pilot groups (14 and 22, no sample-size calculation) are used for causal statements ('crucial role', 'significant role') and a treatment recommendation. The authors do acknowledge small size and call the work a pilot, but the conclusions are worded more strongly than that supports.

issues.title: Third time point has 8 of 22 MRQ patients, selected by residence; MR arm not followed; lung tests cover 10/14 and 14/22
issues.explanation: The 'stepwise' further gain from continued ubiquinol comes from 8 patients who lived near the laboratory, with no comparison arm at that time point. Lung function tests were done in only 10 of 14 MR and 14 of 22 MRQ patients, with no reasons given. Because completers may differ from the full arms, the MRQ3 and lung results are fragile. The analysis is also not intention-to-treat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline characteristics and MRQ2 values of the 8 MRQ3 patients versus the other 14, and reasons for the missing lung-test patients.

quotes.text: The low number of patients with post C-19 in the MRQ3 group ( N = 8) available for the third time point is another limitation.
Unfortunately, the patients from MR group were not followed up after leaving the Sanatorium.
Only 10 patients from MR group and 14 patients from MRQ group were included in these tests

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states that the third time point covers 8 of 22 MRQ patients, all selected by residence and willingness to travel, that the MR arm was not followed, and that lung tests cover only 10/14 and 14/22. These are disclosed limitations, but they remain real constraints: MRQ3 has no MR comparator, and the reasons for the missing lung tests are not given.

issues.title: Self-reported symptom questionnaire, no blinding or validation described; 51.8% vs 62.8% untested
issues.explanation: Symptom improvement relies on an unvalidated patient questionnaire, in an open-label comparison, and the paper does not state any masking. The difference between 51.8% and 62.8% of symptoms resolved is not tested. Knowledge of receiving a supplement could bias self-report. How much this matters is debatable given the overlap with c7.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A validated, blinded or objectively scored outcome, or a between-arm test showing a robust difference.

quotes.text: Clinical symptoms were recorded by patient questionnaire
Overall, after completing the rehabilitation program 51.8% symptoms disappeared in the MR group and 62.8% in the MRQ group.

issues.title: Registered 2022-01-03, about 8 months after enrolment began (May 2021); five broad primary outcomes
issues.explanation: The paper presents the study as a registered clinical trial, but the registry shows first submission after enrolment had started. The registry lists five broad primary outcome domains, and the paper does not name a primary outcome, so selective emphasis cannot be excluded. The effect on the conclusions is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version dated before May 2021, or documentation of a pre-specified primary outcome.

quotes.text: This study was registered as a clinical trial: ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT05178225.
in May 2021 were randomly divided into two groups

issues.title: Non-significant changes called significant: OXPHOS MRQ3 p=0.072 and MRQ dyspnoea p=0.08
issues.explanation: Results 3.4 says CI-linked OXPHOS 'significantly increased' in MRQ2 and MRQ3, but the MRQ3 p-value is 0.072, above the stated 0.05 threshold. Discussion 4.1 says exercise dyspnoea was reduced in both groups, but the MRQ change has p = 0.08. The same section calls the MRQ walking gain clinically significant against a 70 m benchmark that the 61.4 m gain does not reach. These wording slips make the ubiquinol arm look better than the tests support. The main mitochondrial result (MRQ2 p = 0.043) is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified alternative alpha, or a corrected analysis showing these comparisons significant at the stated threshold.

p -values < 0.05 were considered statistically signi fi cant.

issues.title: Identical age 51.3 ± 2.3 years given for control (n=15) and MR group (n=14)
issues.explanation: The healthy control group and the MR patient group are both described with exactly the same mean age and SEM. This could be a coincidence or a copying slip, and it cannot be resolved from the paper. It affects only baseline description.

10.3389/fneur.2024.1393371.headline_claim: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation is a potential therapeutic approach for improving persistent cognitive, mood, sleep and fatigue symptoms in females with Long COVID.
10.3389/fneur.2024.1393371.overall: The paper is candid that this is a small uncontrolled pilot, and its conclusion is framed as preliminary, but the title and results language ('improves', 'significant changes') still imply efficacy that a single-arm, open-label design with no multiplicity control across outcomes cannot establish. The within-person changes are best read as a hypothesis-generating signal that justifies a sham-controlled trial, not as evidence that t-VNS improves Long COVID symptoms.

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post pilot (n=24) cannot separate t-VNS effect from expectation, time or regression to the mean
issues.explanation: All 24 participants received active t-VNS and were compared only with their own baseline, with no sham or untreated arm and open-label delivery. Improvements in cognition (including practice effects on repeated NIH Toolbox testing), mood, sleep and fatigue are therefore confounded with expectation, retest learning and natural fluctuation. The title states that t-VNS 'improves' symptoms, whereas the design supports only a hypothesis-generating signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham-controlled or waitlist arm showing the same change, or a title and conclusions worded purely as preliminary signal.

quotes.text: Participants underwent 10 consecutive days of auricular vagal neuromodulation therapy
However, due to the lack of a control group, we cannot exclude the possibility of other factors contributing to the observed improvements.
Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation improves Long COVID symptoms in a female cohort: a pilot study

second_reader.what_stands: The single-arm, open-label, pre-post design with no control or sham arm (also reflected in the registry as allocation NA and no masking) cannot separate a t-VNS effect from expectation, time, practice or regression to the mean, and the paper's arguments from effect size and symptom chronicity only partly mitigate this. The authors do state this limitation openly in the Discussion and Conclusion and recommend sham-controlled randomised trials, but the title's verb 'improves' is stronger than the design supports.

issues.title: Placebo 'less likely' and 'universality' to males asserted from an uncontrolled all-female sample
issues.explanation: The authors argue that moderate-to-large within-group effect sizes make placebo effects less likely, but within-group effect sizes in an open-label, subjectively assessed single-arm study are exactly what expectation and practice effects can produce. Likewise, an all-female sample cannot support any statement about male patients, and the discussion says effects 'may also extend to male patients'. The hedged wording softens this, but the placebo argument remains a reasoning gap that supports a more positive reading than the design allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A placebo-controlled comparison showing effects beyond sham, or male participants showing the same response.

quotes.text: the robust responses in our female cohort hint at the potential universality of
the moderate to large effect sizes observed make significant placebo effects less likely

issues.title: Open-label self-report mood, sleep and fatigue outcomes (BAI, BDI-II, PROMIS, FSS) reported as improvements
issues.explanation: Anxiety, depression, sleep and fatigue were measured by questionnaires completed by participants who knew they were receiving active stimulation, with no sham arm. Such outcomes are most susceptible to expectation effects, and the paper counts them among the 'significant changes'. The cognitive primary outcome is performance-based and less affected, so the problem is narrower than the candidate states.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded sham comparison, or objective measures corroborating the self-reported changes.

quotes.text: depression (Becks Depression Inventory-II [range 0-63])
we observed significant changes in cognition, mood, sleep

issues.title: About 11 outcomes tested with no across-outcome correction; several results near p=0.02-0.04
issues.explanation: Bonferroni correction was applied only to the three pairwise timepoint comparisons within each outcome, not across the five cognitive subdomains, the composite and the five secondary scales. Several claimed improvements have adjusted p-values only just below 0.05 (LSWM 0.029, depression pre vs post 0.025, sleep 0.036 and 0.021), so they would be fragile under a family-wise correction. The conclusion lists cognition, mood, sleep and fatigue as findings without noting this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecified single primary endpoint with gatekeeping, or results that remain significant under a correction across outcomes.

quotes.text: For analyzing changes in cognitive scores, the uncorrected standard score was used.
but did not survive multiple comparisons correction

issues.title: Composite and 3 of 5 subdomain follow-up cognition analyses use 18 of 24 (25% missing, remote-testing limit)
issues.explanation: The Friedman composite and Flanker, PCPS and DCCS follow-up comparisons use n=18 because the other six were assessed remotely and only two tests could be given. Missingness is driven by logistics rather than outcome, and the authors report that all-24 pre-post results were similar. The residual issue is that the 1-month cognitive claims (the 'sustained or progressing' benefit) for most subdomains come from a subset with different test availability, and mixed n across tests (18 versus 24) complicates interpretation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis on the full 24 at all timepoints showing identical conclusions.

quotes.text: Due to limitations in remote testing for six participants, only 18 participants completed all cognitive and smell assessments at follow-up.
We additionally analyzed pre and post cognition scores available from all 24 patients and found similar results as the 18 patients but with slightly higher significance.

10.3389/fneur.2024.1419134.headline_claim: Patients with PACS/PACVS show notable cognitive deficits, and the study indicates spontaneous remission of cognitive deficits is possible; phosphatidylcholine and CCT effectiveness was inconclusive.
10.3389/fneur.2024.1419134.overall: The central message (inconclusive efficacy; improvement over time in all arms) is hedged and broadly in line with the data, but the open-label, no-placebo design with 5-10 patients per arm cannot separate spontaneous remission from practice, expectation or placebo effects, and it cannot show 'no effect' either. The numeric errors found (14/18 'half', 36.7%, alpha labels, subdimension count) are minor and do not change any result.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: No placebo and open-label, so time improvement cannot be attributed to spontaneous remission or placebo
issues.explanation: Group C had no therapy and no placebo, and patients knew their allocation. The pooled improvement over time (F(1,25) = 28.22) could therefore reflect practice or retest effects, expectation or regression to the mean, not just spontaneous remission, and a placebo effect was never measured. The Discussion's 'no effect beyond the placebo effect' and the Conclusion's evidence for spontaneous remission go further than this design allows. The authors do call the design suboptimal for demonstrating efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A placebo or sham-training arm showing no change, or normative retest data showing no practice effect with the parallel forms.

quotes.text: Group C (cross-over treatment scheme) received no therapy for 4 weeks after the initial neuropsychological testing
Patients were always aware of which group or therapy scheme they belonged to.
spontaneous remission of cognitive deficits in PACS and PACVS may be possible

second_reader.what_stands: The study has no placebo arm and is open-label for patients (Limits 4.5), and it has no way to separate true spontaneous remission from retest/practice effects or regression to the mean, so 'spontaneous remission' is only one possible explanation for the improvement. It is not true that spontaneous remission or time improvement cannot be considered: the untreated group C also improved over the first 4 weeks (+5.0 and +8.6 points), and the conclusion is worded cautiously ('may be possible'). The Discussion phrase 'no effect beyond the placebo effect' is unsupported, since no placebo was given.

issues.title: Arms of 5-10 with no power calculation, yet absence of interaction read as 'no effect' of treatment
issues.explanation: No sample-size calculation is reported and the arms contain 9, 10, 5 and 5 patients. Non-significant interactions (p = 0.438 to 0.775) are then interpreted as the treatments having no effect beyond placebo, and CCT being not responsible for improvement. With this power, moderate differences could not have been detected, so the data are compatible with a benefit as well as none. The authors do say the sample size may cause statistical limitations. This understates rather than overstates any treatment benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation or confidence intervals on the interaction/treatment effects excluding clinically meaningful benefit.

quotes.text: Unlike previous studies, the improvement in cognitive performance cannot be attributed to cognitive training or CCT programs (73).
A small sample size can lead to several issues that compromise the reliability and validity of the results.

issues.title: 'Half of these patients (14 out of 18)' is 77.8%, not half
issues.explanation: The Results call 14 of the 18 patients with insufficient energy 'half', but 14/18 is about 78%. The figure 14 would be half of all 28 respondents, so the denominator or the word is wrong. The same sentence prints 18/28 as 64.2% (64.3% rounded), a small slip too. This is a descriptive QoL detail and does not affect the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the sub-count is 9 of 18, or a text that defines the base as all 28 respondents.

quotes.text: Half of these patients (14 out of 18) indicated experiencing little to no enjoyment in life

issues.title: Many uncorrected within-group tests on groups of 5-10; mixed parametric and non-parametric methods
issues.explanation: The paper reports dozens of within-group p-values (Table 3 and WHOQOL results) with alpha 0.05 and no multiplicity adjustment, on groups as small as 5. Normality testing is unreliable at such sizes, so the choice between t-tests and rank tests is itself fragile. Because the paper's conclusions rely on the omnibus interaction and time main effects, the impact is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated multiplicity strategy, or sensitivity analyses showing the same conclusions with exact or nonparametric tests throughout.

quotes.text: Group comparisons employed parametric tests when normal distribution was confirmed, and non-parametric tests when normal distribution was not established.

issues.title: No trial registration; described as prospective, observational and randomised in different places
issues.explanation: The paper reports an ethics number but no registry entry, so outcomes and analyses cannot be checked against a prespecified plan. The design is called a prospective study, an observational study (ethics) and a randomised allocation (Methods), which makes its status unclear. The conclusions are hedged, so the impact is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (or protocol) with the primary outcome and analyses prespecified before enrolment in May 2023.

quotes.text: This prospective study aimed to evaluate cognitive deficits in patients with PACS and PACVS
approved the observational study under protocol number 03/2023

issues.title: Group A physical-health WHOQOL gain (p=0.032) reported, but Discussion says no significant changes
issues.explanation: The Results report a significant physical-health improvement in group A (p = 0.032) among roughly 20 uncorrected within-group tests. The Discussion then says there were no significant relevant changes across time points, without addressing this one result or the lack of multiplicity control. The summary is defensible as 'no consistent change', but it is worded more absolutely than the Results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 'relevant' as clinically meaningful, with the group A change shown to be below it.

quotes.text: from the first to the second assessment point ( p A =  0.032)
There were no significant relevant changes in the WHOQOL-BREF scores

issues.title: Methods say each domain has three subdimensions; memory is described and tabulated with four
issues.explanation: Section 2.2 states every COGBAT domain is divided into three subdimensions. The same section and Table 2 list four memory subdimensions. This is a descriptive inconsistency that affects no result.

quotes.text: Each of these domains is divided into three subdimensions.
Memory performance was assessed through tests for learning ability, short- and long-term recall

issues.title: Alpha 0.79 called 'good' although Methods define 0.60-<0.80 as adequate; 0.93 called 'good' not excellent
issues.explanation: Methods define 0.60 to under 0.80 as adequate, 0.80 to under 0.85 as good and 0.85 or more as excellent. The Discussion calls the psychological domain (0.79) good, using an unstated alpha > 0.7 cutoff. The overall 0.93 is described as 'good' although the stated scale makes it excellent. These are labelling inconsistencies in a secondary reliability description.

the psychological and environmental domains exhibited good internal consistency
revealing coefficients of 0.66 for physical health, 0.79 for

issues.title: Self-esteem category 4: 10 of 28 printed as 36.7%, should be 35.7%
issues.explanation: Table 4 prints 10 (36.7%) for self-esteem scale point 4 with n = 28. 10/28 is 35.7%. The row percentages then sum to 101.0% (3.6+21.4+21.4+36.7+17.9), whereas with 35.7 they sum to 100.0%. A one-digit typo that affects nothing else.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A count of 11 rather than 10 in that cell, with the counts still summing to 28 (not the case as printed).

script.explanation: 10/28 = 35.71%, but the paper prints 36.7, outside the rounding interval [36.65, 36.80]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 27.2 rather than 28.

10.3389/fneur.2024.1486751.headline_claim: Indoor rehabilitation in specialized centers generally benefited patients with post-COVID-19 condition, with group-level and some individual improvements in attention and fatigue.
10.3389/fneur.2024.1486751.overall: The descriptive findings of high attention-deficit and fatigue prevalence and of improvement from admission to discharge are reasonably reported. The claim that rehabilitation caused or provided a benefit is not supported by a single-arm design with repeated identical tests, 35% attrition and baseline-selected subgroups prone to regression to the mean. Remaining problems are small numeric inconsistencies (the MoCA denominator shift, an implausible infection interval, a mis-stated p-value).

primary_outcome.name: TAP alertness reaction time (median without warning signal), admission vs discharge

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design described as 'controlled'; benefit from rehabilitation asserted without comparator
issues.explanation: All patients received rehabilitation and were compared only with their own admission scores. Improvement cannot be separated from natural recovery, repeated testing with the same MoCA and TAP versions, or regression to the mean. Yet the Methods call the study 'controlled', and the Discussion and Conclusion say the study 'provided evidence' that rehabilitation leads to improvement and that patients 'generally benefited'. The limitation paragraph does not change that headline wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control, or a natural-history comparison cohort showing smaller change.

quotes.text: The PoCoRe study is a prospective, non-randomized, controlled longitudinal study in Germany.
Further, we provided evidence that a rehabilitation program can lead to improvements on a group level
PCC patients who generally benefited from indoor rehabilitation in specialized centers

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design (the authors admit 'absence of a control group'), so describing it as 'controlled' in the Methods is inaccurate. The claims that rehabilitation 'can lead to improvements' and that patients 'generally benefited' rest on within-group change only; the authors partly mitigate this with an explicit limitation and 'group level' wording, but the argument against spontaneous remission is unsupported by comparator data and regression to the mean, practice effects and attrition remain unaddressed for causal attribution.

issues.title: MoCA normalisation 63% is based on 115 of 177 impaired patients but described as applying to all 27%
issues.explanation: Results give 177 impaired at admission, but the improvement figures use 115 patients, and the paper does not say these are the ones with a discharge MoCA. The Discussion then says 'Of the 27% ... 63% improved', which silently shifts the base to the 65% of impaired patients who were re-tested. The remaining 62 impaired patients have no stated outcome, and MoCA dropouts scored lower at baseline, so the 63% may be inflated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 115 is the subset of the 177 with a discharge MoCA, plus an analysis (or counts) of the 62 impaired patients without follow-up.

quotes.text: which normalized in 72 out of 115 (63%) at follow-up on discharge
Of the 27% of participants with suspicious scores on the MoCA at admission, 63% improved to a normative level during rehabilitation

issues.title: 35% of recruited participants (385 of 1,086) excluded from complete-case analysis without sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Only 701 of 1,086 recruited participants had complete TAP alertness data at both timepoints. Dropouts had lower baseline MoCA scores, and comparisons with completers are limited to baseline variables. The authors argue bias is small, but no analysis of the missing discharge data (imputation or sensitivity) supports that, so the size of the improvements is uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (for example multiple imputation or worst-case) showing the improvements are robust to the 385 missing patients.

quotes.text: Out of the 1,086 recruited participants, a total of N = 701 participants were included into data analysis
we observed baseline differences in MoCA scores, with T2-dropouts showing lower performance than the analyzed complete sample

issues.title: Larger gains in subgroups selected on abnormal baseline T-scores are partly regression to the mean
issues.explanation: The deficit subgroups are defined by a low T-score at admission, so their re-test scores are expected to rise toward the mean even without any treatment effect. The paper nonetheless presents the larger subgroup effects (r = 0.52 to 0.70 versus 0.20 to 0.50 overall) as especially large rehabilitation effects. With no control group there is no way to separate treatment from selection artefact, and this affects the headline claims about patients with impairments.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A control group or a test-retest design showing comparable change in an equivalent baseline-selected untreated subgroup, or an analysis adjusting for regression to the mean.

quotes.text: The treatment effects for sustained attention, working memory and divided attention were even larger when we took only those participants into account
especially large effects among those admitted with impairments

issues.title: Maximum infection-to-admission interval of 50 months predates the pandemic given March 2022 to December 2023 admissions
issues.explanation: The paper reports infections up to 50 months before admission, yet admissions ran only from March 2022 to December 2023. Fifty months before December 2023 is about October 2019, and before March 2022 it is about January 2018. This implies at least one infection date or interval is wrong, though the mean of 29 months is unaffected in practice.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the interval is measured from a different reference date, or a corrected maximum.

quotes.text: The initial infection occurred on average 29 months ago (range: 9 to 50, SD = 8.11).
insured persons could take part from March 2022 to December 2023

issues.title: Chi-squared = 10.602, df = 1 printed with p = 0.0001; the statistic implies p of about 0.0011
issues.explanation: A chi-squared of 10.602 on 1 df corresponds to z of about 3.26 and a two-sided p of about 0.0011, not 0.0001. The significance conclusion stands, so this is a small reporting slip in the dropout comparison of MoCA impairment (27% versus 38%).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different chi-squared value or df in the source data that gives p = 0.0001.

quotes.text: This proportion is significantly different from the 105 out of 277 individuals (38%) within the dropouts

script.explanation: The printed chi2 = 10.602 supports p no smaller than 0.00112904, but the paper reports p = 0.0001 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

10.3389/fneur.2025.1523814.headline_claim: C1-INH treatment improves depression, fatigue and pain symptoms in patients with SARS-CoV-2 post-viral fatigue syndrome, indicating C1-INH may be a potential therapeutic target.
10.3389/fneur.2025.1523814.overall: The paper's descriptive finding of low TLR signaling vs healthy controls is separate from its efficacy claim, which is not well supported: only within-arm changes were tested, placebo also improved depression, and fatigue is described as improving when the printed FSS values rose on a higher-is-worse scale. The depression signal is nominally strong but cannot be attributed to C1-INH without a between-treatment analysis, so the headline 'C1-INH can improve depression, fatigue and pain' should be treated as hypothesis-generating at most.

primary_outcome.name: BDI-II depression score (headline outcome; the paper designates no primary outcome)

issues.title: Drug benefit inferred from within-arm change from baseline; no C1-INH vs placebo comparison; placebo arm also improved
