issues.explanation: All efficacy tests compare each arm with its own baseline. The Week 16 tests in a crossover also mix carry-over and time effects. Placebo produced a 22.8% BDI-II fall (p = 0.0132) and Arm 1 kept its gains after switching to placebo. Within-arm changes therefore cannot isolate an effect of C1-INH, yet the abstract says improvements were observed with C1-INH.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A paired C1-INH-versus-placebo comparison, with period and carry-over effects handled, showing a treatment difference.

quotes.text: Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test for depression, fatigue, and pain scores
Improvements in depression, fatigue, and pain were observed with C1-INH treatment
decreasing by 22.8% (4.5 points) from baseline; p = 0.0132

second_reader.what_stands: The reported inference of benefit rests on within-arm change from baseline (Wilcoxon, baseline vs Week 8/16); no C1-INH vs placebo comparison is reported, and the placebo period in Arm 2 also improved significantly on BDI-II. Baseline BDI-II differs between arms (27.2 vs 19.7), and the paper calls these 'trends', which partly tempers but does not remove the problem.

issues.title: 'C1-INH can improve' fatigue and pain, though FSS rose and fatigue/pain p-values were 0.06-0.63
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that treatment can improve depression, fatigue and pain. The fatigue and pain results are all non-significant for C1-INH periods, except an FSS rise that signals worse fatigue. Only the within-arm BDI-II changes are nominally significant, and placebo also improved BDI-II. The data are exploratory and from 36 patients with no power calculation, so a causal 'can improve' statement is stronger than the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled between-treatment analysis showing significant benefit on fatigue and pain.

quotes.text: treatment with C1-INH can improve associated symptoms of depression, fatigue, and pain
This ongoing, exploratory, proof-of-concept study used descriptive statistics.
(increasing by 0.6 points from baseline; p = 0.5337)

second_reader.what_stands: The causal wording ('can improve') for fatigue and pain is not supported: FSS values rose (worse on the stated scale), pain changes were small with p-values 0.17-0.63 in C1-INH periods, and no drug-vs-placebo test exists. The point is slightly overstated in that one FSS p-value (0.0078) is below 0.05 and the Discussion does hedge with 'trends' and a call for confirmation, and the depression claim has nominally significant within-arm changes.

issues.title: FSS rises (0.6, 1.1, 1.3, 2.1 points) are described as fatigue improvement though higher FSS means worse
issues.explanation: The Methods say higher FSS scores indicate worse fatigue. The Results describe FSS 'increasing' by 0.6, 1.1, 1.3 and 2.1 points and call these improvements, and the abstract lists the 0.6 among improvements. As printed, fatigue scores rose or worsened in both arms, including the one nominally significant result (Arm 2, p = 0.0078). So the fatigue-improvement claim contradicts the printed direction of change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data or a corrigendum showing the FSS changes were decreases and the minus signs were lost in the text.

quotes.text: mean FSS score (0.6 points)
(increasing by 0.6 points from baseline; p = 0.5337)
FSS scoring ranges from 1 to 7

second_reader.what_stands: As printed, every FSS change is an increase on a scale where higher means worse fatigue, yet the paper labels them 'improved' and 'continued improvement' and the abstract cites 0.6 points as a favourable trend. The direction is internally contradictory; I could not check the figure, so a sign error in the text rather than in the data cannot be fully excluded.

issues.title: Arm 2 Week 16 BDI-II: 7.4 points on baseline 19.7 is 37.6%, paper prints 19.1%
issues.explanation: The two other BDI-II percentages equal points divided by baseline mean, but this one does not. The 19.1% is also smaller than the 22.8% at Week 8 although the text says the score 'improved further'. If points are right the change is larger than printed, so this probably understates the effect; either figure may be a typo.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-patient data showing the mean of individual percent changes is 19.1%.

quotes.text: by 19.1% (7.4 points) from baseline; p = 0.0036

issues.title: Fatigue and pain, not registered outcomes, support the conclusion; registered BRIEF-A/RBANS showed no benefit
issues.explanation: The registry lists BRIEF-A, RBANS and BDI-II as primary outcomes with no secondary outcomes. The conclusion names fatigue and pain as well, which are not registered. The registered cognitive measures were negative. The negative results are disclosed, so this is selective emphasis rather than hidden reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing fatigue and pain as outcomes.

quotes.text: including in executive function (BRIEF-A)
treatment with C1-INH can improve associated symptoms of depression, fatigue, and pain

issues.title: Multiple scales and timepoints tested at p < 0.05 with no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: Several scales, two timepoints and two arms were tested at an unadjusted 0.05 level. The depression results are strong enough to likely survive a correction, but secondary findings such as FSS p = 0.0078 would not carry much weight. This weakens secondary results only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction, or a clear statement that all p-values are descriptive only.

quotes.text: p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
decreasing by 32.0% (8.7 points) from baseline; p = 0.0010

issues.title: Safety section says no SAEs were observed, then reports one SAE (fatigue) in Arm 2 placebo
issues.explanation: Two consecutive sentences in the safety section contradict each other. The reader cannot tell whether the SAE count is 0 or 1. The SAE occurred on placebo, so it does not change the C1-INH safety message much.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'no SAEs' referred to treatment-related events only.

quotes.text: No SAEs were observed.
One SAE (fatigue) was observed in the Arm 2 placebo group.

issues.title: COI statement declares no commercial relationships despite Pharming grant and funded medical writing
issues.explanation: The Funding section discloses an educational grant from Pharming, the maker of the C1-INH product. The Conflict of interest section says there were no commercial or financial relationships. These two statements are inconsistent, although the funding itself is transparent. Readers should weigh the efficacy claims with the sponsor relationship in mind.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected COI statement or confirmation that no author has any relationship with Pharming.

quotes.text: This study was funded by an educational grant from Pharming Healthcare Inc.
could be construed as a potential conflict of interest

10.3389/fnins.2025.1627462.headline_claim: OAA may contribute to earlier improvements in symptom burden and cognitive function in long COVID and may offer clinically meaningful benefits, although the primary CFQ fatigue outcome was not significant.
10.3389/fnins.2025.1627462.overall: The primary fatigue outcome was null in a trial smaller than its own sample-size target. The positive conclusions rest on unadjusted secondary and exploratory comparisons, a post hoc within-arm association, and some overgeneralised timing claims. Table 4 also has safety-reporting inconsistencies. The abstract's hedged wording is reasonable, but the Discussion and Conclusion overstate what the evidence supports.

primary_outcome.name: Change in Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ) total score, Visit 1 to Visit 3

issues.title: Unadjusted testing across many secondary outcomes underpins the cognitive and symptom conclusions
issues.explanation: The paper tests dozens of outcome-visit comparisons at p < 0.05 with no correction, and the primary outcome was null. The conclusions of 'robust cognitive benefit' and 'clinically meaningful benefits' rest on a handful of nominally significant exploratory results. With this many tests, a few such results are expected by chance, so the findings are hypothesis-generating at most.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis in which the cognitive results remain significant.

quotes.text: indicating a robust cognitive benefit relative to the control group.
All statistical tests were two-tailed, with significance defined as a p -value < 0.05.

second_reader.what_stands: The cognitive and symptom conclusions rest on many unadjusted secondary and exploratory tests at p < 0.05, with no multiplicity control or acknowledgment of it. Most of the DANA and DSQ-SF p-values (0.007 to 0.028) would not clear a Bonferroni threshold for the number of related tests, so 'robust' is stronger than the evidence supports. The authors do label DANA as exploratory and hedge the overall conclusion.

issues.title: Null primary outcome in an underpowered trial (69 vs 90 required) is framed as supporting OAA benefit
issues.explanation: The primary outcome was null (CFQ effect size -0.093). The trial enrolled 69 of the 90 participants its own calculation required. The Discussion and Conclusion nonetheless say the secondary and exploratory results show clinically meaningful benefit and therapeutic activity, and blame the CFQ's sensitivity for the null result. These findings are hypothesis-generating, and the confident framing in the body text goes beyond what the design supports. The abstract's hedged wording is closer to what the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion that explicitly limits the findings to hypothesis generation, with the sample-size shortfall acknowledged where the benefit claims are made.

quotes.text: the required sample size was estimated to be 45 participants per group
Overall, while the primary outcome was not met
No significant difference in the CFQ-measured fatigue reduction was observed between the groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial enrolled 69 of the 90 required and had 62 completers, and the primary result was null with a negligible effect size. The paper states the null openly, but then gives an overall verdict of 'encouraging evidence of OAA's therapeutic activity' based on secondary and exploratory outcomes. It attributes the null to CFQ insensitivity and does not acknowledge the shortfall against the target as limiting the primary analysis. The primary result itself is not presented as supporting benefit.

issues.title: One OAA SAE called 'possibly related' in text but tabulated as 'Not related' (Table 4)
issues.explanation: The Results say the single serious adverse event in the OAA arm was reported as possibly related. Table 4 puts that same event under SAE 'Not related' (1) and shows 0 under SAE 'Possibly related'. The Discussion then says no serious event was attributed to the intervention. The safety summary therefore depends on which of the paper's own statements is correct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the event was reclassified as not related after Visit 2, or a corrected Table 4.

quotes.text: which was reported as possibly related at Visit 2
Possibly related 0 (0%) 0 (0%) 0 (0%)
quotes.location: Table 4, SAE block, Possibly related row

issues.title: DANA percent-change comparisons use t-tests despite stated non-normality and outliers
issues.explanation: The authors say the DANA data are non-normal with outliers, yet compare groups with independent t-tests. The Results mention an LMM interaction term, but the p-values are annotated as t-test results. Percent change from baseline is also skewed and sensitive to low baselines. A rank-based or permutation test would show whether the significant p-values (0.007 to 0.021) survive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with Mann-Whitney or permutation tests giving the same significant results.

quotes.text: Between-group comparisons were conducted using independent t -tests for each visit.

issues.title: Symptom-cognition link 'stronger under OAA' rests on significant vs non-significant slopes, no interaction test
issues.explanation: The authors infer a stronger symptom-cognition association in the OAA arm because that regression was significant and the control regression was not. They do not test whether the two slopes differ. Responder status is defined after randomisation, so the association does not show that OAA acted on cognition through symptom relief. The Conclusion nonetheless cites it as support for biological activity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A responder x treatment interaction test showing a significant difference between arms.

quotes.text: the association between the DSQ-SF response and DANA improvement was weaker and not statistically significant
further supports the potential biological activity of OAA

issues.title: Table 4 TEAE-by-relationship arm counts (9+7, 4+3) do not add to the totals (22, 10)
issues.explanation: In the relationship block of Table 4, the OAA and control counts do not add to the Total column in either the 'Not related' row or the 'Possibly related' row. The text repeats the total of 10 possibly related. The arm-level tolerability comparison therefore cannot be relied on for relatedness. It cannot be told whether the totals or the arm cells are wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing arm cells that sum to the totals.

quotes.location: Table 4, relationship block, Not related row

quotes.text: Possibly related 4 (11%) 3 (9%) 10 (14%)
quotes.location: Table 4, relationship block, Possibly related row

issues.title: Discussion says Go/No-Go gains emerged by Visit 2, but Results show it only at Visit 3 (p = 0.547 vs 0.017)
issues.explanation: The Discussion groups procedural reaction time, Go/No-Go and total efficiency together as emerging by Visit 2, implying a rapid response. The Results show Go/No-Go separated from control only at Visit 3. PRT and total efficiency were nominally significant at Visit 2. The error is limited to one of the three measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors stating that the sentence refers only to PRT and total efficiency.

quotes.text: emerged by Visit 2, suggesting a relatively rapid treatment response
There were no differences in GNG at Visit 2 ( p = 0.547)

issues.title: Day-21 benefit on total DSQ-SF claimed, but only the fatigue Visit 2 post hoc test is reported
issues.explanation: The abstract and Discussion say OAA gave significantly greater improvement in fatigue and total symptom burden at day 21 / Visit 2. The Results report a Visit 2 Tukey comparison only for fatigue. The total score has an omnibus interaction but no reported Visit 2 comparison, so the timing claim is not shown for total burden.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported Visit 2 post hoc test for total DSQ-SF showing p < 0.05.

quotes.text: fatigue scores were significantly lower in the OAA group compared to the control group at Visit 2
detected significantly greater reductions in fatigue and total symptom burden in the OAA group by Visit 2

10.3389/fnins.2025.1637838.headline_claim: Pyridostigmine rapidly improves hand grip strength in patients with ME/CFS and reduces the orthostatic heart rate increase on standing.
10.3389/fnins.2025.1637838.overall: The finding that grip strength fell on repeat testing without PS and was higher after PS is observed, but it comes from a fixed-order, unblinded, uncontrolled two-visit comparison in 20 patients, so a drug effect cannot be separated from order and practice effects. The orthostatic heart-rate result rests on 13 patients, and the claim that it holds regardless of POTS is unsupported by any subgroup analysis. The conclusion is best read as hypothesis-generating, not as demonstrated efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: Maximum hand grip strength (Fmax) 1 h after pyridostigmine vs. without pyridostigmine

primary_outcomes.measure: Physiologic Response - Oxygen Uptake Efficiency Slope (OUES)

issues.title: Fixed-order, unblinded, uncontrolled two-visit comparison used to claim PS rapidly improves grip strength
issues.explanation: The no-PS visit always came first and the PS visit second, with no placebo, randomisation or blinding. The headline 'about 1.5-fold higher with PS' compares Fmax2/Fmean2 across these two visits, so visit order, familiarity, expectation and day-to-day variability are all confounded with the drug. Mentioning the lack of a control group in one limitations sentence does not support the Discussion's 'demonstrates' wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the visit order was randomised or counterbalanced, or a placebo or blinded control arm showing the same decline without PS.

quotes.text: the non-controlled design without randomization of the treatment order and the lack of a control group
This study demonstrates that PS can rapidly improve HGS in patients with ME/CFS.
the same tests were performed both before and 1 h after PS administration

second_reader.what_stands: The study has a fixed order (no-PS visit first, PS visit second), no placebo, no randomization and no stated blinding, so PS effects cannot be separated from order, practice, visit-to-visit or expectation effects; the authors list the non-randomized order and lack of control group as limitations. Even so, the Discussion opens with 'demonstrates' and the Conclusion with 'provides evidence', so the claim of rapid improvement is stated more strongly than this design supports. (The 32% versus about 28.5% mismatch is a side observation and was not part of the point.)

issues.title: 'Regardless of POTS' claim rests on 2 POTS patients; abstract states an established immediate effect
issues.explanation: The Conclusion asserts that heart-rate reduction occurs regardless of POTS, yet no analysis is reported by POTS status and only 2 of 13 tested patients had POTS (11 did not). This cannot show equivalence across subgroups. The abstract also says PS 'exerts an immediate effect' without noting the uncontrolled, fixed-order design (see the design issue above).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified or reported subgroup analysis by POTS status showing a consistent effect with adequate numbers.

quotes.text: Furthermore, PS significantly reduced the standing heart rate increase in ME/CFS patients, regardless of the presence of POTS.
Pyridostigmine exerts an immediate effect on muscle strength and orthostatic function.

second_reader.what_stands: The only evidence for a POTS-independent effect is the pooled analysis of 13 patients, of whom only 2 were reported to have POTS, and no subgroup result or interaction test is given, so 'regardless of POTS' is not supported by a comparison. The abstract's 'exerts an immediate effect on muscle strength and orthostatic function' rests on a single-arm-order, uncontrolled 1 h comparison in 20 patients (13 for orthostatic function), so it states as established what the paper's own limitations show is only suggestive.

issues.title: No sample-size justification or multiplicity control; 20 patients, p-values of 0.007-0.03, confident wording
issues.explanation: The paper gives no power calculation and tests several related HGS and heart-rate outcomes at an unadjusted alpha of 0.05. In a sample of 20 this makes the modest p-values (0.01, 0.017, 0.03) fragile. The wording 'demonstrates' and 'exerts an immediate effect' is stronger than a pilot of this size supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome with a sample-size justification, or multiplicity-adjusted p-values that remain significant.

quotes.text: Twenty of them fulfilled the inclusion criteria for this study.
A p -value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Limitations of our study include the small sample size

issues.title: Orthostatic heart rate result based on 13 of 20 patients; 7 declined the test, 2 could not complete it
issues.explanation: Only 13 of 20 patients (65%) had the standing test, and those who declined may differ systematically, for example by fear of symptom worsening or prior testing. Two patients stopped early at baseline, and the heart-rate change after early termination is not clearly defined. The conclusion nevertheless generalises to 'ME/CFS patients'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis showing the heart-rate result is robust to the missing patients and to the two early terminations.

quotes.text: The PST to assess orthostatic function was performed in 13 out of 20 patients.
only one of these patients discontinued the test prematurely

issues.title: POTS defined as >30 bpm increase, yet a patient at exactly 30 bpm is counted as POTS
issues.explanation: The Methods require a sustained increase of more than 30 bpm, but one of the two patients classed as POTS had an increase of exactly 30 bpm. Either the threshold is misquoted (the usual criterion is 30 bpm or more) or the patient was misclassified. Only the count of 2 POTS patients is affected, which matters little for the main findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the criterion applied was 30 bpm or more, or an unrounded value above 30 bpm for that patient.

quotes.text: sustained pulse increase of more than 30 bpm
persistent orthostatic heart rate increase of 34 bpm and 30 bpm, respectively

issues.title: No trial registration reported for this prospective drug-administration study
issues.explanation: The study gave a drug to patients prospectively but reports no registry identifier. The only identifier cited, from the registry record, belongs to a different randomised trial (LIFT), so it cannot be used to check outcomes or analysis plans for this study. Without registration, outcome selection and the many HGS endpoints cannot be checked against a prespecified plan.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (e.g. DRKS or ClinicalTrials.gov) for this study, or confirmation that it was an unregistered clinical audit.

quotes.text: protocol EA2/170/23, date of approval: 29 September 2023
A RCT of PS in ME/CFS patients with orthostatic intolerance is currently being conducted at the Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (NCT06366724).

issues.title: Percent changes in grip strength do not follow from printed medians (32% vs 28.5%; 12.6% vs 14.3%)
issues.explanation: The reduction in Fmax from 16.5 kg to 11.8 kg is 28.5%, not the printed 32%, and the Fmean2 increase from 13.3 to 15.2 kg is 14.3%, not 12.6%. The abstract's own median fall of 4.65 kg is also smaller than the 32% figure implies (about 5.3 kg). This is likely a median-of-percentages artefact, but the method is not stated and the main claims are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the percentages are medians of individual patient percentage changes.

quotes.text: which corresponds to a reduction of 32%
with an increase of 1.9 kg (12.6%)

10.3389/fnut.2022.1034169.headline_claim: The nutraceutical formulation is a safe and significantly efficient option to reduce multiple symptoms of long COVID.
10.3389/fnut.2022.1034169.overall: The paper shows that self-rated symptoms improved from baseline in 51 completers, but a single-arm, open-label design with subjective outcomes cannot show that the supplement caused this, so the 'safe and significantly efficient' conclusion is not supported as stated. The sponsor's role is incompletely described. The mouse-dose unit discrepancy is a text-extraction artefact.

primary_outcome.name: Change in self-rated severity of 12 long-COVID symptoms from baseline at 2 and 4 weeks

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from a single-arm, open-label study with self-rated symptoms and no control group
issues.explanation: All 51 participants took the supplement and rated their own symptoms, compared only with their own baseline. With no control arm, no blinding and subjective outcomes, improvement cannot be separated from natural recovery, regression to the mean or expectation effects. The paper acknowledges there was no placebo but still concludes the product is 'safe and significantly efficient', and the argument that prior treatments failed does not rule out placebo-type responses. Also, the p<0.01 results are paired within-person changes and say nothing about causation. Adverse events are listed without rates or a described collection method, so the 'safe' claim is also weakly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent placebo or active control arm showing a between-group difference in the same symptom scores.

quotes.text: While there was no placebo in this clinical study, every patient had tried and failed numerous nutraceutical and pharmaceutical products
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph on comparison to baseline

quotes.text: The new combination of nutraceuticals including the compounds listed in Table 1 was tested in a one-arm, open-label clinical trial.
Our data indicate that the use of this nutraceutical product is a safe and significantly efficient option to reduce multiple symptoms of long COVID.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy conclusion rests on a single-arm, open-label design with participant-rated symptom scores and no control group, and the abstract states efficacy without any caveat. The authors do note the lack of placebo and add a brief 'within the limitations' clause, but they argue that prior treatment failure and symptom duration make coincidence unlikely, which does not rule out placebo, expectation or reporting effects, so the causal wording ('efficient option') goes beyond what the design supports.

issues.title: Commercial sponsor's role in the clinical study not described; authors hold stock and patent rights
issues.explanation: The Conflict of interest section says the clinical study was sponsored in part by NTN Enterprises LLC, in which two authors own stock and which acquired the patent rights of two authors. The Funding section lists only the ISF grant and AARDS internal funding, and nowhere is the sponsor's role in design, data analysis or reporting stated. The conflict is declared, so this is incomplete rather than hidden, but it matters because the paper is an uncontrolled study with a positive conclusion about the sponsor's product.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sponsor had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or the decision to publish.

quotes.text: The clinical study has been sponsored in part by NTN Enterprises LLC.
internal research funding (clinical study) from the AARDS (NG).

10.3389/fnut.2023.1131192.headline_claim: Oral ketone esters acutely increased global longitudinal strain versus placebo and suggest a direct improvement in left ventricular myocardial function in people previously hospitalised with COVID-19.
10.3389/fnut.2023.1131192.overall: The study is a small acute crossover pilot whose pre-specified primary outcome (LVEF) was null. The claimed benefit rests on one borderline secondary result (GLS p = 0.04, CI lower bound 0.1) tested among many uncorrected comparisons, and the Conclusion's wording about improved ventricular function and a treatment principle goes beyond that. The numeric slips are minor, but the headline conclusion should be treated as hypothesis-generating at best.

primary_outcome.name: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)

primary_outcomes.measure: In-hospital mortality during hospitalization and a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis
Incident ARDS (Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome) and intensive care unit admission during hospitalization and a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis
Incident hypoxic respiratory failure during hospitalization and a confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis

issues.title: Null primary outcome (LVEF, p = 0.66) but conclusion claims improved left ventricular function from secondary GLS (p = 0.04)
issues.explanation: The pre-specified primary outcome, LVEF, showed no difference (mean difference −0.7, 95% CI −4.0 to 2.6). The paper nevertheless concludes there is a 'direct improvement in left ventricular myocardial function' and that the study 'demonstrates' improved systolic function. This rests on a single secondary measure whose CI barely excludes zero, and cardiac output and the other systolic measures were not significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or a corrected analysis making GLS a confirmatory outcome, with consistent effects on other systolic measures.

quotes.text: oral ketone esters had no effect on LVEF with a mean difference of −0.7 (95% CI: −4.0 to 2.6)%
quotes.location: Results, Effect of ketone esters on echocardiographic parameters

quotes.text: Our study suggests a direct improvement in left ventricular myocardial function in subjects previously hospitalized for COVID-19.
The present study is the first to demonstrate that oral ketone esters acutely improve left ventricular systolic function in post-hospitalized COVID-19 patients

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome (LVEF) was null (p = 0.66), and the claim of improved left ventricular function ('direct improvement'; 'first to demonstrate … acutely improve left ventricular systolic function') rests on the secondary outcome GLS (p = 0.04, CI lower bound 0.1). The null primary is disclosed and the Conclusion uses 'suggests', so concealment is not the issue; the 'first to demonstrate' wording is stronger than a single borderline secondary result in 12 participants supports.

issues.title: Conclusion rests on one uncorrected secondary result (GLS p = 0.04) among ~25 comparisons
issues.explanation: The primary outcome was null, so the benefit claim depends on GLS at p = 0.04 with a CI lower bound of 0.1. No multiplicity adjustment is described across secondary and exploratory outcomes. Covariate adjustments were chosen post hoc and applied to significant results, so the stronger p < 0.01 cannot be read as confirmatory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statistical analysis plan designating GLS as a hierarchically tested confirmatory outcome after LVEF, or an adjusted analysis that remains significant.

quotes.text: GLS was significantly improved after oral ketone esters compared with placebo
quotes.location: Results, Effect of ketone esters on echocardiographic parameters

quotes.text: For the echocardiographic outcomes, significant associations were further adjusted for change in heart rate, as this might affect results.
quotes.location: Methods, Statistical methods and sample size calculation

quotes.text: Echocardiographic outcomes were adjusted for sequence post hoc.
quotes.location: Methods, Statistical methods and sample size calculation

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's conclusion about improved left ventricular function depends on one secondary result (GLS, p = 0.04, CI 0.1 to 3.6) from a 12-participant crossover, with no multiplicity correction among roughly 25 comparisons. The primary outcome was null, and the heart-rate adjustment (applied only to significant results) and sequence adjustment (post hoc) are not independent confirmation. In mitigation, GLS was a prespecified secondary outcome, and only about 3 comparisons were prespecified as secondary (about 12 echo comparisons in all), so the full count of 25 overstates the multiplicity for th

issues.title: Four-person abnormal-GLS subgroup (p = 0.6; interaction p = 0.2) used to propose normalising impaired GLS
issues.explanation: The subgroup comparison was non-significant and the interaction test showed no evidence that the effect differs by baseline GLS. Despite this, the Discussion proposes normalisation of impaired GLS and 'a larger effect' in those with abnormal GLS. The abnormal group was selected using the placebo-period echo, which makes regression to the mean a plausible contributor to the observed rise.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Independent baseline-based classification of abnormal GLS (not from the placebo echo) with a significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction.

quotes.text: we propose that oral ketone esters could normalize impaired GLS in in patients with asymptomatic subclinical myocardial dysfunction
quotes.location: Discussion, Improvement in cardiac function following treatment with oral ketone esters

quotes.text: Ketone esters elevated GLS to above the cut-off value of 16% for 2 out of 4 participants with abnormal GLS, yet results were insignificant (p = 0.6)
quotes.location: Results, Effect of ketone esters on echocardiographic parameters

issues.title: Single-dose, 12-person acute crossover framed as a treatment principle for COVID-19 sequelae
issues.explanation: The study gave one dose to 12 participants and measured echo and blood values within hours, with no clinical outcome. The limitations section concedes the effect may not be specific to COVID-19 hospitalization, but the Conclusion and Implications still speak of COVID-19 sequelae and a novel treatment principle. The hedged wording ('may') limits the overreach.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longer-term, larger trials with clinical or symptom outcomes in post-COVID-19 patients.

quotes.text: Oral ketone esters may represent a novel treatment principle in combatting the impending rise in COVID-19 sequela following the pandemic and other conditions with subclinical cardiac injury.

the results of the present study should be interpreted as the effect of oral ketone esters on patients with asymptomatic subclinical myocardial dysfunction and not specifically in patients previously hospitalized with COVID-19

issues.title: Power for GLS asserted but not calculated; sample size based on an 8% LVEF effect from heart-failure data
issues.explanation: The sample size of 10 (12 enrolled) was based on LVEF, with an assumed 8% effect and SD 8% taken from a trial in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. The limitations say there was power for GLS, yet no GLS calculation is given. The observed GLS CI (0.1 to 3.6) is wide, so the size of any GLS effect is highly uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported power calculation for GLS based on the actual crossover variance.

quotes.text: A limitation is the relatively small sample size, although we did have power to demonstrate effects on GLS.
the sample size required to demonstrate a significant effect with a power of 80% and type 1 error of 5% was 10 participants
quotes.location: Methods, Statistical methods and sample size calculation

issues.title: Overall age in text (60 ± 10) differs from Table 1 total (59 ± 8); time since admission 18 vs 17 months
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the age of the same 12 participants as 60 ± 10 years, but Table 1 gives 59 ± 8, which is what the arm values imply. The text also gives 18 ± 5 months since hospitalization, whereas the Table 1 total is 17 ± 5. These are descriptive slips with no bearing on the treatment comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or the source data showing that 60 ± 10 is the correct overall age.

quotes.text: We included 12 participants (5 women) with a mean ± SD age of 60 ± 10 years.
quotes.location: Results, Study participants and intervention, para 1

issues.title: Product donated by KetoneAid; role of supplier in design, analysis and reporting not stated
issues.explanation: The supplier gave the active product and the matched placebo, and the paper does not say whether it had any role in study design, analysis or writing. The supply is disclosed, so concealment is not shown. The absence of a statement on the supplier's role is a small transparency gap.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the supplier had no role in design, conduct, analysis or reporting.

quotes.text: Ketone ester and taste-matching placebo for the study were donated by the company KetoneAid by initiative of the research group.
The remaining authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

issues.title: GLS 95% CI upper bound 3.6 in text vs 3.7 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The GLS mean difference of 1.9 has an upper CI bound of 3.6 in the Results and 3.7 in Table 2. This is a small discrepancy that does not change significance, but it is on the paper's key result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded bounds showing that both printings are correct roundings of the same value.

quotes.text: This corresponded to a mean difference of 1.9 (95% CI: 0.1 to 3.6)%
quotes.location: Results, Effect of ketone esters on echocardiographic parameters
Table 2, Absolute global longitudinal strain row

issues.title: Washout gap between morning and afternoon interventions stated as 3.5 h (Methods) and 4 h (Discussion)
issues.explanation: The paper describes the same 2 h washout design but gives the interval between the last morning sip and the afternoon start as 3.5 h in one place and 4 h in another. The difference is small and the carry-over argument is not materially affected, but the actual gap is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol timeline showing that 3.5 h and 4 h measure different intervals.

quotes.text: a washout period of 2 h leading to the last part of the morning intervention being ingested 3.5 h before commencing the afternoon intervention
including a wash-out period of 2 h leading to the last part of the morning intervention being ingested 4 h before commencing the afternoon intervention

issues.title: TAPSE labelled in mm in Table 2 (2.4 ± 0.6) but thresholded in cm (<1.7 cm) in Methods
issues.explanation: Table 2 labels TAPSE in millimetres, but 2.4 is a plausible value only in centimetres, and the Methods define abnormal TAPSE as <1.7 cm. This is a labelling error. It does not affect the null TAPSE result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; the label can simply be corrected to cm.

quotes.text: TAPSE, (mm)

10.3389/fnut.2026.1731306.headline_claim: Creatine monohydrate at 6 g/day was associated with improved fatigue and peripheral muscle strength in patients with post-COVID-19 condition, with a favorable safety profile.
10.3389/fnut.2026.1731306.overall: The fatigue result at 6 g/day (p = 0.005) is the paper's principal finding. It comes from a small pilot with no stated registration or sample-size justification, and the 18 g arm showed no effect, so it is best read as preliminary. The handgrip and safety claims in the conclusion are weaker: the handgrip result is an uncorrected secondary finding, and the 'favorable safety' statement is contradicted by the printed nausea rates and the creatinine rises. The numeric slips (eligibility threshold, female percentage, CI sign) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Piper Fatigue Scale-Revised (PFS-R) score, difference-in-differences vs control (6 g/day arm)

issues.title: Handgrip gain (p=0.037) is one of ~68 uncorrected Table 2 comparisons yet is stated as a conclusion
issues.explanation: Table 2 tests 34 outcomes in each of 2 arms (68 comparisons), plus laboratory tests, all at an uncorrected 5% level. Only three Table 2 results fall below 0.05: PFS-R, handgrip in the 6 g arm, and one ultrasound value in the 18 g arm. About three or four such results are expected by chance at that level. A p of 0.037 would not survive even a correction for the two arm comparisons, yet the Abstract and the final conclusion state improved muscle strength as a finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical testing plan or multiplicity adjustment under which handgrip was tested at an unadjusted level.

quotes.text: significant differences in handgrip strength in the 6 g/day group, with a mean difference (DiD estimate) of 4.40 kgf (95% CI: 0.27 to 8.52; p = 0.037)
A two-sided significance level of 5% was adopted.
Creatine supplementation at 6 g/day was associated with improvements in fatigue and peripheral muscle strength in patients with PCC

second_reader.what_stands: Handgrip (p=0.037) is one of about 66 secondary comparisons (68 including the primary) tested at an unadjusted 5% level. It is a secondary outcome with no prespecified hierarchy, and 2 nominal secondary hits is about what chance would give. It is nonetheless stated as a finding in the abstract and conclusion. The authors do add a general caution about multiplicity for secondary outcomes, but it is not applied to the handgrip claim.

issues.title: 'Favorable safety' claim vs nausea 42.8% (18 g) vs 4.7% (control) described as non-significant
issues.explanation: The paper says the AE comparison between groups was not significant, but nausea was reported in about 9 of 21 people on 18 g/day against 1 of 21 on placebo, a difference that is clearly significant on a simple test. Serum creatinine also rose significantly in both creatine arms, and this is dismissed as clinically irrelevant without a measure of kidney function that separates the two explanations. A 4-week study of this size cannot support a firm 'favorable safety profile' conclusion, although the 6 g arm's AEs were mild.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Exact AE counts per arm and a stated test showing no difference, together with kidney-function data (cystatin C or eGFR) unchanged in the creatine arms.

quotes.text: In the 18 g/day group, a greater number of events were observed, notably nausea (42.8%)
The comparison between groups revealed no statistically significant difference ( p > 0.05)
Overall, the intervention was well tolerated, presenting a consistent safety profile throughout the 1-month follow-up

script.explanation: The paper prints p > 0.05, but recomputed from every convention tried on this table (Pearson, Yates, Fisher, McNemar, likelihood ratio, Fisher-Freeman-Halton where they apply) p is at most 0.01121, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

second_reader.what_stands: Taking the printed 42.8% vs 4.7% nausea at face value, a simple two-group or three-group test gives p of roughly 0.004 to 0.014, so the paper's 'p > 0.05' is not reproducible for nausea. The test used and the denominators are not stated, so the discrepancy cannot be fully resolved. The safety wording is also stronger than a 28-day, small pilot with no formal safety endpoints supports, although the events were reported as mild, transient and without serious adverse events.

issues.title: Pilot with no sample-size calculation (18-21 completers/arm); fatigue effect rests on one arm, 18 g null
issues.explanation: There is no sample-size justification, and each arm contributed about 18 to 21 completers. The fatigue benefit is seen only at 6 g/day, while 18 g/day showed none, so there is no dose-response support. Estimates from such small groups tend to be imprecise and possibly inflated (the 95% CI for fatigue runs from -3.47 to -0.63). The wording is hedged in places, but the Abstract states an 'improvement' and a 'favorable safety profile' in firm terms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample-size calculation targeting the fatigue difference, or replication in an adequately powered trial.

quotes.text: A total of 58 completed the protocol: 21 in the 6 g/day group, 19 in the 18 g/day group, and 18 in the placebo arm.
The reduced sample size may have limited the statistical power to detect additional differences between groups

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported; 'a priori' primary outcome cannot be verified
issues.explanation: The paper gives an ethics approval number but no trial registration for a randomized trial enrolling from October 2023. The claim that fatigue was the primary outcome defined a priori therefore rests on the authors' statement alone. This matters because several other outcomes and arms were examined and only some turned out positive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prospective registry record (for example ReBEC or ClinicalTrials.gov) dated before enrolment that lists fatigue as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: the study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Botucatu Medical School (CAAE: 65312822.8.0000.5411)
quotes.location: 2.1 Study design, participants and ethical approval

quotes.text: Fatigue, defined a priori as the primary outcome

issues.title: Analyses are called intention-to-treat but results describe the 58 of 67 who completed the protocol
issues.explanation: The Methods say analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle, and Table 1 shows 67 randomized (21/24/22). The Results and Abstract describe the 58 completers (18/21/19), and no handling of the 9 missing participants is described. If the DiD models used completers only, the analysis is per-protocol and the ITT label is wrong. Attrition was equal across arms (3 each), which limits but does not remove the concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement or CONSORT figure showing that all 67 participants were included in the models (for example via a mixed model or imputation).

quotes.text: Analyses were conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle.
58 individuals completing the protocol (74% women, aged 52 ± 12 years)

issues.title: Fatigue eligibility threshold is score ≥4 in the Abstract but >4 in the Methods
issues.explanation: The Abstract says participants had a PFS-R score of at least 4, while the Methods define fatigue as a score above 4. Someone scoring exactly 4 would be eligible under one definition and not the other. The effect on the results is probably small, but the inclusion criterion is not stated consistently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or supplement showing a single threshold and a one-sided typo in one place would settle which is correct, though the printed inconsistency would remain.

quotes.text: score ≥ 4 on the revised Piper Fatigue Scale (PFS-R)
with fatigue defined as a score > 4

issues.title: Abstract's 76.6% female for 67 randomized does not match Table 1 (49/67 = 73.1%)
issues.explanation: The 74% in the Results refers to the 58 completers (43/58 = 74.1%) and is fine. The Abstract's 76.6% is said to describe the 67 randomized participants. Table 1 counts 49 women among them (73.1%), and 76.6% cannot be produced by any whole number of women out of 67.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different, stated denominator (for example screened participants) for which 76.6% is attainable.

quotes.text: Participants were predominantly female (76.6%)
Female sex, n (%)

issues.title: Adverse-event percentages imply denominators (21, 22, 21) matching neither randomized nor completer counts
issues.explanation: The AE percentages fit denominators of 21 (control), 22 (6 g) and 21 (18 g). The randomized groups were 21, 24 and 22, and the completers were 18, 21 and 19. Nothing in the paper explains which participants the AE denominators represent, so the AE rates cannot be traced to a defined population.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated safety-population definition giving 21, 22 and 21 participants in the three arms.

quotes.text: one case of nausea (4.7%) and one case of headache (4.7%)

issues.title: Eosinophil % CI printed as '1.21 to -0.09', which excludes the estimate -0.66 (likely a missing minus)
issues.explanation: The printed interval runs from a positive 1.21 to -0.09 and so does not contain the estimate of -0.66. With a negative sign on 1.21 the interval, estimate and p-value agree. This is a small typographical slip in a secondary laboratory result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The Supplementary Table 1 value showing '-1.21 to -0.09', which would make this an extraction artefact only.

10.3389/fphar.2024.1394810.headline_claim: MYP (Myelophil) significantly alleviates Long COVID-related fatigue, suggesting potential therapeutic value in managing Long COVID-induced fatigue.
10.3389/fphar.2024.1394810.overall: The large pre-post improvements are plausible as descriptive observations, but the single-arm, open-label design with self-reported outcomes means the efficacy conclusion is only tentative at best, and the cross-trial placebo comparison adds overreach. The numeric inconsistencies are minor SD slips that do not alter the findings.

primary_outcome.name: mKCFQ11 score change at 4 weeks

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot separate MYP effect from recovery, regression to mean or placebo
issues.explanation: All evidence is within-patient change over 4 weeks in patients selected for high fatigue scores, with no control group. Spontaneous recovery from Long COVID, regression to the mean after threshold selection and expectancy effects would all produce improvement without any drug effect. The paper calls the anti-fatigue efficacy 'strongly supported', which the design cannot establish.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group with matched selection and follow-up showing much smaller change.

quotes.text: Utilizing a single-arm design, participants were orally administered MYP (2,000 mg daily) for 4 weeks.
this anti-fatigue efficacy of MYP is strongly supported by other measurements using fatigue-related tools

second_reader.what_stands: The single-arm pre-post design cannot separate an MYP effect from natural recovery, regression to the mean (enrolment on high scores) or placebo response. The authors acknowledge the lack of a control group as a limitation, but still describe the efficacy as 'strongly supported' and 'significant effects' using only within-arm secondary measures that share the same bias.

issues.title: Open-label study with entirely self-reported fatigue outcomes; only objective marker unrelated to symptoms
issues.explanation: Participants knew they were taking MYP and rated their own fatigue, so expectancy can inflate the improvement. The only objective measure, cortisol, did not correlate with symptom change. This adds to the single-arm problem rather than standing as a separate reason the conclusion fails.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded or objectively measured outcome showing consistent benefit.

quotes.text: the open-label nature of the study could introduce bias, as participants' awareness of the treatment might affect their symptom reporting.
The primary outcome was the change in mKCFQ11 scores after 4 weeks of MYP administration

second_reader.what_stands: All five efficacy outcomes (primary and secondary) are self-reported in an open-label, uncontrolled study, and the only objective marker (cortisol) was not correlated with symptom change (r = 0.15). The authors acknowledge possible reporting bias in the limitations, so the point is true but is disclosed rather than concealed.

issues.title: Cross-trial comparison with placebo arms used to suggest MYP benefit beyond placebo
issues.explanation: The Discussion compares MYP's uncontrolled change on a different 99-point scale with placebo-arm changes in other trials using a 33-point scale, then says MYP 'may offer benefits beyond those attributable to placebo'. Such an indirect comparison across populations, instruments and durations cannot support that statement. It is hedged but still tilts the reader toward efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A head-to-head randomized comparison with placebo using the same instrument.

quotes.text: When compared to placebo effects reported in prior RCTs, our findings suggest a potentially greater efficacy of MYP.
These comparisons suggest that MYP may offer benefits beyond those attributable to placebo

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does use an informal cross-trial comparison of its uncontrolled pre-post change against placebo arms of other trials to suggest benefit 'beyond those attributable to placebo', which is not valid because populations, scales, durations and baselines differ and no concurrent control exists. The authors hedge the wording and call for controlled trials, but the inference is not supported by their data.

issues.title: Baseline mKCFQ11 SD printed as 11.7 (abstract, 3.2) and 11.9 (3.1)
issues.explanation: The baseline mKCFQ11 score for the 49 ITT participants is given as 66.9 ± 11.7 in the abstract and Results 3.2, but 66.9 ± 11.9 in Results 3.1. One of the two SDs is wrong. This has negligible effect on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the two figures refer to different samples or time points (e.g., 50 enrolled vs 49 analysed).

quotes.text: with scores of 66.9 ± 11.7 on mKCFQ11
an average mKCFQ11 score of 66.9 ± 11.9

issues.title: Post-treatment fatigue VAS SD printed as 1.7 (abstract) vs 1.9 (Results 3.3)
issues.explanation: The abstract reports post-treatment fatigue VAS of 3.4 ± 1.7, whereas Results 3.3 reports 3.4 ± 1.9. The two cannot both be right, but the difference is small and does not change the significance or direction of the reported improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or supplement showing the SD is the same in both places.

quotes.text: fatigue VAS dropped from 7.4 ± 1.0 to 3.4 ± 1.7
Fatigue VAS changed from 7.4 ± 1.0 to 3.4 ± 1.9

issues.title: 'ITT' set defined as completers with >75% adherence; BOCF is moot but labelling is imprecise
issues.explanation: Results 3.1 says all 49 who finished 4 weeks and kept adherence above 75% were analysed as ITT, which is a completer definition rather than all enrolled. Because only one participant left (before the first dose), no one appears to have been dropped for low adherence, so bias is probably small. The label and the BOCF description do not match what was analysed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that no participant was excluded for adherence below 75%.

quotes.text: maintained an adherence rate above 75%, all were considered for the ITT analysis.

issues.title: Registration date and registered primary outcome not stated; enrolment ended before registration plausible
issues.explanation: The paper gives the registry number but no registration date or the registered outcomes. Enrolment ran December 2021 to April 2023 and the paper says 'prospective', so readers cannot verify that the registration preceded enrolment or that mKCFQ11 was the prespecified primary outcome. This cannot be resolved from the paper alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry entry showing registration before first enrolment with mKCFQ11 change as primary outcome.

quotes.text: the study was registered in the Clinical Research Information Service of the Republic of Korea (KCT0008948).

10.3389/fphar.2025.1508276.headline_claim: FZHY tablets attenuate pulmonary fibrosis and inflammation in convalescent patients with COVID-19, with promising safety profiles.
10.3389/fphar.2025.1508276.overall: The fibrosis-regression difference is nominally significant in both the FAS and PPS, but the Abstract and Results headline the larger PPS numbers, and the outcome is a loosely defined, non-validated imaging score. The functional co-primary was null in a very small spirometry subset, and the favourable week-8 result is a secondary time point, so the broad conclusion that FZHY attenuates fibrosis is more confident than the evidence supports. The numeric slips found (Table 1 denominator, Table 4 fatigue percentage) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Regression rate of pulmonary fibrosis by HRCT score at week 24, plus spirometry (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC) change at 24 weeks

primary_outcomes.measure: The improvement proportion of pulmonary fibrosis

issues.title: Co-primary 24-week lung function was null; a week-8 FEV1/FVC subgroup result is emphasised instead
issues.explanation: The trial's second primary outcome, lung function at 24 weeks, showed no significant difference, and spirometry was done in only about 21-22 patients per arm. The Abstract highlights a week-8 FEV1/FVC difference from a different time point in a small subset, with no multiplicity control, and the Conclusion omits the null co-primary. The conclusion of attenuating fibrosis rests on the semi-quantitative HRCT outcome alone, and the lung-function evidence does not support a functional benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified week-8 spirometry analysis, and an Abstract and Conclusion that report the null 24-week lung function co-primary.

quotes.text: After 24 weeks of treatment, no significant difference in FVC or FEV1 was observed between the two groups
FZHY tablets attenuate pulmonary fibrosis and inflammation in convalescent patients with COVID-19, with promising safety profiles.
Limited spirometry data revealed higher FEV1/FVC in the FZHY group than in the placebo group at week 8

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports that 24-week FVC and FEV1 did not differ, and the week-8 FEV1/FVC difference (p = 0.018, small unadjusted comparison, n = 22 vs 25) is highlighted in the abstract and discussion as suggesting early benefit, with no multiplicity adjustment. However, the authors openly state that spirometry was limited to a few patients, call the finding 'possible' and 'may promote', and list the limitation, so the emphasis is hedged. The 24-week FEV1/FVC result is not given in the text I could read, and the conclusion does not mention the null lung function result.

issues.title: Headline fibrosis regression (71.2% vs 49.2%, p=0.011) is the PPS result, not the stated primary FAS (66.7% vs 47.1%)
issues.explanation: The Methods name the FAS as the primary dataset, with dropouts counted as ineffective. The Abstract, Results text and Discussion report the per-protocol numbers (66 vs 63 patients) as if they were the primary result and do not say which set they come from. The FAS effect is smaller (about 19.6 vs 22.0 percentage points) and has a weaker p-value. The finding remains significant, so this inflates the effect size and certainty rather than overturning the result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the Abstract and Results that the 71.2% vs 49.2% figures are the PPS and that the FAS result is the primary analysis.

quotes.text: The FAS was used as the primary dataset.
the regression rate of pulmonary fibrosis was higher in the FZHY group than in the placebo group (71.2% [47/66] vs 49.2% [31/63]; p = 0.011)
| Regression rate of pulmonary fibrosis (n, %, FAS) | 48/72 (66.7) | 33/70 (47.1) | 0.019   |

issues.title: Fibrosis 'regression' appears to mean any decrease in a 10%-granularity semi-quantitative HRCT score
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is a manually scored, non-validated percentage-extent score for fibrosis. The paper gives no clinically meaningful threshold for regression and appears to count any decrease. The authors acknowledge possible subjective bias. This weakens the interpretation of the 'regression rate' as meaningful fibrosis regression, though blinded multi-reader scoring limits bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified responder threshold with reader-agreement statistics showing the score is reproducible.

quotes.text: A decrease in these scores was considered an improvement.
the chest CT scoring in this study used an artificial semi-quantitative method, which may introduce subjective bias in the results

issues.title: Table 4 fatigue, FZHY: 19 of 33 is 57.6%, printed 63.3% (which equals 19/30)
issues.explanation: The count and denominator printed in the fatigue row do not give the printed percentage. The percentage matches a denominator of 30, so either n = 33 or the percentage is wrong. The outcome is non-significant either way and is a secondary symptom endpoint.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or the source data showing that 19 of 33 and 63.3% both hold under a different definition.

script.explanation: 19/33 = 57.58%, but the paper prints 63.3, outside the rounding interval [63.25, 63.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 30.0 rather than 33.

issues.title: Planned n of 160 had no power calculation; 142 enrolled and sample size not adjusted
issues.explanation: The authors give a planned size of 160 without a formal power calculation and enrolled 142. This limits what can be read into the null secondary outcomes and the small spirometry subsets. The primary fibrosis comparison was still significant, so this mainly affects the interpretation of non-significant results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol-level power calculation showing 142 patients gives adequate power for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: with a planned sample size of 160 patients (80 in each group)
the sample size was not adjusted since the wile type COVID−19 epidemic was quickly diminished during the implementation of this study

issues.title: Table 1 FZHY clinical classification counts sum to 71 of 72; percentages use a denominator of 71
issues.explanation: The four FZHY classification counts add to 71, but the column header says n = 72. The printed percentages correspond to 71, so one patient appears to be missing from this row with no footnote. This is a minor reporting slip and the group comparison is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote or supplement stating that one FZHY patient had a missing classification.

10.3389/fphys.2023.1219252.headline_claim: An 8-week multi-professional intervention (nutrition, psychoeducation, concurrent exercise) is an efficient tool for reversing the inflammatory process and improving daily activities and quality of life in overweight COVID-19 survivors, with benefits described across severity groups.
10.3389/fphys.2023.1219252.overall: The headline claim of efficacy against inflammation and safe use is weakly supported: the design is non-randomised with no untreated comparator, about half of participants were lost, and the primary outcome was null. Reporting is also inconsistent (participant flow, Abstract p-values, duplicated control-group statistics, CIs that include zero). The study is best read as a small exploratory pre-post series, and its positive conclusions should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Body composition (BMI, lean mass, fat mass, body fat %, skeletal muscle mass)

issues.title: No untreated comparator: all three groups got the intervention, so pre-post changes are not attributable
issues.explanation: Allocation was by symptom group, not randomised, and the 'control' group (no COVID-19) received the same program. The study therefore only shows pre-post change within groups, with no contrast against no intervention. Conclusions that the program reverses inflammation, supported by CRP falling in the control group by a similar amount, do not follow from this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or usual-care group, or external evidence that the changes would not occur without intervention.

quotes.text: the self-reported signs and symptoms were considered for the non-randomized allocation of participants in the experimental COVID-19 groups
a factor that reinforces the effectiveness of physical exercise in reversing the in fl ammatory process

second_reader.what_stands: All three groups received the full program, so the paper has no untreated comparator and the pre-post changes (including the CRP fall) cannot be attributed to the intervention. The non-COVID control group is a comparison by severity, not a no-intervention arm, and the CRP statement in the Discussion is a causal claim the design does not support.

issues.title: Conclusion of efficacy and safety, while stated primary outcome (body composition) was null and no adverse events reported
issues.explanation: The Abstract conclusion says the program is efficient for reversing inflammation and improving daily activities, but the stated primary outcome showed no improvement and the Abstract results do not say so. 'Safely used regardless of symptomatology' is stated without reporting any adverse events or safety data in 35 completers. These conclusions go beyond what a non-randomised, uncontrolled, high-attrition study can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecified safety reporting showing no adverse events in all 69 participants, and a controlled design showing inflammation reduction.

quotes.text: can be an ef fi cient tool for reversing the in fl ammatory process
this study provides a concurrent training model that can be safely used in individuals affected by COVID-19
Consequently, the study ' s hypothesis was not con fi rmed.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract and final considerations assert efficacy ('efficient tool for reversing the inflammatory process') and safety, yet the primary outcome (body composition) was null, the efficacy evidence is secondary and uncontrolled, and no adverse-event data are reported. The authors do acknowledge the failed hypothesis and the limitations, so the conclusion is overstated rather than unqualified.

issues.title: About half lost (34 of 69), completers only, and final groups (7/17/11) below the sample-size target
issues.explanation: Only 35 of 69 volunteers finished and results are completer-only, with no intent-to-treat analysis. The severe group ended with 7 participants, below even the 9 per group the sample-size calculation required. The authors concede low power for several analyses, yet draw positive conclusions per group. Differential drop-out may bias the pre-post changes either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all enrolled participants (or dropout comparison at baseline) showing the same results.

quotes.text: but only 35 fi nished the longitudinal protocol
a minimum of 14 patients should be recruited for each study group
lost follow-up among groups because the participants did not return for the fi nal evaluations to perform a possible intent-to-treat analysis

second_reader.what_stands: About half were lost (34 of 69, or 25 by the paper's own dropout count, which is internally inconsistent), analyses are completers only, and the severe group (n=7) is below the stated power sample of 9 while the control (11) and severe groups are below the 14 recruitment target. The authors disclose the attrition, absence of an intent-to-treat analysis and reduced power, but the participant-count figures (89, 71, 69, 25 dropouts) do not reconcile.

issues.title: Dozens of outcomes and per-group t-tests uncorrected; group-specific claims rest on non-significant interactions
issues.explanation: Roughly twenty outcomes were each tested in three groups with an alpha of 0.05 and no correction across outcomes. Interaction terms were non-significant for nearly all outcomes (e.g. CRP p = 0.86, albumin p = 0.06), yet the Abstract highlights which group improved on which measure. Several p-values are borderline (0.04 to 0.05).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan limiting the confirmatory outcomes, or corrected p-values that survive.

quotes.text: The signi fi cance level established was p ≤ 0.05.
The isolated t-test con fi rm this difference for the severe COVID-19 ( t 7 = 2.346; p = 0.05

issues.title: Paired t-test df imply 8 severe and 12 control participants, not the 7 and 11 reported
issues.explanation: The completer counts are 7 (severe), 17 (moderate) and 11 (control), totalling 35. But many per-group paired tests carry df 7 for severe and df 11 for control, implying 8 and 12 participants, plus moderate df up to 17 (18 participants). Together these would exceed 35, so the analysed sets are unclear. The stated n cannot be matched to the analyses.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow chart or table showing the analysed numbers for each test (e.g. 8, 18 and 12 participants with data).

quotes.text: severe ( n = 7), moderate ( n = 17)
moderate COVID-19 ( t 17 = 3.460; p = 0.003

issues.title: Control-group t = 4.498, CI 4.404 to 13.05 and d = 0.16 printed for both chair-stand and sit-up tests
issues.explanation: The control group's paired t, confidence interval and effect size are identical for the 30-s chair-stand and the sit-up test, which measure different quantities. At least one of the two lines is therefore wrong. The abstract and discussion claim that the control group improved on sit-ups, and that claim rests on this line.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing both tests truly produced identical statistics (which is implausible).

issues.title: Participant flow does not reconcile: 71 vs 69 enrolled, 25 dropouts reported but 34 lost (69 to 35)
issues.explanation: The Methods say 71 volunteers were accepted, but the group sizes sum to 69. The text says 25 participants dropped out, yet only 35 completed, which implies 34 (or 36) were lost. The flow of participants cannot be audited from the text, and the true attrition (about 49%) is understated by the stated 25.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The CONSORT flow chart (Figure 1) showing stage-by-stage counts that reconcile 71, 69, 25 and 35 (e.g. other exclusions).

quotes.text: Seventy-one volunteers were accepted to participate in the program
Over the 8 weeks, 25 participants dropped out of the project
but only 35 fi nished the longitudinal protocol

script.explanation: The 69 volunteers, 25 dropouts, 35 finished does not reconcile: 'allocated' (n=69) minus its 1 stated exclusion(s) (25) leaves 44, but 'completed' reports 35 -- 9 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

issues.title: Severe-group SBP (p = 0.04) and CRP (p = 0.05) described as significant though 95% CIs include zero
issues.explanation: For final SBP in the severe group, the paper prints p = 0.04 and calls the drop significant, yet the 95% CI runs from -28.273 to 0.3034, which includes zero. The CI implies p slightly above 0.05. The severe-group CRP drop is likewise called significant with p = 0.05 and a CI of -15.52 to 0.3268. Both claims are borderline at best, and the discussion treats the SBP result as 'highly positive'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired SBP data giving t = 2.5 with a CI excluding zero, showing a typographical CI error.

quotes.text: The isolated t-test con fi rm this difference for the severe COVID-19 ( t 7 = 2.346; p = 0.05

issues.title: Abstract p-values disagree with Results: albumin/HDL-c swapped (0.005/0.002), control sit-up 0.008 vs 0.0011
issues.explanation: The Abstract gives p = 0.005 for severe-group albumin and p = 0.002 for HDL-c, but the Results give 0.002 for albumin and 0.005 for HDL-c. The Abstract gives p = 0.008 for the control-group sit-up improvement, while the Results give 0.0011. Every one of these p-values is below 0.05, so the significance conclusions are unchanged. They are reporting errors in the headline summary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version or erratum showing the Abstract values were from a different, declared analysis.

quotes.text: higher values of albumin ( p = 0.005) and HDL-c ( p = 0.002)
an improvement in sit-up repetitions ( p =0.008)

issues.title: Moderate-group memory deficit 8 of 17 printed as 45.1% (should be 47.1%)
issues.explanation: Eight of seventeen is 47.1%, not 45.1%. The same wrong figure appears in the Results text. It is a small reporting slip that does not affect any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for this row stated in the paper (none is).

quotes.text: memory de fi cit (severe: 85.7%; moderate: 45.1%)

script.explanation: 8/17 = 47.06%, but the paper prints 45.1, outside the rounding interval [45.05, 45.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 17.7 rather than 17.

10.3389/fphys.2024.1416639.headline_claim: Supervised tailored exercise is safe and effective in post-COVID-19 condition, improving physical capacity, physical activity and systemic oxidative stress/plasma proteome markers.
10.3389/fphys.2024.1416639.overall: The exploratory finding that supervised exercise was feasible and without evident harm in PCC is reasonably supported, but the claim of effectiveness rests on two interaction p-values near 0.04 in a small, non-randomised, unblinded comparison with baseline imbalance and no multiplicity handling. The text also contradicts its own tables on several points (6MWT significance, control-group PASE direction, p < 0.001 wording), so the efficacy conclusion should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Physical capacity (STS-30 and bicep curl tests; no single primary outcome named)

issues.title: Sequential non-random allocation (15 vs 10) with baseline imbalance underlies the between-group efficacy claims
issues.explanation: Participants were allocated sequentially, not randomised, to exercise or usual care, with unblinded outcomes and baseline differences in weight and BMI. Between-group differences in STS-30, bicep curl and PASE could reflect allocation, timing or self-selection rather than the programme. The authors acknowledge it is a pilot, but the effectiveness conclusion rests on exactly this comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of concealed allocation and balanced baseline characteristics, or adjusted analyses showing robust effects.

quotes.text: The study was not a controlled randomized trial (No-PCC group was not included). It was a pilot intervention study.
participants were allocated sequentially to one of the two groups: control (usual care) or exercise (8 weeks of mixed tailored supervised exercise)

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was sequential and non-random (15 vs 10), and baseline differences existed (weight and BMI by the authors' own statement, waist and baseline PASE by the printed means), so the between-group interaction results are open to selection and baseline confounding. The authors state the non-randomised design plainly and list the small sample as a limitation, but they do not discuss allocation bias or adjust for baseline differences; this was checked from printed means only, as no baseline test statistics are given.

issues.title: Abstract concludes 'safe and effective' from a 25-person non-randomised pilot with p ≈ 0.04 results
issues.explanation: The efficacy conclusion rests on two interaction p-values near 0.04 in a small non-randomised, unblinded study with no sample size calculation, and the 6MWT, grip strength, symptoms and fatigue showed no significant benefit. Safety in 15 exercisers is only weakly informative. The limitations section calls for a more robust trial, so the confident abstract wording is stronger than the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation in an adequately powered randomised trial.

quotes.text: Supervised exercise adapted to the level of fatigue and ability is safe and effective in PCC patients in improving their general physical capacity and
Two obvious limitations of this study are the small sample size, the short duration of the exercise intervention and absence of long-term follow up of the participants.
quotes.location: 6. Limitations and strengths of the study and future research

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract does conclude 'safe and effective' from a 25-person non-randomised pilot whose key between-group results are p=0.040 and 0.043 with no multiplicity correction, so 'effective' is stronger than the evidence supports; the limitations section does acknowledge small size and short duration but not the non-random allocation or multiplicity. 'Safe' is a more defensible claim for this cohort (no adverse events, fatigue not worse), though still based on 15 exercisers who excluded people with prior PEM.

issues.title: Discussion says no-exercise PASE 'improved' but Results show a fall from 229.20 to 202.80
issues.explanation: The Results report that PASE fell in the control group, while the Discussion says the score also improved in the no-exercise group and concludes that physical capacity improves over time in PCC patients. This is contradicted by the authors' own numbers. The inference about spontaneous improvement over time is therefore unsupported, although the exercise-group interaction result is not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Discussion refers to a different measure, or that the Results figures are transposed.

quotes.text: The score also improved, although less dramatically, in the no-exercise group

issues.title: 6MWT time effect called a significant improvement in Discussion; Results give p = 0.057 (alpha 0.05)
issues.explanation: Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, and the 6MWT time effect has p = 0.057. Despite this, the Discussion groups 6MWT with 'significant improvements' and later argues the result supports clinical utility on the basis of the MCID. The paper contradicts itself on this outcome, and the cardiorespiratory claim is stronger than the data support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different alpha prespecified for time effects or a corrected 6MWT p-value below 0.05.

quotes.text: the observed signi fi cant improvements in STS-30, biceps curl (time and interaction effects) and 6MWT (time effect)
over time for 6-MWT ( p = 0.057)

issues.title: Ambiguous '(all p < 0.001)' beside interaction p-values of 0.043 and 0.040 for STS-30 and bicep curl
issues.explanation: The sentence gives p = 0.043 and p = 0.040 for the exercise-vs-control comparisons and then closes with '(all p < 0.001)'. The latter probably refers to the time effects, but this is not stated, so a reader cannot tell which p applies to which effect. The between-group interaction results themselves are only modestly significant (about 0.04).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or table showing the time-effect p-values for STS-30 and bicep curl are < 0.001 and that '(all p < 0.001)' refers only to them.

quotes.text: sit-to stand test (+31% vs. +11%; p = 0.043)

issues.title: No trial registration identifier reported for a prospective intervention study
issues.explanation: Only an ethics approval number is given, so prespecified outcomes and analyses cannot be checked. With six physical tests and many other outcomes, the selection of STS-30 and bicep curl as highlighted results cannot be verified. This weakens, but does not invalidate, a pilot study.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: This study was approved by the ethics review board of the Centre de Recherche du Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Sherbrooke (protocol # 2022 -4415).

issues.title: Seven of 10 no-exercise proteomic pairs stated, but sex breakdown 1/2 + 5/8 sums to 6
issues.explanation: The text says seven of ten paired samples showed no significant difference, but the male and female counts given in brackets add to six. One of the numbers is misprinted. This affects only a descriptive side-result in the proteomics section.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The underlying proteomic dataset showing 2/2 males (or another consistent breakdown).

quotes.text: seven out of 10 paired samples
(1/2 males and 5/8 females)

issues.title: Resting heart rate called significantly decreased in both groups; Table 2 time effect p = 0.057
issues.explanation: The Results say resting heart rate decreased significantly in both groups, but the only p-value printed for the time effect is 0.057, which is above the stated 0.05 threshold. No within-group tests are reported to support the text. This is a minor secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Within-group tests showing p ≤ 0.05 in both groups.

quotes.text: Resting heart rate decreased signi fi cantly in both groups

10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1436691.headline_claim: Tele-yoga has demonstrated potential as an effective intervention to mitigate stress, anxiety, and insomnia in adults who had COVID-19 in the past year and report moderate psychological stress.
10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1436691.overall: The headline claim that tele-yoga is effective rests on uncontrolled within-group change in a single open-label arm with about 64% attrition at week 16, so it supports only feasibility and hypothesis generation. The Abstract and title overstate this, and there are internal inconsistencies in safety reporting and in a few statistics (IES-R p-value, correlation significance).
