The Conclusion's hedged wording is more defensible than the Abstract's.

primary_outcome.name: Perceived Stress Scale (PSS)

issues.title: Single-arm uncontrolled pre-post design reported as proving programmes useful to counteract stress/anxiety
issues.explanation: All efficacy evidence is within-group change from baseline in one open-label arm of people recovering from COVID-19, assessed by self-report. This cannot separate the programme from natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectancy or time. The authors concede that without a control arm they cannot draw definitive conclusions about efficacy, yet the Abstract says the programmes 'proved' useful and the title promises efficacy. The same problem applies to the repeated within-group tests across several scales and two time points.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control comparison, or Abstract/title wording limited to feasibility and uncontrolled pilot findings.

quotes.text: Both tele-yoga programs proved safe, useful tools to counteract perceived stress, anxiety and insomnia.
Without a control arm, we cannot draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy of the module
Tele-yoga has demonstrated potential as an effective intervention to mitigate stress, anxiety, and insomnia

second_reader.what_stands: The design is single-arm and uncontrolled, and the abstract's wording ('proved ... useful tools to counteract') goes beyond what a pre-post design can show, including for the two programmes separately. The paper is not unaware of this: the limitations paragraph concedes that efficacy cannot be concluded and the Conclusion says 'potential', so the problem is an overstated abstract and title inconsistent with the paper's own caveats, not an unacknowledged design flaw.

issues.title: 64% attrition by week 16 with dropout related to baseline severity and early response; no sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Only 31 of 86 remained at week 16, and completers differed from dropouts on several baseline measures. Dropouts also had larger early stress reductions than those who stayed. Week-16 results therefore rest on a self-selected minority, and the mixed model assumes missingness is explained by observed data without testing that. Week-16 findings should be regarded as tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pattern-mixture or multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis showing week-16 estimates are stable.

quotes.text: with a 63% attrition rate by the 16-week mark
31 subjects remained in the trial and continued their yoga practice
those who remained in the trial had significantly more distress

second_reader.what_stands: Attrition is about 64% (55/86, reported as 63%), and the paper itself shows dropout was related to baseline severity (Table 2) and to larger early stress reduction (-9.85 vs -6.35). No sensitivity analysis for missing data is reported, so the week-16 estimates, based on 31 observed completers, rest on an untested MAR assumption. Some Table 2 p-values (notably IES-R) also do not reproduce from the printed means and SDs, which weakens the severity comparison for that scale but not the overall pattern for GHQ and HADS.

issues.title: Safety: Results report 3 subjects with untoward effects; Discussion and Abstract say none/no side effects
issues.explanation: The Results list 3 subjects with untoward effects (2 giddiness, 1 fall). The Discussion states that none of the participants reported any adverse effects, and the Abstract says the 31 remaining subjects practised without side effects. The safety claim is stated inconsistently and the Discussion version understates the events actually recorded. The safety conclusion rests on informal qualitative feedback from an unclear number of respondents.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion refers only to serious adverse events, or a corrected Results count.

quotes.text: only 3 subjects (3.70%) reported untoward effects
none of the participants reported any adverse effects from the tele-yoga practice

issues.title: Table 2 IES-R baseline difference printed p=0.01 but means/SDs imply p≈0.4
issues.explanation: For IES-R, completers (22.10 ± 19.25, n=31) and dropouts (18.61 ± 20.27, n=55) differ by 3.49 points with SDs near 20. This gives t of about 0.8 and p of about 0.4, not 0.01. The text cites more distress at baseline in completers, and IES-R is one of the supporting measures, so that claim is partly unsupported. Other rows also look off (e.g. age p 0.81 vs about 0.95 recomputed).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Different IES-R summary statistics in the source data, or a correct p reported in a corrigendum.

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

issues.title: Correlation r = -0.16 (HADS anxiety) called significant at p<0.05 although not significant at n ≤ 86
issues.explanation: The Results state significant negative correlations for PSS, GHP, HADS anxiety (r = -0.16) and ISI (r = -0.23). With n=86 the critical |r| at p<0.05 is about 0.21, and with n=31 about 0.35. So -0.16 cannot be significant, and -0.23 is significant only if n is 86 and not 31. The n for these correlations is not stated, and the dose-response support for benefit is weaker than described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated n and p for each correlation showing significance, or a corrected r.

quotes.text: HADS anxiety (r = -0.16), and ISI (r = -0.23), respectively

script.explanation: The printed r = -0.16 supports p no smaller than 0.117616, but the paper reports p = 0.05 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

issues.title: Observed 31 completers fell below the calculated 43; non-significant week-16 results read as absence of effect
issues.explanation: The calculation assumed 50% attrition but 64% occurred, leaving 31 at week 16, below the calculated 43. The authors interpret non-significant week-16 depression and trauma-distress changes as effects that did not sustain, although precision was reduced. The calculation is for a stress outcome and its test is not specified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Power or precision calculations showing adequate power with 31 completers.

quotes.text: Experience in the pilot study suggested an attrition rate around 50% after 16 weeks, so our sample size was set at 86 subjects.

issues.title: Discussion's moderate-severe depression (22%) and anxiety (45%) differ from Results (26.7%, 46.5%)
issues.explanation: The Results give moderate-to-severe anxiety, depression and insomnia as 46.5, 26.7 and 22%. The Discussion says 45% had moderate-to-severe anxiety and only 22% moderate-to-severe depression, which is the insomnia figure. The 'ceiling effect' explanation for the lack of sustained depression change leans on the mis-stated contrast between anxiety and depression. The anxiety discrepancy (45 vs 46.5) is too large to be simple rounding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors confirming different cut-offs used in the Discussion figures.

quotes.text: 46.5, 26.7 and 22% of subjects, respectively, reported anxiety, depression, and insomnia
experienced moderate to severe depression
with 45% classified as having moderate

issues.title: Safety percentage 3.70% matches 3/81, not 3/86 enrolled; denominator undefined
issues.explanation: 3 of 86 gives 3.49%, while 3.70% corresponds to 3 of 81. No group of 81 is defined anywhere in the paper. The likely reading is that a subset gave safety feedback, but the denominator for the safety analysis is not stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 81 participants provided safety feedback.

quotes.text: only 3 subjects (3.70%) reported untoward effects

script.explanation: 3/86 = 3.49%, but the paper prints 3.7, outside the rounding interval [3.70, 3.71]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 81.1 rather than 86.

10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1441018.headline_claim: The multimodal group-based IVR intervention (cognitive training, physical exercise, mindfulness) improved cognition and depressive symptoms in adults with post-COVID-19 condition compared with usual care, and the authors frame it as a pioneering step warranting larger RCTs.
10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1441018.overall: The headline claim that the IVR programme improved cognition and depressive symptoms is only tentative support at best. It rests on a non-randomised, unblinded pilot with large baseline imbalances, 13 vs 13 analysed participants and unexplained loss of 5 of 31, and the significance claims do not clearly withstand the stated multiplicity correction. The numeric slips (r(98), table sums, percentages) are minor, but the abstract overstates the attention result and the Discussion's efficacy language outruns the design.

primary_outcome.name: Global cognition (MoCA), attention, processing speed, verbal episodic memory and subjective memory complaints (MFE-Q), listed collectively as primary measures

issues.title: Non-randomised, unblinded study with large baseline imbalance; causal efficacy language not supported
issues.explanation: Allocation was sequential, outcome assessors were un-blinded, and key outcomes were subjective or practice-sensitive. The groups differed at baseline: the experimental group scored far lower on RAVLT (Sum 37.3 vs 55.5) and had higher PHQ-9 (14.4 vs 9.3). The 'interactions' therefore partly reflect regression to the mean and baseline imbalance. The conclusions in the Discussion ('showed significant efficacy', 'reverse cognitive impairments') are stronger than a pilot with 13 vs 13 analysed and no power calculation can support. The authors' own limitations section acknowledges these problems but the conclusions do not carry the caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomised allocation, blinded assessors, or analyses adjusted for baseline scores that still show the group effect.

quotes.text: Participants were sequentially assigned to two groups.
All the primary and secondary measures were assessed by two un-blinded clinical neuropsychologists
RAVLT-Sum b

second_reader.what_stands: The study is non-randomised with unblinded outcome assessors, and the groups differed markedly at baseline (RAVLT-Sum, with PHQ-9 also higher in the EG). Several significant interactions, notably RAVLT, may reflect baseline differences and regression to the mean, and no baseline-adjusted analysis was done. Phrases such as 'our intervention produced significant improvements' and 'significant efficacy in reducing depressive symptoms' therefore go beyond what the design supports. The authors do disclose these limitations and describe the work as preliminary and pilot, which softens but does not r

issues.title: 31 enrolled (15 vs 16) but 13 vs 13 analysed; only one exclusion is described, leaving 5 unexplained
issues.explanation: Methods allocate 15 to the experimental group and 16 to controls, and describe one experimental exclusion (leaving 14). Tables 1 and 2 analyse 13 per group (26 total), and the ANOVA degrees of freedom (22 to 24) match 26 or fewer. The text never explains the other 4 lost participants (1 experimental, 3 control), so attrition by arm is not reported. The sex percentages in Section 2.2 (76.92%/23.08%) are also 20/26 and 6/26, matching the Table 1 counts, not the stated 31. The analysis is a completers-only analysis with differential, unexplained dropout.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow diagram (Figure 1) showing the reasons and numbers lost per arm, with the sex percentages computed on the analysed sample.

quotes.text: Participants in the experimental group who did not reach this threshold, specifically one individual

second_reader.what_stands: In the text, 31 are enrolled and 26 analysed with only one dropout (EG, n = 1) explained. At least 4 further participants (1 EG, 3 CG) have no stated reason for exclusion. The claim of 5 unexplained is off by one, because the described exclusion is one of the 5. Some outcomes also appear to be analysed on fewer than 13 per group, and the 26-person demographics are not reconciled with '31 participated'. Whether Figure 1 itemises these dropouts cannot be checked from the extracted text.

issues.title: About 20 outcomes tested; claimed Bonferroni correction does not square with reported p of 0.03 to 0.05
issues.explanation: Around 20 outcomes were tested with an alpha of 0.05. Several interactions are declared significant at p = 0.03 to 0.04, and one at p = 0.05, which would not survive a Bonferroni correction across outcomes. The paper states Bonferroni corrections were used without saying over which family, and marginal results (TMT-A p = 0.059, Stroop p = 0.05) are interpreted as findings. Only the results with p of about 0.003 (RAVLT Sum, RAVLT delayed recall) are robust to correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Bonferroni family was limited to pairwise comparisons, plus a pre-specified single primary outcome.

quotes.text: reached marginally statistically significant group*time interactions
with Bonferroni corrections

issues.title: Abstract lists simple attention as a significant group*time interaction; Results show only TMT-A p = 0.059
issues.explanation: The abstract says significant interactions (p < 0.05) occurred in simple attention, among others. The Results report only a marginal attention interaction (TMT-A, p = 0.059) and no significant simple-attention interaction. The abstract therefore overstates the attention finding; the within-group TMT-A change is the only significant attention result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant (p < 0.05) group*time interaction for an attention measure (e.g., Digit Span Forward or CPT) reported in the paper.

quotes.text: significant group*time interactions in global cognition, simple attention,
reached marginally statistically significant group*time interactions

issues.title: Correlation reported as r(98) although the experimental group has n = 13 (df should be 11)
issues.explanation: A Pearson correlation with 98 degrees of freedom implies 100 pairs, but Table 3 is computed in the experimental group of 13. The printed p of 0.03 fits df = 11, so the df is a misprint rather than a wrong analysis. The result is only a minor reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the correlation was computed on about 100 observations (e.g., sessions pooled across participants).

issues.title: Experimental-group vaccination and comorbidity counts each sum to 12, not the 13 stated
issues.explanation: The vaccination categories (2, 4, 6) and the comorbidity categories (4, 4, 4) each sum to 12 in the experimental group, while the control group sums to 13 in both. Possibly one participant has missing data on both items, but no note says so. The error is small and does not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table note stating one experimental participant had missing vaccination and comorbidity data.

quotes.text: 2 or 3 doses
1 or 2 comorbid disorders

issues.title: Same 9/13 printed as 69.23% (sex) and 69.20% (ethnicity, severity); 6/13 printed as 46.20%
issues.explanation: The same share is printed with inconsistent precision across Table 1 rows. 9/13 is 69.23%, but two rows give 69.20%; 6/13 is 46.15%, printed 46.20%. No reader would be misled, but it shows that percentages were rounded by hand.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: n/a (cosmetic)

quotes.text: White-Caucasian

10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1582742.headline_claim: Tablet-based cognitive and mental training may be partially effective, reducing subjective cognitive complaints and depressive symptoms and stabilising the MoCA Memory Index in post-Covid-19 condition.
10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1582742.overall: The paper shows only a tentative signal in a small, unblinded waitlist-controlled pilot, with self-reported outcomes and no clear primary outcome. The three reported effects (complaints, depression, MoCA memory index) rest on nominal 2x2 interaction p-values between 0.017 and 0.025 among 19 subtests, despite a stated Bonferroni correction, so the claim that training improves memory and mood is not firmly supported. The larger merged pre-post gains are exploratory and uncontrolled.

primary_outcome.name: No single primary outcome is named; headline outcomes are subjective cognitive complaints (FSKB [QPC]) and depression (ADS-L) from the 2x2 ANCOVA group x time interaction

issues.title: Three interaction p-values (0.017-0.025) among 19 subtests, despite stated Bonferroni correction of all p-values
issues.explanation: The Methods state Bonferroni correction was applied to all p-values, but the three reported interactions are far above any corrected threshold for 19 tests and appear unadjusted. The 2x2 analyses were also introduced after the original 2x3 test showed no group x time effect other than digit span. The headline claims on memory, complaints and depression rest on these three nominal results, which are best viewed as exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported adjusted p-values below 0.05 for these interactions, or a documented single primary outcome limited to one of them.

quotes.text: Bonferroni correction was applied to all p -values
MoCA memory index score ( p = 0.017), subjective cognitive complaints ( p = 0.022), and depression (ADS-L; p = 0.025)

second_reader.what_stands: The Methods say Bonferroni correction was applied to all p-values, but the Table 2 interaction p-values (0.017, 0.022, 0.025) would not survive correction across the 19 subtests (threshold about 0.0026; adjusted p about 0.32-0.48), so they appear to be uncorrected, or the correction applied only to post hoc comparisons, which the paper does not state. The significant findings are therefore not multiplicity-protected as the Methods imply.

issues.title: Waitlist control and unblinded participants for self-reported complaint and depression outcomes
issues.explanation: The control group received nothing, and participants knew their arm, while the two outcomes carrying the efficacy claim are self-report questionnaires. Expectancy, attention and demand effects could therefore explain the between-group differences. The authors themselves recommend an active control, yet the Conclusion states a significant reduction compared with controls without this caveat. The benefit is therefore a tentative signal, not evidence for the training content.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded or objective outcome showing the same group difference, or an active-control comparison.

quotes.text: due to the study design, blinding of the participants was not possible. Therefore, participants knew whether they were receiving the intervention or not.
include an active control group in their study design

second_reader.what_stands: The control was a waitlist (no training) and participants knew their allocation, and the two outcomes with a significant group x time interaction that concern symptoms (subjective complaints, ADSL depression) are self-reported, so expectation and non-specific effects could contribute. The paper discloses this and recommends an active control, but its conclusion does not discount the self-report findings accordingly. The assessor was blinded, which does not cover the questionnaires.

issues.title: Conclusion says training improves memory; the controlled result is only a non-decline in one MoCA item set
issues.explanation: The controlled analysis found no improvement in memory in the intervention arm, only a non-significant change (p=0.496) against a decline in controls. The merged-group gains are uncontrolled and exploratory. The conclusion that training can improve memory and serve as add-on therapy therefore goes beyond what the design shows. The final overall sentence about improving cognition repeats this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, controlled analysis showing improved memory scores in the intervention arm relative to controls.

quotes.text: Tablet-based training programs can help improve subjective complaints, depressive symptoms, and memory and may serve as an additional therapy option.
These results should therefore not be overinterpreted.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract and conclusion state that training can improve memory, but the only controlled memory finding is stable MoCA 5-word recall in the intervention group versus a decline in the waitlist group (IG +0.32 vs CG -1.43), with no significant effect on the four NAB word-list memory measures. The body text correctly says 'no decline', so the headline conclusion overstates what the Results show; the 'overinterpreted' caveat refers to the exploratory merged analysis.

issues.title: Headline within-arm p<0.001 values; FU1 between-group differences non-significant (p=0.065, p=0.452)
issues.explanation: The abstract highlights within-arm changes (p<0.001) and a non-significant change called 'stable'. The between-group contrasts at follow-up were not significant for complaints (p=0.065) or depression (p=0.452). The supportive evidence is the interaction test, which is itself weak (see c6). The memory result may partly reflect a baseline imbalance and decline in the control group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group contrasts at FU1 that reach significance after adjustment for baseline.

quotes.text: a significant improvement was observed in individuals assigned to the intervention group ( p < 0.001)
the values in the intervention group remained, on average, stable ( p = 0.496)

issues.title: Retrospective registration, no registry ID and no named primary outcome
issues.explanation: The authors state the study was only registered retrospectively and give no registry identifier. The hypotheses cover essentially every domain, so no single primary outcome is defined. This leaves open that the three significant outcomes were selected after the data were seen.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment naming complaints, depression or MoCA memory index as primary outcomes.

quotes.text: this study was only registered retrospectively and not prospectively, which we encourage future studies to do

issues.title: Table 3 short-delayed recall t=1.25 conflicts with p=0.057 and d=0.36 (and ADSL t=7.69 with d=0.63)
issues.explanation: In Table 3, the short-delayed recall row prints t(30)=1.25 beside p=0.057 and d=0.36. A t of 1.25 at 30 df gives p of about 0.22 and d of about 0.22, while the printed p and d both imply t of about 2.0. The ADSL row has the same kind of mismatch (t=7.69 would imply d of about 1.4 and p<0.001). The affected analysis is exploratory and the row is not discussed in the text, so the headline claims are not affected, but the table cannot be fully trusted as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or the raw data showing t=2.0 for short-delayed recall, with the printed 1.25 a typo.

script.explanation: The printed t = 1.25 supports p no smaller than 0.217383, but the paper reports p = 0.057 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

10.3389/fpubh.2022.945988.headline_claim: Yogic breathing (SBT/LBDT) lowered D-dimer and improved exercise capacity in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 cases, supporting its integration into COVID-positive and post-COVID management.
10.3389/fpubh.2022.945988.overall: The headline claim that breathing lowered D-dimer and reduced COVID severity is weakly supported: it rests on a within-group change in one small subgroup with a high baseline, in an unblinded usual-care comparison with no power calculation and no clinical severity endpoint. The exercise-capacity claim is partly supported within groups but not versus controls in COVID-positive patients. Results are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: D-dimer (biochemical parameters)

issues.title: Conclusion that breathing 'was capable of reducing severity' rests on D-dimer alone, with no severity outcome
issues.explanation: No clinical severity outcome was measured; D-dimer is used as a surrogate. Day-15 D-dimer was not clearly different from controls in the COVID-positive or recovered groups, and the COVID-positive groups' D-dimer rose in both arms (CYG 0.22 to 0.30, CCG 0.26 to 0.50, p 0.46 and 0.23). Severe cases were excluded, and the recommendation to integrate into care goes beyond a small, uncontrolled-for-attention pilot.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clinically defined severity outcome showing between-group benefit.

quotes.text: Hence, the intervention was capable of reducing severity in mild to moderate cases of COVID-19.
The study could not include severe COVID-19 cases

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's statement that the intervention 'was capable of reducing severity in mild to moderate cases' rests on D-dimer, a surrogate, with no severity outcome measured. The D-dimer effects appear in recovered and healthy groups, not in the active COVID-positive arm, where there was no significant change and no difference from controls. The authors do note that severe cases were excluded and that further study is needed.

issues.title: RYG baseline D-dimer 0.54 vs RCG 0.31; chit-picking, no concealment; D-dimer fall may be regression to mean
issues.explanation: Allocation used manual chit-picking with no concealment or sequence generation described, and randomization happened after group recruitment with small subgroups. The recovered yoga group started with a much higher D-dimer (0.54) than its control (0.31) and fell to 0.21, so the within-group drop is confounded by regression to the mean. The between-group comparison on day 15 (adjusted p = 0.19) does not show a difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of concealed allocation and a between-group day-15 or change-score comparison, adjusted for baseline, favouring yoga.

quotes.text: each group was randomly divided into two subgroups by manual chit-picking method
D-dimer was found high in RYG at baseline, which was reduced after the intervention
quotes.location: Results, Effect of intervention on blood parameters

second_reader.what_stands: The baseline D-dimer values (0.54 vs 0.31) are as stated, with a baseline difference of p=0.01 (0.02 adjusted). Allocation is described only as manual chit-picking, with no concealment reported. Most of the RYG fall (-0.33) comes from starting high, and the day-15 between-arm difference is not significant (p=0.19). Regression to the mean is therefore a plausible explanation that the paper does not address, but it cannot be proven from the data.

issues.title: About 12 per arm, no sample-size calculation, yet confident efficacy conclusions; corrected threshold 0.003 rarely met
issues.explanation: Six arms of 11-12 participants (6MWT arms 7-12) with no power calculation cannot reliably detect effects across 18 biomarkers. The authors set a Bonferroni threshold of 0.003, but the D-dimer within-group result (p = 0.002) is the only headline one that meets it, and no yoga-vs-control D-dimer difference survives at day 15 in COVID-positive or recovered groups. The conclusion nonetheless states the intervention reduced severity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified power calculation justifying the sample and effects surviving the stated correction.

quotes.text: The sample size of the study was small due to a significant number of patients dropping out
Significance was observed at ≤ 0.05/18 = 0.003 after the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparison.

second_reader.what_stands: The arms contain about 12 people each and no sample-size calculation is reported. Almost no comparisons clear the paper's own 0.003 threshold, and the only yoga-vs-control D-dimer result cited (p=0.01) does not. The authors acknowledge small size as a limitation, but the Conclusion still states that D-dimer was lowered and that the intervention 'was capable of reducing severity' without qualification.

issues.title: D-dimer singled out from 18 'primary' markers and 6MWT headlined despite non-significant CYG vs CCG difference
issues.explanation: The primary outcome is an 18-marker panel, yet the abstract calls D-dimer 'the primary outcome'. The conclusion also claims exercise capacity improved, although the COVID-positive yoga vs control 6MWT difference was not significant and 6MWT was secondary. Most other markers showed no benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registered statement naming D-dimer as the single primary outcome with a corresponding analysis plan.

quotes.text: Although a greater covered distance was observed in CYG than in CCG
quotes.location: Results, Breathing technique improves exercise capacity

quotes.text: D-dimer was the primary outcome, which remained below 0.50

second_reader.what_stands: The Methods define all 18 biochemical markers as primary, while the Abstract singles out D-dimer as 'the primary outcome'. The CYG-vs-CCG difference in D-dimer is not significant (p=0.71), and the one in 6MWT is stated as not significant, yet both are headlined as benefits. Whether D-dimer was the registered primary outcome could not be checked.

issues.title: Usual-care controls without attention control or blinding for 6MWT, a effort-dependent outcome
issues.explanation: Controls got nothing and were not wait-listed, and no blinding of participants or outcome assessors is described. The 6MWT depends on effort and motivation, so expectancy could contribute to the improvement. Reasonable choice for a pragmatic design, but it limits causal claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 6MWT assessors were blinded and an attention-matched comparison.

quotes.text: Controls were under usual clinical care and were not wait-listed for intervention.

10.3389/fpubh.2023.1115393.headline_claim: VR-based exercise is an attractive and safe rehabilitation tool that could enhance exercise performance and benefit long-post-COVID-19 patients with respiratory and cognitive symptoms.
10.3389/fpubh.2023.1115393.overall: The paper can support only the modest statement that, in 20 patients, momentary self-rated dyspnea was somewhat lower after one open-label VR cycling session than after the same session without VR. The VR vs no-VR result is uncorrected, unblinded and non-randomised, and the safety and cognitive/affective benefit claims are not backed by measured data. The 1,001.6 mmHg value is a trivial printed error.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; heart rate, SpO2, leg fatigue and dyspnea measured immediately after exercise trials

issues.title: Open, non-randomised single-session comparison; VR benefit rests on self-rated Borg dyspnea (0.5 vs 1.1)
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they wore the VR headset and rated their own dyspnea and leg fatigue. The VR advantage (dyspnea 0.5 vs 1.1 on a 0-10 scale, one uncorrected t-test, p = 0.004) is therefore open to expectation and distraction effects. No order randomisation or counterbalancing is described. Leg fatigue showed no VR versus no-VR difference. The statement that VR lowers dyspnea can be only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that condition order was randomised or counterbalanced, plus an objective corroborating measure (for example ventilation or HR) that also differed between VR and no-VR.

quotes.text: Dyspnea was recorded to be lower during exercise with VR than during exercise without VR.
The results showed differences between the VR and no-VR trials

second_reader.what_stands: Supported: the VR vs no-VR contrast is a single-group, unblinded comparison with no described randomisation or counterbalancing, and the VR-specific benefit rests on the self-rated Borg dyspnea (0.5 vs 1.1, paired p = 0.004), while HR, SpO2, leg fatigue and MAP showed no VR vs no-VR difference. Not settled: whether the sessions were literally on one day, and whether order was varied, since the paper does not say. A related inconsistency is that the Discussion claims lower leg fatigue with VR, which the Results do not support.

issues.title: Conclusion calls VR safe and beneficial for respiratory and cognitive symptoms; none measured beyond one session
issues.explanation: The conclusion that VR is safe and benefits patients with respiratory and cognitive symptoms rests on one 10-minute session in 20 patients and an open, self-rated comparison. No adverse-event data are reported. The Discussion also claims benefits for anxiety and depression compared with non-specific VR content, but no such outcome or comparator was measured. The data support at most a small difference in momentary self-rated dyspnea during the session.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported adverse-event monitoring and measured anxiety, depression and cognitive outcomes showing benefit relative to a comparator.

quotes.text: In conclusion, VR applications seem to be an attractive and safe tool for implementing rehabilitation.
has beneficial effects on factors, such as tiredness, shortness of breath, anxiety, and depression compared with non-specific VR content

second_reader.what_stands: Supported: the Conclusion's claim of benefit for cognitive symptoms and the Discussion's claims about anxiety, depression and tiredness have no matching measurement in the paper, and nothing was measured beyond a single session per condition, with no follow-up. Not supported as stated: the respiratory part, since a within-session dyspnea difference was measured (0.5 vs 1.1), and safety rests on acute HR and SpO2 values with no adverse-event reporting described, so the safety claim is thinly evidenced rather than contradicted.

issues.title: Headline VR vs no-VR dyspnea p = 0.004 is an uncorrected t-test among 4 outcomes; % differences inconsistent with means
issues.explanation: The Methods describe repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc testing, but the key VR vs no-VR dyspnea contrast is a separate paired t-test with no stated correction across four outcomes and six pairwise contrasts. With about 24 comparisons, p = 0.004 would not clearly survive a Bonferroni correction. The percent differences against the 6MWT (18.2% for VR, 58.3% for no-VR) do not follow from the printed means (2.3 vs 0.5 vs 1.1). The SDs of 40-50 percentage points on these values also show that they are unstable ratios of small ordinal scores.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated pre-specified primary contrast or Tukey-adjusted p for VR vs no-VR dyspnea below 0.05, and an explanation of how the percentage differences were computed.

quotes.text: was used to locate any differences between the means.
The 6MWT showed a higher score in dyspnea than with exercise with VR at 18.2 ± 40.5%

issues.title: 6MWT mean arterial pressure printed as 1,001.6 mmHg; other conditions are 101.9-103.0 mmHg
issues.explanation: The results give the post-test mean arterial pressure for the 6MWT as 1,001.6 mmHg, which is physiologically impossible. The other three conditions are about 102 mmHg with similar SDs, so this is almost certainly a typo for about 101.6. Nothing in the conclusions depends on this value, because blood pressure showed no differences between conditions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version or the raw data showing a value near 101.6 mmHg would show it is a pure typo (which still leaves a printed error).

issues.title: Sample-size calculation (14 patients, 86% power) names no outcome or effect size; 20 recruited
issues.explanation: The paper states 86% power and 5% type I error and obtains 14 patients, but does not say which outcome, effect size or variance was used. The 20 recruited exceed 14, so the study is not underpowered by its own figure, but the number cannot be verified. It also does not address the several outcomes and contrasts analysed. This weakens confidence in secondary results more than the main conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated primary outcome, effect size and SD from which n = 14 follows.

quotes.text: A value for 14 patients was obtained. However, because this is a new exercise method, we recruited 20 patients.

10.3389/fpubh.2023.1121554.headline_claim: A 3-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program improved exercise performance in people with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, with VR-led rehabilitation showing similar effectiveness to traditional rehabilitation for exercise performance and stress.
10.3389/fpubh.2023.1121554.overall: The paper supports only that 6MWT distance improved in both arms of a small (18 vs 14) preliminary trial with no untreated comparator. It does not show that the programme itself caused the improvement, nor that VR and traditional rehabilitation are equivalent, and the stress and regression conclusions are weaker still. Table 2 contains several arithmetic slips and the registered primary outcomes do not match what is reported.

primary_outcome.name: Exercise performance (6MWT distance), reported alongside lung function and stress level

primary_outcomes.measure: Individual's perception of quality of life

issues.title: Programme effect on exercise and stress inferred from pre-post change in both arms; no untreated comparator
issues.explanation: The abstract concludes that the 3-week programme improved exercise performance and reduced stress. This rests on within-arm pre-post tests (6MWT p < 0.001 in each arm; PSS-10 p = 0.015 and 0.004), and both arms received the same intensive programme. There is no arm without the programme, so test learning effects, natural recovery 3-6 months after infection, and regression to the mean remain unexcluded. Between-group differences were non-significant, so the data support only 'both groups improved', not 'the programme caused it'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A usual-care or waiting-list control group, or external evidence of the expected spontaneous change in 6MWT over 3 weeks at this stage after COVID.

quotes.text: The analysis of the results showed a statistically significant improvement in both groups with regard to exercise performance expressed as 6MWT distance.
Furthermore, the program was shown to reduce patients' stress levels.
The between-group comparison revealed a non-significant change with a small effect size

second_reader.what_stands: The claims that the programme improved exercise performance and reduced stress rest on pre-post changes in two arms that both received the rehabilitation programme, with no untreated or usual-care comparator, so the changes cannot be attributed to the programme over natural recovery, practice effects or regression to the mean. The paper does not list this as a limitation. The within-group changes themselves are as reported and the 6MWT gains (about 40-57 m) are real descriptive findings.

issues.title: 'Similar effectiveness' of VR and traditional rehab claimed from non-significant tests in 18 vs 14 patients
issues.explanation: The abstract concludes that traditional and VR rehabilitation show similar effectiveness. The evidence is non-significant Mann-Whitney comparisons of change (6MWT p = 0.264, d = -0.411; PSS-10 p = 0.719), with no equivalence margin and a very small sample. A 6MWT difference of about 17 m (56 vs 39) with a small-to-moderate effect size is compatible with a real difference in either direction. The data are inconclusive, not shown to be equivalent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified non-inferiority/equivalence margin with a confidence interval for the between-arm difference lying inside it.

quotes.text: A comparison of the traditional form of rehabilitation to the novel form using VR, shows similar effectiveness in terms of exercise performance and stress levels.
Thus, it can be preliminarily concluded that rehabilitation conducted in virtual reality yields similar results as the traditional form.

second_reader.what_stands: 'Similar effectiveness' is inferred from non-significant between-group tests in a small sample (18 vs 14) without an equivalence or non-inferiority design, margin or confidence interval; absence of significance is not evidence of similarity, and the 6MWT effect size of d = -0.411 is not negligible. The authors do soften this with 'preliminary' and with the statement that VR was 'not shown to be more effective', so the narrower claim of no demonstrated superiority is supported, but the abstract and Discussion wording of similar effectiveness goes beyond the data.

issues.title: Conclusion promotes a single stepwise stress-dyspnea model (R2 = 0.135, p = 0.026) not specified in Methods
issues.explanation: The Methods say the regression tested whether baseline stress determined 6MWT improvement, and the Results say it did not. The Conclusions instead emphasise that baseline stress predicted change in end-exercise dyspnea, a model not described in the Methods, from a stepwise procedure in 32 patients explaining 13.5% of variance. This is a hypothesis-generating result, not a basis for clinical recommendations about addressing stress.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry prespecifying baseline stress as a predictor of dyspnea change.

quotes.text: Multiple linear regression (stepwise) was used to determine whether baseline stress was a determinant of 6MWT improvement in the two study groups.
Analysis of the change in 6MWD revealed no correlation with the initial values.
the finding that baseline stress level was a significant predictor of changes in endexercise dyspnea highlights the importance

issues.title: About ten outcomes tested at alpha = 0.05 with no correction; VR stress p = 0.015 and dyspnea p = 0.033 would not survive
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports pre-post and between-group tests for about ten outcomes, each at a nominal 0.05 level, with no correction or hierarchy among the three stated primary outcome domains. The 6MWT result is robust, but the stress and dyspnea within-group findings in the VR arm are borderline and would not remain significant after a correction. Because the stress claim already rests on within-group change only (see c7), this weakens it further.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or correction method for the secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: The statistical significance level was set at α = 0.05.
The analysis of the stress level showed a statistically significant improvement in both groups (CG: p < 0.004; VR: p < 0.015)

issues.title: Registered primary outcomes (anxiety/depression, quality of life) unreported; 6MWT not in registered primary list
issues.explanation: The current registry entry lists five primary outcomes, including anxiety and depression and quality of life, which the paper does not report at all. The paper's headline outcome, 6MWT distance, is not among the registered primary measures, and dyspnea is registered but presented as part of the 6MWT. This may reflect partial reporting of an ongoing trial or a registry entry that was updated. The paper does not explain the difference, so a reader cannot rule out selective reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing 6MWT was registered as a primary or secondary outcome from the start and a statement that anxiety/depression and quality of life will be reported separately.

quotes.text: Primary outcomes included analysis of lung function, exercise performance and stress level.
registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05244135)

issues.title: Table 2 total-column percentages wrong: 20/32 printed 68.75 (62.5), 4/32 printed 1.50 (12.5), 21/32 printed 65.25
issues.explanation: Several percentages in the Total column of Table 2 do not match their own counts over n = 32. Female is printed 68.75% where 20/32 is 62.5%, so the Female and Male percentages sum to 106.25%. Divorced is printed 1.50% where 4/32 is 12.5%, and 'Professionally active' 21 is printed 65.25% (with Retirement 34.75%) where 21/32 is 65.63% and 11/32 is 34.38%. These are baseline-table slips that change no efficacy result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or errata showing the printed values were typographical, or a different denominator for these rows.

quotes.location: Table 2, Marital status, Divorced, Total column
Table 2, Current employment status, Professionally active, Total column

script.explanation: 20/32 = 62.50%, but the paper prints 68.75, outside the rounding interval [68.75, 68.76]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 29.1 rather than 32.

issues.title: Table 2 'Married' total 27 exceeds VR 16 + control 9 = 25; marital totals sum to 34, not 32
issues.explanation: The Total column for married participants (27) is not the sum of the two arms (16 + 9 = 25). The four marital categories in the Total column add to 34, more than the 32 participants. The arm columns each sum to their arm size, so the total should have been 25 (78.1%). This is a baseline-table error that does not touch the outcome analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level data showing 27 married participants (which would break the arm columns).

issues.title: 1:1 randomisation yields 18 VR vs 14 control; no participant flow or explanation of the split
issues.explanation: The Methods describe 1:1 randomisation, yet Table 2 shows 18 VR and 14 control participants. A chance imbalance of this size is plausible with simple randomisation, but without a flow diagram readers cannot tell whether anyone was excluded or dropped after allocation. The sample is also described as 'preliminary' of an ongoing project, with no account of how these 32 were selected from the intended larger enrolment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow diagram showing allocation of 18 and 14 with no post-randomisation exclusions.

quotes.text: Randomization was performed using the Research Randomizer (ratio 1:1)
VR group ( n = 18)
Control group ( n = 14)

issues.title: Text says spirometry unchanged/improved, but VR FEV1 %VC fell 84.3 to 81.4 (within-group p = 0.028)
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion say lung function showed a non-significant improvement and that the programme did not change spirometric values. Table 3 shows a nominally significant within-group fall in FEV1 %VC in the VR arm (p = 0.028), and the VR arm's value moves in the opposite direction from the control arm (82.4 to 83.2). With nine lung-function tests and a between-group p of 0.100 this may be chance, but the text should have said it. It is a secondary result and does not change the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified multiplicity adjustment or a note in the paper that the FEV1 %VC fall is chance and not clinically relevant.

quotes.text: The results also showed that the program did not change spirometric values.
non-statistically significant improvement after the completion of the rehabilitation program

10.3389/fpubh.2025.1688592.headline_claim: The multimodal MICOM day clinic, including whole-body hyperthermia, is a promising approach that could help alleviate fatigue, improve well-being and enhance self-efficacy in Post-COVID syndrome.
10.3389/fpubh.2025.1688592.overall: The descriptive qualitative findings (symptom burden, dissatisfaction with GP care, perceived changes) are reasonable as participants' perspectives. The efficacy and WBH-benefit statements go beyond an interview-only, single-arm, retrospective design and should be read as perceived effects, pending the separately published RCT results. Two small participant-descriptor inconsistencies (age, working hours for P 2) do not affect the findings.

primary_outcome.name: Not reported in this paper; the RCT's quantitative primary outcome is said to be published separately (fatigue measured by MFI-20 at weeks 0 and 12)

issues.title: Interviews of 20 intervention participants only are used to claim 'demonstrating the efficacy' of the programme
issues.explanation: The data are post-programme telephone interviews with the 20 intervention-arm participants; the waiting control group was not interviewed and no outcome data are shown here. Participants' perceived improvements (11 of 20 reported symptom improvement) cannot show efficacy, since they are subject to expectation, recall and social-desirability effects and have no comparison. The Discussion nevertheless states efficacy was demonstrated and that the programme 'can improve symptoms', and the limitations section does not name the missing control as a limitation. Efficacy claims should wait for the separately reported RCT.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled quantitative RCT results in the same paper showing a between-group benefit, or efficacy wording being limited to participants' perceptions.

quotes.text: The integrative day clinic suggests a holistic approach for addressing Post-COVID syndrome, demonstrating the efficacy of the concept aimed at enhancing self-efficacy and self-care.
Therefore, only the intervention group was interviewed.
it is unclear whether the changes in symptoms and attitudes or lifestyle mentioned show long-term effects

second_reader.what_stands: True: the sentence 'demonstrating the efficacy of the concept' in 4.3 rests only on interviews with the 20 intervention participants, with no control-group data and no quantitative outcomes in this paper, so self-reported, uncontrolled, short-term accounts cannot demonstrate efficacy. Narrower and fairer: the paper labels itself a qualitative sub-study, includes limitations on generalisability, short follow-up, recall bias and attribution, and elsewhere uses weaker wording ('seems to be a promising approach', 'could help'); the efficacy claim is also scoped to self-efficacy and self-care, whic

issues.title: WBH 'additional therapeutic benefits for the majority' rests on 14/20 retrospective reports without comparator
issues.explanation: The closing Discussion states that WBH appears to provide additional therapeutic benefits for most patients. The only support is that 14 of 20 retrospectively reported positive effects, while 3 reported none and 3 reported deterioration. WBH was given inside a multimodal package, so its separate contribution cannot be identified, as the authors' own limitations and the call for a WBH RCT acknowledge. The wording is hedged ('appears') but 'additional benefit' goes beyond what the design can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A WBH-versus-no-WBH comparison within the trial showing benefit, or rewording as participants' perceptions only.

quotes.text: Using WBH appears to provide additional therapeutic benefits for the majority of patients.
the majority (14 out of 20) retrospectively reported <italic>positive effects</italic>
effects cannot be attributed to individual therapy modules

issues.title: P 2 works 'four hours' in interview but Table 2 lists 30 h/week
issues.explanation: P 2's quotation says they only work four hours, whereas Table 2 records patient 02 as currently working 30 h/week after starting reintegration 6 weeks ago. The units and timing of the quote are not given, so it may refer to daily hours or an earlier stage, but the paper does not reconcile them. This is a small descriptive inconsistency that does not affect the qualitative themes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that the quote refers to daily hours or an earlier time point and Table 2 is correct.

quotes.text: because I only work four hours
Start of reintegration process 6 weeks ago, currently working 30 h/week

issues.title: P 2 age printed as 51 in quotation but 50 in Table 2 (patient 02)
issues.explanation: The interview excerpt attributed to P 2 labels the participant as 51 years old, while Table 2 lists patient 02 (male) at age 50 at the time of interview. This is a minor internal inconsistency in participant descriptors. Nothing in the findings depends on it, though it may indicate imprecise labelling of quotations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that quotation labels use age at a different date than Table 2.

quotes.text: (P 2, male, 51 years)

10.3389/fresc.2022.1093871.headline_claim: Multimodal rehabilitation is helpful and safe for post-COVID patients, who benefit significantly from inpatient rehabilitation.
10.3389/fresc.2022.1093871.overall: The descriptive findings (post-COVID patients are less psychologically burdened than the other groups and improve on several scales and the 6MWT during a five-week stay) are plausible. However, the 'benefit significantly' and 'safe' conclusions are not supported by an uncontrolled retrospective design with no adverse-event data and incomplete 6MWT data, as the authors partly concede. The numeric slips are minor..

primary_outcome.name: BDI-II and HEALTH-49 symptom scores, change from admission to discharge (no primary outcome designated)

issues.title: Admission-to-discharge change in uncontrolled groups presented as significant rehabilitation benefit
issues.explanation: Benefit is inferred from within-group change over about five weeks with no untreated control. Natural recovery, regression to the mean and time effects cannot be separated from treatment, as the authors themselves say in the limitations. The Summary and Conclusion nevertheless state that patients 'benefit significantly' and 'improve significantly', and the post-COVID 6MWT gain has no comparator at all. The data support a description of improvement during a stay, not of treatment benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waiting-list control group, or natural-course data for post-COVID patients showing smaller spontaneous improvement over five weeks.

quotes.text: Thus, causal statements on the actual effectiveness of rehabilitation are not possible.
In conclusion it can be stated that patients with post-COVID syndrome benefit significantly from rehabilitation.
patients with post-COVID-syndrome improve significantly during the stay in rehabilitation.

second_reader.what_stands: The evidence for benefit is solely admission-to-discharge change in uncontrolled groups, and the Summary ('benefit significantly from rehabilitation') and Conclusion ('improve significantly') use effect-attributing wording despite the paper's own limitation that causal statements on effectiveness are not possible and natural recovery cannot be excluded. The Conclusion's 'improve significantly during the stay' is closer to descriptive, and the limitations are disclosed, so the problem is the inconsistency between hedged limitations and the unhedged 'benefit' claim in the Summary, not concealmen

issues.title: Safety conclusion rests on no adverse event reporting and 6MWT data for only 39 of 51 patients
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that rehabilitation is 'safe' and that there was no post-exercise malaise or deterioration. The paper reports no adverse events, no symptom monitoring after exertion and no reasons why 12 post-COVID patients lack comparable 6MWT data. 'Not a single patient deteriorated' applies to the 39 with data, who may differ from the 12 without. A small, uncontrolled, short-term sample cannot rule out less frequent harms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Systematic adverse-event and post-exertional symptom data for all 51 patients, and an explanation showing the 12 missing 6MWTs were unrelated to health deterioration.

quotes.text: In the 6MWT out of 51 post-COVID patients, comparable data could be used in 39 cases (76%).
In summary of the results it can be assumed that multimodal rehabilitation is not only helpful, but also safe for post-COVID patients.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that rehabilitation is 'safe' rests on absence of deterioration in 6MWT (39 of 51, 76%), activity/participation (46 of 51) and self-reported scales, with no systematic adverse-event reporting, dropout accounting, or explanation for the 12 patients without comparable 6MWT data, so those who might have deteriorated or left early are not visible. The paper does examine post-exercise malaise indicators, so the safety claim is not unsupported, but it is broader than what the sample (n=51, no control) and the unreported adverse events can establish.

issues.title: Conclusion attributes discharge work inability to cognitive deficits that were not recorded
issues.explanation: Conclusion point 4 says about 50% of post-COVID patients were discharged unable to work 'mainly due to persistent cognitive deficits'. The limitations state that neurocognitive disorders were not systematically recorded, and no data on reasons for work inability are shown. Table 1 also gives 35.3% able to work at discharge (about 65% not), and 47.1% total return to work (about 53% not), so the 'about 50%' is only loosely tied to the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Recorded neurocognitive assessments linking cognitive deficits to the work-ability decisions at discharge.

quotes.text: about 50% of post-COVID patients were discharged unable to work, mainly due to persistent cognitive deficits.
In this study, neurocognitive disorders were not yet systematically recorded

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; about 50 patients per group with strong efficacy wording
issues.explanation: Each group has about 50 patients and no power calculation is given, and the conclusions describe 'strong' improvement. Within-group effects are large, so statistical power is less of a concern than precision and generalisability of the group comparisons. The authors acknowledge the small samples.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size justification or confidence intervals showing adequate precision for the group comparisons.

quotes.text: Second, there is a relatively small sample sizes with 51 post-COVID patients, compared to 50 psychocardiological patients and 49 psychosomatic patients.

issues.title: Groups matched only on gender; baseline differences not adjusted when comparing improvement
issues.explanation: The three subsamples differ at baseline in marital status, prior outpatient psychotherapy, education and admission symptom levels, and only gender was matched. The cross-sectional 'lower burden' finding is largely descriptive. The statement that post-COVID patients benefit 'in the same way' as the others compares changes from different starting points without stated adjustment, so it is only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses of change adjusted for baseline score and the Table 1 covariates showing the same group pattern.

quotes.text: Due to the significantly higher risk of developing post-COVID in women, case-control matching for gender was performed.
Post-COVID patients in inpatient rehabilitation show a lower psychological burden than psychosomatic or psychocardiological patients

issues.title: Text gives 52.32 (SD 9.16) as post-COVID age; Table 1 shows 51.29 (9.89); 52.32 is the pooled mean
issues.explanation: The Results sentence attributes a mean age of 52.32 years to the post-COVID subgroup, but Table 1 gives 51.29 for that group. The sample-size-weighted mean of the three Table 1 columns is 52.32, so the text number appears to describe all 150 matched patients. A separate sentence also gives 51.95 (SD 9.89) for the 'matched sample', so the age figures in the text are not internally consistent. No conclusion depends on this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 52.32 figure refers to the pooled sample, or Table 1 being corrected to 52.32.

quotes.text: In the post-COVID subgroup the average age was 52.32 years (SD = 9.16).

quotes.location: Table 1, Mean age (SD) row, Post-COVID column

issues.title: Social stress cited as a discharge difference though Methods say it is not reported and Table 2 omits it
issues.explanation: The Methods state that HEALTH-49 social support and social stress results are not reported. The Results nevertheless say that post-COVID patients were less burdened at discharge on social stress. No data for this scale appear in Table 2, so the statement is unverifiable and contradicts the stated reporting scope.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Table 2 row or supplement showing social stress results, or a correction of the sentence.

quotes.text: Results of the HEALTH-49 scales social support and social stress are therefore not reported.
exept for HEALTH-49 phobia, interactionel difficulties and social stress.

10.3389/fresc.2024.1411344.headline_claim: Resonant breathing via the Meo Health online program is feasible and beneficial for self-reported symptoms and wellbeing in people with Long COVID, and warrants larger prospective controlled studies.
10.3389/fresc.2024.1411344.overall: The data show self-reported improvement over time in a self-selected, uncontrolled group of completers, and the Conclusion's wording ('potential') is appropriately modest. They cannot attribute the changes to resonant breathing or support the autonomic-mechanism claim. One table row (anxiety) has an unreconciled printed difference, which does not change the overall picture.

primary_outcome.name: Self-reported symptoms and wellbeing (Likert 1–5 survey items, baseline vs follow-up)

issues.title: Uncontrolled retrospective before-after data (n = 99) used to infer benefit; no comparison group or between-group test
issues.explanation: All 99 participants received the program and are compared only with their own baseline, using paired within-person tests. Any change over a median of 95 days could reflect natural course, other treatments, regression to the mean or placebo/expectancy, so the data cannot show the program caused the improvements. The paper hedges its conclusion, but the Discussion still treats the changes as 'positive outcomes' supporting a mechanism. This also covers the candidate about within-group inference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group with a between-group comparison, or evidence that the paired changes exceed expected natural change.

quotes.text: with no prospective study design or control group
Other therapies being used were not considered and therefore could not be controlled for in the analysis

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a retrospective single-arm before-after analysis of 99 completers, with no comparison group and no between-group test; the authors state this limitation and call for controlled studies. Despite the hedged wording, the Discussion and Conclusion still infer possible benefit and a mechanism from these uncontrolled data.

issues.title: Anxiety row: means 3.62 → 2.66 imply −0.96, but the printed mean difference and CI centre on −0.61
issues.explanation: In Table 1 the anxiety baseline and follow-up means differ by 0.96, yet the mean difference is printed as −0.61 and its CI is centred on −0.61. Every other row reconciles within rounding, so one of the anxiety means (probably the baseline) or the difference is misprinted. The direction of the anxiety improvement is unaffected, but the reported size is uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 or the raw data showing the anxiety means are consistent with a −0.61 paired difference.

quotes.location: Table 1, Anxiety row, Mean diff. column

issues.title: All outcomes are single-item 1–5 ratings from a vendor-designed survey, unvalidated and unblinded
issues.explanation: Symptoms and wellbeing were measured with single 1–5 items from a survey created by the program provider, with no validation or reliability data. Participants knew they were receiving the program and rated themselves, so expectancy can move the scores. Percentage changes on a 5-point scale (e.g. 61.8% with SD 96.0%) are also hard to interpret.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of the survey items, or concordant results on validated instruments.

quotes.text: A survey designed for the program by Meo Health was administered prior to commencement
self-reported symptoms and wellbeing on a Likert scale (1–5, 1 = Very low, 5 = Very high)

issues.title: Completers-only sample (n = 99) with the number of starters and dropouts not reported
issues.explanation: Only people who finished at least 4 weeks and both surveys were analysed, and the paper gives no count of those who enrolled or left. If non-responders or those who felt worse dropped out, the improvements are overstated. The size of the bias cannot be judged from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow count showing few dropouts, or baseline comparison of completers with non-completers.

quotes.text: Participants were included in the analysis if they completed at least 4 weeks of the Meo Health program and completed both baseline and follow up surveys.

issues.title: Discussion says results support an autonomic-function mechanism although no autonomic measures were collected
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that the symptom improvements support improved autonomic function as the mechanism, yet the paper collected only self-reported ratings and says objective autonomic measures were beyond its scope. The Discussion also reads the link between weekly use and stress control as showing the need for consistency in practice, which an uncontrolled correlation cannot show. The final Conclusion is appropriately cautious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Objective autonomic data (e.g. HRV) collected in the same participants showing change.

quotes.text: support the hypothesis of improved autonomic function as the possible mechanism
Obtaining objective measures of autonomic function was also beyond the scope of this study

issues.title: Data from the vendor's own survey; author with prior vendor advisory role credited with formal analysis
issues.explanation: The evaluated program and its survey belong to a company with which one author previously held an advisory role, and that author is credited with formal analysis. The tie is declared, and the paper reports no funding. The paper does not describe who extracted or analysed the data or whether the company reviewed the manuscript.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the analysis was done independently of the company, with no vendor input on analysis or reporting.

quotes.text: JW previously held a non-financial advisory role with Stasis HP.
JW: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal Analysis, Methodology

issues.title: Stress p = 0.0389 exceeds the stated Bonferroni alpha of 0.0056 but stress is cited as an improvement
issues.explanation: The Methods set a corrected alpha of 0.0056 for 9 t-tests, and the p column footnote says Bonferroni was applied. Stress, with p = 0.0389, does not meet that threshold, yet the Discussion lists stress among the outcomes that improved and the '89% improved' statement counts it. Whether the printed p-values are raw or adjusted is also unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that p = 0.0389 is a raw value and that stress is not claimed as a significant improvement.

quotes.location: Table 1, Stress row, Mean diff. column
