10.3389/fresc.2025.1588940.headline_claim: Both a spa-resort and a home-based balance rehabilitation programme improved balance in Long Covid, with the home-based programme improving faster and the spa-resort programme giving more gradual, sustained gains.
10.3389/fresc.2025.1588940.overall: The headline claim that both programmes improved balance, with the home programme acting faster and the spa programme more durably, is only weakly supported: it rests on a handful of nominally significant terms from many uncorrected tests in a completer-only analysis with no untreated comparator and no within-group result for the spa arm. The numerical slips (sample sizes, text-table mismatches) are minor, but the 'sustained benefit' conclusion exceeds the evidence and should be treated as a hypothesis.

primary_outcome.name: Centre-of-pressure sway parameters with eyes closed (SD OAP and mean stay time ST), T0 to T1 and T1 to T2; no single primary outcome is labelled

issues.title: 'Both programmes improved balance' is not supported: no within-group result for the spa arm, no untreated comparator
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say both programmes improved balance-related parameters. The only significant within-group time effects reported (SD OAP decreasing, ST increasing) are for Group B. For Group A, no change estimate is given, and the only significant between-group terms either favour Group B (ST at T1) or are relative to B (SD OAP T1-T2). The design also has no untreated arm, so even real within-group change could reflect time, familiarisation with the test, or regression to the mean.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported within-group estimates for Group A showing a significant improvement, and a comparison against an untreated or usual-care control.

quotes.text: Both the spa resort and home-based rehabilitation programs resulted in improvements in balancerelated parameters, with each approach yielding distinct outcomes.
A signi fi cant and positive Time effect in ST values, suggesting an increase in the value of mean stay time from T0 to T1 for Group B;
quotes.location: Results, list of post hoc findings

second_reader.what_stands: Only Group B has a reported significant within-group improvement (T0 to T1, EC condition, SD OAP and ST). For the spa arm the implied T0 to T1 changes are near zero, and no within-group test or confidence interval is reported. With no untreated comparator, the statement that both programmes improved balance is not supported by the paper's results. Because the extracted tables lost some signs, the Group A figures above are inferred.

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 44 of 60 randomised analysed (26.7% lost), unequal losses, no ITT
issues.explanation: Sixteen of 60 randomised participants are not in the analysis, 9 from the spa arm and 7 from the home arm, and all five who dropped out after T0 were in the home arm. Only participants with usable data at each pair of time points are analysed (N = 44, then 34-35), and no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is given. Differential losses mean the between-group comparisons may reflect who completed rather than the programmes themselves.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or multiple-imputation analysis giving the same results, or evidence that the excluded participants had similar baseline characteristics across arms.

quotes.text: Five of the subjects recruited (all from Group B) participated in only one session (T0) and were therefore considered dropouts.
Therefore, twenty-one subjects for Group A and twenty-three subjects from Group B were considered for further analysis.
Data from T3 were not considered in the statistical analyses due to the substantial attrition.

second_reader.what_stands: Only 44 of 60 randomised participants (26.7% excluded) entered the analysis, with different exclusion counts per arm (9 vs 7) and no intention-to-treat analysis. Most exclusions were for technical or compliance reasons rather than true dropout. The paper also gives inconsistent analysed numbers (Group B n = 22 vs 23; Figure 3 n = 47).

issues.title: 'Sustained' spa benefit rests on one uncorrected interaction (b = -1.826, N = 34) among many tests
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state that the spa programme led to more gradual and sustained improvement, but the only support is a single significant time:Group term for SD OAP between T1 and T2 in the eyes-closed condition. About 16 parameter-condition models were fitted per time window, all at alpha 0.05 with no multiplicity correction and no designated primary outcome, so one significant term is within what chance would produce. Follow-up beyond 3 months was dropped, so 'sustained' is not tested. The authors' own Discussion calls for longer follow-up, yet the Conclusions and Abstract do not carry that caution.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and analysis plan naming SD OAP at T2, or the effect surviving multiplicity correction and replicated at 6 months.

quotes.text: The home-based program showed more rapid improvements, while the spa resort program led to more gradual and sustained improvements in postural stability.
Data from T3 were not considered in the statistical analyses due to the substantial attrition.
using alpha = 0.05.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of sustained spa benefit rests on one significant interaction (SD OAP, EC, b = -1.826, N = 34) among about 16 T1 to T2 tests, with no multiplicity correction and with T3 data excluded. That is about what chance would produce (0.8 expected at alpha 0.05). The paper also does not test Group A's change from baseline. The authors hedge this as a hypothesis in the Discussion, but the Conclusions state it as established.

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a randomised trial recruited January-April 2023
issues.explanation: The paper describes a randomised trial of two programmes, with ethics approval but no registry name or identifier. Without registration, the outcomes and analyses cannot be compared against a prespecified plan, which matters given the many outcomes tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (with identifier and prespecified outcomes) dated before the first enrolment.

quotes.text: Recruitment took place from January 2023 to April 2023.
received approval from the Ethics Committee of Azienda Ospedale Università Padova (359n/AO/23)

issues.title: Text claims on significance and EO-to-EC direction contradict Tables 2 and 4
issues.explanation: The Results say significant effects in EC occurred only for SD OAP and ST, but Table 4 stars Group for SA, Time for AE and Time for SD, plus SD OAP Group, none of which the text lists. The Results also say that all parameters rose from EO to EC at T0, yet mean stay time (ST) fell in both groups in Table 2. The table, not the text, appears to be the source data, so the narrative understates how many terms were nominally significant. This affects how the post hoc findings are summarised, not the data themselves.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text refers only to Time:Group interactions and the ST decrease is not counted as an 'increase' in the same sense; the ST row would still contradict 'all parameters increased'.

quotes.text: only in the EC condition and only for the SD OAP and ST parameters
Before treatment (T0), values of all parameters increased from the EO to the EC condition for both groups

issues.title: No sample-size calculation reported; 44 analysed of 60, with 'potential' framed cautiously in the Discussion
issues.explanation: The paper reports no power calculation, and only 44 participants were analysed for T0-T1 and 34-35 for T1-T2. The authors admit the number is limited and speak of 'potential', which is appropriately cautious. The problem is mainly that the Conclusions do not carry this caution.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry with a stated sample-size justification.

quotes.text: Even with a somewhat limited number of participants, results were able to highlight the potential of offering interventions to improve balance for Long Covid patients in non-hospital settings.

issues.title: Analysed sample sizes disagree: Group B n = 23 vs 22 (Table 2), and 47 in Figure 2 vs 44 in Table 4
issues.explanation: The Results and Figure 1 give 23 analysed participants in Group B, but the Table 2 header gives 22. The Figure 2 caption says the EC plots include 47 individuals, whereas the corresponding mixed-model tables use N = 44, which is also the total after exclusions. The paper does not say which count is correct, so the reader cannot tell who contributes to each table or figure. The conclusions do not depend on this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that one Group B participant lacked T0 data for Table 2, and that Figure 2 includes participants excluded from the models.

quotes.text: twenty-three subjects from Group B were considered for further analysis

quotes.location: Table 2, column header for Group B

quotes.text: The plots include values from n = 47 individuals.

10.3389/fresc.2026.1927300.headline_claim: Tailored individual follow-up was not more effective than a standard one-day group course in improving HRQoL (EQ-5D-5L index) in post-COVID-19 condition, and both CBT-based interventions were associated with improvements in several secondary outcomes.
10.3389/fresc.2026.1927300.overall: The null primary result (no superiority of individual follow-up over a one-day course) is broadly supported, though it comes from a small, possibly underpowered, unblinded trial, and the printed CI for the primary difference is internally wrong. The Abstract and Conclusions give prominence to uncontrolled within-group improvements across many untested-for-multiplicity outcomes, and these should be read as exploratory. The registered primary outcome differs from the reported one in the current registry record, which warrants checking against the protocol.

primary_outcome.name: EQ-5D-5L index score at 6 months

issues.title: Null superiority result read as 'no difference'/'suitable' despite acknowledged low power and wide CI
issues.explanation: The trial was powered for a superiority test and the authors concede it may have been underpowered. The wide uncertainty around the 0.07 difference (the MCID) cannot exclude a clinically relevant difference in either direction. The practical-implications text nevertheless suggests the one-day course is a suitable option, which needs equivalence-type evidence the study does not provide.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority or equivalence margin and analysis showing the CI lies within it.

quotes.text: underpowered to detect clinically meaningful differences between two interventions
Larger studies are needed to confirm these results.

issues.title: Uncontrolled within-group improvements and uncorrected multiple tests emphasised in Abstract and Conclusions
issues.explanation: Between-group differences were null on all outcomes, yet the Abstract and Conclusions highlight significant within-group improvements in fatigue, EQ-VAS, symptoms and neuropsychological tests. Without a no-treatment control these changes cannot be attributed to either intervention, as the authors themselves note elsewhere. Many outcomes and timepoints were tested with no stated multiplicity correction, so isolated within-group significances are more likely chance findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A multiplicity-adjusted analysis, or conclusions that clearly label the within-group changes as uncontrolled and hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: within both treatment groups
Given the limited sample size, the analyses were considered exploratory.

issues.title: Primary-outcome difference 0.07 lies outside its printed 95% CI [-0.18, 0.04]
issues.explanation: The reported score difference of 0.07 cannot be inside a CI of -0.18 to 0.04. The group means and CIs in Table 3 (0.75 vs 0.68) imply a difference of 0.07 with a CI of about -0.04 to 0.18, and a one-sided p near .11, matching the printed p. The printed interval therefore appears to be mis-stated (sign or bound error) in the headline result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the interval refers to a different contrast or scale, or corrected values showing the printed CI is correct.

script.explanation: the estimate 0.07 lies outside its own CI [-0.18, 0.04]

issues.title: Registry lists primary outcome 'Symptom reduction' at 3 months; paper reports EQ-5D-5L index at 6 months
issues.explanation: The ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT06085911) shows one primary outcome, symptom reduction at 3 months. The paper's primary outcome is the EQ-5D-5L index at 6 months, with symptom count treated as secondary. The paper refers to its protocol but does not say whether or when the primary outcome was changed, so a switch cannot be ruled out or confirmed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history or the published protocol showing EQ-5D-5L at 6 months was the primary outcome before enrolment.

quotes.text: For more details, see the protocol (24).

issues.title: Table 2 gender coefficient 0.009 (SE 0.05) printed with p = .11; implied p about .86
issues.explanation: A coefficient of 0.009 with SE 0.05 and CI -0.09 to 0.11 is nowhere near significance and implies a p of about .86. The printed p of .11 is inconsistent with the coefficient and its own interval. The error does not change the conclusion (no gender effect) but is a reporting mistake in the adjusted model table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or output showing p = .11 is right for this coefficient.

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.8600 (reachable range [0.7727, 0.9405] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.11 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Complete-case analyses only; unbalanced neuropsychology losses (8 vs 2 of 10) in secondary outcomes
issues.explanation: The primary analysis excluded only 2 of 60 participants, so the label 'per-protocol' changes little for the primary null result. For secondary outcomes, missing data were simply excluded. Neuropsychological follow-up was 50/60, with 8 of the 10 losses in the intervention arm, so within- and between-group neuropsychological comparisons rest on unbalanced completers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis with imputation or ITT showing the same secondary and neuropsychological results.

quotes.text: only  per-protocol  analyses  were  performed.

issues.title: Safety inferred from no reported adverse events in a 60-participant trial with unspecified AE ascertainment
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the treatments appear safe because no adverse events were reported. The Methods say only that adverse events were 'recorded', with no definition or systematic method. In a small trial the absence of reports gives little reassurance, particularly as post-exertional malaise was not examined.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described systematic adverse-event ascertainment procedure, with a confidence bound showing the safety claim is supported.

quotes.text: suggesting that the treatments are safe for patients with PCC

10.3389/fresc.2026.1946566.headline_claim: Health resort-based and home-based rehabilitation are both effective for post-COVID-19 syndrome, with the health resort option providing additional benefits.
10.3389/fresc.2026.1946566.overall: The finding that both programmes were followed by improvement is plausible, but without an untreated control it cannot be called effectiveness, and the claim of additional benefit from the Health Resort rests on a small number of uncorrected interactions, differential loss of Group B participants and retrospective registration. The abstract also misstates the primary outcome and pain results as 'comparable', and the Discussion misdescribes baseline anxiety and depression. Treat the conclusions as exploratory.

issues.title: 'Both effective' and 'additional benefits' conclusions exceed a pilot with no untreated control or sample-size basis
issues.explanation: The conclusion states both rehabilitation modalities are effective and the Health Resort option adds benefit, yet the design has no no-treatment arm, no sample-size calculation, heavy differential attrition and uncorrected multiple comparisons. Pre-post improvements cannot show effectiveness without a control, and the between-group result for the primary outcome appears at one time point only. The study supports hypothesis generation rather than the confident conclusions in the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A usual-care or waitlist control arm, or a pre-specified powered comparison of the two programmes on the primary outcome.

quotes.text: with the Health Resort-based rehabilitation option providing additional benefits.
effective modalities of care delivery for Post-COVID-19 syndrome management
recruitment was based on the number of eligible participants available during the study period.

second_reader.what_stands: Without an untreated control arm the paper cannot show that either programme is 'effective'; the within-group changes could partly reflect natural recovery. 'Additional benefits' of the Health Resort option rests on a small pilot with no sample-size basis, uncorrected multiple tests, attrition concentrated in the home arm, baseline imbalances, and a bundle of differences between the arms. The Abstract Conclusions are stronger than the pilot design supports, although the Methods and Discussion do describe the work as exploratory.

issues.title: Differential attrition: 8 of 33 Group B excluded after randomisation; 15 of 33 remain at 3 and 6 months vs 31 of 33 in A
issues.explanation: Eight Group B participants were excluded before analysis and a further 10 were lost by 3 months, so only 15 of 33 randomised Group B participants have 3- and 6-month data, against 31 of 33 in Group A. The analysis is a completers-style mixed model with no ITT or sensitivity analysis. The 6-month between-group differences, including the primary outcome's only significant interaction, rest mainly on 15 Group B participants who may differ systematically from those lost. This weakens the follow-up comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (multiple imputation or ITT) showing the same between-group results with all randomised participants.

quotes.text: 25 at T0 and T1, 15 at T2 and T3 for Group B
8 individuals were lost to follow-up before completion of treatment

second_reader.what_stands: All 8 post-randomisation exclusions and the 10 later losses are in Group B, leaving 15 of 33 (45%) at 3 and 6 months against 31 of 33 (94%) in Group A. The analysis is not intention-to-treat, and the large imbalance in attrition between arms limits the between-group comparisons at the follow-up points. The paper gives no sensitivity analysis for this.

issues.title: About 36 uncorrected between-group interaction tests; most headline differences have p between 0.011 and 0.047
issues.explanation: Roughly a dozen outcomes were each tested at three time points for group differences with no multiplicity control, while within-group contrasts were Holm-adjusted. Several of the differences the abstract reports (hand grip, anxiety, pain) rest on interaction p-values of 0.017-0.047 that would not survive even a modest correction. With this many tests, a few such results are expected by chance, so the claim of additional benefit is tentative apart from the dyspnea score at T1.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or adjusted p-values still showing significance for grip, anxiety and pain.

quotes.text: No  multiplicity  adjustment  was applied across the between-group tests for the different outcome measures.

quotes.location: Table 3, Hand Grip Dx row, T3:group column

second_reader.what_stands: There are about 39 uncorrected between-group interaction tests, and the paper says no multiplicity adjustment was applied across them. Most of the 10 nominally significant ones (8 of 10) lie between p = 0.011 and 0.047, which is close to what chance alone could produce among that many tests. Only the BDS T1 result is clearly robust to a conservative correction. The authors do acknowledge the exploratory design and multiple outcomes.

issues.title: Abstract calls QoL and pain gains 'comparable' though PCS-12 (p=0.004) and NRS (p=0.039) T3 interactions favour Group A
issues.explanation: The abstract says both groups had comparable improvements in pain and quality of life. Table 3 shows significant time x group interactions at 6 months for the primary outcome PCS-12 (p = 0.004) and for NRS pain (p = 0.039), both favouring the Health Resort group. The abstract therefore misreports the primary outcome result and understates the between-group findings it otherwise uses to claim 'additional benefits'. Because it says 'comparable' for the primary outcome, readers of the abstract get the wrong picture of the one pre-specified primary comparison. Duplicate c2 (pain) is covered here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract or errata wording stating that the primary PCS-12 outcome and pain differed at 6 months between groups.

quotes.text: Both groups showed comparable improvements in fatigue, pain,

issues.title: Discussion says Group A had lower baseline anxiety/depression; Table 3 shows higher (BAI +11.65, BDI +8.25)
issues.explanation: The Discussion claims Group A had significantly lower baseline anxiety, depression and fatigue, but Table 3 coding (Group A = 1) and Table 2 show the reverse for anxiety and depression, and no difference for fatigue. The imbalance is real and sizeable, and the models adjust only for age and hospitalisation, not baseline symptom level. Greater improvement in anxiety and depression in the group that started with worse scores may partly reflect regression to the mean rather than treatment. The abstract's anxiety claim is therefore less secure than stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that Group A was coded 0 for these models or that the BAI/BDI scale direction is reversed, which the Methods contradict.

quotes.text: Interestingly, at baseline Group A exhibited significantly lower anxiety, depression, and fatigue than Group B.

issues.title: Registered 2024-04-18 after treatment ended (Dec 2023); seven registered primaries vs one primary in paper
issues.explanation: The paper reports registration without a date, and the registry shows it happened after all treatment cohorts finished, so the registered outcomes cannot be taken as a prospective plan. The registry lists seven primary outcomes while the paper designates only the SF-12 physical component as primary; the abstract's headline benefits are in outcomes the paper treats as secondary. This limits confidence that the reported emphasis was pre-specified, though the PCS-12 choice is compatible with the registered 'SF-12'. Duplicate c11 is covered here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing an earlier prospective version naming PCS-12 as the sole primary outcome.

quotes.text: ClinicalTrials.gov under Identifier NCT06379737
Short Form Health Survey (SF-12) physical component

issues.title: Table 4 BDS Group B 5.09 (-0.42, 10.60) paired with unadjusted p=0.027; CI seems adjusted but unlabelled
issues.explanation: The Table 4 CI includes zero while its unadjusted p is 0.027, and Table 3 gives a CI excluding zero for the same estimate. The pattern across Table 4 suggests the CIs are adjusted for multiplicity but sit beside unadjusted p-values without saying so. This is a labelling ambiguity that may mislead a reader about which contrasts are significant; it changes no main conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table note stating that Table 4 CIs are Holm- or simultaneity-adjusted.

10.3389/fspor.2022.877188.headline_claim: Telerehabilitation (tele-R) with therapeutic education is a viable, efficacious alternative to face-to-face rehabilitation for post-COVID fatigue, with improved physical capacity and fatigue, without adverse events.
10.3389/fspor.2022.877188.overall: The data support only that fatigue and fitness measures were better after one month in both groups of a very small, non-randomized pilot; no efficacy of tele-rehabilitation, equivalence with face-to-face care, or safety can be concluded. The authors' pilot framing helps, but the discussion's wording of 'demonstrated benefits' and 'good alternative' goes beyond the evidence.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder Fatigue Score (CFS-11) change from baseline to 1 month

issues.title: Non-random allocation by equipment access and no untreated control; pre-post changes cannot be attributed
issues.explanation: Patients lacking equipment or internet were put in the comparison group, so the groups differ by access and possibly by socioeconomic status. Neither arm is untreated, so improvements over time (fatigue, VO2max and others) could reflect natural recovery after COVID, regression to the mean or practice effects. The study cannot show that either program caused the improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or randomised comparison group showing the same improvements attributable to the programs.

quotes.text: there was no randomization for tele-R and trad-R (the allocation was made arbitrarily based on a patient's sports and computer equipments)
we lack a control group without rehabilitation to compare changes over time and evaluate the interest of this early management for patients

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by equipment access (non-random) and there was no no-rehabilitation arm, and the authors say so in their limitations. Even so, the within-group pre-post changes cannot be attributed to rehabilitation, because spontaneous recovery is not separable, yet the Discussion still says early intervention 'can improve physical function and reduce fatigue'.

issues.title: Efficacy for fatigue and fitness inferred from within-group time effects without between-group differences
issues.explanation: The primary outcome (CFS-11) improved over time with no group difference, and the physical outcomes likewise show time effects but no time*group interaction. Time effects in an uncontrolled before-after design cannot show efficacy, yet the discussion says the pilot 'demonstrated benefits' and that exercise could be an effective solution for fatigue. The data show only that scores were lower after one month in both groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group or controlled analysis showing the change exceeds that expected without rehabilitation.

quotes.text: showing a significant time effect (p = 0.010) without a difference between groups.
Managing fatigue through exercise could be an effective solution for these patients with persistent symptoms.
this pilot study has demonstrated benefits of telerehabilitation on several parameters of physical capacities

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy statements for fatigue and fitness rest on within-group time effects with no between-group difference and no untreated comparator, so they do not show an effect of exercise. 'Demonstrated benefits' is stronger than a pilot with n = 9 and 6 and no control supports, although the fatigue statement is hedged with 'could be'.

issues.title: 'Good alternative' and safe conclusion drawn from 9 tele-R patients without non-inferiority design or safety monitoring data
issues.explanation: The conclusion presents tele-R as a good alternative to face-to-face rehabilitation and free of adverse events. With 9 tele-R and 6 trad-R patients, no equivalence margin, and no stated adverse-event ascertainment method, neither comparability nor safety can be established. A zero count in 9 patients is compatible with a substantial true event rate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified non-inferiority analysis with adequate sample and systematic adverse event surveillance.

quotes.text: seems to be a good alternative rehabilitation program when a face-to-face program is not possible
No adverse events were declared.

second_reader.what_stands: The 'good alternative' and 'without adverse events' conclusions come from 9 tele-R patients, with no non-inferiority or equivalence design, and with no described adverse event ascertainment beyond 'none declared'. The conclusion is hedged ('seems to be', 'in our sample') and some safety procedures are described, but the data cannot establish equivalence or safety.

issues.title: Pilot of 15 analysed (9 vs 6), no sample-size calculation; null group comparisons uninformative
issues.explanation: No sample-size calculation is reported and only 15 patients were analysed, with many outcomes tested. Absence of between-group differences cannot be read as equivalence of tele-R and trad-R, and the many time-effect p-values are unadjusted. The authors acknowledge the size but still draw positive conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample-size justification with adequate power for the equivalence or non-inferiority question.

quotes.text: Our pilot study presents limitations and the first is the reduced size of our sample.
The level of significance was set at p < 0.05.

issues.title: Trial registered 2022-02-10, about a year after study start (2021-02-01); not disclosed as retrospective
issues.explanation: The registry record was first submitted after recruitment ended, so the outcomes were not publicly fixed beforehand. The paper cites the registration without noting the timing. The current registered primary outcome matches the paper's, so no outcome switching is evident, and the risk is mainly of undisclosed flexibility among 6 secondary outcomes and many analyses.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier dated registry version predating recruitment with the same outcomes.

quotes.text: is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov
Patients were recruited from March to July 2021

issues.title: Intro calls fatigue most persistent at 53.1% while citing exercise capacity at 56.3%
issues.explanation: The introduction says fatigue is the symptom that mostly persists at 12 months (53.1%), but the same sentence lists reduced exercise capacity at 56.3%, which is higher. The statement is internally contradictory, though it concerns background literature and not the study's own results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The cited source (Seeßle et al.) reporting fatigue as the most frequent persistent symptom, with 56.3% attached to a different symptom in the list order.

quotes.text: it is always the fatigue that mostly persists (53.1%)
sleeping problems (56.3, 37.5, 39.6, and 26%, respectively

issues.title: Two of 8 trad-R patients (25%) lost; completers-only analysis of 15 of 17
issues.explanation: Both dropouts were in the comparison arm and only completers were analysed, with no reasons given. With such small numbers this could shift the trad-R means, but the loss is small overall and openly reported. It is a minor weakness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reasons for dropout unrelated to treatment or outcome and a sensitivity analysis imputing their data.

quotes.text: Two trad-R patients did not return for post-testing.

10.3389/fspor.2025.1549132.headline_claim: The 24-week multicomponent training program is effective in reducing fatigue, including mental fatigue, in individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2, though results were not superior to physical activity recommendations for functional capacity, body composition, and physical activity levels.
10.3389/fspor.2025.1549132.overall: The trial shows no ITT superiority on its primary outcome (6MWT), and its favourable results come from a small, asymmetrically defined per-protocol set and from within-group changes. The fatigue conclusion is the most defensible finding but is secondary, uncorrected for multiplicity, and the Abstract's mental-fatigue CI is internally inconsistent. The headline claim of effectiveness should be read as tentative and hypothesis-generating..

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance change

issues.title: Abstract concludes the program 'was effective in improving fatigue' on within-group changes, with no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: The fatigue result is the only favourable ITT finding, and the Abstract and Conclusion state it as effectiveness. It is a secondary outcome, among many tested without correction for multiple comparisons, and the mental fatigue CI printed in the Abstract does not contain its own estimate (see the separate issue). The physical fatigue domain improved in both groups. The conclusion should have been worded as a tentative signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified fatigue endpoint or a multiplicity-adjusted between-group test showing a robust effect.

quotes.text: This program was effective in improving fatigue in patients previously significantly affected by COVID-19.
We concluded that the 24-week multicomponent physical training is effective in reducing one of the most prevalent persistent symptoms

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract and conclusion state fatigue effectiveness without hedging, based on within-group improvements in IG and post-intervention group differences in some domains, with no multiplicity adjustment across the many secondary outcomes. Several of the printed CIs for these results are inconsistent with the quoted p-values, and some p-values are borderline (0.047). The paper does report some between-group post-intervention differences, so it is not purely within-group inference.

issues.title: Positive functional/body-composition claims rest on asymmetric PP sets (9 IG adherers vs 10-12 CG completers)
issues.explanation: On the primary 6MWT outcome the ITT analysis shows no superiority of the intervention. The favourable results come from a per-protocol set in which the IG is limited to the 9 participants attending at least 70% of sessions, while the CG includes everyone who was assessed. Adherence is related to prognosis and motivation, so PP differences cannot be attributed to the training. The Discussion's statement that high adherence 'brought greater benefits' is therefore a causal claim the design cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, symmetric PP definition or a CACE/instrumental-variable analysis that preserves randomisation and shows the same effect.

quotes.text: the patients  who  completed  at least  70%  of  the  proposed  sessions  in  the  IG  and  those  who attended  the  24-week  evaluations  in  the  CG  were  included

second_reader.what_stands: The positive PP findings (6MWT, TUG-m, body fat, visceral fat) come from sets of 9 IG adherers against 10-12 CG completers, built with different inclusion rules and with large baseline differences. The CG PP counts also fall short of the 14 implied completers, and the 9 versus 12 adherer figures are inconsistent. The authors acknowledge the small PP sample as a limitation but still describe the PP results as superiority.

issues.title: PP 6MWT 'superiority' of IG inferred from within-group change (p=0.001) and ES 0.61, not a between-group test
issues.explanation: The Results report that in the PP analysis 'only the IG improved', citing a CI and p that describe the IG's own change from baseline. The Discussion then reads the effect size of 0.61 as showing superiority of the IG and clinical relevance. The groups differed at baseline in the PP set, the CG also improved in the ITT analysis, and the 6MWT is not in Table 3 with a between-group interaction p. A significant change in one arm and a non-significant change in the other does not show a difference between the arms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported group-by-time interaction test for the PP 6MWT with p < 0.05 and adjustment for the baseline imbalance.

quotes.text: in the PP  analysis,  only  the  IG  improved  (ES:  0.61;  95%  CI:  50.6124.4; p = 0.001)
the moderate effect size (ES: 0.61) indicates superiority of the IG

second_reader.what_stands: The p = 0.001 and the CI are for the IG's within-group change, and the text reports no between-group test or CI for the PP 6MWT. The 'superiority' claim rests on a point-estimate effect size of 0.61 with no inferential support in the text (Figure 3 not seen), with a baseline imbalance and 9 IG participants. It is not true that ES 0.61 is purely a within-group figure.

issues.title: Mental fatigue CI (-0.5 to 3.5) does not contain the estimate (-1.7) and conflicts with p = 0.005
issues.explanation: The Abstract gives the ITT mental fatigue change for the IG as -1.7 points with a CI of -0.5 to 3.5, which excludes the estimate and spans zero. The Results print the same bounds with p = 0.005. The PP interval is also printed as -3.6 to 0.7 for an estimate of -2.0 with p = 0.017. A correctly reported interval for a significant reduction should lie entirely below zero, so the CI bounds appear to be misprinted. The results for the key fatigue claim therefore cannot be verified from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors' source tables showing the correct CI bounds (for example -3.5 to -0.5).

quotes.text: mental  fatigue  ( -1.7  points,  95%  CI: -0.5  to  3.5)

issues.title: Abstract says 6MWT improved in both ITT groups, but both within-group CIs include zero
issues.explanation: The Abstract states that the primary outcome improved in both groups in the ITT analysis. The printed intervals for both arms span zero, so neither change is shown to be distinguishable from no change in that analysis. The Results repeat the claim without giving a test statistic or p for the ITT 6MWT. This slightly overstates the primary outcome result in the paper's own favour, although the claim applies equally to both arms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported significant time effect for the ITT 6MWT (p < 0.05) in a table or figure.

issues.title: CG ITT 6MWT change printed as 37.4 m in Abstract but 32 m in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Abstract reports the control-group ITT change in 6-minute walk distance as 37.4 m (95% CI -5.26 to 80.2). The Discussion gives 32 m for the same group and analysis. The CI midpoint (about 37.4) supports the Abstract figure, so the Discussion value is likely wrong. Because this is the primary outcome, the discrepancy matters for how large the control improvement looks.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion figure is a different quantity, such as an unimputed or adjusted estimate, or a table giving 32 m.

quotes.text: (IG:  35 m;  CG:  32 m)

issues.title: 20% attrition (3/21 IG vs 5/19 CG) with ML imputation; pulmonary data in only 34 of 40
issues.explanation: Eight participants did not attend the 24-week assessment, and more were lost from the control group. Missing post-intervention data were imputed using a maximum likelihood approach whose assumptions (missing at random) are not discussed. Pulmonary outcomes were analysed in 34 participants, and a PP analysis was not possible. The loss is within the planned 30% allowance, so this is a moderate limitation, not a defect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (complete case or multiple imputation with a missing-not-at-random scenario) giving the same results.

quotes.text: three participants withdrew from  the IG, and five participants from  the  CG did not participate in the 24-week  evaluations
For  missing  post-intervention  data,  a  maximum  likelihood  estimate  was  used  for  imputation.

issues.title: Randomised 40 vs required 44 (target 60); null ITT results inconclusive, 32 completers
issues.explanation: The calculation required 22 per group (44), inflated to 60 for loss. Only 40 were randomised and 32 completed the 24-week assessments, so the trial is below its own required size. The ITT null result on the primary outcome and the many non-significant secondary outcomes cannot be read as showing no benefit, and the PP groups (9 vs 10-12) are very small. The shortfall is not discussed as a power problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power statement showing 80% power at the achieved sample size, or a precision-based argument.

quotes.text: the recruitment target was set at 30 participants per group
Thus, 40 participants were randomized, 21 in the IG and 19 in the CG.

issues.title: Results text gives 21 male + 18 female = 39 of 40; Abstract and Table 1 imply 19 women
issues.explanation: The Results sentence says the 40 participants were 21 male and 18 female, which sums to 39. The Abstract (19 women) and Table 1 (10 + 9 women) both give 19 women. This is a one-word typo in the Results text and does not affect any analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing needed; the typo is confirmed by Table 1, so only the text would need correcting.

quotes.text: Forty participants [age = 52.00 (12.93) years, 19 women]
of  the  40 participants  (21  male  and  18  female)

10.3389/fspor.2026.1797346.headline_claim: A 12-week tailored exercise regimen altered the plasma proteome of people with post-COVID condition, with the changes interpreted as improved vascular integrity and a balanced protease-antiprotease response.
10.3389/fspor.2026.1797346.overall: The headline claim that exercise drives distinct proteomic signatures and improves vascular regulation is not supported by the analysis. It rests on separate within-arm pre/post tests with no between-arm comparison, in a very small sample, and the control arm changed almost as much. The paper's own Discussion hedges this as proof-of-principle, so the data are best read as hypothesis-generating. The remaining problems are small inconsistencies in duration, counts and the stated significance criterion.

primary_outcome.name: Plasma proteins differentially expressed pre vs post intervention (adjusted p-value criterion), SomaScan 1,500-protein panel

issues.title: 'Exercise-specific' proteins (25 vs 11) come from separate within-arm pre/post tests, not an arm comparison
issues.explanation: Each arm is tested pre versus post, and proteins significant in only one arm are called exercise-specific or no-exercise-specific. Being significant in one arm and not the other does not show the arms differ, particularly with unequal and small groups. Many changes also occurred in the control arm, which points to time, batch or visit effects. The causal statement that exercise 'drives' distinct signatures is not supported by this analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A group-by-time interaction or direct between-arm comparison of change scores showing the 25 proteins differ significantly between arms.

quotes.text: This distribution demonstrates that exercise drives both activation and suppression of distinct proteomic signatures
Comparisons were made between post-exercise (PostE) and pre-exercise (PreE) samples and the no-intervention (no-exercise NE) groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The 25 'exercise-specific' and 11 'no-exercise-specific' proteins are set differences between two separate within-arm pre/post significance lists (Fig 2A Venn), not the result of a between-arm or group-by-time test, so 'specific' means only 'significant in one arm and not in the other'; this is a difference in significance status and does not show that exercise caused the difference. The paper's own statement that the arms are compared is loosely worded, and the Fig 1 counts (61 and 48 with 34 shared) do not reconcile with the Fig 2 counts (25 and 11 unique) without an explanation.

issues.title: Small pilot (15 vs 10), no sample-size calculation, with 1,500 proteins tested
issues.explanation: The study has 25 participants, no power calculation and 1,500 proteins tested. Individual protein findings are therefore fragile. The authors acknowledge this and call the work proof-of-principle, so the problem is mainly the stronger Results wording rather than the design alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a defensible pilot design whose limits are disclosed.

quotes.text: While it is not possible to come to definite conclusions from the observed differences, this study provides proof-of-principle
Some of the major limitations of this study is the small sample size

issues.title: 'Improved vascular integrity' inferred from GO enrichment of within-arm protein lists
issues.explanation: The Results conclude that enriched terms point to improved vascular integrity in exercising patients. No vascular function or integrity outcome was measured, and enrichment of terms does not indicate the direction of benefit. The protein lists also come from the within-arm analysis criticised in c4. This is a speculative interpretation presented as a result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Measured vascular or endothelial outcomes that improve with exercise relative to control.

quotes.text: These biological processes collectively point to improved regulation of vascular integrity in PCC individuals following the exercise intervention.

issues.title: Intervention length given as 8 weeks in Introduction but 12 weeks in Methods and Results
issues.explanation: The Introduction describes the earlier study of the same samples as an 8-week regimen. The Methods state 12 weeks of supervised training, and the Results state a 12-week interval between samples. Both cannot describe the same intervention, so one is a reporting error. It is probably a slip and does not alter any proteomic result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The earlier study's report showing a different 8-week exercise phase, with the samples here taken after 12 weeks.

quotes.text: an 8-week tailored exercise regimen in PCC patients
supervised training in the laboratory setting for 12 weeks in addition to standard care

issues.title: Figure 1 totals (61 exercise, 48 non-exercise) exceed Venn totals (59 and 45) for the same comparisons
issues.explanation: Figure 1 gives 61 changed proteins after exercise (45 up, 16 down) and 48 without exercise (41 up, 7 down). The Venn caption gives 34 shared plus 25 unique (59) for exercise and 34 plus 11 (45) for non-exercise. The 2 and 3 missing proteins are not accounted for, so the list behind the '25 exercise-specific' claim is not fully traceable. The gap is small, but the same count error would also affect the overlap percentages.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Figure 2 collapses duplicate or unmapped aptamers to unique gene symbols, reducing 61 to 59 and 48 to 45.

quotes.text: highlighting 45 upregulated and 16 downregulated proteins, with a donut plot summarizing 61 total changes
indicating 41 upregulated and 7 downregulated proteins, and a donut plot summarizing 48 changes
A total of 34 proteins (48.6%) overlapped between the two groups, while 25 proteins (35.7%) were unique to the exercise group and 11 proteins (15.7%) were unique to the non-exercise group.

issues.title: Differential-expression criterion printed as adjusted p > 0.05 but used as < 0.05 elsewhere
issues.explanation: The text defines differentially expressed proteins as those with adjusted p above 0.05, which would select non-significant proteins. The next sentence and the figure legend use adjusted p below 0.05. This is probably a typo, but the stated criterion is wrong as printed. The Methods also do not say how the adjustment was done.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary tables showing the protein lists were selected with adjusted p < 0.05.

quotes.text: (Log2 fold cut range 0.5 to −0.5) were considered as differentially expressed
The volcano plot demonstrates robust changes, with several proteins reaching high statistical significance

10.3390/app12084084.headline_claim: Adding L-acetyl-carnitine (ALC) to physical rehabilitation is a promising and effective treatment for post-COVID syndrome, especially for musculoskeletal pain, depression and quality of life.
10.3390/app12084084.overall: Pain, depression and SF-12 differences between arms look numerically strong from the printed summary statistics, but they come from an open-label comparison on self-reported scales with an unregistered protocol and 60 patients, so 'effective' goes further than the design allows. The Discussion's arm-specific claims rest on within-arm p-values that appear to treat paired data as independent. Several baseline table entries (age and BMI totals, control oxygen percentages) and one PHQ-9 value in the text are internally inconsistent, but these are minor reporting errors.

primary_outcome.name: Perceived musculoskeletal pain (NRS) and degree of dyspnea (Barthel Dyspnea Index)

issues.title: 'Effective' conclusion from an open-label, 60-patient study with self-reported outcomes and no placebo
issues.explanation: The control group received the same rehabilitation without any drug or injection, and blinding is not described. The outcomes (NRS, PHQ-9, SF-12) are all patient-reported, so expectation effects could account for part of the extra improvement. The conclusion calls the combination 'effective' while the Discussion concedes that the sample size and short follow-up prevent generalizing. 'Promising' is supported; 'effective' is not established by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of blinded outcome assessment, or a placebo injection and tablet in the control arm.

quotes.text: Combining exercise with ALC is a promising and effective treatment in the management of Post-COVID syndrome
who underwent the same rehabilitation protocol without drug therapy
the small sample size and the lack of long-term follow-up are the main ones

second_reader.what_stands: The paper concludes ALC plus exercise is an 'effective treatment' from 60 patients with no placebo or described blinding and with mainly self-reported outcomes, and the limitations paragraph names only small sample and no long-term follow-up. It does not mention the lack of blinding or placebo as a limitation. 'Open-label' is my inference from what is not described, not a statement in the paper.

issues.title: Arm-specific effects inferred from within-arm p-values: no exercise-only comparator, pre/post data apparently tested as independent
issues.explanation: The Discussion says exercise alone improves function and quality of life, and that adding ALC additionally improves pain and depression, because the within-arm p-values differ between arms. A within-arm change without an untreated comparator cannot show an exercise effect, and a difference in significance between arms is not a test of the between-arm difference. The control-arm p-values reproduce from independent-samples t-tests on the pre and post means, which ignores the pairing and understates the control-arm improvement in pain and depression. The two-arm contrast in the Discussion is therefore weaker than presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods stating that paired tests were used for T0 vs T1, together with raw paired data giving the printed p-values.

quotes.text: We have observed that physical exercise alone is shown to improve functional capacity and quality of life.
However, if it is combined with ALC therapy, an improvement in musculoskeletal pain and depression is also achieved.

quotes.location: 3.3 Effects of Functional Rehabilitation Alone in Control Group

second_reader.what_stands: The discussion draws arm-specific conclusions ('exercise alone improves functional capacity and quality of life'; pain and depression improve only with ALC) from within-arm significant vs non-significant p-values. The study has no no-exercise or exercise-only comparator for those statements, and the within-arm p-values appear to treat paired T0/T1 data as independent samples, which would make them too conservative; a paired test on the control arm's pain and depression change would likely be significant. The between-arm NRS and PHQ-9 comparison in Table 4 does give a proper basis for the ALC-v

issues.title: No trial registration reported; randomised drug study labelled 'observational case-control'
issues.explanation: No registry identifier is given, so the primary outcomes (pain and dyspnea) and analysis plan cannot be verified as prespecified. The design is also mislabelled: patients were randomised to a drug add-on, which is an interventional trial rather than an observational case-control study. Without registration, selective emphasis on depression and quality of life cannot be ruled out.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment listing the same primary outcomes.

quotes.text: The local ethics committee, 'Palermo 1', approved the study, with the reference number 11/2021.
We conducted an observational case-control study on patients with Post-COVID syndrome.

issues.title: Sample size of 60 justified with a single-proportion precision formula (error margin 0.13), not a group comparison
issues.explanation: The calculation gives 56.8 using a worst-case proportion of 0.5 and an arbitrary error margin of 0.13. It says nothing about power to detect differences between the two arms in pain, dyspnea or depression scores. The text then states that 60 patients was sufficient to prove the thesis, which overstates what the calculation shows. The null secondary comparisons (e.g. FIQ, p = 0.07) cannot be read as evidence of no effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power calculation for a two-group continuous comparison on the primary outcomes showing 33 vs 27 is adequate.

quotes.text: The denominator # = 0.13 is the maximum error acceptable to the researcher, and the choice of # is arbitrary.
Consequently, the number of 60 patients considered was sufficient to prove our thesis.

issues.title: Dyspnea (NPI) scale described as 0 = none, 100 = maximum, yet scores of 83-86 rising at T1 are read as 'improvement'
issues.explanation: The Methods say NPI runs from 0 (no dyspnea) to 100 (maximum dyspnea). Both arms start at about 83-84 and rise by about 2 points at T1, and the Results discuss this as a (non-significant) 'improvement'. Under the stated direction dyspnea would be near maximum and slightly worse after treatment; under the opposite direction, the scale description is wrong. The direction of change in a primary outcome is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation from the authors that higher NPI scores mean less dyspnea in their instrument version.

quotes.text: The overall score ranges from 0 (no dyspnea) to 100 (maximum level of dyspnea)
No statistically significant improvement was observed for NPI scores (83.3 ± 6.5 vs. 85.30 ± 6.02; p = 0.21)

issues.title: Treatment-group T1 PHQ-9 printed as 10.84 in the text but 9.84 in Table 2 and implied by Table 4
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the treatment group's T1 PHQ-9 as 10.84 ± 3.1, while Table 2 gives 9.84 ± 3.02. The change of 3.19 in Table 4 matches the Table 2 value, so the text is the outlier. This is a reporting slip; the text value would shrink the apparent improvement by one point.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement from the authors that 10.84 is a different quantity (e.g. a different time point or subset) from the Table 2 T1 value.

issues.title: Total mean age 58.7 is below both group means (61.3 and 59.8); weighted mean should be about 60.6
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives a total mean age of 58.7 ± 5.4 (repeated in the text), but the treatment and control means are 61.3 and 59.8. A pooled mean cannot be lower than both group means. Either the total or the group means are misreported. The baseline-comparability statement therefore rests on a table with an internal inconsistency, though the effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that the total was computed on a different set of patients than the two group columns.

quotes.text: The population under examination had a mean age of 58.7 ± 5.4 years

quotes.location: Table 1, Age row, Treatment Group column
Table 1, Age row, Control Group column

issues.title: Control oxygen-therapy percentages (59.3/40.7) do not match counts 17/27 and 10/27 (63.0/37.0)
issues.explanation: Table 1 prints 17 (59.3%) and 10 (40.7%) for the control arm of 27. The counts give 63.0% and 37.0%. The printed percentages duplicate the control gender rows. This is a copy error in a baseline table and does not affect efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing 63.0/37.0, or a different control denominator.

quotes.location: Table 1, Oxygen therapy Yes row, Control Group

quotes.text: a control group comprising 27 patients

script.explanation: 17/27 = 62.96%, but the paper prints 59.3, outside the rounding interval [59.25, 59.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 28.7 rather than 27.

issues.title: Five outcomes tested with no multiplicity control, though the main between-group results would likely survive it
issues.explanation: The paper tests five scales within and between groups at an uncorrected 0.05 and reports most p-values only as 'p < 0.05'. A correction is not described. Recomputing from the Table 4 summary statistics, the pain, SF-12 and PHQ-9 differences are far below a corrected threshold, so this weakens the paper less than it might appear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not needed; the issue is already narrow. Exact p-values below 0.01 would remove it.

quotes.text: Results were considered statistically significant with a p value < 0.05.

issues.title: Total mean BMI is 28.2 in the text but 28.8 in Table 1, outside the range of the group means (27.9, 28.4)
issues.explanation: The text reports a total mean BMI of 28.2 while Table 1 prints 28.8. A total mean must lie between the two group means (28.4 and 27.9), so 28.8 is impossible. The group-size-weighted mean is 28.2, so the table cell is the likely slip. No result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; arithmetic from the printed group means rules out 28.8.

quotes.text: Their mean BMI was 28.2 ± 3.2

10.3390/app15084111.headline_claim: Multimodal immersive VR training (cognitive, exercise, mindfulness) in adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome produced a temporary HRV reduction at mid-intervention that recovered by the end, which the authors read as transient stress followed by adaptation; going from 16 to 24 sessions gave no added HRV benefit, so they suggest session intensity may matter more than session number.
10.3390/app15084111.overall: The paper's main finding is modest: a significant fall in some time-domain HRV measures from baseline to mid-term, in an 18-person uncontrolled two-dose study. The abstract's inferences about restoration, resilience and session intensity go beyond what the data show. Several reporting inconsistencies (identical Group 2 SDSD and RMSSD rows, participant counts that do not reconcile, an impossible study end date) reduce confidence in the data handling.

primary_outcome.name: HRV time- and frequency-domain measures (no single primary outcome named; hypothesis was improvement across baseline, mid-term and end)

issues.title: Abstract infers 'adaptation and increased resilience' from HRV that was not significantly different at any later point
issues.explanation: The only significant finding is a fall from baseline to mid-term. Mid-term to end and baseline to end were both non-significant, so no statistically supported 'restoration' was shown. No resilience, stress or adaptation measure was collected. The reading that early demands 'induced physiological stress' is speculation, and the abstract states it as a conclusion without a control group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant mid-term to end increase in HRV and an independent measure of resilience or stress.

quotes.text: The subsequent restoration of HRV suggested adaptation and increased resilience.
No other statistically significant differences were found between the mid-term and the end of the intervention assessments

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract's 'restoration' of HRV and the inference of 'adaptation and increased resilience' are not supported by a significant mid-to-end change; the paper itself reports no significant difference between mid-term and end, and end values stay below baseline in the means. The Discussion words the recovery more cautiously ('likely'), but the Abstract states it as a conclusion without that qualification.

issues.title: Abstract concludes session intensity matters more than session number, which was not tested
issues.explanation: The two arms differed only in number of sessions (16 vs 24) with the same structure, and no intensity measure was recorded. A non-significant difference between arms in a very small sample cannot support a claim about what matters more. The statement is speculation and should not appear as an abstract conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data on session intensity or an arm in which intensity was varied.

quotes.text: The absence of enhanced HRV with extended training suggests that session intensity may be more influential than the number of sessions in modulating HRV among PCC patients.
Although the specifics of each session varied, the structure and timing of the activities remained constant.

second_reader.what_stands: Session intensity was neither varied nor measured, so the Abstract's statement that intensity 'may be more influential' than session number is speculation not tested by the data; the non-significant group-by-time results in a sample of 18 do not support it. The Discussion presents the idea more tentatively and cites outside literature, but the Abstract frames it as something the absence of an effect suggests.

issues.title: Table 2: Group 2 SDSD and RMSSD rows identical at all three timepoints (six mean/SD pairs)
issues.explanation: In Group 2 the SDSD and RMSSD rows give exactly the same mean and SD at baseline, mid-term and end. In Group 1 the two rows differ clearly, so the measures are not interchangeable in this dataset. One of the two Group 2 rows is probably mis-entered, which puts the SDSD and RMSSD time effects (two of the three significant results) in doubt.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the Group 2 SDSD and RMSSD values truly coincide to three decimals at all three timepoints.

issues.title: Sex percentages (42.1/57.9%) imply 19 people; stated n is 18 (9+9), and Table 1 means imply 10 and 8
issues.explanation: With 18 participants no whole count gives 42.1% (7/18 = 38.9%, 8/18 = 44.4%), but 8/19 = 42.1% and 11/19 = 57.9%. Separately, several Table 1 group means fit n = 10 and n = 8, not the stated 9 and 9; for example, a mean of 9.10 on an integer scale is not possible with n = 9. The true sample size and group allocation are therefore unclear. This is a reporting inconsistency and it does not by itself change the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow showing 19 enrolled with one excluded from HRV data, and group sizes matching the Table 1 means.

quotes.text: with 42.1% women and 57.9% men

issues.title: No untreated comparator, so HRV changes over time cannot be attributed to the intervention
issues.explanation: Both arms received the intervention, so any HRV change over 8 to 12 weeks could reflect time, measurement familiarity or regression to the mean as well as the programme. The authors acknowledge this. The effect on the conclusions is covered under the interpretation issue on resilience.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a design feature that the authors disclose.

quotes.text: the absence of a control group that did not receive the intervention, or which received standard care, made it difficult to isolate the impact of the multimodal IVR intervention on HRV

issues.title: Time-effect p-values of 0.022 to 0.037 for three of eight HRV measures; correction scope unclear
issues.explanation: Eight outcomes were tested across three timepoints and the significant time effects are modest. If they were not adjusted across outcomes they would not survive a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/4 = 0.0125 or 0.05/8 = 0.006. The three significant measures are highly correlated, which weakens the case for strict correction. The central 'temporary reduction' finding is therefore fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted p-values across all outcomes that remain below 0.05.

quotes.text: Mixed ANOVAs with Bonferroni corrections were performed
there were main effects of time in SDSD ( F (2, 32) = 3.674, p = 0.037, partial η 2 = 0.187)

issues.title: Drop described as 'particularly marked' in the extended arm despite no group-by-time interaction
issues.explanation: All group-by-time interactions were non-significant, so the data do not show the two arms changed differently. The statement about the extended arm rests on eyeballing within-arm means, with 9 per group. It also supports the secondary conclusion that dose did not matter in the way the authors say.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant group-by-time interaction or planned within-arm contrasts.

quotes.text: Mixed ANOVA analyses did not show any statistically significant interactions between group and assessment time in any of the measures
were particularly marked among participants who underwent the extended multimodal training

issues.title: Device manufacturer's marketing staff thanked for study support; Broomx's role not described
issues.explanation: The intervention hardware is made by Broomx, and its marketing and business development officer is thanked for guidance throughout the study. The paper declares no conflicts and does not describe what Broomx did. This is a transparency gap, not evidence of influence on the results, which are in any case null or negative for the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Broomx had no financial relationship with the authors and no role in design, analysis or reporting.

quotes.text: The intervention was delivered using MK360 IVR hardware developed by Broomx Technologies
The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

issues.title: Study period stated as ending September 2025, but the paper was published 8 April 2025
issues.explanation: The Methods say the study ran until September 2025, yet the paper was received in December 2024 and published in April 2025. The date is wrong, probably a typo for 2024. It does not affect the results but weakens confidence in the reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction giving the actual data collection dates.

quotes.text: The study was conducted between January 2023 and September 2025.
Published: 8 April 2025

issues.title: Table 1 age row: t = 2.39 does not fit p = 0.814; the means and SDs imply t of about 0.23
issues.explanation: A t of 2.39 would be significant, but the printed p is 0.814 and the group means differ by under 1 year. The means and SDs give t near 0.23, so the printed t is probably a typo for 0.239. This is a minor slip and the baseline-equivalence statement still holds.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source table showing t = 0.239.

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

10.3390/arm91060037.headline_claim: A supervised comprehensive rehabilitation program (breathing, aerobic, strength/endurance exercise) is an effective intervention that improves physical capacity after COVID-19 treatment.
10.3390/arm91060037.overall: The pre-post gain of about 120 m in 6MWT distance is internally consistent and plausibly real. The claim that the programme is effective is not supported by a single-arm design in which spontaneous recovery cannot be separated out. The subgroup advice rests on unadjusted analyses and an under-specified null regression, and there are minor reporting slips: the mislabelled 23.83% and the 140 vs 146 counts.

primary_outcome.name: 6MWT distance (m), before vs after rehabilitation

issues.title: Efficacy and causal wording drawn from a single-arm pre-post study with no control group
issues.explanation: All 146 patients were assessed before and after a 2-6 week programme, with no control group, no blinding and no registration. The authors concede that fitness 'may spontaneously improve over time', yet the conclusion calls the programme effective and the Discussion says it 'significantly improves' health indicators. The 120 m gain is real as a before-after difference, but it cannot be attributed to the programme, and programme duration varied by clinician decision.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control group showing smaller gains over the same period.

quotes.text: Our study did not include a control group.
is an effective intervention that can improve the physical capacity of patients after COVID-19 treatment
The results suggest that physical fitness may spontaneously improve over time.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design with an acknowledged lack of a control group, yet the Conclusion calls the program 'an effective intervention' and the Discussion says it 'significantly improves' performance, which are causal efficacy claims the design cannot support. The authors do concede the absence of a control group and that fitness may improve spontaneously, but they rely on an external study to support efficacy, and the Limitations section and Conclusion do not carry that caveat.

issues.title: Text gives 6MWT distance gain as 23.83%; Table 2 means imply 32.5%, and 23.83 is the %predicted change
issues.explanation: The Results say distance rose 'by an average of 23.83%'. The Table 2 distance means (370.03 m to 490.47 m) give a rise of about 32.5%. The number 23.83 matches the change in %predicted points, a different quantity, so the sentence misdescribes the distance gain. The Discussion's 120 m improvement is consistent with the table, so the effect itself is not in doubt.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition of the 23.83% as the change in %predicted, or per-patient percent changes whose mean is 23.83%.

quotes.text: After rehabilitation, patients achieved a longer 6MWT distance by an average of 23.83%.
There was a significant improvement in 6MWT results by an average of 120 m.

issues.title: Advice to focus on elderly and comorbid patients rests on unadjusted analyses; adjusted model is null
issues.explanation: The subgroup claims come from unadjusted comparisons of post-rehabilitation distances (Table 3) and bivariate correlations with change (Table 4). The adjusted regression is described as showing no statistically significant associations, which the Conclusions do not mention. Age, BMI, diabetes and hypertension are strongly linked, so these univariate findings may be confounded. The recommendation is tentative at best. The same Conclusions sentence also covers c8.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A formal test of change scores by subgroup, adjusted for baseline distance and duration, showing a significant difference.

quotes.text: As age and BMI increased, the difference in the 6MWT distance before and after rehabilitation decreased.
The analysis did not reveal statistically significant correlations between examined variables.
special attention should be paid to the elderly, as well as people with coexisting diabetes, hypertension, and obesity.

issues.title: Logistic model described with MCID as 'predictor'; Table 5 odds ratios for categorical levels have implausibly narrow CIs
issues.explanation: The Methods say the 30 m MCID is the 'predictor' of improvement, yet it should be the outcome. Table 5 reports categorical terms (male sex, overweight, 1st-degree obesity) with ORs of about 1.0 and CIs spanning only about 0.008. Such intervals are typical of continuous per-unit terms, not binary comparisons. Reference categories and the number achieving a 30 m gain are not given, so the null adjusted result cannot be interpreted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of the outcome, coding and reference categories showing the variables were continuous per-unit terms.

quotes.text: A multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed with the minimum clinically important difference of 30 m for chronic respiratory diseases as the predictor of improvement in the 6MWT distance.

issues.title: Results say men did better on 6MWT; Discussion says women did, citing %predicted not shown in any table
issues.explanation: The Results say men achieved a better post-rehabilitation 6MWT (515.54 m vs 469.2 m, p = 0.027). The Discussion says women recorded better results and that the authors' data show a similar relationship, relying on %predicted values that appear in no table. The two statements use 'better' in different senses without saying so. This confuses a secondary finding and does not affect the main result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table of %predicted by sex with a statement that 'better' there refers to %predicted.

quotes.text: After rehabilitation, the men achieved a better 6MWT result.
women recorded better results in the 6MWT study after rehabilitation
Our research shows a similar relationship.

issues.title: Hospitalization and pneumonia counts sum to 140, not the 146 analysed; percentages use 146
issues.explanation: In Table 1 the Yes/No counts for hospitalization (101 + 39) and pneumonia (107 + 33) each sum to 140, while all other binary variables sum to 146. The percentages are calculated on 146, so 6 patients are silently absent from these rows. Both variables are covariates in the adjusted model, so the paper does not say how those patients were handled. The effect on the main result is minor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote stating that data on hospitalization and pneumonia were missing for 6 patients.

quotes.text: In total, 146 patients were included in the study, taking into account all inclusion and exclusion criteria

10.3390/biomedicines11113092.headline_claim: A multidisciplinary rehabilitation program including whole-body cryostimulation is safe and feasible for patients with obesity and post-COVID condition, and WBC may serve as an adjuvant booster in rehabilitation.
10.3390/biomedicines11113092.overall: This is a small single-arm feasibility study (n = 16) and supports only feasibility and hypothesis-generating pre-post changes. The abstract's claims of effectiveness, WBC as a booster and safety exceed what an uncontrolled, unpowered, multiplicity-uncorrected design can show. Several reporting slips, including the 6MWT p = 0.093 called significant and the HDL fall counted as lipid improvement, further overstate the benefit.

primary_outcome.name: Safety and feasibility (no primary efficacy outcome is designated)

issues.title: Abstract and Conclusions claim effectiveness and a WBC 'turning point' from uncontrolled pre-post data (n = 16)
issues.explanation: This is a single-arm study of 16 patients with no control group, no randomisation and no component-level analysis, so improvements in weight, lipids and pain cannot be separated from natural recovery, the inpatient diet and exercise, or regression to the mean. The abstract says the improvements 'demonstrate' effectiveness, and the Conclusions call WBC a 'turning point for all participants' and a 'booster'. The authors' own limitations paragraph says the contributions of WBC and the programme cannot be separated. The study supports feasibility and preliminary signals only. The small, unpowered sample (no sample size calculation) adds to this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison (for example, the same programme with and without WBC) showing an advantage for WBC.

quotes.text: The overall improvements demonstrate that multidisciplinary rehabilitation was effective on post COVID patients
the introduction of WBC was a turning point for all participants in terms of subjective and objective improvements in health and function

In the absence of a control group, our results do not fully clarify the extent to which WBC, the multidisciplinary rehabilitation program, or a combination of the two may account for the observed improvements.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract states that the improvements 'demonstrate' effectiveness of the rehabilitation, and the Conclusions call WBC 'a turning point for all participants'. Both rest on an uncontrolled single-arm pre-post comparison of 16 patients with only two time points. The limitations section itself says the design cannot separate WBC from the rest of the program, and the 'all participants' claim is not supported by any individual-level data. The paper does partly mitigate this: the main-text Conclusions use 'possibly an effective tool', and the Discussion calls the evidence preliminary and asks for

issues.title: 6MWT change called significant in text and abstract, but Table 2 gives p = 0.093 (alpha 0.05)
issues.explanation: The Results text lists 6MWT distance as a significant improvement, and the abstract says physical performance improved significantly. Table 2 reports p = 0.093 for 6MWT (Wilcoxon), which is above the stated 0.05 threshold. The 6MWT result therefore does not meet the authors' own criterion, so one of the two performance outcomes is overstated. TUG (p = 0.009) still supports part of the claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 showing p < 0.05 for 6MWT, or a stated alpha above 0.093 for that outcome.

quotes.text: There was a significant improvement in performance capacity as measured by TUG and distance walked on the 6MWT

issues.title: 'Safe' conclusion rests on zero adverse events in 16 patients with no structured safety reporting
issues.explanation: Safety is supported by a single sentence reporting no adverse events. With 0 events in 16 patients, the upper 95% confidence bound for the event rate is roughly 17-19%, so serious but uncommon harms cannot be excluded. The Discussion says the study 'demonstrates the safety'. This is a preliminary signal, not evidence of safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified adverse-event protocol and a larger sample with a confidence bound that excludes clinically important harm rates.

quotes.text: No adverse events occurred during the intervention period.
The present study demonstrates the safety and the feasibility of a multidisciplinary rehabilitation program combined with WBC

issues.title: 17 outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 with no adjustment; borderline results (p 0.013-0.047) reported as significant
issues.explanation: Seventeen paired comparisons were each tested at p < 0.05, with no correction or prespecified primary outcome. The strongest changes would withstand correction, but several reported as significant (SBP p = 0.046, SpO2 p = 0.047, and CRP, total cholesterol and HR at p ≈ 0.013-0.014) would not. The abstract's blanket statements of significant improvement in lipid, inflammatory and cardiovascular profiles are therefore weaker than presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome, or adjusted p-values showing the borderline findings remain significant.

quotes.text: The level of significance was set at p < 0.05.
Biochemical analyses showed a significant decrease in CRP, HDL, LDL, Tot Col, GLU at T10.

issues.title: HDL fell significantly (49.4 to 43.7 mg/dL) yet is counted among 'reductions in lipid profiles' and metabolic improvements
issues.explanation: The abstract presents significant reductions in lipid and inflammatory profiles as a benefit, and the Conclusions credit 'hematological and metabolic parameters' with improving. HDL, the protective lipid fraction, decreased significantly (p < 0.001), which is an unfavourable change, and TG did not change. This is the largest lipid change in Table 2 by p-value and goes against the benefit narrative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the HDL decrease reflects an expected effect of weight loss and a stated judgement that it is not harmful.
