quotes.text: Biochemical analyses showed significant reductions in lipid and inflammatory profiles.
The overall improvement in physical performance, hematological and metabolic parameters, psychological and general well-being, and pain

issues.title: Adherence described as 'four weekly sessions' while WBC comprised ten sessions over two weeks
issues.explanation: The feasibility paragraph says participants attended all four weekly sessions, whereas the Methods describe ten WBC sessions over two weeks plus twice-daily physiotherapy. The unit of 'session' is unclear, though it most likely refers to the four-week programme. This is wording ambiguity with little bearing on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'sessions' means programme weeks, or a log showing attendance at all ten WBC sessions.

quotes.text: All 16 participants attended all four weekly sessions of the program
All patients underwent ten sessions of WBC over a 2-week period

10.3390/biomedicines12102221.headline_claim: Supplementation with a marine oil enriched in monohydroxylated SPMs produces a clear enrichment of serum SPMs at 500 mg/day and a clear improvement in fatigue and dyspnea in patients with post-COVID syndrome.
10.3390/biomedicines12102221.overall: The finding that serum monohydroxylated SPMs rose on supplementation is plausibly supported by large within-group changes, though without a placebo-controlled between-group test. The clinical claims of 'clear improvement' in fatigue and dyspnea at 500 mg are not supported: between-group tests were null, the 500 mg arm was open-label, and the placebo arm was tiny. Treat the paper as an exploratory pilot.

primary_outcome.name: Serum concentrations of monohydroxylated SPMs (14-HDHA, 17-HDHA, 18-HEPE), described under Primary Endpoint as blood samples from patients with PCS

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from within-arm change; between-group tests null (dyspnea p=0.509, mMRC p=0.600)
issues.explanation: The SPM rises are significant versus baseline 'in all groups' but not between groups, so placebo-controlled effect is not demonstrated. Dyspnea differences among the four arms were non-significant (p=0.509 at week 12). The fatigue and dyspnea 'improvement' could reflect natural recovery, which the authors concede.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified placebo-controlled comparison showing significant between-group differences in SPMs or symptoms.

quotes.text: The difference between starting the treatment (baseline before intake of the product) and the end of treatment was significant in all groups ( p -value = 0.002) but not between the groups.
For the differences between baseline and week 12, Xsquared = 8.2496 and p -value = 0.509

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy is inferred from baseline-to-end changes within arms, and the between-group tests are null (mMRC p = 0.509 at week 12 and p = 0.600 at week 4; no significant between-group difference for fatigue or lipid mediators), with the placebo arm also improving. The point's two 'dyspnea' and 'mMRC' p-values are in fact the same scale at two time points. The authors do state the p-values and note that natural improvement is a limitation, but the conclusions still treat the within-arm change as evidence of effect.

issues.title: 'Clear improvement' in fatigue/dyspnea at 500 mg and PCS management claim not supported by null comparisons
issues.explanation: No significant between-group differences were found for fatigue or dyspnea, the 500 mg arm was open-label and uncontrolled, and the placebo arm had about 5 patients. Concluding clear improvement and that the oil 'represents an approach to managing' PCS goes beyond the data. The 500 mg preference was inferred from absence of dose differences.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled between-group analyses showing significant symptom benefit at 500 mg versus placebo.

quotes.text: Similarly, a clear improvement in fatigue and dyspnea was observed with this dosage.
Given that there were no statistically significant differences between the dosages of 500 mg, 1500 mg, and 3000 mg, a clear trend of favoring a 500 mg dosage per day can be postulated.
Supplementation with this marine oil enriched in SPMs hence represents an approach to managing patients with PCS.

second_reader.what_stands: 'Clear improvement' in fatigue and dyspnea at 500 mg, a 'clear trend favoring 500 mg', and the statement that supplementation 'represents an approach to managing patients with PCS' are not supported by the paper's own null between-group results and the improving placebo arm. The wording goes beyond the data, and it is stronger than the paper's own 'slight' and 'trend' descriptions elsewhere. The authors do acknowledge natural improvement and small size as limitations, but the conclusions do not carry that caution.

issues.title: The 500 mg arm (Group X) was unblinded and uncontrolled while the headline improvement relies on self-rated scales
issues.explanation: Group X received unmasked product and was not part of the placebo-controlled comparison, yet the Abstract and Conclusions highlight improvement at 500 mg. Fatigue (FSS) and dyspnea (mMRC) are patient-reported, so expectation effects and natural recovery are uncontrolled for this arm. The paper's 'double-blind' description therefore applies only to arms A, B and C.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that group X outcomes were assessed blind and compared with a concurrent placebo.

quotes.text: except for group X, who were not blinded, for whom the products were thus not masked.
but a clear trend in improvement can be seen in group X, which used 500 mg of marine oil per day.

second_reader.what_stands: The 500 mg arm was open-label and described as non-controlled, and its reported clinical improvement (FSS and mMRC) rests on subjective, self-reported measures, so expectation effects are not excluded. The headline 'clear improvement' at 500 mg is therefore the least protected against bias. The lipid-mediator results are objective measures and are not affected by this concern, and the paper does not say who scored the mMRC.

issues.title: No multiplicity adjustment across many analytes/timepoints; ratio result (p=0.025) is marginal
issues.explanation: The Methods say both that multiple-testing corrections were used and that there was no adjustment, so the analysis is unclear. Dozens of mediators, sums, ratios and two symptom scales were tested. The strong SPM increases would likely survive correction, but the ratio benefit (p=0.025) and any symptom signal would not be robust.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary endpoint and adjusted p-values showing the ratio result survives correction.

quotes.text: p -values below 0.05 were rated statistically significant as there was no adjustment for multiple testing. The data presented here are merely explorative and descriptive.
Changes from the baseline were calculated using the ANOVA test, using multiple testing corrections

issues.title: Table 3 week-12 dyspnea totals (A=15, C=4) are below allocated sizes (16, 5) with no flow or dropout report
issues.explanation: Methods allocate 16 to Group A and 5 to placebo Group C, but Table 3 analyses 15 and 4. No participant flow, dropouts or missing-data explanation is given, so analysed numbers (and whether analysis was ITT) cannot be established. Effect is small but one missing placebo patient is 20% of that arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow diagram or statement showing one Group A and one placebo patient lacked week-12 mMRC data.

quotes.text: Group C: Placebo N = 5 patients;

10.3390/biomedicines12102254.headline_claim: One month of at-home slow-paced breathing (respiratory vagus nerve stimulation) may be beneficial in reducing long-COVID symptoms in healthcare workers, and the authors call for a randomised controlled trial to confirm this.
10.3390/biomedicines12102254.overall: The conclusion that slow-paced breathing 'may be beneficial' rests on an uncontrolled, unblinded pre-post change in 33 of 58 enrolled cases, analysed as completers only, with uncorrected multiple symptom comparisons. The authors hedge and call for an RCT, so it is at most hypothesis-generating. Minor internal inconsistencies (39 vs 38 items, inpatient vs out-patient) do not affect the findings.

primary_outcome.name: No primary outcome designated; headline results are the Nijmegen dysfunctional-breathing score and the long-COVID symptom checklist, both pre-post within the cases

issues.title: Benefit claimed from uncontrolled pre-post change in 33 completers; no long-COVID control group
issues.explanation: The only evidence of benefit is the T0 to T1 change in self-reported symptoms in 33 people receiving the intervention, with no concurrent long-COVID comparison group and no blinding. Natural fluctuation, regression to the mean, expectation and weekly researcher contact cannot be separated from a breathing effect. The authors' hedged wording and their argument that long-standing symptoms rarely improve do not substitute for a control, so the 'may be beneficial' conclusion is only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist long-COVID control group showing no comparable symptom change.

quotes.text: Moreover, we lack a long-COVID control group.
indicated that this approach may be beneficial in reducing the symptoms associated with long COVID

second_reader.what_stands: Benefit is inferred from an uncontrolled pre-post comparison in 33 completers with no long-COVID control group, as the authors themselves acknowledge. The conclusion is hedged ('may be beneficial', RCT needed), but the abstract's 'overall improvement' wording and the unsupported assumption that symptoms would not have diminished without treatment go beyond what this design can show.

issues.title: 25/58 (43%) enrolled cases lost; completers-only analysis with 36% non-adherence among completers
issues.explanation: Of 58 enrolled cases, only 33 were re-evaluated and analysed, with no intention-to-treat or imputation. Dropouts refused re-evaluation, so their outcomes are unknown and completers may be the more responsive. Even among completers, about a third seldom or never adhered, and adherence was not analysed against change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis imputing or including all 58 cases, or baseline data showing dropouts were similar to completers.

quotes.text: N = 33 completed the study and their data were included for the final analysis.
In total, 63% of them reported that they adhered completely/closely to the protocol, while 36% seldom/never adhered.

second_reader.what_stands: 25 of 58 enrolled (43%) were lost, and the analysis is of the 33 completers only, with no dropout-versus-completer comparison or sensitivity analysis. About 36% of completers (about 12 of 33) reported seldom or never adhering, yet the main text gives no results by adherence, so the reported improvements may not reflect people who actually practised the protocol. The 43% attrition is explained by refusal rather than hidden, and the adherence figures are self-reported.

issues.title: Many symptom comparisons at p<0.05 without multiplicity adjustment; conclusion names the significant items
issues.explanation: Methods set a single 0.05 threshold and no adjustment, while many symptoms, NQ items and sub-scores were compared pre/post. The conclusion names asthenia, cognitive decline, headache and confusion, which are those reaching nominal significance. Individual p-values are not in the main text, so the weight of the claim is hard to judge.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary results showing the named symptoms survive correction for the number of tests.

quotes.text: Values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
including asthenia, cognitive decline, headaches, and confusion

issues.title: Interventional study with no trial registration or prespecified primary outcome reported
issues.explanation: No registry entry or prespecified primary outcome is given, and the study is described as exploratory. Which outcomes were primary cannot be checked, which increases the risk of selective emphasis. This is a modest transparency concern rather than a demonstrated defect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: This interventional study was approved by the FVG's Unite Research Ethics Committee
Concurrently, this study was initiated as exploratory

issues.title: M.U.S. described as 39 items in Methods but item comparison uses 38 items (26/38 = 68%)
issues.explanation: Methods say the M.U.S. has 39 items, but the Results compare cases and controls on 26 of 38 items. No exclusion or scoring rule explains the one-item difference. This concerns the baseline case-control comparison, not the intervention effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one M.U.S. item was not scored or compared (e.g. a non-symptom item).

quotes.text: It consists of 39 items exploring the physical, psychological, cognitive and emotional domains.
in 26 out of 38 items (68%)

issues.title: Follow-up assessment called 'inpatient' in Results but 'out-patient' in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Results say completers received a second inpatient assessment, while the Discussion says out-patient. The setting is described inconsistently, but nothing in the analysis depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that both terms refer to the same clinic visit.

quotes.text: received a second inpatient assessment
received a second out-patient assessment

10.3390/biomedicines12112445.headline_claim: Twelve weeks of individualized, controlled exercise training improved fatigue and exercise capacity in outpatient Long-COVID patients and demonstrated efficacy.
10.3390/biomedicines12112445.overall: The finding that fatigue, sit-to-stand and workload scores improved from baseline to 12 weeks among the 41 completers is reasonably supported as a descriptive result. The claim that the programme 'demonstrated efficacy' is not supported by an uncontrolled single-arm design with a third of eligible participants lost and completers-only analysis. Several small numeric inconsistencies (group sizes, workload changes, df) and fragile subgroup findings add further caution without changing the direction of the main results.

primary_outcome.name: not_prespecified_single_primary; FACIT-Fatigue, 1MSTST and workload all reported as main outcomes

issues.title: Efficacy and effectiveness claimed from a single-arm, uncontrolled, 41-patient pre-post study
issues.explanation: The study is a single-arm pre-post design with no comparison group, and all efficacy evidence is change over time within the same participants. Improvement in fatigue or sit-to-stand performance over 12 weeks could reflect natural recovery, expectation or practice effects, so training effect cannot be separated from these. The Abstract and Conclusions nonetheless say the programme 'demonstrated efficacy' and show 'the success of the program', while the paper itself calls the severity findings preliminary. The data support improvement during participation, not efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group, or a waitlist period showing stable outcomes before training began.

quotes.text: This study followed a single-arm pre-test-post-test design over an initial 12 weeks of the ongoing TRIBAL intervention.
The individualized and controlled training approach demonstrated efficacy in reducing fatigue and enhancing exercise capacity among outpatient LC patients.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is a single-arm, uncontrolled, 41-patient pre-post study, yet its abstract and conclusions use causal and efficacy language ('demonstrated efficacy', 'led to', 'demonstrates', 'effectiveness'), and it never acknowledges the missing control group as a limitation. The design is disclosed accurately, but the strength of the claim goes beyond what a pre-post design can support.

issues.title: 22 of 67 eligible participants withdrew and 4 lacked data; results are completers only (41/67, 61%)
issues.explanation: Of 67 eligible participants, 22 withdrew and 4 had missing data, so 26 (39%) are absent from every analysis. No reasons, no comparison with completers and no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis are given. Improvement rates (95.1% workload, 82.9% fatigue and 1MSTST) therefore describe people who stayed and trained, and probably overstate what an enrolled patient would experience.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reasons for withdrawal unrelated to the intervention/outcomes, or an analysis imputing outcomes for the 26 missing participants that gives similar results.

quotes.text: Sixty-seven participants met the inclusion criteria, with twenty-two withdrawing and data from four missing.
quotes.location: 2.1 Ethical Approval, Recruitment, and Study Cohort

quotes.text: led to improvement rates of 95.1% in the workload and 82.9%

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports that 22 of 67 eligible participants withdrew and 4 had missing data, and all results, including the 95.1% and 82.9% improvement rates, are for the 41 completers (61% of those eligible) with no ITT or missing-data analysis. The numbers are disclosed and reconcile, but the improvement rates describe completers only and could be optimistic as a statement about everyone who entered the programme.

issues.title: PCS severity groups: 25 moderate/16 severe in Methods and Fig 3 vs 24/17 in Table 1 and Table A2
issues.explanation: The Methods text and the Figure 3 caption split the 41 participants into 25 moderate and 16 severe. Table 1, the Discussion (41.5% severe) and Table A2 use 24 moderate and 17 severe. One person is classified differently depending on where you look, so it is unclear which group sizes the severity comparison (t(39), p = 0.013) was run on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one participant was reclassified between the analyses, or a corrected table and caption showing identical group sizes.

quotes.text: 61% (n = 25) were moderately affected and 39% (n = 16) were severely affected.
severe (>26.25) with n = 16, and moderate (10.75-26.25) with n = 25

issues.title: Workload gains in Discussion (24.50 W, 43.03 W) differ from Table A1 means (23.69 W, 41.47 W)
issues.explanation: The Discussion reports mean workload increases of 24.50 W at six weeks and 43.03 W at twelve weeks. Differences of the Table A1 means give about 23.69 W and 41.47 W. The sample-weighted Table A2 change scores (about 41.46 W) agree with the table, not with the text, so the text figures are unexplained overstatements of about 0.8 and 1.6 W. The direction of the effect is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text figures were computed on a different set of participants or from unrounded session-level data.

quotes.text: with a mean increase of 24.50 watts in the first six weeks and of 43.03 watts over the twelve weeks

quotes.location: Table A1, T0 row, WL column
Table A1, T2 row, WL column

issues.title: No primary outcome and unadjusted alpha 0.05 across many subgroup tests; PCS (p = 0.013) and CTS (p = 0.027) results fragile
issues.explanation: The paper tests three time-course outcomes plus PCFS, then sex, severity and training-session subgroups and a correlation matrix, all at p < 0.05 and with no designated primary outcome. The authors acknowledge the 'substantial number of analyses'. The subgroup findings that are interpreted (greater workload gain in moderately affected patients, in patients with more sessions) rest on single p-values of 0.013 and 0.027 that are fragile under any correction. The main time effects are highly significant and would survive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and analysis plan, or an adjustment across outcomes that preserves the subgroup findings.

quotes.text: Significance level for all tests was set at p < 0.05.
Given the substantial number of analyses, only statistically significant results will be presented in detail in the results section.

issues.title: CTS ANOVA reported as F(2, 40) implies 43 participants; groups total 41
issues.explanation: A one-way ANOVA with 3 groups and 41 participants has 2 and 38 degrees of freedom, but the paper prints F(2, 40). The three CTS groups in Figure 2 and Table A2 sum to 41, so the printed df do not match the analysed sample. This is likely a reporting slip, but it means the reported F and p cannot be reproduced from the stated group sizes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 43 participants entered the CTS analysis, or a correction showing the df are F(2, 38).

quotes.text: <21 CTS with n = 13, 21-24 CTS with n = 17, and >24 CTS with n = 11

issues.title: No trial registration or protocol identifier reported for the prospective intervention study
issues.explanation: Only an ethics reference number is given. There is no registry entry or published protocol, so selective outcome reporting cannot be ruled out, though the outcomes appear to be a natural set for the question. This weakens confidence in secondary and subgroup findings rather than the main time effects.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (e.g. DRKS/ClinicalTrials.gov) with prespecified outcomes dated before enrolment.

quotes.text: This study was approved by the ethical review board of the German Sport University Cologne (Reference Number 171/2022).
quotes.location: 2.1 Ethical Approval, Recruitment, and Study Cohort

10.3390/biomedicines13092267.headline_claim: A neurorehabilitation programme produced significant improvements in memory, attention, executive function and self-reported cognitive complaints in people with long COVID, and is a viable treatment option.
10.3390/biomedicines13092267.overall: The claim that the programme improved long-COVID cognitive symptoms rests on uncontrolled pre-post change in 18 completers; the comparison group was tested once and showed no post-intervention difference. The within-group gains are statistically strong, but they cannot be attributed to the intervention, so 'successful' and 'viable treatment' are not supported by this design. The numeric slips (ageusia percentage, CCQ normative wording) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Neuropsi Atención y Memoria-III and BANFE-III normalized scores, pre vs post intervention (within experimental group)

issues.title: Efficacy claim rests on uncontrolled pre-post change in 18 treated patients; controls tested once
issues.explanation: Improvement was tested only by paired t-tests of the treated group's baseline versus 6-month scores. The control group was assessed once at recruitment and was not a symptomatic, randomized or re-tested comparator, so change over time cannot be attributed to the programme. Practice effects, regression to the mean, spontaneous recovery and unblinded self-reported CCQ responses are all uncontrolled. Despite this, the Conclusions call the intervention 'novel and successful' and a viable treatment, and the limitations section does not mention the lack of a control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from a concurrent symptomatic control group re-tested at 6 months, or an analysis of between-group change.

quotes.text: the normalized scores were compared to those obtained at the baseline
Significant differences were not found between the post-intervention scores of the experimental group and the control group.
In the present study, a novel and successful neurorehabilitation intervention is presented

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy claim ('novel and successful', 'significant improvement') rests on uncontrolled pre-post paired comparisons in the 18 completers. The 15 controls, who are non-long-COVID subjects, were tested once and offer no comparison of change, and the only between-group result is a non-significant post-intervention difference. The paper does not address practice effects, spontaneous recovery or regression to the mean, and the Discussion's limitations section does not mention the missing control for change.

issues.title: Only 18 of 23 enrolled treated patients analysed (21.7% excluded); no ITT analysis
issues.explanation: Five of 23 recruited participants were removed: 2 for adherence under 90%, 2 for respiratory infection and 1 for HIV. Results are for completers only and no intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is given. Dropping low-adherence patients can inflate the apparent benefit, although with only 2 adherence exclusions the effect is probably small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including all 23 recruited participants, or baseline and follow-up scores of the excluded five showing no difference.

quotes.text: 2 subjects were excluded because they did not show 90% adherence to the intervention
18 subjects completed the neuropsychological rehabilitation overall

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 18 completers vs 15 controls, yet a confident efficacy conclusion
issues.explanation: The paper reports no power calculation, and the final sample is small. A small pilot is acceptable, but the conclusions are written as if efficacy is established. Limited sample size also reduces generalizability, which the limitations passage only touches on as lost participants.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation, or conclusions worded as exploratory.

quotes.text: Atotal of 23 subjects were recruited for the experimental group
could be viable treatment option in the near future

issues.title: CCQ 'better than normative' claim fails for Orientation (1.46 vs 0.76) and marginally Praxis (1.69 vs 1.66)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says post-rehabilitation CCQ levels were better than normative data for healthy subjects. In Table 2 the post means for Orientation and Praxis and gnosis are higher than the normative means, which means more complaints if lower is better. The paper states no statistical test was done on the normative values, and the baseline total (17.00) was already close to the normative total (16.90). The claim therefore holds for most domains but is overstated as a blanket statement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the normative claim applies only to the domains where post scores are below normative values, or a CCQ scoring direction in which higher is better for these domains.

quotes.text: they reached better levels than the normative data for healthy subjects

quotes.location: Table 2, Orientation row, Normative Values column

issues.title: Control Ageusia printed as 4 (29.67%) but 4/15 = 26.67%
issues.explanation: Table 1 lists 4 of 15 controls with ageusia and a percentage of 29.67. Four of fifteen is 26.67%, the value printed for other rows with a count of 4. This looks like a transcription slip in a baseline characteristic with no bearing on the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A control denominator other than 15 for this symptom, which the paper does not give.

script.explanation: 4/15 = 26.67%, but the paper prints 29.67, outside the rounding interval [29.67, 29.68]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 13.5 rather than 15.

issues.title: Many CCQ, Neuropsi and BANFE component tests at alpha 0.05 with no multiplicity correction
issues.explanation: Seven CCQ tests plus several Neuropsi and BANFE components were each tested at 0.05 with no correction. Most results would survive correction, but the Orientation result (p = 0.04) would not. This weakens only a secondary result, and the main claims depend mostly on small p-values.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated pre-specified primary outcome or a correction applied across the tests.

quotes.text: orientation ( p = 0.04), executive function ( p < 0.001), memory ( p < 0.01)

issues.title: No trial registry entry reported; only ethics protocol 03/23 (approved 22 May 2023)
issues.explanation: Only an institutional ethics approval is given. Without a registered protocol, the pre-specification of outcomes and analysis cannot be checked, though no inconsistency is evident.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry identifier registered before enrolment.

quotes.text: This study was approved by the Ethics and Research Committee of INR-LGII with protocol number registration 03/23

10.3390/biomedicines9111540.headline_claim: Persistent long-COVID symptoms are accompanied by immune alterations that revert after a short prednisone course, and corticosteroids may be effective for long-COVID.
10.3390/biomedicines9111540.overall: The immunophenotyping descriptions are plausible as hypothesis-generating pilot data, but the causal claims that prednisone reduces symptoms and normalises immunology are not supported by an uncontrolled, unblinded study of eight treated patients. The title and conclusions are stronger than the design allows, and the minor internal inconsistencies (time since infection, CD11b/CD11c) do not change that.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; immune profile differences (PCA/flow cytometry populations) between PSP, TTP and NSP

issues.title: Steroid benefit inferred from uncontrolled before/after change in 8 symptomatic patients
issues.explanation: All eight symptomatic patients received prednisone and were compared with their own pre-treatment state; the only comparison group (NSP) is asymptomatic and untreated. Symptom recovery and immune normalisation therefore cannot be attributed to the drug rather than time, regression to the mean or expectation. The title and conclusions state a causal benefit that this design cannot show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent placebo or untreated symptomatic comparison group showing the same immune and symptom changes only with prednisone.

quotes.text: After completion of the treatment, all patients described complete or partial recovery of their symptoms.
suggests that corticosteroids may be effective in this situation.

second_reader.what_stands: Benefit is inferred from an uncontrolled before/after change in 8 treated patients, with no concurrent control, so regression to the mean, natural recovery, placebo effect and the 4-day timescale cannot be separated from a steroid effect. The paper does hedge ('may be effective') and lists small sample size and selection as limitations, so the claim is cautious in the conclusion, but the Abstract and Title are stronger than the design supports.

issues.title: Symptom response self-reported, unblinded and without a validated instrument
issues.explanation: Clinical response is described as patients 'described' recovery, with improvement counts for arthralgia, myalgia and asthenia and no scale, blinding or predefined criterion. Such outcomes are highly susceptible to expectation effects after a known steroid course. This weakens the clinical half of the headline claim, independent of the lack of a control group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded assessment with a validated symptom instrument showing the same improvement.

quotes.text: Clinical symptoms were evaluated before and after treatment.
the symptoms that improved the most after treatment were arthralgia (6/7 TTP, 86%), myalgia (6/8 TTP, 75%) and asthenia (4/7 TTP , 57%).

second_reader.what_stands: The main text reports symptom change as patient-described improvement in simple counts, with no validated instrument, no stated blinding, and no definition of 'complete' versus 'partial' recovery. I could not check Table S1, so whether the supplement uses a structured assessment is unknown; the open-label, unblinded nature follows from the single-arm design.

issues.title: Title and conclusions assert steroid effect and immunopathogenic basis from an uncontrolled pilot
issues.explanation: The title states a corticosteroid course 'reduces' symptoms and immunological alterations, and the Conclusions claim an immunopathogenic basis for long-COVID. The data are cross-sectional associations in 9 vs 5 people and an uncontrolled before/after change in 8, which show correlation at best. The authors' own limitations paragraph says the conclusions are limited, yet the final paragraph is not so qualified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data showing the immune changes mediate symptom response to steroids.

quotes.text: The current study provides an immunopathogenic basis for long-COVID and suggests that corticosteroids may be effective in this situation.
A Short Corticosteroid Course Reduces Symptoms and Immunological Alterations Underlying Long-COVID

second_reader.what_stands: The Title asserts a steroid effect on symptoms and on underlying immunological alterations, and the Conclusion claims an 'immunopathogenic basis', from an uncontrolled study of 9 patients (8 treated) with a 5-person comparison group and no multiplicity adjustment. The abstract and the 'may be effective' phrasing are more cautious and a limitations paragraph exists, but the Title and the 'provides an immunopathogenic basis' sentence go beyond what the design can show.

issues.title: n=9/8 patients vs 5 controls, dozens of unadjusted comparisons, no sample-size rationale
issues.explanation: The study compares 34+ immune populations and markers in 9 patients versus 5 controls using Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests, with p<0.05 as threshold and no multiplicity correction or sample-size calculation. With n=8 paired, the smallest attainable two-sided Wilcoxon p is about 0.008, so findings are fragile and some may be chance. The limitation is acknowledged, but the conclusions are not correspondingly tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis plan with multiplicity control or independent replication in a larger cohort.

quotes.text: The reduced number of patients in each cohort and the selection of PSP who reported particularly severe myalgia and/or arthralgia, together with other symptoms, limit the conclusions of our study
Differences were considered statistically significant when p -value < 0.05.

issues.title: 4-month maintenance claim rests on 6 of 8 treated patients, reasons for loss not given
issues.explanation: Only six of eight treated patients were sampled at 4 months and the paper does not say why two were not. The conclusion says both immune and clinical improvements 'were maintained', although a relapse of arthralgia or myalgia occurred in 4 of 6. The denominators are disclosed, so this narrows rather than invalidates the claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two patients were unavailable for reasons unrelated to outcome, with their status.

quotes.text: A second post-treatment sample was obtained in six patients with persistent symptoms (TTP+4M) 4 months after the course of corticosteroids.
Four out of six patients (66.7%) referred to at least a relapse of arthralgia or myalgia

issues.title: 'Over a year' after infection claimed though mean time since infection was 9 months (range 3-13)
issues.explanation: Results state patients were on average 9 months from infection, range 3 to 13 months. The Conclusions and Section 3.3 say alterations were seen over a year after infection, which holds for at most a few patients. The wording overstates the chronicity of the findings, but no analysis depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-patient data (Table S1) showing most patients were more than 12 months post-infection at sampling.

quotes.text: on average 9 months ago (range 3 to 13 months)
These alterations were observed over a year after acute infection

issues.title: cDC marker labelled CD11c+ in text but CD11b+ in Figure 2 legend
issues.explanation: The Results call the expanded population CD11c+ cDC while the Figure 2 legend labels it CD11b+ DC. The methods list an anti-CD11c antibody and no anti-CD11b, so the legend is the likely error. It is a cosmetic inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the discrepancy is in the printed text.

quotes.text: conventional CD11c+ dendritic cells (cDC; p < 0.01)
conventional dendritic cells (CD11b+ DC)

10.3390/brainsci13050791.headline_claim: A multidisciplinary in-hospital rehabilitation program enhanced with daily individualized neuropsychological (cognitive stimulation) treatment improved cognitive function in post-acute COVID-19 patients with brain fog, and the authors suggest rehabilitation and psychological intervention could be effective strategies for PACS brain fog recovery.
10.3390/brainsci13050791.overall: The finding that MoCA scores rose during a 30-day rehabilitation stay is probably real, but the study has no comparison arm, so it cannot show that the neuropsychological treatment caused the gain. Several baseline counts in the text and tables disagree (male 42 vs 22, opioids 24 vs 4, LMWH 63 vs 60), which lowers confidence in the data handling without affecting the MoCA change directly. The abstract and conclusion state efficacy more firmly than the design allows.

primary_outcome.name: MoCA overall score, admission vs discharge

issues.title: Cognitive gain (20.4 to 24.7) attributed to the psychological add-on with no control for recovery or practice effects
issues.explanation: All 56 impaired patients received both standard rehabilitation and the cognitive treatment, so the admission-to-discharge MoCA gain cannot be separated from spontaneous post-COVID recovery, repeat-test practice effects, regression to the mean or the physical programme. The 'untreated' comparison is the 8 patients with normal MoCA, who were selected on the outcome and had no room to improve, so it cannot isolate a treatment effect. The adjusted MANOVA models only adjust for confounders of within-person change, not for the missing counterfactual. The authors call this comparison preliminary, but the treatment-specific inference (the Barthel argument and the 'driven by cognitive stimulation' discussion) rests on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group with matched baseline cognitive impairment receiving standard rehabilitation alone.

quotes.text: the lack of a control group (non-rehabilitated patients and/or rehabilitated without psychological treatment)
since the improvement in cognitive function was higher only in the patients treated, it is plausible that cognitive recovery was primarily driven by cognitive stimulation treatment

second_reader.what_stands: The 20.4 to 24.7 gain comes from an uncontrolled before-after design in which no comparison group received rehabilitation without cognitive stimulation, so recovery over time, practice effects and the effect of the physical programme cannot be separated from the psychological add-on. The authors do disclose this limitation and call the treated-versus-untreated comparison preliminary, but the Discussion still calls it 'plausible' that the cognitive stimulation drove recovery and suggests an 'additive effect', which the design does not support.

issues.title: Abstract and conclusion credit the psychological intervention as effective from an uncontrolled before-after study
issues.explanation: The abstract says the study 'provides evidence of the effects' of the neuropsychological programme, and the conclusion calls psychological intervention an effective strategy. The study is an uncontrolled observational series in which the add-on cannot be distinguished from rehabilitation or spontaneous recovery. The caveat that RCTs are needed appears only in the limitations paragraph, not alongside these claims. The wording is hedged in places, so this is overreach in emphasis rather than an outright misstatement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Abstract and conclusion explicitly limited to 'associated with improvement', with the uncontrolled design stated alongside the claim.

quotes.text: In conclusion, our study provides evidence of the effects of multidisciplinary rehabilitation enhanced with neuropsychological treatment
seem to suggest that both rehabilitations, as well as psychological intervention, could represent effective strategies to obtain PACS brain fog recovery

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract says the study 'provides evidence of the effects' of the rehabilitation enhanced with neuropsychological treatment, and the Conclusion names psychological intervention as a possibly effective strategy, both based on an uncontrolled before-after comparison that cannot attribute the gain to that component. The Conclusion is hedged ('seem to suggest', 'could'), and the Discussion openly states the lack of a control group and the need for RCTs, so the overreach lies mainly in the Abstract's wording and in the omission of this limitation from both summary passages.

issues.title: Text counts disagree with Tables 1-2: male 42 vs 22, CV 33 vs 23, LMWH 60 vs 63, opioids 24 vs 4, duplicate O2 rows
issues.explanation: Several baseline counts in the Results text cannot be reconciled with the tables. Table 1's male row sums to 22 while the text and abstract give 42 (65.6%, 66%). The text gives 33 patients with cardiovascular disease but 35.9%, which is 23/64, and the table sums to 23. Table 2's LMWH row sums to 63 with 37 patients in a 36-patient group, versus 60 in the text, and opioids sum to 4 versus 24. Table 2 also has two O2 therapy rows with different counts. The Table 1 male row is the most substantive of these, so the baseline description is unreliable, but the MoCA change is not directly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 and Table 2 from the source data in which group counts sum to the text totals.

quotes.text: forty-two (65.6%) patients were male
60 (93%) with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH)
24 (38%) with opioids

issues.title: Baseline IES-R mean is 16.6 in the text but 19.6 in Table 4 (same SD 15.6)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the admission IES-R mean as 16.6 ± 15.6, whereas Table 4 gives 19.6 (15.6) at admission. The SD agrees, so a digit has probably been transposed. The IES-R change was non-significant, so no main conclusion depends on it, but one of the two baseline values is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing which admission mean is correct, with the other identified as an acknowledged typo.

quotes.text: the IES-R score for post-traumatic distress means values was 16.6 ± 15.6

10.3390/brainsci14070693.headline_claim: The 12-week exercise program enhanced fitness and cognition in both groups, with the hybrid group favoured in the visuospatial domain and the tele-exercise group in memory, and tele-exercise is presented as an effective, low-cost option.
10.3390/brainsci14070693.overall: The paper supports only that both groups improved over 12 weeks with good adherence; with no untreated comparator, even that cannot be attributed to the programs. Claims of group-specific cognitive effects and of tele-exercise being effective and low-cost go beyond what the data show, resting on uncorrected within-arm tests, a baseline-driven DLCO result and no cost data. Table 2 also has internal inconsistencies, so the reported secondary numbers should be treated cautiously.

primary_outcome.name: No primary outcome designated; the stated aim is feasibility of tele-exercise versus hybrid exercise, with fitness, respiratory, cognitive and oxidative-stress outcomes reported

issues.title: Enhancement of fitness and cognition inferred from uncontrolled within-arm pre-post changes
issues.explanation: Both arms received exercise and there was no non-exercise control, so the paper cannot separate the program's effect from recovery over time or retest effects. The conclusion that the 12-week program enhanced fitness and cognition is causal language the design does not support. This is more serious for the small MoCA gains (about 0.5 to 1 point), which are within typical practice-effect size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A non-exercise or usual-care control arm, or external evidence that MoCA and fitness do not change over 12 weeks in comparable untreated patients.

quotes.text: the 12-week exercise program enhanced fitness indicators and cognition in both groups.
Our data showed differences in both groups before and after 12-week ERP on fitness indicators, body composition, and pulmonary function indicators.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that the programme 'enhanced fitness indicators and cognition in both groups' rests on within-arm paired pre-post tests, with no non-exercise control to attribute the change to the intervention. The cognitive gains are also small (+0.5 to +1.0 MoCA points), and the paper gives no handling of retest effects or missing data. The authors do not hedge this causal wording in the conclusion.

issues.title: Domain-specific cognitive 'differences between groups' rest on uncorrected tests and significant-versus-nonsignificant contrasts
issues.explanation: Many outcomes were each tested at 0.05 with no multiplicity correction. The claimed advantage of hybrid exercise for visuospatial function and of tele-exercise for memory comes from within-group p-values, not from a direct between-group test of change. The single between-group domain result (attention, p=0.014) would exceed 0.05 after a simple Bonferroni correction across six domains. The abstract headlines these domain findings even though the authors admit the study was not powered for them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy limiting the cognitive analyses, a group-by-time interaction test for visuospatial and memory change, or corrected p-values that remain significant.

quotes.text: For all tests, a p -value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
with the hybrid group being favored in the visuospatial domain and the tele-exercise one in memory.
our study was the first to indicate some between the two groups, despite not being powered to detect them

second_reader.what_stands: The domain-specific 'differences between groups' (visuospatial favouring hybrid, memory favouring tele-exercise) come from separate within-arm paired tests judged significant or not at an uncorrected 0.05, not from a group-by-time interaction test, and the paper's own between-group d is 0.00 for visuospatial and about 0.63-0.65 for memory both at baseline and at 12 weeks. The authors do concede the study was not powered for these contrasts, but the Abstract and Conclusions still state them as findings. Only the attention comparison is a direct between-group test, and it too is uncorrected and

issues.title: Tele-exercise called effective and low-cost although no cost data, no control arm and no equivalence test
issues.explanation: The stated purpose was to show tele-exercise is a feasible alternative. The final discussion paragraph goes further, calling it effective and a beneficial low-cost way to promote exercise. Cost was never measured, and 'no difference between groups' with 24 and 25 patients is not evidence of equivalence. Feasibility, adherence and safety are supported; effectiveness and cost-benefit are not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority margin with a supporting confidence interval, and a cost analysis showing lower cost.

quotes.text: could be an effective and beneficial low-cost way to promote exercise in patients who have difficulty or no access to rehabilitation centers
the purpose of our study was to obtain evidence whether an unsupervised tele-exercise program via an online platform is a feasible alternative

issues.title: DLCO 'between-group difference' (p<0.001) is a within-arm change driven by lower TE baseline; 12-week values nearly equal
issues.explanation: The abstract lists the DLCO result as a between-group difference after 12 weeks. Table 2 shows the groups at 12 weeks are almost equal (80.9% vs 79.7% predicted), while TE started about 10 points lower at baseline (67.7% vs 77.3%). The larger TE gain therefore reflects the baseline imbalance and does not show a benefit of tele-exercise. Presenting it as a group difference misleads.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted between-group comparison of DLCO change showing a significant difference at 12 weeks.

quotes.text: the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (HEgroup increased the percent of predicted values at 0.5 ± 32.3% and TEgroup at 26.0 ± 33.1%, p < 0.001)

issues.title: Identical %Change values and SDs in both arms for FEV1, FVC and PEF; FEV1 TE sign contradicts its means
issues.explanation: In Table 2 the '%Changes within Group' entries for FEV1, FVC and PEF are identical in magnitude and SD across two independent arms. The TE FEV1 change is printed as -6.3% although the mean rose from 92.4 to 100.2. These cells cannot all be right, so the percent-change column is unreliable for respiratory outcomes. The group-level means are not directly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level data showing these values, or a corrected Table 2.

issues.title: MoCA t-test df swapped between arms (HE t(24), TE t(23)); attention between-group t(23) should be df 47
issues.explanation: With n=24 (hybrid) and n=25 (tele), paired tests should have df 23 and 24 respectively. The MoCA total scores print the opposite, while other paired tests in the same section are correct. The independent-groups attention test prints df 23 although 49 patients imply df 47. The p-values still fit the correct df, so this is a reporting error that leaves the findings unchanged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-test analysed Ns showing that 25 HE and 24 TE patients contributed to the MoCA total tests, or a corrected table.

quotes.text: The TEgroup showed a higher score (4.8 ± 1.5 versus 3.6 ± 1.8 score t (23) = -2.562, p = 0.014
HEgroup: n = 24, age 60.0 ± 9.5 years

10.3390/brainsci14121212.headline_claim: Online EMDR delivered via an AI-powered remote platform is as effective as in-person EMDR for PTSD symptoms in long/post-COVID patients, and is a valid alternative to in-person administration.
10.3390/brainsci14121212.overall: The headline claim that online EMDR is equally effective and a valid alternative rests on non-significant ANOVAs with no equivalence margin, no CI, no untreated control and no follow-up. The groups' descriptive results are similar, but the study cannot show non-inferiority and the stated conclusions go further than the data. Several reporting slips (6.08 vs 6.80, 22 vs 30 items, effect sizes) do not change the main picture but lower confidence in the table.

primary_outcome.name: SUDs, PCL-5 and IES-R (three co-primary outcome measures; post-treatment and change scores compared by ANOVA)

issues.title: Equivalence/non-inferiority concluded from non-significant ANOVAs, with no margin or CI
issues.explanation: The authors conclude that the two formats are 'equally effective' and that online EMDR is not worse, based only on p-values above 0.05 from one-way ANOVAs. No non-inferiority margin was set, and no confidence interval for the between-group difference or equivalence test is given. The study was sized to detect d = 0.418, so differences of up to about 0.4 SD remain compatible with the data. The conclusion is therefore stronger than the analysis supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority margin with a between-group CI whose bound lies inside it, or a TOST result.

quotes.text: These results reinforce the conclusion that both formats of EMDR therapy were equally effective in reducing the symptoms of PTSD and distress.
confirming our hypothesis that the actuation of EMDR in an online setting does not provide worse results than a standard in-presence session

second_reader.what_stands: The paper concludes equivalence ('equally effective', 'does not provide worse results') solely from non-significant ANOVAs, with no prespecified margin and no confidence interval. The intervals reconstructed from its own summary statistics are fairly wide, and on SUDs under the text values they allow a deficit for online of roughly half an SD. Its power analysis was for detecting a difference, not for equivalence.

issues.title: Conclusion calls online EMDR 'valid' and 'effective' for a broader population on short-term, unblinded data
issues.explanation: The conclusion calls the approach a 'valid and applicable alternative' that opens effective care to a 'broader population'. The evidence is three sessions with immediate post-treatment self-report. There is no follow-up, no adverse-event reporting, and no untreated control to attribute the pre-post change to EMDR. The Introduction even says the study 'demonstrates' equal effectiveness, and the sample is a narrow age band of confirmed-COVID participants. The claim is stronger than this design allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Follow-up data, adverse-event reporting and a wider sample supporting generalisation.

quotes.text: consolidating our approach as a valid and applicable alternative to in-person administration
opens up new possibilities for delivering effective mental health interventions to a broader population
Our study demonstrates that EMDR is just as effective when delivered remotely via AI-powered platforms as it is in person

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusions and Section 1.1 present online EMDR as proven valid and effective, including for a broader population. The evidence is short-term (end of three sessions), self-reported, unblinded, drawn from a narrow screened sample, and probably delivered with participant and therapist co-located, with no follow-up. The limitations in the Discussion are not reflected in the strength of the conclusion.

issues.title: Randomization method and allocation concealment not described; run test used as proof of independence
issues.explanation: The paper says participants were randomly allocated but gives no method of sequence generation, no allocation concealment and no blinding of outcome assessment. It then uses a Wald–Wolfowitz run test on the sequence of scores as evidence of independence, which does not test how allocation was done. Baseline balance is good, so this weakens trust in the design rather than invalidating it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or supplement describing computer-generated sequences with concealed allocation.

quotes.text: participants were randomly allocated to one of two experimental groups
we applied the Wald–Wolfowitz test in order to evaluate the randomness of our data sequences

issues.title: Between-group Cohen's d in Table 1 (e.g. '<0.01' for PCL-5) does not match the printed means and SDs
issues.explanation: The 'Difference (Cohen's d)' rows report values such as <0.01 for every PCL-5 comparison. The printed means and SDs imply d of about 0.12–0.13 for pre-treatment and for the decrement. The SUDs decrement d of 0.04 also falls short of the roughly 0.12 implied by Table 1's own means. The understated effect sizes make the groups look more alike than the printed data show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative d computation (for example from an ANOVA on different data) that reproduces these values.

quotes.text: Difference (Cohen’s d)

issues.title: Online SUDs decrement printed as 6.08 in text but 6.80 in Table 1 (pre−post gives 6.80)
issues.explanation: Section 3.4 gives the online group's SUDs decrement as 6.08, but Table 1 gives 6.80. The printed pre and post means (8.55 and 1.75) support 6.80, so the text figure looks like a digit transposition. It also makes the IP–OL gap look like 0.47 points in the text but 0.25 in the table, and the quoted ANOVA F of 1.51 matches neither gap exactly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the mean decrement is 6.08, which would then make the pre and post means in Table 1 wrong.

quotes.text: and OL (Mean = 6.08, SD = 2.09) groups

issues.title: IES-R described as 30 items in Section 2.1 but 22 items in Section 2.4
issues.explanation: Section 2.1 says the IES-R has 30 items, while Section 2.4 says 22. The 0–88 score range given in 2.4 is consistent with 22 items, so 2.1 is the wrong statement. This is a factual slip that does not change any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a 30-item IES-R variant was actually administered, which would contradict the 0–88 range.

quotes.text: is a standardized psychometric tool with 30 items
The IES-R contains 22 items related to the symptoms

issues.title: No trial registration identifier reported for a prospective two-arm comparison
issues.explanation: The paper describes a prospective allocation of 160 participants to two arms but gives no registry number or registration date. Without registration, the three outcome measures (SUDs, PCL-5, IES-R) cannot be checked against a pre-specified primary outcome. The paper states ethics consent but not approval, funding or conflicts, so this cannot be resolved from the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record dated before enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: All participants provided informed consent before beginning the study.

10.3390/brainsci15050510.headline_claim: Both groups improved over time, so the authors attribute the changes to a possible placebo effect; superficial neuromodulation appears safe but its efficacy is unconfirmed and needs larger trials.
10.3390/brainsci15050510.overall: The paper's own conclusion is null and cautious: both arms improved and no specific benefit is claimed. However, the abstract's SDNN and PPT numbers do not match the tables, the safety claim has no supporting data, and the primary outcomes differ from the registry. The results should be treated as exploratory pilot data.

primary_outcome.name: Composite of outcomes listed in the abstract as primary (HRV, pain threshold, cortisol, fatigue, sleep quality, quality of life); the paper names no single primary

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from Baseline Pain Pressure Threshold at 1 year

issues.title: Abstract SDNN means (30.42→39.11; 31.88→28.73 ms) do not appear in Table 2 (49.06→69.68; 84.65→42.26)
issues.explanation: The abstract reports SDNN values for both groups that appear nowhere in the results table. The table has higher values in both arms, and the control arm falls from 84.65 to 42.26 ms, a much larger drop than the abstract shows. The abstract also presents SDNN as a group-specific benefit, but the table's time-by-group interaction is not significant (p = 0.567). The headline HRV result is therefore unreliable as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract values come from a different measurement (e.g. a different subset or time point) with matching data.

quotes.text: Heart rate variability (SDNN) increased in the experimental group (30.42 to 39.11 ms) but decreased in controls (31.88 to 28.73 ms)

second_reader.what_stands: The SDNN means given in the abstract do not appear in Table 2, and the paper offers no explanation (adjustment, different time point, units) that reconciles them. Only the direction of the T0 to T2 change (EG up, CG down) is consistent between the two.

issues.title: Abstract C5-C6 PPT (2.1→3.5 kg/cm2) differs from Table 2 (EG 1.43→1.87 kg); control not 'stable'
issues.explanation: The abstract's experimental-arm PPT values do not match Table 2's C5-C6 row. The abstract also says controls remained stable, but the table shows control PPT rising 1.52 to 1.92, a similar change to the EG's 1.43 to 1.87. The cited p = 0.032 is the overall time effect, not a group difference. The abstract thus implies a treatment-specific gain the data do not show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the abstract values for C5-C6 in kg/cm2 at another time point.

quotes.text: Pain threshold at C5-C6 improved in the experimental group (2.1 to 3.5 kg/cm 2 ) but remained stable in controls ( p = 0.032).

quotes.location: Table 2, PPT C5-C6 row, EG T0

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's C5-C6 values (2.1→3.5) do not match Table 2 (EG 1.43→1.87), and the control group in Table 2 rose by about the same amount (+0.40 vs +0.44), so describing controls as stable and attaching p = 0.032 to a group contrast misstates the table. The p = 0.032 is the pooled time effect, and the body text itself reports no group or interaction differences.

issues.title: Technique called 'safe and well tolerated' with no adverse-event or tolerability data reported
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Conclusions state the device appears safe and well tolerated. The Methods and Results report no adverse-event monitoring or tolerability outcome, and 16 participants cannot establish safety. The claim is unsupported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adverse-event records or a tolerability measure from the trial.

quotes.text: Superficial neuromodulation appears safe, but further studies with larger samples are needed to confirm efficacy.
despite being a safe and welltolerated therapeutic modality for post-COVID-19 condition patients

issues.title: Two of 9 control participants withdrew after randomization (none in EG); 'no participants lost' statement
issues.explanation: Withdrawals after randomization occurred only in the control arm and were analysed as per-protocol with no ITT analysis. The Results sentence that no one was lost conflicts with this unless it refers only to after treatment began. With a small sample this imbalance could alter the comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow diagram showing the withdrawals occurred before randomization.

quotes.text: Before intervention initiation, two CG participants withdrew due to recommendations from their primary care physicians, leaving seven participants in the CG.
No participants were lost during the study.

issues.title: Six primary outcomes reported vs one registered primary (PPT at 1 year); follow-up only 2 months
issues.explanation: The registry lists pain pressure threshold at 1 year as the sole primary. The paper declares six primary outcomes and measures only through two months, with no mention of the registered primary or the change. The paper never discusses the deviation. Because the conclusion is null, the effect on the headline is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing these six primaries with 2-month follow-up.

quotes.text: Primary outcomes included heart rate variability, pain threshold, cortisol levels, fatigue, sleep quality, and quality of life

issues.title: Large time-effect eta-squared values (0.32-0.39) used to suggest clinical relevance in a 16-person pilot
issues.explanation: Sample size was planned at 60 but 16 were analysed. The Discussion reads time-effect eta-squared values as signalling potentially meaningful change beyond placebo, though they reflect change in both arms and are unstable at n = 16. The final conclusion is cautious, so the damage is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group effect sizes with intervals supporting the claim.

quotes.text: these effect sizes point toward potentially meaningful changes that may have clinical relevance, even in the absence of significant between-group differences.

issues.title: About 20 outcome-by-effect tests with no multiplicity correction in a pilot
issues.explanation: Many outcomes and three effect types were tested at p < 0.05 without correction. Because no efficacy claim is made, the issue mainly affects reading isolated significant results such as SDNN between-group p = 0.021.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchy or single primary test.

quotes.text: no formal correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni) was applied

issues.title: Discussion rMSSD p = 0.193 matches Table 2 HR between-group p, not rMSSD (p = 0.411)
issues.explanation: The p-value attached to the rMSSD group comparison is the one printed for heart rate in Table 2. The rMSSD between-group p is 0.411. Neither is significant, so the conclusion is unchanged, but the statement is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 0.193 is a separate rMSSD test not shown in Table 2.

quotes.text: Interestingly, rMSSD values increased from T0 to T2 in the experimental group but decreased in the control group ( p = 0.193)

issues.title: Discussion calls SF-36 bodily pain (p = 0.004) and vitality (p = 0.026) changes non-significant
issues.explanation: The Discussion cites p-values below 0.05 and then says the changes were not statistically significant, while the Results call them significant. The time effects are significant but the between-group and interaction effects are not, so the sentence mixes the two. It is an internal contradiction in the reporting of a secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that the sentence refers to between-group effects only.

quotes.text: both groups showed improvement in bodily pain ( p = 0.004) and vitality ( p = 0.026) dimensions, though these changes were not statistically significant

issues.title: Results' '13 to 21 points' fits bodily pain only; vitality rose 6.7 (EG) and 9.8 (CG)
issues.explanation: The Results lump bodily pain and vitality together under a 13-21 point increase. This matches bodily pain but not vitality, whose T0-to-T2 changes are 6.67 and 9.81. Minor imprecision.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Text specifying the 13-21 range applies only to bodily pain.

quotes.text: with increases of 13 to 21 points at T2 compared to T0

issues.title: Discussion gives PSQI time p = 0.002 (the MFIS value); Table 2 gives p ≤ 0.001
issues.explanation: The PSQI p-value in the Discussion matches the fatigue (MFIS) row rather than the PSQI row. Both are significant so nothing changes, but it is a reporting slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A separate PSQI test giving p = 0.002.

quotes.text: Both groups showed improvement over 15 treatment sessions ( p = 0.002)

10.3390/covid3090091.headline_claim: Individuals recovering from severe COVID-19, including previously ventilated patients, made significant functional and quality of life gains during inpatient rehabilitation.
10.3390/covid3090091.overall: The finding that patients improved markedly in function and quality of life between admission and discharge is well supported descriptively. The claim that rehabilitation is crucial or justified goes beyond a single-arm design without controls. The remaining problems are internal inconsistencies (ventilated n = 43 vs 37, the admission start date) and a modestly over-interpreted unadjusted vaccination comparison. The 6-month results rest on 76% of the cohort.

primary_outcome.name: Admission-to-discharge change in functional independence (IRF-PAI GG) and 6-minute walk distance; no single primary outcome is named

issues.title: Single-arm admission-to-discharge change used to call rehabilitation 'crucial' for recovery
issues.explanation: The study has no control group and compares only pre and post values over a roughly 14-day stay. Natural recovery, which is expected after acute COVID-19, cannot be separated from any rehabilitation effect. The authors admit they cannot assess the specific impact of rehabilitation, yet the abstract and conclusions assert that rehabilitation is crucial and justified. The data support recovery during the rehabilitation stay and nothing more specific.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control group showing smaller functional gains without inpatient rehabilitation.

quotes.text: Inpatient rehabilitation represents a crucial component for recovery from severe COVID-19.
COVID-19 patients were not compared to matched controls, limiting the analysis of the specific impact of inpatient rehabilitation on outcomes within this population.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that inpatient rehabilitation is 'crucial' for recovery rests on single-arm admission-to-discharge changes with no control group, so spontaneous recovery, acute-care carryover, regression and the passage of time cannot be separated from a rehabilitation effect; the authors' own Limitations section concedes this. The data show that patients improved during the stay, but the necessity ('crucial') wording in the Abstract and the 'underscores the importance' wording in the Conclusions go beyond what this design can establish, and the Limitations caveat is not carried into the Abstract or

issues.title: Ventilated group is n = 43 in the Results but 37 (38%) in Table 1 and the Discussion
issues.explanation: The ventilated versus non-ventilated comparison uses 43 and 55 patients, which sum to 98. Table 1 and the Discussion say 37 patients (38%) were ventilated. One of the two numbers is wrong, and the group sizes for the ventilated-subgroup comparison are uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition that explains why the ventilated subgroup (n = 43) is larger than the Table 1 ventilated count (37).

quotes.text: ventilated during their acute care stay ( n = 43)
and 38% ventilated

issues.title: 6-month results rest on 74 of 98 patients with no comparison of completers and non-completers
issues.explanation: About a quarter of patients are missing from the 6-month analyses, and available-case pairing is used with no check for differences between responders and non-responders. The 86% prevalence of post-COVID condition and the follow-up gains could be biased in either direction. The paper does state the loss and lists it as a limitation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison showing completers and non-completers had similar baseline characteristics and discharge outcomes.

quotes.text: Seventy-four individuals in total completed the survey (Tables 3-6), representing an overall completion rate of 76%.
incomplete pairwise data were excluded on an assessment-by-assessment basis

issues.title: Unadjusted vaccinated (n=23) vs unvaccinated (n=51) symptom counts read as protective effect
issues.explanation: The symptom counts (3.4 vs 5.2, p = 0.014) come from a Mann-Whitney comparison with no adjustment for confounders. The Discussion interprets the difference as a possible protective effect of vaccination. The association is reported accurately, but the causal interpretation goes beyond what an unadjusted comparison of this size supports. The abstract keeps the claim to an association.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A multivariable analysis adjusting for age, comorbidity and severity that retained the difference in symptom counts.

quotes.text: Individuals vaccinated prior to their illness exhibited fewer post-COVID-19 condition symptoms on average than their unvaccinated counterparts (3.4 and 5.2, respectively, p = 0.014, Table 6).
indicating the potential protective effect of vaccination even in individuals with severe disease

issues.title: 5xSTS: 43 'improved' but only 19 had timed results at both admission and discharge
issues.explanation: The text says 43 patients (46%) improved on the 5xSTS, but only 19 completed it at both time points. If improvement needs two timed results, 43 is impossible. If 'unable to complete' at admission counts as worse than a timed result at discharge, 43 is possible but undefined. The authors drop this test as uninformative, so the effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition stating that patients unable to complete the test at admission but able at discharge were classed as improved, with a denominator of 93.

quotes.text: While 43 patients (46%) showed an improvement from admission to discharge, only 19 were able to complete the test at admission and discharge
quotes.location: Results 3.2, 5 x Sit to Stand paragraph

issues.title: Admission window is July 2021 in Results 3.1 but September 2021 in Methods and Discussion
issues.explanation: The study period is given as September 2021 to March 2022 in the Introduction, Methods and Discussion, but the Results start it in July 2021. The inclusion window is therefore unclear. This affects how the cohort is described, not the outcome numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or protocol showing that the July start date is correct and the Methods text is a typographical error.

quotes.text: between July 2021 and March 2022 with a COVID-19 diagnosis
from September 2021 to March 2022 with a COVID-19 diagnosis

10.3390/covid5070107.headline_claim: The MTRP demonstrated promising potential as an effective intervention that enhanced participants' sense of coping and perceived reduction in dyspnea in adults with long COVID.
10.3390/covid5070107.overall: The paper is an honest small, single-arm feasibility study, but its Conclusions use causal wording ('effective', 'enhanced coping') that an uncontrolled design with a self-rated primary outcome and uncorrected secondary tests cannot support. The within-person MRC improvement of about 0.6 points is a signal worth testing, not evidence of efficacy. The Figure 1 cross-reference slip is cosmetic.

primary_outcome.name: MRC Dyspnea Scale (self-reported)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design (N=24, no control) cannot attribute MRC and CRQ Mastery change to the intervention
issues.explanation: All 24 participants received the same 8-week protocol and were compared with their own earlier scores. Improvement in a self-rated dyspnea scale could reflect natural recovery, expectation or regression, none of which can be separated here. The stable pre-baseline scores weaken the natural-recovery explanation a little but do not address expectation or attention effects. Efficacy claims need a control arm; at most the data support feasibility and a signal worth testing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist arm showing no comparable change in MRC over the same period.

quotes.text: utilizing a full within-subject experimental design, comprising a 16-week study
the lack of a control group and the small sample size limit the generalizability of the results

second_reader.what_stands: The study has a single group of 24 with no control condition, so the MRC and CRQ Mastery changes cannot be attributed to the intervention as opposed to time, expectancy, attention or natural recovery; the authors acknowledge this in the Discussion. The stable pre-baseline MRC values give some support against simple drift but do not remove these alternative explanations, and the -4 week CRQ Mastery value showed a trend away from baseline (delta = 0.34, p = 0.08). Some wording in the paper ('treatment effects', 'in response to the MTRP', 'effective intervention') is stronger than the design supp

issues.title: Conclusion says the MTRP 'enhanced' coping and was 'effective' on an uncontrolled, exploratory, uncorrected basis
issues.explanation: The Conclusions describe an effective intervention that enhanced coping and reduced dyspnea, while the Discussion says the control-group lack and the uncorrected multiple comparisons limit interpretation. The coping claim rests on CRQ Mastery alone; no coping or resilience measure (CD-RISC) changed. The 'promising potential' wording tempers this, so the problem is the causal verbs, not the whole conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data, or a pre-specified coping outcome, showing the same improvement.

quotes.text: The MTRP demonstrated promising potential as an effective intervention that enhanced participants' sense of coping and perceived reduction in dyspnea
this analytic choice limits the interpretability of p -values and raises the risk of false-positive findings

issues.title: 13 secondary outcomes with no multiplicity control; the coping claim rests on one CRQ Mastery result
issues.explanation: The paper tested 13 secondary measures across several timepoints, with only LSD pairwise comparisons and no experiment-wide correction. Two reached p ≤ 0.01 or 0.03 on the baseline-to-post contrast. With this many tests, one or two nominal hits are expected by chance. The authors disclose this, but the conclusion still uses CRQ Mastery as evidence for enhanced coping.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy placing CRQ Mastery as a key secondary outcome, or a correction that leaves it significant.

quotes.text: Because these are exploratory analyses, we did not correct for experiment-wide multiplicity error.
CRQ Mastery scores showed steady gains, with a significant overall Time effect

issues.title: Self-rated primary outcome in an open single-arm study; expectation effects not addressed
issues.explanation: The primary outcome, the MRC Dyspnea Scale, is self-reported by participants who know they are receiving the therapy. The authors acknowledge the reliance on self-report but do not discuss expectation effects. Because a single-arm design offers no comparator, the subjective outcome compounds the lack of control. This is a real weakness, though largely shared with the single-arm issue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An objective or assessor-rated co-primary outcome showing concordant change.

quotes.text: The selfreported score on the MRC Dyspnea Scale was collected bi-weekly
the reliance on self-report data limited insights into potential biophysiological changes

issues.title: Missing-at-random assumed but not shown; 5 of 24 (20.8%) stopped responding and 11/24 'achieved MCID' counts all
issues.explanation: The Methods say no imputation was needed 'beyond establishing that the data were missing at random', but no test or description supports this. Five participants stopped responding to surveys, and the MCID proportion (11 of 24) takes everyone as the denominator, so non-responders count as non-achievers. If non-responders were those who did less well, or those who improved and lost interest, the effect estimates move in either direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported missing-data analysis showing completers and non-completers did not differ in baseline or trajectory.

quotes.text: The response rate to the surveys declined from 24 participants at the start to 19 by the end of the study, resulting in a 79% adherence rate to survey completion.
no estimation of missing data (e.g., imputation) was necessary beyond establishing that the data were missing at random

issues.title: No trial registration reported; the MRC primary outcome cannot be checked against a prior record
issues.explanation: The paper reports IRB approval but no registry number or protocol reference. For a single-arm feasibility study registration is not universally expected, so this may be acceptable. It does mean the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be verified as pre-specified, which matters because many secondary outcomes were tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry with a date before enrolment that names the MRC scale as primary.

quotes.text: Institutional Review Board Statement: The study was approved by the IRB of Mount Sinai Medical System.

issues.title: Results cites Figure 1 for MRC means, but Figure 1 is captioned as a participant flow diagram
issues.explanation: The Results text says the mean MRC scores with 95% CIs are in Figure 1. The Figure 1 caption describes a participant flow diagram, and the MRC means figure is captioned Figure 2. This is a cross-referencing error. Readers can work out the intended figure, so no result is affected. It also leaves the paper without a visible participant flow diagram to account for the 24 enrolled and the 19 completing surveys.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A figure list in which Figure 1 shows the MRC means.

quotes.text: Mean MRC scores with 95% confidence intervals are presented in Figure 1.
Figure 2. Mean and 95% CI by Bi-Weekly Assessment of the MRC Dyspnea Scale.

10.3390/covid6010005.headline_claim: Balneotherapy, whether ambulatory, inpatient, or combined with nature therapy, was associated with significant within-group improvements in musculoskeletal symptoms, functional, and psychosocial domains in adults with a history of COVID-19 and persistent symptoms, supporting balneotherapy as a complementary modality for post-COVID recovery.
