10.3390/covid6010005.overall: The short-term within-group improvements are probably real, but the between-group evidence for the primary MSK outcomes is mostly null, and the paper's comparative conclusions rest on within-group change and non-significant patterns against an unblinded no-treatment control. Registration came after data collection, outcomes were designated primary without a registered substudy plan, and several Table 4 MDs and text statistics conflict with the tabulated means. The headline that balneotherapy enhances MSK health relative to no treatment is only tentative.

primary_outcome.name: MSK pain frequency (between-group comparison)

issues.title: Superiority over controls claimed from within-group change and non-significant between-group primary outcomes
issues.explanation: The title and conclusions say balneotherapy enhances MSK health and gives more rapid and clinically meaningful gains than controls. For most primary outcomes (pain frequency p = 0.916, spasm p = 0.626, grip, flexibility) the between-group tests show no difference. The 'more durable relief' claim relies on within-group p-values that differ across arms. A significant change in one arm and not another is not evidence that the arms differ. Only some T1 between-group contrasts (pain intensity, neck tension, fatigue, sleep quality) support a short-term advantage.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant group-by-time or between-group tests at the 3- and 6-month follow-ups for the primary outcomes.

quotes.text: Between-group differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.916)
quotes.location: Section 3.1.1, Change in MSK Pain Frequency

quotes.text: These findings indicate that BT supports more durable MSK pain relief than no intervention, despite modest betweengroup statistical differences.
intervention groups showed more rapid and clinically meaningful gains compared with controls.

second_reader.what_stands: For MSK pain frequency (the outcome quoted), the between-group test was non-significant (p = 0.916; NS at all time points) and the control group also improved significantly by 3 months (p = 0.018), so the 'more durable relief than no intervention' statement rests on within-group significance and is not a tested between-group result. The Conclusion's 'more rapid and clinically meaningful gains compared with controls' is supported by significant between-group contrasts at T1 for several outcomes (pain intensity, neck tension, fatigue, sleep) but not for pain frequency, spasm, grip strength, FFD

issues.title: Unblinded no-treatment control with mainly self-reported outcomes cannot separate BT from expectation and attention effects
issues.explanation: Controls received nothing and could not be blinded, while most outcomes are self-rated Likert or numeric scores. Differences from controls at T1 therefore include expectation, attention and spa-stay effects as well as any specific effect of balneotherapy. The control arm was also told not to use symptomatic medication, which affects the analgesic outcome. The conclusion that balneotherapy itself produced these gains is only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention or sham-treatment control arm, or an objective-outcome-only analysis showing the same between-group effects.

quotes.text: Control-No therapeutic intervention-Participants in this group followed their usual routine without receiving any active or rehabilitative treatment.
participant blinding was not feasible

second_reader.what_stands: The control group received no treatment and no attention-matched or sham comparator, participants were unblinded, and most outcomes (8 of 11) were self-reported, so the design cannot separate balneotherapy's specific effect from expectation, attention and setting effects; the limitations section mentions only that participant blinding was not feasible and does not discuss this confounding. The objective measures (grip, FFD) did not differ between groups, and one clinician-rated outcome (neck tension) did differ, but the paper does not clearly state whether that assessor was blinded.

issues.title: Five MSK outcomes called 'primary' do not match the registered primary outcomes of the parent trial
issues.explanation: The paper designates MSK pain, spasm, neck tension, grip strength and trunk flexibility as primary outcomes. None is among the registered primary outcomes, which are stress measures. Because this is a substudy, the paper's 'a priori' substudy claim cannot be checked against any registered substudy protocol. Readers cannot tell whether these outcomes were chosen before the data were seen.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated protocol or registry history listing the COVID substudy and its MSK primary outcomes before analysis.

quotes.text: Primary outcome parameters included: (1) musculoskeletal (MSK) pain (frequency and intensity)
The substudy was defined a priori to evaluate MSK and functional outcomes

issues.title: Trial registered 30 Aug 2023, after all assessments (baseline Jan, last follow-up 5-13 Aug 2023) were done
issues.explanation: The paper's assessment timetable shows baseline in late January and the six-month follow-up in mid-August 2023. The registry entry was submitted on 19 August and the paper gives 30 August as the registration date. Outcomes and analyses could not have been fixed in advance by a registration, so the 'a priori' framing of the outcomes cannot be checked. The paper does not call the registration retrospective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registration record dated before January 2023.

quotes.text: six-month follow-up (T3; 5 and 12-13 August)
registered in ClinicalTrial.gov (Identifier: NCT06018649, on 30 August 2023)

issues.title: Power claim (80% at n ~ 51, d = 0.4) is for a paired effect, not the between-group comparisons that carry the conclusions
issues.explanation: The sample-size justification says about 51 participants gives about 80% power for a paired effect of d = 0.4. The conclusions concern between-group differences versus controls, for which groups of 38-51 (fewer after 20% attrition) are underpowered for d = 0.4. The numerous null between-group results are therefore uninformative rather than evidence of similarity or of benefit. The authors acknowledge the shortfall but still draw comparative conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group power calculation showing at least 80% power at the analysed sample sizes.

quotes.text: A subgroup of approximately 51 participants provides ~80% power to detect a moderate paired effect (d ≈ 0.4)
Subgroup sizes closer to n = 38 retain adequate power to detect larger effects (d ≥ 0.5) but are underpowered for smaller effects (d ≈ 0.32).

issues.title: Outcomes differ significantly at baseline across arms; no baseline adjustment and completers-only analysis after 20% attrition
issues.explanation: The post hoc subgroup was formed after randomization, and outcomes such as analgesic use (ABT 2.95 vs 1.58-1.81 in the other arms), sleep disturbance and sleep quality differ significantly at baseline. The analysis is an unadjusted repeated-measures GLM, with no handling of the 20% dropouts. Larger falls in the arm with the highest baseline (ABT analgesic use) are partly expected from regression to the mean. The statement that groups were well matched applies only to demographics.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA or mixed-model) results with missing data handled, showing the same between-group effects.

quotes.text: Significant between-group differences were found only at baseline ( η 2 = 0.155, medium)
Thirty-four participants (20%) were lost to follow-up due to various reasons

issues.title: ABT results in text disagree with Table 4: spasm at 6 months (p = 0.039 vs NS) and pain intensity (p < 0.001 vs 0.003)
issues.explanation: The text reports a further significant 0.5-point reduction in spasm for ambulatory BT at 6 months. Table 4 shows the T3 mean identical to baseline (1.96), MD 0.00 and NS. The text also gives p < 0.001 for the ABT pain-intensity reduction, while Table 4 prints 0.003. Either the text or the table is wrong, and the claimed sustained spasm benefit for ABT is not supported by the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors' output showing a 6-month ABT spasm mean about 1.46 with p = 0.039, and a pain-intensity p between 0.001 and 0.003 described by the text as p < 0.001 by mistake.

quotes.text: additional significant improvement by 6 months ( -0.5 points; p = 0.039)
1.21 post-treatment ( -1.9 VAS, -61%, p < 0.001)

issues.title: Baseline ABT+NT vs Control contrasts in text (QoL MD -0.681; analgesic MD 0.740) not reproducible from Table 4 means
issues.explanation: The text reports significant baseline differences for ABT+NT vs Control in quality of life (MD -0.681, p < 0.001) and analgesic use (MD 0.740, p = 0.008). The Table 4 baseline means differ by only 0.13 and 0.23 respectively. The text also gives the QoL difference a sign (<) at odds with the higher ABT+NT score in the table. The statistics in the text and the table do not describe the same data, so the baseline-imbalance description cannot be verified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the post hoc contrasts were adjusted estimates from a completers-only model, with the adjusted means that give MD = 0.681 and 0.740.

quotes.text: ABT+NT < Control: MD = -0.681, p < 0.001
ABT+NT > Control: MD = 0.740, p = 0.008

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

issues.title: Table 4 T3 MD values contradict printed means: IBT spasm 0.15 (means give 0.39), IBT analgesic 0.07 (0.23), ABT QoL 0.13 (0.31)
issues.explanation: In several Table 4 cells the printed change from baseline does not equal baseline minus follow-up mean, although the other cells in the same columns do. Three T3 values are affected: IBT spasm, IBT analgesic use and ABT quality of life. Control QoL at T3 is a fourth, 0.04 vs 0.00. Because the paper uses these MDs to describe significant versus non-significant within-group change, the errors change reported results for individual groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction or raw data showing that the MD column is from a different analysis set, or that the T3 means (not the MDs) are the wrong entries.

issues.title: Table 3 sex counts sum to 50 (ABT+NT, header 51) and 37 (Control, header 38)
issues.explanation: The Woman and Man counts in the ABT+NT and Control columns sum to one fewer than the group sizes in the header. The percentages are computed on 50 and 37. Missing sex data is a plausible cause, but the paper does not say so. Nothing in the results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A footnote or the CONSORT diagram stating that one ABT+NT and one Control participant had missing sex or demographic data.

quotes.text: ABT+NT, n = 51

10.3390/covid6010022.headline_claim: An eight-week moderate-load inspiratory muscle training protocol increased respiratory muscle strength, improved functional capacity, and enhanced quality of life in individuals recovering from post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.3390/covid6010022.overall: The MIP difference (p = 0.036) is arithmetically consistent with the printed means, but the paper's primary outcome does not match the registry and the analysis ignores a large baseline imbalance, so the strength conclusion is tentative. The functional-capacity and sleep-quality claims are stronger than the data support (non-significant 6MWD; two uncorrected secondary results), and the safety percentages are not whole-number counts. The 19-person trial supports only a cautious, hypothesis-generating reading.

primary_outcome.name: Maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP)

issues.title: Registered sole primary outcome (radioaerosol deposition) not reported; paper's primary is MIP
issues.explanation: The registry lists radioaerosol pulmonary deposition at 3 minutes as the primary outcome with no secondary outcomes, while the paper reports no such measure and states that MIP was the primary outcome. The Methods never name a primary outcome; this appears only in the limitations paragraph. The headline strength claim therefore rests on an outcome that does not match the registration, and the change is not explained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing MIP was registered as primary before enrolment, or a report of the radioaerosol outcome elsewhere.

quotes.text: an a priori sample size calculation was performed based on maximal inspiratory pressure, which was defined as the primary outcome.
This study demonstrated that an eight-week IMT protocol increased respiratory muscle strength

second_reader.what_stands: The registry's sole primary outcome (radioaerosol pulmonary deposition) is not reported in the paper, and the paper designates MIP as its primary outcome without acknowledging a change from the registration. The caveat is that only the current registry record was available, so I cannot say when the registered outcome was entered or whether it was ever changed.

issues.title: Conclusion states functional capacity improved though 6MWD difference was not significant (p = 0.103)
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state that IMT improved functional capacity. Neither 6MWD (p = 0.103) nor %predicted (p = 0.058) differed significantly between groups, and both confidence intervals include zero. The Discussion treats the 58.36 m point estimate as exceeding the MCID, which ignores that the interval spans no effect. The safety wording is a separate matter, covered under c2.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority or equivalence framework, or a significant between-group 6MWD result.

quotes.text: This study demonstrated that an eight-week IMT protocol increased respiratory muscle strength, improved functional capacity, and enhanced quality of life in individuals recovering from post-COVID-19 syndrome.
values were not significantly different between groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions say functional capacity improved although the between-group 6MWD difference was not significant (58.36 m, 95% CI -13.08 to 129.81, p = 0.103; %pred p = 0.058). The Results text and the Discussion's power caveat acknowledge the non-significance, but the Conclusions state the improvement as demonstrated rather than as uncertain.

issues.title: Adverse-event percentages 8%, 12%, 4% cannot be whole-number counts in groups of 10 and 9
issues.explanation: Adverse events are given as proportions of participants, but with 10 participants in the IMT group a count can only be 0, 10, 20% and so on, so 8% and 12% are unattainable. In the sham group of 9, 4% would be 0.36 of a person. The safety statement therefore rests on figures that do not match the stated group sizes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the percentages use a different denominator (for example training sessions) and the corresponding counts.

quotes.text: a small proportion of participants reported transient dizziness (8%) or mild muscle pain (12%)
IMT Group (N = 10)

issues.title: MIP compared on post values by t test without baseline adjustment despite 23 cmH2O baseline gap
issues.explanation: The Methods use independent t tests on post-intervention values for MIP, and adjust for baseline only for quality of life. The groups differed at baseline in MIP (68.10 vs 91.22) and age (43.6 vs 57.1 years), and the Results call the post-value difference 'changes in MIP'. The primary comparison therefore does not account for baseline, and its size and direction of bias are unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or change-score analysis for MIP giving the same conclusion.

quotes.text: Between-group comparisons of baseline characteristics, inspiratory muscle performance, lung function, functional capacity, and sleep parameters were performed using independent-samples t tests.
Some baseline differences between groups were observed for age, maximal inspiratory pressure, and EDSS scores.

issues.title: Sleep-quality conclusion rests on 2 of 15 uncorrected Table 2 comparisons; neither survives Bonferroni
issues.explanation: Table 2 contains 15 between-group tests at an unadjusted 0.05 level. The Conclusions call the sleep improvement 'substantial', based on sleep efficiency (p = 0.005) and PSQI (p = 0.011). Total sleep time, latency, time in bed, awakenings and EDSS were not significant, and the two positive results are not labelled exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity plan designating sleep efficiency and PSQI as key secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: Notably, the IMT group also exhibited substantial improvements in sleep quality, as evidenced by both objective and subjective measures.
The significance level adopted was p < 0.05.

issues.title: Printed Cohen's d values are about half of d recomputed from Table 2 (MIP 0.50 vs about 1.05)
issues.explanation: Recomputing d from the printed group means, SDs and sizes gives values roughly double those reported for the significant outcomes. The printed values therefore label large effects as small or medium, which understates the standardised effect sizes the paper itself uses to interpret its results. The p-values and confidence intervals do reconcile with the means and SDs, so the error appears to be in the effect size column.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative effect-size formula that reproduces the printed values from the same data.

quotes.text: mean difference: 31.83 cm H2O; 95% CI: 2.43 to 61.32; p = 0.036, Cohen's d = 0.50
mean difference: -4.60; 95% CI: -7.99 to -1.20; p = 0.011, Cohen's d = 0.60

issues.title: Sleep efficiency Cohen's d printed as 0.60 in one Results sentence and 0.62 in the next (Table 2: 0.62)
issues.explanation: The Results give Cohen's d = 0.60 for the sleep efficiency difference in one paragraph and d = 0.62 for the same comparison (same p = 0.005) in a later paragraph. Table 2 prints 0.62, so the 0.60 appears to be the slip. It is a small internal inconsistency that changes no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Showing that the two sentences refer to different comparisons or different effect size estimators.

quotes.text: Changes in sleep efficiency (actigraphy) showed significant differences between the groups (mean difference: 8.42; 95% CI: (2.97 to 13.88); p = 0.005, Cohen's d = 0.60)
sleep efficacy (90.48 vs. 82.06%, p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.62)

issues.title: Paper gives registration date 21 Sept 2021; registry first submission is 7 March 2022, after study start
issues.explanation: The paper states the trial was registered on 21 September 2021, but the registry record shows first submission on 7 March 2022, six days after the listed start. The paper's date appears incorrect, and registration was effectively at or just after the start of enrolment. This is a small reporting discrepancy, but it matters for the claim of prospective registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing an earlier registration date of 21 September 2021 or an explanation that this is the ethics approval date.

quotes.text: and registered at clinicaltrials.gov (ID: NCT05282199), 21 September 2021.

10.3390/diagnostics13050882.headline_claim: Adaptive force (AFisomax) is a sensitive functional parameter that was substantially impaired in long COVID and normalised with health improvement, and may support diagnosis and treatment choice; the authors state causality for the treatments cannot be judged.
10.3390/diagnostics13050882.overall: The central finding, a large within-patient rise in AFisomax from pre to post/end, is supported in the 17 selected patients. The paper has no comparison group, selects only recovered patients, and relies on unblinded testers, so claims of normalisation, diagnostic value and therapy guidance are stronger than the design allows. Several small numerical misprints (trial counts, an impossible percentage, a median, a CI, a df) are real but do not change the main results.

primary_outcome.name: AFisomax (maximal isometric Adaptive Force), pre vs post and pre vs end

issues.title: Diagnostic and therapy-guidance conclusions exceed a 17-patient uncontrolled, unblinded series
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusions say AFisomax could support diagnosis, follow-up, and the choice of individual therapy, and that the holding capacity 'returned to normal function'. The study has no healthy comparison group, no diagnostic accuracy analysis, no control for repeated testing, and no comparison of therapies. The immediate pre-to-post change after one treatment could not be separated from tester expectation or the test being repeated, and the authors note that instability returned at later appointments, without objective measurement. The data support a large pre-to-end change in recovered patients, not a validated clinical use.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled study with healthy and non-recovering comparators, and a diagnostic accuracy or randomized treatment-guidance analysis.

quotes.text: The findings revealed a substantially impaired maximal holding capacity in long COVID patients, which returned to normal function with substantial health improvement.
This should be used to identify a treatment tailored to the patient's individual conditions and requirements.
MMTs at following treatment appointments showed a fallback to muscular instability for the most patients; however, this was not verified by objective measures.

second_reader.what_stands: The claims that AFisomax 'might support diagnostics', can 'support therapy process' and 'should be used to identify a treatment tailored to the patient' go beyond what 17 recovered, selected, uncontrolled, unblinded patients can show. No diagnostic accuracy or treatment-selection analysis was done. The post-treatment stability reportedly relapsed on later appointments (unmeasured), and the paper concedes lack of specificity and that treatment causality cannot be judged. This is narrower than a blanket overreach: the authors label the work a pilot and call for a clinical study next, and the 'mi

issues.title: Unblinded testers applied the force ramp and rated MMTs; 'not influenced by lack of blinding' is overstated
issues.explanation: The tester knew whether each patient was at pre, post or end and applied the force increase themselves. The authors argue that similar slope and AFmax values show the assessment was not affected by non-blinding. A similar slope does not rule out subtle differences in how force was applied or when the limb was perceived to yield, and the hip slope test was close to significance (p = 0.071). The agreement between tester ratings and measured AF also cannot be read as independent validation, since the ratings were unblinded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded or automated force-application and an independent rater, or data showing identical force profiles at all time points.

quotes.text: Furthermore, the study was not blinded. The testers were aware of the patients' health state.
This strongly indicates that the AF assessment was not influenced by lack of blinding.
For the latter, the RM ANOVA was close to significant.

issues.title: Only the 17 of 37 patients who reported recovery were analysed, so AFisomax cannot be shown to track recovery
issues.explanation: Patients entered the analysis only if they reported substantial improvement by July 2022, so every 'end' value is by definition from a recovered patient. Twenty patients who were still in therapy or dropped out were excluded (54% of 37). No end-point AF values exist for patients who did not improve, so the claim that AFisomax normalises with recovery and is suitable for follow-up has no negative comparison. The pre findings (100% unstable) are supported for all 37.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: End-of-follow-up AF measures in non-recovered patients showing persistent instability.

quotes.text: Seventeen patients were included in this study since they reported a substantially improved or regained health state by July 2022.
100% of the patients showed initially clear instability (this was also the case for the other 20 patients measured in long COVID state, but who were not included in the study)

issues.title: Discussion says AFosc was significantly higher pre vs post/end, but elbow pairwise tests were non-significant
issues.explanation: Hypothesis 3 predicted significantly higher AFosc at pre than at post and end. Results show this only for hip flexors; for elbow flexors only the omnibus ANOVA was significant and the pairwise Bonferroni comparisons missed significance. The Discussion states the finding without restricting it to hip flexors and says the hypothesis was met. This overstates a secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Discussion text restricting the claim to hip flexors, or elbow pairwise tests that were significant.

quotes.text: The pairwise comparisons missed significance after the Bonferroni correction (Figure 5a,d).
AFosc was significantly higher for pre vs. post and pre vs. end, as was hypothesized.

issues.title: Discussion MMT counts (84 pre; 164+4+6 = '173' post/end) do not match Table 1 (87 pre; 175 post/end)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says 84 pre MMTs were rated unstable and that 164 stable, 4 unstable and 6 unclear ratings make up 173 post/end MMTs. The three components add to 174, not 173. Table 1 gives 87 pre trials and 175 post/end trials, with 5 unstable. Excluding invalid trials could account for part of the gap, but the paper never says so and the 174 vs 173 sum cannot be explained that way. The conclusion that tester ratings matched the measured AF is not materially changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Discussion counts are restricted to evaluable trials, with a breakdown in which 164 + unstable + unclear sums to the stated total.

quotes.text: The MMTs at post and end were rated as 'stable' in the majority of trials (164 of 173), as 'unstable' in four of 173 cases and as 'unclear' in six of 173 cases.
All 84 MMTs at pre were assessed as 'unstable' by the testers.
In total, 144 MMTs were performed using the handheld device for hip flexors and 118 for elbow flexors.

issues.title: 30.33% of n = 12 patients is not a possible share (4/12 = 33.33%, 3/12 = 25.00%)
issues.explanation: The text reports the share of patients rating job-related stress at least 2 at the end as 30.33% with n = 12. No whole count out of 12 gives 30.33%. The likely intended value is 33.33%. This is a descriptive, secondary figure and nothing in the main findings depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for this percentage (for example a per-measurement rather than per-patient base).

quotes.text: they amounted to 30.33% and 50.00% (n = 12), respectively

issues.title: Median acute-infection severity of 2.25 (n = 16) is impossible for an integer 0-6 scale
issues.explanation: Severity was rated on integer categories 0-6. With 16 responses the median is the mean of the 8th and 9th values, so it must be a multiple of 0.5. The printed 2.25 is probably a mean. A median of 2 would be 'moderate', which fits less well with the text's 'mild' description. This is a descriptive baseline detail.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the severity scale allowed non-integer ratings.

quotes.text: The median of acute infection severity was 2.25 (n = 16).
degree of severity (0 = symptom free, 1 = mild, 2 = moderate, 3 = severe but without hospitalization

issues.title: Hip AFmax pre 95% CI printed as 148.77; 148.77 around mean 174.98 (SD 50.03, n = 17)
issues.explanation: The confidence interval has identical lower and upper limits, which is impossible for a mean of 174.98 with SD 50.03. The upper bound should be about 200-201. Nothing in the conclusions depends on this cell.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source-data table (Supplementary Table S8) showing the CI as printed.

quotes.location: Table 2, hip flexors, AF max, pre CI

issues.title: Text applies n = 11 to both before-COVID stress percentages; Table 3 gives n = 12 for personal stress
issues.explanation: The sentence gives one n = 11 for both before-COVID stress percentages. Table 3 lists n = 11 for job-related and n = 12 for personal-life stress. Only the denominator label for the personal-stress figure is wrong, and 100% is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; a cosmetic label error.

quotes.text: rated with an intensity of ≥ 2 in 90.91% and 100%, respectively (n = 11)

issues.title: Hip pre-vs-end AFosc/AFisomax test printed as t(17) although n = 17 paired data imply t(16)
issues.explanation: All other hip paired tests are reported with 16 degrees of freedom, as expected for 17 patients. The pre vs. end test is printed with t(17). The effect size d = 2.178 equals 8.979/sqrt(17), so the test used n = 17 and the df is a misprint.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: None needed; cosmetic.

10.3390/healthcare11182561.headline_claim: A telerehabilitation intervention combining education with respiratory and motor rehabilitation helped improve global functionality and self-care, with clinical and functional impacts in people with long COVID in hospital-community transition.
10.3390/healthcare11182561.overall: The directional signal in the intervention group is large, but the paper cannot show that the programme caused it. Controls were self-selected and imbalanced at baseline, assessment was unblinded, and the Methods inclusion criteria contradict the printed baseline means. Table 2 p-values contain clear errors, and the claims of evident benefit and equivalence to face-to-face care go beyond a small feasibility pilot.

primary_outcome.name: not designated as primary in the paper; outcomes include PCFS, FACIT, mMRC, LCADL, HADS, STS, SpO2, heart rate

issues.title: Self-selected, imbalanced usual-care controls and unblinded assessment by the treating nurse
issues.explanation: Controls were people who refused the programme or lacked digital literacy, so they differ systematically from participants. Baseline age (63.9 vs 50.2 years) and SpO2 (97.6 vs 93.9) differ strongly, and between-group results are unadjusted comparisons of post values. The same nurse who delivered the programme assessed the largely patient-reported outcomes with no blinding. Group differences therefore cannot be attributed to the programme, and the control group itself changed on some measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted analyses for baseline and demographics, or blinded assessment, showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Although they had access to the telerehabilitation program, they were not part of the program because they refused or because they lacked digital literacy.
O2 saturation (SPO2) values were higher in the control group ( p < 0.0001).
The evaluation was performed at both times by the rehabilitation nurse who carried out the program.

second_reader.what_stands: Controls were not allocated at random: they were people who refused or lacked digital literacy, and the groups differ at baseline in age (about 14 years), sex mix and SpO2 (3.7 points), plus two other variables. The treating nurse assessed outcomes at both time points with no stated blinding. The paper acknowledges non-randomisation and the lack of a true control group as limitations. It does not discuss assessor bias or adjust for the imbalances.

issues.title: Pilot with non-equivalent controls concluded to show 'evident' benefits 'identical' to face-to-face care
issues.explanation: The authors present a small pilot (24 vs 25) with self-selected controls as having shown evident benefits, and say they equal those of face-to-face rehabilitation. The study had no face-to-face comparison, so the equivalence statement rests on citing other literature. The Conclusions also say the programme can be safely replicated and improves quality of life, which was not measured. These claims go well beyond a feasibility pilot.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A face-to-face comparator arm or a prespecified equivalence analysis in the study.

quotes.text: The benefits of telerehabilitation intervention are evident, and they are identical to the results of face-to-face rehabilitation, as corroborated by the literature [9].
The program has the potential to be safely replicated, promoting the improvement of clinical and functional indicators in people with long COVID.
The sample was intentional, following the guidelines that indicate that, in general, sample size calculations are not required for some pilot studies [19].

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that benefits are 'evident' and 'identical' to face-to-face rehabilitation is not supported by the data, since no face-to-face arm was studied and the comparison rests on a citation. A small pilot with non-equivalent controls, large baseline differences, unadjusted multiple tests and no blinding cannot establish 'evident' benefit. The Conclusion is more cautious ('potential to be safely replicated'), and the Limitations section does name the design weaknesses, but the Discussion wording still overstates what was shown.

issues.title: Ethics approval dated 18 March 2022, after the stated Nov 2021 to Jan 2022 study period
issues.explanation: The Results and Methods say participants were enrolled and assessed between November 2021 and January 2022. The only ethics approval cited is dated 18 March 2022, after data collection ended. The paper also describes a 14-week programme, which does not fit comfortably inside a window ending in January 2022 for late enrollees. Either the dates are wrong or approval was retrospective, and the paper does not say which.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier approval or waiver covering enrolment, or a correction of the study dates.

quotes.text: Forty-nine people were included in the study between November 2021 and the end of January 2022.
Resolution no. 1209/2022 of 18 March 2022

issues.title: Baseline PCFS (2.5) and FACIT (29.8 / 26.9) means contradict the stated inclusion criteria
issues.explanation: Inclusion required PCFS of 3 or more and FACIT of 26 or less. The intervention-group baseline PCFS mean is 2.5 (control 2.8), which is below the minimum eligible value. The intervention-group baseline FACIT mean is 29.8 (control 26.9), which is above the maximum eligible value. So not all participants met the stated criteria, or the criteria were misreported. This raises doubt about who was actually enrolled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that eligibility was judged on a different screening measure or time point than Table 1 baseline.

quotes.text: Post-COVID-19 Functional Status Scale (PCFS) ≥ 3
Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy Fatigue Scale (FACIT) ≤ 26

issues.title: Table 2 prints p=0.005 for rows whose Z (3.6-5.9) implies p<0.001; text says p<0.0001
issues.explanation: In Table 2, PCFS, FACIT, mMRC, STS, Borg_sts and HADS Depression all show p = 0.005, even though their Z values (4.1 to 5.9) imply p far below 0.001. The text correctly reports p<0.0001 for most of these, so the table and text disagree. For depression, Z = 3.568 implies p of about 0.0004, so the text's p<0.0001 is also overstated. The conclusions are not affected, but the printed table cannot be trusted as given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Table 2 p-values are exact-test or adjusted values, which the paper does not state.

quotes.text: better post-COVID functionality (PCFS) ( p < 0.0001)

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.005, but recomputed from the printed z = 5.874 p is at most 4.267e-09, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show. This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: About 16 outcomes tested at p<=0.05 with no correction; several secondary findings marginal
issues.explanation: Each of roughly 16 outcomes was tested in three families of comparisons at an unadjusted 0.05 level. The strongest results are far below any corrected threshold. The marginal ones (heart rate p=0.039, personal care p=0.034, and control-group SpO2, PCFS, effort-labelled and physical activity changes at p=0.021 to 0.045) could easily arise by chance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or correction method, or confirmation that marginal results are not used for conclusions.

quotes.text: In all situations, the significance level adopted was p ≤ 0.05.

issues.title: Text gives p=0.045 for control-group perceived effort; Table 3 Borg_sts is p=0.397 (0.045 is mMRC)
issues.explanation: The Results text says the control group had decreased perceived effort with p = 0.045. In Table 3 the Borg_sts row gives p = 0.397, and p = 0.045 belongs to the mMRC (dyspnoea) row. The text therefore misattributes a significant result to a measure where the change was not significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different Table 3 value for Borg_sts showing p = 0.045.

quotes.text: decreased perceived effort ( p = 0.045)

issues.title: Aerobic block given as 5-20 min in one place and progressing to 30 min in another
issues.explanation: The session structure lists aerobic training as 5-20 min. A later paragraph says it started at 5 min and increased to 30 min. The upper limit is therefore reported inconsistently, which makes the dose description unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that 20 min is the typical session length and 30 min the maximum reached.

quotes.text: aerobic training (5-20 min)
throughout the program, it increased to 30 min

10.3390/healthcare12181864.headline_claim: A 4-week pulmonary telerehabilitation program (breathing and aerobic exercises) is feasible and effective for young adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.3390/healthcare12181864.overall: The finding that the exercise group improved more than the control group on HR, RR, sit-to-stand and 6MWT is a tentative, hypothesis-generating signal at best, since allocation was by convenience (despite the Abstract's 'randomized'), the control did nothing, assessment was open and n = 8 per arm. The claim of 'effective' treatment, and the SpO2 benefit in particular, goes beyond the evidence. The reported statistics also contain several text/table inconsistencies and an apparent HR/RR label swap, so exact values should not be relied on.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; multiple outcomes (SpO2, HR, RR, BP, sit-to-stand, 6MWT, Borg)

issues.title: Abstract says 'randomized'; Methods show convenience allocation to a no-activity control, with open assessment
issues.explanation: The Abstract states that 16 students were randomly allocated to two groups, but the Methods say they were assigned by convenience after committing to the programme. The control group did nothing, so the comparison cannot separate the programme from selection, attention, expectation and spontaneous recovery (which the authors themselves invoke for the CG). Baselines also differ (6MWT 403.3 vs 461.6 m; SBP 122.5 vs 107.8 mmHg), consistent with non-random allocation. The efficacy conclusion is therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a genuine random allocation procedure with concealment, or an outcome assessor blinded to group.

quotes.text: The subjects were assigned by convenience into a control group (CG) (8 subjects) and experimental groups (EG) (8 subjects), after their commitment to continue the program.
Sixteen university students were randomized allocated in two groups (control=CG/experimental=EG).

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract calls allocation randomized, but Methods describe convenience assignment after a commitment to continue, to a no-activity control, with no randomization procedure. Assessor blinding is not reported, so the assessments appear open, though the paper does not state this explicitly.

issues.title: Eight per arm, no sample-size calculation, yet Conclusion says programme is 'effective in treating'
issues.explanation: The study has 16 participants, no sample-size justification, no randomisation and no blinding, and the authors themselves describe it as a pilot providing 'preliminary data'. The Conclusion nevertheless asserts that the programme is 'feasible and effective in treating' post-COVID-19 syndrome. The data support at most a preliminary signal of feasibility, not effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation justifying n = 16 for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: The aim of this pilot study was to analyze the effects of a respiratory TR program
feasible and effective in treating post-COVID-19 syndrome in young patients

second_reader.what_stands: With 8 participants per arm, no sample-size calculation, non-random allocation and an untreated control, the data cannot support the Conclusion that the programme is 'effective in treating' post-COVID-19 syndrome; at most, they are preliminary. The authors do label the study a pilot and call for larger studies, which partly softens but does not remove the strong wording.

issues.title: SpO2 improvement claimed from within-EG p=0.042 despite non-significant interaction (p>0.143)
issues.explanation: The group-by-time interaction for SpO2 was not significant (F(1,14)=2.4128, p > 0.143), meaning no evidence that the EG changed differently from the CG. Yet the Abstract reports a significant SpO2 increase (p < 0.042) and the Conclusion lists SpO2 among improvements, relying on the EG's own pre-post p-value. The CG's SpO2 also rose (0.7), so a within-group test is not evidence of a programme effect. For perceived effort, the highlighted significance is also within-group (both groups improved).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group (interaction or adjusted) test for SpO2.

quotes.text: did not reveal a significant interaction (F(1,14)=2.4128, *p* > 0.143) for the SpO2 variable
a significant increase in SpO<sub>2</sub> (p < 0.042)
can lead to improvements in SpO2, physical and cardiorespiratory capacities

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract and Conclusion report an SpO2 increase based on the within-EG p=0.042 although the group-by-time interaction was non-significant (p>0.143), so a differential effect of the programme on SpO2 is not supported. The Discussion's EG change of 2.3 also differs from the 3.0 implied by Table 3.

issues.title: About ten outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 with no primary outcome or multiplicity correction
issues.explanation: The Methods apply a single significance threshold of p < .05 across roughly ten outcomes, with no primary outcome and no correction. Table 3 within-group p-values of 0.012, 0.028 and 0.042 would not stay below a corrected threshold such as 0.05/7 (about 0.007). The strongest interaction results (RR, 6MWT, sit-to-stand) are likely to hold up, but SpO2 and borderline findings are less secure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and hierarchy, or correction-adjusted p-values.

quotes.text: A value of p < .05 was considered statistically significant.
significant decrease of RR and HR (p < 0.012) accompanied by a significant increase in SpO<sub>2</sub> (p < 0.042)

issues.title: Table 3 RR and HR rows appear swapped (RR about 73, HR about 21)
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports respiratory rate as about 73 and heart rate as about 21, which are physiologically implausible and look like heart rate and respiratory rate swapped. The Discussion then describes decreases of HR = 4 and RR = 8.7 using the same labels, so the text inherits the error. The pattern of the result (a decrease in the EG) is unaffected, but the reported vital-sign effects are attached to the wrong variable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that RR was measured in unusual units, or a corrected table with the labels exchanged.

quotes.location: Table 3, RR row, Control Group Pre
Table 3, HR row, Control Group Pre

issues.title: Discussion attributes CG changes (1.7 reps, 7.5 m) to the EG, whose Table 3 changes are 4.9 and 217.5 m
issues.explanation: One Discussion sentence says the EG improved sit-to-stand by 1.7 and 6MWT by 7.5 m, and the next says the EG improved by 4.9 and 217.5 m. Table 3 shows 4.9 and 217.5 are the EG changes, and 1.7 and 7.5 are the control-group changes. The first sentence is therefore mislabelled. The text also says the EG did better, so this does not change the direction of the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 1.7 and 7.5 are a different EG quantity (for example a different time interval) rather than the CG change.

quotes.text: The EG increased the number of times it could stand up and sit down from a chair by 1.7 and the distance covered after 6 minutes by 7.5 meters.
The EG significantly increased physical (4.9) and cardiorespiratory (217.5 mts) capacity to perform these activities.

issues.title: Post hoc p-values in Results (<0.001, <0.031, <0.002, <0.001) differ from Table 3 (0.012, 0.012, 0.012, 0.028)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives within-EG post hoc p-values for heart rate (<0.001), respiratory rate (<0.031), sit-to-stand (<0.002) and 6MWT (<0.001). Table 3 prints 0.012, 0.012, 0.012 and 0.028 for the same four EG comparisons, and the Abstract repeats the Table 3 values. The text also gives the same F(1,14)=15.121 for the physical and cardiorespiratory interactions, but with different p-values (<0.006 and <0.002), which cannot both be right. All values are significant at 0.05, so the qualitative conclusion holds, but the reported statistics are not reliable as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 3 p-values come from a separate test (e.g. Wilcoxon) from the Tukey results in the text, and corrected F values for the two interactions.

quotes.text: significant decrease in heart (*p* < 0.001) and respiratory rates (*p* < 0.031)
in the EG after treatment (*p* < 0.002)
A significant interaction (Group X Measurement) was found for the comparison of physical (F(1,14)=15.121, *p* < 0.006)

issues.title: Abstract prints the non-significant 6MWT Borg result as 'p < 0.106'; Results print 'p > 0.106'
issues.explanation: The Abstract writes the 6MWT Borg interaction as 'p < 0.106', which as written would read as a bound on a p-value. The Results print 'p > 0.106', and the F statistic implies p of about 0.106, so the Results are the correct form. This is a wrong inequality sign with no effect on conclusions, since 0.106 is non-significant either way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing plausible; the sign is simply inconsistent between sections.

quotes.text: only for physical but not for cardiorespiratory capacity (p < 0.106)
did not show any significant interaction (F(1,14)=2,9929, *p* > 0.106)

issues.title: Described as retrospective file review but reported as an allocated intervention; no registration
issues.explanation: Section 2.1 calls the study retrospective and based on student records, while the Abstract and Methods describe allocation, a scheduled intervention and face-to-face assessments at set times. No registration or protocol is cited, so prespecification of outcomes and analyses cannot be checked. This weakens confidence in how outcomes were chosen but does not by itself invalidate the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registration record or protocol dated before data collection.

quotes.text: A longitudinal, retrospective study was conducted on students of the University.

issues.title: EG SpO2 rise stated as 2.3% in Discussion; Table 3 means differ by 3.0 points
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives the EG oxygen saturation increase as 2.3, using the same units as the CG value of 0.7, which matches Table 3 exactly. For the EG, Table 3 means (91.3 to 94.3) differ by 3.0, not 2.3. The EG gain is therefore understated in the text, and no reading of the table reproduces 2.3.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded individual data giving a mean EG change of 2.3 (not possible given printed means to one decimal unless the table means are wrong).

quotes.text: increased in both groups at the end of treatment (CG: 0.7%; EG: 2.3%)

10.3390/healthcare12232344.headline_claim: Health resort treatment improves functional status, physical performance and fatigue in long COVID patients and should be recommended as a supplement to standard treatment.
10.3390/healthcare12232344.overall: The data show that patients' self-rated fatigue, PCFS and SPPB scores were better at discharge than at admission. The paper's causal statements that the treatment improved functioning, and its recommendation, are not supported by an uncontrolled retrospective pre-post design with subjective outcomes. There are also two minor numerical inconsistencies (men's 63% fatigue reduction, and the 4% versus 10% SPPB age gap) and an unexplained step from 150 eligible to 116 analysed records.

primary_outcome.name: No single primary outcome designated; SPPB physical performance, PCFS functional status and fatigue were each reported as pre/post changes

issues.title: Causal efficacy and recommendation claimed from an uncontrolled pre-post series with self-rated outcomes
issues.explanation: All 116 patients had the same individually tailored multi-component stay, and change was measured only from admission to discharge, with no control group. Fatigue (0-10) and PCFS are patient-rated and unmasked. Large, significant pre-post differences therefore cannot be attributed to the treatment. The conclusion that treatment improved functioning, and the recommendation to use it as a supplement to standard care, go beyond what this design supports. The limitations discuss neither the missing comparator nor the subjective outcomes. This covers candidates c3, c4 and c5.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group with matched baseline status, or evidence on the expected natural course of fatigue and function over the same period.

quotes.text: Health resort treatment improved functioning in patients with persistent COVID-19 symptoms by reducing fatigue, improving their functional capacity and physical performance.
It should be recommended as a supplement to the standard treatment because of its complexity.
Patients also assessed their fatigue on a 0-10 scale

second_reader.what_stands: The paper draws causal conclusions ('improved functioning by reducing fatigue...') and a recommendation to use the treatment from a single-arm pre-post records review, where two of the three outcomes (fatigue, PCFS) are patient-rated and unblinded, and the stated limitations do not mention the lack of a control group or alternative explanations for the change. The pre-post differences themselves are reported accurately, and the SPPB is a performance-based measure, but the SPPB baseline was near ceiling, and a significant within-group change cannot support the causal and recommendation claims m

issues.title: Men's fatigue reduction stated as 63% in text; Table 2 means give 54.7%
issues.explanation: The Results say fatigue fell by about 63% in men. Table 2 gives men's fatigue as 4.46 before and 2.02 after, a fall of 2.44 points or about 55%. Table 3 also lists a men's change of 2.44. The text figure is therefore inconsistent with the tables and makes men's improvement look larger. It also hides that men and women improved by similar amounts. The main findings are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 63% is the mean of individual percentage changes, with individual-level data supporting it.

quotes.text: Fatigue was reduced by approximately 56% in women and about 63% in men.

issues.title: Records fall from 239 to 150 to 116 with no flow or reasons for the last 34 exclusions
issues.explanation: The Methods report 239 records reviewed and 150 meeting the inclusion criterion, but the Results analyse 116. The 34 missing records (about 23% of 150) are not accounted for, although the exclusion criteria may partly explain them. Without a flow of records, readers cannot judge whether selection affected the pre-post results. This weakens the generalisability of the findings but does not by itself invalidate them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow of records stating how many were excluded under each listed exclusion criterion, accounting for all 34.

quotes.text: The eligibility criteria for inclusion were the complete medical records of patients who underwent the health resort treatment for long COVID ( n = 150).
The medical records of 116 people (66 women and 50 men) aged 42-79 years

issues.title: Pre-treatment SPPB gap, ages 40-59 vs 70-79: 10% in Results, 4% in Discussion; Table 4 gives about 10-11%
issues.explanation: The Results say the youngest group scored about 10% better on the SPPB before treatment than the oldest. The Discussion says about 4% higher for the same comparison. Table 4 (10.94 vs 9.83) gives about 10-11%, so the Discussion figure is wrong. It is a minor internal inconsistency that nothing else depends on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explanation that the Discussion figure refers to a different measure or time point.

quotes.text: people aged 40-59 had about 10% better SPPB scores than patients aged 70-79
the SPPB score was about 4% higher in patients aged 40-59 years than in those aged 70-79

10.3390/healthcare13020196.headline_claim: Health resort treatment mitigates neuropsychiatric symptoms in long COVID patients and should be integrated into standard long COVID treatment, with balneological factors improving symptoms to a greater extent.
10.3390/healthcare13020196.overall: The descriptive within-patient improvements are probably real in direction, but the paper's causal claims (that treatment mitigates symptoms, that balneology gives greater benefit, and that it should be integrated into standard care) are not supported by an uncontrolled, unblinded, self-rated before/after record review. The balneology comparison is confounded by baseline imbalance and unadjusted. Several text and table numbers also disagree (headache and memory severity counts, age, group differences, sleep mean), though these are individually minor.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; pre-post change in 0-10 neuropsychiatric symptom severity scores

issues.title: Efficacy and 'integrate into standard care' conclusions rest on uncontrolled within-group pre-post changes
issues.explanation: Every patient received the resort treatment, and the whole-cohort result is a before/after change in self-rated 0-10 scores tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. With no comparison group, improvement cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than natural recovery, regression to the mean or rating expectancy. The paper's own limitations section calls for randomized trials, yet the abstract and conclusions state efficacy and recommend broad adoption.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group with matched baseline showing smaller change, or wording restricting the claim to association.

quotes.text: Health resort treatment mitigates neuropsychiatric symptoms, as it is a complex approach.
Intragroup comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
Health resort treatment should be widely recommended as a complementary approach to the standard treatment of COVID-19 sequelae.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy claim and the recommendation to integrate the treatment into standard care rest on uncontrolled within-group pre-post changes (Wilcoxon signed-rank on the same patients, no untreated comparator). The limitations section does not acknowledge that this design cannot separate treatment effect from natural recovery, regression to the mean or expectation, so the causal wording ('mitigates') and the broad recommendation go beyond what the design supports.

issues.title: Balneology superiority claim rests on a non-randomised, baseline-imbalanced, unadjusted comparison
issues.explanation: Group I had higher baseline concentration, paresthesia and depression scores and longer treatment, so its larger change scores are expected even without a treatment advantage. The analysis used unadjusted delta comparisons with no baseline adjustment and no multiplicity correction across 8 symptoms. Headache, dizziness, sleep and anxiety did not differ, and the borderline findings (p = 0.02, 0.02, 0.04) would not survive correction. The claim that balneological factors improve outcomes to a greater extent is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA/regression) analysis showing a persistent between-group difference after multiplicity control.

quotes.text: Patients included in group I reported more severe long COVID symptoms at admission.
Treatment that includes balneological factors improves symptoms to a greater extent.
The implementation of balneological factors in the treatment course improves treatment effectiveness.

second_reader.what_stands: The superiority claim comes from a non-randomised comparison in which group I had significantly higher baseline symptoms for concentration, paresthesia and depression, and the delta comparisons are unadjusted, with identical post-treatment scores in several symptoms (e.g., memory 1.00 vs 1.00). Larger changes in group I are therefore equally consistent with more room to improve, regression to the mean or confounding by indication. The statement in the abstract and Section 5 that balneological factors improve effectiveness is stronger than the evidence allows, and four of eight symptoms showed

issues.title: Women's excess concentration problems stated as 16%; Table 4 means give about 37%
issues.explanation: The Results state that women had about 16% more concentration problems. The women and men means in Table 4 (2.93 and 1.84) give about 37% on the same base the paragraph uses for its other comparisons. The slip affects one descriptive figure only, but it is a wrong number in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative metric (e.g. a median-based or adjusted difference) that yields 16%.

quotes.text: women had approximately 16% more concentration problems

issues.title: Self-rated, unblinded 0-10 numeric scale used for all outcomes, acknowledged as possibly unreliable
issues.explanation: All outcomes are single-item patient ratings made before and after a treatment the patient knows they received. The authors note the scale may have low reliability for neuropsychiatric symptoms. This adds to the risk that the large percentage reductions reflect expectancy or response shift, but the problem is largely an inherited limitation of the data source.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of validity and responsiveness of this single-item scale in long COVID, or concordant validated instruments.

quotes.text: we used a numeric rating scale to evaluate the severity of symptoms, which may have low reliability when assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms.

issues.title: 30 of 150 eligible records (20%) excluded for incomplete data; no comparison with analysed patients
issues.explanation: Twenty percent of eligible records were dropped for incomplete data, and the paper does not say which items were missing or how excluded patients differed. If missing post-treatment scores were related to outcome, the complete-case estimates could be biased. The effect on the conclusions cannot be settled from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison showing excluded and included patients had similar baseline characteristics, or that the missing items were unrelated to outcome.

quotes.text: Due to incomplete data, 30 medical records of patients undergoing health resort treatment were excluded.

issues.title: Headache mild share printed 35.5% (Table 3) and 25.5% (text); 24/120 = 20%, and moderate (26) outnumbers mild
issues.explanation: Table 3 lists 24 mild headaches with 35.5%, but 24 of 120 is 20%. The Discussion gives yet another figure (25.5%) and says mild was the most common severity, yet the table has more moderate cases (26) than mild (24). The headache severity profile is therefore misreported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing mild as the largest severity category with matching counts.

quotes.text: with most of them assessing the severity as mild (25.5%)

script.explanation: 24/120 = 20.00%, but the paper prints 35.5, outside the rounding interval [35.45, 35.60]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 67.6 rather than 120.

issues.title: Table 3 memory-disorder counts sum to 110, not 120; mild '26 (30%)' should be 36
issues.explanation: The memory row lists 38, 26, 42 and 4 patients, which total 110 of 120. The printed 30% for mild corresponds to 36 patients, and the Discussion's 68.3% with memory disorders also requires 36 mild cases. The mild count is a misprint, and the table is internally inconsistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source record showing 26 mild cases with 10 patients unaccounted for for stated reasons.

quotes.text: Overall, 68.3% of patients reported memory disorders upon admission

issues.title: Text says only diastolic BP differed between Groups I and II; Table 6 shows duration p<0.05 and diastolic p>0.05
issues.explanation: The Results say the only difference between the balneology and non-balneology groups was diastolic blood pressure, but Table 6 gives p>0.05 for that variable and p<0.05 for treatment duration. Group I stayed longer (25.19 vs 23.4 days), which is an unmentioned imbalance that could favour Group I in the delta comparisons. The authors also report that Group I had higher baseline symptoms, so 'only difference' is not accurate either.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the table's p labels are transposed and duration did not differ.

quotes.text: The only difference between the groups was diastolic blood pressure at admission
quotes.location: Results, Groups I and II paragraph
Table 6, Treatment duration row, Group I
Table 6, Treatment duration row, Group II

issues.title: Sleep whole-group pre-treatment mean 2.47 ± 2.23 duplicates paresthesia and mismatches sleep subgroups (about 2.52)
issues.explanation: The whole-group sleep and paresthesia rows both print 2.47 ± 2.23. Paresthesia's subgroup means reproduce 2.47, but sleep's subgroup means (2.77 and 2.18) average about 2.52, and the Table 7 sleep groups also point to about 2.51. The Abstract repeats the 2.47 figure for sleep, so the headline 'greatest improvement' number is slightly off, though the direction of change is not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the whole-group sleep mean is 2.47 (which would require subgroup means that average to 2.47).

quotes.text: sleep disorders (2.47 ± 2.23 points vs. 0.86 ± 1.25 points

issues.title: Discussion says no patient had severe depression; Table 3 lists 2 (1.7%)
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that no patient experienced severe depression symptoms. Table 3 reports 2 patients with severe depression, and these two are included in the 50.83% with any depression. The text contradicts the table on a small descriptive point.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the two severe cases were scored on a different instrument or excluded from the text's statement.

quotes.text: though no patient experienced severe depression symptoms

issues.title: Discussion gives men's mean age 63.45 ± 8.78 as the whole-cohort mean; Results give 64.21 ± 8.67
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the mean age of participants was 63.45 ± 8.78 years. The Results report 64.21 ± 8.67 for all 120 patients, and 63.45 ± 8.78 is the men-only value in Table 1. The age argument for headache prevalence is unaffected, but the number is attributed to the wrong group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: None likely; the men-only figure is printed in Table 1.

quotes.text: In our study, the mean age of participants was 63.45 ± 8.78 years
mean age: 64.21 years ± 8.67 years

issues.title: Correlations r = 0.01 reported with 'p < 0.05' while described as no correlation (n = 120)
issues.explanation: The authors say they saw no correlation between age and headache severity, and likewise for BMI and sleep, but print p < 0.05 beside r = 0.01. With 120 patients, r = 0.01 is nowhere near significant (p about 0.9), so the p-value sign appears to be misprinted. The substantive conclusion (no correlation) is probably right.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the intended notation was p > 0.05 (no effect on conclusions).

quotes.text: we did not observe a correlation between age and headache severity

script.explanation: The printed r = 0.01 supports p no smaller than 0.828351, but the paper reports p = 0.05 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

issues.title: Treatment duration up to 47 days exceeds the stated 2-6 week (42 day) program rule
issues.explanation: Methods state the program stipulated 2 to 6 weeks, but Results report durations up to 47 days. A few stays slightly exceeded the rule, and the paper does not explain the exceptions. This has little bearing on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A program provision allowing extensions beyond 6 weeks.

quotes.text: stipulated an intervention of 2 to 6 weeks
Treatment duration ranged from 17 to 47 days

10.3390/healthcare13222914.headline_claim: In mild-to-moderate post-COVID-19 condition, supervised motion-controlled video game-based VR exercise reduces pain and improves selected secondary outcomes compared with conventional exercise.
10.3390/healthcare13222914.overall: The pain finding (VAS interaction -1.37, p < 0.001) is internally consistent with Table 2 means but rests on an unblinded self-rated outcome, so its size is probably overstated; the direction is plausible. The secondary claims are weaker: Table 2 FSS change scores do not match the printed means, there is no multiplicity control, and the functional statements go beyond null interactions.

primary_outcome.name: Pain intensity (VAS, 0-10 cm)

issues.title: FSS change scores in Table 2 (-8.16, -3.97) do not match week-8 minus baseline means (-7.3, -5.5)
issues.explanation: The Table 2 change columns for FSS disagree with the printed means. The printed change difference (-4.19) matches the Table 3 interaction, so the significant FSS time × group result (p = 0.004) rests on change scores the printed means do not reproduce. The printed means imply a between-group difference in change of only about -1.8. HADS-A in the control group (-1.19 vs -0.8) and 6MWT (27.8 vs 28.2) also differ, but those results are not significant or the gap is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level FSS data or a note showing the change columns and Table 3 are model-based estimates from a different dataset than the printed means.

quotes.text: (mean difference in change = -4.19, 95% CI -6.99 to -1.39;

second_reader.what_stands: The printed FSS change scores (-8.16 and -3.97) do not equal the differences between the printed week-8 and baseline means (-7.3 and -5.5), and the gap (up to 1.5 points) is well beyond rounding. The Table 3 interaction (-4.19) matches the printed change scores, so the means and the change/model figures are not mutually consistent; with per-protocol n of 37 per group, no denominator difference is stated that would explain it, and the paper does not explain the discrepancy.

issues.title: Self-rated pain (VAS) primary outcome with participants aware of their exercise type; only evaluator blinded
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they played VR games or did conventional exercise, and the primary outcome is their own VAS rating. Instructing them not to disclose allocation to the evaluator does not remove expectation or enjoyment effects on the rating. The VAS difference of -1.37 may partly reflect that, and the limitations section does not discuss it. The registry's masking entry (DOUBLE) also does not match the paper's evaluator-only blinding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that participants were unaware of which arm was expected to be superior, or a blinded objective pain measure showing the same effect.

quotes.text: This study is a single-center, randomized, evaluator-blind intervention study
Participants were instructed not to disclose their group assignment or intervention type during evaluations.
Participants were asked to mark the intensity of their pain over the past week on a 10 cm line.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary outcome is a self-rated VAS and participants necessarily knew which exercise they performed, so only the evaluator was blinded and the pain result is open to expectation and performance effects; the limitations section does not discuss this. However, the paper does not claim participant blinding, it states the design as evaluator-blind, and the instruction to participants not to disclose allocation is a reasonable but partial safeguard that cannot remove bias in a self-reported rating.

issues.title: Discussion claims VR 'may be more advantageous' and 'comparable' for function despite null 6MWT/SF-12 tests
issues.explanation: The functional-capacity and quality-of-life interactions were not significant (6MWT p = 0.175, SF-12 p = 0.926 and 0.388). The Discussion nevertheless says VR may be more advantageous for function and gives comparable gains to aerobic exercise. A non-significant interaction does not show equivalence or advantage. The 'both groups improved' statements also lack an untreated control to attribute the improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence or non-inferiority analysis for function, or a significant functional between-group difference.

quotes.text: Considering these multidimensional aspects of functionality, VR exercises may be more advantageous than traditional exercises.
However, the group effect favoring VR in pain, fatigue, and depressive symptoms did not translate into functional outcomes as expected.
The time × group interaction was not statistically significant for 6MWT [ F (1, 48.8) = 1.90, p = 0.175]

issues.title: SF-12 F VRG change repeats the SF-12M value (6.23 ± 9.91); its own means imply about 6.9
issues.explanation: Two different outcome rows show the identical VRG change and SD. For SF-12 F the week-8 and baseline means give a change of 6.9, not 6.23. The duplicated cell looks like a copy error. The SF-12 comparison is not significant, so only one reported value is affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level data showing a mean change of 6.23 (SD 9.91) for SF-12 physical in the VRG.

issues.title: Six secondary outcomes tested at uncorrected 0.05; HADS-D (p = 0.009) would not survive Bonferroni
issues.explanation: No multiplicity adjustment is described for the six secondary outcomes, yet the Discussion states VR gave larger reductions in depression and fatigue. HADS-D misses a six-test Bonferroni threshold. FSS would pass it, but its change data are internally inconsistent. The secondary benefits should be read as exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or adjustment plan for secondary outcomes, or adjusted p-values below threshold.

quotes.text: Also, time × group interaction was observed in favor of VRG for FSS
We observed greater improvements in pain and larger reductions in depressive symptoms and fatigue severity in the VRG.

issues.title: CTG SD for time since COVID-19 diagnosis is 1.3 in the text but 3.2 in Table 1
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the control-group value as 8.7 (1.3) months, but Table 1 gives 8.7 (3.2). The two cannot both be right. Neither SD reproduces the printed p = 0.67 for a t-test with n = 37 per group, so the baseline-balance statement for this variable cannot be fully checked. The effect on the trial's conclusions is negligible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text value is a typo, with the raw SD confirmed as 3.2, and that the p-values came from a different test.

quotes.text: In the CEG, the corresponding values were 8.7 (1.3) and 7.3 (1.7) months

quotes.location: Table 1, Duration since COVID-19 diagnosis, CTG column

issues.title: Analysis described as per protocol (74 of 79); arm of withdrawals and model inclusion not stated
issues.explanation: The analysis is labelled per protocol, and the 5 withdrawals are not shown as contributing data. The paper does not give their arms or baseline data. With only 6.3% attrition and a large pain effect, this is unlikely to change the main result. It still departs from intention-to-treat for a superiority claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all 79 randomized participants (or a statement that LMM included withdrawals' baseline data) with the same pain result.

quotes.text: Statistical analyses were performed per protocol using the SPSS v22 computer program
Five participants withdrew from the study for reasons unrelated to the interventions.

10.3390/healthcare14121630.headline_claim: Incentive spirometer training appears to improve dyspnea, functional status and exercise tolerance in long COVID compared with usual care, and prior NRICM101 use may be associated with greater improvement, which the authors present as hypothesis-generating.
10.3390/healthcare14121630.overall: The paper reports a small (n=49, only 9 controls), unblinded, retrospectively registered study whose primary outcomes differ from the registry. Its conclusions are already hedged as preliminary and hypothesis-generating, which is appropriate, but the IS efficacy claim rests on self-reported outcomes against a no-intervention control and the NRICM101 claim on subgroup significance contrasts, so both should be treated as exploratory.

primary_outcome.name: Dyspnoea-12 (D-12) total score and PCFS functional status, described as primary; Section 2.4 also calls the 6MWD the primary outcome

issues.title: Primary outcomes differ from registry and are internally inconsistent (D-12/PCFS vs 6MWD vs oxygen/blood values)
issues.explanation: The registry record lists 'Oxygen requirements, blood draw values' as the primary outcome. The paper names dyspnea (D-12) and functional status (PCFS) as primary and exercise capacity as secondary, yet later calls 6MWD 'the primary outcome'. The prespecified primary endpoint is not reported as such, and the paper's own primary endpoint is ambiguous, so the positive findings cannot be read as confirmatory. The registry shows 90 actual enrolments against 49 analysed in the paper, which is a further unexplained discrepancy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing D-12/PCFS as primary, or a protocol document showing the outcomes were prespecified.

quotes.text: The primary outcomes included subjective dyspnea and functional status, while the secondary outcomes comprised exercise capacity and pulmonary oxygenation indices.
The primary outcome was the six-minute walk distance (6MWD)
quotes.location: Section 2.4 Outcome Measures, exercise capacity paragraph

second_reader.what_stands: The paper designates D-12/PCFS as primary and oxygenation as secondary/exploratory, which does not match the registered primary (oxygen requirements, blood draw values), and it separately calls 6MWD 'the primary outcome' in the same section, so the primary outcome is internally inconsistent. Because only the current registry record was retrieved and the registration was retrospective, whether the registered outcome was changed over time cannot be established; the mismatch with the current record is what is verified.

issues.title: Randomisation undescribed, design called quasi-experimental, 9 vs 40 split, baseline CVD imbalance (p=0.006)
issues.explanation: The paper says participants were first randomized but also calls the study quasi-experimental and gives no method or concealment. The control group has 9 participants against 40 in the intervention arms, and cardiovascular disease and post-recovery duration differ significantly across groups at baseline. The EG1/EG2 and NRICM101 contrasts are not randomised, and no adjustment was made, so the between-arm differences are confounded and the efficacy estimates are tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described concealed allocation procedure and a flow diagram showing the 9/40 split arose from the randomisation.

quotes.text: Participants were first randomized to either the intervention group or the control group.
This study was designed as a quasi-experimental study.
the distribution of cardiovascular diseases showed a statistically significant difference ( p = 0.006)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper says participants were 'first randomized' but gives no randomization procedure, calls the design quasi-experimental, ends up with a 9 vs 40 control-to-intervention split, and reports a significant baseline imbalance in cardiovascular disease (p = 0.006, 4 cases, 3 of them in the EG1 NRICM101 subgroup); EG1/EG2 are defined by time since recovery, not by randomization. The authors do disclose the CVD imbalance and the lack of a randomized design for subgroup analyses and say adjustment was not feasible, so this is acknowledged but unresolved rather than concealed.

issues.title: Registered 2023-12-09, about 5 months after enrolment began on 1 July 2023
issues.explanation: The paper reports enrolment starting 1 July 2023, and the registry record was first submitted on 2023-12-09. Registration was therefore retrospective, so the outcomes and analyses could not be fixed in advance, which matters given the mismatch with the registered primary outcome. The paper does not state the registration date or acknowledge the delay.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry audit trail showing an earlier submission before July 2023.

quotes.text: from 1 July 2023 to 11 May 2024
The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06165835).

issues.title: Self-reported primary outcomes (D-12, PCFS) vs no-intervention usual care, no blinding or attention control
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they were doing IS training, and the control group received no additional intervention or attention. D-12 and PCFS are self-reported, so the observed D-12 and PCFS improvements may partly reflect expectation and extra contact. The paper does not mention blinding of participants or assessors, and the authors' conclusion is worded cautiously.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors were blinded, or an objective primary endpoint driving the conclusion.

quotes.text: Subjective dyspnea was assessed using the Dyspnoea-12 (D-12) scale
while the CG received usual care without additional pulmonary rehabilitation interventions

issues.title: NRICM101 'trend' rests on significant-vs-nonsignificant subgroup contrasts, n=4-13 per cell, no multiplicity control
issues.explanation: Each subgroup is compared to the same small control group (n = 9), and the NRICM101 benefit is inferred from one subgroup crossing p<0.05 while another does not. For PCFS the two interaction estimates are close with overlapping intervals, and for CaO2 the one nominally significant result (p = 0.042) is among many tests. No formal NRICM101-vs-no-NRICM101 interaction is reported in the GEE tables. The conclusion's wording is hedged, so the harm is limited to the secondary NRICM101 claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported direct NRICM101 × time interaction test between the two EG subgroups showing a significant difference.

quotes.text: the coefficient of time multiplied by group was not significant for both the No NRICM101 EG (B = -0.324, p = 0.527) and CG (B = 0.685, p = 0.129)
a trend toward greater improvements was observed among patients who had previously used NRICM101 (e.g., PCFS and CaO2)

issues.title: Table 1 hypertension 'No' row prints 41 (49%) where 41/49 = 83.7%
