issues.explanation: The 'All' column for hypertension 'No' gives 41 participants as 49%. With n = 49 this is 83.7%, and the 'Yes' row (8, 16.3%) implies the complement. It is a printing slip that does not affect any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the table was correct as originally typeset.

quotes.location: Table 1, Hypertension, No row, All column

script.explanation: 41/49 = 83.67%, but the paper prints 49, outside the rounding interval [48.50, 50.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 83.7 rather than 49.

10.3390/ijerph18083978.headline_claim: A physiotherapy-guided outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program after COVID-19 is tentatively feasible and may confer benefits to a small subgroup of patients.
10.3390/ijerph18083978.overall: This is a small, openly hedged feasibility series; its feasibility conclusions (12 enrolled, 25% dropout, high tolerability) are broadly supported, with several minor count inconsistencies between abstract, text and tables. Claims of benefit rest on uncontrolled pre-post data in 12 patients and should be read as tentative, and registration was retrospective.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility outcomes (recruitment, dropout, adherence, tolerability)

issues.title: Benefit wording drawn from 12-patient uncontrolled pre-post data despite no-causality caveat
issues.explanation: The abstract suggests the programme may confer benefits and the discussion says the changes indicate possible positive effects on recovery. The data are 12 patients without a control group, so improvement cannot be separated from natural recovery after COVID-19. The language is hedged and the limitations are disclosed, so the overstatement is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or removal of the benefit language.

quotes.text: We tentatively suggest from these preliminary findings that the PR protocol used may be both feasible, and confer benefits to a small subgroup of patients recovering from COVID-19.
These clinically relevant changes indicate the possible positive effects of the outpatient PR program on recovery.
Finally, the lack of a control group means that there is no benchmark against which to compare any clinical changes following the intervention.

issues.title: Progressive intensity increase: 9/12 (75%) in results vs 83% in abstract and discussion
issues.explanation: Results report progression of intensity in 9 of 12 patients, which is 75%. The abstract and discussion say 83% (10/12). The headline tolerability figure is therefore overstated by one patient's worth in two places.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 10 of 12 progressed intensity.

quotes.text: A progressive increase in the intensity of training was achieved in 9/12 patients
83% progressive increase of intensity
In 83% of patients, progression of exercise intensity was achieved.

script.explanation: 9/12 = 75.00%, but the paper prints 83, outside the rounding interval [82.50, 84.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 10.8 rather than 12.

issues.title: Dropout session range: abstract 11-19 vs results 8, 11 and 19 sessions
issues.explanation: The abstract states the three dropouts occurred after 11-19 sessions. The results list them as after 8, 11 and 19 sessions, so the lowest value is 8, not 11. The abstract understates how early one dropout occurred, a small feasibility detail.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction showing the 8-session dropout was a typo for another value.

quotes.text: Three dropouts (25%) were reported after 11-19 sessions.
Three dropouts (25%) were reported after 8, 11 and 19 sessions.

issues.title: Registered 2020-05-04 after recruitment began in April 2020 (registry start 2020-03-15)
issues.explanation: The registry record was first submitted after the stated study start and after patients were being assessed. Because primary outcomes could therefore have been shaped after data began accruing, the registered outcomes carry less weight as a pre-specification. The effect on feasibility findings is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence enrolment began after 4 May 2020.

quotes.text: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04375709).
Between April 2020 and June 2020, a total of 65 patients were discharged home from the study site

issues.title: Recruitment denominators inconsistent: 60 vs 48 assessed, 14 eligible, 9/14 participating vs 12 enrolled
issues.explanation: The recruitment rate is computed on 48 patients assessed (14 eligible, 9 participated), but 12 trained after three patients below the eligibility threshold were admitted, and the discussion rebases to 60 candidates. The 'recruitment rate' therefore mixes denominators, and the 25% dropout rate means the 'retention 100%' claim applies only to post-training assessment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing the denominators explicitly.

quotes.text: Of the 48 patients assessed, 29% (n = 14) met eligibility criteria for the current outpatient PR program (Figure 1). Of these, 64% participated in the training program (n = 9/14).
A final recruitment of 12 out of 60 emphasizes that such outpatient PR is appropriate for a select subgroup

issues.title: EQ-5D VAS <80%: text says 10 patients, Table 2 says 9 (75%)
issues.explanation: The results text states HRQoL was below 80% in 10 patients, while Table 2 gives 9 (75%). The two cannot both be right. It affects descriptive baseline only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that the text refers to a different threshold or population.

quotes.text: The HRQoL was below 80% in 10 patients.
EQ-5D-5L VAS < 80%, n (%)

issues.title: Responder session range 11-24 may conflict with 8-session dropout and 25-session completer
issues.explanation: The discussion says 9 responders trained 11-24 sessions. If non-responders had 12, 24, 24 sessions, the 8 and 25 session patients must be responders, outside 11-24. Without individual data this cannot be confirmed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual patient session counts.

quotes.text: after 11 to 24 training sessions
despite 12 (n = 1) and 24 (n = 2) training sessions

issues.title: Methods name unpaired rank-sum for paired pre-post data; figure cites signed-rank
issues.explanation: Methods describe the Wilcoxon rank sum test for pre-post comparison, which is unpaired, while Figure 2 cites a signed-rank test for the norm difference. The test for the HRQoL claim is not stated, and no test statistics or exact p values are given. The likeliest reading is a naming slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that signed-rank was used for all paired comparisons.

quotes.text: The non-parametric Wilcoxon rank sum was applied to analyze continuous variables and Fisher's exact test for categorical variables for pre-post-training comparison.
Difference Norm of 6MWD (%) was obtained from Wilcoxon-sign rank test.

issues.title: Registry lists HRQoL and 6MWT as primary; paper frames feasibility as the main aim
issues.explanation: The registry record lists EQ-5D-5L and the 6-minute walk test as primary outcomes, whereas the paper presents feasibility outcomes as its evaluation and the clinical outcomes as preliminary. Both sets are reported, so nothing is hidden. The difference is in emphasis and cannot be settled from the current registry record alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registry versions showing feasibility as primary.

quotes.text: Feasibility outcomes included: recruitment and dropout rates, number of training sessions undertaken, and tolerability for dose and training mode.
The following aspects of feasibility were evaluated

issues.title: Baseline 6MWD %norm maximum: Table 2 gives 100, text gives 103
issues.explanation: Table 2 prints the baseline range as 50-100 while the results text prints 50-103. Same quantity, different maximum. Trivial effect on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the table value is a rounded or capped display.

quotes.text: Median percentage norm of 6MWD changed from 80% (range 50-103%)
Initial 6MWD%Norm, (%)

issues.title: PCFS >=2: text counts nine (PCFS 2 and 3), Table 2 and later text give 10
issues.explanation: The sentence in 3.1 says nine patients had PCFS 2 and 3, whereas Table 2 gives 10 (83%) with PCFS >=2 and 3.3 refers to 10 patients with restrictions. A PCFS 4 patient could explain it but is not mentioned. Minor.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A PCFS 4 patient in the data.

quotes.text: Nine patients perceived moderate to severe COVID-induced restrictions (PCFS 2 and 3).
Initial PCFS ≥ 2, n (%)

10.3390/ijerph19041992.headline_claim: Fourteen days of home-based molecular hydrogen (H2) inhalation improves physical and respiratory function in acute post-COVID-19 patients and may be considered an efficient rehabilitation approach.
10.3390/ijerph19041992.overall: The large 6 MWT difference (64 m vs 9 m) is internally consistent on recomputation, so the printed numbers mostly hold, apart from small text/table slips (sex split, one CI limit). The conclusion is weaker than stated: blinding of assessors is unclear, baseline BMI/body fat differ and are unadjusted, there is no sample-size justification or registration, and the respiratory claims rest on uncorrected secondary tests. Treat it as a promising pilot signal for walking distance rather than evidence of an efficient rehabilitation approach.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test distance (m)

checklist.blinding: single (participant-level likely; assessor blinding not described)

issues.title: Single-blind design leaves effort-dependent 6 MWT and spirometry open to detection bias
issues.explanation: The paper does not say who was blinded, and it concedes that detection bias cannot be ruled out. The primary outcome (6-minute walk distance) and spirometry depend on effort and on how the tester encourages the participant. If the tester knew the allocation, the 64 m vs 9 m difference could be inflated. The authors disclose this in the limitations, but the conclusion does not temper its wording because of it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors and the spirometry/6 MWT technician were blinded to allocation.

quotes.text: for logistical reasons, there was only single blinding and, therefore, detection bias cannot be ruled out
Participants could not distinguish between the inhalation of H

issues.title: Baseline BMI (p = 0.002) and body fat (p = 0.006) differ by arm; 6 MWT change comparison not adjusted
issues.explanation: Two anthropometric baseline variables differ clearly between arms despite stratified block randomisation. The merged between-group tests of change in Table 6 do not adjust for them, and the authors dismiss the imbalance without analysis. Baseline outcome values were balanced, so the practical impact is probably small but cannot be quantified from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis of 6 MWT change adjusted for BMI/body fat showing the same effect.

quotes.text: randomization can be considered successful because it is not possible to control all variables simultaneously

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 'irrespective of sex and age' and subgroup merging rest on underpowered tests
issues.explanation: No sample-size justification is given. The authors merged sexes and dropped age because sex and age factors were non-significant (p ≥ 0.18) with only 10–16 per cell. They then state the effect holds irrespective of sex and age, while conceding in the Discussion that this may reflect insufficient sample size. Absence of significance is not evidence of homogeneity, and the data-dependent analysis switch is a further caution.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation or an interaction analysis with confidence intervals excluding clinically relevant sex/age differences.

quotes.text: However, this result should be interpreted with caution as it may be due to insufficient sample size.
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph on law of initial values

quotes.text: Therefore, it was possible to merge both sexes into one group and remove the age factor.

issues.title: Conclusion extends efficacy to respiratory function and other settings beyond one small trial with ~11 uncorrected outcomes
issues.explanation: The conclusion endorses H2 for both physical and respiratory function. The respiratory support is FVC p = 0.005 and FEV1 p = 0.028 among about 11 outcomes tested at an uncorrected 0.05. A single 14-day, 50-person trial with detection bias that cannot be excluded supports a tentative signal on 6 MWT rather than a recommended rehabilitation approach. The Discussion also extrapolates to spa and telerehabilitation use and to superiority over supervised exercise training.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified multiplicity strategy showing the respiratory outcomes remain significant, or replication in a larger blinded trial.

quotes.text: may be considered as an efficient rehabilitation approach for improving both physical and respiratory function in acute post-COVID-19 patients.

issues.title: Methods state 26 males/24 females; Table 1 subgroup n (16+13 male, 10+11 female) gives 29/21
issues.explanation: The Methods give a 26/24 sex split. The Table 1 subgroup sizes add to 29 males and 21 females. One of the two is wrong, so the sex-stratified subgroup sizes behind Tables 1, 3 and 5 are uncertain. Total n = 50 is unaffected and the main results are not obviously changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that three participants changed sex category, or a corrected Methods/Table 1 with matching counts (e.g. from the raw data in Table S1).

quotes.text: included 26 males and 24 females

issues.title: No trial registry entry reported for a prospective randomised trial
issues.explanation: The paper reports no registration number, so the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be compared with a prespecified protocol. The funding statement also names a project labelled a 'retrospective study', which is confusing for a prospective trial. The 6 MWT is declared as primary in the Methods, which partly mitigates the concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry identifier with registration date and prespecified primary outcome matching the 6 MWT.

quotes.text: The achieved distance in 6 min was the primary outcome.
This parallel, single-blind, placebo-controlled study with block randomization included 26 males and 24 females

issues.title: Placebo FVC (%) 95% CI upper limit is 2.2 in text but 2.0 in Table 6
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the placebo FVC (%) change as −0.2% (95% CI −2.4 to 2.2). Table 6 gives −2.4 to 2.0 for the same cell. Recomputing from the table's mean and SD supports 2.0, so the text value is a slip. No conclusion depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the two printed values disagree and the recomputation favours the table.

10.3390/ijerph19159566.headline_claim: A 4-week individualised digital physiotherapy programme produced a statistically significant improvement in functional capacity in people with Long COVID-19 and appears to be a promising, feasible and safe strategy.
10.3390/ijerph19159566.overall: The finding that scores rose from baseline to week 4 among completers is arithmetically coherent, but the single-arm design cannot support the Discussion's 'proven effective' or the safety wording. Unreported registered quality-of-life outcomes and an ambiguous licence/conflict statement add moderate concerns. Treat the result as a hypothesis-generating feasibility signal, not evidence of efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: Functional capacity (1-min STS and SPPB)

primary_outcomes.measure: Functional Capacity (SPBB) short performance physical battery test
Functional Capacity (SPBB) short performance physical battery test
The Short Form Health Survey SF-12
The Short Form Health Survey SF-12 Quality of Live
European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions EQ-5D
European Quality of Life-5 Dimensions EQ-5D

issues.title: Effectiveness claimed from a single-arm 4-week pre-post study with no control group
issues.explanation: The only comparison is baseline versus week 4 in one group, so improvement cannot be attributed to the programme. Natural recovery and repeated testing could produce the same change. The wording 'proven to be an effective method' and the title go beyond what this design can show, even though the Conclusions are more cautious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group showing no comparable change over 4 weeks.

quotes.text: A quasi-experimental pre-post study assessed initially and at the end of the 4-week intervention
the results of this research have proven to be an effective method of intervention in Long COVID-19 patients

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does base a claim of effectiveness ('have proven to be an effective method') on a single-arm 4-week pre-post study with no control group, per-protocol analysis and no way to attribute the changes to the intervention. This is partly mitigated because the authors state that the lack of randomisation limits causal inference and call for randomised trials with control groups, and the Abstract and Conclusions use more hedged wording ('promising strategy', 'feasible, safe'), but the title and the Discussion sentence still overstate what this design can show.

issues.title: Registered primary outcomes SF-12 and EQ-5D are neither described nor reported in the paper
issues.explanation: The registry lists SF-12 and EQ-5D at baseline and 4 weeks as primary outcomes alongside functional capacity. The paper reports only 1-min STS and SPPB and never mentions the quality-of-life measures. Readers cannot tell whether they were collected, or whether results were unfavourable. The functional results themselves are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper or a companion publication that SF-12 and EQ-5D are reported separately, or an earlier registry version without them.

quotes.text: assessed initially and at the end of the 4-week intervention the functional capacity (1-min STS and SPPB)

issues.title: Software supplied 'by exclusive license by the principal researcher' while funding and conflicts are declared nil
issues.explanation: The intervention platform is described as provided and financed through an exclusive licence held by the principal researcher, and the vendor is thanked in the Acknowledgments. Yet the paper states no external funding and no conflicts of interest. If the licence carries a financial interest, the declaration is incomplete. The paper's wording is too ambiguous to settle this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the licence is an institutional or purchased licence and the researcher has no financial interest in the vendor.

quotes.text: The software and the mobile application for such an intervention were provided and financed by exclusive license by the principal researcher.
The authors declare no conflict of interest.

issues.title: 'Safe' concluded from absence of spontaneous adverse-effect reports in 32 patients, with no safety data shown
issues.explanation: The Methods say adverse incidents were noted daily, but the Results give no adverse-event counts or any statement on dropouts' reasons beyond 'personal'. The safety conclusion rests on patients not reporting adverse effects. In a small, short, uncontrolled study this supports tolerability at best, not safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A tabulated adverse-event log showing systematic recording, including for the four dropouts.

quotes.text: patients have not reported any adverse effects during the intervention
We consider our intervention feasible, safe and consistent with our objectives.

issues.title: Table 2 category counts sum to 46; Figure 4 text implies at least 56 comorbidities
issues.explanation: The text gives 19 participants with two comorbidities, 5 with one, 3 with three and 1 with more than three, which implies at least 56 conditions. The Table 2 rows sum to 46. If Table 2 counts participants per category, the two can legitimately differ, but the paper does not say so. Nothing in the efficacy results depends on this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 2 counts participants once per category, not per individual condition.

quotes.text: 19 participants who had two comorbidities, 5 had only one comorbidity, 3 had three comorbidities and only one participant had more than three comorbidities

issues.title: Completers-only analysis of 32 of 36 enrolled (4 dropouts, 11.1%) without sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: The results describe only those who finished the programme. Dropouts are not represented, so the estimates may be slightly optimistic. Because the exclusion is disclosed and attrition is low, this weakens the result only marginally.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline data for the dropouts showing they resembled completers, or a worst-case imputation analysis giving the same result.

quotes.text: This study performed a per-protocol analysis, where only information from patients who completed the study protocol was taken

issues.title: Effect sizes use pooled pre/post SD, not paired differences, labelling 1-min STS 'small' (d = 0.45)
issues.explanation: For a paired design the effect size usually uses the SD of the differences. With the printed correlations, the standardised change is about 0.74 for 1-min STS and 0.87 for SPPB, not 0.45 and 0.66. The authors' 'small to medium' labels therefore understate the within-group change, though this does not change significance and the design still limits any causal reading.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors stating that d was deliberately computed on the pooled SD and giving the paired-difference SDs.

quotes.text: and the effect size was analysed using Cohen's d.
The results of the digital physiotherapy interventions show a medium effect size for the SPPB test and a small effect size for the 1-min STS test.

10.3390/ijerph191610398.headline_claim: Using an EMG-driven rehabilitation robot in patients with post-COVID post-viral fatigue 'can be feasible and safe', and larger studies are needed to establish effectiveness.
10.3390/ijerph191610398.overall: The paper's feasibility conclusion is reasonably supported, with no efficacy claim made, but the 'safe' claim is stronger than a 15-patient exposure with self-reported events can show. Several reporting problems (impossible FIM and FAS ranges, retrospective registration, an unreported registered co-primary outcome, and a manufacturer-derived unvalidated fatigue index) limit confidence in the effect estimates and data quality.

primary_outcome.name: Muscle fatigue measured by EMG-robot assessment (change from baseline to 6 weeks; % slope of frequency curve)

issues.title: Table 2 FIM range 136 max and minimums of 8 and 5 fall outside the 18-126 possible range
issues.explanation: The Methods define FIM as 18 items scored 1-7, so totals must lie between 18 and 126. Table 2 prints an IG post-intervention maximum of 136 and minimums of 8 (IG pre) and 5 (CG post), which are impossible under that scoring. This indicates data-entry or reporting errors in the FIM data, though the main conclusion (feasibility) does not rest on FIM.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that FIM totals were computed on a different scoring basis, or a corrected table.

quotes.text: Each item is scored on a 7-point ordinal scale (ranging from 1 to 7)

issues.title: Registered co-primary isokinetic force and 3/8-week timepoints not reported; paper uses 6 weeks only
issues.explanation: The registry lists muscle fatigue and isokinetic force as primary outcomes at 3 and 8 weeks. The paper names muscle fatigue as main outcome, assesses at admission and 6 weeks, and never reports isokinetic force despite saying it was derived. The paper's aim is also reframed as safety and feasibility, which is not a registered outcome. The result is a selective-reporting concern for the effect results, though the null fatigue finding is not exaggerated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing the outcomes and timepoints were amended before data analysis or a report of isokinetic force.

quotes.text: The main outcome measure was muscle fatigue during the two types of rehabilitation treatment.
Both groups were assessed on admission and after six weeks of rehabilitation.
yielding isokinetic force and EMG (real-time activity) surface signal analysis

issues.title: Trial registered 2021-09-03, after the registry start date of 2021-08-01 and paper's January 2021 start
issues.explanation: The registry record shows first submission about one month after the listed start, and the paper states the study ran from January 2021, so registration came after enrolment began. This means the outcomes and timepoints were not locked before data collection, which is relevant given the unreported registered primary outcome. The paper's text gives the registration number without noting it was retrospective.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that enrolment began after registration.

quotes.text: Apilot prospective clinical study was conducted in the Neuro-rehabilitation Ward of the Provincial Hospital in Poznan, Poland, between January and November 2021.
The study has been registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, ID: NCT05130736.

issues.title: 'Feasible and safe' conclusion rests on 15 exposed patients with participant-reported absence of adverse effects
issues.explanation: Safety is inferred from the absence of spontaneously reported adverse effects in 15 robot-exposed patients, with no described systematic adverse-event collection or monitoring. The Discussion states the protocol 'is feasible and safe' as a demonstrated result, which this sample cannot establish. Feasibility (all completed 45 min daily, no dropouts) is better supported than safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described systematic adverse-event monitoring protocol with results.

quotes.text: Our study demonstrated that implementing an EMG robot-rehabilitation protocol in PVF patients is feasible and safe.
No adverse effects of the exercises on EMG-rehabilitation robot (such as musculoskeletal pain, numbness, or deterioration of physical function) were reported by the participants.

issues.title: Primary muscle-fatigue measure is a robot-model EMG index with no reported validation
issues.explanation: The primary outcome comes from the manufacturer's fatigue model, processed with external Python software, and no reliability or validity data are given. The reported values (negative medians, ranges like -55.4 to 34.7) are hard to interpret clinically. Because the authors do not claim efficacy, the effect is limited to making the null fatigue finding uninformative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of the robot's fatigue index in this population.

quotes.text: muscle fatigue assessment model using the LUNA Rehabilitation Robot
frequency analysis was performed using external Python-based software

issues.title: Randomisation method described only as 'selection of the hospital computer'; no concealment reported
issues.explanation: The paper calls the trial randomised but gives no sequence generation, concealment or blinding details. With 15 per arm and no concealment, selection bias cannot be excluded. Baseline tables show no significant differences, which partly reassures, but the effect comparisons are secondary to the feasibility aim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of computer-generated sequence and concealed allocation.

quotes.text: allocation based on the selection of the hospital computer
The study participants were randomly assigned to two groups

issues.title: Control-group therapy time given as 45 min PNF/Bobath and 120 min per day; wording ambiguous
issues.explanation: The Methods say PNF or Bobath was 45 min per day, then say the IG had training for 75 min and the CG for 120 min. This can be read as total training time being matched (IG 75 + 45 robot = 120), but the text does not make this clear. The ambiguity matters because CG received more conventional therapy time, which the authors list only briefly as a limitation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors clarifying that 120 min is the CG total and 45 min a component.

quotes.text: PNF or Bobath therapy was conducted 45 min per day
the CG had this form of therapy for 120 min a day

10.3390/ijerph192214899.headline_claim: A pulmonary and functional rehabilitation program improved functional capacity, pulmonary function and respiratory muscle strength in post-COVID-19 patients, restoring their quality of life.
10.3390/ijerph192214899.overall: The finding that patients improved on 6MWT, MEP and several questionnaires after the programme is plausible, but a 29-patient single-arm design with no control cannot attribute the changes to rehabilitation. Several text statements overstate the tables (100% TUGT independence, 'majority reached predicted'), the spirometry percent rows are implausibly scaled, and the quality-of-life and generalisation claims go beyond the evidence.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test distance (m)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design with no control; title and abstract make causal efficacy claims
issues.explanation: All 29 patients received the programme and were compared with themselves before and after about two months. Spontaneous recovery after COVID-19 over that interval, test familiarity and unblinded assessment all offer alternative explanations. The title states the programme 'improves' outcomes, and the abstract states it 'provided an improvement', which the design cannot establish.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control cohort showing no comparable improvement over the same interval.

quotes.text: the impossibility of a control group for ethical reasons
The pulmonary and functional rehabilitation program provided an improvement in the functional capacity, pulmonary function and respiratory muscle strength

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design with no control group, and the title ('Improves') and abstract Conclusions ('provided an improvement') use causal efficacy wording. The authors do acknowledge the lack of a control group and the small sample in the Discussion and speak of 'intra-group benefits', but this does not remove the causal framing in the title and abstract. Without a control, spontaneous post-COVID recovery, learning effects on the tests and regression to the mean cannot be separated from any programme effect.

issues.title: Abstract claims restored quality of life and Discussion extrapolates from 29 uncontrolled patients
issues.explanation: The abstract concludes the programme restored patients' quality of life, but QoL was not measured with a post-COVID-validated instrument and post-programme CAT remained at 8.1, not a normal level. The Discussion says the sessions 'could be extrapolated to other patients', which a 29-patient single-centre uncontrolled pilot cannot support. The conclusion section is more modest than these statements.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison or normative data showing the post-programme CAT is within normal range, plus larger multi-site replication.

quotes.text: restoring their quality of life
could be extrapolated to other patients affected by COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract says the programme restored quality of life, but the paper only shows a lower CAT score (15.4 to 8.1) in an uncontrolled group, using a COPD-specific instrument, with no pre-COVID or reference comparison. The Discussion's statement that the findings 'could be extrapolated to other patients affected by COVID-19' goes beyond 29 uncontrolled patients from one referral list who completed fewer sessions than planned and fell short of the planned sample size of 42.

issues.title: TUGT: '100% totally independent' (≤10 s) contradicts post-intervention mean of 10.4 s (SD 6.3)
issues.explanation: The Methods define 'fully independent' as 10 s or less. The Results say 100% of patients met this after the programme, yet the post-intervention mean is 10.4 s with SD 6.3. A mean above the cut-off means at least one patient exceeded 10 s, so the 100% claim cannot be correct. The claim overstates the functional-mobility gain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level TUGT data showing all values at or below 10 s with a mean of 10.4 s (arithmetically impossible), or a different classification rule.

quotes.text: In TUGT, after the intervention, 100% of the patients were classified as totally independent, and the final mean was 10.4 s
Atotal of 10 s or less: fully independent

issues.title: 6MWT: 82.6% mean percent-of-predicted described as share of patients reaching predicted value
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives 82.6 ± 28.2 as the mean percent of predicted 6MWT distance. The Results describe it as showing that the majority reached the predicted value, which conflates a mean ratio with a proportion of patients. A mean below 100% implies the average patient remained below predicted, so the text overstates recovery.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A count of patients reaching ≥100% of predicted equal to a majority of 29.

quotes.text: the majority reached the predicted value (82.6%) in the post-intervention evaluation

issues.title: 29 analysed vs 42 required; non-significant MIP (p=0.117) still counted as improved muscle strength
issues.explanation: The sample-size calculation required 42 patients, but only 29 completed the programme (with 12.7 sessions on average versus 16 planned). The non-significant MIP result (p = 0.117; MIP% p = 0.088) is explained away as a sample size effect, yet the abstract and conclusion state respiratory muscle strength improved. This weakens the muscle-strength conclusion specifically; no efficacy test is reliable for the unmet target.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A report of how many were enrolled and a power analysis showing 29 adequate, or a conclusion restricted to MEP.

quotes.text: the minimum number of subjects calculated is 42 individuals
Although the MIP results did not reach significant values, there was an increase in the values after the intervention, which can be explained by our sample size

issues.title: Spirometry (%) rows of 3.7 and 2.9 are implausible as percent-of-predicted, unlike MIP/MEP (%) and FEV1/FVC
issues.explanation: FVC (%) is 3.7 ± 0.9 and FEV1 (%) is 2.9 ± 0.7, while MIP (%), MEP (%) and FEV1/FVC (%) are 100+ or 80. A mean FVC of 3.7% of predicted is not physiologically possible for patients walking and completing the programme, and the FVC litre values (2.9-3.2 L) are inconsistent with it. The rows are probably ratios or mislabelled, so the discussion's claim of improved lung function 'in relation to the mean of the predicted values' is not supported by these data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors' clarification that these rows are ratios rather than percentages, with the headings corrected.

10.3390/ijerph192214905.headline_claim: Online forest bathing produced significant improvements in anxiety, rumination, social connection and Long-COVID symptoms and could be considered an accessible adjunct therapy for Long-COVID patients.
10.3390/ijerph192214905.overall: The headline claim of significant improvement attributable to online forest bathing rests on a fixed-order waitlist-then-intervention comparison in 16 completers, using unblinded self-report and partly non-validated measures. The data support feasibility and a signal worth testing in a controlled trial. Causal efficacy and the adjunct-therapy recommendation are not supported by this design.

primary_outcome.name: Feasibility (retention) and pilot effectiveness on anxiety, rumination, social connection and Long-COVID symptoms; no single primary outcome named

issues.title: Fixed-order waitlist-then-intervention pre/post design with unblinded self-report cannot isolate an intervention effect
issues.explanation: All 22 participants went through the waitlist period and then the intervention in that order, with no concurrent control group. Outcomes are self-reported by participants who knew they were receiving the intervention, and the guides who delivered it were also authors. Any change over time, expectancy, social contact or response to repeated surveying is therefore indistinguishable from an effect of forest bathing. The abstract nonetheless states that online forest bathing 'resulted in' significant improvements, a causal claim this design cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or randomised control group, or counterbalanced order, showing the same changes beyond those seen in controls.

quotes.text: Paired-samples t -tests were conducted for all survey variables between the waitlist control period (baseline) and post-intervention.
Online Forest bathing resulted in significant improvements in well-being and symptom severity

second_reader.what_stands: The fixed-order waitlist-then-intervention design, with unblinded self-report, complete-case analysis (16 of 22) and no randomisation or counterbalancing, cannot isolate a causal intervention effect, so the Abstract's 'resulted in significant improvements' overstates what the design supports. The paper partly tempers this by calling itself a pilot offering 'early evidence' and by using 'associated with' in the Conclusions, but it does not list the fixed order, lack of blinding or expectancy as limitations.

issues.title: Impact analysis limited to 16 of 22 participants; 27% attrition tied to illness, with no missing-data sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Only participants who gave post-intervention data (16 of 22) can contribute to the paired comparisons. Reasons for dropping out included feeling too unwell, which is related to the outcomes, so missingness is likely informative. Because no analysis addresses the missing data, the improvements may overstate what would be seen in all who started.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including all 22 participants (mixed model or imputation) giving similar effects.

quotes.text: Following completion of surveys during the waitlist control period, 27% of participants did not complete post-intervention surveys.
Sixteen participants completed surveys post-intervention and six participants completed surveys at one-month follow-up.

issues.title: Confident efficacy and 'adjunct therapy' wording from 16 analysed participants, four unadjusted tests, no sample-size rationale
issues.explanation: The study had no sample-size calculation, analysed 16 people, and ran four paired tests without correction. The p-values are very small for most outcomes, so the multiplicity concern is modest. The effect sizes are very imprecise and probably inflated by selection and the design. The abstract and conclusion still recommend the intervention as an adjunct therapy, which goes beyond what a pilot of this kind shows, even though the Discussion is more cautious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size rationale and confirmation in an adequately powered controlled study.

quotes.text: could be considered an accessible and inexpensive adjunct therapy for Long-COVID patients
suggest a fully powered controlled trial might offer further generalisable evidence

issues.title: Long-COVID symptom outcome is a 15-item author-made scale (alpha 0.86), with single-item rumination and connection measures
issues.explanation: The symptom score was built from a WHO symptom list and has only an internal consistency estimate. Rumination and social connection are single items. Without validation or minimal important differences, the reported 22% symptom decrease and 48-78% changes cannot be read as clinically meaningful. Percent change in an ordinal 1-7 score also exaggerates apparent size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of the scale against established Long-COVID measures.

quotes.text: In the absence of a concise measure of Long-COVID symptoms, the authors took the symptoms list from the WHO (World Health Organization) website
found to be very reliable ( α = 0.86)

issues.title: Three authors delivered the intervention; disclosed, with analysis separated from delivery
issues.explanation: Three authors were the guides who delivered the intervention, and two of them recruited participants. This is declared, and the authors state they did not analyse the data. Because outcomes are unblinded self-reports collected after sessions the guides led, some bias in responses cannot be excluded. This is a minor concern and mostly adds to the open-label issue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Independent data collection or outcome assessment shown to give the same results.

quotes.text: Three of the authors are forest bathing guides who delivered the intervention.

issues.title: Seven withdrawals listed in Results versus six participants lacking post-intervention data (22 to 16)
issues.explanation: Results list three participants leaving after baseline, two after session one and two after session two, totalling seven. The Methods and Results give 22 completing waitlist surveys and 16 post-intervention, which implies six non-completers. The paper does not explain which participants counted as having post data or how the 16 were defined. The unit of analysis for the paired tests (last survey, average of four surveys, or any survey) is also unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of which participants had post-intervention data, showing the 16 includes some who withdrew after sessions 1-2.

quotes.text: Three participants withdrew from the study after only providing baseline data, two participants withdrew following their first session and two withdrew after their second session.
( N = 16 completed surveys)

10.3390/ijerph20021361.headline_claim: Neuro-meditation (Rebalance) is an effective, non-pharmacological treatment that reduces cognitive impairment, fatigue, mood disturbance, pain and sleep problems in long COVID patients.
10.3390/ijerph20021361.overall: The large self-reported improvements in G-Int are probably real in direction, but with an untreated control, unblinded self-report outcomes and no registration, they cannot be attributed to the program itself. The cognitive reaction-time claims rest on within-group change, and Post2 exists only for G-Int. The headline 'effective treatment' conclusion should be read as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: Co-primary set: five PEBL cognitive tasks, Chalder fatigue scale, perceived stress and POMS mood

issues.title: No sham or attention control; large self-reported gains cannot be separated from expectancy and contact effects
issues.explanation: The control arm received nothing, while G-Int received ten supervised sessions with a coach and device. Fatigue, mood, pain, anxiety and sleep outcomes are all self-reported by unblinded participants, so expectancy, attention and demand effects are confounded with the program. The Conclusions state effectiveness versus a control without this caveat. The size of the fatigue changes (physical fatigue -13 points versus -0.6) is also what expectancy might inflate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham or attention-matched control arm showing similar gains, or objective blinded outcomes corroborating the self-reports.

quotes.text: The G-Int group members followed a Rebalance ® Program while the G-Con and G-Nor groups did not receive any treatment.
Neuro-meditation provided an effective, non-pharmacological treatment to combat subjective and cognitive impairment in long COVID patients.

second_reader.what_stands: There was no sham or attention-control condition and no blinding is described, so the large self-reported improvements in G-Int cannot be separated from expectancy, contact or attention effects. The limitations mention only the missing classical-meditation arm and do not discuss expectancy or contact.

issues.title: Conclusions assert an effective treatment despite untreated control and only 7-day follow-up
issues.explanation: The Conclusions describe the program as an effective treatment and say it improved outcomes versus control, while the Discussion states the design cannot isolate the neuromodulation effect or show persistence beyond 7 days. Post2 data exist only for G-Int. The abstract's 'initial evidence' and 'promising' wording is more appropriate than the Conclusions' definitive claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusions restated as preliminary, or follow-up data with a comparator beyond 7 days.

quotes.text: Neuro-meditation provided an effective, non-pharmacological treatment
yet was not sufficient to conclude whether the observed benefits are persistent over time i.e., beyond 7 days

second_reader.what_stands: Section 5 asserts that the program 'provided an effective' treatment on the strength of a small, unblinded trial with an untreated control and a one-week, intervention-only follow-up, which is stronger than the evidence allows. The abstract and discussion are more cautious and the authors do state that persistence beyond 7 days is unestablished, so the overreach is in the Conclusions wording rather than throughout the paper.

issues.title: Cognitive gains attributed to G-Int from within-group change; Post2 measured in G-Int only
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results claim that only G-Int sped up on reaction-time tasks, based on significant within-group change versus non-significant change elsewhere. A difference between significant and non-significant is not a between-group test, and the G-Con arm also improved numerically on CRT RT (-6.1% vs -9.8%). The Post2 assessment, where the headline RT figures come from (e.g., 521 ms), was done only for G-Int, so no control comparison exists for it. The cognitive claim is therefore weaker than stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A direct between-group test (G-Int vs G-Con change) showing a significant difference, with a G-Con Post2 comparison.

quotes.text: only the G-Int group revealed shortened reaction times in the choice reaction time
Post hoc tests indicated that only the G-Int had a significant reduction in RTs
a second post-assessment was carried out one week after the first session for the G-Int only

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's headline Post2 results (CRT, Simon, pattern comparison) are within-group changes in G-Int alone, with no control data at Post2, so they cannot show a between-group difference. At Post1 there is a significant group x time interaction for CRT, but 'only G-Int' still relies on a significant-vs-non-significant contrast (G-Con also fell 6.1%) with no reported direct G-Int vs G-Con test of change.

issues.title: Corsi total score: text credits +22.4% to G-Int, but Table 4 shows it for G-Nor (G-Int -4.8%)
issues.explanation: The Results say G-Int alone significantly increased its Corsi total score by 22.4%. Table 4 shows that increase belongs to the healthy normative group, while G-Int fell 4.8%. The Discussion itself says the memory task showed no benefit of the program, so the text sentence is a misattribution. It is a reporting error on one secondary outcome and does not change the main claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 4 showing G-Int with +22.4% on Corsi total score.

quotes.text: a significant increase in score between the Pre-Post sessions for G-Int only (+22.4%, p < 0.001)

quotes.location: Table 4, Corsi Total score row, Change Post1-Base

issues.title: No sample-size justification (17 per arm); definite efficacy wording in Conclusions
issues.explanation: The paper reports no power calculation and randomizes 17 patients per arm. The abstract is appropriately tentative, but the Conclusions and Discussion state effectiveness outright. The small, unjustified sample supports a preliminary conclusion rather than a firm one. This is a modest additional weakness beyond the control and spin problems.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation supporting the 17-per-arm design.

quotes.text: Thirty-four patients with long COVID and fifteen healthy participants were recruited for this study
Neuro-meditation provided an effective, non-pharmacological treatment

issues.title: Many outcomes at alpha 0.05 without correction; reaction-time interactions are marginal (p < 0.05)
issues.explanation: The study tests five cognitive tasks with multiple parameters and a dozen questionnaire subscales, all labelled primary, at an uncorrected 0.05 level. The very large fatigue and mood effects are unlikely to be due to multiplicity, but the cognitive RT interactions are only modestly significant (e.g., CRT interaction p<0.05, Simon IN RT no interaction). The Conclusions highlight faster response speed while two of five tasks (Corsi, pursuit rotor) showed no benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy of outcomes or corrected p-values showing the RT results survive.

quotes.text: statistical significance was accepted at p < 0.05
as well as faster response speed in cognitive tasks simulating time-pressure scenarios

issues.title: No trial registration; abstract lists perceived stress as primary outcome but no PSS results reported
issues.explanation: The paper does not give a registry identifier, so the outcome plan cannot be verified. The abstract names the Perceived Stress Scale as a primary outcome, but the questionnaire list in Methods and Tables 2-3 contain no PSS. The omitted outcome and the label 'primary' for nearly every measure leave outcome selection unverifiable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry with matching outcomes, or PSS data reported in the paper or supplement.

quotes.text: perceived stress ( perceived stress scale )
approved by a local Ethics Committee (South-East, France, 09/10/2021)

issues.title: Program duration given as five weeks in the Abstract, four weeks in Methods and title (3-4 in Discussion)
issues.explanation: The Abstract describes the ten sessions as spread over five weeks, whereas the title, Methods and Introduction say four weeks and the Discussion says 3-4 weeks. This is an internal inconsistency in the stated intervention duration. Nothing in the results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol statement that the program ran five weeks for some participants.

quotes.text: ten 30-min sessions of Rebalance ® over a period of five weeks
The Rebalance program included a total of ten 30-min sessions spread over four weeks

10.3390/ijerph20021468.headline_claim: Inpatient post-COVID rehabilitation improved physical performance and neuropsychological health in workers with work-related COVID-19, and the authors state this confirms the feasibility and efficacy of post-COVID rehabilitation, although work ability did not change.
10.3390/ijerph20021468.overall: The finding that physical performance and several neuropsychological scores improved between admission and discharge is reasonably supported descriptively, but the paper's claim that efficacy is 'confirmed' is not supported by a single-arm design over about four weeks. Minor numeric inconsistencies (one WAI subscale, ICU mean, T2 fatigue prevalence) do not change the main results.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; the study reports pre/post changes across physical, neuropsychological and work-ability measures (6MWD listed first)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot separate rehabilitation effect from recovery, yet efficacy is 'confirmed'
issues.explanation: All improvements come from T1-to-T2 changes in one uncontrolled cohort over about 4 weeks. Natural recovery, practice effects on performance tests and regression to the mean cannot be separated from the programme effect. The authors concede this in Limitations but the Conclusions still say the findings confirm efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control group showing the improvements exceed those without rehabilitation.

quotes.text: The results should be interpreted carefully under consideration of an observational study design without a control group.
Taken together, the described findings can confirm the feasibility and the efficacy of post-COVID rehabilitation

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post observational design, and the Conclusions say the findings 'confirm' efficacy without any caveat, although a no-control design cannot separate rehabilitation effect from natural recovery or other time-related changes. The Limitations section does acknowledge the absent control group and natural recovery, but resolves the issue by citing external work rather than data from this study, so the limitation is flagged but not carried through into the strength of the conclusion.

issues.title: Text says no WAI subscale changed, but Table 3 'Work requirements' shows p = 0.010 (z = -2.584)
issues.explanation: Results 3.3.3 states no WAI subscale differed significantly between T1 and T2. Table 3 reports a significant change for the 'Work requirements' subscale (p = 0.010, r = -0.239) under the paper's own p < 0.05 criterion. The medians are identical (7) but the IQR upper bound moved from 9 to 8, so a small shift exists. The error is confined to one sentence and does not alter the main conclusion of no overall WAI change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated stricter alpha or multiplicity correction under which p = 0.010 is not significant.

quotes.text: No significant difference was found between T1 and T2 in any subscale of the work ability index.
• Work requirements

issues.title: Fatigue at T2: 76.1% moderate/severe in Results vs 70% in Discussion
issues.explanation: Results report 53.0% moderate and 23.1% severe fatigue at discharge, totalling 76.1%. The Discussion twice uses 70% as the T2 prevalence and builds explanations (handgrip, work capacity) on it. The 70% figure is not supported by the Results, though the qualitative point that fatigue remained high holds.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of moderate-to-severe fatigue under which 70% is correct.

quotes.text: At rehabilitation discharge, the prevalence of fatigue (BFI score) was 53.0% for moderate and 23.1% for severe symptoms.
As 70% of the patients were categorized as moderately to severely fatigued at T2

issues.title: Mean ICU stay given as 10 days in text but 10.83 days in Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results give a mean ICU duration of 10 days, while Table 2 prints 10.83 for the same variable. Ordinary rounding would give 11, so the text value is truncated or wrong. This is a descriptive variable unrelated to rehabilitation outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the text refers to a different statistic (for example a median) for ICU duration.

quotes.text: In total, 10 patients were treated in an ICU for a mean duration of 10 (5–21) days.

10.3390/ijerph20043100.headline_claim: A self-administered, personalized computerized cognitive training programme based on gamified tasks could be an effective way to ameliorate cognitive dysfunction in persons with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19.
10.3390/ijerph20043100.overall: The paper documents a within-person rise in scores on a repeated online battery among 73 adherent completers (28% of eligible volunteers), but with no control group it cannot support the abstract's claim of an effective treatment. The numerical reporting is largely internally consistent apart from one wrong percentage (memory 82% vs 86.3%). Read as a feasibility pilot generating hypotheses, it is reasonable; the efficacy wording is not supported.

primary_outcome.name: Change in z-scored cognitive performance across five domains (CAB) from baseline to 8 weeks

issues.title: Effectiveness conclusion drawn from uncontrolled single-arm pre-post pilot of 73 completers
issues.explanation: The abstract concludes that the training could effectively ameliorate cognitive dysfunction in PASC, and the discussion says the control group was unnecessary for judging effectiveness. The design has no comparator, so improvement on a repeated online test cannot be attributed to the training. The data support only that scores rose after the programme in completers, and that the pilot was feasible for some volunteers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist arm showing the same change, or a design able to exclude practice and spontaneous-recovery effects.

quotes.text: It is concluded that a self-administered CCT based on gamified cognitive tasks could be an effective way to ameliorate cognitive dysfunction in persons with PASC.

Considering that the focus was on determining whether the intervention could be implemented and whether it was effective in improving the targeted outcomes, the use of a control group was not deemed necessary.
This before-and-after study constitutes the first piece of evidence suggesting that a home-based digital therapeutic program could ameliorate cognitive dysfunction in PASC.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does draw an effectiveness-leaning conclusion from an uncontrolled, single-arm pre-post design of 73 completers, and the wording 'effective', 'could ameliorate' and 'beneficial effects' goes beyond what that design can show, given practice effects, natural recovery and attrition. This is partly offset by the authors' explicit labelling as a feasibility pilot, their caution statement and their call for randomized controlled trials, so the conclusion is hedged rather than unqualified.

issues.title: Only 73 of 262 eligible volunteers (28%) analysed; completers with at least 10 sessions only
issues.explanation: Participants who did not finish both assessments or did not complete 10 training sessions were excluded after enrolment. The reported gains therefore describe a self-selected, adherent minority. Drop-outs and low engagers may have done worse, so effect size and feasibility are likely overstated. This weakens the main result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis including all 262 enrolled (or all 103 with both assessments) showing similar gains, or a feasibility report treating this attrition as a result.

quotes.text: From an initial sample of 262 eligible candidates who volunteered to enter the study, only 103 of them completed the initial and final cognitive assessment
and 73 of them completed also a minimum of 10 training sessions (i.e., second exclusion criterion)

second_reader.what_stands: Only 73 of 262 volunteers (about 28%) were analysed, and they are completers of both assessments with at least 10 training sessions; the paper reports this openly and calls these criteria a priori. The consequence is that results reflect a self-selected, adherent subset, and no analysis of the 189 excluded is given (no intention-to-treat analysis), so effect estimates may be optimistic.

issues.title: Kruskal-Wallis (independent-groups test) used as non-parametric check of paired pre-post scores
issues.explanation: The authors call the Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA a validation of the parametric results, but it treats pre and post scores as independent groups. It therefore does not properly confirm the within-person analysis, and the per-domain ε² values are not paired effect sizes. Because it ignores pairing it is, if anything, less powerful, so the significant results are likely to hold under a correct paired test. The robustness claim is weakly supported rather than the findings being wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the test was run with a repeated-measures specification (e.g., Friedman or Wilcoxon signed-rank) and mislabelled.

quotes.text: a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA was run to validate the results.
All the pre-test vs. post-test comparisons across Domains were significant

issues.title: Memory improvers printed as 63 (82%) of 73; 63/73 is 86.3%
issues.explanation: The Results text gives 63 of 73 participants improving in memory as 82%, but 63 out of 73 is 86.3%. The other four domains are consistent with their counts. The error is small and, if anything, understates the memory result, so the main conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different memory-improver count (about 60 of 73) in the underlying data.

quotes.text: 63 (82%) in memory
quotes.location: Results, paragraph beginning 'Moreover, most of the participants'

script.explanation: 63/73 = 86.30%, but the paper prints 82, outside the rounding interval [81.50, 83.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 76.8 rather than 73.

issues.title: Intervention, outcome battery and norms supplied free by CogniFit; its role not stated
issues.explanation: The training software, the assessment battery and the normative data used to compute z-scores all come from one commercial provider, which supplied them free of charge. The paper says no conflicts exist but does not state whether the company influenced design, analysis or reporting. This cannot be settled from the paper alone and does not itself show bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that CogniFit had no role in study design, analysis or reporting and that no author has a financial tie to it.

quotes.text: The authors are grateful to Cognifit Inc. for providing access to and information about the platform, the CAB, and its normative dataset free of charge.
The authors declare no conflict of interest.

issues.title: Registered 2022-10-03, after enrolment (Oct–Dec 2021) and after the last participant finished (Feb 2022)
issues.explanation: The paper reports registration without a date. According to the registry, the record was first submitted about eight months after the last participant finished, so the registration could not constrain analysis choices in advance. The registered primary outcome is generic, so the paper's choice of z-score domains cannot be checked against a pre-specified plan. The effect on the conclusion is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version or other dated protocol showing the outcomes and analysis were specified before data collection.

quotes.text: The study was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov with the identifier NCT05571852.
The first participant completed the study in December 2021 and the last one in February 2022.
quotes.location: Section 2.2, Settings, Sampling Frame, and Timelines

10.3390/ijerph20156513.headline_claim: Exercise rehabilitation with strength and endurance training improves physical performance in long COVID patients, similarly to coronary and fibromyalgia patients, without post-exertional symptom exacerbation.
10.3390/ijerph20156513.overall: The finding that long COVID patients improved VO2, power and handgrip after 4 weeks is plausible, but it rests on an uncontrolled pre-post design and non-randomised, non-comparable comparator groups. The claims of equal effectiveness and of safety with respect to post-exertional symptom exacerbation go beyond the data, which include no adverse-event or PESE monitoring and no equivalence test. Numeric slips are minor..

primary_outcome.name: Cardiorespiratory and muscular performance (VO2 at VT1, VO2 peak, MAP, handgrip force); no single primary outcome is stated

issues.title: Long COVID improvement is an uncontrolled pre-post change; comparator groups are not a control for it
issues.explanation: The long COVID group has no untreated or usual-care control, so the 4-week gains cannot be separated from natural course, test familiarity or follow-up effects. The coronary and fibromyalgia groups show that similar gains occur elsewhere, but they received different programs and differ in age, sex and smoking. The conclusion that rehabilitation benefits long COVID patients is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or usual-care long COVID control showing no comparable change.

quotes.text: the main one being the absence of a control group for long COVID patients
Cardiorespiratory and muscular parameters were enhanced after exercise rehabilitation in the three groups ( p < 0.001).

second_reader.what_stands: The long COVID improvement is an uncontrolled pre-post change. The coronary and fibromyalgia groups are other diseases on different programmes, so they cannot show what the long COVID patients would have done without rehabilitation (natural recovery, regression to the mean, effects of follow-up, familiarity with the tests). The authors state this limitation in the Discussion. However, the Abstract and Conclusions still describe the study as 'with control groups' and as having 'confirmed' benefit, which overstates what the design can show.

issues.title: 'As effective' and 'without PESE' conclusions rest on non-significant interactions and no PESE or adverse-event data
issues.explanation: The Discussion says rehabilitation was 'as effective' as in other patients, based on non-significant time-by-group interactions (p = 0.517, 0.756, 0.059) in small groups, which does not establish equivalence. The abstract endorses caring for patients 'without post-exertional symptom exacerbation', yet PESE and adverse events were not assessed during or after the program and patients with PESE at baseline were excluded. The authors do concede small samples limit conclusions, but the headline wording is stronger than the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecified equivalence margins met, and systematic PESE/adverse-event monitoring reported.

quotes.text: demonstrating that exercise rehabilitation for long COVID patients without PESE was as effective as exercise rehabilitation for other patients.
we confirm and reinforce the interest of caring for long COVID patients without post-exertional symptom exacerbation

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that the programme was 'as effective' rests on non-significant interaction tests in a small sample (n = 38 per group), without an equivalence analysis, and the VO2 peak gain differed between long COVID and coronary patients. The paper reports no PESE or adverse-event outcomes during or after the programme, so the statement that rehabilitation was safe or suitable for long COVID patients 'without PESE' is based only on baseline exclusion of reported PESE, not on any follow-up evidence of absence of exacerbation.

issues.title: Comparison groups are the last 38 patients from other trials, with large baseline differences in age, sex and smoking
issues.explanation: The coronary and fibromyalgia comparators come from separate studies with different programs, periods and populations, selected by enrolment order. Age (46.9 vs 61.4 vs 47.4 y), sex (55% vs 24% vs 92% women) and smoking (37% vs 76% vs 29%) differ markedly, and adjustment cannot remove all non-comparability. Between-group claims such as 'similar improvement' and the VO2 peak difference are therefore weak.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecified matching or harmonised protocols across the three source studies.

quotes.text: However, the methodological choice of the last patients included in each group should not represent a selection bias a priori.

second_reader.what_stands: The coronary and fibromyalgia groups are the last 38 randomised patients from other trials, and they differ substantially from the long COVID group in age, sex and smoking (all p < 0.001), as well as in baseline physical capacity. The authors acknowledge non-comparability but say the 'last patients' rule should not introduce selection bias, which does not deal with differences caused by the different diseases. The long COVID group is not described as 'last' patients, and the registry shows 17 actual enrollees against 38 in the paper, which the paper does not explain. Adjustment for age, sex an

issues.title: Registered primary outcome (fatigue at 1 month) is not reported; paper analyses physical and autonomic outcomes
issues.explanation: The registry lists fatigue evaluation as the only primary outcome, and the paper reports no fatigue measure and designates no primary outcome. The reported outcomes are CPET, handgrip and HRV, which may be among the registered secondary outcomes. Because the registry enrollment (17) also differs from the paper's 38 and only the current record was seen, the discrepancy cannot be resolved from the paper alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing CPET/handgrip/HRV as registered primary outcomes, or that the analysed cohort comes from a different record.

quotes.text: Efficacy of exercise training was assessed by a cardiopulmonary exercise test, a handgrip force test, and a supine heart rate variability recording at rest before and after the rehabilitation program.

issues.title: Table 2 footnote gives post hoc threshold p < 0.005, but the reported post hoc p is 0.046
issues.explanation: The Table 2 footnote marks the COVID vs coronary VO2 peak difference with a threshold of p < 0.005, while the text reports that same post hoc test at p = 0.046 and the Methods set alpha at 0.05. The footnote threshold is almost certainly a typographical slip for 0.05, but as printed it is inconsistent with the reported p-value. The only claim affected is the single VO2 peak between-group difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation from the authors that the footnote is a typo for p < 0.05.

quotes.text: Post hoc test, COVID significantly different from Coronary in POST, p < 0.005.
the post hoc test identified a significant difference between the COVID and the coronary groups after their rehabilitation ( p = 0.046)

issues.title: Text says all baseline parameters differed except BRS; Table 2 group p is >0.05 for handgrip, LF, HF, LF/HF
issues.explanation: The Results say significant baseline differences were found for all parameters except BRS. Table 2 shows group-effect p-values of 0.121 (handgrip), 0.231 (LF), 0.419 (HF) and 0.224 (LF/HF), and no PRE-only test is given. The statement is therefore not backed by anything printed, though the column is not strictly a baseline test.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A PRE-only one-way ANOVA showing significant differences for all those variables.

quotes.text: Significant baseline differences were found for all parameters except BRS

issues.title: Long COVID study registered about a year after its stated start; outcome analysis described as retrospective
issues.explanation: The registry record was first submitted on 2022-02-10, after the listed start of 2021-02-01, so outcomes could not be verified as prespecified. The paper itself states that the outcome analysis was retrospectively gathered. This limits confidence in prespecification but does not by itself show any result is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registration or protocol with prespecified outcomes.

quotes.text: These patients were enrolled in a combined prospective study and had a retrospectively gathered outcome analysis.

10.3390/ijerph21101385.headline_claim: Face-to-face Mat Pilates training is an effective intervention to reduce persistent long COVID fatigue and improve functional capacity, while online Mat Pilates is not.
10.3390/ijerph21101385.overall: The functional-capacity findings for face-to-face Pilates (endurance, trunk flexion, 6-minute walk) are supported by significant group x time interactions in a small trial. The headline claim about fatigue and the contrast with online training are weaker, because the fatigue scores are reported only as within-group changes without a between-group test. Several Abstract and Discussion statements also do not match the tables.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Assessment Scale total score (no primary outcome explicitly designated)

issues.title: Fatigue benefit rests on within-group significance; no group x time test for FAS reported
issues.explanation: The fatigue (FAS) results are given only as within-group pre-post changes (face-to-face 33.5 to 26.7, p < 0.01). Differences between arms are not tested or reported, even though the control and online groups also changed numerically. A significant change in one arm and a non-significant change in another does not show that the arms differ. The claim that face-to-face but not online Pilates reduces fatigue is therefore not shown by the reported analysis. The functional outcomes are better supported by the printed interactions, though the TUG and handgrip results are weaker.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported group x time interaction for FAS total, physical and mental scores, or a direct between-group comparison showing face-to-face differs from control and online.

quotes.text: only the face-to-face Mat Pilates group showed a significant reduction in the total (33.5 ± 5.5 to 26.7 ± 7.1, p < 0.01)
No difference was found in other groups over time.

second_reader.what_stands: In the extracted text, the fatigue claim rests on within-group pre-post p values for the face-to-face group and a statement of no change in the other groups, and no group x time test for FAS is reported, unlike the other outcomes in Tables 2-4. A between-group interaction p might appear in Figure 2, which could not be read from the extracted text. The inference that the benefit is specific to face-to-face Pilates (the 'only' claim in the abstract and conclusion) therefore lacks a reported between-group comparison, and 'significant in one group, not in the others' is not itself evidence of a di

issues.title: 21 losses stated, but all analyses show n = 49 despite the claimed intention-to-treat with imputation
issues.explanation: The paper reports 21 participants lost during the study, with only a general statement that the losses were unrelated to training. The Methods say multiple imputation was used in the intention-to-treat analysis. Every table and the Abstract report only 49 participants. It is unclear whether the 49 are completers or whether imputation restored the full randomised sample, and the losses per arm are not given in the text. If the arms lost participants unevenly, the between-group comparisons could be biased.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing balanced losses across arms, with the 49 analysed after imputation being the full randomised sample.

quotes.text: During the study, there were 21 losses, but these were not related to the training protocol.
The multiple imputation technique was used in the intention-to-treat analysis for missing data.

issues.title: Discussion credits face-to-face Pilates with TUG improvement; TUG improved in all arms (interaction p = 0.24)
issues.explanation: The Discussion lists TUG among the tests improved by face-to-face Mat Pilates. Table 3 shows TUG time improvements in all three arms, no significance marker for any arm, and a group x time p of 0.24. The data therefore do not show a face-to-face effect on TUG, and the improvement is likely a time effect shared with the control group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A post hoc test showing face-to-face TUG improvement exceeds that of control.

quotes.text: We found improvements in a variety of tests, including TUG, upper limb endurance, trunk flexion isometric endurance, and the 6 min walk test.

issues.title: Face-to-face baseline fatigue categories total 13 (8 + 5), but the group is n = 15
issues.explanation: In Table 1 and the Results text, the face-to-face group has 8 with fatigue and 5 with extreme fatigue, which is 13 of the 15 participants. The printed percentages (61% and 38%) are based on 13, not 15. Two participants are unaccounted for, and the text says all participants had fatigue. This is a baseline reporting error that does not change the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two face-to-face participants had missing baseline FAS data, or a corrected table with counts that sum to 15.

quotes.text: face-to-face Mat Pilates n = 8 (61%)
face-to-face Mat Pilates n = 5 (38%)

script.explanation: 8/15 = 53.33%, but the paper prints 61, outside the rounding interval [60.50, 62.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 13.1 rather than 15.

issues.title: Table 2 hip circumference group x time p = 0.04 contradicts 'no significant interaction' in the text
issues.explanation: The text says no significant group x time interaction was found for the anthropometric outcomes, and the Abstract says hip circumference did not change. Table 2 prints p = 0.04 for hip circumference, which meets the paper's own p ≤ 0.05 criterion. Online Pilates rose from 114.9 to 122.7 cm while face-to-face fell from 116.7 to 111.7 cm. This is a secondary outcome, and the effect on the main conclusion is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A declared correction for the interaction tests that raises the hip circumference interaction p above 0.05.

quotes.text: No significant interaction (group × time) was found among groups.

quotes.location: Table 2, Hip Circumference, Online Pilates row

issues.title: Abstract says no significant BP or lipid changes; Table 4 shows control BP rises and interactions p ≤ 0.03
issues.explanation: The Abstract says no significant changes were seen in blood pressure or the other cardiometabolic markers (p > 0.05). The Results and Table 4 show significant rises in control-group systolic (114 to 122 mmHg) and diastolic (75 to 81 mmHg) pressure. Group x time p values are < 0.01 (systolic), 0.03 (diastolic) and 0.01 (HDL-c). The training-arm findings are largely null, so the discrepancy is a misstatement of the results, not a reversal of the trial's conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Abstract wording limited to the exercise arms, together with an explanation of the significant interaction terms in Table 4.

quotes.text: No significant changes were observed in blood glucose, glycated hemoglobin, triglycerides, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, or blood pressure ( p > 0.05).

quotes.location: Table 4, Systolic Blood Pressure, Control row

issues.title: Allocation concealment not described; independent sequence generation only
issues.explanation: The Methods say an independent researcher ran block randomisation, but they do not say how assignments were hidden from those enrolling participants. Missing concealment details are a common reporting gap and cannot be settled from the paper. The claim about falling below the target group size does not hold, since each arm reached at least 15.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry record or protocol describing concealment (for example central or sealed allocation).

quotes.text: The process was carried out by an independent researcher who had no involvement with the participants.

issues.title: Control LDL-c post SD printed as 2.7 against pre SD 44.4 in Table 4
issues.explanation: The control group's LDL-c is 135.5 ± 44.4 before and 126.6 ± 2.7 after. A sixteen-fold drop in SD is implausible in 18 people over 12 weeks, and it does not fit the printed Cohen's d of 0.18. It is probably a typographical error, with no effect on the paper's conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source data showing a true post SD of 2.7.

10.3390/ijms25158305.headline_claim: A moderate-intensity Nordic walking program improves physical capacity in people with COVID-19 and long COVID syndrome, with genotype-dependent lactate responses that may support individualised exercise prescription.
10.3390/ijms25158305.overall: The headline claim that Nordic walking improves physical capacity, with genotype-specific effects, is not supported: there is no pre-post fitness measure, no untreated comparator, an unadjusted nonrandomized group comparison, uncorrected post hoc testing, and tiny genotype cells. The numeric slips (swapped group sizes, a '90' cell, a mismatched allele frequency) are minor. At best the paper offers exploratory pilot observations on lactate.

primary_outcome.name: Lactic acid concentration during Nordic walking sessions

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Changes from baseline and at the end of procedure (12 weeks)
