issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence from a concurrent usual-care comparison group showing less improvement over the same 3 months.

quotes.text: A notable limitation was the absence of a control group of patients not undergoing any rehabilitation, leaving the extent of the improvements that might occur naturally over time unclear.
Both low-intensity and high-intensity cardiopulmonary rehabilitation programs play a pivotal role in improving cardiopulmonary parameters in patients recovering from severe COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no untreated comparison arm, yet the Conclusions assert that both programmes play a 'pivotal role' in improving cardiopulmonary parameters, which is a causal attribution that pre-post change alone cannot support. The authors do acknowledge the missing control in Section 4.2, but that caveat is not carried into the Conclusions or the Abstract, so the causal wording is only partly offset.

issues.title: Abstract says training intensities are 'proven' sufficient and improve long-term health after 3 months, uncontrolled
issues.explanation: The abstract uses the word 'proving' and refers to long-term cardiopulmonary health, yet the design is an uncontrolled 3-month before-after comparison. No between-arm comparison of improvement is tested, and the authors admit no long-term data exist. The language is stronger than the evidence supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data with a control group and longer follow-up supporting sustained benefit.

quotes.text: proving both low-intensity and high-intensity training as sufficient to improve heart and lung function if performed correctly and over a relatively short duration of 3 months.
This study provides evidence that personalized, targeted rehabilitation strategies can improve long-term cardiopulmonary health in patients recovering from severe COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract's 'proving' and 'sufficient' overstate what an uncontrolled 3-month pre-post study can show, and describing a 3-month measurement as evidence for 'long-term' cardiopulmonary health conflicts with the paper's own limitation that long-term effects were not studied. The Abstract does name the 3-month duration, so the time frame is not hidden, but sufficiency and long-term benefit are not supported by the design.

issues.title: Abstract claims work-intensity gain in both groups; high-intensity gain is 43 to 47 W, p = 0.135
issues.explanation: The abstract states work intensity improved substantially in both groups. Table 8 and the Results give p = 0.135 for the high-intensity group, which is not significant at the paper's 0.05 threshold. The claim is true only for the low-intensity group; the high-intensity change is small (4 W) and unsupported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract refers only to the low-intensity group, or a corrected p-value below 0.05 for the high-intensity group.

quotes.text: The work intensity also demonstrated substantial improvements from the initial testing to the 3-month mark in both groups.
while the high-intensity group increased from 43 (IQR 41-46) to 47 (IQR 44-51), ( p -value = 0.135)

issues.title: Within-group pre-post changes tested with unpaired Mann-Whitney U instead of a paired test
issues.explanation: Tables 7 and 8 compare baseline and 3-month values in the same patients with the Mann-Whitney test, which treats them as independent groups. A paired test (Wilcoxon signed-rank) is needed, so the reported p-values are not valid for these comparisons. Because ignoring pairing usually lowers power, most significant results likely remain significant, but the high-intensity work result (p = 0.135) and borderline values (0.045, 0.030) could change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods stating that the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test was actually used and mislabelled in the footnotes.

quotes.text: Data reported as median (IQR) and calculated using Mann-Whitney u-test

issues.title: Randomisation method not described; baseline work capacity differs 27 vs 43 W (p < 0.001) between arms
issues.explanation: The paper states stratification into intensity groups by randomisation, with no method or concealment described, and also describes matching. Baseline work capacity differs markedly between arms, which is unusual under true randomisation and means between-arm comparisons of change are confounded by starting level. Within-arm results are less affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a concealed random sequence and an explanation of the baseline work difference.

quotes.text: by randomization, resulting in two equal study groups
there was a significant difference ( p < 0.001) between the low- and high-intensity groups, which exhibited median values of 27 (22-29) and 43 (41-46), respectively

issues.title: Results text swaps the 3-month work medians between groups (38 W vs 47 W) relative to Tables 6 and 8
issues.explanation: The paragraph describing Table 6 says the high-intensity group had the higher median at 38 W versus 47 W for low intensity, which is self-contradictory. Table 6 and Table 8 give low = 38 W and high = 47 W. This is a labelling slip in the text; the tables are consistent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Original data showing the group labels in the Table 6 paragraph are correct and the tables are wrong.

quotes.text: with a higher median for the high-intensity group (38W, IQR 36-44) compared to the low-intensity group (47W, IQR 44-51)
from a median of 27 (IQR 22-29) to 38 (IQR 36-44), ( p -value < 0.001)

issues.title: Prospective study of assigned interventions with no registration reported
issues.explanation: The study allocates patients to two interventions but reports no registry entry or protocol, so outcomes and analyses cannot be checked against a prior plan. Whether registration was expected depends on how the study is classified, which the paper leaves unclear. The effect on the conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or published protocol predating enrolment.

quotes.text: This study was a prospective analysis conducted for one year, between September 2021 and September 2022, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

10.3390/jcm12196244.headline_claim: An eight-week, twice-weekly supervised water-based or land-based exercise programme improved exercise capacity in children aged 10-12 with post COVID-19 condition, with no effect on fatigue and parent-reported HRQoL improvement in the training groups.
10.3390/jcm12196244.overall: Exercise capacity appears to have risen in the trained arms, but the effect against control is imprecise. The text and table disagree on which contrast is significant, the claim that AQUA beats LAND is unsupported (equal +2.6 gains), and the HRQoL claim for both training groups goes beyond the data. Analysis is limited to 74 of 86 completers and open-label, so the conclusions should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Exercise capacity (VO2max, modified Balke treadmill) and fatigue (CFSQ)

issues.title: Both arms 'improved' on within-group tests; 'greater AQUA improvement' not supported (change +2.6 in both)
issues.explanation: The conclusion that both programmes improved exercise capacity leans on within-group pre/post p-values (AQUA 0.001, LAND 0.004). The between-group evidence against CONTROL is marginal for LAND and null for AQUA, and AQUA vs LAND is not significant. The Discussion's claim that AQUA improved capacity 'to a greater degree' than LAND is contradicted by the table: both arms gained 2.6 mL/kg/min. Capacity gains were observed, but the superiority claim is unsupported and the effect size vs control is imprecise.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group (change-score or ANCOVA) test showing AQUA > LAND and both > CONTROL.

quotes.text: The absolute maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) values increased after both AQUA ( p = 0.001) and LAND ( p = 0.004) interventions.
Our data also indicates that the AQUA training improved exercise capacity to a greater degree than the LAND training

second_reader.what_stands: For relative VO2max, the change is identical in both exercise arms (+2.6 mL/kg/min), and no direct AQUA-vs-LAND comparison shows an advantage, so the Discussion claim that AQUA improved exercise capacity 'to a greater degree' (and the 'most significant improvement' in the first paragraph) is not supported. The within-group significance of AQUA p = 0.001 vs LAND p = 0.004 is the only basis, and a difference in p-values is not a difference in effect. The abstract's within-group statement is accurate, and I could not check the absolute VO2max change by arm because the table rows are not legible.

issues.title: Text names AQUA vs CONTROL as the only significant post VO2max contrast; table shows LAND vs CONTROL
issues.explanation: The Results say the only significant post-intervention VO2max difference was AQUA vs CONTROL (p = 0.023). In Table 2 that contrast is 1.4 (-2.6 to 5.4), which spans zero, while LAND vs CONTROL is 4.3 (0.01 to 8.6). The text and table disagree on which arm differed from control. This weakens the AQUA-favouring reading of the result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction or the CONSORT/figure data showing the p = 0.023 contrast is AQUA vs CONTROL with a CI excluding zero.

quotes.text: The only significant difference in post-intervention VO2max values was observed between the AQUA and CONTROL groups

quotes.location: Table 2, VO2max Post row, LAND vs. CONTROL column

issues.title: HRQoL improvement claimed for both training groups; significant only in LAND parents, no between-group effect
issues.explanation: The Conclusions and Abstract say parents in the training groups noted HRQoL improvement. The Results report a significant within-group change only in LAND parents. No between-group effect was found for the PedsQL total score in children or parents (group x time p = 0.094 for parents). The AQUA claim rests on a threshold change without significance, and the control group also moved by +1.2. The wording is stronger than the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant AQUA within-group or between-group parent PedsQL result.

quotes.text: HRQoL improvement was observed by the parents of the children in the training groups.
A significant improvement was found in the PedsQL reported by the parents in the LAND group.

issues.title: Analysis limited to 74 of 86 randomised children (14% lost); no ITT analysis, pairwise deletion
issues.explanation: Of 86 randomised children, 74 completed and are the basis for all reported analyses; Table 1 group sizes (25/23/26) sum to 74, not 86. Missing data were pairwise deleted and no intention-to-treat analysis is reported. If dropout differed by arm, completer effects could be biased toward benefit. Arm-wise randomised numbers and reasons for dropout are not stated in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis including all 86 children showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Of the 179 children assessed for eligibility, 86 met the inclusion criteria and were randomized.
Missing data were pairwise deleted.
A total of 74 of the 86 children completed the intervention and attended the post-intervention assessment.

issues.title: No blinding of staff or participants; effort-dependent VO2max test and fatigue questionnaire exposed to bias
issues.explanation: Participants and physiotherapists were not blinded, and the control group received no attention-matched activity. Fatigue is self-reported, but its null result is not threatened by bias in favour of treatment. The larger concern is the exhaustion-based treadmill test with encouragement, an effort-dependent primary outcome whose assessor blinding is not described. The registry says masking was 'single', which the paper does not describe.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that VO2max tests were run and scored by assessors blind to allocation.

quotes.text: Due to the nature of exercise interventions, it was not possible to blind the physiotherapist or participants.
Standardized verbal encouragement was given throughout the test.

issues.title: Baseline 'no significant differences' vs unadjusted pre-intervention CIs excluding 0 (e.g. 6.3, 0.8 to 11.9)
issues.explanation: The text says there were no between-group differences at baseline for any parameter. Table 2 shows pre-intervention contrasts whose CIs exclude zero (6.3 (0.8 to 11.9) and 6.4 (0.8 to 11.9); 6.4 (0.4 to 12.5) for LAND vs CONTROL in the row above). The CIs appear unadjusted while post-hoc testing used Tukey, so the paper cannot be shown to be wrong. The statement is not demonstrated for those parameters. The affected variable is unlabelled in the extracted table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Tukey-adjusted baseline p-values above 0.05 for these contrasts.

quotes.text: No significant differences were found between groups before the intervention for any measured parameter

quotes.location: Table 2, pre-intervention row 48.6/55.0/55.0, AQUA vs. LAND

issues.title: Allocation sequence selected from five random versions by lowest baseline MANOVA F
issues.explanation: The allocation was chosen from five generated versions as the one with the lowest baseline MANOVA F. This is a restricted randomisation that the paper does not analyse or justify. It is not pure random allocation, and standard p-values may be slightly off. The reported baseline groups are broadly similar, so the effect on conclusions is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; a statement that analyses accounted for the restricted allocation would settle it.

quotes.text: Group allocation was prepared in 5 random versions.
The allocation providing the lowest F value for MANOVA comparing the basic characteristics of the study subjects was used.

issues.title: Table 1 LAND body mass SD of 1.6 kg implausible beside SDs of 14.1 and 9.5 in other arms
issues.explanation: LAND mean body mass is printed as 43.4 (1.6) kg. The other arms show SDs of 14.1 and 9.5, and LAND BMI SD is 3.7, which implies a mass SD of roughly 8 kg. An SD of 1.6 is therefore very unlikely and probably a transcription error. No conclusion depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or a correction giving a LAND body mass SD near 8 kg.

10.3390/jcm12196253.headline_claim: HBO may provide a safe and feasible therapeutic tool for mitigation of LCS-related symptoms, with physical functioning and physical and emotional role improving significantly and sustainably.
10.3390/jcm12196253.overall: The study supports only that HBO was feasible and well tolerated in a small open-label cohort with within-patient improvements on self-report scales. The headline claim of significant and sustained improvement of physical and emotional role is contradicted by the paper's own tables, and the long-term claim rests on 18 self-selected patients without a control group.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 domains (physical functioning, physical role, energy, emotional role, emotional well-being, social functioning, pain, general perception of health, limitation of activities) with VAS as secondary self-report

issues.title: Single-arm uncontrolled before-after design cannot attribute improvements to HBO
issues.explanation: All results are within-patient pre-post changes without a control or sham, so placebo effect, natural recovery of long COVID and regression to the mean cannot be separated from any HBO effect. The Abstract and Conclusions nonetheless report significant and sustained improvement and the Discussion says results resemble a sham-controlled trial. The study can show feasibility but not efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or sham control showing the same improvements only in HBO.

quotes.text: This is why we had to conduct the current study without a control group.
our results resemble those of the prospectively randomized, sham control, double-blind study by Zilberman et al.

second_reader.what_stands: A single-arm before-after design with unblinded self-reported outcomes cannot attribute the changes to HBO, and the paper concedes the missing control group. What is not fully fair is that the paper does not hide this limitation, but its wording ('confirm', 'resemble' a sham-controlled trial, 'promising') still goes further than the design supports.

issues.title: Emotional role called significantly improved in conclusions but p = 0.26 (and 0.06, 0.16, 0.56 elsewhere)
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Conclusions say emotional role improved significantly and sustainably. In every analysis set emotional role is non-significant: p = 0.26 in the 59 patients, 0.06 and 0.16 in the 22/18 patients, and 0.56 in the 37 patients. The claim is contradicted by the paper's own tables.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported significant emotional role result in any analysis set.

quotes.text: Physical functioning and both the physical and emotional role improved significantly and sustainably
Improvement that failed to reach statistical level of significance was found for emotional role ( p = 0.26)

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions say emotional role improved 'significantly and sustainably', yet every reported p-value for emotional role (0.26, 0.06, 0.16, 0.56) is above 0.05, and the Results text itself calls the change non-significant. The claim is contradicted by the paper's own data.

issues.title: Physical role claimed sustained at 3 months but Table 2 gives p = 0.07 (Wilcoxon 0.13)
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say physical role improved significantly even during long-term follow-up. Table 2 gives p = 0.07 (0.13 by Wilcoxon) at 3 months, and Section 3.6 does not list physical role among the significant 3-month changes. The Discussion itself lists only physical and social functioning and activity limitation as persisting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant 3-month physical role test in the 18-patient set.

quotes.text: physical functioning and both the physical and emotional role improved significantly and sustainably even during long-term follow-up

second_reader.what_stands: Physical role at 3 months is not significant by either test (p=0.07 t-test, p=0.13 Wilcoxon), and the Results and Discussion do not list it among the persisting effects, so 'sustainably even during long-term follow-up' is not supported for it. The point estimate rose by 14.8 points in 18 patients, but the data are compatible with no change at alpha = 0.05.

issues.title: Long-term claim rests on 18 of 70 enrolled patients, a self-selected subset (37 continued, 4 lost)
issues.explanation: Only 18 patients were evaluated at 3 months. The 37 who wanted more sessions were excluded after session 10, and 4 of the remaining 22 did not return. Patients with better response were likely to continue, so the 18 may differ systematically, and the paper itself notes the two groups responded differently after 10 sessions. The abstract's claim of intention-to-treat analysis does not fit this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Follow-up data on the 37 who continued, or on all enrolled patients.

quotes.text: Out of the 22 remaining patients, 18 entered the final evaluation at 3 months, whilst 4 declined to show up for the investigation (Figure 1).

second_reader.what_stands: The long-term claims do rest on 18 of 70 enrolled (26%) and 18 of 59 evaluable patients, a subset defined by not asking for further treatment, and the authors acknowledge this in their limitations. However, the point's wording is slightly off: the 37 were not lost to follow-up but were deliberately excluded because they continued HBO, and only 4 of the 22 eligible patients were truly lost (about 82% follow-up in the eligible group).

issues.title: About 14 outcomes in three sets tested with no multiplicity correction
issues.explanation: Many paired tests were run without correction, which the authors disclose as exploratory. The strongest findings (p < 0.001) would survive correction, but borderline ones such as physical role (p = 0.01, Wilcoxon 0.02), pain (0.01) and 3-month physical functioning (0.05) may not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pre-specified primary outcome or adjusted analysis showing results hold.

quotes.text: Since it is an exploratory study, we did not apply any correction for multiple comparisons.

issues.title: 3-month physical functioning p = 0.05 in text vs <0.001 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The text gives p = 0.05 and calls it significant, whereas Table 2 gives <0.001 for the same comparison. The two cannot both be right, and p = 0.05 does not meet the stated p < 0.05 criterion. Because the 3-month physical functioning result is a headline claim, the discrepancy matters.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired data or an erratum confirming which p is correct.

quotes.text: physical functioning ( p = 0.05), social functioning ( p <0.001) and limitation of activities ( p =0.02) improved even after 3 months

issues.title: Section 3.7 omits pain, which Table 3 gives p < 0.001 in the 37-patient subgroup
issues.explanation: Section 3.7 lists significant SF-36 domains without pain and then says all further parameters were not significant, yet Table 3 reports p < 0.001 for pain. The Discussion's count of nine improved categories only works if pain is included. This is an internal text-table inconsistency with little effect on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the discrepancy is visible in the text.

quotes.text: All further SF-36 parameters also improved, yet without reaching statistical significance.

issues.title: Physical role called significant at p = 0.05 in 37-patient subgroup (threshold p < 0.05)
issues.explanation: The text labels physical role significant at p = 0.05, whereas the stated criterion is p < 0.05. Rounding could place the true value either side of 0.05, so the label is borderline rather than clearly wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded p below 0.05.

quotes.text: Physical role improved significantly ( p = 0.05)

issues.title: Discussion gives 18 on-schedule patients at 10 sessions; Results and Table 2 give 22
issues.explanation: The Discussion attributes the post-10-session comparison to 18 patients, but those results come from the 22-patient set; 18 is the 3-month subset. It is a labelling inconsistency with no effect on any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable.

quotes.text: the 18 patients who finished HBO according to schedule displayed no statistically significant effect on heart rate
Among these 22 patients, the circulation parameters changed

10.3390/jcm12196428.headline_claim: IA has efficacy in a subset of patients and, thus, AABs play an important role in the pathomechanism of SARS-CoV-2-triggered ME/CFS.
10.3390/jcm12196428.overall: The finding that 7 of 10 patients gained at least 10 SF36-PF points is arithmetically supported by Table 1, apart from an abstract slip in the responder range (10 to 35 vs 10 to 45). It cannot show efficacy, because there is no control and the sample is a 10-patient interim set with a borrowed responder threshold. The mechanistic conclusion about autoantibodies is contradicted by the paper's own data, and registration followed the start of recruitment.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 Physical Function (SF36-PF) score 4 weeks after first IA

primary_outcomes.measure: Improvement in Physical Function (PF) as measured by the Short Form 36 Health Survey Questionnaire (SF-36)

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from an uncontrolled single-arm series of 10 patients on a patient-reported outcome
issues.explanation: All ten patients received IA and were compared only with their own baseline SF-36 PF, a self-reported measure, with no control arm or sham. Gains at 4 weeks cannot be separated from placebo or expectation effects, natural course or regression to the mean, particularly after an intensive 5-session procedure. The sample is only 10 patients with no sample-size justification and no confidence intervals. The Conclusions nonetheless state that the data provide evidence of efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or untreated control group showing a difference in SF36-PF change.

quotes.text: Limitations of our study include the low number of patients having completed therapy so far and the non-controlled treatment.
the first data from our study provide evidence that IA has efficacy in a subset of patients

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does draw an efficacy conclusion from 10 uncontrolled patients using an unblinded, patient-reported primary outcome, so the causal wording 'IA has efficacy' is stronger than the design supports (no control, placebo response, regression to the mean and expectation effects cannot be separated). It is only partly a problem because the authors openly name the non-controlled treatment and small numbers as limitations, restrict the claim to 'a subset', call it first/interim evidence, and state that sham-controlled RCTs are the next step.

issues.title: Conclusion that AABs play an important pathomechanistic role contradicts the paper's own AAB findings
issues.explanation: The Conclusions infer from apparent efficacy that autoantibodies play an important role. The Results report no correlation between AAB levels and response, and AAB levels fell and rebounded similarly in responders and non-responders. The Discussion itself says there is no direct evidence that ADRB2 AAB depletion drives response. IA removes all immunoglobulins, and the design cannot isolate AABs, so the inference does not follow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data showing AAB reduction predicts response, or a controlled comparison that isolates antibody depletion.

quotes.text: AABs play an important role in the pathomechanism of SARS-CoV-2-triggered ME/CFS
However, we found no correlation in the levels of AABs before or after treatment and the treatment response.
we have no direct evidence that the depletion of ADRB2 AABs plays a role in clinical response

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's causal 'thus, AABs play an important role in the pathomechanism' does not follow from, and runs against, the paper's own findings of no association between AAB levels and response and the authors' admission of no direct evidence for ADRB2 AAB depletion mattering. The Discussion is more careful than the Conclusion, and the small sample means the null correlation is weak evidence either way.

issues.title: Study described as prospective but registered (2022-11-14) after recruitment began (Oct 2022)
issues.explanation: The paper calls the study prospective and gives a registration number, but says patients were recruited from October 2022. The registry record shows first submission on 2022-11-14 and labels it retrospective, with a recorded study start of 2022-08-28. Registration after enrolment began weakens the protection against post hoc choice of outcomes and responder thresholds. The registered primary outcome does match the paper's, which limits the concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Dated documentation that no patient was enrolled or treated before the registry submission on 2022-11-14, or an earlier registry version.

quotes.text: Patients were recruited from October 2022 to February 2023
in our prospective observational IA study of patients with SARS-CoV-2-triggered ME/CFS

issues.title: Responder cut-off of 10 SF-36 PF points taken from a paediatric MCID study; two 'responders' gained exactly 10
issues.explanation: The 7/10 responder count depends on a minimum threshold of 10 points justified by a paediatric CFS/ME study. It is not shown to apply to adults with post-COVID ME/CFS. Two of the seven responders (patients 3 and 6) gained exactly 10 points, so a slightly stricter cut-off would lower the count. The threshold is defensible but borrowed, and the paper gives no evidence it was fixed before enrolment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry dated before enrolment fixing the 10-point threshold, plus adult MCID evidence in the same range.

quotes.text: Therefore, we defined an increase of at least 10 points at four weeks after IA as the minimum threshold for considering a patient's response as positive.
Defining the minimally clinically important difference of the SF-36 physical function subscale for paediatric CFS/ME

issues.title: Symptom improvements (muscle pain, immune score, p<0.05) tested only in the 7 responders selected on PF gain
issues.explanation: Muscle pain and immune-score improvements are reported as significant only among the seven patients selected for improving SF36-PF. Selection on one self-reported outcome biases tests on correlated self-reported outcomes toward improvement. There is no all-patient analysis of these symptoms and no correction across the four symptom measures plus FSS. The Discussion's statement that IA improves symptoms therefore relies on a selected subset.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Symptom analyses in all 10 patients, or in a pre-specified subset, showing the same improvement.

quotes.text: Improvements in muscle pain and the immune score were significant after four weeks
provides first evidence that IA can improve physical function and symptoms in a subset of patients

issues.title: Abstract gives responder SF36-PF gain as 10 to 35 points; Table 1 and Results show 10 to 45
issues.explanation: The abstract says the seven responders had gains of 10 to 35 points. Table 1 and the Results show the largest gain was 45 points (patient 7, 25 to 70), and patient 10 gained 40. The abstract therefore understates the top of the responder range. The responder classification itself is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Table 1 in which no responder gained more than 35 points.

quotes.text: with seven responders defined by an increase of between 10 and 35 points in the Short-Form 36 Physical Function (SF36-PF) at week four after IA
Seven patients reported an increase in SF36-PF by 10 to 45 points at week 4 after IA

10.3390/jcm12216739.headline_claim: Moderate-intensity continuous and interval aerobic training are equally effective in improving physical exercise capacity in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome during inpatient rehabilitation, and PCS patients improve comparably to CAD patients.
10.3390/jcm12216739.overall: The paper shows that patients improved on cardiopulmonary measures and questionnaires over inpatient rehabilitation, but its design cannot attribute the gains to aerobic training: there is no non-training control, and the CAD cohort is a non-randomized benchmark. The claim that interval and continuous training are equally effective rests on a non-significant p = 0.157 in a PP sample smaller than planned (IT 45 vs 65), with no equivalence margin and ITT results not shown. Registration was retrospective, though the registered primary outcome matches.

primary_outcome.name: Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak, mL/min/kg, percent-predicted change)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Baseline and week 4 (i. e. before discharge)

issues.title: Training benefit claimed without a non-training control; only within-arm changes and a non-randomized CAD cohort
issues.explanation: The conclusion that PCS patients 'benefit from aerobic endurance training' rests on T0 to T1 changes inside two arms that both trained, plus a comparison with a separate CAD cohort. Both arms also received strength, respiratory, cognitive and psychological therapy, and natural recovery, regression to the mean and non-ergometer therapies are not separable from the cycling. The between-arm test was null (p = 0.157), so the randomized comparison gives no evidence of benefit from either training. The CAD comparison shows only similar percent-predicted changes between differently treated diseases, not efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomized or concurrent no-training or usual-care comparison showing a between-group difference in change in peak VO2.

quotes.text: we provide evidence that PCS patients benefit from aerobic endurance training
A group of 96 patients with a diagnosis of CAD enrolled in a prospective cohort study on the effectiveness of medical rehabilitation was used for comparison.
Patients received individual medical rehabilitation including a combination of strength, respiratory, and cognitive training, as well as physio-, psycho-, and nutrition therapy as indicated.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no non-training control. Evidence for 'benefit from aerobic endurance training' rests on within-group pre-post change in a bundled rehabilitation program, plus a non-randomized, differently managed CAD cohort used as a benchmark. The CAD comparison shows similar change, not a training effect. The paper does mention differing programs as a limitation, but the conclusion still states the causal wording without qualification.

issues.title: Primary analysis on 110 of 139 randomized (21% excluded), arms 45 vs 65; ITT results not shown
issues.explanation: 139 patients were randomized but the outcome tables use only 110, with IT 45 and CT 65. Reasons for exclusion and the split of the 29 exclusions by arm are not given in the text, and only 2 are explained (CPET not available). If allocation was roughly 1:1, the 45 vs 65 split implies more exclusions in the IT arm. The ITT analysis is mentioned in one sentence with no numbers. The equivalence conclusion therefore rests on completers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram giving reasons for exclusion by arm and full ITT estimates with CIs showing results unchanged.

quotes.text: In total, 139 PCS patients were randomized and analyzed according to intention to treat (ITT). The per-protocol (PP) analysis included 110 PCS patients.
Data were analyzed per protocol (PP) using SPSS
the skewed group sizes and implementation error may have affected the comparability of both groups

second_reader.what_stands: Correct that the tables and primary conclusions are from 110 of 139 randomized (about 21 % excluded) with arms 45 vs 65, and that no ITT numbers are shown, only a sentence saying ITT results were similar. Not correct that ITT is wholly absent, since the paper says it was done with imputation; also the paper itself flags the skewed group sizes as a limitation, and I cannot verify the reasons for exclusion from the text.

issues.title: 'Equally effective' concluded from p = 0.157 with no equivalence margin; IT arm 45 of 60 planned
issues.explanation: The calculation planned 60 per group (120) to detect a difference, using an effect size from interstitial lung disease, but analysed only 110 (IT 45). A non-significant superiority-type test does not show equivalence, and no margin or CI for the between-arm difference is given. The observed peak VO2 change was 0.8% for IT vs 4.1% for CT, a 3.3-point difference whose interval is wide relative to the 2.7% overall gain. The conclusion that the modalities are 'equally effective' and 'interchangeable' is stronger than the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified equivalence or non-inferiority margin with a between-group CI lying inside it.

quotes.text: suggesting a sample size of 120 patients (60 per group, alpha = 0.05, 1-beta = 0.9, per protocol, two-way repeated measures ANOVA)
moderate-intensity aerobic continuous and interval training are equally effective
may be used interchangeably considering patients’ preferences

second_reader.what_stands: 'Equally effective' and 'interchangeable' are concluded from a non-significant p=0.157 with no equivalence or non-inferiority margin, in a trial powered for a difference and with the IT arm at 45 of 60 planned. The confidence interval for the between-arm difference (roughly 0 to 2.2 mL/min/kg by my crude calculation) does not exclude a clinically meaningful advantage for CT.

issues.title: Trial registered 2023-08-28, about two years after the August 2021 start; not disclosed in the paper
issues.explanation: The paper cites NCT06016192 and says the trial ran from August 2021 to November 2022, but the registry shows first submission on 2023-08-28, after enrolment finished. The paper does not say registration was retrospective, so prespecification of the primary outcome and analysis cannot be verified from registration timing. The primary outcome as registered does match the paper, which limits the practical concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registration record, or an ethics-approved protocol dated before enrolment that specifies peak VO2 as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: A randomized controlled trial (Clinical Trial: NCT06016192) was performed at Clinic Königsfeld between August 2021 and November 2022

issues.title: Section 3.4 swaps VT1 and peak VO2 % changes (2.7% is peak, 3.1% is VT1 in Table 3)
issues.explanation: Section 3.4 says the improvements at 'submaximal and peak' oxygen uptake were 2.7 ± 11.0% and 3.1 ± 10.0% respectively. Table 3 shows 2.7 ± 11.0% for peak VO2 and 3.1 ± 10.0% for VT1, so the order is reversed. The same section later correctly gives ΔVO2peak as 2.7 ± 11.0%. This is a labelling slip that does not change any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 'respectively' was meant to pair peak with 2.7% and submaximal with 3.1% (a wording slip only).

quotes.text: submaximal and peak oxygen uptake of 2.7 ± 11.0% and 3.1 ± 10.0%

quotes.location: Table 3, Peak exercise, VO2 Δ overall

10.3390/jcm13020425.headline_claim: The authors conclude that the specialised outpatient rehabilitation programme is highly effective and safe for respiratory function after COVID-19, and that the added inspiratory muscle trainer is not necessary.
10.3390/jcm13020425.overall: The main randomised contrast (IMT versus sham IMT on PImax) is null, and the 'highly effective' conclusion depends mostly on before/after changes in two arms that received the same exercise programme. Analysis was restricted to adherent participants after a differential, mostly control-arm exclusion, and Table 2 counts do not match the stated 59. The secondary spirometry advantages are nominal, uncorrected and partly overstated in the abstract, so the findings are tentative at best.

primary_outcome.name: Maximum inspiratory pressure (PImax)

primary_outcomes.measure: Physical endurance improvement assessment of 6 MWT distance and outcome of treadmill stress test.

issues.title: Programme called 'highly effective' from pre/post changes; between-arm PImax difference null (p=0.28)
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusions attribute gains to the programme using within-group p<0.001 values. Both arms did the same exercises, so the only randomised contrast tests the IMT add-on, and for the primary outcome PImax it is null (median change 24 vs 23.5, p=0.28). Without an untreated control, the pre/post change cannot be assigned to the programme. The Results sentence that PImax and others changed 'between the two groups' also blurs within- and between-group findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison against a no-exercise control, or a justification that spontaneous recovery and test learning cannot account for the pre/post change.

quotes.text: The applied rehabilitation program improved respiratory muscle strength in both the study and control groups ( p < 0.001).
is highly effective in improving the functional parameters of the respiratory system.

second_reader.what_stands: The 'highly effective' conclusion and the abstract's 'improved in both groups' rest on within-group pre/post changes of PImax; the between-arm difference is null (24 vs 23.5 cmH2O, p = 0.28), so no added benefit of IMT is shown. Without a no-intervention comparator, the pre/post gains cannot be attributed to the programme itself, and per-protocol exclusions and the lack of a pre-specified non-inferiority or equivalence test further limit this. The authors do note IMT is 'not necessary', which is a fair reading of the null, but the strong effectiveness claim is not supported by the design.

issues.title: Per-protocol analysis after mostly control-arm exclusions turned 1:1 allocation into about 2:1, with no ITT
issues.explanation: Only participants with more than 12 of 18 sessions were analysed, and most of those excluded came from the control arm, so the final split was about 39:22 instead of 1:1. No intention-to-treat analysis is given and the randomised total is not stated in the text. Between-group comparisons therefore rest on a post-randomisation filtered sample, and the direction of bias cannot be determined from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 numbers showing balanced, small exclusions, or an ITT/sensitivity analysis giving the same between-group results.

quotes.text: The large majority of excluded participants were those from the control group, as shown in the flow diagram (Figure 1).
Despite the assumed allocation of respondents to groups in a 1:1 ratio, the final distribution of participants was closer to a 2:1 ratio.
Patients included in the analysis were those with adherence above 12 out of the planned 18 training sessions.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does state that exclusions were mostly from the control arm, that allocation ended up closer to 2:1 (39 vs 22), and that only patients with more than 12 of 18 sessions were analysed, so the analysis is per-protocol and no ITT analysis is reported. What cannot be verified here is the exact exclusion counts per arm (Figure 1 is not in the text). The Results also say all 59 'completed' the programme. The imbalance is disclosed, so it is a limitation the authors acknowledge, but differential post-randomisation exclusion may bias the between-arm comparison and the authors do not weigh thi

issues.title: Table 2 arms (39 + 22 = 61) and women (26 + 13 = 39) exceed the stated 59 patients and 37 women
issues.explanation: The abstract and Results say 59 patients (37 women, 22 men) were analysed. Table 2 lists 39 study and 22 control patients, which sum to 61, and 26 + 13 = 39 women. The male counts do match (13 + 9 = 22), so the study arm appears to be overstated by 2 patients, or the text understated. Which analysed n applies to the Table 3 and 4 tests cannot be told from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 2 or Figure 1 showing 37 study and 22 control analysed patients, with 24 and 13 women.

quotes.text: A total of 59 patients (37 women and 22 men)
A total of 59 patients under treatment following COVID-19 were randomly divided into two groups.

issues.title: 'Proven effective and safe' and preventive use claimed from 59 analysed patients with existing symptoms over 6 weeks
issues.explanation: The abstract says the programme 'has proven' effective and safe, based on a small, partly preliminary analysed set and short follow-up. Participants already had post-COVID syndrome, so the suggestion of use as a preventive measure against long-term symptoms is outside what was tested. Safety is judged from narrative reports in completers only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prevention-focused outcomes in a population without post-COVID syndrome.

quotes.text: has proven to be effective and safe.
the findings suggest potential benefits for patients who adopt the presented rehabilitation program as a preventive measure against long-term COVID-19 symptoms.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation (target 60 'arbitrary'); null PImax result with ~22 controls read as 'device not necessary'
issues.explanation: With no power calculation and a control arm of about 22, a null between-arm PImax difference cannot show that the IMT add-on is unnecessary. The paper is framed as preliminary, which tempers but does not remove the confident conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified power or non-inferiority analysis, or a CI for the between-arm PImax difference excluding a meaningful benefit.

quotes.text: a minimum group size of 60 participants was arbitrarily assumed.
The primary outcome showed that the use of additional resistance training devices is not necessary to achieve satisfactory results.

issues.title: About 20 between-group tests at p<0.05 without correction; four nominal spirometry results are highlighted
issues.explanation: The methods set a single alpha of 0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment across many secondary outcomes. The few nominally significant between-group spirometry results (p 0.009 to 0.022) would not survive a Bonferroni threshold of about 0.0025. The secondary findings should be read as exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that secondary outcomes are exploratory, or adjusted p-values still below threshold.

quotes.text: We assessed the data for statistical significance, which was determined by p < 0.05.

issues.title: Two of three registered primary outcomes (6MWT/treadmill, quality of life) not reported; 6-month vs 6-week time frame
issues.explanation: The registry record lists 6MWT/treadmill, quality of life and respiratory muscle force as primary, with a 6-month time frame. The paper reports only PImax as primary at 6 weeks and states that outcomes were not modified. The mismatch may reflect staged reporting, but it is not explained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registry versions listing PImax as primary, or a separate publication of 6MWT and quality-of-life results.

quotes.text: The primary outcome in relation to the effectiveness of post-COVID-19 rehabilitation was maximum inspiratory pressure (PImax).
Nochanges or modifications to trial outcomes were performed after the trial commenced.

issues.title: Abstract credits 'greater improvement' with within-group p-values; PEF change is larger in controls (9.97% vs 9.67%)
issues.explanation: The abstract gives study-arm percentage gains with within-group p<0.001 as evidence that the study group improved more. For PEF this is contradicted by Tables 3 and 4 (control 9.97% vs study 9.67%, between-group p=0.301). The abstract also omits the null primary between-arm PImax result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group test showing greater PEF improvement in the study arm.

quotes.text: Spirometric parameters improved in both groups, with the study group showing a greater improvement: 8.02% in FEV1 ( p < 0.001), 13.24% in FVC EX ( p < 0.001) and 9.67% in PEF ( p < 0.001).

10.3390/jcm13040938.headline_claim: Personalized six-week post-COVID-19 rehabilitation improved body composition, muscle strength and functioning in patients with PCS, and the benefits were regardless of gender.
10.3390/jcm13040938.overall: The finding that patients improved on fatigue, dyspnoea and physical-capacity measures over six weeks is plausible, but the single-arm design means that improvement cannot be attributed to the programme. The sex-specific claims in the abstract are not supported by the paper's own between-sex tests, and several delta and p-value printings in the abstract and tables are inconsistent, though none change significance conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline to six weeks in body composition, muscle strength and functioning, compared by gender (no single primary outcome is named)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post cohort with no control group supports causal 'improved' and 'effective' claims
issues.explanation: All 90 patients received the same programme and are compared only with their own baseline six weeks earlier. Post-COVID symptoms often improve spontaneously, and tests such as the 6MWT, 30 CST and SPPB show learning effects, so the gains cannot be attributed to rehabilitation. The paper nonetheless calls rehabilitation an effective tool and says it improved outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Inclusion of a concurrent untreated or usual-care comparison group showing differential change.

quotes.text: The effectiveness of the rehabilitation program was assessed by comparing the differences between two time points, i.e., during the initial visit and the final visit after six weeks.
Therefore, it is an effective tool to reduce the symptoms of PCS regardless of gender.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm before/after cohort of completers with no control group, yet the Discussion concludes the program 'is an effective tool' and the abstract says outcomes 'were significantly improved after the rehabilitation'. The design supports an observed improvement over 6 weeks, not a causal effect, and the limitations section does not mention the missing control group.

issues.title: Sex-specific effects claimed from within-group p-values although between-sex delta tests are all p > 0.05
issues.explanation: The abstract states that fat decrease and muscle gain occurred 'only in females' and grip gains 'selectively in males'. These statements compare significant versus non-significant within-group tests; the direct test of difference between the sexes (p-value for deltas) is non-significant for every parameter, for example 0.80 for abdominal fat, 0.35 for skeletal muscle mass and 0.13 for right-hand grip. Biological explanations in the Discussion therefore explain a difference that the data do not demonstrate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant sex-by-time interaction for these outcomes.

quotes.text: A decrease in fat tissue volume and an increase in skeletal muscle mass were observed only in females, while an increase in grip strength was noticed selectively in males.
In all analyzed parameters, the deltas did not differ between the genders ( p > 0.05).

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract and Discussion present effects as sex-specific ('only in females', 'selectively in males') based on within-group p-values, while every between-sex test of deltas is non-significant (p from 0.08 upward). The authors do state that deltas did not differ, but the sex-specific framing and the physiological explanations are not supported by a test of difference between the sexes.

issues.title: 'Rehabilitation should be applied in all patients with PCS' generalised from 90 uncontrolled completers
issues.explanation: The conclusion recommends rehabilitation for every PCS patient. The sample consists of 90 completers referred by general practitioners with clinically relevant dyspnoea, with no comparator, no safety reporting and no cost or harm assessment. The data support, at most, that outcomes improved in similar patients who completed the programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled evidence in a comparable population, or narrowing the recommendation to the studied population.

quotes.text: Rehabilitation should be applied in all patients with PCS regardless of gender-related differences in outcomes.

second_reader.what_stands: The recommendation to apply rehabilitation 'in all patients with PCS' goes beyond the evidence, which comes from 90 uncontrolled completers from one centre, selected by referral, symptom and exclusion criteria, in a narrow age band (mean about 62 years), with no control arm or safety data. A narrower recommendation, such as that the program was followed by improvements in similar patients and merits controlled testing, would match the data.

issues.title: Female delta values in Tables 3-4 do not equal after minus before (6MWT 47.82 vs 51.71; SPPB 1.53 vs 1.65)
issues.explanation: In Table 4 several female deltas differ from the printed after-minus-before means: 6MWT 47.82 vs 51.71, SPPB 1.53 vs 1.65, MFIS -10.12 vs -9.84, Borg -1.72 vs -1.67. Differences are small and could arise from pairs with missing values, but the paper does not say so. In Table 3 the female grip deltas are larger discrepancies (see c8-c10). All are directionally consistent, so conclusions are not affected, but the tables cannot be fully reconciled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that deltas were computed on a subset with complete paired data.

issues.title: Table 3 grip-strength deltas inconsistent with means; non-dominant female delta has wrong sign; delta SDs all 0.00
issues.explanation: Female deltas in Table 3 do not match after minus before: right hand 0.02 vs 0.06, dominant hand -0.06 vs -0.25, non-dominant +0.21 vs -0.19 (sign opposite). The SDs of all grip means are integers and every delta SD is printed as 0.00, which is implausible for paired changes. The grip-strength rows therefore cannot be relied on as printed, although the male increases and the main sex-specific pattern are directionally unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source data tables showing correct deltas and SDs, with the printed table being an extraction fault.

issues.title: Abstract and Table 2 swap p-values for skeletal muscle mass (0.001 vs 0.01) and abdominal fat (0.01 vs 0.001)
issues.explanation: The abstract gives p = 0.001 for skeletal muscle mass and p = 0.01 for abdominal fat volume. Table 2 prints 0.01 for skeletal muscle mass and 0.001 for abdominal fat volume. The two p-values appear transposed between abstract and table. Both remain below 0.05, so the significance conclusions are unchanged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version or raw data showing the abstract and table p-values are consistent.

quotes.text: Rehabilitation was associated with an increase in skeletal muscle mass (24.11 kg vs. 24.37 kg, p = 0.001)
Skeletal muscle mass, [kg] 24.11 ± 6.61 24.37 ± 6.61 0.01
with a reduction in abdominal fat tissue volume (3.03 L vs. 2.85 L, p = 0.01)

issues.title: Completers-only analysis: 7 of 97 patients who started (7.2%) excluded from outcome analysis
issues.explanation: Only patients who finished all six weeks are analysed. Seven patients who began the programme are excluded, and their reasons and outcomes are not described in the text. With 7% attrition the bias is likely small, but efficacy estimates describe completers only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 or supplementary data showing reasons for withdrawal unrelated to outcome and an analysis including them.

quotes.text: Only patients who underwent the complete rehabilitation program were included in the final analysis of the PCR-SIRIO 8 study.
of which 97 started the rehabilitation and 90 were included in the final analysis (49 women and 41 men)

10.3390/jcm13040970.headline_claim: Multidisciplinary group telerehabilitation results in beneficial outcomes in functioning and activities/participation (ICF) in people with post-COVID-19 condition.
10.3390/jcm13040970.overall: The conclusion of beneficial telerehabilitation outcomes is not supported by the between-group comparisons, which are almost entirely null, and rests on within-group counts of significant changes in an unvalidated self-report measure that was not the registered primary outcome. Six-month results are further weakened by 50% waiting-list loss and complete-case analysis. The numeric slips (Table 1 count, CCQ scale, retention percentage) are minor by comparison.

primary_outcome.name: ICF functioning and activity (Functional Compass COVID-19 questionnaire)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in health-related quality of life measured by Short Form-36
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Investigators expect changes at 6 months follow-up after rehabilitation

primary_outcomes.measure: Changes in heart rate variability during physical tests
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Investigators expect normalisation at 6 months follow-up

issues.title: Benefit claimed from within-group ICF changes while between-group comparisons are null
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion say telerehabilitation gives beneficial outcomes, based on more ICF categories improving within the rehabilitation group. The between-group tests were non-significant on the ICF categories at the start and at eight weeks, with only breathing (favouring the waiting list) and olfaction at six months differing. Counting within-arm significant changes does not show superiority over the waiting list, and no multiplicity adjustment is described across 38 categories. The conclusion is not supported by the comparisons reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group test showing a significant group-by-time effect on the ICF outcome.

quotes.text: The results indicate that a larger number of ICF body functions and activity/participation categories had improved in the rehabilitation group after eight weeks and six months.
No significant differences were obtained between the groups at the start and after eight weeks.
However, no differences have been found between the groups, except for more improved breathing functions after eight weeks

second_reader.what_stands: The claimed benefit rests on a larger number of significant within-group Wilcoxon results in the rehabilitation group, while the between-group comparisons are null (apart from breathing, which favoured the waiting list), and the abstract and conclusion state beneficial outcomes without a between-group test supporting this. The authors do disclose the null between-group results in the Discussion and temper the conclusion about residual symptoms.

issues.title: Paper's primary outcome (ICF) differs from registered primaries (SF-36, heart rate variability)
issues.explanation: The registry lists SF-36 quality of life and heart rate variability as primary outcomes. The paper declares ICF functioning and activity as primary, and does not report SF-36 or HRV. The abstract says multiple outcomes were collected, so the reported ones may be a selected subset. The headline therefore rests on an outcome that is not the registered primary, with no explanation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing ICF functioning as primary, or a protocol amendment.

quotes.text: Primary outcomes were the functioning and activity according to the ICF questionnaire.
Multiple outcomes included self-scored questionnaires and physical tests before and after eight weeks, and at six months follow-up.

second_reader.what_stands: Against the current registry record, the paper's stated primary outcome (ICF functioning and activity) differs from the registered primaries (SF-36 and HRV), and the paper neither reports those nor explains the difference. Whether the registry was edited after the trial began cannot be checked, as earlier versions were not retrieved.

issues.title: Six-month follow-up: 60/67 (90%) rehabilitation vs 21/42 (50%) waiting list; complete-case analysis
issues.explanation: Half of the waiting-list participants have no six-month data versus about one in ten in the rehabilitation arm. The waiting-list remainder was also significantly older (50 vs 43 years). The six-month analyses use only completers, so durable-benefit claims rest on non-comparable groups. The authors note the loss and advise caution but still state benefit at six months in the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or multiple-imputation analysis showing the same six-month results.

quotes.text: At six months follow-up, 60 participants from the rehabilitation group and 21 from the waiting list completed the data.
Therefore, we were able to collect less six-month follow-up data than planned.

second_reader.what_stands: Six-month follow-up retention was about 90% (60/67) in rehabilitation versus 50% (21/42) on the waiting list, and the analysis uses only participants with data (complete case) with no stated handling of missingness. The authors disclose reduced waiting-list follow-up and advise caution at six months; the stated 88% in the text differs slightly from 60/67.

issues.title: CCQ in Table 4 (means 15-20, max 45) cannot be the 0-6 item average described in Methods
issues.explanation: The Methods state the CCQ is the sum of 10 items scored 0-6 divided by the number of questions, which bounds it at 6. Table 4 reports means around 15-20 and ranges to 45, which exceeds the bound. The scale used is therefore unclear, so the CCQ results cannot be interpreted as described. This is a secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors stating the CCQ was reported as a sum or rescaled score.

quotes.text: The total score of the domains is calculated by adding all the scores together and dividing this sum by the number of questions.

issues.title: Unblinded waiting-list control with self-reported outcomes; high expectancy in treated arm
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation and the control arm received no attention component, while outcomes are all self-scored. The paper reports high and rising credibility and expectancy in the treatment arm only, so expectancy effects cannot be separated from the programme. The limitations section does not mention this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment or objective outcomes showing a similar effect.

quotes.text: The waiting list controls were informed that they would be offered telerehabilitation in the next round.
Credibility and expectancy were high at both measurements and increased after eight weeks.

issues.title: Primary outcome questionnaire not validated for post-COVID-19 conditions
issues.explanation: The Functional Compass COVID-19 questionnaire is a new adaptation of the Functional Barometer and the authors say it has not been validated for post-COVID-19. It is self-scored. The headline benefit conclusion relies on it without qualification, so the measure's sensitivity to change is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published validation of the instrument in a post-COVID-19 population.

quotes.text: The Functional Compass COVID-19 questionnaire has not been validated among post-COVID-19 conditions and was collected as self-scored data.

issues.title: Table 1 Children 'No' in telerehab column printed 30 (30%); Yes+No = 77, not 67
issues.explanation: In the 8-week telerehabilitation column (n = 67), Children Yes is 47 (70%) and No is printed as 30 (30%). 47 + 30 = 77 exceeds the group size. The percentage 30% fits 20 of 67, so the count appears to be a typing slip. No main result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary table showing 30 participants without children with a different denominator.

quotes.text: Telerehab (n = 67)

script.explanation: 30/67 = 44.78%, but the paper prints 30, outside the rounding interval [29.50, 31.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 100.0 rather than 67.

issues.title: Six-month retention printed as 88% vs 60/67 = 89.6% from abstract and Table 1
issues.explanation: The text says 88% provided data at six months, yet the abstract and Table 1 give 60 of 67 completers, which is 89.6%. The seven non-responders reported also agree with 60 of 67. The discrepancy is about 1.6 percentage points and changes no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A denominator of 68 or a stated reason that the percentage was taken over a different base.

quotes.text: provided post-treatment data after eight weeks and 88% at six months follow-up
At six months follow-up, 60 participants from the rehabilitation group and 21 from the waiting list completed the data.

script.explanation: 60/67 = 89.55%, but the paper prints 88, outside the rounding interval [87.50, 89.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 68.2 rather than 67.

10.3390/jcm13041035.headline_claim: Nordic Walking aerobic exercise therapy increased post-exercise lactate in Long-COVID patients versus non-Long-COVID controls, and reduced fatigue (MFIS) and improved quality of life (SF-36, EQ-5D) relative to controls after 12 weeks.
10.3390/jcm13041035.overall: The finding that Long-COVID participants had higher post-walk lactate than healthy volunteers is supported only as a cross-sectional group difference in a small non-randomized study; the claim that the programme increased lactate or that anaerobic pathways predominate is not. The fatigue-reduction claim relative to controls contradicts the paper's own non-significant MFIS interaction, and QoL improvements lack an untreated Long-COVID comparator. Several reporting inconsistencies (age, dates, Discussion p-values) reduce confidence further.

primary_outcome.name: Lactate concentration after exercise (group effect)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Changes from baseline and at the end of procedure (12 weeks)
Changes from baseline and at the end of procedure (12 weeks)
Changes from baseline and at the end of procedure (12 weeks)
Changes from baseline and at the end of procedure (12 weeks)

issues.title: Healthy non-randomized controls cannot support intervention-effect claims on fatigue and QoL
issues.explanation: Controls are healthy volunteers recruited separately via advertisements, with very different baseline fatigue (MFIS total 59.56 vs 17.58). Both groups received the same programme, so there is no untreated Long-COVID comparator. Group differences reflect disease status, and improvement claims after 'exercise therapy' cannot be attributed to the programme.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Long-COVID comparison arm not receiving the programme.

quotes.text: The healthy control group was recruited through advertisements and flyers in the Madrid region.
Long-COVID group presented a decrease in fatigue with respect to the control group according to the MFIS scale

second_reader.what_stands: Non-randomised, unmasked healthy controls recruited by a different route, who also received the exercise, cannot isolate an intervention effect on fatigue or QoL; baseline MFIS differs by about 42 points. The authors acknowledge the non-randomised design as a limitation, but their conclusions still use causal, intervention-effect wording and a comparison to controls. The controls are reasonable only for the lactate group comparison.

issues.title: Conclusion that anaerobic pathways predominate and that the programme raised lactate goes beyond the data
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the programme 'increased' lactate and that anaerobic pathways are predominant in Long-COVID. The design has no pre-programme lactate, no metabolic pathway measure, and no session differences. Lactate was higher in Long-COVID than in healthy controls, which is not an effect of the programme, and the meter exceeded its range in some measures.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Direct measurements of oxidative versus non-oxidative metabolism.

quotes.text: These results also suggest that anaerobic pathways in Long-COVID patients are the predominant ones
The Nordic Walking program increased blood lactate concentration during aerobic exercise in individuals with Long-COVID syndrome

second_reader.what_stands: Both conclusions go beyond the data. The finding is a higher post-exercise lactate in the Long-COVID group than in controls, with no session or group x session effect, so it does not show that the programme raised lactate. Lactate alone, without oxygen uptake, gas exchange or other measures, does not establish that anaerobic pathways predominate. The out-of-range readings and repeat punctures add measurement uncertainty.

issues.title: MFIS fatigue decrease 'relative to controls' claimed despite non-significant time and group x time effects
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusions say the Long-COVID group decreased in fatigue compared with controls. The MFIS group x time interaction is p = 0.234 and the time effect p = 0.160; only the group main effect (baseline difference) is significant. The claim rests on uncorrected within-group pre/post tests in one arm, which do not test a difference from controls.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant between-group change comparison for MFIS.

quotes.text: group × time (F = 1.584; p = 0.234) interaction on the MFIS scale
The Long-COVID group presented a decrease in fatigue with respect to the control group according to the MFIS scale

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract, Discussion and Conclusions say fatigue decreased relative to controls, but the paper's own MFIS tests show no significant time effect (p=0.160) and no group x time interaction (p=0.234). Only the Long-COVID within-group post hoc changes are nominally significant, which does not support a between-group claim.

issues.title: Abstract age 25.5 ± 7.1 years contradicts Table 1 (46.13 and 46.92) and the 30-60 inclusion range
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the mean age of all 29 participants as 25.5 years. Table 1 gives group means of about 46 years, and eligibility required age 30 to 60, so a mean of 25.5 is impossible. This is a reporting error that does not alter the main findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or data showing the abstract figure refers to a different quantity.

quotes.text: Twenty-nine patients (25.5 ± 7.1 years)

issues.title: Unadjusted baseline imbalance in sex (6.2% vs 30.8% male) and reinfection (25% vs 0%)
issues.explanation: Groups differ in sex and reinfection, and the 2x12 and 2x2 ANOVAs include no covariates. With 29 participants, p-values of 0.114 and 0.069 do not show balance. This weakens between-group comparisons, though the sex distribution is acknowledged in the limitations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Covariate-adjusted analyses showing unchanged results.

quotes.text: Baseline characteristics were similar age, height, weight, hospital admission rate, reinfection, and pneumonia as shown in Table 1.
The gender distribution could impact the generalizability of the study

issues.title: Study timeline inconsistent: recruitment March 2021 vs Feb-Apr 2022, approval Feb 2022, sessions Feb-May 2023
issues.explanation: Methods say Long-COVID patients were recruited in March 2021, which is before ethics approval on 3 February 2022. Results say recruitment ran February to April 2022, and sessions are stated as February to May 2023. The registry gives a March 2022 start. The actual conduct dates cannot be established from the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement from the authors giving the true dates.

quotes.text: Patients in the Long-COVID group were recruited during March 2021
were interested in participating from February to April 2022
Nordic Walking sessions were completed outdoors weekly from February to May 2023

issues.title: Discussion claims lactate differences at sessions 4 and 9 (p < 0.005); Results report none
issues.explanation: The Discussion says lactate was higher in Long-COVID especially in the fourth and ninth sessions with all p < 0.005. The Results state no session effect (p = 0.121), no interaction (p = 0.414) and no differences across sessions. No session-specific tests are presented, so the claim is unsupported by the reported analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported post-hoc per-session comparisons with those p-values.

quotes.text: especially in the fourth and ninth sessions (all p < 0.005)
No differences were found in the sessions (Figure 1)

issues.title: Enrolled 29 vs stated target 40; power calculation covers lactate only, not fatigue/QoL claims
issues.explanation: The calculation required 15 Long-COVID patients, which was met, yet a target of 40 was stated and 29 enrolled. No power calculation supports the fatigue and QoL claims, which are stated confidently in the abstract. The authors do acknowledge small sample size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power calculation covering the fatigue and QoL outcomes.

quotes.text: A target sample size of 40 participants was determined.
The sample size was small because getting patients with Long-COVID to follow exercise programmes is complicated

issues.title: Trial registered 12 July 2022, after the March 2022 start; registered primaries are all reported
issues.explanation: The paper reports registration on 12/07/2022, and the registry lists a March 2022 start, so registration was retrospective. The registered outcomes (lactate, EQ-5D, SF-36, MFIS) are all reported, so outcome switching is not shown, but prespecification cannot be checked against the original record.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing an earlier submission.

quotes.text: The study has been registered at the Registry of Clinical Trials (NCT05453188 on 12/07/2022)

issues.title: Non-Long-COVID SF-36 social functioning identical at pre and post (89.58 (15.84))
issues.explanation: The control group's social functioning mean and SD are identical at both timepoints, unlike all other rows. This may be a copy error. If so, the time main effect and interaction (p = 0.024, 0.042) for this subscale would rest on a wrong cell.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the control values truly are identical.

10.3390/jcm13061543.headline_claim: Hand exoskeleton-based robotic rehabilitation holds promise to optimise rehabilitation outcomes following severe COVID-19, with significant improvements in hand range of motion, self-care, and several SF-36 domains.
10.3390/jcm13061543.overall: The paper is a small uncontrolled pilot, and its claim that the exoskeleton produced positive outcomes is not supported beyond hypothesis generation: total BI and FIM were non-significant, many sub-item tests were uncorrected, and the registration was retrospective. Several reporting slips (units for flexion, ICU stay, study duration) do not change the main results but reduce confidence in the reporting.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated in the paper; registry lists Barthel Index, FIM, SF-36 and range of motion as primary outcomes

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design (n=13) cannot separate therapy effect from natural recovery
issues.explanation: All 13 patients received the same intervention, with measurements before and after only. Patients were recruited 1 to 8.5 months after infection, some had recent strokes, and other care was not described, so recovery over six weeks would be expected anyway. The paper acknowledges the missing control group but still attributes the gains to the exoskeleton.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group showing less improvement over the same period.

quotes.text: the absence of a control group in the study design limits the ability to make direct comparisons and draw conclusions about the causative effects of rehabilitation
the range of motion of the fingers of the patients significantly increased after the rehabilitation with the RobHand exoskeleton

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design with 13 patients, and it cannot separate the exoskeleton effect from spontaneous recovery, which is plausible given the subacute timing after COVID-19 and stroke. The authors acknowledge the absence of a control group as a limitation, but the goniometry paragraph and the Discussion still attribute the ROM and functional gains to the rehabilitation.

issues.title: ~25 uncorrected paired tests; significant items emphasised while total BI (p=0.0514) and FIM (p=0.0636) are null
issues.explanation: About 25 outcome tests were run at p<0.05 without correction and no primary outcome was named. The two summary scales (total BI and total FIM) were not significant, but the Discussion highlights the significant sub-items and SF-36 domains. Most of those p-values (0.005 to 0.04) would not survive even a modest correction, so positive findings may partly be chance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a correction or hierarchical testing plan for the secondary items.

issues.title: Conclusions assert positive outcomes and reduced clinician burden from an uncontrolled 13-patient pilot
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the exoskeleton yielded positive outcomes for physical and psychological well-being and relieves healthcare professionals. The study had no comparator, did not measure staff time or costs, and the total BI (p=0.0514) and total FIM (p=0.0636) were not significant. The language is stronger than a pilot with uncorrected sub-item tests can support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data showing benefit on prespecified outcomes and measured reductions in staff time.

quotes.text: The utilization of a hand rehabilitation exoskeleton yielded positive outcomes, contributing to the physical and psychological well-being of patients.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions assert positive outcomes with causal wording and state that robotic systems relieve the burden on healthcare professionals, but the study is uncontrolled with 13 patients, the overall BI and FIM totals were not significant, and clinician time was not measured. The Abstract's 'suggest ... hold promise' is more measured than the Conclusions section.

issues.title: Trial registered 2023-11-16, about 16 months after start (2022-07-01) and after completion; timing not disclosed
issues.explanation: The registry shows the record was first submitted nine months after the study ended, so the outcomes could not have been pre-specified publicly. issues.title: Active flexion gain 28.7 ± 11.2 printed as both % and mm; passive sentence says mm but gives %

issues.title: Fall-prevention claim rests on a static index (OSI EO, R=0.533); fall-risk index effect (R=0.354) was moderate
issues.explanation: The Discussion calls the between-group FRI 6-2 effect moderate and says only OSI EO shows a large effect. It then concludes that resistance training is 'effective in preventing falls' on the basis of 'the large effect size'. OSI EO is a static platform stability measure, not a fall-risk index, and falls were not recorded, so the fall-prevention conclusion goes beyond the data. The Conclusions also say fall risk fell 'in both intervention groups', which is a within-group result. The between-group FRI 6-2 comparison is significant only at p=0.0418 and has the weaker effect size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prospectively recorded fall incidence, or a between-group FRI result with a large effect size.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's own Discussion rests its fall-prevention conclusion on OSI EO, a static eyes-open stability index (R = 0.533). It describes the effect on the dynamic fall-risk index FRI 6-2 (R = 0.354) as moderate. No falls were measured, so 'effective in preventing falls' is an inference from a posturographic index. The authors do note that static tests are incomplete, but they still draw the conclusion from the static index.

issues.title: Roughly 15 between-group tests at uncorrected alpha 0.05; QoL findings at p=0.028 and 0.040 drive conclusions
issues.explanation: The paper tests nine stability indices and six QoL scores (four domains plus two single items), plus sex-specific within- and between-group comparisons, all at an unadjusted alpha of 0.05, and names no primary outcome. Several headline findings sit close to the threshold (FRI 6-2 p=0.0418, DOM3 p=0.0403, DOM2 p=0.0282). They would not survive even a modest correction. The abstract conclusion of benefit to postural stability and psychological well-being rests on this selected subset.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary outcome, or a stated multiplicity correction under which the main findings remain significant.
