social relationship domain (DOM3) (Z = 2.051, p < 0.0403, R = 0.361)

second_reader.what_stands: About 14 increment comparisons are tested at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05, plus further sex-stratified and within-group tests. The psychological (p = 0.028) and social (p = 0.040) domain findings would not survive a Bonferroni or Holm correction. The QoL conclusion about psychological well-being rests on them. The general-health item Q2 (p = 0.0009) would survive correction, and no multiplicity limitation is mentioned.

issues.title: Only adherent intervention participants analysed; no ITT analysis or flow diagram (46 analysed of 51 randomised)
issues.explanation: The analysis includes only participants who finished pre- and post-testing, and intervention participants must also have missed no more than three sessions. Dropouts (2 intervention, 3 control) are not analysed, and the number excluded for missing sessions is not stated. A per-protocol set in an open exercise trial can favour the intervention. With modest attrition the likely bias is small, but the result is not an intention-to-treat estimate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow showing all randomised participants analysed, or a sensitivity analysis including those with more than three missed sessions and dropouts.

issues.title: QoL gains in an unblinded trial with a usual-activity control; no attention control
issues.explanation: Participants in the intervention group received twice-weekly supervised group sessions, whereas controls only continued usual activity. The psychological, social and general-health differences are self-reported and could reflect expectation or group contact. The Discussion itself credits the group format for social benefits. The Conclusions also credit 'a longer period' of exercise, though the programme lasted 8 weeks. The QoL conclusion should be tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control or blinded or objective QoL-related outcomes showing the same pattern.

issues.explanation: The registry lists dynamic muscle strength and balance assessments as primary outcomes, with only one secondary outcome. This paper reports balance indices and WHOQOL-BREF scores and no strength outcome, and says that other data from the same group appeared elsewhere. issues.title: Safety claim and standard-care recommendation without adverse-event reporting (n=46, 8 weeks)
issues.explanation: The abstract presents the protocol as 'safe' and the Conclusions recommend including it in the standard management of seniors with post-COVID-19 symptoms. The paper reports no adverse-event data except two dropouts for pain, and the Limitations section acknowledges that symptoms were not systematically tracked. The data are from one site, a small sample and a short follow-up with a higher-functioning group, so they support a feasibility signal and not a standard-care recommendation. (The fall-prevention part of this concern is under c1.)
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Systematic adverse-event data showing no excess events, and replication in a larger multi-site trial.

10.3390/jcm13185563.overall: The finding that symptom scores were lower at discharge is plausible, but this uncontrolled, unblinded, self-rated before-after series cannot show that the resort treatment caused it or that it should enter standard care. The conclusion is therefore tentative at best. Several reporting slips (Table 5 dyspnoea rows, the 67% figure, the sex-difference wording, duration percentages) do not change the main direction but reduce confidence in the tables.

primary_outcome.name: mMRC dyspnoea scale change (pre- vs post-treatment)

issues.title: Efficacy and routine-use recommendation drawn from an uncontrolled, open, self-rated before-after series
issues.explanation: All 122 patients received the same programme and were compared only with their own admission scores. The scores were self-rated and unblinded, and measurement stopped at discharge with no follow-up. Natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectation and the general effect of an inpatient stay all fit the observed falls. The conclusion that the treatment is effective and should be added to standard care therefore goes beyond what this design can show. It can only show that symptoms were lower at discharge.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or usual-care comparison group, or blinded objective outcomes with follow-up.

quotes.text: The cardiopulmonary symptoms of long COVID were assessed twice: before and after health resort treatment.
so it should be implemented into the standard treatment course for COVID-19 survivors as a continuation of therapy.
Firstly, the assessment of symptom severity was subjective.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy conclusion and the routine-use recommendation rest on an uncontrolled, open, self-rated before-after series of 122 completers from a single resort, with no comparator, no blinding, and discharge tied to confirmed improvement. The limitations section acknowledges subjectivity and comorbidity but not the lack of a control group or natural recovery, and the Abstract and Conclusions still say 'effectively mitigates' and 'should be implemented into the standard treatment course'. The Discussion's call for a future clinical trial partly tempers this, but not in the headline claims.

issues.title: 28 of 150 eligible patients (18.7%) excluded for incomplete data; completers-only, no comparison
issues.explanation: Of 150 patients eligible by the exclusion criteria, 28 were dropped for incomplete data, leaving 122. The paper does not say what was missing (admission or discharge scores) or whether those patients differed. Records missing discharge scores may come from patients who left early or did not improve, which would favour the treatment. The screen's 49% figure is not attrition; the 89 criteria exclusions are a normal screening step.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison of the 28 excluded with the 122 analysed showing similar baseline severity and course, or reasons unrelated to outcome.

quotes.text: An additional 28 participants were excluded from the analysis because of incomplete data to mitigate the risk of sampling bias.

issues.title: Subgroup efficacy claims rest on significant vs non-significant within-group p-values, with no correction
issues.explanation: The paper says palpitations improved 'only in women' (p = 0.03) versus men (p = 0.62), and that treatment was 'least effective' at 60-69 years because fewer symptoms reached p < 0.05. A difference in significance is not evidence that effects differ, and the sex comparison for this item was not tested directly. The Abstract's 'Age does not mediate the efficacy' rests on non-significant tests in groups of about 40 (ΔmMRC 1.00 vs 0.64 vs 0.91, p = 0.11). Dozens of unadjusted tests were run, so isolated p-values of 0.02-0.04 are weak.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Formal interaction tests with adequate power, or multiplicity-adjusted subgroup results.

quotes.text: palpitations decreased significantly after health resort treatment only in women (68% diminishment)
Age does not mediate the efficacy of health resort treatment.

issues.title: Table 5 dyspnoea-at-rest age-group means (weighted 1.37 / 0.52) cannot match Table 3 overall (1.11 / 0.31)
issues.explanation: A pooled mean must lie between its subgroup means, but Table 3 gives an overall baseline of 1.11, below all three age-group means (1.23 to 1.49). The sex and treatment-strategy splits reproduce 1.11 (and 0.31 after treatment). The age-group rows instead weight to 1.37 and 0.52, which are the overall mMRC means printed in the text. The Table 5 dyspnoea-at-rest block seems to hold the wrong variable or wrong values, so that block cannot be relied on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 5 whose weighted means equal 1.11 and 0.31, or a statement that those rows are a different measure.

quotes.location: Table 5, Dyspnoea at Rest, Group II, before
Table 5, Dyspnoea at Rest, Group I, before

issues.title: Abstract says symptoms do not differ by sex; mMRC was higher in women at admission (p = 0.007)
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Conclusions say persisting symptoms are independent of gender. The Results show significantly higher baseline mMRC in women (p = 0.007), with severe dyspnoea in 54.9% of women against 27.5% of men, and a larger ΔmMRC in women (p = 0.03). The claim holds for the 0-10 symptom items but not for the dyspnoea measure the paper emphasises. The statement is too broad.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Abstract wording restricted to the 0-10 symptom items, with the mMRC difference stated.

quotes.text: Persisting COVID-19 symptoms do not differentiate between women and men.
In women, the mMRC scale scores were statistically higher compared to men during the measurement performed at admission ( p = 0.007).

issues.title: Text says palpitations unchanged in both groups; Table 6 shows Group A p = 0.04 (0.25 to 0.09)
issues.explanation: The Results say heart palpitations remained unchanged in both treatment-strategy groups. Table 6 reports a significant pre-to-post fall in Group A (p = 0.04). Only Group B (p = 0.37) is non-significant, so the text misdescribes the table. This is a minor reporting slip, and the Group A result is in the direction of benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 6 showing Group A palpitations p above 0.05.

quotes.text: In both groups, heart palpitations remained unchanged after the health resort treatment.

issues.title: Text gives 67% fall in dyspnoea at rest; Table 3 means 1.11 to 0.31 imply 72%
issues.explanation: The Results report that dyspnoea at rest fell by about 67%. The Table 3 means give a fall of about 72%. The other symptoms in the same paragraph (sputum, cough, chest pain, tightness, exercise dyspnoea) match their Table 3 means, so this one is an isolated discrepancy. The treatment effect for this symptom is slightly understated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alternative computation (e.g. mean of individual percentage changes) that yields 67%.

quotes.text: Dyspnoea at rest diminished by about 67%

issues.title: Discussion prevalences 15.53% (chest pain) and 31.25% (chest tightness) unattainable with n = 122
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives two symptom prevalences as shares of the 122 participants. Neither can be produced by a whole number of participants out of 122. The likely cause is a typing slip or a different denominator. Only the comparison with other studies is affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different, stated denominator for these prevalences.

quotes.text: In the study group, 15.53% of participants declared chest pain to be present
31.25% of participants declared chest tightness severity ≥ 1 point during pre-treatment measurement

issues.title: Treatment-duration shares 3.28%, 54.92% and 44.8% sum to 103%, not 100%
issues.explanation: The three exhaustive categories (shorter than 21 days, exactly 21 days, longer than 21 days) sum to 103%. Replacing 44.8% with 41.8% gives 100% and matches 51/122. This is a cosmetic slip with no bearing on the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A fourth duration category that is not mentioned.

quotes.text: The most frequently health resort treatment lasted 21 days (54.92% of participants).
In 3.28% of participants, it was shorter than 21 days, while in 44.8% of patients, it was longer.

issues.title: Methods describe a five-point mMRC but give its top anchor as 'ten'; Results use 0-4
issues.explanation: The Methods call the mMRC a five-point scale, then define its endpoints as zero and ten. The Results score it from 0 to 4. The 'ten' appears to be carried over from the 0-10 symptom scale. This does not change any result, but the scale definition is wrong as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a 0-10 mMRC variant was actually used.

quotes.text: Zero means 'dyspnea during intensive effort', and ten means 'inability to wear and leave home because of dyspnea'
participants assessed their dyspnoea with an mMRC scale from 0 to 4 points

10.3390/jcm13185590.headline_claim: Exercise training was safe, increased cardiorespiratory fitness, and substantially improved patient-reported outcomes (mental health, well-being, depression, symptoms) in long COVID, without adverse immunologic effects.
10.3390/jcm13185590.overall: The headline claim of benefit and safety from exercise training rests on an uncontrolled, open-label pre-post study of 14 completers, with many uncorrected tests and retrospective registration, so it supports feasibility and an association with improvement but not the causal efficacy the Conclusions assert. Table 2 has several printing errors, mainly wrong % changes for peak VO2 and work rate (which understate the gains), an implausible p for % predicted VO2, and inconsistent activity-monitor change columns. The raw changes in the main CPET outcomes appear internally consistent.

primary_outcome.name: Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) change after 10-week aerobic training

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in aerobic capacity (Peak Oxygen Uptake) at 10 weeks after rehabilitation comprehensive (normal intensity) pulmonary rehabilitation program.

issues.title: Uncontrolled open-label 14-person pilot concludes hypothesis 'affirmed', training 'substantially improved' outcomes and 'appears safe'
issues.explanation: All results are before-after changes in the same 14 completers, with no control group and unblinded self-reported outcomes. The Conclusions nonetheless state that the hypothesis was affirmed and that training substantially improved mental health and well-being. Safety is judged on those who passed screening and started training, with no powered safety estimate. The data fit 'associated with improvement' and 'feasible', not a causal efficacy claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or wording limited to association in a feasibility pilot.

quotes.text: Our hypothesis that LC patients would benefit from a comprehensive moderate aerobic endurance exercise training program prescribed using a baseline CPET was affirmed.
no control group (subjects were their own control pre/post training)
Exercise training substantially improved patient-reported outcomes of mental health, well-being, and symptoms of depression

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is a single-arm, uncontrolled, unblinded pilot (registry: allocation NA, masking NONE) with 14 completers of 21 consented, no multiplicity correction and no sample-size calculation, yet its Conclusions say the hypothesis was 'affirmed', that training 'substantially improved' mental-health, well-being and depression outcomes, and that training 'appears safe'. The limitations section discloses the lack of a control group, but the efficacy wording is stronger than a pre/post design can support. The 'appears safe' claim is hedged with screening and flexible-dosing conditions, and the imp

issues.title: Dozens of outcomes tested at uncorrected p < 0.05; several reported 'improvements' have p between 0.010 and 0.030
issues.explanation: The paper tests CPET, activity, questionnaire, immune cell and cytokine outcomes, all at p < 0.05, without correction or a designated primary outcome. The strongest questionnaire findings are robust. The fitness results (p = 0.017, 0.030) and several secondary improvements (mMRC, MMSE, PCFS, general health) sit in the range where a correction would remove significance. The paper's confident wording does not reflect this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A designated primary outcome and a stated adjustment for the secondary tests.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was accepted at
As this was a pilot study, no formal a priori sample size calculation was performed.

issues.title: Table 2 peak VO2 % predicted: change 6 ± 1.0 (n = 14) printed with p = 0.815
issues.explanation: A mean change of 6 with SD 1.0 in 14 participants gives t of about 22 and p far below 0.001, not 0.815. The row's change and p cannot both be right. The mL/kg/min row, with a similar relative change, has p = 0.030. This likely understates the significance of the predicted-VO2 improvement, or the SD is misprinted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The correct SD of change and p from the raw data.

quotes.location: Table 2, Peak Oxygen Uptake, % Predicted row

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.815, but recomputed from the printed t = 22.5 p is at most 8.797e-12, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Table 2 % change for peak VO2 (7.4%, 7.4%) and work rate (10.3%) disagree with its own pre/post values and the text
issues.explanation: The primary-outcome rows of Table 2 print % changes that do not follow from the printed pre and post means. L/min: 0.15 on 1.88 is 8.0%, but the table says 7.4% and the text says 7.9%. mL/kg/min: 1.6 on 19.3 is about 8%, but the table says 7.4% (the same figure as the row above). Work rate: 16 on 139 is 11.5%, matching the text, but the table says 10.3%. The absolute changes and p-values are consistent, so the table understates the improvement in the headline outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition of % change (e.g. mean of individual percentage changes) with individual data reproducing 7.4% and 10.3%.

quotes.text: increasing by a mean of 150 ± 200 mL/min (7.9% increase

quotes.location: Table 2, Peak Oxygen Uptake, L/min row

issues.title: PEM-affected sessions given as 3 of 30 in Results but 3 of 20 in Discussion; programme had 20 sessions
issues.explanation: Results report lingering fatigue in an average of 3 sessions out of 30, while the Discussion says 3 of the 20 training sessions. The programme was 10 weeks x 2 sessions per week, so 30 sessions did not exist. The rate of symptom flare-ups is a safety figure, and the two versions differ by 50% (10% vs 15%).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that participants had 30 scheduled sessions.

quotes.text: this occurred an average of 3 sessions out of 30 (range 0–7)
PESE/PEM on average in 3 of the 20 training sessions per participant

issues.title: mMRC: text reports an MCID reduction, Table 3 labels it 'Below MCID' (median 2 to 0.5, MCID 1 unit)
issues.explanation: The text says there was an MCID reduction in mMRC. Table 3 labels the same change 'Below MCID' although the median fell by 1.5 against a 1-unit MCID. One of the two statements is wrong; the numbers favour the text. It is a labelling slip in a secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level change data showing the median individual change was under 1 unit.

quotes.text: There was an MCID reduction in the mMRC dyspnea score after exercise training
mMRC (Lower is Better) 2 1 0.5 2 Below MCID 1 unit

issues.title: Exercise intolerance 6 of 14 printed as 46%; 6/14 = 42.9%
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives 6 of 14 completers with exercise intolerance as the primary symptom and prints 46%. Six of 14 is 42.9%. The other rows in that column use the correct denominator of 14. It is a minor descriptive slip.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a different denominator applied to this row.

quotes.text: Exercise Intolerance 6 46 4 57

script.explanation: 6/14 = 42.86%, but the paper prints 46, outside the rounding interval [45.50, 47.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 13.0 rather than 14.

issues.title: Medical referrals 5 of 21 stated as 25%; 5/21 = 23.8%
issues.explanation: The Discussion says screening identified 5 of 21 patients (25%) needing medical referral. Five of 21 is 23.8%. The error is small and does not affect the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator of 20.

quotes.text: identified 5 of 21 patients (25%)

script.explanation: 5/21 = 23.81%, but the paper prints 25, outside the rounding interval [24.50, 26.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 20.0 rather than 21.

issues.title: Registered 2022-05-10, about 3 months after the 2022-02-02 start; no primary outcome designated in the paper
issues.explanation: The registry shows the trial was registered after enrolment began. The paper cites the NCT number without noting this, and does not designate a primary outcome. Outcome selection therefore cannot be checked against a pre-enrolment record. The registered primary outcome (peak VO2) is the one the paper reports first, which limits the concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing a pre-enrolment submission.

quotes.text: ClinicalTrials.Gov Identifier: NCT05398692
This was a single-center, pilot clinical trial conducted between February 2022 and December 2023.

issues.title: Table 2 activity-monitor change columns do not follow from pre/post values (sign flips, 0:18 vs 0:15)
issues.explanation: Several activity rows are internally inconsistent. Sedentary time rises from 18:16 to 18:29 (+0:13) but the change is printed as -0:04 (-0.2%). Total energy expenditure rises 2758 to 2772 (+14, about +0.5%) yet the % change is -1.2%. Moderate activity falls 1:09 to 1:03 (-0:06) but is printed -0:03. Vigorous activity goes 0:10 to 0:25 (+0:15) but is printed 0:18. Missing wear-time data may explain some of this, but the table does not say so. All these outcomes were non-significant, so the conclusions are barely affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that rows used different valid-data subsets, with n per row.

quotes.text: Sedentary Time (hours/minutes) 18:16 3:06 18:29

quotes.location: Table 2, Total Estimated Energy Expenditure row

issues.title: Baseline peak Borg values swapped: text dyspnoea 5.9 / legs 6.0, Table 2 dyspnoea 6.0 / legs 5.9
issues.explanation: The Results text gives baseline peak RPE-dyspnoea as 5.9 and RPE-legs as 6.0. Table 2 gives dyspnoea 6.0 and legs 5.9. The difference is 0.1 on a 0-10 scale in a non-significant outcome, so nothing depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the table and text columns are labelled differently.

quotes.text: 5.9 ± 2.3 and RPE
Peak RPE1dyspnea 6.0 2.3 5.4 2.0

10.3390/jcm13195817.headline_claim: A proportion of long COVID patients develop persistent long COVID consistent with a long-term condition, with significant overlap with ME/CFS, in patients discharged from a specialist community service.
10.3390/jcm13195817.overall: The descriptive finding that most responding patients remained symptomatic and had low EQ-5D scores is plausible as printed, but it comes from a 24% self-selected, uncontrolled sample and applies only to responders. Causal statements that the service was effective or stabilises patients, and the 'significant' changes without any tests, are not supported, and the post-discharge EQ-5D comparison is misstated in the text.

primary_outcome.name: Not identified; outcomes are descriptive PROM status at follow-up (EQ-5D-5L index, C19-YRSm, NICE ME/CFS criteria)

issues.title: Uncontrolled pre-post cohort used to claim the service was effective and stabilises the condition
issues.explanation: All data come from one uncontrolled cohort with no comparison group. The Discussion asserts that interventions 'were effective' and that the service stabilises the condition and avoids deterioration. Improvement from entry to discharge could reflect natural recovery or regression to the mean, and the post-discharge decline cannot be attributed to loss of service input. The causal language exceeds what the design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A matched or historical comparison group showing different trajectories.

quotes.text: This demonstrates that targeted interventions used within the LLCRS were effective in reducing symptom burden and improving the functional levels of individuals who engaged with clinicians.
This highlights the value of the service in stabilising the long-term condition

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is an uncontrolled before-after cohort of self-selected responders, yet the Discussion states the data 'demonstrate' the interventions 'were effective' and that the service stabilises the condition, which is a causal claim the design cannot support. The post-discharge data (EQ-5D index back to 0.53 vs initial 0.52) actually show the discharge gain was lost on average, so the 'stabilising' interpretation is not supported by a comparison of any kind.

issues.title: 24% response (112/460) from selected discharged patients; headline prevalence applies only to responders
issues.explanation: Only 112 of 460 eligible patients (24%) were analysed, from 2124 discharged, and the authors acknowledge responders are likely those still struggling. The 90.2% persistent-symptom figure and the 'long-term condition in the majority' conclusion therefore cannot be generalised to discharged patients, and the abstract wording is qualified only by 'who responded'. The caveat is disclosed, so this is a weakening of the main claim rather than an error in the numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Non-responder data showing similar outcomes to responders.

quotes.text: As this is a self-selected sample (24% response rate), it is likely that those patients who are still struggling with PLC have responded.
Out of 460 patients contacted, 112 (average of 37.6 months since infection and 9.8 months post-discharge) completed the PROMs.

second_reader.what_stands: The 90.2% (101/112) persistent-symptom figure and the 43% ME/CFS figure come from a 24.3% (112/460) responder subset drawn from a further selected group (460 of 2124 discharged), so they describe responders only and cannot be read as the proportion of discharged patients with persistent LC; the abstract's wording 'patients who responded' is appropriately limited. The limitation is acknowledged, but the Discussion and conclusion still extend the finding to 'the majority of patients' treated in a specialist service.

issues.title: Text says follow-up EQ-5D-5L fell 0.12 below initial score; Table 2 shows 0.53 vs 0.52 (0.01 higher)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says post-discharge EQ-5D-5L dropped below initial scores by 0.12. Table 2 gives 0.52 initial and 0.53 post-discharge, so follow-up is marginally above entry. The 0.12 matches the fall from discharge (0.65) to follow-up (0.53), so the comparator is misstated. This exaggerates the framing of deterioration relative to baseline, though the drop from discharge is real as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 0.12 refers to a different comparison explicitly stated, or that Table 2 initial value is misprinted.

quotes.text: Average EQ-5D-5L index scores after discharge dropped below initial EQ-5D-5L index scores by 0.12

issues.title: 'Significant' changes asserted without tests; 13 to 15.1 rise is below the stated MCID of 4
issues.explanation: No paired tests, confidence intervals or p-values are reported for any change over time, yet changes are called significant. For some statements the authors rely on MCID, but the symptom-severity rise from 13 to 15.1 (2.1 points) is under their own MCID of 4 and is still called significant. Also, different respondents may contribute to different time points, so means at each time point may not be directly comparable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported paired tests, or a statement that 'significant' denotes only a clinical threshold met.

quotes.text: average symptom severity increasing significantly from 13 to 15.1 after discharge
The Minimal Clinical Important Difference (MCID) has been estimated to be 4 points for the Symptom Severity subscale

issues.title: Discussion gives 40% with >3 comorbidities; Table 1 count is 40 of 112 = 35.7%
issues.explanation: Table 1 reports 40 participants (35.7%) with more than three significant co-morbidities. The Discussion states 40% for the same quantity, which appears to confuse the count with the percentage. A small reporting error that does not alter conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator (e.g. 100 respondents with data) explicitly stated for the 40%.

quotes.text: with 40% reporting more than three other significant health problems
Co-morbidities (>3) significant co-morbidities4035.7

10.3390/jcm13206237.headline_claim: Adding progressive muscle relaxation to pulmonary rehabilitation significantly enhances mental health outcomes, particularly reducing anxiety and improving sleep quality, in patients with long-term COVID-19 symptoms.
10.3390/jcm13206237.overall: The large post-intervention differences in anxiety, depression, general health and sleep favouring PR plus PMR are probably real in direction, but the self-reported outcomes cannot be blinded and there is no attention control, so the effect attributable to PMR itself is uncertain. Several text-table inconsistencies (lung-function claims, PSQI figures, a male-percentage error) show careless reporting without overturning the main result. The Conclusions and Discussion go beyond the data in claiming fatigue reduction and well-being benefit from a 21-day trial.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated as a single primary outcome; the registry lists lung function, exercise capacity, anxiety, depression, sleep quality and psychological well-being as primary

primary_outcomes.time_frame: At inclusion and at the end of the study

issues.title: Self-reported mental-health outcomes in a trial where participants cannot be unaware of the extra daily PMR sessions
issues.explanation: The headline benefit is measured with self-administered questionnaires (GHQ-12, PHQ-9, GAD-7, PSQI). Group 2 received 20 extra minutes of guided relaxation daily and Group 1 received no attention control, so the claim that participants were unaware of arm is implausible. Expectation, extra contact time and reporting bias could account for part of the large between-group differences, so the effect specific to PMR is uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham or attention-matched control arm, or objective sleep and anxiety measures showing the same effect.

quotes.text: the participants were unaware of whether they were assigned to the PR group or the PR-combined-with-PMR group
is a self-administered instrument used to diagnose major and subthreshold depression

second_reader.what_stands: Participants in the PR+PMR arm necessarily knew they were doing extra daily relaxation sessions, and no sham or attention control is described, so the claim that participants were unaware of allocation is not credible as written. All the mental-health outcomes that show the large between-group differences are self-reported, so they are open to expectation and performance bias that assessor blinding does not remove, and the paper does not discuss this in its limitations or in its conclusion that PMR 'significantly enhances' mental health outcomes. This does not show the effect is absent, only t

issues.title: Abstract says both groups improved lung function at p<0.0001; Table 5 shows Group 2 FVC% p=0.198, FEV1/FVC p=0.922
issues.explanation: The abstract states that both groups improved in lung function with p < 0.0001. Table 5 prints no p-value below <0.001, and two Group 2 lung-function rows are not significant (FVC % p = 0.198; FEV1/FVC p = 0.922). Other rows, such as FVC (L), are only p = 0.001. The abstract therefore overstates the within-group lung-function result, although the secondary physical findings still show broad improvement in the other rows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 5 showing p < 0.0001 for every lung-function row in both groups.

quotes.text: both groups had noteworthy improvements in lung function, exercise capacity, and sleep quality with statistical significance ( p < 0.0001)

issues.title: Conclusions and Discussion claim fatigue reduction and elimination of sleep problems after a 21-day unblinded trial
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the combination 'decreased fatigue' although no fatigue measure is reported, and says PMR 'effectively eliminate[s]' sleep problems. The conclusion recommends PMR as a valuable approach for overall well-being from a 21-day study of 61 people with no follow-up, no adverse-event reporting and no attention control. The limitations paragraph notes short duration but does not temper the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A fatigue scale in the outcome set and longer follow-up data with adverse events.

quotes.text: this combination significantly improved sleep quality and decreased fatigue and anxiety in patients with COVID-19
A 21-day program may not provide a sufficient timeframe to observe the full extent of improvement in symptoms

issues.title: Discussion PSQI figures (median 8.35 -> mean 4.96, drop 4.74) do not match tables; 4.96 is the GAD-7 mean
issues.explanation: The Discussion gives Group 2's PSQI as moving from a median of 8.35 to a mean of 4.96, a reduction of 4.74 points. Tables 5 and 6 give Group 2 PSQI medians of 8 [8; 9] and 4 [3; 4.75], and 4.96 appears only as the GAD-7 mean. The quoted 'clinically relevant' PSQI reduction exceeding the 3-point MCID is thus not traceable to the tables. A similar slip occurs for GHQ-12: the 4.9-point 'reduction' equals the between-group difference (17.06 - 12.16), not a within-group change. The effect is still large on the table values (median 8 to 4), so the main result stands.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary table giving PSQI means of 8.35 and 4.96 for Group 2.

quotes.text: to a mean score of 4.96, indicating no more poor sleep quality
this group went from a median score of 8.35

issues.title: Randomization described two ways (MedCalc block-4 vs online tool); allocation concealment not described
issues.explanation: Section 2.1 reports pre-generated block-of-4 sequences from a statistical package, while Section 2.10 refers to an online randomization tool and allocation 'upon enrollment'. No concealment mechanism is reported, so selection bias cannot be excluded. Baseline tables look reasonably balanced, so this weakens rather than invalidates the comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Trial protocol or registry detail describing central or opaque allocation concealment.

quotes.text: Participants were randomized using MeldCalc with a block size of 4
Werandomly assigned the 61 patients to two groups using the an online randomization tool.

issues.title: Between-group comparison uses post-scores only with no baseline adjustment; lung function has no between-group test
issues.explanation: Table 6 compares post-intervention values only, so differences present at baseline (for example PSQI baseline p = 0.07, GHQ-12 baseline medians differing in IQR) are not accounted for. Lung-function results are given only as pre/post within each arm, yet the abstract headlines them. Within-group significance says nothing about the added value of PMR.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: ANCOVA or change-score between-group analyses showing the same result, plus lung-function between-group tests.

quotes.text: The sleep quality in the patients in the group that performed PMR increased significantly compared to the group that only performed PR.
Comparison of patients' analyzed parameters post-PR for group 1 and post-PR-and-PMR for group 2.

issues.title: Variables declared non-normal are summarised as mean ± SD in some tables and median [IQR] in others
issues.explanation: The Methods say GHQ-12, PHQ-9, GAD-7 and PSQI departed from normality and required non-parametric tests. Table 4 reports baseline PHQ-9 as mean ± SD and Table 6 reports post GHQ-12 and GAD-7 as mean ± SD, while Table 5 gives medians for the same variables. Which test produced each p-value cannot be determined, but the effects are so large that conclusions are unlikely to change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the test used for each variable, with the summary statistics matching it.

quotes.text: the parameters age, FVC, FEV1, GHQ-12, PHQ-9, GAD-7, and PSQI showed a significant departure from normality

issues.title: Discussion claims significant 6MWT gains in both groups, then says no significant functional-capacity change
issues.explanation: The first paragraph of the Discussion says PR alone and PR with PMR both significantly improved 6MWT, and Table 5 supports this (p < 0.001 in each group). A later paragraph says the study showed no significant changes in functional capacity in both groups. The later sentence is probably meant as a between-group statement, but as written it contradicts the data and the earlier text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors clarifying the sentence refers only to the between-group comparison.

quotes.text: This study showed no significant changes in functional capacity in both groups.
led to significant improvements in exercise capacity, evaluated by the 6MWT

issues.title: Group 2 males: 22/31 printed as 74.19%, but 22/31 = 70.97% (74.19% would be 23/31)
issues.explanation: Results and Table 4 give 22 of 31 Group 2 participants as male, 74.19%. 22/31 is 70.97%; 74.19% corresponds to 23/31. Either the count or the percentage is wrong, a small baseline error that does not affect the outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 23 men in Group 2.

quotes.text: Of the total of 31 subjects from group 2, 22 (74.19%) were male.

script.explanation: 22/31 = 70.97%, but the paper prints 74.19, outside the rounding interval [74.19, 74.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 29.7 rather than 31.

10.3390/jcm14010174.headline_claim: Eight weeks of moderate-intensity resistance training is not a sufficient stimulus to improve body mass and body composition in post-COVID-19 elderly adults, and BIA may serve as a viable alternative to DXA for measuring longitudinal body composition change.
10.3390/jcm14010174.overall: The null finding on body composition is plausible but is overstated as proof that the programme is insufficient, since the study is small and reports no intervals or equivalence tests. The claim that BIA is a viable DXA alternative for change is weakly supported, because the paper itself reports a significant BM-change discrepancy and wide baseline disagreement. Small BIA table inconsistencies and an unflagged departure from the registered primary outcomes further reduce confidence.

primary_outcome.name: Body mass and body composition by DXA and BIA (BM, FM, %FAT, FFM, BMI), group x session interaction

primary_outcomes.measure: Muscle strength under dynamic conditions first
Muscle strength under dynamic conditions second

issues.title: BIA declared a viable DXA alternative for change despite a significant BM-change difference and no equivalence test
issues.explanation: The Results report that BIA and DXA body-mass changes differed significantly in the intervention group (p = 0.0093). The abstract and conclusion nonetheless recommend BIA for longitudinal change, based on non-significant FM and FFM comparisons. A non-significant Wilcoxon test in small groups does not show agreement. The same paper finds wide baseline limits of agreement (FM -3.20 to 9.63 kg) and does not assess agreement of changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence analysis or agreement analysis of change scores showing differences within a clinically justified margin.

quotes.text: BIA recorded a significantly greater difference in BM pre- and post-experiment than DXA in the Intervention Group ( p < 0.01).
We also conclude that BIA may serve as a viable alternative to DXA for measuring longitudinal changes in body composition in elderly people.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports a significant BIA-DXA difference in BM change (p = 0.0093) in the Intervention group and still concludes BIA is a viable alternative for longitudinal change, using non-significant FM/FFM comparisons without any equivalence test or margin. What is narrower: the supporting evidence the authors cite is specifically FM and FFM, the BM discrepancy is small (about 0.3 kg), and the Results text does disclose it; but the Conclusions and Abstract do not mention or qualify it, and the Discussion does not reconcile it.

issues.title: Non-significant ANOVAs (n = 15 vs 26) are stated as training being 'not a sufficient stimulus'
issues.explanation: All group-by-time tests are non-significant, and the authors turn this into a definitive claim that 8 weeks of training is not sufficient. With 41 analysed participants, no confidence intervals and no equivalence testing, the data show only that no effect was detected. The Discussion itself offers alternatives, such as too little frequency or diet, which the study cannot separate. The conclusion is stronger than the design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confidence intervals for group-by-time effects excluding clinically relevant improvements, or a pre-specified equivalence margin.

quotes.text: Based on our results, we conclude that moderate-intensity resistance training lasting 8 weeks (2 × /week; 60 min per session) is not a sufficient stimulus
There were no statistically significant changes in body mass (BM) and body composition measured by DXA and BIA in both Intervention and Control groups (Tables 3 and 4).

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions and title state training 'is not a sufficient stimulus' on the basis of non-significant interaction tests in a small, unbalanced sample (15 vs 26) powered only for a medium effect, with no confidence intervals or equivalence testing, so the data show no detectable effect rather than demonstrate absence of one. The statement is scoped to the specific protocol, and the Discussion offers cautious explanations and limitations, which softens but does not remove the over-reach.

issues.title: BIA body-mass changes in Table 6 (-0.38, -0.81 kg) differ from Table 4 before/after means (-0.42, -0.76 kg)
issues.explanation: Table 4 BIA body-mass means imply changes of -0.42 kg (intervention) and -0.76 kg (control). Table 6 prints -0.38 and -0.81 kg. The DXA deltas reconcile with Table 3, so the discrepancy is specific to BIA. The same pattern appears in BIA fat mass (control -0.39 implied vs -0.41 printed). The gaps are small, but the BIA body-mass delta is the one that carries the reported significant DXA-vs-BIA difference (p = 0.0093).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that some participants lacked a complete pre/post BIA body-mass pair, so that the Table 6 deltas use a smaller n than Table 4.

quotes.location: Table 4, BIA Body mass row, Intervention Before/After
Table 6, ∆ Body mass row, Intervention, BIA
Table 6, ∆ Body mass row, Control, BIA

issues.title: Paper's primary outcome (body composition) is not among the registered primaries (strength, balance)
issues.explanation: The registry lists eight primary outcomes, all strength or balance measures. This paper calls body mass and body composition its primary purpose and does not mention the registered primaries or the change. This is probably a multi-paper trial rather than a hidden switch, but the paper does not say so. A reader cannot tell that the primary here was not pre-specified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version listing body composition as a primary or secondary outcome, or a statement that this paper reports a pre-specified secondary analysis of the trial.

quotes.text: Therefore, the primary purpose of our study was to assess the changes in body mass and body composition of post-COVID-19 elderly adults who participated in an 8-week Resistance Training protocol.
The study protocol was registered on clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05934279).

issues.title: Groups 26 vs 15 with baseline age and body-mass differences; 51 recruited vs 41 analysed unexplained in text
issues.explanation: Table 1 lists 51 recruited participants but only 41 are analysed (about 20% fewer), and the Results text does not say who was lost or from which arm. The arms are unequal (26 intervention, 15 control). Baseline differences in age and body mass are significant in some subgroups, for example women's body mass 65.3 vs 75.9 kg (p = 0.048) and men's age 69.5 vs 76.2 years (p = 0.0205). With a mixed ANOVA and no baseline adjustment, these imbalances could bias the group-by-time estimates in either direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A legible CONSORT diagram reconciling 51 to 41 by arm with reasons, and a sensitivity analysis adjusting for baseline age and body mass.

quotes.text: Total ( n = 51)
The data from the 41 post-COVID-19 elderly adults were analyzed.

10.3390/jcm14020486.headline_claim: Multidisciplinary group telerehabilitation is beneficial for long COVID sufferers, improving health- and pain-related parameters and emotional symptoms after an eight-week programme and at six-month follow-up.
10.3390/jcm14020486.overall: The paper's claim that telerehabilitation is beneficial, including at six months, is not supported by its own between-group results, which were null apart from one anxiety measure at eight weeks, and the waiting list improved on several measures too. The benefit rests on within-group change, an unblinded self-reported design, and a reduced and older waiting-list sample at six months. Several small reporting inconsistencies (N of 24 vs 21, PHQ-9 totals) and a registry mismatch in primary outcomes further weaken confidence.

primary_outcome.name: Pain-related and health-related symptoms, including pain-related ICF categories (paper's stated primary outcomes); no single primary outcome is named in the Methods

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in health-related quality of life measured by Short Form-36
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Investigators expect changes at 6 months follow-up after rehabilitation

primary_outcomes.measure: Changes in heart rate variability during physical tests
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Investigators expect normalisation at 6 months follow-up

issues.title: Conclusion claims benefit over waiting list although between-group comparisons were null on health and pain outcomes
issues.explanation: The authors report no between-group differences in SF-36, pain intensity, pain sites or ICF pain categories at eight weeks or six months; the only significant difference was reduced anxiety risk on HADS at eight weeks. The Discussion nevertheless says SF-36 improved 'to a larger extent compared to the waiting list' and that telerehabilitation 'clearly shows' improvement. The Conclusion states benefit at six months. The waiting list improved on several of the same measures, so the data do not support a confident efficacy conclusion. This also conflicts with the authors' own sentence that no significant group differences were found.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified between-group analysis of change scores showing significant differences favouring telerehabilitation on the primary outcomes.

quotes.text: Our results show that multidisciplinary group telerehabilitation is beneficial for long COVID sufferers and improves health- and pain-related parameters
Telerehabilitation improved health-related quality of life as measured by the SF-36 to a larger extent compared to the waiting list.
Twelve pain-related ICF b-categories were analysed, revealing no differences between the groups after either eight weeks or six months

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion states benefit on health- and pain-related parameters at 8 weeks and 6 months, while the Results report null between-group comparisons for SF-36, pain intensity and the ICF pain categories, with the only between-group signals being HADS anxiety caseness at 8 weeks and one uncorrected pain-site comparison. The Discussion's opening acknowledges the null between-group findings, but the Conclusion and the sentence 'improved ... to a larger extent compared to the waiting list' are not supported by the between-group results presented.

issues.title: Benefit inferred from within-arm paired tests; between-group tests use absolute values with no baseline adjustment
issues.explanation: Cohen's d and significance are derived from paired pre-post tests within each arm. The between-group comparison is a one-way ANOVA on absolute values. No analysis of change scores or baseline-adjusted comparison is reported, even though baseline pain differed numerically (4.6 vs 3.9) and the waiting list improved on several SF-36 domains and HADS depression. Within-arm improvement in a self-reported, unblinded trial cannot separate treatment effect from spontaneous recovery, regression to the mean or expectancy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A change-score or baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA/mixed model) group-by-time analysis showing a significant intervention effect.

quotes.text: For health-related parameters, absolute values for SF-36 were analysed with no differences between the groups (one-way ANOVA).
Participants on the waiting list showed significant improvements in physical functioning, social functioning, and mental health

second_reader.what_stands: Between-group SF-36 comparisons used absolute values by one-way ANOVA with no baseline adjustment shown, and the effect sizes cited as evidence of benefit are within-arm paired values; the waiting list also improved significantly on several subscales. The paper does not report a between-group, baseline-adjusted or group-by-time estimate, so within-arm change is carrying the inference of benefit.

issues.title: Six-month comparison rests on 60 vs 21 participants (81 of 109), unplanned subset and older waiting list
issues.explanation: Six-month data exist for 81 of 109 participants, with waiting-list data from only 21 of 42, because of a change in protocol after recruitment. The six-month waiting-list subset was on average 7 years older than the telerehabilitation group (3 years at eight weeks) and the paper reports this only as 'results not presented'. No analysis addresses the missing data. The claim that effects 'last at six months' therefore rests on an unbalanced, non-randomly reduced control group, and the authors' limitations also mention possible waiting-list drop-out to other treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline characteristics and outcome data showing the six-month waiting-list subset is comparable to the full randomised waiting list, or a sensitivity analysis handling the missing data.

quotes.text: This resulted in a lesser amount of data for the waiting list at the six-month follow-up.
participants on the waiting list were 3 and 7 years older than the telerehabilitation group at the eight-week and six-month follow-up, respectively

second_reader.what_stands: The six-month between-group comparison rests on 60 TR versus 21 WL participants (81 of 109), where the WL data come from a single later group after an ethics amendment rather than the planned design, and the WL was older by 7 years in that subset, with age results not presented. The reason is disclosed and acknowledged as a limitation, but the subset is far below the planned size (about 21 vs 63 per group) and the paper gives 24 rather than 21 for the WL in the Section 3.5 model without explanation.

issues.title: Paper's primary outcomes (pain, ICF pain categories) differ from registered primaries (SF-36, heart rate variability)
issues.explanation: The registry lists SF-36 change at six months and heart rate variability as the primary outcomes, with only two secondary outcomes. The paper names pain-related symptoms and ICF pain categories as primary, powers the study for pain intensity, treats anxiety and depression as secondary, and does not report heart rate variability. Without earlier registry versions or an explanation, it is unclear whether the primary outcomes were changed or which outcomes were prespecified, which matters because the pain outcomes were null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registry versions or the published protocol listing pain intensity and ICF pain categories as primary outcomes, with an explanation for omitting heart rate variability.

quotes.text: Primary outcomes were health- and pain-related symptoms, including ICF categories related to pain.

issues.title: Table 1 PHQ-9 six-month: arms 26 + 10 = 36 but 'All' row prints 33
issues.explanation: The two arms are mutually exclusive and make up the whole sample, yet their counts sum to 36 while the All row says 33. The waiting-list percentage (10 = 50%) implies a denominator of 20, not the 21 used elsewhere, and 33 (43%) implies a denominator of about 77, not 81. The PHQ-9 six-month row is therefore internally inconsistent, though the pathological-score counts are secondary data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table footnote showing that the All row excludes participants with incomplete PHQ-9 data, or a corrected row.

quotes.location: Table 1, PHQ-9 All row, After Six Months
Table 1, PHQ-9 Waiting list row, After Six Months

issues.title: Waiting-list six-month N is 24 in the GLM gender analysis but 21 elsewhere (Fig 3, pain paired test, Table 1)
issues.explanation: The three-time-point GLM reports N = 60 and 24 for telerehabilitation and waiting list. Everywhere else the six-month waiting-list sample is 21 (pain paired test, Figure 3 caption, Table 1 total of 81). The GLM sample size therefore cannot be reconciled with the rest of the paper, so it is unclear which participants entered that model. This affects only the secondary gender/age analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the GLM drew on three extra waiting-list participants with six-month data not counted elsewhere, or a correction of 24 to 21.

quotes.text: Results showed gender having an impact on pain intensity (N = 60 and 24, F = 8.1
For the six-month follow-up, n = 60 for telerehabilitation group (TR) and n = 21 for the waiting list (WL).

issues.title: Discussion says only HADS depression improved on the waiting list, but PHQ-9 also improved at six months (d = 0.6)
issues.explanation: The Results report a significant six-month waiting-list improvement on PHQ-9, another depression measure. The Discussion says only HADS depression improved. The sentence is therefore not accurate as worded, though it is a small summary slip. It also means spontaneous improvement in the control arm was somewhat larger than the Discussion conveys.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 'only' referred to the HADS instrument alone, excluding PHQ-9.

quotes.text: Among those on the waiting list, only depression scores measured using HADS improved after eight weeks and six months
while the waiting list showed improvements when followed up after six months, with a Cohen’s d effect size of 0.6

10.3390/jcm14041391.headline_claim: A trend towards improvement in fatigue was observed in patients with long COVID or PCC who were prescribed hochuekkito, indicating a potential benefit of hochuekkito for general fatigue in such patients.
10.3390/jcm14041391.overall: The headline claim of a potential benefit of hochuekkito rests on a 4.7-point within-group FAS decrease in 13 of 20 patients with no control, 35% missing primary data and a CI (0.5 to 8.9) whose lower bound is below the 4-point MCID. It can support only a hypothesis-generating signal, not benefit attributable to the drug. The two table inconsistencies are minor reporting errors.

primary_outcome.name: Japanese version of the Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) score at 8 weeks, change from baseline

issues.title: Single-arm before-after design cannot separate hochuekkito effect from natural recovery
issues.explanation: The only efficacy evidence is the change from baseline to 8 weeks in one uncontrolled arm. The authors themselves note long COVID fatigue improves over time. Without a comparator, regression to the mean and natural recovery cannot be separated from any drug effect, so the benefit conclusion is tentative at best. The pilot label reduces but does not remove this issue because the abstract and conclusions still imply benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control arm showing less improvement.

quotes.text: The aim of this single-arm pilot study was to confirm observable improvements in fatigue symptoms
some patients may have experienced a natural improvement in fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: A single-arm before-after design cannot separate a hochuekkito effect from natural recovery, and the paper has no control or counterfactual estimate. The authors acknowledge this in Limitations and call for a randomized trial. Yet the Conclusions still speak of a 'potential benefit of hochuekkito', which is only partly tempered by the disclosure.

issues.title: 7 of 20 enrolled (35%) lack week-8 FAS and the primary estimate is complete-case only
issues.explanation: Thirteen of 20 patients contribute to the primary outcome, and the other seven are excluded with no imputation or sensitivity analysis. The authors note one dropout improved, which would bias toward underestimation, but the direction of bias for the others is unknown. The lower CI bound is 0.5, so modest bias could remove the signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (e.g., multiple imputation) giving a similar estimate.

quotes.text: Seven subjects with missing baseline or week 8 data were excluded.
Subjects with missing values at the baseline and at week 8 were excluded from the analysis

second_reader.what_stands: 7 of 20 enrolled patients (35%) are excluded for missing data and the primary estimate is complete-case only, with no imputation or sensitivity analysis. The loss is disclosed, and the authors argue it may cause underestimation. They give no evidence for that direction, and the missingness could also run the other way. The 'FAS' here is the Fatigue Assessment Scale, not a full analysis set. Strictly, the missing data are at week 8 rather than baseline.

issues.title: Conclusions credit hochuekkito and call 4.7 'improvement' though CI lower bound 0.5 is below the 4-point MCID
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusions state a potential benefit of hochuekkito from an uncontrolled change. The Discussion says the 4.7 decrease 'indicated improvement' because it exceeds the 4-point MCID, yet the CI runs from 0.5 to 8.9 and includes changes far below the MCID. Combined with the sample (13), the evidence supports only a hypothesis-generating signal. Also covers the Kampo qi-deficiency and 'appropriately indicated' statements that no result in the paper tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison showing a benefit exceeding the MCID.

quotes.text: indicating a potential benefit of hochuekkito for general fatigue in such patients.
This indicated improvement of general fatigue in the clinical setting.
for which hochuekkito is appropriately indicated.

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion says the 4.7 decrease 'indicated improvement of general fatigue in the clinical setting' without noting that the lower CI bound of 0.5 is far below the 4-point MCID, so clinically meaningful improvement is not established. The Abstract and Conclusions use hedged terms ('trend', 'potential benefit'), but the benefit is still attributed to hochuekkito despite no control group. The claim that hochuekkito is 'appropriately indicated' for qi deficiency is not tested by the data.

issues.title: Limitations report nine males among 13 analysed, but Table 2 has only eight males among all 20
issues.explanation: The Limitations describe an unbalanced gender distribution of nine males and four females. Table 2 and the Results show 8 males and 12 females among all 20 enrolled, so nine males is impossible in any subset. The error does not affect the primary result but undermines the confounding argument made there.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Table S1 showing 9 or more males, which would mean Table 2 is wrong.

quotes.text: unbalanced gender distribution (nine males and four females)

issues.title: Disease-duration categories in Table 2 sum to 18, not 20
issues.explanation: The four duration categories print counts of 1, 6, 2 and 9, totalling 18 against the table's n = 20. No missing category or footnote accounts for two participants. This is a minor reporting gap on a covariate not used in the primary analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note or Table S1 showing two participants with missing duration data.

quotes.text: Number (%) n = 20
More than 3 months

issues.title: No registry entry reported for this prospective study; only a future RCT is cited
issues.explanation: The study is described as prospective observational but no registration identifier is given, so the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be compared with a prior version. The primary endpoint is clearly stated in the methods, and exploratory observational pilots are often unregistered.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier for this study dated before enrolment.

quotes.text: was conducted as a prospective observational study
There is a plan to conduct a randomized controlled trial for these two groups [45].

10.3390/jcm14113802.headline_claim: Among seven ME/CFS patients with elevated GPCR autoantibodies, higher β2-adrenergic and M3-muscarinic receptor antibody concentrations are associated with worse EQ-5D-5L quality of life, supporting a potential pathophysiological role and PE+IVIG as a direction for future trials.
10.3390/jcm14113802.overall: The headline association between β2/M3 autoantibodies and EQ-5D-5L rests on seven patients, imputed data and results that did not survive Bonferroni correction, so it is exploratory at best. The paper shows no significant clinical improvement or antibody reduction, so its therapeutic implications are not supported.

primary_outcome.name: Association between repeat-measured autoantibody concentrations and clinical outcomes (EQ-5D-5L index, ISI, FSS, HADS)

issues.title: Headline 'significant association' stated though both results failed Bonferroni correction (p 0.014, 0.002)
issues.explanation: Results state that the two nominally significant associations did not remain significant after Bonferroni adjustment. The Discussion and Conclusions nonetheless say the study identified a significant association and build on it. With seven patients and many antibody-outcome comparisons, the associations are exploratory and not supported as stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusions and abstract stating the result as exploratory and not significant after multiplicity correction.

quotes.text: However, these results did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni adjustment for multiple testing.
This study identified a significant association between elevated levels of β 2-adrenergic receptor antibodies/M3-receptor antibodies, and clinical outcomes in patients with ME/CFS.

second_reader.what_stands: The Results state that both associations lost significance after Bonferroni adjustment, yet the Discussion and Conclusions (and the abstract) describe a 'significant association' without that qualifier. The paper does say elsewhere that it is a hypothesis-building pilot, which softens but does not remove the inconsistency. I could not verify the number of tests or adjusted p-values because Supplementary Table S2 is not in the text.

issues.title: Conclusions endorse B-cell therapy and combined treatment despite no significant improvement or antibody change
issues.explanation: Results show no significant clinical improvement across time points and no significant antibody change after PE. The Conclusions nevertheless say that integrating PE, IVIG and B-cell therapies could improve quality of life and that B-cell depletion would enhance treatment efficacy. This goes beyond an uncontrolled association in seven patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusions confined to hypothesis generation without therapeutic recommendations.

quotes.text: Integrating plasma exchange, human immunoglobulin administration, and eventually B-cell-targeted therapies could possibly significantly improve the quality of life of individuals suffering from ME/CFS.
None of the antibodies showed a significant change in concentration levels between the two measurement time points.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions say the findings suggest B-cell depletion 'could further reduce' antibodies and 'enhance overall treatment efficacy', and that combined PE, IVIG and B-cell therapy could 'possibly significantly improve' quality of life, although the study found no significant antibody reduction, no significant clinical improvement, and tested no B-cell therapy. The hedging and call for RCTs temper this, but the stated basis ('Our findings') is not supported by the reported data.

issues.title: Uncontrolled seven-patient series cannot support the 'Effect ... of PE and IVIG' framing
issues.explanation: All patients received PE plus IVIG with no comparator, and no significant clinical improvement was found. The title and conclusions imply treatment effects and therapeutic promise, which this design cannot establish.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or framing limited to association and feasibility.

quotes.text: The patients were treated based on best clinical practice, without a placebo group
There were no statistically significant improvements in clinical outcomes across T1, T2, and T3.

second_reader.what_stands: An uncontrolled series of seven patients with no significant change in any clinical outcome cannot support an 'effect' of PE plus IVIG on quality of life; the title wording and 'positive trend' language overreach the design. The authors do disclose the absence of a control group and call the work a pilot, so the limitation is stated, but the title does not reflect it.

issues.title: Seven patients versus 56 required (10% power); association claim drawn from a few tests
issues.explanation: The authors' own calculation needed 56 patients for 80% power; they enrolled seven and report 10% power. A pilot is acceptable, but the confident association and mechanism claims are not supported at this sample size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Framing of the result as hypothesis-generating only, without efficacy or mechanism conclusions.

quotes.text: the study design required a total of 56 patients for an expected 80% statistical power
This pilot study, with a statistical power of 10%, included seven patients

second_reader.what_stands: The study is clearly far below the planned 56 patients (7 vs 56, with the paper itself quoting 10% power), so the two nominally significant associations rest on very little data and are fragile. However, the small size is intentional and disclosed as a pilot, and the t-test degrees of freedom (504, 110) are unexplained and cannot be reconciled with 7 patients from the main text alone.

issues.title: Reported df t(504) and t(110) are unexplained for 7 patients with up to 3 time points
issues.explanation: The paper includes seven patients with at most two antibody and three clinical measurements each, yet reports t(504) and t(110). Pooling over imputations or stacking outcomes may explain larger df, but the paper does not say so, and 504 observations is not reachable from this design. The two significant results therefore rest on an unexplained inference base.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of how the df were obtained (e.g. stacked outcomes or pooled imputed datasets) showing the model fitted had that many rows.

quotes.text: included seven patients, with five being male and two being female

issues.title: Two of six analysed patients had one-third to two-thirds of outcomes imputed; one excluded
issues.explanation: Two patients terminated early and had one-third and two-thirds of clinical data missing, which were imputed, and another patient was excluded. In a sample this small, imputation can drive the associations. This is disclosed, but it adds uncertainty to the reported estimates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Sensitivity analysis on complete cases showing the same associations.

quotes.text: two patients prematurely terminated the study after T1 and T2, meaning we are lacking two-thirds and one-third of their clinical outcome data, respectively
One patient had to be excluded, because he/she lacked baseline and follow-up clinical outcome data. Two patients were analyzed after data imputation.

issues.title: Early termination: two patients (Results) vs three cases (Discussion), not reconciled
issues.explanation: The Results report two patients leaving after T1 and T2, while the Discussion says deterioration led to premature termination in three cases. The paper gives no flow of enrolment, exclusion and completion, so the reader cannot tell who stopped and why.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow statement showing the third case is a different event (e.g. therapy stopped but follow-up continued).

quotes.text: two patients prematurely terminated the study after T1 and T2
This deterioration of clinical status led to the premature termination of therapy in three cases.

10.3390/jcm14124225.headline_claim: A hybrid pulmonary rehabilitation programme (8 outpatient plus 24 home-based sessions) proved beneficial for long COVID patients, with cardiorespiratory adaptations, muscle strength, functional capacity and quality-of-life gains.
10.3390/jcm14124225.overall: The within-group improvements in peak work rate and VO2 in the PR group are large and statistically strong, but the evidence comes from a small, self-selected, non-randomised comparison with baseline imbalances and no adjustment. The conclusion that the programme 'proved beneficial' across several domains is stronger than the design and several non-significant interaction tests support. The reporting inconsistencies between tables and text are minor by comparison.

primary_outcome.name: Peak work rate (WRpeak) on incremental cycle CPET

issues.title: Self-selected UC comparator, imbalanced at baseline (sex 15/12 vs 4/11, age 53.6 vs 60.1), no adjustment
issues.explanation: Usual-care patients were those who could not attend for transport or work reasons, so group membership reflects self-selection. The groups differ in sex mix, age (53.6 vs 60.1 years) and baseline exercise capacity (Table 2 marks baseline PR-versus-UC differences with # for WR, VCO2, VE and HR, e.g. WR 94 vs 68 W). The text nonetheless says there were no baseline differences. The study is called 'propensity-matched', but no matching or covariate adjustment is described, so the time × group effects cannot be attributed to the programme alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described propensity or covariate-adjusted analysis showing the time × group effects persist after adjustment.

quotes.text: Those who were unable to attend the supervised sessions due to transport constrains or work commitments were offered to participate in the usual care group
There were not any significant differences in baseline characteristics between the intervention and UC groups at the outset of the study.
This feasibility, single-centre, propensity-matched study assessed the effect of a hybrid PR programme

second_reader.what_stands: The UC group was formed by self-selection (transport or work constraints) and not by allocation or a described matching procedure, and the analysis used no covariate adjustment for the sex and age differences. Those differences (about 56% vs 27% male, 6.5 years apart) are non-significant (p about 0.07-0.09) but sizeable with n = 42. Baseline peak work rate and VCO2 also differ significantly between groups per Table 2. The 'propensity-matched' label is not supported by any described method.

issues.title: Feasibility, non-randomised study concludes the programme 'proved beneficial' across several domains
issues.explanation: The design is a small, self-selected, non-randomised feasibility comparison, yet the Conclusions state the programme 'proved beneficial' with adaptations in muscle strength, functional capacity and quality of life. Many of these statements rest on within-group pre-post tests with UC non-significance (for example, QF and handgrip, SPPB, 6MWT), not on between-group tests. Time × group ANOVA was not significant for several outcomes the conclusion implies are improved (e.g. EQ-5D p = 0.101, steps p = 0.109, SPPB total p = 0.065). The evidence supports a tentative signal of improvement, not proof of benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusions restricted to a feasibility signal, with between-group tests for each claimed domain.

quotes.text: proved beneficial for long COVID patients, leading to significant cardiorespiratory adaptations, enhanced peripheral muscle strength, improved functional capacity and a better quality of life.
The present study consisted of a relatively small sample size, and randomization was not feasible due to ethical considerations.

second_reader.what_stands: A small, non-randomised study with a self-selected comparator concludes that the programme 'proved beneficial' with significant cardiorespiratory, strength, functional and quality-of-life gains. The Conclusions section carries none of the limitations stated in 4.1 or the call for RCTs in 4.2, so the wording is stronger than the design supports. Several secondary outcomes (SPPB total, HADS, EQ-5D, steps) showed no significant group-by-time effect. The authors do disclose the limitations elsewhere in the paper.

issues.title: Discussion claims SPPB gains from specific components that Results report as non-significant
issues.explanation: The Results say the SPPB total showed only a trend (ANOVA p = 0.065) and none of its components changed significantly. The Discussion nonetheless states that the SPPB total score increased because of better 4-metre gait and sit-to-stand performance. The Discussion also describes 'clinically meaningful reductions' in peak dyspnoea and fatigue, although the time × group p-values are 0.699 and 0.291. These statements go beyond the reported tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests showing significant SPPB and component changes.

Either the text or the table is wrong, which affects how the iso-work PR-versus-UC contrast is read.

10.3390/jcm14134533.headline_claim: A two-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program is feasible and effective in improving pulmonary function, reducing systemic inflammation, and enhancing quality of life in hospitalized patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.3390/jcm14134533.overall: The paper shows consistent within-patient improvements in pulmonary function and inflammatory markers, but the single-arm 14-day design cannot separate any program effect from spontaneous recovery, regression to the mean or practice effects. The causal 'effective' and 'clinically meaningful' conclusions and the tolerability claim go beyond the data and the authors' own caveats. The primary outcome differs from the registration, and registration came after the trial started.  Table 2 also contains implausible TLC and DLCO values.

primary_outcome.name: Pulmonary function (spirometry, plethysmography, lung diffusion, gasometry)

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in the quality of life
primary_outcomes.time_frame: at baseline, immediately after rehabilitation completion, and 3 months after rehabilitation completion

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from an uncontrolled 14-day pre/post series of 77 patients, with no comparator
issues.explanation: All 77 participants received the program and were measured at day 0 and day 14, with no non-rehabilitation group. Spontaneous recovery, regression to the mean and learning effects on spirometry and questionnaires cannot be separated from any program effect. The authors concede this, yet the Conclusions say the program 'is feasible and effective'. The Wilcoxon tests are called 'between-group' but are paired pre/post comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group, or conclusions worded as within-patient change only.

quotes.text: An additional limitation of this study is its non-randomized design and the absence of a control group of COVID-19 patients who did not undergo rehabilitation
This study demonstrates that a comprehensive pulmonary rehabilitation program is feasible and effective in improving pulmonary function

second_reader.what_stands: The design is a single-arm, uncontrolled 14-day pre/post series of 77 patients, and the Conclusions and parts of the Discussion state efficacy ('demonstrates... effective', 'demonstrate the effectiveness') without the caveat that spontaneous recovery and regression to the mean cannot be excluded. The paper does openly disclose the lack of a control group and the resulting inability to infer causality in its limitations paragraph, so the problem is a mismatch between that disclosure and the stronger causal wording in the conclusions, not an undisclosed design.

Only men showed a significant rise (p < 0.05) in the supplementary analysis, so the unqualified statement misstates one reported result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the pooled WBC test was in fact significant, or that the sentence was explicitly restricted to men.

issues.title: Table 2 shows physiologically impossible post-rehabilitation TLC (max 505.9%) and DLCO (max 561.5%)

The data therefore need cleaning and the means re-derived. The Wilcoxon p-values are robust to such outliers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing these values are correct or a corrigendum for the entry errors.

10.3390/jcm14155363.overall: The paper's own framing is cautious (feasibility, exploratory), and the feasibility findings (5.56% overall dropout, high satisfaction) stand. The efficacy hint on fatigue rests on one p = 0.043 from a quasi-randomised, baseline-imbalanced 17-person comparison of a post hoc categorical outcome that differs from the registered primaries and is untested for multiplicity, so it is at most hypothesis-generating. Numerous transcription errors in the tables and text further reduce confidence in the reporting.

issues.title: Alternating (quasirandom) allocation; baseline severe fatigue 4/8 vs 2/9 in the arm that 'improved'
issues.explanation: Allocation was alternate and consecutive, so it was predictable and offers no protection against selection bias, yet the paper states the method 'ensured balance'. The only significant result, fatigue remission, can only occur in people severely fatigued at baseline, and the experimental arm had twice as many (4 vs 2 of 8 and 9). The fatigue contrast is therefore confounded by baseline imbalance and cannot be read as a treatment effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Concealed allocation and evidence the imbalance arose by chance with an adjusted analysis showing the same effect.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by alternation (quasirandom), not true randomisation, and the paper asserts it 'ensured balance' even though baseline severe fatigue was 4/8 vs 2/9 and sex was 62.5% vs 100% female; a non-significant Fisher p-value in 17 people does not demonstrate balance. The 'improved' arm did start with more people in the severe-fatigue category, which leaves more room for category transitions (the control arm had only 2 at risk of remission, which is why 0 remissions there is less informative), but the paper does not claim the imbalance explains the result and that direction of bias is not

10.3390/jcm14176066.overall: The paper shows within-arm HRV changes after a single OMT session, but it reports no group x time or between-arm results, so superiority over sham is not demonstrated, and the sham arm itself had reported significant changes.
