issues.title: OMT-vs-sham effect inferred from within-arm changes; no group×time or between-group result is reported
issues.explanation: The Results report within-arm Hedges' g with CIs for OMT across t1, t2, t3 and say sham stayed 'largely stable'. No group x time interaction or between-group estimate is given, although Methods describe both. Comparing a significant change in one arm with a non-significant change in the other is not a test of whether OMT outperformed sham. The Discussion says sham showed no comparable changes, yet the Results report sham declines in LF/HF (g = -0.53) and mean RR (g = -0.79, CI -1.43 to -0.03). The claim that effects were not due to placebo or expectation is therefore not demonstrated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported group x time interaction results or between-arm effect sizes with CIs for the key HRV outcomes showing OMT superior to sham.

second_reader.what_stands: The OMT-versus-sham conclusion is drawn from within-arm changes (OMT arm significant, sham arm largely not); no group×time interaction result or between-group effect size/CI is reported in the text, despite the methods describing such an analysis. The sham arm also showed within-arm changes in LF/HF and mean RR, so 'no comparable changes' is stated without a formal comparison. Figures were not available in the text, so a between-group result shown only graphically cannot be excluded.

The paper never says which participants were dropped from which analysis, or why, or how missing HRV data were handled. The analysed set therefore differs by outcome, and the reader cannot tell whether the headline effects rest on a selected subset.

rose from t1 (mean: 146 ms 2 ± 207, n = 14)
No subjects were excluded during enrollment.

issues.title: About nine HRV outcomes at three time points reported with no multiplicity handling or primary HRV metric
issues.explanation: The paper names no single primary HRV measure and states no correction across the metrics. Conclusions of 'consistent' effects lean on RMSSD, SDNN, stress index, mean RR, LF and HF changes, while others (pNN50, NN50, Poincaré) are not reported. Because the paper emphasises effect sizes and CIs over significance, this weakens a secondary reading rather than invalidating the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary HRV metric, or a stated correction applied across outcomes.

quotes.text: the consistent group-level patterns and medium-tolarge effect sizes support the reliability of the observed responses to OMT

issues.title: Conclusion says the study 'demonstrates' OMT induces autonomic improvement, despite pilot status and no between-group test
issues.explanation: The closing conclusion states a causal demonstration, while the Discussion calls the study a pilot with a small sample and says results are preliminary. The firm wording is not backed by a reported between-group comparison (see c10). The hedges are present but sit beside a conclusion that still reads as demonstration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group results with CIs that exclude zero for the main HRV outcomes.

quotes.text: In conclusion, while this study demonstrates that OMT can induce short-term autonomic improvements in patients with long COVID-19
It is crucial to consider the study as a pilot one.

issues.title: Outlier count given as five, 4+2=6, and six in Table 2; Table 2 totals 35 not 42; '75%' fits none
issues.explanation: The Results say five outliers, four in the osteopathy arm and two in sham, which adds to six. Table 2 lists 6 outliers, but the Discussion and Figure 4 say five. Table 2's 'entire study population' of 29 plus 6 outliers gives 35, not 42. The Discussion's '75% hospitalised' is a whole number of people only for 4 (3/4) or 8, not for 5 or 6. Which participants were treated as outliers, and whether they were kept in the HRV analyses, cannot be determined.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of exactly which participants were outliers, how many per arm, and how Table 2's 29 relates to 42.

quotes.text: Five outliers were identified in the dataset, four of them in the osteopathy group, and two in the sham group
Interestingly, 75% of these outliers had been hospitalized during the acute phase of COVID-19
Table 2. Outliers in comparison to entire study population.

issues.title: Methods claim no significant baseline differences; Table 1 prints p = 0.02, and the row's stats imply p ≈ 0.002
issues.explanation: The Methods say baseline comparisons showed no significant group differences, yet Table 1 lists p = 0.02 for loss of self-control and p = 0.05 for anxiety, with the sleep p-value blank. The printed means and SDs for loss of self-control (1.7 ± 2.7 vs 4.7 ± 3.1, n = 21 each) give t of about 3.3 and p of about 0.002, not 0.02. The sham mean and SD there duplicate the following 'lack of drive' row, suggesting a copying slip. Baseline imbalance in symptom scores (the sham arm was worse) matters little for the HRV outcomes but contradicts the stated comparability.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw baseline data showing the correct sham value for loss of self-control and the correct p-value, plus a corrected Methods statement.

quotes.text: These tests confirmed no significant baseline differences between groups across demographic and clinical parameters
Loss of self-control

issues.title: Discussion cites an LF/HF reversal t2→t3 after OMT, but Results say LF/HF was unchanged in the OMT group
issues.explanation: Results say the LF/HF ratio stayed statistically unchanged at all time points in the osteopathy group, and the only reported LF/HF change is in the sham group. The Discussion lists LF/HF among stress markers that reversed between t2 and t3 after OMT, interpreting this as 'a return to sympathetic predominance'. That reading of the OMT arm is not supported by the paper's own results, and it makes the autonomic story look more consistent than the data show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported OMT-arm LF/HF analysis showing a significant t2 to t3 change.

quotes.text: The LF/HF ratio remained statistically unchanged across all time points within the osteopathy group.
stress-related markers (e.g., mean HR, stress index, LF/HF ratio) also showed a reversal between t2 and t3

issues.title: Time since infection: text (12.5 and 17.2 months) does not match Table 1 (433.1 and 543.7 days) after conversion
issues.explanation: Converting Table 1 gives about 14.2 months (sham) and 17.9 months (OMT), versus 12.5 and 17.2 in the text. The table's ± values appear to be standard errors though they are not labelled as such, while the same table uses SDs elsewhere. This is a minor reporting inconsistency in a baseline covariate and does not affect the HRV findings directly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data giving the infection-to-intervention interval per participant in a single unit.

quotes.text: In the sham group, this interval was 12.5 ± 1.2 months, compared to 17.2 ± 1.9 months in the OMT group.

quotes.location: Table 1, Duration since SARS-CoV-2 infection row (Sham)

10.3390/jcm14196861.headline_claim: Add-on multimodal short-term treatment (corticosteroids, inhaled corticosteroids, hyaluronic-acid inhalations, voice therapy) may enable full recovery of post-COVID dysphonia, with HSV showing objective improvement in vocal fold oscillation.
10.3390/jcm14196861.overall: The data are a small, uncontrolled, descriptive pre-post series and support only tentative statements about improvement in HSV indices and patient-reported voice scores after combined treatment. The claims of 'full recovery' and HSV superiority over videostroboscopy are not supported by any analysis in the paper. The reported significance is also less secure than described, because raw p-values appear to have been used despite a stated FDR correction.

primary_outcome.name: Pre-post change in a priori selected HSV parameters sensitive to glottal insufficiency (e.g., OQ or left-right phase asymmetry)

issues.title: Conclusions claim HSV superiority over videostroboscopy and 'full recovery' that the data do not test or show
issues.explanation: No result compares HSV with videostroboscopy: VLS findings are not reported or analysed. The Conclusions nonetheless state that HSV is more precise. 'Full recovery' is also not supported: post-treatment mean VHI was still 33.71, the Discussion speaks of 'partial restoration of vibratory function', and several HSV indices did not change significantly. Both statements go beyond a small uncontrolled pre-post series.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported head-to-head analysis of HSV against VLS (for example, diagnostic yield or agreement) and post-treatment data showing normalisation of VHI and HSV indices.

quotes.text: The HSV technique provides greater precision for reliable laryngeal evaluation and assessment of phonatory function than laryngeal videostroboscopy.
our findings suggest that add-on multimodal short-term treatment may enable full recovery
indicating partial restoration of vibratory function

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's claim that HSV is more precise and reliable than videostroboscopy is not tested by any data in the paper, and VLS results are never reported. 'Full recovery' conflicts with the paper's own data (residual VHI handicap, post-treatment perturbation values still elevated, no normal comparison) and with the Discussion's 'partial restoration', although the phrase is hedged with 'may' and a call for controlled studies.

issues.title: Uncontrolled pre-post study of 14 patients with bundled, unblinded treatments cannot attribute improvement
issues.explanation: There is no control group, and patients received a clinician-chosen mix of systemic and inhaled steroids, hyaluronic-acid inhalations and voice therapy. Inflammatory dysphonia often improves on its own over 6-8 weeks, so the improvement cannot be assigned to the treatment or to any component. The self-reported VHI and V-RQOL changes are open to expectation effects, and the sample (14, no power calculation) is too small for firm inference. The study can support a descriptive, hypothesis-generating statement only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or natural-history data showing little spontaneous recovery over the same 6-8 weeks in comparable patients.

quotes.text: This was a single-center observational pre–post study
were administered by clinical judgment.
The pre–post design also leaves room for regression to the mean and spontaneous improvement.

second_reader.what_stands: With 14 patients, no control group, treatments bundled and chosen by clinical judgment, and unblinded patient-reported outcomes, the paper cannot attribute the improvement to any treatment or to treatment at all. The authors disclose this, and the HSV raters were blinded to timepoint, but the causal wording in the Results and Discussion goes beyond what the design supports.

issues.title: Stated FDR control not reflected in tables (raw p<0.05 used); pre-specified primary outcomes non-significant
issues.explanation: Methods say the false discovery rate was controlled, yet the tables flag 11 of 23 parameters as significant at raw p < 0.05, and the Discussion lists multiplicity as unaddressed. Applying Benjamini-Hochberg to the 23 printed p-values leaves about 8 significant, and AmplAsymAvg (0.02176), Jita (0.02771) and Jitt (0.03924) would not survive. The a priori primary outcomes (OQ, phase asymmetry) are not significant (OQAvg p = 0.66035, PhaseAsymAvg p = 0.45919), but the abstract-level narrative reports the significant secondary indices as the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary output showing the printed p-values are already FDR-adjusted, or that BH was applied within separate STV and LTV families with the same significant set.

quotes.text: For multiple HSV indices, the false discovery rate was controlled (Benjamini–Hochberg).
The primary outcome was the pre–post change in a priori selected HSV parameters sensitive to glottal insufficiency (e.g., OQ or left-right phase asymmetry).
Finally, multiple comparisons across numerous parameters may inflate type-I error

second_reader.what_stands: The Methods state Benjamini–Hochberg control, but the Results and tables use and report only raw p<0.05, and re-applying BH to the printed p-values removes at least AmplAsymAvg, Jitt and Jita from the significant list. The named primary-outcome examples (open quotient and phase asymmetry) are all non-significant, while the highlighted findings are secondary indices. The primary outcome is described only by examples, so which parameters were primary cannot be fully pinned down from the paper.

issues.title: Screening text accounts for 165 of 230 non-analysed patients; 65 of 244 screened are unexplained
issues.explanation: The Results state that of 244 screened patients, 150, 8 and 7 were excluded, which leaves 79, yet only 14 were analysed. The remaining 65 patients (probably dysphonia combined with other symptoms) are not described in the text. The analysed sample is small and selected, so the incomplete flow matters for judging selection bias. It does not change any reported result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing an exclusion box (for example dysphonia with other symptoms, n≈65) that closes the 244 to 14 cascade.

quotes.text: Of these, 150 were excluded due to non-laryngeal primary complaints, 8 due to structural laryngeal lesions, and 7 for incomplete records.
A total of 14 patients presented isolated dysphonia and completed both baseline and 6–8-week assessments (pre–post set).

script.explanation: The Screening cascade 244 to 14 as described in Results 3.1 does not reconcile: 'screened' (n=244) minus its 3 stated exclusion(s) (165) leaves 79, but 'analysed pre-post set' reports 14 -- 65 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

10.3390/jcm14228193.headline_claim: LLLT and TENS are both very beneficial for erectile dysfunction after COVID-19, with LLLT moderately better than TENS, and the combined LLLT plus TENS treatment is more effective than either alone.
10.3390/jcm14228193.overall: The finding that active treatment is associated with improvement in IIEF scores is plausible, but the paper never tests active versus sham, analyses completers only, and reports an unreconciled participant flow and a discussion that misstates two of its own comparisons. The claims that LLLT is moderately better than TENS and that the combination is superior across all domains rest on borderline or untested contrasts without multiplicity control. Treat the results as exploratory.

primary_outcome.name: Erectile function domain of IIEF-15 (EFD)

issues.title: Efficacy of LLLT and TENS rests on within-arm change; no active-vs-sham between-group test is reported
issues.explanation: The paper reports significant before/after changes in each active arm and 'no notable changes' in the sham arm. It never tests active versus sham for any outcome. The between-group tests reported are LLLT vs TENS and combined vs single therapy. The conclusion that both therapies are 'very beneficial' therefore compares significant with non-significant within-group changes rather than comparing the groups directly. Baseline values were also adjusted by unspecified transformations. This leaves the size of the true treatment effect over sham, and the possibility of a placebo response, untested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group (ANCOVA or t-test on change scores) comparison of each active arm against sham.

quotes.text: After treatment, no notable changes were observed in the control group.
the improvement in erectile function after the combined use of LLLT and TENS was 64.2%
According to IIEF-15 dynamics, LLLT and TENS are both very beneficial in the treatment of erectile dysfunction following COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy claims for LLLT, TENS and the combination rest on within-arm pre/post tests and on active-vs-active comparisons; no active-vs-sham (control) between-group test is reported in the text, and the control arm's lack of change is stated without a statistic. The Conclusions' 'very beneficial' wording is therefore not supported by a direct comparison against sham, although the randomised sham arm and similar baselines make a between-group test possible in principle.

issues.title: Arm sizes (23+22+23+23 = 91) and treatment-phase attrition do not reconcile with 93 randomized
issues.explanation: The text says 93 were randomized, but the four printed arm sizes sum to 91. Adding each arm's completers and its withdrawals/losses gives arms of 23, 24, 24 and 22 (sum 93), which differ from the printed sizes in three arms. So at least one stage of the flow (randomized, treatment completers, or the withdrawal and loss counts) is misreported. The CONSORT flow cannot be audited, but the efficacy conclusions are not directly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT diagram (Figure 1) showing arm sizes of 23, 24, 24 and 22, or a corrected withdrawal and loss list that reconciles with the printed arm sizes.

quotes.text: The remaining 93 patients were randomized into four groups
The number of patients who completed treatment was 22 in the control group, 21 in the LLLT group, 22 in the TENS group, and 21 in the LLLT + TENS group.

script.explanation: The participant flow does not reconcile: the arms of 'randomized' sum to 91, but the stage reports n=93 -- 2 participant(s) appear or vanish between the total and its own breakdown.

issues.title: LLLT-over-TENS ED advantage (p = 0.049) is a borderline result among many uncorrected contrasts
issues.explanation: The claim that LLLT gives a 'moderately better' outcome than TENS rests on one contrast with p = 0.049 and a difference of 8.2%. The paper tests two primary and three secondary outcomes with several pairwise contrasts each, without multiplicity control. The same pair also shows opposite and equally borderline results elsewhere (TENS better on intercourse satisfaction, p = 0.048). With this many uncorrected tests, a p just under 0.05 is weak evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or hypothesis for the LLLT vs TENS ED contrast, or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis in which the contrast stays significant.

quotes.text: Comparisons between two groups do not require the application of the Bonferroni correction.
with LLLT showing a moderately better outcome than TENS

issues.title: 'Much more successful in enhancing all IIEF domains' conflicts with non-significant combined-vs-TENS result
issues.explanation: The conclusion says the combination was much more successful across all IIEF domains. In Results, combined vs TENS for intercourse satisfaction is not reliable (p = 0.123), and the orgasmic and overall-satisfaction advantages are reported only against LLLT. Where the combination was compared with TENS (for ED and hypoesthesia) the paper reports no significant ED gain over TENS. The blanket statement goes beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported combined-vs-TENS tests showing significant advantages in every domain.

quotes.text: Nevertheless, the combination of LLLT and TENS proved to be much more successful in enhancing all IIEF domains
but these results did not reach the level of reliability

issues.title: Hypoesthesia endpoint is a subjective 10-point scale rated with an unblinded investigator
issues.explanation: Hypoesthesia is a co-primary endpoint on an unvalidated ten-point scale that the authors themselves call relatively subjective. Only participants were blinded; the investigator knew each allocation. The conclusion that only TENS reliably reduced hypoesthesia rests on this measure and on the contrast between a significant TENS result and a non-significant LLLT result (p = 0.08). The hypoesthesia findings are therefore less secure than the IIEF-based ones.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded assessment of the sensory outcome, or validation of the scale in this population.

quotes.text: Another limitation was the use of a relatively subjective method of determining penile tactile sensation, using a ten-point scale.
Only after TENS did genital hypoesthesia reliably regress

issues.title: Analysed sample appears to be the 82 completers of 93 randomized; no ITT analysis or missing-data handling
issues.explanation: Table 1 and the follow-up counts show 82 participants in the analysis, 11 fewer than were randomized. The paper gives no intention-to-treat analysis, no handling of missing data and no description of the analysed set. Dropouts from different arms may differ in outcome, so relative efficacy estimates rest on completers only. The effect on the conclusions is likely modest given 11.8% attrition.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis giving the same effects, or a statement that all 93 were analysed.

quotes.text: Completed follow-up: In total, 20 patients in the control group, 21 patients in the LLLT group, 21 patients in the TENS group, and 20 patients in the LLLT + TENS group completed three months of post-monitoring.

issues.title: Unspecified data transformation, normalization and outlier limitation applied to baseline values
issues.explanation: The Methods say that data transformations, normalization and outlier limitation were performed to address baseline differences between groups. Table 1 shows no baseline differences (p 0.78 to 0.99), and no rule is given for outlier limitation or which outcomes were processed. The reported percentage changes may therefore be based on altered data, which prevents verification. Direction of any bias is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of the exact transformations and outlier rules, with results on untransformed data.

quotes.text: data transformations, normalization, and outlier limitation were performed

issues.title: Section 4.6 misattributes the 20% (ED) and 25% (hypoesthesia) gains and reverses LLLT-vs-TENS directions
issues.explanation: Results attribute the 20% erectile-function gain (t = 3.16) to the combination over LLLT alone, and say LLLT beat TENS by 8.2%. Section 4.6 says erectile function was 20% stronger with TENS than with LLLT. Likewise, Results attribute the 25% tactile gain (t = 2.032) to the combination over TENS, and say TENS beat LLLT by 36.9%. Section 4.6 says tactile sensation was 25% better with LLLT than with TENS. The discussion therefore reverses the direction of two between-arm findings, including the main hypoesthesia contrast.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that these were different comparisons from those in Results, which no passage gives.

quotes.text: Erectile function turned to be stronger by 20% ( t = 3.16, p -value = 0.003, Cohen's d = 1.05) in TENS compared to LLLT results
This result was 20% ( t = 3.16, p -value = 0.003, Cohen's d = 1.05) higher than after the use of LLLT alone
tactile sensation was better by 25% ( t =2.032, p -value = 0.0491, Cohen's d = 0.64) in LLLT compared to TENS therapy

issues.title: Control-group baseline hypoesthesia: text 3.90 vs Table 1 3.60 (same SD 0.92)
issues.explanation: The Results give the control group's pre-treatment hypoesthesia as 3.90 while Table 1 gives 3.60. The text value duplicates the TENS group's 3.90, suggesting a copying slip. It is a baseline value for a primary endpoint, but it does not change any reported conclusion. The text's overall mean of 3.57 is also below every group mean in Table 1 (3.60 to 3.90).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing which value is correct and that the other is a typo, which would still be a printed error.

quotes.text: Hypoesthesia prior to treatment was 3.90 ± 0.92 points in the control group

quotes.location: Table 1, Hypoesthesia row, Control Group column

issues.title: Overall baseline SDs in text (ED 1.2, age 4.4) are smaller than every group SD in Table 1
issues.explanation: The text gives overall pre-treatment SDs of 1.2 for the erectile function domain and 4.4 for age. Every group SD in Table 1 is larger (3.25 to 3.75 and 6.0 to 7.7), which an overall SD cannot be. The same holds for disease duration (1.2 vs 1.6 to 1.9) and hypoesthesia (0.65 vs 0.91 to 1.23). The overall means also differ (ED 15.3 and 15.2 in the text vs a group-mean average near 15.9). The overall figures seem to be a different or mislabelled statistic. They do not affect the efficacy comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the quoted overall figures are SDs of group means or standard errors, rather than pooled SDs.

quotes.text: Before treatment, the mean level of ED was 15.3 ± 1.2 points

quotes.location: Table 1, erectile function domain row, Control Group column

quotes.text: The mean age of the participants was 41.4 ± 4.4 years

issues.title: Sample-size calculation states both a type I error of 0.01 and a significance level of 0.05
issues.explanation: The sample-size paragraph gives two different alpha values for one calculation, so the stated n = 19 per group cannot be reproduced from the text. Analyses use p <= 0.05. The practical impact is limited because accrual reached about 20 per arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The ClinCalc inputs (alpha, power, effect size) used for the n = 19 figure.

quotes.text: a type I error rate of 0.01
an expected significance level of 0.05

issues.title: Hypoesthesia inclusion lower bound given as 3 points in criteria but 2 points in Section 2.1.5
issues.explanation: The eligibility list requires hypoesthesia of 3 to 7 points, while the demographics section says the mandatory condition was two to seven points. It is unclear which threshold was applied. This has little effect on the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry stating the threshold actually used.

quotes.text: Hypoesthesia in the penis area from 3 to 7 points;
The mandatory condition for inclusion was the presence of hypoesthesia from two to seven points

10.3390/jcm14248786.headline_claim: A 12-week, 24-session core-focused plank (MORETA) non-aerobic exercise program significantly reduced body fat and improved physical and psychosocial fatigue in women with Long COVID, and alleviated pain/discomfort.
10.3390/jcm14248786.overall: The paper shows within-person changes in fat, physical/psychosocial fatigue and EQ-5D pain in 17 women, but with no control group these cannot be attributed to the exercise programme, and the effectiveness and safety wording in the Discussion and Conclusions goes beyond that design. There are also a few printed inconsistencies (the 'all regions' fat claim, the IPAQ-1 effect size, an impossible r/p pair), but these are minor and do not change the picture. The results are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Body fat percentage (total body) and MFIS fatigue; the paper names no single primary outcome

issues.title: Uncontrolled single-group pre-post design (n=17, paired t-tests only) cannot show the program caused the changes
issues.explanation: All findings come from within-person pre/post comparisons in 17 women with no comparison group, and the statistics are paired t-tests only. Changes in fat, fatigue and pain may reflect time, expectancy, natural fluctuation or measurement conditions rather than the exercise. Despite this, the paper concludes the program 'significantly reduced' fat and 'reinforce[s] the effectiveness' of the intervention. At most the data show associations with the programme period, to be tested in a controlled study.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist group showing the same change would be needed to separate the programme effect from time and expectancy.

quotes.text: An exploratory pre-post non-controlled intervention study was conducted involving women diagnosed with LC
To evaluate changes in body composition, MFIS, EQ-5D-5L, IPAQ and TSK-11 preand post-intervention paired t -tests were used.

second_reader.what_stands: The design is a single-group, uncontrolled pre-post study of 17 women analysed with paired t-tests (plus FDR correction, correlations and regressions on change scores), so it cannot establish that the program caused the changes; regression to the mean, natural fluctuation, time effects and expectation effects are not separable. The 'paired t-tests only' wording is slightly too narrow since Section 2.5 also describes FDR adjustment, correlations and regressions, and the authors do label the study exploratory and list the design as a causality limitation.

issues.title: Conclusions state the program 'significantly reduced' fat and 'reinforce the effectiveness', beyond an uncontrolled n=17 study
issues.explanation: The Conclusions use causal, efficacy language ('significantly reduced body fat and improved ... fatigue') and the Discussion says the findings 'reinforce the effectiveness' of the intervention and 'support the integration' into rehabilitation protocols. An exploratory, uncontrolled study of 17 women with no sample-size calculation can support only a hypothesis-generating statement. The claim that no adverse effects occurred also rests on a very small sample and on informal reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusions worded as exploratory associations, or controlled replication data.

quotes.text: A12-week non-aerobic therapeutic exercise program significantly reduced body fat and improved physical and psychosocial fatigue in women with LC
These findings reinforce the effectiveness of individualized therapeutic non-aerobic exercise-based interventions as a rehabilitation strategy in women with LC.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions say the program 'significantly reduced' body fat and 'improved' fatigue, and the Discussion says the findings 'demonstrate' and 'reinforce the effectiveness' of the intervention. This causal and efficacy language goes beyond what an uncontrolled n = 17 pre-post study can support, even though a limitations paragraph acknowledges the design restricts causal inference.

issues.title: Fat reduction called significant 'across all regions' but both legs are non-significant (p = 0.089, 0.069)
issues.explanation: The first Results sentence says body fat fell significantly in all measured regions, attaching p = 0.003 (the total-body figure). Two sentences later the text says fat reduction was not evident in either leg, and Table 2 agrees. Only total, arm and trunk fat changes are significant, so the summary sentence overstates the breadth of the effect. The discussion's focus on trunk and upper limb is accurate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'all regions' meant only the regions listed as significant, or table values showing leg p-values below 0.05.

quotes.text: The intervention produced significant reductions in body fat across all measured regions
fat reduction was not evident in the lower limbs, both in the right leg ( p = 0.089, ES = 0.574)

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective intervention study; no primary outcome specified
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval but no trial registration or pre-specified primary outcome, although the aims name fat mass and fatigue. With 25+ outcomes tested, readers cannot verify which analyses were planned. The FDR correction partly mitigates the multiplicity concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry created before recruitment that lists the same outcomes.

quotes.text: The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Hospital Universitario Fundación Alcorcón (approval code: 21/173)

issues.title: IPAQ-1 effect size is -0.698 in the text but -0.798 in Table 5
issues.explanation: The Results text gives ES = -0.698 for vigorous activity days per week, while the Table 5 row for the same comparison prints -0.798 with the same p = 0.048. One of the two is wrong. Neither value equals the t-derived paired effect size either. It affects one secondary effect size, not the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or the raw data showing the intended value and which printing is correct would settle which is wrong, but the two printings would still disagree as published.

quotes.text: significantly increased from 0.77 to 1.85 days per week ( p = 0.048, ES = -0.698)

issues.title: Correlation r = -0.84 reported with p = 0.765 at n = 17; the two cannot both be right
issues.explanation: With 17 participants, a correlation of -0.84 would be highly significant (p well below 0.001), yet the paper prints p = 0.765 and calls it non-significant. The pair is internally impossible; a decimal slip in r (e.g. -0.084) would explain it. It is a minor reporting error in an exploratory analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing r = -0.084 would make this a typo only; it would not make the printed pair consistent.

quotes.text: changes in MFIS (r = -0.84, p = 0.765)

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.765, but recomputed from the printed r = -0.84 p is at most 3.04e-05, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show, and on the other side of alpha = 0.05 (a decision error). This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Text says arm muscle rose, but left-arm muscle fell 1.99 to 1.97 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The text states slight increases in muscle in the arms, legs and trunk. Table 2 shows right arm up but left arm down by 0.02. The generalisation is therefore slightly inaccurate for one region. Since the text itself says none of the muscle changes were significant, this has no effect on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the table value is printed.

quotes.text: Although slight increases were observed in total body muscle (from 39.74% to 40.11%) and in specific regions such as the arms, legs, and trunk

quotes.location: Table 2, Left arm (%) muscle row, post-intervention

10.3390/jcm15041468.headline_claim: Three months of epicatechin-enriched supplementation (ECES) significantly reduces perceived fatigue and improves quality of life and inflammatory/glycocalyx markers in adults with long COVID compared with placebo.
10.3390/jcm15041468.overall: The headline claim that ECES improves fatigue, quality of life and inflammation in long COVID is weakly supported. The trial is small, has no sample-size calculation, tests many outcomes without correction, and relies on within-group tests for most results. The numeric slips (Tables 1 and 2) and the 6-month versus 15-day inconsistency reduce confidence in the data handling, though they do not themselves overturn the efficacy findings.

primary_outcome.name: Self-reported fatigue (NRS) change; registry lists IL-1b, IL-6, TNF-alpha, syndecan-1 at 0 and 90 days

issues.title: Conclusions of therapeutic/pharmaceutical use go beyond a small single-centre trial with within-group tests
issues.explanation: The paper concludes that the supplement improves strength, endothelial function and fatigue and proposes it as a therapeutic approach. This rests on 46 patients, unadjusted tests and no safety data. The call for further studies is made in the limitations rather than in the headline claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmatory multicentre trial data with a prespecified primary outcome and safety reporting.

quotes.text: the results reported in this work provide a nutraceutical and potentially pharmaceutical alternative for the treatment of long COVID
Therefore, it may be proposed as a therapeutic approach to restore physical performance in people with long COVID.

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion says the results 'provide a nutraceutical and potentially pharmaceutical alternative for the treatment of long COVID' and the Conclusions say it 'may be proposed as a therapeutic approach'. This goes beyond a 46-participant single-centre trial with unadjusted t-tests, largely within-group, no multiplicity control and registration after the start. It is softened by hedging words and by a stated limitations paragraph and a call for multicentre confirmation, so the overreach is in the wording of the claim and not an absence of caveats. The Discussion also says the double-blind, pla

issues.title: Efficacy for QoL, biomarkers and VAS items inferred from significant-vs-nonsignificant within-group tests
issues.explanation: For quality of life, VAS subdomains and biomarkers the paper contrasts a significant paired change in the ECES arm with a non-significant change in the placebo arm. The difference between a significant and a non-significant result is not itself a test of a treatment effect. Placebo also improved significantly in some outcomes, and no baseline-adjusted between-group analysis is reported for them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group (ANCOVA or interaction) tests on change from baseline for QoL, VAS and biomarker outcomes showing significant differences favouring ECES.

quotes.text: treatment with the ECES increased the quality of life as compared with the placebo-treated group, where a non-significant change was noted (Figure 3)
IL-6 also significantly decreases in the placebo group (Figure 7D).

second_reader.what_stands: For QoL (VAS), the VAS sub-items and the four biomarkers, the paper infers an ECES advantage from a significant change in the ECES arm versus a non-significant change in the placebo arm, and no between-arm test is reported for them. A difference between significant and non-significant is not itself a significant difference. For IL-6 the placebo arm also fell significantly, which the text reports but does not use to temper the efficacy statement. The fatigue and handgrip outcomes are an exception, as they do have between-group tests in Figs 2C, 5C and 6C.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 46 participants analysed, yet results described as demonstrating efficacy
issues.explanation: The paper reports no power calculation or target sample size, and only 23 per arm were analysed. The authors list the small sample as a limitation but then treat significance as strengthening the findings. A small unplanned sample makes significant results more prone to exaggerated effect sizes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol with a justified sample-size calculation for a prespecified primary outcome that the study reached.

quotes.text: The number of patients included was low, and the study was monocenter
However, the results were statistically significant, and the trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled, which strengthens the findings.

issues.title: Roughly 15+ outcome tests with unadjusted t-tests and no designated primary outcome
issues.explanation: The paper tests fatigue, quality of life, several VAS subdomains, handgrip in men and women separately, and four biomarkers, each within and between groups. The only stated threshold is p < 0.05, with no correction and no primary outcome. The findings that reach significance could include chance results, and the conclusion rests on that subset.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis plan naming one primary outcome with a gatekeeping or correction strategy for the secondary outcomes.

quotes.text: statistical analyses (simple or paired t -tests) were performed using Prism version 10.0
A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

issues.title: Mean time since symptom onset 15.4 ± 9.4 days contradicts the 6-month minimum inclusion criterion
issues.explanation: Eligibility required at least 6 months since symptom onset, yet Table 1 gives a mean of 15.4 days, with an SD of 9.4 days, in both arms. Either the unit is mislabelled or the inclusion criterion was not applied as written. This matters because it leaves the true duration of illness in the sample unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 showing the unit as months (or the time since a different event, such as the latest infection) with values of 6 or more.

quotes.text: post-COVID19 patients with at least 6 months after symptom onset

quotes.location: Table 1, Time since symptoms onset (days) row, All column

issues.title: Table 1 'All' means fall outside the arm means: age 52.72 (arms 52.87, 55.35); infections 1.87 (1.78, 1.52)
issues.explanation: With 23 per arm the overall mean should be the average of the arm means. For age that is 54.11, not 52.72. For infections it is 1.65, not 1.87. The overall column or the arm columns are therefore misreported, which casts doubt on the accuracy of the baseline table. It does not directly change the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Participant-level data showing that the arm columns or the All column in Table 1 were computed on different participants than printed.

quotes.text: The average age of recruited patients was 52.72 ± 8.19 years

quotes.location: Table 1, Number of COVID-19 infections row, All column

issues.title: Headline is fatigue/QoL, while registry lists four biomarkers as primary; no primary outcome stated in paper
issues.explanation: The registry lists IL-1b, IL-6, TNF-alpha and syndecan-1 as primary outcomes, but the paper emphasises self-reported fatigue and quality of life and names no primary outcome. All biomarkers are reported, so this is a shift of emphasis rather than omission. The fatigue result, the paper's lead finding, therefore has the status of a secondary or exploratory outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing that fatigue and quality of life were added as primary outcomes before enrolment, or a protocol naming them as the primary endpoints.

quotes.text: Interestingly, self-reported fatigue levels decreased by a significant 51% in the ECEStreated group (Figure 2A)
would significantly improve measures of fatigue, quality of life (QOL), and serum markers of inflammation and glycocalyx damage

issues.title: Table 2 headache: All column prints 36/46 but arms (17+17) sum to 34; 73.9% fits 34/46
issues.explanation: The Headache row gives 36 of 46 overall, but the two arms each have 17 cases, which total 34. The printed 73.9% matches 34/46 (73.9%), not 36/46 (78.3%), so the 36 is the wrong figure. It is a reporting slip in a baseline table and does not affect efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A data listing showing 36 participants with headache, with arm counts other than 17 and 17.

script.explanation: 36/46 = 78.26%, but the paper prints 73.9, outside the rounding interval [73.85, 74.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 48.7 rather than 46.

issues.title: Registry start date (2023-08-01) precedes registration (2023-10-02); paper says study ran from October 2023
issues.explanation: The registry record gives a study start two months before the first submission, which would indicate registration after the start of the study. The paper gives October 2023 as the start and says the study followed registration, which would be prospective. The paper does not address the discrepancy, so the timing of registration relative to enrolment is uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing that the August 2023 start was an anticipated date, or enrolment records starting on or after 2 October 2023.

quotes.text: it was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06064838, posted on 2 October 2023) in accordance with trial reporting requirements
from October 2023 to June 2024

issues.title: Table 2 percentages misprinted: cough ECES 12/23 shown as 53.17 (52.17); confusion placebo 15/23 as 62.22 (65.22)
issues.explanation: Two arm-level percentages in Table 2 do not match their own counts. The counts are consistent with the All column, so these are most likely typos. They affect only a baseline symptom table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing different denominators for these cells, such as 22 or 24 participants.

quotes.location: Table 2, Confusion/lack of concentration row, Placebo column

script.explanation: 12/23 = 52.17%, but the paper prints 53.17, outside the rounding interval [53.16, 53.18]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 22.6 rather than 23.

10.3390/jcm15062263.headline_claim: Disequilibrium, rather than POTS, is the primary determinant of orthostatic intolerance in patients with long COVID.
10.3390/jcm15062263.overall: Disequilibrium and failure of the standing test clearly co-occur in this small series. The causal and comparative conclusion that it is the primary determinant of OI over POTS is not supported by an uncontrolled sample with only 7 OI cases. Table 2's headers are apparently swapped and the POTS CI is inconsistent with its p-value, so readers need to rely on the text rather than the table.

primary_outcome.name: Association of disequilibrium (Romberg/tandem gait) with orthostatic intolerance on the active 10-min standing test

issues.title: 'Primary determinant' conclusion drawn from an uncontrolled cross-sectional series with only 7 OI cases
issues.explanation: The conclusion calls disequilibrium the primary determinant of OI and speaks of an etiologic role. The design is a single-clinic cross-sectional series of 32 patients, only 7 of whom failed the standing test, analysed by a 6-covariate regression. The authors admit causal evidence is lacking and that the small sample may destabilise coefficients. The association is clear, but the causal and comparative conclusion (disequilibrium over POTS) is stronger than the design allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger, prospective or controlled study showing disequilibrium predicts OI independently of POTS, or an intervention study with a comparison group.

quotes.text: In conclusion, disequilibrium, rather than POTS, appeared to be the primary determinant of OI in patients with long COVID.
First, the direct evidence showing the causal role of disequilibrium for OI is still lacking.
which may destabilize regression coefficients, inflate correlation estimates

second_reader.what_stands: The 'primary determinant' wording in the conclusion rests on a single-clinic, single-time-point series of 32 patients with only 7 OI cases. The model has 6 predictors (about 1.2 events per variable), and the treatment data are an uncontrolled pre/post series. Disequilibrium and OI were clearly associated (6/7 versus 3/25), but the data cannot rank determinants or show causation, which the Limitations concede. 'Uncontrolled' is imprecise because an internal OI-versus-no-OI comparison exists. There is also no healthy or untreated control group, and blinding of the examiner is not stated.

issues.title: Table 2 OI (+)/(-) column headers appear swapped: n=25 labelled OI-positive, but text and Table 1 give 7 OI patients
issues.explanation: The text says seven patients failed the standing test, and Table 1 lists exactly seven. Table 2 labels the 25-patient column as orthostatic intolerance (+) and the 7-patient column as (-). Its row contents fit the opposite assignment: all 8 POTS patients completed the test, and disequilibrium is 86% in the 7-patient column. As printed, Table 2 says POTS is more common and fibromyalgia less common in people with OI, contradicting the text. Readers must correct the headers themselves, and the printed statement is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the 25-patient group actually failed the standing test, which would contradict Table 1 and every other statement in the text.

quotes.text: seven patients discontinued standing due to symptoms of OI before completing the test
Notably, none of the patients with POTS failed to complete the test.
Clinical characteristics of patients with and without orthostatic intolerance (unable to complete the active 10-min standing test).

issues.title: Post-treatment 'resolution' of OI in 7 open-label patients has no control group and no blinding
issues.explanation: Treatment outcomes come from seven patients retested in the same clinic after minocycline, with rTMS added in one. There is no control arm, no blinding, and no objective measure beyond the same standing test. Natural recovery over 6 weeks, placebo effects and co-interventions cannot be separated from treatment. The treatment results cannot support the claim that improving disequilibrium resolves OI, though the paper frames them as supporting evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo comparison group showing a difference in OI resolution.

quotes.text: OI associated with disequilibrium resolved in five of six treated and retested patients
OI resolved in association with improvement of disequilibrium following treatment with oral minocycline or rTMS.

issues.title: POTS coefficient -0.38 (p=0.049) has CI -0.62 to -0.31, inconsistent with p; compensation reading untested
issues.explanation: For the POTS term the printed CI excludes zero by a wide margin, which a p of 0.049 cannot produce. A p of 0.049 implies the CI should nearly touch zero (about -0.76 to 0.00). The disequilibrium CI (0.32-0.96 around 0.64) is symmetric and fits its p. The Discussion also treats this borderline negative coefficient as evidence that POTS acts as a compensatory mechanism; the design cannot test that, and it follows from the fact that no POTS patient (0/8) had OI.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Output from the regression software showing a POTS CI consistent with p=0.049, with the printed bounds being a typesetting error.

quotes.text: whereas POTS was significantly negatively associated (partial regression coefficient: -0.38, p = 0.049
indicates that sympathetic activation associated with POTS serves as a compensatory mechanism necessary for maintaining an upright posture

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0000 (reachable range [0.0000, 0.0000] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.049 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Figure 1 gives Patient #3 as 51 years old; Table 1 lists the same patient as 59/M
issues.explanation: The Figure 1 caption describes Patient #3 as a 51-year-old man. Table 1 lists Patient #3 as 59/M, and both agree on 3 months of disease. One age is a transcription error. It affects a single descriptive detail and does not alter any analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction showing the caption and table refer to different patients, or that one age was a typo with the other confirmed.

quotes.text: Representative case of a 51-year-old male patient with long COVID for 3 months (Patient #3 in Table 1)

issues.title: Section 3.4 attaches the unretested patient to the disequilibrium group, but Table 1 shows it is Patient 7 (no disequilibrium)
issues.explanation: The text says OI resolved in five of six treated and retested patients, and that one patient recovered without a repeat test. Table 1 shows seven treated patients. Patients 1-6 (all with disequilibrium) were retested, and 5 of 6 completed the test. Only Patient 7, who had no disequilibrium, was not retested. The wording suggests the unretested patient was among the disequilibrium group, and it blurs that the 'resolution' denominators differ. The effect is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing further is needed; the issue is wording. It would fall away if the authors state that the unretested patient is Patient 7, who lacked disequilibrium.

quotes.text: although one patient experienced symptom recovery without a repeat standing test
not done

issues.title: Minocycline 'therapeutic trial' added mid-project with no registration or adverse-event reporting
issues.explanation: The IRB statement says a minocycline therapeutic trial was added during the main project. No registration or prespecified outcome is reported, and no adverse events are described. Treatment findings are therefore post-hoc observations. The effect on the main conclusion is small, because the treatment data is a secondary part of the paper.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registration record or a protocol dated before treatment began, or an explicit statement that the treatment data are a retrospective case series.

quotes.text: 'Minocycline therapeutic trial' was added during the process of the main project

10.3390/jcm15186970.headline_claim: Respiratory retraining (Papworth method) improves orthostatic intolerance symptoms and dysfunctional breathing in long COVID, independent of changes in end-tidal CO2.
10.3390/jcm15186970.overall: The finding that scores improved in the 13 patients who completed the programme is reported credibly, but the conclusion that breathing retraining has therapeutic potential in long COVID rests on an uncontrolled before-after comparison of a self-selected 42% of referred patients. It should be read as hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; pre-post change in Malmö POTS score and BPAT score were the reported significant outcomes

issues.title: Benefit of breathing retraining inferred from a single-arm pre-post comparison in 13 completers
issues.explanation: The study has no control group; improvements in Malmö POTS (59.3 to 42.3) and BPAT (5.7 to 2.1) are paired before-after changes in 13 patients. Spontaneous recovery of long COVID, regression to the mean (patients were selected for persistent symptoms), and non-specific effects of attention cannot be separated from the effect of the programme. Significance is judged only by a within-patient paired t-test, which cannot show attribution to the intervention. The conclusion that the findings show therapeutic potential is therefore only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control group showing a smaller improvement than the treated group.

quotes.text: the lack of a control group, which may limit the generalisability of our findings
To compare the baseline and final readings, a paired <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test was carried out
These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted respiratory physiotherapy and rehabilitation in autonomic dysfunction and OI in LCS.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, uncontrolled pre-post comparison of 13 completers (41.9% of the 31 referred), analysed by paired t-tests, yet the closing paragraph speaks of 'therapeutic potential' and 'clinical benefits of respiratory rehabilitation'. The paper does acknowledge no control group and non-causal design, and uses 'associated with' in one sentence, so the problem is partly tempered, but the benefit language still outruns what this design can show (natural course, regression to the mean, and completer-only selection are not addressed).

issues.title: Outcomes reported only for 13 of 31 referred patients (41.9%); 2 starters dropped out, no ITT
issues.explanation: Results are given only for the 13 who completed. Two who began but did not finish contribute no data, and the 16 who never started (10 for symptom resolution, 6 for logistics) were not followed. Completer-only analysis can inflate apparent benefit, though most non-starters never received the intervention, so only the 2 dropouts are a true loss to treatment analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Outcome data for the 2 dropouts showing similar improvement, or an ITT analysis of those who started.

quotes.text: A total of 41.9% (13 of the 31) of patients completed the programme
A total of 6.5% (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 2/31) of patients started but did not complete the programme.

issues.title: About ten outcomes tested at unadjusted p < 0.05; headline results would mostly survive correction
issues.explanation: No multiplicity correction is stated for about ten outcomes. The two key outcomes remain significant under a Bonferroni-type correction for ten tests, so the main claim is not threatened, but the secondary blood-pressure findings are more fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecification of Malmö POTS and BPAT as the only primary outcomes.

quotes.text: where a <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> < 0.05 was considered significant.

10.3390/jpm14050515.headline_claim: A supervised 8-week physiotherapy program (interval aerobic plus strengthening exercise) improves muscle strength, dyspnea and functional status in Long COVID patients compared with those who did not undergo the program, and intermittent exercise training is safe and effective in this population.
10.3390/jpm14050515.overall: The headline claim of benefit over non-participants is not supported. All between-group tests were non-significant in a 10-vs-10 non-randomised comparison, and the control group improved as much on the 60 s-STS. What remains is a tentative, within-group pre-post signal whose p-values appear to be one-tailed and uncorrected, so the right-quadriceps result is not significant at two-sided alpha 0.05.

primary_outcome.name: No primary outcome designated; quadriceps strength, 60-s sit-to-stand rises and Borg dyspnea reported as outcomes

issues.title: Conclusion claims superiority over non-participants, but all between-group tests were non-significant (n=10 per arm)
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the programme improves strength, dyspnea and function compared with those who did not undergo it. The Results report no significant between-group differences at baseline or final measurement, and no group-by-time analysis was done. The conclusion rests on within-group pre-post changes, and the control group also improved on the 60 s-STS. With 10 per arm and no sample-size calculation, the null between-group tests are also uninformative either way. The data support only a tentative, hypothesis-generating signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group comparison of change scores (or ANCOVA on final values) showing significant differences favouring exercise.

quotes.text: can lead to improvements in muscle strength, dyspnea, and functional status in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome compared to those who did not undergo the program

One-way ANOVA analysis and Mann-Whitney U test showed no statistically significant differences for the variables of muscle strength, functional status, and dyspnea between the two groups at baseline and final measurements.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion claims improvement compared with non-participants, but the paper's own between-group tests were all non-significant and no group-by-time test was reported. Controls also improved on 60 s-STS by the same amount. The comparative claim is not supported by the reported data, and the small-sample caveat does not remove this.

issues.title: Paired t-test p-values (e.g. t=-2.17, n=10, p=0.03) match one-tailed, not two-tailed, p-values
issues.explanation: With 10 participants per group (df = 9), a t of 2.17 gives a two-sided p of about 0.058, not 0.03. The other paired t-tests also give two-sided p-values about twice as large as printed. The paper never says the tests were one-tailed, and its Wilcoxon p matches a two-sided test. The right-quadriceps result, one of the four 'significant' within-group findings, is therefore not significant at the stated alpha.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that one-tailed tests were prespecified, or raw data giving a different t or df.

script.explanation: The printed t = 2.17 supports p no smaller than 0.0571745, but the paper reports p = 0.03 -- more significance than the statistic earns at its printed precision.

second_reader.what_stands: For df = 9, the printed p-values (0.03, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01) match one-tailed rather than two-tailed probabilities for the printed t statistics. The paper does not state that one-tailed tests were used. If two-tailed tests are the intended standard, the right quadriceps result (t = -2.17, p about 0.058) would not be significant at 0.05.

issues.title: Discussion says controls did not improve on 60 s-STS, but controls rose by 3.7 rises (p=0.01), same as exercisers
issues.explanation: The Discussion states the control group showed no similar improvement in the 60 s sit-to-stand. Results and Table 3 show the control group also improved significantly, by 3.7 rises, which is the same gain as the exercise group. The functional-status benefit therefore cannot be attributed to the programme, and the Discussion misstates the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the control rise was not significant, or a between-group test of change showing a clear advantage for exercise.

quotes.text: The control group in the present study did not show similar improvements in the 60 s-SST

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion statement that controls did not show similar 60 s-STS improvements contradicts the paper's own Results and Table 3. Controls gained 3.7 rises (p = 0.01), the same as the exercise group. The Results text does say the control gain was significant, but the Discussion and Conclusions do not take it into account.

issues.title: Non-randomised, self-selected control group (unable to attend; transport and pessimism) limits comparability
issues.explanation: Allocation depended on ability and willingness to attend the hospital, not on chance. The authors themselves note that transport difficulty and a pessimistic view of rehabilitation drove participation. These factors could relate to outcomes, and Table 1 shows imbalances (employed 80% vs 40%, ICU days 20 vs 50.5), so baseline similarity cannot be assumed at n=10 per arm. Any between-group inference is therefore confounded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that allocation factors were unrelated to outcomes, or an analysis adjusting for baseline covariates with similar results.

quotes.text: whereas patients who were unable to participate (due to logistical/transport issues) comprised the control group ( n = 10).
Beyond the participants' willingness, difficult transportation to the hospital and a pessimistic view of the benefits of rehabilitation played a significant role

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was non-randomised and based on ability or willingness to attend, with transport difficulty and pessimism about rehabilitation named as drivers. This leaves room for selection bias and confounding between arms. The authors list this under limitations but do not discuss it as a threat to the between-group comparison, and they still draw a comparative conclusion.

issues.title: 'Safe and effective' claimed from 10 exercisers; no adverse events, but monitoring method not described
issues.explanation: Safety is supported only by a statement of no adverse events in 10 exercisers, with no description of how events were ascertained. Ten participants cannot exclude uncommon harms. The effectiveness part of the sentence repeats the unsupported between-group claim. The authors also cite literature on symptom exacerbation from exercise in Long COVID.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified adverse-event monitoring protocol with systematic ascertainment, or a larger sample.

quotes.text: Furthermore, intermittent exercise training has been shown to be safe and effective in this population.
There were no adverse events during the training sessions.

issues.title: Four outcomes tested within each arm at alpha 0.05 with no primary outcome or correction; p-values 0.01-0.03
issues.explanation: Four outcomes were tested in each group with no stated primary outcome or multiplicity control. Two of the four exercise-group results (p = 0.03 and 0.02) would not survive a Bonferroni threshold of 0.0125. The problem weakens the within-group findings, which are the only positive evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or a statement that the analysis was exploratory.

quotes.text: Paired samples t -tests and Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test were performed to examine any differences between the two measurements at the beginning and at the end in each group.
with a statistical significance level of α = 0.05.

issues.title: Age SDs in Participants text (overall 4.5, control 4.76) contradict Table 1 (15.04, 14.42) and the age range
issues.explanation: The text gives an overall age SD of 4.5 years, and a control-group SD of 4.76, for a sample ranging from 21 to 79 years. Table 1 gives the control SD as 15.04 and the exercise SD as 14.42. An overall SD cannot be smaller than the within-group SDs, so the text values are wrong. This is a descriptive reporting error and does not affect the outcome analyses.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw age data showing an overall SD of about 4.5 years, which is incompatible with the printed range.

quotes.text: aged from 21 to 79 years old (M = 52.8 years, SD = 4.5 years)
aged from 28 to 79 years old (M = 54.70 years, SD = 4.76 years)

10.3390/jpm15060217.headline_claim: A personalized, supine plank-based exercise program improved fatigue and body fat percentage in women with long COVID, and could be an effective strategy for LC patients.
10.3390/jpm15060217.overall: The data show lower fatigue and body fat scores after 12 weeks in 17 women, but with no control group, no blinding and subjective outcomes, the claim that the program is an effective strategy for LC patients is not supported. The paper also has several internal inconsistencies (a Discussion sentence contradicting the Results, misaligned Table 2 p-values, inconsistent dates and duration), and these do not change the direction of the findings.

primary_outcome.name: Overall fatigue (MFIS) and total body fat (%)

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from uncontrolled, non-blinded single-arm pre-post study of 17 women
issues.explanation: All results are paired within-group changes in one arm with no comparator, no blinding and no sample-size calculation. Fatigue is a subjective outcome, so the changes cannot be attributed to the exercise program. The Abstract and Conclusions nonetheless say the program could be an effective strategy for LC patients, and the Discussion says it 'significantly improved' fatigue. The data support only that scores were lower after 12 weeks in this small sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or waitlist arm showing a between-group difference.

quotes.text: single-arm non-blinded exploratory case study, with a pre-post format was carried out
It could be an effective strategy to achieve improvements for LC patients.
This trial has some limitations such as the absence of a control group

second_reader.what_stands: True: the paper's own design is an uncontrolled, non-blinded, single-arm pre-post study of 17 women, and it nonetheless states that the program 'significantly improved fatigue', 'showed rapid improvements', and 'could be an effective strategy', while the Discussion also says 'can effectively improve fatigue, reduce fat tissue'; the limitation is acknowledged only briefly and the causal wording is not tempered by it. Not wrong: the design is plainly disclosed in the abstract and Methods, the limitation of no control group is named, and the abstract and conclusion use the hedged 'could be', so t

issues.title: Discussion says physical/psychosocial MFIS did not decrease; Table 3 shows significant decreases
issues.explanation: The Discussion states the patients did not decrease their physical and psychosocial MFIS sub-scales. Table 3 and the Results report decreases of 8.65 and 1.70 points (p ≤ 0.001). The sentence contradicts the paper's own data and conclusion, probably through a wording error, and a reader could be misled about which sub-scales changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Context showing the sentence refers to something other than the change in MFIS scores over the program.

quotes.text: Our patients did not decrease their physical and psychosocial sub-scales according to the MFIS.
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'The severity of fatigue is influenced'

quotes.text: with particularly notable improvements in the physical ( -8.65) and psychosocial ( -1.70) sub-scales

issues.title: Post-training trunk fat–fatigue correlations read as 'decrease in trunk fat' reducing fatigue
issues.explanation: The correlations are between post-training levels of trunk fat and fatigue across 17 women. The text interprets them as showing that as participants lost trunk fat their fatigue diminished, which is a statement about change. The 'high r-values' in Table 2 are also described as evidence of a significant impact of the program, although they are not effect sizes. These readings support the paper's mechanistic story more than the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correlation between pre-to-post change in trunk fat and change in fatigue, which the paper does not report.

quotes.text: These findings indicate that as participants experienced a decrease in trunk fat, their levels of fatigue also diminished (Figure 2).
The high r-values suggest that the exercise program had a significant impact on reducing the total body fat (r = 0.73)

issues.title: Table 2 p-values for right leg, left leg and trunk do not match their t statistics (df 16)
issues.explanation: A paired t of 2.49 on 16 df cannot give p = 0.000, and a t of 4.35 cannot give p = 0.022. The p-values for the right leg, left leg and trunk rows appear to belong to different rows. All three results remain significant at 0.05, so the effect on the conclusion is small, but the table is wrong as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or output showing the printed p-values correspond to these rows, for example via a different test.

script.explanation: The paper prints p = 0.022, but recomputed from the printed t = 4.35 p is at most 0.0005014, allowing for the rounding of every printed input: the paper reports LESS significance than its own numbers show. This is a reporting inconsistency, not the over-claiming direction, and not evidence of fabrication.

issues.title: Discussion dates trial start to June 2022, after the Methods' last patient exit in May 2022
issues.explanation: The Methods say screening began in January 2022 and the last patient exited in May 2022. The Discussion refers to the start of the trial in June 2022. The two dates cannot both be right, but nothing in the results depends on which one is correct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explanation that 'start of the trial' in the Discussion refers to a different event, or a corrected date.

quotes.text: Screening started in January 2022, and the last patient exit occurred in May 2022.
throughout the start of the trail in June 2022
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'However, in our study we reported'

issues.title: Program duration given as 12 weeks/3 months elsewhere but '2-month' in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Methods describe a 12-week (24-session) program. One Discussion sentence attributes the fatigue improvement to a '2-month program'. This is a factual slip about the intervention length with no effect on the reported numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the fatigue assessment was actually made at 2 months.

quotes.text: The twelve-week program included two weekly sessions.
after the 2-month program, the patient sample improved significantly compared to the baseline
quotes.location: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In relation to fatigue'

10.3390/life13071563.headline_claim: A single session of transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation over T5 and T10 improves respiratory functional performance in post-COVID-19 patients by activating spinal respiratory networks.
10.3390/life13071563.overall: The data show only that some spirometric flow measures changed between two tests 15 minutes apart in 10 patients, with no sham or untreated comparison and uncorrected, borderline p-values. The conclusions that stimulation improves respiratory performance by activating spinal networks, and is suited to rehabilitation, are not supported by this design. The results are hypothesis-generating at best.

primary_outcome.name: Respiratory flow and timing measures (PIF, PEF, tPIF, tPEF; FVC reported as unchanged); no single primary outcome is designated

checklist.control: unmatched healthy control group that also received scts; no sham or non-stimulated control

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from one uncontrolled pre/post session; healthy group also stimulated and unmatched
issues.explanation: All 18 participants received the real stimulation, and the outcome is the change between a pre and a post spirometry test within one visit. There is no sham or non-stimulated group that went through the same setup. The healthy group is unmatched, differs greatly at baseline (PIF about 476 vs 94 L/min), and itself changed in the opposite direction for PEF. Practice effects, repeated-effort variability, expectation and regression to the mean therefore cannot be separated from any stimulation effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sham-stimulation or no-stimulation arm, or a test-retest session without stimulation, showing no comparable change in PIF, PEF, tPIF and tPEF.

quotes.text: This study included unmatched controls with a notable difference in baseline parameters
using a simple 'pre-/post-acute effect' study design where baseline data sets served as self-controls
A paired t -test and signed rank test were used to assess normally and non-normally distributed outcomes, respectively.

second_reader.what_stands: Both groups received the same single scTS session and were measured only before and after it, so no unstimulated or sham comparison exists and the pre-post change cannot be separated from test-retest variation, learning or effort effects. The healthy group is stimulated, differs greatly in age, sex and baseline spirometry, and therefore cannot serve as a control for the COVID group. The authors do acknowledge the unmatched controls and call for test-retest and matched controls, so the limitation is disclosed, but the abstract and conclusions still read the changes as an intervention effect.

issues.title: Mechanism and rehabilitation benefit asserted from one session, 10 patients, indirect spirometry outcomes
issues.explanation: The conclusions state that stimulation works 'via activation of the spinal neural networks' and 'leads to improved respiratory functional performance', and that it could be used in rehabilitation. The data are single-session spirometry changes in 10 patients, with no sham arm, no neural measurement, no follow-up and no sample-size calculation. The healthy group's PEF fell significantly, which is not consistent with a uniform facilitation effect. The mechanism is inferred rather than measured, and 'improvement' beyond 15 minutes is untested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data with direct neurophysiological measures and sustained functional outcomes showing the same effect.

quotes.text: A single session of scTS applied over the thoracic spinal cord in post-COVID-19 patients leads to improved respiratory functional performance via activation of the spinal neural networks.
scTS facilitates excitation of both inspiratory and expiratory spinal neural networks leading to an immediate improvement of respiratory functional performance.

second_reader.what_stands: The mechanistic claim (activation of spinal networks, excitation of inspiratory and expiratory networks) and the rehabilitation claim rest on one session in 10 patients, with only indirect spirometric outcomes, no sham or unstimulated comparison and no direct neurophysiological measure. The wording of the Abstract and Conclusions is stronger than these data allow, although the Discussion and Limitations partly soften it by calling the findings initial and asking for further trials. An improvement in peak flows 15 min after stimulation is not evidence of a lasting rehabilitation benefit.

issues.title: Five outcomes x two groups tested at alpha 0.05 uncorrected; COVID findings at p = 0.013-0.049
issues.explanation: Ten within-group tests (5 outcomes x 2 groups) were run at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05. The four 'significant' COVID results have p = 0.040, 0.049, 0.035 and 0.013. With a Bonferroni threshold for five outcomes (0.01), none would pass. Several of the tests are on skewed flow data with SDs near or above the mean change, so the results are fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single primary outcome or a declared multiplicity adjustment under which the COVID results remain significant.

quotes.text: The statistical significance threshold was set to α = 0.05.
significantly increased PIF ( p = 0.040) and PEF ( p = 0.049) in association with significantly decreased tPIF ( p = 0.035) and tPEF ( p = 0.013)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states a single alpha of 0.05 with no multiplicity adjustment across five outcomes in each of two groups, and the four significant COVID results lie between p = 0.013 and 0.049. None of them would pass a Bonferroni or Holm adjustment over the five COVID outcomes. The outcomes are correlated and the study is exploratory, so the correction would be less severe than the independent-test figure suggests, but the paper does not discuss the issue.

issues.title: Conflicts statement says no financial interest yet an author holds shares in the device maker
issues.explanation: The conflicts section opens by saying no author is affiliated with any organization with a financial interest in the subject matter. It then states that one author is a shareholder in Cosyma, the producer of the Biostim-5 stimulator used in the study, and in NeuroRecovery Technologies. The interest is disclosed, so this is an internal inconsistency rather than concealment. The study is uncontrolled and unblinded, so such an interest matters more.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected statement removing the contradictory first sentence.

quotes.text: The authors have no affiliation with any organization with a direct or indirect financial interest in the subject matter discussed in the manuscript.
Yury Gerasimenko holds shareholder interest in NeuroRecovery Technologies and Cosyma (producer of a Biostim-5 device used in this study).

issues.title: No registration or pre-specified primary outcome reported for interventional study
issues.explanation: The paper gives ethics approval but no trial registry entry or pre-specified outcome. Five respiratory outcomes were analysed and the paper does not say which was primary. Together with c2 this leaves room for outcome selection, though registration for a pilot physiology study is debatable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry made before enrolment that names the primary outcome.

quotes.text: Data collection occurred between December 2020 and March 2022.

10.3390/life14070864.headline_claim: The authors conclude that a home-based motor and respiratory tele-rehabilitation programme after hospital rehabilitation appears to be a potentially viable, safe and effective strategy for patients with long COVID.
10.3390/life14070864.overall: The data show clear gains in walking and respiratory measures between baseline and the end of the combined programme, but the single-arm design and non-significant home-phase changes mean the effectiveness of tele-rehabilitation itself is not established. Conclusions are hedged but still call the approach effective and safe, and there are minor text-table and attrition-reason inconsistencies and a retrospective registration.

primary_outcome.name: Walked distance on the instrumented 6-minute walk test (i6MWT), T0 to T2; the paper says it 'typically serves as the primary outcome measure' and reports within-session changes only

primary_outcomes.measure: Change from baseline balance and functional mobility.
Change from baseline in several respiratory measures.
Change from baseline in the pulmonary function test.

issues.title: Single-arm design cannot separate tele-rehabilitation effect from hospital rehab and natural recovery
