issues.explanation: All 23 patients had a 4-week hospital programme followed by 3 weeks of home tele-rehabilitation, with no control group. Most of the gain occurred T0 to T1 in hospital, and the T1 to T2 home phase was mostly non-significant. Improvements cannot be attributed to tele-rehabilitation versus the hospital programme or natural recovery, and the paper itself states the contributions cannot be quantified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group receiving hospital rehabilitation alone, or a home-phase comparison showing a significant effect.

quotes.text: Another limitation is the absence of a control group, as reported in previous studies
since patients underwent hospital-based before tele-rehabilitation, quantifying their respective impacts on patients’ recovery is difficult

second_reader.what_stands: The single-arm sequential design cannot separate the tele-rehabilitation effect from the preceding hospital rehabilitation or from natural recovery, and the authors say so themselves in the limitations. The paper acknowledges this, but it still limits any causal attribution to tele-rehabilitation.

issues.title: 'Effective' tele-rehabilitation claimed though T1-T2 motor changes were non-significant
issues.explanation: The home phase is the only interval attributable to tele-rehabilitation. For gait parameters the paper says T1 to T2 change was not significant, with no plus marker for any motor outcome; only FVC and MVV @25 carry one. The Conclusions nevertheless call the approach effective and the Discussion describes 'constant improvement' and a 'positively synergic' hybrid effect. A non-significant home-phase trend, in an uncontrolled design, does not support efficacy of the tele-rehabilitation component.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled or formally tested T1-T2 analysis showing a significant home-phase benefit.

quotes.text: Although the variation between T1 and T2 was not significant, a consistent increasing trend could be observed for all parameters, indicating constant improvement.
the tele-rehabilitation approach proposed in this study appears to offer a potentially viable, safe and effective strategy in addressing rehabilitation needs.

second_reader.what_stands: The motor changes during the tele-rehabilitation phase (T1-T2) were non-significant and below the 30 m clinical threshold the authors cite, yet the text interprets them as 'constant improvement' and the conclusion calls the approach 'effective'. This is softened by hedged wording ('appears to', 'potentially'), by significant T1-T2 gains in FVC and MVV@25, and by the lack of a control group being acknowledged; the effectiveness claim is still not supported for the motor outcomes of the tele-rehab phase.

issues.title: Text places T1-vs-T2 significance on MVV @34; Table 2 marks it on FVC and MVV @25 only
issues.explanation: The Results say the MVV test differed significantly between T2 and T1 for 'FVV @34' (an apparent typo for MVV @34). In Table 2 the MVV @34 row carries only a single asterisk at T1 and T2, with no T1-vs-T2 marker, while FVC and MVV @25 carry the plus marker. The text and table disagree about which respiratory measures changed during the home phase. The effect is on one reported result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement or supplementary table showing the T1-T2 test for MVV @34 was significant and the plus marker was omitted from the table.

quotes.text: variations both between T0 and T1 (i.e., MVV @25 and MVV @34) and T2 and T1 (i.e., FVV @34)

issues.title: 'Safe' claim rests on zero reported adverse events in 23 completers, with 5 dropouts uncharacterised
issues.explanation: Safety is inferred from the absence of reported adverse events among 23 completers, with adverse incidents recorded informally. Five of 28 starters left and three of them for non-cooperation, with no stated safety follow-up for them. With 23 patients, zero events only excludes a fairly high event rate, so 'safe' is weakly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified safety monitoring protocol covering all 28 starters showing no events.

quotes.text: the absence of adverse events supports the proposed program as a safe solution for managing patients with long COVID.

issues.title: Trial registered 2023-02-20, after the 2022-07-26 start and after enrolment began 16 May 2022
issues.explanation: The registry shows first submission on 2023-02-20, after the registered study start of 2022-07-26, and the paper says evaluation began 16 May 2022. The registered outcomes therefore cannot be shown to precede data collection. The paper does not disclose the retrospective registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registry version dated before enrolment began.

quotes.text: The two rehabilitation centers evaluated 40 patients from 16 May 2022 to 15 August 2023.
trial registration: NCT05739552

issues.title: Registered balance/mobility primary outcome not reported; primary outcome not formally designated
issues.explanation: The registry lists balance and functional mobility among five primary outcomes, yet the paper reports no balance measure and designates walked distance only loosely as the usual primary. Because only the current record was retrieved, it cannot be shown whether the outcome set changed. Selective reporting is possible but unproven.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing balance was never a registered outcome, or the paper reporting balance results.

quotes.text: which typically serves as the primary outcome measure for assessing changes in patients’ performance

issues.title: 'Significance in all inter-session variations' of respiratory measures contradicted by Table 2 markers
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion say all respiratory parameters improved significantly in all inter-session comparisons. Table 2 shows FVC unmarked at T1 (3.60) and MVV @34 without a T1-T2 marker, and the text itself says FVC only reached significance at T2. The blanket wording overstates what the table shows, though the main T0-T2 respiratory improvements are marked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-comparison p-values showing significance for every respiratory parameter in every pairwise comparison.

quotes.text: Regarding respiratory parameters, significance (p < 0.05) was found in all inter-session variations.

issues.title: Five withdrawals: all 'personal reasons' in Results vs three for non-cooperation in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Results attribute all five withdrawals to personal reasons unrelated to the rehabilitation programme. The Discussion says three of the five dropped out for lack of cooperation and only the other two for personal reasons. These accounts differ, and the Results version supports the claim that attrition was unrelated to the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that non-cooperation was unrelated to the programme (for example, reasons outside the intervention).

quotes.text: Five participants withdrew from the study due to personal reasons unrelated to the rehabilitation program
Among these, three dropped due to a lack of cooperation, while the others withdrew from the program due to personal reasons

issues.title: About 11 outcomes x 3 comparisons tested with uncorrected paired t-tests; no primary outcome
issues.explanation: The authors ran ANOVA then paired t-tests for T1-T0, T2-T1 and T2-T0 on gait, strength and respiratory outcomes, and report no correction or exact p-values. Isolated findings such as cadence at T2 only are vulnerable. The larger improvements (walked distance, MVV) are unlikely to be artefacts of multiplicity, so the weakening is partial.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated correction (for example Bonferroni or Tukey) or a single pre-specified primary outcome with hierarchical testing.

quotes.text: followed by post hoc analyses including paired t-tests between the observed time points (i.e., T1–T0, T2–T1, T2–T0).

10.3390/life14111518.headline_claim: Combining spinal cord transcutaneous stimulation (scTS) with respiratory training (RT) yields significant improvements in respiratory function in post-acute COVID-19 patients, with an average effect size about twice that of RT alone.
10.3390/life14111518.overall: The headline claim that scTS adds significant, clinically comparable benefit to respiratory training is not supported by this design: a fixed-order, uncontrolled, unblinded cohort of 5 cannot separate scTS from time, extra training and early recovery, and the significant results do not meet the Bonferroni threshold the authors say they used. The data are at most a hypothesis-generating pilot signal, with unexplained inconsistencies in the reported PEF, PIF and baseline FVC values.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated as a prespecified primary outcome; FVC is the stated endpoint in Methods (2.3) and the Results report FVC, PIF, PEF, tPIF and tPEF

issues.title: Fixed-order single cohort of 5: scTS effect confounded with time, cumulative training and natural recovery
issues.explanation: All five participants had RT first and then RT plus scTS, with no sham, no concurrent control and no counterbalancing. Any difference in the second phase could come from the extra 10 sessions of training, spontaneous recovery in early post-COVID (about 2 months after diagnosis), or practice with spirometry. The Conclusions nevertheless state that the study 'demonstrates' significant benefits of scTS.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent RT-only or sham-scTS control arm, or randomized/counterbalanced order of the two phases.

quotes.text: The study included one cohort of participants (n = 5) who underwent two different interventions: RT alone and RT combined with scTS.
The study’s small sample size and lack of a control group limit the scope for robust conclusions.
This study demonstrates that combining scTS with RT offers significant benefits for respiratory rehabilitation in post-COVID-19 patients.

second_reader.what_stands: All five participants received RT first and then scTS+RT, with no control arm, randomisation or counterbalancing, so any extra gain in the second block cannot be attributed to scTS rather than to further training or ongoing recovery. The authors do list the missing control group as a limitation, but the Conclusions and Discussion still state that scTS produced the benefit.

issues.title: Conclusions claim benefit comparable to or exceeding rehabilitation and bronchodilators from 5 uncontrolled patients
issues.explanation: The paper concludes that scTS+RT offers 'clinical benefits comparable to or exceeding traditional rehabilitation methods' and may reduce mortality, but no bronchodilator or rehabilitation comparator, no mortality data, and no control arm exist. The limitations mention the lack of a control group, yet the Conclusions section still says the study 'demonstrates' significant benefit. The evidence supports only a hypothesis-generating pilot signal.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison with a rehabilitation or bronchodilator arm, or outcome data on symptoms and mortality.

quotes.text: The results from this study suggest that neuromodulation combined with respiratory muscle training could yield clinical outcomes comparable to those observed with bronchodilators or traditional pulmonary rehabilitation programs.
offering clinical benefits comparable to or exceeding traditional rehabilitation methods.
These improvements may translate into meaningful clinical benefits, such as symptom alleviation, improved respiratory function, and potentially reduced mortality.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of benefit 'comparable to or exceeding' traditional rehabilitation and bronchodilator response is made from five patients without any control or active comparator, using changes that are confounded with time and prior training. The Discussion uses softer wording and the limitations are acknowledged, but the Conclusions state the comparison without qualification and the mortality statement has no supporting data in the study.

issues.title: Bonferroni correction stated but significance called at unadjusted p = 0.013 to 0.034 (α = 0.05)
issues.explanation: The methods say multiplicity was Bonferroni-adjusted, but the number of comparisons is not given and every significance call uses an unadjusted threshold of 0.05. The three significant scTS+RT results (p = 0.034, 0.023, 0.023, 0.013) would fail even a modest Bonferroni threshold across the five outcomes (0.05/5 = 0.01). So the claim of significant benefit does not survive the correction the authors say they applied.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that reported p-values are Bonferroni-adjusted, or the pre-specified number of comparisons and an adjusted threshold that these p-values meet.

quotes.text: We adjusted for multiple testing using the Bonferroni correction
The statistical significance threshold was set to α = 0.05.
led to a significant decrease in tPEF from 0.56 ± 0.46 to 0.43 ± 0.36 sec (p = 0.013)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper says Bonferroni correction was used but states no adjusted alpha, and calls results significant at the unadjusted 0.05 level (p = 0.013 to 0.034). With any plausible family of 6 to 12 comparisons none of these p-values would meet a Bonferroni threshold. The correction may have been used only in planning the sample size, but the paper does not say so.

issues.title: scTS superiority over RT inferred from significant vs non-significant pre-post changes, no direct test
issues.explanation: The paper compares each phase against its own start value and concludes scTS+RT is better because one phase reached p < 0.05 and the other did not (for example FVC p = 0.131 versus 0.034). No test compares the change in phase 2 with the change in phase 1. The 'twice as large' effect size claim is an average over five outcomes with SDs of 0.70 and 0.38, from n = 5. This overlaps with the confounding by fixed order and is the analytic step behind the headline claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A paired comparison of the phase-2 change against the phase-1 change per participant showing a significant difference, with the effect-size difference's confidence interval.

quotes.text: Following the scTS + RT intervention, FVC outcomes significantly increased compared to post-RT levels
The average effect sizes of the RT and scTS + RT interventions accounted for all outcome measures were 0.78 ± 0.70 vs. 1.46 ± 0.38

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that scTS+RT is superior rests on one block having mostly significant p-values and the other having none, together with a descriptive comparison of average effect sizes. No direct test comparing the two blocks is reported. The paper does give effect sizes for both blocks, so it is not based on p-values alone, but the effect-size contrast is not accompanied by any interval or test.

issues.title: PEF and PIF scTS+RT start values (1.52, 1.21) do not match post-RT values (1.38, 1.40)
issues.explanation: For FVC, tPIF and tPEF the starting value of the scTS+RT step equals the post-RT value. For PEF the post-RT value is 1.38 L/s but the next step starts at 1.52 L/s. For PIF the post-RT value is 1.40 L/s but the next step starts at 1.21 L/s. The likeliest cause is a mix of median/MAD and mean/SD summaries, but the paper does not say so, so the reader cannot tell which values are right. This affects two secondary flow outcomes, not the FVC results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary data showing the post-RT PEF and PIF means equal 1.52 and 1.21, with the 1.38 and 1.40 values being medians, plus a statement that the summary statistics differ.

quotes.text: PEF changed from 1.15 ± 0.37 to 1.38 ± 0.04 L/s
significantly increased from 1.52 ± 0.49 to 2.11 ± 0.49 L/s
PIF changed from 1.58 ± 0.80 to 1.40 ± 0.52 L/s

issues.title: Baseline FVC % predicted 48.9 ± 16.23 (Results) vs 67 ± 3 (Table 1) unexplained
issues.explanation: Table 1 lists FVC % predicted for the five participants as 65 to 71 (mean 67 ± 3), whereas the Results give the pre-intervention FVC as 48.9 ± 16.23% predicted. The two may come from different measurements, but the paper does not say so. The discrepancy bears on how severe the baseline impairment was and on how large the later gains (54.4 to 69.6%) really are relative to baseline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 1 reports screening values from a different spirometer or date, or corrected values.

quotes.text: from 48.9 ± 16.23 to 54.38 ± 15.52% predicted

issues.title: Sample size of 5 rests on pilot effect size (d = 0.77) and ignores the stated Bonferroni correction
issues.explanation: The target of 5 was reached, so there is no shortfall. But the calculation uses a single effect size from a 10-person pilot with a different design (single-session change in tPEF), and it was computed at an unadjusted 5% level even though Bonferroni correction is said to be used. Under the stated correction, power would be well below 80%. The authors call the study preliminary, which limits the concern, yet the Conclusions are stated confidently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power calculation that incorporates the multiplicity correction and still gives n <= 5.

quotes.text: a sample size of 5 participants is required
accounted for potential data loss by planning to enroll 7 participants

issues.title: Conflict statement denies financial-interest affiliations but then discloses device-maker shareholdings
issues.explanation: The Conflicts of Interest section opens by saying the authors have no affiliations with organisations that have a financial interest in the subject, and then discloses that two authors hold shares in Cosyma, the maker of the stimulation device, and intellectual property rights. The disclosure is present, so the issue is an internal contradiction rather than concealment. Readers should weigh the favourable, uncontrolled, unblinded results with that interest in mind.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected statement clarifying that the first sentence refers only to funding sources.

quotes.text: The authors declare no affiliations with any organization that has a direct or indirect financial interest in the subject matter of this manuscript.
Yury Gerasimenko holds shareholder interests in Neurorecovery Technologies and Cosyma, Inc. (manufacturer of the Neostim-5 device used in this study).

10.3390/medicina59071211.headline_claim: Ultrasound-guided hydrodistension with physiotherapist-guided exercise was clinically effective for post-COVID-19 adhesive capsulitis (phase 1) in terms of movement recovery and pain reduction.
10.3390/medicina59071211.overall: The 16-patient single-arm series shows large pre-post improvements, but with no control group, no blinding, no sample-size justification and a Table 3 that does not reconcile with Table 2, the stated conclusion of demonstrated effectiveness is not supported; at most it is a hypothesis-generating pilot. The direction of change is plausible, but its size cannot be attributed to the combined treatment.

primary_outcome.name: Not designated in the paper; active ROM, VAS, SPADI and DASH are all reported

issues.title: Uncontrolled 16-patient series concludes the strategy is effective; no control, no sample size, no blinding
issues.explanation: All 16 patients received the same combined treatment with no comparator, so natural recovery of a self-limiting condition, the corticosteroid effect alone, and regression to the mean cannot be separated from the effect of the strategy. Outcomes are unblinded patient-reported and clinician measures. The abstract says the study 'demonstrated' effectiveness, which this design cannot support. This also covers the small sample and lack of sample-size calculation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control arm showing smaller improvement under natural course or injection alone.

quotes.text: the absence of a control group consisting of patients with adhesive capsulitis developed in post-COVID-19 syndrome not subjected to treatment
The study demonstrated that the management of adhesive capsulitis (phase 1) developed in post-COVID19 syndrome

second_reader.what_stands: It is true that this is an uncontrolled 16-patient series with no stated sample-size calculation and no stated blinding of assessors, yet the Abstract and Conclusions say the strategy 'represented an effective treatment strategy' and was 'clinically effective' without a caveat in the Abstract. The limitations (small size, no control group) are acknowledged in the Discussion, Limitations and Conclusions, so the paper is not silent on them. Blinding and sample size are simply not addressed, and the causal wording is stronger than a single-arm design supports.

issues.title: Table 3 'mean differences' (e.g. flexion 13.81, VAS -19.39) contradict Table 2 means (+45, -5.4)
issues.explanation: Table 3 is titled mean differences, but its values do not equal the differences between the Table 2 means. Flexion rose from 55 to 100 degrees (+45) yet Table 3 shows 13.81, and VAS fell 5.4 points yet Table 3 shows -19.39. The Table 3 VAS entry for pre to 20 sessions (-18.42) is smaller than pre to 10 sessions (-19.39) although VAS kept falling. The p-values rest on a table whose quantities are unidentified, so the reported statistics cannot be verified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 3 reports t statistics or another derived quantity, with data showing it reconciles with Table 2.

quotes.text: Pre to 10 sessions 13.81 p < 0.00001
Table 3. Mean differences and pairwise comparisons with t -test.

second_reader.what_stands: The Table 3 entries labelled 'mean differences' do not equal the differences between the Table 2 means (flexion +45 vs 13.81, VAS -5.4 vs -19.39), and the VAS value exceeds the 0-10 scale range. The entries are probably test statistics or some other quantity, but the paper does not say so, so the labelling and the table cannot be reconciled from the text. I cannot tell from the paper what the numbers actually are.

issues.title: Many uncorrected pairwise t-tests (7 outcomes x 3 contrasts); borderline VAS 10-to-20 week p<0.02
issues.explanation: Twenty-one pairwise t-tests were run with no correction, and the type of t-test (paired or unpaired) is not stated; the methods describe it as testing 'correlations between the means'. Most p-values are extremely small and would survive correction, so only borderline contrasts such as VAS 10 to 20 sessions (p<0.02) are really vulnerable. This weakens a secondary result rather than the main one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified correction or primary outcome, or paired-test details showing the borderline contrasts survive adjustment.

quotes.text: Correlations between the means of outcome measures pre-treatment and post-treatment were analyzed with a t -test; p < 0.05 was considered significant.
between after 10 sessions and after 20 sessions ( p < 0.02) for VAS

issues.title: Interventional study reports ethics approval but no trial registration
issues.explanation: The paper calls the study interventional and gives ethics approval dated 20/07/2022 but no registry entry, and does not state enrolment dates. Prespecification of outcomes therefore cannot be checked. This has little bearing on the conclusion given the other limitations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry predating enrolment, or confirmation that registration was not required.

quotes.text: This interventional study was approved by the local ethics committee (379/2022/Sper/ IOR, and approved date: 20/07/2022).

issues.title: SPADI scale described as 0-130 yet reported as percentage; baseline 55.5% in text vs 55 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The methods define SPADI as 13 items each scored 0-10, giving a 0-130 range, but also call it a percentage score. The baseline is 55.5% in the text but 55 in Table 2. The scale definition is internally inconsistent (13 items x 10 = 130, while the standard SPADI has 0-100), which makes the stated MCID of 10 harder to interpret. Effects are large enough that the conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the SPADI is rescaled to a percentage and the 55 vs 55.5 difference is rounding of a different statistic.

quotes.text: The percentage score can vary from 0 to 130
before treatment patients had a mean score of 55.5% ± 16.12

10.3390/medicina62010210.headline_claim: A 12-week core-focused plank exercise program can effectively reduce fatigue and improve self-perceived health status in women with Long COVID, and may serve as a safe rehabilitation option for individuals with PESE.
10.3390/medicina62010210.overall: The headline claim that the programme effectively reduces fatigue is not supported: total MFIS showed no group × period difference and the control group improved slightly more, and the few significant interactions (psychosocial MFIS, EQ-VAS) are uncorrected across about 30 tests. The non-randomized allocation by ability to commit further prevents causal attribution, and the safety claim is unsupported by presented data. Reporting slips (19.6% vs 19.1%, repeated F/p values) add to the unreliability, so the paper is at best exploratory.

primary_outcome.name: MFIS total score (fatigue); the paper does not clearly name a single primary outcome

issues.title: Total MFIS shows no group × period effect (p = 0.551; control 16.3% vs 14.2%) yet conclusion says fatigue is reduced
issues.explanation: For total fatigue, the group × period interaction was non-significant, and the control group improved slightly more than the intervention group. The significant period effect (p = 0.002) reflects improvement in both arms, which is consistent with natural change, regression to the mean or expectation effects. The Conclusions nevertheless state that the programme 'can effectively reduce fatigue'. The total-score data do not support that claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome on which the intervention differs significantly from control, or an adjusted analysis showing a total-MFIS benefit.

quotes.text: no statistically significant interaction during intervention for group × period (F = 0.369, p = 0.551), with an improvement in the intervention group of 14.2% vs. 16.3% in the control group
This study demonstrates that a 12-week core-focused plank exercise program can effectively reduce fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: The total MFIS shows no group × period effect (p = 0.551) and a slightly larger percentage improvement in the control group (16.3% vs 14.2%), so the data do not show the program reduces overall fatigue beyond what the control group experienced. The conclusion that the program 'can effectively reduce fatigue' is therefore stronger than the total-score result supports, even though the authors do mention in the discussion that the total difference was non-significant.

issues.title: Allocation by ability to commit to sessions, with a no-intervention control, confounds the group comparison
issues.explanation: Participants who could commit to two supervised sessions a week went to the intervention, and those who could not formed the control. Motivation, availability and health status therefore differ systematically between groups, and the control group receives no attention or contact. Any between-group difference in subjective outcomes (fatigue, EQ-VAS) cannot be attributed to the exercise itself. The Conclusions still say the study 'demonstrates' effectiveness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Covariate-adjusted analyses or baseline-adjusted models showing the same interaction results, plus evidence that groups were comparable on motivation and availability.

quotes.text: participants who could commit to attending two supervised sessions per week for 12 weeks were assigned to the intervention group, while those unable to commit were placed in the control group
statistical analyses accounted for observed differences where relevant

second_reader.what_stands: Assignment by ability to commit to twice-weekly sessions, with an untreated control group, makes the intervention effect inseparable from availability, motivation or health status, and no covariate adjustment is described despite the claim that analyses accounted for differences. The authors do state the selection-bias limitation in 2.3, in limitation (xii) and in the conclusions, so the issue is disclosed but not resolved.

issues.title: Conclusions highlight uncorrected subdomain/EQ-VAS interactions (p = 0.014, 0.046) and a non-significant physical domain
issues.explanation: Of about 30 ANOVAs across body composition, MFIS and EQ-5D-5L, only the 2-item psychosocial MFIS domain and the EQ-VAS reach significance for the interaction, with no multiplicity control. The physical-domain claim rests on a larger percentage change (39.1% vs 16.7%) whose interaction was not significant (p = 0.187). The EQ-5D-5L total interaction was null (p = 0.919), so the EQ-VAS result is not corroborated by the instrument it belongs to. The Conclusions treat these selected findings as established benefits.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-registered plan naming the psychosocial MFIS and EQ-VAS as primary outcomes, or multiplicity-adjusted results that remain significant.

quotes.text: participants in the intervention group experienced meaningful improvements in the physical and psychosocial domains of fatigue
There was no statistically significant interaction during intervention of group × period (F = 1.882, p = 0.187)
There was a statistically significant interaction between the group × period (F = 4.347, p = 0.046)

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusions present physical-domain improvement as meaningful although its interaction test was non-significant (p = 0.187), and they rely on two nominally significant interactions (psychosocial p = 0.014, EQ-VAS p = 0.046) that would not survive a simple multiplicity correction; no correction or primary outcome is stated. The paper does include general caveats about sample size and non-randomisation, but not about multiplicity.

issues.title: Weight and total body fat report identical F and p for group, time and interaction; other values also repeat
issues.explanation: The weight paragraph and the total body fat paragraph give the same three F values and p values (0.291/0.597, 1.249/0.279, 0.786/0.388). The right-arm and right-leg fat interaction values (0.690, 0.417) also match, and the total muscle mass 'group' result (F = 0.369, p = 0.551) equals the total MFIS interaction result. At least some of these are likely transcription errors, so the body composition statistics cannot be taken at face value. The null body composition finding is probably unaffected, but the reporting is unreliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The raw data or figure values showing that weight and total fat genuinely yield identical ANOVA statistics, or a correction from the authors.

quotes.text: No statistically significant differences were observed between groups or across time points (F = 0.291, p = 0.597 for group; F = 1.249, p = 0.279 for time; group × time: F = 0.786, p = 0.388).
For total body fat (Figure 2a), no significant differences were found between groups or over time (F = 0.291, p =0.597 for group; F = 1.249, p =0.279 for time; group × time: F = 0.786, p = 0.388).
For total muscle mass (Figure 4a), no significant differences were observed (F = 0.369, p = 0.551 for group

issues.title: Pilot of 39 (20/19) with no sample-size calculation, against 100-120 needed, yet concluded as effective
issues.explanation: The authors state that a fully powered trial would need about 100-120 participants and that their 39 should be treated as exploratory. The Conclusions nonetheless say the programme 'demonstrates' effectiveness. Because the sample is below what the authors consider adequate, the few significant interactions are fragile. The Methods framing is appropriate; the mismatch lies in the conclusion wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Conclusion wording limited to hypothesis-generating language consistent with the Methods.

quotes.text: therefore, no formal sample size calculation was performed
would require approximately 100-120 participants in total

issues.title: Safety for people with PESE asserted without adverse-event methods, adherence or PESE data (n = 20 exercising)
issues.explanation: The Discussion claims 'absence of adverse events and the avoidance of PESE', and the Conclusions call the programme a safe option for individuals with PESE. No method for recording adverse events or PESE is described, and no adherence, attendance or dropout figures are shown. With 20 exercising participants, even a true absence of events leaves wide uncertainty about safety. The aim to 'explore safety and feasibility' is not matched by reported data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described adverse-event/PESE monitoring protocol with attendance and dropout data showing no events.

quotes.text: The intervention's safety profilemarked by the absence of adverse events
This program may serve as a safe rehabilitation option for individuals with PESE.

issues.title: EQ-VAS improvement in intervention group printed as 19.6% in Results but 19.1% in Discussion
issues.explanation: The Results report a 19.6% EQ-VAS improvement in the intervention group, while the Discussion reports 19.1% for the same comparison against the same 1.1% control figure. The two cannot both be correct. The gap is small and does not change the significance claim, but it is a reporting error in a headline secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two figures are computed differently (for example mean of individual changes vs change of group means), or a corrected figure.

quotes.text: with an improvement in the intervention group of 19.6% vs. 1.1% for the control group
HRQoL, assessed through the EQ-VAS, improved by 19.1% in the intervention group compared to only 1.1% in the control group

10.3390/medicines8090047.headline_claim: A 14-day supplementation with ImmunoSEB plus ProbioSEB CSC3 resolves post-COVID-19 fatigue and is effective as an early intervention in COVID-19 recovery.
10.3390/medicines8090047.overall: The direction of the day-14 difference (91% vs 15% fatigue-free) is large, but the trial supports only a short-term, self-reported symptom improvement, not durable resolution of fatigue. Sponsor employment, an inconsistent funding statement and thin statistical reporting further limit how far the unqualified conclusion can be relied on.

primary_outcome.name: Proportion of patients showing improvement in physical and mental fatigue on CFQ-11 at day 14

issues.title: Conclusion that supplement 'resolves' fatigue rests on a 14-day, single-trial, self-reported outcome
issues.explanation: The conclusion states flatly that the regimen resolves post-COVID fatigue and recommends adding it to multidisciplinary care. The data are a single 14-day trial with no follow-up, a self-reported scale, and a population enrolled a median of about 3 weeks post infection, so durability and effect on chronic fatigue are not shown. The authors acknowledge the lack of follow-up only in the limitations, not in the conclusion; the study supports a short-term symptom-score benefit at day 14, not resolution of fatigue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Follow-up data showing sustained fatigue resolution beyond day 14, or a conclusion explicitly limited to short-term symptom reduction.

quotes.text: This study demonstrates that a 14 days supplementation of ImmunoSEB + ProbioSEB CSC3 resolves post-COVID-19 fatigue.
The treatment period in our study was a one-time intervention of 14 days with no long-term follow up.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does base 'resolves' on one 14-day trial with a self-reported CFQ-11 outcome and no follow-up after day 14, and the Conclusions generalise to long-lasting post-COVID fatigue beyond the early-stage population actually enrolled (mean about 3 weeks, maximum 87 days). The authors do disclose the short duration and lack of follow-up in the limitations, and the blinded placebo-controlled design with a large between-arm difference supports 'reduced' fatigue at day 14 better than it supports durable 'resolution'.

issues.title: No effect sizes/CIs, unadjusted multiple outcomes, and primary endpoint not matching reported headline result
issues.explanation: The paper reports percentages and means with p < 0.001 but no between-group differences with confidence intervals, no per-arm SDs for the efficacy scores, and no multiplicity handling across many time points, subscales and 11 items. The stated primary endpoints (improvement in physical and mental fatigue proportions) differ from the headline outcome (fatigue-free by bimodal total score). With effects this large the direction is unlikely to change, but the size and its precision cannot be judged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-registered protocol specifying fatigue-free status as primary, and reporting of effect sizes with CIs and adjusted p values.

quotes.text: proportion of patients showing improvement in physical fatigue on CFQ-11 and the proportion of patients showing improvement in mental fatigue on CFQ-11 on day 14
The data were analyzed using z test statistics.

issues.title: Funding statement 'no external funding' conflicts with industry sponsorship and employee authors
issues.explanation: The Funding section says the research received no external funding, yet the Acknowledgments say Advanced Enzyme Technologies sponsored the study and the Conflicts section says two authors are its paid employees. Sponsorship and employment are disclosed elsewhere, so the conflict is not concealed, but the funding line is internally inconsistent. The sponsor's role in analysis and reporting is not stated, only that the supplier had no role in design and conduct.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the sponsor is treated as internal funding and that the sponsor had no role in analysis, interpretation or reporting.

quotes.text: This research received no external funding.
A.R. and S.J. are paid employees of Advanced Enzyme Technologies, which sponsored the study

10.3390/medsci14020222.headline_claim: Inspiratory muscle training added to multicomponent exercise did not produce significant between-group differences, but structured exercise programs (with or without IMT) support recovery in severe COVID-19 survivors and IMT may be effective for quality of life and functional status.
10.3390/medsci14020222.overall: The paper supports only that function improved over six weeks in people doing supervised exercise; with no non-exercise comparator and both arms exercising, the 'demonstrated' benefit and any added benefit of IMT are not established. Between-group tests are null in a 15 vs 14 pilot-scale trial, so the IMT claims in the Results go beyond the data, though the Discussion is more careful. Numerous table errors (impossible SDs, inverted CIs, implausible p-values, mis-starred significance) lower confidence in the printed numbers but do not themselves overturn the main findings.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: No untreated control: 'demonstrated' benefit of exercise rests on pre-post changes in both exercising arms
issues.explanation: Both arms received the full exercise programme, so the pre-post gains cannot be separated from natural recovery, learning effects on the tests or regression to the mean. The authors acknowledge this, yet the Conclusions say the study demonstrated that structured exercise supports recovery. The data support only that function improved over six weeks in people doing exercise.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent no-exercise or usual-care arm showing smaller change, or wording limited to describing within-group change.

quotes.text: this trial was designed as a pragmatic, two-arm comparison of rehabilitation strategies rather than a no-intervention control trial
This study demonstrated that structured physical exercise programs can support recovery in COVID-19 survivors

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no untreated control, so 'demonstrated' that exercise supports recovery rests on pre-post changes in both exercising arms, which cannot separate exercise from natural recovery or practice effects. The authors openly flag the missing control group as a key limitation and say improvements may reflect natural recovery, so the problem is the strength of the verb 'demonstrated' in the first Conclusions sentence rather than concealed design information.

issues.title: Results attribute benefits to IMT from within-arm significance although between-group tests are null
issues.explanation: The Results say IMT yielded significant benefits including symptom reduction, and that the magnitude of change was greater in the IMT arm. These statements compare p-values within arms (for example PCFS symptoms p = 0.544 in GEm vs 0.013 in GEmTMI) rather than testing the difference between arms, which was not significant (p = 0.275 at the second assessment). The Conclusions then call the benefits 'clinically meaningful' despite non-significance. The data do not show an added effect of IMT, and the study cannot exclude one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-group (interaction or ANCOVA) analysis showing an advantage of IMT, or wording restricted to 'no evidence of added effect'.

quotes.text: These findings suggest that IMT may be an effective intervention for improving quality of life and functional status in similar populations.
Although between-group differences were not statistically significant, the findings suggest clinically meaningful benefits

second_reader.what_stands: For the PCFS and SF-36 outcomes, the Results text credits IMT with significant benefits based on within-arm p values (significant in GEmTMI, not in GEm) although every between-group test is null, and it claims an IADL improvement that is not significant in GEmTMI (p=0.307). The IPAQ outcomes are an exception, since the between-group difference at time 2 is significant (p=0.002), though no test of change between groups is reported. The Discussion and Conclusions partly hedge, so the overattribution is concentrated in the Table 3 paragraph.

issues.title: Table 1 starred p = 0.048 for hypertension/obesity contradicts text and the counts (8/15 vs 6/14; 10/15 vs 9/14)
issues.explanation: Table 1 prints p = 0.048 with a significance star on the merged hypertension/obesity row. The Results say there was no significant between-group difference in disease prevalence, and the Discussion calls the groups well balanced. The printed counts (hypertension 8/15 vs 6/14, obesity 10/15 vs 9/14) are far too similar to give p near 0.05, so the p-value or the label is wrong. This is a reporting error in a baseline table and does not change the efficacy conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explicit statement of which test produced 0.048 and on which comorbidity, with counts that reproduce it, or a corrected table.

quotes.text: Hypertension ( n ) Obesity ( n ) | 14 19 | 8 10 | 6 9 | 0.048 *
there was no statistically significant evidence of between-group differences in age, sex, weight, height, BMI, or disease prevalence

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 15 vs 14 analysed, so null between-group results cannot show comparability
issues.explanation: The authors explain why no power calculation was done and repeatedly note the limitation. With 15 and 14 per arm, only large differences could be detected, so 'no significant difference' cannot support the claim of 'comparable effectiveness' in the Results. The honest framing in the Discussion mostly addresses this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported power analysis or CIs for the between-group differences that rule out clinically relevant effects.

quotes.text: Therefore, this small sample size should be interpreted as an important limitation, particularly with respect to detecting between-group differences.
No significant between-group differences were observed, suggesting comparable effectiveness of the interventions.

issues.title: Table 1 total weight/height means lie outside both group means; baseline p-values do not match means and SDs
issues.explanation: The total mean weight (93.35 kg) exceeds both group means (92.04 and 83.33), and the total mean height (166.07 cm) exceeds both group means (159.92 and 163.08). That is arithmetically impossible, so a group or total column is mis-printed. Several between-group p-values also do not fit the printed means and SDs, such as weight (p = 0.905) and BMI (p = 0.655), and the peak VO2 comparison in Table 4 (p = 0.45 for 20.70 ± 6.78 vs 13.22 ± 2.61). This leaves it unclear whether the baseline comparability claim is reliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Original data showing the group columns or totals were swapped or mis-typed, with p-values from rank tests that reproduce those printed.

issues.title: Table 5: 6MWT baseline differs between arms (p = 0.043, 344.0 vs 415.54 m) but text says no between-group differences
issues.explanation: Table 5 stars the baseline 6MWT between-group comparison as significant. The Results say no significant between-group differences were observed. A baseline gap of about 71 m in the key functional outcome shows the arms were not comparable at the start, which weakens the 'comparable effectiveness' reading. No baseline adjustment was made. The size of the issue is limited to one outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the baseline difference was tested with a rank test and that the text refers only to post-intervention comparisons.

quotes.text: No significant between-group differences were observed, suggesting comparable effectiveness of the interventions.

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

issues.title: Table 2: several 95% CIs are inverted or exclude their own mean (e.g. 56.81 [98.96/74.67])
issues.explanation: For total emotional role limitations at the 2nd assessment the interval is printed backwards and excludes the mean of 56.81. Other cells show the same kind of fault, such as mental health 58.52 [51.36/56.88] and GEm vitality 45.36 [55.65/55.05]. These CIs cannot be trusted as printed. The p-values and main conclusions do not rest on them, so the damage is limited to this table's reliability.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original tables or SPSS output showing correct intervals, which would show these are typesetting errors.

quotes.location: Table 2, Role Limitations due to Emotional Problems row, Total 2 a
Table 2, Mental Health row, Total 1 a

issues.title: Table 2 SDs of 90.28 (pain) and 55.88 (role-physical) exceed the maximum possible for a 0-100 scale
issues.explanation: Methods say SF-36 domain scores range from 0 to 100, so no SD can exceed about 50. Table 2 prints an SD of 90.28 for GEmTMI pain at the first assessment and 55.88 for total role limitations due to physical health at the second. The printed CIs imply much smaller SDs, so these are probably typos. They are wrong facts in Table 2 and do not affect the main conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing SDs below 50 for these cells (a transcription error), which would still be a correction rather than a refutation.

quotes.location: Table 2, Pain row, GEMTMI 1 a column
Table 2, Role Limitations due to Physical Health row, Total 2 a column

quotes.text: Domain scores range from 0 (worst) to 100 (best).

issues.title: 30 'allocated' vs arms of 15 + 14 = 29; the dropout's arm is not stated and the analysis is completers only
issues.explanation: The text says 30 patients were allocated to groups of 15 and 14, which sum to 29. One patient was excluded for transport difficulties, so the arm sizes are probably the analysed numbers. The paper does not say which arm the dropout belonged to, and the analysis excludes that person (not intention-to-treat). The effect on results is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing 15 and 15 allocated with one dropout from GEmTMI.

quotes.text: The 30 eligible patients were allocated to two rehabilitation groups: the physical exercise group (GEm; n = 15) and the physical exercise plus inspiratory muscle training group (GEmTMI; n = 14).
One patient was excluded from the study due to absences related to transportation difficulties

issues.title: Table 5 legend describes a 30 s sit-to-stand test; Methods describe 60 s, and the table reports a 5-repetition time
issues.explanation: Methods describe a single 60 s sit-to-stand test. The Table 5 legend mentions repetitions per 30 s and per 1 min, while the table rows show a 5-repetition time and a 1-minute count. The five-repetition test is never described in Methods. Readers cannot tell exactly which tests were run, but the main result (1-minute count) is clear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Methods description of both a 5-repetition test and a 30 s test.

quotes.text: completed as many sit-to-stand repetitions as possible in 60 s.
sit-to-stand test (STS; repetitions/30 s and 1 min)

10.3390/metabo16080594.headline_claim: Six weeks of supplementation with Lactobacillus helveticus Rosell-52 and Bifidobacterium longum Rosell-175 improves mood and reduces anxiety and depressive symptom severity in people with post-COVID anxiety/depressive symptoms, with changes associated with fecal SCFA concentrations.
10.3390/metabo16080594.overall: The large between-group differences on HADS, GAD-7, BDI and some SCL-90 subscales give plausible support for symptom improvement in the 56 completers. The wording 'unequivocally' and 'leads to' overstates a small, completers-only, uncorrected trial. The prevalence analyses are within-arm only and their p-values do not reproduce, the SCL-90 GSI scale is unexplained, and the SCFA link rests on one scale.

primary_outcome.name: Change in perceived anxiety/depression measured with the Polish Hopkins Symptom Checklist (SCL-90); Global Severity Index reported

issues.title: 'Unequivocally demonstrated' and 'leads to improved mood' overstate a small 56-completer 6-week trial
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the trial unequivocally demonstrated improvement, and the Conclusions say supplementation leads to improved mood. The evidence is 28 completers per arm, one site, six weeks, completers-only analysis, no multiplicity control, and a sample-size assumption that is not coherent. The SCFA 'association' is correlational, as the paper itself says elsewhere. A tentative claim of benefit fits; 'unequivocal' does not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger or replicated trial with a corrected, intention-to-treat primary analysis showing the same effect.

quotes.text: unequivocally demonstrated that the administration of
leads to improved mood and a reduction in the intensity of psychological symptoms
The study was conducted with a relatively small sample size

second_reader.what_stands: The wording 'unequivocally demonstrated' and 'leads to improved mood' is stronger than a 6-week, 56-completer, single-site trial analysed on completers only (6 of 62 lost, 4 vs 2 between arms), with self-report outcomes, many unadjusted tests and no multiplicity correction, can support; the authors do acknowledge small sample size in the limitations and open the Conclusions with 'may benefit', but they do not carry that caution into the Discussion's first sentence or the Conclusions' main statement. The effect sizes on the scales are large, so the direction of the finding is not in question, o

issues.title: SCL-90 Global Severity Index printed as 10.5 (mean item score cannot exceed 5; subscales all below 1.8)
issues.explanation: The Methods define the SCL-90 as an average over five-point items, and an average above 2 is called high. Table 2 reports baseline GSI means of 10.5 and 11.7 and follow-up values of 6.5 and 10.2, while every Table 3 subscale mean is at or below 1.8. The GSI cannot be the item average the Methods describe, so the units are unexplained and the GSI result cannot be interpreted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the GSI in Table 2 is a summed or otherwise transformed score, with its range.

quotes.location: Table 2, SCL-90 Global severity index row, PG baseline

quotes.text: An average score of greater than 2 points for any group of items is considered high.

issues.title: No multiplicity control across ~15 outcomes and SCFA correlations; SCFA-link claim rests on one scale (HADS-A)
issues.explanation: All tests used alpha 0.05 with no correction, across HADS, GAD-7, BDI, nine SCL-90 subscales, three SCFAs and several correlations. The psychological effects are large enough to survive correction, but the Conclusion that the changes were associated with SCFA changes rests on correlations with HADS-A only. The Discussion itself says this was not confirmed with other tests. The Discussion also says the SCL-90 confirms improvement, though only some subscales differed at follow-up.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction showing the SCFA-symptom association and the secondary results still hold.

quotes.text: Hypotheses were tested at a significance level of 0.05.
The observed changes were associated with changes in short-chain fatty acid concentrations in feces.

issues.title: Prevalence reductions tested only within arms; control arm also fell (HADS-A 27→15 of 28)
issues.explanation: The reported prevalence reductions come from before/after chi-square tests inside the PG, with no PG vs CG comparison. Control-arm counts also fell, notably HADS-A from 27 to 15 of 28, which is significant by the authors' own method. A within-arm drop therefore does not show an effect of the psychobiotic. Yates chi-square also treats the same participants at two time points as independent groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-arm comparison of follow-up or change in case counts, with a paired or adjusted method, favouring the PG.

quotes.text: was observed after the supplementation period in the PG.
* statistically significant differences.

issues.title: Completers-only analysis: 56 of 62 randomized analysed (4 PG, 2 CG lost), no ITT or sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: All efficacy tables use 28 per arm, not the 32 and 30 randomized. The six dropouts did not attend the final visit and gave no reason. No intention-to-treat analysis or missing-data sensitivity analysis is reported, although the paper claims CONSORT conformity. The effect sizes make a reversal unlikely, so this weakens rather than undermines the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or multiple-imputation analysis of all 62 randomized participants giving similar between-group differences.

quotes.text: Ultimately, 56 patients completed the study (90.3%).
None of the patients who completed the study reported any adverse events.

issues.title: Prevalence p-values (0.0044, 0.0219, 0.0011) do not match Yates chi-square on Table 4 counts
issues.explanation: The Methods state Yates-corrected chi-square tests on the prevalence data. Applying that test to the PG baseline vs follow-up counts in Table 4 gives p-values different from those printed: much smaller for HADS-A and GAD-7, and larger for BDI. This suggests a different or paired test, or a table or reporting error, and the method is not specified. The direction of each result holds except that the BDI p is about 15 times larger than printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods or supplementary output showing the test actually used (for example McNemar or an exact test) and reproducing the printed p-values from the counts.

quotes.text: a chi-square test with Yates’ correction for continuity was conducted to examine the impact of the psychobiotic intervention on the psychological test outcomes
was observed after the supplementation period in the PG.

issues.title: Table 5: two 95% CIs cannot contain their means (acetic 34.7 vs 26.4–31.1; propionic 11.5 vs 7.8–5.3)
issues.explanation: Two Table 5 intervals are mis-printed. The PG follow-up acetic acid mean of 34.7 ± 21.5 (n = 28) implies a CI of about 26.4 to 43.0, but the printed CI is 26.4–31.1, with an upper bound below the mean. The CG baseline propionic acid CI (7.8–5.3) is reversed and fits 7.8–15.3 with a lost leading digit. These are reporting slips in secondary SCFA data; none changes a significance result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data or a corrigendum showing the intended upper bounds are 31.1 and 5.3 under a different interval method.

quotes.location: Table 5, Acetic acid row, PG follow-up mean
Table 5, Acetic acid row, PG follow-up 95% CI
Table 5, Propionic acid row, CG baseline 95% CI

10.3390/microorganisms14040734.headline_claim: Multi-strain probiotic supplementation modulated gut microbiota taxonomic composition and predicted functional potential, with more evident effects in individuals with long COVID.
10.3390/microorganisms14040734.overall: The headline conclusion that the probiotic promoted microbiota modulation, especially in long COVID, rests on a non-randomised, no-placebo comparison with non-equivalent arms and on a handful of unadjusted nominal p-values in small subgroups. Global diversity and structure showed no effect, and the biochemical findings were all non-significant. The study is best read as exploratory, hypothesis-generating work, and the reporting inconsistencies (sex counts, severity counts, Prevotella_9 direction) lower confidence further without changing that reading.

primary_outcome.name: Change (t1-t0) in gut microbiota composition, genus-level differential abundance, probiotic vs control (no primary outcome is named in the text)

issues.title: Non-random, no-placebo comparison with non-equivalent arms (control is 25/40 healthy) supports causal wording
issues.explanation: Allocation was non-random and the control group received nothing, so the 'double-blind' label cannot hold. In the whole-cohort comparison, the control arm is mostly healthy people with a different baseline microbiota, versus infected participants in the probiotic arm. The arms also differ by clinical group and sex. Any difference in change over time can reflect group differences, regression to the mean or season rather than the probiotic. The causal conclusion that probiotics 'promoted' modulation is therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses restricted to infected participants with covariate adjustment (clinical group, sex, baseline abundance), or evidence that the control group received a matching placebo.

quotes.text: Due to non-random allocation and unequal distribution of participants, the study was analyzed as an interventional study, rather than a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
while participants in the control group did not receive probiotic supplementation

second_reader.what_stands: The arms are non-equivalent (62.5% of controls are healthy never-infected people, none in the probiotic arm), there is no placebo, and allocation was non-random; this is acknowledged in Methods 2.1 and the limitations. Wording is largely associational ('associated with', 'causality cannot be inferred'), but 'probiotic intervention was responsible for', 'promoted the modulation' and 'selectively enriched' are causal, and the 'double-blind' label is inconsistent with an untreated control arm.

issues.title: Hundreds of genus, pathway and correlation tests at unadjusted p<0.05, with p<0.1 read as trends
issues.explanation: The Methods define significance as p < 0.05 and report 0.05-0.1 as trends, with no correction for the many genera (323), pathways and correlation pairs tested. In the long COVID subgroup of 13 vs 10, a handful of nominal hits (p = 0.013-0.028) is within what chance would produce. The functional 'signature' rests on essentially one pathway family (identical estimates 0.893, SE 0.445, p = 0.048-0.049). These results are exploratory and cannot support the stated taxonomic and functional modulation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: FDR-adjusted q-values in Tables S1-S3 showing the highlighted genera and pathways remain significant after correction.

quotes.text: Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05, while results with 0.05 < p < 0.1 were reported as trends
This analysis identified a set of functional pathways significantly enriched in long COVID individuals receiving probiotics ( p < 0.05; Table 5).
a total of 217 significant correlations were detected

second_reader.what_stands: Hundreds of genus, pathway and correlation tests are interpreted at unadjusted p<0.05, with p<0.1 reported as trends, and the Methods describe no multiplicity correction. The exact number of tests is not printed in the main text, and the Discussion does call the trends tentative, but the headline significant findings (e.g. p = 0.013-0.028 among 323 genera) would not be expected to survive correction.

issues.title: Conclusion highlights 'more evident' long COVID effects from unadjusted subgroup counts (13 vs 10)
issues.explanation: The conclusion says probiotics modulated composition and function, with more evident effects in long COVID. That comparison is based on the number of nominally significant genera in a 13 vs 10 subgroup, not on a formal subgroup-by-treatment interaction test. Global community structure showed no change. The subgroup result is hypothesis-generating at best, and the conclusion presents it as a finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified subgroup hypothesis and a significant treatment-by-group interaction test for the genera highlighted.

quotes.text: with more evident effects in individuals with long COVID.
PERMANOVAbased on Bray-Curtis distances showed no differences between probiotic and control groups (F = 0.83, p = 0.422)

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of 'more evident effects in individuals with long COVID' rests on a larger number of nominally significant genera in a 13 vs 10 subgroup, without any test of whether the effect differs between long COVID and other participants, and alongside null global diversity results. The subgroup has a different comparator (long COVID controls rather than a mixed healthy-dominated control group), so the count comparison does not demonstrate a stronger effect.

issues.title: Conclusion treats non-significant CRP/ALT/AST/ferritin trends (p 0.058-0.099) as support for host homeostasis
issues.explanation: None of the biochemical differences reached p < 0.05, and the ferritin trend runs in the opposite direction from the others. The abstract-level conclusion nonetheless cites a 'consistent trend of inflammatory and metabolic markers decrease' as support, and suggests probiotics may restore host homeostasis. Nothing in the study measures host homeostasis or symptoms. The conclusion goes beyond what these data can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted analyses with pre-specified biochemical endpoints reaching significance, or symptom and homeostasis measures showing benefit.

quotes.text: Although none of these differences reached statistical significance, effect size estimates indicated moderate effects across the evaluated biomarkers
These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions may contribute to the restoration of gut ecosystem stability and host homeostasis during long COVID recovery.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion treats non-significant biochemical trends (p 0.058-0.099, from a 13 vs 10 subgroup among many markers) as support for restored 'host homeostasis' and 'a consistent trend of inflammatory and metabolic markers decrease', although ferritin rose and no marker reached p<0.05. The Results and Discussion do label them non-significant, so the overstatement is mainly in the Conclusion.

issues.title: Female count is 61 in Table 2 but 58 in Table 3 for the same 74 participants
issues.explanation: Table 2 splits the 74 analysed participants by clinical group and gives 61 women. Table 3 splits the same 74 by intervention arm and gives 58 women. A participant's sex cannot change between tables, so at least one table is wrong by 3 people. This affects the sex-balance comparison in Table 3, which is the one that matters for the confounding discussion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or a statement that Table 2 and Table 3 use different participant sets or sex definitions.

issues.title: Prospective human intervention with no trial registration or pre-specified outcomes reported
issues.explanation: The study is described as an interventional study with a 12-week probiotic given to people, yet no registry number is reported. The primary outcome is also never defined. It is therefore impossible to tell which of the many genus, pathway and biochemical outcomes were planned and which were chosen after seeing the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (or protocol) dated before enrolment that lists the same outcomes.

quotes.text: This study was designed as a double-blind, single-center, double-arm interventional study, with a previously published cross-sectional analysis of the same cohort
The study was approved by the University Hospital Medical Centre 'Bežanijska kosa' Ethics Committee (approval number 2237/2)

issues.title: Between-group biochemical comparison described as Wilcoxon signed-rank; r and p imply N of about 22
issues.explanation: Table 6's legend says group differences in Δ values were assessed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which is for paired data, not for comparing a probiotic group with a control group. It is not clear which test produced the p-values. If r = Z/√N, then p = 0.058 (Z ≈ 1.89) and r = 0.405 imply N ≈ 22, far fewer than the 74 participants said to be analysed. The number of participants with biochemical data per arm is not reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that a rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) test was used and a table giving the n per arm for each biochemical marker.

quotes.text: Differences between groups were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test applied to ∆ values.
Biochemical parameters were evaluated by comparing within-group paired sample changes ( ∆ , t1-t0) using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

issues.title: Prevotella_9 'lower' after probiotic, yet printed change is +0.019 vs -0.030 in controls
issues.explanation: The Results text says Prevotella_9 was lower with probiotics, but the printed Δ values show a rise in the probiotic group and a fall in controls. The targeted test (p = 0.013) would then indicate an increase, not a decrease. The Discussion repeats the beneficial reading ('not stimulated... exhibited decreasing trends'). Either the numbers or the description is wrong, and the direction of a genus labelled 'potentially pathogenic' matters for the claimed benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data or Figure 4 showing the probiotic Δ is negative and the control Δ positive, i.e. a transposition error in the text.

quotes.text: a lower relative abundance of Prevotella
∆ probiotic = 0.019, ∆ control = -0.030, p = 0.013

issues.title: Table 4 probiotic severity counts sum to 12, but the group has 13 participants
issues.explanation: The probiotic long COVID column is headed n = 13, but mild, moderate and severe counts add to only 12. The percentages are computed on 13 and total 92%. One participant has no severity category and this is not explained. The severity comparison (p = 0.74) is therefore based on an unstated 12 versus 10.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that one participant's severity was missing, or a corrected count for one category.

quotes.text: Probiotic (n = 13)

issues.title: Figure 5 caption gives ρ > 0.4 while text and panel title use |ρ| > 0.3
issues.explanation: Section 3.6 defines significant correlations as |ρ| > 0.3 with p < 0.05, but the Figure 5 caption says ρ > 0.4. The supplement shows the authors used different thresholds for different outputs, so this may be a display choice. It is still not stated for Figure 5 which threshold produced the plotted and counted associations. This is a minor labelling inconsistency with no effect on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Figure 5 uses a stricter display threshold than the 0.3 used for counting significant correlations.

quotes.text: Correlations with | ρ | > 0.3 and p < 0.05
ρ > 0.4, p < 0.05; Green indicates positive correlations

10.3390/neurosci3020021.headline_claim: Long COVID may be explained by oxidative stress and parasympathetic/sympathetic dysfunction, and autonomic therapy produces positive outcomes and may restore quality of life.
10.3390/neurosci3020021.overall: The descriptive finding that autonomic classifications and symptom counts worsened after COVID and were lower at follow-up is plausible as a hypothesis-generating observation. The causal claims (oxidative-stress mechanism, therapy effect, restored quality of life) are not supported by an uncontrolled, single-device retrospective series, and several follow-up percentages and p-values cannot be reconciled with the stated N=152 or with the Results text.

primary_outcome.name: Autonomic dysfunction prevalence and symptom count (no single prespecified primary outcome identified)

issues.title: No control group: improvement after therapy cannot be attributed to autonomic treatment
issues.explanation: All 152 patients are compared only with their own earlier tests, with no untreated or alternatively treated group. Regression to the mean is likely because follow-up followed abnormal tests, and natural recovery, time since infection, concurrent care and repeat-testing effects are also possible. The statements that therapy 'has been shown' to improve outcomes and quality of life are therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or sham comparison group, or a validated quality-of-life measure showing change beyond that expected from natural course.

quotes.text: Autonomic therapy has been shown to provide positive outcomes and improvement in patients quality of life.
Further studies are needed, including blinded, controlled studies.

second_reader.what_stands: The study has no control group, so the improvements after therapy cannot be attributed to autonomic treatment, yet the Conclusions say therapy 'has been shown to provide positive outcomes' and improve quality of life. The authors do label the study hypothesis-generating and call for blinded, controlled studies, which partly tempers the claim, but the causal wording in Conclusions and Discussion is not supported by the design (and quality of life was not measured directly; only P&S tests and a symptom count were reported).

issues.title: Conclusions assert oxidative-stress mechanism, 'all' long-COVID symptoms and restored quality of life
issues.explanation: The data are device-based autonomic classifications and symptom counts in 152 selected patients with prior autonomic disease, without controls. No oxidative stress marker and no quality-of-life measure was collected. The claims that oxidative stress causes the dysfunction, that it may explain all long-COVID symptoms, and that therapy restores quality of life go well beyond these data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Oxidative stress biomarkers, a validated quality-of-life instrument and a comparison group in the same cohort.

quotes.text: may explain all of the symptoms of long-COVID syndrome
patient quality of life may be restored

second_reader.what_stands: The study provides no data on oxidative stress or quality of life, so the Abstract's oxidative-stress mechanism and 'all of the symptoms' claim, and the Conclusions' statement that mitochondrial damage 'leads to' P&S dysfunction, go beyond what was measured, and the cohort was pre-selected for autonomic dysfunction with no comparison group. The claims are phrased with 'may' and the study is described as hypothesis-generating, so the paper does not assert them as established, and the Abstract's 'SARS-CoV-2, via its oxidative stress, can lead to' is the least hedged part.

issues.title: All autonomic outcomes come from one proprietary monitor; classification thresholds not validated here
issues.explanation: Sympathetic withdrawal, parasympathetic excess and the AAD/CAN categories all come from a single commercial monitor made by the corresponding author's company. The paper asserts it is 'uniquely capable' but offers no validation, reliability or cut-off justification beyond self-citations. Whether this matters depends on external validation the paper does not show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Independent validation data for the monitor's cut-offs in post-COVID populations, or test-retest reliability data.

quotes.text: P&S monitoring differs from the other autonomic monitors, in that it is uniquely capable of independently and simultaneously measuring the two individual autonomic branches
AAD and DAN indicate an increased morbidity risk and CAN indicates an increased mortality risk.

issues.title: Table 3 follow-up percentages do not match counts over N=152 (e.g. 41 = 27.2%, 25 = 16.2%)
issues.explanation: Table 3 is headed N=152, and the baseline and post-COVID rows agree with that. Several pre-COVID follow-up and post-COVID follow-up cells do not: 41/152 is 27.0 (printed 27.2), 25/152 is 16.4 (printed 16.2), and 11/152 is 7.2 (printed 7.5). This suggests some follow-up tests had fewer patients, with the actual denominators unreported, so the paired comparisons may rest on a different set of patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that all 152 patients were tested at every timepoint, with corrected percentages, or the stated per-timepoint denominators.

quotes.location: Table 3, Pre-COVID-19 Follow-up row, SW column
Table 3, Post-COVID-19 Follow-up row, PE column

issues.title: Statistical methods undefined: test, pairing, comparison and multiplicity unspecified for ~18 p-values
issues.explanation: The methods say only that 'Pearson correlation and Student's t-test' were run in SPSS. The paper does not say which timepoints each p-value compares, whether tests were paired, how prevalence percentages were tested, or whether any adjustment was made for about 18 p-values. Some p-values for symptom counts also differ between the Results text and Table 3. The directional findings are likely robust, but the p-values cannot be verified as reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement specifying paired tests for each comparison, with SDs and adjusted p-values, and a reconciled p-value table.

quotes.text: The Pearson correlation and Student's t -test statistics are based on SPSS v. 20.

issues.title: Discussion gives pre-COVID sympathetic withdrawal as 45.7%; Table 3 and 69/152 give 45.4%
issues.explanation: The Discussion quotes 45.7% for pre-COVID sympathetic withdrawal. Table 3 prints 69 (45.4), and 69 of 152 is 45.4%. The error is small and does not change the finding that sympathetic withdrawal was more common than parasympathetic excess.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 45.7% comes from a different denominator or subset (e.g. 69/151 = 45.7%) that the paper defines.

quotes.text: patients presented to the clinics with more sympathetic withdrawal (45.7%)

issues.title: Headache/migraine 71/152 printed as 46.9% in Table 2 and Results; arithmetic gives 46.7%
issues.explanation: Table 2 and the Results prose both give 71 patients (46.9%) with headache or migraine. Seventy-one of 152 is 46.7%, which is how the same count is printed in Table 3. This is a trivial reporting slip that affects no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A defined subset size for which 71 gives 46.9% (about n = 151.4, not an integer) or a correction to the table.

quotes.text: nearly half (46.9%) reported generalized pain

script.explanation: 71/152 = 46.71%, but the paper prints 46.9, outside the rounding interval [46.85, 47.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 151.4 rather than 152.

10.3390/nu14112203.headline_claim: Fermented papaya and noni syrups (FFS) are clinically effective for post-COVID syndrome, improving symptoms, heart and lung function, and immune/metabolic markers versus placebo honey.
10.3390/nu14112203.overall: The headline claim of clinical efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness is not well supported: the design is unblinded in practice or unreported, randomization and analysis methods are unclear, and no safety or cost data exist. Several text-table contradictions (Borg direction, p-value signs, symptom counts) further reduce reliability, and the placebo arms also improved on most measures.

primary_outcome.name: not specified as primary; total average symptom score from 22-item self-assessment questionnaire

issues.title: Conclusion claims clinical effectiveness, safety and cost-effectiveness without adverse event or cost data
issues.explanation: No adverse events or costs are reported, yet the conclusion calls the approach safe and cost-effective. Heart and lung improvement is asserted although Borg dyspnea rose in all groups and ECG improvements occurred in placebo arms as well, with no between-arm test. The strength of the conclusion exceeds the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported adverse event and cost data supporting safety and cost-effectiveness.

quotes.text: This approach could be considered as safe and cost-effective way to address post-COVID patients’ quality of life

second_reader.what_stands: The Results contain no adverse event, tolerability or cost data, so the conclusion that the approach is safe and cost-effective rests only on background statements and cited literature, not on data from this trial. The claim of clinical effectiveness is also stated more strongly than the evidence supports (see the Borg and multiplicity issues), though the safety and cost wording is softened by 'could be considered'.

issues.title: Ordinal 0-2 scores summarised as mean±SD and tested with Fisher/t-test despite stating non-normal data
issues.explanation: The methods say data were non-normal so nonparametric tests were used, then apply Student's t-test to connected data and Fisher's exact test to mean scores. Fisher's test requires counts, not means, and the tables print only mean±SD (some odd, e.g. 0.04±0.01 and 0.2±0.02). The symptom p-values cannot be verified or matched to a coherent method.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw item-level data and a clear, appropriate test for each comparison.

quotes.text: Since the distribution of the data was significantly different from normal, nonparametric statistics were used.
To evaluate the difference between connected data, the two-tailed Student’s <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>-test was applied

second_reader.what_stands: The paper summarises ordinal 0-2 scores as mean ± SD and states that a Student's t-test (a parametric test) was used for paired data while also saying the data were non-normal and nonparametric methods were applied; it also reports Fisher's exact p-values without any counts or contingency tables. The methods are internally inconsistent and the printed SDs look implausibly small for such scores (they resemble SEMs), though the paper does not show which test produced which reported p-value.

issues.title: 22 symptom tests with no multiplicity control; 'more effective for all 22' contradicts non-significant rows
issues.explanation: Twenty-two items were tested at p<0.05 in each of two strata, with no correction. The Discussion claims FFS was more effective for all 22 symptoms, but several rows (body weight, hair loss, anxiety, dryness in severe, and many in moderate) show no difference. The overall conclusion is overstated relative to the table.
