issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary outcome or an adjusted analysis keeping the findings.

quotes.text: Collectively, for all 22 clinical symptoms analysed, FFS was remarkably more effective than placebo.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports roughly 22 item-level tests per cohort with an uncorrected alpha of 0.05 and no multiplicity control or primary outcome, and the statement that FFS was more effective for all 22 symptoms is contradicted by its own tables, where several rows (e.g. hair loss, bodyweight, and in the moderate cohort 10 or more items) show no significant difference. The Discussion itself concedes no effect on bodyweight and hair loss.

issues.title: No blinding statement; main outcome is patient-reported and placebo differs in taste
issues.explanation: The paper never states who was blinded. The FFS syrup is described as sweet, acidic, slightly bitter and unpleasant, whereas the placebo is honey in water, so patients may infer allocation. The primary symptom outcome is self-reported, so expectation effects could produce the symptom differences.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of double-blind procedures with matched placebo.

quotes.text: The questionnaire containing 22 questions on patients’ subjective opinions was recommended to be filled out in the beginning and at the cessation of the trial.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper contains no statement that participants, treating clinicians or outcome assessors were blinded, and the placebo (diluted honey) plausibly tastes different from the described FFS syrups, while the main reported effects come from a patient-reported questionnaire. The risk of bias from unmasking is therefore real and unaddressed, though the paper does not show that unblinding actually occurred.

issues.title: Group 3 Borg 'significantly improved' but Table 5 shows 10.8 rising to 11.8 and vs placebo
issues.explanation: The text calls the Group 3 Borg change an improvement, while the table shows a higher score after the trial with significance marks versus baseline and versus placebo. Under the standard scale this is worse dyspnea in the FFS arm, the opposite of the claim. Values above 10 also exceed the stated 1-10 range. Duplicate-adjacent to c2 but concerns a different group and a significance claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the Borg scale was reversed or the table columns swapped.

quotes.text: Borg’s score was statistically significantly improved as compare to the beginning of the trial in Group 3

second_reader.what_stands: The tabulated Borg scores in Group 3 went up (10.8 to 11.8) and are higher than placebo (11.8 vs 10.8), which on a dyspnea scale means worse or no better, so calling this a significant improvement contradicts the table. The text also describes Groups 1 and 2 as 'diminished' when the printed values rose, and several values exceed the stated 1-10 range; the paper does not explain these inconsistencies (the p-value flags show significance of a change in the unfavourable direction).

issues.title: Symptom outcome is a 22-item questionnaire developed for the study, with no validation reported
issues.explanation: The symptom score is built from a new, unvalidated questionnaire. This weakens interpretation of the symptom results but is common in exploratory trials.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Published validation of the instrument.

quotes.text: A special questionnaire for the self-assessment of post-COVID patients was developed and recommended to be filled up by all participants of the trial.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation reported; placebo arms of 27 and 29 with efficacy claimed in each stratum
issues.explanation: No power calculation is given. Placebo arms are small and the conclusion claims efficacy in both strata. Small arms mainly make the sparse significant findings fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation.

quotes.text: clinically effective improving deteriorated heart and lung functions

issues.title: No trial registration identifier reported for a randomized placebo-controlled trial
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval but no registry ID, so outcome selection among many symptom items cannot be checked against a prior plan.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry with prespecified outcomes.

quotes.text: The study protocol was scrutinized and approved by the local Ethical Committee

issues.title: Borg dyspnea said to diminish in groups 1 and 2, but Table 5 shows rises (7.1→9.4, 7.3→9.1)
issues.explanation: The text says dyspnea was equally diminished in both severe-COVID groups. Table 5 shows scores increasing significantly in both (superscript 1), which on the usual scale means worse dyspnea. Methods also say scores run 1 to 10, yet values reach 9.4 to 11.8, so the scale is unexplained. Dyspnea therefore gives no support for the lung-benefit claim and may indicate worsening in all arms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Borg was scored on a reversed scale (higher = better) or that the table columns are mislabelled.

quotes.text: subjective dyspnea assessed by a Borg’s score was equally diminished for both the experimental and the placebo groups

issues.title: Product manufacturer named but no funder role or conflicts statement in the text
issues.explanation: The supplement is made by Carica Ltd. and no funding or conflict statement appears in the provided text. It may be in omitted back-matter, so this cannot be settled from the text alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A funding and conflict-of-interest statement.

quotes.text: manufactured by Carica Ltd., in Manila, The Philippines

issues.title: Randomization unexplained; arms are 64/27 and 68/29, about 70:30 splits, with no method or concealment
issues.explanation: The paper says only that patients were randomly placed into four groups. No sequence generation, concealment or allocation ratio is given, and the unequal FFS vs placebo sizes are unexplained. Without these, allocation bias cannot be excluded, and the causal reading of FFS vs placebo differences is weakened.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol describing a 70:30 allocation with concealed central randomization.

quotes.text: were randomly placed into four groups

issues.title: ECG and symptom benefit rests partly on within-arm before/after change; placebo arms also improved
issues.explanation: Symptom tables compare after-trial scores between arms (not change from baseline), and ECG/lung claims compare percentages before vs after within arms with no between-arm test. Placebo arms also improved on most items, so within-arm change cannot be attributed to FFS. The between-group symptom comparison is partly present, so the issue is narrower than stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified between-arm test of change on ECG measures.

quotes.text: Fisher’s exact test was used to determine the significance of the differences between the beginning and cessation of the trial

issues.title: Results text gives p > 0.05 for 'significantly different' total score; Table 3 prints p < 0.05
issues.explanation: The text says total average scores differed significantly between FFS and placebo but prints p > 0.05, contradicting itself and Table 3 (p < 0.05). The table value is likely right, so this is a typo-level inconsistency. It changes no conclusion but is a visible error in a headline sentence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the intended p was indeed above 0.05 and the table is wrong would change which printing is wrong, but not that they conflict.

quotes.text: Total average scores of all symptoms together were significantly different for FFS and placebo groups (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> > 0.05)

issues.title: Text reports 11 significant less-pronounced symptoms; Table 2 shows 10 (baseline 0.6-1.4)
issues.explanation: Table 2 has ten p<0.05 rows with baseline 0.6-1.4 outside the three top symptoms. The text says 11. The ambiguity in defining the group makes this a minor count discrepancy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A defined 11th row meeting the stated criteria.

quotes.text: statistically significant differences between FFS and placebo groups were obtained for 11 symptoms

issues.title: Text reports 4 trending symptoms in moderate-COVID groups; Table 3 shows 3
issues.explanation: Only memory impairment, attention concentration and headache carry 0.05<p<0.1 in Table 3. The text counts four. A small count discrepancy with no bearing on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A fourth Table 3 row with 0.05<p<0.1.

quotes.text: A trending difference between the groups after the trial was observed for 4 symptoms.

issues.title: Discussion lists anxiety/depression as trend-level; tables show p<0.05 (Table 2 depression) or p>0.05
issues.explanation: The Discussion says anxiety/depression had a trend, but no table gives a trend for them. The results section names dizziness as a trend, which the Discussion omits. A minor text-table inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table row giving 0.05<p<0.1 for anxiety or depression.

quotes.text: Perception of changes in memory and attention impairment as well as anxiety/depression, and headache had a trend to statistical difference between FFS and placebo groups

issues.title: Methods text codes symptom presence as 0 and absence as 1; tables code Yes=1, No=0
issues.explanation: The Results text states the reverse of the coding shown in the tables. Reading by the text would invert the direction of the binary items. Likely a wording slip, but the scoring definition is unreliable as written.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the table labels, not the text, are reversed.

quotes.text: existences or absences of a symptom were scored as 0 and 1, respectively

10.3390/nu14153004.headline_claim: 1-MNA supplementation significantly improved physical performance in a 6-minute walk test and reduced the percentage of patients with severe fatigue after COVID-19.
10.3390/nu14153004.overall: The walking-distance benefit is plausible but rests on a non-random alternating allocation, no placebo and no stated blinding, and its size is reported inconsistently between text and Table 2. The fatigue claim is weaker: mean FSS did not differ, the 1-MNA count with FSS≥4 was unchanged, the Discussion contradicts itself, and the baseline counts conflict with the reported medians. Registration was retrospective and the primary/secondary status of FSS differs from the registry, so conclusions should be treated as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance

issues.title: Fatigue claim rests on a Phase 1 FSS≥4 count (5 vs 14); mean FSS not different and 1-MNA count unchanged
issues.explanation: The abstract and Conclusions say 1-MNA reduced severe fatigue, based on a Phase 1 comparison of 5/25 vs 14/25 patients with FSS≥4. Mean FSS did not differ between arms, fatigue scores rose in both, and the 1-MNA count did not change from baseline (5 to 5). The Discussion says both that fewer patients had fatigue and that supplementation did not reduce the number reporting fatigue. The claim is better stated as 'fewer 1-MNA patients had worsening fatigue relative to a no-treatment control'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis showing a between-arm difference in FSS change, or a different reading of the Discussion statement.

quotes.text: 1-MNA supplementation did not result in a reduction in the number of people reporting fatigue.
As in the comparison of FSS in Phase 1, the differences between Gr NO-1-MNA and Gr 1-MNA were not statistically significant.
significantly fewer patients reported significant fatigue, defined as an FSS score ≥ 4, after one month of supplementation

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of reduced severe fatigue rests on a Phase 1 threshold count (5 vs 14) that arises from an increase in the control arm, not a decrease in the 1-MNA arm. Mean FSS did not differ significantly between groups and rose in both. The paper's own Discussion says that 1-MNA did not reduce the number of people reporting fatigue, which conflicts with its Abstract and Conclusion.

issues.title: Baseline FSS medians (4.44, 4.54) incompatible with only 5 and 6 of 25 patients having FSS ≥ 4
issues.explanation: Table 1 reports median baseline FSS of 4.44 and 4.54, so at least 13 of 25 patients in each arm must have scored at or above those values. The text says only 5 (20%) and 6 (24%) had FSS ≥ 4 at baseline. One of these sets of figures is wrong. Because the fatigue conclusion rests on the FSS≥4 counts, this undermines trust in that binary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual FSS data or a corrected table showing medians below 4 or counts of 13 or more with FSS ≥ 4.

quotes.text: In Phase 0, five pts (20%) in Gr 1-MNA had an FSS score ≥ 4.
In Gr NO-1-MNA the number of patients with an FSS score ≥ 4 was six (24%) (NS).

second_reader.what_stands: The baseline medians in Table 1 (4.44 and 4.54) require at least 13 of 25 patients per group to have FSS ≥ 4. The text reports only 5 and 6. The two statements cannot both be correct, and the paper does not say which is wrong. Which number is in error cannot be determined from the paper.

issues.title: Alternating allocation by entry order described as randomization; no concealment
issues.explanation: Patients were assigned one to 1-MNA, the next to control, and so on. This is predictable allocation, not randomization, and it offers no allocation concealment. Enrolling clinicians could know the next assignment and influence who enters which arm. The between-group claims are therefore from a non-randomized comparison, even though Table 1 shows balanced baselines.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a concealed, computer-generated sequence was used and the alternating description is wrong.

quotes.text: Pts were randomized according to the order in which they entered the study-one patient to the 1-MNA group, the next patient to NO-1-MNA, etc.
The groups were randomized: Gr NO-1-MNA-25 pts

second_reader.what_stands: The paper calls an alternating, entry-order allocation 'randomization'. The sequence was predictable by anyone who knew the previous assignment, and the paper describes no allocation concealment. The study is better described as quasi-randomized, with a risk of selection bias.

issues.title: No-supplement control with unblinded self-reported FSS; placebo effect acknowledged but not reflected in conclusions
issues.explanation: The control arm received nothing, with no placebo and no described blinding. The FSS is a self-completed questionnaire, so expectation effects can drive it. The authors concede a placebo effect cannot be ruled out, yet the abstract and Conclusions state the fatigue benefit without that caveat. The 6MWT is also effort-dependent and the assessor was not stated to be blinded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of blinded outcome assessment and a sham or placebo control.

quotes.text: Gr 1: NO-1-MNA-without supplementation;
It cannot be ruled out that the 1-MNA group experienced a placebo effect.

second_reader.what_stands: The control group got no supplement and no placebo, and the paper does not describe blinding. FSS is self-reported, and the 6MWT depends on patient effort. The placebo limitation is acknowledged in the Discussion, but the Abstract and Conclusions state efficacy without that caveat, so the limitation is only partly reflected in the conclusions.

issues.title: Registered about six months after study start (registry: start 2021-01-08, submitted 2021-07-12)
issues.explanation: The paper cites registration as if prospective but does not state that it was done after enrolment began. Registry dates show submission about 6 months after the recorded start. This limits confidence that the outcomes, thresholds and analyses were set in advance, which matters given the primary/secondary discrepancy and the FSS≥4 emphasis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the protocol and outcomes were fixed before the first enrolment, for example earlier registry history or a protocol date.

quotes.text: Patients from registered ClinicalTrials.gov identifier-NCT04961476 were included in the analysis.
The study enrolled 50 consecutive patients who met the inclusion criteria for the study.

issues.title: Walking claim cites within-arm p = 0.000034; Table 2 p-values sit in mislabelled rows
issues.explanation: The abstract's evidence for walking benefit is the 1-MNA arm's change from baseline (p = 0.000034), which cannot be attributed to treatment. The between-arm test of change (p = 0.0016) is in Table 2, but the table's other p-values (0.000034, 0.068) are within-arm tests shown against between-group rows. The difference in change is modest (about 29 m) and not adjusted for baseline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted between-group analysis and a corrected Table 2 showing the 28.72 m difference with its proper test.

quotes.text: in Gr 1-MNA, the 6MWT distance was significantly higher after 1 month of supplementation with 1-MNA, compared with the beginning of the study
Mean distance in phase 0515.80519.243.440.000034

issues.title: 6MWT change in text (18.14/38.86 m; 47 m; baseline 515.18) disagrees with Table 2 (13.28/42.00; 515.80)
issues.explanation: The Results text and abstract give mean 6MWT gains of 18.14 m (control) and 38.86 m (1-MNA), plus a mean of 47 m and a baseline of 515.18 m. Table 2 prints 13.28 m, 42.00 m and 515.80 m. The paper cannot be right in both places, so the size of the headline walking benefit is unclear. The table values are the ones consistent with the printed phase means.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values are medians or improvers-only means, with data that reproduce 18.14, 38.86 and 47.

quotes.text: mean Gr NO-1-MNA was 18.14 m vs. 38.86 m in Gr 1-MNA
515.18 m in Phase 0 vs. 557.8m in Phase 1
Mean difference between distances42.0013.28

issues.title: FSS registered as a primary outcome but called secondary in the paper
issues.explanation: ClinicalTrials.gov lists both 6MWT and FSS as primary outcomes at 1 month. The paper declares only 6MWT primary and FSS secondary, while the conclusion gives fatigue equal prominence. The discrepancy cannot be fully settled because earlier registry versions were not seen. If FSS was co-primary, its null mean-score result should carry primary-outcome weight.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing FSS was originally registered as secondary.

quotes.text: The primary endpoint was improvement in performance as assessed by the 6MWT test, and the secondary endpoint was defined as reduction in fatigue by FSS assessment.
reduced the percentage of patients with severe fatigue after COVID-19

issues.title: Discussion says 95% improved walking distance; Results give 23 of 25 (92%)
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that 95% of 1-MNA patients increased walking distance. The Results and abstract give 23 of 25, which is 92%. With 25 patients, 95% is not attainable (24/25 = 96%, 23/25 = 92%). It is a small overstatement of a secondary claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator or time point for the 95% figure stated in the paper.

quotes.text: As many as 95% of the pts with 1-MNA supplementation showed an increase in walking distance
(23 out of 25 pts, equal to 92%)

issues.title: Gr 1-MNA baseline FSS 4.23 in text vs 4.28 in Table 1
issues.explanation: The Fatigue results give the baseline mean FSS in the 1-MNA group as 4.23, while Table 1 gives 4.28. This is a small transcription inconsistency. Nothing in the conclusions depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: n/a

quotes.text: Gr 1-MNA FSS = 4.23 in Phase 0

10.3390/nu14153027.headline_claim: Personalized rehabilitation after ICU-level COVID-19 hospitalisation was associated with a clear beneficial effect on autonomy, symptoms and nutrition, with fatigue persisting in most patients at 6 months.
10.3390/nu14153027.overall: The descriptive findings (large loss of autonomy and weight after ICU COVID-19, persistent fatigue in about 70%) are plausible, but several percentages do not fit n = 37 and some text statements disagree with the tables. The claim of a 'clear beneficial effect' of rehabilitation rests on an uncontrolled before-after series of 37 patients and is not supported as a causal conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; autonomy (GIR 5-6 classification) and weight/BMI change were the main reported outcomes

issues.title: 'Clear beneficial effect' of rehabilitation claimed from a single uncontrolled cohort of 37 with no comparator
issues.explanation: All 37 patients received individualised rehabilitation and there is no control group, so recovery of autonomy, weight and symptoms after the nadir cannot be attributed to rehabilitation as opposed to natural recovery. The mixed-model tests and the *** in Figure 3 compare time points within the same patients (Figure 3 compares each phase to before the illness), so none of them measures a rehabilitation effect. The programmes were also heterogeneous and not described. The descriptive findings (loss of autonomy and weight, persistent fatigue) are reasonable, but the stated causal benefit is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison with matched ICU survivors not rehabilitated, or an analysis separating the rehabilitation-period change from expected spontaneous recovery.

quotes.text: This non-interventional (with no control group) study analyzed each patient's clinical and biological chart data
Rehabilitation significantly improved such parameters
a clear beneficial effect from personalized rehabilitation

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single uncohort of 37 with no control group and no description of the individualized programs, yet the abstract calls the effect of rehabilitation 'clear' and the conclusions say rehabilitation 'significantly improved' the parameters. Improvement over time (autonomy, weight, symptoms) is shown, but it cannot be attributed to rehabilitation rather than natural recovery. The limitations section acknowledges the missing comparison group but the headline wording does not reflect it.

issues.title: GIR percentages in abstract/Table 2 (39%, 30.5%, 80%) do not fit n = 37; Table 5 gives 15/37 = 40.5% in GIR 1-2
issues.explanation: The abstract and Table 2 say 39% of patients were in GIR 1-2 at admission, but Table 5 puts 15 of the 37 patients there, which is 40.5%. Table 2's admission figures (30.5/30.5/39) match a denominator of 36, not 37. The same pattern appears in the text: 11 patients are called 30.5% (11/37 = 29.7%) and 30 patients are called 80% (30/37 = 81.1%). The differences are small and the story is unchanged, but the headline dependence figure cannot be reproduced from the stated cohort.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one patient lacked an admission GIR score (denominator 36) and that the other percentages used the same base.

quotes.text: but upon admission to the rehabilitation center (CRM), 39% of them became highly dependent
the number of autonomous patients grew from 11 (30.5%) to 30 (80%) 6 months after returning home

script.explanation: 15/37 = 40.54%, but the paper prints 39, outside the rounding interval [38.50, 40.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 38.5 rather than 37.

issues.title: Abstract's 'significant correlation' between malnutrition and autonomy (p < 0.05) has no described test or statistic
issues.explanation: The abstract reports a significant correlation between malnutrition and autonomy, but the statistical methods name no test for it and the Results give no coefficient, test statistic or p-value. Table 5 shows counts only, with 30 of 37 patients severely malnourished, leaving little variation in the malnutrition categories. The reader cannot verify or interpret the claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described test (e.g. chi-squared or trend test) with its statistic and p reported in the supplement or main text.

quotes.text: with a significant correlation being observed between malnutrition and autonomy ( p < 0.05)
Interestingly, we observed that when patients presented with the lowest degree of autonomy (GIR 1-2), they often also presented with malnutrition and fatigue (Table 5).

issues.title: Text gives 20% in GIR < 5 at discharge; Table 2 discharge column gives 25% + 6% = 31%
issues.explanation: The Results sentence describes the discharge time point (69% in GIR 5-6) and then says 20% were in GIR < 5. Table 2 shows 31% in GIR < 5 at discharge. The 20% belongs to the 6-month column. This understates residual dependence at discharge and leaves the text unreliable about which time point is meant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the 20% in the sentence refers to the 6-month assessment.

quotes.text: (20% were in GIR < 5)
GIR at discharge from theCRM 69% 25% 6%

issues.title: Text says fatigue and lack of appetite occurred in 'all' patients; Table 4 gives 97.3%; Discussion says 'about 90'
issues.explanation: The Results say fatigue and lack of appetite were present in all individuals during hospitalisation, yet Table 4 gives 97.3% (36/37) for both. The Discussion describes fatigue falling 'from about 90 to 70%', which does not match 97.3% to 70.2%. These are small wording and rounding inconsistencies with no effect on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: None needed; the wording is simply imprecise.

quotes.text: the fatigue identified subjectively in all of the individuals during their hospitalization
A lack of appetite was present in all of the individuals at the time of hospitalization
the percentage of patients complaining of fatigue decreased only from about 90 to 70%

issues.title: Methods claim 'complete data' at 6 months; dietary questionnaire has 36 responses for 37 patients, unexplained
issues.explanation: The Methods say the 6-month phone questionnaire provided complete data, but Table 6 rests on 36 responses with no reason given for the missing patient. This may also explain why Table 2's percentages fit 36 rather than 37 (see the GIR percentage issue). The effect on results is negligible, but the denominators are not reconciled anywhere.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one patient lacked a dietary questionnaire but all other data were complete.

quotes.text: a questionnaire was completed by a health staff member, thereby providing complete data
The 36 responses obtained from the questionnaire are presented in Table 6.

10.3390/nu14234984.headline_claim: Oral L-arginine plus vitamin C for 28 days improved exercise capacity, muscle strength, endothelial function and fatigue in adults with long COVID, and may be proposed as a remedy.
10.3390/nu14234984.overall: The primary walking-distance result is statistically strong, but the small trial's stated power calculation does not hold, and the placebo fatigue percentage is printed wrongly (80.1% vs 91.3%). Secondary results at p = 0.03 are uncorrected, and the 'remedy' conclusion and NO-mechanism claim go beyond what a preliminary single-centre, assessor-blinded trial supports. The primary finding is best read as promising rather than confirmed.

primary_outcome.name: Change from baseline to day 28 in 6-minute walk test distance (m)

primary_outcomes.measure: 6 minute walking test to evaluate Fatigue

issues.title: 'Remedy' conclusion and NO-synthesis claim go beyond a preliminary 46-participant, 28-day, single-blind trial
issues.explanation: The authors acknowledge that a small single-centre sample makes the results preliminary, yet the Conclusions propose the supplement as a remedy for long COVID. Masking is single (assessors only), so the self-reported fatigue outcome is open to bias. The mechanism is stated as 'increasing NO synthesis', but nitric oxide or its metabolites were not measured. The disclosure in the limitations paragraph does not temper the headline conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion worded as hypothesis-generating, or direct NO measurements supporting the mechanism.

quotes.text: may therefore be proposed as a remedy to restore physical performance and relieve persistent symptoms in people with long COVID
our results should be considered preliminary.
through increasing NO synthesis

second_reader.what_stands: The claim is accurate as to the paper: the Conclusions call the combination a 'remedy' for long COVID on the basis of 46 participants, 28 days and single-blind assessment, without repeating the 'preliminary' caveat from the Discussion. The Discussion also says FMD improvement occurred 'through increasing NO synthesis' although NO synthesis was not measured and FMD is only 'at least partly' NO-mediated, so this is an inference. The authors do acknowledge the preliminary nature and the need for larger trials in the limitations paragraph, so the overreach is in the Conclusions and mechanistic wor

issues.title: Placebo fatigue 21 printed as 80.1%, but 21/23 = 91.3% (same sentence uses n = 23 for 2 = 8.7%)
issues.explanation: The results give fatigue as 2 (8.7%) in the active arm and 21 (80.1%) in the placebo arm. With 23 per arm, 21 participants is 91.3%, not 80.1%. The printed percentage cannot be reconciled with the printed count, so one of the two is wrong. The error understates the contrast, and the significant result probably survives.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or supplementary table showing a placebo analysis denominator of about 26 with 21 fatigued, or a corrected count of about 18.

quotes.text: fatigue was reported by two participants (8.7%)
21 (80.1%) in the placebo group

script.explanation: 21/23 = 91.30%, but the paper prints 80.1, outside the rounding interval [80.05, 80.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 26.2 rather than 23.

issues.title: Handgrip and FMD (each p = 0.03) credited in conclusion with no multiplicity adjustment across secondary tests
issues.explanation: The trial tested a primary outcome, three prespecified secondary outcomes, serum arginine and multivariate models, with an unadjusted alpha of 0.05. Handgrip and FMD each reach only p = 0.03, which would not survive even a simple correction across four secondary tests (0.05/4 = 0.0125). The conclusion nonetheless states these as established improvements. These are best treated as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical or gatekeeping testing plan, or a stated alpha adjustment for the secondary endpoints.

quotes.text: Flow-mediated dilation was greater in participants who received
improved exercise capacity, muscle strength, endothelial function, and fatigue in adults with long COVID.

issues.title: Stated 80% power for 21 per arm does not fit the inputs (d = 0.7 needs ~32 per arm; 21 gives ~62%)
issues.explanation: With a two-sided alpha of 5%, SD 50 m and a 35 m difference, about 32 per arm are needed for 80% power. The planned 21 per arm gives about 62% power. The Discussion then asserts the study was adequately powered. The primary result is significant, so the practical effect is that the estimated effect size is more likely to be inflated and the claim of adequacy is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different SD or effect size in the cited reference (Chetta et al.) that yields 80% power at 21 per arm.

quotes.text: A sample size of 42 participants, 21 per intervention arm, was estimated to provide 80% power to detect a between-group difference of at least 35 m
The sample size was adequately powered for the primary outcome.

10.3390/nu15173701.headline_claim: PEALUT (palmitoylethanolamide co-ultramicronized with luteolin) supplementation improved patient-reported symptoms, pain, anxiety, depression, fatigue and brain fog in Long COVID patients, supporting a role for non-resolving neuroinflammation and the GP as the setting for early management, with randomized controlled trials said to be needed to confirm the preliminary observation.
10.3390/nu15173701.overall: The data are an uncontrolled, open-label, retrospective before-after series, so the reported improvements cannot be attributed to PEALUT, and the Abstract's causal and mechanistic wording goes beyond that design. There are also unexplained differences in analysed N across tables and an inconsistent PGIC percentage breakdown. At most the paper supports a hypothesis-generating observation.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Single-arm, open-label, self-reported before-after data cannot attribute improvement to PEALUT
issues.explanation: All 49 patients received PEALUT, with no comparator and no blinding. Outcomes are patient-reported symptom scores, symptom counts and global impression. Natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectation effects and the retrospective chart basis could each produce the large falls reported. The Abstract nonetheless says supplementation 'helped to improve' all symptoms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo comparison group showing the same outcomes diverge, or blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: The lack of a control group is the main limitation of this analysis
Supplementation with PEALUT helped to improve all patient-reported symptoms
patients were evaluated through a battery of validated self-administered tool

second_reader.what_stands: A single-arm, open-label, retrospective before-after series of self-reported outcomes cannot attribute the observed improvement to PEALUT, and the authors themselves say natural recovery cannot be excluded. The Abstract's 'helped to improve all patient-reported symptoms' is causal phrasing that the design does not support, and the radiating-pain figures (36.2% to 38.1%) do not show improvement.

issues.title: Mechanistic and 'strongly support' claims go beyond an uncontrolled retrospective series
issues.explanation: The Abstract says the results highlight the pathogenetic role of non-resolving neuroinflammation, and the Conclusions say the findings strongly support preclinical studies. The study measured no neuroinflammation markers and had no control arm, so it cannot test mechanism. The recommendation that PEALUT is a valid tool for GPs rests on the same uncontrolled improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled data with inflammatory biomarkers linking PEALUT to symptom change.

quotes.text: these results highlight the pathogenetic role of 'non-resolving' neuroinflammation in Long COVID development
The current clinical findings strongly support previous preclinical studies
PEALUT might represent a valid tool for the General Practitioners in their daily clinical practice

second_reader.what_stands: The paper measured only symptom questionnaires in an uncontrolled retrospective series, so it provides no evidence on neuroinflammation as a mechanism, and 'highlight the pathogenetic role' and 'strongly support previous preclinical studies' go beyond the data. The authors do label the results preliminary and 'might' appears in the practice recommendation, which softens but does not remove the overreach.

issues.title: Analysed N varies unexplained across tables (49/46/42 vs 47/46/45); no flow or missing-data account
issues.explanation: The pain-pattern table gives N = 49, 46 and 42 at T0, T60 and T90. The symptom table gives 47, 46 and 45 for the same visits. The paper never explains the differences, reports no dropouts or reasons, and does not say how missing data entered the mixed models. Results are therefore for whoever was available at each visit, and the reader cannot judge selective attrition. This is a reporting gap rather than a wrong result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A patient flow or per-instrument completion table stating who was missing each questionnaire at each visit and why, with analyses showing the results hold for all 49.

issues.title: PGIC categories sum to 99.1% (103.9% with 'unchanged') vs stated 95.3% improved
issues.explanation: The paper says 95.3% felt improved, made up of 32.4% extremely, 38.1% much and 28.6% minimally improved. Those three add to 99.1%, not 95.3%. With the 4.8% reported unchanged, the categories exceed 100%. At least one printed PGIC percentage is wrong, so the PGIC breakdown cannot be relied on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The Figure 5 counts showing categories that sum to 95.3% of a stated N.

quotes.text: According to PGIC results, at the end of the therapy 95.3% of patient felt improved
Only 4.8% of them declared they felt 'unchanged' and no patients complained of being worse

issues.title: Symptom-count outcome is a non-standardised checklist; no primary endpoint specified
issues.explanation: The number of symptoms is built from an ad hoc list rather than a validated instrument, and no primary outcome is named. Many outcomes are tested, with no multiplicity statement beyond Tukey-Kramer for time contrasts. This weakens interpretation of the symptom-count result but not the overall pattern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified protocol naming the primary outcome, or validation of the checklist.

quotes.text: patients presented a mean of 5.4 ± 0.26 symptoms at T0

10.3390/nu16101529.headline_claim: HRW might be an effective strategy for alleviating fatigue and improving cardiorespiratory endurance, musculoskeletal function, and sleep quality, but does not ameliorate dyspnea in Long-COVID patients.
10.3390/nu16101529.overall: The paper's headline, that HRW alleviates fatigue and improves endurance, muscle function and sleep, rests on uncorrected secondary percent-change comparisons in a 32-person pilot. The primary group and interaction effects were all null. Several reporting inconsistencies add to this: a misprinted PSQI CI, a 6MWT p-value and CI tighter than the descriptive data allow, and mislabelled percent-change columns. The findings are best read as hypothesis-generating, and the dyspnea null result is the most reliably supported statement.

primary_outcome.name: FSS score (fatigue)

issues.title: Efficacy claimed in title and conclusions although no primary group or interaction effect was significant
issues.explanation: The authors' primary models (group x time with covariates) show no significant group or interaction effect for FSS (p = 0.122, 0.184), 6MWT (p = 0.279) or 30s-CST (interaction p = 0.221). The title, abstract and conclusions nevertheless say HRW alleviates fatigue and improves endurance and muscle function. These claims rest on secondary percent-change comparisons in a 32-participant pilot. The headline conclusion is stronger than the primary analysis allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecification that the percent-change comparison was the primary analysis, or a primary group-by-time effect that is significant.

quotes.text: significant main effects of time ( p = 0.001) but not group ( p = 0.122) and interaction ( p = 0.184) on FSS score
This study demonstrated that HRW might be an effective strategy for alleviating fatigue
The findings of this pilot study demonstrate that the daily intake of HRW provides promising benefits for alleviating fatigue

second_reader.what_stands: The primary mixed-model interaction for FSS (p = 0.184) and the group effect (p = 0.122) are not significant. The fatigue benefit in the title, abstract and Discussion rests on a secondary, covariate-adjusted comparison of change scores at p = 0.046, which the paper does not weigh against the null primary test. The conclusion's 'might be' and the stated limitations soften this, but the title and Discussion do not.

issues.title: Sleep benefit comes from an exploratory 19-person subgroup (interaction p = 0.064) but is a general abstract claim
issues.explanation: The PSQI result is from an exploratory subgroup of 19 participants who reported difficulty sleeping. The abstract presents it as a general improvement in sleep quality alongside the primary outcomes. In that subgroup the mixed model shows no group effect (p = 0.909) and only a marginal interaction (p = 0.064). The 'significant' result rests on the secondary percent-change test, p = 0.012. The abstract and conclusions therefore overstate what the subgroup analysis supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sleep-quality hypothesis in the full sample, or a significant interaction in the subgroup.

quotes.text: marginally significant effects of interaction ( p = 0.064), but not group ( p = 0.909), on sleep quality
Additionally, the exploratory analysis showed that sleep quality improved significantly after HRW consumption compared to PW consumption for those with difficulty sleeping.
we also performed exploratory subgroup analyses on those who had difficulty sleeping or anxiety and depression

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's PSQI result (p = 0.012, d = 1.274) is the 19-person exploratory subgroup, whose interaction was not significant (p = 0.064), yet the abstract and Conclusion state improved sleep quality as a general finding. The subgroup label appears only in the Results and Discussion. The PSQI confidence interval as printed appears to have lost a minus sign on its upper bound.

issues.title: About 20 tests at p < 0.05 with no correction; FSS (p = 0.046) and PSQI (p = 0.012) are borderline
issues.explanation: The paper runs many tests across outcomes, analysis types and subgroups, each at an unadjusted 0.05 level. The fatigue benefit (p = 0.046) is a borderline secondary result that would not survive any plausible adjustment. This adds to the weakness described under the primary-versus-secondary issue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical testing plan or an adjustment procedure described in the paper.

quotes.text: For all statistical tests, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
FSS score, mMRC score, total distance in 6WMT, and total times in 30s-CST were the primary outcomes for fatigue, dyspnea, cardiorespiratory endurance, and musculoskeletal function, respectively.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper uses an uncorrected alpha of 0.05 across roughly 20 or more tests, with no multiplicity adjustment or stated hierarchy, and FSS at p = 0.046 is borderline and would not survive any plausible correction. Calling PSQI p = 0.012 'borderline' is less apt: it would pass a four-outcome Bonferroni threshold of 0.0125 but not a threshold across about 20 tests, and its main weakness is that it comes from an exploratory subgroup.

issues.title: 6MWT: p < 0.001 and CI 41.97-61.89 are much tighter than Table 2 SDs allow (about p = 0.008)
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives the 6MWT change as 69.33 +/- 57.10 (HRW) versus 18.90 +/- 41.54 (PW), n = 16 each. These data give a difference of 50.43 with a standard error near 17.6, so a p of about 0.008 and a 95% CI of roughly 14 to 87 m. The paper reports p < 0.001 and a CI of 41.97 to 61.89, which implies an SE of about 5. The reported significance for the endurance outcome is stronger than the printed descriptive statistics support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level data or a model output showing an adjusted SE of about 5 m for the group difference.

quotes.text: percent change in the total distance in the 6WMT ( p < 0.001, [95% CI = 41.972, 61.891], d = 1.010)

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

issues.title: No trial registration reported, so primary outcomes cannot be checked against a prior plan
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval (2 March 2023) but no trial registry entry. Without a registered primary outcome, readers cannot check whether the percent-change comparisons that carry the headline were prespecified. The paper itself designates the FSS, mMRC, 6MWT and 30s-CST models as primary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier and registration date preceding enrolment, with matching outcomes.

quotes.text: The Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Sport University approved the study protocol (Approval number: 2023301H)
The approval date is 2 March 2023.

issues.title: PSQI 95% CI printed as -5.169 to 0.742 spans zero, yet p = 0.012 and 'significant'
issues.explanation: The paper prints the PSQI percent-change CI as -5.169 to 0.742, which includes zero, and calls the result significant at p = 0.012. Both cannot hold. The Table 3 group difference of -2.97 sits near the centre of -5.169 to -0.742, so the upper bound is probably missing a minus sign. As printed, the interval contradicts the claimed significance in the abstract and Results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or the authors' output showing the upper bound is -0.742.

quotes.text: percent change in PSQI score ( p = 0.012, [95% CI = -5.169, 0.742], d = 1.274) from baseline

issues.title: Table 2/3 'Percent Changes (%)' columns are raw post-minus-pre differences, not percentages
issues.explanation: The columns labelled percent change equal absolute post minus pre differences in each scale's units. For FSS, 21.69 - 38.13 = -16.44, which is printed as the 'percent change'; the true percent change would be about -43%. The secondary analyses on which the headline depends are therefore described as percent changes but appear to be raw changes. This mislabels the secondary outcome and makes the effect sizes harder to interpret.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the percent-change columns hold absolute changes, or recomputation showing the printed values are percentages.

issues.title: Days-after-COVID SDs (8.87 PW, 6.95 HRW) exceed the maximum possible for a 21-35 day window
issues.explanation: Inclusion required diagnosis 21-35 days before participation. Values confined to 21-35 with the printed means cannot have SDs as large as those in Table 1. Either the variable was measured differently from the eligibility definition, or some participants fell outside the window. The effect on the main findings is probably small, but the eligibility description does not match the reported data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that this variable was measured at a different time point or that the window was relaxed.

quotes.text: having been diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 infection 21-35 days prior to participation

quotes.location: Table 1, Days after COVID-19 row, PW column

script.explanation: Both interpretations exceed the plausibility ceiling (7.23). Labeled SD = 8.87; implied SD under SE interpretation = 35.48.

issues.title: PSQI d = 1.274 labelled 'moderate' though the paper's own 1.20-2.0 band is 'large'
issues.explanation: The Methods define 1.20 to 2.0 as a large effect. The Abstract describes the PSQI effect, d = 1.274, as moderate. This is a labelling slip that, if anything, understates the claimed effect. Nothing else depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different effect-size banding stated elsewhere in the paper.

quotes.text: 0.60~1.20 indicates moderate, 1.20~2.0 indicates large
d = 1.274) compared to PW were of a significantly moderate effect size

10.3390/nu16223840.headline_claim: Severe COVID-19 leaves persistent gut-lung axis alterations, and a six-month multispecies probiotic (Pro-Vi 5) partially modulates some of these biomarkers in a randomized, placebo-controlled pilot study.
10.3390/nu16223840.overall: The baseline severe-vs-mild differences are plausible but are unadjusted for large imbalances in age, BMI and comorbidity, so attribution to severe infection is weak. The probiotic effects are exploratory, rest on 8 vs 13 completers, include within-arm inference and an abstract claim (L-DOPA at 3 months) that the Results contradict, so they support hypothesis generation only.

primary_outcome.name: Gut-lung axis biomarkers (no single primary outcome stated in the paper; registry lists microbiome, barrier and cytokine primaries)

issues.title: Richness 'improved by probiotic' rests on within-arm p-values (n=8); no between-arm test; RDA null
issues.explanation: The abstract credits the probiotic with improving microbial richness, but the evidence is a significant change in the probiotic arm (p = 0.047 and 0.014) versus 'not observed' in placebo. A difference between significant and non-significant arms is not itself a test of treatment effect. The paper's own overall microbiome analyses found no significant influence of the intervention over time, and the Discussion goes on to say 'we could show an increase in microbial richness'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported interaction or between-arm test of richness change that is significant.

quotes.text: showed a significant improvement in microbial richness after 3 months ( p = 0.047) and 6 months ( p = 0.014) of intervention, which was not observed in the placebo group
but did not detect a significant influence of the probiotic intervention on the microbiome over time (variance = 0.008, F = 0.28, p > 0.999)

second_reader.what_stands: The richness claim rests on p-values reported for the probiotic arm (n = 8) versus a statement of non-significance in placebo, and no between-arm test of richness change is printed in the main text. The RDA and PERMANOVA nulls for the intervention are accurately quoted. What I could not establish is whether the Figure 6 mixed model, whose results are not shown, includes an arm-by-time term, so I cannot say that no between-arm test exists. The abstract's 'significantly improved by probiotic intervention' is stronger than the printed evidence supports.

issues.title: Severe-vs-mild differences unadjusted for age, BMI, comorbidity (n=21 vs 10) yet attributed to severe infection
issues.explanation: The two groups differ in age (56 vs 38 years), BMI (28 vs 23), obesity, hypertension, comorbidity index and days since infection (318 vs 221). All comparisons are unadjusted univariate tests, so differences in microbiome, metabolome and immunity cannot be separated from these factors. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless present them as long-term alterations after severe infection.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Covariate-adjusted analyses showing the main severe-vs-mild differences persist after adjusting for age, BMI and comorbidity.

quotes.text: Patients after severe COVID-19 infection were older, had a higher BMI/were more often obese
potential confounding factors, such as detailed medication regimens, baseline microbiome compositions, and pre-infection body weight and composition, could not be accounted for
The study provides evidence of long-term alterations of the gut-lung axis after severe COVID-19 infection

second_reader.what_stands: The severe-versus-mild comparisons are unadjusted for age, BMI and comorbidity, and the groups differ markedly on all three, as well as on time since infection. The authors acknowledge confounding by obesity, comorbidity and missing pre-infection data in the Discussion and Conclusions, so the limitation is not hidden. However, the abstract's wording still attributes the alterations to severe infection without that caveat, and age and time since infection are not named among the confounders.

issues.title: Differential dropout 5/13 probiotic vs 0/13 placebo; completers-only analysis of probiotic effects
issues.explanation: Five of 13 probiotic participants (38%) left the study, four for reasons related to the product or study burden, while no placebo participant did. Only completers were analysed (8 vs 13), so randomization no longer guarantees comparable arms. Probiotic effects are estimated on tolerant survivors, with no sensitivity analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or imputed analysis giving the same probiotic effects.

quotes.text: five patients in the probiotic group dropped out during the study
Eight patients in the probiotic and thirteen patients in the placebo group finished the study according to the protocol and were included in the analysis

second_reader.what_stands: Dropout was 5/13 in the probiotic arm versus 0/13 in placebo, and all probiotic-effect analyses use the 8 vs 13 completers only, so they are not ITT. The authors report the imbalance and its stated reasons, which are mostly product-related. They do not describe any sensitivity analysis for the missing participants, and the post-randomisation exclusion could bias the probiotic-versus-placebo comparisons.

issues.title: Abstract claims stool L-DOPA rise at 3 months; Results report no 3-month stool change and no L-DOPA
issues.explanation: The abstract says L-DOPA increased after 3 months of intervention. The Results state there were no stool metabolome changes at 3 months, and the 6-month stool findings list DOPAC but not L-DOPA. The abstract therefore reports a finding the Results do not support, and the 6-month stool changes were also said not to withstand multiplicity control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A supplementary table or figure (e.g. Figure S13/S14) showing a 3-month L-DOPA increase that the Results text omits.

quotes.text: an increase in L-DOPA after 3 months and butyrate after 6 months of intervention could be observed
There were no changes in the stool metabolome after 3 months of intervention

issues.title: Four registered 6-month cytokine outcomes (TNF-alpha, IL-1b, IL-6, IL-6R) not reported in the paper
issues.explanation: The registry record lists TNF-alpha, IL-1b, IL-6 and IL-6R among eight primary outcomes at 6 months, and the paper reports none of them. It instead reports many additional immune and metabolic markers and does not declare primary outcomes. Because only the current registry record was seen, whether the outcomes were changed cannot be determined from the paper alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Cytokine results reported elsewhere (e.g. supplement) or registry history showing those outcomes were added after the analysis.

quotes.text: The main aim was to explore which biomarkers of the gut-lung axis are altered in patients after mild versus severe COVID-19 infection and which of these biomarkers can be modulated by a probiotic.
we also observed improvements in innate and adaptive immune markers

issues.title: CD4 T helper cells: Results say higher in severe (p=0.013); Discussion says severe lowers them
issues.explanation: The Results report fewer CD3+CD4+ T helper cells in mild than in severe patients, meaning higher counts after severe disease. The Discussion asserts a persistent decrease in CD4+ cells after severe infection and cites this as supported by the baseline data. The two statements contradict each other, and the Results say the baseline immune differences did not withstand multiplicity correction. Together with c3 and c4 this is a single problem: the Discussion's description of the T and B cell findings does not match the Results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence in Table S6 or Figure 4 that CD4+ counts are lower in the severe group, i.e. that the Results sentence has the groups reversed.

quotes.text: We observed a lower number of CD3+CD4+ T helper cells ( p = 0.013) in patients after mild infection as compared to patients with severe infection
Severe COVID infections lead to a persistent decrease in CD4+ T helper cells even after several months

issues.title: Quality-of-life benefit claimed from uncorrected ARTIQ p=0.014 (3 mo) and 0.022; 6-month only p=0.07
issues.explanation: The claimed improvements in tiredness (p = 0.014) and psychological burden (p = 0.022) come from many questionnaire items and timepoints with no multiplicity control reported for them. The tiredness effect did not persist at 6 months (p = 0.07) and rests on 8 vs 13 completers. The Discussion presents these as shown clinical improvements, while the study is only exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the ARTIQ tiredness comparison was a pre-specified single primary endpoint, or that a multiplicity correction was applied to it.

quotes.text: felt significantly less tired in the ARTIQ questionnaire after 3 months ( p = 0.014
Clinically we could show statistically significant improvements in quality of life, namely in the perception of tiredness and the psychological aspect of the ARTIQ.

issues.title: Two authors hold grants/honoraria from the probiotic maker; supplier's role in the trial not stated
issues.explanation: The tested product is made by Institut Allergosan, and two authors, including the senior author, declare research support or speaker honoraria from the company. The funding statement does not say whether the company supplied the product or placebo or had any role in design, analysis or reporting. This is declared, so it is a transparency gap rather than concealment, and it matters because the conclusions favour the product.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the company had no role in design, conduct, analysis or reporting, with product supplied independently.

quotes.text: Angela Horvath and Vanessa Stadlbauer have received research grants, other research support, and/or speaker honoraria from the Institute Allergosan and Winclove Probiotics.
The project was conducted at the Center for Biomarker Research in Medicine (CBmed), a COMET K1 center funded by the Austrian Research Promotion Agency (Project 3.23).

10.3390/nu17020304.headline_claim: Vitamin K2/D3 supplementation for 24 weeks improves long COVID symptoms (total symptom count and RECOVER Research Index), attenuates hyper-inflammatory state, and reduces gut permeability and fungal translocation, and is safe.
10.3390/nu17020304.overall: The trial is an open-label, no-placebo, single-site study with self-reported outcomes and uncorrected testing of many biomarkers. Its symptom benefit and mechanistic claims should be treated as preliminary and not demonstrated, and the gut-permeability conclusion goes beyond the reported data. Several printed numbers (baseline vitamin D percentages, p < 0.01 summary, adjusted p-values, the glucose contradiction) are inconsistent with the paper's own tables and need correction.

primary_outcome.name: Not designated as primary; headline outcomes are total number of LC symptoms and RECOVER LC Research Index

issues.title: Open-label, no-placebo control for self-reported symptom outcomes; benefit stated as demonstrated
issues.explanation: Controls received no placebo, so participants and assessors were presumably aware of allocation. The main outcomes are the number of self-reported symptoms and a questionnaire-based index. These are open to expectation and reporting bias. The placebo limitation is only partly acknowledged, and the Conclusions still say the trial 'demonstrated' improvement. Effects are therefore tentative until tested against placebo.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded outcome assessment or objective outcome showing the same effect, or a placebo-controlled replication.

quotes.text: did not receive any study drug or placebo as part of their participation in the study
participants randomized to the control arm or SOC arm did not receive a placebo
we demonstrated that a daily dose of 2000 IU of vitamin D3 and 240 µg of vitamin K2 over 24 weeks could help improve symptoms of long COVID

second_reader.what_stands: The control arm received no placebo and the symptom outcomes are self-reported, so participant expectation could influence them. The limitations paragraph addresses only outside vitamin use, not unblinded self-report bias, while the Discussion says 'Our results confirm the beneficial and safe role' and the Conclusions say the trial 'demonstrated' improvement, which is stronger than an open-label design supports, though the Conclusions do also call for confirmatory studies.

issues.title: About 20 biomarkers tested at alpha 0.05 with no correction; mechanistic claims rest on p = 0.01 to 0.03
issues.explanation: The Methods list around 17 or more biomarkers, plus symptom outcomes, all judged at p < 0.05 with no correction or hierarchy. Only four markers are reported as improved, with p-values of 0.001, 0.01, 0.02 and 0.03. Several would not survive even a modest correction. The conclusions on attenuated hyper-inflammation and fungal translocation are therefore hypothesis-generating only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical or correction procedure, or a registered primary biomarker outcome showing significance after adjustment.

quotes.text: Changes in markers of inflammation (ICAM, TNF-RI, oxLDL, and sCD163) were modeled separately from each other.
Reductions in oxidized LDL, sTNF-RI, sCD163, and the fungal translocation marker (1,3)-β-d-glucan (BDG) were observed in the vitamin K2/D3 arm compared to the SOC arm

second_reader.what_stands: No multiplicity correction is stated, and with roughly 14 to 21 biomarkers examined, three of the four reported findings (p = 0.01 to 0.03) would not survive a standard Bonferroni correction. The Discussion nonetheless draws mechanistic inferences from them, although Table 2 shows no association between these markers and symptom index; the exact number of tests is not fully reported, so 'about 20' is approximate.

issues.title: Conclusion says supplementation was 'effective in reducing gut permeability'; only an association is reported
issues.explanation: No between-arm Zonulin comparison is presented. Table 3 reports Zonulin only as a covariate associated with symptom change, with an adjusted CI that includes zero. The statement that the intervention reduced gut permeability is therefore not shown. The 'safe' wording is based on a small single-site open-label trial with a rise in glucose and one myocardial infarction leading to discontinuation, and should be more cautious.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-arm Zonulin change favouring K2/D3 with an interval excluding zero.

quotes.text: Vitamin D3 and K2 supplementation was also effective in reducing gut permeability and fungal translocation
This safe intervention has the potential for global impact

second_reader.what_stands: For gut permeability, the paper reports only an association between Zonulin change and symptom count, with no treatment-arm Zonulin comparison, so 'effective in reducing gut permeability' is not supported, and the adjusted CI (-1.4, 0.2) is inconsistent with the listed p = 0.02. For fungal translocation, a between-arm BDG difference (p = 0.03, uncorrected, with baseline imbalance) is reported, so that part is a weaker claim rather than unsupported; 'significantly improving quality of life' is also not measured.

issues.title: Baseline LC Research Index higher in controls (median 16 vs 11, p = 0.01); baseline not in listed covariates
issues.explanation: The headline outcome differed at baseline between arms. Because the control arm started higher, regression to the mean could contribute to a larger apparent fall in the treatment arm. The listed covariates do not include baseline LC Index, though the cLDA model may handle it. The paper does not discuss this imbalance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis adjusting explicitly for baseline LC Index that gives a similar treatment effect.

issues.title: Adjusted LC Index effect −3.2 (−5.5, −0.9) is given p = 0.04; the CI implies about 0.006
issues.explanation: The adjusted K2/D3 versus SOC estimate has a CI that sits well away from zero, which corresponds to p of about 0.006. The printed p is 0.04. The text repeats p = 0.04 for the headline adjusted result. The headline adjusted effect is likely stronger than the p suggests, or the interval is wrong. The unadjusted row (−3.1, p = 0.01) is consistent with its CI.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the p-value comes from a different test than the Wald CI, or a corrected CI.

quotes.location: Table 2, K2/D3 vs. SOC row, Adjusted column

quotes.text: the mean difference in the LC Research Index was 3.2 points lower in the vitamin K2/D3 arm compared to the SOC arm

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0064 (reachable range [0.0046, 0.0086] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.04 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Four biomarker reductions summarised as p < 0.01; printed p-values are 0.001, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03
issues.explanation: Section 3.6 groups oxLDL, sTNF-RI, sCD163 and BDG under p < 0.01. Only oxLDL (p = 0.001) is below 0.01. sTNF-RI is p = 0.01, sCD163 p = 0.02 and BDG p = 0.03. The summary therefore overstates the strength of three of the four findings, and the sCD163 and BDG results are only marginal at the nominal 0.05 level.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated analysis (for example a model-based joint test across 24 weeks) that yields p < 0.01 for all four markers.

quotes.text: Reductions in oxidized LDL, sTNF-RI, sCD163, and the fungal translocation marker (1,3)-β-d-glucan (BDG) were observed in the vitamin K2/D3 arm compared to the SOC arm
sTNF-RI decreased by 106.3 ± 239.0 pg/mL [vs. SOC (−91.9 ± 244.4);

issues.title: Adjusted Zonulin estimate −0.7 (−1.4, 0.2) crosses zero but is given p = 0.02
issues.explanation: For a single coefficient, a 95% CI that includes zero is incompatible with p = 0.02. The footnote about the interaction model may explain the mismatch, but the paper never says which test the p belongs to. The text then reads this as Zonulin improvement being associated with fewer symptoms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that p = 0.02 is the joint test of the Zonulin interaction terms and that −0.7 (−1.4, 0.2) is one contrast within that model.

quotes.text: In adjusted models, Zonulin was modeled as a three-way interaction with treatment group and time.

issues.title: Glucose said to show no between-arm change, yet a K2/D3-versus-SOC contrast gives p = 0.001
issues.explanation: Section 3.5 says metabolic parameters showed no significant between-arm change. The next sentence reports glucose rising 5.4 mg/dL on K2/D3 against a fall of 6.3 mg/dL on SOC, with p = 0.001. Either the 'no changes' statement or the p-value is wrong, and a possible adverse metabolic signal is described as stable. The Discussion mentions the glucose rise but also says the intervention did not affect metabolic markers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that p = 0.001 relates to a different comparison (for example, a time effect) and that the between-arm glucose test was non-significant.

quotes.text: with no significant changes observed between treatment arms
increased by 5.4 ± 21.1 mg/dL vs. a decrease of 6.3 ± 26.5 mg/dL

issues.title: Adjusted-model covariates described inconsistently (changes in BMI, lipids, D-dimer, BDG vs baseline values)
issues.explanation: Table 2's footnote says the adjusted models include changes in BMI, lipids, D-dimer and BDG, which could themselves be affected by treatment. The Methods list the same variables without 'changes' and add baseline vitamin D. It is unclear which model was run. Because the unadjusted and adjusted treatment estimates agree, the headline LC Index difference is not much affected, but the reporting prevents confidence about what was adjusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis code or a supplement showing that only baseline values of these covariates were used.

quotes.text: Adjusted models included treatment arm, age at baseline, sex, race, and changes in BMI, lipids, D-dimer, and BDG.
Adjusted models included treatment arm, age, serum vitamin D at baseline, sex, race, BMI, lipids, D-dimer, and BDG.

issues.title: Baseline <20 ng/mL: text gives 19.2% and 8.6%, Table 1 gives 26.5% and 30.2%
issues.explanation: The Results text says 19.2% of the K2/D3 arm and 8.6% of the SOC arm had 25(OH)D below 20 ng/mL. Table 1 prints 26 (26.5%) and 16 (30.2%) for the same row. Neither text figure is a whole-number share of the arm sizes (98 and 53). The text also reverses the direction of the baseline imbalance. The error is confined to a baseline description and does not touch the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Table S1 showing a different defined subset (for example a different timepoint or population) for which 19.2% and 8.6% are the correct shares.

quotes.text: At the time of treatment allocation, 19.2% of the vitamin K2/D3 arm and 8.6% of the SOC arm had serum 25(OH)D levels of

10.3390/nu17040723.headline_claim: Curcuma and Boswellia phospholipid supplementation with a low-FODMAP diet produces positive effects on abdominal bloating and pain in subjects with post-COVID-19 IBS-like symptoms, similar to those without prior COVID-19.
10.3390/nu17040723.overall: The study shows bloating and pain scores fell in both cohorts of a 30-day open-label supplement-plus-diet regimen, but with no placebo or randomised comparator it cannot show that the supplement caused the improvement. The claim of similar effects in PCIBS and IBS conflicts with the paper's own significant between-cohort bloating difference, and the correlation statistics contain reporting errors. Treat the findings as preliminary, hypothesis-generating pilot observations.

primary_outcome.name: Reduction in severity of abdominal bloating

issues.title: No placebo or randomised control; open-label self-rated bloating outcome supports no causal efficacy claim
issues.explanation: The PCIBS arm (n=16) is a single-arm, open-label pre/post comparison; the comparator is a non-randomised IBS cohort that received the same active supplement plus a low-FODMAP diet. Bloating and pain were patient-reported and unblinded, and everyone also received dietary advice. Expectation, natural recovery 60-120 days after COVID, and the diet cannot be separated from any supplement effect, yet the Discussion says the findings 'prove' efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent placebo or diet-only comparator in PCIBS patients showing a larger bloating reduction on supplement.

quotes.text: This two-cohort open-label study was conducted at the University of Pavia’s Department of Public Health in Italy.
the absence of a post-COVID-19 randomized control group with IBS-like symptoms who received a placebo and another group who received only an LFD
The reduction in the severity of stomach bloating was the primary outcome.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper has no placebo, randomised or LFD-only comparison, and its primary outcome is a self-rated bloating score in an open-label design, so the data cannot support a causal efficacy claim. The authors list the missing control as a limitation and use some hedged wording ('correlated with', 'promising'), but they also write 'prove' and 'shows positive effects', which go beyond what the design allows.

issues.title: 'Similar' effects in PCIBS and IBS claimed despite significant between-cohort bloating difference (−0.899, p<0.001)
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say the effects in PCIBS are similar to those in non-COVID IBS, and the Discussion says the findings 'prove' efficacy. The authors' own comparison shows the bloating reduction was significantly smaller in PCIBS (−1.950 vs −2.850), and indican fell only in controls. With 16 PCIBS patients, no placebo arm and no test of equivalence, both 'proved efficacy' and 'similar effects' go beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence analysis, or a controlled PCIBS comparison showing an effect not different from that in IBS.

quotes.text: These results are similar to those observed in subjects with IBS without previous COVID-19 infection.
These findings prove that supplementation of a rational premix combination

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's own comparison shows a statistically significant difference in bloating change between cohorts (−0.899, CI −1.270 to −0.528), yet the Conclusion calls the results 'similar' to the non-COVID IBS group. This is partly softened because both groups improved significantly and the Discussion acknowledges a more prominent effect in controls, but the Conclusion itself omits that qualification, and the baseline bloating imbalance (adjustment only for age and gender) is not considered.

issues.title: Bloating differs at baseline (2.96 vs 2.63, p=0.010) on a 0-3 scale; between-cohort ANCOVA not baseline-adjusted
issues.explanation: The primary outcome differed between cohorts at baseline, and the model adjusted only for age and sex. With a 0-3 scale and controls starting at 2.96, change scores are bounded by baseline, so the between-cohort difference (−0.899, p<0.001) cannot be read cleanly as a difference in effect. Baseline indican also differed numerically (90.6 vs 75.2) and was not adjusted for.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA adjusted for baseline bloating that gives the same between-cohort difference.

quotes.text: Only the abdominal bloating score differed at baseline between the two cohorts

issues.title: PCIBS pain-bloating correlation r = 0.456 (n=16) called significant but implies p about 0.08
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion state that in the PCIBS cohort the fall in pain was significantly correlated with the fall in bloating. For r = 0.456 with 16 patients the two-sided p is about 0.08, above the paper's 0.05 criterion. The printed 'p > 0.01' hides this, and the Discussion extends the claim to both cohorts.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A printed p below 0.05 for this correlation, or a larger n than 16 for this analysis.

quotes.text: significantly correlated with the decrease in abdominal bloating (r = 0.456;

issues.title: Correlations printed as negative 'r2' (−0.547, −0.532) with 'p > 0.01' for results called significant
issues.explanation: A squared correlation cannot be negative, so 'r2' must be r. The same sentence reports 'p > 0.01' for associations described as statistically significant, which is the wrong inequality. The correlations are secondary and the direction is clear from the text, so this is a reporting slip rather than a threat to the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original figure 2B labelling r (not r²) and p < 0.01.

quotes.text: r2 = −0.547, control group
r2 = −0.532, PCIBS group

issues.title: No trial registration identifier reported; primary endpoint cannot be checked against a protocol
issues.explanation: The Methods give an ethics code but no registry entry, so the pre-specification of bloating as the primary outcome cannot be verified. This matters mainly because the efficacy wording is strong. It is a transparency gap rather than a demonstrated outcome switch.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prospective registry record listing bloating as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: After receiving approval from the local independent ethics committee, the study was carried out in compliance with the ICH Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice

10.3390/nu18030521.headline_claim: Vitamin D replacement therapy guidance (vitamin D3 25 µg, dietary and sun-exposure guidance, exercise) added to alfacalcidol reduces ME/CFS symptoms in patients with PVS or PASC and vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency, and may be an effective therapeutic approach.
10.3390/nu18030521.overall: The finding that the package arm reported fewer checklist symptoms than the control arm at Week 12 is large and statistically clear within this trial, but it comes from an open-label trial with a subjective count endpoint and a multi-component intervention. The specific claims that inactive vitamin D3 is preferable, and that the approach is effective for ME/CFS generally, go beyond what the design can show. The sample-size inconsistencies in the Figure 3 and 7 tables look like extraction artefacts and do not affect the conclusions.

primary_outcome.name: Change in number of ME/CFS symptoms from screening to Week 12 (MMRM)

issues.title: Open-label trial with clinician-recorded symptom-count primary endpoint; effect of -5.6 may be inflated
issues.explanation: Participants and clinicians knew the allocation. The intervention arm also received extra lifestyle and supplement counselling, and the control arm received only general guidance. The primary outcome is a count of symptoms ticked on a checklist, so expectancy and observer bias could produce much of the difference. The authors acknowledge this possibility, but the Conclusions still describe an effective approach without that caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment, or an objective or validated functional endpoint showing a comparable benefit.

quotes.text: This study is a randomized, open-label, multicenter trial.
Because this study employed an open-label design, the effects of placebo response, observer bias, expectancy effects, and reporting bias cannot be completely excluded
The primary endpoint was the change in the number of ME/CFS symptoms from screening to Week 12.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label, the primary endpoint is an investigator-recorded symptom count, and the authors themselves say placebo response, observer bias, expectancy and reporting bias 'may have influenced the results, potentially inflating perceived benefits'. The size of any inflation cannot be estimated from the paper. The control arm also received alfacalcidol and general guidance, but not the diet, sun and exercise components. The comparison is therefore not attention-matched, so non-specific effects of the guidance are inseparable from vitamin D. The limitation is disclosed and weighed in

issues.title: 'Inactive vitamin D3 is preferable' is not tested: both arms got alfacalcidol and AEs were not compared
issues.explanation: Both arms received alfacalcidol, and the intervention arm added 25 µg D3 and lifestyle advice, so the trial never compared D3 against alfacalcidol. The claim of a better risk profile rests on external literature, and adverse events are reported only descriptively. The Discussion also interprets the lack of 25(OH)D rise in the control arm as an alfacalcidol effect. The Conclusions extend to ME/CFS after PASC or vaccination in general, from a single open-label trial in which 71 of 85 analysed participants (83.5% of the 85) came from one site.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomized comparison of D3 versus alfacalcidol with prespecified, arm-wise safety outcomes.

quotes.text: we conclude that treatment with inactive vitamin D3 is preferable.
quotes.location: 4. Discussion, paragraph on differential effects on 25(OH)D levels

quotes.text: may represent an effective therapeutic approach for ME/CFS following PASC or COVID-19 vaccination.

second_reader.what_stands: The trial did not compare inactive D3 against active D, because both arms received alfacalcidol and the intervention arm added D3 plus lifestyle guidance. The statement that D3 is 'preferable' on efficiency and adverse-event risk rests on external references and a dose argument, not on a tested comparison. The main text gives no arm-by-arm adverse event or calcium comparison, though Supplementary Table S1 could contain one and I could not check it. The Conclusions section is more cautiously worded than the Discussion.

issues.title: Intervention is a bundle (D3 25 µg plus diet, sun, exercise guidance) versus general guidance; components not separable
issues.explanation: The two arms differ in a vitamin D3 supplement, dietary, sun-exposure and exercise advice, and the amount of clinician contact. The trial can show that the package outperformed the control, but not whether the effect comes from vitamin D3, the lifestyle advice or extra attention. The Discussion nevertheless attributes the symptom decrease to the rise in 25(OH)D from the supplement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An arm receiving only the D3 supplement, or attention-matched lifestyle guidance, showing the supplement alone drives the effect.
