quotes.text: The investigational treatment was defined as a combination of active vitamin D preparation and vitamin D replacement therapy guidance.
The control treatment was defined as a combination of active vitamin D preparation alone and general guidance.

issues.title: Primary endpoint is an unvalidated checklist symptom count that does not capture severity or QOL
issues.explanation: A count of present or absent symptoms treats mild and severe symptoms alike and has no established minimal important difference. A reduction of 5.6 symptoms may not translate into clinical benefit. The authors acknowledge this and defer functional outcomes to a later publication.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Concordant improvement on a validated severity or function scale at Week 12.

quotes.text: Another limitation of this study is the use of a simple symptom count as the primary endpoint, which does not directly reflect symptom severity or quality of life (QOL).

10.3390/nu18111706.headline_claim: Three months of L-citrulline supplementation reduced ICAM-1 concentrations and increased aerobic capacity in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.3390/nu18111706.overall: The ICAM-1 reduction and the 6MWT improvement are reported from a small, open-label trial registered about 4 years after it ended, with about 20 uncorrected tests and unexplained mismatches between Table 1 and Table 2 baselines and between printed changes and means. The conclusions should be read as hypothesis-generating, and the ICAM-1 result is borderline under any multiplicity correction. The 6MWT finding is a secondary outcome, and the control group also improved substantially.

primary_outcome.name: Endothelial function biomarkers (ICAM-1 is the headline result)

issues.title: Trial registered in April 2026, nearly 4 years after the study ended (Feb 2021 to May 2022)
issues.explanation: The paper reports registration on 22 April 2026, while enrolment and follow-up ran from February 2021 to May 2022. Outcomes, the primary endpoint and the analysis plan could not be verified before the data existed. This matters because several outcomes were tested without correction and the registry's outcome list differs from the paper's. The registry's first-submitted date (7 April 2026) also differs from the paper's 22 April.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prospectively dated protocol or registration that predates enrolment.

quotes.text: Registration date: 22 April 2026.
The study was carried out between February 2021 and May 2022

second_reader.what_stands: The trial was registered retrospectively, in April 2026, about 3 years 11 months after the stated end of the study in May 2022 (and roughly 5 years after it started), so the primary and secondary outcomes could not have been prospectively pre-specified in the registry. The paper does not acknowledge this in its limitations.

issues.title: ~20 outcomes tested at p<0.05, no correction; ICAM-1 group×time p=0.034 and 6MWT p=0.011 are the only hits
issues.explanation: Table 2 tests about 20 outcomes at an unadjusted 0.05 level. Only ICAM-1 (p = 0.034) and the 6MWT (p = 0.011) reach significance in the group-by-time test, and neither is adjusted for multiplicity. The Discussion says the findings should be read cautiously, but the Conclusions state both effects as established. With 5 endothelial markers, the ICAM-1 result is borderline under any correction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified single primary endpoint with a hierarchical testing plan.

quotes.text: A p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
only ICAM-1 showed a significant group × time effect

second_reader.what_stands: About 20 group × time tests were run at an uncorrected p < 0.05, and the two significant results (ICAM-1 p = 0.034 and 6MWT p = 0.011) would not survive a Bonferroni threshold of 0.0025 across all tests. The point is slightly weakened because the ICAM-1 test was the basis of the sample size calculation and the authors do urge caution about it, but multiplicity is never mentioned, and the conclusion states both findings without qualification.

issues.title: Baseline means in Table 2 differ from Table 1 for the same groups: 6MWT 421.14 vs 414.38 (IG), 433.94 vs 440.13 (CG)
issues.explanation: Table 1 and the 'Pre' columns of Table 2 should show the same baseline values, but they differ for the 6MWT in both arms, and also for handgrip and control-group ASMMI. The paper does not say Table 2 uses a different sample. The 6MWT is the basis of the aerobic-capacity conclusion, and the arms' baseline gap flips direction between tables (IG 12.8 m lower in Table 1, 25.8 m lower in Table 2). The analysis population for Table 2 is therefore unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 2 uses a different analysis set or adjusted means, with the n for each column.

quotes.location: Table 1, Six-minute walk test row, IG
Table 2, Six-minute walk test row, IG pre
Table 2, Six-minute walk test row, CG pre

issues.title: 6MWT/body composition called secondary in paper but listed as primary in the (retrospective) registry
issues.explanation: The registry lists endothelial markers, body composition and physical functionality as primary outcomes, and no secondary ones. The paper calls the 6MWT and body composition secondary, yet presents improved aerobic capacity as a main finding and conclusion. Because registration was retrospective, the registry cannot confirm which outcomes were fixed in advance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier prospective protocol or registry version that labels the 6MWT as secondary.

quotes.text: with secondary objectives to assess the effect of this supplementation on body composition and the six-minute walk test (6MWT)
The main finding of our study was that supplementation with L-citrulline was associated with decreased ICAM-1 levels and improved aerobic capacity.

issues.title: Discussion credits L-citrulline with LVEF/endothelial function gains not measured here; Conclusion omits control-arm 6MWT gain
issues.explanation: The Discussion says L-citrulline significantly improved ejection fraction, endothelial function and functional class, none of which this trial measured, and the other endothelial markers did not differ between groups. The Conclusion says supplementation increased aerobic capacity without noting that controls improved by 67.7 m, which the authors elsewhere attribute partly to natural recovery. The trial was open-label and the conclusion rests on an uncorrected, secondary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clear statement that the cardiac sentence refers to previously published work, and a Conclusion that notes the control-arm improvement.

quotes.text: in our experience, L-citrulline significantly improved left ventricular ejection fraction, endothelial function, and functional class
These findings may partially reflect the natural recovery process after severe COVID-19

issues.title: E-selectin baseline imbalance (72.31 vs 82.55, p=0.015); unclear whether Table 2 estimates are adjusted
issues.explanation: Despite randomisation, the arms differed at baseline in E-selectin, and hospital stay differed at p = 0.064. The Methods say the models were additionally adjusted for these, but Table 2 gives no adjusted estimates or notes. It cannot be confirmed that the ICAM-1 and 6MWT between-group results hold after adjustment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table showing adjusted and unadjusted ICAM-1 and 6MWT group×time estimates.

quotes.text: Participants in the intervention group exhibited significantly lower E-selectin levels (72.31 ± 13.07 vs. 82.55 ± 12.77; p = 0.015)
additionally adjusted for variables with p -values < 0.10, such as E-Selectin and hospital stay, using bivariate analysis.

issues.title: Table 2 changes often differ from post minus pre means: ICAM-1 CG -2.31 vs +1.28; 6MWT IG 141.2 vs 138.46
issues.explanation: In several rows the printed change is not the difference of the printed means: control ICAM-1 has opposite sign, 6MWT IG is 2.7 m off, 6MWT CG is 67.70 vs 61.00, and handgrip rows differ by 0.09 and 0.30. The authors may have reported adjusted model estimates, but Table 2 does not say so. Readers cannot tell which figures the p-values and the 6MWT group difference rest on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table note stating that Δ values are covariate-adjusted model estimates.

issues.title: Total body water: IG and CG share one CI (-2.78 to 1.92) and IG estimate 0.97 is off-centre; Lipids CI also repeated
issues.explanation: The intervention-group change of 0.97 has exactly the same CI as the control group's -0.43, and 0.97 is not near its midpoint (-0.43). The printed means imply a change of 0.30, not 0.97. The Lipids row repeats a CI the same way (IG 2.43 with -7.78 to 5.82, the same as CG). These look like printing errors in secondary results and do not touch the headline findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors' source output showing that IG TBW has a different CI.

quotes.location: Table 2, Total body water row, IG

script.explanation: the estimate 0.97 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-2.78, 1.92] (expected about -0.4300) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

10.3390/ph15010043.headline_claim: HRG80 Red Ginseng produced marked improvements in energy, sleep, mental clarity, pain relief and well-being in people with CFS and fibromyalgia, including post-viral CFS/FMS.
10.3390/ph15010043.overall: The one-month, open-label, single-arm pilot cannot establish that HRG80 caused the reported improvement, and the headline figures come from a subgroup selected on a post-treatment self-rating. The analysis also excludes about 27% of applicants and the conflict statement is inconsistent with the funding disclosure. The data support only a tentative, hypothesis-generating signal, as the authors partly acknowledge in calling for a placebo-controlled replication.

primary_outcome.name: VAS composite score (sum of energy, well-being and mental clarity), pre- to post-treatment

issues.title: Causal efficacy claimed from an open-label, uncontrolled pre-post design with self-rated outcomes
issues.explanation: All participants took HRG80 and rated themselves before and after, with no placebo or comparison group and no blinding. Improvement could come from expectation, natural fluctuation, regression to the mean after selecting people with low baseline scores, or concurrent treatments (which were allowed to continue). Yet the abstract and Discussion state that HRG80 'resulted in' marked improvement. The Conclusions call for replication but still state efficacy. The main conclusion is therefore not supported as a causal claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent placebo or untreated control arm with blinded outcome assessment showing the same improvement difference.

quotes.text: No placebo group was used as this was an open trial
The design (a prospective, open, unblinded trial)
Our study showed that HRG80 red ginseng root powder resulted in a marked improvement in people with CFS and fibromyalgia.

second_reader.what_stands: The design is single-arm, open-label and pre-post with self-rated outcomes, so it cannot separate a treatment effect from placebo response, expectation, regression to the mean or natural fluctuation. Even so, the Abstract and Conclusion say the product 'resulted in' improvement and 'showed' marked improvement. The Discussion limitations and the call for a placebo-controlled replication soften this but do not remove the causal wording.

issues.title: 27% of 258 applicants (70) excluded from analysis with no ITT or sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Of 258 applicants, 6 withdrew and 64 did not return the post-study questionnaire, leaving 188 analysed. Their data were dropped, and the authors acknowledge that loss may relate to side effects or non-response. A further 19 completers reported persistent side effects. Without an ITT or worst-case analysis, the reported improvement (and 60.1% 'improved') applies only to people who stayed and responded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or sensitivity analysis showing the improvement persists when non-completers are imputed as unchanged or worse.

quotes.text: Despite repeated requests for follow-up information, 64 participants did not fill out the post-study questionnaire or offer any information as to why they did not.
It is possible that they did not offer post-study data because of observed side effects or a lack of response to the intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: About 27% of the 258 applicants (70 people: 64 who did not complete follow-up plus 6 reported dropouts) are absent from the analysis. No ITT, imputation or sensitivity analysis is reported. The authors acknowledge the loss and its possible link to side effects or non-response, but they do not test how it affects the results. The Methods also describe 188 as having 'qualified' and agreed to complete post-questionnaires, which sits awkwardly with the 258 figure.

issues.title: Abstract headline gains (58%, 67%, 72%) come from the outcome-defined improver subgroup (113/188), not the full sample
issues.explanation: The abstract and Discussion report 58% composite, 67% energy and 72% stamina improvement from the 113 participants who rated themselves 'better' or 'much better' afterwards. That subgroup is selected on a post-treatment outcome, so large changes within it are expected by construction. The full-sample primary results are smaller (composite 40.2%, energy 50.0%, stamina 45.5%) and are not stated in the abstract. Readers are given an inflated sense of the typical effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract that reports the full-sample primary result as the headline, with the improver figures clearly labelled as post hoc subgroup results.

quotes.text: 58% average composite improvement in the previous three measurements (primary outcome measure)
The group that improved reported an average 67% increase in energy, 72% increase in stamina

second_reader.what_stands: The 58%, 67% and 72% figures do come from the 113 improvers (Table 3), not the full sample, where the corresponding gains are 40.2%, 50.0% and 45.5% (Table 2). The Abstract labels them as an 'in this group' result but gives no full-sample figures. The improver group is defined by the participants' own post-treatment global rating, which is itself an outcome, so its larger gains are partly built in by selection.

issues.title: 'No conflict of interest' declared despite advisory role with the distributor, free product and paid statistician
issues.explanation: The funding statement says the lead author sits on the scientific advisory board of EuroPharma, which markets HRG80, and that EuroPharma supplied the product and paid the statistician and publication fees. The Conflicts of Interest statement nevertheless says there are none, and the funding line says the author provided funding. The facts are partly disclosed but the formal declaration is inconsistent with them. This does not alter the numbers but matters given an open-label, subjective-outcome positive study of a sponsor's product.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conflicts statement that lists the advisory role and company support, or evidence that the journal's form treats these as non-conflicts.

quotes.text: He is an unpaid member of the scientific advisory board of EuroPharma, the company with distribution and marketing rights for HRG80 in North America.
EuroPharma supplied the supplement and shipping to the study subjects at no charge and reimbursed the cost of the statistician and publication fees.
The authors declare no conflict of interest.

issues.title: Generalisability to the US CFS/FMS population asserted from a self-selected, 89% female, 188-person sample
issues.explanation: Participants were invited from the lead author's practice and newsletter, and only people willing to commit to the post-study questionnaire were counted. The authors nonetheless say the findings should generalise to the US population. Self-selection, a very female sample and completer-only analysis limit what can be extended beyond this group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of representative sampling or comparison of participants with the national CFS/FMS population.

quotes.text: The study population reflected a diverse population of people in the United States suffering with CFS and fibromyalgia.
The author (J.T.) invited his patients as well as readers of his newsletter to participate in this study.

issues.title: Table 3 well-being 'percent improvement' (43.6%) does not match its means (3.8 to 6.3 = 65.8%)
issues.explanation: In the improver subsample, well-being rises from 3.8 to 6.3, which is a 65.8% increase by the same method used in every other row. The table and abstract report 43.6% and 44%. Either the percentage or one of the means is wrong, and the composite sums fit the printed means. This understates the improver well-being effect; it is a reporting error affecting one reported result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The percentage being a mean of individual percent changes rather than computed from group means, stated as such (the other rows contradict this).

quotes.text: 44% average increase in overall well-being

issues.title: 'Qualified' used for 188 (Methods) and 258 (Discussion); stated loss of ~25% omits the 6 dropouts
issues.explanation: Methods says 188 participants 'qualified', but Results and Discussion show 258 met the inclusion criteria and only 188 completed. The counts reconcile once 6 dropouts and 64 non-responders are subtracted. The Discussion's '~25% (64)' loss leaves out the 6 dropouts, so total non-completion is about 27%. The effect is small, but the Methods wording hides the true size of the starting group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram text stating that 188 is the number of completers out of 258 eligible applicants (Figure 2 is not legible in this text).

quotes.text: A total of 188 participants qualified for the study by meeting the inclusion criteria below
of the 258 people who initially qualified for the study

10.3390/ph15030345.headline_claim: Overall, this pilot study demonstrates that Chisan®/ADAPT-232 can increase physical performance in Long COVID, and might be useful for preventing the progression of renal failure associated with increasing creatinine.
10.3390/ph15030345.overall: The headline claim that ADAPT-232 increases physical performance is a nominal secondary result in a 100-patient pilot, set against a null primary duration outcome and many uncorrected tests. The renal claim is weaker still. Several internal inconsistencies (dropouts 22 vs 1, unlabelled SEs, mislabelled units, an implausible SD) reduce confidence in the data handling, but none destroys the null primary finding.

primary_outcome.name: Duration of symptoms of Long COVID (average of all symptoms, Table 2)

primary_outcomes.measure: Duration of symptoms of Long COVID:
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from baseline during the period of the treatment and follow up (from Day 1 to Day 14 and day 21 after randomization)
Change from baseline during the period of the treatment and follow up (from Day 1 to Day 14 and day 21 after randomization)

primary_outcomes.measure: Length of home stay/ sick listed
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from baseline during the period of the treatment and follow up (from Day 1 to Day 14 and day 21 after randomization)

primary_outcomes.measure: Severity of the Long COVID symptoms
primary_outcomes.time_frame: Change from baseline during the period of the treatment and follow up (trough 21 days after randomization)

issues.title: Conclusion claims increased physical performance though the primary duration outcome was null (p = 0.5375)
issues.explanation: The primary outcome, average duration of all symptoms, is 7.640 days with ADAPT-232 versus 7.463 days with placebo (p = 0.5375), and fatigue, headache and other durations also show no difference. The one headline positive finding is the walk-time result, seen in a figure, in a pilot of 100 patients. Table 1 shows baseline walk time was already higher in the ADAPT group (5.534 vs 5.162). The abstract-level claim that the product 'can increase physical performance' goes beyond a nominal secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy naming walk time as the primary outcome with a significant adjusted result.

quotes.text: Overall, this pilot study demonstrates that Chisan®/ADAPT-232 can increase physical performance in Long COVID.
Average duration of all symptoms, days

second_reader.what_stands: The duration outcome (p = 0.5375) and the home-stay outcome (p = 0.9839) are indeed null, and the Conclusion states physical performance 'can increase' with the stronger verb 'demonstrates' for a pilot trial. But the claim rests on a separate outcome (daily walk time, Figure 1) which the Methods list as a primary measure, so it is not strictly contradicted by the null duration result; the walk-time result itself could not be verified from the text provided (no p-value or numbers given). Most symptom-severity differences are described as non-significant.

issues.title: About a dozen outcomes and many timepoints tested at 5% with no multiplicity control; few nominal hits drive conclusions
issues.explanation: The paper tests twelve listed outcomes, many symptoms, and several visit days, including row-by-row multiple t-tests, all at 5%. Only a few nominal results are reported as significant (walk time, cough, creatinine, day-9 pain, day-11 fatigue, IL-6 at p = 0.0487). With this many tests, a handful of p < 0.05 results is expected by chance, so these should be read as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan or adjusted p-values for the reported significant findings.

quotes.text: The level of statistical significance was set at 5% in all methods.
multiple t-tests

second_reader.what_stands: The paper sets alpha at 5% for all methods and describes no multiplicity correction, despite about a dozen outcomes, multiple visits and many symptom-level tests. Several conclusions (IL-6 p = 0.0487, fatigue p = 0.0157 on a single day, creatinine, walk time) rest on isolated nominal significance, and the authors do not discuss multiplicity as a limitation, although the study is labelled a pilot.

issues.title: Dropouts stated as 22 in Methods 4.2.3 but as 1 (99 of 100 completers) in Methods 4.1
issues.explanation: Section 4.2.3 says 22 participants dropped out. Section 4.1 says 99 of 100 completed and one stopped, and the analysis tables use nearly the full sample. If 22 were true, attrition would be about 22% and the 'observed data' efficacy analysis would rest on far fewer patients than reported. If 1 is true, the 22 is a wrong statement. The paper does not say which, so the reliability of the completer-based between-group estimates cannot be judged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow chart or text showing 22 dropouts, or a statement that 22 is a planned or template figure rather than an observed count.

quotes.text: There were 22 cases of participant dropouts from the study.
In total, 99 patients (99%) completed their respective treatment cycles according to protocol

issues.title: Walk time called 'objective' in Discussion but listed as patient-reported in Table 3, with no validation
issues.explanation: The headline physical-performance claim rests on walking minutes and a questionnaire score. The paper describes the walk time as objectively recorded but schedules it among patient-reported outcomes and does not describe how it was measured or validated. Table 1 values (5.534 min, SD 0.0628) are also unusually tight. This limits how far the finding can be read as physical performance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of device-based or validated measurement of daily walk time.

quotes.text: increasing their physical activity and workout (daily walk time) was recorded by objective measures
Workout, min

issues.title: Table 2 placebo fatigue-duration SD (0.648) repeats the Table 1 baseline fatigue SD and is implausible
issues.explanation: Mean fatigue duration is 12.98 days in placebo with SD 0.648, against SD 4.899 in the ADAPT group at 11.96 days. A tenfold smaller spread is implausible and the figure equals the baseline fatigue score SD in Table 1. This points to a transcription error in the fatigue-duration row, so its p-value (0.2662, Mann-Whitney) cannot be checked from the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing a placebo SD of 0.648 days for fatigue duration.

quotes.text: Fatigue, days

issues.title: Renal-protection claim rests on one creatinine comparison in patients with normal baseline creatinine
issues.explanation: Creatinine was a secondary biomarker, patients had normal levels (about 77 vs 75.5 μM), and the follow-up was 21 days. The paper gives no effect size or p-value for the creatinine difference in the text and no kidney outcomes. A small shift within the normal range does not show prevention of renal failure progression.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported creatinine between-group estimate with a pre-specified analysis and a clinically meaningful difference.

quotes.text: It also suggests that Chisan®/ADAPT-232 might be useful for preventing the progression of renal failure associated with increasing creatinine.
ADAPT-232 significantly decreased blood creatinine compared to placebo, suggesting prevention of renal failure progression in Long COVID.

issues.title: IL-6 'normal level' is < 30 in Methods but < 5.186 in Table 1
issues.explanation: Two different reference limits are given for IL-6. The Table 1 value is a pooled mean from the literature, not a clinical cut-off. This changes how many patients look abnormal at baseline but not any trial result. Other limits are also odd (CRP 'normal < 350 mg/L', D-dimer in pg/L).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the table label gives the healthy-donor mean rather than a cut-off.

quotes.text: IL-6 (mean 6.1 pg/mL, normal level
The pooled estimate of IL-6 was 5.186 pg/mL

issues.title: Baseline IL-6 dispersion in text (1.548, 0.554) is the SE of Table 1's SDs (10.95, 3.919), unlabelled
issues.explanation: The text and table give different spreads for the same baseline means. The text values match the table SDs divided by sqrt(50), so they are SEs shown as if they were SDs. The mislabelling makes the IL-6 groups look much more homogeneous than they are. The post-treatment IL-6 'significance' (p = 0.0487) rests on multiple t-tests across rows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated label of SEM in the Discussion.

issues.title: Blinding described as quadruple in Methods 4.3.1 and double-blind in Methods 4.3.4
issues.explanation: The paper uses two blinding labels. The registry says quadruple, so this is probably loose terminology. The paper does not describe how outcome assessors were blinded, and the QP, sponsor and PI handled the code lists.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A single consistent blinding statement naming who was masked.

quotes.text: The treatment regime was quadruple-blinded
and the study was double-blind.

issues.title: Neutrophil count (60.89) exceeds total WBC (8.96), both labelled 10^3 u/L; differential rows sum to ~99
issues.explanation: Neutrophils cannot exceed total leukocytes, so the unit on the differential rows is wrong. The five differential values sum to about 99, which fits percentages. This is a labelling slip in baseline data and does not affect efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the unit label is wrong either way.

quotes.text: Total Leukocyte count, WBC
Absolute Neutrophil count

10.3390/ph16040537.headline_claim: Recombinant human IL-2 treatment restored NK cell count and functional potential in patients with post-COVID syndrome, and its effectiveness has been proven in patients with low NK cell levels.
10.3390/ph16040537.overall: The finding that NK cell counts rose after rhIL-2 in this single-arm cohort is descriptive and plausible, but the paper's claim that effectiveness is 'proven' is not supported by an uncontrolled, open-label, 29-patient design with patients selected for low NK counts. Several text-table inconsistencies and uncorrected multiple subset tests further weaken the secondary subset claims.

primary_outcome.name: NK cell count and functional potential (no single primary outcome labelled)

issues.title: Abstract states rhIL-2 effectiveness 'has been proven' from a 29-patient uncontrolled open-label study
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion say effectiveness has been proven, based on laboratory NK values before and after treatment in a single uncontrolled group. The limitations section notes open-label design and small sample but does not qualify this wording. Clinical benefit is not assessed formally, and the claim is stronger than the design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomized controlled comparison or qualified wording of efficacy.

quotes.text: In general, the effectiveness of using rhIL-2 in treatment of post-COVID syndrome has been proven in patients with low levels of NK cells.
In addition, the study treatment design was open-label.

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract and Conclusions say effectiveness 'has been proven' on the basis of an uncontrolled, open-label study of 29 patients with surrogate immunophenotype endpoints. That wording is stronger than the design supports, and the Limitations section does not mention the lack of a control arm. The claim can be read as referring only to NK cell numbers and phenotype, but even that is not shown to be caused by rhIL-2.

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute NK cell change to rhIL-2; selected low-NK patients
issues.explanation: All 29 patients received rhIL-2 with basic therapy, and the only comparison is before vs after plus a healthy reference group. Patients were selected for low NK counts, so regression to the mean and co-treatment are alternative explanations. The abstract's conclusion of restoration due to rhIL-2 goes beyond this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo patient group with the same selection and measurements.

quotes.text: all patients with post-COVID syndrome received recombinant human IL-2 (hrIL-2) at a dose of 0.5 mg
NK cell absolute count less than 0.07 × 10 9 cells/L, and/or relative number less than 5% out of lymphocyte population

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design in patients selected for low NK cell values, with no untreated patient comparator. Rises in NK cell counts therefore cannot be attributed causally to rhIL-2, because regression to the mean, the concurrent basic therapy and natural recovery are not excluded. The large size of the changes and the known biology of IL-2 make a real drug effect plausible but not demonstrated by this design.

issues.title: Dozens of NK subset tests in Tables 2-6 with no multiplicity correction or primary outcome
issues.explanation: Tables 2-6 report many subset comparisons against controls and before/after, and the statistical analysis section describes no correction or prespecified primary outcome. Some borderline p-values (0.047, 0.049, 0.022) would not survive correction. Strong effects (p < 0.001) would likely survive, so the weakening is mainly for secondary subset claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome and correction method in a protocol.

quotes.text: The significance of differences for quantitative parameters from unrelated samples was assessed using the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test.

issues.title: Text says pre-treatment CD16+CD56dim CD8+ NK >5-fold above controls; Table 5 medians 0.21 vs 0.24
issues.explanation: The Results state the pre-treatment level of CD16+CD56dim CD8+ NK cells was more than 5-fold higher than controls, and the Discussion says it was significantly higher. Table 5 gives 0.21 before treatment versus 0.24 in controls, with no p-value flag. The text description is not supported by the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original table showing a before-treatment median about 1.2 or higher for this subset.

quotes.text: before treatment was more than 5-fold higher than in the control group

issues.title: Control group size: 35 volunteers in Methods vs n = 30 in Figure 1 and 2 captions
issues.explanation: Methods say 35 age-matched volunteers were examined, but both figure captions give the healthy control group as n = 30. No exclusion or flow explanation is given. The control size behind the Mann-Whitney comparisons is therefore unclear, though this affects only the reference group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 5 controls were excluded or had missing data for the figures.

quotes.text: As a control group, 35 age-matched volunteers were examined.
healthy control group (HC, n = 30)

issues.title: Prospective rhIL-2 treatment study reports ethics approval but no trial registration
issues.explanation: The study treats all patients prospectively with an interventional drug, but no registry or registration number appears. Outcomes and analysis cannot be checked against a prespecified plan. Practice norms vary, so this is a limited concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier for this study.

quotes.text: An observational therapeutic prospective clinical study was conducted with patients undergoing rehabilitation

issues.title: Abstract p = 0.001 for CD57+ NK cells matches no Results value (percentage p < 0.001; count p = 0.004/0.011)
issues.explanation: The abstract gives p = 0.001 for CD57+ NK cells. The Results report p < 0.001 for the percentage and p = 0.004 and 0.011 for the absolute count. The abstract value matches neither exactly, a small reporting inconsistency that does not alter the direction of the finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source table showing p = 0.001 for the CD57+ comparison cited in the abstract.

quotes.text: decreased count of CD57 + ( p = 0.001)

issues.title: Discussion says CD56+CD94+ reduced >30-fold; Table 6 medians give about 26-fold
issues.explanation: The Discussion claims a reduction of more than 30-fold versus controls. Table 6 medians (5.25 vs 0.20) give about 26-fold. The reduction is real and large, so the error is a minor exaggeration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Mean-based ratios or unrounded medians giving a ratio above 30.

quotes.text: was reduced by more than 30-fold compared to the control group

script.explanation: Control/before-treatment median ratio vs claimed >30-fold: 5.25 / 0.2 gives 26.25, not the printed 30. For the printed value to hold the denominator would have to be 0.175, not 0.2.

issues.title: Text calls pre-treatment CD16+CD56dim increase significant; Table 2 (0.97 vs 0.69) shows no p-value
issues.explanation: The Results say both CD16+CD56dim and CD16-CD56dim cells were significantly increased before treatment. Table 2 gives a p-value only for the CD16-CD56dim row; the CD16+CD56dim row (0.97 vs 0.69) has none. The text overstates one comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A p-value below 0.05 for this comparison in the source table.

quotes.text: the count of CD16 + CD56 dim and CD16 -CD56 dim NKcells was significantly increased (Table 2)

issues.title: Inclusion required WHO score 3-7, but Table 7 lists 13 of 29 patients in the 1-3 band
issues.explanation: The inclusion criteria require WHO scores of 3 to 7, yet Table 7 groups 13 patients (44.83%) as 1-3. If all 13 scored exactly 3 this is consistent; the banding hides it. The paper cannot settle whether patients below the stated criterion were enrolled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level scores showing all 13 in the band had score 3.

quotes.text: prior acute COVID-19 (severity ranging from 3 to 7 score according to the WHO criteria)

10.3390/ph17040463.headline_claim: The oral food supplement (Echinacea angustifolia, rosehip, propolis, royal jelly, zinc) shows beneficial effects on the inflammatory state, fatigue and quality of life in long COVID patients.
10.3390/ph17040463.overall: The headline claim of anti-inflammatory and anti-fatigue benefit rests on a small, 33-patient crossover with no primary outcome, no multiplicity control and an undefined between-period analysis, so it is at best hypothesis-generating. Several reporting errors (CRP unit, BMI outlier, polyphenol units) add to concerns about data quality, though they do not by themselves overturn the nominal results.

primary_outcome.name: Not specified; CRP, NLR, MLR, vitamin D and FSS are reported as the main findings

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from within-period significance; no described between-period test; vitamin D also rose on placebo
issues.explanation: The text frames effects as occurring 'only' in the OFS period, but a significant change in one period and non-significant in another is not a test of difference between them. Vitamin D also rose in the placebo period (31.20 to 33.98), and the single p-value per row is not defined in terms of which comparison it tests. A crossover with period and carry-over effects needs a within-subject treatment contrast, which is not described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement that the p-values test OFS-versus-placebo change differences, with period and sequence effects handled.

quotes.text: we observed a statistically significant improvement in fatigue monitored by the FSS questionnaire, exclusively in the period of the OFS treatment
Data expressed as mean ± standard deviation; applied test: t -test for paired data.

second_reader.what_stands: The FSS efficacy claim ('exclusively in the period of the OFS treatment') rests on a within-period p = 0.0001, with no described between-period test or interaction test, and the Methods name only ANOVA and chi-squared. Vitamin D also rose on placebo (+2.78 vs +6.58 on OFS), so 'only after OFS adoption' overstates it; the table p = 0.0005 is not defined as a between-period test, and I could not verify the FSS placebo values from the text.

issues.title: ~40 outcomes tested at p ≤ 0.05 with no correction or primary outcome; NLR p = 0.0455 borderline
issues.explanation: The paper tests dozens of endpoints without a declared primary outcome or any multiplicity adjustment. Only four laboratory results reach nominal significance, and one is p = 0.0455. Several of these would not survive correction, so the inflammatory conclusion is tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or hierarchical testing plan.

quotes.text: Values of p ≤ 0.05 are considered statistically significant.
(neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, p = 0.0455; monocyte to-lymphocyte ratio, p = 0.0005; C-reactive protein, p = 0.0145)

second_reader.what_stands: About 38 table outcomes (more including questionnaires) were tested at p ≤ 0.05 with no stated primary outcome or multiplicity adjustment, and NLR p = 0.0455 and CRP p = 0.0145 would not survive a Bonferroni threshold of about 0.0013. The NLR result is borderline at the nominal alpha.

issues.title: Conclusion claims confirmed benefit, QoL gain and synergy; SF-36 is only a descriptive 'trend', ingredients not tested
issues.explanation: Quality-of-life improvement is supported only by a described trend in figures with no test. The synergy claim cannot be assessed because only the combined product was given. The conclusion therefore goes beyond what the reported data show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported SF-36 domain statistics with a between-period comparison, and ingredient-level data.

quotes.text: The charts show an increasing trend at the end of the treatment (T1) only during the OFS treatment.
thanks to the synergistic effect of NBCs contained in the tested OFSs

second_reader.what_stands: The SF-36 result is described only as a visual 'increasing trend' with no statistical test, yet the Conclusions state a 'noticeable improvement' in quality of life and that the trial 'would seem to confirm' benefit. The 'synergistic effect' of ingredients is asserted although only the combined product was compared with placebo, so synergy was not tested; the stated limitations (sample size, unmeasured zinc and vitamin C) do not address this.

issues.title: Methods name chi-squared and ANOVA; tables report paired t-tests; the comparison behind each p is undefined
issues.explanation: The statistical section says a Chi-squared test was used for inference on categorical variables, yet all outcomes are continuous means and the footnotes say paired t-test. No test is described for the OFS-versus-placebo comparison quoted in the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods clarification of the test applied to each outcome.

quotes.text: The Chi-squared test was carried out for the execution of the inferential statistical analysis

issues.title: Placebo T1 BMI 30.68 ± 35.91 inconsistent with other BMI cells (~24 ± 3) and the 18.5-25 inclusion range
issues.explanation: An SD of 35.91 for BMI is implausible, and the mean is far from all other BMI cells, including the placebo T0 value of 24.19. This indicates a data error or outlier in the dataset; weight (67.80 ± 11.10) and height (1.67) in the same column imply BMI near 24. It suggests data quality problems but does not affect the significant findings directly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing an extreme outlier is genuine and a corrected value.

quotes.text: Body mass index (BMI) between 18.5 and 25 kg/m 2

issues.title: 33 patients, no sample size calculation; abstract states benefits without hedging
issues.explanation: With 33 patients and no power calculation, the study can only be exploratory. The limitation is acknowledged, but the abstract still states 'This study showed the OFS's beneficial effects'. This weakens the main result to tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation supporting n = 33.

quotes.text: The study population included 33 patients, 14 males and 19 females
This study showed the OFS's beneficial effects on the inflammatory state, fatigue and quality of life in long COVID patients.

issues.title: Randomization and allocation concealment not described; groups 'divided' to be homogeneous
issues.explanation: The trial is called randomized, but the method of sequence generation and concealment is not given, and the wording suggests deliberate balancing. This cannot be settled from the paper. It matters for a crossover because order effects and carry-over are unassessed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of computer-generated randomization with concealed allocation.

quotes.text: The study population was divided into two homogeneous groups (group A and group B) for age, sex and BMI.

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported; only the ethics protocol code
issues.explanation: The paper gives an ethics approval code but no registry entry, so prespecified outcomes cannot be checked. This is relevant given multiple outcomes and no declared primary endpoint. It may be an omission rather than a lack of registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment with matching outcomes.

quotes.text: protocol code RS 150.21, approved on 4 November 2021

issues.title: CRP unit inconsistent: mg/dL in Results text, mg/L in Table 2, for the same 2.77 and 1.44 values
issues.explanation: The Results text reports CRP as 2.77 and 1.44 mg/dL, while Table 2 labels the same values mg/L. These differ by a factor of 10. The numbers themselves match, so this is a labelling error that does not alter the reported significance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the assay unit was converted between text and table.

quotes.text: the CRP decreased significantly (2.77 ± 2.5 mg/dL vs. 1.44 ± 1.70 mg/dL)
CRP (mg/L)

issues.title: Polyphenol 43.98 given as mg/g in Abstract but as mg per capsule in Table 6 (400 mg capsule)
issues.explanation: The same figure of 43.98 is reported with two different units. Given a 400 mg capsule, the two units imply different quantities (about 17.6 mg vs 43.98 mg per capsule). This is a reporting inconsistency in the product characterization, not in the clinical outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods stating the capsule mass or conversion that reconciles both figures.

quotes.text: The OFS's total polyphenol content was 43.98 mg/g gallic acid equivalents.
Total Polyphenols for Capsule, Expressed as Gallic Acid (mg)

10.3390/pharmacy11020061.headline_claim: Community pharmacist counselling with proposed self-medication 'led to a significant improvement' in the condition of patients with post-COVID symptoms, with median self-reported severity falling from 3 to 1.
10.3390/pharmacy11020061.overall: The descriptive findings (symptom frequencies, referral and follow-up patterns) are usable, though Table 2 and Table 3 contain several small numerical inconsistencies and the abstract's respiratory 51.2% does not match its own count. The headline claim that the pharmacists' intervention 'led to' significant improvement is not supported, because the study has no comparator, relies on unblinded self-rated severity from a non-psychometrically validated scale, and analyses only the 69.5% who returned. At best the data show symptoms were rated lower 3-4 weeks after counselling.

primary_outcome.name: Patient self-reported symptom severity (1-5 scale), first visit vs follow-up visit

issues.title: Uncontrolled before-after cohort cannot support 'pharmacists' intervention led to significant improvement'
issues.explanation: All 871 patients received the intervention and only their own first-visit and follow-up severity ratings are compared. There is no comparator group, so natural recovery over 3-4 weeks, regression to the mean and other care cannot be separated from the pharmacist's effect. The authors concede this in the limitations, yet the abstract states the intervention 'led to' improvement and the conclusions say symptoms were 'efficiently ... treated and controlled'. The improvement is real as a before-after description, but attributing it to the intervention is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical untreated comparison group, or natural-history data showing post-COVID symptom severity does not fall over 3-4 weeks without treatment.

quotes.text: The pharmacists' intervention led to a significant improvement in the post-COVID patients' condition.
It was not always possible to determine if the improvement in symptoms in the postCOVID period for patients was a direct result of pharmacist recommendations only
A large spectrum of post-COVID symptoms could be efficiently identified, treated and controlled in the self-medication process

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm before-after cohort with no control group, with outcomes self-reported on a 1-5 scale and about 30% lost to follow-up. It therefore cannot show that the pharmacists' intervention caused the improvement, and the abstract's 'led to a significant improvement' and the Conclusions' 'efficiently ... treated and controlled' overstate it. The paper's own limitations section acknowledges that time or other factors could explain the change, which weakens but does not remove the problem, since the abstract and Conclusions are not hedged accordingly.

issues.title: Severity ratings (1-5) self-reported to the same pharmacist who delivered the advice, unblinded
issues.explanation: The key outcome is a 1-5 patient rating of symptom severity, collected by the counselling pharmacist at both visits. Patients' expectations and social desirability can move such ratings in the direction of the intervention. This is partly inherent to a patient-reported outcome, and the authors acknowledge the subjectivity, so it weakens the efficacy reading rather than creating a separate error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that ratings were entered by patients independently of the counselling pharmacist, or corroborated by an objective measure.

quotes.text: a section for patients' subjective descriptions of their symptom intensity and severity marked on a scale of 1-5
One of the limitations of this study was the use of patient-reported subjective data

issues.title: Severity scale built for the study and piloted on 5 pharmacists, yet later described as 'validated'
issues.explanation: The questionnaire was developed by the programme leads and checked only by a one-week pilot with five pharmacists for clarity and content. No reliability, construct validity or responsiveness data are reported. Section 4.3 nonetheless describes triage using a 'validated questionnaire'. The 1-5 scale is anchored only at 'lowest' and 'highest', so its sensitivity to change is untested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A published psychometric validation of this questionnaire or its severity scale in a comparable population.

quotes.text: The standardized questionnaire was developed by the lead members of the SMART Pharmacist Program, based on a review of the available literature in November 2021
triage using a validated questionnaire
quotes.location: Section 4.3, Impact of Education on Application in Practice

issues.title: 30.5% did not return; change analysed only in returners with no comparison of those lost
issues.explanation: Only 69.5% of the 871 patients came back, and the improvement analyses use patients who reported at the second visit. The paper gives no baseline comparison of returners and non-returners and no sensitivity analysis. About 266 patients' outcomes are unknown, so the median fall from 3 to 1 describes a self-selected subset. The Discussion calls the follow-up rate 'really high', which does not acknowledge this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison showing returners and non-returners had similar baseline severity and symptoms, or an analysis imputing the missing outcomes.

quotes.text: and 69.5% returned to the pharmacist for a follow-up visit
for patients who reported the changes in the second visit
quotes.location: Section 3.1, Analysis of the Most Frequent Symptoms

issues.title: Immunity status: female count 117 does not match its 33.1% (117/534=21.9%); F+M=217 vs All 280
issues.explanation: In Table 2 the immunity row gives 117 females at 33.1%, but 117 of 534 is 21.9%. The female and male counts sum to 217 against an overall 280. A 177 in place of 117 would reconcile the percentage and nearly the total, so this looks like a typographical error. One table row is wrong, and the main conclusions are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source data showing 117 females at 21.9% with a different, consistent overall count.

script.explanation: 117/534 = 21.91%, but the paper prints 33.1, outside the rounding interval [33.05, 33.20]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 353.5 rather than 534.

issues.title: Table 2 'All' counts exceed female+male in many rows; respiratory 476 prints 51.2% where 476/871=54.7%
issues.explanation: Female plus male is 871, yet in most rows the overall count is larger than the two sexes added together. Behavioural changes show 121 vs 111, respiratory 476 vs 472, digestive 254 vs 251, skin/hair/nail 239 vs 236, cognitive 243 vs 241, insomnia 170 vs 169 and one symptom 300 vs 299. Table 5 age-group totals agree with the sex sums rather than the 'All' column (respiratory 471, digestive 250, behavioural 111). The abstract's headline respiratory figure of 51.2% does not match 476/871 = 54.7% (or 472/871 = 54.2%). These are reporting errors in a descriptive table and do not change the efficacy conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A note that some patients were counted in the 'All' column but not allocated to either sex or age group, with 51.2% computed on a different base.

quotes.text: mostly related to the respiratory system (51.2%)

script.explanation: 476/871 = 54.65%, but the paper prints 51.2, outside the rounding interval [51.15, 51.30]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 929.7 rather than 871.

issues.title: Table 3: several referral % and a follow-up % do not match the printed counts (e.g. 7/115 printed 5.0)
issues.explanation: In Table 3 several percentages disagree with the counts beside them. Memory referrals are 7 of 115 but printed 5.0% (computed 6.1%). Dehydrated skin is 2 of 93 printed 1.8% (computed 2.2%), and daily sleepiness 9 of 90 printed 7.8% (computed 10.0%). The hair loss follow-up rate is 130/163 = 79.8%, printed 81.3. The discrepancies are small and affect secondary descriptive figures only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator for the referral percentages under which all four rows reconcile, and a hair loss follow-up N other than 163/130.

quotes.location: Table 3, Memory, ability to remember row

script.explanation: 7/115 = 6.09%, but the paper prints 5.0, outside the rounding interval [4.95, 5.10]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 140.0 rather than 115.

issues.title: 871 patients nested in 53 pharmacists analysed as independent; many unadjusted symptom-level tests
issues.explanation: Patients are clustered within 53 pharmacists whose counselling style and recording may differ, but the Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests treat patients as independent. Dozens of symptom and age-group tests are also run without a multiplicity correction. P-values are therefore somewhat too small, though the large reported shifts are unlikely to be erased.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A mixed-model or cluster-robust analysis with pharmacist as a random effect giving the same conclusions.

quotes.text: In total, 871 patients with post-COVID symptoms were included in the study, served by 53 pharmacists.
Changes in data between two repeated observations were analysed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

issues.title: Discussion says study 'confirmed' fatigue is more common in females; Table 2 shows 29.8% F vs 31.4% M (p=0.620)
issues.explanation: The Discussion cites studies finding fatigue more common in females and says 'This study confirmed that pattern.' Table 2 shows fatigue slightly more common in males, and the difference is not significant. Only the skin/hair finding supports the female pattern. This is a secondary claim and does not affect the main conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'pattern' refers only to alopecia/hair changes, with fatigue explicitly excluded.

quotes.text: This study confirmed that pattern.

issues.title: Table 6 prints a follow-up rate of 10 (Sight, ≤43) while text says the lowest was 60% (hearing)
issues.explanation: The Results state that the lowest follow-up rate across age groups was 60% (hearing, younger patients). Table 6 prints 10 for the youngest sight group. This is probably a truncated 100, but as printed it contradicts the text. The text also says follow-up was 'similar' across groups, which sits uneasily with values from 60 to 100.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source table showing the Sight ≤43 follow-up as 100.

quotes.text: with the lowest being for younger patients with hearing changes (60%)

quotes.location: Table 6, Sight row, follow-up rate columns

10.3390/s23135880.headline_claim: Active tDCS (anode FPz, cathode IZ, 0.5 mA) improved olfactory performance in post-COVID anosmia/hyposmia, with the authors noting the progression did not reach statistical significance.
10.3390/s23135880.overall: The paper is a small pilot (15 completers, 2 anosmic) whose Conclusions are appropriately hedged, but the Discussion's statement that stimulation was effective only for anosmic subjects is not supported: it rests on two active-arm subjects with no anosmic sham and null interaction tests. Several internal inconsistencies (C38 data, classification labels, the stimulation montage, and the ANOVA error structure) further reduce confidence in the reported group results. Treat the findings as exploratory and hypothesis-generating only.

primary_outcome.name: Sniffin' Sticks TDI score (threshold, discrimination, identification) before vs after stimulation

issues.title: 'Effective only for anosmic' rests on 2 active-arm subjects' pre-post change; interaction p=0.87–0.98, no anosmic sham
issues.explanation: The Discussion says active stimulation was effective only for anosmic participants. That rests on two subjects whose mean TDI rose from 15.38 to 17.00, with no anosmic subjects in the sham arm and non-significant pairwise changes. The treatment-relevant group×assessment interactions are all null (TDI p=0.8727). The 'all p<0.05' statement reflects the group main effect, i.e. baseline differences, and one cited p is 0.0502. The text also says hyposmic active subjects declined with only one improving by under a point, but C22 rose 7.75 and C30 rose 0.75. Regression to the mean and test repetition are unaddressed, and the Conclusions' wording is correspondingly stronger than the data allow.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-arm test including sham anosmic subjects, or a significant group×time interaction, showing greater change in anosmic active subjects.

quotes.text: active stimulation was found to be effective only for individuals with anosmic scores.
those with hyposmic values exhibited a decrease in performance (only one of them improved their TDI score, but by less than one point
It is noteworthy to mention that the anosmic group could not be included in this study due to the limited number of available samples, which comprised only two cases.

second_reader.what_stands: The 'effective only for anosmic' statement rests on the pre-post change of two active-arm subjects (+2.5 and +2.25 TDI points). There is no anosmic sham group, no interaction test supports a group difference (p = 0.87 to 0.98 for THR, ID and TDI, with discrimination at 0.39), and the paper itself reports no significant change. The text's claim that only one hyposmic active subject improved, and by under a point, is contradicted by Table 3, where C22 improved by 7.75. The printed anosmic initial TDI (15.38 ± 0.18) also does not match the Table 3 values (14.875). The authors do caveat non-signif

issues.title: 20 allocated, 15 analysed (25% loss); arm of dropouts and ITT analysis not reported
issues.explanation: Twenty patients were allocated to stimulation but only 15 completed, with dropouts described as declining to continue. The arms the five came from are not stated and no intention-to-treat analysis is shown. Differential dropout could shift the small active/sham comparison. The paper discloses the loss only in the EEG discussion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing dropouts balanced across arms and an ITT analysis with similar results.

quotes.text: Initially, a sample of 20 patients was allocated to stimulation, but this was later reduced to 15 after some patients declined to continue with the experimental procedure.

issues.title: C38 baseline (ID 7, TDI 14.25) in Tables 1/3 conflicts with Table 5 (ID 7.5±0.71, TDI 15.38±0.18); C38 difference 2.25 too
issues.explanation: The anosmic subjects' initial TDI values in Table 3 (15.5 and 14.25) give a mean of 14.88 and an SD of 0.88, not the 15.38±0.18 in Table 5 and the text. The Table 5 figures fit C38 having ID 8 and TDI 15.25. Separately, C38's printed TDI difference is 2.25, but 16 minus 14.25 is 1.75 (and 0.75 on the Table 5 value). The anosmic mean change (+1.62) is the headline benefit, so the row error matters modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing C38's initial ID and TDI values and which table is correct.

quotes.text: TDI Initial 15.38±0.18
ID Initial 7.5±0.71

issues.title: Classification inconsistent with 30.75 cut-off and text: C33 (31.25), C06 (33.25), sham C21/C23 labelled hyposmic
issues.explanation: C33 (TDI 31.25) is described as normosmic in the text but labelled Hyposmia in Table 1, and it is counted in the 'hyposmic' active group. The text calls C06 hyposmic, while Table 1 gives 33.25 (normosmia). The sham group is called hyposmic although C21 (31.75) and C23 (33.25) are normosmic by the stated cut-off. Group labels used in Tables 4–5 are therefore not cleanly defined by the stated classification. The labels affect subgroup means rather than the arm comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated rule assigning classification by percentile rather than TDI, applied consistently to all subjects.

quotes.text: C21, C23, C25, and C33 were in the opposite situation, obtaining a normosmic score
(3) patients classified as hyposmic who received sham stimulation
sorted those scores higher than 30.75 as normosmia

issues.title: Stimulation electrodes listed (FP1, FP2, O1, O2, IZ) match Model 2, not the selected Model 3 (FPZ anode, IZ cathode)
issues.explanation: Methods list five stimulation electrodes at FP1, FP2, O1, O2 and IZ. Results say Model 3 (anode FPZ, cathode IZ) was selected for the tDCS strategy. FPZ is not among the listed electrodes, whereas Model 2 uses exactly FP1/FP2 as anodes and O1/O2/IZ as cathodes. It is therefore unclear which montage participants actually received, which weakens interpretation of the intervention and the electric-field simulation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of the montage actually delivered, or a corrected electrode list consistent with Model 3.

quotes.text: The 5 electrodes selected for stimulation were positioned following the 10–10 distribution of the international system at FP1, FP2, O1, O2, and IZ.
Model 3: Anode electrodes, FPZ; cathode electrodes, IZ.

issues.title: 'Repeated measures' ANOVA has residual df 24 = 30 obs − 6 cells, i.e. pre/post treated as independent
issues.explanation: The ANOVA is described as repeated measures across three groups of 15 subjects. Every residual has 24 df, which fits an independent-observations two-way model on 30 data points rather than subject-level error terms (12 and 12). Pre/post scores from the same person are then treated as independent, so the F tests and p-values (e.g. TDI group p=0.0013, ID p=0.0502) are not valid as labelled. Group effects and interactions are affected in different directions, so the effect on conclusions is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Output of a mixed model showing subject-level error terms, or the authors' statement of how the 24 df arose.

quotes.text: a two-way repeated measures ANOVA was conducted to compare the initial and final olfactory assessments across three distinct groups
a Mauchly’s test was performed to verify the assumption of sphericity

issues.title: Placebo 'almost 20%' improvement attributed to C31 and C35, active-arm subjects whose TDI fell
issues.explanation: The Discussion cites C31 and C35 as placebo responders with almost 20% improvement. Both received active stimulation per Table 3, and their TDI differences are −4.5 and −0.75. Sham subjects C21 and C37 improved about 17–18%, so the subject IDs or the measure may be wrong. This affects only an illustrative remark.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification of which measure and subjects the 20% refers to.

quotes.text: This can be seen in the case of patients C31 and C35, who achieved an improvement of almost 20%.

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective sham-controlled stimulation study
issues.explanation: Only ethics committee approval is given; no registry identifier appears. Without registration the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be verified against pre-specification. This is a reporting gap rather than evidence of a changed outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry predating recruitment.

quotes.text: The Ethics Committee for Drug Research of the Department of Health of Alicante—General Hospital approved the present study

issues.title: Text says anosmic group (n=2) 'could not be included', yet ANOVA's group 2 is anosmic active
issues.explanation: Results 3.4 says the anosmic group could not be included because only two cases existed. Later the three analysed groups include 'patients classified as anosmic who received active stimulation', and Table 5 reports their means. Likely the statement refers to the absence of a sham anosmic group, but as worded it contradicts the analysis. This affects how readers understand the group structure behind the main claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors clarifying that the sentence refers to a sham anosmic group.

quotes.text: (2) patients classified as anosmic who received active stimulation

10.3390/s23167238.headline_claim: Telerehabilitation through the ARC Intellicare system is usable and safe for home rehabilitation in subjects with chronic motor and respiratory disabilities, with preliminary data suggesting promising effectiveness in post-COVID-19 condition or PD.
10.3390/s23167238.overall: The feasibility findings (high adherence, good usability, completion by all 21 enrolled) are broadly supported, though several reported numbers are inconsistent between text and tables. The claim that treatment efficacy was 'demonstrated' is not supported by an uncontrolled, 21-person, 4-week pre–post design with within-group tests, and the study was registered retrospectively without this being stated. The conclusions are reliable only as preliminary feasibility data.

primary_outcome.name: Adherence to home rehabilitation program (Adherence-Days and Adherence-Repetitions) and safety (device-related adverse events)

primary_outcomes.time_frame: Daily evaluation performed on each patient using ARC during 30-day study period

issues.title: 'Efficacy demonstrated' from an uncontrolled 21-person pre–post study with within-group tests only
issues.explanation: The Discussion says efficacy was demonstrated by significant improvement on pre–post scores. The design has no control group, and inference is by within-group Wilcoxon tests across many outcomes with no multiplicity handling. Such changes cannot be separated from time, recovery, expectancy or co-intervention. Safety is also asserted as established on the basis of 21 participants over 4 weeks with a single adverse-event sentence. The feasibility and adherence findings are less affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group, or an explicit reframing of the clinical results as exploratory descriptive changes without causal wording.

quotes.text: is a pilot single-center, not controlled, prospective, pre–post-intervention study
Treatment efficacy was demonstrated by a homogeneous and statistically significant improvement
Pre–post-treatment within-group changes were checked by using the Wilcoxon rank test for the whole sample as well as for each study group.

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion states 'Treatment efficacy was demonstrated' on the basis of a single-arm 21-person pre–post study analysed only with within-group Wilcoxon tests, so changes cannot be attributed to the intervention (no control for regression to the mean, natural recovery of post-COVID, medication effects, or expectation) and no multiplicity adjustment is stated. The word 'homogeneous' is also not borne out by the subgroup results. This is partly tempered by the authors' own limitations paragraph and the Conclusions ('preliminary', 'promising', RCT needed), and by the clinical outcomes being sec

issues.title: Registered 2021-10-08, about 4 months after enrolment ended (2021-05-30); not disclosed as retrospective
issues.explanation: The registry record (NCT05074771) was first submitted on 2021-10-08 and is labelled retrospective. The paper's own dates put enrolment between 26 March and 30 May 2021, before registration. The manuscript gives the identifier without noting this. The registered primary outcomes match the paper, which limits the practical harm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An earlier registration record or version with a date before 26 March 2021.

quotes.text: were enrolled between 26 March 2021 and 30 May 2021
Trial registration: the trial ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier is

issues.title: Whole-sample adherence in text (80% days, 77% reps) differs from Table 4 (82.2, 75.0)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives mean adherence as 80% by days and 77% by repetitions. Table 4's Total rows give 82.2 and 75.0. The days figure is understated and the repetitions figure overstated. The primary-outcome headline numbers are therefore not reported consistently, although both days figures meet the 80% target and the repetitions figures (75.0 and 77) both exceed the 70% target.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition of the text figures as a different summary (for example a median or a pooled rather than per-person mean) would explain the difference.

quotes.text: the whole sample of subjects achieved 80% adherence calculated on days and 77% on repetitions

issues.title: Adherence-Repetitions endpoint: '15 (76%)' of 21 is 71.4%
issues.explanation: The count of 16 for Adherence-Days is consistent with 76% of 21. For Adherence-Repetitions the text gives 15 subjects but also 76%, which is the percentage for 16. Fifteen of 21 is 71%. The number of people reaching the secondary adherence endpoint is therefore uncertain by one person.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual-level adherence data showing 16 of 21 participants at or above 70% repetitions adherence.

quotes.text: 15 (76%) reached the endpoint of 70%
sixteen subjects (76%) reached the endpoint

script.explanation: 15/21 = 71.43%, but the paper prints 76, outside the rounding interval [75.50, 77.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 19.7 rather than 21.

issues.title: Results 3.4 text swaps BDI/BAI statistics and differs from Table 5 on BFI p and 2MWT Z
issues.explanation: The text attributes Z = 3.1, p = 0.002 to mood (BDI) and Z = 2.5, p = 0.01 to anxiety (BAI). Table 5 gives these as BAI (−3.1; 0.002) and BDI (−2.6; 0.01) respectively. The BFI p-value is 0.005 in the text and 0.0005 in the table, and the 2MWT Z is −3.2 in the text and −3.3 in the table. Every one of these outcomes is significant either way, but the text cannot be trusted as a summary of the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Original software output showing which scale each Z and p belongs to, and confirming the printed Table 5 rows are correctly labelled.

quotes.text: Mood state (BDI) (Z = 3.1
according to the BFI (Z = 3.5

issues.title: Women among 21 enrolled: text says 8 (3 in pwPD), Table 3 says 7 (2 in pwPD)
issues.explanation: The Results text reports 8 women overall and 3 among the 10 pwPD. Table 3 gives 7 F/14 M overall and 2 F/8 M in pwPD. The sex distribution of the sample is therefore reported inconsistently; no result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement from the authors that the pwPD count of 2 or 3 is correct, with the other value shown to be a typo, would settle which is right but would not remove the inconsistency.

quotes.text: 10 were pwPD (mean age 65 ± 4 years [range: 59–70], 3 women)

issues.title: Technology difficulty 'less than 5%' of trained participants, but 2 of 23 is 8.7%
issues.explanation: The Discussion says difficulty or non-acceptance of the technology occurred in under 5% of people receiving training. The Results report 2 of the 23 trainees as unsuitable because of technology limitations. That is 8.7%, so the Discussion understates how often training failed on usability grounds.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated denominator (for example 40+ trainees) under which 2 events are under 5%.

quotes.text: less than 10% of the whole sample and less than 5% among people receiving training
2 were defined as unsuitable due to limitations in the use of technology

issues.title: 67 of 78 printed as 83%; 67/78 is 85.9%
issues.explanation: The Discussion says 67 of 78 examined people needed rehabilitation and gives 83%. The ratio is 85.9%. Nothing in the study's conclusions depends on this figure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated different denominator for the 83% (for example 81 people).

quotes.text: sixty-seven out of seventy-eight (83%)

script.explanation: 67/78 = 85.90%, but the paper prints 83, outside the rounding interval [82.50, 84.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 80.7 rather than 78.

issues.title: Sample-size CI 'width 0.8' but bounds 0.44–0.97 give width 0.53
issues.explanation: The sample-size justification states an interval width of 0.8 and then the interval 0.44–0.97. These two cannot both be right. The calculation covers only the adherence precision of a pilot and does not alter any result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The authors defining 'width' as something other than upper minus lower bound.

quotes.text: with an interval width of 0.8 (IC95% 0.44–0.97)

issues.title: Reasons for declining consent sum to 14 (7 COV19), but 13 decliners (6 COV19) are stated
issues.explanation: The text says 13 people declined, 6 COV19 and 7 pwPD. The listed COV19 reasons (1, 2, 2 and 2) add to 7, giving 14 decliners in total. The pwPD reasons (4 + 3) do match 7. One COV19 reason count appears to be overstated by one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reason category whose 2 COV19 participants overlap with another category (for example a person giving two reasons) would explain the extra count.

quotes.text: 13 (36%)—6 COV19 and 7 pwPD, respectively—declined
no time to perform rehabilitation (2 COV19)

10.3390/s23198120.headline_claim: EMG-driven rehabilitation robots are effective for post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome, and substituting part of conventional rehabilitation with robotic rehabilitation did not negatively alter outcomes.
10.3390/s23198120.overall: The headline claim that the robot was shown effective is not supported: both groups improved similarly, interaction tests were essentially null, and the abstract's between-group p-values (0.015, 0.023) contradict Table 2 (0.076, 0.118). Table 2 also contains misplaced or inconsistent values, and the unreported registered fatigue outcome and lack of power or equivalence analysis further weaken the conclusions. At most the data suggest comparable improvement when robot time substitutes for part of usual therapy.

primary_outcome.name: Not named in the paper; headline between-group change in FIM and mean extensor strength

issues.title: Abstract FIM and extensor-strength between-group p-values (0.015, 0.023) absent from results; Table 2 gives 0.076, 0.118
issues.explanation: The abstract says the intervention group improved better on FIM (p=0.015) and mean extensor strength (p=0.023). Table 2 gives the group x time p-values for these as 0.076 and 0.118, and the Discussion says only the FIM motor subscale interaction was significant and neither approach is more beneficial. No analysis producing 0.015 or 0.023 is described, so the abstract's between-group claims are unsupported and contradict the paper's own results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described additional analysis (e.g. t-test on change scores) that yields p=0.015 and 0.023 for these outcomes.

quotes.text: the intervention group improved better in terms of Functional Independence Measure ( p = 0.015)
ANOVA showed significant group × time interaction only in the summary score of the motor subscale.

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's p = 0.015 (FIM) and p = 0.023 (mean extensor strength) do not appear in the Results or tables, and the Table 2 interaction p-values are 0.076 and 0.118; the Discussion says only the FIM motor subscale interaction was significant. The Methods describe no change-score comparison that could produce the abstract values, so their source cannot be determined from the paper, though an unreported change-score analysis cannot be ruled out.

issues.title: Table 2 extension-strength control values misplaced: 16.65 ± 10.52 sits in mean-extension post; peak pre shows 6.99
issues.explanation: Control-group baseline peak extension strength is 16.65 ± 10.52 in Table 1, but Table 2 prints 6.99 ± 4.91 for that cell. The 16.65 ± 10.52 value instead appears as the control post value of the mean extension row, whose baseline was 5.95 and whose intervention post was 7.36. The pattern indicates transposed or wrongly entered cells, so the control mean-extension post and peak-extension pre values, and the associated group x time p-values (0.118, 0.572), cannot be trusted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the control mean-extension post value really is 16.65 ± 10.52 and the peak pre is 6.99.

quotes.text: Peak extension strength 15.31 ± 9.11 30.39 ± 26.08 6.99 ± 4.91
Peak extension strength 15.31 9.11 16.65 10.52

second_reader.what_stands: Two control-group cells in Table 2 are inconsistent with Table 1: peak extension Pre is printed 6.99 ± 4.91 (Table 1 gives 16.65 ± 10.52), and 16.65 ± 10.52 appears in the mean-extension Post cell. Whether this is a typesetting/extraction shift or an error in the published table cannot be determined, but as printed the values are misplaced and a sensible mean-extension post value for control is missing.

issues.title: Conclusion that robot rehabilitation is effective rests on within-group gains; between-group tests show no difference
issues.explanation: Both groups improved on all measures, and group x time interactions were non-significant except the FIM motor subscale (p=0.047), which the authors call almost insignificant and which showed no post hoc between-group difference. The Discussion concludes neither approach is more or less beneficial, yet the abstract and conclusions say the robot was shown to be effective. At most the data support comparable improvement with a robot substituting part of therapy, not superior or demonstrated effectiveness; no equivalence margin or power calculation backs even that.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified non-inferiority or equivalence analysis with margin supporting the claim.

quotes.text: The use of EMG-driven robots in the rehabilitation of post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome patients was shown to be effective.
neither approach is more or less beneficial than the other.
post hoc analysis showed no statistical significance in the comparison of post-intervention measures between groups.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim of effectiveness rests on within-group improvements that are also seen in the standard-care control group, and the between-group tests show no reliable difference (the Discussion itself says neither approach is more or less beneficial). However, the Conclusions also frame the result as the robot not worsening outcomes when substituted for part of usual therapy, so the claim is better described as unqualified wording than as contradicting the paper's own Discussion; no formal non-inferiority analysis is reported.

issues.title: Baseline FIM differs between Table 1 (77.71, 83.59) and Table 2 pre (79.76, 84.13) for the same groups
issues.explanation: Table 1 and Table 2 are both headed n=42 and n=39, yet the baseline FIM means and SDs differ. All other rows of Table 1 match Table 2 pre values exactly, so this row is an isolated inconsistency. It affects the FIM interaction result that underlies the headline claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the ANOVA used a different analysis set or imputed values for FIM.

issues.title: 18 outcomes with 3 tests each and no multiplicity control; sole significant interaction p=0.047
issues.explanation: Table 2 tests 18 outcomes for group x time interaction at alpha 0.05 without correction (Tukey is only for post hoc comparisons within the ANOVA). The only significant interaction is 0.047 on one of several overlapping FIM subscales; with 18 tests an isolated p just under 0.05 is expected by chance. The authors themselves discount it, so the issue weakens a secondary finding rather than a stated main claim.
