10.38109/2225-1685-2023-1-86-92.headline_claim: In patients with unstable angina after COVID-19, combined atorvastatin and curcetin reduced inflammatory biomarker concentrations compared with atorvastatin monotherapy.
10.38109/2225-1685-2023-1-86-92.overall: The conclusion that the combination lowered inflammatory biomarkers more than atorvastatin alone rests on small, open-label subgroups with unreported allocation, baseline imbalance, no effect size or baseline adjustment, and a within-group significance contrast. The 'confirmed synergy' claim is not supported by the design, and the Results mislabel the percentage figures. The results are at best tentative.

primary_outcome.name: hsCRP and IL-6 (inflammatory biomarkers); no primary outcome is named in the paper

issues.title: Efficacy rests on within-arm significance contrast; between-arm effect unquantified, unadjusted, baseline hsCRP differs
issues.explanation: The Abstract contrasts a significant fall in the combination arm with a non-significant fall on monotherapy, which does not by itself show the arms differ. The only between-arm evidence is a significance marker on post-treatment values in Table 3, with no estimate, CI or exact p. Baseline hsCRP was 6.2 versus 4.5 and Apo B 85.1 versus 117.4 in the two arms, and no baseline adjustment was done. The unqualified conclusion 'compared with atorvastatin monotherapy' is stronger than this supports. The arms are small (43 and 34) and no sample-size calculation is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted between-arm estimate with CI (for example ANCOVA or a change-score comparison) showing a clear difference in hsCRP and IL-6.

quotes.text: atorvastatin monotherapy (n = 43) did not have a significant effect after two months of treatment
combination treatment with atorvastatin and curcetin reduced concentrations of inflammatory biomarkers compared with atorvastatin monotherapy

quotes.location: Table 3, вчCРБ row, II subgroup, 2 months

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract's headline percentages are within-arm changes, and the Results text mislabels them as between-arm differences. The 'effective vs not significant' contrast across arms is in itself not a test of difference. A between-arm P<0.05 at 2 months is flagged with ^, but no effect size, CI, change-score comparison or baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA-type) estimate is given, and the baseline hsCRP medians differ (6.2 vs 4.5). The claim that no between-arm test exists is not correct.

issues.title: Discussion says study 'confirmed synergy' of curcumin and quercetin, but no single-component arms exist
issues.explanation: Synergy needs arms for each component alone and in combination. This study compares atorvastatin alone with atorvastatin plus a fixed curcumin-quercetin mixture, so any benefit could come from either component or from the mixture. The claim of confirmed synergy is not supported by the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Arms or analyses isolating curcumin and quercetin separately from the combination.

quotes.text: вызванного инфекцией COVID-19 у больных ИБС

second_reader.what_stands: The study has no curcumin-only or quercetin-only arm, so it cannot show synergy between the two components. At most it compares atorvastatin plus the mixture with atorvastatin alone, so the Discussion's 'confirmed synergism' is not supported by the design.

issues.title: Randomization of COVID-exposure groups is implausible; subgroup allocation undescribed, open-label, baselines differ
issues.explanation: Patients were 'randomized' into groups defined by whether instability followed COVID-19, which cannot be randomized. No method of sequence generation or concealment is given for the atorvastatin versus combination subgroups, and the study is open-label. Baselines differ in Apo B, Apo B/Apo A-I and diabetes, so the arms may not be comparable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a concealed random allocation sequence for the two treatment subgroups and balanced baselines in prognostic variables.

quotes.text: Больные, рандомизированные в подгруппы, не отличались по возрасту, полу

quotes.location: Table 3, Апо В row, II subgroup baseline

second_reader.what_stands: Prior COVID-19 exposure cannot be randomized, and the paper does not describe how patients were allocated to atorvastatin alone or with curcetin. The abstract calls the study open-label, and the subgroups differ at baseline in Apo B (85.1 vs 117.4, t about 4.9) and ApoB/ApoA-I (0.60 vs 0.80). The Apo B subgroup means also do not reconcile with Table 1 (99.4 vs 105.5), so a transcription problem cannot be ruled out.

issues.title: Results call 49%/40% between-subgroup differences; they are subgroup II within-arm falls (between-arm: 51%/47%)
issues.explanation: The Results say post-treatment hsCRP and IL-6 in subgroup II were 49.0% and 40.0% lower than in subgroup I. Table 3 medians give 51.1% and 46.9% for that comparison. The 49.0% and 40.0% instead match subgroup II's change from baseline (4.5 to 2.3 and 8.5 to 5.1). The Abstract and Results therefore describe the same numbers as two different comparisons, which muddles the central between-arm claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that percentages were computed from means or individual-level data rather than the printed medians, and that they refer to the between-arm difference.

quotes.location: Table 3, вчCРБ row, I subgroup, 2 months
Table 3, вчCРБ row, II subgroup, 2 months

issues.title: About 13 outcomes at two timepoints in Table 3 with no multiplicity control; inflammatory markers are the stated aims
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports many lipid, apolipoprotein, glucose and inflammatory variables with no adjustment described. The two inflammatory markers are stated aims, so the concern mainly affects secondary lipid claims such as the Apo B difference. The between-arm markers are significant only at nominal P < 0.05.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or hierarchical testing plan naming hsCRP and IL-6 as co-primary.

quotes.text: Dynamics of blood lipids, glucose, biomarkers of lipid metabolism and inflammation in the study groups

issues.title: Randomized interventional study reports no trial registry identifier
issues.explanation: The study is presented as a randomized comparative trial of a drug combination, but no registry entry is given. Prespecified outcomes and the allocation plan cannot be checked. The grant number is not a registration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier (ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN, etc.) with a registration date before enrolment.

quotes.text: Протокол исследования одобрен комитетом по этике

10.3831/kpi.2023.26.3.238.headline_claim: Complex rehabilitation with acupuncture is effective for hospitalised post-COVID-19 patients, improving respiratory function, daily activity and exercise tolerance compared with complex rehabilitation alone.
10.3831/kpi.2023.26.3.238.overall: The headline claim that acupuncture is effective is only weakly supported: the evidence is an open-label comparison with self-rated outcomes, baseline imbalances, an unclear ANCOVA specification and an argument based on within-arm significance. The authors' own Conclusion concedes that superiority over complex rehabilitation alone cannot be asserted, which contradicts the abstract. Several printing errors (dose description, a percentage, a total, anthropometric SDs) add to the doubts but are individually minor.

primary_outcome.name: Barthel index (BI); the Discussion calls BI a primary outcome without defining the primary outcome in Methods

issues.title: Abstract states acupuncture is 'effective'; body says data insufficient and superiority cannot be asserted
issues.explanation: The abstract's conclusion that rehabilitation with acupuncture is effective is not matched by the body, which says it is impossible to say with certainty that acupuncture adds benefit and that the data are insufficient to assert effectiveness. Elsewhere the Discussion still concludes acupuncture 'served to improve the effectiveness of rehabilitation', so the paper's messages conflict. Given the open-label design and unclear analysis, the stronger abstract claim is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract conclusion restricted to feasibility, with the superiority claim removed or qualified.

quotes.text: Rehabilitation with acupuncture is possible and effective in patients recovering from post-COVID-19.
However, it is impossible to say with certainty that the use of acupuncture with CRM is more effective than the CRM alone.
our data are insufficient to assert the effectiveness of acupuncture in rehabilitation for PCC

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract states acupuncture rehabilitation is 'effective' without the caveat, whereas the Discussion says the data are insufficient to assert effectiveness and the Conclusion says superiority to CRM alone cannot be asserted; the paper's own conclusions are internally inconsistent (the Discussion also concludes acupuncture improved rehabilitation effectiveness).

issues.title: Baseline outcome scores and covariates differ between arms despite 'similar' claim (e.g. Barthel 86.8 vs 90.6)
issues.explanation: The Results state the groups were similar at baseline, but Table 3 shows baseline differences on every outcome, with p < 0.001 for Barthel and 6-MWT, and Table 1 shows imbalance in sex (31% vs 17.5% male), headache, joint pain, bronchitis, motor-system disease and weight. For a 1:1 randomized trial of 160 this is unexpected and raises questions about how allocation was carried out. It also makes the unadjusted within-arm and post-treatment comparisons hard to interpret, and ANCOVA on baseline scale values cannot fix the other imbalances.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Before-row p-values compare something other than the baseline arms, plus tests showing no baseline imbalance.

quotes.text: all of which were similar between the groups

quotes.location: Table 3, Barthel index, Before, CRM without acupuncture
Table 3, Barthel index, Before, CRM with acupuncture

second_reader.what_stands: Baseline Barthel scores differ by 3.8 points (about 1 SD, p < 0.001 as printed), and baseline Borg, mMRC and 6MWT also differ significantly per Table 3, along with several Table 1 covariates (weight, BMI, sex, headache, comorbidities), so 'similar between the groups' is not accurate. The ANCOVA adjusts for baseline outcome values, but not for these other covariates, and the paper does not acknowledge the imbalance.

issues.title: Efficacy argued from within-arm significance (all four scales vs two) rather than a between-arm effect
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Discussion present the result as acupuncture reaching significant improvement on all scales and the control on only two. A difference in within-arm significance is not evidence of a between-arm difference, and the paper gives no between-arm effect sizes or confidence intervals for change. Table 3 column b does give ANCOVA p-values, but with no adjusted differences or CIs and an unclear model, the claimed benefit cannot be quantified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-arm adjusted mean differences with CIs from a clearly specified model showing benefit on each scale.

quotes.text: We found statistically significant improvement after the rehabilitation course with acupuncture in the all scales.
The 6-MWT and the BI scores were significantly improved in the acupuncture group only
Therefore, we conclude that the use of acupuncture as an additional method served to improve the effectiveness of rehabilitation.

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract, Results and the Discussion's main argument lean heavily on within-arm significance (4 scales vs 2) and on 'significant in one arm but not the other', which is not a between-arm test. A between-arm ANCOVA is reported (p < 0.001) but without effect estimates or CIs, so the claim is not purely within-arm, though the presentation of efficacy rests mainly on it.

issues.title: No blinding or sham/attention control; subjective outcomes (MDS, Borg) drive the conclusion
issues.explanation: Patients knew they were receiving the extra acupuncture sessions, and dyspnoea and exertion scales are self-rated. The Limitations say this 'may have affected the results' and that psychological expectation could contribute. The abstract and Conclusion nevertheless state the effect as real, which the design cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Blinded outcome assessment or a sham/attention-control arm showing similar effects.

quotes.text: First, because the acupuncture group was a control group, no blinding was performed, which may have affected the results.
The Borg scale requires patients to rate the difficulty of their breathing

second_reader.what_stands: There was no blinding, no sham or attention control, and the largest effects are on patient-rated scales (MDS, Borg), so expectation bias is a real concern; however, the authors state the lack of blinding and expectation effects as limitations, and the conclusion is not driven only by subjective outcomes since the 6MWT and Barthel are also reported.

issues.title: Abstract says adverse events were monitored and documented, but none are reported
issues.explanation: The abstract states that adverse events were monitored and documented. The Results, tables and Discussion contain no adverse event data for either arm, not even a statement that none occurred. The conclusion that acupuncture is 'possible' and the earlier claim of established safety cannot be assessed from this report.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or statement of adverse events by arm in the published paper or supplement.

quotes.text: Adverse events also were monitored and documented.

issues.title: ANCOVA model and test designs unclear: acupuncture called a covariate, ANCOVA p-values given for baseline rows
issues.explanation: The statistical methods say ANCOVA was used with acupuncture as a 'covariate' and a two-sample t-test was used for normality, while the Results use paired t-tests and describe treatment as a covariate. Table 3 also shows ANCOVA p-values (column b) for the baseline rows, which cannot be an adjusted post-treatment test. This leaves the main between-group inference without a reproducible specification and with no adjusted estimates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis code or output showing post-treatment scores modelled with group as a fixed factor and baseline as covariate, with adjusted differences.

quotes.text: to measure the effect of pre-treatment scale values, with acupuncture as a covariate on post-treatment values.
the two-sample t-test was used from baseline to the end of treatment
taking into account the type of treatment as a covariate, and identified a significant difference between the two groups

issues.title: Acupuncture dose unclear: once daily for 10-14 days vs 7-10 sessions 'every day' (mean 9.5)
issues.explanation: The Participants section says acupuncture was given once a day for 10-14 days. The Intervention section says 7-10 sessions were given 'every day'. Table 1 gives a mean of 9.5 sessions, which fits a total course of 7-10 sessions rather than daily sessions for 10-14 days. The exposure actually delivered is therefore not reproducible from the text, though the conclusion does not hinge on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol statement that sessions were daily on weekdays only, or a total of 7-10 sessions within the 10-14-day stay.

quotes.text: Acupuncture was performed once day for 10-14 days.
7-10 treatment sessions conducted every day

issues.title: Table 1 BMI SD (0.22 in control arm) implausibly small given weight SD 13.92 kg; height printed 1.6 ± 7.52
issues.explanation: A BMI SD of 0.22 for a group whose weight SD is 13.92 kg is not feasible, since weight variation alone would give a BMI SD of several units. Height is printed as a mean of 1.6 (metres) with an SD of 7.52, mixing units. These anthropometric rows therefore appear mis-transcribed or mis-computed, which lowers confidence in the table's reliability.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing BMI SDs of this size, or a corrected table.

quotes.location: Table 1, Body mass index, CRM without acupuncture

issues.title: Total saturation 96.1% is not the average of arm means 96.2% and 95.6% (95.9%)
issues.explanation: With equal arm sizes the pooled mean must be the average of the two arm means. The Total column prints 96.1% while the arms give 95.9%. Other Table 1 rows reconcile, so this cell is out of line. A small reporting error with no bearing on the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that saturation was missing for some participants in either arm.

quotes.location: Table 1, Saturation upon admission, CRM without acupuncture
Table 1, Saturation upon admission, CRM with acupuncture

issues.title: Coronary heart disease 31/80 printed as 46.6%; should be 38.8%
issues.explanation: The count of 31 in the 80-patient control arm gives 38.8%, not 46.6%. The Total column (76, 47.5%) is consistent with 31 and 45, so the percentage is the misprinted part. It affects only one baseline cell, but it is one of the baseline comparisons being used to claim similarity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing 46.6% with a matching count and denominator.

script.explanation: 31/80 = 38.75%, but the paper prints 46.6, outside the rounding interval [46.55, 46.70]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 66.5 rather than 80.

10.3897/pharmacia.69.e82596.headline_claim: Adding thiotriazoline to basic therapy for 30 days in post-COVID-19 syndrome produced a hepatoprotective effect and improved endothelial, anticoagulant and safety-related markers, and so can increase the safety of the drug treatment.
10.3897/pharmacia.69.e82596.overall: The biomarker differences favour the thiotriazoline group on several measures, but the design is unrandomised with no per-arm baselines and no adjustment. The conclusion goes beyond the data to thrombus prevention, myocardial benefit and safety, which were not measured. Treat the findings as exploratory, hypothesis-generating signals only.

primary_outcome.name: Not designated; the stated aim is a combined effect on anticoagulant, antiplatelet, endothelioprotective and hepatoprotective parameters

issues.title: Non-randomised add-on comparison (37 vs 20), no group baselines or adjustment, with causal efficacy conclusion
issues.explanation: Patients got basic therapy alone or with thiotriazoline, but the paper does not say how they were allocated. Baselines are given only for the pooled 57 patients, so the two groups cannot be compared at the start. Differences at day 30 could reflect case-mix, route of administration (tablet or suppository), concomitant drugs or natural recovery. The conclusion that thiotriazoline 'led to' benefit is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of randomised or concealed allocation, plus a baseline table by arm showing balance.

quotes.text: Of these, 20 patients received basic therapy (antibiotics, anticoagulants, acetylsalicylic acid)
contributed to the prevention of thrombus formation

second_reader.what_stands: The paper describes a two-arm add-on comparison (37 vs 20) with no stated randomisation or allocation method, no per-group baseline data and no adjusted analysis, yet concludes in causal terms that thiotriazoline 'led to' improvements. I did not verify how patients were actually assigned, only that the paper does not report it.

issues.title: Conclusion claims thrombus prevention, myocardial benefit and increased safety; none was measured
issues.explanation: The conclusion says thiotriazoline prevented thrombus formation, improved the myocardium and increased treatment safety. The study measured only symptoms, a few lab markers and platelet aggregation. There were no thrombotic events, no cardiac tests (ECG, troponin, echo) and no adverse-event reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported thrombotic, cardiac and adverse-event outcomes by arm.

quotes.text: contributed to the prevention of thrombus formation while improving the condition of the myocardium and vascular endothelium
the appointment of thiotriazoline in the complex therapy of post-COVID syndrome can increase the safety of the proposed drug treatment.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion's claims of thrombus prevention, myocardial improvement and increased safety are not backed by any directly measured endpoint: no thrombotic events, cardiac measures or adverse events are reported, only laboratory surrogates (D-dimer, platelet aggregation, eNOS, liver enzymes). The safety statement is partly hedged ('can increase') in paragraph 1, but the myocardial and thrombus statements in paragraph 2 are stated as findings.

issues.title: About ten biomarkers tested at p<0.05 with no primary outcome or multiplicity control
issues.explanation: The aim lists four activity domains, and the Results report many marker comparisons against one uncorrected 0.05 threshold. Some effects are large, but the marginal ones, such as ferritin 388 vs 409 and bilirubin, would be fragile under any correction. Exact p-values are never given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary endpoint, or adjusted p-values that stay significant.

quotes.text: Evaluation of the complex therapeutic effect of thiotriazoline (anticoagulant, antiplatelet, endothelioprotective, hepatoprotective action) in patients with post-COVID syndrome in comparison with basic therapy.
quotes.location: Introduction, The aim of the study

quotes.text: For all analyzes, negatives р<0.05 (95%) were considered statistically significant.

issues.title: 20 vs 37 patients, no sample-size rationale, yet effect is said to be 'demonstrated'
issues.explanation: The comparator arm has only 20 patients and the paper gives no sample-size calculation. Small unrandomised groups can support a tentative signal, but not a demonstrated hepatoprotective effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sample-size justification or a conclusion framed as hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: The studies involved 15 relatively healthy volunteers and 57 patients aged 30 to 65 with post-COVID syndrome.
reduced disorders of the hepatobiliary system caused by both the disease itself and side effects of basic therapy

issues.title: Text gives basic-therapy platelet aggregation 99.4% and platelet SD 54.8; Table 4 prints 100.4 and 53.6
issues.explanation: The Results text and Table 4 disagree for the same group. Aggregation is 99.4% in the text but 100,4 in the table, and the platelet-count SD is 54,8 in the text but 53,6 in the table. The reported 32% fall in aggregation matches the table value, so the text figures look like slips. This affects no conclusion, but it shows the text and tables were not checked against each other.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text values come from a different measurement set than Table 4.

quotes.text: averaged 99.4% versus 60% of relatively healthy patients (Table 4; Fig. 1A, B).
quotes.location: Results and discussion, platelet aggregation paragraph
Table 4, basic therapy row, platelet aggregation
Table 4, basic therapy row, platelet count

issues.title: INR and eNOS 'increases' of 50%/35% and 55%/42% do not match Tables 2-3 as relative changes
issues.explanation: The text reports INR rising 50% vs admission and 35% vs basic therapy, and eNOS rising 55% and 42%. Computed from baseline, the table values give about +102% and +53% for INR and +124% and +72% for eNOS. The text numbers only appear if the difference is divided by the treated-group value, whereas the D-dimer and ferritin percentages use baseline as the denominator. The percentages are therefore on inconsistent bases and the INR/eNOS gains are understated. Separately, an admission INR of 0.44 is physiologically odd and its calling a rise to 0.89 'normalization' is not explained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition of percentage change that applies to INR and eNOS but not D-dimer and ferritin.

quotes.text: a significant increase in relation to the group of patients when staying by 50% and in relation to the group of basic therapy - by 35%

issues.title: Text says complaints 'disappeared' and were present in 'all' patients; Table 1 shows 2-3 remaining and 54-55 of 57
issues.explanation: The text says palpitations, weakness and fatigue disappeared after thiotriazoline. Table 1 shows 3, 2 and 2 of 37 patients still reporting them. The text also says all patients had weakness, fatigue, palpitations and fever on admission, but Table 1 gives 54-55 of 57. The overall pattern still favours the treated group (for example weakness 2/37 vs 17/20), so this is overstated wording rather than a reversed finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 'disappeared' as resolution in most patients.

quotes.text: complaints of palpitations disappeared, blood pressure stabilized (without additional correction with antihypertensive drugs), weakness and fatigue disappeared
Upon admission, all patients complained of severe weakness, increased fatigue, palpitations, fever from 37.2 to 38.3 °C.
Heartbeat
quotes.location: Table 1, Heartbeat row (admission 55, Group 2 after treatment 3)

10.4025/arqmudi.v27iespecial.68175.headline_claim: The water aerobics (hydrogymnastics) program improves the double product only in the comparison group, is an adequate program to lower blood pressure, and would need to last longer than 16 weeks to produce significant body-composition changes.
10.4025/arqmudi.v27iespecial.68175.overall: The headline claims of improved heart rate and double product and of an adequate blood-pressure-lowering program are not supported: the design is uncontrolled and non-randomised, Table 2 post-test values duplicate Table 1 pre-test values for all nine variables, the cited significant SBP drop has p=0,118, and the CG heart rate actually rose. The stated analysis method (Pearson) also cannot produce the printed p-values reliably, so little of the inferential content survives.

primary_outcome.name: Not stated; hemodynamic (HR, SBP, DBP) and anthropometric variables reported

issues.title: Comparison-group post-test means/SDs identical to intervention-group pre-test values on all nine variables
issues.explanation: Every post-test mean and SD in Table 2 (Comparison Group) equals the pre-test mean and SD in Table 1 (Intervention Group), e.g. weight 108,89 (18,24), BMI 40,10 (5,99), HR 77,77 (9,21). Two independent groups of different sizes (14 vs 26) cannot produce identical post-test and pre-test summary statistics for nine variables. This indicates a table-construction or data-handling error, so the Comparison Group post-test results, and every conclusion that rests on them (the SBP drop, double product, HR rise), cannot be relied on. Text and Table 2 also differ in the HR post value (9,21 SD in table, matching IG pre).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing the CG post-test values genuinely equal the IG pre-test values, or an erratum correcting Table 2.

second_reader.what_stands: All nine CG post-test means and SDs in Table 2 match the IG pre-test values in Table 1 exactly. This is unexplained in the paper, and it casts doubt on the CG post-test data and on every CG change score, p-value and effect size derived from them.

issues.title: Text reports significant SBP drop in CG; Table 2 gives p = 0,118 (alpha 0.05)
issues.explanation: The Discussion cites a significant drop in SBP in the Comparison Group and builds the double-product conclusion on it, but Table 2 gives p = 0,118 for that comparison, above the stated 0.05 level. The conclusion that the program improves the double product only in the CG therefore rests on a non-significant result (and on values that duplicate Table 1, see c1).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected analysis showing p<0.05 for CG SBP.

quotes.text: the significant drop in SBP in the CG

second_reader.what_stands: The Results text and Conclusion describe a 'significant drop in SBP in the CG', but Table 2 gives p = 0,118, which is non-significant at the paper's own alpha of 0.05. Only the effect-size label ('Largo') supports a large change, and in a sample of 14 that estimate is imprecise.

issues.title: Efficacy claims rest on uncontrolled pre-post changes; both groups received the program, non-random groups
issues.explanation: Both groups were exercised for 16 weeks and compared only with their own baseline, with no untreated control, no randomisation and no between-group test. Changes cannot be attributed to the program, and the conclusion that it 'improves' responses and is 'adequate to lower blood pressure' is stronger than this design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent non-exercising control group or a randomised comparison.

quotes.text: The analysis was descriptive between pre and post test (GI= 26 and GC=14).
The results reveal that there is an improvement in both groups regarding the hemodynamic response of blood pressure and heart rate.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy conclusions rest on within-group pre-post changes, with no untreated control, no randomization and no between-group analysis. The groups are defined by COVID history, so they differ systematically. The authors flag sample size but not the absence of a control or the non-random allocation, so 'effectiveness' and 'adequate program' are not supported by this design.

issues.title: Conclusion says program lowers BP and improves double product; data show non-significant CG SBP (p=0,118)
issues.explanation: The conclusion asserts improvement in the double product and lower blood pressure, but no double product is reported, CG SBP is non-significant, IG SBP did not fall, and only IG DBP changed significantly. The conclusion also cites reduced CC and 'HC' (not measured) as body-composition gains although all those changes were non-significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported double product with significant change in a controlled analysis.

quotes.text: it is an adequate program to lower blood pressure
the water aerobics training program improves the response of the double product
The reduction of PG%, CC and HC indicate improvements also in body composition parameters

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion states that the program improves the double product (only in the CG) and lowers blood pressure, but the only SBP change cited for this is non-significant (p = 0,118). No double product was tested, and means-based estimates show a larger fall in the IG. The body-composition 'reductions' are also all non-significant, and the hedge about needing more weeks does not cover the double-product claim.

issues.title: Text claims HR improved in both groups; CG heart rate rose 74,36 to 77,77 (p = 0,012)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says both groups improved in blood pressure and heart rate. In Table 2 the CG heart rate increased significantly, which is the wrong direction for improvement. Only the IG shows a reduction (77,77 to 74,62).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that higher HR is the desirable direction here, or corrected Table 2.

quotes.text: there is an improvement in both groups regarding the hemodynamic response of blood pressure and heart rate

second_reader.what_stands: The Results sentence says heart rate improved in both groups, but the CG's heart rate rose significantly (74,36 to 77,77, p = 0,012). The Conclusion limits the HR improvement to the IG, so the inconsistency sits in the Results/Discussion wording rather than in the final claim.

issues.title: Pearson's test named for pre-post differences; p-values do not track effect sizes
issues.explanation: A correlation test does not assess change in means, so the stated method cannot produce the printed p-values for improvement. Several rows are inconsistent with each other: CG BMI d=0,26 has p=0,811 while CG PGC d=0,16 has p=0,097, and SBP d=0,85 has p=0,118. The significance conclusions are therefore unverifiable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data and a stated paired t/Wilcoxon analysis reproducing the p-values.

quotes.text: Pearson's test, for repeated samples, was used to determine the differences between pre and post test.

second_reader.what_stands: Naming 'Pearson's test' as the test of pre-post differences is incorrect or at best ambiguous, since a correlation does not test mean change. The actual test (likely a paired t-test) is not stated, and some printed d values do not reproduce exactly from the printed means and SDs. The claim that p-values 'do not track effect sizes' is not an error in itself, because paired p-values depend on unreported SDs of differences and the printed values are plausible.

issues.title: Text says only HR improved significantly in IG, but Table 1 shows DBP (p=0,027) and HR (p=0,048)
issues.explanation: The sentence introducing Table 2 says participants 'only reported significant improvements in HR', although Table 1 shows both DBP and HR significant, and the sentence is also misattributed (Table 2 is the Comparison Group, where HR actually worsened). The paper's own earlier text gives the correct DBP and HR exception, so this is a reporting inconsistency affecting one result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: n/a; the discrepancy is printed in the paper.

quotes.text: Intervention participants only reported significant improvements in HR
with the exception of DBP and HR

issues.title: Pilot with 26 and 14 participants and no sample-size calculation
issues.explanation: No sample-size justification is given and the groups are small and unequal, so null findings are uninformative and significant ones unstable. The authors admit this as a limitation and call the work a pilot, so the issue mainly amplifies the overreaching conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation supporting these sample sizes.

quotes.text: However, it has some limitations that must be recognized, such as the sample size.
The analysis was descriptive between pre and post test (GI= 26 and GC=14).

issues.title: No ethics committee approval or informed consent statement reported
issues.explanation: Only adherence to the Declaration of Helsinki is stated; no approval body, number or consent procedure appears for an interventional study with human participants. This is a reporting gap and does not alter the numerical results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ethics approval number and consent statement.

quotes.text: The study was guided by the Declaration of Helsinki.

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a pragmatic clinical trial
issues.explanation: The paper calls itself a pragmatic clinical trial but gives no registry identifier, so outcomes and analysis cannot be checked against a prior plan. With nine outcomes tested and no primary outcome named, selective emphasis is not excluded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record with prespecified outcomes.

quotes.text: This study is characterized as a pragmatic clinical trial

10.4081/ejtm.2022.10698.headline_claim: Aquatic walking exercises, delivered in tap water or mineral-water pools as part of a multidisciplinary rehabilitation programme, can help correct impaired upright posture and normalise walking pattern in patients with Long COVID.
10.4081/ejtm.2022.10698.overall: The headline claim that the programme corrects posture and normalises gait rests on an uncontrolled 12-patient pre/post study, and its own tables show most post/pre percentages above 100% with one median that does not match its printed values. The Stage 2 randomised trial is small, unregistered and open-label, and shows exercise-tolerance gains only within each arm, so it gives no evidence that the aquatic or mineral-water component is responsible. The conclusions should be treated as preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated. Stage 2 reports 6-minute walking test (within-group change) alongside spirometry, Borg scale, cardiointervalography, laser Doppler flowmetry and EQ-5D.

issues.title: Posture and gait conclusion rests on an uncontrolled 12-patient pre/post study with no gait measure or p-values
issues.explanation: Stage 1 enrolled 12 patients with no control group and compared stabilometry before and after about two weeks of training, alongside basic therapy. The conclusion says the programme corrects posture, significantly reduces head and neck oscillations and normalises walking. No gait-pattern outcome is reported, no p-values are given and Stage 2 has no posture or gait measure. A single-arm comparison cannot separate the exercise from basic therapy, natural recovery and repeated testing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison or reported test statistics and p-values for gait outcomes showing the effect against a control.

quotes.text: evaluated in an open descriptive study that enrolled 12 patients
statistically significantly reducing the amplitude of head and neck oscillations and normalizing the walking pattern

second_reader.what_stands: The final conclusion about significantly reduced head and neck oscillation and a normalized walking pattern rests on an uncontrolled 12-patient before/after study. No gait measure and no p-values are reported. The tables show no neck data, and the head Z and X results do not clearly show reduced oscillation (see i2). The paper does call the study preliminary, but the closing sentence states the result firmly.

issues.title: Text claims reduced deviation in all three planes, but most Table 1/2 percentages exceed 100%
issues.explanation: The Results state that body-axis deviation fell in all three spatial planes, and the Discussion says head and neck oscillations were significantly reduced. In the tables, most post/pre percentages are above 100% (Body X 306,5%, Body Angle 1973,86%, Head X 163,04%, Head Z 173,34%). Several medians change sign and several get larger in magnitude. The tables do not show a uniform decrease. The percentage definition and any test statistics or p-values are missing, so the significance asterisks cannot be checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition of the percentage column under which values above 100% denote reduced deviation, together with the individual-level data and p-values.

quotes.text: in all the three spatial planes was observed
quotes.location: Results and Discussion, Aquatic exercises methods
Table 2, Me row, Head X column
Table 2, Me row, Head Z column

second_reader.what_stands: The percentages are after/before ratios, and 16 of 21 exceed 100%. Head X (sign flip, larger magnitude) and Head Z (magnitude 8.59 to 14.89) moved away from zero, which contradicts the statement that deviation fell in all three planes. The paper does not define 'deviation' or the reference value, and the Body Z median percentage (112.68%) does not match its own before and after values (about 98%).

issues.title: Exercise-tolerance gain shown only within arms (p=0.047 in each); no between-arm comparison of change
issues.explanation: The 6-minute walk improvement is tested separately in each arm using the Wilcoxon test. No comparison of change between mineral-water and tap-water arms is given. Both arms had the full rehabilitation programme, so the improvement cannot be attributed to the aquatic component or to the mineral water. The two identical borderline results (T=8, p=0.047 in both groups) with multiple unadjusted outcomes make it weaker still.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group analysis of change (or ANCOVA) in 6-minute walk distance, or a stated primary outcome with a correction.

quotes.text: has been recorded in both groups considered

second_reader.what_stands: Exercise-tolerance gains are shown only as within-arm pre/post tests, each with T=8, p=0.047, and no between-arm comparison of change is given. Both arms received aquatic exercise within a larger multidisciplinary programme and there is no non-aquatic control, so the gain cannot be attributed to aquatic exercise or to mineral water. The authors do not claim a between-arm difference, and the p=0.047 values are borderline.

issues.title: Table 1 Body Z median 'deviation' of 112,68% does not match medians 388,1 to 380,96 (implies 98,2%)
issues.explanation: Every other percentage in Table 1 equals the post-intervention value divided by the pre-intervention value, ignoring sign. The Body Z median is the only exception: 380,96/388,1 is about 98,2%, not 112,68%. Either the percentage or one of the medians is misprinted. The cell sits in a table whose significance asterisks are the paper's only evidence for the Stage 1 result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the percentage is computed differently for medians (for example a median of individual patient ratios), or a corrected table.

quotes.location: Table 1, %of the deviation from the original value, Me row, Body Z column

issues.title: Stage 2 randomised comparison of 14 per arm, no sample-size calculation reported
issues.explanation: The Stage 2 trial randomised 14 patients per arm and 23 completed. No power calculation is given. The authors say that non-significant trends in spirometry and Borg scores are probably due to the small number of patients. The sample cannot support firm between-arm conclusions, though the paper does not make one.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation or a statement that Stage 2 was a pilot.

quotes.text: the small number of patients involved in the study
the intervention group (n = 14)

issues.title: Prospective randomised Stage 2 reports no trial registration and no designated primary outcome
issues.explanation: Stage 2 is described as a prospective randomised study, but only an ethics committee approval is given. No registry or protocol is cited and no primary outcome is stated. Many outcomes are tested at p<0.05 and the paper highlights those that reached significance, so selective reporting cannot be ruled out.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry entry or protocol with pre-specified outcomes.

quotes.text: open-label, prospective, randomized, parallel-group study was carried out between July 2021 and March 2022
Statistical significance was considered for p < 0.05.

issues.title: Open-label Stage 2 with patient-reported EQ-5D and Borg outcomes
issues.explanation: Participants and staff knew the water type, and subjective outcomes could be influenced by expectation. The only significant EQ-5D finding favoured the tap-water group and the Borg score was non-significant, so there is no evidence of inflated benefit for the tested intervention. The open design nonetheless adds uncertainty to the subjective results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that outcome assessors or participants were blinded to water type.

quotes.text: open-label, prospective, randomized, parallel-group study
in the comparison group after the treatment with a mean value of 3

10.4081/monaldi.2021.1981.headline_claim: Systemic corticosteroids lead to clinical and radiological improvement in a selected subset of long-COVID patients with radiological changes and either hypoxia at rest or exertional desaturation.
10.4081/monaldi.2021.1981.overall: The descriptive data suggest many patients improved over about 12 weeks. The causal headline that steroids lead to clinical and radiological improvement is not supported by an uncontrolled, retrospective before-after series with no safety data. The numeric slips are minor, though Table 2 understates the significance of the desaturation and hypoxia changes.

primary_outcome.name: not prespecified; change in clinical symptoms, chest X-ray and HRCT findings, and 6MWT outcomes after treatment

issues.title: Causal steroid benefit claimed from an uncontrolled retrospective before-after series (n=24 treated)
issues.explanation: Improvements are shown only as pre/post changes in treated patients, with no control group. Natural recovery from COVID over 12 weeks is documented and the authors cite it. The treatment was also given to patients selected on clinician criteria (hypoxia, desaturation, HRCT abnormality) who were then analysed without adjustment. McNemar and Wilcoxon tests show a change, not that steroids caused it. No adverse events are reported. The conclusion that steroids 'lead to' improvement is therefore not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A contemporaneous or matched untreated comparison group showing a smaller improvement.

quotes.text: we did not have a control group for better interpretation of results
Again, this resolution can be spontaneous or effect of the treatment given or both.
We found systemic corticosteroids lead to clinical and radiological

second_reader.what_stands: The study is an uncontrolled retrospective before-after series of 24 steroid-treated patients, and the Conclusions state 'We found systemic corticosteroids lead to clinical and radiological improvement' and the Discussion says 'We found systemic corticosteroids to be helpful', which are causal wordings the design cannot support. The paper does acknowledge the missing control group as a limitation and says the resolution 'can be spontaneous or effect of the treatment given or both', and it frames steroids as a trial in a selected subset, so the problem is overstated causal language and not an a

issues.title: Table 2 marks desaturation (24 to 10) and hypoxia (7 to 2) as NS, but the same counts are p=0.02 or imply p<0.001
issues.explanation: Table 2 labels the fall in six-minute-walk desaturation (24 to 10 of 49) and in resting hypoxia (7 to 2) as not significant. Table 3 shows these are the same patients, with all changes in one direction. Resting hypoxia is p=0.02 in Table 3, and the desaturation change implies a McNemar p well below 0.001. The labels contradict the paper's own method and understate the improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient-level data showing the 10 patients desaturating at follow-up are not among the 24 desaturating at presentation.

quotes.text: xi. Desaturation in six-minute walk test (>4% from baseline)
vii. Desaturation in 6-minute walk test (>4% from baseline)
the prevalence of exertional desaturation in these patients decreased from 100% to 41.6%

issues.title: Only patients with at least 12 weeks of records analysed; number of long-COVID attenders lost is not reported
issues.explanation: Inclusion required file records at least 12 weeks after presentation. The paper gives only 4,542 OPD patients in total and 49 analysed, and does not say how many long-COVID patients met the case definition but were excluded. Patients who returned for follow-up may differ in severity or recovery from those who did not. The size and direction of the resulting bias cannot be judged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A report that all long-COVID attenders in the period had 12-week records, or the number excluded with comparable baseline data.

quotes.text: Only those patients of long-COVID, with available file records of at least 12 weeks after the first presentation to the OPD of the study unit, were included in the study.

issues.title: Table 1 respiratory comorbidity percentages (2.85%, 5.71%) use a denominator of 35, not n=49
issues.explanation: Table 1 is captioned n=49, and every other percentage in it uses 49. Three respiratory comorbidity rows (1, 2 and 2 patients) show 2.85%, 5.71% and 5.71%, which are percentages of 35. The correct values are 2.04% and 4.08%. This is a printing error in baseline data and does not affect the treatment results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that these three rows use a subgroup of 35 as denominator.

quotes.location: Table 1, row c. Bronchial asthma with allergic rhinitis
Table 1, rows d (COPD only) and e (ILD)

script.explanation: 1/49 = 2.04%, but the paper prints 2.85, outside the rounding interval [2.85, 2.86]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 35.1 rather than 49.

10.4081/mrm.2022.886.headline_claim: Nebivolol 2.5 mg once daily, given for one week, increases pulmonary capillary blood volume and reduces dyspnoea in patients 'radiologically recovered' from COVID-19 pneumonia, and is well tolerated.
10.4081/mrm.2022.886.overall: The headline claim that nebivolol raises capillary blood volume and relieves dyspnoea rests on eight patients, one week of treatment, and within-arm pre-post tests with no direct between-treatment comparison, so it is at best a tentative pilot signal. The Conclusions also contain a reversed-direction wording error about dyspnoea, an unexplained DLCO figure, and an uncomputed correlation claim. Claims of clinical effectiveness and tolerability go well beyond the evidence.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from significant pre-post change on N versus non-significant on P; no N vs P comparison
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion conclude that nebivolol, 'but not placebo', works because the nebivolol pre-post test was significant and the placebo one was not. A difference in significance does not show a difference between treatments, and no direct between-treatment test is reported. Multiple endpoints (about 9) were tested at p<0.05 with no adjustment, and several p-values sit near 0.03-0.04. There is no handling of period or carryover effects in the crossover.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported N-vs-P comparison of the changes (paired or mixed model with period and sequence terms) that is significant.

quotes.text: N, but not P, improved significantly
while P was completely ineffective from this point of view

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy ('N, but not P, improved significantly'; 'P was completely ineffective') rests on one arm reaching p<0.05 within itself and the other not, with no direct N-vs-P comparison, crossover analysis or interaction test. The raw changes (e.g. Vc +7.8 vs -0.6; dyspnoea score -1.9 vs +0.1) point the same way, but a difference in significance is not evidence of a difference between treatments, and the paper does not test one.

issues.title: Effectiveness and tolerability claimed from 8 patients, 1 week, no adverse-event data or power calculation
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say nebivolol 'proved effective' and offers a 'novel and effective option' in clinical practice, and that it 'was well tolerated'. The evidence is eight patients, one week at one dose, with within-arm significance tests only and no sample-size calculation. Tolerability rests on a single remark that blood-pressure and heart-rate changes were tolerated, with no adverse-event reporting. The data support a hypothesis-generating signal, not a confident efficacy and safety conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size justification and systematic adverse-event data showing tolerability, or conclusions worded as preliminary.

quotes.text: Nebivolol seems to provide a novel and effective option against these pulmonary abnormalities in clinical practice, even if still off-label.
nebivolol was well tolerated in all patients investigated though normo-tensive
i) the small sample of patients investigated

second_reader.what_stands: The effectiveness and tolerability conclusions ('proved effective', 'novel and effective option', 'well tolerated in all patients') rest on 8 patients treated for one week, with no reported adverse-event data and no power calculation. The paper does acknowledge the small sample, dose and duration as limitations and calls for further studies, which softens the effectiveness claim somewhat. The tolerability claim has no supporting data beyond a one-line statement, and the lack of safety data is not listed as a limitation.

issues.title: Crossover order randomisation, concealment and carryover handling not described (n=8, 2-week gap)
issues.explanation: The paper says the treatments were randomly administered for one week each with a two-week interval. It does not say how the order was generated or concealed, how many patients received each order, or why two weeks is an adequate washout. With eight patients, order imbalance or carryover could matter, and the paper reports no check for either.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocol or supplement detailing the sequence generation, blinding procedure and a carryover or period analysis.

quotes.text: both randomly administered for one week, with a two-week interval in between

issues.title: Text reports DLCO rise of 8.5 after nebivolol; Table 2 means imply 5.1 points (7.2%)
issues.explanation: The Results state nebivolol improved DLCO 'by 8.5'. Table 2 gives 70.9 before and 76.0 after nebivolol, a rise of 5.1 points or 7.2%. The other percentages in the paragraph (Vc 17.7%, eNO 17.6%) do match the table, so this figure stands out as unsupported. The reported significance (p=0.04) is borderline, so the size of the effect matters.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of the 8.5 figure (for example a different subset or unit) that reproduces it from the data.

issues.title: Discussion claims Vc gain 'strictly correlated' with dyspnoea drop; no correlation analysis reported
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the effect on capillary blood volume was strictly correlated with the fall in dyspnoea score. The Statistics section lists only t-tests and no correlation, regression or coefficient appears in the Results or tables. With n=8, such a correlation would also be imprecise. This is used to support the mechanistic story and the 'confirmed hypothesis' claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported correlation (r, p, n) between individual Vc change and DS change.

quotes.text: proved strictly correlated to the drop in patients

issues.title: Conclusions say nebivolol increased dyspnoea; Table 3 shows the score fell from 2.5 to 0.6 (-76%)
issues.explanation: The Conclusions state that nebivolol was effective in 'increasing' pulmonary capillary blood volume 'and the corresponding dyspnoea'. The Results and Table 3 show dyspnoea score falling by 76% after nebivolol. The sentence as written says the opposite of the data. The intended meaning is probably clear to a reader, but the headline sentence is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition showing the dyspnoea score is scored so that higher means better, which Table 3 and the Results text contradict.

quotes.text: proved effective in increasing pulmonary capillary blood volume and the corresponding dyspnoea substantially
Only N minimized DS by 76% from the corresponding mean basal value

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective placebo-controlled crossover study
issues.explanation: The paper gives ethics approval before recruitment but no registry identifier. Without registration, the pre-specified primary outcome and analysis cannot be checked against what is reported. That matters more here because many outcomes were tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry made before enrolment that matches the reported outcomes.

quotes.text: The study was approved by the Ethical and Scientific Commission of the National Centre for Respiratory Pharmacoeconomics and Pharmacoepidemiology

10.4103/0970-2113.341091.headline_claim: Pulse steroid therapy in severe COVID-19 pneumonia is associated with improved survival and less need for oxygen at discharge compared with standard low-dose steroids.
10.4103/0970-2113.341091.overall: The collected abstracts are small, mostly descriptive and largely retrospective. The pulse-steroid survival claim rests on an unadjusted non-randomised comparison with baseline imbalance, so it supports only an association. The two numeric slips (an SD likely an SE, a smoking percentage that does not match its count) are minor and do not affect any main conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: mortality (survival)

issues.title: Retrospective non-randomised pulse vs standard steroids; unadjusted RR 0.5 with baseline imbalance, causal wording
issues.explanation: The two steroid regimens were compared in a retrospective, non-randomised cohort, and the abstract states the pulse group had higher CT severity and inflammatory markers at baseline. No adjustment, matching or allocation rule is described, yet the Results say pulse steroids 'significantly reduced mortality'. Differences in severity, timing and treatment era could move the RR in either direction, so the causal wording is not supported by the design. The Conclusion's 'associated with' is more appropriate.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full paper showing an adjusted analysis (e.g., multivariable or propensity-weighted) with a similar effect, and a clear allocation rule independent of prognosis.

quotes.text: Patients in pulse steroid group had significantly higher CT severity index (CTSI) as well as pro-inflammatory markers (IL-6, CRP) compared to standard dose steroid group.
Pulse steroid therapy significantly reduced mortality in severe CVOVID-19 pneumonia patients (RR 0.5 [95% CI 0.35-0.73]
This retrospective study included 198 patients of severe COVID-19 admitted and managed from June 2020 to December 2020
quotes.location: Pulse steroid abstract, Materials and Methods

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract confirms a retrospective, non-randomised comparison (101 standard vs 97 pulse) in which the pulse group had higher CTSI, IL-6 and CRP at baseline, and it reports an RR of 0.5 (0.35-0.73) with no mention of adjustment, and the Results use causal wording ('significantly reduced mortality'). The CI and P value are internally consistent, the conclusion is hedged as 'associated with', and the imbalance is toward worse severity in the pulse group. Whether the RR is unadjusted cannot be confirmed from the abstract, which states no adjustment method, and the full paper may contain one.

issues.title: Age dispersion 2.2 cannot be an SD for n=17 with range 45-75; likely an unlabelled SE
issues.explanation: The abstract gives ages of 45-75 years with mean 58.1±2.2 in 17 people. With observed values at 45 and 75 the SD must be at least about 5.3, so 2.2 cannot be an SD. It is plausible as a standard error (SD about 9), so the issue is an unlabelled dispersion measure in a descriptive statistic.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 2.2 is an SE, or that the range refers to a different set of participants than the 17 completers.

quotes.text: Age group of participant was 45-75 years (Mean= 58.1±2.2)

issues.title: Ever smokers 58 of 468 printed as 16.2%; the count gives 12.4%
issues.explanation: The abstract says 58 of the 468 patients were ever smokers and gives 16.2%. 58/468 is 12.4%. The mismatch could reflect a smaller denominator (about 358) for smoking data, but none is stated. This is a descriptive baseline figure in a different abstract from the headline claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that smoking status was available for only about 358 patients.

quotes.text: Ever smokers comprised 58 (16.2%) patients.
quotes.location: Post COVID-19 lung sequelae abstract, Results

script.explanation: 58/468 = 12.39%, but the paper prints 16.2, outside the rounding interval [16.15, 16.30]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 358.0 rather than 468.

10.4103/ayu.ayu_271_23.headline_claim: The authors state that CPP alone proved superior to WHO rehabilitation on all assessment parameters in post-COVID syndrome, improving symptoms, 6MWT, PCFS and QoL, and that CPP is safe at the prescribed dose.
10.4103/ayu.ayu_271_23.overall: The direction of the finding (larger symptom, 6MWT and QoL gains with CPP plus rehabilitation than with placebo plus rehabilitation) is plausible, but the open-label design with subjective outcomes, no multiplicity control and an unvalidated symptom scale make the size of the effect uncertain. The Conclusion overreaches ('proved', 'all parameters', 'safe') relative to the design and to the authors' own non-significant taste and smell results. Remaining numeric discrepancies are minor labelling inconsistencies.

primary_outcome.name: Improvement in symptoms (cough, dyspnea, fatigue, headache and associated symptoms)

issues.title: Open-label trial with subjective symptom, QoL and function-scale outcomes; blinding and concealment not described
issues.explanation: The trial is described as open-labeled although it uses a placebo, and no blinding of participants or outcome assessors is reported. Symptom grades, PCFS and WHO QoL are patient- or clinician-rated. Expectation and assessor bias could inflate the very large between-group differences. The authors still state that superiority was 'proved'.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods stating that participants and outcome assessors were masked to allocation, with allocation concealment described.

quotes.text: The study was a prospective open-labeled placebo-controlled interventional clinical trial
quotes.location: Materials and methods, Selection of patients

second_reader.what_stands: The paper states the trial was 'open-labeled', does not describe who was blinded, how allocation was concealed, or whether outcome assessors were masked, and its main outcomes are symptom grades, QoL questionnaires and PCFS, which are subjective or self-reported (6MWT is performance-based but effort-dependent). A placebo capsule was used, so participants may have been masked in practice, and the 'open-label' wording is internally inconsistent with 'placebo-controlled'; this cannot be resolved from the text. I did not check the trial registry record for this point.

issues.title: Conclusion says CPP 'proved' preeminent over rehabilitation and 'safe'; design is add-on and open-label
issues.explanation: Both arms received WHO rehabilitation, so the trial compares CPP+rehab with placebo+rehab, not CPP with rehabilitation. The study is open-label with subjective outcomes and no multiplicity control, so 'proved' is too strong. 'No adverse reaction was reported' is stated without any described AE ascertainment or counts. A sample of 56 per arm with no AE monitoring method cannot establish safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods section describing systematic AE monitoring, with event counts per arm, and conclusions worded as add-on efficacy.

quotes.text: The present clinical study proved the preeminence of CPP over rehabilitation in all the assessment parameters in PCS
No adverse reaction was reported in the present study, which reveals that the trial drug CPP is safe in the prescribed dose

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's wording is stronger than the design supports: the comparison is add-on (CPP plus rehabilitation versus placebo plus rehabilitation), not CPP versus rehabilitation, so 'preeminence of CPP over rehabilitation' misdescribes it (the paper's own Discussion says the effect is combined), and 'proved' is strong for a single open-label trial of 110 analysed participants with subjective outcomes. 'Safe' rests on an unreported adverse-event method and about 8 weeks of exposure in 56 participants, so it is not demonstrated beyond 'no adverse reaction reported'; the laboratory values being

issues.title: 'All parameters' significant claims contradicted by non-significant taste and smell results
issues.explanation: The Conclusion, and the Results sentences on group A and on intergroup differences, say CPP was superior or significant in all parameters. The Results themselves report no significant intergroup difference for loss of taste and smell. The Discussion also says intragroup effects were seen on all symptoms except taste and smell. The blanket claim is therefore stronger than the authors' own data support, although it affects only symptoms with very few patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Results text restricting the claim to symptoms with adequate numbers, with taste and smell explicitly excluded in the Conclusion.

quotes.text: proved the preeminence of CPP over rehabilitation in all the assessment parameters in PCS
Although there were no significant differences
quotes.location: Results, paragraph on loss of taste and smell

quotes.text: Statistically highly significant results were obtained in all the subjective and objective parameters of group A

issues.title: Many symptom and timepoint tests, no multiplicity control, parametric tests on ordinal grades
issues.explanation: About 14 symptoms, three timepoint contrasts, 6MWT, PCFS and four QoL domains are tested with no stated correction or primary hierarchy. The 'all parameters' superiority claim rests on this unadjusted set. Because the main P values are very small, the headline direction likely survives. Marginal 'P<0.05' within-group results are weaker, and ordinal grades analysed with ANOVA/ANCOVA add uncertainty.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single primary outcome with hierarchical testing, or adjusted P values that remain significant.

quotes.text: For intragroup analysis, data were categorized into three levels

issues.title: Scoring of the four primary symptoms not described in Methods; ad hoc ordinal scale for others
issues.explanation: The primary objective is symptom improvement, assessed for cough, dyspnea, fatigue and headache. The Methods give only a rationale for choosing them and do not define their scoring range, anchors or assessor. References to gradation tools exist but no validation is claimed. This limits how far the primary outcome result can be trusted or replicated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of the scoring scale and its validation or its source for each of the four symptoms.

quotes.text: Hence, these four symptoms were selected for assessment in the present study
using an ordinal scale of no/mild/moderate and severe complaint

issues.title: Text places 3 group A recoveries 'after the 2nd week'; Table 5 puts them in the 4th-week column
issues.explanation: The Results text says three group A patients recovered after the 2nd week. Table 5 shows 0 in the 2nd-week column and 3 in the 4th-week column. The counts add up (49 complete relief), so this is a timing label discrepancy only and no result changes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'after the 2nd week' means the 4th-week visit, or a corrected Table 5.

quotes.text: Among them, three patients recovered after the 2 nd week
24 got recovered after the 6 th week

issues.title: Group B 6MWT 'deterioration of 0.2%' not reflected in Table 2 means (230.09 to 230.08)
issues.explanation: The Discussion describes a mild 0.2% deterioration in group B walking distance at follow-up and builds an interpretation on it (the body cannot maintain the effect after stopping rehabilitation). Table 2 means are essentially identical at AT and AF. The tabulated change is 0.01 m, about 0.004%, and the AT-AF statistic is non-significant. The point is minor and does not affect the CPP comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-patient data showing a mean percentage decline of 0.2% between AT and AF in group B.

quotes.text: The mild deterioration of 0.2% in walking distance AF visit
quotes.location: Discussion on results obtained in group B

issues.title: Two group A patients reporting complete relief excluded from analysis (110 of 112); likely understates effect
issues.explanation: Two group A patients withdrew saying they had complete relief and were excluded from effect analysis, leaving 110 analysed. They would plausibly have counted as successes, so excluding them if anything understates CPP's effect. The attrition is small and an intention-to-treat analysis is not reported. The deviation is a departure from ITT but is unlikely to alter conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT analysis (for example last observation carried forward with the two patients as complete relief) giving the same conclusions.

quotes.text: two patients were considered dropouts as according to these two patients, they had complete relief, and as per their view
whereas for the assessment of the effect of therapies, 110 patients were analyzed

10.4103/ipj.ipj_234_23.headline_claim: Patients with post-COVID-19 depression showed better improvement with medications plus CBT than medications alone.
10.4103/ipj.ipj_234_23.overall: The paper supports only that patients given medication plus CBT had lower post BDI-II scores (8.34 vs 15.06) than those on medication alone in an open-label comparison with unclear allocation and a self-report outcome. The numeric slips (25.23 vs 25.13, SD 7.57 vs 7.52, a 0.06 mismatch in the control means) are minor, but the 'very effective' and 'eliminates symptoms' wording is stronger than the design allows. Medication regimens by arm are also unreported.

primary_outcome.name: BDI-II post-intervention score (between-group comparison)

issues.title: 'Eliminates the symptoms' and 'very effective' overstate an unblinded add-on comparison; within-group change used as support
issues.explanation: The Results cite within-group improvement in both arms as suggestive of how CBT helps, but the control arm improved by 21 points without CBT. The text then says CBT 'eliminates the symptoms of depression' and the Conclusion calls it 'very effective' and 'proved', although the design is unblinded and self-reported, has no attention control, and has no remission data or follow-up. The supported finding is a lower BDI-II mean with medication plus CBT than with medication alone at one time point.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Remission or response rates, a blinded outcome measure and follow-up data supporting the strong wording.

quotes.text: The overall improvement in both groups on depression was suggestive
CBT proved to be a very effective and fruitful management technique for patients

second_reader.what_stands: Wording such as 'eliminates the symptoms' is not supported since the experimental post-mean was 8.34 on the BDI-II, and 'very effective' rests on an unblinded add-on comparison with no attention control; the Results also invoke improvement in both groups as evidence for CBT although the control group improved by about 21 points. The core conclusion of better improvement with CBT plus medication than medication alone is a correct reading of the Table 3 post-intervention difference, and the paper does flag that CBT cannot be separated from drug effect.

issues.title: Chit randomisation with no concealment or allocation ratio; unexplained 92 vs 64 split
issues.explanation: Allocation is described only as 'chit randomization'. There is no mention of concealment, who drew the chits, or why group sizes are unequal (92 vs 64), and recruitment is called purposive sampling. Chit draws are easily subverted when open, so selection into the CBT arm cannot be ruled out. Baseline BDI-II means were not significantly different, which partly reassures, but the comparison is weaker than the label 'randomised' suggests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or description showing a concealed random sequence with a planned unequal allocation ratio (about 3:2).

quotes.text: Through chit randomization methods, patients are allocated into two groups
Through purposive sampling, a total
quotes.location: Material and Method, Sample of the Study

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports chit randomisation but gives no allocation ratio, no description of sequence generation or allocation concealment, and no explanation for the 92 vs 64 split, which is somewhat improbable under 1:1 simple randomisation (z about 2.2). It is not shown that the split is wrong, only that it is unexplained and the method is unconcealed or undescribed.

issues.title: Open-label add-on CBT vs treatment as usual, self-report BDI-II, no attention control or assessor masking
issues.explanation: The experimental arm received eight CBT sessions on top of medication, and the controls received only usual treatment with no psychological contact. The only outcome is a self-report scale and no masking of the person collecting it is described. Part of the 6.7-point difference in post-scores may therefore reflect expectancy and extra attention rather than CBT content. The comparison supports 'CBT package plus medication did better than medication alone', not a CBT-specific effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that BDI-II was administered by an assessor blind to allocation, or an attention-matched comparison arm.

quotes.text: The control group was on treatment as usual
Depression was assessed by applying the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) pre- and post-intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: The comparison is open-label CBT plus medication versus medication as usual with no attention control, and the sole outcome is self-reported BDI-II with no stated blinding, so non-specific effects of therapist contact and expectation are confounded with CBT. The limitations section does not acknowledge this.

issues.title: Medication type, dose and adherence not reported by arm; Limitation about CBT vs antidepressants is unclear
issues.explanation: Both arms are said to have received 'appropriate pharmacotherapy', but the drugs, doses and adherence are not tabulated by arm, and the analysis is not adjusted for baseline score or medication. Differences in medication between arms could contribute to the post-score gap. The Limitation says CBT and antidepressant effects cannot be separated, which does not follow from a design in which both arms took medication.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table showing equivalent medication regimens and adherence in the two arms, or an adjusted analysis giving the same difference.

quotes.text: Further, since CBT was combined with pharmacotherapy, we cannot differentiate whether the improvement achieved is due to the intervention of  CBT or due to antidepressants.

issues.title: Experimental pre-post mean change: text 25.23 vs Table 2 and Table 3 means giving 25.13
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the experimental group's pre-post mean change as 25.23, but Table 2 prints 25.13. The Table 3 means (33.47 pre, 8.34 post) give 25.13, so the text is the mistaken one. This is a small transcription slip and the finding is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing a mean change of 25.23 and different pre or post means from those printed in Table 3.

quotes.text: The difference between pre and post of the experimental group on the level of  depression was M = 25.23
Pre- and post-score of exp. on BDI-II

issues.title: Baseline severity percentages (59.78/25/15.21%) match the 92 experimental patients, not all 156
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Discussion report depression severity percentages for 'patients' without naming a group. They reproduce exactly as counts out of 92 (the experimental arm), not out of 156. No severity breakdown is shown for the 64 controls, so baseline severity balance cannot be judged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table giving severity categories for all 156 patients that reproduces these percentages.

quotes.text: 59.78% of patients report severe levels

issues.title: 'Receiving treatment for more than 7 months' vs a July 2021 to January 2022 study period
issues.explanation: The Results say patients received treatment for more than 7 months, yet the study ran from July 2021 to January 2022 and the intervention was eight sessions. Per-patient duration cannot exceed the study window. The sentence is unclear and no treatment duration or timing of the post-assessment is given anywhere else.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the figure refers to something other than treatment duration, such as time since COVID-19 infection.

quotes.text: The period of study was from July 2021 to January 2022
for more than 7 months

issues.title: Control means 36.06 and 15.06 differ by 21.00, not the 21.06 change reported in Table 2
issues.explanation: The control group's pre and post means (36.06 and 15.06) give a change of 21.00, but Table 2 and the text report 21.06. The reported t statistics for both the change and the between-group post comparison fit 21.06 and a post mean near 15.00. One printed mean, probably the 15.06 post value, is therefore off by 0.06. The effect is trivial and the conclusion is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data confirming a control post mean of 15.06 and a mean change of 21.06 (this would require a non-additive handling of missing data).

issues.title: Control pre-post SD: text 7.57 vs Table 2 7.52 (the printed t = 22.40 supports 7.52)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the control group's SD of the change as 7.57, while Table 2 prints 7.52. Back-calculating from the reported t and n = 64 gives about 7.52, so the text figure is the likely slip. It is a minor reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing an SD of 7.57 for the control change scores.

quotes.text: was M = 21.06 with SD = 7.57
