Several baselines (depression, stress, situational anxiety) differ significantly under the SD reading although they are reported as p>0.05. The methods call the ± a standard error of the mean, which cannot be right for the stress and depression values. The p-values may have come from raw data that is not shown.

issues.title: No-training, unblinded, non-randomised control for self-reported outcomes; allocation not described
issues.explanation: Controls had only the pre and post tests, with no sham or attention condition, and all outcomes are questionnaires. Allocation to 24 versus 16 is not described, and baseline stress and depression were higher in the trained group. A between-group difference at the end cannot be attributed specifically to alpha-rhythm neurofeedback.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of random allocation and an attention-matched or blinded control condition.

quotes.text: Участники контрольной группы не проходили курс тренинга по БОС
quotes.location: Materials and methods, control group paragraph

quotes.text: В контрольной группе также было отмечено небольшое улучшение состояния

second_reader.what_stands: The control group received no training and no sham, and the paper does not describe allocation, randomisation or blinding. The outcomes that are reported are self-reported, and participants who trained could not have been blind to it. The paper does not state the word 'unblinded', but nothing in the design could have blinded the trained group.

issues.title: Treatment effect judged from unadjusted endpoint comparison and pre-post change, with differing baselines
issues.explanation: The effect is judged from the pre-post drop in the trained group and from endpoint comparisons only. No baseline adjustment or comparison of change scores is shown. The trained group started higher on stress and depression, so larger falls could partly reflect regression to the mean.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or change-score comparison between groups showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Stimulation of the alpha rhythm in the frequency range 8-14 Hz helped to change the psychoemotional state of the subjects.

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy statement rests on unadjusted endpoint comparisons and unadjusted pre-post changes, while baselines differ between the groups (stress by 22 points, depression by 13). The paper reports no baseline-adjusted or change-score test. The baseline imbalance for stress favours the control group, so it is not clear that it inflates the apparent effect there. For depression the endpoint difference is smaller than the baseline difference, which makes the endpoint comparison hard to interpret.

issues.title: Two authors affiliated with Neurobotics (Zelenograd) while evaluating 'Neuro V' (Zelenograd); no COI statement
issues.explanation: Two authors list Neurobotics in Zelenograd, and the device is described as made in Zelenograd. The paper has no funding or conflict-of-interest statement, and the link is inferred from location only. If the company makes the device, the favourable unblinded evaluation carries an undisclosed interest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Neurobotics has no commercial interest in Neuro V, or a COI declaration.

quotes.text: ALEXANDER A. ZONOV - Lead Researcher, Neurobotics, Russia, Moscow, Zelenograd
The equipment "Neuro V" (Zelenograd, Russia) was used for neuro-biofeedback training.

issues.title: Whole-sample mean age 42.25 is the main-group mean; pooled mean from Tables 1-2 is about 45.9
issues.explanation: The abstract and Methods give 42.25±2.59 as the mean age of all 40 participants. Table 2 shows this is the 24-person main group only. The 16 controls average 51.37, so the pooled mean is about 45.9. The Methods' '12 younger than 40' also matches the main group only (control has 2 more), and the 25% 'under 30 days' matches the main group (pooled 11/40 = 27.5%).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 'sample' statistics in the abstract and Methods refer to the main group only.

quotes.text: the mean age was 42.25±2.59 years

issues.title: Minimum participant age is 25 in the abstract but 23 in the Methods
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the age range as 25 to 73 years, while the Methods give 23 to 73 years for the same 40 participants. One of the two is wrong. Nothing in the efficacy results depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the abstract range refers to a subset, for example completers only.

quotes.text: The age of the participants ranged from 25 to 73 years
в диапазоне от 23 до 73 лет

issues.title: Control-group anxiety values swapped between scales in the text relative to Table 4
issues.explanation: The text lists personal then situational anxiety and gives 47.2 and 48.1 'respectively'. Table 4 gives 47.2 for situational and 48.1 for personal anxiety. The values are swapped in the prose. The differences are small, so the effect on conclusions is negligible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Table 4 rows being mislabelled rather than the text.

quotes.text: (47,2±11,7 и 48,1±9,8, соответственно

10.47197/retos.v59.105417.headline_claim: Multicomponent exercise improved anxiety, sleep quality, cognitive function, and functional capacity in post-COVID-19 adults in Danlí, Honduras, compared with a WHO-recommendations control group.
10.47197/retos.v59.105417.overall: The headline claim that exercise improved anxiety, sleep and cognition versus control cannot be relied on. No between-group test is reported, the control arm is only advice, and on the printed scales the exercise arm's anxiety and PSQI scores rose more than control. The sample size is also inconsistent (48 vs 49), and ethics approval was not completed beforehand.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; anxiety (STAI), sleep quality (PSQI), cognition (MMSE) and functional tests are reported as main outcomes

issues.title: Claims of significant between-group effects rest on descriptive means with no test reported
issues.explanation: The Results and Conclusions state significant differences between exercise and control on anxiety, sleep, cognition, SF-36 and function. The paper reports no between-group test, no effect estimate or confidence interval, and no p values. Tables 2 and 3 have no SDs. The SF-36 text calls experimental pre-post changes (25, 50, 50, 55, 50) differences 'compared with control', but the between-group differences in Table 3 would be much smaller (for example 5 for physical functioning). The conclusion of significant superiority is not supported by what is shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported between-group tests (for example ANCOVA or t-tests on change scores) with p values and CIs supporting the stated differences.

quotes.text: Los resultados muestran diferencias significativas entre los grupos de control y experimental
La intervención experimental demostró mejoras significativas en la reducción de la ansiedad, la mejora del sueño y el aumento de la función cognitiva en comparación con el grupo de control.

second_reader.what_stands: The claims of 'diferencias significativas' between groups (Discusión, Conclusión 3) are supported only by pre/post means in Table 2, with no SDs, test statistics, p-values or CIs reported, even though the Methods name a t-test and a p<0.05 threshold. The wording 'significant' is therefore unverifiable from the paper. This is also a narrower point than the direction problem: for anxiety and sleep the 'effect' is a larger rise on scales where higher means worse.

issues.title: Anxiety, sleep and depression scores rose in both arms but are described as improvements or stability
issues.explanation: The Abstract and Results describe the experimental group's anxiety rise (30 to 70) and PSQI rise (8 to 20) as improvement or reduction. The Methods say higher PSQI means worse sleep, and higher STAI conventionally means more anxiety. On the printed numbers the exercise arm worsened more than control (anxiety +40 vs +22, sleep +12 vs +9). Depression rose from 3 to 6.25, which is called stable. Unless the scoring was reversed, the headline claims of benefit on anxiety and sleep point the wrong way.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the authors used reversed or transformed scoring for STAI and PSQI so that higher means better.

quotes.text: el grupo experimental reportó mejoras notables en ansiedad (de 30 a 70 puntos), calidad del sueño (de 8 a 20 puntos)
puntajes más altos indican una peor calidad de sueño
la depresión se mantuvo estable en un promedio de 3 en el pre test y 6.25 en el post test

second_reader.what_stands: By the paper's own scale definitions (PSQI higher = worse stated explicitly; STAI and Goldberg are conventionally higher = worse and no reversal is stated), anxiety, sleep and depression scores all rose in both arms, and the experimental arm rose more on anxiety and sleep. Yet the Abstract and Results describe these as 'mejoras notables', 'reducción notable' and 'estable' (3 to 6.25 is a doubling). Only the MMSE change is a real improvement. The narrower caveat is that the STAI and Goldberg direction is not stated in the paper, so it rests on convention; for PSQI it is stated in the paper.

issues.title: Authors state the ethics committee application for this experimental study was not completed in time
issues.explanation: The Procedure section states that the ethics application for the 'experimental study' modality could not be completed beforehand. No approval or waiver is reported. The study enrolled people with persistent COVID-19 into a supervised exercise programme, so absence of documented prior review is a significant compliance concern. The scientific findings are unaffected, but the report's ethical standing is.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ethics committee approval letter dated before enrolment, or a documented waiver.

quotes.text: no ha sido posible culminar con la debida antelación la solicitud de informe en el Portal de Ética

second_reader.what_stands: The authors themselves state that the ethics-portal application for this 'experimental study' was not completed in time, and the paper reports no committee approval. The text mentions informed consent and Helsinki principles, but I could not find any statement that approval was granted, so the ethical review status remains unreported rather than affirmatively shown to be absent.

issues.title: Randomisation sequence generation and allocation concealment not described
issues.explanation: The paper says participants were randomly assigned but gives no method, no concealment, and no flow diagram. The total (48 or 49) is not reconciled with the 24/24 split. Allocation bias cannot be excluded or confirmed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or CONSORT statement describing computer-generated sequence and concealed allocation.

quotes.text: Los participantes fueron asignados aleatoriamente a uno de estos dos grupos

issues.title: Open-label trial with self-reported outcomes (STAI, PSQI, SF-36) and no blinded assessment
issues.explanation: Participants knew their arm, and most outcomes (anxiety, sleep, quality of life, depression) are self-reported. No blinded outcome assessor is described. Reported benefits on these scales may be inflated by expectation, though blinding was hard to achieve.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors were blinded and that objective measures drove the conclusions.

quotes.text: calidad de sueño (Pittsburg); El índice de calidad de sueño de Pittsburgh

issues.title: Control arm got only written advice and self-recording, so exercise cannot be separated from supervision
issues.explanation: The exercise arm received 24 supervised sessions, whereas the control arm received a document and was asked to record its own activity. Any difference therefore mixes exercise with attention, supervision and expectation. The authors concede a more active control might have changed results, but the Conclusions still credit the exercise programme directly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the control arm received equivalent contact and supervision time.

quotes.text: los participantes del grupo control registraron las actividades físicas moderadas o vigorosas que pudiesen realizar en su día a día
la falta de un grupo de control más activo puede haber influido en los resultados

issues.title: Sample size derived from a survey-style formula (population 56, 5% margin), not from effect-size power
issues.explanation: The target of 49 comes from confidence level and margin of error for a population of 56, not from expected effects or variability. It gives no assurance of power to detect between-group differences. The 48 vs 49 discrepancy is covered by c2.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A power calculation based on an expected between-group effect size and SD.

quotes.text: el tamaño de la población fue de 56 donde se obtuvo un tamaño muestral de 49 participantes

issues.title: Table 1 counts sum to 49 and percentages use n=49, but N=48 is stated throughout
issues.explanation: The Abstract, Participants section, and Table 1 header give N = 48 (24 per arm). The Table 1 counts sum to 49 for sex (30+19), marital status (2+47), residence (9+40), education (34+7+8) and employment (8+28+13). The printed percentages were computed on 49, and the Design section also says 49. The paper never explains the missing or extra participant, so the true sample and the arm sizes are uncertain. This is a reporting inconsistency that does not itself change the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A participant flow account showing 49 enrolled and 48 analysed, with Table 1 percentages explicitly based on 49 enrolled.

quotes.text: Hombre3061, 2
Mujer1938, 8
una muestra de 49 sujetos con síndrome post COVID-19

script.explanation: 30/48 = 62.50%, but the paper prints 61.2, outside the rounding interval [61.15, 61.30]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 49.0 rather than 48.

issues.title: No trial registration identifier reported for a randomised exercise trial
issues.explanation: No registry or identifier is cited, so prespecified outcomes cannot be checked. This matters because many outcomes were measured and a subset is highlighted in the conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment with matching outcomes.

quotes.text: Un estudio aleatorizado simple y controlado que evalúa dos intervenciones

10.47660/cbr.2021.1877.headline_claim: tDCS combined with aerobic exercise is safe and effective in significantly reducing pain and fatigue in patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases and post-COVID-19 syndrome.
10.47660/cbr.2021.1877.overall: The headline claim that tDCS plus exercise is effective is not supported by an uncontrolled, open-label, nine-patient pilot with self-reported outcomes, and the large pre-post changes cannot be attributed to tDCS. The safety statement rests on five sessions in nine patients, and the printed medication percentages are impossible for this sample, which raises questions about data transcription. Results are best read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Pain VAS and fatigue VAS, pre- vs post-tDCS (paper names no primary outcome)

primary_outcomes.measure: Frequency of treatment-emergent adverse events [safety and tolerability]

issues.title: Uncontrolled single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute pain and fatigue reductions to tDCS
issues.explanation: All patients received tDCS plus aerobic exercise, and outcomes are compared only with their own baseline in nine patients. Without a control or sham group, any change could reflect exercise, expectation, natural recovery or regression to the mean (patients were enrolled for being symptomatic). The efficacy conclusion is therefore not supported by this design. Further, the title and conclusion credit the combination, so the specific contribution of tDCS is undetermined; open-label self-reported outcomes (candidate c3) and the unsupported conclusion (c5) are part of this same problem.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent sham or exercise-only control arm showing a smaller change.

quotes.text: After tDCS intervention, the VAS for pain and fatigue reduced significantly (Table 1).
The patients were evaluated in three periods: within one week before and after tDCS intervention, as well as 30 days after the intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, open, uncontrolled pre-post design with 9 patients, so the pain and fatigue reductions (about 5 points on a 0-10 VAS each) cannot be attributed to tDCS rather than to exercise, natural course, expectation or regression to the mean. The paper does label itself a pilot open study, but its wording of 'after tDCS intervention' and 'effective' still implies attribution.

issues.title: Conclusion declares tDCS plus exercise 'safe and effective' from nine uncontrolled, unblinded patients
issues.explanation: The conclusion asserts efficacy and safety with no mention of the missing control, open-label self-reported outcomes, or small sample (nine patients, no precision estimates). Safety conclusions from nine patients over five sessions cannot exclude uncommon adverse events. A cautious reading would call the results hypothesis-generating. This also covers the overlapping open-label and underpowered concerns (c3, c4).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion hedged as preliminary, with limitations acknowledged where the claim is made.

quotes.text: The present pilot study shows that tDCS associated with aerobic exercise was safe and effective in significantly reducing the fatigue and pain
A PILOT OPEN STUDY

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion calls tDCS plus exercise 'safe and effective' on the basis of nine unblinded patients with no control group, and does not state these limitations there. The safety statement is weakly supported (0 events in 9 is compatible with up to about 33% true rate), and the efficacy statement is not supported by this design, though the title does flag the open pilot nature.

issues.title: Twelve uncorrected pre-post tests in Table 1; none of the p values below 0.004
issues.explanation: Table 1 presents twelve pre-post tests with no multiplicity correction and no primary outcome declared. Under a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/12 = 0.0042, none of the reported p values (smallest 0.005) would be significant. All results, including non-significant ones, are shown, which limits selective reporting, but the claims of significance rest on uncorrected tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or a stated adjustment plan.

quotes.text: Moreover, the physical domains of the fatigue and physical function improved significantly.

issues.title: Registered primary outcome (adverse events) not the paper's headline; efficacy outcomes not registered as primary
issues.explanation: The registry record lists treatment-emergent adverse events as the primary outcome at four time points, up to 60 days. The paper does not name a primary outcome, headlines pain and fatigue efficacy, and reports safety in a single sentence with no 60-day data. This is a mismatch between registered and emphasised outcomes rather than a demonstrated outcome change, since earlier record versions were not checked.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Registry history showing pain and fatigue were primary outcomes, or a protocol designating them as such.

quotes.text: No adverse effects or disease relapses were observed in all protocols, which had 100% of patients' adherence.
Clinical trials: NCT04890483.

issues.title: Medication percentages 50.6% and 5.9% are impossible for a sample of nine patients
issues.explanation: The Results state that 50.6% used prednisone and 5.9% used immunosuppressants, but the study had nine patients. With nine patients, any share is a multiple of about 11.1%, so neither figure can occur. This suggests the percentages come from a different population or were mis-transcribed, and the true medication use is unknown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that percentages refer to a different denominator (e.g. a larger source cohort), or corrected counts out of nine.

quotes.text: 50.6% were using prednisone (6.0 [IQR 0.0-6.0] mg/day) and 5.9% were using immunosuppressive drugs
that included nine patients

10.47750/jptcp.2023.30.07.016.headline_claim: Pulmonary rehabilitation improved dyspnea, respiratory function, oxygen saturation and 6MWT in severe post-hospitalization COVID-19 patients, and it is very important alongside medical treatment.
10.47750/jptcp.2023.30.07.016.overall: The direction of benefit (better dyspnea, spirometry and walk distance with rehabilitation than with medication alone) is plausible, and the between-group post-values are reported. However, the open-label design, retrospective registration, entry of patients who met an exclusion criterion, and several unreconciled values between Tables 3 and 4 mean the size of the effect cannot be relied on. The conclusion is better treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Dyspnea (mMRC) and spirometry measures after 6 weeks (registry primary outcomes; paper does not name a single primary outcome)

issues.title: Unblinded usual-care control with subjective, effort-dependent outcomes; conclusion stated without caveat
issues.explanation: Control patients received only their medications, and the paper does not describe blinding of outcome assessors; the registry lists no masking. The dyspnea score, 6MWT and incentive-spirometer-based spirometry all depend on patient effort and rater judgement, so expectation and attention effects could inflate the apparent benefit. The Limitations section does not discuss this, yet the conclusion is stated flatly. The direction of benefit is plausible, but its size is uncertain.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation of assessor blinding or objective outcome measurement by independent staff.

quotes.text: Both groups continued their medications.
Pulmonary rehabilitation improved dyspnea, respiratory function, oxygen saturation and 6MWT in severe post hospitalization COVID- 19 patients.

second_reader.what_stands: The control group received usual care only (medications), the registry records masking as NONE, the paper does not describe assessor blinding, and the main outcomes (mMRC, 6MWT, effort-dependent spirometry) are subjective or effort-dependent, yet the Conclusion is stated without any caveat and the Limitations section does not mention lack of blinding. Participant blinding was not feasible, and oxygen saturation is less susceptible to bias, so the concern is about unacknowledged bias risk rather than the design being avoidable.

issues.title: Post-program values differ between Table 3 and Table 4: 6MWT 266.6 vs 278.7 m, 169.5 vs 187.4 m; SO2 also differs
issues.explanation: The same post-program measurements for the same 50+50 patients are printed with different values in Tables 3 and 4. The 6MWT distance is 266.6 m vs 278.7 m in the experimental group and 169.5 m vs 187.4 m in the control group. The control-group SD (73.7 vs 71.7) and several SO2 means or SDs also differ between tables. The between-group test in Table 3 and the within-group tests in Table 4 therefore cannot both rest on the same data. Readers cannot tell which 6MWT result is correct, and the control group's change (169.9 to 169.5 m, essentially none, vs to 187.4 m, p=0.02) depends on which table is right.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Tables 3 and 4 use different analysis sets or time points, or corrected tables showing identical post-program values.

quotes.text: 6MWT distance (m)266.668.7169.573.7

issues.title: All 100 patients analysed with no flow diagram or adherence data, despite stated non-adherence
issues.explanation: Every table reports N=50 per arm with complete outcomes, and no screening, exclusion, dropout or adherence figures are given. The Limitations section says some patients lacked commitment to the exercise program and had difficulty learning it. No analysis population (ITT or per-protocol) is defined, and no sample size calculation or adverse events are reported. Completeness of follow-up and exposure to the intervention cannot be verified.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flow diagram or adherence log showing no dropouts or missing outcomes.

quotes.text: Lack of commitment of some Patients to follow the exercise program.
each  group  consisted  of  50  patients.

issues.title: 7 of 100 patients had normal baseline spirometry despite exclusion of normal pulmonary function tests
issues.explanation: The Methods say enrolled patients had restrictive impairment and that normal pulmonary function tests were an exclusion criterion. Table 2 nonetheless lists 3 experimental and 4 control patients with normal spirometry at baseline. These patients could not improve on spirometry and may dilute or distort the spirometry comparison. The paper does not explain how they were eligible. The effect on the conclusions is small because the numbers are few and balanced.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol definition showing that 'normal' in Table 2 is a grading on a different measure from that used for eligibility, or a note that these patients met another inclusion route.

quotes.text: The exclusion criteria were mild or moderate COVID infection, normal pulmonary function tests
Normal36%48%

issues.title: Post-values compared between arms without baseline adjustment; within-group p-values also cited as benefit
issues.explanation: Table 3 tests post-program values between arms, which is acceptable under randomization, but no change-from-baseline or baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA) comparison is presented. Baseline 6MWT and mMRC were not identical between arms. The Results also say both groups improved with p<0.05, and the within-group p-values in Table 4 say nothing about the treatment effect. The between-group conclusion is probably directionally sound, but its size is not well estimated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted or change-score between-group analysis giving results consistent with Table 3.

quotes.text: Post  COVID  -19  cases  in  each  group  show improvement in all respiratory function with pvalue <0.05.

issues.title: Retrospective registration: first submitted 2022-07-23, after the 2021-05-15 start; registry named inconsistently
issues.explanation: The registry record was first submitted more than a year after the study start, and the program period reported in the paper (May 2021 to May 2022) had already ended or nearly ended. The paper gives no registration date and does not disclose that registration was retrospective. It also attributes an NCT number to the Pan African Clinical Trials Registry. Retrospective registration means the outcomes could not be verified as prespecified, although the registered primaries (dyspnea, spirometry) match what the paper reports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated prospective registration record, such as an earlier PACTR entry, made before enrolment began.

quotes.text: Pan African Clinical Trials Registry no is (NCT05476835).
for 6 weeks from May 2021 to May 2022

10.47750/pnr.2023.14.s02.87.headline_claim: Active cycle of breathing technique added to conventional physiotherapy is an efficient modality that improves ABG parameters, fatigue and 6MWT in post-COVID syndrome patients.
10.47750/pnr.2023.14.s02.87.overall: The direction of the result, with Group B improving more than Group A, is internally supported by Tables 2 and 3. The percent-change figures reproduce from the printed means, apart from small prose typos and a mismatched sex count. The causal and practice-recommending conclusion is only tentative, because randomization and concealment are undescribed, blinding is unspecified for subjective outcomes, there was no registration or sample-size calculation, and no safety data are reported.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly named; outcomes are ABG (PaO2, SaO2, PaCO2), six-minute walk test and fatigue level

issues.title: Random sequence generation and allocation concealment not described; ID numbers 'divided' into two groups
issues.explanation: The Randomization section is mostly about SPSS and then says unique ID numbers were divided into two equal groups of 30. It does not say how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was hidden from the enrolling team. The trial is also unregistered and reports no sample-size calculation. The large between-group differences therefore cannot be attributed to ACBT with confidence, because allocation bias cannot be excluded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or registry entry describing computer-generated random sequences with concealed allocation.

quotes.text: Each participant was assigned a unique identification number. These numbers were divided into two equal groups (n=30).

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does not describe how the random sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed; it only says ID numbers were 'divided' into two equal groups of 30, which does not establish randomization. The trial is labelled randomized, but the method is unreported, so the risk of selection bias in allocation cannot be assessed from the text.

issues.title: Blinding not specified; self-reported fatigue (FAS) and effort-dependent 6MWT may carry expectation effects
issues.explanation: The design is called 'single-blinded' with no statement of who was blinded. The fatigue outcome is a 10-item self-rated scale, and the 6MWT depends on effort. Group B knowingly received an additional breathing programme. The large fatigue difference (post-treatment mean difference 9.97 points) may therefore be partly expectation or attention effect. The blood-gas outcomes are less exposed to this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors were blinded, with fatigue collected by an independent blinded assessor.

quotes.text: A prospective, single-blinded, before and post-test, randomized controlled trial was used in the investigation design.

issues.title: Abstract concludes ACBT is 'efficient' and should be incorporated; design is small, unregistered, no safety data
issues.explanation: The abstract calls ACBT an efficient modality to add to conventional protocols. The evidence is 60 patients at one hospital with undescribed randomization, unclear blinding, no registration and no adverse-event reporting. The control arm gave no equivalent extra contact time. The recommendations section itself says more research is needed, which sits uneasily with the confident abstract conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registered protocol, a sample-size calculation, an attention-matched control, and safety data supporting routine use.

quotes.text: which is an efficient modality that may be incorporated into conventional physical therapy protocols.
More research is required to decide how effective it is in cases post-COVID.

issues.title: Group A fatigue decline printed as 34.92% in Results but 35.92% in Abstract and Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results text says Group A's fatigue fell by 34.92%. The Abstract and Table 2 give 35.92%, and Table 2's own mean difference and baseline mean also give 35.92%. This is a one-digit slip in the prose. It does not change the finding that Group B improved more.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different baseline mean or mean difference for Group A that yields 34.92%.

quotes.text: Group A demonstrated a 34.92% decline
(Decrease fatigue 35.92% PaCO2 4.35%)

issues.title: Table 1 sex counts (35 women, 25 men) contradict stated 31 women and 29 men
issues.explanation: The text says 31 women and 29 men. Table 1 shows 18 and 17 women, which sum to 35, and 12 and 13 men, which sum to 25. One of the two descriptions of the sample is wrong. The Table 1 sex comparison between arms is therefore unreliable, but the treatment results do not depend on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the table or the text refers to a different sample.

quotes.text: Sixty patients were selected as convenient studies of both sexes (31 women and 29 men)

issues.title: Table 1 sex-distribution p = 0.19 does not match printed counts (recomputed chi-square p about 0.79)
issues.explanation: Table 1 gives 18/12 versus 17/13 and reports p = 0.19 for the sex comparison. A chi-square test on these counts gives chi2 of about 0.07 and p of about 0.79. The printed p is not reproducible from the printed counts. The conclusion that the groups are balanced on sex is unaffected, but the table has a further inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different sex count or test that yields p = 0.19.

quotes.text: There was no statistically substantial difference between groups concerning the distribution of ages and sex (p > 0.05).

issues.title: Group A SaO2 change printed as 2.75 in Results but 2.7% in Abstract and 2.70 in Table 3
issues.explanation: The Results prose gives 2.75 for Group A's SaO2 increase. The Abstract and Table 3 give 2.7 and 2.70, and the table's own mean difference reproduces 2.70%. The prose value is a transcription slip that nothing else depends on.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Unrounded data giving 2.75% for Group A.

quotes.text: Group A demonstrated a 2.75 increase in SaO2

10.48035/tesis/2454/53703.headline_claim: Six weeks of supervised power-oriented resistance training (PRT) safely improved cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, and mental health in people with post-COVID-19 conditions.
10.48035/tesis/2454/53703.overall: The primary result, a 2.10 mL/kg/min gain in peak VO2 with strength gains, is internally consistent and probably real as a short-term effect, though the 3–5 day washout may have biased it toward the null. The abstract has several reporting errors (the distress P value, two swapped P values, a reversed TMT-A direction, and a blanket 'no period effects' claim), and the mental-health and symptom claims rest on unblinded, uncorrected, per-protocol secondary analyses. The conclusions on safety and one-year persistence go beyond the data.

primary_outcome.name: Change in peak VO2 (ml/kg/min), ITT, crossover treatment effect

issues.title: Seven of 22 symptoms 'reduced' and mental-health claims rest on uncorrected nominal tests, several borderline
issues.explanation: The paper tests 22 symptoms and many secondary outcomes at α=0.05 without correction. Of the seven symptoms called reduced, four have CI upper limits of 0.97–0.99. The conclusion that the programme improves symptoms and mental health relies on these nominal results. The authors accept that multiple analyses limit interpretability, but this is not reflected in the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity adjustment under which these symptoms remain significant.

quotes.text: exercise program reduced seven of the 22 long-COVID symptoms
multiple analyses reduced the interpretability of the secondary outcomes

second_reader.what_stands: The seven 'reduced' symptoms and several mental-health findings (K10, MoCA, TMT-A, symptom CIs ending at 0.97–0.99) rest on uncorrected nominal tests, several of them borderline. Across 22 symptom tests the chance of at least one false positive is about 68%. The authors name multiplicity as a limitation, but the Abstract and conclusions state the effects without that qualification. The depression (CES-D) result is strong and is not undermined by this.

issues.title: 'Safely' and '1-year persistence' conclusions go beyond descriptive AE data and an uncontrolled follow-up
issues.explanation: Adverse events were reported only descriptively. Some participants discontinued because of exercise-related events such as palpitations and pain, and one had angina-type symptoms. The study was not designed to show safety. The claim that benefits persisted for one year rests on an uncontrolled extended follow-up. These stronger statements are not supported by the design, although the short-term fitness and strength results are.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified comparative safety analysis showing no excess adverse events, and a controlled 1-year follow-up.

quotes.text: A supervised 6-week PRT intervention program safely improved
This demonstrates safety and efficacy
Adverse events were reported descriptively.

second_reader.what_stands: 'Safely' and 'demonstrates safety' rest on descriptive, spontaneously collected adverse-event counts with no comparator and no formal safety estimate. Some exercise-related events and discontinuations did occur. The claim that benefits persist for 1 year rests on an uncontrolled, post hoc follow-up where everyone had received the intervention, and the EQ-5D did not mirror it. The one place the paper labels this 'exploratory' is not carried into the concluding paragraph.

issues.title: 3–5 day washout; absence of carry-over inferred from an underpowered non-significant test
issues.explanation: Participants had only 3–5 days between 6-week exercise and usual-care periods. The authors accept in the limitations that this may not remove exercise effects, but they still say the crossover contrasts are clean. Their only evidence is a non-significant carry-over test with very wide CIs. The AB group retained gains in the usual-care period and many outcomes show significant period effects, so the crossover estimates are less certain than presented. Residual carry-over would bias toward the null for the primary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence margin for carry-over with adequate power, or first-period-only analyses giving the same effects.

quotes.text: The 3–5-day washout may have been insufficient to eliminate the exercise effects.
indicated no carry-over effects, confirming sufficient “wash-out” (3-5 days)

second_reader.what_stands: The absence of carry-over is inferred from a non-significant between-group sum test whose CI is very wide (about -6 to +4 mL/kg/min). That interval is compatible with carry-over comparable to the treatment effect, and Group 1 stays above baseline after the usual-care period. The authors do acknowledge the washout may have been insufficient, but the Methods' 'confirming sufficient wash-out' and the Abstract's 'no carry-over' overstate what a non-significant test can show.

issues.title: Abstract gives P<0.001 for psychological distress; K10 effect -2.28 has P=0.028 in text and Table 2.2
issues.explanation: The abstract says psychological distress fell significantly with P<0.001. The Results and Table 2.2 report the same effect (-2.28, 95% CI -4.30 to -0.25) with P=0.028, and that P fits the CI. The abstract therefore overstates the strength of evidence for a mental-health result that is part of the headline conclusion. The effect is still nominally significant.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different, stronger analysis of K10 (for example a mixed model) that the abstract reports and that is not the one in Table 2.2.

quotes.text: Signiﬁcant decreases were found in psychological distress scores (P<0.001).
Psychological distress score by −2.28 [95% CI −4.30 to −0.25], P = 0.028.
quotes.location: Results, Crossover Analysis for the Secondary Endpoints

issues.title: Unblinded exercise vs usual care weakens the self-reported mental-health and symptom results
issues.explanation: Participants knew when they were exercising and most secondary outcomes are patient-reported, so expectation effects could explain part of the differences. The primary fitness outcome and the strength outcomes are objective and are much less affected. The limitation is acknowledged but the conclusion on mental health is stated without hedging. This weakens the secondary results rather than the primary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched or sham control, or objective measures of the mental-health outcomes showing similar effects.

quotes.text: First, blinding of participants was not possible, which may have introduced placebo effects that partially explain the benefits.
Owing to the nature of the study, patients cannot be blinded to the exercise training modality.
quotes.location: Material and methods, Randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding

issues.title: Secondary outcomes analysed per-protocol only; missing-data method described as both BOCF and multiple imputation
issues.explanation: Table 2.2 labels all secondary outcomes as per-protocol, with 42–47 participants per cell. The Methods say the study followed ITT with baseline observation carried forward, and later say multiple imputation was used for peak VO2. The secondary results that support the mental-health and strength claims therefore come from completers who adhered to at least 80% of sessions, and the imputation approach is unclear. Attrition itself (11%) is modest.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: ITT analyses of the secondary outcomes with a clearly stated imputation method giving similar estimates.

quotes.text: Secondary outcomes (PP)
The study followed an intention-to-treat principle with the use of baseline observation carried forward imputation

issues.title: P values for VAS quality of life (0.041 vs 0.005) and ALM/height² (0.005 vs 0.041) are swapped in text/abstract
issues.explanation: The Results text and abstract give P=0.041 for the VAS effect and P=0.005 for ALM/height². Table 2.2 gives the opposite, P=0.005 for VAS and P=0.041 for ALM/height², and the table values match the printed CIs. So the abstract understates the evidence for VAS quality of life and the text overstates it for lean mass. No main conclusion changes, but two reported results are wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the text P values come from different analyses of these outcomes than Table 2.2.

quotes.text: Quality of life increased in VAS scores by 4.65 points [95% CI 1.45 to 7.85], P = 0.041.
quotes.location: Results, Crossover Analysis for the Secondary Endpoints

quotes.text: ALM/height2 changed by 0.06 kg/m2 [95% CI 0.00 to 0.12], P = 0.005.
quotes.location: Results, Crossover Analysis for the Secondary Endpoints

script.explanation: the p-value recovered from the CI is 0.0044 (reachable range [0.0043, 0.0045] across the printed precision of the estimate and its bounds), but p = 0.041 is reported -- this recovery inverts a WALD interval, so if the paper used a bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood or Fieller interval the two numbers are not comparable; confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: TMT-A effect of +1.60 s (higher = worse) reported as improved cognitive performance
issues.explanation: The authors define higher TMT-A times as greater impairment. The treatment effect is +1.60 s with P=0.036, and the period means show longer times after exercise than after usual care. The abstract and Results nonetheless say the intervention improved cognitive performance. The direction is reversed. This is a secondary outcome, but it is listed in the abstract as a benefit.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that Table 2.2 reports usual care minus exercise for this row, so that +1.60 means a shorter time with exercise.

quotes.text: cognitive performance by 1.60 points [95% CI 0.11 to 3.09], P = 0.036 more than usual care.
quotes.location: Results, Crossover Analysis for the Secondary Endpoints

quotes.text: higher scores indicate greater impairment

issues.title: Abstract says no period effects detected, but Table 2.2 shows significant period effects for several outcomes
issues.explanation: The abstract states that no carry-over or period effects were detected. Table 2.2 lists period-effect P values below 0.0001 for pectoral press, leg press and knee extension, and 0.002 for back press, which are the strength outcomes the abstract highlights. A significant period effect means the outcome changed between periods regardless of treatment, which complicates the simple crossover contrast. The statement holds for the primary outcome only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the abstract sentence is limited to the primary outcome.

quotes.text: No carry-over or period eﬀects were detected.

issues.title: Table 2.2 carry-over CIs misprinted: depression 2.15 (-1.03 to -5.33), ALM/height² 0.52 (-1.77 to -0.74)
issues.explanation: Two carry-over cells in Table 2.2 have CIs that cannot contain their point estimates. For depression the CI is reversed (-1.03 to -5.33), and the midpoint and P show it should be -1.03 to 5.33. For ALM/height² the CI -1.77 to -0.74 excludes 0.52 and is incompatible with the printed P=0.414. The carry-over conclusions are not changed, but the carry-over table cells are unreliable as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source table showing the corrected CIs and a text-extraction cause for the signs.

issues.title: Abstract study period starts March 1, 2021; Results say recruitment began May 1, 2021
issues.explanation: The abstract gives March 1, 2021 as the start of the study, but the Results say recruitment and data collection began on May 1, 2021. This is possibly a difference between study start and first enrolment, but the paper does not say so. It is a minor reporting inconsistency.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that March 1 marked project start and May 1 marked first participant enrolment.

quotes.text: from March 1, 2021, to September 30, 2022
Recruitment and data collection took place from May 1, 2021, to September 30, 2022.

10.48047/13z65272.headline_claim: PARAM, a VR and pain-neuroscience-education exposure intervention, is a feasible and clinically relevant digital therapeutic for chronic musculoskeletal pain in Long COVID, with improvements in FABQ, PCS and PSEQ scores.
10.48047/13z65272.overall: The headline conclusion that PARAM is effective is not supported: the trial is described in a few sentences, with no allocation method, arm sizes, baselines or between-group test, only within-arm percentage changes. The paper is mainly a conceptual description of the intervention, and the 'revolutionize' and cost-effectiveness statements go well beyond its data. At best the data suggest a hypothesis for a properly controlled trial.

primary_outcome.name: unclear

issues.title: Non-randomized comparison with standard physiotherapy, no allocation method, baselines or between-group test
issues.explanation: The comparison of PARAM with standard physiotherapy rests on a quasi-experimental design with no description of how participants were assigned, how many were in each arm, or whether the groups were comparable at baseline. The 48% vs 16% FABQ reductions are within-arm percentage changes with no between-group estimate, CI or p-value. Without these, confounding by selection and regression to the mean cannot be excluded, and the effectiveness conclusion is not supported by this design as reported. The paper also describes itself as a review of the intervention framework, so the trial is reported only as a brief summary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A full trial report giving the allocation procedure, arm sizes, baseline comparability, and an adjusted between-group estimate with CI showing a difference favouring PARAM.

quotes.text: The  mean  fear-avoidance  beliefs  questionnaire  (FABQ)  scores  reduced  by  48%  in  the PARAM group in contrast to just 16% in the standard physiotherapy group (SP).
The improvements in outcome measures suggest that the intervention was effective in changing maladaptive pain beliefs and restoring functional confidence among the study participants.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper describes the study as quasi-experimental and gives no allocation method, no baseline values, no group sizes and no between-group test. It nonetheless states that the intervention 'was effective in changing maladaptive pain beliefs', which rests on unadjusted percent changes alone. The PCS and PSEQ improvements are given without any comparator. What is not established is whether the original trial report contains these details; this text does not.

issues.title: Effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and 'revolutionize' claims exceed a feasibility-level, non-randomized pilot
issues.explanation: The text claims PARAM is effective, scalable and cost-effective and may revolutionize pain management, yet no cost data, recruitment/retention/adherence figures, safety data or between-group analyses are reported. Feasibility is asserted without any feasibility metrics. The claims go well beyond what a 70-person, non-randomized, unreported-methods study can show, and the paper itself says long-term efficacy and safety remain to be established.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported feasibility metrics, cost analysis and a controlled between-group effect estimate supporting these claims.

quotes.text: As such, PARAM may represent  a  new  frontier  in  the  treatment  of  chronic  pain  and  has  the  potential  to revolutionize the way we approach pain management in the future.
PARAM could serve as a cost-effective and efficient modality to address both the physiological and psychological components of chronic pain.

second_reader.what_stands: The claims that PARAM is 'cost-effective' and could 'revolutionize' pain management go beyond a small non-randomized pilot with no cost data and no between-group testing. The wording is hedged ('could', 'may', 'has the potential') and the Conclusion does call for more research on long-term efficacy and safety, so the overreach is in the strength of the framing rather than in flat assertions of proven benefit.

issues.title: No trial registration or protocol reported for the 70-participant quasi-experimental study
issues.explanation: The paper reports no registry number, protocol, ethics approval or prespecified primary outcome for the trial. Reported outcomes (FABQ, PCS, PSEQ) therefore cannot be checked against a plan, and selective reporting cannot be ruled out. This is a modest concern given the study's pilot status.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or protocol with prespecified outcomes predating enrolment.

quotes.text: PARAM was used in a quasi-experimental trial involving 70 silk weavers with Long  COVID -related

10.5114/ada.2024.144522.headline_claim: Blue light therapy reduces fatigue and improves quality of life in COVID-19 survivors and may be used as adjunctive treatment of fatigue in long COVID.
10.5114/ada.2024.144522.overall: The within-patient improvements in FSS, SF-36 and DLQI are large and statistically clear, but the single-arm, unblinded design with subjective outcomes cannot show that blue light caused them, so the efficacy claim in the title and discussion is overstated. The metabolite and serotonin mechanism statements rest on uncorrected tests in 20 patients and are tentative. The numeric slips (SF-36 direction wording, small delta mismatches) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS)

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from uncontrolled single-arm pre-post study of 43 patients with subjective outcomes
issues.explanation: All 43 participants received the same blue light and were compared only with their own baseline, with self-reported outcomes and no blinding or control. Improvement in post-COVID fatigue over weeks can occur spontaneously, and expectation effects are likely. The title and discussion nonetheless describe the therapy as improving and successfully treating fatigue, which this design cannot support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or placebo arm showing the same improvement difference.

quotes.text: All participants underwent 10 full-body blue light irradiation using Phlecs Full Body Blue 1.0
this is the first report describing successful use of blue light therapy in treatment of fatigue in long COVID patients
another study with a placebo group is needed to establish a possible causal explanation for these phenomena

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is an uncontrolled single-arm pre-post study of 43 patients whose primary outcomes (FSS, SF-36 Vitality, DLQI) are subjective, and the Discussion's wording 'first report describing successful use' goes beyond what this design can show. However, the authors do acknowledge the lack of a placebo group as a limitation, say the findings should be taken with caution, and frame the conclusion as 'could be used as adjunctive treatment' and 'requires further investigation', so the efficacy claim is tempered rather than unqualified.

issues.title: Unadjusted tests on metabolites and 28 correlations; tryptophan, kynurenine and DLQI-KA findings fragile
issues.explanation: The paper tests several outcomes, five serum metabolites and a correlation matrix at an unadjusted 0.05 level. Tryptophan (p=0.0251) and kynurenine (p=0.0152) would not survive a five-test correction, and the single significant correlation (rho 0.463, n=20) is one of about 28 pairs. The clinical scale results are robust, and the serotonin finding is hedged, so the effect is on the secondary mechanistic claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction showing these results remain significant.

quotes.text: A pvalue below 0.05 was deemed significant.
A statistically significant moderate correlation was found between the kynurenic acid serum concentration and DLQI
Taken together, our results suggest that blue light therapy may increase serotoninergic transduction

issues.title: No adverse events or dropout reported; analysed n per outcome not stated for 43 enrolled
issues.explanation: The paper does not state how many of the 43 participants completed the regimen or were analysed for each scale, nor whether any adverse events occurred. Combined with the small mismatches between delta and mean differences, the analysed denominators are unclear. Safety statements rely on the literature rather than this cohort.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow count and adverse-event statement for the 43 participants.

quotes.text: The study comprised of 43 adults, 7 males (mean age: 45.00 ±11.10), 36 females (mean age: 38.00 ±12.82)
blue light therapy has minimal side effects compared to antidepressant medications

issues.title: Discussion says SF-36 decreased; Results and Table 1 show it rose from 57.10 to 76.07
issues.explanation: The Discussion states that both FSS and SF-36 decreased significantly. Results and Table 1 show SF-36 vitality increased (higher is better), while only FSS decreased. This is a wording error in one sentence; the data and the direction of benefit are clear elsewhere.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper defining SF-36 scoring as reversed, which is not present.

quotes.text: In our study a significant decrease was observed in both FSS and SF-36 scales

issues.title: SF-36 and DLQI mean changes differ from after-minus-baseline (18.74 vs 18.97; -3.85 vs -3.67)
issues.explanation: Table 1 prints a mean SF-36 change of 18.74 while the printed means differ by 18.97, and a DLQI change of -3.85 versus -3.67 from the means. Small gaps like these arise when some participants have missing data at one time point, but the paper gives no per-scale n. The discrepancies are small and do not change the direction or significance.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported n per scale showing complete pairs for all 43 participants, which would make the mismatch unexplained.

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective interventional study
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval and consent but no registry or protocol identifier. Outcomes (FSS, SF-36, DLQI, metabolites) cannot be checked against a pre-specified plan. Impact is limited because the design is already exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before enrolment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: The approval of the Bioethical Commission (No. RNN/312/20/KE) was obtained before conducting the study.

issues.title: Device manufacturer's co-operation is stated but its role and any interests are not described
issues.explanation: The conflict section names the manufacturer of the tested device as a co-operating party without saying what it provided or whether it had any role in design, analysis or reporting. The paper has no explicit statement of whether authors have interests in the product. This leaves a possible commercial influence unassessable, though nothing shows it affected results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the manufacturer supplied only equipment with no role in design, analysis or reporting and that authors have no interests.

quotes.text: The research was conducted with co-operation with Phlecs (Eindhoven, Netherlands).
The paper is funded by research grant of Medical University of Lodz

10.5114/areh.2022.119900.headline_claim: Low-level laser photobiomodulation appears to increase functional performance, ADL activities and fatigue perception in elderly people after COVID-19, with greater improvement than placebo.
10.5114/areh.2022.119900.overall: The fatigue (FSS) between-group difference is nominally supported, but the functional (KATZ) claim is not, since the between-group result is p = 0.071 and placebo also improved. The cited registration belongs to a different trial, and Table 1 BMI values contradict the stated inclusion range, so the population and pre-specification cannot be verified. The headline conclusion should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) and Katz ADL index (no primary outcome designated)

primary_outcomes.measure: Effect of the upper body ergometer on arthrogenic index ( triglyceride/ high density lipoprotein)
primary_outcomes.time_frame: after one month of the trial application

issues.title: Cited registration NCT04676074 describes an unrelated ergometer trial (n=40, AIP outcome), not this PBM trial (n=100)
issues.explanation: The paper cites NCT04676074 as its registration, but the registry record is for an upper-limb ergometer trial in post-menopausal obese women with arthrogenic index as primary outcome and 40 participants. This paper tests photobiomodulation on FSS and Katz in 100 older post-COVID adults. The trial therefore has no verifiable prospective registration or pre-specified primary outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correct registry ID for this PBM trial with pre-specified FSS/KATZ outcomes registered before enrolment.

quotes.text: it was listed on clinicaltrials.gov with the number NCT04676074

second_reader.what_stands: The registry number cited in the paper points to an ergometer trial (n=40, atherogenic-index outcome), not to this PBM trial (n=100, FSS/KATZ outcomes), so the paper's registration claim is not supported by the cited record. I cannot say whether a separate correct registration exists, or why the number differs.

issues.title: Functional (KATZ) benefit rests on within-arm change; between-group post-treatment KATZ p = 0.071
issues.explanation: For fatigue the between-group post-treatment comparison is significant (p < 0.05), so that part is supported on its face, though only post scores, not change from baseline, were compared. For function, the KATZ between-group comparison is p = 0.071 and placebo also improved significantly, so a treatment-specific functional effect is not shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group analysis of KATZ change scores (or ANCOVA adjusted for baseline) showing a significant difference.

quotes.location: Table 4, KATZ score, between groups post-treatment

quotes.text: between pre- and post-intervention FSS and KATZ scores in the PBM group

second_reader.what_stands: The between-group post-treatment KATZ comparison is not significant at the stated alpha (p = 0.071), and the significant within-group KATZ improvement occurred in both PBM and placebo arms, so it does not show a PBM-specific functional benefit. The Discussion and Conclusion nonetheless state a greater functional improvement with PBM. The conclusion on function is therefore stronger than the between-group result supports. The FSS between-group difference (p < 0.05) is a separate matter and was not affected by this check.

issues.title: Table 1 mean BMI 27.27 and 27.44 is impossible for an inclusion range of BMI 30-35 kg/m2
issues.explanation: The Methods say participants' BMI was 30 to 35 kg/m2, so any group mean must lie within 30-35. Table 1 reports group means of 27.27 and 27.44, below the lower bound. Either the eligibility criterion or the table is wrong, so the described population is unclear; the efficacy results are not directly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction or erratum showing the inclusion range was different (e.g. BMI 25-35) or that Table 1 reports a different quantity.

quotes.text: their BMI was 30 to 35 kg/m2

issues.title: No sample size justification, no designated primary outcome, FSS/KATZ analysed as unadjusted post scores
issues.explanation: The paper reports no sample size calculation and designates no primary outcome among FSS and KATZ. Between-group tests compare post scores only, without adjusting for baseline, and the paper reports no flow numbers for analysis or adverse events. This weakens confidence in the secondary and the main results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome and sample size calculation in the trial protocol or correct registration.

quotes.text: P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

issues.title: Results text states no age/BMI difference 'p < 0.05' whereas Table 1 gives p = 0.807 and 0.506
issues.explanation: The text says no significant difference was noted, but attaches p < 0.05, which would mean the opposite. Table 1 gives p = 0.807 and 0.506, so this is a wrong inequality sign in the text. It misleads no one who reads the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: n/a: the table values are clearly non-significant.

quotes.text: between the two groups (p < 0.05), as shown in Table 1

10.5114/biolsport.2024.139072.headline_claim: An ambulatory cardiopulmonary rehabilitation programme improves submaximal exercise capacity (6MWD), dyspnoea and resting heart rate in Tunisian patients with long COVID-19, with the 6MWD and mMRC changes exceeding MCIDs.
10.5114/biolsport.2024.139072.overall: The direction of the main finding, more improvement in 6MWD with rehabilitation than with sedentary control, is plausible and large, but it rests on 30 completers from 36 in an unblinded design with a no-activity comparator and no ITT analysis. Several reporting slips (Borg values below the scale minimum, 13/20 printed as 75%, conflicting Δ sign definitions, conflicting 6MWW statements) and a sample-size calculation that does not reproduce from its inputs lower confidence in the reporting. The conclusions are best read as tentative evidence of benefit, not a firm demonstration of efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), change from pre to post CPRP (m)

issues.title: Completers-only analysis: 30 of 36 randomised analysed, with no ITT and no arm-level attrition
issues.explanation: Patients who missed any session or the final evaluation were excluded from analysis, so the efficacy results come from 30 of the 36 who agreed to take part. The paper does not say how many of the 6 exclusions came from each arm, nor how many were randomised to each. No intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is given. For an intervention requiring 18 supervised sessions, completers can differ systematically from dropouts, so the 168 m effect may be overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing dropouts split by arm and an ITT or imputed analysis giving similar results.

quotes.text: Files of patients who missed any session of the CPRP or did not attend the final evaluation were excluded from the final statistical analysis.
However, only 30 (20 in the IG, 10 in the CG) completed the protocol.

second_reader.what_stands: The analysis is explicitly completers-only: 30 of 36 who agreed were analysed, with no ITT or sensitivity analysis and no handling of missing outcomes. The claim of 'no arm-level attrition' is only partly supported: the text gives no per-arm number randomised or lost (Figure 1 may), so differential dropout cannot be assessed from the text.

issues.title: Patient-rated dyspnoea and effort-dependent walk test in an intervention-vs-no-activity design with unblinded patients
issues.explanation: Patients could not be blinded, and the comparator was only an instruction to stay sedentary, with no attention-control. Borg and mMRC are self-rated, and the 6MWD depends on patient effort, so expectation can inflate improvements. The paper also asserts that patients did not know their group, which is hard to reconcile with attending the programme. The conclusions nevertheless cite the Borg and mMRC reductions as evidence of efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of an attention-control comparator or objective outcomes that agree with the patient-reported ones.

quotes.text: Meanwhile, although blinding for patients could not be achieved, patients were unaware of the other treatment modalities.
participants in the IG experienced significantly greater decreases in Borg and mMRC scales

second_reader.what_stands: Patients knew, or could easily infer, their allocation, and the main outcome (6MWD) and the dyspnoea scores depend on effort or self-report. The paper admits patient blinding was not achieved but still labels the trial single-blinded, does not list this as a limitation, and states the dyspnoea conclusions without qualification. Blinded assessors reduce, but do not remove, this risk. Whether the assessors stayed truly unaware of allocation cannot be verified.

issues.title: Borg means of 5.2 (pre) and 1.8/3.8 (post) fall below the stated 6-20 scale minimum of 6
issues.explanation: The Methods say the Borg scale runs from 6 to 20, so no group mean can be below 6. Table 2 reports a pre-CPRP IG mean of 5.2, a post-CPRP IG mean of 1.8 and a post-CPRP CG mean of 3.8. Either the wrong scale is described or the data were recorded on a different (0-10) scale. The Borg change of -3.5 vs -1.3, quoted in the abstract and conclusions, cannot be interpreted until this is resolved.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 0-10 category-ratio Borg scale was actually used, or raw data showing scores of 6 or higher.

quotes.text: The Borg scale was used to rate dyspnoea from 6 (i.e. no exertion at all) to 20 (i.e. maximal exertion)

quotes.location: Table 2, Borg scale row, IG Pre

issues.title: Effects labelled 'small' although reported effect sizes and their own scale indicate large ones
issues.explanation: The abstract and text describe the 6MWD and heart-rate effects as having 'small effect sizes'. The paper's own scale calls anything above 1.30 'very large', and the 6MWD change difference gives a standardised difference of about 1.9. The reported partial eta-squared values (0.104 for 6MWD in metres, 0.157 for % predicted) are medium to large by usual benchmarks. The label therefore misdescribes the results, and it understates the observed effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition under which 'small' refers to a different quantity, such as the ANOVA interaction after adjustment, with the calculation shown.

quotes.text: albeit with small effect sizes
An effect size of ≤ 0.2 was described as a small effect, around 0.5 as a medium effect, around 0.8 as a large effect, and more than 1.30 as very large effect

issues.title: IG post-CPRP 6MWD below LLN: 13 of 20 is 65%, but 75% printed in Table 4, Results and Discussion
issues.explanation: Table 4 gives 13 (75) for IG patients with an abnormal 6MWD after the programme, but 13 of 20 is 65%. The Δ of -7 from 20 patients agrees with a count of 13. The 75% is repeated in the Results and the Discussion. The correct decrease is from 100% to 65%, so the paper understates the improvement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 15 patients, not 13, were below LLN, together with a corrected Δ.

quotes.text: it decreased from 100% (pre-CPRP) to 75% (post-CPRP) in the IG (Table 4)

script.explanation: 13/20 = 65.00%, but the paper prints 75, outside the rounding interval [74.50, 76.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 17.3 rather than 20.

issues.title: Text calls 6MWW changes comparable; Table 4 gives Δ vs Δ p = 0.001 but ANOVA p = 0.078
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the groups had comparable 6MWW changes. Table 4 shows a large IG change (14153) against a CG change of -379, with p = 0.001 for the Δ vs Δ comparison. The ANOVA interaction for the same row is p = 0.078. The ANOVA interaction p-values are also far larger than the Δ vs Δ p-values for 6MWD (0.013 vs 0.001) and resting HR (0.014 vs 0.007). This suggests the ANOVA was not a repeated-measures model, which the paper does not describe.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods description showing the ANOVA is the pre-specified test of between-group change, and a statement that the Δ vs Δ t-tests are exploratory.

quotes.text: The two groups in our RCT showed comparable changes in 6MWW

issues.title: Sample size of 28 does not reproduce from the stated formula with r = 0.5 (about 41 expected)
issues.explanation: The authors give N = (r+1)(Zα/2+Z1-β)²δ²/(r d²) with r = 0.5, 90% power and inputs of 80 ± 126 vs 0.05 ± 26 m. With a pooled SD of about 91, this gives about 41 total patients. The reported 28 is what the same formula gives for equal allocation (r = 1), yet the trial used a 2:1 split. The study may therefore have had less power than stated, though the large observed effect partly offsets this. The result depends on how δ was pooled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A worked calculation showing 28 follows from the stated formula and inputs with r = 0.5, for example with a different definition of δ.

quotes.text: r = 0.5 gives a sample size distribution of 0.5:1 for the CG and IG
Insertion of the aforementioned data into the formula resulted in a total sample of 28 patients (19 in the IG and 9 in the CG).

issues.title: Allocation concealment only partly described; the randomising PI also took part in recruitment
issues.explanation: The allocation sequence was generated with free software and run by the principal investigator after consent, and the enrolling evaluator is said to have had no access. However, the recruitment phase names RK, the investigator who ran the sequence, and AK as the investigators who explained the protocol. The paper does not say how allocation was communicated or whether it could be foreseen. The risk is real but unproven.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of how allocation was concealed, such as sealed envelopes or central allocation.

quotes.text: The evaluator who enrolled and assessed patients ( EZ in the authors' list) had no access to the randomization sequence.
the investigators (RK and AK in the authors' list) explained the protocol's content

issues.title: Methods define ΔCPRP as pre minus post; tables and results use post minus pre
issues.explanation: The Methods define the change as pre minus post-CPRP, but the table footnotes define it as post minus pre. All printed values follow the footnote. The Methods wording is therefore a definitional error, and it would reverse every sign if applied literally. A reader can still recover the right interpretation from the tables.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this is a stated-definition inconsistency, partly mitigated by the explicit footnotes.

quotes.text: Δ CPRP = preminus post-CPRP
Δ : Post minus Pre.

10.5114/reum/172575.headline_claim: Adding L-arginine, L-carnitine and quercetin to the standard therapeutic complex for post-COVID musculoskeletal lesions gives better and faster pain relief, tolerance and remission than the comparison group, and is advisable in rehabilitation.
10.5114/reum/172575.overall: The descriptive findings on post-COVID musculoskeletal symptoms are plausible, but the treatment recommendation rests on a self-selected, non-randomised comparison with no baseline data and unexplained significance marking. The causal and 'autoimmune' conclusions are not supported by the data reported, so the headline conclusions should be treated as tentative at best.

primary_outcome.name: Time to reduce joint ache by half (with related effectiveness criteria)

issues.title: Self-selected comparison group (102 supplemented vs 40 who declined) with no baseline data or adjustment
issues.explanation: Patients chose whether to take the supplements, and no baseline table by group, randomisation, blinding or adjustment is given. Differences in time to pain reduction and NSAID use may reflect who chose treatment (motivation, severity, adherence) rather than the supplements. The recommendation to add the supplements rests wholly on this comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline characteristics and severity by group showing balance, or an adjusted analysis giving a similar effect.

quotes.text: Other patients (40  individuals),  who  did  not want to take them, were in the comparison group.
Both groups of patients were representative in the age and gender aspects.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by patient preference (102 took the supplements, 40 declined), and the paper presents no baseline comparison between the groups beyond the unsupported statement of age and sex representativeness. No adjustment for confounding is described; only unadjusted t-tests are used. Baseline VAS, joint counts, inflammatory markers and comorbidity are not compared between groups, so the differences in Table IV may reflect who chose treatment.

issues.title: Recommendation to add L-arginine, L-carnitine and quercetin stated without noting design limits
issues.explanation: The Conclusions advise including the three supplements in rehabilitation, but the Discussion never mentions the self-selected control, lack of randomisation or blinding, or that only a fraction of patients (52, 64, 26) were followed at each check-up time. The recommendation is stronger than this design supports. This is separate from c3 in that it concerns how the conclusion is worded rather than the comparison itself.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A limitations discussion in the paper, or randomised evidence in the same population.

quotes.text: it is advisable to include pharmacological agents with multiple action into the rehabilitation complex, in particular, L-arginine, L-carnitine and quercetin.

second_reader.what_stands: The recommendation to add L-arginine, L-carnitine and quercetin is given in the Conclusions without any mention of the non-randomised, self-selected, unblinded, placebo-free design or the small comparison group. The only hedge is a generic statement that further investigation is needed. The wording 'advisable' is moderate, but the design limits that bear on it are not weighed.

issues.title: Causal claim of long-term inflammatory, metabolic and autoimmune response not supported by uncontrolled data
issues.explanation: The first conclusion attributes a long-term inflammatory, metabolic and autoimmune response to acute COVID-19. The data are a single-arm case series with an unexplained laboratory control, CRP/ESR only, and no reported autoimmune or metabolic results. Causation and the 'autoimmune' and 'metabolic' components are not supported by what is shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An uninfected comparison cohort and reported autoimmune/metabolic results.

quotes.text: contributes to the occurrence of a long-term unfavorable inflammatory,

second_reader.what_stands: The causal claim of a long-term inflammatory, metabolic and autoimmune response is not supported by the data presented. Only early (4-6 weeks) inflammatory markers against a reference value are reported, with no uninfected control, no metabolic data and no autoimmune results, and the design is uncontrolled for this question. The raised early markers in Table III do support a narrower statement of short-term inflammation.

issues.title: Table IV significance symbols unexplained, no p-values; multiple outcomes tested at uncorrected 0.05
issues.explanation: Table IV reports six effectiveness criteria in two age strata against one comparison group, flagged only with * and # without a legend or exact p-values. No multiplicity correction is described and 'reliably better' is claimed. The differences are large relative to the reported errors (e.g., 10.2 vs 19.2 days), so multiplicity alone probably does not change the direction, but the relapse comparison (2/65 vs 4/40) is likely not significant and is not tested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A legend defining the symbols with exact p-values and a stated correction.

quotes.text: The statistical significance level was set at p < 0.05.
which  was  reliably  better  concerning  the  group of comparison (Table IV).

issues.title: Text gives top VAS as 54.4 ±3.12 cm; Table I gives 54.8 ±3.12 mm; units also conflict
issues.explanation: The Results text quotes the highest pain score as 54.4 ±3.12 cm, but Table I shows 54.8 ±3.12 for the same cell, labelled in mm. The digits disagree, and the text's 'cm' is implausible for a VAS (54 cm would exceed any VAS length). One reporting error affecting a descriptive value; the main claims are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected version or source data showing the two values refer to different cells or subgroups.

quotes.text: The VAS score ranges from 39.2 ±1.68 cm to 54.4 ±3.12 cm with arthritis available.

quotes.location: Table I, VAS row, older than 50 males

issues.title: Text's 3-5-fold CRP rise exceeds Table III mean ratios of 1.9 and 2.5 versus control
issues.explanation: The Results state a 3-5-fold CRP increase, but the group means in Table III are 9.1 and 12.2 mg/l against a control of 4.9 mg/l. This is about 1.9- and 2.5-fold. The text may refer to individual ranges or a different reference value, which the paper does not say, so the fold change as written overstates the tabulated difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Statement that the fold change refers to individual patient ranges or a different reference limit.

quotes.text: a 3-5-fold increase of C-reactive protein levels

10.51737/2766-5003.2021.021.headline_claim: Oral L-arginine supplementation could improve quality of life and exercise tolerance in patients with long COVID symptoms.
10.51737/2766-5003.2021.021.overall: The paper reports large before-after gains in exercise measures in 10 uncontrolled patients; these cannot be attributed to L-arginine. The quality-of-life and safety statements in the Discussion and Conclusions have no reported data behind them, so only a hypothesis-generating reading is supported.

primary_outcome.name: Exercise capacity (time to exhaustion, min) on graded maximal exertion test

issues.title: Uncontrolled 10-patient before-after series used to infer L-arginine benefit in long COVID
issues.explanation: All 10 patients received L-arginine and were compared only with their own baseline about one month later. Natural recovery (mean acute illness 45 days, symptoms of fatigue), regression to the mean, practice effects on repeat exercise testing and expectation effects cannot be separated from a drug effect. With no control group, no blinding and no sample-size justification, the conclusion that supplementation improves quality of life is not supported as a causal statement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untreated or placebo control group showing no comparable improvement over the same interval.

quotes.text: were enrolled in a short-term observational follow-up
Treatment with LArginine 20 mL (Bioarginina® Farmaceutici Damor SpA) of an 8,3% oral solution (1,66 gr) twice day was initiated in all patients.
Our results suggest that oral L-arginine supplementation could improve the quality of life of patients with long COVID symptoms.
