second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports a single-arm, uncontrolled series of 10 patients with only baseline and 1-month measurements, and draws a benefit conclusion for L-arginine from the before-after change. Without a control group, spontaneous recovery, learning effects on the exercise test and placebo effects cannot be separated from a treatment effect, and the paper does not acknowledge this.

issues.title: Quality-of-life improvement claimed in conclusion but no quality-of-life measure is reported
issues.explanation: The Results assert an improvement in quality of life and NYHA class, and the Conclusions state that L-arginine could improve quality of life, but no questionnaire, score or data for quality of life are given. The reported objective results concern exercise capacity, which is not the same construct. The headline quality-of-life conclusion therefore has no documented outcome behind it. Also, the Statistical Analysis refers to PCS, mMRC and comorbidity mediation analyses that are not reported anywhere.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported scores from a validated quality-of-life instrument at baseline and follow-up.

quotes.text: The positive effects of L-arginine were also associated with an improvement in NYHA functional class and quality of life
Our results suggest that oral L-arginine supplementation could improve the quality of life of patients with long COVID symptoms.

second_reader.what_stands: No quality-of-life instrument or score is defined or reported; the Results state a QoL improvement and the Conclusions build on it, but the only data are exercise-test results, NYHA class and six-minute walk distance. The QoL claim could at most be inferred indirectly from functional measures, and the PCS and mMRC mentioned in the statistics section are never presented.

issues.title: Safety ('no side effects', no contraindications) and endothelial-mechanism claims unsupported by reported data
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the treatment worked 'without any side effects' and has 'the absence of contraindications', yet the Methods and Results describe no adverse-event assessment, and with 10 patients rare events could not be excluded. The Conclusions also elevate endothelial dysfunction as a priority therapeutic target although no endothelial function measure (e.g., flow-mediated dilation) was taken. These statements go beyond what the reported data can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described systematic adverse-event assessment and an endothelial function measurement in these patients.

quotes.text: in a short time and without any side effects. It is also a natural therapy characterized by low cost, easy availability and the absence of contraindications.
endothelial dysfunction should become one of the priority targets of future COVID therapies

issues.title: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement despite a named commercial product
issues.explanation: The treatment is identified by brand and manufacturer, yet the paper has no funding or competing-interest statement, so the manufacturer's role cannot be judged. Nothing in the paper indicates sponsor involvement, so this is a disclosure gap only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A funding and conflict-of-interest statement showing no sponsor involvement.

quotes.text: Treatment with LArginine 20 mL (Bioarginina® Farmaceutici Damor SpA)

10.51793/os.2022.25.2.005.headline_claim: Adding the combined probiotic Bifiform to standard treatment for post-COVID-19 post-infectious IBS produced more pronounced clinical relief and better quality of life than standard treatment alone.
10.51793/os.2022.25.2.005.overall: The direction of the main finding (higher symptom-based efficacy with the probiotic) may be real, but the paper does not show how patients were allocated, uses unblinded subjective outcomes, and prints a chi-square and several percentages that do not match its own counts. The questionnaire superiority claim rests on within-group tests only. The conclusion is worded cautiously, so it should be read as a tentative, hypothesis-generating result.

primary_outcome.name: Overall treatment efficacy (clinical response category)

issues.title: Allocation to probiotic vs control arms not described; no baseline table; causal conclusion drawn
issues.explanation: The paper says only that patients were 'divided into 2 groups', with no randomisation method, concealment or allocation rule. It gives no baseline comparison of age, sex, disease duration or IBS subtype between arms. Differences in outcome could therefore reflect who was chosen for which arm rather than the probiotic. The authors nonetheless conclude the probiotic leads to more pronounced regression of symptoms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registration or protocol describing concealed random allocation and a baseline characteristics table by arm showing balance.

quotes.text: Пациенты были разделены на 2 группы.
Группу контроля составили 35 пациентов, в лечение которых не включался пробиотик.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does not describe how patients were allocated to the probiotic or control group, and it gives no baseline characteristics by arm; only pre-treatment IBS-SSS and IBS-QOL means per arm appear, in Tables 2 and 3. Without an allocation method or arm-level baseline comparability, the better outcomes in the probiotic arm are attributed to the probiotic more firmly than the design supports, although the wording ('interesting combination', 'contributes to') is somewhat hedged and the paper contains no explicit statement that allocation was non-random.

issues.title: Table 1 chi-square 8.712 not reproducible from counts 29/35 vs 19/35 (about 6.63); p 0.004 vs 0.003
issues.explanation: Using the printed efficacy counts, the chi-square for effective vs non-effective is about 6.6 (p about 0.01), not 8.712 (p about 0.003). The table prints p = 0.004 while the text prints p = 0.003 for the same chi-square. The group difference remains significant with the correct figure, so the direction of the result holds, but the printed test statistic does not match its own table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different 2x2 table or analysis set that yields chi-square 8.712, or an exact test explicitly named in the Methods.

quotes.text: Межгрупповое сравнение показало значительно более высокую общую эффективность

script.explanation: Reported χ² = 8.712 matches NEITHER convention: Pearson gives 6.6288 and Yates-corrected gives 5.3693 (both tried, window ±0.5). The mismatch is not explained by the continuity-correction convention. McNemar's was also tried (6.7600 uncorrected, 5.7600 corrected), in case the table is paired.

issues.title: Table 1 percentages do not match counts of n=35 (comparison arm: 56.9 vs 54.3, 34.1 vs 31.4, 43.1 vs 45.7)
issues.explanation: Both arms have 35 patients, but several Table 1 percentages do not equal count/35. The comparison arm is off by up to 2.7 points. The headline 56.9% also appears in the abstract and results, while 19/35 is 54.3%. Main-arm cells 82.7 and 17.3 are also slightly off (82.9 and 17.1). The efficacy gap is therefore about 28.6 points rather than 25.8, so the shift is small and does not change the direction of the finding. It does show that the counts and percentages were not generated from the same data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that percentages were computed on a different denominator or from a different patient set, or corrected counts that reproduce the printed percentages.

script.explanation: 19/35 = 54.29%, but the paper prints 56.9, outside the rounding interval [56.85, 57.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 33.4 rather than 35.

issues.title: Symptom-graded efficacy and questionnaire outcomes with no placebo and no blinding reported
issues.explanation: The primary outcome (efficacy grade) comes from patients' reported symptoms (pain, bloating, defecation) and an interview. The IBS-SSS and IBS-QOL are also self-reported. With no placebo or blinding mentioned, expectation effects could inflate the apparent benefit in the arm that received the extra capsule. This weakens the size of the reported difference but does not by itself show that it is absent.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcome assessors and patients were blinded, or a placebo-controlled design.

quotes.text: Оценка клинической эффективности лечения пациентов проводилась в соответствии с их основными симптомами (боль в животе, вздутие живота, дефекация).
Степень 1 - пациенты с выявленными симптомами после опроса.

issues.title: IBS-SSS/IBS-QOL superiority claimed with only within-group pre/post tests (Tables 2-3)
issues.explanation: Tables 2 and 3 give a t and p for each arm's change from baseline, all p < 0.001. The abstract and text then say the 'most significant' improvement was in the main group, but no between-group test is shown. A significant change in both arms does not show that one changed more than the other. The questionnaire superiority claim is therefore not formally supported by what is printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group comparison of post-treatment scores or change scores (with adjustment for baseline) reaching significance.

quotes.text: однако самый низкий показатель нарушения качества жизни после проведенного лечения был также зафиксирован в основной группе по сравнению с группой сравнения (табл. 3).
однако самым низким показатель был в основной группе по сравнению с группой сравнения (табл. 2).

issues.title: No ethics committee approval or trial registration reported
issues.explanation: Patients gave informed consent, but the paper does not name an ethics committee or approval number and gives no registration. For a prospective comparison of two treatments, readers cannot verify oversight from the text alone. This does not affect the numerical results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ethics committee approval number or protocol registration for this study.

quotes.text: подписавшие форму информированного согласия после полного информирования о цели и процессе исследования.

issues.title: No sample-size justification for 35 patients per arm
issues.explanation: The paper does not say why 35 per arm was chosen. The primary efficacy difference is statistically significant, so power is not the main concern for that result. The lack of justification matters mainly for how stable the effect size is, and it is a small issue in this study.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sample-size calculation in a protocol or registration.

quotes.text: Нами были обследованы 70 пациентов с ПИ-СРК, развившимся после перенесенной инфекции COVID-19.

10.51793/os.2025.28.10.009.headline_claim: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as a pulmonary rehabilitation method was effective for long-term respiratory outcomes of COVID-19 in patients with chronic bronchoobstructive disease (asthma or COPD).
10.51793/os.2025.28.10.009.overall: The conclusion that HBO is effective rests on within-group significance in a small, retrospective, unblinded, non-randomised comparison with a subjective primary-type outcome and no between-group test. Several printed numbers are inconsistent (the 1.5-fold claim, ferritin SD, FEV1/FVC, DLco n), which further reduces reliance. At most the data are hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: mMRS dyspnoea index (within-group change at 3 months)

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from within-group p-values; no between-group test reported for any outcome
issues.explanation: Benefit is argued from a significant change in the HBO arm versus a non-significant change in the comparison arm. A difference in significance is not a significant difference, and no between-group test, effect size or confidence interval is printed. Baselines also differ between groups (e.g. FEV1/FVC 80.6 vs 117.7, ferritin SD), so groups are not clearly comparable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group comparison of change scores (or ANCOVA) showing significant differences for the key outcomes.

quotes.text: тогда как у пациентов группы сравнения статистически значимого изменения этого показателя не отмечалось (p = 0,61)
функциональные тесты показали улучшение показателя бронхиальной проходимости по сравнению с контрольной группой

second_reader.what_stands: No between-group comparison (of change scores or of 3-month values) is reported for any outcome; the claims of benefit versus control rest on 'significant in the HBO group, not significant in the comparison group' (e.g. mMRS p=0.002 vs p=0.61, FEV1 p<0.001 vs none). The comparison group's own MSCT lesion change was also p<0.001, so the within-group contrast does not support superiority even on that outcome. The Methods name a Mann-Whitney test but none is reported.

issues.title: Retrospective non-randomised cohort with no blinding or control for confounding concluded to show HBO effective
issues.explanation: Patients were not randomised; how they came to receive HBO is not stated, and no adjustment for confounders is made. The outcome that most drives the conclusion (mMRS) is subjective and unblinded, and the comparison group received no sham or equivalent attention. The categorical statement of effectiveness is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Description of a pre-specified allocation rule or adjusted analysis addressing confounding, plus acknowledgement of limitations.

quotes.text: было проведено ретроспективное когортное наблюдательное исследование в двух параллельных группах пациентов
гипербарическая оксигенация как метод пульмореабилитации оказалась эффективной в лечении отдаленных респираторных исходов COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The study is described as a retrospective observational cohort, with no randomisation, no blinding, no adjustment for confounders (only univariate Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon), and no stated allocation mechanism, yet the Conclusion states HBO 'proved effective'. The paper does not discuss these limitations; the similarity in Table 1 characteristics is not a substitute for confounder control, and baseline lung function differed between arms.

issues.title: Comparison-group FEV1/FVC of 117.7% and 116.1% inconsistent with its own FEV1 (78.0) and FVC (83.5)
issues.explanation: FEV1 78.0 and FVC 83.5 (% predicted) imply a ratio near 93% of predicted, not 117.7. The main group's values are consistent (84/91.1 = 92%, versus 80.6 printed in a different scale), so the table mixes scales or contains an error. This undermines confidence in the spirometry table and its between-group comparability.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors stating the ratio is expressed on different scales in the two groups, or correcting the entries.

issues.title: mMRS fall described as 'more than 1.5-fold' but 2.4 to 1.8 is a 1.33-fold (25%) reduction
issues.explanation: The text says the dyspnoea index decreased by more than 1.5 times, but the printed means give a ratio of 1.33. Even allowing for rounding of both means (2.35/1.85 = 1.27 to 2.45/1.75 = 1.40), 1.5 is not reachable. The magnitude of the dyspnoea improvement is overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing a mean ratio of at least 1.5 with the printed means being rounded from different values.

quotes.text: среднее значение индекса одышки по шкале mMRS уменьшилось более чем в 1,5 раза (с 2,4 до 1,8 балла, p = 0,002)

script.explanation: mMRS baseline / 3-month, main group: 2.4 / 1.8 gives 1.33333, not the printed 1.5. For the printed value to hold the denominator would have to be 1.6, not 1.8.

issues.title: CT: comparison group described as 'almost unchanged' despite a significant fall (27.4% to 21.5%, p<0.001)
issues.explanation: The text says the comparison group's lung involvement 'almost did not change' yet prints a p<0.001 for a fall of about 6 percentage points, and the conclusion claims faster resolution without a between-group test. The larger fall in the HBO group (29.7 to 2.7%) is suggestive, but the contrast is not formally tested and the description of the comparison group contradicts its own p-value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group comparison of CT change showing a significant difference in favour of HBO.

quotes.text: в то время как в группе сравнения оно почти не изменилось и соста-
способствовало более быстрому разрешению остаточных рентгенологических изменений в легких

issues.title: DLco analysed n (21 and 18) differs from 23 and 20 with no stated reason for 6 missing patients
issues.explanation: Table 5 uses 21 and 18 patients while every other table and the text use 23 and 20. The paper never says why 2 and 2 patients lack DLco data. The DLco result is non-significant, so the effect on conclusions is small, but the attrition is unexplained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that DLco could not be measured in 4 patients (e.g. technical failure or inability to perform).

quotes.text: Основная группа , n = 21
Основная группа , n = 23

issues.title: Baseline ferritin SD printed as 22 in Abstract but 221.0 in Table 3
issues.explanation: The abstract gives baseline ferritin 436 ± 22 and follow-up 427 ± 217, while Table 3 gives 436.0 ± 221.0 and 427.0 ± 217.0. The abstract SD for baseline is ten times smaller than the table's and would make the change look far more precise. It appears to be a typographical slip, but it is a wrong printed figure in the abstract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the abstract and table are the same value in the published layout.

issues.title: Roughly 25 within-group tests at p < 0.05 without correction; only significant markers highlighted
issues.explanation: Seven blood markers, four spirometry indices, DLco, mMRS and CT were each tested at 0.05 without any multiplicity control and no primary outcome was named. Headline results with p<0.001 would probably survive a correction, so the practical effect is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome or a multiplicity-adjusted analysis.

quotes.text: Разница между показателями считалась статически значимой при p < 0,05.

10.51847/ugvstnjdmp.headline_claim: Neuro-stimulating exercises (oriental gymnastics combined with volleyball) restore cognitive functions and eliminate post-COVID syndrome symptoms among students.
10.51847/ugvstnjdmp.overall: The headline conclusion of proven efficacy and eliminated post-COVID symptoms cannot be relied on: allocation was non-random to a non-comparable control, and superiority over control was never tested between groups. The arithmetic slips (Abstract 20.15%, 'times' for point gains, a mean above the scale maximum) are secondary but show weak reporting. The data are consistent with a larger improvement in the experimental group, but that is not established.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly named; anxiety (STAI personal/situational), HADS, and cognitive/psychophysical tests are all reported as outcomes

issues.title: Superiority claims over control rest on within-group p-values; no between-group test reported
issues.explanation: Every p value in Tables 1-4 is a within-group comparison of baseline against 9 months, and both groups reach P<0.01. The text nonetheless states that the experimental group improved 'compared to the control one' and that the results are significant versus control. A between-group test of change (or of endpoints adjusted for baseline) is never shown, so superiority is asserted rather than tested. The control improving significantly too also means the within-group tests do not isolate the technique. No multiplicity handling across about 10 outcomes is stated either.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group test (e.g. t-test on change scores or ANCOVA) with its p values showing a difference between arms.

quotes.text: Note: p - is the mathematical significance of the differences in indicators inside the group.
The testing in May 2022 showed a significant improvement in the indicators among the students of the experimental group (P<0.01) compared to the control one.

second_reader.what_stands: Every p-value in Tables 1-4 is, by the table notes, a within-group (pre/post) test. The claims of significant improvement in the experimental group 'compared to the control one' are made in the text without any reported between-group test, test statistic or interaction/difference-in-change analysis. The control group also improved significantly within-group, so the within-group p-values cannot show superiority. The size of the differences in change is large and might well be significant if tested, but the paper does not show this.

issues.title: Non-random allocation: post-COVID students vs. a separate first-year class with unstated COVID status
issues.explanation: The experimental group was selected for having had COVID-19 with post-COVID symptoms, while the control group is described only as 25 first-year students. The control group's COVID history and symptoms are not described, and the groups differ in selection, class, and teaching, so the arms differ at the outset in unmeasured ways. Baseline similarity in test scores does not remove this, and regression to the mean and natural recovery over 9 months cannot be separated from the intervention.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description showing that controls were also post-COVID symptomatic and allocated by a concealed random or matched procedure.

quotes.text: there was one control group of 25 first-year students (n=50)

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was non-random: the experimental group was defined by having had COVID-19 with post-COVID symptoms, while the control group is described only as 25 first-year students, with no stated COVID or post-COVID status. The paper does not say whether the control group had post-COVID symptoms, so the comparison is not shown to be like-for-like. Close baseline means on the outcome scales partly mitigate this, but they do not remove the problem. The claim that the control students were from a separate class is an inference; the paper says only 'one control group of 25 first-year students'.

issues.title: Conclusion that post-COVID symptoms were eliminated and efficacy 'proven' is not supported
issues.explanation: The conclusion says no post-COVID symptoms remained in the experimental group, the cognitive consequences were eliminated, and efficiency was proven. The paper reports no symptom-level reassessment, no individual-level data, no between-group test, no sample-size justification, and a non-comparable control. Recovery over 9 months also occurs naturally, and the control group improved too. The data at most suggest a larger improvement on several scales in a small, non-randomised sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified symptom measure with individual-level resolution data and a valid between-group comparison.

quotes.text: no symptoms of the post-COVID syndrome among the students of the experimental group
There  has  been  proven  efficiency  of  the authors' technique.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusions that no post-COVID symptoms remained and that the effect on cognition was 'eliminated' and 'proven' are not supported: symptoms were not assessed at follow-up with a defined measure, only group means of anxiety, depression and psychomotor tests are shown, the control group also improved, and there is no between-group test or random allocation. At most the data show larger pre-to-post changes in the experimental group than in the control group in a small, non-randomised sample.

issues.title: Lower-pass mean of 20.5 'out of 20' exceeds the stated maximum of 20
issues.explanation: Table 4 labels the lower-pass indicator as 'the number of passes out of 20 times' yet the experimental mean at 9 months is 20.5, above the possible maximum. The text also says 96.2% managed more than 20 passes. Either the scale description or the data are misreported, so the lower-pass result and its 111.7% gain cannot be interpreted as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods description showing the passes test has no cap at 20 (for example, 20 is a threshold, not a maximum).

quotes.location: Table 4, lower pass row, experimental 9 months

quotes.text: more than 20 times (May 2022)

issues.title: Personal anxiety decrease printed as 20.15% in Abstract but 20.55% in Results; Table 1 gives about 20.56%
issues.explanation: The Abstract reports a 20.15% decrease in personal anxiety in the experimental group, while the Results text reports 20.55%. Table 1 means (50.25 to 39.92) give a 10.33-point fall, which is about 20.56% of baseline, so the Results figure fits and the Abstract figure is a slip. The effect is small and does not change any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Abstract refers to a different quantity, such as a different subgroup or time point, than the Results figure.

issues.title: No registration or protocol reported for a prospective study with about ten outcomes
issues.explanation: The study ran from September 2021 to May 2022 and reports ethics approval but no registry entry or protocol. With many outcomes and no stated primary one, selective emphasis cannot be excluded. Whether registration was expected for this type of study is debatable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or protocol dated before enrolment naming the primary outcome.

quotes.text: The pedagogical experiment was started in September 2021

issues.title: Free-throw and lower-pass gains labelled 'times' (2.41, 10.82) are point differences; % figures are correct
issues.explanation: The text says free throws increased 'by 2.41 times (50.3%)' and lower passes 'by 10.82 times (111.7%)'. A 2.41-fold increase would be 141%, but Table 4 means show absolute gains of 2.41 and 10.82 points, which match the stated percentages. The error is one of units, not of the underlying data, so only the wording misleads.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that 'times' was meant as 'points'; no change to the numbers would then be needed.

quotes.text: increased by 2.41 times (50.3 %)
increased by 10.82 times (111.7%)

issues.title: Table 4 baseline 'no significant differences' printed with P<0.01 instead of P>0.01
issues.explanation: For the volleyball baseline the text says the groups did not differ significantly but gives P<0.01, which under the paper's own threshold means significant. Every other baseline statement uses P>0.01, so this is almost certainly a sign slip. It is a cosmetic inconsistency, though it leaves unclear whether baseline volleyball skills were balanced.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing needed; the inconsistency is on the page. It would be moot if the baseline P values were shown to exceed 0.01.

quotes.text: differences (P<0.01)

10.51910/ijhdr.v25icf.1532.headline_claim: The pilot trial confirms the feasibility of future homeopathic studies in Long COVID and suggests there may have been a biological difference in response between verum and placebo, possibly related to homeopathic aggravations.
10.51910/ijhdr.v25icf.1532.overall: The null between-group result at each time point is reasonably supported, although Table 2's baseline SDs are wrong and the MYMOP direction is misdescribed. The suggestion of a biological difference tied to aggravations rests on uncorrected exploratory interaction tests and untested counts, so it should be treated as hypothesis-generating only. Retrospective registration is disclosed and the primary outcomes match, so it is a minor concern.

primary_outcome.name: Co-primary: Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS), SF-36 Physical Composite Score (PCS), SF-36 Mental Composite Score (MCS)

issues.title: Biological-difference/aggravation interpretation rests on one exploratory interaction and untested aggravation counts
issues.explanation: There was no significant between-group difference at any time point and no main group effect (p=0.811). The 'biological difference' idea rests on a group-by-time interaction for two of three outcomes and on aggravation counts (19 vs 10 events, with six verum participants having repeat events) that were not tested. Aggravations were physician-reported and not linked to later outcomes. An equally plausible explanation is chance, or baseline and posology differences, so the causal story is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified analysis linking aggravation to early outcome trajectories, or a corrected interaction test that remains significant.

quotes.text: possibly related to the phenomena of homeopathic therapeutic aggravations
The finding of almost twice as many reported aggravations in the verum group might account for the slower improvement of the verum group early in the study.
There were no significant differences in the means of the FAS, PCS, or MCS between placebo and verum at each of the four time-points

second_reader.what_stands: The aggravation interpretation rests on one exploratory interaction (FAS and PCS, not MCS) and on raw counts of physician-reported events with no statistical test and no link to the outcome trajectories. The 'almost twice' figure counts events; by participants the rates are similar (at least 11 vs 10 of 36 per arm). The authors do use hedged wording and list limitations, but the Conclusion still refers to a 'biological difference' in response.

issues.title: Interaction p-values 0.021/0.022 across three co-primary outcomes with no multiplicity adjustment
issues.explanation: Three co-primary outcomes were each tested for main effects and interaction at 0.05 with no correction. A Bonferroni threshold for three outcomes is 0.0167, and both reported interaction p-values (0.021, 0.022) exceed it. The interaction findings are therefore fragile, and the paper builds its conclusion on them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical or gatekeeping testing plan, or an adjusted analysis in which the interaction remains significant.

quotes.text: in favor of placebo for both FAS (F(3, 210)=3.3, p=0.021) and PCS (F(3, 210)=3.28, p=0.022)
Statistical significance was set at 0.05

second_reader.what_stands: Two interaction p-values (0.021, 0.022) from three co-primary outcomes were interpreted at an unadjusted 0.05, and neither would pass a Bonferroni (0.0167) or Holm correction. The paper states no multiplicity adjustment or hierarchy. The authors do call the study a pilot and the finding unexpected, which tempers but does not remove the issue.

issues.title: Table 2 baseline SDs (FAS 2.2/2.3, PCS 6.6/5.7, MYMOP 0.3) disagree with the Supplement and with Table 2's own p-values
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives baseline SDs far smaller than the Supplement does for the same means (FAS 2.2 vs 6.8, PCS 6.6 vs 20.4, MCS 5.4 vs 16.7, MYMOP 0.3 vs 1.0). The p-values printed in Table 2 are reproduced by the Supplement SDs, not by the Table 2 SDs. The Table 2 SDs are therefore most likely wrong. The baseline-balance statement is unaffected, but the table is unreliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 2 reports a different dispersion measure (e.g. SE or a within-person SD) that reproduces its printed p-values.

quotes.location: Supplemental Materials B, FAS Baseline row, placebo column

issues.title: MYMOP symptom 2 trend (p=0.058) called 'in favor of placebo' though verum mean is lower (1.0 vs 1.7)
issues.explanation: At 12 weeks the placebo mean for MYMOP symptom 2 is 1.7 and the verum mean is 1.0. Scores fall from about 4.4 at baseline, so lower means better, and the numerical difference favours verum. The text says the trend favours placebo. The first MYMOP symptom (1.6 placebo vs 1.3 verum) also leans toward verum, so the secondary outcomes do not support the 'placebo improved sooner' narrative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the MYMOP scores in this study were coded so that higher values mean better status.

quotes.text: A positive trend (p-value 0.058) in favor of placebo was found for the second listed MYMOP symptom.

quotes.location: Supplemental Materials C, MYMOP2 12-weeks row, placebo column
Supplemental Materials C, MYMOP2 12-weeks row, verum column

issues.title: Registered 28 Oct 2021, six weeks after the 15 Sep 2021 study start; disclosed, primary outcomes match
issues.explanation: The trial was registered after enrolment began, so the registration cannot prove outcomes were fixed in advance. The paper discloses this and the registered primary outcomes agree with those reported, which limits the concern. Because the main result is null, the practical risk of outcome switching is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing no outcome changes and enrolment of the first participant only after registration.

quotes.text: registered during enrollment at ClinicalTrials.gov on October 28, 2021 (NCT05104749 ID: 0012021).
quotes.location: Methods, Ethical Approval and Trial Registration

quotes.text: The study was carried out between September 15, 2021 and April 22, 2022.

10.5195/ijt.2023.6560.headline_claim: Eight weeks of telerehabilitation is an efficient way to improve physical fitness and mental health in people recovering from COVID-19.
10.5195/ijt.2023.6560.overall: The headline conclusion that telerehabilitation improves fitness and mental health is only partly supported. Several fitness outcomes and depression differ between groups, but handgrip and anxiety do not, the get-up-and-go result runs in the wrong direction as printed, and analysis is on completers only after about a third of participants were lost. Participant-flow and Table 1 numbers also contain several internal inconsistencies, so the trial supports a tentative rather than a confident effect.

primary_outcome.name: No single primary outcome is named; physical fitness tests (handgrip, flex-arm, sit-up, get-up-and-go, 6MWT) and depression/anxiety scores (BDI, BAI) are reported together

issues.title: Only 16 completers per arm analysed after 15 of 47 allocated were lost (about 32%); no ITT
issues.explanation: About a third of those allocated dropped out or were removed for 'medical restrictions', and all analyses use the 16 completers per arm. No intention-to-treat or missing-data analysis is reported. Dropout may be related to outcome, especially in a home exercise programme. Efficacy conclusions are therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis reaching the same conclusions.

quotes.text: ending the study with 16 individuals in each group
due to dropouts and medical restrictions

second_reader.what_stands: About 32% of allocated participants (15 of 47) were lost and only the 16 per arm completers were analysed, with no ITT or imputation described, which risks bias in a completer-only analysis. Attrition was similar across arms, and the text gives 45 evaluated against 47 by arithmetic, a minor inconsistency.

issues.title: Get-up-and-go time in TG rose 6.65 to 7.75 s yet is reported as an improvement vs CG
issues.explanation: The get-up-and-go test is timed in seconds, so a lower value is better. The TG mean rose from 6.65 to 7.75 s, while the CG barely changed (7.22 to 7.35), yet the Results and Discussion present this as a TG improvement and as superior agility. Either the table has a data or labelling error, or the TG got slower and the text is wrong. The reported difference of 1.00 also does not equal 7.75 - 6.65 = 1.10. The agility claim is not supported as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or a corrected table showing TG time fell from pre to post.

quotes.text: there was an improvement in fitness only in the indices of flex arm (p=0.00), sitting up (p=0.00), 'get up and go' (p=0.02)

quotes.location: Table 2, 'Get Up and Go' (seconds), TG Post
Table 2, 'Get Up and Go' (seconds), TG Pre

second_reader.what_stands: As printed, TG time rose by about 1.1 s while CG was essentially unchanged, which on a timed task indicates slower performance, yet the paper describes it as an improvement and as TG superiority in agility. Unless the values are mis-entered or the measure is not a time, the direction is mislabelled; the paper does not resolve this.

issues.title: Conclusion of improved fitness and mental health overlooks null between-group handgrip and anxiety results
issues.explanation: Between groups, only depression (p=0.00), flex arm, sitting up, get-up-and-go and 6MWT differed. Handgrip improved similarly in both groups, and anxiety did not differ (p=0.26). The Discussion nonetheless says all outcomes improved and that all fitness indices increased in the TG versus CG, and it leans on pre-post anxiety change. The concluding sentence generalises to physical fitness and mental health as a whole. This is stronger than the between-group results support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A conclusion restricted to the outcomes with significant between-group differences.

quotes.text: statistical differences were found for depression (p=0.00), but not for anxiety (p=0.26)
we observed an increase in all physical fitness indices and a reduction in depression levels in the TG
eight weeks of training by telerehabilitation is an efficient way to improve the physical fitness and mental health in patients affected by COVID-19.

second_reader.what_stands: The first Discussion paragraph's claim of an increase in all fitness indices vs CG contradicts the handgrip null reported in the same paper, and the final conclusion of improved mental health rests on depression alone while the between-group anxiety result was null. The handgrip and anxiety nulls are disclosed in the body, so they are not hidden, but the conclusion does not carry them forward.

issues.title: Results say 45 allocated, but arms 24+23 and 75 minus 28 both give 47
issues.explanation: The Results state that 75 people were recruited, 28 excluded and 45 allocated. The stated arm sizes (24 and 23) sum to 47, and 75 minus 28 is also 47. The attrition counts (8 of 24, 7 of 23) lead to the 16 and 16 completers, so 45 is the figure that does not fit. This is a reporting error in the participant flow. It makes the attrition percentage (15/45 versus 15/47) ambiguous.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing 45 allocated with different arm sizes, or 47 allocated with 45 being a different stage.

quotes.text: Forty-five individuals were evaluated and then allocated into the Telerehabilitation Training (TG n = 24) and Control (CG n = 23) groups
Of 75 individuals clinically recovered from COVID-19 and initially recruited in this study, 28 were excluded

script.explanation: The participant flow does not reconcile: 'recruited' (n=75) minus its 1 stated exclusion(s) (28) leaves 47, but 'allocated' reports 45 -- 2 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic. the arms of 'allocated' sum to 47, but the stage reports n=45 -- 2 participant(s) appear or vanish between the total and its own breakdown.

issues.title: Unblinded, no-exercise control with self-reported mood scales; lectures given to both arms
issues.explanation: Both arms received lectures, but only the TG received supervised sessions with an exercise specialist. Depression and anxiety are self-reported, and blinding is not described. The depression between-group difference could therefore partly reflect expectation or contact time. The authors list self-report as a limitation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of blinded outcome assessment or an attention-matched sham-exercise control.

quotes.text: The control group did not perform the physical training program.
the self-reported survey that can lead to type I or type II error

issues.title: About 7 between-group tests at p<0.05 uncorrected; get-up-and-go (p=0.02) and 6MWT (p=0.01) borderline
issues.explanation: Five fitness tests and two mood scales are compared between groups with no multiplicity correction and no designated primary outcome. The strongest results (p=0.00) are likely robust. The p=0.02 and p=0.01 results would not survive a conservative correction, and the conclusion does not qualify them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome or adjusted p-values still below 0.05.

quotes.text: The main limitations of this study were the relatively small sample size, multiple tests, and the self-reported survey that can lead to type I or type II error.

issues.title: Sample size calculation reported without effect size or target n; 32 analysed
issues.explanation: The Methods claim 80% power but give no outcome, effect size or required sample, so adequacy of 16 per arm cannot be assessed. The authors name small sample as a limitation, but the conclusion is stated confidently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated target n and effect size matching the achieved sample.

quotes.text: The sample size was calculated to have 80% statistical power, with a two-tailed alpha level of 0.05, to detect a between-group difference.
The main limitations of this study were the relatively small sample size

issues.title: Table 1 counts do not reconcile: mild+severe is 19 of 16 in both arms; other totals off by one
issues.explanation: Mild and Severe are exclusive categories, but they sum to 19 in both arms of 16 (percentages 62.5 + 56.3 = 118.8%). Several other rows also fail to add up: hospitalization (7 + 9 = 16 against a total of 15), dyspnea (7 + 11 = 18 against 17), and O2 support, where TG 7 is printed as 20.0%. Table 1 is the only description of the baseline groups, so its reliability is reduced. The efficacy results are not directly affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 or protocol data showing the classification and symptom counts do reconcile.

quotes.text: Mild, (n, %)
Hospitalization, (n, %)
Dyspnea, (n. %)

issues.title: Hypertension 7/16 in TG vs 2/16 in CG; baseline imbalance not discussed or adjusted
issues.explanation: Hypertension is more common in the TG, as are some other baseline differences, and no covariate adjustment is made. The imbalance is probably chance, but with 16 per arm it cannot be ruled out as influencing the results. The paper only reports p-values for demographics.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An adjusted analysis showing unchanged effects.

quotes.text: Hypertension, (n, %)
matched for sex and disease severity

10.52403/ijhsr.20230305.headline_claim: Aerobic exercise (walking plus diaphragmatic breathing) is effective in improving peak expiratory flow rate, exercise capacity and quality of life in post COVID-19 patients, with the experimental group showing significantly higher improvement than the diaphragmatic-breathing control group.
10.52403/ijhsr.20230305.overall: The paper reports large within-group and between-group differences, and the printed t statistics are internally consistent. But the design is a 30-patient non-randomised convenience sample with unreported allocation, unblinded effort-dependent outcomes, unequal contact time and imbalanced baseline characteristics. The conclusion of effectiveness and superiority is therefore tentative, and the claim about preventing complications is unsupported.

primary_outcome.name: not stated as a single primary outcome; peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR), exercise capacity (6MWT) and SF-36 quality of life are all reported as outcomes

issues.title: Non-randomised convenience-sample study with unreported allocation; superiority claimed from 30 patients
issues.explanation: Thirty patients were chosen by convenience sampling and split into two groups of 15 with no stated method of allocation, randomisation, concealment or blinding. The groups differ in age, sex mix and BMI, and nothing is adjusted for. The control arm also received much less contact time (10 vs 50 minutes per session), so the comparison cannot isolate the effect of aerobic exercise. The conclusion that aerobic exercise is effective and superior is therefore only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described random allocation procedure with concealment, or an adjusted analysis showing the same between-group effect.

quotes.text: Pre and Post Experimental study
Convenient sampling

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a convenience-sample, two-group pre-post design with no stated allocation method, no randomisation and no blinding, and only 30 participants. Despite this, it concludes that aerobic exercise is effective and superior, using unadjusted post-test comparisons; the allocation method is not reported, so selection and confounding cannot be excluded.

issues.title: Conclusion claims prevention of pulmonary complications and cost-effectiveness, which were not measured
issues.explanation: The conclusion says aerobic exercise will help prevent pulmonary complications and plays an important role in rehabilitation. The study only measured PEFR, 6-minute walk distance and SF-36 scores over 5 weeks in 30 non-randomly allocated patients. Complication prevention and cost-effectiveness were not assessed. The limitations section does not state that effectiveness conclusions are tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported complication rates or a cost analysis supporting these statements.

quotes.text: which will help to prevent pulmonary complications and improve quality of life.
Cost effective programme.

second_reader.what_stands: The claim that the programme will 'prevent pulmonary complications' is not supported, because no complication or incidence outcome was measured and there was only a 5-week pre-post assessment. 'Cost effective' is asserted without any cost data or economic analysis. The quality-of-life part of the conclusion is supported by SF-36 results, subject to the design limits noted under i4.

issues.title: Effort-dependent outcomes (PEFR, 6MWT, SF-36) measured unblinded with a self-reported questionnaire
issues.explanation: Participants knew which arm they were in, and the paper does not describe blinded outcome assessment. The outcomes are effort-dependent or self-reported, and the walk test used verbal encouragement. This can inflate the apparent benefit of the more intensive arm. The paper does not discuss it beyond a note on manual measurement error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that assessors were blinded to group allocation.

quotes.text: As the measurements were taken manually

issues.title: Within-group pre-post significance read as proof of effect; between-group test uses post scores only, unadjusted
issues.explanation: The paper says significant paired pre-post changes 'prove' the effect of each exercise, but such changes also reflect natural recovery, practice and regression to the mean. The between-group comparison uses post-test scores without adjusting for baseline, and the MCS baseline difference of 5.66 points is not trivial. The groups were similar at baseline on the tests reported, so this weakens the secondary inferences more than the main between-group result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ANCOVA or change-score comparison between groups showing the same difference.

quotes.text: exercise in peak expiratory flow rate among Post COVID-19 patients.

issues.title: Total study duration printed as 6 months and as 5 weeks (5 weeks is the intervention period)
issues.explanation: The study duration section gives 6 months in total and 5 weeks for the intervention. The sampling procedure then calls 5 weeks the 'total study duration'. This is most likely loose wording for the intervention length, but it leaves the real recruitment and enrolment timeline unclear. No result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the 6 months includes recruitment and analysis and that 5 weeks refers only to the intervention.

quotes.text: Total study duration-  6  months
The  total  study  duration  was  5  weeks

issues.title: Table 3 gender percentages (33.35/66.65, 53.35/46.65) differ from counts over 15 (33.33/66.67, 53.33/46.67)
issues.explanation: With 15 per group, 5/15 is 33.33%, 10/15 is 66.67%, 8/15 is 53.33% and 7/15 is 46.67%. The table prints figures that differ by 0.02 in each cell. This is a trivial cosmetic error that does not change the finding that sex was imbalanced across groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; the arithmetic is unambiguous, though it is trivial.

script.explanation: 5/15 = 33.33%, but the paper prints 33.35, outside the rounding interval [33.34, 33.36]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 15.0 rather than 15.

10.52403/ijhsr.20230310.headline_claim: An 8-week balloon blowing technique programme is effective in improving PEFR, exercise tolerance and quality of life in post-COVID-19 survivors.
10.52403/ijhsr.20230310.overall: The direction of the findings (larger improvements in PEFR, 6MWT and SGRQ with balloon blowing) is plausible and the main t-statistics reconcile with the printed means and SDs. However, allocation was non-random and unblinded, and the experimental arm exercised four times as long per day, so the claim that the technique itself is 'effective' is only tentative. The Results text also states the QOL direction wrongly, and several tables contain transcription slips.

primary_outcome.name: Not explicitly designated; PEFR, exercise tolerance (6MWT) and QoL (SGRQ) all reported as outcomes

issues.title: Non-random convenience allocation, unblinded, with 40 vs 10 min/day dose; between-group superiority is confounded
issues.explanation: Participants were 'conveniently divided' into two groups of 15, with no randomisation, concealment or blinding described. The experimental arm received four times the daily exercise time (40 vs 10 minutes), so any difference could reflect training volume or attention and not the balloon technique. Outcomes are the patient-effort-dependent 6MWT and peak flow, and the QOL questionnaire is self-reported, so open-label assessment can bias them. Post-test group comparisons are unadjusted, so the superiority claim is only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of concealed random allocation, blinded outcome assessment, and a matched-time control arm.

quotes.text: Then conveniently divided equally in two groups
Duration  was10  minutes  per day for 8 weeks.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was by convenience with no randomisation, concealment or blinding reported, and the experimental arm received 40 min/day versus 10 min/day in control, so any between-group difference cannot be attributed to the balloon technique rather than to more total exercise time, attention or expectation. The paper does not list this design weakness among its limitations.

issues.title: Pre-post significance described as 'proving' the effect, and effectiveness concluded from a non-randomised design
issues.explanation: Each within-group paired t-test is followed by 'This proves the effect' of the technique, and the control arm's significant change is treated the same way. Pre-post change in an uncontrolled arm can come from time, learning effects on the 6MWT, or regression to the mean. The conclusion that the programme 'is effective' relies on unadjusted post-test comparisons in a convenience-allocated sample of 30. The wording is stronger than the design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A randomised, blinded design with a matched-dose control and a between-group analysis of change adjusted for baseline.

quotes.text: This  proves  the  effect  of  Diaphragmatic breathing  exercise  in  exercise  tolerance  among  Post COVID-19 patients.
Hence Balloon blowing technique is effective in PEFR among Post COVID-19 patients

second_reader.what_stands: Significant pre-post p-values are described as 'proving' the effect of the exercise, and 'effective' is concluded from a non-randomised, unblinded two-group comparison with unequal exercise dose; significance testing does not prove an effect, and pre-post change without a valid comparator cannot be attributed to the intervention. The t and p values for Table 12 recompute correctly, so the problem is the inferential wording and design, not the arithmetic.

issues.title: Results say experimental QOL scores were 'significantly higher'; Table 18 shows 49.79 vs 58.37 (lower)
issues.explanation: The Results text for the post-test QOL comparison says the experimental group's scores were significantly higher than controls'. Table 18 gives 49.79 for the experimental group and 58.37 for controls, and the Discussion says 'lower'. On the SGRQ lower means less impairment, so the text states the opposite of what the data show. Read literally it would mean the intervention worsened QOL, though the conclusion itself rests on the correct direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A version of the paper in which the Results sentence reads 'lower', or a statement that QOL was scored so that higher is better.

quotes.text: The scores in the experimental group were significantly lower than that of the control group.
100: Maximum health impairment

issues.title: Sample-size formula printed without inputs or calculated n; 15 per arm
issues.explanation: The paper prints a generic sample-size equation but not the SD, effect size or resulting n, so the choice of 15 per arm cannot be verified. With n = 15 per arm the estimates are imprecise, and several outcomes are tested without correction. This weakens confidence in the size of the effects more than in their direction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol or worked calculation showing 15 per arm gives adequate power for a stated difference.

quotes.text: Equations were used in;

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective interventional study
issues.explanation: The study is a prospective intervention with three outcomes but reports no registry entry, so pre-specification of the primary outcome and analysis cannot be checked. No primary outcome is designated, so any of the three significant results could be presented as the main finding. This is a transparency gap with limited bearing on the numbers themselves.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry entry dated before enrolment listing these outcomes.

quotes.text: Total study duration: 6 months

issues.title: Exercise tolerance t-value printed as 0.029 in text but 2.29 in Table 15 (0.029 is the p-value)
issues.explanation: The Results and Discussion paragraphs on post-test exercise tolerance give 't-value 0.029'. Table 15 gives t = 2.29 and p = 0.029. A t of 0.029 would mean essentially no difference. The reported significance is unaffected, because the table values reconcile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing in the paper supports a t of 0.029. The check would fail only if the raw data gave a t near 0.03.

quotes.text: 0.029 shows p-value < 0.05

issues.title: Several transcription errors in control-group tables: QOL pre-test 58.98/58.93, SD 1.19, and SDs 918/968
issues.explanation: The control pre-test QOL mean is 58.98 in Table 10 but 58.93 in Tables 17 and 19. The control pre-test QOL SD is 1.19 in Table 17 against 11.19 elsewhere. The Table 14 pre-test exercise-tolerance SDs print as 918 and 968, against 59.88 and 47.82 elsewhere. The printed 0.552 mean change fits 58.93 and not 58.98 (difference 0.61). The pattern points to careless transcription, and the headline results are unaffected, but the tables are unreliable as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 58.98 as the true control baseline and a QOL SD of 1.19.

quotes.text: QOL scores (58.98 and 58.37)
EXPERIMENTAL 475 59.8 530 57.8

10.52403/ijshr.20230256.headline_claim: Physiotherapy rehabilitation improved dyspnoea, SpO2, oxygen requirement, mobility and independence in post-COVID-19 patients, which the authors describe as concrete proof of efficacy.
10.52403/ijshr.20230256.overall: The descriptive before-after improvements are large, but the paper cannot attribute them to physiotherapy because it has no comparator and no inferential statistics, so 'concrete proof of efficacy' is not supported. Discharge denominators are inconsistent (26 vs 30, 22 vs 30), and there are several minor numeric slips.

primary_outcome.name: Dyspnea grade (MMRC), SpO2 and oxygen requirement, as described in Methods

issues.title: Efficacy of physiotherapy inferred from an uncontrolled before-after series of 30 inpatients
issues.explanation: All patients are one group measured at admission and discharge with no comparator, no statistical test, and no adjustment for concurrent medical treatment or natural recovery after COVID-19. The paper states that the study reaffirms efficacy and gives 'concrete proof', which this design cannot support. Missing discharge data (26 or 30 patients) and no sample-size calculation weaken it further.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent comparison group or analysis separating physiotherapy effects from natural recovery.

quotes.text: This is a retrospective observational cohort study.
The study revealed concrete proof of the efficacy of the physiotherapy recommendations
Despite the limited study population, we were able to demonstrate significant results

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is an uncontrolled before-after series of 30 inpatients. Efficacy is inferred from admission versus discharge changes alone. There is no comparison group, and the paper does not address natural recovery, regression to the mean, or co-interventions such as diet and medical care. The 'concrete proof' and 'significant results' wording is not supported, because no inferential test is reported, and the authors' only caveats are the small sample and the need for further research.

issues.title: Discharge denominators inconsistent: N=30 in text/Tables 3-6 vs N=26 in Tables 1-2 and 22 vs 30 discharged
issues.explanation: Discharge SpO2 is N=30 in the text but N=26 in Table 1, and Table 2 reports 4 patients with discharge data not available. Tables 3-6 nonetheless give discharge percentages over N=30, and the Conclusion states both 'a sum of 22 patients was discharged' and '30 patients were discharged independently'. The analysed denominator at discharge is therefore unclear, and the 4 missing patients are counted as if assessed in some tables, which could overstate the proportion improved or not.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow description showing which patients had discharge measurements for each scale.

quotes.text: The  Mean  of  SpO2  levels  among  subjects  (N=30)  during  discharge  was  0.97
A  sum  of  22  patients  was discharged
Data Not Available

issues.title: Stated maximum oxygen flow of 4 L/min contradicted by 4 patients on 5 or 6 L in Table 2
issues.explanation: Methods say the maximum oxygen considered was 4 L, yet Table 2 and the Results report 2 patients on 5 L and 2 on 6 L during admission. One of the two statements is wrong. This does not change the before-after pattern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A clarification that the 4 L maximum refers to something other than admission flow.

quotes.text: The maximum oxygen taken into consideration was 4 lit and the minimum was 1lit.
6 litre O 2

issues.title: Table 1 age range 46-84 years lies outside the stated 50-80 year eligibility
issues.explanation: Methods restrict the sample to 50-80 years, but Table 1 reports a minimum of 46 and maximum of 84. Some patients thus did not meet the stated criterion, or the criterion was misreported. The effect on the findings is probably small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the range was applied to a different variable or that eligibility was defined differently.

quotes.text: age  group  of  50-80  years
Maximum 84.00

issues.title: MMRC grade 3 at admission: text gives 30.30% but 9/30 and Table 3 give 30.00%
issues.explanation: The Results text prints 30.30% for 9 patients at MMRC grade 3, while Table 3 prints 30.00%. With N=30, 9 patients is exactly 30.00%, so the text value is a typo. Nothing depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing; the count and denominator are printed.

quotes.text: subjects  (30.30  %)  scored  the  value  of  3

script.explanation: 9/30 = 30.00%, but the paper prints 30.3, outside the rounding interval [30.30, 30.31]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 29.7 rather than 30.

10.5334/ijic.icic23285.headline_claim: A 3-month hybrid integrated care programme (outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation followed by home-based, ICT-supported follow-up) improves exercise tolerance, quality of life and functional capacity compared with usual care in patients with long COVID-19 syndrome.
10.5334/ijic.icic23285.overall: The claim that the programme improves outcomes compared with usual care is not supported by what is reported: allocation is unexplained and unadjusted, and only within-group changes are tested. The PR group's improvements from baseline look sizeable, but without a controlled between-group analysis they may reflect natural recovery. Feasibility (95% compliance) is the better supported finding.

primary_outcome.name: Exercise tolerance (work rate at cardiopulmonary exercise test to limit of tolerance, Tlim)

issues.title: Superiority over usual care inferred from within-group changes; no between-group test reported
issues.explanation: Results give change from baseline within the PR group (all p=0.001) and note that in UC only mMRC changed. A difference in significance within each group does not show the groups differ from each other. The headline claim of improvement 'compared to UC' therefore has no direct statistical support in the reported results. Also, the UC arm's changes for the other outcomes are not given, so the size of any difference cannot be judged.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group (group-by-time or adjusted) comparisons in the full paper favouring PR.

quotes.text: compared to baseline, FACIT, CAT, and mMRC scores were improved following PR in the PR group by 15±9 (p=0.001)
only mMRC was improved at 3 month assessment compared to baseline by 0.7±0.6 (p=0.008)

second_reader.what_stands: The superiority claim 'Compared to UC' rests on the contrast between significant within-group changes in PR and mostly non-significant changes in UC, and no between-group test is reported in the abstract. Both groups improved on mMRC, and a difference in significance between groups is not itself evidence of a difference between them.

issues.title: Unequal allocation (27 vs 15), no stated randomisation or baseline adjustment, yet causal 'compared to UC' conclusion
issues.explanation: Patients were 'allocated' to rehabilitation (n=27) or usual care (n=15) with no randomisation, concealment or blinding described, and no baseline comparison or adjustment is given. If allocation was by choice or availability, differences in motivation, severity or access could drive any difference. The conclusion nonetheless states that the programme improves outcomes compared with usual care.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Full-paper evidence of concealed random allocation, or baseline-adjusted between-group analyses showing the same effect.

quotes.text: were allocated to PR (n=27) or usual care (UC) (n=15) groups
Compared to UC, application of a 3-month hybrid IC programme improves exercise tolerance, QoL and functional capacity

second_reader.what_stands: The abstract does report unequal groups (27 vs 15), says only 'allocated', and gives no randomisation method, no baseline comparability by group and no adjustment, yet concludes causally 'Compared to UC ... improves'. The unequal ratio itself is not a flaw, and the abstract format may simply have omitted design details, so what can be said is that the allocation method is unreported and the causal wording is not supported by anything shown here.

issues.title: Small study (42 patients, 15 controls), no sample-size calculation, confident efficacy conclusion
issues.explanation: Only 15 patients form the comparison group and no power calculation is reported. Small samples give imprecise estimates, and the conclusion is worded confidently. The point is secondary to the allocation and analysis problems already raised.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample size calculation supporting these group sizes.

quotes.text: were allocated to PR (n=27) or usual care (UC) (n=15) groups

issues.title: About 15 outcomes across several domains with no primary outcome or correction stated
issues.explanation: Roughly a dozen questionnaires and tests are listed with no primary outcome and no correction. However, the reported within-group p-values are very small, so multiplicity alone would probably not overturn the within-PR improvements. It matters mainly for any between-group claim across all domains.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome (e.g. Tlim) with the other outcomes labelled secondary.

quotes.text: FACIT, CAT, EQ-5D, mMRC, BECK, HADS and Impact Event Scale -Revised (IES-R) questionnaires

issues.title: 'Well accepted' rests on 95% home-session compliance only; no acceptability measure
issues.explanation: Compliance and contact counts show adherence, which is related to but not the same as patient acceptance. No satisfaction or acceptability data are given, and drop-outs from the programme are not reported. The feasibility claim is reasonable; the acceptance wording is slightly beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Patient satisfaction or acceptability data, or low drop-out reported in the full paper.

quotes.text: Compliance with the home -based follow up programme was 95%.
application of a hybrid PR programme is feasible and well accepted from the patients with long COVID-19 syndrome

10.53365/nrfhh.605.headline_claim: Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization (DNS) significantly improves balance and gait problems over six weeks in people with post-COVID condition, supporting its effectiveness as a targeted physiotherapy neuromuscular rehabilitation intervention.
10.53365/nrfhh.605.overall: The balance result (4.17-point gain in the DNS arm against a 3-point MDC, with a significant time-by-group interaction) is reasonably supported for a small six-week trial. The gait benefit is statistically significant but clinically small and below the MDC, and the conclusion overstates it. The conclusion also extends to unmeasured outcomes (pain, brain fog), and the blinding, group-count and registration descriptions are inconsistent, so the headline effectiveness claim should be read as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Tinetti Balance and Gait Assessment score (balance and gait subscales)

issues.title: Conclusion says DNS significantly improves gait though neither arm reached the 3-point MDC (2.55 vs 1.69)
issues.explanation: The Results report that experimental gait improved by 2.55 points and control by 1.69, both under the stated MDC of 3, and that this may not be clinically significant. The abstract conclusion nevertheless states that DNS significantly improves balance and gait problems and supports its effectiveness. Statistical significance is presented as clinical benefit for gait, and the paper's own caveat is missing from the conclusion. The balance result (4.17 vs MDC 3, control 2.07) is better supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a smaller MDC applies to this population, or a conclusion that qualifies the gait result as not clinically significant.

quotes.text: However, neither group reached the MDC threshold.
DNS significantly improves balance and gait problems over six weeks

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does report that neither arm reached the 3-point MDC (2.55 and 1.69), and its own Results caution that gait gains may not be clinically significant, yet the abstract conclusion states DNS 'significantly improves' gait and supports its 'effectiveness' with no mention of this. What is not wrong is the statistical claim: the time and time-by-group effects for gait are statistically significant as reported, so 'significantly' is accurate in the statistical sense only.

issues.title: Conclusion cites pain and brain-fog benefits that were not measured; 'first' claim conflicts with own ref 21
issues.explanation: The only outcomes were Tinetti balance and gait scores. Yet the conclusion refers to potential improvements in pain, and the implications section claims influence on cognitive symptoms including brain fog. The paper also says the work may be the first to test this approach in this population, while its reference 21 is a randomized trial of DNS in post-COVID-19 patients. These statements go beyond a single-centre, six-week trial with two Tinetti outcomes in adults aged 18-45.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Pain or cognitive measures in the trial data, or a clarification that ref 21 is not a comparable post-COVID DNS trial.

quotes.text: demonstrates potential improvements in pain, balance, and gait mechanics
The work may be the first to systematically test the novel approach on this population
not only physical outcomes but also cognitive symptoms, including brain fog
quotes.location: Implications for Physiotherapy Practice and Research

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion refers to improvements in pain and the Implications section to cognitive effects including brain fog, although neither was measured in this study; both are unsupported by the reported data. The 'first' claim, though hedged with 'may', sits alongside the paper's own ref 21, which by its printed title is a prior RCT of DNS in post-COVID patients, so the novelty claim is overstated or at least needs narrowing.

issues.title: 'Double-blind' claim contradicts assessor-blinded design; participants cannot be blind to exercise vs TENS
issues.explanation: The Methods say both participants and assessor were kept blind, yet the same section calls the study assessor-blinded, and the interventions (DNS exercise versus isometrics with TENS) are visibly different. Participant blinding is therefore not credible, and expectation or motivation effects could inflate performance scores on the Tinetti tests. Assessor blinding limits but does not remove this risk, and the blinding procedure itself is not described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A described method by which participants were unaware of their allocation, or a statement that participant blinding was not claimed.

quotes.text: A double-blind trial design was maintained throughout the investigation by keeping both participants and the result assessor blind.
This assessor-blinded randomized control trial (RCT)

issues.title: Abstract leads with pooled time effects; no direct between-group contrast at Week 6, gait interaction small
issues.explanation: For gait, the abstract reports only the main effect of time (F=124.82), which shows both arms improved and says nothing about DNS versus conventional therapy. The differential effect appears only in the Results (interaction p=.006, ηp²=.09), and no Week 6 between-group difference or confidence interval is given. The raw Week 6 gait difference is small (about 0.7 points, 11.38 vs 10.69). The interaction supports some differential benefit, but its size and certainty are not shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported between-group differences at Week 6 (or in change scores) with confidence intervals showing a meaningful advantage for DNS.

quotes.text: Similarly, gait outcomes showed a significant main effect of time, F(2,112) = 124.82, P < .001
The main effect of group was not statistically significant, F(1,56) = 0.06, p = .803
quotes.location: Results, Analysis of the Tinetti Balance Score

issues.title: Text cites Table 3 for experimental-group differences (+2.34, +4.17, +1.83); Table 3 shows pooled -1.62, -3.12, -1.5
issues.explanation: The Results attribute Bonferroni differences of +2.34, +4.17 and +1.83 to the Experimental group and cite Table 3. Table 3 instead prints pooled, negative-signed differences (-1.62, -3.12, -1.5) for both groups combined. The experimental-group pairwise tests and p-values are not shown anywhere, so the claim of significant within-group gains for the experimental group cannot be checked against a table. The numbers reconcile arithmetically, but the sourcing is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A group-specific post-hoc table showing +2.34, +4.17 and +1.83 for the experimental group.

quotes.text: Day 1–Week 3 ≈ +2.34
quotes.location: Results, Tinetti Balance Score, paragraph after Table 2

quotes.text: Bonferroni Post-hoc-Tests RM Factor for Tinetti Balance score

issues.title: Trial registration and ethics numbers printed as placeholders ('XXX'); registration cannot be verified
issues.explanation: The paper states that the protocol was registered and ethically approved, but the identifiers are placeholders. Readers cannot check whether the outcomes were prespecified, and the Methods label all measures as 'primary' with no hierarchy. The efficacy findings cannot be checked against a registered protocol.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A valid registry identifier with a protocol dated before enrolment that lists the same outcomes.

quotes.text: The study protocol was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (XXX)

issues.title: Two arms (n=29 each) in abstract and Methods, but 'three' groups in sample size and baseline results
issues.explanation: The trial has two arms (Group A conventional, Group B DNS), but the sample-size calculation refers to 'three intervention groups' and the baseline comparison to 'three study groups'. This suggests text carried over from another design. The power calculation may not match the analysis actually run, and no third arm is described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a third arm existed, or a correction of the text to two groups.

quotes.text: allocated randomly to two groups (n = 29)
no significant differences between the three study groups
among the three intervention groups

issues.title: Methods name Tukey's HSD post hoc; Abstract and Results report Bonferroni, and no group-by-time contrasts shown
issues.explanation: The Statistical analysis section says Tukey's HSD was used after significant interactions, but every reported post-hoc table is Bonferroni on the time factor. No Tukey contrasts between groups at Week 3 or Week 6 are shown. The mismatch is mostly descriptive, but it means the between-group comparison at each time point was never reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported Tukey group contrasts at each time point, and a Methods statement naming Bonferroni for time contrasts.

quotes.text: Tukey's HSD post hoc analysis was performed
Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc analyses were used for pairwise comparisons

issues.title: Overall age SD 2.33 is impossible given group SDs 8.31 and 9.15; overall mean 31.83 also off
issues.explanation: The Results give the overall age as 31.83 with a spread of 2.33, but Table 1 shows group SDs of 8.31 and 9.15. The pooled SD must be about 8.7, so 2.33 cannot be an SD. The overall mean is also slightly different from the group means' average. This is a minor descriptive error that does not affect the efficacy results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw age data showing an overall SD of 2.33 (impossible given the group SDs).

quotes.text: 58 participants (mean age: 31:83
with a mean age of 31.38 ± 8.31 years

10.53445/batd.1277497.headline_claim: Medicinal leech therapy (MLT) can be used to improve cognitive, autonomic and sleep disorders in patients with post-COVID-19 neurological symptoms.
10.53445/batd.1277497.overall: The conclusion that leech therapy improves cognitive, autonomic and sleep disorders cannot be relied on: it rests on an uncontrolled before-after comparison with unblinded, largely self-reported outcomes and no reported safety data. The same ISI outcome is printed with different values in Tables 2 and 5, and the statistical reporting gives no test statistics or p-values.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; MoCA, PSQI, ISI, ESS and ISSD all presented as outcomes

checklist.control: healthy controls only, no untreated patient comparator

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from uncontrolled pre-post change in 83 treated patients; no untreated patient comparator
issues.explanation: All 83 patients received leech therapy and were compared with themselves over 11 days; the only comparator is a group of 50 healthy people. Natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectation effects and co-interventions cannot be separated from any leech effect. The causal conclusion of benefit is therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data from a concurrent untreated or sham-treated post-COVID group followed over the same period.

quotes.text: the control group - healthy individuals without pathology from the central nervous system and the main group  -  COVID-19  patients
all cognitive, autonomic and sleep disorders of COVID-19 patients were managed using  MLT  in  a  full  11-day  course

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy conclusions rest on before-and-after change in the same 83 treated patients; the only comparator is a healthy control group (n=50) measured once, which cannot show what would have happened to untreated post-COVID patients over 11 days. Table 2 does include a healthy control group, so the paper is not strictly without any comparison group, but it has no untreated patient comparator.

issues.title: Conclusion that MLT managed all disorders and suits neurorehabilitation exceeds uncontrolled data with no safety reporting
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that all cognitive, autonomic and sleep disorders were managed and that MLT can be used for rehabilitation, based on a single-arm study with no concurrent control. No adverse events in the 83 treated patients are reported, although the Discussion itself lists allergy, bleeding and infection as known risks. The claims of efficacy and use go beyond what the design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified safety record for the 83 patients showing few or no adverse events, together with controlled efficacy data.

quotes.text: all cognitive, autonomic and sleep disorders of COVID-19 patients were managed using  MLT  in  a  full  11-day  course
Nevertheless, it should be noted its side effects: allergic reactions, bleeding and infections.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's statement that all disorders were managed, and that MLT is suited to neurorehabilitation, goes beyond uncontrolled before-and-after data, and the paper's own tables show several scales still above healthy-control values at day 11. The paper reports no adverse events from its own patients; the Discussion lists side effects (allergy, bleeding, infection) only generically from the literature, so safety is not evaluated in this cohort.

issues.title: ISI for the same 83 patients differs between Table 2 (18.4/11.5/6.9) and Table 5 (17.5/13.1/8.6)
issues.explanation: Tables 2 and 5 report the Insomnia Severity Index for the same 83 patients at the same three time points, yet baseline, day-6 and day-11 means and SDs all differ. The text says ISI fell by 67%, which fits Table 2 (18.4 to 6.9 = 62.5%) poorly and Table 5 (17.5 to 8.6 = 50.9%) not at all. Which ISI result is correct cannot be determined, so the sleep outcome is unreliable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the two tables used different ISI versions or subsets of patients.

quotes.text: as evidenced by a decrease in the ISI by 67%

issues.title: Paired t-test also used for control-vs-patient comparisons; no test statistics, p-values or multiplicity control
issues.explanation: The Methods say differences between groups and within a group were both tested by the paired t-test, but the healthy controls (n=50) and patients (n=83) are independent groups, so a paired test is inappropriate for that comparison. No test statistics, exact p-values or effect sizes are given; significance appears only as asterisks undefined in any footnote. Many outcomes and two time points are tested with no multiplicity adjustment, weakening the secondary results.
