issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported test statistics and p-values showing an independent-samples test was used for group comparisons, with a stated correction for multiple testing.

quotes.text: The  statistical  significance  of  the  differences between groups and the difference between two variables for the same group was determined by the paired t-test.

10.53625/jirk.v5i3.11105.headline_claim: QFPDT herbal therapy is clinically effective as a supportive therapy for alleviating joint pain in patients with Han Shi Zheng (cold-damp syndrome), and is safe with no serious adverse effects.
10.53625/jirk.v5i3.11105.overall: The finding that VAS fell from baseline in all 30 patients is plausible, but the single-arm, open, 7-day design cannot show that the herbal formula caused the improvement or that it is safe. The headline mean reduction of 3.1 is also inconsistent with the paper's own subgroup means, which imply about 2.5. The 'clinically effective' conclusion should be read as a tentative pilot observation at best.

primary_outcome.name: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) joint pain score, pre vs post 7-day QFPDT

issues.title: Efficacy and causal effect claimed from 30 untreated-comparator-free patients, 7 days, within-group Wilcoxon only
issues.explanation: All 30 patients received the herbal formula with no control group, no randomisation and no blinding, and efficacy rests on a paired before/after Wilcoxon test (Z=4.828). Such a test shows that scores changed, not that the herbal formula caused the change, because natural fluctuation, regression to the mean (patients were enrolled in pain), co-treatment and expectation effects are not separated. The paper nonetheless states that the therapy is clinically effective and has a significant effect, and the Methods describe the design as identifying cause-effect relationships. The conclusion is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or placebo arm with a between-group comparison of VAS change, or explicit reframing of the study as hypothesis-generating only.

quotes.text: These findings demonstrate that QFPDT is clinically effective
Subjek tidak dibagi secara acak
Karena terdapat perbedaan maka dapat disimpulkan bahwa terapi Qing Fei Pai Du Tang berpengaruh signifikan dalam menurunkan nyeri sendi

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's design is a single-arm, non-randomised, 30-patient, 7-day pre-post study analysed only with a within-group Wilcoxon test (Z = 4.828, p < 0.001), which shows only that scores changed. Even so, the Abstract states the findings 'demonstrate that QFPDT is clinically effective', the Methods say the design identifies cause and effect, and the Wilcoxon section concludes the therapy has a significant effect on joint pain. Those claims go beyond what a design with no comparator can support, and no limitation is discussed beyond a brief suggestion to run an RCT in future. The paper's wording

issues.title: Headline mean VAS reduction 3.1 contradicts printed subgroup means (2.875, n=24; 1, n=6), which imply 2.5
issues.explanation: The paper reports an overall mean VAS fall of 3.1 points. It also reports mean falls of 2.875 in the 24 effective patients and 1 in the 6 non-effective patients. An overall mean must lie between its subgroup means, and these weighted means give 2.5, not 3.1. The headline effect size is therefore about 0.6 points too large, or the subgroup table is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired VAS data or Table 6.5 showing a mean fall of 3.1 across all 30 patients, with the subgroup means printed differently (for example, in different units or on a different subset).

quotes.text: Penurunan rata-rata skor VAS sebesar 3,1 poin menunjukkan respon yang kuat secara klinis.
quotes.location: Hasil dan Pembahasan, 1. Hasil Analisis Statistik

quotes.text: rata-rata penurunan nyeri pada pasien efektif
quotes.location: Hasil dan Pembahasan, 4. Pembahasan Hasil Antar Variabel (continues: 2.875 ± 0.899 effective, 1 ± 0 not effective)

quotes.text: 24 pasien efektif dan 6 pasien tidak efektif
quotes.location: Hasil dan Pembahasan, 4. Pembahasan Hasil Antar Variabel

issues.title: Safety and acceptability asserted from a 7-day, 30-patient open study with no adverse-event methods or data
issues.explanation: The conclusion and recommendations call the therapy 'safe' and 'well accepted', and the abstract says no serious adverse effects were reported. The paper contains no description of how adverse events were monitored, no counts or tables of events, and no tolerability or adherence data. With 30 patients followed 7 days, a statement of safety goes beyond what was measured. At most the data support that no serious events were noted.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Methods or tables showing systematic adverse-event collection (for example, daily symptom checks and lab monitoring) with event counts reported.

quotes.text: serious adverse effects were reported
Secara umum, terapi ini aman

issues.title: Text says data are normal as the reason for Wilcoxon, contradicting its own non-normality conclusion
issues.explanation: The normality section concludes the data are not normally distributed (pre-therapy Sig. 0.006). The next sentence says 'because the data are normally distributed' the Wilcoxon test was used. This is self-contradictory, but the test chosen matches the non-normal conclusion. It is a cosmetic error with no effect on the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable. The contradiction is on the page, though a 'tidak' omitted in typing would explain it.

quotes.text: dapat diputuskan bahwa data tidak berdistribusi normal
Karena data berdistribusi normal, maka pengujian menggunakan uji wilcoxon.

10.53730/ijhs.v6ns8.12876.headline_claim: Deep breathing exercise is effective in reducing respiratory problems and complications in post-COVID patients.
10.53730/ijhs.v6ns8.12876.overall: The headline claim that deep breathing exercise is effective is not well supported. The design is a single-group pre-post study with no control, no blinding and a poorly described outcome, so the observed fall in median dyspnoea score (1.00 to 0.00) cannot be attributed to the exercise. The text also cites non-significant chi-square tables (p = 0.24-0.79) as evidence of effectiveness, and has a few internal labelling errors.

primary_outcome.name: Dyspnoea score, pre- vs post-intervention (Wilcoxon signed-rank, within group)

issues.title: Single-group pre-post design with no control cannot support the claim that the exercise is effective
issues.explanation: All 60 patients got the intervention and were compared only with their own baseline. Post-COVID symptoms often improve on their own, and the paper reports no control, blinding, or time frame for reassessment. The Wilcoxon p<0.001 shows that scores changed, not that the exercise caused the change. The conclusion that the exercise is effective and 'reduces complications' goes beyond what this design shows, and complications were not measured.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group, or evidence that symptoms in comparable untreated patients did not improve over the same interval.

quotes.text: preexperimental pre-test post-test one group design was chosen for the study.
This study concludes that the practice of deep breathing exercise is an effective

second_reader.what_stands: The paper uses a one-group pre-test/post-test design with no control group and still states causally that deep breathing exercise 'is effective'. This design can show that scores fell after the intervention, but cannot attribute the fall to the exercise, because natural recovery, regression to the mean and other time-related changes are not controlled. The authors do not acknowledge this as a limitation beyond a suggestion to use a quasi-experimental design in future.

issues.title: Text calls Table 2.1 significant at p<0.05 and infers effectiveness; its p-values are 0.24-0.79
issues.explanation: After Table 2.1 the paper says the result is significant at p<0.05 and therefore the exercise is effective. The table's chi-square p-values are all above 0.05 (cold 0.62, cough 0.79, chest pain 0.24). The test relates symptoms to dyspnoea category and does not compare pre- and post-intervention status. The sentence is unsupported by its own table, and it is repeated in the Discussion. The Wilcoxon result in Table 2.2 is the only inferential result bearing on change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated alpha above 0.24, or a pre-post test that the sentence was clearly referring to.

quotes.text: This shows result is significant at
The Chi square and p value shows the association between the respiratory problems and dyspnoea category

issues.title: Dyspnoea outcome: reliability method named but no kappa value or scoring rules reported
issues.explanation: The paper names an inter-rater observation method with Cohen's kappa but never gives the kappa value. It also does not say how the dyspnoea category was scored. The 'self-instructed' tool and an unblinded investigator-assessed outcome leave room for measurement bias in the pre-post change. The reader cannot judge how reliable the outcome is.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported kappa with a scoring definition and a statement that assessors were independent of the intervention delivery.

quotes.text: inter-rater observation method and it was measured by

issues.title: Results text says 70% had chest pain; Table 1, Abstract and Discussion give 30% (18/60)
issues.explanation: The sentence under Table 1 says 70% of patients reported chest pain and 30% did not. Table 1 shows the reverse: 18 yes (30.0%) and 42 no (70.0%). The Abstract and Discussion agree with the table, so only this sentence is wrong. It is a reporting slip that does not touch the main finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or data source showing that 70% reported chest pain.

quotes.text: Majority 70% patient were reported chest pain and 30% of patient had not chest pain problem.
according to the study majority 30% patients were complained of chest pain

issues.title: No ethics approval or participant consent statement in an intervention study of 60 patients
issues.explanation: Patients received an intervention and were assessed before and after. The text contains no statement of ethics committee approval or informed consent. This could be an omission and cannot be resolved from the paper. It does not alter the numerical results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ethics committee approval number or consent statement from the authors or the journal record.

quotes.text: The study concluded that the deep breathing exercise was effective in terms of reducing the respiratory problems and complications in post covid patients.

issues.title: 43.3% age group labelled 35-60 years in Discussion but 36-50 years in Results and Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results and Table 2 put 26 of 60 patients (43.3%) in the 36-50 band. The Discussion gives the same 43.3% as the group aged 35-60. A 35-60 band would also overlap other bands and would not give 43.3%. This is a minor labelling error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different age banding defined elsewhere in the paper under which 43.3% corresponds to 35-60 years.

quotes.text: 43.3%  patient  from  age  group  of  35-60  years
majority 43.3% patient from age group of 36-50 years

10.54033/cadpedv21n6-080.headline_claim: Individualized, supervised physical rehabilitation program (PRP) produces large improvements in peripheral and respiratory muscle strength and cardiorespiratory fitness in post-COVID-19 survivors, while heart-rate-recovery-based mortality risk did not change.
10.54033/cadpedv21n6-080.overall: The data show large improvements in strength and estimated fitness in 18 completers, but the single-arm, completers-only design cannot attribute these to the rehabilitation programme, so the 'great effect' and 'essential' claims are overstated. Several printed effect sizes do not reproduce from the tables, and the labels are inconsistent between the abstract and the tables. The direction of the main findings is probably real, but their size and causal attribution are weakly supported.

primary_outcome.name: Peripheral and respiratory muscle strength and exercise capacity (pre- vs post-PRP); primary objective stated as effect of PRP on muscle strength and exercise capacity

issues.title: Causal 'great effect' of PRP and 'essential' claim rest on a single-arm, 18-completer pre-post cohort
issues.explanation: All results compare baseline with post-PRP in one uncontrolled group, so natural recovery, learning on the step test and regression to the mean cannot be separated from the programme's effect. The Conclusion nevertheless emphasises the 'great effect' of PRP and calls such strategies 'essential' to mitigate COVID-19 sequelae. The authors list the missing control group only as a limitation. At most the data show improvement over time in a self-selected group of completers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical control group, or analysis of stable pre-programme baselines, showing no spontaneous improvement over the same period.

quotes.text: we did not have a control group for comparing the intervention, which may introduce bias
are essential to mitigate and /or resolve the sequelae left by COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The causal 'great effect' and 'essential' statements rest on an uncontrolled single-arm pre-post study of 18 completers. The authors do disclose the lack of a control group, but the conclusion does not temper its wording to match, and spontaneous recovery and learning effects are not discussed.

issues.title: Printed Cohen's d values (HGS 2.7, MEP 2.7, 6MST 1.6) do not reproduce from the tabulated means and SDs
issues.explanation: The paper does not state how d was computed. Dividing each mean change by the SD of the change gives about 1.1 for HGS, 1.3 for MEP and 1.4 for the 6MST, against printed values of 2.7, 2.7 and 1.6. The HGS and MEP rows print the identical d and CI (2.7, 2.0-3.4) despite different data, which suggests a copy error. The 'huge' label for these outcomes, repeated in the abstract and Discussion, is not supported by the tabulated data. The effects remain large by any of these calculations.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated d formula (for example one using a different SD) that reproduces 2.7 for both HGS and MEP from the raw data.

quotes.text: (47.2±33.4 number of steps)

second_reader.what_stands: The printed Cohen's d values for HGS (2.7), MEP (2.7) and 6MST (1.6) cannot be reproduced from the tabulated means and SDs under either a pooled-SD or a paired definition. The reproduced values are about 0.5 to 1.1 for HGS, 0.7 to 1.3 for MEP and 1.2 to 1.4 for 6MST. HGS and MEP share an identical d and CI despite different data, and the Methods do not say which d formula was used.

issues.title: 10 of 28 included patients (35.7%) excluded as dropouts; analysis is completers only; 50 selected vs 28 included unexplained
issues.explanation: Only the 18 patients who finished the programme are analysed, with no intention-to-treat or missing-data handling. Dropouts are likely to be those with worse tolerance or outcomes, which would inflate the average gains. The Methods also state that 50 subjects were selected, but the cohort is 28, and the gap of 22 is not explained in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram showing that the 22 extra subjects never met inclusion criteria, plus baseline data showing dropouts resembled completers.

quotes.text: 28 patients post COVID-19 were included in the study; however, 10 patients withdrew from treatment
We selected 50 subjects diagnosed with COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The 35.7% attrition (10 of 28) is correct, and all analyses are completers-only with no ITT or imputed analysis and no comparison of dropouts with completers. The gap between 50 selected and 28 included is not explained in the text, though Figure 1 may account for it and is not available in the extracted text.

issues.title: About 20 uncorrected secondary tests; SpO2 and RR benefits claimed at p = 0.015-0.039
issues.explanation: The paper states that p < 0.05 was significant for all tests, with no multiplicity control, across dozens of outcomes in Tables 2 and 3. The Conclusion cites improved oxygen saturation and breathing work, which rest on p-values around 0.02 to 0.04. With this many tests, some of those would be expected by chance. The main strength and fitness findings are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy limiting primary tests to the strength and fitness outcomes, with SpO2 and RR labelled exploratory.

quotes.text: Values of p <0.05 were considered statistically significant for all tests.
Cohen's d test was used to calculate the effect size, when a statistically significant difference was reached.

issues.title: No a priori sample size; post hoc power of 0.999 derived from the observed 6MST effect (n = 18)
issues.explanation: The authors report a post hoc power of 0.999 using the observed 6MST difference, which merely restates the p-value and does not show the study was adequately designed. No pre-specified sample size or target is given, and the test is described as a 'two-way independent t-test' although the data are paired. The 'large sample power' wording overstates the strength of the evidence from 18 patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registered protocol with an a priori sample size calculation.

quotes.text: a post hoc calculation of the power of the sample was performed for the results of the comparison between baseline and post-PRP period for patients (n=18)
This was a single center study with a small sample size.

issues.title: VO2peak is a questionnaire-derived estimate (0.43 x DASI + 9.6), not measured, yet presented as fitness gain
issues.explanation: The headline 'cardiorespiratory fitness' gain (estimated VO2peak 17.2 to 27.8) is computed from patient-reported daily-activity scores, not from an exercise test with gas analysis. Patients who know they completed rehabilitation may report more activity. The formula is a published one, but the paper gives no evidence of its accuracy in post-COVID patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Measured VO2peak (cardiopulmonary exercise test) in the same patients, or validation of the DASI equation in post-COVID cohorts.

quotes.text: VO2peak = 0.43 x DASI + 9.6
The VO2peak value was estimated according to the level of physical activity described by the patient

issues.title: Portuguese abstract labels d = 2.3 (VO2peak) and d = 2.7 (MEP) 'Muito grande'; Tables 2-3 classify both as huge
issues.explanation: The Portuguese abstract calls the VO2peak (d 2.3) and MEP (d 2.7) effects 'Muito grande' (very large). The Results and Tables 2 and 3 call both 'huge', and the Methods scale puts d of 2.0 or more at huge. The Spanish abstract uses 'Enorme' for these results. The slip is confined to the Portuguese abstract labels. It affects the effect-size wording, not the estimates.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Portuguese-language scale in the paper that defines 'Muito grande' to include d of 2.0 or more.

quotes.text: PEmáx IC95% 2,7 (2,0-3,4), p=0. 001, Muito grande
MEP ( p =0.001, huge)

issues.title: Table 3 resting SpO2: means 94.9 and 96.2 imply change 1.3, but delta printed as 1.6
issues.explanation: The resting SpO2 means before and after PRP differ by 1.3 points, yet the delta column prints 1.6. For the paired data with n = 18 these should agree to rounding. Other rows of the table reconcile, so this looks like a transcription error in one number. It is a small secondary outcome and does not change the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired data showing a mean change of 1.6, for example because the means were calculated on different subsets.

issues.title: Table 1 CT percentages (33.3, 38.9) use a base of 18, but the footnote says CT was available in 13
issues.explanation: The CT counts (6 and 7) sum to 13, matching the footnote. The printed percentages are computed over 18, so the rows sum to 72.2% rather than 100%. Over the 13 patients with CT they would be 46.2% and 53.8%. It is a descriptive baseline table and no result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the CT percentages are deliberately over all 18 patients with 5 missing.

quotes.text: # CT: chest computed tomography n= 13 subjects

quotes.location: Table 1, pulmonary involvement by CT, <= 50% row

10.54033/cadpedv21n7-221.headline_claim: A six-week cardiopulmonary rehabilitation protocol improved lung function, respiratory muscle function and dyspnea in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome compared with a control group.
10.54033/cadpedv21n7-221.overall: The respiratory muscle strength, endurance and dyspnea benefits are supported by significant between-group differences, though dyspnea is subjective and unblinded. The headline claim that rehabilitation improved lung function, the primary outcome, rests on within-group change; the between-group comparison was null and baseline-imbalanced. Several small table and flow errors (control-group changes, 78 vs 79, a 6.71 percentage) are reporting slips that do not change the main findings.

primary_outcome.name: Lung function (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, PEF)

issues.title: Lung-function improvement claimed from CRG change over baseline; between-group FVC, FEV1, PEF differences not significant
issues.explanation: Lung function is the primary outcome, and Table 3 shows no significant between-group difference for any lung-function variable. The Abstract and Conclusion nonetheless say the protocol improved lung function, based on the CRG's change from baseline in an unblinded trial. Within-group change cannot be attributed to the intervention. The recommendation for clinical use rests on secondary outcomes only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group test of change from baseline (or baseline-adjusted) showing a significant lung-function effect.

quotes.text: A intervenção melhorou a CVF, VEF1 e PEF dos pacientes após seis semanas de reabilitação.
Although the CRG presented increased lung function (FVC, FEV1, and PEF) after six weeks, values did not differ from CG.
The cardiopulmonary rehabilitation improved lung and respiratory muscle function and reduced perceived dyspnea

second_reader.what_stands: The Abstract and Conclusion present improved lung function (FVC, FEV1, PEF) as an effect of the intervention, but the support is only the CRG pre-post change; the paper's own Results say the between-group differences did not differ from CG (all CIs include zero). The Results and Discussion state the within-group basis accurately, so the problem lies in the unqualified Abstract and Conclusion wording; also, the CG's own change over baseline was not significant, but no between-group test supports a lung-function effect, and lung function was the declared primary outcome.

issues.title: Self-reported Borg dyspnea difference (-2.48) from unblinded participants against an attention-control lecture arm
issues.explanation: Participants knew they were receiving exercise rehabilitation or lectures, and the dyspnea score is subjective. The Conclusion lists placebo effects among limitations but still states that perceived dyspnea was reduced. The dyspnea result is therefore likely overstated, though the size of the effect makes some real benefit plausible.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of participant blinding or a sham-controlled design.

quotes.text: Dyspnea was assessed after the respiratory muscle endurance test using the modified Borg scale
whereas the CG participated in remote lectures (twice a week for six weeks)

issues.title: Table 3 'intergroup difference' column equals the six-week between-group difference, not the change difference; FVC baseline imbalance 2.04 vs 2.67 L
issues.explanation: The column is headed 'Six weeks - Baseline', but its values equal the difference of six-week means (FVC 2.36 - 2.58 = -0.22), not the difference in change. CRG started with much lower FVC than CG, so the endpoint comparison favours CG and may hide a CRG improvement. A difference in change would be 0.31 - (-0.08) = 0.39 L. This affects the non-significant lung-function comparison, whose direction of error is toward understating the effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Model output showing the interaction (group x time) estimates, which would be the baseline-adjusted comparison.

quotes.text: Intergroup difference

issues.title: Table 3 control-group changes disagree with printed means: dyspnea -0.60 vs -0.06, FEV1 0.08 vs 0.01, FEV1/FVC 3.34 vs 4.34
issues.explanation: In three control-group rows of Table 3 the six-weeks-minus-baseline change does not equal the difference of the printed means. The dyspnea CI is centred on -0.06, not -0.60, so the printed change appears to be a slip. The FEV1 and FEV1/FVC rows have the same kind of mismatch. These are reporting errors in the control arm; none changes the significance pattern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction or supplementary data showing the printed changes derive from the model with different underlying means.

quotes.location: Table 3, Dyspnea row, CG intragroup difference
Table 3, FEV 1 (L) row, CG intragroup difference
Table 3, FEV 1 /FVC (%) row, CG intragroup difference

script.explanation: the estimate -0.6 is not the arithmetic midpoint of [-1.08, 0.96] (expected about -0.0600) -- note that bootstrap, exact, profile-likelihood, bias-corrected and Fieller intervals are all legitimately asymmetric, and this paper does not say which method it used, so confirm the method before treating this as a finding

issues.title: Sample size calculation gives no effect size or target n; trial of 34 (33 analysed) likely underpowered for between-group lung-function tests
issues.explanation: The authors say the effect size could not be calculated and cite a single study of older patients. They give no target sample size or effect size. With 17 and 16 per arm, the wide CIs on lung-function differences cannot rule out meaningful effects either way, so the non-significant results are inconclusive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported G*Power input (effect size, target n) showing the achieved sample was adequate for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: Randomized clinical trials with patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome are scarce, hampering the effect size calculation.
We recommend studies with larger sample sizes and different patient populations

issues.title: Equal randomization of 34 plus one CRG dropout would give CRG 16/CG 17; tables print CRG 17/CG 16
issues.explanation: The Methods say patients were equally randomized, and the Results say one CRG patient dropped out of 34. A 17/17 split would therefore leave CRG 16 and CG 17, the reverse of Tables 2 and 3. Unequal allocation (18/16) would explain the tables, but the paper's text does not give the randomized arm sizes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing 18 randomized to CRG and 16 to CG.

quotes.text: Patients were equally randomized (www.random.org) into cardiopulmonary rehabilitation
One patient from the CRG dropped out

issues.title: Table 2 CRG ICU 'No' percentage printed 6.71; 11/17 gives 64.71
issues.explanation: The ICU counts sum to the hospitalized subgroup, which is a sensible denominator for counts. The percentages are taken over the whole group, though, and the CRG 'no' percentage 6.71 matches neither basis. It is most likely a typo for 64.71. Nothing else in the paper depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table showing 64.71, or a stated different denominator reproducing 6.71.

quotes.location: Table 2, ICU admission row, CRG column

script.explanation: 11/17 = 64.71%, but the paper prints 6.71, outside the rounding interval [6.71, 6.72]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 163.9 rather than 17.

issues.title: Flow text: 78 assessed, 45 excluded, 34 included does not add up (79)
issues.explanation: The Results say 78 patients were assessed, 45 excluded and 34 included, which sums to 79. One of the three numbers is off by one. The trial's randomized and analysed totals are otherwise consistent with 34 and 33, so this is a small reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 1 showing 79 assessed, or 33 included.

quotes.text: Seventy-eight  patients  were  assessed  for  eligibility.  Of  these,  45  were excluded

script.explanation: The participant flow does not reconcile: 'assessed' (n=78) minus its 1 stated exclusion(s) (45) leaves 33, but 'included' reports 34 -- 1 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

10.5455/njppp.2024.14.04187202411052024.headline_claim: Nintedanib might have therapeutic benefits in improving pulmonary function in patients with lung fibrosis following COVID-19 disease.
10.5455/njppp.2024.14.04187202411052024.overall: The headline claim of improved spirometry with nintedanib rests on a small, unblinded study with unclear allocation and an unverified control arm whose day-90 values replicate baseline. The disease-modification conclusion goes well beyond 90 days of spirometry. Only a tentative signal of benefit can be taken from the paper.

primary_outcome.name: Spirometric parameters (FEV1, FVC, PEFR, FEV1/FVC) at day 90

issues.title: Category-2 day-90 values in Table 4 are identical to its day-1 values in Table 2 for 7 of 8 variables
issues.explanation: Table 4's control-arm means and SDs for FEV1, FVC, FVC%, PEFR, PEFR%, FEV1/FVC and FEV1/FVC% match the day-1 values in Table 2 exactly, with only FEV1% differing slightly (28.3 vs 28.33). Real repeat spirometry in 25 patients over three months would not reproduce every mean and SD to two decimals. Since the between-group day-90 comparison is the main evidence of benefit, it cannot be trusted until the control data are verified; the discussion's 'significant difference in both categories' also has no supporting analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source spirometry records showing the control group's day-90 values happen to equal their baseline values.

quotes.location: Table 2 (Cat-2 FEV1, day 1) and Table 4 (Cat-2 FEV1, day 90)
Table 2 FVC% day 1 and Table 4 FVC% day 90, Category-2

second_reader.what_stands: Category-2 day-90 means and SDs in Table 4 are exactly identical to the day-1 values in Table 2 for 7 of 8 variables, with the eighth (FEV1%) differing only by 0.03 in the mean (28.30 vs 28.33) and having the same SD. The paper gives no explanation, and no within-group Category-2 comparison is reported, so whether this is a true absence of change or a tabulation problem cannot be determined, but the identity itself is present.

issues.title: Conclusion of disease modification drawn from one 90-day spirometry comparison in 50 patients
issues.explanation: The data are two spirometry measurements 90 days apart in 25 patients per arm, with no imaging, symptoms, mortality or longer follow-up. A short-term rise in spirometry values does not show that progression of fibrosis was prevented or that the disease outcome was modified. The same short follow-up (c5) is covered here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Longer-term follow-up with progression endpoints (serial imaging, FVC decline over 12 months) showing a durable difference.

quotes.text: establish the possible role of nintedanib in preventing the progression of the disease process and thus modify the disease outcome
The patients of both categories were instructed to report again on day 90.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion that the findings help establish a role in preventing progression and modifying disease outcome rests on a single 90-day spirometry comparison in about 50 patients, with no progression or clinical outcome measures and no longer follow-up. The wording is partly hedged ('might', 'possible role') and the small sample is acknowledged, but the disease-modification inference goes beyond what the data can show.

issues.title: Allocation described as random in a study labelled observational; method, concealment and blinding not given
issues.explanation: The Methods call the study observational and prospective yet say patients were randomly distributed into two equal categories. No sequence generation, concealment or blinding of the spirometry operator is described, and the controls received no placebo. If allocation was by clinicians or convenience, the groups may differ in unmeasured ways (weight and BMI already differ), so the day-90 differences cannot be attributed to nintedanib.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a concealed random sequence and blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: The total number of study subjects was randomly distributed into two equal categories.
This observational prospective study

second_reader.what_stands: The paper labels the study observational yet says subjects were randomly distributed into two equal groups, and gives no randomisation method, allocation concealment or blinding. The design is therefore unclear, and the comparison cannot be treated as a randomised one.

issues.title: Benefit supported by within-group day 1 vs 90 change in nintedanib arm; no between-group change analysis
issues.explanation: Table 3 tests only the nintedanib group against its own baseline, and the Results and Discussion cite this as evidence of benefit. Without the control group's own change, recovery over time or learning effects on spirometry cannot be separated from drug effect. The between-group day-90 comparison is the relevant test, but it is not an analysis of change and it is undermined by the Table 4 problem noted separately.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group analysis of change from baseline (or ANCOVA on day-90 values adjusted for baseline) showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Comparison of spirometry variables in patients of Category-1 between day 1 and day 90
Significant improvement of all the spirometric parameters was observed on day 90 in comparison to day 1.

issues.title: No sample size calculation; 25 patients per arm, acknowledged as main limitation
issues.explanation: No power calculation is reported and each arm has about 25 patients. The authors acknowledge this, and the conclusion is hedged, so this alone weakens rather than invalidates the findings. The larger issues are the unclear allocation and the Table 4 values.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample size calculation in a protocol.

quotes.text: The main limitation of our study was the small sample size

issues.title: Baseline p-values (weight 0.213, BMI 0.253, PEFR% 0.24) do not match their means and SDs at n≈25 per arm
issues.explanation: Recomputing a pooled t-test from the printed means and SDs (assuming 25 per arm) gives about p=0.04 for weight, 0.07 for BMI and 0.04 for PEFR%, versus printed 0.213, 0.253 and 0.24. The group sizes are inferred, not printed, so this is tentative. If correct, baseline imbalance in weight and PEFR% is larger than the paper reports, undermining the claim of matched groups.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Group sizes very different from 25, or a different test being used to produce these p-values.

issues.title: No registration or ethics approval identifier reported for a prospective drug comparison
issues.explanation: The paper says only that it followed institutional ethics committee guidelines; no approval number or registry entry is given. Because the primary outcome is not defined in advance, the choice of eight spirometry variables cannot be checked against a plan. The impact on the conclusion is limited.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or protocol with a primary outcome defined before enrolment.

quotes.text: abiding by the guidelines of the institutional ethics committee

10.5535/arm.23060.headline_claim: A telerehabilitation pulmonary exercise program is superior to no rehabilitation for exercise capacity and health-related quality of life in young females after mild-to-moderate long COVID-19, with no effect on lung function.
10.5535/arm.23060.overall: The finding of a larger 6-minute walk distance and higher self-reported SF-36 scores in the exercise arm is internally consistent: the percentages, mean differences and Table 1 t-values recompute correctly. However, the 6MWT was not a registered primary outcome, and the SF-36 benefit comes from unblinded participants compared with a minimal-contact control. The conclusions should be read as tentative evidence from a small, single-site trial in young women.

primary_outcome.name: 6-minute walk distance (6MWT); SF-36 HRQOL and spirometry also reported

primary_outcomes.measure: Health-related quality of life, Medical Outcomes Study short-form (SF-36)
Health-related quality of life, Medical Outcomes Study short-form (SF-36)

issues.title: Self-reported SF-36 benefit from an unblinded exercise program versus a 10-minute education control
issues.explanation: SF-36 is a registered primary outcome and is completed by participants who know they got the supervised program. The control arm got only brief written and verbal education, so contact time, attention and expectation differ greatly between arms. The limitations section does not mention this. The HRQOL conclusion is therefore tentative, likely overstated, and not isolated to the exercise content.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of participant-blinded or attention-matched control, or an objective corroborating outcome for HRQOL.

quotes.text: It was not possible to blind the treating therapists who participated in the study due to the nature of study procedures.
The participants in the control group got written instructions on an explanatory note and prescribed educational presentations from physiotherapists for 10 minutes.
After therapy, the intervention group's HRQOL significantly improved when compared to the control group's (p=0.001).

second_reader.what_stands: The SF-36 outcome is self-reported by participants who knew they were receiving a supervised exercise program rather than a 10-minute education session, and the paper reports blinding only of the evaluating therapist. The control group is not attention-matched, and the limitations section does not discuss participant unblinding or expectation effects on a self-reported outcome. This is a risk of bias, not proof that the effect is bias. The unblinded self-report design and the minimal control may account for some of the 11.87 to 17.68 point between-group differences. The abstract and conclusion

issues.title: Sample size and headline rest on 6MWT, which is not a registered primary outcome (SF-36, respiratory function)
issues.explanation: The registry lists SF-36 and respiratory function at baseline and 6 weeks as the primary outcomes. The paper names no primary outcome, powers the trial on the 6MWT, and puts the 6MWT first in the abstract and title. All registered outcomes are reported, including the null lung-function result, so this is a mismatch in emphasis and pre-specification rather than hidden outcomes. The 6MWT result cannot be treated as a pre-specified primary finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing the 6MWT was registered as a primary outcome, or a paper statement designating the primary outcomes consistently with the registry.

quotes.text: based on data of 6-minute walk test (6MWT) derived from pilot study conducted on 5 subjects in each group
The investigation was prospectively listed on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05172102).

10.55572/jms.v2i2.51.headline_claim: Structured cardiopulmonary exercise training at moderate or high intensity increases functional capacity in post-COVID health workers compared with a control group, with no significant difference between the two intensities, and this improvement is said to improve quality of life.
10.55572/jms.v2i2.51.overall: The finding that VO2 rose in the trained groups and not in the control is plausible, but it rests on small, non-randomised, age-unmatched groups with no baseline comparison or power calculation. The 'no difference between intensities' statement is weak evidence given 10 per arm, and the quality-of-life conclusion is unsupported. Baseline tables also contain internal inconsistencies, which lowers confidence in the reporting overall.

primary_outcome.name: VO2 (ml/kgBB/menit) as the measure of functional capacity

issues.title: Non-randomised, unblinded no-training control of mixed age (20-58) compared with age-split training arms
issues.explanation: Participants were enrolled consecutively and by quota, with no randomisation or allocation concealment, and the control group spans 20-58 years while training arms are split by age. Control and treated groups were not shown to be comparable at baseline, and no baseline VO2 or adjustment is reported. The finding that training raises VO2 is plausible, but the between-group p-values cannot be attributed to training alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of random allocation or a baseline-adjusted analysis showing comparable groups.

quotes.text: Kelompok kontrol terdiri dari usia 20-58 tahun.
Kelompok perlakuan pertama usia 20-40 tahun.

second_reader.what_stands: The control group is non-randomised, received no training, and has no stated blinding or any other control for expectation; its stated age range (20-58) spans both treatment age bands, whereas the treatment arms are split by age (20-40 and 41-58). However, the printed control ages show it is almost entirely young (9 of 10 aged ≤40, mean 34.5), so it is not truly mixed in age and resembles treatment A rather than B; the compared B-moderate arm (mean 47.22) therefore differs in age from its comparator, and the paper does not adjust for age. The point is true about the design and the stated age r

issues.title: Moderate-vs-high intensity 'no difference' rests on 10 per arm, no power calculation, p=0.496
issues.explanation: The sample size of 10 per group was set by quota, with no calculation of power to detect a difference between intensities. A non-significant result in such small groups does not show the intensities are equivalent, yet the abstract and discussion treat it as supportive evidence of equal effect. The B-group high-intensity arm has a single participant, so no comparison is possible there.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified equivalence margin and power analysis, or a confidence interval for the intensity difference excluding a clinically relevant effect.

quotes.text: Sehingga besar sampel minimal yang dibutuhkan ialah 10 Tenaga kesehatan
Pada kelompok B intensitas tinggi dilaporkan terdapat selisih VO2 (1.75 ml/kgBB/menit) namun hanya terdapat 1 orang sampel (Case Report).

issues.title: Conclusion asserts improved quality of life, but no quality-of-life outcome was measured
issues.explanation: The abstract and conclusion state that the increase in functional capacity will improve quality of life in post-COVID patients. The study measured only VO2 and reports no quality-of-life or symptom outcome. This claim is an extrapolation, not a result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A quality-of-life instrument administered and analysed in this study.

quotes.text: Peningkatan kapasitas fungsional akan meningkatkan kualitas hidup pada penderita Sindroma Pasca COVID 19.

issues.title: No ethics approval or trial registration statement in a prospective intervention study
issues.explanation: The study ran from May to October 2021 with informed consent and a 12-session intervention. The paper contains no ethics approval or registry statement, so prospective registration and the pre-specified outcome cannot be checked. This may be a reporting omission rather than a failure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ethics approval number or registry identifier dated before enrolment.

quotes.text: Waktu yang diperlukan untuk penelitian ini dimulai dari bulan Mei sampai bulan Oktober 2021.

issues.title: Methods list t-tests but Results use Mann-Whitney for control comparisons; test for Table 3 unstated
issues.explanation: The Methods name paired and unpaired t-tests, but the control comparisons use Mann-Whitney, and the test behind the Table 3 p-values (including p=1.0 for control) is not stated. The conditional wording in Methods makes a nonparametric switch plausible, but normality testing is not reported. Table 4 is also called 'multivariate' although it contains pairwise tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement naming the nonparametric tests and normality assessment used for each table.

quotes.text: T-test tidak berpasangan untuk
dengan Uji Mann Whitney didapatkan bahwa Selisih VO2

issues.title: Baseline sex and complaint counts in text/Table 2 disagree with Table 1 for group A (e.g. 8 vs 4 females)
issues.explanation: For group A moderate intensity the text and Table 2 give 8 females and 2 males, but Table 1 rows A1-A10 show 4 females and 6 males. For group A high intensity the text gives 1 female and 9 males, but Table 1 shows 5 and 5. Complaint percentages also differ: fatigue is 100% for A moderate in the text but only 9 of 10 in Table 1 (A7 lists headache only), and 60% for A high in the text versus 8 of 10 in Table 1. These are baseline descriptors, so the VO2 results are not directly affected, but the baseline description cannot be trusted as printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected or alternative Table 1 coding showing 8 females in A1-A10 and 1 female in A11-A20.

quotes.text: laki -laki sebanyak 2 sampel dan Perempuan ialah 8 sampel
laki -laki sebanyak 9 sampel dan Perempuan ialah 1 sampel

10.5606/kbbu.2024.88700.headline_claim: Long-term olfactory training is an effective treatment for persistent olfactory dysfunction after COVID-19, increasing olfactory sensitivity over 3 to 12 months.
10.5606/kbbu.2024.88700.overall: The paper shows that self-rated smell scores are higher at 3 to 12 months than at a baseline of 0, but the single-arm, open-label design, completer-only analysis and subjective outcome mean it cannot show that training caused the improvement. The conclusion that training is effective is not supported as stated; the data are best read as descriptive of a self-selected group of adherent patients.

primary_outcome.name: Patient-rated olfactory VAS score (0-10) at 3, 6 and 12 months

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from single-arm before-after data; 12-month recovery not separable from natural course
issues.explanation: All patients received olfactory training and were compared with a baseline score of 0, so improvement over 3 to 12 months cannot be attributed to training rather than continued spontaneous recovery. The authors note the lack of a control group but argue that requiring 2 months of persistence reduced spontaneous recovery, which does not remove it over a further year. The conclusion that training increases olfactory sensitivity is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent untrained control group, or historical data showing minimal recovery beyond 2 months in comparable patients.

quotes.text: The lack of a control group can be considered another limitation.
In conclusion, OT  treatment  in  patients with persistent  PIOD  that  developed  after  COVID-19 infection  increases  olfactory  sensitivity.

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy is claimed (Abstract: 'effective treatment'; Conclusion: OT 'increases olfactory sensitivity') from a single-arm before-after series with no control group, so gains over 12 months cannot be separated from natural recovery. The authors acknowledge the missing control group and the 2-month persistence criterion, but that criterion only partly reduces the problem and does not support a causal conclusion.

issues.title: Patient-rated, non-validated 0-10 smell VAS in an open-label study, with no objective olfactory test
issues.explanation: The only outcome is a self-rated 0-10 score given by patients who know they are being trained, so expectation effects can inflate improvement. No validated psychophysical smell test was used, and the scale was also used to classify recovery categories. This weakens the size of the effect more than its existence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Objective validated olfactory testing (e.g. Sniffin' Sticks) showing concordant improvement.

quotes.text: scored from a total of 10 points by the patients
Patient evaluations were made with a subjective questionnaire rather  than  objective  and  specific  smell  tests.

second_reader.what_stands: The only outcome is a patient-rated 0-10 smell VAS, with no validation cited and no objective olfactory test, in an open-label single-arm study; the authors openly state the lack of objective testing as a limitation. The paper does not describe blinding or a validation of the scale, and the conclusions do not scale back to reflect the subjective outcome.

issues.title: Completer-only analysis: 37 of 120 (30.8%) excluded, mostly non-attenders, no ITT or sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: Results cover only the 83 patients who attended and trained regularly, and the conclusion of effectiveness is drawn without considering what happened to the 35 who dropped out. Dropout related to lack of benefit would inflate the improvement. No worst-case or intention-to-treat analysis is shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Outcome data for the 35 non-attenders, or an analysis showing results hold under missing-not-at-random assumptions.

quotes.text: 35 who could not comply with the OT treatment and did not attend follow-up appointments
Patients  who  did  not  perform  the training regularly were excluded from the study.

second_reader.what_stands: 37 of 120 patients (30.8%) were dropped, 35 of them for non-compliance or non-attendance, and only the 83 completers were analysed, with no ITT, imputation or sensitivity analysis. This can inflate the apparent recovery, since patients without benefit may be more likely to stop; the paper does not discuss this attrition as a limitation. The 'two for new hypertension' exclusion is a minor, defensible part of the 37.

issues.title: Kruskal-Wallis used on repeated measures at 3, 6, 12 months; p=0.0001 does not test change from baseline
issues.explanation: The single p-value comes from a test for independent groups applied to repeated measurements in the same 83 patients, and it compares only the three post-treatment time points. It therefore says nothing formal about improvement from the baseline of 0, and the claim that longer training increases recovery rests on a mismatched test. Ignoring pairing usually makes the test conservative, so the direction is uncertain, but the reported inference is not valid as stated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A repeated-measures analysis (Friedman or mixed model) reproducing the significance, with baseline included.

quotes.text: the nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance was used in the comparisons
The mean VAS score after starting treatment was 6.95±2.28 at three months, 7.59±2.13 at six months, and 7.96±1.97 at 12 months (p=0.0001; Table 1).

10.5606/tftrd.2023.11605.headline_claim: An eight-week yoga-based exercise program could be an effective, reliable and complementary treatment for post-COVID-19 healthcare professionals, improving functional capacity, dyspnea, QoL, depression, anxiety and sleep.
10.5606/tftrd.2023.11605.overall: The conclusion that yoga is an effective treatment is not well supported: allocation was by availability, baselines differed markedly, and most between-group tests were null, while the Discussion states several advantages over controls that the Results contradict. Within-group improvements in the yoga arm are plausible but cannot be attributed to the program. Numeric slips (the SD of change for anxiety, the control percentage, the 6MWT change) are minor but show weak internal checking.

primary_outcome.name: Not named by the authors; the 6-minute walk test (functional capacity) is reported first

checklist.control: non-intervention group (not allocated at random), not 'none'

issues.title: Non-random, self-selected controls with large baseline imbalance (6MWT 430 vs 469 m; anxiety 16.2 vs 10)
issues.explanation: Controls were staff who could not commit to the sessions, so allocation depended on availability and motivation. At baseline the yoga group had a much lower 6MWT, higher anxiety, and lower general health and vitality, leaving more room to improve and exposing it to regression to the mean. No covariate adjustment was done. Any difference in change cannot be attributed to yoga, and the final null between-group 6MWT may reflect catch-up rather than absence of effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Randomised allocation, or analyses adjusted for baseline showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Twenty-two health professionals who stated that they could not provide continuity due to personal causes

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation to the control group was non-random and based on participants' stated inability to attend, and the groups differed substantially at baseline (6MWT 430.1 vs 469 m, p=0.006; Beck anxiety 16.15 vs 10, p=0.001; also SF-36 and mMRC measures), with the yoga group being worse off. Analyses were not adjusted for baseline and the limitations section does not address the imbalance, so between-group comparisons are susceptible to confounding and regression to the mean.

issues.title: Conclusion of effectiveness rests on within-group changes; most between-group tests are null
issues.explanation: The Discussion and Conclusion say yoga improved strength, flexibility, function, QoL, depression and anxiety, and was an 'effective, reliable' treatment. For grip, flexibility, 6MWT, mMRC, depression (interaction p=0.0504), role restriction, general health and vitality after-scores, the between-group comparison was not significant, and the control group also improved on 6MWT. Only a few outcomes (IPAQ, anxiety, some SF-36 domains) show a group difference, in a non-randomised design with imbalanced baselines. The claimed effectiveness is stated more confidently than the between-group evidence allows.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests (adjusted for baseline) showing significant advantage for yoga on the outcomes named in the conclusion.

quotes.text: there were significant improvements in muscle strength, flexibility, functional capacity, physical activity level, QoL, anxiety, and depression levels
A statistically significant improvement was observed for YBEG in the within-group assessment with the hand grip strength test
provide an increase in the functional capacity, physical activity level, and QoL of health professionals and reduce depression and anxiety

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion that YBE increases functional capacity and QoL and reduces depression rests mainly on within-group changes; the between-group tests for 6MWT, mMRC, grip, flexibility, depression (interaction p=0.0504) and most SF-36 domains are null. Only physical activity (IPAQ) and, with a baseline imbalance, anxiety show a between-group difference, so the effectiveness conclusion is stronger than the between-group evidence, and no multiplicity correction was applied.

issues.title: Discussion claims between-group advantages (6MWT, mMRC, grip, flexibility, 'all parameters') that Results show are null
issues.explanation: The Discussion says 6MWT and mMRC improved significantly versus the NIG, that the NIG had significant deterioration, and that YBEG clearly out-gained the NIG on grip. The Results report no significant between-group difference for 6MWT (p=0.578 after), mMRC (p=0.354), grip (p=0.713) and the flexibility tests. The Discussion also says all parameters improved in both groups, yet control anxiety rose (10 to 10.46), general health fell (-3.0) and vitality fell (-1.0). The functional-capacity benefit over control is therefore not supported by the authors' own tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group test (interaction or post-hoc) showing significantly greater 6MWT/mMRC/grip change in YBEG than NIG, or a statement that the Discussion refers only to within-group change.

quotes.text: The significant improvement in mMRC values and the walking distance at the 6MWT after the YBE program compared to the NIG supported
When evaluated between groups, no significant difference was found
When both groups were analyzed, improvement was observed in all parameters during the eight-week follow-up period

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion makes explicit comparative claims against the NIG for 6MWT, mMRC and hand grip ('compared to the NIG', 'higher gains than the NIG'), and the Discussion also says flexibility deteriorated significantly in the NIG compared to the YBEG, while the Results report null between-group tests for these (p=0.354, 0.713, 0.058, 0.796, 0.969, and 6MWT between-group p>0.05 with post-values 485.5 vs 480.2 m, p=0.578). The wording 'improvement was observed in all parameters' is also too broad (for example, the NIG changed in the wrong direction on several measures, and PSQI and mental health di

issues.title: About 15 outcomes tested at p<0.05 with no primary outcome or multiplicity control; powered 6MWT is null between groups
issues.explanation: The methods use an unadjusted threshold of 0.05 for all outcomes and for several tests per outcome. Marginal findings (anxiety after-score p=0.041, sleep group p=0.049, social functioning group p=0.044) would not survive correction. The outcome the study was powered on (6MWT) shows no between-group difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary outcome with a hierarchical testing plan, or corrected p-values keeping the key results significant.

quotes.text: was considered statistically significant
a minimum sample size of at least 15 subjects, with a power of 80%

issues.title: YBEG Beck anxiety change SD 0.46 is below the minimum 1.19 allowed by the before/after SDs
issues.explanation: For paired data the SD of the change cannot be smaller than the difference between the baseline and follow-up SDs. Table 3 gives SDs of 7.23 and 6.04, so the minimum is 1.19, yet the text prints 0.46. The printed paired p of 0.015 also implies an SD of roughly 5, not 0.46. The SD is almost certainly mis-printed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw paired data showing an SD of change of 0.46 (mathematically impossible with these SDs).

quotes.text: -2.57±0.46 in the YBEG

quotes.location: Table 3, Beck's anxiety, Before, Yoga group
Table 3, Beck's anxiety, After, Yoga group

issues.title: Differential dropout (4/30 = 13.3% vs 7/22 = 31.8%) with completer-only analysis of 41 of 52
issues.explanation: Eleven of 52 participants (21%) left, more than twice as often in the control arm, and only completers were analysed. Reasons for dropout and baseline data on dropouts are not given, so bias cannot be gauged. This weakens, but does not by itself overturn, the comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis including dropouts with similar results.

quotes.text: However, four individuals from the YBEG and seven individuals from the NIG could not complete the study.

issues.title: YBEG 6MWT mean change 56.57 m in text vs 55.41 m implied by Table 3 means (430.12 to 485.53)
issues.explanation: The text gives the mean YBEG change as 56.57 m, but the before and after means in Table 3 differ by 55.41 m. For the same participants these must agree. The control group matches (11.26 vs 11.2), so the yoga figures are internally inconsistent. The discrepancy is small and does not alter the direction of the result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Table 3 means were computed on a different set of participants than the change score.

quotes.text: 56.57±33.15 m (range, 0 to 114 m) in the YBEG

issues.title: Control hospitalization 1 of 15 printed as 14.3% (should be 6.7%)
issues.explanation: Table 2 lists one hospitalised control among 15, which is 6.7%, but prints 14.3%. All other control percentages use n=15. This is a printed error with little bearing on conclusions, but the printed p of 0.179 may have been computed from the wrong table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A defined subgroup of 7 controls to which the hospitalization count refers.

quotes.text: Control group (n=15)

script.explanation: 1/15 = 6.67%, but the paper prints 14.3, outside the rounding interval [14.25, 14.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 7.0 rather than 15.

10.5606/tftrd.2025.14301.headline_claim: Both continuous training (CT) and low-intensity interval training (LIIT) mild-moderate aerobic protocols improve functional capacity, dyspnea, tachycardia, QoL, depression and anxiety in post-COVID-19 patients with residual symptoms, and LIIT may be an option for patients with poor functional capacity.
10.5606/tftrd.2025.14301.overall: The paper shows that patients improved on both exercise protocols over a few weeks, but with no untreated comparator and no adjustment for large baseline differences it cannot establish that either protocol caused the improvement or that interval training is better in poor-function patients. The text-table inconsistencies (resting MBD p, SpO2 direction, baseline HR) are minor and do not change results. The efficacy conclusions should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: not specified as primary; 6MWT distance and functional capacity are the main reported outcomes

issues.title: Efficacy of each protocol claimed from uncontrolled pre-post change; no untreated comparator, no between-group evidence
issues.explanation: The study randomised patients between two active exercise protocols. Claims that each one improves functional capacity, dyspnea, QoL, anxiety and depression rest on within-arm pre-post tests, which cannot separate treatment effect from natural recovery, learning on the 6MWT or regression to the mean. Post-treatment values did not differ between arms and most delta comparisons in Table 3 were non-significant. The stated conclusion of effectiveness is therefore not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent no-treatment or usual-care comparison arm, or between-arm results showing both protocols outperform it.

quotes.text: a control group was lacking
none of the patients were followed without treatment

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy of both protocols is concluded from uncontrolled pre-post change; no untreated comparator exists and the between-group analyses compare only the two active arms. The authors acknowledge the missing control and natural recovery in the limitations, but the conclusion still states causal improvement without qualification.

issues.title: Marked baseline imbalance (6MWT 254 vs 371 m, O2 need 60% vs 15%) with unadjusted between-arm change comparisons
issues.explanation: The LIIT group had worse baseline severity, shorter 6MWT distance, higher resting HR and greater oxygen need. A group starting lower has more room to improve and regresses upward, so larger LIIT deltas in 6MWT, mMRC and resting HR cannot be attributed to the protocol. Table 3 compares raw change scores with no baseline adjustment, and randomisation method is not described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted (ANCOVA) between-group analysis showing the same LIIT advantage, or demonstration of balanced prognostic factors.

quotes.text: 60% in the LIIT group and 15.2% in the CT group (p<0.001)

second_reader.what_stands: Baseline imbalance is real (6MWT 254 vs 371 m, p=0.004; O2 need 60% vs 15.2%, p<0.001, plus disease severity, ICU stay, resting HR and mMRC), and the between-arm delta comparisons in Table 3 are unadjusted for it. The authors acknowledge that the greater LIIT gains may reflect the initial difference, which softens but does not remove the problem.

issues.title: 63 analysed of 76 enrolled (17.1%); below the 68 required; completers-only analysis
issues.explanation: The sample size calculation required 68 participants and was inflated to 76 for dropout, but only 63 were analysed, so the study finished underpowered for its stated 90% power. No intention-to-treat or sensitivity analysis is described for the 13 missing patients, and arm-wise losses are not stated in the text. Selective dropout could bias the group comparisons, though the paper's main claims are mostly within-arm.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flowchart showing balanced, reasoned losses and a sensitivity analysis including all randomised patients.

quotes.text: The study was completed with a total of 63 patients
The patient number was increased to 76 due to the possibility of dropout.

issues.title: LIIT recommended for poor-function patients from 3 of ~22 uncorrected, baseline-confounded delta tests
issues.explanation: The Conclusion recommends interval training for patients with poor functional capacity. This rests on a few secondary delta comparisons (mMRC 0.032, resting HR 0.026, 6MWT 0.010) that are unadjusted for multiplicity or baseline imbalance. Post-treatment outcomes were similar between arms, so the claim is at most hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified primary analysis or interaction test showing greater LIIT benefit in poor-capacity patients after adjustment for baseline.

quotes.text: The other parameters showed no significant difference.
for patients with poor functional capacity

issues.title: Baseline resting HR differs between Table 1 and Table 2 (90.7 vs 89.55 CT; 99.1 vs 99.47 LIIT)
issues.explanation: Table 1 and the Results text give baseline resting HR of 90.7±12.52 (CT) and 99.1±17.43 (LIIT), while the pretreatment columns of Table 2 give 89.55±12.81 and 99.47±17.23. The small differences, which also appear for resting BP, may reflect a different measurement session (the exercise test), but the paper does not say. This affects no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 2 resting HR is the resting value recorded at the ergometric exercise test, distinct from the Table 1 baseline reading.

quotes.location: Table 2, Resting HR row, CT pretreatment

issues.title: LIIT resting MBD p given as 0.002 in text but 0.008 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The Results text reports the LIIT pre-post change in resting modified Borg dyspnea as p=0.002, whereas Table 2 gives 0.008 for the same test. The text value appears to have been copied from the 6th-minute MBD row (0.002). Significance is unchanged either way, so this is a minor reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An erratum or table version showing 0.002 for the resting MBD LIIT test.

quotes.text: resting  MBD  (p=0.002)

issues.title: LIIT 6-min SpO2 listed as 'decreased' in text but rose from 88.57 to 91.23 in Table 2
issues.explanation: The text lists SpO2 (p=0.003) among 6MWT variables that 'decreased significantly after PR' in the LIIT group. Table 2 shows 6th-minute SpO2 rising from 88.57±5.09 to 91.23±4.57. The direction is misdescribed, though the underlying result is favourable and the p-value matches.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the sentence refers to a different SpO2 measure (e.g. desaturation) that fell.

quotes.location: Table 2, 6th min SPO2 row, LIIT posttreatment

10.56199/dpcsms.sjjq1180.headline_claim: Osteopathic treatment is effective for astheno-neurotic syndrome in post-COVID patients and its inclusion in rehabilitation treatment is recommended.
10.56199/dpcsms.sjjq1180.overall: The headline claim that osteopathic treatment is effective is only weakly supported. All inference is from within-arm before/after tests against an untreated, unblinded comparison group, with no between-group test, and the comparison arm itself improved on SAS. The recommendation for routine rehabilitation overreaches what 40 patients and a brief conference report can show.

primary_outcome.name: not explicitly designated; reported outcomes include asthenia (SAS), vegetative status (Kerdo index), SF-36 quality of life, complaint frequency and somatic dysfunction incidence

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from within-arm paired tests; no between-group comparison reported
issues.explanation: All reported p-values are before/after tests (paired t-test, chi-square) within each arm. The paper never tests treated against untreated, even though its third objective is a comparative analysis. Concluding effectiveness from one arm's significance versus the other's non-significance is a recognised error. Repeated chi-square tests on paired counts, with no multiplicity handling, add further uncertainty.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group test of change scores (or interaction) showing a significant difference favouring treatment.

quotes.text: Student's t-test for linked samples were used from the data analysis package.
The results of the research indicate the effectiveness of osteopathic treatment in patients with post-COVID astheno-neurotic syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy is inferred from separate within-arm paired tests, and no between-group comparison (for example of change scores or an adjusted model) is reported. The SAS result in the comparison group is itself statistically significant (p = 1.30E-3), which contradicts the idea that the untreated arm was unchanged. The conclusion that treatment is effective therefore rests on 'significant in one arm, not significant in the other', which is not valid evidence of a treatment effect.

issues.title: Untreated, unblinded comparison with no sham; subjective and palpatory outcomes open to expectation effects
issues.explanation: The comparison group received no intervention and no sham or attention control. Most outcomes are self-reported (complaints, SAS, SF-36) or examiner-palpated (craniosacral rhythm, somatic dysfunctions), and no blinding of patients or assessors is reported. Contact time, expectation and examiner knowledge could explain much of the improvement. No reliability is reported for the palpatory findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A report that assessors or patients were blinded, or that a sham or attention control was used.

quotes.text: the comparison group was observed without conducting treatment
the indicators of the craniosacral mechanism such as rhythm, amplitude and strength were assessed
The SF-36 questionnaire was used to assess life quality.

second_reader.what_stands: The comparison group received no treatment and no sham, and the paper does not describe blinding of participants, therapists or assessors. The outcomes are self-reported (SAS, SF-36, complaints) or examiner-judged palpatory findings (craniosacral rhythm, amplitude, strength, suture mobility), so expectation and observer effects are plausible and unaddressed. 'Unblinded' is inferred from the absence of any blinding statement, not from an explicit statement of open-label design.

issues.title: Recommendation for routine rehabilitation from 40 patients, untreated control and no safety data
issues.explanation: The abstract and practical recommendations advise including osteopathic treatment in post-COVID rehabilitation. The evidence is 20 treated patients, an untreated, unblinded comparison, no between-group test, no adverse-event reporting, no registration and no follow-up beyond treatment. The conclusion is stated as established effectiveness rather than preliminary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group results, safety data and a larger confirmatory trial supporting the recommendation.

quotes.text: The effectiveness of the therapeutic measures allows recommending the inclusion of osteopathic treatment in rehabilitation treatment of patients with post-COVID syndrome.

second_reader.what_stands: A recommendation to include osteopathic treatment in rehabilitation is drawn from 40 patients, an untreated comparison group and within-arm tests, with no reported safety or adverse-event data and no stated limitations. The 'routine' wording is the point's own gloss; the paper says 'inclusion in rehabilitation treatment' and 'complex rehabilitation treatment', which is close enough that the concern applies.

issues.title: Randomisation method, concealment and baseline data not described
issues.explanation: The paper says patients were randomly split 20/20 but gives no sequence generation, concealment or baseline table. Comparability rests on a bare statement of no significant differences. This is a reporting gap that weakens confidence in the comparison but does not by itself show bias.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of a concealed random sequence and a baseline table showing balance.

quotes.text: Patients were randomly split into two groups
(without significant differences between the groups)

issues.title: Comparison group SAS fall is significant (p=1.30E-3) yet text says indicators did not change
issues.explanation: Section 3.3 reports a significant SAS decrease in the comparison group of 0.8 points (p=1.30E-3). Conclusion 3 says that in the comparison group these indicators did not change significantly. The untreated arm therefore did improve on the primary asthenia scale, which narrows the apparent treatment contrast and contradicts the summary.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction showing the comparison-group SAS p-value was misprinted.

quotes.text: the decrease was 0.8 points on the SAS scale (p:1.30E-3)
In the comparison group, these indicators did not change significantly.

issues.title: Thoracic segment is Th10-Th12 (73%) in Results but Th11-Th12 in Conclusion
issues.explanation: Results section 3.1 lists Th10-Th12 dysfunction in 73% of patients. The Conclusion lists Th11-Th12 as among the most common dysfunctions. It also omits Th4-Th5, which the Results report at 70%. This is a small reporting inconsistency and does not affect the efficacy claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the conclusion deliberately pools or relabels segments, or that the Results label is a typo.

quotes.text: Th10-Th12 - in 73%
Th11-Th12 segments, first rib

issues.title: Same chi-square (26.19) for two outcomes with different baselines (100% vs 95%)
issues.explanation: Occipital-mastoid/petro-jugular (baseline 100%) and thoracic diaphragm (baseline 95%) both show an 85% reduction with chi-square 26.19. Other outcomes with the same percentage reduction but different baselines have different chi-squares (55%: 10.23 vs 10.67). The identical value could be coincidence or a copying slip, and the missing counts prevent a check. The tests also treat before and after as independent samples, although the data are paired.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw before/after counts showing both outcomes have the same 2x2 table.

quotes.text: dysfunctions of the occipital-mastoid and petro-jugular sutures decreased by 85% (χ2 = 26.19; p<0.001)
the incidence of somatic dysfunctions of the thoracic diaphragm decreased by 85% (χ2 = 26.19; p<0.001)

10.56726/irjmets49482.headline_claim: Pulmonary rehabilitation has a significant positive impact on pulmonary function, exercise capacity and symptoms in long COVID patients within a Bangladeshi tertiary healthcare setting.
10.56726/irjmets49482.overall: The headline claim of a significant positive impact of pulmonary rehabilitation is not supported: the study is a single-arm admission-versus-discharge comparison of bare means with no variance, tests or comparator, and the sustained-recovery claim exceeds the roughly 20-day data. Several printed percentages and subgroup counts are wrong (880.9%, 26.57%, 65.90%), which are minor in themselves but indicate poor reporting quality.

primary_outcome.name: Respiratory function (FEV1, FVC, DLCO)

issues.title: Efficacy inferred from single-arm admission-to-discharge change; no comparator, variance or tests reported
issues.explanation: All 126 participants received rehabilitation and outcomes are only first-day versus last-day means (e.g., male FEV1 3.2 to 4.5 L), with no control group, no SDs, no confidence intervals and no significance tests. Spontaneous recovery, learning effects on the walk test and regression to the mean cannot be separated from any rehabilitation effect. The claim of 'significant' impact therefore rests on descriptive means only.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control group or paired analyses with variance accounting for natural recovery.

quotes.text: Physical capacity was measured at admission and discharge from the hospital
the aim of this multicenter retrospective study was to report the effectiveness of pulmonary rehabilitation in subjects recovering from COVID-19 in a real-world setting.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, uncontrolled before/after series (all 126 received PR, measured at start and end of a ~20-day program), yet it draws conclusions of 'effectiveness', 'efficacy' and 'significant positive impact'. For its own data, only group means or counts are given, with no variance measures, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests; the SDs and p-values in the Discussion belong to a cited study. The lack of a control group is not listed as a limitation, so improvement cannot be attributed to PR rather than natural recovery, regression to the mean, or other factors.

issues.title: 'Robust and sustained recovery' claimed from measures taken only at about 20 days
issues.explanation: All outcomes were measured at admission and at the end of a roughly 20-day programme. The Discussion nonetheless says rehabilitation facilitates a 'robust and sustained recovery', despite acknowledging that follow-up was too short to capture long-term trajectory. Durability is untested.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Post-discharge follow-up data showing maintained gains.

quotes.text: facilitating a robust and sustained recovery for individuals grappling with the protracted effects of COVID-19
The relatively short duration and follow-up period in our investigation may not capture the long-term trajectory of recovery in long COVID survivors.

issues.title: Another study's results (p<0.001, PG/LG groups) sit in the Discussion among the authors' own findings
issues.explanation: The Discussion quotes pulmonary rehabilitation gains with p-values for groups 'PG' and 'LG', which do not exist in this single-group study. They are attributed to Spielmanns et al., but a reader could take them as this cohort's results. The authors' own data have no p-values, yet the text claims 'significant increase' in FVC.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analyses in the paper testing the FVC change in this cohort.

quotes.text: The significant  increase  in  forced  vital  capacity  (FVC)  observed  in  our  cohort  mirrors  previous  research
The improvements in the 6MWT in the pre to post comparison were on average 180 (±101) meters for PG and 102 (±89) meters for LG (p < 0.001).

issues.title: Male fatigue counts sum to 104 of 105; mild 65 printed as 65.90% (65/105 = 61.90%)
issues.explanation: The male fatigue categories (65, 34, 5) add to 104, not 105. The mild share printed as 65.90% does not match 65/105 = 61.90%, and the three printed percentages sum to 103.04%. Female fatigue counts have a similar gap (see c4). These are reporting errors in a descriptive outcome.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table showing one male participant with missing fatigue data and 65.90% as a typo.

script.explanation: 65/105 = 61.90%, but the paper prints 65.9, outside the rounding interval [65.90, 65.91]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 98.6 rather than 105.

issues.title: Rehabilitation type percentages 880.9% and 11.09% do not match 111/126 (88.1%) and 15/126 (11.9%)
issues.explanation: The paper prints 880.9% for 111 of 126 center-based participants, which is impossible as a percentage. The companion 11.09% for 15 participants should be about 11.90%.
