The two printed shares also sum to 892%, not 100%. This is a typographical error with no bearing on the efficacy claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table or figure showing the correct values with the text being a reproduction artefact.

quotes.text: where the percentages was 880.9% and 11.09% respectively.

script.explanation: 111/126 = 88.10%, but the paper prints 880.9, outside the rounding interval [880.85, 881.00]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 12.6 rather than 126.

issues.title: Design described inconsistently as retrospective multicenter, cross-sectional, and interview-based
issues.explanation: The Introduction calls the study multicenter and retrospective (borrowed wording from another study), while Methods describe a cross-sectional design with face-to-face structured interviews at one named centre. Design labels therefore conflict, making it unclear how the pre-post outcomes were obtained. No registration is reported, which is not unusual for observational work.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement clarifying the design and data source.

quotes.text: Cross sectional study design is to be followed in this study.
Data was collected through face-to-face interview using a structured questionnaire.

issues.title: Unmarried 26.57% does not match 36/126 = 28.57%; married + unmarried sum to 97.99%
issues.explanation: 36 of 126 is 28.57%, but the paper prints 26.57%. Married (71.42%, 90 participants) plus unmarried then sum to 97.99% though the paper says there were no divorced cases. A single-digit typo with no effect on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A source table showing 26.57% was an intended different base.

quotes.text: and 26.57% were unmarried (36 participants)

script.explanation: 36/126 = 28.57%, but the paper prints 26.57, outside the rounding interval [26.57, 26.58]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 135.5 rather than 126.

issues.title: Female fatigue categories cover 19 of 21 women (percentages sum to 90.46%)
issues.explanation: The female fatigue counts 12, 5 and 2 total 19, and the printed percentages total 90.46%, leaving two women unaccounted for. This may be an unreported 'no fatigue' category or missing data, which the paper does not say. The impact is limited to this descriptive table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that two women had no fatigue.

quotes.text: severe 2 (9.52%) participant

issues.title: Muslim 90.74% is not a whole-number share of 126 (114/126 = 90.48%); shares sum to 100.26%
issues.explanation: 9.52% matches 12/126, so Muslim should be 114/126 = 90.48%, not 90.74%. The two shares sum to over 100%. A trivial slip with no effect on conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A count showing a different denominator.

quotes.text: 90.74% were Muslim

10.56936/18290825-2.v19.2025-82.headline_claim: Adding aerophytotherapy with sage essential oil to comprehensive sanatorium rehabilitation contributes to further improvements in functional and emotional status, vitality and general health in patients after COVID-19.
10.56936/18290825-2.v19.2025-82.overall: The paper is a non-randomised, unadjusted comparison of 54 treated with 181 untreated patients, so the claim that aerophytotherapy adds benefit is at best tentative. Several results the text calls significant meet only p<0.1, 25 enrolled patients are unaccounted for, and the conclusion leans on within-group changes and uncorrected tests. Only the descriptive finding that both groups improved with comprehensive rehabilitation is reasonably supported.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; Table 1 reports about 25 outcomes, and the headline rests on SF-36 vitality and general health

issues.title: Non-randomised 54 vs 181 comparison with no adjustment, described as 'qualitative randomization'
issues.explanation: A 54-patient subgroup 'prescribed' aerophytotherapy is compared with 181 other patients. The paper gives no allocation rule, no blinding, and no adjustment for baseline differences, which exist in Table 1 (for example FEV1 96.6 vs 98.3, physical function and several symptom scores). Selection into the treated group could explain differences, so the claim of an added benefit of aerophytotherapy is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A documented randomisation or concealed allocation procedure, or a baseline-adjusted analysis showing the same benefit.

quotes.text: allowed us to talk about qualitative randomization
The additional inclusion of aerophytotherapy with sage essential oil in the rehabilitation program contributes to further improvements

second_reader.what_stands: The 54 vs 181 comparison is not shown to be randomised, and 'qualitative randomization' is not an accepted design feature. Table 1 shows baseline imbalances (for example VAS, roughly z = 4.7 if the ± values are SEMs) and no adjustment is made. The conclusion that aerophytotherapy 'contributes to further improvements' is therefore a causal claim the design cannot support, and the aerophytotherapy and audio-relaxation components cannot be separated.

issues.title: Results called significant where Table 1 gives only p<0.1 (FVC between groups, FEV1, household activity)
issues.explanation: The stated significance level is p<0.05, yet the text describes the between-group FVC difference as significant and FEV1 as significantly improved in the experimental group, while Table 1 prints p2<0.1 for FVC and p1<0.1 for experimental FEV1. The 'household activity' EQ-5D between-group difference is also called significant, and its row (label missing) shows p<0.1. These results do not meet the paper's own threshold, and the FVC and FEV1 claims are part of the 'functional status' conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An explicit statement that p<0.1 was accepted as significance, or exact p-values below 0.05 for these comparisons.

quotes.text: These differences were statistically significant in favor of the group
FEV1 increased statistically significantly only in the experimental group.

second_reader.what_stands: The text calls the between-group FVC difference significant, calls FEV1 significant in the experimental group, and calls the household-activity difference significant. Table 1 supports only p<0.1 for each, which is above the stated alpha of 0.05. The within-group FVC improvements are genuinely p<0.05 or lower.

issues.title: Conclusion's added benefit rests on within-group significance, uncorrected multiple tests and a non-significant emotional trend
issues.explanation: The text credits the experimental group with significant vitality and general-health gains, though the table shows the control group improving significantly on the same domains and most between-group p2 values are >0.1. Roughly 36 between-group comparisons were run at p<0.05 without correction, and only 4 reached p<0.05, close to the 1.8 expected by chance; no primary outcome was declared. The conclusion also claims better 'emotional status' although the Results say emotional-role change was insignificant in both groups, and it omits that the dyspnea measures showed no between-group difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Between-group tests for vitality and general health that remain significant after multiplicity adjustment, and a pre-declared primary outcome.

quotes.text: vitality and general health scores significantly increased in the experimental group
although a positive, albeit statistically insignificant, trend was noted in the group receiving aerophytotherapy
was chosen to be p<0.05

second_reader.what_stands: The 'emotional status' and 'functional status' parts of the added-benefit conclusion are not supported at p<0.05 between groups: the emotional item is a stated non-significant trend and the FVC/FEV1 evidence is only p<0.1. The 36 between-group tests have no multiplicity correction. The vitality and general-health claim is better supported than the point suggests, since two SF-36 rows (probably those) have between-group p2<0.05, but this is nominal and uncorrected, and one of those rows is also significant in the control group. The row mapping is inferred because the labels are missing.

issues.title: 260 patients enrolled but only 54 + 181 = 235 in the comparison; 25 unaccounted for
issues.explanation: Methods and Results say 260 patients were included, but the two arms analysed in Table 1 total 235. No exclusion, missing-data or selection reason is given for the 25 patients (9.6%). The paper also does not say how patients came to be in the 54-patient aerophytotherapy subgroup rather than the control group.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram or sentence explaining who the 25 patients were and why they were left out of the group comparison.

quotes.text: The study group included 260 people.
The experimental group consisted of 54 patients and the control group - 181 patients

script.explanation: The 260 enrolled vs 54+181 compared balances arithmetically but 1 transition(s) drop participants with no stated reason: 25 participant(s) drop between 'enrolled' and 'analysed in group comparison' with no stated exclusions. Not itself an error -- papers legitimately omit attrition reasons -- but the reader cannot audit the loss.

issues.title: Oxygen price diagram: text says control improved more, but table change is larger in experimental (1.104 vs 0.785)
issues.explanation: The text groups mMRC and the oxygen price diagram as improving more in the control group. For mMRC that fits (change 0.246 vs 0.178), but for the oxygen price diagram the experimental group rose more. The between-group p is only <0.1, so the practical effect is small and the error understates the aerophytotherapy result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that a lower oxygen price score means improvement, or that the text refers only to mMRC.

quotes.text: more pronounced in the control group, but reliable differences between the groups were not revealed

10.5812/archcid-144280.headline_claim: Vitamin B1 (600 mg daily for 8 weeks) alongside supportive therapy significantly reduced the duration of post-acute COVID-19 symptoms and is recommended to enhance recovery rates.
10.5812/archcid-144280.overall: The headline claim that vitamin B1 significantly reduces the duration of post-acute COVID-19 symptoms is not supported: the trial is open-label with no placebo, self-rated outcomes, no duration analysis, large unadjusted baseline imbalances, and apparently retrospective registration. Several reported P values cannot be reproduced from the printed summaries. At best the data suggest a possible benefit that needs a blinded, adequately powered replication.

primary_outcome.name: post-acute COVID-19 symptom severity (VAT 0-10) and duration

issues.title: 'Significantly reduced duration' claimed with no duration or time-to-recovery analysis
issues.explanation: The paper reports only cross-sectional t-tests of symptom scores at weeks 1-3 and week 6 and descriptive recovery percentages. No time-to-resolution analysis or survival-type comparison supports the stated conclusion that duration was significantly reduced. The week 1-3 comparison shows higher scores in the intervention arm for several symptoms, and the roughly 6 versus 8 week onset-interval imbalance sits across this comparison. The conclusion goes beyond what the reported analysis can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified time-to-resolution analysis with a significant result adjusted for onset interval.

quotes.text: Our study findings indicate that administering vitamin B1 can significantly reduce the duration of postacute COVID-19  syndrome.
By the seventh week, 67% of symptoms had resolved in the intervention group, compared to only 33% in the control  group.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper concludes that vitamin B1 'significantly' reduces duration, but it reports no duration or time-to-recovery analysis. The word 'significantly' is not backed by a test of recovery rates or of duration. The only recovery data are untested descriptive percentages whose denominator (symptoms rather than patients) is not defined, and the nine-week follow-up window limits any duration claim.

issues.title: Open-label, no-placebo trial with self-rated 0-10 symptom scores as the only efficacy outcome
issues.explanation: Patients knew their allocation and rated their own symptoms on an ad hoc 0-10 scale. Controls got only supportive care, with no placebo or sham. Differences in self-reported scores and recovery therefore cannot be separated from expectation, attention and natural recovery. The conclusion that vitamin B1 reduces symptom duration is stated confidently despite this.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A blinded or placebo-controlled replication, or objective outcome measures showing the same difference.

quotes.text: This study was conducted as an open-label trial without blinding.
The control group received only the supportive therapy prescribed for the intervention group.
which may have led to reporting bias

second_reader.what_stands: The trial is open-label with no placebo, and the only efficacy outcomes reported are patient-rated 0-10 symptom scores. The authors do flag subjectivity and reporting bias, but they do not discuss the absence of blinding or placebo as a limitation, and the conclusion is stated without qualification.

issues.title: Tables 2-3: headache week-6 P < 0.0001 and myalgia P = 0.72 do not match printed means and SDs
issues.explanation: For week-6 headache the arms are 1.00 ± 0.00 and 0.73 ± 1.11, yet the printed P is < 0.0001. A t-test on these summaries gives about 0.17. In Table 2, myalgia 6.00 ± 1.52 vs 5.36 ± 0.91 is printed with P = 0.72, whereas a t-test at n = 33 per group gives about 0.04. The per-symptom n is never stated, so these results cannot be reproduced, and the very significant week-6 findings that carry the efficacy claim are not verifiable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-symptom sample sizes and raw data reproducing the printed P values.

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

second_reader.what_stands: The headache week-6 P < 0.0001 cannot be reproduced by any sample size up to 33. The printed values give P ≈ 0.17, and the control mean is lower than the intervention mean, so the entry is wrong or mis-keyed. The myalgia P = 0.72 does not match the printed means and SDs at n = 33 (P ≈ 0.04), but it might be reconcilable with an unreported smaller n, so that part is not settled.

issues.title: Large baseline imbalance in onset interval (6.3 vs 8.2 weeks), neutrophils, lymphocytes, CRP; not adjusted
issues.explanation: The groups differ markedly on time since onset and on inflammatory markers despite reported random allocation with no concealment described. The authors say they could not control for these confounders, and the analysis is unadjusted t-tests. Because a duration-of-symptoms conclusion depends on disease stage at entry, the comparison is not reliable. The CRP P value of 0.003 also cannot be reproduced from the printed summaries, so even the imbalance table has errors.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Adjusted analyses (ANCOVA or regression) including onset interval and showing the same effect, or evidence of an allocation error in the random table.

quotes.text: the interval from symptom onset (P < 0.0001), neutrophil percentage (P < 0.0001)
we were unable to control for confounding variables, including the interval from symptom onset

second_reader.what_stands: Large baseline imbalances in onset interval (6.3 vs 8.2 weeks), neutrophil % and lymphocyte % are real and reproduce from the printed numbers. The analyses are unadjusted, as the authors admit. The CRP imbalance is not supported: the printed means and SDs give P ≈ 0.48, not 0.003, and the CRP SD in the first group is about twice its mean. Either the P-value or the CRP summary values are in error.

issues.title: Registration (IRCT20221229..., Dec 2022) appears about 14 months after enrolment began (Oct 2021)
issues.explanation: The IRCT code points to registration at the end of 2022, while recruitment is reported from October 2021 to November 2023. The trial therefore looks retrospectively registered, so outcomes and analyses could not be fixed before data were seen. The paper also says the protocol was 'approved by' the registry, which is not what registration means.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record showing an original registration date before October 2021.

quotes.text: from October 2021 to November 2023
The study protocol was approved by the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20221229056979N1)

issues.title: About 15 symptoms at several timepoints tested at uncorrected P < 0.05 with no primary outcome
issues.explanation: No primary outcome is named and no multiplicity correction is applied across 15 symptoms and several timepoints. Some marginal findings (cough P = 0.038, headache P = 0.022, sleep P = 0.022) would not survive correction, but the very small week-6 P values might.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified primary outcome, or corrected analyses retaining the key results.

quotes.text: The significance level for this study was set at P < 0.05.

issues.title: 66 participants, no sample size calculation, confident efficacy conclusion
issues.explanation: No power calculation is reported and 66 patients were randomized. The Discussion asks for larger studies while the Conclusions recommend vitamin B1. The conflict between a tentative sample and a confident recommendation weakens the conclusion, but it is largely covered by the open-label and analysis problems.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified power calculation or a protocol showing the target n was met.

quotes.text: Future studies with larger sample sizes are recommended to further validate these findings.

issues.title: Table 1 corticosteroid counts in the intervention arm sum to 28 of 33; percentages imply n = 29
issues.explanation: The intervention-arm corticosteroid Yes and No counts (3 and 25) add to 28, not the 33 participants randomized. The percentages (10.3 and 86.2) only fit a denominator of 29 and sum to 96.5%. The control column sums correctly, so the baseline comparison (P = 0.151) rests on an inconsistent intervention column. This is a small baseline-table error that does not touch the main outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 showing a complete intervention column of 33 with matching percentages, or a stated 4 missing or unknown corticosteroid records.

script.explanation: 3/33 = 9.09%, but the paper prints 10.3, outside the rounding interval [10.25, 10.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 29.1 rather than 33.

issues.title: Table 2 anosmia identical in both arms (4.90 ± 0.57); per-symptom n not given
issues.explanation: Mean and SD are identical in both arms for anosmia, with P > 0.999. With a small number of symptomatic patients this can occur by chance. The underlying problem is that the table headers say n = 33 per group while the symptom rows clearly cover smaller subsets, which is not explained.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Per-symptom n and raw data showing distinct values in each arm.

issues.title: Symptom outcome measured with an uncited, unvalidated 0-10 Visual Assessment Tool
issues.explanation: All symptom outcomes use a visual 0-10 scale with no validation cited. PSQI is validated but no PSQI results are reported anywhere in the Results. The main claims therefore rest on an unvalidated instrument.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Citation of a validated version of the tool, or reported PSQI results.

quotes.text: using a Visual Assessment Tool (VAT)

issues.title: Table 1 prints P '> 0.0001' for onset interval and neutrophils; text says P < 0.0001
issues.explanation: Table 1 uses a greater-than sign for two highly significant baseline differences, while the Results text calls them P < 0.0001. This is a wrong inequality sign that no reader would be misled by.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original table showing a '<' sign.

quotes.location: Table 1, Interval from symptom onset (w) row

quotes.text: interval from symptom onset (P < 0.0001)

10.5812/asjsm-158465.headline_claim: Selected-exercise-rehabilitation (SER) can help reduce consequences after COVID-19 by improving immune function, reducing muscle damage factors, and enhancing oxidative stress processes, mitochondrial activity, physical fitness, and mental and social health.
10.5812/asjsm-158465.overall: The headline claim that SER reduces post-COVID fatigue and improves many biological processes is weakly supported: the comparison uses a usual-care control with self-reported outcomes, only completers are analysed (35 of 47), and the reported statistics are pooled with no group-level estimates. An impossible FEV1/FVC scale and conclusions about unmeasured oxidative and mitochondrial mechanisms further reduce reliability. The pre-post improvement is likely partly natural recovery after hospitalization.

primary_outcome.name: Chalder Fatigue Scale

issues.title: Conclusions credit SER with improving oxidative stress and mitochondrial activity, which were not measured
issues.explanation: Only CRP, WBC, FEV1/FVC, walk, handgrip and questionnaires were measured. The Conclusions state, based on the obtained data, that SER improves immune function, oxidative stress and mitochondrial activity. No such measures exist in the study, and there is no sample size calculation, so the broad efficacy claims go well beyond the evidence.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported oxidative stress and mitochondrial measurements in the study.

quotes.text: enhancing oxidative stress processes,  mitochondrial  activity,  and  physical  fitness, while also improving mental and social health
Based on the obtained  results  and  data,  SER  can  help  reduce  the consequences  after  COVID-19

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions credit SER with effects on oxidative stress and mitochondrial activity, but no such outcome was measured, and the Discussion supports these only with literature citations. The statement is introduced as following from 'the obtained results and data', so it is not clearly marked as a hypothesis.

issues.title: FEV1/FVC means of 288.69 (pre) and 147.86 (post) are impossible for a ratio or percentage
issues.explanation: Table 2 lists FEV1/FVC means of 288.6857 and 147.8571, but the Methods describe it as the ratio of FEV1 to FVC. A ratio cannot exceed 1 (or 100 as a percentage). The variable is therefore mis-scaled, mislabelled or mis-entered, and the discussion's inference about respiratory muscle strength from 'changes in FEV1/FVC' rests on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that this column is a different quantity (e.g. a sum, or a scaled score) with its units.

quotes.text: and their ratio (FEV1/FVC), were examined at the respiratory clinic of Al-Zahra Hospital

second_reader.what_stands: The printed FEV1/FVC means (288.69 pre, 147.86 post) are outside the possible range of a ratio or percentage, and the paper gives no unit or definition that would make them valid. The row also shows a fall of about 141 units, which is unexplained and which the Discussion cites as evidence of benefit ('as indicated by changes in FEV1/FVC').

issues.title: Table 3 p-values lack test, df and group-by-time interaction; eight outcomes, LSD post-hoc, no group data
issues.explanation: Table 2 reports pooled 'Total' pre and post means without separating the two groups, and Table 3 gives only p-values per column with no statistic, df or effect sizes. The claimed between-group effect cannot therefore be seen. Eight outcomes are tested with LSD post-hoc and no correction. Effect sizes (0.63 to 1.93) are within-group, pooled and are not treatment effects against control.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Group-specific means, interaction F-tests and adjusted between-group differences with CIs.

quotes.text: Post-hoc analyses (Tukey  and LSD) were performed to further explore significant main effects and interactions
P-values are lower than 0.005 in the  table  of  tests  of  between-subject  effects

second_reader.what_stands: Table 3 gives only p-values, with no test statistic, df, group means or group-by-time interaction, so the paper does not show that the intervention changed outcomes more than usual care. Table 2 pools both groups, and the between-subject effect described in the text is not the interaction test. The printed p-values would survive a Bonferroni correction for 8 outcomes (0.0009 < 0.00625), so the multiplicity concern is limited to the unstated correction and the use of LSD post-hoc tests.

issues.title: Usual-care-only control with largely self-reported outcomes; non-specific effects and natural recovery unaddressed
issues.explanation: The control group received standard care without any attention or sham comparator, and the outcomes (fatigue, depression, quality of life) are self-reported. The authors admit expectation effects but the conclusions state benefit unqualified. CRP and WBC were measured during resolving acute illness, so improvement is expected with time alone. Combined with the unblinded participants, the between-group effect cannot be attributed to exercise specifically.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control or blinded objective primary outcome showing the same benefit.

quotes.text: Participants in exercise groups were aware of their active engagement, potentially generating positive expectations that contributed to self-reported benefits.
the control group received  standard  care  without  the  structured exercise program for eight weeks

second_reader.what_stands: The control group was usual care only, with no attention or sham comparator, and three of eight outcomes are self-reported. The authors do acknowledge expectation effects and call for sham or active controls in future work. The paper does not address natural recovery over the 8 weeks after an acute-phase baseline, even though it states that CRP and WBC normalised by the post-test. So the point is narrower than stated: non-specific effects are acknowledged, natural recovery is not.

issues.title: 12 of 47 randomized (25.5%) excluded, with data 'deemed incorrect' dropped; completer analysis only
issues.explanation: Thirty-five of 47 randomized patients were analysed. Losses include non-adherence, absence from the final test, and data judged incorrect and excluded, with no per-arm numbers in the text. Analysing only completers while calling it analysis by original assignment can bias the comparison, since non-adherers are likely to differ. No sensitivity analysis is reported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT figure with per-arm numbers and a sensitivity analysis including all randomized patients.

quotes.text: Ultimately,  data  from  35  patients  were  included  in the  statistical  analysis
Additionally,  data  were  deemed incorrect upon evaluation and were subsequently excluded from the analysis.

script.explanation: The participant flow balances arithmetically but 1 transition(s) drop participants with no stated reason: 12 participant(s) drop between 'randomized' and 'analysed' with no stated exclusions. Not itself an error -- papers legitimately omit attrition reasons -- but the reader cannot audit the loss.

issues.title: Intervention delivery split is inconsistent: remote 3 weeks, 4 weeks, or 5 weeks across sections
issues.explanation: The Methods say the first three weeks were remote and in-person began in week four, then say the first four weeks were remote and the final four in person. The Discussion refers to individual sessions in the first 5 weeks and group sessions in the last 3. The intervention cannot be reproduced exactly from the text, but no result depends on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A protocol clarifying that different components were delivered on different schedules.

quotes.text: For the first three weeks of the SER
training  sessions  in  the  first  four weeks  were  conducted  remotely

issues.title: Table 1 covers 6 of 8 weeks (20-40 min) while text says 15 to 60 min over the program
issues.explanation: The text says session duration rose from 15 to 60 minutes, but Table 1 lists only six weeks, starting at 20 and ending at 40 minutes. Weeks seven and eight, and any 15 or 60 minute sessions, are not shown, so the dose actually delivered cannot be verified. The frequency entries ('5 to 4 days') are also reversed ranges.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A complete eight-week schedule showing 15-minute and 60-minute sessions.

quotes.text: gradually increased from fifteen to sixty minutes
Sixth week (3 to 4 days a week for 40 min)

issues.title: Walk test is a 6-minute test in Methods but a 2-minute test in Results, Table 2 and Discussion
issues.explanation: The Methods list the 6-minute walk test as an outcome, but every reported result refers to a two-minute walk test. Reported values (62.5 pre, 81.1 post) cannot be interpreted without knowing which test was done. The fitness outcome is therefore not clearly defined.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A correction stating which walk test was actually done.

quotes.text: The 6-minute walk test
Two minutes' walk test

issues.title: Baseline timing stated as 2-3 days before discharge in Methods and about 1 day in Results
issues.explanation: The Methods place baseline testing about two to three days before discharge and the Results about one day before. The difference is small and both are approximate. It matters little, except that baseline CRP and WBC were taken during resolving acute illness, so regression to normal is expected regardless of treatment.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Records showing the actual interval was within both ranges.

quotes.text: approximately two to three days before hospital discharge
conducted approximately one day before each patient's hospital discharge

10.58727/jshr.107257.headline_claim: An 8-week circuit of aerobic, strength and breathing exercise effectively enhances pulmonary function, and improves oxygen saturation, in women with post-COVID-19 syndrome compared with the control group.
10.58727/jshr.107257.overall: The directional finding that the programme may improve some spirometric measures is plausible, but the headline of established efficacy is overstated: four of eight outcomes show no treatment effect, no multiplicity correction was applied, only FEV1/FVC survives Bonferroni and that outcome has baseline imbalance, and no registration is reported. The Discussion also credits MRf with a benefit its own results refute, and Table 2 contains several misprinted intervals..

primary_outcome.name: Pulmonary function and SpO2 (eight measures; no single primary outcome designated)

issues.title: Eight outcomes tested at alpha 0.05 uncorrected; only FEV1/FVC (p = 0.006) survives Bonferroni (0.00625)
issues.explanation: The paper tests eight outcomes at 0.05 with no correction and designates no single primary outcome. The claimed gains in SpO2 (p = 0.041), FEV1 (0.010) and PEF (0.009) are near the threshold and do not pass a Bonferroni or Holm correction. Only FEV1/FVC (0.006) does, and that outcome is affected by baseline imbalance. The headline of improvement across several measures is therefore only tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified hierarchical testing plan or a single designated primary outcome with the rest declared exploratory.

quotes.text: with a significance level of 0.05
a significant interaction effect between time and treatment (F(1,58) = 4.353, p = 0.041)
The main outcomes of this study were pulmonary  functions.

second_reader.what_stands: Eight outcomes were each tested at an uncorrected alpha of 0.05 with no designated primary outcome. At the printed precision only the FEV1/FVC interaction (p = 0.006) is below the Bonferroni threshold of 0.00625, and that margin is very small. The spO2, FEV1 and PEF interactions (p = 0.041, 0.010, 0.009) would not survive correction.

issues.title: 'Has established' efficacy claimed from a 60-person trial where 4 of 8 outcomes show no treatment effect
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the study has established that circuit training improves oxygen saturation and pulmonary function, and the Conclusions say it effectively enhances pulmonary function. Four of eight outcomes (FVC, MVV, MRf, MVt) show no interaction effect. The conclusion also describes control-group improvements as smaller, though FVC and MVV improved equally. The three remaining positive interactions are near-threshold and uncorrected, so the confident wording is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Prespecified, multiplicity-adjusted evidence of treatment benefit on a designated primary outcome.

quotes.text: This study has established that circuit training
While the control group also showed some improvements in pulmonary functions by the end of week

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion says the study 'has established' that circuit training improves oxygen saturation and pulmonary functions, from 60 participants with unblinded participants and no allocation concealment. Half of the outcomes (FVC, MVV, MRf, MVt) show no treatment-by-time effect, and the Conclusions' 'smaller magnitude' for the control group is not borne out for FVC and MVV. The Discussion also cites MRf as improved versus control despite p = 0.259. The limitations section is real but omits sample size, multiplicity and the lack of allocation concealment, so 'established' overstates the evidence.

issues.title: Discussion credits MRf with a treatment-vs-control gain; Results show interaction p = 0.259 and no extra benefit
issues.explanation: The Discussion lists MRf among metrics that improved with the programme compared with control, and later cites it as evidence of better breathing efficiency. The Results report a significant time effect only (p = 0.003), with no treatment effect (p = 0.215) and no interaction (p = 0.259). They state the treatment gave no additional benefit for MRf. The Discussion therefore contradicts the paper's own analysis and overstates the effect.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A between-group MRf comparison favouring treatment that is not reflected in the printed interaction p-value.

quotes.text: and  MRf  among  participants  who  engaged  in  the  8-week  exercise  program
the treatment did not provide an additional benefit for MRf beyond the improvements

issues.title: FEV1/FVC benefit partly rests on control-arm decline from a higher, imbalanced baseline (86.0 vs 79.1)
issues.explanation: Interaction tests are reported, so the main claims do use a between-group comparison. For FEV1/FVC, however, the arms differed at baseline (p = 0.039), and the control arm fell from 86.0 to 76.1 while treatment rose from 79.1 to 82.7. That pattern is what regression to the mean would produce, and the paper cites the control decline as supporting the programme. The conclusion's description of control gains as 'of smaller magnitude' also conflicts with the equal FVC and MVV improvements.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An analysis of post-test FEV1/FVC adjusted for baseline showing a treatment difference, with the control decline not driving the result.

quotes.text: except for FE1/FVC%, which exhibited a lower value in the treatment group than the control group [p=0.039]
the treatment was effective in maintaining or improving the FEV1/FVC

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a randomised trial run April-July 2022 with eight unranked outcomes
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval but no registry identifier or protocol. With eight outcomes and no designated primary, readers cannot tell whether the highlighted outcomes were prespecified. This weakens confidence in the selective emphasis on SpO2, FEV1, FEV1/FVC and PEF.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry entry dated before recruitment listing the same outcomes.

quotes.text: from the Semarang State University Research Ethics Commission under reference number 008/KEPK/EC/2022.

issues.title: Abstract omits control-group FEV1/FVC effect size whose CI [0.09, 0.84] excludes zero
issues.explanation: The abstract says that in the control group effect sizes were significant only for FVC and MVV. Table 2 gives the control FEV1/FVC effect size as 0.47 [0.09, 0.84], an interval that excludes zero. The paper itself discusses a control-group decline in FEV1/FVC, so the abstract's list is incomplete. This is a small reporting slip that does not change the main interpretation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the abstract or methods that its 'significant effect sizes' refer only to improvements, not declines.

quotes.text: mientras que en el grupo de control solo se observaron en FVC y MVV

quotes.location: Table 2, FEV1/FVC (%) row, Effect Size line, Control column

issues.title: Table 2 Total-column effect sizes misprinted: FEV1/FVC -0.16 [-0.10,0.41], PEF -0.33 [-0.59,-0.67]
issues.explanation: The Total-column effect-size cells in Table 2 contain intervals that do not match their estimates. FEV1/FVC is printed as -0.16 [-0.10, 0.41], where the interval centres on about +0.16. PEF is printed as -0.33 [-0.59, -0.67], where the upper bound is below the lower bound; -0.07 would centre on -0.33. A similar pattern appears in the MVt Total cell and the FEV1 treatment cell [-1.05, 0.26]. These look like typographical errors that do not change any conclusion but reduce trust in the table.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The source PDF showing the cells as +0.16 [-0.10, 0.41] and -0.33 [-0.59, -0.07], which would make this an extraction artefact.

quotes.location: Table 2, FEV1/FVC (%) row, Effect Size line, Total column
Table 2, PEF (l/sec) row, Effect Size line, Total column

script.explanation: the estimate -0.16 lies outside its own CI [-0.1, 0.41]

10.58727/jshr.111605.headline_claim: Water-based exercise may be especially helpful for promoting psychological healing, reducing fatigue and preserving functioning in people recovering from mild to moderate COVID-19.
10.58727/jshr.111605.overall: The headline claim that water exercise helps reduce fatigue and promotes mental-health healing is not supported: no fatigue measure improved, some worsened, and the anxiety/depression change was a non-significant two-person shift in a single-arm study with 71% loss. The data support at most that completers showed no clear change over 8 weeks.

primary_outcome.name: MFI-20 total fatigue score (no primary outcome designated in the paper)

issues.title: Conclusion says water exercise reduces fatigue, but MFI scores rose (female total 52.20 to 56.40, p=0.04)
issues.explanation: Higher MFI scores mean more fatigue. Total-sample reduced motivation rose from 10.05 to 11.14 (p=0.04) and female MFI total rose from 52.20 to 56.40 (p=0.04). No fatigue measure improved, yet the Conclusions say the programme may help in reducing fatigue. The data point the opposite way or show no change, and the Discussion's own finding is of no significant change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Data showing a decrease in fatigue scores, or a conclusion reworded to 'no worsening of fatigue'.

quotes.text: reducing  fatigue and preserving functioning in people recovering from mild
In females,  the MFI  total  score  significantly  increased  at  the postintervention testing  point.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions say water exercise may help in 'reducing fatigue', yet no fatigue measure improved and the only significant changes (female MFI total, total-sample reduced motivation) were increases, i.e. more fatigue. The paper is not wholly inconsistent, since it elsewhere describes fatigue as 'mostly unchanged' or stable, but the 'reducing fatigue' wording is not supported and the significant rises are not weighed in the Conclusions.

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post design cannot attribute changes to the programme
issues.explanation: With no comparison group, any change over 8 weeks cannot be separated from time, regression to the mean or expectation. The Conclusions nonetheless credit the programme with mental-health and functioning benefits and 'stability' as evidence of value. Stability without a control cannot show the programme preserved anything.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or waitlist control group showing differential change.

quotes.text: The fact that we included only an experimental group
These results suggest that water exercise may be especially helpful for promoting

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm pre-post design, so changes cannot be attributed to the programme, and the paper says so openly in the Limitations and final Conclusions sentence. What remains is that earlier Conclusions sentences still use benefit-attributing language ('benefits', 'evidenced by... improvements') that the design cannot support, though 'may be' hedges some of it.

issues.title: Only 21 of 72 enrolled (29%) analysed; 71% attrition not handled or discussed
issues.explanation: Results come only from participants who completed both testing points. Those who dropped out may differ in fatigue and health, so the completers may not represent the enrolled group. The Limitations section does not mention attrition, and conclusions are applied to people recovering from COVID-19 generally.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Baseline data and reasons for dropout showing completers resemble non-completers.

quotes.text: Out of the 72 participants who were initially  enrolled,21  (15 female, 6 male)

second_reader.what_stands: Only 21 of 72 enrolled (about 29%) were analysed, a completers-only analysis with roughly 71% non-completion that is neither analysed for bias nor listed among the limitations in the text. Reasons for dropout may appear in Figure 1, which could not be read, so that detail cannot be checked; the unexplained n=20 in Table 3 is a further small gap.

issues.title: Non-significant anxiety/depression change (11 to 9 of 20 with an issue) presented as a mental-health benefit
issues.explanation: Table 3 shows 11 of 20 with an anxiety/depression issue before and 9 of 20 after, a two-person change with no test and no control. The Conclusions say the benefits for mental health were highlighted and mention improved emotional wellbeing. Other EQ-5D domains worsened (mobility issues 6 to 9, pain 9 to 11), which is not mentioned.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant test of the anxiety/depression change versus a control.

quotes.text: The benefits of water-based exercise for mental health were highlighted
Although  not  significant,  the decrease  in  the  incidence  of  anxiety  and  depressive

second_reader.what_stands: A 2-person net change (11 to 9 of 20), with no test reported and an exact p of at least about 0.5 under the most favourable assumption, is presented in the Conclusions as a demonstrated mental-health benefit and 'improvements in emotional well-being', and the Conclusions drop the Discussion's 'not significant' caveat. Changes of similar size in the opposite direction for mobility and pain/discomfort are not given comparable weight.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 21 completers too few to support the stated benefit conclusions
issues.explanation: No power calculation is reported, and 21 participants (6 males) give little ability to detect change. Non-significant results are interpreted as stability or benefit rather than as inconclusive. The authors do acknowledge the small sample, so this mostly weakens secondary results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample-size calculation showing adequate power for the key outcome.

quotes.text: The second drawback is the comparatively small sample size

issues.title: Programme described as 'safe' with no adverse-event reporting and 51 of 72 lost
issues.explanation: The Conclusions call the programme safe, but the paper reports no adverse events or safety monitoring. Dropouts might include people who stopped for harm-related reasons, and this is not addressed. Stable scores in completers are weak support for safety.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A report of adverse-event monitoring and reasons for the 51 dropouts showing none were harm-related.

quotes.text: As a safe and inclusive type of rehabilitation, water-based activities

issues.title: Table 3 percentages use a denominator of 20 while analysed sample is stated as 21
issues.explanation: Every Table 3 row sums to 20 participants (e.g. 14+6), and percentages are computed on 20, yet the analysed sample is stated as 21. The missing participant is not explained. This affects only the descriptive quality-of-life frequencies, not the main claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that one participant had missing EQ-5D-5L data at one or both time points.

quotes.text: Total (n=21)

issues.title: No trial registration reported for a prospective intervention study
issues.explanation: The paper gives an ethics approval but no registry entry or protocol, so planned outcomes cannot be checked. Outcome reporting seems to match the stated Methods variables, which limits the practical concern.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry dated before recruitment.

quotes.text: with identical assessments conducted at the start and end

10.58854/jicm.1223171.headline_claim: Inhaled eucalyptus (E. globulus) essential oil aromatherapy is effective for post-COVID syndrome symptoms of dyspnea, back pain and anxiety and is recommended as complementary treatment.
10.58854/jicm.1223171.overall: The paper shows that 15 patients reported lower mMRC, VAS and BAI scores 4 weeks after starting the oil. It cannot show that the oil caused the improvement, because there was no control group. The 'effective' conclusion and the recommendation to use the oil are not supported by this design. The BMI discrepancy and the reference date are minor reporting slips.

primary_outcome.name: mMRC dyspnea score (with VAS back pain and BAI anxiety also reported as outcomes; no single primary outcome is designated)

issues.title: Single-arm pre-post study of 15 patients cannot show efficacy; no control, no sample-size justification
issues.explanation: All 15 patients were measured before and after 4 weeks of oil inhalation, with no comparator and no blinding. Post-COVID symptoms commonly improve over time, and self-reported dyspnea, pain and anxiety are open to expectation effects. The within-group p-values (<0.001) therefore cannot be attributed to the oil. The sample is tiny and no sample-size calculation is reported, so the effect estimates are imprecise. Only 'effective' as a hypothesis is supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent control or placebo arm, or natural-history data from the same population showing no spontaneous improvement over 4 weeks.

quotes.text: the absence of a control group.
Eucalyptus aromatherapy oil inhalation was found to be effective

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-arm, 15-patient pre-post pilot with no control group and no sample-size justification, so it cannot establish efficacy, and its improvements could reflect natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectation or other co-interventions. The authors do acknowledge small size and no control group as limitations, but the Conclusion's statement that the oil 'was found to be effective' goes beyond what the design supports.

issues.title: Conclusion recommends clinical use of the oil on the basis of an uncontrolled 15-patient pilot
issues.explanation: The Conclusion states that the oil was effective and recommends it in the complementary treatment and follow-up of post-COVID patients. An uncontrolled pilot of 15 patients with no safety reporting can generate a hypothesis, but it cannot support a treatment recommendation. The call for randomized trials at the end of the Conclusion conflicts with the recommendation just before it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled evidence of benefit from the same intervention in this population, or a conclusion worded only as hypothesis-generating.

quotes.text: we recommend the use of this aromatherapy oil in the complementary treatment
There is a need for randomized controlled clinical studies with a larger sample size.

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion does recommend clinical (complementary) use of the oil on the basis of an uncontrolled 15-patient pilot, and links the recommendation to a claim of effectiveness the design cannot support. It is partly tempered by the restriction to complementary use and by the explicit call for randomized controlled studies, so the recommendation is hedged rather than unqualified.

issues.title: Mean BMI is 37 (±4.4) in the abstract but 24.7±3.4 in Results and Table 2
issues.explanation: The abstract gives the mean BMI of the 15 patients as 37 (SD 4.4). The Results text and Table 2 give 24.7 (SD 3.4). Both cannot be right. A BMI of 37 would mean obesity and 24.7 is normal weight, so the sample description differs. The efficacy results do not depend on BMI.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that the abstract BMI refers to a different subgroup or time point.

quotes.text: the mean BMI was 24.7±3.4 (Table 2)

issues.title: No ethics committee approval for a prospective study; 'pilot' given as the reason
issues.explanation: Patients were advised to use a specified oil regimen and were assessed before and 4 weeks after. No ethics committee review is reported, and no informed consent is mentioned. 'Pilot study' is not normally an exemption from review. The paper discloses this, and local rules may allow it, so the paper alone does not show a violation. Readers should note the gap.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that the local regulator or ethics body exempted this work, or a statement of patient informed consent.

quotes.text: Ethics committee approval was not obtained

issues.title: Reference 10 access date (22 Nov 2023) is later than the acceptance date (30.12.2022)
issues.explanation: The article lists acceptance on 30.12.2022. Reference 10, the effect-size calculator website, was accessed on 22 November 2023, nearly a year later. A page cannot be consulted after the article was accepted. This is probably a typo, and it affects no result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the article was revised or re-accepted after November 2023.

quotes.text: Kabul Tarihi: 30.12.2022
Accessed 22 novomber 2023.

10.5960/dzsm.2023.570.headline_claim: Respiratory muscle training with an app-based device improves persistent shortness of breath, and patients benefit from intense, regular RMT over one month, after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
10.5960/dzsm.2023.570.overall: The SGRQ and subjective-health improvements are large and statistically strong within the trial group, but the paper cannot show that RMT caused them. There is no between-group or period-adjusted comparison, the control is unblinded and untreated, and the control period is described inconsistently between text, table and Discussion. The CPET subgroup claims are exploratory and contain printed statistics that do not reconcile.

primary_outcome.name: Dyspnea symptoms (SGRQ total score; visual analogue scale for subjective health status)

issues.title: Efficacy claimed from within-arm pre-post Wilcoxon tests; no between-group or period comparison, n=7 control
issues.explanation: All p-values are paired Wilcoxon tests of change from baseline. The pooled intervention effect (n=15) is never tested against the control-period change (n=7) or against the concurrent control arm, and period and order effects are not examined. The causal claim in the title and Discussion rests on non-significance in a seven-person control period, which is weak evidence of no change. The limitations section says efficacy against a control group still needs evaluation, yet the title and conclusion state that RMT improves breathlessness.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group or crossover (period-adjusted) analysis of SGRQ and subjective health showing the intervention effect exceeds the control-period change.

quotes.text: To compare intervention-related changes paired Wilcoxon-Tests were conducted.
larger studies are needed to fully evaluate the efficacy of RMT compared with a control group
The effect was associated with the training intervention since there was no score reduction at all during the control period.

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy is inferred from within-arm pre-post Wilcoxon tests, with no between-period or between-group test, and the control period has only 7 patients. The authors do concede in Limits that larger studies are needed to evaluate efficacy against a control group, so the weakness is partly acknowledged, but the title and Discussion wording are stronger than the analysis supports.

issues.title: Control period misreported: subjective health +14.14 (text, significant) vs -7.3 (Table 1); 'no SGRQ reduction' vs -3.1
issues.explanation: The Results text reports a significant control-period rise in subjective health of 14.14 points, about the same size as the 12.43-point intervention effect. Table 1 shows -7.3±17.3 with no significance marker. The Discussion also says there was 'no score reduction at all' in the control period, yet the control SGRQ changes were Total -3.1, Symptoms -2.4, Activity -1.2 and Impacts -4.5, all in the improving direction. The main argument for attributing the effect to training is that the control period was flat, and the paper describes that period inconsistently.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An author correction showing which subjective-health value is right and that SGRQ control-period changes are negligible relative to the intervention effect.

quotes.text: Although there was a significant change in subjective health (14.14±10.25, p=0.011, d=1.38, 95% CI [0.29, 2.42])

quotes.location: Table 1, Subjective health row, control column

quotes.text: The effect was associated with the training intervention since there was no score reduction at all during the control period.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper gives two incompatible control-period values for subjective health (+14.14±10.25, p=0.011 in the text versus -7.3±17.3 in Table 1), and this cannot be reconciled from the paper. The SGRQ claim is only partly right: the control-period SGRQ total fell by 3.1 points (not significant), so 'no score reduction at all' overstates it; 'no significant reduction' would be accurate.

issues.title: Unblinded, no-sham waitlist control for patient-reported primary outcomes (SGRQ, subjective health VAS)
issues.explanation: The control condition is one month without RMT, with no sham device or attention control. The primary endpoints are the SGRQ and a health-status VAS, both self-reported by patients who know they are training. The paper reports no blinding of patients or assessors. Expectation, attention and spontaneous-recovery effects are therefore confounded with the training effect, which limits the claim that RMT itself improved symptoms.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that outcomes were assessed blind or evidence of an attention-matched sham condition.

quotes.text: underwent an additional month without RMT as a control period and started RMT after a second examination at T1.
Primary endpoint: Improvement of dyspnea symptoms through breathing training (SGRQ, visual analog scale for subjective health status).
The treating physicians, the authors were aware of the identity of the individual patients during and after data collection.
quotes.location: Material and Methods, Study Design Participants

second_reader.what_stands: The control was a no-intervention waiting period without a sham, the study was open-label, and the primary endpoints are patient-reported, so expectation effects could contribute to the improvements. The paper does not state a blinding procedure for patients or outcome assessment, and the Limits section does not discuss this as a source of bias.

issues.title: Planned N=20, analysed 15 (16 randomised); no explanation, benefit stated confidently
issues.explanation: The a priori calculation required 20 patients but only 15 were analysed. The paper does not say why recruitment stopped at 16 or why one participant was excluded after randomisation because of low baseline symptoms. Small samples with large reported effects tend to overstate effect size, and the null whole-group CPET findings are uninformative at this size. The authors acknowledge the small sample in Limits, yet the Summary conclusion states that patients benefit without qualification.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Explanation that the target was met or a power analysis showing N=15 retains adequate power for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: N=20 patients are necessary for the study.
The significance of the findings of this study is limited by the small sample size.

issues.title: Post hoc subgroup (n=9) with uncorrected p=0.022/0.013 headlined after null whole-group VO2peak and power
issues.explanation: Whole-group relVO2peak (p=0.076) and relPmax (p=0.075) were not significant. The abstract instead leads with significant gains in a post hoc low-VO2peak subgroup, with no multiplicity adjustment among the roughly eight CPET variables and several SGRQ domains tested at alpha 0.05. The subgroup statistics are also printed inconsistently (see c6). The conclusion's wording is hedged, but the abstract emphasis overstates what an exploratory subgroup can show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified subgroup analysis in the registration (DRKS00028645) or multiplicity-adjusted results.

quotes.text: Exercise capacity and V ˙ O 2peak significantly increased in a subgroup of patients with low V ˙ O 2peak values at study inclusion
A subanalysis of N=9 patients within the study who had impaired
An α -level of 0.05 was considered significant.

issues.title: Table 1 significance markers contradict the text: relVO2peak p=0.076, relPmax p=0.075, SGRQ Symptoms p=0.013, BF max
issues.explanation: Table 1 marks whole-group relVO2peak (p=0.076) and relPmax (p=0.075) with * although the text calls both non-significant. It marks SGRQ Symptoms with ** (p<0.01) while the text gives p=0.013. It also stars the control-period BF max change although the text says only VE max changed in the control period. HR max is starred in the table with no matching text result. A reader using the table would conclude the whole-group CPET gains were significant, contrary to the text and the authors' own conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Authors' confirmation that the starred table cells refer to a different analysis, with matching p-values.

quotes.text: All other CPET parameters showed no significant differences after the control-period

issues.title: Subgroup CPET statistics inconsistent: relVO2peak 2.98±5.79 copied from whole group; relPmax d=0.95 outside CI
issues.explanation: The subgroup (N=9) relVO2peak change is printed with the same mean and SD as the whole group (2.98±5.79) but a different p and d, which the numbers cannot support. The subgroup relPmax effect size d=0.95 is printed with a 95% CI of [1.13, 1.72] that excludes it, and the control Activity CI [-0.83, -0.67] excludes its d=-0.09. These errors sit in the subgroup results quoted in the abstract, so those figures cannot be taken at face value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing the subgroup relVO2peak change truly has mean 2.98 and SD 5.79 and the printed CIs are correct.

issues.title: Intervention fatigue change: text -0.93±3.34 (d=+0.28) vs Table 1 +0.9±3.3
issues.explanation: The text reports a fatigue change of -0.93 but a positive effect size of 0.28, while Table 1 lists +0.9±3.3 for the same intervention change. The direction of the fatigue change is therefore unclear. The result is non-significant either way, so this is a minor reporting error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clarification that the text and table use different sign conventions.

quotes.text: while fatigue remained unchanged (-0.93±3.34, p=0.317, d=0.28, 95% CI [-0.81, 0.26])

10.61186/jps.23.144.13.headline_claim: Computer-based cognitive rehabilitation, alone and combined with tDCS, significantly improved quality of life in post-COVID-19 recovered patients, and the two approaches can affect quality of life.
10.61186/jps.23.144.13.overall: The sample-size, age-range and sex-count discrepancies are extraction artefacts of garbled Persian digits and do not stand. The main problem is that the efficacy conclusion rests on within-arm improvement, while the group-by-time interaction was null and the sham arm improved similarly, so the paper does not show that either treatment, or tDCS in particular, improves quality of life. The small sample, unreported allocation details and absent registration further limit what can be relied on.

primary_outcome.name: SF-36 physical and mental health subscales (quality of life)

issues.title: Efficacy conclusion rests on within-arm gains; stage*group interaction null (p=.708, .735) with sham arm improving too
issues.explanation: All three arms improved over time (Table 1, each within-arm F significant, and the sham arm improved comparably). The stage*group interaction was not significant (p = .708 physical, .735 mental), and the authors say the hypothesis was not confirmed. The Conclusion nonetheless says both methods, including the tDCS combination, significantly affect quality of life. With no non-intervention control and no between-arm difference, the data support only that scores rose over time, not that either treatment caused it, and there is no evidence that tDCS adds anything.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified within-arm estimand with a non-intervention control group, or a between-arm contrast showing the active arms beating sham.

quotes.text: the interaction effect of stage*group was not significant for  any  of  the  variables  (p  >  0.05)
Initially, the current research demonstrated that both intervention methods

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusion's claim that both CBCR alone and CBCR+tDCS 'had a significant effect' rests on within-arm time effects (Table 1). The only between-arm test, stage*group (p = .708, .735), is null, and the sham arm improved significantly too (p <= .001, partial eta2 .588 and .485), so the within-arm gains cannot be attributed to the tDCS or to the cognitive training itself. The authors do report the null interaction and say the group-difference hypothesis was not confirmed, so the weakness lies in the Conclusion's wording rather than in concealment. The raw arm means were not available, so the ch

issues.title: 15 per arm is small for a three-arm interaction test; null between-arm result is uninformative
issues.explanation: The authors enrolled 15 per group, above their calculated 10, so the screen's 'below target' reading is wrong. However, no effect size is stated for the group*time interaction. With 15 per arm, a non-significant interaction (partial eta2 about .02) cannot exclude a clinically useful difference between arms. The paper reads the null as a finding of no difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated target effect size and power for the interaction contrast, or a confidence interval showing the between-arm difference is small.

quotes.text: A total of 45 participants were  selected  through  convenience  sampling

issues.title: Allocation method, concealment and blinding not described (convenience sample, 'randomly assigned')
issues.explanation: The paper says participants were randomly assigned but does not describe sequence generation or concealment. The limitations note the study was not double-blind. This makes the sham comparison harder to trust, though the main between-arm result was null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of the randomisation sequence, concealment and who was blinded.

quotes.text: randomly assigned to three groups of 15 individuals each

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported for an interventional study
issues.explanation: Only an ethics approval code is given. Without registration, the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be checked against a prespecification. The effect on the conclusion is small because the key result is null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry (for example IRCT) made before enrolment.

quotes.text: IR.IAU.TJ.REC.1401.041

10.61453/intij.202228.headline_claim: Combined body weight, abdominal strengthening and breathing exercise produced greater improvement in abdominal muscle thickness, upper limb strength and lower limb strength than general breathing and separate limb strengthening exercises in post-LSCS women.
10.61453/intij.202228.overall: The headline claim that the combined exercise programme is superior is not reliably supported: allocation was by alternation, groups differed at baseline, and no between-group statistic is reported, so the superiority rests on unadjusted post-test means from 30 women. The within-group improvements are plausible but say nothing about which programme is better. The post-COVID framing is also not backed by the eligibility criteria.

primary_outcome.name: Abdominal muscle thickness (ultrasonography), upper limb strength (dynamometer), lower limb strength (sit-up test)

issues.title: Allocation by odd-even alternation is labelled randomization; no concealment, yet 'double-blind' claimed
issues.explanation: The paper states randomization was done by the odd-even method and that subjects were divided into two groups of 15 this way. Odd-even assignment is alternation, which is predictable, so it is not true random allocation and allocation concealment is not possible. Baseline imbalance is visible too (ultrasound 1.33 vs 2.00, dynamometer 13.60 vs 17.13), so the between-group comparison of post-test values is open to selection bias. The claim of double blinding is also doubtful, as participants performing visibly different exercise programmes cannot realistically be blinded.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A documented concealed random sequence, or evidence that allocation was not predictable to the enrolling investigator.

quotes.text: Randomization was done by using the odd-even method of sampling.
Using the oddeven method of sampling, subjects were divided into 2 groups
In this study, the investigator and subjects were blinded.

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation by odd-even alternation is a predictable, non-random (quasi-random) method that the paper calls randomization, and it describes no allocation concealment. The claim that investigator and subjects were blinded is not explained and is hard to reconcile with such clearly different exercise programmes; the paper also does not use the term 'double-blind' for any specific masking procedure beyond that sentence.

issues.title: No between-group test reported; superiority rests on post-test means and unadjusted baseline-imbalanced data
issues.explanation: Every p-value printed (p<0.0001) is for pre-to-post change within a group. The between-group claim relies on comparing post-test means (e.g. sit-up 9.13 vs 11.40) with no test statistic, SD, p-value or CI shown. Group B also started higher on all three outcomes, so a higher post-test value does not by itself show a greater treatment effect. The conclusion that Group B is superior is therefore not demonstrated in the reported results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Printed between-group tests (with SDs) on change scores or baseline-adjusted post-test values showing a significant difference.

quotes.text: Quantitative data analysis revealed that there is a significant difference between group A&B and within the groups.
The study's findings demonstrated a statistically significant difference between the pre- and posttest interventions.

second_reader.what_stands: No between-group test statistic, p-value, effect size or CI is reported, and the superiority claims rest on post-test means from groups that differed at baseline, with no adjustment or analysis of change scores. The change-score gaps are smaller than post-test gaps (especially sit-up, 0.74 vs 2.27), though the upper-limb dynamometer change is still clearly larger in B; whether any difference is statistically significant cannot be verified.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation; 15 per arm used to claim superiority of the combined programme
issues.explanation: The trial enrolled 30 women with no stated sample-size justification. The conclusion asserts that the combined programme gave a higher level of benefit than the comparator. With 15 per arm and unequal baselines, such a confident conclusion is not supported by the design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified sample-size calculation showing adequate power for the between-group difference.

quotes.text: 30 subjects were selected using a randomized sampling technique.
group B with combined body weight, abdominal strengthening, and breathing exercise produced a higher level of beneficial result

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports no sample-size calculation and has only 15 participants per arm, yet concludes the combined programme is superior. It does not describe the study as a pilot or acknowledge the small sample as a limitation.

issues.title: Post-COVID framing not supported by inclusion criteria; 'shorter period' claim unsupported by 12 weeks in both arms
issues.explanation: The title and Discussion refer to post-COVID LSCS women, but the eligibility criteria list age, LSCS, 8 weeks postpartum and postnatal exercise, with no COVID-19 requirement or documentation. Both arms exercised for 12 weeks, so the claim of benefit over a shorter period rests only on the shorter daily session time, not on a shorter time to benefit, which was not measured. The results therefore cannot be said to apply to a post-COVID population.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that all participants had confirmed COVID-19 or post-COVID symptoms, and time-to-benefit data.

quotes.text: Women aged 20 to 40 years, who underwent LSCS, women who crossed 8 weeks of postpartum
combined exercises had a significant influence on enhancing fast strength than completing the exercises independently and for a shorter period of time.

second_reader.what_stands: The post-COVID framing (title, Discussion) is not supported by the inclusion criteria, which contain no COVID-related requirement and report no COVID status of participants. The 'shorter period' claim is unsupported if it means programme duration (12 weeks in both arms), but it is accurate for per-session time (about 7.5 min in B versus 43 min in A).

issues.title: Described as a randomized controlled trial with no registration reported
issues.explanation: The paper reports ethics approval but gives no trial registry or number. Without a registration the prespecified primary outcome and analysis cannot be checked, and no primary outcome is designated among the three measured. The effect on the conclusions is limited given the other, larger problems.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registration record with prespecified outcomes.

quotes.text: This is a double-blind randomized controlled trial conducted on post-LSCS women

10.61453/intij.202342.headline_claim: Body-weight exercises (push-ups, squats, plank, burpees) improved muscle strength more than stretch-band strengthening exercises in COVID-19 survivors, and both groups showed positive outcomes.
10.61453/intij.202342.overall: The headline claim that body-weight exercises are superior for muscle strength is not reliable. No strength outcome was measured, the groups differed hugely at baseline on the 6MWT with similar within-group gains, and several p-values (0.05, 0.98, <0.0001 for the sit-and-reach) cannot be reconciled with the printed means and SDs. Together with n=30 and no described randomisation, the data support at most a tentative statement.

primary_outcome.name: Six-minute walk test (sit-and-reach test also reported; no primary outcome named)

issues.title: Allocation not described; 6MWT baseline differs 4.3 vs 5.38 and post-test gap mirrors it
issues.explanation: The Methods say participants 'were allotted' to groups from a convenience sample, with no randomisation, concealment or blinding described. Baseline 6MWT differs by 1.08 (about 2.7 SDs), and the post-test gap of 1.01 is almost the same, while group A in fact improved slightly more (0.97 vs 0.90). The between-group comparison of post-test values does not adjust for baseline, so the claimed superiority of body-weight exercises is not supported by this design.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Description of a concealed random allocation, or a baseline-adjusted analysis showing a between-group difference in change.

quotes.text: They were divided into 2 groups that is group-A
pre-test and post-test mean and standard deviation of group A was 4.3(0.41) and 5.27 (0.2) respectively
While the pre and post-test mean and standard deviation of group B was 5.38 (0.37) and 6.28(0.37) respectively.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper does not describe how participants were allocated to the groups, and the groups differ markedly at baseline on 6MWT (4.3 vs 5.38, p<0.0001 by my calculation). The post-test gap (1.01) is almost the same as the baseline gap (1.08), and group A's improvement (0.97) was slightly larger than B's (0.90), so the post-test comparison does not show a benefit of body weight exercises. No baseline comparison or adjustment is reported. As a side note, the reported between-group p=0.05 for post-test 6MWT does not match the printed means and SDs (t is about 9.3), which I did not need for this poi

issues.title: Sit-and-reach between-group p<0.0001 cannot arise from post-test means 3.8 vs 4.15 with SD 9.4 each
issues.explanation: The post-test sit-and-reach means differ by only 0.35 with identical SDs of 9.4 in groups of 15. These values give a t statistic near 0.1 and a p of about 0.9, not p<0.0001. The claimed significant between-group difference on this outcome is therefore not supported by the printed numbers.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or a different stated analysis showing the p<0.0001 refers to something other than the post-test means (or a corrected SD/mean in the text).

quotes.text: the post-test means and standard deviation was 3.8(9.4) and 4.15 (9.4)
there was a significant change in-between the group A and group B among the values of p<0. 0001

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

second_reader.what_stands: With the printed means (3.8 vs 4.15), SDs (9.4 each) and n=15 per group, an unpaired t-test gives t of about 0.10 and p of about 0.9, not p<0.0001. The reported significance cannot be reproduced from the reported summary statistics, so either the p-value or the summary values are wrong or misreported.

issues.title: Group B 6MWT pre-post change 5.38 to 6.28 (SD 0.37) reported as p=0.98, unlike group A's similar change
issues.explanation: Group B improved by 0.90 with SDs of 0.37 at both time points, almost the same as group A's 0.97 change which is reported as p<0.0001. Even with no pre-post correlation, a 0.90 change with these SDs would give a very small p, not 0.98. The p-value is therefore not reconcilable with the means, and the authors then still describe group B as markedly improved.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Confirmation that P=0.98 is a transcription error for a different value, or raw data showing the printed means/SDs are the errors.

quotes.text: While the pre and post-test mean and standard deviation of group B was 5.38 (0.37) and 6.28(0.37) respectively.
The statistical analysis shows that there was no significant difference in-between the pre and post-test with the p values (P=0.98).

second_reader.what_stands: A 0.90 rise with SDs of 0.37 and n=15 cannot yield p=0.98 under any paired or unpaired t-test; the result should be highly significant, like group A's. The p=0.98 and the statement of no significant pre-post difference in group B are inconsistent with the paper's own means and SDs, and also with its conclusion that both groups improved.

issues.title: Conclusion claims improved muscle strength but only 6MWT and sit-and-reach were measured
issues.explanation: The Results state two outcome measures, the six-minute walk and sit-and-reach tests. The Conclusion says body-weight exercise improved muscle strength more than stretch-band exercise, though no strength measure was taken. The Discussion itself describes these tests as measuring functional capacity and flexibility.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A muscle strength outcome (e.g. dynamometry) reported in the paper.

quotes.text: They were assessed by using two outcome measures.
group-B with Body Weight exercises showed higher level of positive outcome in improving muscle strength when compared with group-A.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion that group B was better 'in improving muscle strength' is not supported because muscle strength was not measured; only 6MWT (functional capacity) and sit-and-reach (flexibility) were. The conclusion also rests on post-test comparisons that are statistically problematic (see the other points).

issues.title: Between-group 6MWT post-test p=0.05 conflicts with p<0.001 in Discussion and with means 5.27 vs 6.28
issues.explanation: The Results give p=0.05 for the post-test between-group six-minute walk comparison, while the Discussion says p<0.001 for both outcomes and the Results summary lists p<0.0001 for the second outcome only. Recomputing from the printed means and SDs (n=15 per group) gives a p well below 0.0001, so the printed 0.05 does not match the data either. The between-group result is therefore reported inconsistently, and the reader cannot tell which p-value belongs to the analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated different test or adjusted analysis (e.g. ANCOVA on baseline) that yields p=0.05, together with an explanation of why the Discussion states p<0.001.

quotes.text: there was a significant difference in-between the group A & B among the values of p=0.05
the p value for both the outcomes are less than 0.001(P< 0.001)

issues.title: No sample-size justification for 15 per arm; conclusion states group-B superiority without caveat
issues.explanation: Thirty convenience-sampled participants (15 per arm) were studied with no sample-size calculation. The Conclusion states group B had a higher level of positive outcome without hedging, while the Discussion only suggests larger samples as future work. A study of this size supports at most a tentative, hypothesis-generating statement.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation showing adequate power for the primary outcome.

quotes.text: Convenient sampling method was used in the study, 30Covid-19 survivors were selected for the study
Number of samples can be increased and this study  with  large  sample  size  can  be  recommended

issues.title: No trial registry identifier reported for a 16-week interventional study
issues.explanation: The paper reports institutional ethics approval and a prospective 16-week intervention but gives no registry identifier. The planned outcomes and analysis therefore cannot be compared with a prior record. This is a transparency gap rather than a demonstrated error.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A trial registry entry predating enrolment.

quotes.text: After receiving IRB certificate from NRI College of Physiotherapy, NRI Academy of Sciences, the subjects were fully explained about the study
