10.61919/mjxane13.headline_claim: A structured six-week low-histamine diet was associated with higher MoCA cognitive performance, fewer self-reported cognitive failures, lower fatigue, and lower plasma histamine and hs-CRP than habitual-diet standard care among adults with post-COVID brain fog.
10.61919/mjxane13.overall: The reported statistics (CIs, Hedges' g, F-to-eta-squared, correlation CI and p) are internally consistent, and the authors frame the conclusion cautiously. However, unblinded participants, an unmatched control, complete-case analysis, no registration and very large effects for a six-week diet mean the findings are tentative and likely overstated.

primary_outcome.name: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score at post-intervention

issues.title: Complete-case analysis of 60/64 drops 2 intervention dropouts who could not sustain the diet; no sensitivity analysis
issues.explanation: All efficacy results use 60 completers. Two intervention participants stopped because they could not keep to the diet, which is a tolerability signal and likely related to outcome, and their exclusion may flatter the intervention. With only 4 of 64 missing, the bias is probably small, but no sensitivity analysis (for example worst-case imputation) is given, and the authors acknowledge that the analysis is not ITT.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT or worst-case sensitivity analysis showing similar effects.

quotes.text: two participants in the intervention group discontinued because they were unable to maintain the dietary restrictions
The analysis excluded four randomized participants without post-intervention data and consequently did not constitute a full intention-to-treat analysis.

issues.title: Unblinded participants and unmatched counselling contact leave CFQ/FSS (and MoCA) open to expectation effects
issues.explanation: Participants knew their allocation, and the intervention arm received biweekly dietitian counselling while controls received only weekly phone contact. The self-reported CFQ (diff -12.70) and FSS (diff -11.70) are therefore susceptible to expectation and attention effects, and these can also affect effort on MoCA. The authors acknowledge this, but the Conclusion still lists fewer cognitive failures and lower fatigue as findings, and the huge effects (g about -1.9 to -2.2) are not plausibly attributable to diet alone.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control arm or sham-diet comparator showing the same effects.

quotes.text: Blinding of participants and the dietitian was not feasible because the intervention required active dietary modification
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, randomization and blinding

quotes.text: Attention, expectation and behavioural-support effects may therefore have contributed to the observed differences.

issues.title: No trial registration reported; multiple outcomes without prespecified hierarchy or multiplicity control
issues.explanation: The report gives no registry identifier or protocol reference, so the primary outcome (MoCA) and the analysis plan cannot be checked against a prespecified record. Several co-primary-looking outcomes (MoCA, CFQ, FSS, histamine, hs-CRP) were tested at p<0.05 with no correction, and the authors themselves call for a prospectively defined outcome hierarchy. This weakens confidence in the secondary results more than in the MoCA finding.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry record dated before enrolment listing MoCA as the primary outcome.

quotes.text: Larger preregistered trials using standardized interventions, active comparison conditions, intention-to-treat analyses and longer follow-up are required
prospectively defined outcome hierarchy

issues.title: Article history lists receipt (17 Nov 2026) after acceptance (24 Jan 2026) and publication (28 Feb 2026)
issues.explanation: The article-history line gives a receipt date later than both the acceptance and publication dates. These cannot all be correct, so at least one date is misprinted. This does not affect any trial result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected article history showing a receipt date before acceptance.

quotes.text: Received: 17 November 2026; Accepted: 24 January 2026

10.63144/ijt.2025.6716.headline_claim: Physiotherapist-supervised synchronous telerehabilitation is more effective than asynchronous telerehabilitation for adults with post-COVID-19 syndrome in a low- and middle-income country.
10.63144/ijt.2025.6716.overall: The central claim that synchronous telerehabilitation is more effective than asynchronous is weakly supported: the single between-group primary signal was not confirmed post hoc, and the secondary 'effects' are within-arm changes that cannot be separated from natural recovery. Participant counts do not reconcile and mean imputation was used with markedly differential attrition, so the analysed data are uncertain. The result should be read as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Five Times Sit-to-Stand Functional Test (FTSTS)

issues.title: Superiority and 'safe, effective' conclusions exceed a non-confirmed primary result and a one-line safety report
issues.explanation: The only between-group signal is an omnibus F test on the FTSST (p = 0.0269) that the Tukey post hoc did not confirm. Baseline FTSTS was also lower in STR (11.02 s vs 12.62 s). Superiority of STR is therefore tentative at best, and it is further weakened by the attrition and imputation problems. The statement that TR is safe and effective rests on no control group and a brief 'no exercise-related issues' sentence in a small trial, yet it is used to support routine clinical integration.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant pre-specified pairwise or interaction contrast on FTSTS robust to the missing-data handling, and a systematic adverse event collection in both arms.

quotes.text: A significant between-group difference (F = 5.936; p = 0.0269) was found in the FTSST by mixed-model effects, but in the post hoc, this difference was not found.
In short, a TR offers a safe, accessible, and effective alternative.
No exercise-related issues occurred.

second_reader.what_stands: The primary result is only partly confirmed (the omnibus group effect was significant but the post hoc comparison was not), and the Discussion's statement that STR 'offers more positive clinical outcomes' and the closing 'safe, accessible, and effective' go beyond it. Safety rests on a one-line report with hospitalization as the only predefined event, with no monitoring in the ATR arm. The Conclusions' wording 'seems more effective' is hedged, and the omnibus primary test was nominally significant, so the claim is overstated rather than unsupported.

issues.title: Losses of 8 and 13 imply 15 and 8 analysable, but 17 and 14 (n=31) are analysed 'intention-to-treat'
issues.explanation: The Results say 23 and 21 were randomized and 8 and 13 were lost. That leaves 15 and 8 participants, yet 17 and 14 are reported as the final count. The implied losses from the final counts are 6 and 7, not 8 and 13. Calling a 31-person set 'intention-to-treat' also conflicts with 44 randomized. The true analysis population, and so the size of the primary and secondary analyses, cannot be established from the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A CONSORT flowchart showing a stage-by-stage count in which 17 and 14 follow from 23 and 21 with the stated exclusions, and a clear definition of what 'lost' means.

quotes.text: we successfully randomized 44 consecutive participants, with 23 assigned to the STR group and 21 to the ATR group
resulting in the loss of 8 participants from the STR group and 13 from the ATR group during follow-up
which yielded a final participant count of 17 in the STR group and 14 in the ATR

script.explanation: The participant flow does not reconcile: 'randomized' (n=44) minus its 1 stated exclusion(s) (21) leaves 23, but 'analysed' reports 31 -- 8 participant(s) unaccounted for by the paper's own arithmetic.

second_reader.what_stands: The stated losses (8 and 13) and the stated final counts (17 and 14) cannot both be right: 15 and 8 would remain, not 17 and 14. Describing the 31 analysed participants as 'intention-to-treat' is also inconsistent with ITT, which would retain all 44 randomized. I could not check Figure 1, so I cannot say which set of numbers is correct.

issues.title: Differential loss (8/23=35% vs 13/21=62%) handled by average imputation, with 31 of 44 analysed
issues.explanation: Loss to follow-up was much higher in the asynchronous arm. Mean imputation shrinks variance and pulls missing values toward the arm mean, which can distort between-group and within-group tests. The ATR group's adherence could not be monitored, so missingness is likely related to outcome. The primary between-group F test is therefore fragile, and no sensitivity analysis is given. The counting inconsistency itself is reported under c1.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis (multiple imputation, mixed model on all available data) giving the same between-group result, or evidence that missingness was unrelated to outcome.

quotes.text: Intention-to-treat (missing data handled using the average imputation method) was performed for all outcomes.
attrition occurred, resulting in the loss of 8 participants from the STR group and 13 from the ATR group during follow-up

second_reader.what_stands: By the paper's own figures, loss was much higher in the ATR arm (62% vs 35%). The analysis was nominally ITT with average (mean) imputation, but only 31 of 44 randomized participants appear in the analysis. Mean imputation understates variance and shrinks between-group differences. The attrition assumed in the sample size calculation (20%) was exceeded, and the paper reports no sensitivity analysis for missing data.

issues.title: Arm-specific 'positive effects' drawn from within-arm change; no secondary between-group test was significant
issues.explanation: The Conclusions credit STR with improving dyspnea, fatigue, stress and quality of life and ATR with only fatigue and anxiety. These statements rest on post hoc within-arm contrasts against baseline, with significance in one arm and not the other. A difference in significance does not show a difference between arms, and the between-group p values are 0.67, 0.82, 0.74, 0.65, 0.58 and 0.30. The uncontrolled before-after changes also cannot be separated from natural recovery, which the authors acknowledge.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Significant group-by-time interaction tests for these outcomes, or conclusions limited to within-arm descriptions.

quotes.text: In contrast, asynchronous telerehabilitation only positively affected perceived fatigue and anxiety.
There was no significant difference between groups, only intra-group (F = 6.192; p = 0.0123) on the mMRC scale.

second_reader.what_stands: No secondary between-group comparison was significant, yet the Conclusions credit STR with positive effects on dyspnea, fatigue, stress and quality of life and ATR with fatigue and anxiety, all from within-arm change over time. Within-arm change without a no-treatment control cannot separate treatment effect from natural recovery, which the authors acknowledge in the limitations. The difference between an arm that changed and one that did not is not itself tested, so the arm-specific contrast is unsupported.

issues.title: Secondary outcomes tested at P<.05 with no across-outcome correction; several post hoc p values sit near 0.05
issues.explanation: Six secondary outcomes were each tested at the 0.05 level with no adjustment across outcomes. A few of the cited within-group contrasts are marginal (p = 0.0483, 0.0336, 0.0270), so the claims that STR improved stress and ATR improved anxiety would not survive even a modest correction. This weakens the secondary within-group conclusions rather than the primary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction across the secondary outcomes, under which these contrasts remain significant.

quotes.text: The level of significance was P<.05.
initial assessment vs. eight weeks of intervention for the STR group (95% CI = 0.03745-12.90; p = 0.0483)
quotes.location: Results, Self-reported Stress, Anxiety, and Depression

10.63278/1342.headline_claim: Hypoxytherapy is an effective rehabilitation method for post-COVID-19 respiratory dysfunction and improves pulmonary function, supporting its inclusion in post-COVID-19 rehabilitation protocols.
10.63278/1342.overall: The headline claim that hypoxytherapy is an effective rehabilitation method is weakly supported: the design is an uncontrolled before/after comparison with no reported untreated patient arm, the sample size and effect sizes are left as placeholders, and key significance statements do not match the tables. The conclusion also extends benefit to obstructive disease that the authors say was absent. Results should be treated as preliminary.

primary_outcome.name: No primary outcome designated; FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC and PIC are all reported

checklist.control: healthy controls only; untreated post-covid arm described in abstract but not reported

issues.title: Abstract claims benefit over untreated patients; results are uncontrolled before/after plus healthy controls
issues.explanation: The abstract claims treated patients did better than untreated post-COVID patients, but no untreated post-COVID arm is reported. The data are paired before/after values in treated patients (Wilcoxon) and comparisons with healthy controls. Without a concurrent untreated comparator, spontaneous recovery over time cannot be separated from a treatment effect, yet the conclusion recommends adoption into protocols.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported data and a between-arm analysis for a concurrent untreated post-COVID group.

quotes.text: showed better respiratory outcomes than those who did not receive treatment
P2→3 (Wilcoxon test)

second_reader.what_stands: The paper's evidence for benefit is an uncontrolled before/after comparison in the same patients, plus comparison with healthy controls; no concurrent untreated post-COVID group appears in the results tables. The abstract wording 'than those who did not receive treatment' is not supported by the reported analyses.

issues.title: Sample size left as placeholder; abstract effect sizes 'X%, Y%, Z%' unfilled; no power calculation
issues.explanation: The Results state 'n = [insert sample size]' and the abstract gives effect sizes as X%, Y% and Z%, so the number analysed and the size of effects are not reported in the text. No sample-size justification is given. Table 8 percentages suggest roughly 17 patients, but a confident recommendation cannot rest on an undeclared, small sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported analysed n and sample-size justification.

quotes.text: The post-COVID-19 cohort (n = [insert sample size])
The FVC and FEV1 values increased by an average of X% and  Y%

second_reader.what_stands: The sample size is left as a placeholder ('[insert sample size]', '[X]') and the abstract's effect sizes are unfilled ('X%', 'Y%', 'Z%'); no power calculation is reported. Group sizes can only be inferred from Table 8 (27 controls, 17 patients), and the 55.9%/44.1% split implies n=34 rather than 17, a further unexplained inconsistency.

issues.title: FEV1/FVC 'increase after therapy' P=0.00004 is the control-vs-after comparison; before/after Wilcoxon P=0.023
issues.explanation: The text attributes P=0.00004 to the rise in FEV1/FVC after hypoxytherapy. In Table 3 that value belongs to the Mann-Whitney comparison of controls with treated patients, not to the before/after change. The actual within-patient test is P=0.023, so the treatment effect is far less significant than the text implies, and a between-group comparison is presented as evidence of change from treatment. The paper also admits the treatment has 'limited direct' effect on this ratio.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that 0.00004 is the before/after test result and Table 3 labels are swapped.

quotes.text: this ratio increases after hypoxytherapy sessions (P=0.00004)
P2→3 (Wilcoxon test)

second_reader.what_stands: The P=0.00004 printed in Table 3 belongs to the Mann-Whitney control-vs-after comparison (P1→3), not the before/after test; the before/after Wilcoxon P is 0.023. The text attaches 0.00004 to an 'increase after therapy' and cites Table 4, which is a normality table.

issues.title: Conclusion claims 'substantial benefits' in obstructive disease; no such patients studied, FEV1/FVC little changed
issues.explanation: The Conclusion says hypoxytherapy gives substantial benefits to obstructive pulmonary disease patients and improves quality of life and gas exchange. The Discussion states these patients had no emphysema, chronic bronchitis or asthma, and no quality-of-life or gas-exchange outcome is reported. The conclusion also admits little effect on FEV1/FVC. The abstract further recommends incorporation into protocols from an uncontrolled sample.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported obstructive-disease subgroup data or quality-of-life/gas-exchange outcomes.

quotes.text: Hypoxytherapy  provides  substantial  benefits  to  obstructive  pulmonary  disease  patients
emphysema, chronic bronchitis and bronchial asthma were not

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion claims 'substantial benefits' in obstructive pulmonary disease patients, yet the Discussion states that emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma were absent, so no such patients were studied. The 'little change in FEV1/FVC' statement also does not match Table 3, which shows a rise from 73.8 to 94.6 (P=0.023), and gas exchange and life quality were not measured.

issues.title: PIC 'significantly lower' than controls at P<0.00001 in text; Table 7 gives P=0.06 for that comparison
issues.explanation: The text says post-COVID PIC was significantly lower than controls (P<0.00001). Table 7 reports P=0.06 for control vs patients before treatment, which is not significant at 0.05. The text overstates the baseline deficit that the treatment is meant to correct, and no table value matches the quoted P.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different, unreported analysis giving P<0.00001 for this comparison, or a corrected Table 7.

quotes.text: was significantly lower than that of the control group (P<0.00001)
P1→2 (Mann-Whitney test)

issues.title: Methods report written consent; consent statement says consent waived (retrospective); no ethics approval named
issues.explanation: Section 2.2 says participants gave written consent before the research began, whereas the end matter says informed consent was waived due to the retrospective design. A study cannot be both prospectively consented and retrospective without explanation, and no ethics committee or approval number is given. This is a reporting inconsistency about study conduct rather than about the results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ethics approval and clarification of which consent applied.

quotes.text: The study participants provided written consent before the research began
Consent statement: Due to the retrospective nature of the study, informed consent was waived

issues.title: FEV1 'elevated to normal' with P>0.05; abstract presents FEV1 increase as improved expiratory efficiency
issues.explanation: The text says hypoxytherapy elevated FEV1 to normal levels (P>0.05). If the P value is the before/after test, this is a non-significant change described as a benefit; if it compares with normal values, it is consistent with 'normalised'. Table 2 is too garbled to tell, so the abstract's claim of improved expiratory efficiency is not clearly supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Clear Table 2 showing a significant before/after FEV1 change.

quotes.text: Hypoxytherapy sessions elevated the FEV1 index to normal volume levels (3.4±0.5, P>0.05)

issues.title: Table 3 control FEV1/FVC mean 101.72 (Q3 120.26) is impossible for a ratio; likely % predicted, unlabelled
issues.explanation: Table 3 reports control FEV1/FVC with mean 101.72 and Q3 120.26, which a ratio of FEV1 to FVC cannot reach. The text separately says typical values are 75-85%. The values are probably % of predicted, but the table does not say so, so the scale of the headline ratio analysis is unclear.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that Table 3 values are % of predicted.

quotes.text: an individual typically expels 7585% of air during the first second of exhalation

issues.title: Text on normality contradicts Table 4: post-treatment p=0.708 (normal), control p=0.000 (non-normal)
issues.explanation: The text states the control group shows no departure from normality and that normality decreased after treatment. Table 4 shows the opposite: controls are non-normal (p=0.000), patients before treatment borderline non-normal (0.046), and after treatment normal (0.708). The text misdescribes its own table, which also bears on the choice of tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 4 or text with matching direction.

quotes.text: Posttreatment, the rates of  normalcy  decreased
The control group exhibits no variation from normalcy

issues.title: Methods promise t-tests for normal data; PIC (normal per Table 6) analysed with nonparametric tests
issues.explanation: The Methods say t-tests are used when data are normal, and Table 6 shows PIC normal in every group, but Table 7 reports only Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests, which the Methods never mention. Nonparametric tests are valid here, so this mainly reflects an undocumented analysis choice.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Methods statement that nonparametric tests were used for all comparisons.

quotes.text: Student's  t-test served to analyze data between two groups when the data followed a normal distribution.

10.63682/jns.v14i32s.7381.headline_claim: Adding aerobic and balance exercises to relaxation exercises produced greater reductions in anxiety and greater gains in balance and maximum voluntary ventilation than relaxation alone in patients with COVID-19-related dizziness, so these exercises can be considered safe, affordable and effective complementary treatment.
10.63682/jns.v14i32s.7381.overall: The headline claim that aerobic and balance exercises reduce anxiety, dizziness and improve respiratory function more than relaxation alone cannot be relied on as stated. Dizziness was never measured, the MVV significance is not supported by the printed statistics, the baseline demographics conflict with the stated age range, and the trial is small and registered after its reported conduct. The anxiety and balance gains are the most plausible findings, but only as tentative results from a small trial with baseline imbalance.

primary_outcome.name: Anxiety (Hamilton Anxiety Scale, post-treatment score); the paper does not label a primary outcome

primary_outcomes.measure: SPSS for Windows, version 22 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, Illinois, USA)

issues.title: Post-treatment MVV difference (117.2 vs 108.13) reported as p = 0.0002 but t = 1.68 implies p about 0.1
issues.explanation: The between-group MVV comparison is reported as significant with p = 0.0002. The printed t of 1.67555 on 28 df corresponds to p of roughly 0.10, and the means and SDs give an even smaller t. The data as printed therefore do not show a significant MVV advantage, which undermines the respiratory-function claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data or a corrected table showing a between-group MVV t statistic consistent with p = 0.0002.

quotes.text: The difference between the groups was statistically significant (p = 0.0002).

script.explanation: The reported statistics fit NEITHER Welch's nor Student's t-test on these group statistics, under either tail convention, allowing for rounding of the printed inputs.

second_reader.what_stands: From the printed means, SDs and n, the post-treatment MVV difference (117.2 vs 108.13) is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level (p about 0.1), and the printed t of 1.68 itself implies this. The reported p = 0.0002, and the claim of a significant between-group MVV difference built on it, is inconsistent with the paper's own numbers.

issues.title: Conclusion claims reduced dizziness and safety; no dizziness measure or adverse-event monitoring reported
issues.explanation: The outcomes measured were anxiety (HAMA), balance (BBS) and MVV. No dizziness measure is reported, yet the title, aims and conclusion all say the exercises reduce dizziness. Safety is declared on the basis of a single sentence that no adverse effects were reported. The claims about dizziness and safety are not supported by the data presented.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dizziness outcome measure with results, or a described adverse-event monitoring procedure.

quotes.text: can effectively reduce anxiety and dizziness while enhancing maximum voluntary ventilation
HAMA: The HAMA is a commonly used instrument to evaluate the severity of anxiety symptoms.

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion that the exercises 'reduce dizziness' has no dizziness measurement behind it; only anxiety, balance and MVV were assessed. The safety claim rests on one line saying no adverse effects were reported, with no described monitoring and only 30 participants, so it is weakly supported rather than entirely absent.

issues.title: 15 patients per arm with no sample-size calculation, randomization method or blinding, yet firm efficacy claims
issues.explanation: The trial randomized 30 patients with no power calculation, no description of how allocation was generated or concealed, and no mention of assessor blinding. The Results and Conclusion nonetheless state superior effectiveness and safety. A study of this size and conduct supports only tentative conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified sample-size calculation and a described concealed randomization with blinded outcome assessment.

quotes.text: The patients were randomly divided into two equal groups, each consisting of 15 participants.
The intergroup comparisons highlight the superior effectiveness of the intervention in Group A

second_reader.what_stands: The paper reports 15 patients per arm with no sample-size rationale, no randomization procedure and no blinding, and the registry lists no masking. Its efficacy language is firm given those design limits, and the paper does not discuss them as limitations.

issues.title: Registered primary outcome is a software name; paper names no primary outcome and has no dizziness measure
issues.explanation: The registry lists SPSS version 22 as the primary outcome, which is not a clinical measure, so registered and reported outcomes cannot be compared. The paper's stated primary goal is anxiety and dizziness, yet no dizziness outcome is reported. Earlier registry versions were not seen, so a change in outcomes cannot be shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry history showing a clinical primary outcome that matches one reported in the paper.

quotes.text: The statistical analysis for this study was performed using SPSS for Windows, version 22
The primary goal of this study was to evaluate the effects of aerobic and balance exercises on anxiety and dizziness

issues.title: Reported mean ages (28.4, 29.6 y) are impossible for the stated 45-65 y range; Discussion says 40-60 y
issues.explanation: The Methods say participants were aged 45 to 65 years, and the Discussion says 40 to 60. Table 1 reports mean ages of 28.4 and 29.6 years, which cannot occur if everyone is at least 45 (or 40). The three age descriptions cannot all be right. This raises doubts about whether the baseline table and the cohort description come from the same data, and about the exercise prescription, which is based on 220 minus age.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected Table 1 with ages inside the stated range, or an erratum explaining which age description is correct.

quotes.text: ranging in age from 45 to 65 years
The mean age was 28.4 ± 2.11 years in Group A

issues.title: Baseline BBS difference (26.67 vs 22.2, p = 0.026) called non-significant and labelled NS
issues.explanation: The text and Table 3 call the pre-treatment balance difference non-significant. Yet it has p = 0.026 (t = 2.67), below the paper's own 0.05 threshold. This means the groups were not balanced on the balance outcome at baseline, which undermines the paper's statement that the groups were comparable.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated stricter alpha for baseline tests, or a corrected baseline p-value above 0.05.

quotes.text: with Group A scoring 26.67 ± 5.73 and Group B scoring 22.2 ± 3.59 (p = 0.026)
There was no significant difference between the groups in the pretreatment scores

issues.title: MVV % improvements (77.27%, 42.20%) do not match the printed means (about 13.4% and 8.9%)
issues.explanation: The MVV percentages are far larger than the printed means and mean differences allow. The same calculation applied to the HAMA and BBS rows matches the printed percentages. The inflated MVV percentages exaggerate the benefit in Group A and in the control group, and the stated advantage of Group A is overstated.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated definition of percentage improvement under which 77.27% follows from the printed MVV values.

quotes.text: Group A demonstrated a 77.27% improvement in MVV

issues.title: Registration (first submitted 2021-08-06) postdates the reported May-June 2020 study period
issues.explanation: The paper dates the trial to May-June 2020, but the registry record was first submitted in August 2021 and lists a 2021 start date. The registration is either retrospective by over a year or the study dates are wrong. The registered record also lists a statistics program as its primary outcome, so registration provides no protection against selective reporting.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Earlier registry versions or documentation showing registration before enrolment, or a corrected study period.

quotes.text: This study was carried out between May and June 2020 on a sample of 30 patients
the study was registered with the clinical trial registration number NCT04996225

issues.title: Balance and anxiety group comparisons use post-treatment scores only, with baseline imbalance in BBS
issues.explanation: Between-group tests were run on post-treatment scores with no adjustment for baseline. For balance, Group A started 4.5 points higher than Group B (p = 0.026), so some of the post-treatment gap may reflect the starting difference. The change from baseline was not compared between groups. The balance superiority claim is therefore less certain than stated, although the gain also looks larger in Group A.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A baseline-adjusted or change-score analysis showing the same between-group difference.

quotes.text: An unpaired t -test was used to compare the mean values between the two groups
with Group A scoring 26.67 ± 5.73 and Group B scoring 22.2 ± 3.59 (p = 0.026)

issues.title: Post-treatment BBS between-group p is 0.002 in text but .0002 in Table 3
issues.explanation: The text and Table 3 give p-values for the same comparison that differ by a factor of ten. Both are below 0.05, so the conclusion is unchanged, but the reported statistic cannot be pinned down. The printed t of 3.889 also does not match the p printed in either place.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Corrected text and table showing the same p-value.

quotes.text: A statistically significant difference was observed between the groups (p = 0.002)

issues.title: Table 1 caption says no differences with (p < 0.05); the printed p-values are 0.38-0.81
issues.explanation: The caption says there are no significant differences but attaches p < 0.05, which means the opposite. The table shows p-values of 0.38 to 0.81, so the intended meaning is p > 0.05.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: n/a (trivial wording slip).

quotes.text: revealed no significant differences in average age, weight, height, or BMI (p < 0.05)

10.64719/pb.4500.headline_claim: Stellate ganglion block is a safe, low-risk, minimally invasive and effective procedure for symptoms of long COVID and may be an effective adjunctive treatment for select patients.
10.64719/pb.4500.overall: The paper is an uncontrolled retrospective pre/post series of 17 patients, so the abstract's statements that the block is safe, low-risk and effective, and that all patients improved, go well beyond the evidence. Several reporting errors (a 94% COMPASS-31 figure that should be about 88%, a wrong left-side percentage, a footnote that contradicts the text, and an unreported post-block COMPASS-31) are mostly minor, but they reduce confidence in the data. Only the heart-rate and FSS changes are nominally significant, and these should be read as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: not specified; FSS, GAD-7, PCL-5 and heart rate were all analysed, with FSS and heart rate reported as significant

issues.title: Efficacy and safety asserted from an uncontrolled, retrospective pre/post series of 17 patients
issues.explanation: All efficacy results are within-patient pre/post differences from paired tests in 17 patients, with no comparator, no blinding and symptom-survey outcomes that are patient-reported. Such changes may reflect natural recovery, regression to the mean, expectation or co-interventions. The abstract and Discussion nevertheless state flatly that the block is safe, low-risk and effective, which this design cannot show.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent comparison group, or conclusions limited to describing change observed in an uncontrolled series.

quotes.text: Stellate  ganglion block is a safe, low-risk, minimally invasive, and effective  procedure  in  the  treatment  of  symptoms  for  long  COVID.
This study shows that a stellate ganglion block is a safe, effective procedure that can be used as an adjunctive treatment in patients with long COVID.
lack of a control group

second_reader.what_stands: Efficacy and safety are asserted in the Abstract Conclusions and Discussion paragraph 3 from an uncontrolled, retrospective pre/post series of 17 patients, with two of four outcomes non-significant, partial data on HR and PCL-5, and no comparator; the unqualified 'effective' is not supported by the design. The limitations paragraph and the softer final Conclusion ('may be an effective') do acknowledge this, and the absence of observed complications in 17 patients is accurately reported but is weak evidence of a 'safe, low-risk' profile.

issues.title: Abstract and text say all patients improved, but the Results report 1 of 8 followed patients with no improvement
issues.explanation: The abstract, the Results and the Discussion say all patients reported symptomatic improvement or relief. The subgroup paragraph says one patient followed at 1, 2 and 3 months reported no symptomatic improvement, and that leaves 7 of 8 improving in that subgroup. The universal-response statement is therefore not accurate, and it is one of the paper's most prominent efficacy claims.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the non-improver was among the patients who still reported some improvement elsewhere, or a correction of the subgroup sentence.

quotes.text: All patients reported some degree of symptomatic improvement from the block.
one  patient  reported  no  symptomatic  improvement  post-block

issues.title: Non-significant PCL-5 change (5.3 points, P=0.159, n=10) described as clinically significant
issues.explanation: PCL-5 was available for only 10 of 17 patients, and the mean change of 5.3 points was not statistically significant. The text nonetheless describes it as clinically significant and as lowering scores below the diagnostic threshold, a group-mean statement that says little about individual patients. The Discussion adds that more data might have made it significant, which is not supported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified minimal clinically important difference with individual-level responder data showing the change.

quotes.text: dropping scores below the clinical threshold for PTSD diagnosis
may have been more significant with more data

issues.title: Post-block COMPASS-31 collected and listed for analysis but its results are not reported
issues.explanation: The Methods say COMPASS-31 scores were compared pre and post, and the Results say 16 patients completed it post-procedure. Only the pre-procedure COMPASS-31 is reported. The paper's own autonomic outcome is therefore missing, and the autonomic claim rests on a single heart-rate comparison in 14 patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported post-procedure COMPASS-31 analysis in a table, figure or supplement.

quotes.text: Sixteen patients completed post-procedure COMPASS 31, GAD-7, and FSS surveys

issues.title: COMPASS-31 >20 and >40 percentages (93.7%, 81.2%) fit n=16, not the stated 17; correct values are 88.2% and 76.5%
issues.explanation: Table 1 is headed N = 17 and the text says all 17 completed the pre-procedure COMPASS-31. The printed counts 15 and 13 give 88.2% and 76.5% of 17, not 93.7% and 81.2%. The inflated 94% is carried into the abstract as a headline figure on autonomic dysfunction.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that one patient had no valid pre-procedure COMPASS-31 score, which would make 16 the correct denominator.

quotes.text: All 17 patients completed pre-procedure COMPASS 31, GAD-7, and FSS surveys.

script.explanation: 15/17 = 88.24%, but the paper prints 93.7, outside the rounding interval [93.65, 93.80]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 16.0 rather than 17.

issues.title: 'No complications or untoward effects' stated although 2 patients had Horner's syndrome
issues.explanation: Two patients had unilateral Horner's syndrome that resolved within a week, and the Methods name Horner's syndrome as a potential complication to monitor. The Discussion and abstract nevertheless claim a safe, low-risk procedure with no untoward effects in any patient. The safety statement is slightly overstated, although the events were minor and transient.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition of 'untoward effect' that excludes expected, transient and self-resolving effects.

quotes.text: Two patients experienced unilateral Horner's syndrome
There were no complications or untoward effects from the procedure in  any  patient.

issues.title: Table 2 footnote says 1 patient lacks pre-procedure FSS/GAD-7 data; text says all 17 completed them
issues.explanation: The text says all 17 completed pre-procedure COMPASS-31, GAD-7 and FSS surveys, and that 16 completed them post-procedure. The Table 2 footnote for FSS and GAD-7 instead lists one patient with missing pre-procedure data. This leaves the number of pairs entering the paired tests unclear (16 pairs on one reading, 15 or 16 on the other).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected footnote stating post-procedure missingness.

quotes.text: 1 patient. b Missing pre-procedure data for 3 patients and post-procedure data for 6 patients.
Sixteen patients completed post-procedure COMPASS 31, GAD-7, and FSS surveys

issues.title: Table 1 left-sided block 6 (32.3%) should be 35.3%; blocked-side percentages sum to 97.0%
issues.explanation: Six of 17 is 35.3%, not 32.3%. The three categories in the table (10, 6, 1) account for all 17 patients but their printed percentages sum to 97.0%. This is a small reporting slip that affects no conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A different denominator for this row; none is given, and the other rows use 17.

script.explanation: 6/17 = 35.29%, but the paper prints 32.3, outside the rounding interval [32.25, 32.40]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 18.6 rather than 17.

10.64898/2025.12.30.25343085.headline_claim: Self-administered transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation for 8 weeks reduces post-COVID fatigue, with benefit seen only in the active nVNS group among participants meeting minimum adherence.
10.64898/2025.12.30.25343085.overall: The headline claim that active taVNS, but not sham or placebo, improves post-COVID fatigue is not supported by the analysis reported: it rests on a post-randomisation adherent subset (59/114) and on within-arm significance, while the formal group-by-session VAS interaction was null (p=0.203). The data are compatible with a modest benefit but equally with non-specific improvement; causal and mechanistic claims go well beyond them.

primary_outcome.name: Fatigue visual analogue scale (VAS)

issues.title: Active-only benefit inferred from within-arm p-values; group-by-session VAS interaction p=0.203
issues.explanation: The authors say significant improvement occurred only in the active group, not sham or placebo. But the formal test of whether groups differed (VAS interaction F(4,110)=1.516, p=0.203) was not significant, and control arms improved by 8.0 points versus 11.9 in the active arm. Differences in significance between arms are not evidence of a difference between arms, and the small control arms (19, 16) had little power.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant pre-specified between-group contrast of active versus sham/placebo on VAS.

quotes.text: A repeated measures ANOVA showed no significant interaction between group and session for the visual analogue scale
This change was only significant in the active nVNS, and not sham or placebo group.

second_reader.what_stands: The paper infers an active-only VAS benefit from the contrast between significant within-arm p-values (active p=0.003) and non-significant ones (sham p=0.018 after correction, placebo p=0.141), while its own group-by-session interaction test is null (p=0.203). A difference in significance between arms is not evidence of a difference between arms, and the sham and placebo reductions point the same way as the active one.

issues.title: Efficacy conclusion rests on 59 of 114 randomised after post-randomisation adherence exclusion
issues.explanation: Only participants meeting a usage threshold measured after randomisation were analysed, with no intention-to-treat result. Adherence may differ by arm (for example because of tragus-clip discomfort) and relate to outcome, so the remaining arms may no longer be comparable. The Discussion itself says the changes were only seen after this exclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An ITT analysis of all randomised participants showing the same effect.

quotes.text: Of the 114 participants recruited, 24 dropped out during the study and a further 31 were excluded from analysis for not meeting minimum TENS usage
these significant changes were only seen after excluding participants not meeting a minimum usage criterion

second_reader.what_stands: The efficacy findings rest on 59 of 114 randomised participants (about 52%), selected by a post-randomisation adherence criterion, and the Discussion states the significant changes appeared only after that exclusion. The paper discloses this and labels the analysis per-protocol, but it cannot rule out that selection by adherence differs between arms and affects the comparison.

issues.title: Discussion cites primary VAS improvement as taVNS-specific despite null group-by-session interaction
issues.explanation: The closing paragraph says improvements 'notably include the primary outcome' and were 'not seen after sham or placebo stimulation', without noting that the group-by-session test for VAS was not significant (p=0.203) and that controls also fell by 8 points. Pooled pre/post VAS p<0.001 across arms is also reported as a benefit. The wording is hedged ('may offer', 'promising') but overstates specificity.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, significant between-group VAS result.

quotes.text: The improvements notably include the primary outcome of fatigue VAS
A repeated measures ANOVA showed no significant interaction between group and session for the visual analogue scale

second_reader.what_stands: The Discussion presents the primary VAS improvement as seen with taVNS but not with sham or placebo, although the paper's own interaction test for VAS is null (p=0.203). The data show a same-direction improvement in all arms, so the specificity claim is not supported by the formal test.

issues.title: Causal 'vagal dysfunction contributes to pCF' and renaming claim exceed a null-interaction subgroup result
issues.explanation: The Discussion says the results strengthen the argument that vagal dysfunction actively contributes to pCF and suggests the term 'Sick Vagus Syndrome'. The data are a post-randomisation per-protocol subgroup with a non-significant group difference, and none of the autonomic measures changed after stimulation. Placebo/sham effects, adherence selection and spontaneous recovery are not excluded, so the causal and mechanistic inference is unsupported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Controlled between-group evidence of vagal-measure change mediating the symptom effect.

quotes.text: strengthens the argument that vagal dysfunction is not merely correlated with but actively contributes to pCF
Post-COVID fatigue might therefore more accurately be termed 'Sick Vagus Syndrome'.

second_reader.what_stands: The causal statement that vagal dysfunction 'actively contributes to pCF' and the proposed renaming go beyond what the paper shows: the subgroup result has no significant between-group interaction, no autonomic or vagal measure improved, and the control arms moved in the same direction. The hedged wording ('strengthens the argument', 'might') softens but does not remove this gap.

issues.title: Missed-day denominator of 120 days does not match the 112-day (16-week) trial or 56-day logging period
issues.explanation: The Results report 62.5 missed days out of 120 for low-adherence participants, but the trial is described as 16 weeks (112 days) and the logger as covering 8 weeks. The denominator is never defined, so the figure cannot be reconciled with the stated design. It affects only a descriptive adherence statistic.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement defining the 120-day window (e.g. monitoring period incl. extended follow-up).

quotes.text: and 62.5/120 missed days
over the course of the 16-week trial

10.64898/2026.02.24.26347001.headline_claim: The authors conclude that 15-day nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was safe and well-tolerated, but that no virological or immunological evidence supports its use as a Long COVID treatment in this population.
10.64898/2026.02.24.26347001.overall: The descriptive immunology is mostly consistent, but the headline that no virological or immunological evidence supports NMV/r rests on small, unpowered, exploratory comparisons with differential sample loss, and is stated more firmly than the data allow. Safety and NMV/r-specific hematologic claims are weakly supported within this sub-study, while the Summary wording on IgG and the RANTES finding are minor overstatements.

primary_outcome.name: PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score change at Day 28 (trial primary, as stated in the Introduction; this sub-study reports no primary outcome of its own)

primary_outcomes.measure: Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS)-29 Physical Health Summary Score

issues.title: Flat 'no virological or immunological evidence' conclusion rests on small, unpowered exploratory subgroups
issues.explanation: The conclusion states that no virological or immunological evidence supports NMV/r use. The analyses are of 37 and 45 paired samples, with about 40-55% having detectable S1 at baseline, and no power calculation. The authors themselves say the small Spike-positive number may have reduced the ability to detect subtle changes. Null results here show only that large effects were not seen, so the unqualified conclusion is stronger than the design supports.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Equivalence margins or power calculations showing the sub-study could exclude clinically meaningful immunological or viral changes.

quotes.text: may have compromised the robustness of the analyses
no virological or immunological evidence supports its use as a treatment for Long COVID in this study population

issues.title: Hematologic changes called specific to NMV/r from within-arm tests while between-arm comparison showed no difference
issues.explanation: The paper reports significant within-arm shifts in the NMV/r arm and none in placebo, and then says the changes were observed specifically in the nirmatrelvir arm. The same paragraph states that no differences were observed between arms at day 28. Significant in one arm and not in the other does not show the arms differ. The attribution to NMV/r is not established, though it is stated modestly.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A significant arm-by-time interaction or between-arm comparison of change scores for these parameters.

quotes.text: no within-group changes were detected in the placebo arm. In the NMV/r arm, modest but statistically significant shifts were detected
modest hematologic changes were observed specifically in the nirmatrelvir arm on day 28

issues.title: Differential sample loss (6/51 placebo vs 12/49 NMV/r) with per-protocol-style exclusions not addressed in analysis
issues.explanation: Of 51 placebo and 49 NMV/r participants, 45 and 37 contributed paired samples. Some NMV/r exclusions follow discontinuation or rebound, which could relate to treatment. The sub-study uses available-sample analyses without sensitivity analysis or discussion of this imbalance. This weakens the arm comparisons modestly, and the paper makes no randomized-comparison claim for these outcomes.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A sensitivity analysis including all available participants or showing baseline characteristics of excluded participants were balanced.

quotes.text: Eightytwo participants (n=45 PBO/r; n=37 NMV/r) provided blood samples at baseline (Day 0) and post-treatment (Day 28)
Among 49 participants in the NMV/r subgroup, 2 did not take medication, 1 had 13% compliance, 3 discontinued on day 5

issues.title: Summary says SARS-CoV-2 IgG 'remained constant' though RBD IgG fell significantly in both arms (padj 0.024, 0.0275)
issues.explanation: The Summary says SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG levels remained constant. The Results report significant day-28 declines in RBD-specific IgG in both arms, plus an anti-N change in the placebo arm. Only anti-Spike IgG was unchanged. The declines are small (<0.5 log10) and the Discussion describes them, so this is a Summary wording problem rather than a change to the findings.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Summary that specified anti-Spike IgG only, or data showing the RBD decline was not significant.

quotes.text: SARS-CoV-2-specific  IgG  levels remained  constant
a significant decline in RBD-specific IgG was  observed  on  day  28  compared  to  baseline,  irrespective  of  drug  arms

issues.title: 'Safe and well-tolerated' stated despite dysgeusia in 16/37 NMV/r and hematologic shifts, with no AE analysis here
issues.explanation: The conclusion calls NMV/r safe and well-tolerated, but this sub-study did not analyse adverse events systematically. It reports dysgeusia in 16/37 NMV/r participants versus 3/45 placebo, and significant red cell, platelet and hemoglobin shifts in the NMV/r arm. These were within normal ranges and safety was assessed in the parent trial, so the claim is defensible but is not demonstrated here.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The parent trial's prespecified safety analysis showing comparable serious and overall adverse event rates, cited as the basis for the statement.

quotes.text: although NMV/r was safe and well-tolerated over 15 days
Sixteen out of 37 participants in the NMV/r arm had self-reported dysgeusia
quotes.location: Results, Treatment alters levels of circulating cytokines in both arms

issues.title: Post hoc RANTES-improvement association headlined in Summary; improver definition and many comparisons
issues.explanation: The Summary features RANTES reductions in self-reported improvers. The improver category was defined post hoc from five instruments, and RANTES was one of >100 analytes tested; the same RANTES fall appeared in both arms over time, so it may reflect time or regression to the mean. The Discussion appropriately says causation is unknown, and the paper is labelled exploratory, so the emphasis is mild.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified improvement definition and analysis plan naming RANTES.

quotes.text: We do not know whether this association is a simple correlation or causation.

issues.title: Paired day-0 vs day-28 comparisons labelled 'Wilcoxon Rank Sum', inconsistent with signed-rank Methods
issues.explanation: The Results describe paired baseline-versus-day-28 comparisons as Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests, while Methods and figure legends state the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired data. Rank-sum is for independent groups, so the labelling is inconsistent. The reader cannot tell which test produced the p-values.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Author confirmation that signed-rank tests were used throughout and the Results labels are typos.

quotes.text: Paired comparisons across time points were conducted using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
(Wilcoxon Rank Sum test; padj PBO/r  = 0.024, padj NMV/r  = 0.0275; Fig. 3E)

10.64898/2026.05.11.26352906.headline_claim: CT combined with active tDCS enhanced untrained working memory and visuospatial memory compared with CT plus sham stimulation, whereas CT alone did not improve untrained cognitive performance versus PMR.
10.64898/2026.05.11.26352906.overall: The null primary result (CT vs PMR) is reported honestly, but the headline claim that tDCS-augmented training produces transfer gains rests on uncorrected secondary contrasts in 20 vs 20 participants, only one of which (post-intervention 2-back) is reasonably robust. Treat the tDCS finding as hypothesis-generating, not as confirmed efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: Untrained working memory (N-back accuracy) at post-intervention, CT vs PMR

issues.title: Conclusion states tDCS 'produces significant enhancements' from secondary, unadjusted contrasts (n=20 per arm)
issues.explanation: The primary CT vs PMR comparison was null. The headline claim about tDCS rests on secondary contrasts in 20 vs 20 participants: 2-back (p=0.002, then p=0.037 at follow-up) and VR (p=0.037 at post only), with 1-back, PROPr, PROMIS-Cog and letter updating (trained task, in the opposite direction, p=0.036) not supporting benefit. Phrasing such as 'produces significant enhancements' and 'neuromodulation approaches may be necessary' is stronger than exploratory, uncorrected secondary results from a small phase IIb trial can support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchical testing plan placing the tDCS 2-back contrast as a confirmatory endpoint, or replication in an adequately powered trial.

quotes.text: CT combined with tDCS produces significant enhancements in transfer cognitive tasks
neuromodulation approaches may be necessary for cognitive transfer

second_reader.what_stands: The conclusion's 'produces significant enhancements in transfer cognitive tasks' rests on secondary contrasts (n=20 per arm, not powered for this comparison, no multiplicity correction stated) in which 3 of 6 transfer contrasts had p<0.05; only the 2-back post-intervention result (p=0.002) would survive a simple Bonferroni correction, and the visuospatial effect did not persist at follow-up. The 'unadjusted' part of the point does not stand: the estimates are adjusted for baseline score, age and sex, and the Discussion elsewhere calls results 'preliminary' and lists sample size as a limitation

issues.title: No multiplicity control across ~24 secondary contrasts; VR (p=0.037) and 2-back follow-up (p=0.037) are marginal
issues.explanation: Twelve contrasts per comparison set (six outcomes at two timepoints) are tested at an unadjusted 0.05 level, and the paper describes no correction. Only the post-intervention 2-back result (p=0.002) is clearly stronger than what chance could produce across this many tests; the VR and follow-up 2-back results (p=0.037 each) and the opposite-direction letter updating result (p=0.036) are of the size expected from chance. The tDCS claim for visuospatial memory in particular is fragile.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified gatekeeping or correction procedure in the statistical analysis plan under which these contrasts remain significant.

quotes.text: CT+AtDCS also outperformed CT+StDCS in the virtual reality task at post-intervention ( β = 6.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 12.85, p = 0.037)

10.64898/2026.08.25.26361319.headline_claim: MMT is associated with selective early plasma proteome remodelling, with HHIP the leading protein associated with clinical response among MMT participants, and lower inflammation/injury and higher repair/remodelling biology in responders.
10.64898/2026.08.25.26361319.overall: The paper is candid that this is a small, exploratory, post hoc analysis and its closing conclusion is appropriately modest, but the responder definition is unregistered and unvalidated, and the HHIP and 17-protein findings are selected and tested in the same 30 people, so the reported p-values cannot be read as evidence of a response signature. The ELISA gives only weak agreement with the SomaScan result. The results are best treated as hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Clinician-selected post hoc response phenotype (week 8, at least 2 of 5 components meeting 0.5 SD CIC threshold)

issues.title: Responder definition is post hoc, unvalidated and unregistered; 16/20 vs 3/10 (p=0.0147) is not confirmatory
issues.explanation: Responders were defined after the fact by a clinician-chosen set of five measures, with a 0.5 SD improvement threshold that the authors say is not a validated minimal clinically important difference. The registered primary outcome was treatment completion, so this response result is not a pre-specified efficacy test. The between-group response difference and every responder-versus-nonresponder molecular comparison inherit this flexibility, so they can only be read as hypothesis-generating.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A dated protocol or statistical analysis plan showing the 2-of-5 rule, components and 0.5 SD threshold were fixed before unblinding.

quotes.text: The threshold served as a standardized exploratory criterion rather than a validated measure-specific minimal clinically important difference.
Clinical response was summarized using a post hoc, clinician-selected response phenotype developed specifically for this study.
quotes.location: Results, Study design and plasma proteomic profiling workflow

second_reader.what_stands: The paper itself says the responder rule is post hoc, clinician-selected and not a validated measure-specific MCID. The threshold is 0.5 SD of the cohort's own baseline, and missing components count as non-response. The Fisher p of 0.0147 is arithmetically correct but is a nominal, exploratory result that cannot be confirmatory. The registry's current primary outcome is treatment completion, so this responder rule is not the registered primary. Whether it appears among the 3 unseen secondary outcomes could not be checked, so 'unregistered' is supported only in that limited sense.

issues.title: HHIP and 17-protein pattern selected and tested in same n=30 (4 nonresponders); in-sample p-values are optimistic
issues.explanation: The 17 proteins and HHIP were chosen because they separated responders from nonresponders, then the composite and program scores were tested for that same separation in the same people, so the low p-values are largely built in. Only four MMT participants were nonresponders, and the HHIP permutation p of 0.000413 equals the smallest value that split can produce. No independent validation exists, and the screen used a liberal unadjusted p ≤ 0.20 threshold. The finding is a prioritised hypothesis, not a signature.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Replication of the HHIP and 17-protein pattern in an independent cohort, or cross-validated scores where selection is nested inside the folds.

quotes.text: Because HHIP was selected and evaluated in the same small cohort, these analyses support its prioritization for further study but do not establish monitoring or predictive performance.
The responder screen used an unadjusted two-sided p value threshold of 0.20 and an absolute responder minus nonresponder change difference of at least 0.10 log2(RFU)
The composite score for the exploratory 17 protein response pattern was higher in MMT responders than in MMT nonresponders (p = 0.00289)

second_reader.what_stands: HHIP and the 17-protein set were selected on the responder/nonresponder contrast in the same 30-participant cohort and then evaluated on that contrast, with only 4 MMT nonresponders. The composite p-values (for example 0.00289) are therefore optimistic in-sample results. The HHIP FDR q=0.0066 accounts for screening across assays but not for re-testing the selected marker in the data that selected it. The authors disclose this and do not claim validation.

issues.title: HHIP ELISA (10/14 vs 2/4 decreased) does not reproduce SomaScan's complete separation but is called supportive
issues.explanation: SomaScan showed all 16 responders separated from all 4 nonresponders, yet in the ELISA HHIP fell in half of the nonresponders as well. The orthogonal assay therefore only weakly agrees with the discovery result. The paper still counts it as support in the Discussion and summary, and does not report a test or why only 14 responders were shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Full ELISA change data for all 20 MMT participants showing a significant, consistent separation between responders and nonresponders.

quotes.text: HHIP decreased in 10 of 14 displayed MMT responders and 2 of 4 nonresponders (Supplementary Figure 4).
HHIP was the leading protein associated with response among MMT participants, and the ELISA supported the SomaScan result.

second_reader.what_stands: The ELISA does not reproduce SomaScan's complete separation: 71% vs 50% decreasing, from 14 vs 4 participants, is statistically uninformative (Fisher p about 0.57), and no ELISA test or effect size is reported. The direction is the same as SomaScan, and the Discussion and limitations temper the claim. However, the summary statement that 'the ELISA supported the SomaScan result' is stronger than these data can bear.

issues.title: Title and OrganAge/aging language outrun null responder results (p=0.750, 0.437; q=0.253)
issues.explanation: The title and some Results sentences present a settled response signature and link responders to aging-related protein signatures. The OrganAge treatment effects did not pass FDR (all q = 0.253) and the responder comparisons were far from significant. The closing paragraph is appropriately cautious, but the headline framing is stronger than the exploratory data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Nothing needed beyond rewording; independent replication would support the stronger title.

quotes.text: these findings provide a hypothesis-generating extension of the broader proteomic finding that beneficial clinical responses to MMT were linked to early molecular changes, including protein signatures associated with aging biology
Neither responder comparison was statistically significant.

10.64898/2026.10.05.26364531.headline_claim: Cognitive rehabilitation was not associated with detectable changes in resting-state network connectivity in long COVID-related cognitive impairment, and SN-DMN connectivity may be a marker of network disorganization underlying cognitive dysfunction.
10.64898/2026.10.05.26364531.overall: The central null finding (no detectable intervention effect on connectivity) is reported consistently, but with 39 completers and a minimum detectable d of about 0.7 it is inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect. The brain-behaviour associations are exploratory, uncorrected, and worded more strongly in the conclusion than the data allow. The remaining discrepancies (abstract network label, run length) are minor.

primary_outcome.name: Resting-state functional connectivity (overall network mean and within- and between-network connectivity)

issues.title: Abstract attributes processing-speed association to CEN-DMN; Results report within-CEN and within-DMN
issues.explanation: The abstract says improved processing speed was associated with increased CEN-DMN (between-network) connectivity. The Results report significant DKEFS Word Reading associations with the CEN network mean and DMN network mean (within-network), and Figure 4 marks no CEN-DMN cell as significant. The abstract therefore misstates which connectivity measure was associated, though the finding is itself nominal and exploratory.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table showing a significant CEN-DMN between-network association with a processing-speed measure.

quotes.text: improved processing speed associated with increased CEN-DMN connectivity
DKEFS Word Reading demonstrating positive associations with both

issues.title: Null connectivity result from 39 completers (detectable d about 0.7) is stated without the power caveat in the abstract and conclusion
issues.explanation: With 39 participants, the study had 80% power only for d of about 0.7, so it cannot rule out small or moderate intervention effects on connectivity. The authors say this in Results 3.2, but the abstract and conclusion state the null result without that qualifier. Readers of the abstract could take the study as evidence of no effect rather than as inconclusive.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An abstract or conclusion that carries the power limitation, or an equivalence analysis excluding effects above a small bound.

quotes.text: This pilot (N = 39) was not powered to detect small- moderate effects

issues.title: Uncorrected exploratory associations (8 nominal of ~7x16 tests) are worded as consistent and as neural changes accompanying improvement
issues.explanation: Eight nominal associations at p<0.05 were found among about 7 connectivity metrics by 16 cognitive measures, with none surviving multiple-comparison correction. The conclusion calls SN-DMN a consistent cross-domain correlate, and the Discussion says the associations suggest neural changes do accompany cognitive improvement. This wording is stronger than uncorrected, exploratory associations in 39 people support, and the conclusion omits the correction caveat.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-registered, corrected analysis in which these associations survive.

quotes.text: SN-DMN connectivity emerged as a consistent cross-domain correlate
Although none of these individual associations would survive correction for multiple

issues.title: Imaging analysed in 39 of 58 randomized (19 lost, 32.8%) by complete-case; losses by arm and 67 registered not explained
issues.explanation: Only 39 of 58 participants had usable imaging at both sessions, and mixed models were fitted on complete cases. The paper gives the completer split (19 vs 20) but not the arm-wise losses or any comparison of excluded and included participants. Since exclusion was due to motion or image quality, which may relate to treatment or symptoms, the null between-group result could be affected, though the direction is unknown. The registry lists 67 enrolled, which the paper does not reconcile with 58.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A flow diagram giving arm-wise imaging exclusions and a sensitivity analysis showing excluded participants did not differ by arm.

quotes.text: Fifty-eight participants enrolled; 39 completed both imaging sessions
For participants with complete data at both timepoints, we implemented linear mixed-effects

10.70135/seejph.vi.2132.headline_claim: Jacobson Relaxation Techniques reduce pain compared with control among post-COVID geriatrics with co-morbid illness, offering a valuable non-pharmacological approach.
10.70135/seejph.vi.2132.overall: The large observed pain reduction in the intervention arm is plausible, but the efficacy claim rests on a non-randomised, unblinded usual-care comparison with an unspecified between-group analysis and inconsistent reporting of group sizes, test type and p-value placement. The conclusions about follow-up and quality of life go beyond what was measured, so the finding should be treated as tentative.

primary_outcome.name: Pain intensity (Numeric Pain Rating Scale)

issues.title: Non-randomised, unblinded usual-care comparison for a self-reported pain outcome underlies an efficacy claim
issues.explanation: Allocation was purposive with no randomisation or concealment, the control received only standard care, and pain was self-rated with no blinding. Expectancy, attention and selection effects are indistinguishable from any effect of relaxation. The abstract nonetheless concludes efficacy.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence of randomisation, blinded outcome assessment or an attention-matched control.

quotes.text: Participants in the control group will receive standard care for pain management.
indicating the efficacy of Jacobson Relaxation Techniques in pain management among post-COVID geriatrics with co-morbid illness

second_reader.what_stands: Allocation was purposive and non-randomised, the control received unspecified standard care, blinding is not described (and participant blinding is not feasible), and the outcome is a self-reported NPRS, yet the Abstract Results state the data indicate 'efficacy'. The Discussion's 'may offer a promising approach' and the call for further study temper this somewhat, but the efficacy wording in the abstract is stronger than the design supports.

issues.title: Between-group claim (p<0.05) has no described or reported between-group test; only within-group tests are specified
issues.explanation: The headline claim is a between-group difference after the intervention, yet the Methods specify only paired within-group t-tests and Table 2 gives one unattributed p-value. No test statistic, effect size, confidence interval or baseline adjustment is given for the comparison. Contrasting a significant change in one arm with a non-significant change in the other is not a valid test of difference.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-group test (e.g. ANCOVA or independent t on post scores) with statistic and CI.

quotes.text: The intervention group demonstrated a significant reduction in pain scores compared to the control group post-intervention (p < 0.05)
Utilized paired t-tests to assess differences in pain levels before and after the intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: The Methods specify only paired t-tests, and no between-group test is described there; the abstract's between-group p<0.05 has no stated comparison, statistic or effect estimate. The point overstates in saying none is reported: Table 2 and the Results text mention an independent t-test with p<0.001, but it is attributed to the within-group change and its target comparison is unclear, so the between-group claim is not clearly backed by a described analysis (although the printed means would plausibly give a significant difference).

issues.title: Abstract conclusion claims quality-of-life benefit though only one-week pain scores were measured
issues.explanation: Only pain on the NPRS was measured, once, after one week. Quality of life was not assessed and no longer-term or practice-implementation data exist. The abstract conclusion therefore goes beyond the data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A quality-of-life measure reported in the paper.

quotes.text: Further study recommended on the integration of these techniques into clinical practice can improve the quality of life for this vulnerable population

issues.title: Discussion claims pain reduction at follow-up, but only one post-test at one week was measured
issues.explanation: The Methods and Abstract describe baseline and a single assessment after one week. The Discussion nonetheless claims a significant reduction at both post-intervention and follow-up. No follow-up data are reported, so this statement is unsupported.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Reported follow-up data or a protocol defining a later timepoint.

quotes.text: demonstrated a significant reduction in pain intensity at post-intervention and at follow-up
Pain was assessed for both the groups after one week.

issues.title: Methods give control n=1 (arms sum to 42) while Abstract and Tables give 41 per arm (total 82)
issues.explanation: The Methods state a total of 82 with 41 intervention and 1 control participants, which cannot add up. The Abstract and Tables use 41 per arm, so the Methods figure appears to be a typographical error. It does not change the analysis but is a printed factual error about group size.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Methods text is the correct allocation; or evidence the 1 is an extraction artefact of the original document.

quotes.text: 41 participants in the intervention group and 1 in the control group
allocated to either the intervention group (n=41) or the control group (n=41)

issues.title: Table 2 prints P <0.001 on the control row, contradicting the text saying the control change was non-significant
issues.explanation: The text says the control change did not reach significance, yet the only p-value in Table 2 sits on the control row and the intervention row is blank. This is probably a misplaced cell, but as printed the table assigns the highly significant result to the wrong group and no p-value is reported for the control change.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The original layout showing the P value on the intervention row.

quotes.text: which did not reach statistical significance

issues.title: Pre-post p-value labelled independent t-test in Results but paired t-test in Methods
issues.explanation: The Methods describe paired t-tests, but the Results and Table 2 attribute the pre-post p-value to an independent t-test. Which test was used is unclear, and the between-group comparison behind the abstract's p<0.05 is not described at all. This is folded into the between-group inference issue.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis code or a statement confirming the test used.

quotes.text: with an independent t-test yielding a p-value of < 0.001
Utilized paired t-tests to assess differences in pain levels before and after the intervention.

issues.title: No sample-size calculation reported for a purposively sampled study
issues.explanation: No justification of the sample of 82 is given. With a large observed effect, 41 per arm is likely adequate, so this weakens rather than undermines the finding. The allocation inconsistency is a separate issue (c1).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A stated sample-size calculation.

quotes.text: The sample size is 82, with 41 participants in the intervention group and 1 in the control group.

issues.title: No trial registration or protocol reported; Methods mix future and past tense
issues.explanation: The paper reports no registry entry, so planned outcomes cannot be compared with those reported. Future-tense wording in the Methods suggests protocol text was carried into the report. With a single pain outcome the practical consequence is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry entry or protocol.

quotes.text: Baseline assessment: Participants' demographic information, medical history, and baseline pain intensity will be recorded.

10.7189/jogh.16.04164.headline_claim: Long COVID is marked by a distinct gut microbiome composition versus healthy controls, and short-term montelukast seems to exert transient genus-level effects without broader microbial destabilisation.
10.7189/jogh.16.04164.overall: The case-control finding of a compositional difference (PERMANOVA R2 = 0.081, P = 0.001) is plausible but confounded by a separately recruited healthcare-worker control group, and the named taxa lack stated multiplicity control. The montelukast conclusion is not supported by the reported tests: no significant between-arm differences were found for Bacteroides or Prevotella, so the claimed drug effect rests on visual trends in a small, partly missing sample.

primary_outcome.name: Gut microbiome composition (alpha and beta diversity, taxon abundance) at visit 2

issues.title: Montelukast 'transient genus-level effects' claimed from visual trends; no significant between-group difference
issues.explanation: The Results state that no significant between-group differences in Bacteroides or Prevotella were seen at any time point, and the montelukast pattern rests on visual inspection of stacked bar plots. The Discussion nonetheless says montelukast 'induc[ed]' and 'caused' a Bacteroides reduction, and the Conclusions state a drug effect at genus level. The only significant between-arm finding at visit 2 is Dialister, from an uncorrected LEfSe comparison, so the treatment-effect claim is not supported by the reported tests.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported between-arm or arm-by-time test (with correction) showing a significant Bacteroides difference at visit 2.

quotes.text: no statistically significant differences in relative abundance of <italic>Bacteroides</italic> and <italic>Prevotella</italic> were observed between groups at any time point
in our study, montelukast caused a reduction in <italic>Bacteroides</italic> without a broad disruption of the gut microbial community
short-term montelukast administration seems to exert transient effects at the genus level without causing broader microbial landscape destabilisation

second_reader.what_stands: The paper itself states that Bacteroides and Prevotella did not differ significantly between groups at any visit and bases the pattern on visual observation. Yet the Discussion says montelukast 'caused a reduction in Bacteroides' and 'induc[ed] a transient reduction', and the Conclusions describe 'transient effects at the genus level'. This causal, drug-effect wording goes beyond what an unsupported visual trend can show, even though the Conclusions are hedged with 'seems to'.

issues.title: Separate healthcare-worker control cohort, matched only on age/sex; difference attributed to long COVID
issues.explanation: Controls came from a different, previously published cohort of health care workers, matched on age, sex and size. Patients were symptomatic primary-care patients, and diet, medication, lifestyle and prior treatment are not adjusted for. The PERMANOVA explains 8.1% of variance, and the Conclusions attribute the shift to long COVID itself, which a cross-sectional comparison with this control group cannot establish. The limitation paragraph acknowledges missing metadata but does not temper the Conclusions.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A covariate-adjusted PERMANOVA or control matching on diet, medication and health status that preserves the difference.

quotes.text: matched by age, sex and sample size
quotes.location: Methods, Study design and sample collection

quotes.text: These results suggest that long COVID involves significant structural reorganisation of the gut ecosystem
the lack of detailed metadata remains a potential source of bias

second_reader.what_stands: The control group is a separate published health-worker cohort matched on age and sex only, so disease status is fully confounded with cohort, occupation and any unmeasured lifestyle or technical differences. The authors do state the metadata limitation and the same-institution processing, but the Conclusions still attribute the difference to long COVID without that qualification. The claim that the paper lacks any acknowledgement of bias is not accurate, but the causal attribution is stronger than the design supports.
