issues.title: Cross-sectional LEfSe taxa called at nominal 0.05 with no stated multiplicity control or LDA threshold
issues.explanation: The Bonferroni correction is described only for the longitudinal paired tests; the cross-sectional LEfSe comparison across all phyla and genera uses the nominal 0.05 level. No LDA cutoff, FDR step or effect sizes are given in the text. The PERMANOVA result (single test, P = 0.001) is robust to this, but the specific named taxa in the Conclusions are less secure.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary LEfSe settings showing FDR/Bonferroni-adjusted p-values and LDA thresholds for the named taxa.

quotes.text: We set the significance level at 0.05 (two-sided) for all statistical tests.
To account for multiple comparisons in these longitudinal assessments, we adjusted <italic>P</italic>-values using the Bonferroni correction.

issues.title: Per-arm samples at visits 2 and 3 not reported (45 baseline, 32 and 29 later); no missing-sample handling
issues.explanation: Only 32 of 45 baseline participants have visit-2 samples and 29 have visit-3 samples, but the paper does not give per-arm numbers or reasons for missing samples. Whether the losses are balanced between montelukast and placebo cannot be judged, and the paired analyses silently use available cases. This weakens the reliability of the arm-specific temporal trends described.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Supplementary Figure S1 showing balanced per-arm sample counts with reasons for missing samples.

quotes.text: 45 samples at baseline (visit 1), 32 after treatment (visit 2), and 29 after one year (visit 3)
quotes.location: Methods, Study design and sample collection

quotes.text: Of the 45 participants, 23 received montelukast and 22 received placebo
quotes.location: Methods, Study design and sample collection

10.7326/annals-25-03959.headline_claim: Fluvoxamine reduced fatigue (FSS) versus placebo at day 60 and sustained the benefit to day 90 in adults with long COVID, supporting its potential role in fatigue management; metformin showed no benefit.
10.7326/annals-25-03959.overall: The fluvoxamine fatigue benefit is directionally supported, but the effect estimate comes from a trial stopped early at an interim look and several reported numbers and dates are inconsistent with the stated eligibility and timeline. The quality-of-life claim is stated more strongly than the small, uncorrected secondary results support.

primary_outcome.name: Change in FSS score from baseline to day 60

issues.title: Day-90 fluvoxamine recovery probability: text 99.6% vs Table 2 97.8%
issues.explanation: The Results text says the posterior probability of superiority for recovery at day 90 was 99.6%. Table 2 gives 97.8% for fluvoxamine at day 90 and 99.6% at day 60. The text value appears to be the day-60 figure, so the day-90 recovery evidence is overstated in the text.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected table or erratum showing 99.6% as the true day-90 value.

quotes.text: posterior probability of superiority at day 90 was 99.6%

issues.title: Quality-of-life benefit claimed 'across all time points' from small EQ-5D effects with no multiplicity handling
issues.explanation: The Discussion says quality-of-life improvements were observed at all time points and the summary says the trial supports improving quality of life. EQ-5D-5L gains are 0.06 to 0.10, the day 90 interval reaches 0.00, and no importance threshold or multiplicity adjustment for the many secondary outcomes, timepoints and subgroups is given. The fatigue finding is more directly supported than this secondary claim.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified multiplicity strategy and a stated minimal important difference exceeded by the EQ-5D estimates.

quotes.text: Improvements in health-related quality of life, assessed via the EQ-5D-5L, were also observed across all time points.
this trial offers support for fluvoxamine in reducing fatigue severity and improving quality of life in people with long COVID

issues.title: Participants enrolled up to 10 Feb 2025 cannot have day-90 data by the 19 Feb 2025 stopping date
issues.explanation: The last enrolment (10 Feb 2025) is nine days before the fluvoxamine group was stopped (19 Feb 2025), and even day 60 data are not available by then. Yet Figure 1 says all patients completed their allocated duration and day-60/90 outcomes are reported. Either the analysis used imputed values for recent enrollees, or follow-up ran past the stated dates; the paper does not say, and no analysed n is given.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement of follow-up cut-off dates, or analysed n by timepoint showing late enrollees were excluded or imputed.

quotes.text: We enrolled a total of 399 participants between 18 October 2023 and 10 February 2025
stopping the fluvoxamine group for superiority on 19 February 2025
All patients completed their allocated duration.

issues.title: Median 'time since most recent episode' 692–870 days (IQR from 403) vs eligibility window <365 days
issues.explanation: Eligibility required fatigue persisting 90 to <365 days after a single infection, but Table 1 gives medians of 692–870 days, with lower quartiles of 403–511, all above 365. Either the variable is not time since infection (undefined in the paper) or participants were enrolled outside the stated window. The paper does not define it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A definition showing the variable measures something other than time since infection.

quotes.text: with new or worsening fatigue persisting 90 to less than 365 days after the acute illness

quotes.location: Table 1, Median time since most recent episode

issues.title: Fluvoxamine stopped early for superiority after 2 of 4 interim looks; effect size not discussed as possibly inflated
issues.explanation: The fluvoxamine arm was stopped for efficacy at an interim look, and trials stopped early tend to overestimate effects. The paper states the early stopping reduced precision but not that the −0.43 point estimate may be inflated. Its credible interval (−0.80 to −0.07) approaches the null, and the powered effect was 0.45, so the lower bound is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Analysis showing a bias-adjusted estimate close to −0.43.

quotes.text: 2 of 4 planned analyses were conducted.
stopping the fluvoxamine group for superiority on 19 February 2025

issues.title: No trial registration identifier appears in the paper text
issues.explanation: No registry number or registration date appears in the supplied text, so the primary outcome and analysis plan cannot be checked against a registered record. The paper refers to a protocol and statistical analysis plan on the journal site, and registration details may sit in front matter that is not in this extract.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A registry identifier and a registration date before first enrolment.

quotes.text: The trial was conducted at 22 participating outpatient sites in Brazil between October 2023 and February 2025.

issues.title: Text cites Table 2 for the primary FSS endpoint, but Table 2 shows recovery risk ratios
issues.explanation: The Results state that Table 2 reports the change in FSS to day 60, yet Table 2 contains only recovery (FSS <3) risk ratios. The primary FSS estimates (-0.43, CrI -0.80 to -0.07) appear only in prose, with no table of the primary result. The values are available, so this is a presentation error, not a missing result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table elsewhere in the paper giving the primary FSS effects.

quotes.text: reports the primary end point (change in FSS score from baseline to day 60)
Recovery (FSS Score <3) at 30, 60, and 90 Days

issues.title: Screening FSS minimum 3.00 (fluvoxamine, metformin) and 3.10 (placebo) vs inclusion mean FSS ≥4
issues.explanation: Inclusion required mean FSS ≥4, but Table 1 shows minimum screening FSS of 3.00–3.10 in all arms. Eligibility may have been confirmed at a later baseline visit and Table 1 may show an earlier screening value, but the paper does not say. This does not change the effect estimates, though it bears on who was enrolled.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Protocol showing eligibility FSS was measured separately from Table 1's screening value.

quotes.text: Inclusion required moderate to severe fatigue (mean Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] score ≥4)

10.7326/annals-25-04883.headline_claim: Neither metformin nor ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) significantly improved long COVID recovery at 8 weeks, with the authors concluding that the trial did not show a statistically significant improvement in recovery with either drug.
10.7326/annals-25-04883.overall: The null conclusion for metformin and UDCA on 8-week recovery is supported by the reported counts, which are internally consistent. The Discussion overstates the recovery rate (70% to 80% against 64% to 68%), and the claim that cytokine data strongly support an immune mechanism goes beyond correlational data. The high placebo response, which the authors acknowledge, leaves the trial able to say little about efficacy.

primary_outcome.name: PASC recovery rate at 8 weeks from baseline (PASC score ≥12 at baseline to <12 at week 8)

issues.title: Correlational cytokine changes in recoverers described as strongly supporting an immune-dysregulation mechanism
issues.explanation: The Discussion says cytokine changes alongside symptom improvement 'strongly support' a role for immune dysregulation in long COVID. The data are correlations among participants who recovered, pooled across arms, and no drug effect or treatment-by-time interaction was found. Because roughly two thirds of the placebo group also recovered, the association cannot separate cause from natural resolution or regression to the mean. The conclusion is better described as hypothesis-generating than as strong support.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified mediation or within-arm analysis showing cytokine change predicts recovery beyond time and baseline severity.

quotes.text: strongly support the role of immune dysregulation in the pathophysiology of long COVID
treatment group-by-time interactions were not seen for any of the analyzed cytokines

issues.title: Discussion cites 70% to 80% recovery; Results give 67% overall and 63.6% to 68.2% by arm
issues.explanation: The Discussion says approximately 70% to 80% of participants recovered. The Results report 264 of 396 (67%) overall, with 63.6%, 68.2% and 68.2% in the three arms, and the cytokine section gives 68%. The Discussion range overstates the observed recovery rate, so the high placebo response looks larger than it was. The between-arm comparisons and the null conclusion are not affected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified analysis (for example a per-protocol or sensitivity set in Supplement Table 6) showing recovery of 70% to 80% that the Discussion is explicitly referring to.

quotes.text: approximately 70% to 80% of the study participants experienced recovery from long COVID during the 8-week follow-up period
Overall, 264 (67%) of 396 participants reported recovery from PASC at 8 weeks.

10.7416/ai.2025.2678.headline_claim: MBSR delivered to COVID-19 ICU survivors reduced some chronic symptoms and improved insomnia and psychological symptoms within one year, supporting an annual MBSR programme alongside drug therapy.
10.7416/ai.2025.2678.overall: The headline claim that MBSR improved insomnia and psychological disorders is weakly supported: the trial is open-label with self-reported outcomes, analyses completers only, and several text and table inconsistencies (timeline, eligibility years, control-arm losses, ISI t statistics) are unresolved. The authors themselves call the effects not clinically relevant and possibly unstable, yet the Conclusions say the results 'demonstrate' benefit. At best the results are hypothesis-generating.

primary_outcome.name: Pain intensity (BPI-SF, least pain in last 24 h and related domains)

issues.title: Conclusion 'demonstrates' benefit, but authors call effects not clinically relevant; small open trial, 93 of 105 analysed
issues.explanation: The trial was open-label with self-reported outcomes, stopped at 105 randomised and analysed 93 (target 106 analysable), with non-significant categorical outcomes. The authors themselves say the reductions appear purely statistical and not clinically relevant and may not persist. The conclusion nevertheless says the results demonstrate improvement in insomnia and psychological disorders, recommends an annual programme, and extends to 'healthy individuals', who were not studied.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A larger, blinded or attention-controlled trial showing clinically relevant, sustained effects in this population.

quotes.text: The main results of this RCT demonstrate that the MBSR program reduced some chronic symptoms, improving the patients' insomnia and psychological disorders within one year.
MBSR is a promising modality for Long-COVID among healthy individuals.
the MBSR program does not remain stable over time, at least not up to 1 year

second_reader.what_stands: The Conclusions say the trial 'demonstrates' symptom reduction, while the Discussion says the reductions are not clinically relevant and do not remain stable to 1 year. The trial is small (105 randomised, below the 125 planned; 93 analysed at 6 months, 90 at 12 months) and open-label. The authors do name sample size as a limitation, but the wording of the conclusion is stronger than their own interpretation.

issues.title: Open comparison with usual care only; all outcomes self-reported, no attention control
issues.explanation: Participants knew whether they were attending an 8-week group programme, and the outcomes (pain, HADS, ISI) are self-administered. Expectancy, attention and group-contact effects cannot be separated from MBSR itself. The authors raise this in the Discussion but still conclude the programme improved insomnia and psychological disorders.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An attention-matched control arm, or blinded or objective outcome assessment showing the same effects.

quotes.text: compared MBSR with usual care among patients who survived the acute phase of a SARS-COV-2 infection.
it is possible that participant's expectation towards the practice played a role in their perception of improvements
self-administered tools for the assessment of outcomes

second_reader.what_stands: The control arm received usual care only (no attention or active control), and all outcomes were self-reported questionnaires in an unmasked trial (registry masking NONE). The authors themselves flag expectation and self-report as possible influences, but they do not tie this to the strength of their conclusions.

issues.title: ISI t = -8.801 for 9 vs 13.6 is implausible given the Table 2 score distribution
issues.explanation: For insomnia at 6 months the means are 9 vs 13.6 (difference 4.6), with t = -8.801. This needs a pooled SD of only about 2.5. But Table 2 shows 25 of 47 scoring 0-7 and 8 of 47 scoring 22-28 in the intervention arm, which implies an SD of roughly 7 or more and a t of about 3. The same pattern applies to the 12-month ISI (t = -3.569 for 9.1 vs 11.1) and to the HADS-A result (t = -3.636 for 11.28 vs 13.15). The headline insomnia and anxiety effects rest on these statistics.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Group SDs in Figure 3 (or source data) consistent with t = -8.8, or confirmation that a paired or adjusted analysis was used.

quotes.text: Severe insomnia- 22-28, n (%)

second_reader.what_stands: Given the Table 2 ISI category counts, the standard deviations must be at least about 6, which caps an independent-samples t for 9 vs 13.6 at roughly 3.5, not 8.8. The reported t (and the 12-month t of -3.569) is therefore inconsistent with the table. The paper does not allow us to tell whether the t statistics, the table counts or the means are the incorrect element.

issues.title: About 40 outcome-timepoint tests at nominal 5% with no correction; several significant results are marginal
issues.explanation: The paper tests eight pain domains, anxiety, depression and insomnia categories and mean scores at two timepoints, with the significance level set at 5% and no correction. Several of the reported 'improvements' have p between .007 and .035 and would not survive correction. The HADS and ISI mean-score results with p < .001 are more robust to this criticism.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified hierarchy or correction for multiplicity, or a single pre-specified primary comparison.

quotes.text: with the significance level set at 5% (two-tailed)
No other significant findings emerged.

issues.title: Paper's stated primary outcome (BPI pain intensity) is mostly null, yet conclusions rest on other outcomes
issues.explanation: The registry lists chronic pain, anxiety, depression and insomnia as four primary outcomes. The paper calls BPI pain the primary outcome and bases its sample size on it, while its conclusion emphasises insomnia and psychological outcomes. Pain intensity at 6 and 12 months is non-significant for worst pain, average pain and pain now. The primary outcome designation is inconsistent with the registry and with the weight placed on results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The registry history showing BPI pain intensity as the sole primary outcome at registration, or a protocol specifying the hierarchy.

quotes.text: valutato con il Brief Pain Inventory (risultati primari)
of BPI-pain intensity (four-items) between the MBSR and control groups at 12 months from enrollment.

issues.title: Control arm falls 53 to 46 at 6 months with no stated reason; text accounts for only 8 of 12 exclusions
issues.explanation: The intervention arm reconciles (52 allocated, 5 missed, 47 analysed). In the control arm 7 patients are missing by 6 months and 3 more by 12 months, yet the text mentions only the 3 lost at 12 months. The analysis uses only completers (93 of 105), with no intention-to-treat analysis. The unexplained control-arm losses could bias the comparison.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Figure 2 or the supplement showing reasons for the 7 control-arm losses by 6 months.

quotes.text: included in the analyses (47 in the intervention arm and 46 in the control arm)
five patients in the intervention group did not participate in the 6-month follow-up interviews
lost 3 patients (6.5%) in the control group

issues.title: Recruitment to July 2024, yet all MBSR sessions stated as April-May 2023
issues.explanation: The trial period and recruitment are given as April 2023 to July 2024. The MBSR programme is said to have been delivered in two months, April to May 2023, with follow-up at 6 and 12 months afterwards. Patients cannot have been recruited through July 2024 and still all completed this programme and 12-month follow-up within the stated study period. Either the dates or the description of delivery is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected timeline (e.g. delivery dates per focus group through 2024 and follow-up end date).

quotes.text: The study sample was recruited from one General Hospitals (Department of anesthesia) in Lecco, Italy from April 2023 to July 2024
which took place over a total of 2 months between April and May 2023

issues.title: Inclusion criterion is ICU admission in 2021-2022; Table 1 shows 51 of 93 admitted in 2020 and none in 2022
issues.explanation: The criterion restricts to admissions in 2021-2022. Table 1 shows 51 (54.8%) admitted in 2020 and 42 in 2021, none in 2022. Either the criterion is misprinted or more than half the sample did not meet it, which would also affect the 1-2 years since discharge timing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: The protocol stating 2020-2021 as the eligibility window.

quotes.text: patients hospitalized in intensive care units in the years 2021-2022 for a Sars-CoV-2 infection

quotes.location: Table 1, Year of admission to ICU, 2020

issues.title: Discussion lists pain interference with general work as reduced; Table 2 shows higher MBSR scores (2.08 vs 1.58)
issues.explanation: The Discussion says MBSR reduced interference with general work. In Table 2, general work interference is higher in the MBSR arm at 6 months (2.08 vs 1.58, p = .127) and 12 months (1.97 vs 1.69, p = .501). No reduction was shown.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that the Discussion sentence refers to general activity rather than general work.

quotes.text: in the interference of pain with mood, general work, sleep and interference with enjoyment of life

quotes.location: Table 2, Pain Interference with general work

issues.title: Italian summary gives arm sizes 53 vs 52; Results and Discussion give 52 intervention, 53 control
issues.explanation: The Italian summary says 53 intervention and 52 control patients. The Results say 52 allocated to intervention and 53 to control, and the Discussion also refers to 52 patients in the experimental group. The arm sizes are printed inconsistently, though the total of 105 is unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A corrected summary, or the flowchart showing 53 allocated to intervention.

quotes.text: (53 vs 52 pazienti per gruppo)
(52 allocated to the intervention group and 53 allocated to the control group)

issues.title: Discussion says 16 intervention patients with all four conditions at 1 year; Table 3 and Results give 15
issues.explanation: Table 3 and the Results report 15 (31.9%) intervention patients with all four conditions at 12 months, versus 12 (25.5%) at 6 months. The Discussion says 16. The Discussion then uses the change from 12 to 16 to argue the benefit does not last, though the table comparison between arms is not significant (p = .948).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing 16 patients at 12 months.

quotes.text: (16 patients with all four conditions)
in 15 (31.9%) patients at T1 for the Intervention group

issues.title: Three 6-month depression percentages use the other arm's denominator (8/47 printed 17.4; 5/46 printed 10.6; 12/46 printed 25.5)
issues.explanation: In Table 2 at 6 months, three depression cells give percentages that do not match their own arm's denominator but match the other arm's. The counts sum correctly (8+18+13+8=47; 5+17+12+12=46) and the p-values look driven by the counts. The errors are small and do not change any conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; the arithmetic is fixed by the printed counts and arm sizes.

quotes.text: Absence of depression 0-7, n (%)
Severe depression 15-21, n (%)

script.explanation: 8/47 = 17.02%, but the paper prints 17.4, outside the rounding interval [17.35, 17.50]. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 46.0 rather than 47.

10.7759/cureus.31009.headline_claim: Many COVID-19 patients have impaired HRQoL and dyspnea at discharge, and early institution of a standard pulmonary rehabilitation protocol improves symptoms and HRQoL rapidly over about one month.
10.7759/cureus.31009.overall: The within-group improvement in dyspnea and SGRQ scores over 60 days is plausibly real and the tables are largely internally consistent. The attribution of this improvement to rehabilitation is not supported by a design with no comparator, and the list of 'influencing factors' in the Conclusions goes beyond the non-significant or over-parameterised regressions. The findings should be read as descriptive recovery data.

primary_outcome.name: Change in mMRC, modified Borg and SGRQ scores from day 0 to day 60

issues.title: Uncontrolled single-group pre-post study used to attribute 48-patient improvement to rehabilitation
issues.explanation: All patients were assessed at discharge and at day 60, with no comparison group and only paired t-tests of change. Post-COVID dyspnea and quality of life are expected to improve spontaneously over 60 days, and discharge-day scores are by selection at their worst, so regression to the mean also applies. The data cannot separate rehabilitation from natural recovery, yet the Abstract and Discussion present rehabilitation as the cause. Home physical therapy was also unsupervised and not uniform (43/48).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent non-rehabilitation comparison group, or external evidence that spontaneous recovery over 60 days is negligible in this population.

quotes.text: There was no control group to compare in our study.
Rapid recovery and improvement reflects the effect of regular physical therapy.
Significance of changes in parameters from day 0 to day 60 was evaluated by paired t-test.

second_reader.what_stands: The study is a single-group pre-post cohort of 48 patients with no control group, and the Discussion and Abstract/Conclusions attribute the improvement to rehabilitation/physical therapy ('reflects the effect of regular physical therapy'), which the design cannot establish. This is partly tempered because the authors acknowledge in Limitations that there was no control group and that the role of physical therapy could not be assessed properly, and the Methods describe the study as observational rather than interventional; the problem is the inconsistency between that caveat and the causal word

issues.title: Conclusion lists diabetes, age, smoking, hypothyroidism as affecting recovery; regressions show p>0.05
issues.explanation: The Conclusions say age, smoking, diabetes, hypothyroidism, asthma, oxygen and hospital stay inversely affected recovery and HRQoL change. In the regressions, mMRC and Borg change had no significant predictors, and in the SGRQ model diabetes (p=0.280), age (0.231), smoking (0.227) and hypothyroidism (0.108) are all non-significant. Oxygen and hospital stay were not entered in the models at all. The factor claim is therefore largely unsupported by the paper's own analysis.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A reported analysis showing these factors significantly predict change in scores.

quotes.text: Factors such as age, smoking, diabetes, hypothyroidism, asthma, history of moist oxygen receiving, and prolonged hospital stay inversely affected recovery and HRQoL changes.

issues.title: Regressions fit ~28 terms in 48 patients per outcome with no multiplicity control; isolated p<0.05 reported
issues.explanation: Tables 6-8 each fit a model with about 28 coefficients, including combination terms, in 48 patients. Many tests were run across six outcomes with a 0.05 threshold and no correction, and several coefficient signs and effect sizes look unstable. The few significant associations (BMI, asthma, hypertension, gutkha) are exploratory at best. The 'different influencing factors were identified' claim is therefore tentative.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified, parsimonious model or multiplicity-corrected results showing the same associations.

quotes.text: Different influencing factors were identified.
Multivariate regression analysis was applied to find relationship of mMRC, modified Borg, and SGRQ % change, with selected influencing variables.

issues.title: Text says 'majority' >75% SGRQ impact improvement; Table 5 shows 21/48 (43.8%), a plurality
issues.explanation: The Results text groups modified Borg and SGRQ impact as having a 'majority' with more than 75% improvement. This holds for Borg (52.1%) but not SGRQ impact (43.8%), and 'most' for SGRQ activity <50% (43.8%) is likewise a plurality. The slip is minor and does not change any table value.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence the authors meant 'largest group' rather than more than half.

quotes.text: Majority of the patients had more than 75% improvement in their initial modified Borg and SGRQ impact scores

10.7759/cureus.31281.headline_claim: Post-ICU COVID-19 survivors admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation program maintained good functional recovery at three months, with improvement in respiratory muscle and cough strength.
10.7759/cureus.31281.overall: The descriptive results for MEP, PCF, 1'STST, 6MWT and FAS are internally plausible, with some inconsistencies (FAS T1 text vs table, a Discussion claim about Brief-BESTest that the data do not show). The causal framing that the findings reinforce the importance of rehabilitation is not supported by a single-arm follow-up that begins after the program ended. Treat the paper as a descriptive follow-up of 36 completers rather than evidence of rehabilitation benefit.

primary_outcome.name: not designated; the paper reports several T1 vs T2 outcomes (MEP, PCF, 1STST, 6MWT, FAS, MIP, brief-BESTEST, TUG)

issues.title: Single-arm follow-up after discharge cannot support the claim that findings reinforce rehabilitation
issues.explanation: All 36 patients are compared with themselves from discharge (T1) to three months later (T2), with no comparison group. Gains in MEP, PCF, 1'STST and 6MWT over this window may reflect natural recovery, post-discharge outpatient or home exercise (86% had some), or measurement familiarity. The authors acknowledge this in the limitations yet conclude that the findings reinforce the importance of rehabilitation; the data support only a descriptive follow-up.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent comparison group, or conclusions restricted to describing outcomes without attributing them to rehabilitation.

quotes.text: due to the absence of a control group, it is not possible to report on the causality of the observed conclusions
These findings reinforce the importance of rehabilitation in this population.

second_reader.what_stands: A single-arm, uncontrolled follow-up cannot show that rehabilitation caused the observed improvement, and the authors concede this in their limitations. The Conclusions sentence 'These findings reinforce the importance of rehabilitation' is therefore stronger than the design supports. It is not wholly unsupported, because the Discussion hedges between natural recovery and rehabilitation benefit and the paper's main claim concerns post-discharge monitoring. The paper also reports no association between type of post-discharge rehabilitation and change, and almost every patient (31 of 36) had som

issues.title: T1 FAS in Results text (18.60±2.65) disagrees with Table 3 (median 19.00, IR 4.30)
issues.explanation: The Results text gives the T1 final FAS as 18.60±2.65, but Table 3 gives 19.00 with an interquartile range of 4.30 for the same cell. The T2 value is identical in both places, so the T1 mismatch cannot be a change of statistic. The direction of the FAS finding (T2 higher than T1) survives either value, but one of the two printed T1 summaries is wrong.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text reports mean±SD for T1 while the table reports median/IQR, with the T2 value also differing between the two, or a corrected table.

quotes.location: Table 3, FAS - median; IR row, T1 column

issues.title: Discussion links acute hospital stay to Brief-BESTest improvement; only 1'STST correlated in Results/Table 4
issues.explanation: The Results and Table 4 report a single significant correlation (ρ = 0.397, p = 0.027) between the 1'STST change and acute hospital length of stay. The Discussion instead says longer acute stay was associated with greater improvement in Brief-BESTest, which was not analysed in Table 4 and showed no T1-T2 difference. The Discussion statement is unsupported by any reported result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A Brief-BESTest correlation analysis with acute hospital LOS reported in the paper or its supplement.

quotes.text: only a low positive correlation was found between 1'STST and acute hospital LOS
Longer acute hospital stay length was associated with greater improvement in Brief-BESTest.

issues.title: 6 of 42 (14.3%) lost to follow-up plus 2-8 missing values per test, with completers-only analysis
issues.explanation: Six patients who did not attend the three-month visit were excluded, and only 36 were analysed. Table 3 shows further missing test data (4 at T1 and 2 at T2 for most outcomes; 8 and 7 for 6-MWT percent predicted). No comparison of completers with non-completers or sensitivity analysis is reported, so the T2 results may be biased if those lost were less recovered or more recovered. This weakens the generalisability of the favourable results but does not overturn them.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A comparison showing completers and non-completers had similar baseline and discharge outcomes, or a sensitivity analysis giving the same results.

quotes.text: Six patients were excluded because they did not attend the three months follow-up consultation and tests.
quotes.location: Materials and methods, Subjects and study design

issues.title: Table 4 reports 30 uncorrected correlations; the single hit (p = 0.027) would not survive correction
issues.explanation: The primary T1-T2 comparisons are robust to a conservative correction. The correlation analysis tests 30 pairs, and the only nominally significant one (ρ = 0.397, p = 0.027) is well above a corrected threshold of about 0.0017 (0.05/30), and about one false positive would be expected by chance at 0.05. The paper treats this as a finding and discusses it, which weakens that secondary result.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified single correlation hypothesis or an adjusted analysis in which this association remains significant.

quotes.location: Table 4, Δ 1´-STST row, Acute hospital LOS column

10.7759/cureus.52935.headline_claim: The authors state that the case collection provides strong evidence for amifampridine's efficacy in post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS)-associated fatigue, with a randomized double-blind study planned to provide absolute proof.
10.7759/cureus.52935.overall: The five-case series shows within-patient improvement in a subjective score, with a small and unanalysed two-patient withdrawal test, but it cannot support the stated 'strong evidence' of efficacy or the call for an urgent indication extension. Outcomes were open-label and recorded by a patient-author with a planned patent, and no adverse events are reported. The date inconsistencies and a small SD mismatch are minor and do not change this.

primary_outcome.name: Bell score (fatigue/vigilance/resilience/occupational activity scale), change in five patients

issues.title: 'Strong evidence' of efficacy drawn from five uncontrolled cases and a two-patient discontinuation test
issues.explanation: The main result is a before-after rise in Bell score in five open-label patients, tested only with a within-patient paired t-test (mean 28 to 82, p=0.00265). This shows change over time, not an effect of the drug, and a paired p-value in n=5 says nothing about a comparator. The conclusion that the series gives 'strong evidence' and that an extension of the indication would be 'urgent' is not supported by this design. The design supports only a hypothesis worth testing.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A controlled comparison (randomized or at least concurrent) showing the same effect.

quotes.text: The present case collection provides strong evidence for the efficacy of amifampridine in PCS-associated fatigue.
The increase from a mean of 28 ± 16 to 82 ± 20 was highly significant (p=0.00265, paired t-test).
If proven, an extension of the indication of amifampridine for the treatment of PCS-associated fatigue would be urgent.

second_reader.what_stands: Describing five uncontrolled, open-label, selected cases plus a two-patient, fixed-order, 6-day discontinuation test as 'strong evidence' of efficacy is not supported by the design; the paired t-test arithmetic is correct but only quantifies a before/after change in five people. The paper does concede that a randomized trial is needed for 'absolute proof', which softens but does not remove the overstatement.

issues.title: Open-label subjective Bell scores recorded by T.B., a treated patient and planned patent applicant
issues.explanation: The Bell score and sleep time of all patients were recorded by T.B., who is patient 1, received the drug, and has a stated patent interest in the indication. Patients knew they were receiving amifampridine and had been given extensive literature on it, so expectation and recording bias could inflate the before-after change. Blinding was applied only to the six-day discontinuation test.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Documentation that outcomes were recorded or rated by someone independent and blind to treatment.

quotes.text: The Bell score and the need for sleep per 24 hours were documented daily by T.B.
extensive literature on amifampridine was made available to them

second_reader.what_stands: The scores are subjective, the main before/after series (Figure 1) was open-label with patient-reported outcomes in relatives briefed by T.B., and the person documenting scores is a treated patient and planned patent applicant, which is a conflict that the paper itself discloses. However, the discontinuation phase is described as double-blind with blinding done by a colleague, and the paper does not say who recorded the Figure 1 scores, so 'open-label scores recorded by T.B.' is established for the daily documentation but not for every data point.

issues.title: No adverse events or tolerability reported for any of the five treated patients
issues.explanation: The paper reports efficacy outcomes only, and discusses adverse reactions solely from a published 665-patient cohort that included patients with MS, LEMS and other conditions. Doses of up to 20 mg daily were used long term, and the paper never says whether any patient had side effects such as paraesthesia. The statement that adverse reactions 'appear to be justifiable' is therefore not backed by the paper's own patients.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement in the paper that no adverse events occurred in the five patients, with how this was assessed.

quotes.text: In view of the massive impairment caused by PCS, the adverse drug reactions appear to be justifiable if amifampridine proves to be effective against fatigue in further studies.

issues.title: Two-patient 'double-blind' discontinuation test: no sequence method, differing orders, no analysis
issues.explanation: The discontinuation test is the only controlled element, but the paper gives no randomization or sequence method, and the described schedules differ between patients. With n=2, a short 6-day window, no washout and no statistics, it cannot establish a drug effect beyond anecdote. It is still modestly supportive, since symptoms worsened off drug and recovered on it.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of randomized sequence allocation and washout, with blinded outcome ratings.

quotes.text: a double-blind discontinuation trial (3 days verum, 3 days placebo) was conducted at the request of patients 2 and 3
In patient 3, the discontinuation (placebo) led to a reduction in the Bell score to 50-60 from day 1

issues.title: Patient 3 start May 2022 gives 13 months before the June 2023 trial, not the stated two months
issues.explanation: The case description says patient 3 started amifampridine in May 2022, while the Results say the June 2023 discontinuation trial began two months after patient 3's start. Both cannot be right. The error changes how long patient 3 had been on treatment when 'long-term' medication was tested, but it does not alter the Bell score results.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that patient 3 started, stopped and restarted treatment in about April 2023, or a corrected start date.

quotes.text: After taking amifampridine from May 2022, the need for sleep fell to 7-9 hours and the Bell score increased to 80.
two months after the start of treatment for patient 3

issues.title: Planned patent on the indication declared, alongside strong efficacy language from the same author
issues.explanation: The author discloses a planned US/EU patent application for amifampridine in post-COVID fatigue. This is a commercial interest in the very conclusion the paper draws, and the author also records the outcomes in his own case. The disclosure exists, but it is not mentioned in the text and does not temper the 'strong evidence' wording.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Not applicable; this depends on how the interest is judged.

quotes.text: Planned patent for the indication of amifampridine in treating patients with post-COVID fatigue.

issues.title: Baseline Bell score SD of 16 does not match the patient values in the text (computed about 13)
issues.explanation: The baseline Bell scores in the case descriptions are 10, 20-40 (midpoint 30), 40, 40 and 20, giving a mean of 28 as printed. The sample SD of these values is about 13, not 16. The post-treatment mean and SD (82 ± 20) and the p-value are reproducible from the text. The discrepancy is small and does not change the interpretation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Individual baseline values for patient 2 (or others) that give SD 16 with mean 28.

quotes.text: The increase from a mean of 28 ± 16 to 82 ± 20 was highly significant (p=0.00265, paired t-test).
fluctuating fatigue symptoms with a Bell score between 20 and 40

issues.title: Patient 1's SARS-CoV-2 infection dated May 2022 in the Introduction but April 2022 in the Case Presentation
issues.explanation: The same infection in the author/patient 1 is given two different months. It is a small factual inconsistency in the case history, with no effect on the efficacy data.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Evidence that two separate infections are being described.

quotes.text: In May 2022, T.B. contracted SARS-CoV-2
After a SARS-CoV-2 infection in April 2022, severe fatigue occurred

10.7759/cureus.54925.headline_claim: Combined systemic corticosteroid, mesoglycan and diuretic 'may constitute an option' for persistent post-COVID-19 hyposmia and dysgeusia, and early treatment start is recommended.
10.7759/cureus.54925.overall: The study is a retrospective, uncontrolled, unblinded pilot with a subjective VAS outcome, so the recovery cannot be attributed to the regimen; the authors hedge the main conclusion, which keeps it tentative. The early-treatment recommendation and smell-versus-taste claim rest on unadjusted subgroup and within-group comparisons and are weaker still. Reporting slips (smell baseline 2.0 vs 2.21, baseline ANOVA p = 0.026 described as no difference) are small and do not change the picture.

primary_outcome.name: Change in self-rated smell and taste VAS score (0-10) from treatment start (T0) to 12 months (T5)

issues.title: Efficacy framing from a retrospective single-arm study with no control, over a 12-month natural recovery window
issues.explanation: All patients received the same multi-drug regimen and were compared only with their own baseline over 12 months, a period in which spontaneous recovery of post-COVID smell and taste is common. The paper admits this but still frames the aim as evaluating efficacy and concludes the regimen may be a treatment option. The before-after improvement cannot be attributed to the regimen, nor to any individual component.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A concurrent or historical matched control group showing less recovery.

quotes.text: Our study has several limitations inherent to its observational and exploratory nature, including the lack of a control arm.
Data were collected retrospectively from patients presenting at the otolaryngology clinic of the Fidenza Hospital
quotes.location: Materials And Methods, Study design and patients

second_reader.what_stands: The paper is a retrospective single-arm study with no control and a 12-month follow-up, so the pre/post VAS rise cannot be attributed to the treatment, and the efficacy wording ('evaluate the efficacy', 'more effective on smell', 'early treatment start is recommended') goes beyond what that design supports. However, the authors explicitly acknowledge the lack of a control arm and natural recovery as a limitation and hedge their conclusion ('may constitute an option', 'deserves further evaluation'), so the framing is mixed rather than uniformly over-claimed.

issues.title: Latency-subgroup differences are unadjusted, with small groups and 12 separate ANOVAs
issues.explanation: Patients were split by time from infection to treatment (n = 19, 16, 40, 12) and compared by separate one-way ANOVAs at each timepoint with no covariates and no formal group-by-time test. Patients who present later may differ in severity, age or sex, and the smell baseline ANOVA was itself p = 0.026. The statement that earlier treatment led to greater recovery is therefore descriptive of association at best, and the analysis compares final VAS levels rather than change from baseline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: An adjusted model or change-from-baseline analysis showing the same latency gradient.

quotes.text: Post-hoc ANOVA using Tukey's test revealed significant differences between the subgroups
quotes.location: Results, Effects of time and latency range on smell and taste

quotes.text: Patients treated earlier after the onset of infection when neurosensory damage was less pronounced recovered smell and taste more rapidly and to a greater extent
quotes.location: Results, Effects of time and latency range on smell and taste

second_reader.what_stands: The latency-subgroup comparisons are unadjusted for covariates, rest on small groups (B = 16, D = 12), and come from 12 separate one-way ANOVAs with 72 Tukey pairwise tests and no multiplicity correction across ANOVAs. Many differences are strong (p ≤ 0.002), especially A versus D, but several marginal ones (p about 0.04–0.05, e.g. taste T3 and T4) would not survive a correction across the family, and the conclusion that earlier treatment causes better recovery is not supported because latency is confounded with natural recovery time and no covariates were modelled.

issues.title: Baseline smell ANOVA p=0.026 described as no significant difference between subgroups A-D
issues.explanation: Table 2 gives an omnibus F = 3.236, p = 0.026 for smell at T0 across the four latency subgroups, yet the text twice says there are no significant baseline differences. Only the Tukey pairwise comparisons were NS. This matters because baseline imbalance by latency subgroup undermines the claim that earlier treatment caused better recovery, and the omnibus test suggests the groups differed at baseline.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A prespecified corrected alpha below 0.026 for baseline comparisons.

quotes.text: with no significant difference between subgroups A-D
quotes.location: Results, Characteristics of the study population

issues.title: Outcome is a subjective paper VAS with no objective olfactory/gustatory test, in an open study
issues.explanation: Smell and taste were measured only by patient-rated 0-10 VAS selected for ease of use, with no psychophysical test and no blinding. Patients knew they were receiving treatment, so expectation effects may inflate scores. The authors disclose this, and note subjective ratings can also underestimate recovery, so the direction of bias is uncertain, but it limits how far the improvement can be read as true recovery.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Objective olfactory test results showing concordant improvement.

quotes.text: The VAS, which was selected as an assessment tool in this pilot study for its ease of use, was administered to patients in paper format.
quotes.location: Materials And Methods, Outcomes and assessments

quotes.text: The fact that smell and taste recovery were assessed only subjectively is another limitation of the present study.

issues.title: Smell-versus-taste 'more effective' claim based on separate within-group effect sizes, no direct test
issues.explanation: Treatment is said to be more effective on smell than taste from effect sizes computed within each sense. Smell started lower (2.21 vs 3.17) and ended similar (6.9 vs 7.1), so a larger change reflects headroom and score scaling, not differential efficacy, and no formal comparison is reported. The claim is also not about treatment effect since there is no comparator.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A direct paired test of change in smell vs taste, with adjustment for baseline.

quotes.text: based on the effect size analysis, the evaluated treatment was more effective on smell than on taste function.
Cohen's dz statistical test for paired samples.

issues.title: Baseline smell VAS printed as 2.0 in text but 2.21 in Table 1
issues.explanation: The Abstract, Results and Discussion give baseline smell VAS as 2.0, whereas Table 1 gives 2.21 ± 1.99. Rounded to one decimal, 2.21 is 2.2, not 2.0. The discrepancy is small and slightly understates baseline smell, and thus the apparent improvement to 6.9 is marginally overstated in the text (4.9 vs 4.69).
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the text value is a median or uses a different time point or population.

quotes.text: At T0, the mean VAS scores were 2.0 and 3.2 for olfactory and gustatory function, respectively
quotes.location: Results, Characteristics of the study population
Table 1, VAS score at treatment start, Smell row

issues.title: Safety stated as 'always well-tolerated' without adverse event counts or a collection method
issues.explanation: The regimen includes IV dexamethasone, acetazolamide and a 30-day oral steroid taper, yet the paper gives no adverse event counts, no definition of how events were collected in a retrospective chart review, and no dropouts. The statement of no safety problems is therefore an assertion rather than a result. It is a secondary claim and does not drive the efficacy conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table of adverse events or a statement of systematic collection.

quotes.text: No safety problems were identified, and the treatment, already well-established in the specialist field of otolaryngology for sudden hearing loss, was always well-tolerated.

10.7759/cureus.61855.headline_claim: Olfactory training alone and combined with mometasone nasal spray showed no superiority over control for post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction, and the authors suggest patients may improve without intervention.
10.7759/cureus.61855.overall: The central finding, no demonstrated superiority of olfactory training or training plus mometasone over no treatment, is plausible but weakly supported. The trial is very small (10, 10 and 11 patients) with an unreproducible power statement, no concealment description and an unclear between-group test. Several descriptive errors (symptom percentages mislabelled, a duplicated correlation, out-of-range durations) reduce confidence in data handling but do not change the null conclusion.

primary_outcome.name: TIBSIT olfactory test score (with eODQ as secondary)

issues.title: Three arms of 10, 10 and 11 with unsupported power calculation; null findings read as no benefit
issues.explanation: The power calculation gives no outcome, effect size or variance, and was for 30 patients in total, not per arm. With 10 or 11 per arm, only very large differences could be detected, so the non-significant comparisons at 6 months do not rule out a useful effect. The conclusion states that patients improve without intervention, which reads more confidently than the data allow. The authors do acknowledge the group-size limitation.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A pre-specified effect size and SD from which the stated sample size follows, together with confidence intervals for between-group differences excluding clinically important benefit.

quotes.text: A sample size of 30 randomized patients was calculated to be able to provide 80% power for a significance level of 0.05.
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, Study design and patients

quotes.text: the sample size calculation did not consider the number in each group and drop-out rates as it shows the overall total number of samples for the study
This suggests a possibility that patients with post-COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction show improvement in terms of olfactory function and quality of life even without intervention.

second_reader.what_stands: The arm sizes of 10, 10 and 11 are correct as stated, and the power calculation is unsupported: no effect size, variance, outcome or test is given, and the authors themselves concede it ignored group numbers and drop-outs. The 'null findings read as no benefit' part holds only in part: the conclusion says no superiority was shown and only raises a possibility of spontaneous improvement, but with about 10 per arm and an unsupported power calculation, the absence of significant differences cannot show the interventions are no better than control, and the spontaneous-recovery inference is also we

issues.title: TIBSIT-eODQ correlation reported identically at 3 and 6 months (rs = -0.454, p = 0.010)
issues.explanation: The same coefficient and p-value are printed for the 3-month and 6-month correlations between TIBSIT and eODQ scores. Scores changed between visits in all groups, so identical values are unlikely and one is probably a copying error. A coefficient of about -0.45 is also moderate, not 'strong'. This is a secondary analysis that does not drive the conclusion.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Raw data showing both correlations really equal -0.454 with p = 0.010.

quotes.text: Spearman's correlation coefficient, rs = -0.454, p = 0.010

quotes.text: which was statistically significant at six months follow-up (rs = -0.454, p = 0.010)

issues.title: Text symptom percentages (cough 64.5%, fever 58.1%, dyspnoea 19.4%) match the wrong Table 1 rows
issues.explanation: All three symptom percentages in the Results text are reproduced by Table 1, but under different symptom labels. 64.5% is fever, 58.1% is shortness of breath, and 19.4% is cough. Either the text or the table labels are wrong. Descriptive data only, so conclusions are unaffected.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Author confirmation that Table 1 row labels are the ones misassigned, which would still leave an inconsistency but locate it.

quotes.text: Other most common symptoms experienced by patients were cough (64.5%), followed by fever (58.1%) and shortness of breath (19.4%).
quotes.location: Results, Patient demographics and disease characteristics

issues.title: No allocation concealment described; metric for between-group TIBSIT tests unclear with baseline imbalance
issues.explanation: Randomisation is described only as a computer-generated sequence, with no mention of concealment. Baseline TIBSIT medians differ (32.5 in Group 2, 38 in Control), and the analysis does not adjust for baseline. The 3-month Group 2 vs control result is described as higher 'improvement' although the raw medians are slightly lower than control, so it is unclear whether scores or change scores were compared. This weakens interpretation of the secondary between-group comparisons.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A statement that the Mann-Whitney tests compared change from baseline, and a description of concealment (central or sealed opaque envelopes).

quotes.text: randomized into three groups via a computergenerated sequence

issues.title: Table 1 percentages use all 31 patients as denominator, not group sizes of 10, 10 and 11
issues.explanation: The Table 1 header reads 'Number of patients (percentage)' with no stated denominator, but each percentage is the count divided by 31 (for example 4/31 = 12.9%). Within-group shares would be 40% for Dusun in Group 1. This hides baseline differences between arms, which are what a baseline table is meant to show. No result is changed.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A table footnote stating that percentages are of the total sample of 31.

quotes.text: Group 1 consisted of 10 patients, Group 2 consisted of 10 patients, and Group 3 consisted of 11 patients.
quotes.location: Results, Patient demographics and disease characteristics

issues.title: Table 4 lists improvers with COVID-19 symptoms under 7 days although stated range starts at 7 days
issues.explanation: The text gives the range of COVID-19 symptom duration as 7-34 days. Table 4 nevertheless places 1 patient (3 months) and 2 patients (6 months) who improved in a '<7 days' category. The category bins also overlap at the boundaries (7-14, 14-21, and so on). Either the range or the table is wrong. This is a secondary univariate analysis, so the effect on the conclusion is small.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: Source data showing every patient had at least 7 days of symptoms and the '<7' row is a mislabelled category.

quotes.text: Overall, the median duration of symptoms of COVID-19 was 10 days (mean: 12.2 ± 7.2, range: 7-34).
quotes.location: Results, Patient demographics and disease characteristics

issues.title: Smell-disturbance duration range starting at 5 days conflicts with >4-week inclusion criterion
issues.explanation: Inclusion required residual olfactory dysfunction for more than four weeks after recovery, yet the reported range of smell-disturbance duration starts at 5 days. Table 4 also lists patients with duration under 1 month. The paper does not say whether duration was counted from onset or recovery, so the discrepancy may be definitional, but it raises doubt about eligibility or data entry.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A methods statement that duration was measured from COVID-19 onset and that all patients met the more-than-four-weeks-after-recovery criterion.

quotes.text: residual olfactory dysfunction for more than four weeks after recovery
quotes.location: Materials and Methods, Study design and patients

quotes.text: The median duration of symptoms of smell disturbances was 60 days (mean: 77.1 ± 61.2, range: 5-180).
quotes.location: Results, Patient demographics and disease characteristics

issues.title: No placebo or participant blinding; patient-reported eODQ and unsupported 'team blinded' statement
issues.explanation: The control group received nothing, so participants knew their allocation. The eODQ is a self-reported questionnaire and could reflect expectation. The statement that 'the research team was kept blinded throughout' is not explained, since the interventions are visible to those who dispense them. The impact is limited because the paper reports no between-group eODQ comparison and the main result is null.
issues.would_be_refuted_by: A description of how the assessors were masked (for example, a separate tester who did not know allocation) and a placebo or sham arm.

quotes.text: The research team was kept blinded throughout the study.
